mcqs.explanation: Laryngopharyngeal reflux is the cause of the pseudosulcus of the larynx. Pseudosulcus of vocal cords is a depression in the vocal cord mucosa due to chronic irritation from the reflux. Vocal Sulci:550 Types True vocal sulci Pseudosulcus Etiology Sulcus vocalis Sulcus vergetur e Laryngopharyngeal refl ux Epidermal cy sts Developmental defect Treatment PhonosurgeryBreak the fibro us bands underneath Treat acid reflu x

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman presents to you with a common cold. Due to this, her voice has changed . Which of the following conditions does not cause a similar voice change?
mcqs.explanation: Common cold leads to rhinolalia clausa. A large nasopharynx doesn 't cause rhinolalia clausa but instead rhinolalia aperta. Rhinolalia clausa or hyponasality is a lack of nasal resonance for words that are resonated in the nasal cavity. Words with M, N, NG sounds like B, D, G. It is due to the blockage of the nose or nasopharynx. Common causes of rhinolalia clausa are: • Common cold • Nasal allergy • Nasal polypi • Nasal growth • Adenoids • Nasopharyngeal mass • Familial speech pattern.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: What type of speech pathology will be seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Rhinolalia aperta or hypernasality of speech will be seen in this condition of cleft palate . It is seen when certain words which have little nasal resonance are resonated through the nose. The defect is the failure of the nasopharynx to cut off from the oropharynx or abnormal communication between the oral and nasal cavities. Common causes are: • Velopharyngeal insufficiency • Congenitally short soft palate • Submucous palate • Large nasopharynx • Cleft of soft palate551 • Paralysis of soft palate • Post adenoidectomy • Oronasal fistula • Familial speech pattern • Habitual speech pattern. NOTE: • Clausa = Close ; closed nose and nasopharynx • Aperta = Open /aperture ; abnormally open nose and nasopharynx

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Wagner and Grossman theory is related to_____
mcqs.explanation: Wagner and Grossman hypothesis • Explains the position of the cord in recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN ) palsy . • States that "The complete paralysis of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in paramedian cord due to the adduction by intact cricothyroid muscle ". • Since cricothyroid is supplied by SLN, it is spared and causes mild adduction .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following nerves provide the sensory supply to the larynx below the vocal cords?
mcqs.explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve provides the sensory supply to the larynx below the vocal cords. Above the vocal cords, the larynx is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve- a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following muscles is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
mcqs.explanation: Cricothyroid is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It is supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve. All the other muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: While assisting a direct laryngoscopy procedure being done on a patient , you notice that the vocal cords are in a slightly abducted position. Which intrinsic muscle of the larynx is responsible for this?
mcqs.explanation: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx that causes abduction of the vocal cords.552

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: You are a junior resident in the ENT department asked to examine a patient 's larynx. The patient has complete paralysis of vocal cords following a total thyroidectomy procedure . What is the expected position of the vocal cords?
mcqs.explanation: Intermediate (cadaveric) position is seen in complete paralysis of the vocal cord. • This is a neutral position of the cricoarytenoid joint. • Abduction and adduction take place from this position. • It is not always seen in cadavers (misnomer).

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause for bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis?
mcqs.explanation: Surgical trauma is the most common cause of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis. The incidence of permanent RLN paralysis is approximately 1% to 1.5% for total thyroidectomy and less for near-total procedures . Note : Previously, extra laryngeal malignancies had been the most common cause which included lung (50%), esophagus , thyroid, and larynx.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not cause bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy ?
mcqs.explanation: Ortner's syndrome is a rare cause of left (unilateral) recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy due to compression by enlarged cardiac structures such as the left atrium or pulmonary artery. Causes of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy: • Thyroid surgery • Neck trauma • Thyroid malignancy • Cervical lymphadenopathy . Though the risk of bilateral nerve involvement is much less than unilateral, it is possible . Depending on whether the palsy is unilateral or bilateral, findings will differ . Terminologies in vocal cord palsy : • Pure RLN palsy : abductor palsy (the only abductor, posterior cricoarytenoid is affected ) • Pure SLN palsy : rare (only cricothyroid, one of the adductors and the main tensor is affected ) • Complete paralysis: both SLN and RLN are involved.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: What is the most common inflammatory cause for vocal cord palsy ?
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis is the most common inflammatory cause of vocal cord palsy . Lesions include : • Apical553 • Mediastinal scarring • Mediastinal lymph nodes .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following nerves is more prone to injury, causing vocal cord paralysis?
mcqs.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is more prone to injury, causing vocal cord paralysis. The reasons being: • It is longer as it loops around the arch of the aorta to climb back to the larynx. • It is in association with more structures in the mediastinum. Other options : • Right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the subclavian artery and therefore it's shorter and safer. • Unilateral paralysis of the superior laryngeal nerve is rare and they are usually a part of a combined paralysis.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman has undergone a total thyroidectomy procedure and has been shifted to the post -op ward. 2 hours later she develops stridor and dyspnea , but her voice is normal . Which of the following vocal cord lesions is the most likely cause for her condition?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical picture of stridor and dyspnea with a normal voice is most likely due to bilateral abductor paralysis (B/L RLN injury). It is the most dangerous vocal cord lesion. All the other options will have an abnormality in the voice. Normal voice is seen only in B/L RLN injury. In bilateral abductor paralysis, • Both the cords lie in the median or paramedian position, the airway is inadequate causing dyspnea and stridor. This may lead to death if untreated . • The voice is good . • Dyspnea and stridor become worse on exertion or during an attack of acute laryngitis.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A patient in the ICU is aphonic but can maintain respiration. He has a history of recurrent chest infections . Which of the following nerve palsies would you suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical presentation is that of bilateral complete palsy (SLN + RLN ). Both cords are in a cadaveric position, the patient has aphonia but respiration is maintained. Aphonia is suggestive of bilateral complete palsy , unilateral palsy presents with hoarseness of voice. Sensations are lost from supraglottis (supplied by the internal branch of SLN), the patient will develop aspiration and multiple chest infections .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old singer has undergone a subtotal thyroidectomy for thyroid nodules . She presents to you one week later with complaints of difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice when she tries to reach high notes . There is no difficulty in her breathing and her voice is otherwise normal . Paralysis of which muscle is responsible for her condition?
mcqs.explanation: 554 Paralysis of cricothyroid is responsible for the difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice. Cricothyroid is the main tensor of the vocal cords. It is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (branch of the superior laryngeal nerve).

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A patient has been posted for type 1 thyroplasty surgery. What does this procedure involve?
mcqs.explanation: Medialization of the vocal cord is done in type 1 thyroplasty . Note to remember: MLSLType Thyroplasty Uses I Medialization In Complete pal sy II Lateralization In RLN palsy III Shortening (relax the vocal c ord) To reduce pitch IV Lengthening (tighten the voc al cord) To increase pitc h555

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: What is the false statement regarding carcinoma larynx?

options.a: Squamous cell is the most common histological type
options.b: Glottis is the most common site
options.d: Tobacco is an important causative factor

mcqs.explanation: Laryngeal carcinoma is more common in males. Laryngeal cancer • Male :Female ratio is 10 :1 • Risk factors: Smoking tobacco and alcohol • 90-95% are squamous • Most common site : Glottis followed by supraglottis and subglottis .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following cancers presents with hoarseness of voice as its earliest symptom ?
mcqs.explanation: Glottic carcinoma presents with hoarseness of voice as its earliest symptom . Lesions of the vocal cords affect its vibratory capacity . Therefore they are diagnosed early and have a better prognosis. Supraglottic and subglottic growths are often silent . Hoarseness is a late symptom .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not the reason behind the development of hoarseness of voice in laryngeal carcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: Phonotrauma is not the reason behind the development of hoarseness of voice in laryngeal carcinoma . It occurs due to overuse of voice and is associated with the development of benign lesions such as vocal nodules and cysts . Hoarseness in supraglottic cancer and subglottic cancer indicates spread of disease to: • Vocal cords with infiltration of the thyroarytenoid muscle • Involvement of recurrent laryngeal nerve • Cricoarytenoid joint involvement. Hoarseness in glottic carcinoma is early because lesions of the cord affect its vibratory capacity .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with carcinoma limited to the glottis of the larynx. Which of the following lymph nodes would be initially involved?
mcqs.explanation: Tumours limited to the glottis usually do not spread to any lymph node station as there are no lymphatics in the vocal cords. However, if the tumour invades the supra- or the infra- glottic spaces , lymph node spread can occur. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the larynx. Glottis is the most common site of cancer.560

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following laryngeal carcinomas has maximum lymph node involvement?

options.d: All have equal chances of lymph node involvement

mcqs.explanation: Supraglottic carcinoma has the highest chance of lymphatic spread in the larynx. Lymph node enlargement is often a presenting complaint as it occurs early in the course of the disease .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A patient has been diagnosed with laryngeal carcinoma limited to the supraglottis . Which of the following subsites will not be affected ?
mcqs.explanation: The Pyriform sinus is not a subsite of the supraglottis . Epiglottis , false cords, aryepiglottic folds (medial wall of the pyriform sinus), and arytenoids are the subsites of supraglottis . Aryepiglottic folds are shared between the supraglottis and hypopharynx.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man is diagnosed with supraglottic carcinoma . Which of the following lymph node levels is the earliest to be involved?
mcqs.explanation: Level II (upper jugular) and III (middle jugular) lymph nodes are the most common and earliest nodes involved in supraglottic carcinoma.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding supraglottic carcinoma ?

options.a: Epiglottis , false vocal cords are most commonly involved
options.b: Lymphatic spread to upper and middle jugular lymph nodes
options.c: Hoarseness of voice is an early symptom
options.d: Bilateral nodes seen in epiglottic cancer

mcqs.explanation: Hoarseness of voice is a late symptom of supraglottic carcinoma . The most common site of supraglottic carcinoma is the epiglottis followed by false cords and then aryepiglottic folds . Nodal metastases occur early to the upper and middle jugular lymph nodes . Bilateral metastases can be seen in cases of epiglottic cancer. Supraglottic growths are often silent as hoarseness is a late symptom.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A patient has been posted for a surgical procedure to excise cancerous lesions from the vocal cords. Which laser is most commonly used ?
mcqs.explanation: Endoscopic resection with CO2 laser is most commonly used in laryngeal surgeries . Carcinoma of the mobile membranous vocal cords can be precisely excised with the CO2 laser under the microscope . It gives the same result as being traditionally treated with radiotherapy. Laser excision has the advantage of lower cost, lower duration of treatment , and morbidity.561

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presents to you with complaints of weight loss, hoarseness of voice, and difficulty in breathing. On direct laryngoscopy , a mass involving both the vocal cords with extension to the subglottis is seen . Cords are immobile and there is no lymph node involvement. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis of glottic carcinoma . What is the next step in the management of this case?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical picture of glottic carcinoma involving immobile vocal cords with extension to the subglottis suggests that the tumour belongs to the T3 stage . The treatment of choice is concurrent chemotherapy and radiotherapy. TNM classification of glottic carcinoma (American Joint Committee on Cancer, ) Treatment of laryngeal cancers: TLM : Transoral laser microsurgery; RT : Radiotherapy; OPL: Open partial laryngectomy ; CT: Chemotherapy ; CRT : Chemoradiotherapy, TL : Total laryngectomy .Stag e Description T1 Tumour limited to vocal cord (s) with normal mobility T1a Tumour limited to one vocal cord T1b Tumour involves both vocal c ords T2a Tumour extends to supraglot tis and/or subglottis , with nor mal vocal cord mobility T2b Tumour extends to supraglot tis and/or subglottis , with im paired vocal cord mobility T3 Tumour limited to the larynx with vocal cord fixation and/ or invades paraglottic space a nd/or minor thyroid cartilag e erosion T4a Tumour invades thyroid carti lage and/or invades tissue be yond the larynx T4b Tumour invades prevertebral space , encases carotid artery or invades mediastinal struct uresT stage Treatment T1a TLM > RT T1b (mid-cord lesion) RT /TLM > OPL T2a RT /TLM > OPL T2b RT \261 CT > TLM T3 CRT T4a TL > CRT562 T stage Treatment T4b Palliative manageme nt

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions would you not recommend a total laryngectomy as the treatment?

options.a: Glottic carcinoma with invasion of the thyroid cartilage
options.b: Glottic carcinoma involving the posterior commissure
options.c: Transglottic tumours with fixation of the vocal cords
options.d: Tumour involving both vocal cords with normal mobility

mcqs.explanation: Tumour limited to both vocal cords with normal mobility can be classified as stage T1b . Treatment will include radiotherapy or transoral laser microsurgery. There is no indication for a total laryngectomy . Total laryngectomy is indicated in: • All T4 lesions • Invasion of thyroid or cricoid cartilage • Bilateral arytenoid cartilage involvement • Lesions of the posterior commissure • Failure after radiotherapy or conservation surgery • Transglottic cancers with cord fixation. It is contraindicated in patients with distant metastasis . Treatment of T3 cancers is controversial, open vertical hemilaryngectomy and more extensive partial laryngectomies are used in carefully selected cases . Total laryngectomy or CRT is recommended for bulky T3 tumors or tumors not suitable for conservation laryngeal surgery.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: In the oncology ward, four patients have been diagnosed with laryngeal carcinoma . Which of the following patients would you advise for transoral laser microsurgery as the first choice ?

options.a: A patient with vocal cord palsy , with subglottic extension
options.b: A patient with tumor limited to one cord, with normal mobility
options.c: A patient with tumor invading the thyroid cartilage
options.d: A patient with tumor limited to larynx, with fixed cord

mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , a patient with tumor limited to one cord, with normal mobility will be advised for transoral laser microsurgery as the first choice . TNM staging in this patient is T1a . Option A: TNM staging here is T2b and the patient is advised for chemoradiotherapy as the first choice . Option C: TNM staging here is T4a and the patient is advised for total laryngectomy as the first choice . Option D: TNM staging here is T3 and the patient is advised for chemoradiotherapy as the first choice . TNM classification of glottic carcinoma (American Joint Committee on Cancer, ) Treatment of laryngeal cancers: TLM : Transoral laser microsurgery; RT : Radiotherapy; OPL: Open partial laryngectomy ; CT: Chemotherapy ; CRT : Chemoradiotherapy, TL : Total laryngectomy .563 Stag e Description T1 Tumour limited to the vocal c ord(s) with normal mobility T1a Tumour limited to one vocal cord T1b Tumour involves both vocal c ords T2a Tumour extends to supraglot tis and/or subglottis , with nor mal vocal cord mobility T2b Tumour extends to supraglot tis and/or subglottis , with im paired vocal cord mobility T3 Tumour limited to the larynx with vocal cord fixation and/ or invades paraglottic space a nd/or minor thyroid cartilag e erosion T4a Tumour invades thyroid carti lage and/or invades tissue be yond the larynx T4b Tumour invades prevertebral space , encases carotid artery or invades mediastinal struct uresT stage Treatment T1a TLM > RT T1b (mid-cord lesion) RT /TLM > OPL T2a RT /TLM > OPL T2b RT \261 CT > TLM T3 CRT T4a TL > CRT T4b Palliative manageme nt

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an indication of high tracheostomy ?

options.d: Suspicion of Laryngeal carcinoma planned for surgery later

mcqs.explanation: Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy . It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland.564 The disadvantage of a high tracheostomy is subglottic stenosis at the level of the cricoid and perichondritis of the cricoid. However, in laryngeal carcinoma this would be a temporary measure as the definitive management is total laryngectomy . Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea. Functions: • Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction. • Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance • Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood • Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex . • Allows positive pressure respiration • Allows administration of anesthesia Indications: • Respiratory obstruction due to • Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis ) • Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures • Neoplasms • Foreign bodies or edema • Bilateral abductor paralysis • Congenital anomalies • Retained secretions • Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles • Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions • Painful cough • Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema , chronic bronchitis565

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A surgeon is to perform a mastoidectomy procedure for a patient with CSOM. He uses the following instrument during the procedure . What is the name of the given instrument?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows Mollison 's mastoid retractor. It is used in mastoidectomy procedures to retract soft tissues after incision and elevation of flaps . It is self -retaining and hemostatic . Shown below is Jansen's self -retaining mastoid retractor.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: The following instrument is used for:

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old patient is to undergo mastoid surgery. Which of the following instruments will not be present in the operation theatre?
mcqs.explanation: Lempert's trocar does not exist . Option A: Lempert's curette (scoop ) is used for removal of bony septa and granulations in mastoid surgery.573 Option B: Lempert's endaural retractor is used for endaural approach to ear surgery. It has two lateral blades which retract the flaps and a third central blade with holes . The central blade retracts the temporalis muscle . The central blade can be fixed to the body of the retractor by its hole .Option C: Lempert's endaural speculum is used to spread open the meatus when giving the local injection or making an endaural incision.574 Lempert's incision is used in endaural approach. It consists of two parts: Lempert I: It is a semicircular incision, made from 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock position in the posterior meatal wall at the bony-cartilaginous junction. Lempert II : Starts from the first incision at 12 o'clock and then passes upwards in a curvilinear fashion between tragus and the crus of helix. It passes through the incisura terminalis and thus does not cut the cartilage . Both mastoid and external canal surgery can be done.

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman has complaints of reduced hearing on her right side . You perform a diagnostic test using the following instrument. What is the name of this instrument?
mcqs.explanation: The image is of a Digital audiometer . An audiometer is an electronic device that produces pure tones , which can be increased or decreased in 5 dB steps . The amount of intensity that has to be raised above the normal level is a measure of the degree of hearing loss at that frequency. This is charted in the form of a graph577 called an audiogram. The difference in the thresholds of air and bone conduction (A–B gap) is a measure of the degree of conductive deafness . Uses : • To measure the threshold of hearing of air and bone conduction • Helps to predict speech reception threshold • To diagnose the type of hearing loss and measure the degree • For the prescription of hearing aids • Helps to find the degree of handicap for medicolegal purposes • A record can be kept for future reference .

mcqs.subject: ENT
mcqs.question: An objective diagnostic test is performed on a patient who complains of loss of hearing on his right side . The following instrument is used to perform this test . What is this instrument known as?
mcqs.explanation: The image is of a tympanometer . It is used in evaluating the status of the middle ear. It is based on a simple principle that when a sound strikes the tympanic membrane, some of the sound energy is absorbed while the rest is reflected . A stiffer tympanic membrane would reflect more sound energy than a compliant one. mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A victim of child trafficking was brought to you by the police for age determination. Which of the following would you use as an accurate method for determining the same?
mcqs.explanation: From the given options, mineralization of teeth is the more accurate method of age determination in childhood. The relationship between the chronological age and dental age is stronger than between chronological age and skeletal age. Two aspects of tooth development have been used in the estimation of dental age: • The emergence of teeth - superior part of the crown of the tooth appearing level with the surface of the alveolar bone • The stage of mineralization of crowns and r oots during development Estimation of dental age using mineralization stages of crowns and roots of developing teeth includes visualization from a radiographic image. This helps in viewing both erupted and unerupted teeth. It is a more accurate method of estimating age than emergence, because emergence is an event whose exact time of occurrence is not accurately known. The study of dental microstructure is the most accurate method of age determination in childhood . T his involves counting perikymata (incremental lines on the surface of tooth enamel). Note : Eruption is a continuous process by which a tooth moves from its crypt in the jaw bone to its position of occlusion in the mouth. It is different from emergence. Emergence denotes that a tooth has pierced the gingiva.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which o f the following is a superadded permanent tooth?
mcqs.explanation: The 6 molars are called superadded teeth. Permanent dentition refers to the teeth which begin to erupt from 6th year of age and remain throughout the life. They are totally 32 in number. The tooth distribution in each jaw is as follows: • 4 incisors • 2 canines • 4 premolars11 • 6 molars. Thus, each jaw has 16 teeth. Among these 4 incisors and 2 canines and 4 premolars are called as successional teeth, which erupt in the place of predecessor deciduous teeth. The remaining 6 permanent molars (1st, 2nd, and 3rd molar teeth) erupt independently without any predecessor teeth. Hence they are called superadded teeth.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Electron microscopy of the surface of tooth enamel revealed a neonatal line. What is your inference?
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal line is an incremental line found on the surface of tooth enamel, that indicates that an infant was live born. The study of dental microstructure, which involves counting perikymata (incremental lines on the surface of tooth enamel), can provide an accurate method of age determination. One particularly pronounced incremental line, the neonatal line, can be of medicolegal significance in determining whether an infant was live-born or stillborn. It is formed very s oon after birth and can be visualized by light microscopy if the child survived for about 3 weeks or by electron microscopy within 1 or 2 days of birth.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A dentist evaluating a child's teeth notices the presence of mixed dentition. What would be the approximate age of the child?
mcqs.explanation: 6 – 12 years is the age of mixed dentition and the number of teeth remains constant at 24. The period during which both primary and permanent teeth are in oral cavity together is known as mixed dentition period. This is the period where the deciduous teeth get replaced by permanent successors.12

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: While examining the skeletal remains from a bomb blast, a forensic expert decides to use the Gustafson's method for identification of the ages of people killed. Which of the following would you not assess in this method?
mcqs.explanation: Tooth length is not assessed in Gustafson's method. Gustafson's method of estimation of age of an individual is based on physiological changes in teeth. It is mainly useful in adults over 25 years of age. Gustafson's criteria includes: • Attrition - wear and tear changes of occlusal surface • Periodontosis - regression of gums surrounding the tooth resulting in loosening of the tooth and falling • Secondary dentin - deposition of dentin in pulp cavity • Cementum appositi on - deposition o f cementum in the root forming incremental lines • Root resorption - involves both cementum and dentin • Transparency of the root - This is the most reliable criteria. Canals in dentin get filled with mineral and they become less transparent. Gustafson's method has now been largely replaced by Lamendin's method. Other methods of age determination based on teeth: • Lamendin's method - It evaluates root dentine translucency, periodontopathy, and tooth len gth • M iles ' method - Uses transparency of the root as a single criterion • Boyd's method - Determination of age of an infant by counting incremental lines on enamel • Stack's method - Determination of age by measuring dimensions of teeth • Variation in racemization of amino acids (especially aspartic acid) in dental pulp with age • Evaluating the reduction of the pulp chamber through X-rays

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most reliable criterion for age determination from Gustafson's method?
mcqs.explanation: Transparency of the root is the most reliable criterion in Gustafson's method. Gustafson's m ethod of estimation of age of an individual is based on physiological changes in teeth . It is mainly useful in adults over 25 years of age. Gustafson's criteria includes: • Attrition - wear and tear changes of occlusal surface • Periodontosis - regression of gums surrounding the tooth resulting in loosening of the tooth and falling • Secondary dentin - deposition of dentin in pulp cavity • Cementum apposition - deposition of cementum in the root forming incremental lines • R oot resorption - involves both cementum and dentin13 • Transparency of the root - This is the most reliable criteria. Canals in dentin get filled with mineral and they become less transparent.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: When does the fusion of the spheno-occipital suture usually occur in females?
mcqs.explanation: The spheno-occipital suture fuses by about 18–20 years in females and by about 20–22 years in males. The timing of cranial suture closure was one of the first techniques used to estimate the age of adult individuals. The spheno-occipital suture on the skull base is particularly useful for aging young adults. The other cranial sutures show more variation in the timing of closure. Sagittal suture is used for age determination. Sutures ossify on the endocranial surface befo re t hey ossify on the ectocranial surface, and this must also be taken into account when using this method. Overall, this method of age determination is less reliable. mcqs.question: Which among the following is the best indicator that a female is more than 16 years of age?

options.a: Fusion of distal end of ulna
options.b: Fusion of proximal end of ulna
options.c: Fusion of medial end of clavicle

mcqs.explanation: Complete union of the distal ulna is considered as a conclusive evidence of age more than 16 years in females. The appearance of ossification centres is complete by around 5 years. Thus, from birth to 5 years. Thus from birth to 5 years , the calendar of appearance of ossification centres is used for aging. After the age of 5 years, the fusion of epiphyses acts as a calendar up to the age of 25.18 The analysis of the hand and the wrist is the recommended method for living age diagnostics. But, this technique frequently does not provide sufficient evidence to place an individual older than or younger than key threshold ages - 16, 18 or 21. Additional radiographs needed to establish the threshold ages of 16, 18 or 21 can be any of the following: • Proximal humerus • Distal end of the ulna or radius • Distal femur • Proximal tibia • Iliac crest The proximal end of the ulna cannot b e used to conclusively state that the individual is more than years. This is because complete fusion of proximal end may occur earlier than 16 years. Establishment of the age of 21 years can be done by evaluation of the medial end of the clavicle. mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most reliable method for estimation of age in adulthood (>25 years)?
mcqs.explanation: Estimation of age in adulthood (>25 years) is best estimated by degenerative changes in pubic symphysis. Physical anthropology has established several methods for determining age in adults which include macroscopic, microscopic, and biomolecular methods. Macroscopic methods of adult age determination are the most important ones and consist principally in the degree of degeneration of selected articulations such as: • Pubic symphysis • Osteochondral surface o f the 4th rib19 • Auricular surface of the ilium Suchey and Brooks described six phases of degenerative change in the pubic symphysis. Until recently, the most commonly used method for estimating age using the architecture of the pubic symphysis was that of Todd, who described 10 stages of pubic symphysis change during aging. More recently, researchers Suchey and Brooks described six phases of degenerative change in the pubic symphysis. To solve this controversy, the following is suggested: A t wo -step procedure has been developed for estimating age: • If by looking at the skeleton, the age of the individual seems to be within the first 3 phases of the Suchey–Brookes pubic symphysis method, then this should be the method of choice. • If the subject is classified in the last 3 phases, then one should switch to the Lamendin technique in order to assess age more accurately. • Currently, age diagnosis at over 60 remains a problem. In early adulthood, Suchey-Brookes p ubic symphysis method is most accurate. In late adulthood, Lamendin technique of dental age estimation is most accurate.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: The secondary ossification centres that appear before birth include all of the following except:
mcqs.explanation: The ossification centre for distal tibia does not appear before birth. It appears 3 months after birth. Nearly all secondary centers commence ossification after birth, although a few develop in the last few weeks of intrauterine life. Secondary ossification centres which are already present when an infant is born include: • Calcaneus • Talus • Distal f emur • Proximal tibia • Cuboid • Head of humerus Visualization of the secondary ossification centers of the distal femur and the proximal tibia and commencement of ossification in the calcaneus and talus is usually accepted as signifying a full-term fetus.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following statements regarding photosuperimposition is false?

options.a: It may be performed on the pelvis
options.c: It requires an antemortem picture of the victim
options.d: 2D images may be used for this test

mcqs.explanation: Photosuperimposition is only performed on the skull, not the pelvis.22 Photosuperimposition is a well-established technique used for identification. It is done when a potential candidate for the identity of a skull is known to the investigating authority and photographs taken during life are available. Photographs of the skull are taken in exactly the same orientation in 3 planes as the available photograph. These are then enlarged to exactly the same dimensions as the photograph, and either the negative or a positive print is made on tran sparent f ilm. This is then laid over the photograph and adjusted in an attempt to match up the major anatomical landmarks such as: • Nasion • Supraorbital ridges • Angle of the jaw • Nasal aperture • External auditory meatus • Teeth The test is mainly an exclusory one i.e. if the match cannot be made, then the skull is not that of the person in the photograph. If the match is good or excellent, then it may or may not be the same person.23

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be determined using the cephalic index?
mcqs.explanation: Cephalic index is used to determine the race of the individual. Formula to calculate cranial index = maximum skull breadth x 100 / maximum skull length The skull offers the best evidence on racial origins. There are three main racial groups, namely, Caucasian, Mongoloid and Negroid. All the skulls cannot be accurately differentiated into the 3 broad categories because of racial mixing. The skull of an Indian is caucasian with a few negroid features. mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes a skull belonging to an Indian man?
mcqs.explanation: The skull of Indians can be classified as mesaticephalic. This type of skull is of intermediate length and width. The skull of an Indian is caucasian with a few negroid characteristics. Because of racial mixing, the Indian skull cannot be correctly differentiated into the broad categories of dolichocephalic, mesaticephalic, and brachycephalic. Note: This is a controversial question. The use of the cephalic index for the determination of race has been discredited an d t he cephalic index of the entire Indian population cannot be generalized to belong to one category. mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding teeth features and ethnicity?

options.a: In Africanoids the cusps of molars are wide and deep and shovel shaped cusps in incisors
options.c: Upper third molar is most commonly absent in Mongolians
options.d: Prominent lingual ridge and labial ridge in mongols

mcqs.explanation: 32 The cusps of molars are wide and deep and cusps of incisors are shovel-shaped in Mongoloid races. Africanoid races tend to have large teeth and often have more cusps on their molars, even up to eight, with two lingual cusps on the mandibular first premolars as an additional common finding. In Caucasian races, the lateral incisors in the upper jaw are usually smaller than the central. They also have long pointed canine roots. Small nodules on the lingual surface of maxillary molars, c alled Carabelli's cusp are most common in Caucasian races. In mongoloid teeth, enamel pearls and small nodules of enamel on the tooth surface, are much more frequent. The condition of bull-tooth or taurodontism is most common in Mongoloid people. The pulp cavity of molars is wide and deep, and the roots are fused and bent. A congenital lack of the third upper molar is most commonly seen. The lingual and labial ridges are more prominent.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about sex chromatin is false?

options.a: 2 Barr bodies are seen in a person with 47XXY genetic makeup
options.b: Barr body may be seen in a genetic male
options.c: Davidson body seen in neutrophil nucleus
options.d: A common site for sex chromatin sampling is tooth pulp

mcqs.explanation: The number of Barr bodies in someone with 47XXY genetic makeup is 1, not 2. The number of Barr bodies is given by the formula n-1, where n is the number of X chromosomes. Barr body is a small planoconvex mass, lying near the nuclear membrane. It represents the inactivated X chromosome. Barr bodies are seen in 0-4% of genetic males (46XY) and 20-80% of genetic females (46XX). Sites for sampling for sex chromatin include • Buccal mucosa • Tooth pulp • Hair bulb Davidson body is a drumstick-shaped m ass of chromatin hanging down from neutrophil nuclei. It is seen only in females (0-6%).

mcqs.question: You are asked to determine the sex of a person from the skeletal remains found on an empty site. Which of the following bones is most accurate for the same?
mcqs.explanation: The whole pelvis is the most reliable bone for sex determination. Krogman's degree of accuracy in sex determination from adult skeletal remains: • Entire skeleton – 100% • Pelvis plus skull – 98% • Long bones and pelvis >95% • Pelvis alone – 95% • Long bones and skull - 90-95% • Skull alone – 90% • Long bones alone – 80-90%

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the minimum age beyond which sex determination based on skeleton would be highly accurate?
mcqs.explanation: Minimum age of a skeleton beyond which sex determination would be highly accurate is 14–16 years. This is because most marked changes regarding sex differences o ccur in the skeleton post -puberty. In prepubertal skeletons, the chance of a correct sex allocation is only 50%. If the pelvis is present, the chances of correct sex allocation increases to about 80%.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the Bertillon system used for?
mcqs.explanation: The Bertillon system is used for identification based on anthropometry. The origins of forensic anthropology can be traced to the end of the nineteenth century when the French criminologist Alphonse Bertillon devised the first classification and identification system to identify criminals, based on anthropometry.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: You have measured the femur length to be 40cm from the skeletal remains of an unknown person. What is the approximate height of the individual?
mcqs.explanation: The approximate height of the individual is 150 cm. The stature/femur relationship is 3.74. Thus, stature can be calculated by using the formula, stature = femur l ength x 3.74 = 40 x 3.74 = 149.6 cm \037 150 cm The relationship between the mean stature and the mean length of the femur appears to be fairly stable around the world. However, this factor tends to overestimate tall and underestimate short individuals.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be estimated using Pearson's formula?
mcqs.explanation: Pearson's formula is used for the estimation of stature. Methods of determination of stature: 1. Pearson's formula: Any bone may be used, but the measurement of one or more of the six long bones provides the most reliable e stimates. The descending order of usefulness of bones is femur> tibia> humerus> radius.39 2. Trotter and Gleser's method - Formula for stature (cm\ = 1.30 (Femur + Tibia) + 63.29 (+/-2.99) 3. Stature/femur relationship - The relationship between the mean stature and the mean length of the femur appears to be fairly stable around the world which is 3.74. 4. Anatomical method - This is the most accurate method. It consists of the sum of the following parameters: • Basibregmatic height of the skull • Height of the vertebrae from the axis through the first sacral vertebra • B icondylar length of the femur • Physiological length of the tibia • Articulated height of the talus and calcaneus • Constant is added to account for the soft tissues Note: Pearson also introduced the principle of regression.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Crown Rump Length is 21 cm, length of lower limb is 10 cm, gestational a ge of the fetus will be :
mcqs.explanation: Gestational age of this fetus is 6-7 months. Crown rump length + length of lower limb = crown heel length Rule of Haase enables the estimation of the age of the fetus in lunar months from its crown-heel length (in cm). According to the rule, • Age in months = Squ are root of crown-heel length (when the crown-heel length is 25 cm or less/ first 5 months). • Age in months = crown-heel length divided by 5 (when the crown-heel length is more than 25 cm/ last 5 months). Here, crown heel length = Crown rump + lower limb length = 31 cm. Hence, gestational age = 31 / 5 = 6-7 months.

mcqs.explanation: The length of the vertebral column is 35% of the stature of an individualBone % of heig ht Hum erus Tibia 2240 Bone % of heig ht Fem ur Spin e 35

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A forensic expert is examining the pelvic bone and lower vertebrae of an unknown individual, to determine the sex. Which of the following is regarded as the best source of information for the same?
mcqs.explanation: The greater sciatic notch, which is a part of the ilium is the ideal feature to determine sex. The sacrum is the least reliable bone for sex determination. The femur is the most useful long bone for sex determination, due to its length and massiveness. Pearson and Bell's criteria for sexing of the femur are: • Vertical diameter of the femoral head - most useful criterion • Popliteal length • Bicondylar width • Oblique trochanteric length41

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Edmond Locard is most famous for?
mcqs.explanation: Edmond Locard is famous for his theory of exchange or Locard's exchange principle. This theory states that every contact leaves a trace. When two objects come into contact with one another, each will take something from the other object or leave something behind. Locard is also renowned for his contribution to the improvement of dactylography, an area of study that deals with fingerprints. He developed the science of poroscopy, the study of fingerprint pores, and the impressions p roduced by these pores.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: When are the fingerprint patterns determined?
mcqs.explanation: Fingerprint patterns are determined by the 4th month of gestation and remain fixed throughout life. Fingerprints are impressions of patterns that are formed by papillary or epidermal ridges at the fingertips. They begin to appear between 12-16 weeks of intrauterine life. The formation is completed by 24 weeks. At birth, a fine pattern of ridges is seen on the skin of the bulbs of the fingers and thumbs, parts of the palms, and the soles of t he f eet.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the most common fingerprint pattern?
mcqs.explanation: Loops are the most common fingerprint pattern encountered. Patterns of fingerprints: • Loops (60-70%)46 • Radial • Ulnar • Whorls • Concentric • Spiral • Double spiral • Almond shaped • Arches • Plain • Tented • Composite • Central pocket loop • Lateral pocket loop • Twinned loop • Accidentals The image given below shows the different patterns of fingerprints.47

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: While investigating a case of homicide, the forensic team finds that the fingerprints left behind have no delta forma tion. W hich fingerprint pattern is described here?
mcqs.explanation: Plain arches have no delta. Classification of fingerprints into different patterns is based on delta and core formation. Delta is a triangular arrangement formed where three separate ridge line flows come together. Core is the centermost portion of a ridge flow pattern. The number of delta and core for each pattern is given below. The image given below shows the delta and core in the different fingerprint patterns. For each type, the position of the core is marked with a green c ircle, and the delta is marked with a blue triangle.Pattern Delta Core Loop 1 Plain arc h 0 Tented ar ch 1 delta at the base of the upth rust Whorl 2 Accident al >2 Note: Dactylography or dermatoglyphics is the study of fingerprint patterns. The first fingerprint bureau in India was established in Kolkata.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods will be used to make latent fingerprint marks visible?
mcqs.explanation: Latent prints can be made visible by ultraviolet spectrum lighting, application of lead powder and cyanoacrylate fuming. Latent prints are those that are left behind through interaction of hands, palms, and feet with the environment. Occasionally these prints are left cleanly so as to be clearly visible to the unaided eye. It is m ore often the case that the prints are only partially visible or not visible at all without the use of specialized fingerprint-processing methods and equipment. Methods to enhance fingerprints: • Lighting or photoluminescence • White light • Ultraviolet spectrum • Physical method - dusting a surface with a fine powder of contrasting color such as: • White: Lead carbonate • Black: Charcoal • Grey: Aluminium dust or chalk powder + mercury • Chemical • Ninhydrin • Cyanoac rylate f uming • Silver nitrate49

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Up to what depth from the skin surface can fingerprints be obtained?
mcqs.explanation: Histological sections up to a depth of 0.6mm from the surface of the skin give satisfactory fingerprints. Since the ridges extend up to the dermis, fingerprints can be obtained from the dermis as well.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Identical twins have similarities in all of the following except:
mcqs.explanation: Fingerprint pattern differs in identical twins. Fingerprints are formed during intrauterine life due to friction ridges. These ridges are created by pressure on the fingers from touching the surroundings. Hence, it is unique to every individual.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: In a peculiar case of robbery, the forensic team finds that no finger prints were left behind d espite the footage showing that the thief did not wear any gloves. Which of the following medical conditions could he be suffering from?
mcqs.explanation: A person suffering from dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (DPR) has a lack of fingerprint patterns, and hence will not leave fingerprint marks. There are two closely related autosomal dominant ectodermal dysplasia syndromes causing complete absence of fingerprints. They are Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome (NFJS) and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (DPR). A permanent damage of fingerprints also occurs in patients with leprosy, electrical injury, and irradiat ion.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: While reading a forensic report, you notice that the identification of the suspect was done through edgeoscopy. What does this method evaluate?

options.b: Sweat pore openings on fingerprint ridges
options.d: Fissures and grooves on lip print

mcqs.explanation: Edgeoscopy is a method of identification through the examination of the unique details and characteristics found along the edges of individual fingerprint ridges. Methods of identification using different prints: • Dactylography - evaluation of finger prints • Poroscopy - evaluation of sweat pore openings on fingerprint ridges • Cheiloscopy - evaluation of lip prints • Podography - evaluation of foot prints • Rugoscopy - evaluation of palatal rugae • Ridgeolog y - evaluation of friction ridges on fingerprints Note: Locard is known as the father of poroscopy, edgeoscopy and ridgeology.50

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A person of interest in a homicide case is on the run from the police. He wishes to remove the tattoo on his left arm w hich i s very prominent. Which of the following methods may be used for the same?
mcqs.explanation: Methods for deliberate tattoo removal include: • Surgical excision • Scarification with sandpaper • Application of caustic soda • Electrolysis • Q-switch laser method - non-invasive and effective method for removing tattoos without scarring All other methods depend upon damage to the epidermis and dermis, with consequent inflammation and scar formation. The tattoo is removed but replaced with a cicatrix, which will itself indicate that something pre-existed at t hat s ite. Attempts at the deliberate removal of tattoos are common to remove evidence of identity. Note: If the tattoo mark is absolutely invisible or has been removed artificially, the pigments used to produce them may be detected by histological examination of the lymph node.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: In tattoos, which of the following colors is least likely to fade over time?
mcqs.explanation: Black areas in a tattoo are the least likely to fade over years. This is because the black pigment (carbon particles) are more resistant than the other pigments to transportation by the lymphatic system. T hus, they tend to persist in the skin. Colors such as blue, green, or red are scavenged by tissue cells and leached into the lymphatic system after a number of years or decades. Light colors such as white, pink, and blue fade faster. Chemicals used in different tattoo pigments are: • Black pigment - Carbon • Green pigment - Potassium dichromate • Red pigment - Mercuric chloride If the tattoo mark is absolutely invisible or has been removed artificially, the pigments used to p roduce them may be detected by histological examination of the lymph node.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: An unidentified dead body is brought to you for autopsy. You notice a faded tattoo mark on the left arm of the body. All of the following methods would be used to visualize the same except:

options.d: Rubbing the part and examining with a magnifying lens

mcqs.explanation: Ink blotting is not used to visualize tattoos. A faded tattoo mark can be visualized by: • Ultraviolet light • Infrared photography • Rubbing the part and examining it with a magnifying lens51 In decomposed bodies, the tattoo marks can be visualized by removing the epidermis with a moist cloth. The lymph nodes near a tattoo mark also show a deposit of the pigment.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A deceased male was brought to the morgue for a \037post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found on examination. Which of th e following structures would you examine?
mcqs.explanation: The lymph nodes should be examined in this case. Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes. Hence, in cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: A strand of hair is found at a crime scene. Which of the following attributes will indicate that it is of human origin?

options.b: Pigment granules present in cortex and medulla
options.d: Hair scales have a coronal pattern

mcqs.explanation: The cuticle completely covers the hair shaft in human hair. It only partly covers the hair shaft in animal hair. Human hair has 3 parts: • Cuticle - outermost layer • Cortex - middle layer • Medulla - innermost part Human hair can be identified by the following features: • Thick cortex i.e. medullary index <0.3 • Pigment present only in cortex, where it is evenly distributed • Pattern of scales are imbricate or flattened The image given below shows the structure of hair.52 Note: Medullary index = diameter of medulla / diameter of hair.53

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following provisions is included in BNS Section 22/IPC section 84?

options.a: Child under 7 years is not liable for the act
options.b: A person of unsound mind is not liable for the act
options.c: A person who has committed an act under involuntary intoxication is liable
options.d: A person who commits an act under voluntary intoxication is not liable

mcqs.explanation: BNS Section 22 (previously IPC section 84) states that the act of a person of unsound mind is not liable for punishment/ prosecution. The defence under this section requires the following elements to be established: • The accused was suffering from unsoundness of mind at the time of doing the act.61 • The accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he was doing what was either wrong or contrary to law.

mcqs.subject: Forensic Medicine
mcqs.question: According to the Juvenile Justice Act, which of the following pairs correctly refers to a juvenile?
mcqs.explanation: According to Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, juvenile refers to a boy or a girl who has not completed 18 years of age.
