mcqs.explanation: Metabolic derangements like hypercalcemia and hypokalemia lead to the production of large amounts of dilute urine by causing nephrogenic DI. Options C & D: Primary polydipsia is of three types : • Dipsogenic – Due to inappropriate thirst. • Iatrogenic – Due to an increase in fluid intake due to its presumed health benefits . • Psychogenic – Due to psychosis or obsessive -compulsive disorder.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings do you expect to see in a patient with central diabetes insipidus ?

options.a: Low plasma and low urine osmolality
options.b: High plasma and high urine osmolality
options.c: Low plasma and high urine osmolality
options.d: Low urine and high plasma osmolality

mcqs.explanation: Diabetes insipidus of central or nephrogenic origin are characterized by low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality .88 Condition Plasma osmolali ty Urine osmolali ty Sodium concentrati on Central and nephrogenic DI High Low Hypernatremia Psychogenic polydipsia Low Low Hyponatremia SIADH Low High Hyponatremia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 29-year-old lady presented with polydipsia and polyuria. Her symptoms started soon after a road traffic accident 6 months ago. Her blood pressure was recorded at 120 /80 mmHg with no postural drop. The daily urinary output was reported to be between 6-8 liters. Clinical investigation results are given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis for the given clinical scenario would be psychogenic polydipsia . The normal range of urine osmolality is 500-850 mOsm/L and that of plasma osmolality is 280-295 mOsm/L. Hence in the given scenario, both urine and plasma osmolality are low, along with hyponatremia suggestive of psychogenic polydipsia .Condition Plasma osmolali ty Urine osmolali ty Sodium concentrati on Central and nephrogenic DI High Low Hypernatremia Psychogenic polydipsia Low Low Hyponatremia SIADH and cerebral salt wast ing Low High Hyponatremia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with polyuria and polydipsia . She has been on lithium therapy for 6 years for bipolar disorder. Investigations revealed low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality . Which of the following drugs can be used for the treatment of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of lithium-induced nephrogenic DI. Among the given options thiazide diuretics is the best suited answer. Thiazides reduce the kidney's ability to excrete free water by increasing proximal tubular water reabsorption (secondary to volume contraction) and block the ability of DCT to form dilute urine. This effect results in an increase in urine osmolality . Treatment of diabetes insipidus : • Central and gestational diabetes insipidus : • Desmopressin an ADH analog • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus : • Adequate water intake along with a low sodium diet • Thiazide diuretics • Potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene and amiloride): Amiloride is the drug of choice for lithium-induced DI • Prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor (indomethacin)89 • Psychogenic diabetes insipidus : • Behavioral therapy to reduce fluid consumption

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Polyuria characterized by low fixed specific gravity of urine is seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Fixed specific gravity, in which values remain 1.010 regardless of fluid intake, occurs in chronic glomerulonephritis with severe renal damage . In chronic kidney disease , as renal function deteriorates , polyuria can be seen due to the impairment of the kidney's ability to concentrate urine. In diabetes insipidus , although specific gravity is low it is not fixed . Potomania (beer potomania/beer drinker's potomania/ beer drinker 's hyponatremia) is a specific hypo-osmolality syndrome related to massive consumption of beer.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with frequent urination, nocturia, and enuresis . 24-hour urine volume was measured and recorded to be 7 liters. The urine osmolarity was 260 mOsm/L. ADH assay was performed and the recorded values were reported as 0.8 pg /ml. An MRI of the brain was performed and T1 weighted indicated the absence of the bright spot . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The features of frequent urination, nocturia, with polyuria(>3L/day), low urine osmolarity(<280 mosm/L ), low plasma ADH levels and MRI showing absent pituitary bright spot is suggestive of Pituitary Diabetes Insipidus.Diabetes Insipidus(DI) : Treatment: • For Central DI, synthetic analog of ADH Desmopressin (DDAVP ) is used . • For Nephrogenic DI, a low sodium diet with thiazide diuretic and/or amiloride and prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor is used .90 • For primary polydipsia , there are no effective drugs used but for Iatrogenic type patient education is helpful . Other options : Option A: In nephrogenic DI, there is polyuria, low urine osmolarity but the ADH levels will be >1pg/mL. Option B: In primary polydipsia , there is polyuria, low urine osmolarity, ADH levels will be <1pg/mL but a pituitary bright spot present . Option D: In solute loss (mannitol or hypertonic saline infusion), urine osmolality is >300 mOsm/L.Types Primary pathology Caused by Pituitary/ Central DI Primary deficiency of ADH se cretion AVP -Neurophysin II gene (m ost common gene defect ) Primary polydipsia Suppression of ADH secretio n by excessive fluid intake 1. Dipsogenic DI : Following head trauma, TB meningitis, Multiple sclerosis .2. Psychog enic DI : Due to psychosis or OCD3. Iatrogenic polydipsia : Due to motivated health ben efits Gestational DI Deficiency due to Increased d egradation of ADH N terminal aminopeptidase p roduced by placenta Nephrogenic DI Renal insensitivity to ADH or drugs like lithium or genetic mutation defect in gene encoding V2 re ceptor on chXq28(most com mon gene defect )91

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings will you not expect to see in a patient with SIADH?

options.a: Normal serum urea and creatinine levels

mcqs.explanation: SIADH does not cause hypernatremia. SIADH is the most common cause of euvolemic hyponatremia. The excess ADH secreted leads to the gain of water in the body. This stimulates baroreceptors to release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). ANP leads to the loss of water and salt in the urine, leading to urine sodium level of > 20 mEq/L in these patients . Thus, the level of water reaches a steady state (euvolemia) but the urinary loss of sodium continues to occur, giving rise to hyponatremia. SIADH is characterized by low levels of uric acid, normal blood pressure , and normal urea and creatinine levels . SIADH is diagnosed based on the following criteria (Bartter-Schwartz criteria): 1. Reduced serum osmolality 2. Urine osmolality > Serum osmolality 3. Clinical euvolemia 4. Increased levels of urinary sodium 5. Absence of other causes of hyponatremia like pituitary , renal, adrenal, thyroid or liver diseases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old chronic smoker who was diagnosed with small cell carcinoma of the lung presents to the casualty with nausea, confusion, and dizziness. After the initial workup, he is diagnosed to have syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). This condition is characterized by which of the following findings?

options.a: Hyponatremia and urine sodium excretion > 20 mEq/L
options.b: Hypernatremia and urine sodium excretion > 20 mEq/L
options.c: Hyponatremia and urine sodium excretion < 20 mEq/L
options.d: Hypernatremia and urine sodium excretion < 20 mEq/L

mcqs.explanation: The syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is associated with increased urinary excretion of sodium (urine sodium excretion > 20 mEq/L ), and hyponatremia. Small cell lung cancer is commonly associated with SIADH due to the ectopic release of antidiuretic hormone.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: SIADH is not observed in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Primary pulmonary emphysema is not a cause of SIADH. Respiratory causes of SIADH include asthma, pneumothorax and positive -pressure respiration.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old woman presented with headache and nausea. Examination did not reveal any signs of dehydration and investigations revealed the findings shown below . Which of the following drugs does not lead to this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of SIADH and demeclocycline does not cause this condition. Demeclocycline causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and hence is used in the treatment of chronic SIADH. The following features in the given case point towards the diagnosis of SIADH: • Serum osmolality less than 275 mOsm/Kg • Urine osmolality more than 100 mOsm/Kg95 • Urine sodium more than 20 mmol/L • Serum sodium level less than 135 mmol/L

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors is not associated with syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)?
mcqs.explanation: Chromophobe adenoma is a type of pituitary adenoma that causes symptoms of hypogonadism due to pressure effects on the pituitary stalk. It is not a cause of syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A child who underwent ventriculoperitoneal shunt surgery for tubercular meningitis with hydrocephalus, develops polyuria and hyponatremia. What could be the probable cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of cerebral salt wasting . Both SIADH and cerebral salt wasting cause hyponatremia, but polyuria happens in cerebral salt wasting . Cerebral salt wasting results from hypersecretion of atrial natriuretic peptide . It is seen primarily with central nervous system disorders including brain tumors, head trauma, hydrocephalus, neurosurgery , cerebrovascular accidents, and brain death . It is associated with hyponatremia, polyuria and elevated urinary sodium excretion. Treatment is by restoring intravascular volume with sodium chloride and water. Clinical parameters to distinguish between SIADH, cerebral salt wasting , and central diabetes insipidus are:Clinical parameter SIADH Cerebral salt wastin g Central DI Serum sodium Low Low High Urine output Normal or lo w High High Urine sodium High Very high Low Intravascular volume statu s Normal or hi gh Low Low Vasopressin level High Low Low

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient who presented with acute confusion and vomiting was diagnosed to have SIADH. This condition can be best treated by which of the following methods ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of acute symptomatic SIADH and this condition is best treated by the infusion of hypertonic (3%) saline. This mode of treatment also helps in the correction of sodium deficiency that is partly responsible for hyponatremia. The other form of treatment is to help reduce the concentration of body water by giving an AVP receptor -2 antagonist, conivaptan. Conivaptan blocks the antidiuretic effect of AVP and increases urine output .96 DDAVP is a synthetic analog of AVP and should not be used as it will further increase water retention .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the drug of choice for the treatment of chronic SIADH?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for the treatment of chronic SIADH is tolvaptan. Vaptans are selective V2 receptor antagonists that act by increasing urinary water excretion by blocking the antidiuretic effect of AVP . Treatment options for chronic SIADH include : • Restriction of fluid intake to below the level of urine output - This is considered the mainstay of treatment. But it also has certain disadvantages as stated below , and hence adding on a drug like vaptan is necessary in most cases . • Tolvaptan • Demeclocycline • Fludrocortisone Advantages of vaptans over fluid restriction: • Fluid restriction is usually a burden to the patient , unreliable , impractical, and slow to work. • Increased thirst is a frequently observed characteristic of hyponatremia in SIADH, and is particularly difficult to suppress . Hence, water restriction in SIADH frequently leads to non-compliance in the long run.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What causes central pontine myelinolysis ?
mcqs.explanation: Rapid correction of hyponatremia may result in central pontine myelinolysis . Central pontine myelinolysis is an osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), wherein rapid correction of hyponatremia results in water being driven out of the cell which has adapted to a chronic state of hypotonicity , leading to damage to the myelin sheath of these cells . It is characterized by the acute onset of quadriparesis, ataxia, and abnormal extraocular movements.97

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a specific sign for Graves' disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Ophthalmopathy is the specific sign of Graves' disease . Glycosaminoglycan deposition , lymphoid infiltrates and fatty infiltration are responsible for ophthalmopathy and dermopathy . Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder due to the production of TSH-receptor stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) thereby causing hyperthyroidism . It is characterized by the triad of: • Thyrotoxicosis • Infiltrative ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos) • Dermopathy (pretibial myxedema )104 Ophthalmopathy can sometimes precede or follow thyrotoxicosis , accounting for some cases of euthyroid ophthalmopathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with Graves' disease presents with the following finding. Which statement regarding this condition is false ?

options.a: Acropachy is strongly associated with this condition.
options.b: It occurs in more than 50% of patients with Graves' disease .
options.c: It occurs almost always in the presence of moderate or severe form of ophthalmopathy .
options.d: Skin changes can occur after trauma.

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario along with the image is suggestive of thyroid dermopathy . It occurs in <5% of patients with Graves' disease . Thyroid dermopathy is almost always associated with ophthalmopathy . Thyroid dermopathy is most frequently observed over the anterolateral parts of the lower leg . Hence , it is termed pretibial myxedema . Skin changes can occur at other sites , particularly after trauma. The typical lesion is a noninflamed, indurated plaque with a deep pink or purple color and orange peel -textured papules . Thyroid acropachy refers to a form of clubbing rarely observed in Graves' disease . It is strongly associated with thyroid dermopathy . Thyroid dermopathy usually does not need any active treatment , but if necessary , treatment includes topical, high-potency glucocorticoid ointment under an occlusive dressing or octreotide can be useful in some cases . The following image shows thyroid dermopathy and acropachy:

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient from a hilly area was referred with a partial small bowel obstruction confirmed on CECT. Conservative management was tried for a week , but he continued to deteriorate and was taken up for emergency laparotomy. On post -operative day 7, he developed atrial fibrillation. Investigations revealed elevated free T3 and free T4 levels . What is the most probable cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the Jod-Basedow phenomenon , likely due to the administration of an iodine-containing contrast agent during CECT. This phenomenon is characterized by hyperthyroidism due to enhanced thyroid hormone production following the administration of contrast agents and other iodine-containing substances . This occurs in:105 • Patients with autonomous thyroid nodules • Patients with pre-existing subclinical hypothyroidism (endemic iodine deficiency in hilly areas) Option B: Wolff-Chaikoff effect is characterized by the transient inhibition of thyroid iodide organification by excess iodine, thereby decreasing thyroid hormone synthesis . Option C: Basedow disease is another name for Graves' disease . Option D: Plummer disease is another name for toxic multinodular goitre .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common symptom of thyrotoxicosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperactivity and irritability are considered as the most common symptoms of thyrotoxicosis . The following table summarizes the symptoms and signs of thyrotoxicosis in descending order of frequency: Rarely, there can be an associated mid-systolic heart murmur called the Means-Lerman scratch. This is heard in the upper part of the sternum caused by the rubbing of the pericardium and the pleura , due to the hyperdynamic circulation.Symptoms Signs Hyperactivity , irritability, dys phoriaHeat intolerance and s weatingPalpitationsFatigue a nd weaknessWeight loss with increased appetiteDiarrhoea PolyuriaOligomenorrhea, los s of libido Tachycardia, atrial fibrillatio n in the elderlyTremorGoitre Warm , moist skinMuscle wea kness, proximal myopathyLid retraction or lagGynecomasti a

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about thyroid storm?

options.a: Symptoms are vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice and altered mentation
options.b: The mortality rate is 10 % with treatment
options.d: High doses of propranolol decrease T4 \032 T3 conversion

mcqs.explanation: The mortality rate of thyrotoxicosis crisis is almost 30% even with treatment . The usual causes for mortality are: • Cardiac failure • Arrhythmia • Hyperthermia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with amiodarone therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: Silent thyroiditis is not associated with amiodarone therapy . Amiodarone has the following effects on the thyroid gland:106 • Acute , transient suppression of thyroid function i.e., Wolff-Chaikoff effect • Hypothyroidism in patients susceptible to the inhibitory effects of a high iodine load • Thyrotoxicosis may be caused by Jod-Basedow phenomenon due to the iodine load, in the setting of multinodular goitre or incipient Graves' disease . It can also be caused by a thyroiditis -like condition. Painless thyroiditis , or silent thyroiditis, occurs in patients with underlying autoimmune thyroid disease and has a clinical course similar to that of subacute thyroiditis . The condition can occur in up to 5% of women 3–6 months after pregnancy and is then termed postpartum thyroiditis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is false ?

options.a: Type 2 AIT is associated with intrinsic abnormalities of the thyroid gland
options.b: Type 2 AIT is due to lysosomal destruction of thyroid gland.
options.c: Type 1 AIT is due to Jod-Basedow phenomenon .
options.d: Colour flow doppler shows increased vascularity in Type

mcqs.explanation: Type 1 AIT is associated with intrinsic abnormalities of the thyroid gland. Amiodarone is structurally similar to thyroid hormones and contains 39% iodine by weight . Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT ) is the most common manifestation of the effects of amiodarone on the thyroid. Administration of amiodarone should be stopped if possible . Near-total thyroidectomy rapidly decreases thyroid hormone levels and may be the most effective long-term clinical solution .Type 1 AIT Type 2 AIT Anunderlying diseaseis prese nt.E.g., Grave's disease, Mult inodular goitre etc No underlying disease Due to theJod-Basedowphen omenon Due todrug -inducedlysosoma l destruction of thyroid tissue Increased vascularity on colo ur doppler Decreased vascularity on colo ur doppler

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about non-toxic multinodular goitre ?

options.a: It is more commonly observed in women
options.b: It does not occur in iodine-deficient regions
options.c: Most patients with non-toxic MNG have hypothyroidism
options.d: Risk of malignancy is higher than in cases of solitary thyroid nodule

mcqs.explanation: Multinodular goitre (MNG) is more commonly observed in women. It is common in iodine-deficient regions. Most patients are asymptomatic and euthyroid . Sudden pain may occur due to haemorrhage. TFTs should be performed in all patients to exclude thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism . The risk of malignancy due to MNG is similar to that due to solitary nodules . Hoarseness , reflecting the involvement of laryngeal nerves implicate malignancy. Most non-toxic MNGs can be managed conservatively. Levothyroxine if used , should be started at low doses and then increased gradually . Radioiodine therapy is implemented for large goitres as it107 decreases goitre size and can ablate regions of autonomy.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the major difference between non-toxic and toxic multinodular goitre ?
mcqs.explanation: The major difference between toxic and non-toxic multinodular goiter (MNG) is the presence of functional autonomy in toxic MNG. The pathogenesis of toxic MNG appears to be similar to that of non-toxic MNG. In both types , many nodules are polyclonal whereas others are monoclonal and vary in their clonal origins. Most patients with non-toxic MNG are asymptomatic and euthyroid . However, patients with toxic MNG have subclinical or mild hyperthyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common thyroid malignancy?
mcqs.explanation: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy. Prevalence of different types of thyroid malignancies:Type of malignan cy Occure nce Papillary 80-90 % Follicular 5-10% Medullary <10 % Others 1-2%

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The following patients presented with thyroid nodules . Who has the least risk of developing thyroid carcinoma ?

options.a: A 55 -year-old woman with no voice abnormalities and nodule size of 3 cms
options.b: A 65-year-old woman with vocal cord paralysis and hoarse voice and nodule size of 3.5 cms
options.c: A 60-year-old man without any voice abnormalities and nodule size of 2.5 cms
options.d: A 43-year-old woman with no voice abnormalities and nodule size of 4.5 cm

mcqs.explanation: Among the options , the female patient with age between 20 and 65 years and no voice abnormalities and nodule size < 4 cm has the least risk for development of thyroid carcinoma . Risk factors for the development of thyroid carcinoma in patients with thyroid nodules include : • Age less than 20 or greater than 65 years • Male gender • Increased nodule size > 4 cm • Vocal cord paralysis and hoarse voice • New or enlarged neck mass • Family history of thyroid cancer, MEN2, or other syndromes associated with thyroid malignancy (e.g., Cowden's syndrome, familial polyposis , Carney complex )108 • Nodule fixed to adjacent structures • Exposure to radiation in childhood or adolescence • Extrathyroidal extension • Lateral cervical lymphadenopathy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about thyroid hormone resistance ?

options.a: Inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder
options.b: Characterized by elevated thyroid hormone levels and normal or elevated TSH
options.c: Classic forms are caused by mutations in TR -\031 gene

mcqs.explanation: Thyroid hormone resistance is an autosomal dominant disorder. It is characterized by elevated thyroid hormone levels and inappropriately elevated or normal TSH levels . Classic forms of the disease are attributed to the mutation in TR -\031 gene . Patients with this condition are often asymptomatic , as hormone resistance is partial and compensated by the increase in thyroid hormone levels . In most patients , no treatment is indicated .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with what condition present with normal thyroglobulin levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum thyroglobulin levels are normal in patients with thyrotoxicosis factitia, as it is caused by the self -administration of thyroid hormone. Its level is elevated in all other types of thyrotoxicosis . Thyroglobulin (Tg) levels are particularly increased in thyroiditis , implicating destruction of thyroid tissue and release of thyroglobulin . The primary course of action for determining the thyroglobulin levels , however, is in the clinical follow -up of thyroid cancer patients . Following total thyroidectomy and radiofrequency ablation, thyroglobulin levels become undetectable . In the absence of anti-Tg antibodies , measurable levels of Tg are indicative of incomplete ablation or recurrent cancer.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with fever and painful neck swelling . She gives a history of sore throat and cough one week ago. Lab investigations revealed elevated T3 and T4 levels and elevated ESR. Which of the following statements about this condition is false ?

options.a: Treatment of choice is supportive care and NSAIDs
options.b: Women are generally affected three times more often than men
options.c: Both thyrotoxic and hypothyroid phases can be observed

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of De Quervain's thyroiditis , and it is not autoimmune in origin. It is subacute granulomatous thyroiditis that occurs secondary to viral infections . Many viruses such as mumps, influenza, coxsackie, adenoviruses, and echoviruses have been clinically implicated in this condition. Peak incidence is observed at 30-50 years and women are generally affected three times more often than men. Clinically, it presents as a painfully enlarged thyroid and is sometimes accompanied by fever. It has three distinct phases : • Thyrotoxic phase109 • Hypothyroid phase • Recovery phase Treatment includes large doses of aspirin, NSAIDs, steroids and/or beta -blockers to relieve the observable clinical symptoms . Antithyroid drugs do not have any role. In case the hypothyroid phase is prolonged - levothyroxine can be used .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with hypothyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Graves' disease is not associated with hypothyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old baby presented with a history of constipation , lethargy , and has poor activities. Clinical examination reveals jaundice , hypotonia and there was no palpable goitre . Laboratory investigations revealed low T4 and elevated TSH levels . Which of the following is not true about this condition?

options.a: Most common cause is inborn defects in the synthesis of thyroid hormone
options.b: The developmental abnormalities are more common in girls
options.d: High circulating T4 level is needed to normalize TSH

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism . The most common cause of this condition is thyroid gland dysgenesis , seen in about 80-85% of cases of neonatal hypothyroidism . In the remaining cases of neonatal hypothyroidism , it is due to inborn defects in thyroid hormone synthesis and rarely due to TSH receptor antibodies . These developmental abnormalities are twice as common in girls. Clinical features include : • Prolonged jaundice • Umbilical hernia • Enlarged tongue • Hypotonia • Delayed bone maturation Permanent neurological damage results if treatment is delayed . T4 requirements are relatively high during the first year of life . A high circulating T4 level is needed to normalize TSH. Early treatment with T4 results in normal IQ levels by preventing neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with autoimmune hypothyroidism have a higher predisposition for all except :
mcqs.explanation: Autoimmune hypothyroidism is usually not associated with type II diabetes mellitus . Genetic risk factors for autoimmune hypothyroidism has been documented with HLA -DR3 , HLA -DR4, HLA -DR5. A weak association also exists with CTLA4 gene polymorphism. This may explain the relationship between autoimmune hypothyroidism and type I diabetes mellitus , Addison's disease , pernicious anemia, and vitiligo.110 Less commonly encountered clinical associations include : • Celiac disease • Dermatitis herpetiformis • Chronic active hepatitis • Rheumatoid arthritis • Myasthenia gravis • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Sjogren's syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Most common symptom seen in patients with hypothyroidism is?
mcqs.explanation: The most common symptom of hypothyroidism is tiredness and weakness . Symptoms and signs in decreasing order of frequency are given below :Symptoms Signs Tiredness, weaknessDry skin Cold intoleranceHair lossDiff iculty concentrating and poor memoryConstipationWeight gain with poor appetiteDyspn eaHoarse voiceMenorrhagia ( later oligomenorrhea or ame norrhea)ParesthesiaImpaired hearing Dry coarse skin, cool periphe ral extremitiesPuffy face , han ds, and feet (myxedema )Diffu se alopeciaBradycardiaPeriph eral edemaDelayed tendon re flex relaxationCarpal tunnel s yndromeSerous cavity effusio ns

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An elderly patient presents to the ER with symptoms suggestive of myxedema coma. Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperthermia is least likely in this patient . Clinical manifestations of myxedema coma include decreased consciousness , seizures and hypothermia . Myxedema coma is a serious condition with a mortality rate of 20 -40%. The clinical outcomes are independent of the detected T4 and TSH levels . Clinical features of myxedema crisis include : • Impaired cognition, ranging from confusion to somnolence to coma (myxedema coma) • Convulsions and abnormal CNS signs. • Profound hypothermia (can reach 23\260C), hypoventilation , hyponatremia, hypoglycemia , hypoxemia , hypercapnia , and hypotension. • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.111

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient came to the hospital with complaints of lethargy , increased sleep , and weight gain. Investigations revealed low plasma TSH concentration. However, on the \037administration of TRH , the TSH levels increased . Which of the following conditions is likely in this patient ?

options.a: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.b: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.c: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
options.d: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus

mcqs.explanation: The presenting symptoms of lethargy , increased sleep , and weight gain are suggestive of hypothyroidism. An increase in TSH on administration of TRH confirms the lack of stimulus for TSH secretion from the hypothalamus . Although decreased TSH levels can be seen in hyperthyroidism , clinical features such as lethargy , increased sleep and weight gain are not. This pushes the diagnosis in favor of hypothyroidism . If the disease was in the pituitary , there would be no increase in TSH secretion on administration of TRH (Option B). Normally, the thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH ) is released by the hypothalamus . It stimulates the pituitary gland to release the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4 hormones. Administration of TRH does not elevate the TSH levels in this case since the pituitary g land is abnormal Primary disease of the hypot halamus Decreased release of TRH lea ding to decreased TSH and h ypothyroidism Administration of TRH cause s elevation of TSH levels sinc e the pituitary gland is norm al.112

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman with a history of constipation , dry skin and menorrhagia presents to the ER with altered sensorium, non-pitting edema , hypothermia , bradycardia, and hypotension . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history is typical of a case of hypothyroidism and the diagnosis is myxedema coma, which is a serious complication of hypothyroidism . Myxedema coma is a part of a larger clinical picture of myxedema crisis. Myxedema crisis refers to severe, life -threatening manifestations of hypothyroidism . It is often precipitated by the administration of sedatives , antidepressants , hypnotics , anaesthetics , or opioids . Clinical features of myxedema crisis : • Impaired cognition, ranging from confusion to somnolence to coma (myxedema coma). • Convulsions and abnormal CNS signs. • Profound hypothermia (can reach 23\260C), hypoventilation , hyponatremia, hypoglycemia , hypoxemia , hypercapnia , and hypotension. • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury • A high mortality rate Other options : Option A: Without a history of or focus of infection , septic shock is unlikely. Option B: Cardiogenic shock would present with symptoms of left heart failure i.e. pitting pedal edema, abdominal distension , prominence of neck veins, and dyspnea . Option D: Hypoglycemia usually presents with sweating , palpitations , and tachycardia113

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman who presented with tremors, palpitations , weight loss, and menstrual irregularities is diagnosed with Graves' disease . Which of the following statements would be correct with respect to her thyroid function test ?

options.d: Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) at 24 hours below normal

mcqs.explanation: 118 In Graves' disease , the level of serum TSH is low, free T4 is high and serum T3 is high. In patients with thyrotoxicosis , the radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) at 24 hours is characteristically elevated . Grave's disease is characterized by thyrotoxicosis caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs ) synthesized by lymphocytes in the thyroid gland, bone marrow , and lymph nodes . Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies are also seen . This results in excess production of free T3 and free T4 levels and in turn reduces serum TSH levels . RAIU is used to differentiate Grave's from other thyroid disorders, here there is diffuse high uptake. Measurement of TRab and TPOs is also done to confirm the diagnosis if the diagnosis clinically is unclear.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common pattern of thyroid hormone levels in a patient with sick euthyroid syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most common hormone pattern observed in sick euthyroid syndrome (SES) is a decrease in total and unbound T3 levels with normal levels of T4 and TSH. This pattern is called low T3 syndrome. SES is caused by an acute severe illness in the absence of underlying thyroid disease . T4 to T3 conversion via peripheral deiodination is impaired leading to a fall in T3 corresponding to the severity of illness . There is an adaptive increase in the level of reverse T3 (rT3 ). In very sick patients , there can be a dramatic fall in both total T4 and T3 levels . This pattern is called low T4 syndrome and is associated with a poor prognosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: On thyroid function test analysis, TSH value was much higher than normal with a low free T4. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: An elevated TSH value with low free T4 is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism (Option D). Option A: In subclinical hypothyroidism, free T4 levels remain normal despite elevated TSH. Option B: TSH is low in hyperthyroidism.119 Option C: The diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism is made along with a deficiency of other pituitary hormones. TSH levels may be low, normal , or slightly increased . The elevation in TSH levels can be attributed to the secretion of immunoreactive but biologically inactive forms of TSH. To confirm the diagnosis, it is essential to detect a low level of unbound T4. The diagnostic approach to hypothyroidism is given in the flowchart below :

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The radio-iodine uptake scan of a patient evaluated for swelling of the thyroid is shown below . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing localized overactivity (increased uptake ) in the left lobe of the thyroid i.e., hot nodule , with suppression of the remainder of the gland, is suggestive of a hypersecreting adenoma. Other options : Option B: The likelihood of malignancies like papillary Carcinoma thyroid is low (5%) in the case of a hot nodule . Option C: Graves disease shows diffusely increased uptake on a thyroid scan. Option D: Lateral aberrant thyroid presents with swelling of cervical lymph nodes and not thyroid. It is due to skip metastasis from papillary thyroid carcinoma to the ipsilateral cervical lymph nodes . The thyroid scan appearance in different conditions is shown in the image below :120 Diagnostic isotope studies , such as 99mTc -pertechnetate and iodine-123 , are becoming less common in thyroid imaging because some warm swellings (5%) which are actually malignant could be mistaken as benign. Isotope scanning is most valuable when assessing a hyperthyroid patient presenting with a nodule or nodularity in the thyroid. It helps to identify overactivity in the gland, which can differentiate between a toxic nodule that suppresses the rest of the gland and a toxic multinodular goitre with multiple areas of increased uptake .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs can cause the condition shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the absence of scalp hair and skin, along with calvarial defects (skull bone defects ), suggestive of aplasia cutis congenita . This is commonly associated with carbimazole and methimazole . These drugs can also cause other defects such as: • Choanal atresia • Tracheoesophageal fistula • Fetal goiter

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients cannot undergo radioiodine therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: Lactating mothers cannot undergo radioiodine therapy . Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications of radioiodine therapy . Patients can safely conceive 6 months after undergoing radioiodine treatment . Radioiodine therapy in patients with severe ophthalmopathy can be given with caution along with prednisone to prevent exacerbation of ophthalmopathy .121

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations . She informs you that a urine pregnancy test done one week ago was positive . Her investigations reveal hyperthyroidism . Which of the following antithyroid drugs can be prescribed for her?
mcqs.explanation: The patient in the given clinical scenario is in the 1st trimester of pregnancy. Propylthiouracil is used in the 1st trimester of gestation because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole. Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as • Aplasia cutis congenita • Choanal atresia • Treacheosopageal fistula • Fetal goiter However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity . It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy. The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation . This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient undergoing radioactive iodine therapy for a non-toxic multinodular goitre later develops altered sensorium, fever, and vomiting. What is the anti-thyroid drug of choice in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of thyroid storm and propylthiouracil is the drug of choice in this patient. This is due to its inhibitory action on peripheral T4 \032 T3 conversion. PTU is administered in large doses (500–1000 mg loading dose and 250 mg every 4h) administered orally / via nasogastric tube / per rectum. Propranolol is also given to reduce symptoms like tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. However, she has no features of hyperthyroidism. Which of the following statements about her condition is false ?

options.a: It is also referred to as simple goitre or colloid goitre
options.b: Most commonly caused by iodine deficiency
options.d: Thyroid function tests should be performed in all patients with goiter

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of a non-toxic diffuse goitre . Surgery is rarely indicated in this condition, except for cosmetic reasons, tracheal compression or obstruction of the thoracic inlet. It is sometimes called simple goitre - because of the absence of nodules , and colloid goitre - because of the presence of uniform follicles that are filled with colloid . It is most commonly caused by iodine deficiency and is often termed endemic goitre . Most diffuse goitres are benign and asymptomatic . Examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged , non-tender , generally soft gland without palpable nodules . TFTs should be performed in all patients to exclude thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism . If markedly enlarged , it can cause tracheal/oesophagal compression. Substernal goitre may obstruct the thoracic inlet leading to a positive Pemberton's sign i.e., facial congestion on bilateral arm elevation due to venous occlusion .122

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about silent thyroiditis is true?

options.b: Glucocorticoids are not indicated for treatment
options.c: It is not associated with thyrotoxicosis
options.d: It is not associated with hypothyroidism

mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoid treatment is not indicated in silent thyroiditis . The condition is called silent thyroiditis, as it is painless . When it occurs 3-6 months after pregnancy, it is termed postpartum thyroiditis . The condition is observed in up to 5% of women and it is 3 times more common in women with Type 1 diabetes mellitus . Typically , patients experience a brief phase of thyrotoxicosis lasting 2-4 weeks , followed by hypothyroidism for 4-12 weeks , and then clinical resolution . Often , only one phase is apparent. In addition to painless goitre , silent thyroiditis can be distinguished from subacute thyroiditis by a normal ESR value and the presence of TPO antibodies . Severe thyrotoxic symptoms can be managed with a brief course of propranolol, a 20 –40 mg dose administered three or four times daily. Thyroxine replacement may be needed for treating the hypothyroid phase but should be withdrawn after 6–9 months, to enable patient recovery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman with fatigue , depression and weight gain was found to have hypothyroidism. Which of the following statements is false about the treatment of her condition?

options.a: The replacement dose of thyroid is 1.6 �Mg/kg body weight
options.b: Complete relief from symptoms might occur within 3-6 months after initiation of treatment
options.c: TSH responses should be determined 2 months following the initiation of treatment or change in dose
options.d: Once TSH level is stable , TSH measurement is recommended at annual intervals

mcqs.explanation: The clinical effects of levothyroxine replacement are slow to appear. Patients may not experience full relief from symptoms until 3–6 months after normal TSH levels are restored . If there is no residual function, the daily replacement dose of levothyroxine is usually 1.6 �Mg/kg body weight (typically 100 –150 �Mg), ideally taken at least 30 minutes before breakfast. TSH responses are gradual and should be determined 2 months following the initiation of treatment or change in dose . Once the full replacement is achieved and TSH levels are stable , TSH measurement is recommended at annual intervals. In patients who have developed hypothyroidism following treatment of Graves' disease , lower doses are needed for replacement . This is because there is often underlying autonomous function, necessitating lower replacement doses (typically 75 –125 �Mg/d).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks of gestational age presents to your OPD. She is on oral levothyroxine supplementation for hypothyroidism . What is the target TSH level to be maintained in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The target TSH level to be maintained in the first trimester of pregnancy is <2.5 mIU/L . For second and third trimester the target is <3.0 mIU/L. Thyroid function must be evaluated by testing for TSH levels every 4 weeks in the first trimester a nd less frequently after 20 weeks . The levothyroxine dose may be increased by 50% during pregnancy. Following delivery , doses of thyroxine are usually restored to that of pre-pregnancy levels .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An elderly woman with hypothyroidism presents to the ER with decreased consciousness , hypothermia , sinus bradycardia, and hypotension . Her family members reveal that she has not been taking her thyroid medications recently . Investigations reveal elevated TSH levels and reduced T3 and T4 levels . All of the following can be used in the treatment except :
mcqs.explanation: 123 The given scenario is suggestive of myxedema coma. Hypotonic IV fluids are avoided in the course of treatment of this condition. However, hypertonic saline is used . Hypotonic fluids may exacerbate water retention and dilutional hyponatremia secondary to impaired renal perfusion and inappropriate vasopressin. Treatment of myxedema coma includes : • Levothyroxine (T4) can be administered as a single IV bolus of 500 �Mg. Although further doses are strictly not required, it is continued at 50-100 �Mg/day. • An alternative mode of treatment is the IV administration of liothyronine (T3) or via NG tubes with doses ranging from 10 -25 �Mg every 8-12 hours in case T4 to T3 conversion in myxedema is impaired. • Parenteral hydrocortisone should be administered to treat a condition of impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism . • Hypertonic saline or IV glucose may be recommended for treatment . • External warming is indicated only if the temperature is less than 30oC.124

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN ) type 1 is also called as ___________ .
mcqs.explanation: MEN1 is also referred to as Wermer's syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not observed in MEN1 syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Anterior pituitary tumours are associated with MEN1 syndrome, not posterior pituitary tumors.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man presented with abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea. He had a history of hyperparathyroidism and a transsphenoidal prolactinoma resection . Which of the following is the most common functional enteropancreatic tumor seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of MEN1 syndrome and gastrinoma is the most common functional enteropancreatic tumor in MEN1 / Wermer's syndrome. Enteropancreatic tumors in MEN1 syndrome are: • Non-functioning pancreatic tumors (most common overall) • Functioning pancreatic tumors : • Gastrinoma - 50% (most common among functioning pancreatic tumours) • Insulinoma - 30% • Glucagonoma • VIPoma (least common)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the first and second part of duodenum . MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets , and anterior pituitary . Gastrinoma is the most common pancreatic islet tumor in MEN 1 syndrome and if it is associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcers , the condition is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presents to the OPD with complaints of recurrent episodes of weakness , headache , sweating, and fainting after fasting. He tells that the symptoms improve after the consumption of food. There is a history of MEN1 syndrome running in the family. Serum C peptide levels are found to be elevated . What is the definitive treatment of choice in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 129 The given clinical scenario along with elevated serum C peptide levels points towards a diagnosis of insulinoma in a MEN1 patient . The definitive treatment of choice in this patient is surgery. Insulinoma is the second most common functioning enteropancreatic tumor in MEN1 syndrome. Investigation of choice is 72-hour fasting glucose and serum insulin levels . These parameters are measured when the patient develops hypoglycemic symptoms during a supervised 72-hour fasting period . The treatment of choice is surgery, ranging from enucleation of a single tumor to pancreatectomy . Non-surgical management of insulinoma includes frequent consumption of carbohydrate-rich meals , octreotide or diazoxide, which are not always successful . Selpercatinib , a kinase inhibitor was recently approved by the FDA. It is used to treat tumours with a mutation in the RET gene . These are non-small cell lung cancer, medullary thyroid cancer, and other types of thyroid cancers in patients with a mutation in the RET gene .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most frequently observed cutaneous manifestation of MEN1 syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most frequently observed cutaneous manifestation of MEN1 syndrome is angiofibroma. Cutaneous tumors in MEN1 Syndrome are: • Angiofibroma – 85% • Collagenoma – 70% • Lipoma - 33 %

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old man who was diagnosed with MEN1 syndrome presents to your OPD for his annual checkup . Which of the following investigations will you not do as part of annual screening for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Secretin study is not done as an annual screening test in patients with MEN1 syndrome. It is a provocative test for the diagnosis of gastrinoma. Annual biochemical screening tests to be done in patients with MEN1 syndrome are: Other imaging tests like MRI and CT might have to be done for screening of conditions like anterior pituitary tumors or adrenal tumors.Tumor Age to begin screenin g Annual screening test Parathyroid Calcium, PTH Gastrinoma Gastrin(+/- gastric pH) Insulinoma Fasting glucose , insulin Other pancreatic NE Ts <10 Chromogranin A; pancreatic polypeptide , glucagon ,vasoac tive intestinal peptide Anterior pituitary 5 Prolactin, IGF-I130

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common component of Sipple 's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most common component of MEN2A syndrome, which is also called Sipple 's syndrome is medullary thyroid cancer.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with MEN2 syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Pituitary adenoma is not a characteristic feature of the symptom complex of MEN2 and its variants, but it is observed in MEN1 and MEN4 syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with MEN2B syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Meningioma is not commonly seen in MEN2B Syndrome. MEN1 syndrome is associated with meningiomas.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: MEN4 syndrome is caused by a mutation in which of the following genes ?
mcqs.explanation: MEN4 is caused by genetic mutations in CDKN1B (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor), located on chromosome 12 . MEN1 is caused due to MEN1 gene mutation on chromosome 11 . MEN2 is associated with RET proto-oncogene mutation on chromosome 10 .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following malignancies would you not expect to see in a patient with MEN4 syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is not associated with MEN4 syndrome, but it is associated with MEN2 syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with abdominal pain and swelling in his scrotum and was diagnosed to have testicular carcinoma . There is a history of MEN syndrome running in his family. Which of the following conditions is he likely to have?
mcqs.explanation: This patient is likely to have MEN4 syndrome as reproductive organ tumors are a characteristic feature of this condition.131

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The clinical triad of pheochromocytoma includes all of the following symptoms except :
mcqs.explanation: The clinical triad of pheochromocytoma includes the following symptoms : • Headache • Profuse sweating • Palpitation (due to tachycardia) Hypertension is the most predominant sign of pheochromocytoma . Though intermittent hypertension is a classical feature , sustained hypertension is also common.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following would you not see in a patient with pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypercalcemia is seen in patients with pheochromocytoma , not hypocalcemia . This is due to the production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP ) by the tumor.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with pheochromocytoma , which of the following clinical features is least likely to be present ?
mcqs.explanation: Polyuria, not oliguria is seen in patients with pheochromocytoma . Excess catecholamine levels in this condition can cause polyuria and polydipsia due to hyperglycemia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an associated finding that can be seen in patients with pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Caf\351 au lait spots are seen in neurofibromatosis 1, which is a pheochromocytoma -associated syndrome. Pheochromocytoma-associated syndromes include the following : • Neurofibromatosis type 1 • Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 • Von Hippel –Lindau syndrome • Paraganglioma syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following parameters can help you diagnose a patient with a malignant pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Malignant pheochromocytoma refers to tumors that have undergone metastasis to lymph nodes or distant sites .137 They are histologically and biochemically the same as benign ones. Hence , typical histological criteria like cellular atypia, mitotic spindles , and capsular invasion are insufficient to confirm malignancy in pheochromocytomas.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following catecholamines would be elevated in a patient with extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Norepinephrine is exclusively secreted in patients with extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma . The PNMT (phenylethanolamine -N-methyl transferase) enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine . This enzyme is absent in extra-adrenal sites . Hence , extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas secrete only norepinephrine and cannot secrete epinephrine . On the other hand, adrenal pheochromocytomas can secrete norepinephrine , epinephrine , and dopamine in varying amounts depending on the PNMT levels in the tumor. Extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas or catecholamine -secreting paragangliomas are most commonly found in the abdomen. They commonly arise from the organ of Zuckerkandl .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 31 -year-old woman is rushed to the ED with a severe headache and vomiting. Past history includes a total thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer 3 months ago. Her BP is 200 /100 mm Hg and pulse is 110 /min. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the findings shown. Which of the following is likely to be predominantly elevated ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario with a history of thyroid cancer (likely medullary carcinoma ) and the image showing mucosal neuromas points towards MEN2B syndrome. Her current presentation is suggestive of a pheochromocytoma . She is likely to have predominantly elevated levels of epinephrine and its metabolite , metanephrine . This is due to the higher expression of the PNMT enzyme associated with the mutations in MEN2 syndromes (both 2A and 2B ). The higher levels of epinephrine result in a more symptomatic presentation . In contrast, low PNMT expression is seen in von -Hippel -Lindau (VHL ) syndrome. This leads to a predominant elevation of norepinephrine and normetanephrine levels . It is less symptomatic compared to MEN2 syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a suspected case of pheochromocytoma , which of the following would you avoid while making a diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Biopsy and FNAC should be avoided in patients with pheochromocytoma , as it is a highly vascular tumor. CT and MRI have similar sensitivity but T2 -weighted MRI with gadolinium contrast is the optimal test for diagnosis. MIBG (metaiodobenzylguanidine ) scintigraphy can be used to localize the tumor if both CT and MRI are negative. Genetic testing may be performed as nearly 40% of the tumors are associated with familial syndromes like VHL , neurofibromatosis, and MEN2. Note : In cases of malignant pheochromocytoma , biopsy may be indicated to confirm adrenal gland metastasis in other sites .138

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged male patient is being evaluated for recurrent episodes of palpitations , headaches , and profuse sweating . He was found to have elevated blood pressure readings on multiple occasions over the past 2 months. Which of the following tests has the highest sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma . The measurement of 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines has both the highest specificity and sensitivity in the diagnosis of this condition. Imaging modalities like CT and MRI have a sensitivity of around 98-100 % and specificity of 70%.24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines Plasma fractionated metanep hrines Sensitivity 98% 96-100 % Specificity 98% 85-89% False positive s Very rare Can occur due to drugs like l evodopa , TCAs, \030-blockers, \031-blockers, diuretics Procedure Collection of samples over 24 hours may be cumbersome Requires only a single blood sample . May be preferred in children. Uses Preferred first-line test as it i s highly specific Reserved for patients with a high index of suspicion like:F amily historyGenetic syndro mes like MEN2Prior history of pheochromocytoma

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the best method for detecting and localization of tumors associated with pheochromocytomas?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , the fluorodopa -PET scan is the best method for detecting and localization of tumors associated with pheochromocytoma . If biochemical testing for pheochromocytoma is positive , an abdominal MRI must be performed first. If MRI is negative or if multiple tumors are suspected , the tumor can be localized by performing one of the following investigations: • 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET scan - most sensitive , gold standard • Fluorodopa and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET scans - 97% sensitive • MIBG scintigraphy - least sensitive (94%)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of headache , palpitations , and sweating . His blood pressure at presentation was 180/100 mm Hg. Further testing revealed elevated urinary metanephrines . CT abdomen showed a right adrenal mass. What is the drug of choice for the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma . The drug of choice to control blood pressure prior to surgery is oral phenoxybenzamine at 0.5–4 mg/kg of body weight . It is a non-specific \030-blocker and is preferred due to its long action (3-4 days).139 Other \030-blockers like oral prazosin and intravenous phentolamine have a shorter duration of action and can be used to manage paroxysms. IV phentolamine is also used for intra-operative management of BP. \030-blockers are usually given for 7 days. Following this, \031-blockers are started , usually 2-3 days preoperatively . \031-blockers should never be started first because blockade of vasodilatory peripheral \031-receptors with unopposed \030-receptor stimulation can lead to a further elevation in blood pressure . (Mnemonic: A before B)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following should not be used for the initial management, in a patient with pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Beta-blockers like atenolol should never be used as the initial drug or alone in the management of pheochromocytoma. They must be given only after adequate alpha blockade has been established . Blocking beta-receptors may cause unopposed stimulation of alpha-receptors , precipitating a hypertensive crisis. Option A: Prazosin is an alpha-blocker. Option C: Nitroprusside can be used in case of hypertensive emergencies . Option D: Metyrosine inhibits catecholamine synthesis . It can be used when other agents have been ineffective .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a part of Averbuch's chemotherapy protocol ?
mcqs.explanation: Vinblastine is not included in Averbuch's chemotherapy protocol for the treatment of malignant pheochromocytoma.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed with malignant pheochromocytoma . Which of the following is used to treat this condition?
mcqs.explanation: 131I -MIBG (metaiodobenzylguanidine) is used for the treatment of malignant pheochromocytoma . Malignant pheochromocytomas occur in 10 % of cases and are histologically and biochemically the same as benign ones. The diagnosis of malignant pheochromocytoma is based on documentation of metastatic disease . The treatment of choice is nuclear medicine therapy with any of the following : • 131I -MIBG at 200 -mCi doses at monthly intervals (3-6 cycles ) • DOTATOC (a somatostatin receptor analog) labeled with radioactive lutetium or yttrium Chemotherapy can also be given according to Averbuch's protocol . Note : 123I -MIBG and Gallium-DOTATATE are used for imaging.140

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of Cushing's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic due to administration of corticosteroids .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following causes ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Cushing's disease causes ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. It occurs due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding Cushing's syndrome?

options.a: It is commonly associated with MEN1 syndrome
options.b: Bronchial carcinoid is a possible cause
options.d: It is associated with coronary heart disease

mcqs.explanation: Cushing's syndrome is rarely associated with MEN1 syndrome. Bronchial carcinoids are a source of ectopic ACTH secretion resulting in ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. Clinical features of Cushing's syndrome are attributed to the glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid actions of cortisol. mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with Cushing's syndrome is least likely to present with:
mcqs.explanation: Proximal myopathy is commonly seen in Cushing's syndrome, not distal myopathy . Clinical features of Cushing's syndrome are attributed to the glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid actions of cortisol. They include :System Clinical features Body fat Centralortruncal obesity (mos t common)Buffalo hump (fat deposition behind the neck) Moon facies Skin Purple striae (over abdomen & flanks)Acne and Hirsutism Easy bruisingFacial plethora Hyperpigmentation Musculoskele tal Proximal myopathyOsteopor osis Metabolic Poorly controlled hyperglyce miaDyslipidemia Reproductive OligomenorrheaAmenorrhea Renal Hypokalemic alkalosis CVS AtherosclerosisDiastolic Hyp ertensionEdema147 System Clinical features Hematologic Hypercoagulable stateLymph openiaNeutrophiliaEosinope nia CNS DepressionPsychosisAnxiety

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following would not be seen in a patient with Cushing's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Cushing's disease , and all other causes of Cushing's syndrome, can result in a hypercoagulable state . This is due to an increase in procoagulant factors and inhibition of fibrinolysis. Cushing's disease is a form of Cushing's syndrome caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor. The high ACTH levels stimulate melanocytes and cause skin hyperpigmentation . This is especially seen over friction-prone areas like knuckles and elbows . The majority of patients with Cushing's syndrome have psychiatric symptoms such as: • Anxiety, • Depression , and • Frank psychosis Mineralocorticoid action of cortisol may lead to diastolic hypertension , hypokalemia, and edema .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old woman visits a gynecologist with complaints of irregular and infrequent menstrual cycles . She is also upset that she has gained 12 kg over the past few months. Her face appears as shown in the image below . Her blood pressure at this visit is 144/98 mm Hg and she has multiple purple striae over her abdomen. Which of the following investigations should you advise this patient ?

options.c: Serum testosterone levels and abdominal USG

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the image showing moon facies with acne and hirsutism are suggestive of Cushing's syndrome. It can be diagnosed with the help of a single midnight serum cortisol measurement . Option A: Cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test is used for the diagnosis of Addison's disease . Options C and D: Serum testosterone , abdominal USG, and LH : FSH ratio, are used to confirm a diagnosis of the polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Though PCOS can present with similar features , it is not typically associated with moon facies , purple striae, or hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: You can advise any of the following tests for screening of a patient suspected to be having Cushing's syndrome except :
mcqs.explanation: Determination of plasma ACTH levels is not advised as a screening test for a patient with Cushing's syndrome. Plasma ACTH determination is done to distinguish between ACTH-dependent and independent causes . It is done after the screening or confirmation of Cushing's syndrome.148

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In patients with which of the following conditions would you expect to see the highest basal ACTH level ?
mcqs.explanation: Basal plasma ACTH levels are highest in ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors. Plasma ACTH > 15pg /ml is suggestive of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome due to pituitary or ectopic sources . Basal ACTH in pituitary adenoma can be normal or elevated , whereas in an ectopic source the ACTH production is very high. This occurs because a pituitary adenoma retains some sensitivity to the negative feedback mechanism exerted by cortisol, but ectopic tumors remain unaffected . Plasma ACTH < 5pg /ml is suggestive of ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome that can be caused by an adrenal adenoma or exogenous administration of glucocorticoids .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with suspected Cushing's syndrome is found to have elevated ACTH levels . What is the investigation of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: An elevated ACTH level is suggestive of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. The investigation of choice for ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome is MRI brain , to look for the presence of a pituitary tumour. If the MRI brain shows a mass it is suggestive of a pituitary mass of >6 mm in size. However, if the MRI brain does not show a mass it suggests a pituitary tumor of <6mm in size or an ectopic ACTH source .Note : High-dose dexamethasone suppression test and CRH stimulation test are employed to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH syndrome. A definitive cause can be established only by imaging techniques like MRI for pituitary tumors, CT scan of the chest and abdomen for ectopic ACTH sites . Hence MRI is considered the investigation of choice .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old man chronic smoker presented with flecks of blood in his sputum . He is currently on treatment for COPD and hypertension . His BMI is 31 kg/m\262 and he has central obesity . His RBS is 261 mg/dl. During further evaluation, he is found to have high ACTH levels that remained high even after administration of high-dose dexamethasone . What is the underlying cause of this patient 's symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: 149 Elevated ACTH levels that do not get suppressed by a high-dose dexamethasone test are suggestive of Cushing's syndrome secondary to an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor. Considering the patient 's smoking history and presentation with hemoptysis , it is likely to be a lung tumor. Ectopic sources of ACTH include small cell lung cancers and pulmonary carcinoid tumors. The most effective treatment strategy is the management of the underlying SCLC or carcinoid.Dynamic testing for Cushing' s syndrome High dose dexamethasone su ppression test CRH stimulation test Pituitary adenoma Positive (suppressed cortisol) Positive (increase in ACTH a nd cortisol) Ectopic ACTH Negative Negative Iatrogenic: Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected b y dynamic testing Adrenalmass or hyperplasia : Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected by dynamic testing

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Evaluation of a patient with Cushing's syndrome reveals high ACTH levels that are responsive to CRH and suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: CRH responsiveness is seen only in ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism which is due to a pituitary cause . This is because the pituitary tumor contains corticotrophic cells that are responsive to CRH.Dynamic testing for Cushing' s syndrome High dose dexamethasone su ppression test CRH stimulation test Pituitary adenoma Positive(suppressed cortisol) Positive(increase in ACTH an d cortisol) Ectopic ACTH Negative Negative Iatrogenic: Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected b y dynamic testing Adrenalmass or hyperplasia : Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected by dynamic testing150

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman was diagnosed with ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome. As MRI of the pituitary was normal and further testing was unequivocal, she was scheduled for inferior petrosal sinus sampling. It revealed a baseline petrosal :peripheral ACTH ratio > 2. What is the treatment of choice in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Cushing's syndrome with petrosal : peripheral ACTH ratio > 2 at baseline confirms the presence of an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma. The treatment of choice is transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. Radiotherapy is used in case of recurrence of tumors. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is performed to differentiate pituitary and ectopic sources of ACTH when initial imaging and testing are inconclusive.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following would not be used to treat patients with Cushing's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Mitomycin is not used in the treatment of Cushing's syndrome. The drugs used in its management include : • Metyrapone • Ketoconazole • Aminoglutethimide • Trilostane • Cyproheptadine • Mitotane – Mainly in adrenal carcinoma • Etomidate – Severe cortisol excess

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the best adrenolytic agent that can be used in the management of patients with adrenocortical carcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: Mitotane is used in the management of adrenocortical carcinoma due to its adrenolytic properties . Mitotane is an insecticide derivative. It is effective in the treatment of benign Cushing's also, but is rarely used due to its side effects .151

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following complications is associated with bilateral adrenalectomy ?
mcqs.explanation: Nelson 's syndrome is a rare complication of total bilateral adrenalectomy (TBA ). TBA is a procedure used to control hypercortisolism in Cushing's disease (due to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) when resection of the primary tumor is not possible . The loss of feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic -pituitary -adrenal axis following TBA increases CRH. This leads to stimulation of ACTH-secreting corticotroph cells , causing enlargement of the original pituitary tumor or the formation of a new one. Nelson 's syndrome is associated with a clinical triad of: • Hyperpigmentation • Excessive ACTH secretion • Corticotroph adenoma Screening is done with fasting plasma ACTH levels and MRI brain is performed at regular intervals. Prophylactic pituitary irradiation may be recommended to prevent its incidence . The primary treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Patients will also require life -long glucocorticoid replacement , as they do not produce cortisol. The use of steroidogenic inhibitors in the treatment of Cushing's disease has decreased the need for bilateral adrenalectomy these days. Option A: Sheehan 's syndrome refers to postpartum hypopituitarism that is caused by ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary as a result of severe postpartum hemorrhage. Option B: Addison's disease occurs due to autoimmune destruction of adrenal glands. Option C: Waterhouse -Friderichsen syndrome refers to adrenal apoplexy that is caused by fulminant meningococcemia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a cause of pseudo -Cushing's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Malignancy does not cause pseudo -Cushing's syndrome. It may cause ectopic ACTH production , leading to true Cushing's syndrome. Pseudo -Cushing's syndrome refers to functional hypercortisolism caused by chronic activation of the HPA axis. It presents with clinical and biochemical features similar to Cushing's syndrome, making it difficult to differentiate between them. It may occur secondary to the following conditions: • Severe major depressive disorder • Polycystic ovarian syndrome • Insulin-resistant obesity • Obstructive sleep apnea • Chronic alcoholism152 • End-stage renal disease It usually resolves when the underlying condition is treated .153

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Addison's disease is commonly associated with ____
mcqs.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency , also known as Addison's disease , is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis. Tuberculous adrenalitis is still a frequent cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developing countries like India. It is characterized by the loss of glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and adrenal androgen secretion . Glucocorticoid deficiency results in fatigue , lack of energy , weight loss, fever, myalgia, normochromic anemia, and hypoglycemia . Mineralocorticoid deficiency is characterized by nausea, vomiting, low blood pressure , postural hypotension , salt craving , hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Adrenal androgen deficiency manifests as a lack of energy , dry itchy skin, loss of libido, and loss of axillary and pubic hair (in women). Hyperpigmentation is seen in primary adrenal insufficiency due to excess proopiomelanocortin-derived peptides . Hyperpigmentation is not seen in secondary adrenal insufficiency . The diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency can be made with the short cosyntropin test (cortisol level <450-500nmol/L sampled 30 to 60 minutes after ACTH stimulation is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency ). Plasma ACTH, plasma renin, and serum aldosterone can help differentiate primary from secondary causes . Primary adrenal insufficiency will show elevated ACTH and a compensatory elevation in renin levels due to decreased aldosterone in the body. In secondary adrenal insufficiency , ACTH is low with normal renin and aldosterone . Treatment includes glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and adrenal androgen replacement . Other options :159 Option B: Patients with adrenocortical carcinoma present with features of glucocorticoid and adrenal androgen excess , and not adrenal insufficiency . Options C and D: Hypernephroma and medullary carcinoma thyroid are not associated with Addison's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in India?
mcqs.explanation: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in India and other developing countries. Idiopathic atrophy due to autoimmune conditions is the most common cause in developed countries .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with reduced cortisol and elevated ACTH, which of the following would not be part of your differential diagnoses ?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated ACTH and reduced cortisol levels are seen in primary adrenal insufficiency . It is not a feature of MEN 4 syndrome. The following syndromes are associated with primary adrenal insufficiency : • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 • Triple-A syndrome • Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome • Kearns-Sayre syndrome • IMAGe syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and was started on levothyroxine 2 weeks ago. She now presents to your clinic with abdominal pain and dizziness. The left and right images below show her current appearance and her appearance last month, respectively . Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing skin hyperpigmentation in a patient with severe dizziness and a history of autoimmune thyroiditis points to a diagnosis of Addison's disease . Hyperglycemia is not a feature of this condition. Hypocortisolism leads to hypoglycemia in these patients . Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency characterized by the disruption of glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and androgen secretion . Primary adrenal insufficiency is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis and coincident autoimmune disease occurring in these patients most frequently includes thyroid autoimmune disease , vitiligo, and premature ovarian failure. Clinical features of Addison's disease :160 Hormone Clinical features Hypoaldosteronism Abdominal pain, nausea, vo miting, salt craving Dizziness, postural hypotensi on AKI due to volume depletion Hyponatremia Hyperkalemia, metabolic aci dosis Hypocortisolism Anorexia, weight loss, fatigue , myalgia, arthralgia Fever (increased IL -1) Depression Postural hypotension Hypoglycemia Hyponatremia (loss of feedba ck inhibition of ADH) Slightly increased TSH (loss of feedback inhibition) Hypoandrogenism Loss of libido Loss of pubic and axillary hai r Elevated ACTH HyperpigmentationLevothyroxine can precipitate adrenal insufficiency or crisis in undiagnosed patients . In patients with concurrent adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism , a course of steroids must be given before giving thyroid replacement .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common biochemical abnormality seen at presentation in patients with adrenal insufficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: Hyponatremia is the most common biochemical abnormality seen at presentation in patients with adrenal insufficiency . It is observed in 80% of the patients at presentation . Hyponatremia is caused by: • Mineralocorticoid deficiency • Diminished inhibition of ADH release by cortisol, resulting in mild SIADH during secondary adrenal insufficiency Hyperkalemia is diagnosed in 40% of the patients during initial diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea for the past 3 days. She has been excessively tired and dizzy for the past 2 weeks . On examination, there are patches of hyperpigmented skin. Blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg and blood glucose is 50 mg/dl. How will you confirm the diagnosis?
