options.b: Serum Na+, K+, saline suppression test

mcqs.explanation: 161 This clinical scenario is suggestive of adrenal insufficiency . The confirmatory test for diagnosis is the ACTH stimulation test or short cosyntropin stimulation test . Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are seen . Plasma levels of ACTH, renin and aldosterone are used to differentiate between primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman is being evaluated for adrenal insufficiency . You decide to check her serum levels of ACTH, renin, and aldosterone . Which of the following laboratory findings would prompt you to subsequently order a pituitary MRI?

options.a: High renin and low aldosterone levels
options.c: Low renin and high aldosterone levels

mcqs.explanation: Pituitary MRI is indicated in secondary adrenal insufficiency which presents with the following parameters: • Low-normal ACTH level • Normal renin level • Normal aldosterone level The following findings are seen in primary adrenal insufficiency : • High ACTH levels • High renin • Low aldosterone levels Pituitary MRIs are not required in primary adrenal insufficiency . The fact that a pituitary MRI is done itself gives a hint towards secondary adrenal insufficiency .162

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old man collapses during a family vacation. At the hospital , blood pressure is found to be 86/52 mm Hg, and random blood sugar is 49 mg/dl. His wife says that he has been on treatment for Addison's disease for two years but had forgotten to pack his medication for the trip. What is the drug of choice for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of an adrenal crisis triggered by missed medication. In this patient who is a known case of adrenal insufficiency , IV hydrocortisone is the drug of choice . However, in patients with newly diagnosed adrenal insufficiency , dexamethasone is used for the treatment of adrenal crisis. This is because dexamethasone is not measured in cortisol assays and would not interfere with the diagnostic tests , whereas hydrocortisone interferes with cortisol assays. Acute adrenal insufficiency requires the immediate initiation of the following therapeutic strategies : • Rehydration - saline infusion at an initial rate of 1 L/h with continuous cardiac monitoring. • Glucocorticoid replacement - bolus injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone , followed by the maintenance dose of 100 –200 mg over 24h. • Mineralocorticoid replacement - initiated once the daily hydrocortisone dose has been reduced to <50 mg as higher doses of hydrocortisone have sufficient mineralocorticoid action.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient who presented with an adrenal crisis is undergoing treatment with dexamethasone . Which of the following abnormalities will not improve with this treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperkalemia will not improve following administration of dexamethasone . Dexamethasone is a long-acting steroid with glucocorticoid action. It has no effect on hyperkalemia, which is mediated by mineralocorticoids. Hyponatremia is chiefly due to mineralocorticoid deficiency , however, hypocortisolism causes hyponatremia due to loss of feedback inhibition of ADH resulting in SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion ).163 Hypocortisolism can also cause postural hypotension as cortisol regulates vascular tone by potentiating the effects of vasoconstrictors. Thus on administration dexamethasone hyponatremia and postural hypotension will improve as dexamethasone has glucocorticoid action but hyperkalemia will not improve. Dexamethasone is used in patients with newly diagnosed adrenal insufficiency as it does not interfere with serum cortisol measurement.Hormone Clinical features Hypoaldosteron ism Abdominal pain, nausea, vo miting, salt craving Dizziness, postural hypotensi on AKI due to volume depletion Hyponatremia Hyperkalemia, metabolic aci dosis Hypocortisolis m Anorexia, weight loss, fatigue , myalgia, arthralgia Fever (increased IL -1) Depression Postural hypotension Hypoglycemia Hyponatremia (loss of feedba ck inhibition of ADH) Slightly increased TSH (loss of feedback inhibition) Hypoandrogeni sm Loss of libido Loss of pubic and axillary hai r Elevated ACTH Hyperpigmentation

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old woman who was diagnosed with a non-functioning pituitary adenoma develops features of adrenal insufficiency . Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: A non-functioning pituitary adenoma causes hypopituitarism due to compression of the pituitary stalk. This results in secondary adrenal insufficiency . Hyperpigmentation is not a feature . This condition is characterized by an alabaster-like paleness due to the lack of ACTH secretion . In primary adrenal insufficiency , hyperpigmentation occurs as a result of elevated ACTH.164

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect with respect to Addisonian pigmentation ?

options.c: Does not affect the oral mucosa

mcqs.explanation: Addison's disease causes patchy hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa. Hyperpigmentation is also present in areas of increased friction including: • Palmar creases • Dorsal aspect of the foot • Nipples and the axillary region

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of mineralocorticoid excess ?
mcqs.explanation: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is the most common cause of mineralocorticoid excess . It causes primary hyperaldosteronism . Other causes of primary hyperaldosteronism are: • Conn's syndrome – Unilateral adrenal adenoma • Glucocorticoid -remediable hyperaldosteronism (< 1%) Other causes of mineralocorticoid excess are as follows : • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) • Syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess (SAME) • Adrenocortical carcinoma • Progesterone -induced hypertension • Cushing's syndrome Liddle's syndrome is due to a mutation of ENaC subunits . This results in reduced degradation of ENaC channels, causing prolonged mineralocorticoid action.165

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following clinical features will you not expect to see in a patient with Conn's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: In Conn's syndrome, even though there is volume expansion, an underlying salt-escape mechanism leads to the absence of pedal edema . The volume expansion due to hypernatremia leads to right heart dilatation that stimulates the release of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP). This leads to compensatory diuresis and lack of edema despite sodium retention . Features of primary hyperaldosteronism: • Hypokalemia • Hypertension • Metabolic alkalosis • Polyuria (due to ANP) • Polydipsia (consequence of polyuria) • Muscle weakness

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 39-year-old man is referred for evaluation of severe hypertension that has not improved despite being on 3 anti-hypertensive drugs. The presence of decreased plasma renin activity in this patient would point to which of the following diagnoses ?
mcqs.explanation: Conn syndrome is a cause of primary hyperaldosteronism that presents with hypertension and low levels of renin. Elevated aldosterone levels cause negative feedback in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS ) and results in decreased renin production .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the best initial investigation in a patient with hypokalemic hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypokalemic hypertension is suggestive of hyperaldosteronism . The screening test of choice is a measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone levels to calculate the aldosterone -renin ratio (ARR ). ARR must be estimated in patients with hypertension and any one of the following features : • Drug resistance • Hypokalemia • Adrenal mass • Onset before 40 years of age Prior to the determination of ARR , hypokalemia correction must be done. If the patient is on spironolactone , it must be stopped 4 weeks prior to testing . Other blood pressure medication may be continued . ARR screen is considered positive when: • ARR > 750 pmol/L : ng/mL per hour166 • Aldosterone > 450 pmol/L Option A: ACTH stimulation test is used for the diagnosis of Addison's disease . It presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia. Options B and C: If ARR is positive , CT abdomen and adrenal vein sampling are used for confirmation of the diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following tests is not performed in patients with an elevated aldosterone -renin ratio?
mcqs.explanation: An elevated aldosterone -renin ratio (ARR ) is indicative of primary hyperaldosteronism . Metyrapone stimulation test is used in the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency , not hyperaldosteronism . A failure of suppression of aldosterone levels below 140 pmol/L indicates autonomous aldosterone production, which is the hallmark of primary hyperaldosteronism . This principle is used in the following tests : • Saline infusion test - IV administration of 2L of physiological saline over 4 hours • Oral sodium loading test - oral sodium given over 3 days • Fludrocortisone suppression test - given IV over 4 days These tests may be used to confirm the diagnosis in patients with elevated ARR , but are not necessary in cases of overt hypokalemic hypertension , strongly positive ARR , and high aldosterone .167

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a clinical feature of diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: Weight loss is a clinical feature of diabetes mellitus , not weight gain. Diabetes mellitus refers to a group of common metabolic disorders that result in hyperglycemia . It causes the following classical triad of symptoms : • Polyuria - due to osmotic diuresis • Polydipsia - triggered by the resulting hypovolemia • Weight loss - due to catabolic state Note : Obesity is a risk factor, not a symptom of type 2 diabetes mellitus and plays a role in its pathogenesis. Increase in the adipocyte mass leads to an increase in the level of circulating free fatty acids. Free fatty acids impair glucose utilization in skeletal muscles , promote glucose175 production by the liver, and impair beta-cell function.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the OPD by his worried mother as he urinates more than ten times a day and is always drinking water. She also reports that despite eating more than his brother did at that age , he is not gaining any weight . Random blood glucose is 252 mg/dl. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?

options.a: Antibodies against zinc transporters may be present
options.c: It is associated with a strong family history
options.d: Insulin-resistance is the hallmark for pathogenesis

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of type 1 diabetes mellitus . It is an autoimmune disease associated with the following immunologic markers : • Antibodies against zinc transporter (ZnT -8) • Islet cells antibodies (ICA) • Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GAD) • Insulin autoantibodies (IAA )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which chromosome contains the major susceptible gene for type 1 diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: The major susceptibility gene for type 1 diabetes mellitus is located in the HLA region of chromosome 6. Type I diabetes mellitus occurs in genetically susceptible individuals and is usually triggered by infections . The HLA complex is most commonly involved. The common HLA associations include : • Causative - HLA-DQA1*0501 and DQB*0201 • Protective - HLA-DQA1*0102 , DQB1*0602 , DRB1 *1501 Other genomic associations of type I diabetes mellitus include the CTLA -4 gene and IL -2 receptor . Type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with mutations in the calpain-10 gene on chromosome 2. It results in insulin resistance .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following mechanisms is predominantly responsible for an increase in the fasting plasma glucose level of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: In type 2 diabetes mellitus increased fasting blood sugar is predominantly due to increased hepatic gluconeogenesis . In the postprandial period , there is a rise in peripheral blood glucose levels . Due to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes mellitus , there is reduced peripheral uptake of glucose by insulin-sensitive tissues like the liver and skeletal muscles . This results in reduced glucose utilization by skeletal muscles as well as reduced glycogenesis in the liver and skeletal muscles . This results in increased postprandial plasma glucose levels . Increased hepatic glucose output predominantly accounts for increased FPG levels , whereas decreased peripheral glucose utilization results in postprandial hyperglycemia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old woman presents with fatigue and weight loss for the past 6 months. She tells you that her father is also a diabetic . Further evaluation reveals the following . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 176 This clinical scenario is suggestive of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY ). MODY is a monogenic form of diabetes mellitus that is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion. It affects young adults < 25 years of age . It occurs due to reduced insulin secretion . Etiological factors of type 1 and 2 diabetes such as insulin resistance , obesity , and antibodies are not associated with this condition. Stable hyperglycemia is usually seen , hence complications like diabetic ketoacidosis are uncommon. Macrovascular complications like hyperlipidemia or hypertension are not seen . It is treated with sulfonylureas . Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA ) is a form of type 1 diabetes that occurs between 30-50 years of age .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: All of the following are true about maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY ) except :

options.b: MODY 4 is the most common form

mcqs.explanation: MODY 3 is the most common form of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY ), accounting for two -thirds of all the cases . MODY is a monogenic form of diabetes mellitus that is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion. It affects young adults <25 years of age . There are a total of 11 types of MODY based on mutations involves. Some of the affected genes include : • Types 1,3,5: HNF (Hepatocyte nuclear transcription factor) mutation • Type 2: Glucokinase mutation • Type 4: IPF 1 (Insulin Promotor Factor-1) mutation These mutations result in impaired glucose -induced insulin secretion resulting in insulinopenia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following would cause type 1 diabetes in an adult patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Type 1 diabetes mellitus in an adult is suggestive of latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA ). LADA is common in thin-built adults between 30-50 years and is associated with autoantibodies . As the progression of the disease is less rapid than in children, clinical features may mimic type 2 diabetes . However, patients usually require insulin treatment within 5 years. Option A: Patients with latent diabetes become diabetic under stressful conditions. However, upon removal of stress , they become non-diabetic . Option B: MODY or maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic form of diabetes that occurs < 25 years. There is impaired insulin secretion , but no antibodies . Option C : Brittle diabetes is seen in children with type 1 DM. It presents with wide fluctuation in blood sugar levels .177

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Patients with all of the following conditions can develop diabetes mellitus except :
mcqs.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is not associated with diabetes mellitus . Genetic syndromes associated with diabetes include : • Prader-Willi syndrome • Friedreich's ataxia • Wolfram 's syndrome • Down's syndrome • Klinefelter 's and Turner 's syndrome • Huntington's chorea • Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome • Myotonic dystrophy • Porphyria Diseases of the exocrine pancreas causing diabetes : • Hemochromatosis • Pancreatitis • Neoplasia • Cystic fibrosis Endocrinopathies causing diabetes : • Acromegaly • Cushing's syndrome • Glucagonoma • Pheochromocytoma • Hyperthyroidism

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients can be diagnosed with diabetes mellitus ?

options.a: A patient with RBS of 210 mg/dl
options.b: A patient with FBS of 125 mg/dl and 2-hour PPBS of 199 mg/dl
options.c: A patient with symptoms of diabetes and RBS of 192 mg/dl

mcqs.explanation: The patient with HbA1c \037 6.5 % can be diagnosed with diabetes mellitus as this is an independent criterion for diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old man presents to his physician for a routine health evaluation. He is concerned that he might have diabetes as his three brothers have all been diagnosed with diabetes . He does not have any complaints. Which of the following tests can be employed in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: HbA1c and fasting blood glucose are used for screening diabetes mellitus in asymptomatic individuals.178 HbA1c refers to glycated hemoglobin and it serves as a long-term indicator for blood glucose levels (8 to 12 weeks). • Normal < 5.7 % • Abnormal glucose homeostasis : 5.7 to 6.4 % • Diabetes mellitus : \037 6.5% HbA1c also serves as a prognostic indicator for glycemic control.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be termed impaired glucose tolerance ?

options.a: Fasting blood glucose levels between 100 and 125 mg/dL
options.b: Random blood glucose levels between 140 and 199 mg/dL
options.c: Blood glucose levels between 140 and 199 mg/dL following oral glucose tolerance test
options.d: Fasting blood glucose levels between 100 and 199 mg/dL

mcqs.explanation: Impaired glucose tolerance is defined as blood glucose levels between 140 -199 mg/dL following an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Impaired fasting glucose is when the fasting blood glucose is between 100 to 125 mg/dL.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: You are counselling an asymptomatic middle -aged woman regarding screening for diabetes mellitus . Based on the ADA recommendations, what will you tell her?

options.a: All individuals > 35 years must undergo screening every 3 years
options.b: All individuals > 50 years must undergo screening every 5 years
options.c: Oral glucose tolerance test would be performed
options.d: Random blood glucose levels would be checked

mcqs.explanation: The ADA recommends screening for type 2 diabetes mellitus in all asymptomatic individuals > 35 years every 3 years. The tests used for screening are: • HbA1c levels • Fasting blood glucose levels Individuals can be screened earlier if they are overweight with BMI >25 kg/m2 and have one of the following risk factors: • Family history of diabetes • History of cardiovascular diseases • History of gestational diabetes mellitus or delivery of a baby > 4 kg • Obesity (BMI \03725 kg/m2 ) • Physical inactivity • Hypertension (\037140 /90 mm Hg) • HDL cholesterol < 35 mg/dL • Triglycerides >250 mg/dL • Polycystic ovarian syndrome or acanthosis nigricans Note - If an individual has a test result near the margins of the diagnostic threshold , a close follow -up should be done and repeat the test in 3–6 months.179

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus . Her HbA1c level is 11.1%. What is the initial drug of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin is the best initial drug of choice when HbA1c is > 9% at diagnosis. Insulin is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes in the following cases : • Inadequate glycemic control with 2 or more oral agents • HbA1c > 9% at diagnosis In patients with HbA1c < 9%, metformin is the drug of choice .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her relatives after she suffered a brief, seizure -like episode . They tell you that she is taking an oral medication for diabetes . On examination, the patient was disoriented , and CBG was 45 mg/dl. Which of the following drugs most likely played a role in the patient 's current presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: Repaglinide is an insulin secretagogue and hence poses the risk of causing hypoglycemia . Drugs that can cause hypoglycemia (insulin secretagogues ): • Sulfonylureas • Meglitinides : Nateglinide , Repaglinide The following drugs are not directly responsible for stimulating insulin secretion and hence do not cause hypoglycemia : • Metformin • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor • Pioglitazone • DPP-4 inhibitor: SitagliptinManagement of diabetes mell itus Intervention Advantages Disadvantages180 Management of diabetes mell itus Lifestyle changes Reduced complications and mortality Insufficient for most patients within 1st year Metformin Weight neutral GI side effectsContraindicate d when GFR < 45 ml/min Insulin Rapidly effectiveLowers HbA 1c more than other drugs (by 1.5-3%) Weight gainHypoglycemia GLP -1 agonists Weight lossReduces cardiova scular complications GI side effects Pramlintide Weight lossLowers postprand ial glucose GI side effectsHypoglycemia when used with insulin Sulfonylureas Rapidly effective Weight gainHypoglycemia Thiazolidinediones Lowers insulin requirements Weight gain, edema , CHF, fr actures Meglitinides Rapidly effective Weight gainHypoglycemia SGLT -2 inhibitors Weight lossBetter cardiovasc ular and renal outcomes UTI, vulval candidiasisDehyd rationEuglycemic DKA DPP-4 inhibitors Weight neutral Angioedema , urticaria Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors Weight neutral GI flatulenceRise in LFT

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: All of the following drugs can be used in the treatment of patients with type 1 diabetes except :
mcqs.explanation: Metformin can only be used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus . Drugs that can be used for treating both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus include the following : • Acarbose - reduces the breakdown of starch into sugar in the GI tract and lowers the postprandial glucose rise in both types. • Pramlintide - an injectable drug that enhances amylin secretion leading to reduced glucagon levels • Insulin

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus is now diagnosed with hypertension . Which of the following antihypertensive drugs will you not prefer in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Hydrochlorthiazide belongs to the thiazide group of diuretics , that can cause dyslipidemia and hyperglycemia. Hence they are not preferred for use in diabetic hypertensives . The antihypertensive drug of choice in diabetes mellitus include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs).181

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A type 2 diabetic patient who was recently started on treatment complains of frequent urination , fever, and burning micturition. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a urinary tract infection (UTI). This adverse effect occurs as a result of dapagliflozin use . The group of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 or SGLT -2 inhibitors includes drugs like dapagliflozin and canagliflozin. These drugs prevent glucose reabsorption in the renal tubules and cause loss of sodium and glucose . • UTI - due to glucosuria • Dehydration - due to natriuresis and volume loss • Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis - low blood glucose levels due to glucosuria can reduce insulin release SGLT -2 inhibitors must be temporarily discontinued for 3-4 days before any scheduled surgery to avoid potential risk for diabetic ketoacidosis .Management of diabetes mell itus Intervention Advantages Disadvantages Lifestyle changes Reduced complications and mortality Insufficient for most patients within 1st year Metformin Weight neutral GI side effectsContraindicate d when GFR < 45 ml/min Insulin Rapidly effectiveLowers HbA 1c more than other drugs (by 1.5-3%) Weight gainHypoglycemia GLP -1 agonists Weight lossReduces cardiova scular complications GI side effects Pramlintide Weight lossLowers postprand ial glucose GI side effectsHypoglycemia when used with insulin Sulfonylureas Rapidly effective Weight gainHypoglycemia Thiazolidinediones Lowers insulin requirements Weight gain, edema , CHF, fr actures Meglitinides Rapidly effective Weight gainHypoglycemia SGLT -2 inhibitors Weight lossBetter cardiovasc ular and renal outcomes UTI, vulval candidiasisDehyd rationEuglycemic DKA DPP-4 inhibitors Weight neutral Angioedema , urticaria Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors Weight neutral GI flatulenceRise in LFT

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man is hospitalized with pneumonia. He is a known patient of type 2 diabetes . During the hospital stay, his appetite is poor and his oral intake is irregular. The physician decides to administer rapid-acting insulin based on high blood sugar values. Which of the following would he use ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario describes the sliding scale method . Rapid-acting insulins such as glulisine are used .182 Sliding scale refers to the administration of insulin as a bolus dose based on the blood sugar level before the meal. Using this principle , the insulin dose is titrated every time according to pre-meal glucose levels to determine insulin requirement. Hence , rapid-acting insulin is preferred . This method requires a fixed carbohydrate intake at every meal. It is used for the short-term management of hospitalized patients , especially when the frequency or quantity of food intake is very variable. It does not deliver insulin in a physiological manner , hence is not a preferred long-term strategy for glycemic control.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about Afrezza?

options.a: It is available as a powder for inhalation

mcqs.explanation: Afrezza is an inhalational form of insulin that can cause hypoglycemia . It is a rapid-acting form of insulin that is administered at the beginning of each meal. Peak levels are achieved 12 -15 minutes later. Adverse effects include hypoglycemia , cough , throat pain, or irritation . It may cause acute bronchospasm in patients with asthma, COPD, as well as active smokers. Hence , it is contraindicated in these condition.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents to the casualty with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His blood sugar levels are 421 mg/dl and urine ketones are 3+. He is started on IV normal saline and insulin infusion. Which of the following should he be monitored for?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis , which is treated with insulin infusion. Insulin causes an intracellular shift of K+ ions resulting in a decreased extracellular K+ ion concentration. This results in hypokalemia. Non-diabetic clinical applications of insulin include : • Treatment of hyperkalemia • To determine the functions of the anterior pituitary • To examine the completion of truncal vagotomy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Dawn phenomenon is clinically suspected when a patient shows which of the following findings?

options.a: Early morning hyperglycemia with hypoglycemia at 3 am
options.b: Early morning hypoglycemia with normal blood glucose levels at 3 am
options.c: Early morning hyperglycemia with normal blood glucose levels at 3 am
options.d: Early morning hypoglycemia with hyperglycemia at 3 am

mcqs.explanation: Dawn phenomenon refers to normal blood glucose levels at 3 am followed by early morning hyperglycemia. This occurs due to an early morning surge in plasma growth hormone and cortisol levels , which have an insulin-antagonistic action. In normal individuals, this is countered by increased early morning insulin secretion . However, in diabetic patients , insulin secretion is disrupted which results in the unopposed action of growth hormone. Hence , there will be resulting hyperglycemia .183

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A patient is said to have developed insulin resistance when the required insulin dosage is which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: When a patient needs > 200 units of insulin per day, they are said to have developed insulin resistance . Some causes of insulin resistance are as follows : • Werner syndrome • Lipodystrophy syndrome • Ataxia-telangiectasia • Polycystic ovarian disease Insulin resistance can present as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old child who is known to have type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with confusion and drowsiness . Her mother says that she seems to be breathing very fast. On examination, mucous membranes are dry and blood pressure is 70/50 mm Hg. Random blood glucose is 415 mg/dl and urine ketones are 4+. What is the next best step in management?

options.a: 2-3 L of normal saline over 1-3 hours
options.d: Insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg given IV

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and the first step is to assess the arterial blood gas (ABG) levels . This precedes correction of fluid balance, as assessment of the current status of the patient is necessary before beginning treatment . A baseline pH and electrolyte level must be obtained . Diabetic ketoacidosis is the most serious complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus . The symptoms include dehydration, nausea, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness , and coma in severe cases . In DKA, the insulin-to-glucagon ratio is decreased which promotes gluconeogenesis , glycogenolysis , and ketone body formation in the liver. Ketone bodies exist as ketoacids at physiological pH which are neutralized by bicarbonate. As bicarbonate stores are depleted , metabolic acidosis ensues . Increased lactic acid production also contributes to the acidosis. The diagnostic biochemical criteria for DKA includes : • Hyperglycemia (>250 mg/dL) • Venous pH <7.3 • Plasma/serum bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L • Increased anion gap • Ketonemia (beta -hydroxybutyrate [BOHB] >3 mmol/L ) and ketonuria Signs of ketoacidosis : • Kussmaul breathing (deep , heavy, non-labored rapid breathing) • Fruity breath odor (acetone ) • Prolonged Q-T interval • Diminished neurocognitive function • Coma184

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is responsible for the elevated levels of TG and VLDL in diabetes mellitus ?

options.a: Increased activity of lipoprotein lipase and decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase
options.b: Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
options.c: Increase in peripheral function of LDL receptors
options.d: Increased in activity of hepatic lipase

mcqs.explanation: The elevated levels of triglycerides (TG) and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL ) in diabetes mellitus (DM) are due to decreased activity of lipoprotein lipase (LpL ) and increased activity of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL ). Insulin normally has an inhibitory action on HSL and induces LpL on capillary walls . There is an absolute or relative deficiency of insulin in DM. In DM, the activity of LpL is decreased and HSL is increased . The increased activity of HSL results in increased mobilisation of fat stores towards lipolysis releasing fatty acids. These fatty acids are partly cleared by the liver, resulting in increased synthesis of VLDL and TG, resulting in dyslipidemia . They can accumulate in the liver, resulting in steatosis (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease ). The reduced activity of LpL prevents the clearing of TG and VLDL in the bloodstream and their levels remain elevated .185

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Types, Clinical Features and...
mcqs.question: In a PHC, which of the following initial screening tests are used to diagnose diabetes ?
mcqs.explanation: Fasting blood sugar >126 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial blood sugar >200 mg/dl can be used as screening tests for diabetes in a primary health center (PHC). HbA1c estimation is usually unavailable for screening at many PHCs due to low resources . In India, facilities for HbA1c estimation are usually available only at tertiary centers . Random blood sugar >200 mg/dL can be used for diagnosis only if the patient presents with symptoms of diabetes , hence it is not a useful screening test .186

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of diabetic ketoacidosis ?
mcqs.explanation: In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), serum bicarbonate is usually < 15. Serum HCO3 > 15 meq/L is suggestive of alcoholic ketoacidosis . DKA is an acute complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus . It is usually precipitated by absolute or relative insulin deficiency caused by increased metabolic demand (infections ) or insulin noncompliance. The common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain. The common signs include Kussmaul breathing, fruity odor of the breath, dehydration , tachycardia, hypotension, and delirium. The diagnosis of DKA is made based on the following parameters: • Hyperglycemia > 250 mg/dl • Ketosis or ketones in urine • Metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.3 • HCO3 < 15-18 mEq/L • High anion gap due to ketoacids and lactic acidosis Hyponatremia is seen as a result of hyperglycemia (osmotic shift causes dilutional hyponatremia). Normal sodium levels on admission indicate severe dehydration . Despite a total-body potassium deficit , the serum Potassium at presentation may be mildly elevated , secondary to the acidosis and volume depletion .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes is brought to the ER with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Investigations show blood glucose of 520 mg/dl and urine positive for ketone bodies . Which of the following is the drug of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for controlling hyperglycemia in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is short-acting insulin, preferably regular insulin.196 Intermediate (such as lente insulin and NPH), long-acting insulins, and oral hypoglycemic agents are never used in the initial management of DKA. The mainstay of treatment is the administration of normal saline followed by infusion of short-acting insulin. The precipitating event must be identified and treated . Careful monitoring of K+ levels and replacement in the later stages is required, as insulin therapy causes hypokalemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the leading cause of death in children with diabetic ketoacidosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Cerebral edema is the leading cause of mortality in children with diabetic ketoacidosis . The osmolar gradient generated due to the high blood glucose level results in water shift from the intracellular fluid (ICF) to the extracellular fluid (ECF) space and leads to the contraction of cell volume. Correction with insulin and intravenous fluids can result in a rapid reduction in effective osmolarity, reversal of the fluid shift, and result in cerebral edema . Complications of diabetic ketoacidosis include : • Cerebral edema – especially in children • Cardiac arrhythmia - due to electrolyte imbalance • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) • Venous thrombosis • Acute gastric dilation • Acute kidney injury • Intestinal necrosis • Acute pancreatitis • Mucormycosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has severe abdominal pain. Which of the following is the recommended test to rule out acute pancreatitis?
mcqs.explanation: In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), severe abdominal pain can mimic acute pancreatitis . Serum lipase is the best test to rule out this condition. It must then be confirmed by imaging (USG or CT abdomen). Serum amylase is an unreliable indicator as DKA is associated with hyperamylasemia of salivary origin. Serum and urine trypsinogen may be elevated in early pancreatitis but are not used for diagnosis. Fecal elastase is elevated in chronic pancreatitis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 15-year old boy presents with persistent vomiting for one day. Laboratory investigations reveal the following . What is the best sequence of management?

options.a: Start IV fluids , administer IV regular insulin, and then correct hypokalemia
options.b: Start IV fluids , administer subcutaneous bolus of insulin and correct hypokalemia concurrently
options.c: Start IV fluids and correct hypokalemia first, then administer IV regular insulin
options.d: Administer IV regular insulin with KCl first , then start IV fluids once the K+ level is corrected

mcqs.explanation: 197 This clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). On confirming the diagnosis, IV fluids must be started . If the initial serum potassium < 3.3 meq/L , insulin should be administered only after the correction of hypokalemia. This is because treatment with insulin and fluids can worsen hypokalemia by the following mechanisms: • Insulin causes the shift of K+ ions into cells • Resolution of the acidosis also promotes K+ entry into cells • Urinary loss of K+ salts of organic acids

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Distinguishing features between hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state and diabetic ketoacidosis include all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Hypotension and tachycardia are common features of both hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS) and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In DKA, insulin deficiency and an increase in counter-regulatory hormones lead to shunting of free fatty acids to form ketone bodies . The ketoacids increase the anion gap and cause low pH. In HHS, there is still some insulin available . Hence , there are no ketones formed, and the patient has normal pH and pCO2.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: An elderly man is brought to the hospital with confusion and drowsiness . His son says that he has been urinating more frequently than normal and eating very little over the past 1 week . Capillary blood glucose is 800 mg/dl. Which of the following would not be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS). Kussmaul 's breathing is not a feature of HHS. HHS is commonly seen in older adults suffering from type 2 diabetes mellitus . Patients can present with the following features : • Polyuria198 • Polydipsia • Lethargy • Altered sensorium, coma • Seizures • Severe dehydration The following lab values are seen : • Blood glucose of 600 -1200 mg/dl • Serum osmolality > 350 mOsm/L • Prerenal azotemia due to dehydration • Pseudohyponatremia may be seen due to hyperglycemia • Normal pH and ketones The mainstay of management is fluid replacement , IV regular insulin, along with potassium replacement. Heparin can be given prophylactically as volume contraction can increase the risk of venous thrombosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: What is the most common pattern of dyslipidemia associated with diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: Dyslipidemia commonly occurs as a complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus . The most common pattern is as follows : • Increased triglyceride levels - due to increased glucose and free fatty acids, decreased lipolysis of VLDL . • Decreased HDL levels Though diabetes does not increase LDL levels , there is increased atherogenicity as the existing LDL molecules are more easily glycated and susceptible to oxidation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Dyslipidemia is more commonly associated with which of the following ?

options.c: Maturity onset diabetes of the young

mcqs.explanation: Dyslipidemia is more commonly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus . It is less common in type 1 and gestational diabetes . Maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY ) is not associated with dyslipidemia . Note : Saroglitazar is a more advanced drug that reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients . It acts on PPAR alpha and gamma receptors .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: You have started a 40-year-old man on treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia . Which of the following is not an appropriate target for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 199 According to the ADA guidelines , a treatment goal of postprandial plasma glucose < 180 mg/dL must be followed in adults with diabetes . In younger individuals or those with other cardiovascular risk factors, the target blood pressure is < /80 mm Hg. Although not a treatment goal, the ADA also recommends triglyceride levels be maintained at < 150 mg/dl. Note : Saroglitazar is a more advanced drug that reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients . It acts on PPAR alpha and gamma receptors .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A middle -aged patient with type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with essential hypertension . What is the antihypertensive drug of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice in this diabetic patient with hypertension is losartan. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB ) are the first-line drugs in diabetic hypertensives . Among ARBs, the drug of choice is telmisartan (acts on PPAR receptor ). They reduce both macrovascular and microvascular complications and have a nephroprotective effect . However, they are contraindicated in chronic kidney disease as they can cause a further decline in GFR.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy is an increase in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). It occurs as a result of glomerular hyperperfusion and renal hypertrophy . The following sequence of changes are seen in diabetic nephropathy : • Increased GFR • Incipient diabetic nephropathy - microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day albumin) • Diagnostic marker to detect early diabetic nephropathy • Indicator of long-term cardiovascular disease • Overt diabetic nephropathy - macroalbuminuria ( >300 mg/day albumin) • End-stage renal disease200

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy has been on treatment for type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 10 years. His physician decides to begin screening for diabetic nephropathy . Which of the following is not always a reliable indicator of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Albumin of 30-300 mg/day refers to microalbuminuria . It can be unreliable in the diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy . It is not required to diagnose nephropathy as it is very variable. Non-albuminuric diabetic nephropathy may occur in some patients and regression of albuminuria may be seen in type 1 diabetics . Diabetic nephropathy can be diagnosed if the following are satisfied : • Reduced GFR (< 60 mL /min/1.73 m2 ) with or without persistent albuminuria (> 30 mg/day or urine PCR > 30 mg/g) • Long duration of diabetes or established diabetic retinopathy • Other etiologies are ruled out Long duration in type 1 diabetes refers to 5 years after diagnosis. On the other hand, patients with type 2 diabetes are exposed to hyperglycemia and prediabetes for a long time even before diagnosis. Hence , at the time of diagnosis, patients with type 2 diabetes are considered to have had the disorder for a duration sufficiently long to produce kidney disease . However, a clinical diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy can be made in patients with established retinopathy , even if the duration of diabetes is short.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about diabetic nephropathy is true?

options.a: Pancreatic transplantation can improve proteinuria at an early stage
options.b: Strict glycemic control is unlikely to prevent microalbuminuria
options.c: Dietary protein restriction can benefit diabetic patients with albuminuria
options.d: Microalbuminuria is not an indicator of long-term cardiovascular morbidity

mcqs.explanation: Pancreatic transplantation can help improve proteinuria at an early stage . Successful pancreatic transplantation can have the following effects : • Prevention of diabetic nephropathy and regression of albuminuria in early stages .201 • Stabilization and improvement of diabetic neuropathy and retinopathy • Increase in HDL with reduction in LDL and triglycerides Option B: Strict glycemic control can prevent or revert microalbuminuria . Option C: The ADA does not suggest restrictions of protein intake in diabetic patients with albuminuria because studies have failed to prove its benefits . Option D: Microalbuminuria is an indicator of long-term cardiovascular morbidity.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is found to have a 24-hour urinary albumin of 250 mg. Which of the following drugs may be prescribed to reduce the progression of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACEI) inhibitors or angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARB) are recommended to reduce the progression of diabetic nephropathy . It has the following effects : • Reduction of albuminuria • Reduces the associated decline in GFR The mainstay of management of diabetic nephropathy includes control of blood sugar and blood pressure , inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAAS ) system , and inhibitors of SGLT2 to halt the progression of the disease . RAAS inhibitors include ACE inhibitors, ARBs , or direct renin inhibitors.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A pathologist is studying a renal biopsy sample from a patient with suspected diabetic nephropathy . Which of the following biopsy findings is pathognomonic for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The characteristic lesion of diabetic nephropathy is nodular or intercapillary glomerulosclerosis , also called Kimmelstiel -Wilson nodules . It is pathognomonic for this condition. The following image shows Kimmelstiel -Wilson nodules .Other non-specific findings seen on biopsy include :202 • Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) thickening - highly sensitive • Diffuse glomerulosclerosis - most common pattern, due to diffuse mesangial thickening • Fibrin cap - accumulation of hyaline material within the capillary loop • Capsular drop - accumulation of hyaline material attached to the Bowman's capsule • Armani -Ebstein reaction - collection of glycogen clumps within the renal tubules due to tubular injury Renal biopsy is done to rule out other causes of renal failure. The indications for renal biopsy in diabetic nephropathy are: • Absence of diabetic retinopathy • Absence of edema • Absence of frothing and proteinuria • Absence of hypertension • Presence of microscopic hematuria or features of nephritic syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following types of renal tubular acidosis can develop in individuals with diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: Type IV renal tubular acidosis (RTA) may occur in individuals with diabetes mellitus types 1 and 2. Type IV RTA occurs due to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism . Low plasma renin activity is common in diabetic patients due to: • Impaired conversion of prorenin to renin • Volume expansion in diabetic nephropathy suppresses renin release These individuals have a tendency to develop hyperkalemia and acidemia, which can be exacerbated by the use of ACEI and ARBs . Hence , these drugs should be avoided.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus . When should you refer him to an ophthalmologist ?

options.b: Immediately at the time of diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Patients with type 2 diabetes should undergo a comprehensive ophthalmological examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy at diagnosis, followed by an annual examination of the fundus . In patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus , screening for retinopathy is recommended 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. Annual fundal examination is recommended thereafter .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients would you screen for diabetic retinopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Screening for diabetic retinopathy is done at 3-5 years following diagnosis in type 1 diabetes mellitus , whereas, patients with type 2 diabetes must be screened at the time of diagnosis.203 As type 2 diabetes mellitus often has a long asymptomatic period of hyperglycemia before clinical diagnosis, these patients are more likely to have complications at the time of diagnosis itself . Retinopathy develops in nearly 50-80% of patients by 20 years of diagnosis. The presence of diabetic retinopathy often correlates with pathological findings of diabetic nephropathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: What is the most common clinical presentation of diabetic neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common form of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy . It presents with distal sensory loss and pain in a stocking-and-glove distribution and is a risk factor for foot ulceration. Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication and results in the following features : • Postural hypotension • Silent myocardial infarction • Hypoglycemia unawareness • Erectile dysfunction • Overflow incontinence • Gastroparesis • Enteropathy with constipation or diarrhea Mononeuropathy of peripheral (median, ulnar, radial) and cranial (oculomotor) nerves is also seen , as well as mononeuritis multiplex. Diabetic polyradiculopathy is characterized by severe pain along the distribution of one or more nerve roots.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings in a diabetic patient is self -limiting?
mcqs.explanation: Amyotrophy refers to weakness of hip extensors and flexors secondary to polyradiculopathy involving the lumbar plexus and femoral nerve. It is associated with severe pain along the distribution of the nerve roots. It is self -limiting and resolves over 6-12 months. Strict glycemic control can reduce the incidence and prevent the progression of macular edema , peripheral neuropathy , and macroalbuminuria. However, once developed , they cannot be reversed. Intermittent microalbuminuria with normal GFR can be reversed with strict glycemic control.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a 65-year-old diabetic woman who has been admitted following a seizure . On admission, she was unconscious , and random blood glucose at admission was 37 mg/dl. The hypoglycemia was corrected and she regained consciousness . The woman says that she had felt normal and had no other symptoms prior to the onset of seizures . What is the likely cause of this presentation ?

options.a: Medication change from metformin to insulin

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of silent hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient . The most likely cause is autonomic neuropathy .204 Hypoglycemia presents with symptoms like palpitation , tremors, and sweating as a result of sympathetic stimulation. These symptoms are protective and provide advance warning before progression to neuroglucopenia . However, in autonomic neuropathy , there is a reduced release of counterregulatory hormones like catecholamines . Hence , the classical symptoms of hypoglycemia do not occur and the patient directly presents with features of neuroglucopenia . This is called hypoglycemia unawareness . The use of beta -blockers can also cause hypoglycemia unawareness .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: You are counselling a patient with longstanding , poorly-controlled diabetes mellitus . Advising tight glycemic control in this patient would not improve which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: In patients with longstanding diabetes mellitus , tight glycaemic control is beneficial for microvascular complications . However, it has no effect on macrovascular complications like peripheral vascular disease (PVD ), myocardial infarction, and stroke. Good glycemic control improves microvascular complications through primary and secondary prevention. It reduces the incidence of complications as well as stabilizes and prevents further progression in affected individuals. Intermittent microalbuminuria with normal GFR can even be reversed with tight glycemic control.Complication % risk reduction with tight gl ycemic control Retinopathy 47 % Microalbumin uria 39 % Nephropathy 54% Neuropathy 60 %

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which among the following statements explains Legacy effect and metabolic memory?
mcqs.explanation: Legacy effect or metabolic memory can be observed in relation to glycemic control during early disease in patients with diabetes mellitus. Intensive glycemic control during the early stages of the disease has a positive effect on long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications (statement 1) even if this intensive glycemic control is not maintained long term. Similarly, uncontrolled blood glucose levels in the early stages causes an increased risk of these complications (statement 5). This phenomenon is called legacy effect and is attributed to metabolic memory. In patients with longstanding diabetes , intensive glycemic control at later stages can improve microvascular complications but has no effect on macrovascular complications .205

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic diabetes presents to the OPD for his annual checkup . A small painless ulcer is noted over his right foot. His BMI is 33 kg/m2 . All of the following factors can be implicated in the causation of his foot ulcer except :
mcqs.explanation: Venous stasis is not a cause of diabetic foot ulcers and gangrene . They are usually caused by a combination of three factors: • Ischemia - secondary to atheroma • Peripheral neuropathy - leads to trophic skin changes • Immunosuppression - due to excess sugar deposition in tissues , predisposing diabetic patients to infection Common sites of ulcers include : • Great toe • Metatarsophalangeal areas.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old diabetic woman presents to the OPD with the following skin lesions . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing irregular plaques with yellowish discoloration and telangiectasias are suggestive of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. It is an inflammatory granulomatous disorder of the skin due to collagen degeneration and lipid deposition . It is usually seen in young women with diabetes mellitus . The lesions usually begin in the pretibial region. It begins as papules that gradually enlarge and darken to form erythematous plaques with irregular margins, atrophic centers , and central ulceration. Option A: Necrolytic migratory erythema is a feature of glucagonoma . It is a waxing and waning rash that appears as shown below .Option B: Diabetic dermopathy or shin spots are commonly seen in elderly men. It presents as pigmented pretibial papules as shown below .206 Option D: Granuloma annulare presents with small papules arranged in an annular pattern. There is no yellowish discoloration or telangiectasias, as shown below .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Patients with diabetes mellitus are at a higher risk of developing all of the following infections except :
mcqs.explanation: Emphysematous appendicitis is not a complication of diabetes mellitus . The potentially fatal infectious complications of diabetes include : • Malignant otitis externa • Rhinocerebral mucormycosis • Emphysematous pyelonephritis • Emphysematous cholecystitis207

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: A morbidly obese diabetic woman is not responsive to metformin therapy . She has a history of pancreatitis and family history of bladder cancer. She does not want to take injections. Which of the following would be suitable to reduce her glucose levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , canagliflozin (Option C) is the most suitable treatment . It is an oral drug belonging to the class SGLT -2 inhibitors and causes weight loss. Although it increases the risk of urogenital infections , it has no risk of pancreatitis or bladder cancer. Option A: Sitagliptin , a DPP-IV inhibitor, is associated with the risk of acute pancreatitis . Option B: Pioglitazone, a thiazolidinedione , can increase the risk of bladder cancer and can cause weight gain and congestive cardiac failure. Option D: Liraglutide is an injectable GLP -1 receptor agonist. Pancreatitis is a serious adverse effect of this drug. Hence , it is contraindicated in individuals with a history of pancreatitis and should be permanently discontinued if pancreatitis develops .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diabetes Mellitus: Complications and their Mana...
mcqs.question: Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs should be stopped in a patient with a creatinine of 5.6 mg/dL?
mcqs.explanation: Metformin should be stopped in case of elevated creatinine levels (renal insufficiency ) > 1.5 mg/dl in men and >1.4 mg/dl in women. Metformin acts by reducing hepatic glucose production and improves peripheral glucose utilization. Lactic acidosis and Vitamin B12 deficiency are specific adverse effects of metformin. It is not used in patients with a glomerular filtration rate <30 mL /min (moderate renal insufficiency ), acidosis, unstable congestive cardiac failure, liver disease , severe hypoxemia , and patients undergoing contrast studies .208

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of 11 -beta -hydroxylase deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: 11 -beta -hydroxylase deficiency is associated with metabolic alkalosis, not metabolic acidosis. It is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia that presents with the following features : • Glucocorticoid deficiency : • Hypoglycemia • Hyperpigmentation around the genitals due to excess adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion • Mineralocorticoid excess : • Hypokalemia • Hypertension • Metabolic alkalosis • Adrenal androgen excess • Virilization in females • Precocious puberty in males213

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A neonate with ambiguous genitalia undergoes karyotyping and is confirmed to have a 46XY genotype . His blood pressure is 140 /80 mm Hg and serum potassium is 1.9 mEq/L . Which of the following is responsible for these findings?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario with ambiguous genitalia in a male neonate is suggestive of 17 alpha-hydroxylase deficiency . It causes hypertension and hypokalemia due to the accumulation of -deoxycorticosterone , which is a mineralocorticoid causing sodium retention . -hydroxylase deficiency also leads to the accumulation of 11 -deoxycorticosterone .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following abnormalities will you see in a child with salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypoglycemia is a feature of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). It is due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . It results in hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Males typically present with salt-wasting crises as they often go undiagnosed at birth due to the presence of normal genitalia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the drug of choice for the prenatal treatment of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for the prenatal treatment of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is dexamethasone, as it readily crosses the placenta . It is an experimental approach aimed at reducing the virilization of 46XX fetuses by suppressing fetal adrenal steroid and androgen secretion . It may be considered when there is a high risk of CAH due to strong family history. It is effective only when started before 4 weeks of gestation . Hydrocortisone is given in the children at divided doses of 1–1.5 times the normal cortisol production.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A female neonate is noted to have ambiguous genitalia at birth. Further testing reveals elevated 17-(OH)-progesterone levels and a blood glucose of 40 mg/dl. What treatment will you recommend?
mcqs.explanation: Ambiguous genitalia , elevated 17-(OH)-progesterone , and hypoglycemia are suggestive of 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . The drug of choice is hydrocortisone . Hydrocortisone acts as a potent glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid action and thus increases salt absorption from the kidneys as well . Betamethasone , beclomethasone , and dexamethasone have negligible effects as mineralocorticoids.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about galactorrhea?
mcqs.explanation: Galactorrhea or pathological production of milk is not associated with lactation, which is a physiological condition.214 Galactorrhea is the inappropriate discharge of milk-containing fluid from the breast. It may be unilateral or bilateral. It is associated with acromegaly and hyperprolactinemia . Treatment is with dopamine agonists like bromocriptine or cabergoline if it is due to hyperprolactinemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with gynecomastia , you will order all of the following tests except :
mcqs.explanation: Determination of prolactin level is not useful in patients with gynecomastia . For the diagnosis of gynecomastia , serum levels of the following hormones must be checked : • Testosterone • LH • FSH • Estradiol • hCG

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old man is being evaluated for gynecomastia . Laboratory investigations reveal low levels of serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario of gynecomastia with low LH and testosterone is suggestive of a sertoli cell tumor. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is also a possible diagnosis with the above clinical presentation and must be ruled out before diagnosing a Sertoli cell tumor. The differential diagnosis of gynecomastia is as follows : • High LH and low testosterone • Testicular failure • Low LH and low testosterone • Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism • Sertoli cell tumor - increased primary estrogen production • High LH and high testosterone • Androgen-resistant state • GnRH-secreting tumor

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A mother brings her 17-year-old daughter to the gynecologist as she has not started menstruating yet . Examination reveals well -developed breasts and the absence of pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic examination reveals a short, blind-ended vagina . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Clinical features :215 • Female phenotype • Normal breast development • Blind-ended vagina with absent uterus and ovaries • Presence of testes in the abdomen or inguinal region • Scanty pubic and axillary hair • Primary amenorrhea in late adolescence Option A: In Turner 's syndrome, breasts are infantile. Option B: Stein Leventhal syndrome or polycystic ovarian disorder presents with hirsutism and anovulatory menstrual cycles . Option C: Premature ovarian failure presents with secondary amenorrhea.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A baby girl is referred to a pediatric surgeon for suspected bilateral inguinal hernias. Further evaluation reveals the masses to be testes in the inguinal canal. Which karyotype would you expect to find in this child?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical picture is suggestive of androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS). Affected children have a male karyotype or 46 XY with a female phenotype . 46XY individuals with complete AIS (formerly called testicular feminization syndrome) have the following features : • Female phenotype • Normal breast development • Blind-ended vagina with absent uterus and ovaries • Scanty pubic and axillary hair Most patients present with • Inguinal masses in infancy - Due to undescended testes or hernias containing testes • Primary amenorrhea in late adolescence Gonadectomy is a recommended course of treatment due to the possible risks of malignancy.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An 18-year-old boy is brought to the casualty with minor burns following a house fire. He tells you that he did not even smell the smoke. Further probing reveals a history of bilateral orchidopexy at the age of 7. Examination findings include eunuchoid habitus, prepubertal testes , and microphallus. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Anosmia and absent secondary sexual characteristics in this patient are suggestive of Kallman syndrome. It is an X-linked disorder that causes isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism due to defective development of the olfactory bulb. This results in: • Defective migration of GnRH-producing neurons that originate from the olfactory epithelium • Aplasia or hypoplasia of olfactory bulb The clinical features include :216 • Cryptorchidism • Absent or delayed pubertal changes due to GnRH deficiency • Anosmia or hyposmia Options A and B: Klinefelter syndrome is a cause of primary or hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. Option D: Hyperprolactinemia can cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism , but is also associated with gynecomastia, galactorrhea, and bitemporal hemianopia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in males?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism in males is Klinefelter 's syndrome It occurs in males with a 47 XXY karyotype and is associated with testicular dysfunction and male infertility . Causes of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism in males and females : • Congenital • Klinefelter 's syndrome • Turner 's syndrome • Swyer 's syndrome • Premature ovarian failure associated with fragile X syndrome and galactosemia • Acquired • Mumps orchitis • Testicular torsion, trauma • Liver cirrhosis • Ketoconazole • Premature ovarian failure

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following will you recommend in all patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Gonadectomy is clinically recommended in all patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) or testicular feminization syndrome due to the risk of malignancy arising from the abnormally located testes . Options B, C, D: These treatment options may be offered to patients with AIS, but it depends on personal preference and whether they identify as males or females .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old patient is being evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased estrogen , FSH, and LH. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 217 Decreased levels of estrogen , FSH, and LH are suggestive of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism , which is caused by Kallman syndrome. It is an X-linked disorder (KAL gene ) that causes isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and anosmia. Causes of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism: • Congenital • Kallman's syndrome • Isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (IHH) • Prader-Willi syndrome • CHARGE syndrome • Acquired • Pituitary tumors, apoplexy • Hyperprolactinemia • Anorexia nervosa, excess exercise • Irradiation • Infection • Trauma Option A: Asherman syndrome causes secondary amenorrhea due to intrauterine synechiae . Option B: M\374llerian agenesis presents with primary amenorrhea with normal levels of all hormones. Option D: Turner 's syndrome causes primary amenorrhea due to hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.218

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Hypercalcemia is associated with all of the following medical conditions except :
mcqs.explanation: 227 Hypercalcemia is associated with all of the following conditions except hypothyroidism . Hyperthyroidism is however associated with hypercalcemia . Other options : 1) Multiple myeloma is a hemotological malignancy associated with hypercalcemia . 2) Hyperparathyroidism is associated with sub-periosteal bone resorption resulting in hypercalcemia. 3) Sarcoidosis is associated with hypercalcemia due to increased activity of 1 alpha hydroxylase activity in the macrophages .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following can cause hypercalcemia in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin A intoxication can cause hypercalcemia. This is due to high bone turnover. Ingestion of 50,000 –100 ,000 units of Vitamin A daily can increase calcium levels up to 12 –14 mg/dL. Note : Vitamin D intoxication also leads to hypercalcemia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious by her neighbors. She is found to have marked dehydration and serum calcium levels of 16 mg/dl. All of the following can cause this presentation except :
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario with severe hypercalcemia (> 14.8 mg/dl) is suggestive of a hypercalcemic crisis. Pancreatitis causes hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia . Hypercalcemic crisis is often caused by malignancies due to an acute rise in calcium levels following bone resorption due to metastases . It is a medical emergency that presents with polyuria, severe dehydration , gastrointestinal symptoms , and altered consciousness . It can lead to cardiac arrest and coma.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following will not be seen in a patient with hypercalcemia ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypercalcemia is associated with constipation and not diarrhea. Clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia include : The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic 'stones , bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans'.System Clinical features Renal Renal stones (Calcium oxalat e > calcium phosphate ) Nephrocalcinosis Polyuriaand dehydration Renal failure228 System Clinical features Musculoskeletal Bone pain, bone cysts Myalgia and arthralgia Osteopenia , osteoporosis GIT Constipation Nausea ,vomiting, anorexia Abdominal pain Peptic ulcer disease Acute pancreatitis Neuropsychiatric Anxiety,depression , fatigue Cognitive dysfunction Drowsiness , obtundation, co ma Cardiac Short QT interval, bradycardi a Hypertension Others Ectopic calcification

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in patients following excessive intake of calcium?
mcqs.explanation: Excess calcium ingestion is not associated with restrictive cardiomyopathy . It results in milk-alkali syndrome, commonly associated with excessive intake of absorbable antacids such as milk or calcium carbonate. In susceptible individuals, there is a loss of negative feedback , leading to excess calcium absorption when there is excess intake. It results in the following triad of clinical features : • Hypercalcemia • Alkalosis - due to HCO3 reabsorption caused by PTH suppression , natriuresis, and water depletion . • Renal failure - due to damage to renal tubules . It is reversible once ingestion of antacid is stopped . However, in severe cases , a chronic form called Burnett's syndrome can develop. It is associated with irreversible renal damage .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Parathyroid adenomas are the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism . Causes of primary hyperparathyroidism: • Parathyroid adenomas: These maybe229 • Solitary (more common) • Multiple • Part of MEN -1, MEN -2A or MEN -4 • Chief cell parathyroid hyperplasia • Parathyroid gland carcinoma • Lithium use • Hyperparathyroidism -jaw tumor (HPT -JT ) syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following sets of lab values will be seen in a patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism?
mcqs.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism presents with decreased calcium and increased levels of PTH , phosphate , and ALP . In this condition, calcium deficiency leads to reactive stimulation of the parathyroid. It is caused by the following : • Chronic kidney disease • Vitamin D deficiency • Gastrointestinal malabsorption • Liver disease

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: All of the following statements are true about primary hyperparathyroidism except :

options.a: It causes prolongation of QT interval

mcqs.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT ) causes shortening of the QT interval. The asymptomatic form is the most common presentation in the Western population . But in developing countries , the patients are usually symptomatic . The classical symptoms and signs of PHPT are due to hypercalcemia as well as increased parathyroid hormone (PTH ) levels . The features of hypercalcemia are as follows : The features of elevated PTH levels are as follows : • Osteitis fibrosa cystica • Osteopenia /osteoporosis • Hyperuricemia and gout • Pseudogout • Increased production of calcitriol • Nephrolithiasis • Hypophosphatemia • Anemia230 The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic - "bones, stones , groans, moans with fatigue overtones"System Clinical features Musculoskeletal Bone painSkeletal deformitie sPathological fracturesMyalgi a and arthralgia Renal Renal stones (Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate )Nephro calcinosisPolyuria and dehyd rationRenal failure GIT ConstipationNausea , vomitin g, anorexiaAbdominal painPe ptic ulcer diseaseAcute pancr eatitis Neuropsychiatric Anxiety, depressionCognitive dysfunctionIrritabilityHalluc inations Cardiac Short QT intervalbradycardia Hypertension Ectopic calcification Cornea: Band keratopathyExt ravascular tissues : calcinosis Small arteries: calciphylaxis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following would you expect in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Neuropsychiatric changes are seen in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT ). The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic - "bones, stones , groans, moans with fatigue overtones" Note : Though multiple clinical studies have found an increased incidence of gall stones in primary HPT, there is no reference to this in Harrison 's and Williams's endocrinology . Hence , option D would be the most appropriate answer.System Clinical features Musculoskeletal Bone painSkeletal deformitie sPathological fracturesMyalgi a and arthralgia Renal Renal stones (Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate )Nephro calcinosisPolyuria and dehyd rationRenal failure231 System Clinical features GIT ConstipationNausea , vomitin g, anorexiaAbdominal painPe ptic ulcer diseaseAcute pancr eatitis Neuropsychiatric Anxiety, depressionCognitive dysfunctionIrritabilityHalluc inations Cardiac Short QT intervalbradycardia Hypertension Ectopic calcification Cornea: Band keratopathyExt ravascular tissues : calcinosis Small arteries: calciphylaxis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Calcitonin levels are increased in:
mcqs.explanation: Calcitonin levels are increased in hyperparathyroidism. Due to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH ) levels in hyperparathyroidism , there is osteoclast activation. This leads to increased calcium levels in plasma. As a response to this, there is an increase in the level of calcitonin to regulate the high calcium levels . Calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland. Its principal effects are to lower serum calcium and phosphate by its action on bone and kidney. In bone, calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts and reduces bone resorption. In the kidney, it inhibits the reabsorption of both calcium and phosphate .
