Other options Option A: In hyperthyroidism , the direct effect of thyroid hormones can lead to bone resorption and mild hypercalcemia . However, hyperparathyroidism is a better answer. Options B and D: Hypoparathyroidism and Cushing's syndrome will have low serum calcium and hence , will not have increased calcitonin levels .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: The spinal x-ray of a patient with elevated ALP levels is shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above x-ray shows a rugger jersey spine which is a distinct feature of hyperparathyroidism . It is associated with elevated ALP . It refers to the prominent hyperdensities at the endplates of successive vertebrae, which mimics the striped appearance of a rugby jersey . Option A: Paget 's disease causes cortical thickening, which results in increased opacity on all sides of the vertebral body. These are called picture frame vertebrae. Option C: Osteopetrosis presents with normal ALP levels . It results in sclerotic endplates of vertebrae that are termed sandwich vertebrae. Though this finding is similar to rugger jersey232 spine , it is denser and more sharply defined than rugger jersey spine . In addition, there is sclerosis of inner margins of vertebral bodies , resulting in a bone within a bone appearance . Option D: Ankylosing spondylitis produces a bamboo spine appearance due to fusion of vertebral bodies .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presents with worsening pain and an inability to bear weight on her left leg . She says that she had banged her leg against a chair 3 days ago. X-ray reveals a fracture of her left tibia. In view of this finding, a skeletal survey was performed and reveals the following additional finding. What is the likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a pathological fracture of the tibia. The given x-ray shows brown tumors or osteitis fibrosa cystica, which are characteristic of hyperparathyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: This x-ray finding in a patient is characteristic of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: The arrows in this x-ray point to arrow-headed fingers or the spade phalanx sign. It is pathognomonic of acromegaly. Acromegaly is the result of excessive growth hormone (GH) production , most commonly from a macroadenoma of the pituitary . There is osseous enlargement , presenting with spade -like hands and widening of the terminal phalangeal tufts , giving an arrow-head appearance . Other features in the hand include : • Widened joint spaces (due to cartilage hypertrophy ) • Generalized osteoporosis and cystic changes in the carpal bones Option A: Hyperparathyroidism causes subperiosteal bone resorption, which is marked along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers. Option B: Down's syndrome can cause hypoplasia of the middle phalanx of the 5th finger. Option C: Psoriasis causes a pencil -in-cup appearance of the distal phalanx.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not used to treat a patient with hypercalcemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism?
mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoids have no effect on the serum calcium concentration in primary hyperparathyroidism and normal individuals. They are effective in the treatment of hypercalcemia when associated with the following conditions: • Malignancy • Vitamin D intoxication • Sarcoidosis Initial medical management of hypercalcemia involves the following : • Normal saline (200 -500 ml/hour): It is the mainstay treatment to correct dehydration , and titrated to maintain a urine output of >100 ml/hour233 • Pamidronate or zoledronate : These are bisphosphonates and are considered as the drug of choice in primary hyperparathyroidism • Cinacalcet : This is a calcimimetic that increases the affinity of the glands to extracellular calcium, thereby decreasing parathyroid hormone secretion • Denosumab: This inhibits RANK-ligand, which acts on osteoclasts • Calcitonin: This is an activated vitamin D analog that may be used to reduce calcium levels . It should be used within the first 24 hours Forced diuresis refers to aggressive fluid hydration with loop diuretic administration. Although this is an effective method to reduce calcium levels , it requires careful monitoring for adverse effects like fluid overload, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesia . Due to this reason as well as the availability of more effective treatment modalities , forced diuresis is not preferred any longer. The definitive management of primary hyperparathyroidism is the surgical removal of the parathyroid gland.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used in the treatment of hypercalcemia due to Vitamin D toxicity ?
mcqs.explanation: In patients with hypercalcemia due to vitamin D toxicity , glucocorticoids like dexamethasone are the preferred therapy as they decrease 1,25 (OH2) vitamin D (calcitriol) production . This results in reduced intestinal calcium absorption and increased urinary excretion of calcium. Hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and ketoconazole may also decrease calcitriol production and are used occasionally. But the preferred therapy is steroids . Vitamin D toxicity presents acutely with features of hypercalcemia such as confusion, polyuria, polydipsia , anorexia, vomiting, and muscle weakness . Chronic intoxication may cause nephrocalcinosis , bone demineralization, and pain. Lab features include elevated 25 (OH) vitamin D, high calcium, and suppressed PTH . Dexamethasone can also be used in the treatment of hypercalcemia caused by the humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (due to PTHr ) and sarcoidosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: A patient is brought to the emergency department with confusion, drowsiness , and multiple episodes of vomiting. His family members say that he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder several years ago and has been on medication ever since. Further evaluation reveals a serum calcium level of 16 mg/dl. What should be the next step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypercalcemic crisis. The next best step in management is saline hydration. Typically 200 -500 ml/hour fluids are given to correct dehydration and titrated to maintain a urine output of >100 ml/hour. Hypercalcemic crisis is a medical emergency associated with serum calcium >14 mg/dl. It is often caused by conditions causing an acute rise in calcium levels such as malignancies or lithium overdose . It presents with oliguria, severe dehydration , gastrointestinal symptoms , and altered consciousness . It can lead to cardiac arrest and coma. Initial medical management of hypercalcemia involves the following :234 • Fluids are the mainstay treatment • Bisphosphonates • Cinacalcet • Denosumab • Calcitonin

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: In a patient with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia , which of the following will you not suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is associated with hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia Hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia is observed in the following conditions: • True hypoparathyroidism • Hereditary hypoparathyroidism • Acquired hypoparathyroidism – following surgery • Hypomagnesemia • Pseudohypoparathyroidism • Chronic kidney disease • DiGeorge syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: All of the following medical conditions are associated with hyperphosphatemia except :
mcqs.explanation: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is a type of pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A associated with normal calcium and normal phosphate. The clinical features are similar to pseudohypoparathyroidism but there is no PTH resistance . Pseudohypoparathyroidism is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a mutation of the alpha subunit of the Gs protein. This causes PTH resistance . It is associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature , round facies , and short fourth metacarpal). Types of pseudohypoparathyroidism : PHP: pseudohypoparathyroidism , PPHP: pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism , PTH : parathyroid hormoneType PHP 1A PHP 1B PHP 1C PHP PPH P Hypocalcemia Yes Yes Yes Yes No Hyperphosphatemia Yes Yes Yes Yes No PTH levels \027 \027 \027 \027 Nor mal GS \030 subunit deficiency Yes No No No Yes235 Type PHP 1A PHP 1B PHP 1C PHP PPH P Albright hereditary osteodyst rophy Yes No Yes No Yes PTH resistance Yes Yes Yes Parti al No

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought by his mother with with the following abnormality. Serum levels of vitamin D are found to be low. Which of the following would not be seen in this boy?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a windswept deformity of the lower limbs (combination of valgus deformity of one leg with varus deformity of the other leg ). This finding along with low serum vitamin D points to a diagnosis of vitamin D deficiency rickets. It is associated with an increase in parathyroid hormone (PTH ) levels .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to hypocalcemia ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypocalcemia is a feature of secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT ). Hypocalcemia refers to total serum calcium \0268.4 mg/dl. The causes include : • Low PTH • Hypoparathyroidism • High PTH (SHPT ) • Chronic kidney disease • Vitamin D deficiency • Pseudohypoparathyroidism236 • Hyperphosphatemia • Loop diuretics , calcitonin, bisphosphonates • Massive blood transfusions • Hyperventilation • Hypomagnesemia - Mg is essential for PTH release • Severe hypermagnesemia - higher Mg levels suppress PTH secretion Hypocalcemia causes tetany or increased neuromuscular excitability . It can cause paresthesias , cramps, spasms, and seizures . Latent tetany can only be detected by performing Chvostek and Trousseau's signs. A prolonged QT interval is seen on ECG.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: The following sign is elicited in a patient . What is it called ?
mcqs.explanation: The above image indicates Trousseau's sign or carpopedal spasm classically seen in patients with hypocalcemia. Trousseau's sign is elicited by making the forearm ischemic by applying a sphygmomanometer cuff to the arm and keeping the pressure above systolic blood pressure (SBP) for 5 minutes . The hand goes into a painful carpopedal spasm and assumes the accoucheur 's hand position. Hypocalcemia results in tetany or increased neuromuscular irritability. It leads to paresthesia and tingling of extremities and perioral area. Severe hypocalcemia can cause seizures . Option A: Chvostek's sign is also seen in hypocalcemia . Tapping the facial nerve in front of the tragus will cause spasms of the facial muscles . Option C: Tinel's sign is seen in carpal tunnel syndrome. It refers to a tingling sensation on tapping over the median nerve. Option D: Troisier's sign refers to left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in metastatic abdominal malignancy.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Parathyroid and Calcium Homeostasis
mcqs.question: Which of the following agents cannot be used to manage a patient with chronic hypocalcemia ?
mcqs.explanation: Etidronate is not used in the management of hypocalcemia . It is a bisphosphonate used in the management of hypercalcemia . The goal in the management of hypoparathyroidism is to restore the calcium-phosphate balance. The mainstay is calcium and vitamin D supplements . Other underlying conditions must also be treated . Instead of loop diuretics , thiazides can be administered on a low sodium diet as they enhance urinary calcium reabsorption.237

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The hormone leptin is derived from which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Leptin is an adipocyte -derived hormone. It acts through brain circuits (predominantly in the hypothalamus ) to influence appetite , energy expenditure , and neuroendocrine function. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure . The arcuate nucleus in the hypothalamus plays an important role in the regulation of appetite .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old woman has been fasting all day as part of a new diet . Which of the following is a gut peptide that will be increased in this woman?
mcqs.explanation: In the fasting state , high levels of ghrelin are seen . It is a gut -peptide produced in the stomach and stimulates hunger and appetite .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy ate two pieces of cake, a sandwich, and two scoops of ice cream at his friend's birthday party an hour ago. Levels of which of the following are likely to be high in this boy?
mcqs.explanation: This boy is likely to have high levels of \030-Melanocyte -stimulating hormone (\030-MSH). It is a hypothalamic peptide that decreases appetite and hence would be increased in the fed state .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a key transcription factor involved in the differentiation of mesenchymal preadipocytes to adipose cells ?
mcqs.explanation: One of the key transcription factors involved in the differentiation of mesenchymal preadipocytes to adipose cells is the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor \025 (PPAR \025). It is a nuclear receptor that also binds the thiazolidinedione class of insulin-sensitizing drugs used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus . Note : Saroglitazar has a dual action on PPAR \030 and PPAR \037 receptors . It reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding adiponectin ?

options.a: Its levels are increased in obesity

mcqs.explanation: Adiponectin levels are reduced in obesity. It is an abundant adipose -derived protein with the following characteristics: • Its levels are reduced in obesity • It enhances insulin sensitivity and lipid oxidation242 • Has vascular-protective effects On the other hand, resistin and RBP4 levels , which are also secreted by adipocytes , may induce insulin resistance.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old girl is referred to an endocrinologist with severe obesity and insatiable hunger despite adequate nutrition. Due to the early-onset severe obesity , genetic testing was done and revealed inactivating mutations in the leptin gene . Which of the following neuroendocrine abnormalities is this child most likely to develop ?
mcqs.explanation: The most prominent neuroendocrine abnormality seen in obese individuals with inactivating mutations in the leptin (ob gene ) or leptin receptor (db gene ) is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism . Leptin mutations are responsible for a rare form of obesity that runs in families . These mutations prevent leptin from delivering satiety signals. Hence , the brain perceives starvation despite adequate nutrition. It results in morbid, early-onset obesity . Mutations in the following genes can cause obesity in humans: • Lep (ob) • LepR (db) • POMC • PC-1 • MC4R

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Genetic mutations causing pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) deficiency presents with all of the following except:
mcqs.explanation: Cachexia is not a feature of mutations of the pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) gene . It is associated with the following characteristics: • Absence of \030-MSH • Severe obesity - \030-MSH inhibits appetite in the hypothalamus • Pale skin and red hair • Absence of ACTH • Secondary adrenal insufficiency

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The production of which of the following hormones is increased in obesity ?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin levels are increased in obesity . It stimulates the synthesis of fatty acids and TAG and decreases the rate of lipolysis . Thyroxine, growth hormone, and adiponectin have lipolytic effects , hence their levels are reduced in obesity . Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are consistent features of obesity . Insulin resistance is more strongly linked to intra-abdominal fat than to fat in other areas.243 Adiponectin (Option D) is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that is produced by adipocytes . It performs vital functions that are reduced in obesity - like, increasing insulin sensitivity and the inhibition of gluconeogenic enzymes . It also enhances fatty acid oxidation. Insulin resistance in obesity occurs as a result of the following : • Insulin receptor downregulation • Increased FFA (free fatty acids) and capable of impairing insulin action • Intracellular lipid accumulation • Circulating peptides produced by adipocytes such as TNF-\030, IL -6, RBP4 , and resistin modify insulin action.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a child with obesity , hypogonadism , and mental retardation, which of the following would you not suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: Children with Angelman syndrome present with mental retardation but do not have obesity and hypogonadism. It occurs due to the deletion of band q12 of the maternal chromosome 15. The following syndromes present with obesity , hypogonadism , and mental retardation • Prader-Willi syndrome - deletion of band q12 of the paternal chromosome 15. • Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome • Carpenter syndrome • Cohen syndrome The following image shows a child with Prader-Willi syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Obesity is not seen in patients with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Sipple syndrome is characterized by pheochromocytoma which is associated with weight loss.244 Obesity is seen in the following syndromes: • Cushing's syndrome • Prader-Willi syndrome • Pickwickian syndrome • Hypothyroidism • Insulinoma • Craniopharyngioma and other hypothalamic disorders • Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome • Carpenter syndrome • Cohen syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman is being evaluated for high blood glucose levels . On examination, acanthosis nigricans is noted , and her BMI is 34 kg/m\262. How would you classify her weight ?
mcqs.explanation: According to the WHO classification , a BMI of 34 kg/m\262 would be classified as class I obesity . The revised BMI classification for Asians/Indians is as follows : • Underweight - BMI < 18.5 kg/m2 • Normal or lean - BMI 18.5–22 .9 kg/m2 • Overweight - BMI 23 .0 –24 .9 kg/m2 • Obese BMI \03725 kg/m2 Note : As the question does not specify Asian/Indian , the answer is given according to WHO classification.Classification BMI (kg/ m\262) Risk Underweight <18.5 - Normal weight 18.5–24. - Overweight 25–29 .9 Increased Obesity (Class I) 30–34.9 High Obesity (Class II ) 35–39.9 Very high Extreme obesity (Class III ) \037 40 Extremely hi gh

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A known patient of type 2 diabetes mellitus on oral medication presents to your OPD for review . His blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg and his BMI is 28.4 kg/m\262. His fasting glucose is 118 mg/dl and postprandial glucose is 154 mg/dl. He consumes a low-calorie diet and exercises regularly . How will you manage his obesity ?

options.a: Start him on a more intense diet and exercise regimen
options.b: Anti-obesity drugs in combination with proper diet and exercise
options.d: Anti-obesity drugs alone as lifestyle changes have not been effective

mcqs.explanation: 245 This obese man with a BMI of 28.4 kg/m\262 along with comorbidities must be managed with anti-obesity drugs as an adjunct to comprehensive lifestyle modifications. The recommendations for management of obesity are as follows : • Diet , exercise , behavioral therapy : • BMI - 25-29 .9 with comorbidities • BMI \037 • Adjunctive pharmacotherapy: • BMI - 27-29 .9 with comorbidities • BMI \037 • Bariatric surgery: • BMI - 35-39.9 with comorbidities • BMI \037 40

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following anti-obesity drugs is a selective 5-HT2C receptor agonist?
mcqs.explanation: Lorcaserin is a selective 5-HT2C receptor agonist with a functional selectivity ~15 times that of 5-HT2A receptors and 100 times that of 5-HT2B receptors .246

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old child was brought with a history of recurrent episodes of jaundice . Blood investigations were suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis . Which of the following liver function test findings is likely to be seen here?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario describes recurrent hemolysis in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis leading to jaundice . In hemolytic conditions, only the unconjugated / indirect bilirubin is raised and conjugated /direct bilirubin remains normal i.e. <15% of total bilirubin. Bilirubin is synthesized from heme which is released primarily from the breakdown of old RBCs. This bilirubin is in its unconjugated form. It enters the circulation and reaches the liver. It is converted to conjugated bilirubin which is then secreted into the biliary tree . Therefore, in a healthy person, most of the circulating bilirubin is unconjugated /indirect bilirubin. Hence , the normal liver function tests show indirect bilirubin >85% and direct /conjugated bilirubin <15% of the total bilirubin. The normal bilirubin values are as follows : • Total bilirubin levels - 1 to 1.5 mg/dL253 • Direct bilirubin - <0.3 mg/dL

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: A 2-week-old baby presented with yellowish discoloration of the skin. Investigations revealed markedly elevated direct bilirubin levels . Which of the following conditions should be suspected in the newborn?
mcqs.explanation: The raised direct bilirubin levels indicate conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Among the given options, biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Biliary atresia is a disorder characterised by destruction or absence of bile ducts in a newborn. It leads to obstruction to the flow of bile thereby causing leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation. Option B: Physiological jaundice of the newborn occurs due to immaturity of the newborn's liver. It is not able to conjugate the excess bilirubin produced after birth. It leads to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Option C: Breast milk may contain certain factors that inhibit the conjugation of bilirubin leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Option D: Hemolytic disease of the newborn causes excess production of bilirubin due to hemolysis leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Investigations performed in a patient with recurrent jaundice gave the following results. What is the possible cause of jaundice in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of urinary bilirubin and increased total bilirubin indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Among the given options, Dubin Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Only conjugated bilirubin can appear in the urine because it is water-soluble and filterable by the kidney . Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and bound to albumin, hence it cannot be filtered by the kidney. Causes of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: • Increased bilirubin production - • Hemolytic anemias • Hematomas • Impaired bilirubin uptake and conjugation- • Gilbert syndrome • Crigler Najjar syndrome • Drugs - Probenecid, Rifampin Causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: • Hereditary cholestatic syndromes • Dubin Johnson syndrome • Rotor syndrome254 • Biliary obstruction

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

options.d: Stone in the common bile duct

mcqs.explanation: Probenecid causes impaired hepatic uptake of bilirubin which leads to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Amoxicillin-clavulanate, acute hepatitis and stone in the common bile duct are causes that lead to mixed hyperbilirubinemia (both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin elevated ) or predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemias . Levels of conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin are useful in determining pre-hepatic causes of jaundice but are not useful in differentiating between intrahepatic and post -hepatic causes of jaundice .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with jaundice . She had been on OCPs for the past month. Her LFT and liver biopsy findings are given below . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Dubin Johnson syndrome (DJS). The LFT describes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzyme levels . The given image of microscopic examination of liver biopsy shows an accumulation of dark melanin-like pigment in the hepatocytes which is seen in this condition. DJS is an autosomal recessive condition causing defective expression of MRP 2 protein which is important for the biliary excretion of conjugated bilirubin. The patient has icterus but is otherwise asymptomatic . DJS also impairs biliary excretion of various compounds like epinephrine metabolites . The dark melanin-like pigment is derived from these metabolites causing the liver to appear black. Rotor syndrome is also an autosomal recessive condition causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but it does not present with pigmentation of the liver. Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes are characterized by unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: What is the defect seen in patients with Rotor syndrome?

options.b: Mutation in organic anion transport protein

mcqs.explanation: Rotor syndrome occurs due to mutation in OATP (organic anion transport protein) 1B1 and 1B3 . Rotor syndrome is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It is a benign disorder with mild elevation of bilirubin levels . It is similar to Dubin Johnson syndrome but the liver does not show any black pigmentation . No treatment is required for these patients .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: While evaluating a patient with jaundice , all of the following investigations would help you to differentiate between Dubin Johnson syndrome and Rotor syndrome except :
mcqs.explanation: 255 Serum bilirubin levels are not helpful in differentiating between Dubin Johnson syndrome (DJS) and Rotor's syndrome as both these conditions present with mild elevation of serum bilirubin. These two conditions can be differentiated as follows :Test Rotor Syndrome Dubin Johnson syndrome Oral cholecystography Gall bladder is visualized Gall bladder not visualisedIm paired ability to concentrate t he contrast material into bile Total urinary coproporphyrin Elevated NormalIncreased excretion o f coproporphyrin 1 and decre ased excretion of coproporph yrin 3 Bromsulphalein (BSP) cleara nce test Delayed clearance of BSPNo reflux Rise in plasma levels of BSP after 90 minutes of injection Reflux of BSP from hepatocyt es

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: In a patient with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which feature helps confirm the diagnosis of Crigler- Najjar syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Kernicterus is seen in Crigler-Najjar syndrome but not in Gilbert syndrome. Gilbert syndrome does not cause a significant elevation in unconjugated bilirubin to cause kernicterus. Crigler-Najjar syndrome and Gilbert syndrome are both caused by various mutations in the UGT1A1 gene. This leads to decreased activity of bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase enzyme leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Both are predominantly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. These syndromes present with jaundice in infants. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in these syndromes is not associated with any hemolysis . All the other liver function tests are usually normal . Crigler Najjar syndrome may lead to kernicterus causing severe brain damage . Liver transplantation is required without which the infant may not survive beyond 1-2 years of age . Whereas, Gilbert syndrome is a benign asymptomatic condition that does not need any intervention.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: An infant presented with yellow discolouration of the skin, poor feeding , and seizures . Investigations revealed total bilirubin- 40 mg/dL and unconjugated bilirubin- 34 mg/dL. Phenobarbitone was administered while blood was being arranged for an exchange transfusion. However, there was no improvement. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with poor feeding and seizures is indicative of kernicterus. This accompanied with unconjugated hyperbilrubinemia is highly suggestive of Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1. No improvement in bilirubin levels following the administration of phenobarbital further supports the diagnosis.256 Crigler-Najjar syndrome is of two types with type 1 having absent/trace enzyme activity and type 2 having <10 % of the normal enzyme activity. Hence , type 1 is far more severe and leads to kernicterus and neurological damage . Type 2 may also lead to kernicterus occasionally. Kernicterus occurs because the unconjugated bilirubin is lipid -soluble and hence crosses the blood-brain barrier . Phenobarbital is an enzyme inducer. Its administration can be used to differentiate between type 1 and type 2 Crigler-Najjar. • Enzyme induction by phenobarbital leads to improved conjugation of bilirubin leading to a reduction in total bilirubin level in type 2 Crigler-Najjar syndrome. • No improvement is seen in type 1 as the enzyme activity is absent and therefore cannot be induced . Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemias (Autosomal Recessive ) include : Note : Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.Crigler-Najjar type I Crigler-Najjar type II Gilbert Syndrom e UDP-GT Activity Absent Markedly reduced Reduced Serum bilirubin - 45 mg/dl <20 mg/dl Generally <3 mg/ dl Pheno-barbital effect on seru m bilirubin No effect Reduction Reduction Outcome Kernicterus Usually benign, kernicterus i s rare Benign Prevalence Rare Rare CommonThe normal serum bilirubin (between 1 and 1.5 mg/dL) present in serum represents a balance between input from the production of bilirubin and hepatic /biliary removal of the pigment . Isolated elevation of the bilirubin: • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia- >15% conjugated bilirubin • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia- <15% conjugated bilirubin

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old child presents with jaundice and easy fatiguability . He had a history of ear infection which was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Investigations done are shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemolytic jaundice . It can present with the following features : • Low hemoglobin • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia • Pigment gall stones - excess bilirubin in bile257 • Development of cholestasis when the gall stones obstruct the flow of bile . This would result in the elevation of conjugated bilirubin and LFTs show a cholestatic picture . Hepatic and obstructive causes of jaundice are not likely as the other liver function tests are normal. The various causes of jaundice can be differentiated as follows : Inherited hyperbilirubinemias like Gilbert syndrome are suspected when there is no associated hemolysis . It is unlikely in this patient because there are clear hemolytic features .Jaund ice Pre hepatic Hepatic Post hepatic Cause Excessive amount of bilirubi n is presented to the liver Impaired cellular uptake / def ective conjugation/ defective secretion of bilirubin Defective excretion due to m echanical obstruction to the f low of bile LFT Elevated unconjugated biliru bin Elevated conjugated and unc onjugated bilirubinMarked el evated levels of AST and ALT (>1000U /L) Elevated conjugated bilirubin Elevated levels of ALP and G GT Exam ple Hemolytic anaemia Hepatitis Choledocholithiasis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with increased activity of 5'- nucleotidase ?
mcqs.explanation: 5\037-nucleotidase is usually elevated in cholestasis . Enzymes elevated in cholestasis are : • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP ) • 5\037-nucleotidase • \025-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , alanine aminotransferase is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT ) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are indicators of liver cell injury. This is because ALT is found primarily in the liver, whereas , AST is found in the liver, cardiac muscle , skeletal muscle , kidneys, brain , pancreas, etc . GGT and ALP are enzymes that primarily reflect cholestasis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: In a patient with acute viral hepatitis , what level of serum transaminases will you expect ?
mcqs.explanation: 258 In a patient with acute viral hepatitis , serum transaminases are elevated to >1000 IU/L The normal levels of serum transaminases are 10 -40 IU/L. Marked elevation of serum transaminases >1000 IU/L is seen in conditions with extensive hepatocellular injury. These include : • Viral hepatitis • Ischemic injury to the liver in conditions like acute heart failure • Toxin /drug-induced liver injury Minor elevations of serum transaminase levels up to 300 IU/L are non-specific and can be found in any liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: A 64-year-old man with jaundice and abdominal pain was found to have an ALP level of 200 mg/dL. His LFT reports from a month ago had shown an ALP level of 50 mg/dL. What is your inference ?

options.b: Could be due to fatty meal intake

mcqs.explanation: A 4 fold rise of serum ALP (alkaline phosphatase ) is suggestive of cholestatic liver disease . However, serum ALP levels cannot differentiate between extrahepatic and intrahepatic cholestasis . The normal range for serum ALP is considered 40-125 IU/L. Serum alkaline phosphatase is found in the liver, bone, small intestines , and placenta . Hence , a mild increase in ALP , i.e., 1 - 1.5 times normal , can be seen in these conditions: • Following a fatty meal intake - influx of intestinal alkaline phosphatase into the blood. Hence , the patient is advised to fast before the blood sample is collected for the test . • In pregnancy - placental ALP • In children - rapid bone growth • In elderly people over 60 years of age ALP can be raised even in conditions like metastatic bone disease , inflammatory bowel disease , Hodgkin's lymphoma, etc . Hence , it needs to be correlated with raised levels of gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) and 5' nucleotidase which are more specific for liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding liver enzymes is true?

options.a: ALT is raised to >1000 IU/L in cirrhosis
options.b: Absolute levels of aminotransferases correlate with the prognosis
options.c: AST:ALT ratio <1 is seen in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
options.d: AST:ALT ratio >1 is seen in chronic viral hepatitis

mcqs.explanation: AST:ALT ratio <1 is seen in NAFLD (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease ). The AST:ALT ratio can be interpreted as follows : Option A: Patients with cirrhosis have only mildly elevated or even normal levels of serum transaminases. Option B: Absolute levels of aminotransferases are not used for predicting prognosis. This is because there is a poor correlation between the degree of liver cell damage and the levels of aminotransferases.259 AST: ALT Condition <1 Chronic viral hepatitis , Nonal coholic fatty liver disease >1 Cirrhosis >2:1 Suggestive of alcoholic liver d iseaseAlcohol intake is associ ated with the deficiency of py ridoxal phosphate which in t urn leads to decreased levels of ALT enzyme. So, AST>AL T. >3:1 Highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Liver function tests of a patient show isolated elevation of gamma-glutamyltransferase with other liver enzymes within normal limits. All of the following drugs could be responsible for this finding except :
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , penicillin does not lead to elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) levels . GGT is a microsomal enzyme. Hence , drugs that are microsomal enzyme inducers can lead to an increase in GGT levels . However, other liver enzyme levels will be normal . Therefore, an isolated rise in GGT level does not indicate cholestatic liver disease . Drugs that increase levels of GGT are: • Barbiturates • Carbamazepine • Ethanol • Griseofulvin • Rifampicin • Phenytoin

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding prothrombin time is false ?

options.a: Indicates prognosis in acute liver disease
options.b: Indicates prognosis in chronic liver disease
options.c: Measures factors II , V , VIII , X
options.d: Measures factors II , V , VII , X

mcqs.explanation: Prothrombin time (PT) can help in estimating the levels of factors II , V , VII , and X. PT evaluates the extrinsic and the common pathway of coagulation . Factor VII is required in the extrinsic pathway and factors II , V, X are required in the common pathway . Coagulation factors are produced by the liver (except factor VIII ) and they have a short half-life . Hence , they indicate the synthetic function of the liver and are very useful in assessing acute hepatic dysfunction . Factor VIII is produced by vascular endothelial cells .260 Prolonged PT that is not corrected by vitamin K administration indicates poor prognosis in both acute and chronic liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which among the following is a marker of chronic liver disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum albumin is a marker of chronic liver disease because it is synthesized by the hepatocytes and has a long half-life of 18–20 days. Serum albumin is not a good indicator of acute or mild hepatic dysfunction . Hypoalbuminemia is more common in chronic liver disorders such as cirrhosis and usually reflects severe liver damage . In hepatitis, albumin levels <3 g/dL should raise the possibility of chronic liver disease . Prothrombin time is used to assess acute parenchymal liver disease . 5' nucleosidase is elevated in cholestasis . Elevation of ALP (<3 fold) is not specific to liver diseases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be seen in a patient with chronic liver disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic liver disease is associated with hypergammaglobulinemia . Chronic liver diseases with hypergammaglobulinemia include autoimmune hepatitis , primary biliary cirrhosis, and alcoholic liver disease . The liver produces all globulins except gamma globulin which are produced by B cells . In chronic liver diseases like liver cirrhosis, there is impaired reticuloendothelial function in hepatic sinusoids . Hence the liver fails to clear the bacterial antigens. This causes an increased production of gamma globulin .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a marker for liver fibrosis?
mcqs.explanation: Telopeptide is not a marker for liver fibrosis. It is a marker for bone resorption. Various non-invasive markers to detect hepatic fibrosis are given below :Non-invasive test for fibrosis Components tested Fibrotest /FibroSure \0302-macroglobulinHaptoglobi nApolipoprotein A-1GGTTota l bilirubin Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (EL F) assay Hyaluronic acidProcollagen p eptide III (PIIINP )Tissue inhi bitor of metalloproteinase (TI MP) Transient elastography (Fibr oScan) Ultrasound waves are used to measure liver stiffness261 Non-invasive test for fibrosis Components tested Fibrospect II Hyaluronic acidAlpha 2 macr oglobulinTissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (TIMP 1)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
mcqs.question: In which of the following patients planned for a liver biopsy , would you not be required to use the transjugular approach?
mcqs.explanation: Liver biopsy can be performed in a patient with splenomegaly via the percutaneous approach. When the percutaneous approach is not advisable, liver biopsy can be performed via the transjugular approach. In this approach, a cannula is inserted via the jugular vein which is then passed into hepatic veins through which the biopsy sample is taken. Therefore, any bleeding resulting from the procedure will drain into the hepatic veins. Indications of transjugular liver biopsy : • Percutaneous approach contraindicated • Significant ascites • Prolonged INR • Coagulopathies • Difficulty in accessing the liver via the percutaneous route • Morbid obesity262

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of cirrhosis in India?
mcqs.explanation: Alcoholic liver disease is the most common cause of cirrhosis in India. The most common cause of cirrhosis worldwide is chronic viral hepatitis - Hepatitis C and B. NASH is expected to overtake it in the near future .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: What is the minimum amount of ethanol a man must have consumed for him to be at increased risk for alcoholic liver disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The minimum amount of ethanol that leads to an increased risk of developing alcoholic liver disease is 28g/day. In women, the minimum is 14g/day. The risk factors for alcoholic liver disease are: • Quantity of alcohol consumption - The risk of developing alcoholic liver disease increases when alcohol consumption is >14 drinks / week in men and >7drinks/week in women. A standard drink contains 14g of ethanol which is present in - • 120 mL of wine • 350ml of beer • 45ml of spirits (gin, rum, whiskey , vodka , tequilla) • Gender - Women have increased susceptibility to alcoholic liver disease • Hepatitis C infection - Increases the severity and decreases survival in alcoholic liver disease • Genetics - A variation in patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 3 (PNPLA3) gene confers an increased risk of progressive liver disease

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and nausea . His ultrasound abdomen revealed grade 2 fatty liver. Which among the following findings is unlikely to be seen in his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease . It is usually characterized by an AST: ALT > 2. This is because there is a deficiency of pyridoxal 5'- phosphate that is a cofactor for the enzymatic activity of ALT . Therefore, ALT levels fail to rise and there is a reversal of the AST: ALT ratio. Prothrombin time (PT) is prolonged due to the deficiency of coagulation factors and, usually, does not respond to the administration of parenteral vitamin K. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease , which is reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism . Elevated ALP levels are seen due to enzymatic induction by alcohol and mild cholestasis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in patients with Zieve's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Zieve's syndrome is not associated with thrombocytosis .267 Zieve's syndrome is a rare syndrome occurring due to severe alcoholic hepatitis characterized by a triad of: • Cholestatic jaundice • Hemolytic anemia • Transient hyperlipidemia It resolves with abstinence from alcohol.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most specific marker for alcoholism?
mcqs.explanation: GGT (Gamma Glutamyl Transferase) is the most specific marker of alcoholism among the given options. The markers with >60% sensitivity and specificity for heavy alcohol use are gamma-glutamyl transferase (>35 u) and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT), the combination of the two is likely to be more accurate than one. An isolated elevation in serum GGT or GGT elevation out of proportion to that of other enzymes (such as the ALT and ALP ) may be an indicator of alcohol abuse or alcoholic liver disease . ALT (option A) is usually elevated in acute hepatocellular conditions such as hepatitis . Alanine aminotransferase is predominantly found in the liver, hence a more specific marker of liver injury. A ratio of AST/ALT > 2:1 indicates the possibility of alcoholic liver disease and > 3:1 ratio is highly indicative of this condition. In alcoholic liver disease , ALT levels are often normal . ALP (option C) is elevated in cholestasis , \037\037is also elevated when there is rapid bone growth like in children and adolescents because of bone alkaline phosphatase and in normal pregnancies due to placental alkaline phosphatase . LDH (option D) elevation is nonspecific.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: You are using a CAGE questionnaire to screen a patient for alcohol abuse . Which of these is not the correct expansion of this questionnaire?

options.a: C - drink to calm your nerves
options.b: A - criticism over drinking annoys you
options.d: E - had a drink as eye opener

mcqs.explanation: C stands for feeling the need to cut down your drinking in the CAGE questionnaire. The CAGE questionnaire is used for identifying alcohol abuse . It can be expanded as below : • C - Have you ever felt you ought to cut down on your drinking ? • A - Have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking ? • G - Have you ever felt guilty or bad about your drinking ? • E - Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover (eye -opener )? One 'yes ' response raises a suspicion of an alcohol use problem and more than one is a strong indication of abuse or dependence .268

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: What parameters are used in calculating discriminant function?

options.c: Prothrombin time, ascites and hepatic encephalopathy

mcqs.explanation: Discriminant function (DF) is calculated using prothrombin time and bilirubin level . It is also known as the Maddrey score and it assesses the severity and mortality risk in alcoholic hepatitis . DF = 4.6 X (the prolongation of the prothrombin time above control [seconds ]) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL) DF \037 32 indicates severe disease and is an indication for starting glucocorticoids .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: A patient with alcoholic hepatitis has just been admitted to your ward. Prior to starting treatment, the senior doctor asks you to calculate his discriminant function. What is the cutoff value for determining severe disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Severe alcoholic hepatitis is defined as discriminant function (DF) \037 . Severe alcoholic hepatitis is defined as: • Discriminant Function (DF) \037 • Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) score \037 • Presence of hepatic encephalopathy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Which among the following is true about alcoholic cirrhosis?
mcqs.explanation: Alcoholic cirrhosis is characterized by mixed micro-and macronodular. If a mixed pattern is not an option, the best choice is micronodular cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is the late stage of alcoholic liver disease . It is characterised by extensive fibrosis. Alcoholic cirrhosis begins as micronodular cirrhosis. With the cessation of alcohol use , larger nodules may form, resulting in a mixed micronodular and macronodular pattern. The various conditions in which cirrhosis is seen are listed below : • Macronodular cirrhosis- Parenchymal nodules >3 mm • Micronodular cirrhosis- Parenchymal nodules <3 mmMacronodular cirrhosis Micronodular cirrhosis Chronic viral hepatitis \0301 Anti trypsin deficiencyDrugs & tox insHereditary hemorrhagic te langiectasiaCryptogenic cirrh osisWilsons disease (Micro & Macro nodular >> Macronod ular) AlcoholPrimary biliary cirrho sisLarge bile duct obstruction HemochromatosisIntestinal bypassCystic fibrosisIndian c hildhood cirrhosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Prednisolone therapy for alcoholic hepatitis can be started in a patient with all of the following except:
mcqs.explanation: 269 SOFA score >2 indicates sepsis and glucocorticoids are avoided in septic patients . Glucocorticoids are indicated in severe alcoholic hepatitis which is defined as: • Discriminant Function (DF) \037 • Model for End-stage Liver Disease (MELD) score \037 • Glasgow alcoholic hepatitis score \037 • Presence of hepatic encephalopathy Prednisolone is given at a dose of 32 mg orally daily for 4 weeks and then slowly tapered off. Glucocorticoid therapy is avoided in: • Active GI bleeding requiring blood transfusions • Active infection requiring antibiotic treatment • Preexisting chronic renal disease with a serum creatinine level greater than 2 mg/dL • Pancreatitis • Obvious contraindications to glucocorticoid therapy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man presents with yellowish discoloration of the skin, abdominal pain, and fever. He reports consuming one-quarter of whisky every day for the past 10 years. He is a known case of chronic kidney disease . His lab reports are given below . Which of the following is used in his treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe alcoholic hepatitis . Since the patient is a known case of chronic kidney disease , pentoxifylline is used in his treatment . Severe alcoholic hepatitis is defined by a discriminant function \037 . In the given scenario, DF = 4.6 X (the prolongation of the prothrombin time above control [seconds ]) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL) = 4.6 x (16-11 ) + 11 = 34. Thus, the patient cannot be managed by nutritional support alone. Pentoxifylline is a TNF alpha inhibitor used either by itself or along with glucocorticoids in the treatment of severe alcoholic hepatitis. It is preferred in patients with kidney diseases and conditions where glucocorticoids are contraindicated . Glucocorticoid therapy is avoided in: • Active GI bleeding requiring blood transfusions • Active infection requiring antibiotic treatment • Preexisting chronic renal disease with a serum creatinine level greater than 2 mg/dL • Pancreatitis • Obvious contraindications to glucocorticoid therapy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about nonalcoholic fatty liver disease ?

options.a: Results from fat accumulation in more than 5% of hepatocytes
options.b: Strongly associated with obesity and insulin resistance
options.c: Associated with reduced serum ferritin levels
options.d: Diagnosis of NASH requires presence of inflammation

mcqs.explanation: 270 Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is associated with increased levels of serum ferritin. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is defined as hepatic steatosis in the absence of any secondary cause for fat accumulation. Histologically , this requires fat accumulation in more than 5% of hepatocytes and it can be divided into: • Nonalcoholic fatty liver (NAFL)- steatosis without inflammation • Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) - steatosis with inflammation NAFLD is strongly associated with obesity and insulin resistance . Its diagnosis requires demonstration of hepatic steatosis and exclusion of significant alcohol consumption and other causes of hepatic fat accumulation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Alcoholic Liver Diseases and Non-Alcoholic Fatt...
mcqs.question: A non-diabetic patient has been diagnosed with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Which of the following is the first-line therapy for it?
mcqs.explanation: The first-line therapy for nondiabetic patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is vitamin E. Management of NAFLD includes : • Vitamin E - first-line therapy in non-diabetics • Insulin sensitizers - first-line therapy in diabetics • Immunizations for Hepatitis A and B • Weight loss • Abstinence from alcohol Note : The FDA in 2024 has approved Resmetirom, a thyroid hormone receptor -beta (THR -beta ) agonist for noncirrhotic NASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis.271

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following hepatitis viruses is a DNA virus?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B is a DNA virus. The hepatotropic viruses include :Hepatitis viru s Family Genetic materi al A Picorna vir us RNA B Hepadna vi rus DNA C Flavivirus RNA D Deltavirus RNA280 Hepatitis viru s Family Genetic materi al E Hepevirida e RNA

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common route of spread of hepatitis E virus?
mcqs.explanation: The most common route of the spread of hepatitis E is feco -oral. Hepatitis E virus is the most common cause of acute hepatitis in adults , especially in endemic countries like India. The most common cause of acute hepatitis in children is the hepatitis A virus. Routes of transmission of hepatitis viruses:Hepati tis Vertical route Need le Blood transfusion Sexua l Feco -oral Hep B HBeAg positive mother >90 %HBsAg with Anti-HBe mot her 10 -15% 6-30 % 1 in 2 lakh(Most common blo od transfusion-related virus). Varia ble - Hep C 5% 1.8-6 % 1 in 18 lakh 5% - Hep A Nil Nil Rare Rare Most co mmon Hep E Rare Nil Nil Nil Most co mmon

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding hepatitis E?

options.a: Can be fatal in pregnant women
options.b: Can cause chronic hepatitis in immunocompetent
options.c: Most common route of spread is vertical transmission

mcqs.explanation: Fatality due to Hepatitis E is highest in pregnant women. In the general population , hepatitis E can lead to fatal fulminant hepatitis in only 1–2% of cases . However, in pregnant women, this is raised to 20 % of cases . HEV does not have a carrier state and can cause chronic hepatitis only in immunocompromised individuals. Its most common route of spread is feco -oral. Note - HEV is also known as E-NANB, i.e., Enterically transmitted Non-A Non-B hepatitis virus.It often appears in epidemics ; hence , it is also called epidemic NANB.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is associated with the highest risk of developing fulminant hepatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Acute viral hepatitis caused by the hepatitis D virus is associated with the highest risk of developing fulminant hepatitis .281 However, fulminant hepatitis is most commonly caused by hepatitis E, especially in endemic countries such as India. This is due to the greater prevalence of hepatitis E infections compared to hepatitis D.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A pregnant woman comes to your clinic for her first antenatal checkup in her 3rd trimester. Laboratory workup reveals that she is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive . What is the chance of vertical transmission of hepatitis B to the child?
mcqs.explanation: The chance of vertical transmission of hepatitis B from a mother who is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive is >90%. In contrast, when the mother is HBsAg positive but HBeAg negative or HBsAg positive with Anti Hbe, the risk of vertical transmission is low. To prevent vertical transmission of HBV , HBsAg positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA titres should receive tenofovir prophylaxis from the 28th week of pregnancy until birth. Infants born to these women are given hepatitis B immunoglobulin along with the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The presence of HBeAg indicates active replication of HBV . Therefore, HBeAg is the qualitative marker of infectivity . HBV DNA titre is the quantitative marker of infectivity . Routes of transmission of hepatitis viruses:Hepatitis Hep B Hep C Hep A Hep E Vertical route HBsAg and HBeAg positive mother >90%HBsAg positive with Anti HBe mother- -15 % 5% Nil Rare Needle 6-30 % 1.8-6 % Nil Nil Blood transfusi on 1 in 2 lakh(Most common blo od transfusion-related virus) 1 in 18 lak h Rare Nil Sexual Variable Yes Rare Nil Feco -oral - - Most co mmon Most co mmon

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the first marker to rise in a patient with acute hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: The first virologic marker to rise in acute hepatitis B is HBsAg i.e., Hepatitis B surface antigen. It is detectable in serum within 1–12 weeks of infection . Usually , HBsAg becomes undetectable 1–2 months after the onset of jaundice . If it persists beyond 6 months, it indicates chronic hepatitis B. However, very rarely, patients may have an HBsAg negative status even during active infection due to infection with escape mutant HBV . These escape mutants have mutations within the S gene and they are known to be responsible for occult hepatitis B infections .282

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which serological marker can be used to diagnose acute hepatitis B in the window period ?
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis of acute hepatitis B in the window period or serological gap can be made by the detection of the anti-HBc antibody. The window period is the period between the disappearance of HBsAg to anti-HBs seroconversion. During this window period , anti-HBc is the only detectable antibody.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old male patient presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice . His lab reports are given below . What is the likely causative organism for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: Increased viral load and negative HBeAg suggest a pre-core mutant variety of hepatitis B virus. These strains have mutations in the pre-core region of the C gene , leading to a stop codon that prevents HBeAg synthesis . These strains can be detected in the serum by HBV DNA analysis. Infection with hepatitis B mutants is difficult to treat and causes infections of prolonged duration. They have a higher risk of progressing to liver cirrhosis. Types of hepatitis B mutants are:Type Feature Pre-core muta nts Defect in pre-core region CN o HBeAg Escape mutant s Mutation in S regionHBsAg r esists neutralisation by anti- HBsSeen inInfants born to H BeAg positive mothersLiver t ransplant recipientAssociated with passive and active imm unization283 Type Feature YMDD mutati on Mutation in P region i.e. YM DD locus which codes forreve rse transcriptaseSeen in patie nts on lamivudine therapy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The lab report of a 40-year-old man is shown below . What is the most likely cause for this serological picture?

options.b: Hepatitis B in the remote past

mcqs.explanation: The given lab findings are most likely to be in patients who had hepatitis B in the remote past i.e., patients in late convalescence period . In such conditions, the patient will have positive IgG anti-HBc and negative HBsAg.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with acute hepatitis B has recovered from the infection . Identify the serological marker marked in the image:
mcqs.explanation: The serological marker marked in the image which becomes detectable early in the infection and remains elevated for a long period after recovery from the infection is an anti-HBc antibody. Anti-HBc is demonstrable in serum within the first 1–2 weeks after the appearance of HBsAg. It precedes detectable levels of anti-HBs by weeks to months. IgM anti-HBcAg antibody is seen early in the infection for about 6 months and indicates a recent infection . IgG anti-HBcAg antibody is seen later, after 6 months, and indicates remote infection .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An intern sustained a needle -prick injury while establishing an IV line on a patient in the casualty . The patient was subsequently found to be HBsAg positive . The presence of which of the following markers in the intern would reliably indicate an early infection ?
mcqs.explanation: The most reliable indicator of recent HBV infection is IgM anti-HBc in serum. However, the first virologic marker to rise in acute hepatitis B is HBsAg i.e. surface antigen. HBsAg is detectable in serum within 1–12 weeks of infection . Anti-HBc is demonstrable in the serum about 1-2 weeks after this, and may sometimes persist in the serum even longer than an anti-HBs antibody. IgM anti-HBcAg is seen early in the infection and persists for about 6 months. It indicates a recent infection . IgG anti-HBcAg antibody is seen later i.e. after 6 months and indicates remote infection . HBcAg is not detectable in the serum of patients with HBV infection as it is present intracellularly. Note : The risk of transmission of HBV from percutaneous routes (eg ., needle prick) is about 6-30% and it is about 100 times more infectious than HIV .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: During your casualty rotation, you accidentally injure yourself while suturing a patient . You had taken the full schedule of hepatitis B vaccination during your first year of medical school. Which of the following markers will you get measured to determine the need for HBIG administration?
mcqs.explanation: 284 The need for administration of hepatitis B hyperimmune globulin (HBIG ) in a previously vaccinated individual can be determined based on anti-HBsAg levels . It is the marker for determining the efficacy of hepatitis B vaccination . The complete hepatitis B vaccine schedule consists of three intramuscular doses at 0, 1, and 6 months. Post Exposure Prophylaxis: The prophylaxis can be done using the hepatitis B vaccine or hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG).Vaccination status of the exp osed person Recommended prophylaxis Unvaccinated HBIG (0.06 mL /kg) and initi ate hepatitis B vaccine series Known responder to previous vaccination (anti-HBs titer>1 0 mIU/ml) No action required Non-responder to previous v accination (anti-HBs titre <1 0 mIU/ml) HBIG: 2 doses (1 month apar t) OR HBIG: 1 dose + initiate hepatitis B revaccination.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following markers can be used to differentiate between hepatitis D superinfection and coinfection ?
mcqs.explanation: IgM anti-HBc can be used to differentiate between hepatitis D coinfection and superinfection in patients with HBV infection . Co-infection : • Simultaneous infection with both HBV and HDV • IgM anti-HBc detectable in co-infection as its presence indicates recent infection Superinfection : • HDV infection of an individual chronically infected with HBV • IgM anti-HBc will not be detectable • IgG anti-HBc will be present

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A male patient presents with complaints of jaundice , loss of appetite , and weight loss for the past several months. After a full laboratory workup, a liver biopsy was performed which appeared as shown in the given image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given histopathological image shows ground-glass hepatocytes which are a hallmark of chronic hepatitis B infection .285 These ground-glass hepatocytes are liver parenchymal cells that have an eosinophilic , granular, and glassy appearance on light microscopy. This appearance is due to the accumulation of HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum . Liver biopsy findings in viral hepatitis:Virus Liver Biopsy Findings Hepatitis A Hepatocyte swelling , monocy te infiltration, Councilman b odies Hepatitis B Ground glass appearance Hepatitis C Lymphoid aggregates with a f ocal area of macrovesicular st eatosis Hepatitis D Similar to HBV Hepatitis E Patchy necrosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following pairs of viral hepatitis and its management is incorrectly matched ?

options.a: Acute viral hepatitis E - Supportive care
options.b: Acute viral hepatitis B - Antiviral therapy
options.c: Acute viral hepatitis A - Supportive care
options.d: Acute viral hepatitis C - Antiviral therapy

mcqs.explanation: Antiviral therapy is not indicated in acute hepatitis B infection . It is only indicated in chronic hepatitis B. The majority of acute hepatitis (A, B, and E) infections are self -limiting, resulting in viral elimination and complete healing within 6 months. Hence , they need only supportive management. Only 5% of acute hepatitis infections become chronic.286 In acute hepatitis C infection , recovery is rare, and the risk of progression to chronic hepatitis is high(\02485%). Thus antiviral therapy is started irrespective of the disease stage .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an indication for antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B infection ?

options.b: HbeAg negative with HBV DNA <2000 IU/L
options.c: ALT > 2 times upper limit of normal
options.d: Normal Fibroscan report with ALT < 2 ULN

mcqs.explanation: ALT > 2 times upper limit of normal is an indication for antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B infection . The decision to initiate antiviral therapy is primarily based on the presence or absence of cirrhosis, and parameters such as HBeAg, alanine aminotransferase (ALT ) level , and HBV DNA level . The following are the indications for starting antivirals in chronic hepatitis B: • Patients without cirrhosis • HBeAg + with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • HBeAg -ve with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL • Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis Recommended first-line antiviral drugs: • Entecavir • Tenofovir alafenamide • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate Pegylated interferon alfa can also be used . Treatment is aimed at HBeAg seroconversion, but most patients may need to continue antiviral therapy indefinitely .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old man presented with complaints of fatigue for the past 1 month. His lab reports are given below . What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: HBeAg negative and HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL is suggestive of HBV carrier . Serial monitoring of both biochemical and virological parameters is done for such patients . Indications for starting antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B are: • Patients without cirrhosis • HBeAg + with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • HBeAg -ve with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL • Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is recommended as first-line therapy in a patient with chronic hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: 287 First-line drugs used for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B include entecavir and tenofovir. Second -line drugs for this condition include : • Lamivudine • Adefovir • Telbivudine Pegylated interferon can also be used in its treatment .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In which of the following populations should surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma be done?
mcqs.explanation: Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma is recommended for Asian male HBV carriers over the age of 40 years. The most common etiological factor for hepatocellular carcinoma in the world is the hepatitis B virus (HBV ) infection . Surveillance programs have been implemented to screen for HCC in high-risk individuals because it is more cost-effective than the treatment of HCC. Surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is recommended in: • HBV carriers with cirrhosis • Patients with high serum levels of HBV DNA and ongoing liver injury • HBV carriers born in Africa and over the age of 20 • Asian male HBV carriers over age 40 • Asian female HBV carriers over age 50 • HBV carriers with a family history of HCC Note : The CDC recently updated its guidelines for Hepatitis B screening . The report includes screening for all adults >18 years old using the triple -panel test (HBsAg, Anti-HBs, total anti-HBc) and expanded risk -based testing in certain high-risk populations .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old male comes to the OPD with intermittent jaundice for the past 2 months. You suspect acute viral hepatitis . Which of the following will you not evaluate in this patient?
mcqs.explanation: IgM anti-HBe is not one of the markers that are evaluated in a suspected case of acute viral hepatitis . Investigations done in suspected acute viral hepatitis are: • IgM anti-HAV - to detect acute hepatitis A infection which is the most common cause of acute hepatitis in children • HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc - to detect acute hepatitis B infection , where HbsAg is the first marker to rise and IgM anti-HBcAg is the most reliable marker of acute infection • Anti HCV - to evaluate for acute hepatitis C infection288 • IgM anti-HEV (rarely)- to detect acute hepatitis E infection which is one of the causes of acute viral hepatitis in adults .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male chronic smoker presents to the AIIMS OPD with fever, fatigue , yellow -colored urine, and clay-colored stools . For the past few days, he has developed an aversion to cigarette smoking. On examination icterus was present . What investigations would you advise to rule out acute viral hepatitis ? Liver function test results are given below :

options.c: HBsAg, IgM antiHBc, AntiHDV , AntiHCV , Anti HEV

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of jaundice . The tests that should be done in this patient to rule out acute viral hepatitis include: • Anti-HAV • HBsAg • IgM anti-HBc • Anti-HCV We mainly test for hepatitis A, B, and C. Tests for hepatitis D and E are not used routinely . Hepatitis D only occurs concurrently with Hepatitis B, either as a co-infection (when it is clinically indistinguishable from HBV infection ) or superimposed on chronic HBV infection . In the latter scenario, it presents as a sudden worsening of the patient 's condition. IgM anti-HDV , IgG anti-HDV , and HDV RNA assays are useful for diagnosis when hepatitis D is suspected . Hepatitis E is not tested as the majority of patients who acquire hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection spontaneously clear the virus. Acute hepatic failure is more likely in those who are pregnant and in those who are malnourished or have preexisting liver disease . Chronic HEV has been described almost exclusively in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., organ transplantation). The diagnosis of acute HEV is typically based upon the detection of IgM antibodies to HEV. Both false positives and negatives are common with available assays and are thus , not very reliable . Thus, additional serologic testing or HEV RNA testing should be performed to confirm the diagnosis and not be useful as a screening test . [Please note the difference between anti-HBe and anti-HEV]Condition Suspect ed Targetted Test Performed Acute Hepatitis A IgM Anti-HAV Acute Hepatitis B HBsAg andIgM Anti-HBc*1 o r both can be positive . A posi tive IgM AntiHBc with negati ve HBsAg is seen when HBsA g is below the detection thres hold. Acute Hepatitis C Anti HCV

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following groups of individuals need not be screened for Hepatitis C infection ?

options.b: Patients with unexplained elevation of aminotransferase levels
options.c: Patients who have undergone long-term haemodialysis
options.d: Household contacts of patients with hepatitis C

mcqs.explanation: HCV screening is not indicated for household contacts of persons with hepatitis C. However, hepatitis B virus screening is recommended in household contacts of HBV -infected persons.289 Indications of HCV infection screening : • Persons with a history of using injection drugs • Persons with HIV infection • Long term hemodialysis • Persons with an unexplained elevation of aminotransferases • Recipient of blood or organs from a donor found to be positive for hepatitis C • Children born to women with Hepatitis C • Health care, public safety , and emergency medical personnel following needle injury or mucosal exposure to HCV contaminated blood • Sexual partners of persons with Hepatitis C

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen as an extrahepatic manifestation in patients with hepatitis C infection ?
mcqs.explanation: Polyarteritis nodosa is not characteristically associated with hepatitis C infection . However, it is a common extrahepatic manifestation of hepatitis B viral infection .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man who presented with weight loss and abdominal discomfort is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C . All the following factors can determine the progression of liver disease in this patient except :
mcqs.explanation: While HCV RNA is considered the gold standard for establishing a diagnosis of hepatitis C, it has no role in determining the progression of liver disease in patients with chronic hepatitis C. The likelihood of progression of liver disease in patients with chronic hepatitis C is increased by: • Longer duration of infection - most important determinant • Older age • Obesity - patients with a high body mass index are at an increased risk of developing fibrosis • Diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance • Concomitant liver disorder (eg ., alcoholic liver disease , chronic hepatitis B, hemochromatosis) • Concomitant HIV infection . The best prognostic indicator in chronic hepatitis C is the rate of fibrosis and baseline inflammation seen in liver histology .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old man presented with generalized weakness , fatigue , and fever. His lab investigations are given below . What is the preferred treatment regimen for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatitis C for which the preferred treatment regimen is velpatasvir 100 mg and sofosbuvir 400 mg.290 The goal of treatment is a sustained virologic response (SVR ), which is defined as the absence of a virus in the blood (undetectable HCV RNA), 12 weeks after completion of treatment . This can be achieved by the use of pan-genotypic directly acting antiviral drugs, irrespective of the disease stage .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a non-structural protein 5A inhibitor used in the treatment of patients with hepatitis C infection ?
mcqs.explanation: Sofosbuvir is not an NS5A inhibitor but is an NS5B nucleoside /nucleotide polymerase inhibitor. The directly acting antivirals used in the treatment of Hepatitis C infection include :291

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Autoimmune hepatitis is suspected in a woman presenting with fatigue , pruritus, and arthralgia. She has a past history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis . Which of the following is not part of the simplified scoring system for the given condition?
mcqs.explanation: Presence of viral markers is not a part of the simplified scoring system for diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis . The simplified scoring system includes four variables. They are: • Autoantibodies • Elevated serum IgG level • Typical compatible histologic features295 • Absence of viral hepatitis markers The clinical presentation in autoimmune hepatitis is variable and shares features with acute and chronic hepatitis of other aetiologies . They usually present with an insidious onset of non-specific symptoms such as fatigue , anorexia and eventually jaundice . It can then progress to extensive liver necrosis and liver failure. Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with several autoimmune diseases such as: • Rheumatoid arthritis • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Thyroiditis and Grave's disease • Haemolytic anemia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is associated with Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH )?
mcqs.explanation: Minocycline is associated with the development of drug-induced AIH . Other drugs associated with AIH include nitrofurantoin, methyldopa , diclofenac , and possibly statins.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old lady is suspected to have autoimmune hepatitis . Which of the following antibodies is unlikely to be present in her serum?
mcqs.explanation: cANCA is not seen in autoimmune hepatitis . It is positive in Wegner's granulomatosis. pANCA is what is seen in autoimmune hepatitis . There are 2 types of autoimmune hepatitis : Type I (classic) autoimmune hepatitis is often seen in young women. It is linked to HLA -DR3 or HLA -DR4. It responds well to steroids and has a better prognosis. The autoantibodies that are seen in type I are: • ANA - antinuclear antibodies • ASMA - anti-smooth muscle actin • pANCA - perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic • anti-SLA - anti-soluble liver antigen Type II autoimmune hepatitis is often seen in children. It is linked to HLA -DRB1 or HLA -DQB1. It usually leads to fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver failure. The autoantibodies that are seen in type II are: • Anti-LKM 1 - anti-liver kidney microsomes • Anti-liver cytosol 1

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Match the following :
mcqs.explanation: 296 • Anti LKM 1- Autoimmune hepatitis II • Anti SLA - Autoimmune hepatitis I • Anti LKM 2 - Drug-induced hepatitis • Anti LKM 3 - Chronic hepatitis D

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman presenting with abdominal pain is diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis . The mainstay of management in this patient is:
