mcqs.explanation: The mainstay of management in autoimmune hepatitis is glucocorticoid therapy . Glucocorticoids are started at high doses and tapered down to a low maintenance dose . The dose of glucocorticoids is often reduced by combining with azathioprine. The benefits of glucocorticoid + azathioprine combination therapy are: • Reduction in the duration of therapy. • Avoid life -threatening complications of steroids (e.g., cushingoid features , hypertension , diabetes , osteoporosis ).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old female patient with a diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis did not respond well to glucocorticoids . Which among the following is false regarding her further management options ?
mcqs.explanation: Liver transplant is not contraindicated in refractory autoimmune hepatitis even though the risk of recurrence is high. The medical management of refractory autoimmune hepatitis include : • High dose glucocorticoids • Glucocorticoids + high dose azathioprine • Addition of cyclosporine , tacrolimus, or mycophenolate mofetil .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A young lady has been on treatment for autoimmune hepatitis for 2 weeks , she has now come for follow -up investigations. Which of the following suggests a poor prognosis in this patient?
mcqs.explanation: Persistently increased serum bilirubin after 2 weeks of therapy suggests a poor prognosis. Early signs of poor prognosis include : • Failure of serum bilirubin to reduce after 2 weeks of therapy . Early signs of good prognosis include : • An increase in serum albumin. • A decrease in serum bilirubin, globulins and aminotransferases. • Improvement of symptoms . Histopathologic improvement can often take months to years.297

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The most common symptom of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is
mcqs.explanation: The most common symptom of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is fatigue . Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a granulomatous autoimmune condition characterized by the destruction of interlobular hepatic bile ducts . Most patients with PBC are asymptomatic at the time of the diagnosis. Fatigue and pruritus are both common presenting symptoms . However, the most common symptom is fatigue . Other symptoms and signs are - • Right upper quadrant pain • Hyperpigmentation • Xanthomas and xanthelasma • Jaundice • Hepatosplenomegaly .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 44-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is now diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis. Which of the following is false regarding her lab values?
mcqs.explanation: Anti-LKM 2 antibodies are not seen in primary biliary cholangitis . They are seen in drug-induced hepatitis . The laboratory findings of primary biliary cholangitis include : • Liver function tests • Elevated ALP • Elevated GGT and 5'- nucleotidase • Elevated ALT and AST • Serology - • Antimitochondrial antibodies - positive in 95% of patients . These are mostly directed against the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex . • Antinuclear antibodies • Elevated HDL , LDL , and VLDL • Elevated serum IgM Hyperbilirubinemia is seen once cirrhosis has developed .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis has been taking ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) twice daily. She now presents with ascites and variceal bleeding . What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient ?

options.c: Add obeticholic acid to the treatment

mcqs.explanation: 298 The presence of ascites and variceal bleeding suggest decompensated liver disease and the appropriate treatment is liver transplantation. The first-line drug in primary biliary cholangitis is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). It only slows the rate of progression of the disease . It does not provide any symptomatic benefit or cure the disease . Obeticholic acid is another drug used in PBC as monotherapy or in combination with UDCA. It is a farnesoid X receptor agonist. Liver transplantation is considered when there are signs of decompensation or portal hypertension such as ascites , variceal bleeding , encephalopathy , coagulopathy , or malnutrition.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presented with fatigue , pruritis, and xanthomas over the elbows . A biopsy of her bile duct revealed florid duct lesions . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Florid duct lesion is characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). It is the lymphocytes and plasma cells all centered around bile ducts .Primary sclerosing cholangitis has the characteristic "onion-skin" concentric fibrosis surrounding the bile ducts .299

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about primary sclerosing cholangitis is false ?

options.a: Affects both intra and extrahepatic bile ducts
options.b: Liver biopsy definitively establishes the diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Liver biopsy does not establish the diagnosis in primary sclerosing cholangitis . The diagnosis requires imaging with MRCP. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of intra and extrahepatic biliary ducts resulting in strictures and cholestasis . The cause is unknown. Most patients have underlying ulcerative colitis . It has an association with HLA DRw52. Patients present with symptoms of cholestasis such as fatigue and pruritus. The laboratory findings include : • Liver function tests - Elevated ALP and aminotransferases. • Increased serum IgM levels • Positive p-ANCA MRCP is the investigation of choice . It shows multiple strictures in intra and extrahepatic bile ducts . Liver biopsy reveals a concentric "onion skin" fibrosis. This is however not pathognomic of PSC. There is no definitive treatment . It involves the administration of UDCA and liver transplantation. PSC can lead to the development of cholangiocarcinoma The image below shows onion-skin fibrosis in PSC.300

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: In acute liver failure, encephalopathy occurs within ______ of the development of clinical symptoms .
mcqs.explanation: 307 In acute liver failure, encephalopathy occurs within 4 weeks of the development of the clinical symptoms . Acute liver failure is the rapid worsening of the liver function in patients without cirrhosis or any preexisting liver disease . The patient initially suffers from an acute injury to the liver by viruses, drugs, etc . Following this, the function of the liver rapidly worsens and patient develops coagulopathy and encephalopathy within 4 weeks of the development of jaundice or other clinical symptoms .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of acute liver failure in India?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in India is a viral infection . Among the viruses, hepatitis E virus is the most common cause of acute liver failure. In developed countries , acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A small child was rushed to the ED by his parents. He had accidentally consumed wild mushrooms while they were trekking. Examination showed features of encephalopathy and his liver function tests were deranged . Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Amanita phalloides (wild mushrooms) toxicity causing acute liver failure. Hypoglycemia is seen in acute liver failure and not hyperglycemia . It occurs due to impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis . Features of acute hepatic failure are: • Hepatic encephalopathy and cerebral edema - There are increased levels of ammonia (neurotoxin) in the body as a result of decreased elimination by the liver. • Coagulopathy - There is a decrease in the synthesis of coagulation factors leading to the elevated prothrombin time and INR . • Increased risk of infections - It occurs as a result of decreased reticuloendothelial activity, decreased synthesis of complements , acute phase reactants, etc . • Renal failure- This is more commonly seen in drug/toxin-induced hepatic failure. • Metabolic complications like hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A patient is said to have hyperacute liver failure if encephalopathy occurs within?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperacute liver failure is defined as the development of encephalopathy within 7 days of the appearance of symptoms . Acute liver failure can be subcategorized into three groups depending on the time interval between the onset of jaundice and encephalopathy . • Hyperacute - encephalopathy develops within 7 days or less than 7 days • Acute - encephalopathy develops between 8-28 days308 • Subacute - encephalopathy develops between 28 days to 6 months Patients with hyperacute liver failure are more likely to develop coagulopathy and cerebral edema , but most of the patients will recover without the need for liver transplantation. On the other end, patients with subacute liver failure have less severe coagulopathy and cerebral edema , but most of them will need liver transplantation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A young patient with Hepatitis E virus infection develops acute liver failure. Which of the following scores can be used in assessing the prognosis of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In a patient with acute liver failure, MELD score and King's College Hospital criteria can be used to assess the prognosis. Option A: Pitt score is used used to predict mortality in patients having bloodstream infections . Option B: The child-Pugh score is used to assess the severity of cirrhosis. Option D: Maddrey 's Discriminant Function (MDF) score suggests which patients with alcoholic hepatitis may have a poor prognosis and benefit from steroid administration.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A young patient is admitted to the hospital after ingestion of a large number of acetaminophen tablets . To predict the prognosis using King's College hospital criteria in this patient , which of the parameters are not used ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum bilirubin is not included in King's College Hospital criteria in acute liver failure due to paracetamol overdose. The King's College Hospital Criteria is a prognostic tool for patients with acute liver failure (ALF). The criteria is divided into acetaminophen and non-acetaminophen causes of liver failure. Liver transplantation is indicated in acetaminophen -induced ALF if there is a presence of • Either pH <7.3 • Or all of the following • Prothrombin time >100 sec or INR >6.5 • Serum creatinine level >3.4 mg/dL (300 �Mmol/L) or anuria • Grade 3-4 encephalopathy Liver transplantation is indicated in non-acetaminophen causes of ALF if there is a presence of • Either prothrombin time >100 sec or INR >6.7 • Or any three of the following • Unfavorable etiology (seronegative hepatitis or drug reaction) • Age <10 or >40 yr • Acute or subacute category (duration of jaundice >7 days) • Serum bilirubin level >17.5 mg/dL (300 �Mmol/L) • Prothrombin time >50 sec or INR & gt ;3.5309

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: For patients with acute liver failure, which of the following is not an absolute contraindication for liver transplantation?
mcqs.explanation: Portal vein thrombosis is not an absolute contraindication to liver transplantation. This is because portal vein thrombosis can be overcome by constructing a graft from the donor liver portal vein to the recipient 's superior mesenteric vein. Absolute contraindications of liver transplantation are: • Uncontrolled extra-hepatobiliary infection or untreated sepsis • Uncorrectable life -limiting congenital anomalies • Active substance or alcohol abuse • Malignancies - Hepatocellular carcinoma with metastatic spread , incurable malignancies outside the liver, cholangiocarcinoma • AIDS • Advanced cardiopulmonary disease Note : Milan criteria- Patients with primary hepatocellular malignancy can be considered for liver transplantation if there is: • A single lesion \0265 cm. • Up to three separate lesions all <3 cm without any evidence of gross vascular invasion , nodal or distant metastases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the most common indication of liver transplantation in children?
mcqs.explanation: Biliary atresia is the most common indication of liver transplantation in children. Indications of liver transplant in children: • Biliary atresia • Neonatal hepatitis • Congenital hepatic fibrosis • Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency • Wilsons disease • Glycogen storage disorders • Lysosomal storage disorders The most common indication of liver transplant in an adult is the cirrhotic liver. Cirrhosis may be the consequence of viral hepatitis , autoimmune hepatitis , chronic use of alcohol, or biliary cirrhosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: When should a liver transplant assessment be considered in a patient with cirrhosis of the liver?

options.a: When he develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
options.b: When he has ascites which responds to diuretics

mcqs.explanation: 310 Liver transplant assessment should be considered in a patient with cirrhosis of the liver when he develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis . Cirrhosis is the most common indication of liver transplantation in adults . However, not all cases of cirrhosis require liver transplantation. It is considered 1. When the patient either develops the complication of cirrhosis like: • Persistent hepatic encephalopathy • Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis • Portal hypertensive bleeding • Diuretic resistant ascites • Hepatorenal syndrome 2. Or has a poor liver function • MELD score > • Child-Pugh grade C

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A surgeon has removed a part of the liver from the live donor and has stored it in the University of Wisconsin (UW) solution . Which of the following is not a component of this solution ?
mcqs.explanation: Mannitol is not a component of the University of Wisconsin (UW) solution . It is the most commonly used preservation solution during the transplantation of the liver and kidneys. The organ can be stored in this solution for up to 20 hours. Components of UW solution are: • Lactobionate- Prevents cellular swelling and reperfusion injury • Raffinose and hydroxyethyl starch- Prevents endothelial injury • Glutathione and allopurinol- free radical scavengers • Adenosine - required for regeneration of ATP

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding liver transplantation (LT )?

options.a: The ideal graft weight to recipient weight ratio (GRWR ) in living donor transplant is >0.8 %.
options.b: In domino LT , liver grafts with metabolic diseases is used as they are structurally and functionally normal .
options.c: Extended criteria donors and paired-exchange LT decrease waitlist mortality.
options.d: Reduced size LT involves dividing the whole liver into right lobe for an adult patient and left lateral segments for pediatric patients .

mcqs.explanation: The false statement regarding liver transplantation is option D. Reduced -size liver transplantation involves the resection of a full -size liver to appropriately fit in the abdominal cavity of small adults /adolescents . It is reserved only for urgent transplantation. On the contrary, split LT involves dividing the whole donor liver into a left lateral segment (segments II and III ) for a pediatric patient and a right lobe (segments I, IV -VIII ) for an adult patient . Option A: The required graft volume in a living donor transplant is measured by graft weight to recipient weight ratio (GRWR ) or ratio of graft volume (GV) to recipient standard liver volume (SLV ). The ideal GRWR is >0.8 % or GV/SLV is > 35%. The remnant donor liver mass is kept at >30% for safe regeneration .311 Option B: Domino liver transplant involves transplanting a liver from a donor with metabolic disease (eg : familial amyloid polyneuropathy ) to a recipient with end-stage liver disease (eg: hepatocellular carcinoma ). The donor also receives an LT (healthy donor) and is prioritized over the end-stage liver disease recipient . As a liver with metabolic diseases is structurally and functionally normal , it can prolong the recipient 's life by at least 15-20 years as they will not develop the metabolic disease immediately . Option C: Extended criteria donors/ECDs (liver grafts extracted from donors after circulatory death ) and paired-exchange technique are used to decrease waitlist mortality. However, ECDs have poor graft function due to prolonged hypoxia and are associated with higher infection transmission and biliary complications.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: Auxiliary liver transplantation is beneficial in which of the following conditions:
mcqs.explanation: Auxiliary liver transplantation is beneficial in acute liver failure. Auxiliary liver transplantation involves implanting a healthy liver graft heterotopically or orthotopically while leaving the whole or part of the native liver intact. The auxiliary partial orthotopic LT (APOLT ) technique is used in patients with acute liver failure and metabolic diseases (primary hypercholesterolemia, glycogen storage disorders, organic acidemia, etc ). In acute liver failure, this technique helps in native liver regeneration and immunosuppression withdrawal . In children with metabolic liver diseases , this technique helps in future gene therapy . Options B, C, and D are chronic liver diseases not suitable for auxiliary liver transplantation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: Which of the following sentences is true regarding split liver transplantation?

options.a: It is done in living donor
options.b: Left lateral lobe is donated to the paediatric recipient
options.c: It is the most common type of liver transplant
options.d: Caudate lobe is donated to the adult recipient

mcqs.explanation: In a split liver transplant, the left lateral lobe is donated to the pediatric recipient . Split liver donation: This method is done when the liver from the deceased donor is suitable for transplant in an adult as well as a pediatric recipient . The liver is split into two . The left lateral segment (2 and 3) is donated to the pediatric recipient , left medial and right segments (4, 5, 6, 7, and 8) is donated to the adult recipient .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A patient who underwent liver transplantation is started on tacrolimus for immunosuppression. His family physician prescribed him fluconazole for the treatment of a fungal infection . This will lead to

options.c: No effect on both the drugs

mcqs.explanation: In a patient who is on tacrolimus, the addition of fluconazole may lead to toxicity of the tacrolimus. Tacrolimus and cyclosporine are calcineurin inhibitors and are the common agents used for the i mmunosuppression following liver transplantation. They are metabolized by the CYP3A enzyme. Fluconazole can inhibit this enzyme and lead to increased levels of tacrolimus and cyclosporine .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A patient presented with fever and pain abdomen. He had undergone liver transplantation a month ago and is taking immunosuppressants . On examination, abdominal guarding was present and on auscultation , no bowel sounds were heard. Doppler showed hepatic artery thrombosis. Which of the following medications is he most likely on?
mcqs.explanation: 312 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of peritonitis due to hepatic artery thrombosis. Sirolimus is known to cause hepatic artery thrombosis in liver transplant recipients . Sirolimus is an mTOR inhibitor and prevents T cell activation. It is not used commonly in liver transplant recipients because of the increased frequency of hepatic artery thrombosis in the first month posttransplantation . However, they can be used in patients with calcineurin inhibitor-related nephrotoxicity .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: All of the following complications can be seen in patients with liver transplantation except
mcqs.explanation: Patients with liver transplantation are more likely to develop B cell lymphomas and not T cell lymphoma. Complications of liver transplantation • Rejection of the transplanted liver • Hepatic artery thrombosis • Posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorders- It can range from a mild polyclonal proliferation of B cells to B cell lymphomas. • Congestive heart failure and arrhythmias • Increased susceptibility to infections as a result of immunosuppression • Renal dysfunction due to acute tubular necrosis or nephrotoxicity of the tacrolimus and cyclosporine • Seizures are commonly associated with cyclosporine or tacrolimus toxicity .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A liver biopsy is performed in a patient who is suspected to have acute rejection following liver transplantation. Which of the following findings in the biopsy will confirm the presence of acute rejection ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of endotheliitis confirms the presence of acute rejection of the liver transplant. Rejection following liver transplantation can be acute or chronic. Patients usually present with • Malaise • Fever • Right upper quadrant pain Laboratory investigations will show • Elevated levels of serum bilirubin • Aminotransferases • Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidases • Liver biopsy - for confirming the diagnosis and planning the treatment313 Liver biopsy of the acute rejection is characterized by the presence of mixed portal cellular infiltrate, bile duct injury, and endothelial inflammation (endotheliitis ). Chronic rejection is characterized by the presence of focal parenchymal necrosis, mononuclear cell infiltration, progressive cholestasis , and fibrosis. In some patients , this process will lead to the loss of intrahepatic bile ducts , which is called vanishing bile duct syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male patient developed fever, malaise, and anorexia after a month of liver transplantation. On evaluation, he has leukopenia , thrombocytopenia , and deranged liver function tests . Which of the following organisms is most likely to have caused this?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of post -solid transplant infection most likely due to cytomegalovirus (CMV). It is the most common cause of post -solid organ transplants in India. Epstein -Barr virus (EBV), herpes , and varicella are also known to cause infection post -solid organ transplantation but to a lesser extent . CMV disease in recipients can present with fever, leukopenia , thrombocytopenia , malaise, and arthralgia. They usually present within 1-4 months after transplant. The diagnosis of CMV infection is established by nucleic acid testing (NAT) using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Management includes the use of anti-viral drugs like ganciclovir, valganciclovir , foscarnet, cidofovir and intravenous immunoglobulins.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Acute Liver Failure and Liver Transplantation
mcqs.question: Which of the following primary diseases has the higher chance of recurrence, after liver transplantation?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , autoimmune hepatitis has the highest chance of recurrence after liver transplantation. Although some cases of sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cirrhosis recur, data for recurrence of autoimmune hepatitis is more supportive . Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency does not recur after liver transplantation.314

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common gene mutation associated with hemochromatosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most common mutation seen in hemochromatosis is a cysteine to tyrosine substitution at position 282 (C282Y) in the HFE gene. HFE mutations are the most common cause of hereditary hemochromatosis and are inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to develop iron overload?
mcqs.explanation: Thalassemia minor does not result in iron overload. Secondary hemochromatosis or iron overload is characterized by the deposition of iron in parenchymal cells .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following clinical manifestations of hemochromatosis is incorrectly matched with its mechanism of onset ?
mcqs.explanation: Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, impotence , amenorrhea) in hemochromatosis occurs as a result of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. This is due to iron deposition in the pituitary gland, not testes .321 Iron deposition occurs in the following sites :Organ Manifestation Liver Hepatomegaly Skin Slate -grey or bronze skin hyp erpigmentation :increased me lanin synthesisdue to iron de position Pancre as pancreatic diabetes /type 3C d iabetes Pituita ry Hypogonadotropic hypogona dismSecondary hypothyroidi sm Heart Dilated cardiomyopathyCong estive heart failureArrhythmi as Joints Arthropathy is due to:Iron de positionCalcium pyrophosph ate deposition (pseudogout )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy undergoes genetic testing as his brother has been diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. He is found to be homozygous for the C282Y mutation. Which of the following is the strongest indicator that he will develop symptoms of the disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum ferritin > �Mg/L is the strongest predictor of disease expression among individuals homozygous for the C282Y mutation. Many patients with C282Y mutations are initially asymptomatic and do not show features of iron overload. In such patients , serum ferritin can indicate whether they are likely to develop the disease as ferritin levels reflect the total iron stores . As ferritin levels may be high following inflammatory conditions, combined measurement of ferritin and transferrin saturation is done in a practical setting to avoid false positives . It is also repeated once inflammation subsides . If these tests are abnormal , genetic testing for HFE mutations is done.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old diabetic man is worried as the skin over his face , neck, and dorsum of hands has turned greyish over the past two months. He also complains of abdominal and joint pain. On examination, gynecomastia and hepatomegaly are noted . What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of hemochromatosis. The treatment of choice is the removal of excess iron by phlebotomy . Phlebotomy is an inexpensive , convenient, and safe method of treatment . In this process , 500 mL of blood is removed 1-2 times weekly which removes 200 -250 mg of iron. Weekly phlebotomy should be continued until the serum ferritin level is \026100 �Mg/L and every 3 months thereafter . It is contraindicated in severe anemia and hypoproteinemia . Chelating agents bind to iron to form complexes that get excreted and are the drugs of choice . Drugs such as deferoxamine and deferasirox are commonly used . However, they are less effective322 and more expensive than phlebotomy . Liver transplantation is indicated either in end-stage liver disease or in refractory cases . Supportive management includes avoiding iron-containing substances such as red meat, multi-vitamin tablets , etc . Alcohol should be completely avoided as it can aggravate the disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis has been started on weekly phlebotomy . All of the following features will improve with this treatment except :
mcqs.explanation: In hemochromatosis, removal of excess iron through phlebotomy has no effect on arthropathy and hypogonadism.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about Wilson's disease ?

options.b: AP1S1 gene is essential for normal functioning
options.c: Siblings of affected children have 1 in 4 risk of the disease

mcqs.explanation: Wilson's disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene on Chr.13q . The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions: • Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin • Helps excrete free copper in bile . Thus, an ATP7B deficiency leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues . It is an autosomal recessive condition. So, siblings of affected children have a 1 in 4 chance. Intracellular trafficking of ATP7B (Wilson's disease ) and ATP7A (Menke's disease ) genes are regulated by an adaptor protein encoded by the AP1S1 gene . Mutations in this gene result in a syndrome with features of both Wilson's and Menke's diseases . It is called MEDNIK syndrome: • Mental retardation • Enteropathy • Deafness • Neuropathy • Ichthyosis • Keratodermia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following are true regarding KF ring?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options only statements 1 and 5 are true. Kayser -Fleischer (KF) rings are seen in almost all patients of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement. It initially appears as a crescent in the superior pole of Descemet 's membrane and gradually extends inferiorly, eventually becoming circumferential in shape . KF rings occur due to copper deposition in the descemet 's membrane. It is golden -brown to greenish-brown in color and can be best seen by slit-lamp examination.323 The image below shows a KF ring :While it is a characteristic sign of Wilson's disease (statement 2), it can also be seen in: • Primary biliary cholangitis • Primary sclerosing cholangitis • Cholestasis KF rings are present in almost 95% of patients of Wilson's disease with neurological /psychiatric symptoms compared to around 65% of those with hepatic presentations (statement 4). They disappear on treatment with copper -chelating agents like d-penicillamine (while desferrioxamine is an iron chelating agent ) and reappear with disease progression (statement 3).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In patients with Wilson's disease , Kayser -Fleischer rings are most commonly associated with:
mcqs.explanation: The presence of the Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ring in Wilson's disease is most commonly associated with neuropsychiatric manifestations such as dystonia. In majority of the cases , neuropsychiatric manifestations follow hepatic manifestations . It is due to the deposition of free copper in the basal ganglia (leading to bilateral degeneration and atrophy) and cortex. The features include : • Dysarthria (most common): Irregular word spacing, hypophonic or spastic speech • Dystonia: Vacuous smile i.e mask-like face with an open mouth • Parkinsonism : Bradykinesia, postural instability , rigidity • Subcortical dementia : Slow mental processing , memory loss • Psychiatric symptoms : Loss of emotional control, depression , hyperactivity • Decreased scholastic performance: Deterioration in handwriting, clumsiness • Autonomic symptoms : Excessive sweating and salivation, sexual dysfunction324 • Wing beating tremors (seen in advanced disease ): High amplitude tremor that is prominent with arms abducted , elbows flexed and palms facing downward.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old woman is being evaluated in the emergency department for a 3-day history of dark -colored urine and abdominal distension . On examination, she is conscious and oriented . Icterus is present . The following investigations are done. Which of the following would you suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: The given laboratory values indicate hepatic disease and hemolytic anemia (low Hb with high reticulocyte count). These lab findings along with clinical features point to a diagnosis of Wilson's disease . The clinical features of Wilson's disease include : Option A: Hemochromatosis presents with clinical features of iron overload. Serum ferritin and total iron are elevated . Option B: Acute viral hepatitis presents with positive HbsAg, whereas anti-Hbs IgG indicates past infection . There is tender hepatomegaly with very high levels of transaminases (>1000 IU/L). Option C: Primary biliary cirrhosis presents with jaundice , severe itching, and pale stools . There are high levels of direct bilirubin, ALP , and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies .System Clinical features Hepatic (most com mon) JaundiceAbdominal painHep atomegalyFatigueAscitesVari ceal bleedCoagulation defects High AST & ALT with low AL P Neurological DysarthriaDystoniaParkinson ismSubcortical dementiaDep ressionWing beating tremors Decreased scholastic perform ance Ophthalmic Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ringsS unflower cataract Others Hemolytic anemia (Coombs n egative )Acute pancreatitisFan coni's syndromeHyperparath yroidismCardiomyopathySpo ntaneous abortionsInfertility

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A child presents with hepatitis and progressive neurological degeneration . A picture of his eye has been provided below . Among the following options , what would be the initial step regarding the investigations done for this child's diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features of hepatitis , progressive neurological degeneration , and the Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image are suggestive of Wilson's disease . The initial step regarding investigations done for the diagnosis is the measurement of serum ceruloplasmin levels . Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ring is a golden to greenish -brown ring of deposition of copper in the Descemets membrane of the peripheral cornea. Patients with neurological manifestations325 manifest with KF ring in >95% of cases . Lab investigations in Wilson's disease would show: The gold standard technique for diagnosis of Wilson's disease is percutaneous needle liver biopsy for measurement of hepatic copper levels >200 �Mg/g of dry weight .Lab markers Change in Wilson's diseas e Reason Serum ceruloplas min \023\023\023 ATP7B deficiency results in r educed bound copper 24h urinary coppe r \027\027 (>100 �Mg/24h) Excess free copper excreted i n urine Total serum coppe r \023 Due to marked reduction in c eruloplasminOption B: The role of total serum copper in the diagnosis of Wilson's disease is limited . Measurement of serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper is preferred . Option C: ATP7B enzyme assays have shown promise in early studies as a neonatal screening test for Wilson's disease . However, it is not yet part of routine clinical practice . Option D: Karyotyping is done for every asymptomatic 1st and 2nd degree relative of a patient with Wilson's disease . This helps differentiate the carriers (heterozygous ) from the patients (homozygous ) and can lead to early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings would be seen in a patient with Wilson's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The following findings will be seen in a patient with Wilson's disease : • Decreased total serum copper • Decreased serum ceruloplasmin • Increased urinary copper Normally, >90% of copper exists in bound form and <10% in free form. In Wilson's disease , despite elevated levels of free copper , the marked reduction in ceruloplasmin results in a net reduction of total serum copper i.e., \023total serum copper =\027free copper + \023\023ceruloplasminLab markers Change in Wilson's diseas e Reason Serum ceruloplas min \023\023\023 ATP7B deficiency results in r educed bound copper 24h urinary coppe r \027\027 Excess free copper excreted i n urine326 Lab markers Change in Wilson's diseas e Reason Total serum coppe r \023 Due to marked reduction in c eruloplasmin

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought with complaints of abnormal posture . His scholastic performance used to be above average but has deteriorated over the last 3 months. Dystonia and increased muscle tone are noted on clinical examination. The following picture is seen on ophthalmic examination. What is the gold standard for the diagnosis of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ring with sunflower cataract are suggestive of Wilson's disease . The gold standard for diagnosis is the estimation of liver copper following biopsy . A copper level of >200 �Mg/g dry liver tissue is diagnostic for Wilson's disease . It is measured using neutron activation analysis or atomic absorption spectrometry . Sunflower cataract is a rare finding of Wilson's disease . It occurs due to the deposition of copper in the center of the lens.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A pathologist is preparing a tissue sample from the liver biopsy of a patient with Wilson's disease . What stain will he use ?
mcqs.explanation: In Wilson's disease , liver biopsy samples are stained using rubeanic acid to visualize the cytoplasmic copper . Another stain used for copper is the rhodanine stain. However, copper staining is not reliable for diagnosis and a quantitative copper assay must be performed . The given image shows the staining of copper by rubeanic acid.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 17-year-old girl was brought with involuntary, writhing movements of her limbs. On examination , she is anicteric with dystonia and hyperreflexia . Investigations revealed mildly elevated transaminases and low serum ceruloplasmin levels . Which of the following is the safest drug that can be initiated for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 327 This clinical scenario is suggestive of Wilson's disease with predominantly neurological features . The safest drug that can be initiated for this patient is trientine. This is because D-penicillamine can worsen neurological symptoms and would not be tolerated by this patient . The copper chelating agents , D-penicillamine and trientine are the first-line drugs in the management of Wilson's disease . D-penicillamine is the recommended drug due to its availability and cost-effectiveness compared to trientine. However, D-penicillamine can precipitate various adverse effects including aplastic anemia, myasthenia gravis and membranous nephropathy . It can also worsen neurological symptoms . Hence , trientine is administered in those who cannot tolerate D-penicillamine . Elemental zinc is commonly used as a maintenance therapy along with chelating agents . It can also be used as first-line therapy in pregnancy. Tetrathiomolybdate is currently under phase 2 clinical trials. It has been identified to be effective in patients with neuropsychiatric manifestations but is not approved for clinical use . Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for advanced liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: For a patient with Wilson's disease , you would administer pyridoxine along with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: Penicillamine should always be co-administered with pyridoxine (25 mg/day) as it is an antagonist to pyridoxine.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The Nazer's prognostic index for Wilson's disease includes all of the following parameters except :
mcqs.explanation: ALT is not a part of Nazer's prognostic index. Nazer's prognostic index is used to establish disease severity in Wilson's disease patients who present with hepatic decompensation .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Low serum copper levels attributed to ATP7A gene is due to:
mcqs.explanation: Low serum copper level attributed to the ATP7A gene is due to Menke's disease (Option C). Menke's disease or Menke-Kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition occurring due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper -containing enzymes . It presents within 3 years of age and is characterized by: • Depigmented kinky hair • Failure to thrive • Neurodegenerative symptoms like loss of developmental milestones , truncal hypotonia, epilepsyLoose , wrinkled skin • Multiple fractures328 • Poor visual acuity • Recurrent infections . Lab investigations show low serum copper (<65 �Mg/dL) and low ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dl). The disease is fatal as it has no curative treatment . But, administration of L-histidine and copper chloride injections may be beneficial , if started early. Aceruloplasminemia is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by tissue iron overload, mental deterioration, microcytic anemia, and low serum iron and copper concentrations. Option B: Low serum copper and low ceruloplasmin is also seen in Wilson's disease , but is associated with the gene defect ATP7B on chromosome 13 . It is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism with features of hepatolenticular degeneration and Kayser Fleischer ring. Option A: Dubin Johnson Syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired canalicular excretion of bilirubin due to mutation in MRP-2 protein leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Option D: Gilbert's Syndrome is characterized by decreased UDP glucuronyl transferase activity leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which can be autosomal recessive or dominant.329

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is unlikely to lead to cirrhosis in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis A infection is an acute self -limiting condition that does not lead to cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is a late stage of chronic liver disease pathologically characterized by hepatic fibrosis, distortion of hepatic architecture , and formation of regenerative nodules . The causes of cirrhosis are: • Chronic viral hepatitis - Hepatitis B and C • Alcoholic liver disease • Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease338 • Autoimmune hepatitis • Biliary cirrhosis - • Primary biliary cholangitis • Primary sclerosing cholangitis • Cardiac cirrhosis • Inherited metabolic liver diseases - • Cystic fibrosis • Hemochromatosis • Wilson's disease • \0301 Antitrypsin deficiency • Cryptogenic cirrhosis • Drugs - methotrexate , isoniazid

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: While examining a chronic alcoholic patient , you notice the given finding. Which of the following is false regarding it?

options.a: Occurs due to alterations in the metabolism of estrogen
options.b: Presence of even 1 lesion is abnormal
options.c: Commonly seen over the superior vena cava territory
options.d: Compression results in blanching followed by reappearance after release

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows spider telangiectasia and the presence of >2 to 3 of these are considered abnormal. Spider telangiectasias are dilated arterioles with a prominent central arteriole with radiating vessels appearing in the shape of a spider . They are generally seen in the superior vena cava territory. Compression results in blanching followed by reappearance after the release of pressure . They occur due to a hyperestrogenic state which is caused by defective estrogen metabolism in liver cirrhosis. Clinical features seen in cirrhosis include : • Spider telangiectasias • Palmar erythema • Terry's nails - pallor of the proximal nail bed • Clubbing • Gynaecomastia • Caput medusae - dilated abdominal veins. • Parotid enlargement The image below shows Terry's nails.339

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient greater than _____ mm Hg.
mcqs.explanation: Clinically-significant portal hypertension is defined as hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) \03710 mm Hg. HVPG is the difference between the wedged hepatic venous pressure (WHVP ) and the free hepatic venous pressure (FHVP). It represents the pressure difference between the portal vein and IVC . Interpretation of HVPG values:HVPG v alue Interpretation 1-5 mm Hg Normal >5 mm Hg Portal hypertension \03710 mm Hg Clinically significant portal h ypertension , varices can deve lop \03712 mm Hg Risk of variceal bleeding and ascites

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension . Budd Chiari syndrome is a congestive hepatopathy characterized by the obstruction of hepatic venous outflow . The most common cause is due to hepatic vein thrombosis. Obstruction of two or340 more major hepatic veins causes Budd-Chiari syndrome. It is characterized by hepatomegaly , ascites , and abdominal pain.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is used to reduce the intrahepatic resistance in portal hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Carvedilol is used to reduce the intrahepatic resistance in portal hypertension . The pharmacologic management of portal hypertension includes : • Drugs that reduce the portal blood flow • Non-selective \031 blockers - Propranolol and nadolol are preferred • Somatostatin and its analogs - Octreotide , lanreotide , and vapreotide • Vasopressin and analogs - Terlipressin • Drugs that decrease the intrahepatic resistance • Carvedilol - due to its \030 blockade property

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Ascitic tap done on a patient with abdominal distention revealed a SAAG of 1.4g/dL. What is the likely cause of his ascites ?
mcqs.explanation: The serum ascites albumin gradient of \0371.1g/dL is suggestive of portal hypertension . SAAG helps distinguish ascites caused by portal hypertension from other causes of ascites .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with massive abdominal swelling . Paracentesis fluid was sent for lab analysis and results show serum protein to be 3g/dL and ascitic fluid protein to be 1g/dL. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1g/dL [calculated as serum albumin level - ascitic fluid albumin level , which in this case is 3-1=2g/dL] and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL is late Budd Chiari syndrome. Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) can be used to differentiate between ascites due to portal hypertension and non-portal hypertensive ascites . It represents the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient. It is given by the formula: SAAG = Serum albumin level - Ascitic fluid albumin level Interpretation of SAAG: • SAAG \0371.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids . It reflects the presence of portal hypertension . • SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension . It may be due to infection or malignancy. In cases with high-SAAG (\0371.1), ascitic protein level analysis further helps in identifying the etiology :341 • \0372.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites as in early Budd-Chiari syndrome. • <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein as in late Budd-Chiari syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is said to have refractory ascites if the ascites does not resolve even after:
mcqs.explanation: Refractory ascites is defined as the inability to mobilize ascitic fluid despite : • Compliance with dietary sodium restriction • Administration of maximum doses of diuretics - • 400mg of spironolactone per day and • 160mg of furosemide per day

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the minimum absolute neutrophilic count that should be present in the ascitic fluid to diagnose a patient with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is made when the fluid sample has an absolute neutrophil count >250/�ML. SBP is the spontaneous infection of the ascitic fluid without an intraabdominal source . Infection with E.coli and other gut bacteria is most commonly seen . However, gram-positive bacteria like Streptococcus viridans , Staphylococcus aureus, and Enterococcus sp., can also be found. Abdominal paracentesis is the investigation of choice . It can be managed with antibiotic therapy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A cirrhotic patient admitted for ascites complained of abdominal pain on the 2nd day of his hospital stay. On examination, he was febrile . His lab reports are given below . Which of the following is false about his condition?

options.a: E.coli is the most commonly isolated organism
options.b: Prophylaxis against this condition is recommended in upper GI bleed
options.c: Third generation cephalosporins are used for treatment
options.d: Weekly antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended to prevent recurrence

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with ANC \037 250 cells /�Ml in ascitic fluid is suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Daily antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended in patients who have had an episode of SBP to prevent a recurrence. SBP is the spontaneous infection of the ascitic fluid without an intraabdominal source . The most common causative organisms are E.coli and other gut bacteria. The diagnosis of SBP is made when the ascitic fluid has an absolute neutrophil count >250/�Ml. According to the latest recommendations, weekly antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer recommended. For patients with low protein ascites (<1.5 g/dL [15g/L]) along with either impaired renal function or liver failure, we use prolonged outpatient trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (one double -strength tablet daily). Alternatives include ciprofloxacin 500 mg per day or norfloxacin 400 mg per day. For patients on chronic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy , renal function should be monitored by checking serum electrolytes , blood urea nitrogen ( BUN) and creatinine every one to six months depending on the stability of patient . If there is worsening renal function,342 trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be discontinued .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following cannot be used to predict the risk of bleeding of oesophageal varices?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of bleeding in a patient with oesophageal varices cannot be predicted based on the number of varices present . The factors that are used to predict the risk of variceal bleeding are: • Severity of cirrhosis (Child's class, MELD score) • History of a previous variceal bleed • Location of the varices - varices with a thinner layer of supporting tissue are likely to bleed more • Size of the varices - larger varices have a higher risk of bleeding • Endoscopic appearance of varices - Presence of red wale sign, hematocystic spots , diffuse erythema, and cherry red spots are associated with increased risk of bleeding • Variceal pressure

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with which of the following conditions would you not recommend a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt?
mcqs.explanation: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is not recommended in hepatic encephalopathy as it can aggravate its symptoms . TIPS creates a low-resistance channel between the hepatic vein and an intrahepatic branch of the portal vein. It uses a percutaneous approach under angiographic guidance . This reduces portal pressure . It is used in the management of: • Oesophageal varices - in patients who fail medical or endoscopic management and have a poor surgical outcome • Refractory ascites • Gastric varices • Ectopic varices • Portal hypertensive gastropathy • Hepatorenal syndrome • Budd Chiari syndrome343

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man with hematemesis is rushed to the casualty . On examination, he is icteric, PR-122 /min and BP- 88/64 mmHg. The following finding is seen on his abdomen. Which of the following is false regarding his initial management?

options.a: pRBC is used to maintain Hb between 7-9g/dL
options.c: IV octreotide is used to acheive hemostasis
options.d: Upper GI endoscopy is only performed after 12 hours

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the image showing caput -medusae is suggestive of acute esophageal variceal bleeding due to portal hypertension . Upper GI endoscopy is performed within 12 hours after fluid resuscitation in variceal bleeding . The management of esophageal variceal bleeding involves: • Resuscitation with IV fluids , airway protection , and oxygen • Blood transfusion to maintain Hb between 7-9g/dL • Antibiotic prophylaxis with ceftriaxone before endoscopy • An attempt at hemostasis with octreotide or terlipressin or vasopressin • Upper GI endoscopy within 12 hours after fluid resuscitation to confirm the source of the bleed • Endoscopic variceal ligation of sclerotherapy • In case, of failure or rebleeding - TIPS Nonselective beta -blockers like propranolol and nadolol are used in the prophylaxis of variceal bleeding .344

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about the given image?

options.a: Esophageal balloon should be deflated for about 5 mins every 6 hours
options.b: Gastric balloon should be inflated first
options.c: Pressure in the oesophageal balloon should not exceed 60 mm Hg.
options.d: Endotracheal intubation prior to tube insertion reduces the risk of pulmonary aspiration

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Sengstaken -Blakemore tube . Pressure in the oesophageal balloon should not exceed 45 mm Hg. It is used for balloon tamponade in variceal hemorrhage when medical therapy fails or is not available. Initially, only the gastric balloon should be inflated , with 200 – 250 mL of air, as this will usually control bleeding . The oesophageal balloon is used in continued bleeding , it should be deflated for about 5 minutes every 6 hours to avoid oesophageal mucosal damage . Endotracheal intubation prior to tube insertion reduces the risk of pulmonary aspiration.345

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis shows marked confusion and gross disorientation. He is drowsy but responds to pain and voice stimuli. What is the most likely grading of hepatic encephalopathy in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Gross disorientation with an intact response to pain and voice suggest grade 3 hepatic encephalopathy . Hepatic encephalopathy is the alteration of mental status and cognitive function occurring in liver failure. This occurs due to the failure of removal of gut -derived neurotoxins like ammonia by liver. These neurotoxins enter the brain leading to the development of symptoms .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the earliest symptom of hepatic encephalopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest symptom of hepatic encephalopathy is an alteration in sleep pattern. Other signs and symptoms of hepatic encephalopathy include : • Asterixis also called the flapping tremor • Mood changes and inappropriate behavior • Disorientation and confusion

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A cirrhotic patient was admitted following variceal bleeding . On the 3rd day of his hospital stay, he appears to be drowsy and confused . His wife reports that he had been awake throughout the previous night. On examination, flapping tremors were noticed . Which of the following is least likely to have precipitated his symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatic encephalopathy . Antibiotics are unlikely to precipitate hepatic encephalopathy . The common precipitating factors of hepatic encephalopathy are : • Gastrointestinal bleeding • Infections like SBP or UTIs • Peritoneal tap • Constipation • Renal failure • Hypovolemia • Hypoxia • Drugs - sedatives , antidepressants , diuretics • Hypoglycemia • Hypokalemia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following antibiotics could be used in the treatment of patients with hepatic encephalopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Rifaximin can be used in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy . It lowers blood ammonia levels .346 Treatment of hepatic encephalopathy includes : • Correction of precipitating factors • Lactulose - decreased GI transit time due to cathartic actions leading to increased elimination of ammonia • Rifaximin - lowers the blood ammonia levels • L-ornithine L-aspartate - stimulate the urea cycle , with resulting loss of ammonia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not part of the diagnostic criteria of hepatorenal syndrome?

options.a: 50% increase in creatinine from baseline within 7 days
options.b: Rise in creatinine of 0.3 mg/dl in 48 hours
options.d: No recent use of nephrotoxic agent

mcqs.explanation: The absence of shock is a part of the diagnostic criteria for hepatorenal syndrome. Hepatorenal syndrome is a progressive renal failure in patients with acute or chronic liver disease . The diagnostic criteria for hepatorenal syndrome include : • Cirrhosis with ascites • Diagnosis of acute kidney injury (AKI) • Increase in serum creatinine of \037 0.3mg/dL in 48 hours, OR • 50% increase in serum creatinine from baseline within 7 days • Absence of shock • No evidence of recent use of nephrotoxic agents • Absence of intrinsic renal disease

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following clinical features is most likely to be seen in patients with hepatopulmonary syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , platypnea is most likely to be seen in patients with hepatopulmonary syndrome. Hepatopulmonary syndrome is characterized by a triad of liver disease , hypoxemia , and intrapulmonary vascular dilatations. Most patients have dyspnea on exertion. The classic clinical manifestations are: • Platypnea - Increase in dyspnea when the patient moves from supine to upright position • Orthodeoxia - Decrease in arterial oxygen tension when the patient moves from supine to upright position The hypoxemia is due to a ventilation-perfusion mismatch which causes an increased alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient. The most sensitive test for diagnosis is contrast bubble echocardiography . Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment of this condition following which the symptoms subside .347

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old man presents with oliguria, abdominal distension , and pedal edema . His medical records show long-standing cirrhosis with multiple hospitalisations for ascites and hepatic encephalopathy . His lab reports are given below . What is the best treatment for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatorenal syndrome. The best treatment modality for it is liver transplantation. Hepatorenal syndrome is characterised by a rise in: • AST • ALT • Total bilirubin • Serum creatinine • Blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Management of hepatorenal syndrome include : • Norepinephrine • Octreotide • Terlipressin • Midodrine • Intravenous albumin • Liver transplantation- definitive treatment

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not a MELD exception ?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic Hepatitis B is not a MELD exception . MELD (Model for End-stage Liver Disease ) score is used to prioritize patients awaiting liver transplantation. However, there are certain diseases that impair patient survival and are not accounted for in the MELD score. Patients with these diseases are given upgraded MELD points to accurately represent the mortality risk and these conditions are called MELD exceptions . The MELD exceptions include :- • Portopulmonary hypertension • Hepatocellular carcinoma • Familial amyloid polyneuropathy • Primary hyperoxaluria (necessitating liver-kidney transplantation) • Cystic fibrosis with liver disease • Highly selected cases of hilar cholangiocarcinoma. • Hepatopulmonary syndrome • Hepatic artery thrombosis 7–14 days post -liver transplantation.348

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is false ?

options.a: Components of MELD (Model for end stage liver disease ) scoring system are creatinine, bilirubin, International normalized ratio (INR ), serum sodium (mEq/L).
options.b: Components of CTP(Child Turcotte Pugh) score are albumin, bilirubin, INR , ascites , encephalopathy
options.c: Components of CTP (Child Turcotte Pugh ) are creatinine, bilirubin, International normalized ratio (INR)
options.d: MELD score is used to assess and prioritize patients awaiting liver transplantation

mcqs.explanation: The Child Turcotte Pugh (CTP) score does not include creatinine. The components of the CTP score are: • Albumin • Bilirubin • International normalized ratio (INR ) • Ascites • Encephalopathy The Model for End-stage liver disease (MELD 3.0) is used to prioritize patients awaiting liver transplantation and includes : • Female sex • Bilirubin • Albumin • Serum sodium (mEq/L) • INR (International Normalized ratio) • Creatinine

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the Child-Turcotte-Pugh class for the patient who has a serum bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl, serum albumin 3 g/dl, prothrombin time increased by 5 seconds (INR = 2), no encephalopathy , and mild ascites ?
mcqs.explanation: The given patient belongs to Child-Turcotte-Pugh class B. The score can be calculated as follows : Serum bilirubin-2.5mg/dl: Serum albumin-3g/dl: Prothrombin time-5 seconds or INR -2: No encephalopathy : Mild ascites : Therefore, the Child-Turcotte-Pugh score is (2+2+2+1+2)= 9 which is included in Class B.349

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an epithelial mucosal defense mechanism of the gastric mucosa?
mcqs.explanation: Restitution is an epithelial mucosal defense mechanism. It is the process by which healthy surface epithelial cells from the adjoining areas migrate to restore a damaged region of the gastric mucosa. The gastric mucosa has well -established mucosal defense mechanisms against various assaults like HCl, pepsin , alcohol, etc . These include : • Pre-epithelial defense : A layer of mucous over the surface epithelium . This is secreted by the surface epithelium and contains HCO3- which maintains neutral pH at the cell surface • Epithelial defense : It is constituted by the surface epithelial cells and their intercellular tight junctions that perform the following functions • Act as a physical barrier • Restitution is the migration of healthy cells to damaged areas • Rapid renewal of surface epithelial layer • Generating factors that prevent cellular damage such as heat shock proteins • Sub-epithelial defense : • Rich microvascular bed of the gastric submucosa that provides HCO3- and washes away the toxic metabolites .356 • Alkaline tide - It is caused by the release of HCO3- into the gastric capillaries by the parietal cells . This HCO3- helps in the quick neutralization of HCl.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman complains about a burning pain in her chest . She reports using NSAIDs for her constant knee pain. This drug impairs her gastric mucosal defense mechanism primarily by:
mcqs.explanation: The NSAIDs impair the mucosal defense mechanism primarily by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis . NSAIDs also decrease nitric oxide synthesis and have an irritant effect on the gastric mucosa but inhibition of COX enzymes / prostaglandin synthesis is the most prominent factor. Almost all the mucosal defense mechanisms are primarily mediated by prostaglandins synthesized by the gastric mucosal cells . Apart from the prostaglandins, the other factors that play a role in mucosal defense include : • Nitric oxide (NO)- Causes vasodilation thereby increasing the mucosal blood flow . • Several growth factors like EGF, TGF, FGF- Play a role in epithelial regeneration and restitution .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: All of the following are true about the risk factors of NSAIDs associated peptic ulcer disease except :

options.b: H pylori infection increases the risk
options.c: Even low dose of a NSAID can cause ulcers
options.d: Concomitant use of glucocorticoids decreases the risk

mcqs.explanation: Concomitant use of glucocorticoids with NSAIDs increases the risk of peptic ulcer disease . Other risks factors for NSAID-induced PUD include : • H pylori infection • Serious or multisystem disease • Alcohol and smoking • Concomitant use of the following drugs with NSAIDs increases the risk of PUD and its complications: • Glucocorticoids • Anticoagulants • Clopidogrel • Multiple NSAIDs PUD may occur even with low doses of NSAIDs. No dose of NSAIDs is considered completely safe .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: What pattern of gastritis is most common in patients with H.pylori-related duodenal ulcers ?
mcqs.explanation: Antral predominant gastritis is associated with duodenal ulcers . Antral predominant gastritis is associated with increased acid production by the parietal cells . This subjects the duodenum to increased acid exposure , leading to the formation of duodenal ulcers . H. pylori infection may result in the following patterns of gastritis:357 • Non-atrophic pangastritis- mostly asymptomatic and sometimes associated with MALToma . • Corpus predominant gastritis- affects the corpus and causes atrophy. This leads to the loss of acid-producing parietal cells that are primarily found in the corpus. Hence , it is associated with decreased acid production . This is also a predisposing factor for the development of gastric cancer. • Antral predominant gastritis- spares the parietal cells . Hence , it is associated with increased acid production. Option A: Autoimmune gastritis is caused due to autoantibodies against the parietal cells . It is not associated with H. pylori. Option C: Granulomatous gastritis is characterized by the presence of granulomas It is associated with Crohn's disease and sarcoidosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A patient presents with frequent epigastric pain with burning sensation for the past 2 years. The pain usually occurs 2-3 hours after a meal and is relieved by taking food. He also says that he sometimes wakes up at night because of severe pain. The most probable cause for his symptoms is:
mcqs.explanation: Epigastric pain with a burning sensation that usually occurs 2-3 hours after a meal and is relieved by taking food suggestive of duodenal ulcer. The following patterns of pain are usually seen in peptic ulcer disease : • Duodenal Ulcer - Pain occurs 1.5 to 3 hours after a meal and is frequently relieved by antacids or food. Pain may awaken the patient from sleep . • Gastric Ulcer - Pain/discomfort may be precipitated by food. Nausea and weight loss are common. • Perforated ulcer- The bed of the ulcer tunnels through the entire thickness of the gastric wall and opens into the peritoneum . This presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain and leads to peritonitis . Radiography shows gas under the diaphragm. • Penetrating ulcer- It is a type of perforation where the ulcer tunnels into an adjacent organ like the pancreas/liver. In this case, the pain is no longer relieved by food or antacids and might radiate to the back. Many patients with peptic ulcers , especially elderly patients , may not have these symptoms and may directly present with a complication like bleeding or perforation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about gastric ulcers ?
mcqs.explanation: Gastric ulcers are associated with low basal acid production and low stimulated acid production . Gastric acid secretion occurs in two patterns : • Basal acid output - Occurs in a circadian pattern. It is mediated by ACh from the vagus and histamine. • Stimulated acid production - Occurs in response to food . It is mediated by gastrin in addition to other factors.358 Gastric Ulcer Duodenal Ulcer Less common More common Occurs later in life , with a pe ak incidence in the 6th decad e Occurs earlier in life Basal and stimulated acid pr oduction is low/normal, exce pt in type 3 gastric ulcers Basal and nocturnal acid pro duction is increased Can representmalignancyand should be biopsied Rarely malignant Most common site :Antrum(di stal to acid-secreting mucosa) on the lesser curvature Most common site : 1st part o f the duodenum ( within 3cm s from the pylorus ) Painafterfood intake Painbefore food intake, andr eliefontaking food

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: H pylori causes gastric mucosal injury due to the presence of:
mcqs.explanation: H.pylori produces vacuolating exotoxin (Vac A) which causes gastric mucosal injury. Vac A inhibits CD4+ T-cells and disrupts the function of B cells , macrophages & mast cells . Cag A positive strains of H pylori cause an increased risk of gastric cancer.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: You are a first-year resident . You are asked to prescribe an H.pylori eradication regimen to a patient with peptic ulcer disease . Which of the following drugs will you not include in it?
mcqs.explanation: Erythromycin is not effective in H pylori eradication. Note : Vonoprazan , a potassium -competitive acid blocker, has been recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of peptic acid-related disorders.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: In which of the following patients presenting with epigastric pain and discomfort is H.pylori eradication therapy not indicated :

options.a: 46-year-old man with a family history of gastric cancer in the father
options.b: 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on NSAIDs for 5 years
options.c: 58-year-old man with 35-pack years history of smoking
options.d: 36-year-old man with GERD on PPI's for 3 months

mcqs.explanation: The need for H pylori eradication therapy in patients with GERD on long-term PPIs is not well established and is controversial. H pylori eradication therapy is offered to patients diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease (PUD) as it greatly decreases the recurrence of ulcers. In addition to this, it should also be offered to patients at increased risk of PUD and gastric cancer such as: • Patients with long-term NSAIDs usage . Eg . Rheumatoid arthritis • Patients taking gastric acid inhibitors for >1 year359 • Patients with increased exposure to risk factors of gastric cancers. Eg . heavy smokers, exposure to dust , coal • Patients with previous history/family history of gastric neoplasm

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: Eradication of H.pylori infection in patients with peptic ulcer disease is determined by?
mcqs.explanation: Eradication of H. pylori infection can be determined by a urea breath test . A stool antigen test can also be employed .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: H.pylori increases the risk of:
mcqs.explanation: H.pylori increases the risk of gastric MALT lymphoma. H.pylori is protective against the following : • GERD • Barrett's esophagus • Adenocarcinoma of esophagus • Adenocarcinoma of the cardia of the stomach H. pylori are inversely related to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and its sequelae , which include Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma. H.pylori strains positive for Cag A may be particularly protective against the development of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Thus, colonization with H. pylori, particularly Cag A strains, may be protective against the more severe forms of GERD. Eradication of H. pylori is associated with mild worsening of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in patients with corpus-dominant or pangastritis. It improves symptoms in those with antral-dominant gastritis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: The most common complication in patients with peptic ulcer disease is:
mcqs.explanation: GI bleeding is the most common complication of peptic ulcer disease . Other complications : • Perforation- second most common • Gastrocolic fistulas • Gastric outlet obstruction • Rarely malignancy360

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old woman presented to the ER with an altered sensorium. Her husband reported that she has had abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation for the past 4 days. She has been self -medicating for gastritis. Her lab investigations are as shown. Which of the following drugs is she most likely on that could have caused her symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical features indicating hypercalcemia and investigations showing renal insufficiency, metabolic alkalosis are suggestive of milk-alkali syndrome. Long-term use of calcium carbonate can lead to this condition. In susceptible individuals, there is a loss of negative feedback , leading to excess calcium absorption when there is excess intake. It results in the following triad of clinical features : • Hypercalcemia • Alkalosis- due to HCO3 reabsorption caused by PTH suppression , natriuresis, and water depletion • Renal failure- due to damage to renal tubules It is reversible once ingestion of antacid is stopped . However, in severe cases , a chronic form called Burnett's syndrome can develop. It is associated with irreversible renal damage .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A patient is admitted to the ICU after he suffered trauma to his head . This patient is prone to develop what type of gastric ulcers ?
mcqs.explanation: The gastric ulcers associated with head trauma are Cushing ulcers . Head trauma leads to vagal stimulation which in turn leads to increased gastric acid production . Option A: Curling ulcers are seen in severe burns. Option C: Stress ulcers are seen in conditions like shock, sepsis , etc . They are thought to be caused by local ischemia and splanchnic vasoconstriction. Option D: Refractory ulcers are those that do not heal even after adequate medical therapy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: You would diagnose a patient to have a refractory gastric ulcer if the ulcer fails to heal after:
mcqs.explanation: A gastric ulcer is said to be refractory if it fails to heal after 12 weeks . A refractory duodenal ulcer is that which fails to heal after 8 weeks . Management of refractory PUD: • Rule out other diseases or causes • High dose PPI • Surgery

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presents with acidity , abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss for the past few months. Her symptoms are not relieved by taking antacids. An endoscopic evaluation shows ulcers on the second part of the duodenum . Which of the following conditions should be suspected in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario of symptoms not improving with antacids, associated diarrhea, and the unusual location of ulcers are highly suggestive of Zollinger Ellison syndrome.361 Zollinger Ellison syndrome (ZES) is a peptic ulcer disease caused by unregulated gastrin release from a neuroendocrine tumor/gastrinoma. About 60% of the tumors are malignant, hence , it is important to identify ZES. The clinical presentation of ZES is very similar to that of peptic ulcer disease . The features which help in suspecting ZES include : • Unusual locations- the second part of the duodenum and beyond • Refractory to medical therapy • Recurrence after acid-reducing surgery • Presenting with complications like bleeding and perforation • Not associated with H. pylori or NSAID ingestion Patients of ZES often have associated diarrhea and involvement of the esophagus (esophagitis, ulceration, or stricture ).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent duodenal ulcers with poor response to medical therapy. He had a history of hyperparathyroidism and transsphenoidal prolactinoma resection . Which among the following is the next appropriate step ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Zollinger Ellison syndrome (ZES). The next appropriate step to evaluate the patients for ZES is by measuring the serum gastrin levels . History of hyperparathyroidism and transsphenoidal prolactinoma resection indicates MEN1 syndrome. ZES is commonly associated with MEN1. The normal gastrin levels are <150 pg /mL . An increase of >10 times the normal levels is highly suggestive of ZES. Secretin test is a gastrin provocative test . It is done when the gastrin levels and the acid secretory studies are inconclusive for ZES. It is the most sensitive and specific gastrin provocative test for the diagnosis of gastrinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound is done to localize the tumor. It is done after the diagnosis of ZES has been established .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following investigations employs somatostatin analogues to detect gastrinomas?
mcqs.explanation: OctreoScan detects gastrinomas using their property of uptake of somatostatin analogues . OctreoScan detects endocrine tumors that express receptors for somatostatin in conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) and multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN ) syndromes. Other modalities used for localizing the tumor in ZES include : • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS ) • PET/CT with Ga-DOTATATE is the investigation of choice when available. Note : PET/CT with Ga-DOTATATE is the gold -standard test for localizing tumors in pheochromocytoma.362

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses cause infectious gastritis in immunocompromised patients ?
mcqs.explanation: Viruses that cause infectious gastritis in immunocompromised individuals include cytomegalovirus and Herpes simplex virus.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders
mcqs.question: An anemic patient on evaluation showed macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear. Serology revealed anti-parietal cell antibodies . Which of the following is most likely to be associated with her condition?
