mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following are features of Crohn's disease except :
mcqs.explanation: Lead pipe appearance is seen in ulcerative colitis (not Crohn's disease ). This appearance is due to the loss of haustra in the diseased colonic segment . The image below shows the lead pipe appearance of the colon on barium enema:

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A young man presents to the OPD with complaints of chronic diarrhea, right lower abdominal pain, and weight loss. On examination, you note a low-grade fever and a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant . Colonoscopy revealed sparing of the rectum. The following endoscopic findings may also be seen in his condition except :
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Crohn's disease presenting as ileocolitis . Fine granular mucosa is seen in ulcerative colitis , not Crohn's disease . Ileocolitis presents as right lower abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea. Pain is usually colicky and is relieved by defecation . It may mimic acute appendicitis in the early stages . Endoscopic findings in Crohn's disease include : • Aphthous ulcers - Small, shallow ulcers surrounded by erythema394 • Longitudinal ulcers - Linear or serpiginous deep ulcers • Cobblestone appearance - Deep , longitudinal ulcerations interlaced with intervening normal mucosa • Strictures • Fistulas .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the earliest radiographic feature of Crohn's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Aphthous ulcers seen in Crohn's disease are the earliest radiological signs on small bowel follow -through study . They are shallow ulcers that are often multiple and separated by normal intervening mucosa. They are also the earliest macroscopic findings of Crohn's disease . Features on barium small bowel follow-through in Crohn's disease include : • Mucosal ulcers : • Aphthous ulcers initially • Deep ulcers (more than 3 mm depth ) • Longitudinal fissures • Transverse stripes • Severe mucosal ulcers lead to cobblestone appearance • Sinus tracts and fistulae • Creeping fat: widely separated loops of the bowel due to fibrofatty proliferation • Thickened folds due to edema • Pseudo -diverticula formation: due to contraction at the site of ulcer with ballooning of the opposite site • String sign of Kantor: tubular narrowing due to spasm or stricture depending on the chronicity • Rose thorn appearance • Partial obstruction. CT and MR enterography have a higher sensitivity for the diagnosis of Crohn's disease . They may reveal additional features such as: • Fat halo sign - submucosal fat deposition • Comb sign - engorgement of the vasa recta. In gastric Crohn's disease , conical narrowing of the antrum may be seen . This is called Ram 's horn sign. The image below shows aphthous ulcers (focal contrast with surrounding haloes of mucosal edema)395 The image below shows the string sign of Kantor:The image below shows rose thorn appearance :396 The image below shows cobblestone appearance :

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the earliest radiologic change seen on barium enema in ulcerative colitis?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest radiological change of ulcerative colitis seen on barium enema is fine mucosal granularity. Double -contrast barium enema allows for exquisite detail of the colonic mucosa and also allows the bowel proximal to strictures to be assessed . It is however contraindicated if acute severe colitis is present due to the risk of perforation. Early changes in ulcerative colitis : • Mucosal granularity • Fine granular pattern397 • Mucosal stippling • Collar button ulcers • Deep collar stud ulcers . The below contrast radiograph shows granular mucosa typical of ulcerative colitis .Option A: Collar button ulcers are small deep ulcers in which the button surface corresponds to the eroded ulcer base and the button neck corresponds to the undermined and preserved mucosa. They are also seen in ulcerative colitis . Option C: String sign represents circumferential inflammation and fibrosis, resulting in long segments of luminal narrowing as shown below . It is more characteristic of Crohn's disease .Option D: Ram 's horn sign is seen in gastric Crohn's disease .398

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings is seen in patients with ulcerative colitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Pseudopolyps are seen in ulcerative colitis. They are formed due to alternating inflammation and regeneration of the ulcerated mucosal epithelium in ulcerative colitis . Other gross findings in ulcerative colitis include : • Continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon most commonly involving the rectum • Fine mucosal granularity • Collar button ulcers • Pseudopolyps . Rose thorn appearance , skip lesions , and pseudodiverticula are features of Crohn's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 37-year-old man was referred to medical gastroenterology with complaints of chronic bloody diarrhea. Examination revealed blood on rectal examination. A colonoscopy was done as shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: In the above scenario, colonoscopy shows continuous involvement of erythematous rectosigmoid mucosa and has a fine granular surface resembling sandpaper . This along with the clinical features is suggestive of ulcerative colitis. The image below shows a gross specimen of the colon with diffuse involvement of mucosa and ulcers (without skip lesions ) in ulcerative colitis .The image below shows a gross specimen of jejunum showing the cobblestone appearance as seen in Crohn's disease .399

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following complications is unlikely to occur in a patient with ulcerative colitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Fistula is not a complication of ulcerative colitis . It is seen in Crohn's disease . Hemorrhage, malignant change, and toxic megacolon are complications of ulcerative colitis . Note : Stricture formation may be a complication of ulcerative colitis , but it is seen only in 5-10% of patients . They are more commonly seen in Crohn's disease .400

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with the following lesion. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.a: Can occur years before the onset of bowel symptoms

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows pyoderma gangrenosum. It is very difficult to treat and often requires IV antibiotics and IV glucocorticoids . Other drugs used in its management include dapsone , cyclosporine , and infliximab. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a dermatological extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease . It begins as a pustule and progresses to an ulcer with necrotic tissue and exudates . It may occur years before the onset of bowel symptoms and is usually associated with severe disease . Lesions are commonly found on the dorsal surface of the feet and legs but may occur on the arms, chest , and even the face . It responds poorly to colectomy and may even develop years after the surgery. Other dermatological manifestations associated with IBD include : • Erythema nodosum • Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis ) • Perianal skin tags • Psoriasis • Metastatic Crohn's disease (cutaneous granulomas).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 37-year-old man presented with hematuria and dysuria for 5 days. He also complains of chronic diarrhea and weight loss for 6 months. His urine microscopy revealed the following stones . What is the most likely disorder associated with this finding?
mcqs.explanation: The given urinary crystal is the bipyramidal or envelope -shaped crystals of calcium oxalate dihydrate . Calcium oxalate stones are more commonly associated with Crohn's disease . In Crohn's disease (especially post small bowel resection ), fatty acids are not absorbed because of ileal dysfunction. These fatty acids in the gut lumen bind to calcium. Because of this, the dietary oxalates which normally bind to the calcium are now left unbound. This leads to increased absorption of dietary oxalates leading to hyperoxaluria and oxalate stones . Note : Celiac disease is also associated with calcium oxalate stones .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Perianal examination of a patient revealed the following finding. Which condition is this associated with?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a large hemorrhoidal perianal skin tag. These are found in patients with Crohn's disease , especially those with colon involvement.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old man was brought to the casualty with a high fever and abdominal pain for the past 2 days. His history is significant for bloody diarrhea over the past few months. The abdominal radiograph of this patient is given below . Identify the condition.
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon . It is seen in severe ulcerative colitis .409 Abdominal radiography in toxic megacolon shows transverse or right colonic dilation >6 cm and loss of haustrations. Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension or features of sepsis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with ocular pain, photophobia , and blurred vision. Which among the following is the most likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: Uveitis is the most common cause of the given symptoms in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Uveitis is an ophthalmic manifestation of IBD . It is associated with both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease . It can develop during remission and is seen even after bowel resection . Prompt intervention with glucocorticoids is required to prevent scarring and visual impairment. The other common ophthalmic manifestations in IBD are conjunctivitis and episcleritis . Episcleritis , more common in Crohn's, is a benign disorder presenting with mild ocular burning.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man with Crohn's disease presents with red tender swellings on the lower leg as shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of erythema nodosum seen in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Erythema nodosum is a dermatologic manifestation of IBD . It is seen in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease . It manifests as tender erythematous nodules on the anterior surface of the lower legs , ankles, thighs , and arms. Option A: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a dermatological manifestation of IBD . It begins as pustular lesions which then ulcerate with necrotic foci and exudation .Option C: Sweet 's syndrome is acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis , seen in ulcerative colitis .410 Option D: Ecthyma gangrenosum is a skin infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, often seen in immunocompromised patients . It presents as pustules /vesicles which progress to necrotic ulcers .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What are the cardiopulmonary manifestations associated with inflammatory bowel disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The cardiopulmonary manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD ) are: • Endocarditis • Myocarditis • Pleuropericarditis • Interstitial lung disease411 Both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease have an increased risk of venous and arterial thrombosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 36-year-old man presents with worsening fatigue , jaundice , and pruritis for the last 3 months. Past history revealed recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea and weight loss over the past year. Lab investigations show raised ALP , GGT, and bilirubin, and an MRCP is done as shown below . Which of the following is most likely to be associated with his current presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario along with MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic narrowing with alternating areas of normal and dilated segments of bile ducts is suggestive of primary sclerosing cholangitis . PSC is more common in ulcerative colitis than in Crohn's disease . Additionally , recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea with weight loss seen in this patient also point toward a possible diagnosis of ulcerative colitis . Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD characterized by intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct inflammation/fibrosis. Around 50-75 % of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) have inflammatory bowel disease (IBD ) whereas , only 5% of IBD cases develop PSC. Option A: Chronic pancreatitis is associated with a chain of lakes appearance - dilated main duct with clubbing and dilatation of the side branches. Patients can present with steatorrhoea i.e., the passage of offensive -smelling large stools due to fat malabsorption. The image below shows chain of lakes appearance on MRI:Option B: Celiac disease may be associated with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), rather than primary sclerosing cholangitis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: After initiating treatment for patients with IBD , in which of the following extraintestinal manifestations would you expect to see an improvement?
mcqs.explanation: Arthritis worsens with exacerbation of bowel disease and improves with the treatment of bowel symptoms or surgery.412 Ankylosing spondylitis , uveitis, and pyoderma gangrenosum do not correlate with disease activity in the bowel. They may occur during the remission of disease or even after surgery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed with ulcerative colitis on endoscopy . He is hemodynamically stable but currently has 3-4 episodes of blood-tinged loose stools per day. Which of the following drug would you prefer for treating this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of mild ulcerative colitis . The preferred drug for mild ulcerative colitis (UC) is 5-ASA agents (5-aminosalicylic acid). Given below is the Truelove and Witts severity index for ulcerative colitis . Note : Mirikizumab ( an IL -23 inhibitor) was recently FDA approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . It reduces stool frequency, rectal bleeding and bowel urgency .Mild Moderate Severe Bowel movements < 4 per day 4 – 6 per day > 6 per day Blood in stool Small Moderate Severe Fever None < 37.5\272C > 37.5\272C Tachycardia None < 90 mean pulse >90 mean pulse Anemia Mild Hb > 75 % of normal Hb Hb < 75 % of normal Hb ESR < 30mm < 30mm > 30mm Endoscopic appear ance ErythemaDecreased vascul ar markingsFine granularit y Marked erythemaAbsent va scular markingsCoarse gra nularityContact bleedingNo ulcerations Spontaneous bleedingUlcer ationsTreatment of Ulcerative Colit is Mild Moderate Severe Induction 5-AS A 5-ASA + Oral steroids IV steroids + IV anti TNF alp ha + IV cyclosporine Maintainance 5-AS A 5-ASA + Azathioprine/6- MP Oral cyclosporine or inflixim ab

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 36-year-old man presented with complaints of 7-8 episodes of bloody diarrhea per day. He is pale and febrile. Heart rate is 110 bpm and ESR is 50mm. Colonoscopy revealed continuous mucosal involvement with ulcerations and mucosal hemorrhages. Which of the following drugs would you not prefer in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of severe ulcerative colitis . Mesalamine (5-ASA) is ineffective in the management of severe ulcerative colitis (UC). It is used in the treatment of mild-moderate UC. Given below is the Truelove and Witts severity index for ulcerative colitis . Note : Mirikizumab ( an IL -23 inhibitor) was recently FDA approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . It reduces stool frequency, rectal bleeding and bowel urgency .413 Mild Moderate Severe Bowel movements < 4 per day 4 – 6 per day > 6 per day Blood in stool Small Moderate Severe Fever None < 37.5\272C > 37.5\272C Tachycardia None < 90 mean pulse >90 mean pulse Anemia Mild Hb > 75 % of normal Hb Hb < 75 % of normal Hb ESR < 30mm < 30mm > 30mm Endoscopic appear ance ErythemaDecreased vascul ar markingsFine granularit y Marked erythemaAbsent va scular markingsCoarse gra nularityContact bleedingNo ulcerations Spontaneous bleedingUlcer ationsTreatment of Ulcerative Colit is Mild Moderate Severe Induction 5-AS A 5-ASA + Oral steroids IV steroids + IV anti TNF alp ha + IV cyclosporine Maintainance 5-AS A 5-ASA + Azathioprine/6- MP Oral cyclosporine or inflixim ab

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs have no role in the management of patients with ulcerative colitis?
mcqs.explanation: Metronidazole has no role in the management of ulcerative colitis . It is an antibiotic that is useful in active inflammatory, fistulous , and perianal Crohn's disease . Note : Mirikizumab ( an IL -23 inhibitor) was recently FDA approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . It reduces stool frequency, rectal bleeding and bowel urgency .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with Crohn's disease is started on infliximab. Which of the following conditions is the patient is at increased risk of developing?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with Crohn's disease on infliximab are at increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HS-TCL). Infliximab is the first biologic therapy approved for Crohn's disease . It is an IgG1 antibody against TNF-alpha. Drugs used in treatment of Crohn's disease : • Oral budesonide (mainly for mild to moderate ) • Oral prednisolone • Methotrexate • Anti TNF alpha414 • Azathioprine • 6-mercaptopurine • Monoclonal antibodies • Antibiotics Infliximab is also used in the treatment of moderate to severely active ulcerative colitis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Ustekinumab is effective in all of the following conditions except :
mcqs.explanation: Ustekinumab has no role in rheumatoid arthritis. It is effective against both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis . It can also be used in the management of plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. It is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody that blocks the activity of IL -12 and IL -23 . Biological therapy in inflammatory bowel disease : • Anti-TNF therapies : • Infliximab • Adalimumab • Certolizumab • Anti-integrins: • Natalizumab • Ustekinumab • Vedolizumab Note : Mirikizumab (an IL -23 inhibitor) was recently FDA approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . It reduces stool frequency, rectal bleeding and bowel urgency .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs has no role after induction of remission has been achieved in a patient with IBD ?
mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoids play no role in maintenance therapy in inflammatory bowel disease . They are used for induction in Crohn's disease and moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . Once clinical remission has been induced , they should be tapered gradually .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with IBD was brought to the ER with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back. His lab investigations revealed elevated serum amylase and lipase . He gives a history of being started on a new drug for maintenance therapy of his IBD 2 weeks back. The causative drug is most likely to be:
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of pancreatitis . Azathioprine causes pancreatitis in some patients within the first few weeks of therapy . It is completely reversible on discontinuing the drug.415 Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine (purine analogues ) also have an increased risk of toxicity as some individuals may lack the enzyme necessary for their metabolism . This may lead to hepatitis , bone marrow suppression , etc . Hence , the patient should be monitored regularly with blood counts and liver function tests .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is nutritional therapy in inflammatory bowel disease used for?
mcqs.explanation: Nutritional therapy is used for inducing remission in Crohn's disease . Dietary antigens may stimulate an immune response . Hence , nutritional therapies like total parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition (peptide -based preparations), etc . can be used to provide bowel rest in active Crohn's disease . These interventions cannot be used for maintaining remission. Ulcerative colitis does not respond to dietary intervention. Drugs used in treatment of Crohn's disease : • Oral budesonide (mainly for mild to moderate ) • Oral prednisolone • Methotrexate • Anti TNF alpha • Azathioprine • 6-mercaptopurine • Monoclonal antibodies • Antibiotics

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice in a patient with refractory ulcerative colitis ?

options.a: Mucosal proctectomy with ileal pouch –anal anastomosis

mcqs.explanation: The treatment of choice in refractory ulcerative colitis (UC) is mucosal proctectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA ). As ulcerative colitis is a mucosal disease , the rectal mucosa is dissected and removed down to the dentate line of the anus. The ileum is made into a pouch that serves as neorectum .416

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in patients with malabsorption syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Constipation is not a feature of malabsorption syndrome. Malabsorption syndrome refers to a spectrum of conditions of various etiologies that arises due to diminished absorption of one or more dietary nutrients. The general features of malabsorption syndrome are abdominal pain, diarrhea, steatorrhea , and weight loss. Anemia may be present when there is defective absorption of iron, folate , or vitamin B12 . Hypocalcemia and tetany can be seen due to defective absorption of vitamin D.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following tests is useful for the assessment of intestinal mucosal function in a patient presenting with symptoms of malabsorption?
mcqs.explanation: D-xylose test is useful for the assessment of intestinal mucosal function. D-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the intestinal mucosa without undergoing enzymatic digestion .426 The test is performed by administering 25g of D-xylose orally followed by the collection of urine 5h later. The test is considered abnormal (positive ) if urinary D-xylose is <4.5g . A positive D-xylose test indicates abnormal small intestinal mucosa.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The result of a D-xylose test showed urinary excretion of the monosaccharide at 3.6g after 5 hours. Which of the following can be a differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A urinary D-xylose <4.5g after 5 hours of oral D-xylose (abnormal ) can be seen in Crohn's disease . D-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the small intestinal mucosa without undergoing enzymatic digestion . An abnormal (positive ) D-xylose test indicates abnormal small intestinal mucosal absorption. A positive D-xylose test is seen in: • Celiac disease • Whipple 's disease • Tropical sprue • Short bowel syndrome • Crohn's disease The test is of limited clinical value today and mostly has been replaced by small intestinal biopsy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are likely to suffer from malabsorption?
mcqs.explanation: A small bowel diverticulum can result in malabsorption. A small bowel diverticulum is a blind pouch protruding from the small intestine that communicates with the lumen of the gut . It becomes a potential site for bacterial overgrowth which causes malabsorption. The growing gut bacteria depletes vitamin B12 and deconjugates bile acids leading to steatorrhea , diarrhea, and macrocytic anemia. Anterior colon resection , ulcerative colitis, and sigmoid volvulus affect the large intestine and therefore do not cause malabsorption.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of short bowel syndrome in adults ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of short bowel syndrome in adults is mesenteric vascular occlusion . Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorption disorder caused by a lack of functional small intestine . In adults , the common causes are : • Mesenteric vascular disease (e.g: mesenteric vascular occlusion .) • Primary mucosal and submucosal disease (e.g: Crohn's disease ) • Operations without any preexisting small-intestinal disease (e.g: after trauma)427 In children, necrotizing enterocolitis is the most common cause .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to have protein malabsorption?
mcqs.explanation: Homocystinuria is not a protein malabsorption disorder. It is a disorder of methionine metabolism that leads to increased homocysteine levels . Proteins are broken down by pancreatic enzymes and are absorbed as amino acids and peptides . So, protein malabsorption usually occurs only in pancreatic insufficiency . Additionally , there are three rare genetic disorders that lead to protein malabsorption. They are: • Enterokinase deficiency - Defective conversion of the proenzyme trypsinogen to trypsin. It is characterised by: • Diarrhoea • Growth retardation • Hypoproteinemia • Hartnup disease - Defective transport of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids. It is characterised by: • Pellagra-like rash • Neuropsychiatric symptoms • Cystinuria- Defective transport of cystine and other dibasic amino acids. It is characterised by: • Renal calculi • Chronic pancreatitis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A Schilling test was performed on a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency and the results are given below . What is the inference ?
mcqs.explanation: The above findings on Schilling test show reduced absorption of vitamin B12 irrespective of all interventions. This is suggestive of an ileal disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea . D-xylose test was normal and the Schilling test was abnormal . A duodenal biopsy was normal . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario describes a case of malabsorption syndrome (chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea), a normal xylose test and normal duodenal biopsy with abnormal schilling test points towards pancreatic insufficiency . A normal xylose test and normal duodenal biopsy rules out small intestinal pathologies like celiac disease (option A) and intestinal lymphangiectasia (option C), presence of steatorrhea rules out ulcerative colitis (option B) as it affects the large bowel which is not the main site of absorption of fat.428 Ileal disease is also characterized by normal xylose test , normal duodenal biopsy and steatorrhea and abnormal schilling test but among the given options the most appropriate answer would be pancreatic insufficiency due to chronic pancreatitis . Pancreatic insufficiency is characterised by the deficiency of exocrine pancreatic enzymes that result in maldigestion and malabsorption. The features in favor of the diagnosis: • Steatorrhea - a deficiency of pancreatic lipases can lead to undigested fat in stools . • D-xylose test - d-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the intestinal mucosa without undergoing any enzymatic action. Normal d-xylose test denotes intact mucosa. • Schilling test - it is abnormal as pancreatic enzymes are required for the absorption of vitamin B12 . Diagnosis of various malabsorption syndromes:Pathologies D xylose test Duodenal mucosal biopsy Schilling test Celiac disease Decreased Abnormal ; Short or absen t villi; epithelial cell dama ge ; crypts hypertrophy Normal Ileal disease Normal Normal Abnormal Chronic pancreatitis Normal Normal Abnormal ; normal after p ancreatic enzymes substit ution Intestinal lymphangiectasi a Normal Abnormal ; dilated lympha tics, clubbed villi Normal Bacterial overgrowth synd rome Normal or may be abn ormal Usually normal or can hav e diffuse non specific dam age to villi Usually abnormal ; normal after antibiotics administ ration

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An 11 -year-old boy presented with steatorrhea and chronic diarrhea. An evaluation revealed delayed intellectual development and ataxia. Acanthocytes were seen on the peripheral blood smear. Ophthalmological examination showed the following . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image showing retinitis pigmentosa and presence of acanthocytes along with the given clinical features is suggestive of abetalipoproteinemia. Abetalipoproteinemia is a rare genetic disorder in which there is defective chylomicron formation. Chylomicrons are required for the absorption and transport of fats and fat-soluble vitamins . It presents in early childhood with steatorrhoea and diarrhea, hypolipidemia , failure to thrive, ataxia, sensory and motor neuropathies.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The findings associated with abetalipoproteinemia are :
mcqs.explanation: Figure A shows vacuoles (unabsorbed fat) in the cytoplasm of the enterocytes . Figure B shows acanthocytes . These findings are associated with abetalipoproteinemia .429 Figure C shows distended macrophages in the lamina propria and periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive granules as seen in Whipple 's disease . Acanthocytes are abnormal red blood cells with spiked cell membranes due to thorn-like projections. Causes of acanthocytes in peripheral smear are: • Abetalipoproteinemia • Renal disease • Liver disease • Hemolytic anemia430

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All are true about the types of celiac disease except :

options.a: Latent type is associated with HLA DQ 2,
options.b: Atypical type has a negative serology
options.c: Silent type has a positive serology
options.d: Classic type presents with diarrhea and steatorrhea

mcqs.explanation: Atypical celiac disease has a positive serology with atypical symptoms . Serology in celiac disease refers to either anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (anti-tTG) or anti-endomysial antibodies . Note : Tropical sprue and celiac disease have similar clinical, endoscopic and histologic findings. A diagnosis of tropical sprue must be considered with a negative celiac serology .Type of celiac disease Serol ogy Features A Classic + Diarrhea, steatorrhea B Atypical + Iron deficiency anemia, osteo penia, ataxia, peripheral neur opathy , infertility C Silent + No features D Latent - HLA DQ 2,8

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease is dermatitis herpetiformis (DH). DH is characterized by intensely pruritic small papules and vesicles on the extensor surfaces of extremities , buttocks , and neck. It can be considered a celiac disease of the skin. Other extraintestinal manifestations of celiac disease are: • Anemia431 • Low bone density • Ataxia • Peripheral neuropathy • Infertility Celiac disease is often associated with other conditions such as type 1 diabetes mellitus , autoimmune thyroid disease , IgA deficiency, bird fancier's lung, and Down syndrome. The image below shows dermatitis herpetiformis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old girl presented with fatigue , chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, bone pain, and abdominal distension . Investigations revealed iron deficiency anemia and osteoporosis. Which of the following is the single best test to be done for her evaluation?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of fatigue , chronic diarrhea, weight loss and abdominal distention along with investigations showing features of malabsorption (iron deficiency ) lead to the diagnosis of celiac disease or gluten sensitive enteropathy . The single best test for which is checking serum for the presence of IgA tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG ) antibodies (Option D). Celiac disease is a disorder characterized by an immunological response to gluten causing damage to the proximal intestinal mucosa (villous atrophy) and malabsorption of nutrients. Symptoms usually begin 6 to 24 months from the introduction of gluten into diet , although most patients go undiagnosed . The common manifestations are - irritability , abdominal distention , chronic diarrhea, weight loss or muscle wasting and extra-intestinally , the symptoms observed are aphthous ulcers , delayed puberty , iron deficiency anemia and short stature . Screening for celiac disease is by testing for tissue transglutaminase IgA, endomysial , and deamidated antigliadin antibodies . IgA levels in serum are measured to detect false -negative results because of IgA deficiency . Small intestinal biopsy shows characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia , and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes .432 The treatment involves the exclusion of gluten -containing food from diet . Long term complications observed are osteoporosis , anemia, infertility and malignancy (enteropathy related -T cell lymphoma is the most common association) The Marsh classification is used to categorize celiac disease into different types and to quantify severity of disease involvement.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient who presented with severe malabsorption is found to be positive for IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies . What will be the next best step ?
mcqs.explanation: In this patient with positive serology , a biopsy should be done next, to confirm the diagnosis of celiac disease . Tissue transglutaminase Ab (tTG-IgA) is the best screening test . IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA) are most specific . But a small-intestinal biopsy is required to establish a diagnosis of celiac disease , before starting treatment.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presented with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea , and weight loss. IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies were found to be positive . Duodenal biopsy revealed the following . Which of the following complications would you not expect in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario along with the presence of IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies and biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia , lamina propria infiltrates indicate a case of celiac disease . Pancreatic insufficiency is not a complication of celiac disease . The complications of celiac disease are: • Intestinal lymphomas • Intestinal ulcers - also known as ulcerative jejunoileitis • Collagenous sprue - development of a subepithelial collagen layer

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old lady with celiac disease is recommended a gluten -free diet . Which among the following can she consume ?
mcqs.explanation: Rice can be consumed on a gluten -free diet . The primary management of celiac disease is avoiding gluten in the diet .Diet avoided (gluten )"BRO W" Diet Allowed "So M RP" Barley Soya bean Rye Maize Oats Rice Wheat Potato433

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: When will you diagnose a patient with refractory celiac disease ?

options.a: No remission of disease despite gluten free diet
options.d: Development of a subepithelial collagen layer

mcqs.explanation: Refractory celiac disease is diagnosed when there is no remission of disease despite a strict gluten -free diet for 6-12 months. Patients are symptomatic and have persistent small intestinal villous atrophy on biopsy . They respond well to steroids .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Match the following disorders with their respective sites of involvement:
mcqs.explanation: The sites involved in the given malabsorption syndromes are as follows :Disorder Site of involvement Celiac disease Proximal small intestine Whipple 's disea se Proximal > Distal small intes tine Tropical sprue Whole small intestine (panint estine )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All are true about Whipple 's disease except :

options.a: Caused by gram positive organism Tropheryma whipplei
options.b: Culture of organism from biopsy specimen helps in early diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Tropheryma whipplei is difficult to culture from the biopsy specimen . Hence , it cannot be used for the early diagnosis of Whipple 's disease. Whipple 's disease is a chronic multisystem disorder caused by the gram-positive bacteria Tropheryma whipplei . It primarily causes malabsorption along with central nervous system & cardiac problems . It mostly affects men and presents with fever, diarrhea weight loss, and arthralgia. The diagnosis of Whipple 's disease is made through a biopsy which shows the presence of PAS-positive macrophages in the small intestine and other organs with evidence of disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple 's disease is progressive dementia . Other important CNS manifestations in Whipple 's disease are: • Personality and mood changes • Progressive supranuclear ophthalmoplegia • Focal neurologic presentations434 • Oculomasticatory myorrhythmia - an unusual combination of rhythmic eye and jaw movements which is pathognomonic of Whipple 's disease . Whipple 's disease associated with CNS symptoms has a poor prognosis. Note : Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with neuroblastoma.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cardiovascular presentation seen in patients with Whipple 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cardiovascular presentation in Whipple 's disease is culture -negative endocarditis. Other cardiovascular findings include : • Congestive heart failure • Pericarditis • Myocarditis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man presented with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and joint pains. A duodenal biopsy was done. Which of the following drug is used in the maintenance phase of treatment of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages present in the lamina propria. This along with the given features suggests Whipple 's disease . Cotrimoxazole is used in the maintenance phase of the treatment of Whipple 's disease . Treatment of Whipple 's disease : • Induction phase - ceftriaxone or meropenem or penicillin G + streptomycin - 2 weeks • Maintenance phase - trimethoprim / sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) for 1 year. It has high CNS penetration so it is used in maintenance to prevent relapse .435

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man presented with diarrhea, floating stools , and weight loss for 3 months. Celiac serology was negative . Biopsy of the small intestinal mucosa revealed villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia with normal mucosal thickness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The history of malabsorptive symptoms , a negative celiac serology , and the biopsy findings are suggestive of tropical sprue . Improvement in symptoms after folic acid intake is a hallmark of tropical sprue . Tropical sprue is an acquired malabsorptive condition of probable infectious aetiology . It is seen in people from the tropics such as India, Southeast Asia and South America. Tropical sprue and celiac disease have similar clinical, endoscopic and histologic findings. However, a positive celiac serology (anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies ) can be used to rule out tropical sprue .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following would you prescribe for a patient with tropical sprue ?
mcqs.explanation: The treatment of tropical sprue is tetracycline + folic acid. Because of marked folate deficiency , folic acid is most often given together with broad spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 months.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drug is used for the management of a patient with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth?
mcqs.explanation: Rifaximin is the preferred drug for the management of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). The antibiotics are given for around 3 weeks . The other drugs that can be used are : • Tetracyclines • Cephalosporins • Metronidazole • Amoxicillin-Clavulanic acid Rifaximin is the antibiotic used in hepatic encephalopathy to lower blood ammonia levels .436

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An upper GI endoscopy is performed in a patient with dyspeptic symptoms . It shows the presence of thickened gastric folds . Which of the following differential diagnoses would you not consider in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Pancreatic rests are not a differential diagnosis for hypertrophied gastric folds . These usually present as a single lump in the stomach and are formed by ectopic pancreatic tissue .441 Thickened gastric folds can represent a local malignant process , inflammatory process , or hormonal response . The differential diagnoses of large gastric folds include : • Menetrier 's disease • Zollinger–Ellison syndrome - hypergastrinemia leads to parietal cell hyperplasia and prominent folds • Malignancy- lymphoma, infiltrating gastric cancer • Infections- histoplasmosis , tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which part of the stomach is usually spared in Menetrier 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The antrum is usually spared in Menetrier 's disease . Foveolar hyperplasia results in the development of large rugal folds in the body and fundus of the stomach, sparing the antrum. These hypertrophied rugal folds give a cobblestone or cerebriform appearance to the gastric mucosa. The image given below shows the endoscopic appearance of Menetrier 's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old man presented with a history of diarrhea for 5 months, occasional abdominal pain, and weight loss. Upper GI endoscopy showed the following finding. Which of the following is least likely to occur in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario and endoscopy image showing large, rugal gastric folds are suggestive of Menetrier's disease . Among the given options, hematemesis is least likely to occur in this patient . Large, gastric rugal folds in Menetrier 's disease occur due to massive overgrowth of mucous cells (foveolar cells ) lining the stomach. Patients usually present with epigastric pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia, peripheral edema, and weight loss. Occult gastrointestinal bleeding may occur, but overt bleeding is unusual . If overt bleeding is seen , it is usually due to superficial mucosal erosions.442 They develop protein-losing gastropathy , leading to hypoproteinemia as a result of increased secretion of gastric mucus. There is also a decrease in the number of parietal cells which leads to decreased acid secretion (hypochlorhydria) in the stomach. They are at an increased risk of developing gastric carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old child with vomiting, abdominal pain, weight loss, and peripheral edema underwent an upper GI biopsy . Histology showed foveolar hyperplasia and glandular atrophy within the gastric mucosa. Which of the following is most commonly associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of Menetrier 's disease . In children, it occurs commonly due to the infection by cytomegalovirus . The histopathological features of Menetrier 's disease include : • Foveolar hyperplasia - hyperplasia of surface and glandular mucosa • Reduction in oxyntic glands, parietal cells , and chief cells • Dilated , tortuous gastric glands • Elongation of pits of gastric glands • Eosinophilic infiltration in lamina propria The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of Menetrier 's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Overexpression of which of the following causes Menetrier 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Overexpression of TGF-\030 (transforming growth factor-alpha) causes Menetrier 's disease . This overexpression results in overstimulation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway and increased proliferation of mucous cells , resulting in mucous cell (foveolar) hyperplasia .443

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 24-year old woman underwent extensive workup for unexplained weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea. She was suspected to have Menetrier 's disease . Which of the following investigations will confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Menetrier 's disease is confirmed by endoscopic full -thickness biopsy . A full -thickness biopsy allows for the visualization of the cells on the surface as well as the pits of the gastric glands. The histopathological specimen shows the following features : • Foveolar hyperplasia - hyperplasia of surface and glandular mucosa • Reduction in oxyntic glands, parietal cells , and chief cells • Dilated , tortuous gastric glands • Elongation of pits of gastric glands • Eosinophilic infiltration in lamina propria A punch biopsy can only sample the surface of the gastric gland and hence is not preferred . The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of Menetrier 's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man presented with a history of dyspepsia . He has been taking pantoprazole for the last few months, however, his symptoms persisted . Upper GI endoscopy was done, and a full -thickness gastric biopsy was taken. The histopathological appearance is shown below . What is the treatment of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the image showing foveolar hyperplasia are suggestive of Menetrier's disease . The treatment of choice is cetuximab . Increased epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling has been implicated in the pathogenesis of Menetrier 's disease . Cetuximab is an EGFR inhibitor, and blocks this signaling pathway and helps in the improvement of the symptoms . Therefore, it is the first line of treatment . Medical therapy with proton pump inhibitors (lansoprazole) and somatostatin analogues (octreotide ) may also be tried to manage symptoms . If the patient continues to have protein loss despite medical therapy , then total gastrectomy is indicated . The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of Menetrier 's disease .444

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common site for a MALToma ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site for mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT ) lymphoma or MALToma is the stomach. MALToma is a type of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma that most commonly occurs in the stomach and to a lesser extent in the salivary glands, lungs , small intestine , etc . It occurs as a result of the malignant proliferation of B cells in the marginal zone of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT ).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about MALTomas ?

options.b: History of chronic gastritis usually seen

mcqs.explanation: MALToma arises from B lymphocytes present in the marginal zone of the lymphoid tissue . The majority of the cases of MALToma are associated with H. pylori induced chronic gastritis. This infection results in an increased proliferation of lymphocytes in the mucosa of the stomach causing MALToma . It is initially low grade and if the infection is not treated , it later progresses to high grade. The patients usually present with non-specific symptoms like epigastric pain and discomfort. It is usually diagnosed in patients around 60 years of age . It is also associated with autoimmune diseases like Sjogren's syndrome and Hashimoto's thyroiditis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old woman underwent an endoscopic biopsy of a gastric tumor. The biopsy shows dense lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions in the gastric glands. Which of the following investigations will confirm your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and lymphoepithelial lesions seen in the gastric glands is suggestive of MALToma . The diagnosis is confirmed by immunophenotyping .445 Histopathological examination of a MALToma shows the presence of lymphoepithelial lesions. These are caused due to the invasion of gastric glands and crypts by the neoplastic lymphocytes . These lymphocytes are positive for CD19, CD20 and negative for CD5 and CD10. Biopsy or aspiration of the bone marrow is also done to see the bone marrow involvement. Radiological investigations like CT scans, MRIs, and PET scans are useful in identifying the extent of the tumor and infiltration of the tumor to the adjacent organs. Note : Cytogenetic testing will be helpful in identifying chromosomal abnormalities. The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of a MALToma .The below image shows a sample of a MALToma showing positive immunophenotyping for CD20 .446

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Immunophenotyping from a gastric tumor in an elderly man showed the following findings. The tumor was found to be limited to the gastric mucosa. What is the treatment of choice?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of a low-grade gastric MALToma . The treatment of choice for this condition is H. pylori eradication therapy which can be done with the OCM regimen (omeprazole , clarithromycin and metronidazole ). Immunophenotyping in MALTomas shows positive staining for CD19 and CD20 which is suggestive of a B-cell neoplasm . Negative staining for CD5 and CD10 is seen , suggesting it arises from the marginal zone of lymphoid tissues . Chronic infection with H. pylori leads to the development of MALTomas . When these lesions are limited to the mucosa, treatment of the infection alone is sufficient to cause regression of the tumour. In high-grade tumors or the tumors which invade into the adjacent or distant organs, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are required to treat the tumor. Radiotherapy is usually three -dimensional conformal radiotherapy. The chemotherapeutic agents used in the treatment of MALToma are rituximab, cyclophosphamide , fludarabine, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone . Radical gastrectomy has a limited role and is done when the disease is confined to the stomach.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old smoker presents with postprandial abdominal pain and diarrhea for the past 1 year. On examination, she is malnourished, and a bruit is heard in the epigastrium . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of chronic mesenteric ischemia. Chronic mesenteric ischemia occurs due to atherosclerosis of the celiac or mesenteric arteries. It is common in older women, and they usually have a history of smoking, coronary artery disease , cerebrovascular disease , or peripheral artery disease . The important clinical features of chronic mesenteric ischemia are:447 • Postprandial abdominal pain occurs as a result of a mismatch between the increased demand and decreased blood flow to the intestine. This is called intestinal angina • Weight loss- patients avoid eating due to postprandial pain and this leads to significant weight loss • Diarrhea- occurs as a result of decreased absorption • Physical examination may reveal epigastric bruit in almost half of the patients . The gold standard investigation to diagnose the blockade is mesenteric angiography. Once the disease is confirmed, the patients have to be started with antiplatelets and mesenteric angioplasty and stenting should be performed . Option A: Acute mesenteric ischemia present with acute abdomen, bloody diarrhea and nausea. Angiography will show occlusion of superior mesenteric artery. Option C: Wilkie's syndrome occurs due to compression of the third portion of the duodenum by the superior mesenteric artery. It can present similarly, however is associated with vomiting and rapid weight loss. It usually occurs in young, asthenic women. Option D: Nutcracker syndrome occurs due to compression of the left renal vein, between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. It presents with varicoceles and hematuria.448

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of large vessel vasculitis?
mcqs.explanation: Takayasu disease is an example of large vessel vasculitis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Biopsy performed on a patient with suspected vasculitis showed the presence of granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Churg-Strauss syndrome is the most likely diagnosis as it is a granulomatous vasculitis. The vasculitis can be classified as:Granulomatous vasculitis Non-granulomatous vasculiti s Giant cell arteritisTakayasu a rteritisGranulomatosis with p olyangiitisChurg -Strauss syn drome Polyarteritis nodosaKawasaki diseaseBehcet 's diseaseMicr oscopic polyangiitisHenoch -S chonlein purpura454

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man presented with complaints of fever, malaise, and weight loss. His lab investigations showed mild anemia, elevated ESR, and serology was positive for cANCA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) is the most likely diagnosis as it is associated with cANCA.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about giant cell arteritis?

options.b: May lead to ischemic optic neuropathy

mcqs.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is common in older women (>50 years of age ). Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of the large vessels , commonly seen in females over 50 years of age . It usually involves the temporal artery. It is characterized by fever, anemia, and headache . Depending on the artery involved, the patient may have tenderness over the affected artery, scalp pain, tongue and jaw claudication . Untreated patients may develop ischemic optic neuropathy . Laboratory investigations reveal elevated ESR and normochromic normocytic anemia. It shows good response to glucocorticoid therapy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old woman came with complaints of headache for the past 1-month. She also reported aching of the jaw during her meals. Over the last week , she has experienced episodes of painless visual loss which lasted for around 10 minutes . Which of the following is the best investigation for the diagnosis of her condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation of headache , jaw claudication , and painless visual loss is suggestive of giant cell arteritis. The best investigation for the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis is temporal artery biopsy . Histopathology shows panarteritis with the presence of mononuclear cells and giant cells . The biopsy may not be positive in all patients due to patchy histologic findings. Since involvement of the vessel may be segmental , positive yield is increased by obtaining a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens . Note : According to the 21st edition of Harrison 's Medicine , as involvement of the vessel may be segmental , getting a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens would help to increase a positive yield . And Robbin's 10th edition mentions that an adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman presents to your OPD with complaints of pain and stiffness of the shoulders which is worse in the morning . She works as a bus conductor and tells you that she has difficulty raising her shoulders to ring the bell . On examination, there is diffuse tenderness over the shoulders . Which of the following vasculitis is closely associated with her presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation of painful, tender , and stiff shoulders with restricted movement points toward a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica, which is closely associated with giant cell arteritis. Polymyalgia rheumatica is characterized by pain and stiffness (worst in the morning ) in the muscles of the neck, shoulder , back, hips, and thigh. On examination, diffuse tenderness is present without localization to any specific structures . Pain restricts the active range of motion but passive range of motion and muscle strength are normal .455 ESR and CRP are typically elevated in polymyalgia rheumatica whereas creatine phosphokinase (CPK) lies within the normal range. It shows a good response to prednisone therapy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe right-sided throbbing headache . She also gives history of pain and stiffness of the shoulders and hips. Her lab values show an ESR of 80 mm/hr. What is the next best step in her management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation of headache and symptoms suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica with raised ESR points towards a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis (GCA), for which the next best step is initiation of steroids (prednisone ). Although temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic investigation for GCA, it should not delay the initiation of steroids as it helps in reducing symptoms and preventing visual loss. The biopsy findings usually remain positive for at least 1 month after initiation of steroids . Newer drugs used in the treatment of giant cell arteritis are tocilizumab (anti-IL -6 receptor ) and abatacept (CTLA4 -Ig).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which is the most common artery involved in Takayasu arteritis?
mcqs.explanation: The most common artery involved in Takayasu arteritis is the subclavian artery. Patients present with pain, claudication, and weakness of the affected limb. The arterial pulse in the affected limb may be weak or absent. The order of arteries affected in Takayasu arteritis is subclavian artery > common carotid artery > abdominal aorta > renal artery > aortic arch = vertebral > coeliac axis > iliac > pulmonary > coronary artery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman presents to the hospital with fever, malaise, and arthralgia for a duration of 1 month. She also complains of pain, numbness, and weakness in her right arm , which has been increasing over the past 1 week . Clinical examination reveals weak radial pulses , and her laboratory investigations show elevated ESR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical features with a marked weakening of pulse in the upper extremities and laboratory findings of elevated ESR are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis. It is also known as pulseless disease . Takayasu arteritis is a systemic disease and may present with generalized and vascular symptoms . It commonly affects adolescents or young females . Generalized symptoms like fever, night sweats , weight loss, malaise, arthralgias, and anorexia may occur long before vascular symptoms . Vascular symptoms depend on the vessel involved: • Arch of the aorta and its branches: • Subclavian artery (most commonly affected ) - It leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities . Hence , it is also known as pulseless disease . It may also lead to Raynaud's phenomenon . • Carotid arteries- It leads to weak pulses , blindness , and neurological deficits . • Aortic arch- It may lead to congestiv e heart failure.456 • Abdominal aorta, celiac axis, and superior mesenteric artery - leads to abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting • Iliac vessels - leads to claudication of the legs • Renal arteries - leads to systemic hypertension • Pulmonary artery - leads to pulmonary hypertension • Coronary arteries (least commonly affected ) - lead to myocardial infarction Investigations: • Laboratory tests reveal an elevated ESR level , anemia, and elevated immunoglobulin levels . • Arteriography is done as a confirmatory test . Treatment includes glucocorticoid therapy, methotrexate , immunotherapy with anti-TNF agents , and surgery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with suspected Behcet 's disease which of the following tests can be used to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Pathergy test can be used for confirming Behcet 's disease . It is a nonspecific inflammatory skin reaction to scratch or intradermal saline injection and is a specific manifestation. The diagnostic criteria in Behcet 's syndrome are the presence of recurrent oral ulcerations plus two of the following findings: • Recurrent genital ulcerations • Ocular lesions • Skin lesions • Positive pathergy test Option A: Foshay test is used in cat-scratch disease . Option B: Tzanck test is used to diagnose herpes infection . Option D: The cardiolipin antibody test is used to detect antiphospholipid antibodies .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old woman presented with recurrent oral and genital ulcerations . An inflammatory skin reaction was observed after intradermal administration of normal saline. Which of the following statements is incorrect about her condition?

options.b: Associated with painless scarring oral ulcers

mcqs.explanation: Recurrent oral and genital ulcerations with a positive pathergy test are suggestive of Behcet 's syndrome. It is associated with oral ulcers that are painful and heal without scarring. Behcet 's syndrome usually affects young individuals and is associated with HLA -B51 and anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies . The clinical features of Behcet 's syndrome include : • Oral ulcers - painful, non-scarring • Genital ulcers - painful, scarring • Ocular involvement - scarring and bilateral panuveitis457 • Skin involvement - folliculitis , acne-like rashes, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum • Arthritis and peripheral vein thrombosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a medium vessel vasculitis?
mcqs.explanation: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a medium vessel vasculitis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old man presented to the hospital with the findings shown in the image below . He also complained of pain in the upper and lower limbs. On examination, his BP was 160/100 mmHg and his peripheral pulses were palpable . Serology was negative for ANCA. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most probable diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa. The image shows the gangrene of the fingers. The presence of myalgia, the involvement of cutaneous vessels (gangrene with palpable peripheral pulses ), renal vessels causing hypertension and serology negative for ANCA make polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) the most probable diagnosis. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is necrotizing arteritis of the medium-sized blood vessels . It can affect the skin, peripheral nerves, renal vessels , mesenteric vessels , heart, and brain . Lungs are usually spared in PAN. The disease initially starts with non-specific symptoms like fever, malaise, arthralgia, and myalgia. Later, depending on the artery involved , patients may develop the following symptoms : • Skin findings - ulcers , digital gangrene, and livedo reticularis • Renal arteries - hypertension and renal failure • Mesenteric arteries - abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, bleeding , and a bowel perforation Other options : 1) Takayasu arteritis- It is a large vessel vasculitis. Also known as pulseless disease as it may be associated with weak upper extremity pulses . 2) Microscopic polyangiitis - It is a small vessel vasculitis. It is positive for p-ANCA. Presentation is similar to granulomatosis with polyangiitis but without upper airway involvement. 3) Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis- It is frequently associated with hepatitis C. Circulating cryoglubulins and rheumatoid factor can be found in blood. Most common clinical manifestations are cutaneous vasculitis, peripheral neuropathy , glomerulonephritis and arthritis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient diagnosed with polyarteritis nodosa which of the following arteries are characteristically spared ?
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary arteries are characteristically spared in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN). PAN mainly involves renal and visceral arteries. Histopathology of the involved arteries usually shows the following findings: • Transmural necrotizing vasculitis of the arteries and adjacent veins. Venules are spared . • Renal arteries - arteritis without glomerulonephritis458 • Fibrinoid necrosis • Absence of granuloma and eosinophilia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about polyarteritis nodosa?
mcqs.explanation: One-third of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) cases are associated with Hepatitis B. Other options : Option A: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic vasculitis which is associated with necrotizing inflammation of small and medium-sized muscular arteries. Option B: Patients show hypergammaglobulinemia . Option C: PAN is rarely associated with ANCA positivity . There is no serological test for PAN. Most patients exhibit an elevated leukocyte count with a predominance of neutrophils . PAN is usually seen in young adults , characterized by rapidly accelerating hypertension , abdominal pain, bloody stools , myalgias, and peripheral neuropathy . Arterial inflammation is segmental , necrotizing, and transmural , leading to aneurysms and thrombosis. The involved vessels are typically found at arterial bifurcations, spreading to veins but sparing venules . The most commonly affected organs are the kidney, heart, liver, and gastrointestinal tract, in that order. Pulmonary arteries are not involved. Inadequate blood flow leads to ischemia, ulcers , infarcts, atrophy, or hemorrhage. Diagnosis relies on histopathological findings from organ biopsies or the demonstration of aneurysms in small to medium-sized arteries of the renal, hepatic , and visceral vasculature. Untreated PAN has an extremely poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of only 10 to 20 %. Common causes of death include gastrointestinal complications , such as bowel infarcts and perforation, as well as cardiovascular issues . Timely treatment is vital for improved outcomes . Combining prednisone and cyclophosphamide has shown significant benefits in survival rates. Glucocorticoids alone may be sufficient for milder cases . In PAN cases associated with hepatitis B or C, antiviral therapy is combined with glucocorticoids and plasma exchange . Managing hypertension effectively can help reduce vascular complications . Despite successful treatment , relapses occur in approximately 10 -20 % of patients . A histopathological image of PAN showing necrotizing transmural inflammation is given below :459 The image below shows aneurysms in renal vasculature:

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of vasculitis in children in India?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of vasculitis in children in India is Kawasaki disease . Kawasaki disease has a higher incidence in children in the Indian subcontinent . The most common vasculitis worldwide is Henoch-Schonlein purpura, whereas in the Indian subcontinent and other Asian countries the most common vasculitis is Kawasaki disease .460

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings would you not expect in a patient diagnosed with small-vessel vasculitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Ischemic optic neuropathy associated with giant cell arteritis (large vessel vasculitis) can present as visual loss. Small vessel vasculitis is the inflammation of arterioles , capillaries , or venules . It starts with nonspecific symptoms like fever, fatigue, and arthralgia. Since it mainly affects the small vessels and capillaries present in the lungs , kidney, and skin, the majority of the patients will have: • Hemoptysis • Glomerulonephritis (hematuria, proteinuria) • Palpable purpura

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following structures is most commonly involved in cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The structure most commonly involved in cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis is postcapillary venules . Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis is defined as vasculitis which is limited to the small vessels of the skin. There is no systemic vasculitis and glomerulonephritis . It most commonly affects postcapillary venules . It is characterized by the presence of leukocytoclasis (presence of neutrophil debris in and around the blood vessels ).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with cutaneous vasculitis, glomerulonephritis , and peripheral neuropathy . Which investigation should be performed next to help you diagnose the condition?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of cutaneous vasculitis, glomerulonephritis , and peripheral neuropathy are suggestive of small-vessel vasculitis. Investigating for ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies ) should be the next step to aid in diagnosis. Characterized bynecrotizing v asculitiswithglomerulonephri tis(pauci immune, crescentic ) Characterized byasthma,peri pheral and tissue eosinophili a,extravascular granulomafor mation, andvasculitisof multi ple organs. mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which is the most common form of vasculitis associated with connective tissue disorders?
mcqs.explanation: The most common form of vasculitis associated with connective tissue disorders is small-vessel venulitis . Connective tissue disorders that can cause vasculitis are: • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Rheumatoid arthritis • Relapsing polychondritis • Sj\366gren's syndrome

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A pathology resident is examining biopsy specimens of patients with clinical features of vasculitis . In which of the following conditions would he report granulomatous inflammation of the vessels ?
mcqs.explanation: Biopsy findings of giant cell arteritis, Churg-Strauss syndrome, and Takayasu arteritis show granulomatous inflammation of vessels as they are granulomatous vasculitis. The vasculitis diseases can be classified as:Granulomatous vasculitis Non-granulomatous vasculiti s Giant cell arteritisTakayasu a rteritisGranulomatosis with p olyangiitisChurg -Strauss syn drome Polyarteritis nodosaKawasaki diseaseBehcet 's diseaseMicr oscopic polyangiitisHenoch -S chonlein purpura

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain over the forehead aggravated on bending and occasional hemoptysis . Laboratory investigations reveal elevated ESR and red cell casts in the urine. Her serology is positive for cANCA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 467 The given clinical scenario with cANCA positivity is suggestive of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener 's granulomatosis). It is characterized by the involvement of the upper respiratory tract (sinusitis), lower respiratory tract (occasional hemoptysis ), and kidneys (red cell casts). It is a granulomatous, necrotizing vasculitis of the small vessels that mainly affects : • Upper respiratory tract- presenting with sinusitis, otitis media, and nasal septal perforation. • Lower respiratory tract- presenting with hemoptysis . • Kidney (glomerulonephritis )- presenting with proteinuria, hematuria, and hypertension . Apart from these organs, the disease can also affect the eye and skin. Skin lesions present as palpable purpura or subcutaneous nodules . Laboratory investigations show anemia, leucocytosis , elevated ESR, and ANCA positivity . Options A and C: In Goodpasture 's syndrome and microscopic polyangiitis , the symptoms of upper respiratory tract involvement are very rare. Option D: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is commonly seen in children. It presents with palpable purpura, joint pain, abdominal pain, and glomerulonephritis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient who presented with skin rashes, otitis media and hematuria has been diagnosed with granulomatosis with polyangiitis . Which of the following drugs would you not use in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Abatacept is a disease -modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Important drugs used in the management of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) are: • Cyclophosphamide • Rituximab (anti CD20 antibody) • Glucocorticoids • Methotrexate

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presents with hemoptysis , proteinuria, and the clinical presentation given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario showing saddle nose deformity along with hemoptysis , and proteinuria is suggestive of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis). Involvement of upper respiratory tract in granulomatosis with polyangiitis manifests as: • Paranasal sinusitis, serous otitis media • Nasal ulcers , purulent or bloody nasal discharge • Nasal perforation leading to the destruction of septum and saddle nose deformity • Subglottic tracheal stenosis468

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature associated with Wegener 's granulomatosis?
mcqs.explanation: Wegener 's granulomatosis is associated with necrotizing vasculitis. Wegener 's granulomatosis predominantly affects the small blood vessels of the upper respiratory tract, lungs , and kidneys. Lung involvement will show multiple , bilateral cavitating nodules and pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray. The radiograph below shows cavitating nodules in a patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener 's granulomatosis).Renal involvement initially appears as focal or segmental glomerulonephritis on biopsy . If left untreated , it can lead to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). Patients with Wegener 's granulomatosis have an increased incidence of venous thrombosis, like deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis on biopsy . This finding is commonly seen in the tissues obtained from lungs , skin, upper airways, and rarely kidneys.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old man presented with complaints of fever, weight loss, and hemoptysis . His serology was positive for pANCA and biopsy showed small vessel vasculitis with neutrophil infiltration. Which of the following is a feature associated with his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation along with pANCA positivity and biopsy findings of leukocytoclastic (neutrophil infiltration) vasculitis point towards a diagnosis of microscopic polyangiitis . It is associated with fibrinoid necrosis. Microscopic polyangiitis , also known as hypersensitivity vasculitis, causes segmental fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles and venules . It is associated with neutrophil infiltration, and hence also called leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Histopathology of the affected tissue will show necrotizing vasculitis of arterioles, venules , and capillaries without any granulomas. It is caused by ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies ) and is not mediated by the immune complex . It primarily affects the kidneys and lungs .469

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features is not useful to distinguish between microscopic polyangiitis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Both microscopic polyangiitis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis are associated with necrotizing vasculitis. Hence , this feature is not useful to distinguish between them.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A triad of skin lesions , asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex and eosinophilia is seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: A triad of skin lesions , asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex , and eosinophilia is seen in Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis ). It is a necrotizing vasculitis of the small-to-medium-sized vessels and in order to be diagnosed with Churg-Strauss, a patient should have evidence of asthma, peripheral blood and tissue eosinophilia (>1000 cells /�ML), extravascular granuloma formation and clinical features consistent with vasculitis. Common presenting symptoms of this condition are lower respiratory tract symptoms such as severe attacks of asthma, upper respiratory tract symptoms such as allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and nasal polyps , mono neuritis multiplex (a type of peripheral neuropathy affecting at least two nerves) which presents with a complaint of pain, numbness, or weakness in the affected areas and skin lesions like palpable purpura and subcutaneous nodules . Renal involvement is less common and less severe than other small vessel vasculitis. P-ANCA antibodies are present in Churg Strauss syndrome. • Severe attacks of asthma • Mononeuritis multiplex : a type of peripheral neuropathy affecting at least two nerves. Patients will complain of pain, numbness, or weakness in the affected areas. • Skin lesions like palpable purpura and subcutaneous nodules . Glucocorticoids show effective responses in these patients . Other drugs that have been tried are mepolizumab and rituximab. For fulminant multisystem disease , daily cyclophosphamide with prednisolone followed by azathioprine or methotrexate is used . Option A: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy , and glomerulonephritis . It is most commonly associated with Hepatitis C. Option B: Polyarteritis nodosa can also present with mononeuritis multiplex and skin lesions , but they do not have eosinophilia , it has predominant neutrophilia . Option D: Giant cell arteritis manifests with the cardinal symptom of headache localized to the temporal region. Common symptoms include headache , polymyalgia rheumatica , jaw claudication , fever, and decrease in body weight . Laboratory results show increased ESR, CRP levels , normochromic or mildly hypo chromic anemia.470

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old housewife presented with recurrent attacks of asthma and pain and numbness along the distribution of the median and ulnar nerve. Her serology was positive for pANCA. Further evaluation is unlikely to reveal which of the following findings?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of asthma, mononeuritis multiplex , and pANCA positivity is suggestive of Churg-Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis ). It affects small to medium-sized arteries. Laboratory investigations will show peripheral blood eosinophilia . Some patients may be positive for pANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies ). Histopathology will show the presence of necrotizing vasculitis, tissue eosinophilia, and extravascular granulomas. Histopathology of ANCA associated vasculitides can be remembered as: • Microscopic polyangiitis : necrotizing vasculitis • Wegener 's granulomatosis: necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas • Churg Strauss syndrome: necrotizing vasculitis with extravascular granulomas and eosinophilia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the ER with colicky abdominal pain. His mother tells you that he refuses to walk due to knee pain. On examination, palpable purpura is noted . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation of palpable purpura, colicky abdominal pain, and arthritis, point towards a diagnosis of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP) also known as IgA vasculitis. It is a small vessel vasculitis that occurs due to IgA immune complex deposition within the wall of the blood vessels . It is commonly seen in children and is characterized by: • Palpable purpura without thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy . • Arthralgia- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints. • Abdominal pain • Glomerulonephritis : proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, RBC casts in urine. The skin biopsy will show small vessel vasculitis, with IgA and C3 deposition in the affected organs by immunofluorescence .
