It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles , such as coal mines. It is usually benign and less than 10 % of the cases develop progressive massive fibrosis which may lead to pulmonary dysfunction , pulmonary hypertension , and cor pulmonale . Coal workers may also develop emphysema or chronic bronchitis, independent of smoking. Unlike asbestosis , this condition does not predispose to cancer.631

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An old woman presents with a persistent productive cough and clubbing . On auscultation , wheeze and crackles are present . There is no history of fever. Which of the following is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiectasis . HRCT is the investigation of choice - most specific . Bronchiectasis is a suppurative lung disease with abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi. It is an end-stage condition of various diseases (infections , congenital or autoimmune disorders) that result in the destruction of the bronchial wall and its surrounding supporting tissues . Ried's classification divides bronchiectasis into 3 types based on the phenotype of the affected bronchi: • Cylindrical or tubular (most common) • Saccular or varicose • Cystic Traction bronchiectasis is a type of bronchiectasis seen in conditions causing extensive pulmonary fibrosis (tuberculosis , idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). The mechanical traction due to fibrosis pulls apart the adjacent bronchi, making them distorted and abnormally dilated . There is no destruction of the bronchial wall. Clinically, they have a chronic productive cough , clubbing , crackles, and rhonchi.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with a fever and cough . She has a history of repeated chest infections for several years and coughs up yellow -green purulent sputum with some streaky hemoptysis . What could be the underlying condition based on the CT given below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the CT showing signet ring sign is suggestive of bronchiectasis which can be due to cystic fibrosis. A history of repeated chest infections is an indication of cystic fibrosis and a major risk factor for the development of bronchiectasis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an unlikely complication in patients with bronchiectasis ?
mcqs.explanation: Lung cancer is not a known complication of bronchiectasis .639 Complications of bronchiectasis include : • Massive hemoptysis • Empyema and lung abscess • Respiratory failure • Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale • Secondary amyloidosis (AA type ) Chronic and recurrent infections lead to secondary amyloidosis (AA type ) and involve the kidneys.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 58-year-old white man presents with a 6-month history of productive cough , weight loss, fever, and night sweats . HRCT shows a cluster of grapes appearance . A biopsy shows features of a non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection . Cystic fibrosis is ruled out. Which of the following drugs is not to be used in the treatment regimen?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiectasis secondary to a non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection. Mucolytic dornase is recommended routinely in cystic fibrosis (CF)-related bronchiectasis but not in non-CF bronchiectasis . Macrolides (azithromycin or clarithromycin) combined with rifampicin and ethambutol are used in the treatment of non-CF bronchiectasis . Treatment of bronchiectasis : • Antibiotic therapy : This is used to treat exacerbations and is given for 10 -14 days. Commonly administered antibiotics include : • Amoxicillin or clarithromycin: First-line drugs • Ciprofloxacin: For Pseudomonas aeruginosa • Airway clearance: • Postural drainage: This is done by gravity-assisted positioning of the patient and chest physiotherapy. • Mucolytic treatment : only in cystic fibrosis patients • Normal or hypertonic saline (\0373%) nebulization • Humidified air inhalation • Drugs like N-acetylcysteine or carbocysteine • Others : • Inhaled bronchodilators like long-acting \0312 agonists and anticholinergics • Long-term oxygen therapy : In patients with chronic respiratory failure • Pulmonary rehabilitation • Adequate hydration • Resection of a focal area of suppuration , lung transplantation: In refractory cases640

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A college student presents with complaints of fever, chronic productive cough , steatorrhea . There is a past history of recurrent lung infections and multiple hospitalizations with similar complaints. Which of the following is false about this condition?

options.b: Abnormality in CFTR gene leads to defective calcium transport
options.c: Most common mutation is F508 deletion
options.d: Males have infertility in adult life

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Abnormalities in cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein (CFTR) gene lead to defective chloride transport and not calcium transport. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting the epithelial cells of various exocrine glands of the body. It is caused by mutations in the gene coding for CFTR protein. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. The most prominent clinical features of cystic fibrosis are chronic respiratory diseases (fever, productive cough , recurrent lung infections) and pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea ). Male patients with cystic fibrosis usually have infertility due to congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in azoospermia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with an acute respiratory tract infection . He has a history of asthma associated with recurrent respiratory tract infections and sinusitis. Genetic testing in childhood had revealed CFTR mutations. Which of the following is likely to be decreased in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis. In these patients , sperm count is most likely to be decreased . Male patients with cystic fibrosis usually have infertility due to congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in obstructive azoospermia. Option A: Sweat chloride levels are elevated (\03760 mEq/L ) due to abnormalities in the CFTR protein leading to defective chloride transport. Option B: Serum bicarbonate levels are increased due to excessive loss of salt in the sweat resulting in hypochloremic alkalosis. Option D: Immunoreactive trypsinogen levels are increased due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Measurement of these levels is a diagnostic screening test in newborns.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A young boy is being evaluated for cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride shows values of 38 and 44 mEq/L (normal<40). What is the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
mcqs.explanation: DNA analysis is used to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in patients with equivocal (one normal and one abnormal value) or frankly normal sweat chloride values. The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met: • Presence of • Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal , or genitourinary) or • Positive newborn screening or • A sibling with cystic fibrosis • Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by • Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or641 • Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or • An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference Option A: 72-hour fecal fat is not used in the diagnosis of CF. Option B: Measuring the levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen is a screening test in newborns. Option D: Trans epithelial nasal potential difference measurement can be used as an adjunct to sweat test , but it has limited availability and is predominantly used as a research tool.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy has been having recurrent hospitalizations for infections , since 2 years of age. After a detailed evaluation, a diagnosis of Kartagener 's syndrome was made. Which of the following features is not a component of the triad seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Male infertility is typical in Kartagener syndrome, but not a component of the triad. Kartagener 's syndrome is primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of: • Situs inversus • Chronic sinusitis • Bronchiectasis Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility . It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis . As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen, its absence , will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality. Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile , due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Infertility in Kartagener 's syndrome is due to which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Kartagener 's syndrome is a type of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of • Situs inversus • Chronic sinusitis • Bronchiectasis Infertility in Kartagener 's syndrome is due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function), not azoospermia (complete absence of spermatozoa in ejaculate ). Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility . It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis . As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen, its absence will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality.642 Approximately half of the patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia have Kartagener syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which is the most common cause of lung abscess ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of lung abscess is aspirated oropharyngeal secretion . Lung abscess represents necrosis and cavitation of the lung following microbial infection . They are broadly divided into two categories : • Primary lung abscesses : usually arise from aspiration, often caused principally by anaerobic bacteria (most common) • Secondary lung abscesses : arise in the setting of an underlying condition, such as a post-obstructive process (e.g., a bronchial foreign body or tumor) or a systemic process (e.g., HIV infection or another immunocompromising condition)

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A bed -ridden patient with a Ryles tube tried to pull out the tube . This led to aspiration following which he developed fever with chills and cough . X-ray findings were suggestive of lung abscess . Which of the following pathogens is unlikely to have caused it?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a primary lung abscess . Staphylococcus is involved in the formation of secondary lung abscess , not primary. Microbial pathogens causing lung abscess :Clinical conditions Pathogens Primary lung abscess (due to aspiration) Anaerobes (e.g.,Peptostrepto coccusspp .,Prevotellaspp ., Ba cteroides spp .,Streptococcus milleri), microaerophilic stre ptococci Secondary lung abscess (due to underlying conditions) Staphylococcus aureus, gram -negative rods (e.g.,Pseudom onas aeruginosa,Enterobacte riaceae),Nocardiaspp .,Asperg illusspp .,Legionellaspp .,Pneu mocystis jirovecii Embolic lesions Staphylococcus aureus(often from endocarditis ),Fusobacte rium necrophorum(Lemierre' s disease )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 64-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department after being found unconscious due to alcohol intoxication. On physical examination, his dental hygiene was poor. Chest auscultation revealed fixed amphoric breath sounds over the right hemithorax. Which of the following lung lobes is most likely to be affected ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a primary lung abscess due to aspiration. Most common lobes involved in primary lung abscess are posterior upper lobes and superior lower lobes , given the predisposition of aspirated materials to be deposited in these areas.643 The right lung is affected more commonly than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated . In secondary abscesses , the location of the abscess may vary with the underlying cause .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man presents with persistent fever and productive cough for 6 weeks with night sweats and anemia. The following is his CXR. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario described along with the chest X-ray image showing air-fluid level is suggestive of a lung abscess . The patients usually present with complaints of fever, cough with sputum production , and chest pain. Patients with putrid lung abscesses may report foul -smelling sputum . Patients with chronic lung abscesses usually have a history of night sweats , fatigue , and anemia. On physical examination: • Poor dentition /gingival disease • Amphoric and/or cavernous breath sounds on lung auscultation • Digital clubbing • The absence of a gag reflex CXR features of lung abscess : • A lung cavity with an air-fluid level • The cavity wall is thick and irregular, and a surrounding pulmonary-infiltrate is often present • Computed tomography (CT) is more sensitive than chest radiography and is used to detect small cavities The two x-ray images given below show thick-walled cavities with air-fluid levels on lateral and PA views respectively.644

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old male patient presented with 2 weeks of productive cough , fever, and shortness of breath. A chest radiogram was done as shown below . Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?
mcqs.explanation: In the above clinical scenario, the patient most likely has a lung abscess as depicted by the radiograph. Clindamycin is the drug of choice in the treatment of lung abscesses . When there are contraindications to clindamycin, a combination of penicillin and metronidazole is likely to be as effective as clindamycin. Anaerobes of oral origin are the most common causative organism and require broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage. Vancomycin , ciprofloxacin, and cephalexin have no significant activity against anaerobes. Below is a chest X-ray showing a lung abscess (yellow dotted circle) with an air-fluid level (arrow).645

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with fever, productive cough , night sweats , and clubbing is diagnosed with lung abscess . Which of the following is an unlikely complication of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Lung carcinoma is unlikely in patients with lung abscesses . Lung carcinoma may cause lung abscess (in 10 -15% of cases ) but lung abscess is not a premalignant condition. Complications of lung abscess : • Empyema • Pneumatocele • Bronchopleural fistula • Bronchiectasis • Metastatic infections like brain abscess • Life-threatening hemoptysis • Massive aspiration of lung abscess contents

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common presentation of inhalational anthrax ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common presentation of inhalation anthrax is hemorrhagic mediastinitis , which is seen in 38% of the patients . Inhalational anthrax also known as wool sorter's disease is caused by Bacillus anthracis. Infection usually occurs among workers handling contaminated animal wool , hair, and skin in textile and tanning industries . Patients present with malaise, fever, cough , shortness of breath & headache . B. anthracis spores are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages and transported to mediastinal lymph nodes . Hemorrhagic necrosis of the thoracic lymph nodes draining the lung results in hemorrhagic mediastinitis . Pulmonary infiltrates , mediastinal widening , and pleural effusion are other findings. Treatment of inhalation anthrax includes a combination of intravenous ciprofloxacin and clindamycin for at least 14 days, antitoxins (Raxibacumab , Obiltoxaximab), anthrax immunoglobulins and steroids (if associated meningitis is present ). Prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin (500mg twice daily for 2 months) is recommended for anyone at high risk of inhalational exposure to anthrax spores .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a common feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Central bronchiectasis is a typical feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), not distal bronchiectasis . ABPA is an eosinophilic pulmonary disorder caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to the colonization of airways by the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus . It occurs almost exclusively in patients with asthma (~2.5% of patients) or cystic fibrosis (up to 15%). In chronic cases , repeated episodes of bronchial obstruction, inflammation, and mucoid impaction can lead to646 bronchiectasis , fibrosis, and respiratory compromise. While central bronchiectasis is characteristic, some patients can develop chronic cavitary lesions . With the development of ABPA , asthma or cystic fibrosis typically worsens and may manifest with a new or worsening cough or an increase in sputum production or wheezing . Many patients report coughing up thick sputum casts. The presence of hyperattenuating mucus in the airways is highly specific . ABPA is diagnosed serologically , based on the presence of: Serum IgE > 1000 IU/ml Positive skin prick test or IgE levels against A. fumigatus extract Detection of Aspergillus -specific antibodies Eosinophilia >500 cells /�ML Treatment - The use of systemic glucocorticoids is indicated for ABPA , but the course should be tapered by 3-6 months. Antifungal agents like itraconazole, voriconazole, and newer azoles can be used for over 4 months to control disease activity. Monoclonal antibodies against IgE, IL -4, and IL -5 receptors can be used for severe refractory cases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following tests is not used to diagnose a patient with suspected allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis ?

options.d: Culture of Aspergillus fumigatus from sputum

mcqs.explanation: The culture of Aspergillus fumigatus from sputum is not a diagnostic criterion for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The sensitivity of sputum culture in ABPA is low. ABPA is diagnosed serologically , based on the presence of: • Serum IgE > 1000 IU/ml. • Positive skin prick test or IgE levels against A. fumigatus extract. • Detection of Aspergillus -specific antibodies . • Eosinophilia >500 cells /�ML.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia underwent induction therapy . Within the next few days, he developed a cough and fever. On evaluation, HRCT showed a halo sign. Eventually , the patient deteriorated and died due to respiratory compromise. On autopsy , lung histopathology showed infarction and invasion of blood vessels by Aspergillus hyphae . Which of the following is not true about this condition?

options.a: Fungal hyphae are broad and aseptate
options.b: Yeast forms are not seen in infected tissue
options.c: Most of the patients are asymptomatic
options.d: Exposure to hay barns is a risk factor.

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of aspergillosis . Fungal hyphae of Aspergillus species are narrow, septate , and have branching at 45o. Yeast forms of Aspergillus are not seen in infected tissue . Exposure to the high number of conidia that are found in construction sites , hay barns, moldy barks , and composts is a risk factor. Clinical features : • Most of the patients are asymptomatic • Fever • Cough647 • Chest discomfort • Trivial hemoptysis • Shortness of breath Halo sign-on HRCT refers to a localized ground glass appearance representing an area of hemorrhagic infarction surrounding a nodule . It is seen in invasive aspergillosis , a distinct entity where there is a direct invasion of hyphae into the lung tissue . The air crescent sign describes the crescent of air that can be seen in invasive aspergillosis . It usually heralds recovery and is the result of increased granulocyte activity. Monod sign refers to the gas that surrounds a mycetoma (most commonly an aspergilloma ) in a pre-existing pulmonary cavity.648

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: On performing a pulmonary function test , reduction in FEV1/FVC is characteristic of:
mcqs.explanation: Reduction in FEV1/FVC is characteristic of obstructive lung disease . Forced vital capacity (FVC) is the volume of expired air recorded when a person inhales to the total lung capacity and exhales as hard and as completely as possible . The volume of air expired in the first second is called the forced expiratory volume 1 (FEV1). Given below is a graphical representation of FEV and FEV1:FVC is reduced in both obstructive and restrictive lung diseases . In obstructive diseases , the slope of FVC is steady , therefore the FEV1 value is low and the FEV1/FVC ratio decreases . In restrictive diseases , the airflow is fast in the beginning leading to a higher value of FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio increases.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old smoker presented with chronic productive cough and shortness of breath. Physical examination revealed a barrel chest and an expiratory wheeze on auscultation . All of the following findings would be seen in his pulmonary function tests except ?
mcqs.explanation: 654 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is characterized by an increased residual volume. According to Uptodate , decreased vital capacity and increased total lung capacity is indicative of hyperinflation seen in COPD. FVC can be used a proxy for VC in normal individuals but in COPD FVC is less than VC due to air trapping, airflow limitation, and small airway collapse .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with intermittent wheeze and cough . His mother reports that these episodes are precipitated by physical exercise . There is a history of atopic dermatitis in his mother. Pulmonary function tests are performed . Which of the following findings are least likely to be seen in him?

options.a: Decreased forced expiratory volume in one second

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of asthma. The diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) tends to be normal or high in these patients .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Decreased maximum mid-expiratory flow rate is seen in obstruction of:
mcqs.explanation: Decreased maximum mid-expiratory flow rate (MMFR) is seen in obstruction of small airways. MMFR is the average expiratory flow rate during the middle 50% of the vital capacity i.e., forced expiratory flow rate between 25 and 75% of the vital capacity . This is the most sensitive measurement of early airflow obstruction, particularly in small airways.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions is likely to have pulmonary function test findings as given below :
mcqs.explanation: Low FEV1 and FVC with a high FEV1/FVC ratio are characteristics of restrictive lung disease . Among the options , pleural effusion is a restrictive lung disease . • Obstructive lung diseases • Asthma • COPD • Bronchiectasis • Bronchiolitis • Restrictive lung diseases • Intrinsic • Interstitial lung disease • Extrinsic • Myasthenia gravis • Kyphoscoliosis • Pleural effusion655

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 76-year-old retired worker from a granite quarry presents with progressive dyspnea and a chronic cough . He has never smoked cigarettes . His chest X-ray is shown below . Which of the following patterns would you see on his pulmonary function tests ?
mcqs.explanation: The chest X-ray shows calcification of the hilar lymph nodes called eggshell calcification. The clinical scenario along with the chest X-ray is suggestive of silicosis . It is a restrictive lung disease characterized by increased FEV1/FVC and decreased compliance . It is an occupational interstitial lung disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An elderly woman presents with breathlessness on exertion. On auscultation , bilateral basal rales are heard. A chest CT is done and is shown below . Which of the following is likely to be increased in her?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the honeycomb pattern of lung parenchyma due to interstitial fibrosis is suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD ). The alveolar-arterial gradient (PAO2 -PaO2) is increased in ILD . It is a restrictive lung disease . In ILD , the alveolar-capillary bed is damaged and thus there is a decrease in diffusion capacity . Therefore , while the PAO2 (Alveolar O2) remains normal , the PaO2 (arterial) decreases , and the alveolar-arterial difference increases.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide is decreased in patients with:
mcqs.explanation: Diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is decreased in patients with emphysema . DLCO measures the ability of the lungs to transfer gas from inhaled air in the alveoli to the red blood cells in pulmonary capillaries . In general , the DLCO is used to identify the cause of dyspnea or hypoxemia . It is also used to monitor disease progression in interstitial lung disease , and identify pulmonary hypertension in patients at risk , such as those with systemic sclerosis . DLCO is decreased in patients with:656 • Interstitial lung disease • Emphysema (COPD usually have normal DLCO) • Bronchiolitis obliterans • Pulmonary hypertension • Thromboembolic disease • Chronic congestive Heart Failure DLCO is increased in patients with: • Alveolar hemorrhage • Acute Congestive heart failure • Asthma

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath and fatigue . She has a medical history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Her pulmonary function test results are given below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above PFT pattern shows near-normal FVC, increased FEV1%, and markedly decreased DLCO. This along with the given history is suggestive of pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH). It is more commonly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis . Option B: Interstitial lung disease is a restrictive lung disease . In ILD , the FVC is usually ,<80% of the predicted value. It is more commonly associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis . Options C and D: Congestive heart failure and bronchiectasis have obstructive pathology . They would have decreased FEV1% and normal DLCO.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A flow -volume loop of a patient is given below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The likely diagnosis is tracheal stenosis. The flow -volume loop shows flattened inspiratory and expiratory curves, suggestive of fixed upper -airway obstruction.657 A normal flow -volume loop begins on the X-axis (Volume axis): at the start of the test , both flow and volume are equal to zero. After the starting point, the curve rapidly mounts to a peak: Peak expiratory flow (PEF). Then, the PEF the curve descends (=the flow decreases ) as more air is expired . A normal , non-pathological F/V loop will descend in a straight or a convex line from the top (PEF) to the bottom (FVC). The forced inspiration that follows the forced expiration has roughly the same morphology , but the PIF (Peak Inspiratory Flow ) is not as distinct as PEF.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The flow -volume curve after spirometry in patient 1 is given below . The most likely diagnosis in this patient is:
mcqs.explanation: The given flow -volume curve shows decreased lung volumes (total lung capacity , vital capacity , and residual volume) with normal shape , suggestive of a restrictive pattern. The curve is a miniature version of the normal curve with shift towards the right. It is seen in myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis presents with ventilatory restriction due to reduced respiratory muscle strength . Asthma, emphysema , and endobronchial neoplasms present with obstructive flow patterns .658

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is seen in patients with brain stem injury?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with brain stem injury develop type 2 respiratory failure. It is characterized by low pO2 and high pCO2. Acute respiratory failure refers to acute impairment in gas exchange between the lungs and the blood causing hypoxia with or without hypercapnia .662

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man underwent emergency surgery following a road traffic accident . The surgery was performed under general anesthesia . Two days later, he developed features of respiratory failure. Which of the following types is likely to be present in him?
mcqs.explanation: The features of respiratory failure in the perioperative period of this patient is most likely due to lung atelectasis . Type 3 respiratory failure is most likely to be present in him. Type 3 respiratory failure is also known as perioperative respiratory failure. After general anesthesia , there is a decrease in functional residual capacity due to a reduction in muscular tone. This leads to airway closure and the collapse of the dependent lung units. Atelectasis can be treated by frequent changes in position, chest physiotherapy , upright positioning, and control of incisional and abdominal pain. Non-invasive positive -pressure ventilation may also be used to reverse regional atelectasis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is admitted for myocardial infarction complicated by severe mitral regurgitation. He suddenly develops shortness of breath, decreased urine output , and drowsiness . Blood pressure is 86/40 mmHg, pulse 120 bpm, and respiratory rate 24 per minute. Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: Up to 40% of cardiac output may be distributed to the respiratory muscles
options.b: Patient will develop type 2 respiratory failure
options.c: Intubation and mechanical ventilation are treatment of choice
options.d: Batwing appearance can be expected on an x-ray

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cardiogenic shock. He is likely to develop type 4 respiratory failure, not type 2. Patients in cardiogenic shock often have respiratory distress secondary to acute pulmonary edema (batwing appearance on x-ray). This increases the requirement of oxygen delivery to the respiratory muscles from <5% to up to 40% of cardiac output . Hypoperfusion and increased oxygen requirement lead to inadequate perfusion of respiratory muscles which causes type 4 respiratory failure. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are the treatment of choice .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old construction site worker is admitted for fever, nausea, vomiting, and pain abdomen radiating to the back. The next day he develops sudden onset breathlessness and hypoxia. He has been drinking daily for the past 10 years. He had a myocardial infarction 6 months back. His chest X-ray is given below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the chest X-ray finding is suggestive of ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome) secondary to acute pancreatitis . Acute pancreatitis gives rise to inflammatory processes and endothelial damage that results in ARDS. CXR features in ARDS: • Early findings - normal or diffuse alveolar opacities (consolidation), bilateral and which obscure the pulmonary vascular markings • Late findings - these opacities progress to more extensive consolidation that is diffuse Clinical disorders commonly associated with ARDS: • Direct lung injury: • Pneumonia • Aspiration of gastric contents • Pulmonary contusion663 • Near-drowning • Toxic inhalation injury • Indirect lung injury: • Sepsis • Severe trauma- multiple fractures, flail chest , head trauma, burns • Multiple transfusions • Drug overdose • Pancreatitis • Post-cardiopulmonary bypass

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: According to the berlin definition , moderate ARDS is characterized by all, except
mcqs.explanation: Moderate ARDS is characterized by PaO2/FiO2: - 200 mmHg. PaO2/FiO2: - 300 mm/Hg is classified as mild ARDS. Diagnostic criteria in ARDS—Berlin definition :(requires each of the following criteria to be present to diagnose ARDS) • Onset - Acute : Respiratory symptoms must have begun < 1 week of a known clinical insult • Bilateral alveolar or interstitial infiltrates : on a chest X-ray image or CT scan • Respiratory failure must not be fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Objective assessment e.g Echo should be done in cases of no known cause . • Impairment of oxygenation : The severity of hypoxemia defines the severity of ARDS. Note : American-European Consensus Conference (AECC) classification of ARDS is no longer used . Image: Alveolar/interstitial infiltrates in ARDS patientSeveri ty PaO2/FiO2(On ventilator sett ings that include PEEP \0375 cm H2O) Mild > 200 mmHgbut\026 300 mmH g Mode rate > 100 mmHgbut\026 200 mmH g Sever e \026 100 mmHg664

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is least likely to be present in patients with ARDS?
mcqs.explanation: Increased left atrial pressure is not likely to be present in ARDS. ARDS is characterized by • PCWP of \02618 mmHg with normal LA pressure • Decreased pulmonary compliance • Increased pulmonary artery pressure • Severe hypoxemia665

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A fisherman was rushed to the ED following a near-drowning incident. On arrival , he was unconscious and was not breathing. He was resuscitated and stabilized . A few hours later, he developed sudden onset breathlessness and low saturation. Chest X-ray showed diffuse alveolar opacities . He was started on mechanical ventilation. What will be the recommended ventilator setting for him?

options.a: Low tidal volume and high PEEP
options.b: Low tidal volume and low PEEP
options.c: High tidal volume and high PEEP
options.d: High tidal volume and low PEEP

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of ARDS secondary to drowning. The ventilator setting recommended is low tidal volume and high PEEP. Drowning causes direct lung injury. The aspiration of water into the lungs damages the surfactant. This disrupts the alveolar-capillary membrane and leads to alveolar edema , resulting in ARDS. The ventilator settings recommended in ARDS are: • Low tidal volume: To avoid barotrauma due to overdistention of the alveoli. • High PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure ): This prevents the collapse of alveoli at the end of the expiration and improves oxygenation.666

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding lung cancer?

options.a: It is the most common cancer in Indian men
options.b: Tobacco smoking is the most common cause
options.c: Adenocarcinoma is the most common histologic type
options.d: It is the most common cause of cancer death

mcqs.explanation: The most common cancer seen in Indian men is lip and oral cavity cancer, not lung cancer. Most common cancer: • In men globally - Lung cancer • In Indian men- Lip and oral cavity cancer • In women globally - Breast cancer • In Indian women- Breast cancer Tobacco smoking is a primary cause of the development of lung cancer. It increases 10 fold greater risk of developing lung cancer compared to those who have never smoked. It is the most common cause of cancer death .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common type of lung cancer in light smokers?
mcqs.explanation: 671 The most common lung cancer in light smokers (<10 pack-year history) is adenocarcinoma. WHO classification of lung carcinomas: The WHO classification system divides epithelial lung cancers into four major cell types : • Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) • Non-small-cell lung carcinomas (NSCLCs) • Adenocarcinoma • Squamous cell carcinoma • Large-cell carcinoma Adenocarcinoma is most commonly seen in: • Lifetime non-smokers • Light smokers (<10 pack-years history) • Women • Younger adults (<60 years) In smokers, the most common types are small-cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinomas.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man with a 35 pack-year history of smoking presented for a routine check-up. His brother was diagnosed with lung cancer at a similar age . Which of the following would be preferred to screen him for lung cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Low-dose CT/ thin-slice spiral chest CT would be preferred to screen him for lung cancer. He belongs to the high-risk population to develop lung cancer. The high-risk population is individuals whose age is \03760 years and who have a smoking history of \03710 pack-years. Low dose CT scans are shown to detect more lung nodules and cancers than the standard CXR in selected high-risk populations . Also, up to 85% of cancers thus detected are classified as stage I. Early staged cancers are considered potentially curable with surgical resection . Here, the aim is to reduce medical radiation exposure as much as possible , low dose CT is effective in screening for lung cancer, and is thus preferred .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about hypertrophic osteoarthropathy ?

options.a: Platelets have a role in the development of HOA
options.c: HOA is commonly associated with lung malignancies
options.d: Skin changes are more common in secondary HOA

mcqs.explanation: Skin changes are more common in primary HOA, not secondary HOA. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is a condition characterized by the clubbing of the digits . In advanced stages , it is characterized by the periosteal new bone formation and synovial effusion . The exact mechanism of its development is unclear. However, platelets are said to have a role in the development of HOA via platelet -derived growth factor. There are two types of HOA:672 Primary HOA Secondary HOA Inherited autosomal domina nt condition Acquired condition, secondar y toLung neoplasmsMesothel iomaSuppurative lung infecti onsCongenital heart diseaseT hyroid acropachyInflammato ry bowel disease Skin changeslike thickening, seborrhea, excessive sweating are commonly seen Skin changes are unusual The symptomsdisappearinad ulthood The symptoms persist till the underlying cause is treated

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged non-smoker presented with a dry persistent cough and hemoptysis . A CT scan showed a mass in the periphery of his right lung. A biopsy was taken, cells showed an acinar pattern with mucin formation. The cells were positive for thyroid transcription factor 1 and napsin A. What other feature is most likely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the biopsy findings is suggestive of lung adenocarcinoma. It is most commonly associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy . Adenocarcinomas are mainly seen in the periphery of the lung. They grow in various patterns like acinar , lepidic , papillary, micropapillary, and solid with mucin formation. Cells are positive for markers like thyroid transcription factor 1 and napsin A. Option C: Hypercalcemia due to ectopic production of PTH -related peptide is seen in squamous cell carcinoma . Options B and D: However, SIADH, Cushing's syndrome, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome are associated with small-cell lung carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A female patient comes with complaints of unintentional weight loss and right shoulder pain for the past 6 months. She reports that the pain radiates to her arm and is not relieved by NSAIDs. Chest X-ray is given below . Which nerve roots are likely to be compressed ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the X-ray findings is suggestive of Pancoast syndrome / superior sulcus tumor. This affects the C8, T1 , and T2 nerve roots. It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm , often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough , hemoptysis, wheeze , stridor, dyspnea , or post -obstructive pneumonitis. Regional spread can cause • Tracheal obstruction • Esophageal compression with dysphagia • Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness • Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea • Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner's syndrome (enophthalmos , ptosis , miosis, and anhydrosis)673

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A COPD patient presented to the emergency with an acute exacerbation. On evaluation, a chest X-ray revealed a solitary pulmonary nodule . Which of the following patterns of calcification would suggest a likely malignancy in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Asymmetric calcification is suggestive of a malignant lesion.Benign lesion Malignant lesion Lack of growth over a period of >2 years The growth of the lesion is ev ident in comparison with an old X-ray Patterns of calcification:Dens e central nidusMultiple punct ate fociBull 's eye granulomaP opcorn ball hamartomas Patterns of calcification:Asy mmetricLack of calcification Associated chest symptoms a re uncommon chest symptoms like cough , h emoptysis are common Complications are uncommo n Complications like atelectasis , pneumonitis , and effusion ar e common

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice in patients with adenocarcinoma of the lung with EGFR mutation?
mcqs.explanation: Adenocarcinomas with EGFR mutation are exquisitely sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors of the EGFR signal pathway such as gefitinib and erlotinib. Option A: Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody against VEGF. Option B: Paclitaxel- a taxane, is a plant alkaloid and chemotherapeutic agent . Option C: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor effective in the treatment of CML and GIST .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man presents with persistent cough and hemoptysis . The intern notices that he has moon-like facies and purple striae on his abdomen. On evaluation, a chest X-ray revealed a mass in his right lung. Which of the following type of lung carcinoma could be the cause of this patient 's features ?
mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario the patient has features of Cushing's syndrome, secondary to small-cell lung cancer. This occurs due to ectopic ACTH production . It can also seen in pulmonary carcinoids. Most effective management is treating underlying SCLC or carcinoid.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An elderly man was rushed to the ED with confusion and multiple episodes of vomiting. His wife reported that he had increased frequency of urination and constipation for the past days. He is a known case of lung cancer. ECG showed a shortened QT interval. What could be the primary cause of his symptoms ?

options.b: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
options.c: Ectopic secretion of PTH related peptide

mcqs.explanation: The primary cause of his symptoms is ectopic secretion of PTH related peptide . Lung cancers are associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes. Squamous cell lung cancer is associated with hypercalcemia due to ectopic PTH related peptide . Hypercalcemia may present as vomiting,674 abdominal pain, constipation , increased frequency of urination, kidney stones , bone pain and shortened QT interval.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old woman presents with vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased urine output since morning. On the previous day, she received chemotherapy for her stage 4 lung cancer. On examination, she is drowsy , HR-110 /min and RR -30/min. All of the following biochemical findings can be seen in this patient except :
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). It is associated with hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia . TLS is caused by the destruction of a large number of rapidly proliferating neoplastic cells . It is usually seen within 1-5 days of receiving chemotherapy . It has also been observed with the administration of glucocorticoids , letrozole , tamoxifen, rituximab and gemtuzumab . Rarely, spontaneous necrosis of malignancies causes TLS . Clinical features : • Nausea , vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy • Pruritus, renal colicky pain, oliguria • Muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, tetany Biochemical findings: • Hyperuricemia • Hyperkalemia • Hypocalcemia • Hyperphosphatemia Due to these biochemical changes , there is an increased risk of arrhythmias, acidosis, and acute kidney injury.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not used in the management of patients with tumor lysis syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is not recommended in the treatment of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). Urinary alkalinization by sodium bicarbonate decreases the solubility of xanthine, hypoxanthine, and calcium phosphate . This potentially increases the risk of intratubular crystallization. Management of TLS includes : • Aggressive hydration • Allopurinol • Rasburicase - recombinant urate oxidase • Febuxostat - non-purine selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients with non-small lung carcinoma is a suitable candidate to undergo a potentially curative surgical resection :

options.a: 60-year-old smoker with a tumor within 2cm of carina
options.c: 55 -year-old non-smoker with tumor involving the main pulmonary artery
options.d: 57 -year old light smoker with ipsilateral mediastinal node metastases

mcqs.explanation: 675 Patients with ipsilateral mediastinal node metastases are suitable candidates for curative resection . In patients with NSCLC, the following are contraindications to potentially curative resection : • Extra-thoracic metastases • Vocal cord involvement • Superior vena cava syndrome • Involvement of the main pulmonary artery • Cardiac tamponade • Phrenic nerve paralysis • Malignant pleural effusion • Tumor within 2 cm of the carina • Metastasis to the contralateral lung • Metastases to supraclavicular lymph nodes • Contralateral mediastinal node metastases676

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Sleep apnea is defined as a temporary pause in breathing during sleep lasting at least :
mcqs.explanation: Sleep apnea is defined as a temporary pause in breathing during sleep lasting at least 10 seconds . Sleep apneas can be further divided into: • Obstructive apneas - Sleep apnea with persistent respiratory effort . • Central apneas - Sleep apnea with an absence of respiratory effort . The gold standard for the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) is an overnight polysomnogram (PSG).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is referred to the sleep clinic for polysomnography . Which of the following is not a component of it?
mcqs.explanation: Arterial blood gases are not part of polysomnography . However, they are usually measured to rule out alveolar hypoventilation secondary to lung disease or chest wall abnormalities. An overnight polysomnogram is a multi-parametric test and is the gold standard for the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea. It includes: • EEG • Eye movements (EOG ) • Muscle activity or skeletal muscle activation (EMG) • ECG • Respiratory airflow and respiratory effort indicators • Peripheral pulse oximetry • Sleep latency • Sleep efficiency • Arousal index680 Other sleep disorders diagnosed by polysomnography : • Narcolepsy • Idiopathic hypersomnia • Periodic limb movement disorder • REM behavior disorder • Parasomnias

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged obese patient presented with complaints of daytime tiredness and decreased exercise tolerance. Echocardiology revealed reduced ejection fraction. The sleep study showed periods of apnea without respiratory efforts . Which of the following is not true regarding his condition?

options.a: Transient cessation of neural drive to all respiratory muscles
options.c: Is due to decreased sensitivity to pCO
options.d: Can be induced by CPAP at high pressure

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of central sleep apnea (CSA), and it is caused by increased sensitivity to pCO2. Thus changes in pCO2 levels during sleep lead to an unstable breathing pattern that manifests as hyperventilation alternating with apnea. Crescendo -decrescendo breathing pattern known as Cheyne -Stokes respiration is seen . Risk factors for CSA: • Heart failure • Opioid medications • Hypoxia (e.g., breathing at high altitude ) • Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) at high pressures seems to induce central apnea; this condition is referred to as complex sleep apnea.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is not a risk factor for the development of central sleep apnea?
mcqs.explanation: Strychnine is not a risk factor as it does not cause respiratory depression . It is a CNS stimulant. Only drugs that cause respiratory centre depression are risk factors for the development of central681 sleep apnea. Option A: Opioids depress the respiratory centre in a dose -dependent manner . Option C: Barbiturates cause respiratory depression in high doses . Option D: Gelsemium is an ergot -type alkaloid and is a CNS depressant . Often used in homoeopathy, in large doses , paralysis and death from respiratory failure can occur.The pink shaded area shows an apneic period without any respiratory efforts .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient comes to the sleep clinic and the following pattern is seen on polysomnography . What type of breathing pattern is it?
mcqs.explanation: The breathing pattern shown in the image is suggestive of Cheyne -Stokes respiration. It is characterized by progressively deeper and sometimes faster breathing, followed by a gradual decrease that results in a temporary stop in breathing called apnea. It is caused by an increased sensitivity of the respiratory center to arterial PCO2. There is an apneic phase , during which arterial PO2 falls and arterial PCO2 rises. These changes in the arterial blood gas content stimulate the respiratory center , resulting in hyperventilation and hypocapnia , followed by recurrence of apnea. It is present in 40% of patients with advanced HF and usually is associated with low cardiac output .682

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents with daytime sleepiness and impaired concentration and memory. On examination, his BMI is 41 kg/m2 , blood pressure is 160 /100 mm of Hg. His awake arterial blood gas analysis is given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most probable diagnosis of this patient is obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) or Pickwickian syndrome is defined as the presence of awake alveolar hypoventilation in an obese individual which cannot be attributed to other conditions associated with alveolar hypoventilation . Patients with OHS are obese and give a history of daytime hypersomnolence , loud snoring, choking during sleep , fatigue , impaired concentration, and memory. On examination usually , there is a small oropharynx and a thick neck. OHS may be associated with the following findings: • Elevated serum bicarbonate (>27 mEq/L) • Hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) • Hypoxemia (PaO2 <70 mmHg) • Polycythemia Options A and D: In obstructive sleep apnea and central sleep apnea, the awake ABG values are usually normal . Option B: There are no ABG changes in narcolepsy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man is brought to the OPD by his wife for gasping episodes during sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness . She reported that he even dozed off while driving yesterday and nearly caused an accident . He is being treated for hypertension , gastro-oesophageal reflux, and type 2 diabetes . What else would be the ideal therapy for his symptoms ?

options.d: Implantable neuro-stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS). The ideal therapy is continuous positive airway pressure therapy (CPAP).683 Option A: Supplemental oxygenation can improve oxygen saturation but there is little evidence that it improves OSAHS symptoms . Option B: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty is the most common surgery done in OSAHS but it is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP. Option D: Unilateral neuro-stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve through a surgically implanted device is a recently tested therapy for OSAHS. It can be used as an alternative in selected patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of Syndrome Z?
mcqs.explanation: Syndrome Z is defined as a combination of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome with metabolic syndrome. LDL more than 100 mg/dL is not a criterion for the diagnosis of metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed based on The NCEP: ATP III Criteria. Three or more of the following must be present : • Central obesity : waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F) • Hypertriglyceridemia : triglyceride level \037150 mg/dL or specific medication • Low HDL cholesterol : <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively , or specific medication • Hypertension: blood pressure \037130 mmHg systolic or \03785 mmHg diastolic or specific medication • Fasting plasma glucose level \037100 mg/dL or specific medication or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes684

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Urine sample of a patient has been collected for analysis. How soon should it be analyzed?
mcqs.explanation: Urine samples should be analyzed within 2-4 hours after collection to avoid cell lysis and precipitation of solutes . If urine analysis is not possible in the given time, then the sample can be stored at 4-8 oC for a maximum of 12 hours. Urine samples can be collected using the following techniques : • Midstream sample during spontaneous voiding • Fresh specimen from an indwelling catheter • Suprapubic needle aspiration of the bladder , especially in infants

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following determine the color of urine except :
mcqs.explanation: The solubility of solutes is not a determining factor of the color of urine. Determinants of the color of urine are: • Chemical content • Concentration • pH (Normal pH is 4.5-8) The normal color of urine is pale straw due to the presence of urochrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs can cause green -colored urine in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Green urine can be caused by triamterene, a potassium -sparing diuretic .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What value of urine specific gravity is called isosthenuria?
mcqs.explanation: Isosthenuria is defined as a urine specific gravity of 1.010 , which is similar to that of plasma. The normal specific gravity of urine is around 1.020 to 1.030 . Specific gravity and osmolality are measures of the concentration or relative density of urine. • Specific gravity: The weight of a solution relative to that of equal amounts of water. It is measured by refractometry or using reagent strips. • Osmolality : The gold standard for relative density . It is defined as the number of osmoles of solute per kilogram of solvent. It is measured directly with an osmometer . Isosthenuria means that the kidney is neither concentrating nor diluting the urine. This is seen in chronic renal failure (CRF) and acute tubular necrosis (ATN).Abnormality Causes Isosthenuria CRF, ATN690 Abnormality Causes Hyposthenuria (low specific g ravity) Diabetes insipidus Hypersthenuria (high specific gravity) SIADH, Severe dehydrati on

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is being evaluated for the following appearance of his urine. A urine dipstick test is performed and the result is negative . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows reddish discoloration of the urine sample . A negative urine dipstick indicates absence of RBCs and is suggestive of porphyria. A urine dipstick test is the first step to be done in a patient with high coloured urine to help identify true hematuria. A positive dipstick test identifies heme that is present in red blood cells , haemoglobin or myoglobin. A negative dipstick test implies that the reddish discolouration is due to pigments from certain food items (beetroot ), drugs or porphyrias.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients are considered to have significant hematuria based on their urine analysis findings?
mcqs.explanation: Hematuria is defined as the presence of 2-5 RBCs / high-powered field (HPF). It is considered significant or persistent in the presence of one of the following : • RBCs > 3 / HPF on 3 or more occasions • RBCs > / HPF on 1 occasion • Gross hematuria691

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with hematuria, generalized edema , and abdominal distension is suspected to have a glomerular pathology . Which of the following is likely to be seen in the urine?
mcqs.explanation: Acanthocytes are a subtype of dysmorphic red blood cells with protruding blebs that are seen in glomerular disease . The 40-5-1 rule can be used to identify glomerular diseases based on urinalysis: • Dysmorphic RBCs - 40% (can range from 10 -80%) • Acanthocytes - 5% (can range from 2-5%) • Even a single RBC cast Hematuria can be either due to systemic or renal causes . Renal causes can be further subdivided into glomerular and non-glomerular causes as given below :Glomerular Non-glomerular Dysmorphic RBCs seen (abno rmal shape and size) Isomorphic RBCs seen (norm al shape and size) RBC casts may be present RBC casts always absent MCV is reduced (<72 fl) MCV is normal Protein excretion > 1g /day Protein excretion < 1g /day The cause is usually medical The cause is usually surgical

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An 18-year-old boy presents to the clinic with a history of malaise. He was diagnosed with mild sensorineural hearing loss nearly 10 years ago. He also has a history of recurrent hematuria. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of Alport syndrome. The clinical features include : • Recurrent hematuria and nephritic syndrome • Sensorineural hearing loss • Anterior lenticonus Other causes of recurrent hematuria include : • Alport syndrome • IgA nephropathy • Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) • Papillary necrosis • Renal cell carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about proteinuria?

options.a: Proteinuria is always due to glomerular pathology
options.b: Albuminuria upto 150 mg/day is considered normal
options.d: Proteins are reabsorbed in the DCT

mcqs.explanation: Nephrotic -range or heavy proteinuria refers to excretion of > 3.5 g/day or > 1000 mg/m2/day in children.692 Normally, the following mechanisms prevent proteinuria: • The glomerular basement membrane acts as a barrier to prevent the loss of negatively charged and large proteins. • Reabsorption of small proteins in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). The various types of proteinuria are: • Glomerular - increased filtration of proteins due to disruption of basement membrane • Tubular - damage to tubules prevents protein reabsorption in the PCT • Overflow - excess production of low molecular weight proteins such as light chains • Postrenal - infections or stones can lead to secretion of IgA and IgG by the urinary tractType of Proteinuria Total proteinuria (mg/day) Albuminuria(mg/d ay) Normal-range <150MainlyTamm -Horsfallpr otein (70-75 mg/day) < Moderately increased 150-500 30-300 Severely increased > > Orthostatic proteinuria 150-500 —

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following findings in a patient are suggestive of non-glomerular proteinuria except :
mcqs.explanation: Non-glomerular proteinuria is characterized by the presence of N-acetyl glucosaminidase (NAG). This form of proteinuria occurs as a result of tubular injury. N-acetyl glucosaminidase (NAG) is a lysosomal enzyme present in the proximal tubular cells and is released into the urine following any injury to the tubules . Low-molecular-weight proteins such as \0312-microglobulin are normally reabsorbed in the PCT. When there is tubular injury, the proportion of these proteins in urine increases. This lowers the albumin: \0312-microglobulin ratio in urine. In glomerular proteinuria, there is increased filtration of macromolecules like albumin across the glomerular capillary wall. NAG is absent as there is no tubular injury.Glomerular proteinuria Non-glomerular proteinuria Type of protein excreted High molecular weight (Albu min) Low molecular weight (\0312-mi croglobulin) 24 hr protein excretion > 1-2 g/day < 1 g/day RBC casts Present Absent Albumin: \0312microglobulin ra tio (Normal 100 :1) :1 :1 N-acetyl glucosaminidase (N AG) Absent Present693

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with recurrent kidney stones . The microscopic examination of urine is shown below . What is the type of stone seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a hexagonal crystal, suggesting cystine stones . These stones are a recurrent feature in patients with cystinuria. Crystals in urine are usually associated with kidney stones . Crystals form in the urine depends upon a variety of factors including: • The degree of concentration of constituent molecules • The urine pH • The presence of inhibitors of crystallization Calcium oxalate and uric acid crystals can sometimes be found in normal urine that has been left to stand, due to crystal formation ex vivo .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about casts in urine?

options.a: Width of cast depends on the size of tubule in which it is formed
options.b: Casts in urine are specific to kidneys
options.c: Site of formation is proximal convoluted tubule
options.d: Casts are made up of uromodulin

mcqs.explanation: The sites of formation of casts are the collecting ducts and DCTs (distal convoluted tubules ). Casts are cylindrical structures formed by the aggregation of Tamm -Horsfall mucoprotein or uromodulin. This protein is secreted in the thick ascending loop of Henle . They assume the shape and size of the lumen in which they are formed. Several factors favour cast formation, such as urine stasis, low pH and high concentration. Casts are the only elements in urine sediments that are specifically of renal origin.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis was started on amphotericin B. Two days later, he is found to have decreased urine output . Urinalysis reveals granular casts. What could be the possible diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Muddy -brown granular casts are seen in acute tubular necrosis, a type of intrinsic renal failure. ATN can occur secondary to nephrotoxicity or hypovolemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following casts are associated with a poor prognosis?
mcqs.explanation: Broad casts are associated with a poor prognosis. They refer to wider waxy casts that are seen in advanced chronic kidney disease . It implies dilation of the tubules .694

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for chronic kidney disease ?

options.d: Large for gestational age at birth

mcqs.explanation: Small for gestational age (SGA) at birth is a risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD), not LGA. Important risk factors for CKD or chronic renal failure are: • SGA • Childhood obesity702 • Hypertension • Diabetes mellitus • Autoimmune disease • Family history of kidney disease • Previous episode of acute kidney injury • Structural abnormalities of the urinary tract • Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD). The leading causes of CKD in decreasing order of frequency are as follows : • Diabetic nephropathy • Glomerulonephritis • Hypertension -associated CKD • ADPKD (Adult or autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to develop chronic renal failure?
mcqs.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is least likely to cause chronic renal failure. It is a rapidly progressive condition and a cause of acute renal failure.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following parameters are used in the staging of chronic kidney disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD) are stratified by estimated GFR (eGFR) and degree of albuminuria in order to predict the risk of progression of CKD. Serum creatinine is not directly used in the staging of chronic kidney disease .Stages of Chronic Kidney Dis ease based on GFR Stage GFR(ml/min/1.73sq. mt) Description \03790 Normal or increased GFR wit h other evidence of Kidney D amage703 Stages of Chronic Kidney Dis ease based on GFR 60-89 Slight decrease in GFR, with other evidence of kidney dam age 3A 45-59 Moderate decrease in GFR wi th or without other evidence of Kidney Damage 3B 30-44 15-29 Severe decrease in GFR, with or without other evidence of kidney damage <15 Established renal failure, also known asEnd-Stage Renal D isease

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease , at which stage do the complications of kidney failure start appearing?
mcqs.explanation: The features of kidney failure become prominent as the GFR progressively declines to stages 3 and 4. The following complications occur as a result of loss of kidney function: • Volume overload • Hyperkalemia • Metabolic acidosis • Hyperphosphatemia • Mineral and bone disorders • Hypertension704 • Anemia • Dyslipidemia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old woman is being evaluated for new-onset uremic encephalopathy . What is her GFR likely to be?
mcqs.explanation: Clinical features of uremia start to appear in patients with GFR < 15 mL /min/1.73 m2 or end-stage renal disease (ESRD). By this stage , renal clearance is severely impaired and the accumulation of uremic toxins leads to several complications including: • Uremic encephalopathy • Pruritus • Malnutrition • Anorexia, nausea, fatigue • Platelet dysfunction • Sexual dysfunction • Pericarditis, pleuritis • Peripheral neuropathyStages of Chronic Kidney Dis easeStag e GFR(ml/ min/ 1.73 m2 ) Description \03790 Normal or increased GFR wit h other evidence of Kidney D amage 2 60-89 A slight decrease in GFR, wit h other evidence of kidney da mage 3A 45-59 Moderate decrease in GFR wi th or without other evidence of Kidney Damage 3B 30-44 4 15-29 Severe decrease in GFR, with or without other evidence of kidney damage <15 End-stage renal disease705

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about uremic syndrome?

options.a: It occurs due to accumulation of toxins
options.b: There is loss of kidney function and hormone regulation
options.d: Can be eliminated by removing urea through intensive dialysis

mcqs.explanation: Uremic syndrome cannot be eliminated by removing urea alone. It is a complex condition occurring due to the accumulation of multiple toxins. The pathophysiology of uremic syndrome involves the following : • Accumulation of toxins (uremia) - urea, creatinine, other products of protein metabolism like urates, hippurates , polyamines , indoles. • Loss of kidney function leading to fluid and electrolyte imbalance and hormone dysregulation . • Progressive systemic inflammation with vascular and nutritional impairment. Clinical features secondary to loss of kidney function tend to develop in parallel with declining GFR. However the features of uremia and, hence , uremic syndrome, usually occur only in stage 5 or ESRD.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man with CKD has been on dialysis for 3 months. He now presents with intense body pains and muscle pain. He suffered from 2 fractures over the last 2 months. On evaluation, he was found to have decreased PTH levels and normal calcium levels . He has been regularly taking oral vitamin D and calcium tablets . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario in a CKD patient is suggestive of adynamic bone disease . In CKD, metabolic bone disorders (renal osteodystrophy ) can be of three types :Osteitis fibrosa cystica Osteomalacia Adynamic bone disease High bone turnover Low bone turnover Low bone turnover Renal calcium loss Decreased calcitriol formatio n leads to low calcium It is aniatrogenicconditionInc reased intake ofvitamin Dorc alcium-containingphosphate binders or dialysis .706 Osteitis fibrosa cystica Osteomalacia Adynamic bone disease High PTH occurs in response to low calcium (secondary hy perparathyroidism) Low vitamin D leads todefect ivemineralizationDecreased c alcium leads to a mild increa se in PTH , which stimulates osteoblasts . Thus thebone vol umeismaintained . High vitamin D decreases P TH levels , which leads todecr eased bone volume.Mineraliz ationisdefectivebecause of al uminium, which comes from dialysis . Treatment:Vitamin D + calci um Treatment:Vitamin D + calci um Treatment:Withdrawal of off ending agent

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman with chronic kidney disease presents to the OPD with exercise intolerance, fatigue , and shortness of breath. On examination, she is found to have severe pallor. Which of the following is least likely to be a cause for these findings?
mcqs.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is not a feature of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Common causes of anemia in CKD include : • Erythropoietin deficiency • Diminished red blood cell survival • Bleeding diathesis • Iron deficiency • Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency • Hyperparathyroidism (due to bone marrow fibrosis) • Hemoglobinopathy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in patients with chronic renal failure?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperthyroidism is not a feature of chronic renal failure. Option A: Peripheral neuropathy can occur secondary to uremia. Options C and D: In chronic renal failure, calcitriol (vitamin D3) production is decreased , leading to metabolic bone disease , which in turn leads to low serum calcium levels , secondary hyperparathyroidism , and osteomalacia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common neurological disorder seen in patients with CKD?
mcqs.explanation: The most common neurological disorder seen in patients with CKD is peripheral neuropathy . The various neuromuscular manifestations of CKD include : • Memory and concentration impairment • Dialysis dementia - due to aluminum intoxication707 • Restless leg syndrome • Peripheral neuropathy • Hiccups • Cramps • Uremic encephalopathy • Confusion and lethargy • Tremors • Myoclonus • Asterixis • Seizures • Coma

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman goes to her family doctor as she is unable to fall asleep at night. She complains of tingling and crawling sensations over her legs at night. She also feels a strong urge to move her legs , which relieves the symptoms for a while . Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?

options.c: Most common cause is chronic kidney disease
options.d: Most common movement disorder in pregnancy

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of restless legs syndrome (RLS) or Willis-Ekbom disease . Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is not the most common cause of this condition. RLS is a neurological sleep disorder that can be primary or secondary. The primary form is more common. It shows autosomal dominant inheritance in most cases , but can be idiopathic . Secondary RLS is associated with the following : • Iron deficiency • Pregnancy - most common movement disorder • Peripheral neuropathy • Diabetes mellitus • CKD • Parkinson 's disease • Multiple sclerosis It is characterized by an uncontrollable, restless urge to move the legs . It tends to worsen during periods of inactivity and at evening or night. It is accompanied by crawling, tingling or burning sensations . These symptoms show partial or complete improvement with movement. This cycle may continue for a while and result in insomnia. Primary RLS is managed by improving sleep hygiene and dopamine agonists (pramipexole or ropinirole) if symptoms persist . Iron supplements can also be given. In secondary RLS , the underlying cause must be treated .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most likely cause of convulsions in a patient with CKD?
mcqs.explanation: 708 The most likely cause of convulsions in a patient with CKD is water intoxication. Volume overload in these patients as well as damage to the blood-brain barrier by uremic toxins causes cerebral edema and seizures .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is most common cause of mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients at every stage of CKD.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following would be elevated in patients with chronic kidney disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with elevated levels of fibrinogen. CKD is a pro-inflammatory state characterized by altered levels of acute -phase reactants (APR) • Elevated levels of positive APR like CRP and fibrinogen (associated with high ESR). • Reduced levels of negative APR like albumin and fetuin .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the predominant electrolyte abnormality seen in patients with advanced CKD?
mcqs.explanation: High anion gap metabolic acidosis is the predominant electrolyte abnormality in a patient with advanced CKD. In advanced CKD, impaired renal functioning causes decreased urinary excretion of acids. These retained organic acids result in a high anion gap. In early CKD, potassium retention is associated with bicarbonate loss. This gives rise to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap in early CKD. The following electrolyte abnormalities are seen in CKD: • Hyperkalemia • Hypocalcemia • Hyperphosphatemia • Hyperuricemia • Hypermagnesemia Hypokalemia is uncommon in CKD and usually reflects markedly reduced dietary potassium intake, especially in association with excessive diuretic therapy or concurrent GI losses .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the most life -threatening manifestation of CKD?
mcqs.explanation: Of the given options, hyperkalemia is the most life -threatening complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD) as it can result in cardiac arrhythmias and sudden death .709 CKD is staged based on declining glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and albuminuria. The various clinical manifestations occur due to loss of kidney function and accumulation of various uremic toxins (urea, creatinine, and other products of protein metabolism ). Complications of declining kidney function include : • Volume overload • Hyperkalemia • Metabolic acidosis • Hyperphosphatemia • Mineral and bone disorders • Hypertension • Anemia • Dyslipidemia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Patients with CKD have increased levels of all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Serum estrogen levels are low in CKD patients . This leads to menstrual abnormalities and infertility . Option A: Plasma levels of insulin are elevated in CKD patients due to impaired clearance by the affected kidneys. Hence , insulin dose must be reduced in these patients . Option B: Elevated parathyroid hormone levels in CKD are secondary to derangements in the homeostasis of calcium, phosphate , and vitamin D. Option D: FGF-23 (fibroblast growth factor) is part of a family of phosphatonins that promotes renal phosphate excretion. The levels of this hormone increase early in the course of CKD.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the emergency with chest pain that is radiating to his shoulder , shortness of breath, and diaphoresis . He is a known case of chronic kidney disease . Which of the following investigations is best for diagnosis?

options.b: Troponin levels on admission and 1 hour later
options.c: Troponin and CK-MB levels at admission

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myocardial infarction (MI) in a patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD). A serial rise in cardiac troponin levels over 3-6 hours following presentation is needed to make a diagnosis. An interval of 1-hour is not considered sufficient . Minor chronic elevations in serum troponins are commonly observed in patients with CKD even in the absence of cardiovascular disease. Hence , a single elevated troponin value in such patients cannot be used to diagnose MI. CK-MB is far less sensitive and specific than troponins. Hence , it is not preferred .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most sensitive test to detect early diabetic nephropathy in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 710 Microalbuminuria is the most sensitive and earliest finding of diabetic nephropathy . It refers to urine albumin of 30–300 mg/24-hour urine. It is seen in the stage of incipient diabetic kidney disease . However, microalbuminuria is a very variable finding and is not required to diagnose nephropathy. Non-albuminuric diabetic nephropathy may occur in some patients and regression of albuminuria may be seen in type 1 diabetics . Diabetic nephropathy can be diagnosed if the following are satisfied : • Reduced GFR (< 60 mL /min/1.73 m2 ) with or without persistent albuminuria (> 30 mg/day or urine PCR > 30 mg/g) • Long duration of diabetes or established diabetic retinopathy • Other etiologies are ruled out

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease is found to have normal -sized kidneys on ultrasonography. Which of the following diagnoses is least likely?
mcqs.explanation: Hypertensive nephropathy is unlikely in this patient as it usually presents with shrunken kidneys. Longstanding CKD due to most causes results in bilaterally small kidneys. Causes of CKD with normal size kidneys are: • Diabetic nephropathy (kidney size may be increased at the onset ) • Amyloidosis • HIV nephropathy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
