mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Auscultation of a patient with pleuritic chest pain revealed a patch of dullness with increased vocal fremitus beneath the angle of the left scapula . What is this sign called ?
mcqs.explanation: A patch of dullness with increased vocal fremitus beneath the angle of the left scapula due to the compression of the base of the lung by the pericardial fluid is called Ewart's sign. It is seen in pericardial effusion . Acute pericarditis is frequently associated with pericardial effusion . Option A: Auenbrugger 's sign is the bulging of the epigastrium in severe pericardial effusion . Option B: Moschcowitz 's sign is the abrupt transition in percussion from the lungs to the right heart border seen in pericardial effusion . Option C: Dressler's sign is the dullness to percussion of the lower half of the sternum seen in pericardial effusion .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of Beck's triad?
mcqs.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus is not part of Beck's triad. Pulsus paradoxus is seen in cardiac tamponade . However, it is not a part of Beck's triad. Beck's triad is seen in cardiac tamponade and it includes : • Hypotension • Soft or absent heart sounds • Jugular venous distension Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space significant enough to cause an obstruction to the inflow of blood to the ventricles. This reduces cardiac output and arterial pressure causing hypotension . This also causes a greater than the normal reduction in the systolic arterial blood pressure producing pulsus paradoxus. Pulsus paradoxus refers to the fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration. Other causes of pulsus paradoxus include : • Massive pulmonary embolism • Tension pneumothorax • Severe obstructive lung disease • Hemorrhagic shock The echocardiography clip below shows the swinging heart sign, which is characteristic of cardiac tamponade.1013

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax?
mcqs.explanation: The differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax is breath sounds. The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade . The presence of hypotension , distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) suggest a cardiac tamponade . These features can also be seen in tension pneumothorax. Other clinical features pointing towards tension pneumothorax are absent breath sounds , hyper resonance to percussion , and shift of the mediastinum to the contralateral side . Heart sounds can be muffled by structures between the stethoscope and the heart, eg , adipose tissue deposition (obesity ), fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion , pleural effusion ), gas accumulation (pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema ), soft tissue masses can lead to attenuation of heart sounds .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An intern is asked to measure the blood pressure of a patient with cardiac tamponade . He/she should ask the patient to:
mcqs.explanation: The patient with cardiac tamponade is asked to breathe normally to elicit pulsus paradoxus. In a patient with cardiac tamponade , both ventricles share an incompressible pericardial covering due to the fluid . As the right ventricle enlarges during inspiration, the interventricular septum bulges into the left ventricle, reducing the left ventricular volume. This results in reduced stroke volume and hence reduced systolic arterial pressure . As a result , there is a greater than normal (more than 10 mmHg) fall in systolic arterial blood pressure during inspiration, producing pulsus paradoxus. This cannot be elicited if the patient is holding his/her breath, taking long or shallow breaths.1014 Pulsus paradoxus is also seen with effusive constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy and right ventricular myocardial infarction.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An RTA victim is brought with breathing difficulty . On examination, the following is noted . Which of the following JVP findings is most likely to be seen in this patient ?

options.a: Absent x and prominent y descent
options.b: Prominent x and absent y descent

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds , and elevated JVP (Beck's triad) suggest a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade . The JVP finding most likely to be seen is prominent x descent and absent y descent .Note : JVP in constrictive pericarditis is characterized by prominent x and y descents .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with dizziness and breathing difficulty came to the emergency department . The ECG is given below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The ECG shows electrical alternans with sinus tachycardia. This along with the patient 's symptoms suggests a likely diagnosis of cardiac tamponade . Electrical alternans is the beat -to-beat alternation in the ECG waveform. In cardiac tamponade , this is caused by the periodic swinging motion of the heart in a large pericardial effusion .1015 Feature Cardiac tamponade Constrictive pericarditis Restrictive cardiomyopathy Pulsus paradoxus +++ + +/- (Rare) JVP Prominent x desce nt +++ + +++ Prominent y descent - ++ + Kussmaul 's sign - + +/- (Rare) Pericardial knock - ++ - Third heart sound - - + Electrical alternans ++ - - Thickened and calcified perica rdium - +++ -

mcqs.question: A 25-year-old road traffic accident victim presents with chest pain and breathlessness . On examination , his BP was 80/60mmHg.On inspection , his neck veins were distended and on auscultation , his heart sounds were muffled . Which of the following clinical features is likely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The symptoms and signs suggest a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade . mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A young motorist sustained injuries in a road traffic accident . He was found to have fractures of multiple ribs anteriorly on both sides. Radial and femoral fractures were also present . On examination, the following was noted . What should be the immediate intervention?

options.c: Intercostal tube drainage on both sides

mcqs.explanation: The presence of hypotension , distended jugular veins, and absence of heart sounds (Beck's triad) are suggestive of cardiac tamponade. An urgent pericardial tap needs to be done to relieve the tension on the heart chambers. Although these features could be seen in tension pneumothorax as well , the presence of adequate bilateral air entry excludes this diagnosis. Pericardiocentesis , also known as pericardial tap, can be performed with sub-xiphoid, parasternal, or apical approaches . The most common approach is a sub-xiphoid approach under echocardiographic guidance . Option A: Rapid blood transfusion is needed in massive blood loss indicated by hypotension . Although this patient presents with hypotension , it is most likely a result of cardiac tamponade . Although blood transfusion is indicated , it will be effective only when the pericardial tap decompresses the pericardium. Option C: Intercostal tube drainage is done in tension pneumothorax. The presence of adequate air entry bilaterally excludes this diagnosis. Option D: The fixation of femur fracture and femoral artery is not a priority here. The inability to palpate pulses distal to the fracture could be a result of hypotension . This needs to be explored only if the patient fails to improve after the pericardial tap and blood transfusion.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: You're an intern examining a patient in the ICU. While assessing the JVP , you notice a lack of fall during inspiration. Which of the following conditions would you not consider as a differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A rise or a lack of fall in JVP with inspiration is known as Kussmaul 's sign. It is not seen in cardiac tamponade. Normally, in inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure and increased intrathoracic volume , the capacity of the right heart increases and the JVP falls. In conditions where the myocardium or pericardium is poorly compliant, it does not allow the right heart chambers to accommodate more blood and this fall is not seen . In fact, due to an increase in venous return during inspiration, the JVP might rise. This is called Kussmaul 's sign. This is seen in: • Restrictive cardiomyopathy • Constrictive pericarditis • Massive pulmonary embolism • Right ventricular infarcts1017 • Advanced cases of left ventricular systolic failure Kussmaul 's sign is not seen in patients with cardiac tamponade because even though the increase in pericardial pressure exerts an inward force compressing the entire heart during inspiration, the increase in negative intrathoracic pressure is still transmitted to the right side of the heart. This allows for an increase in blood flow to the right atrium. Therefore, the JVP falls as seen in normal conditions.Feature Cardiac tamponade Constrictive pericarditis Restrictive cardiomyopathy Pulsus paradoxus +++ + +/- (Rare) JVP Prominent x desce nt +++ ++ +++ Prominent y descent - ++ + Kussmaul 's sign - +++ +/- (Rare) Pericardial knock - ++ - Third heart sound - - + Electrical alternans ++ - - Thickened and calcified perica rdium - +++ -

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old man presents to the emergency department with respiratory distress and hypotension following a trauma. He has subcutaneous emphysema and there is an absence of air entry into the right side of the lungs . What is the next best step ?

options.a: Start IV fluids with large bore cannula
options.b: Needle decompression into the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
options.c: Take the patient to the ICU and intubate him

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a young male developing respiratory distress with hypotension , subcutaneous emphysema , and unilaterally absent air entry is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. The immediate next step , in this case, would be needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line (as the patient is an adult ). In children, the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is chosen as the site for needle decompression. Needle decompression turns a tension pneumothorax into an open pneumothorax. It has to be followed by tube thoracostomy. An intercostal chest drain (ICD) tube is inserted in the triangle of safety , just anterior to the midaxillary line on the side of the lung injury. The site of insertion is the same in both children and adults . The triangle of safety is bounded by the lateral border of the pectoralis major anteriorly, the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi posteriorly , and the fifth intercostal space inferiorly, with the apex below the axilla. This provides a safe landmark for the insertion of an ICD with minimal risk of tissue injury.1018 Tension pneumothorax is a condition where air accumulates in the pleural space due to a one-way valve air leak, leading to the collapse of the affected lung. This can cause a mediastinal shift, compression of the opposite lung, and decreased venous return, resulting in obstructive shock. It commonly occurs during positive -pressure mechanical ventilation, but can also happen after chest trauma, subclavian/internal jugular venous catheter insertion, or chest wall defects . The diagnosis is clinical, and immediate treatment is necessary without waiting for radiological confirmation. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea , tachycardia, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the side of injury, absent breath sounds on the affected side , cyanosis, and neck vein distention . Patients can also develop subcutaneous emphysema as a complication secondary to the pneumothorax.1019

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of frequent exacerbations of COPD is undergoing right heart catheterization for evaluation of pulmonary artery pressure . What is the mean pulmonary arterial pressure above which the diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension can be made?
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a pathological hemodynamic condition characterized by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP ) >20mmHg assessed by right heart catheterization . Pulmonary hypertension could be a complication of cardiac or pulmonary disease or a primary disorder of small pulmonary arteries. Right heart catheterization is the gold standard investigation in diagnosing pulmonary hypertension . Note : The threshold for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension has been revised from >25 mmHg to >20 mmHg to enable earlier detection .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following genes is the most commonly implicated in hereditary pulmonary arterial hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2 ) mutation is the most commonly implicated gene in hereditary pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The BMPR2 receptor is involved in the regulation of growth , differentiation , and apoptosis of pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells . Due to the mutation, there is enhanced proliferation and reduced apoptosis of vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells leading to pulmonary hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a feature of pulmonary arterial hypertension ?

options.a: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure >20 mm Hg
options.b: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure \026 25 mm Hg

mcqs.explanation: 1022 Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP ) \026 15 mm Hg is a feature of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The table below shows the hemodynamic classification of pulmonary hypertension . mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient diagnosed with pulmonary hypertension , which of the following is an unlikely finding on a chest X-ray?
mcqs.explanation: A focal area of oligemia or Westermark 's sign is seen in pulmonary embolism. The signs seen on chest radiograph in pulmonary hypertension are: • Enlargement of central pulmonary arteries • Rapid tapering of vessels known as vascular pruning • Right ventricular enlargementThe ECG shows features of RV strain in patients with PH. The pulmonary function tests show a reduction in DLCO in PAH.1023

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Echocardiography was done for a patient who presented with severe exertional dyspnea , chest pain, and occasional fainting spells . It revealed a mitral valve area of 1 sq cm, elevated LA pressure , and significant RV hypertrophy with TR . Which is the next best step in the evaluation of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, a mitral valve area of 1 sq cm suggests severe mitral stenosis . This leads to elevated LA pressure and subsequently pulmonary hypertension . Due to pulmonary hypertension , there is compensatory RV hypertrophy (right ventricular-pulmonary hypertension coupling ) and secondary TR . The next step should be to confirm pulmonary hypertension . Right heart catheterization is the gold standard test for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension . Option A: Cardiac MRI is considered the gold standard for assessing RV function. In the case of pulmonary hypertension , it is used for serial follow -ups due to its non-invasive nature. Options B and D: CT angiography and ventilation/perfusion scan are done when pulmonary hypertension is suspected to be due to pulmonary embolism, coagulation disorders, or past history of thrombosis (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension ) which should be followed by right heart catheterization .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old female patient presents with gradually worsening shortness of breath, fatigue , and exertional chest pain. On auscultation , a loud P2 is heard. Pulmonary function tests reveal an isolated reduction in DLCO. Her family history is positive for similar findings in other members and genetic testing has revealed a mutation in the BMPR2 gene . Based on suspicion , which of the following therapies is this patient most likely to benefit from?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension . Vasodilator therapy would be beneficial in this patient . Endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, and prostacyclins are examples of vasodilators. Option A: Since pulmonary arterial hypertension is a vascular disorder, bronchodilation is not beneficial . Option C: Nitric oxide is a vasodilator and inhibitors of nitric oxide would worsen the disease in pulmonary arterial hypertension . Option D: Immunosuppressants are not useful in pulmonary arterial hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following group of drugs can not be used in the management of a patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: ACE inhibitors are not used in pulmonary arterial hypertension .1024

mcqs.question: Aortic aneurysms caused by spondyloarthropathies are most commonly seen in:
mcqs.explanation: 1029 Aortic aneurysms caused by spondyloarthropathies are most commonly seen in the ascending aorta. An aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of a segment of a blood vessel . An aortic aneurysm occurs when the structural components of the aortic wall, that is, elastin and collagen , are damaged . This may occur either due to degradation or abnormal synthesis of these components . mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: What is the most common pathology associated with ascending aortic aneurysm?
mcqs.explanation: The most common pathology associated with ascending aortic aneurysm is medial degeneration . Medial degeneration (cystic medial necrosis) describes the degenerative process of the tunica media of the aorta. There is degeneration of collagen and elastic fibers in the media and loss of medial cells that are replaced by multiple clefts of mucoid material, such as proteoglycans . It is seen in the following conditions and is associated with the corresponding mutations: • Marfan's syndrome- fibrillin 11030 • Loeys-Dietz syndrome- TGFBR1 , TGFBR2 • Ehlers -Danlos syndrome type IV - type III procollagen • Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes- genes associated with actin and myosin eg . ACTA2 , MHC11 • Congenital bicuspid aortic valves • Turner 's syndrome • Hypertension

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man who is a known case of Marfan's syndrome has come for his regular check-up. His chest X-ray is shown below . Following this, he is being taken up for echocardiography to evaluate the given finding further. Which of the following is true regarding the management of this patient ?

options.a: Operative repair if diameter is > 5 cm
options.b: Operative repair if diameter is > 6 cm
options.c: Operative repair if diameter is > 5.5 cm
options.d: Operative repair if diameter is > 4 cm

mcqs.explanation: The X-ray shows a widening of the mediastinum with trachea displaced to the right and dilatation of the ascending thoracic aorta (red arrow) i.e. ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm. In the case of Marfan's syndrome, ascending aortic aneurysm of 4-5 cm is taken up for operative repair. This is because of a higher rate of expansion of the aneurysm in these patients . Management of thoracic aortic aneurysm: • Beta-blockers and angiotensin receptor antagonists reduce the rate of expansion, especially in Marfan's syndrome. • Operative treatment is indicated in: • All symptomatic cases • Ascending aortic aneurysm - \037 5.5 cm in diameter or growth rate of >0.5 cm/year • Descending aortic aneurysm - > 6 cm in diameter or growth rate of >1 cm/year • Marfan's syndrome - 4-5 cm in diameter

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man came with complaints of irregular bowel movements. While undergoing an abdominal ultrasound examination, an abdominal aortic aneurysm of 5.8 cm diameter was noted . There is a history of hyperlipidemia for the past 10 years. What is the next best step in the management of AAA?

options.d: Follow up with serial abdominal ultrasound

mcqs.explanation: Operative repair of the aneurysm is the next best step in management in this case. Operative repair is indicated for both symptomatic or asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysms if they are \037 5.5 cm in diameter . Abdominal aortic aneurysms are mostly asymptomatic and are detected as incidental findings on investigations for other complaints. Sometimes , they present with pain and pulsatile abdominal mass. Rupture of aneurysm presents with acute pain and hypotension . Management of abdominal aortic aneurysms: • Statins- atherosclerosis is the most common pathology associated with abdominal aortic aneurysms. Hence , statins are prescribed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events. • Asymptomatic aneurysms <5.5 cm in diameter - serial abdominal ultrasound to monitor the rate of expansion of the aneurysm. • Operative repair is indicated for:1031 • Aneurysm of any size associated with symptoms • Rapidly growing aneurysms • Aneurysms \0375.5 cm in diameter Note : Medical management with beta -blockers though helps in BP control, it is not effective in reducing the rate of growth of abdominal aortic aneurysms. mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old patient came to the OPD with a complaint of abdominal pain. On further investigations, he was found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which of the following investigations may indicate the etiology of the aneurysm?
mcqs.explanation: Blood cultures may indicate the etiology of the aneurysm. They are often positive in patients with mycotic aneurysms. A mycotic aneurysm is a rare condition that develops as a result of staphylococcal , streptococcal, salmonella or other bacterial or fungal infections of the aorta. The term mycotic aneurysm is usually a misnomer as the causative pathogen is usually bacteria rather than fungi. These aneurysms are usually saccular. These organisms may involve every major artery, but aortic involvement predominates .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: All of the following are predisposing factors for aortic dissection , except :
mcqs.explanation: The third trimester of pregnancy is a predisposing factor for aortic dissection , not second . Predisposition to aortic dissection increases when there are factors associated with: • Medial degeneration - seen in: • Syndromes affecting the connective tissue - Marfan's, Ehlers Danlos syndrome • Vasculitis- Takayasu's arteritis, giant cell arteritis1032 • Increased stress on the aortic wall- seen in: • Hypertension • Third trimester of pregnancy • Other conditions with increased incidence include : • Bicuspid aortic valve • Coarctation of aorta • Aortic trauma • Cocaine use

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presents with acute pain in the chest which radiates to the interscapular region of the back. He is a known hypertensive for the past 10 years. His CT is shown below . Which of the following drug is contraindicated in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the CT image showing double -lumen of the aorta are suggestive of aortic dissection. Isolated use of a direct vasodilator such as hydralazine is contraindicated in acute dissection . It is because these agents can increase hydraulic shear and worsen the dissection by causing vasodilation without reducing the left ventricular ejection force that continues to weaken the arterial wall. Medical therapy for aortic dissection includes beta -blockers and sodium nitroprusside to reduce cardiac contractility and blood pressure. The heart rate is reduced to around 60 bpm and the SBP is lowered to \026 120mmHg . CCBs like verapamil and diltiazem may be used IV if nitroprusside or beta -blockers cannot be employed . Parenteral angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor such as enalaprilat may be considered .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: The image depicting Stanford type A aortic dissection is?
mcqs.explanation: Image D depicts Stanford type A aortic dissection . The classification schemes for aortic dissection are: • Stanford classification • Type A - dissection involves the ascending aorta with or without the involvement of other parts of the aorta • Type B - dissection is limited to the arch and/or descending aorta without the involvement of ascending aorta • DeBakey classification • Type I - dissection involves ascending to descending aorta • Type II - dissection is limited to the ascending aorta or transverse aorta without descending aorta1033 • Type III - intimal tear is located in the descending aorta with distal propagation of the dissectionHence , if the ascending aorta is involved, it is Stanford type A and DeBakey type I or II . If only the aortic arch or the descending aorta is involved, it is Stanford type B and DeBakey type III . From a management standpoint , the classification of aortic dissections into type A or B is more practical and useful , since DeBakey types I and II are managed in a similar manner .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presents with a history of severe pain and numbness in his calf muscles following morning walks. The symptoms subside on taking rest. On examination, thickened toenails , decreased pulses , and reduced temperature of the legs are noted . He has a history of smoking for the past 20 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario describes intermittent claudication . It is the most common symptom of peripheral arterial disease (PAD). The most appropriate advice for this patient is antiplatelet therapy with aspirin. PAD occurs due to atherosclerotic plaques causing stenosis and occlusion of blood flow . The symptoms of inadequate blood flow exacerbate during increased physical activity. The following advice is given to patients with PAD: • Lifestyle modification- regular exercise , discontinue smoking • Statins to treat hypercholesterolemia • Reducing the risk of cardiovascular events: • Controlling hypertension - angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta -blockers • Antiplatelet therapy - aspirin, clopidogrel • Revascularization procedures (catheter-based or surgical)- For patients not improving with medical therapy • Endovascular interventions- percutaneous transluminal balloon angioplasty (PTA ), stent placement , atherectomy1034 • Surgical- aortobifemoral bypass using Dacron grafts, axillofemoral bypass , femoro-femoral bypass Antiplatelet therapy and warfarin is not preferred because of the high risk of bleeding . Intravenous heparin is used to treat acute limb ischemia which most often occurs due to thromboembolic events . Acute limb ischemia presents with loss of pulses distal to the occlusion , cyanosis, or pallor. These symptoms do not subside on taking rest. Hence , this patient has intermittent claudication and not acute limb ischemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: Which of the following collagen vascular diseases has the strongest association with Raynaud's phenomenon ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given collagen vascular diseases , systemic sclerosis has the strongest association with Raynaud's phenomenon . Raynaud's phenomenon occurs in: • 80–90% of patients with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). • % of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). • 30% of patients with dermatomyositis or polymyositis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: Diseases of Aorta and Peripheral Arteries
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman complains of bluish discoloration of her fingertips on exposure to cold. Which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Raynaud's phenomenon . Clonidine is avoided in Raynaud's phenomenon as it worsens the condition. Clonidine acts on central alpha-2 adrenoreceptor in CNS and reduces sympathetic outflow . This causes decreased blood pressure and perfusion that can exacerbate Raynaud's phenomenon or any PVD . Drugs that can be used for the treatment of Raynaud's phenomenon : Primary Raynaud's: • Dihydropyridine CCBs- nifedipine , isradipine, felodipine , and amlodipine • Diltiazem • Prazosin , doxazosin, and terazosin Secondary Raynaud's: • Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors- sildenafil and tadalafil Digital sympathectomy is helpful in some patients who are unresponsive to medical therapy .1035

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient was brought to the emergency with complaints of chest pain, hemoptysis , and severe dyspnea. CT scan showed vessel sign suggestive of pulmonary infarction. Which among the following is typically responsible for this?
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary infarction as suggested by CT is typically due to a small pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary infarction occurs when small thrombi lodge in the segmental and subsegmental vessels . These patients most often have pleuritic chest pain as the site where the thrombus lodges are near the innervation of pleural nerves. Massive pulmonary emboli and saddle emboli that occlude the main pulmonary artery cause hypotension and shock as opposed to infarction. These are caused by larger-sized emboli that lodge more proximally in the pulmonary circulation. Pulmonary embolism is classified based on the degree of reduction of pulmonary vascular blood flow and associated hemodynamic disturbances : • Massive: Hypotension lasting for >15 minutes or BP maintained with inotropes . • Submassive: No hypotension , but features of cardiac injury present . • Non-massive: No hypotension or features of cardiac injury. CT findings associated with pulmonary infarction include a feeding vessel or vessel sign as shown below . It depicts a distinct vessel feeding directly to a lesion, usually of hematogenous origin. However, it is not specific for pulmonary infarction.1042

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with a suspected pulmonary embolism underwent a chest X-ray. It showed an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery. What is this sign called ?
mcqs.explanation: Enlarged right descending pulmonary artery on a chest X-ray in pulmonary embolism is called Palla's sign. The black pleura sign is seen in alveolar pulmonary microlithiasis. It refers to the shadow of the pleura between the extensive alveolar calcification and the adjacent rib cage .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Echocardiography in a patient with pulmonary embolism revealed akinesia of the right ventricular free wall with normal motion at the right ventricular apex. What is this sign called ?
mcqs.explanation: The sign described is called McConnell's sign. It demonstrates right ventricular dysfunction as akinesia of the right ventricular free wall with normal motion at the right ventricular apex. It is the best -known indirect sign of pulmonary embolism on transthoracic echocardiography. Moses ' (Bancroft's), Homan's, and Lowenberg's signs are seen in venous thrombosis. They're not specific to pulmonary embolism.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following biomarker is least likely to be elevated in a patient with pulmonary embolism?
mcqs.explanation: NGAL (Neutrophil gelatinase -associated lipocalin) is a kidney injury marker and not a cardiac injury marker. The following are biomarkers of cardiac injury in pulmonary embolism: • Plasma brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) • Heart-type fatty acid binding protein1043 • Troponins . Serum troponin and plasma heart-type fatty acid-binding protein levels increase because of right ventricular microinfarction . Myocardial stretch causes the release of brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-proBNP.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is likely to show increased D-dimer values?
mcqs.explanation: All of the conditions mentioned above have raised D-dimer levels . D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product . Plasma D-dimer levels commonly rise in DVT and pulmonary embolism due to the breakdown of fibrin by plasmin. D-dimer is more sensitive to pulmonary embolism than DVT . The sensitivity of D-dimer levels in the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism is > 95% but it is is not specific for pulmonary embolism. Normal D-dimer rules out pulmonary embolism in low and intermediate -risk patients . Patients with a high risk of PE should undergo a CT pulmonary angiogram to effectively rule out PE. Conditions which have raised D-dimer levels include : • Myocardial infarction • Pneumonia • Sepsis • Cancer • Postoperative state • Pregnancy- second and third trimester

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset pain in the right leg . The pain is associated with swelling , redness , and tenderness . Which of the following is false regarding the management of this condition?

options.a: Recurrence of this condition despite intensive anticoagulation is an indication for IVC filter
options.b: IVC filters can prevent recurrent PE in patients of right heart failure
options.c: IVC filters reduce the rate of recurrence of this condition
options.d: Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy is done in patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension

mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of deep vein thrombosis (DVT ). IVC filters increase the rate of recurrence of DVT (by providing a nidus for clot formation) even though they usually prevent pulmonary embolism (over the short term). The two principal indications for insertion of an IVC filter are: • Active bleeding (prevents the use of anticoagulation ) • Recurrent venous thrombosis despite intensive anticoagulation Prevention of recurrent PE in patients with right heart failure who are not candidates for fibrinolysis and prophylaxis of extremely high-risk patients are some other indications for filter placement . Patients impaired by dyspnea due to chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension should be considered for pulmonary thromboendarterectomy .1044

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A resident is evaluating a patient , who presented with acute onset of chest pain and dyspnea , for pulmonary embolism. Which of the following imaging test should be performed to confirm this diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: CT pulmonary angiography should be performed as it is the principal imaging test for the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE). Option A: Most patients with acute PE have normal echocardiograms. However, echocardiography is a very useful diagnostic tool for detecting conditions that may mimic PE, such as acute myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade , and aortic dissection . Option C: Ventilation-perfusion (V /Q) scanning has become a second -line diagnostic test for PE, used mostly for patients who cannot tolerate intravenous contrast or in whom the CT results are inconclusive. Option D: MR pulmonary angiography may detect large proximal PE but is not reliable for smaller segmental and subsegmental PE. It is used when neither CT angiography nor ventilation-perfusion scan can be done. The images below demonstrate a pulmonary embolus (marked by arrows). The image of the gross specimen shows saddle thromboembolism.1045

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis in his right limb. Which of the following parameters is a part of Well's criteria that assess the clinical likelihood of pulmonary embolism in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Hemoptysis is a parameter in Well's criteria used to assess the likelihood of pulmonary embolism.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with a Well's score of 1.5, which of the following should be the initial investigation?
mcqs.explanation: A patient with Well's score of 1.5 has a low probability of pulmonary embolism. The initial investigation should be the measurement of D-dimer levels . In a patient with a high probability of pulmonary embolism, the initial investigation is CT pulmonary angiography.1046

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an indication for fibrinolytic therapy in a patient diagnosed with massive pulmonary embolism?
mcqs.explanation: For fibrinolysis (thrombolytic therapy ) in massive pulmonary embolism, the only widely accepted indication is persistent hypotension or shock. It is defined as SBP <90mmHg or a decrease in SBP by \03740 mmHg from baseline for >15 minutes . Alteplase or recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), streptokinase , and urokinase are approved for the treatment of PE. tPA is the most commonly used fibrinolytic, but it is not superior to other agents . Pulmonary embolism is classified based on the degree of reduction of pulmonary vascular blood flow and associated hemodynamic disturbances : • Massive: Hypotension lasting for >15 minutes or BP maintained with inotropes . • Submassive: No hypotension , but features of cardiac injury present . • Non-massive: No hypotension or features of cardiac injury. Contraindications for thrombolysis: • Haemorrhagic stroke • Ischemic stroke in the last 6 months • CNS tumours • Major surgery/trauma in the last 3 weeks • Active bleeding • Bleeding diathesis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old woman with SLE, secondary anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome develops pulmonary embolism. After admission, she is started on anticoagulants . For how long should the anticoagulation therapy be continued ?
mcqs.explanation: 1047 Duration of anticoagulation for DVT and venous thromboembolism secondary to antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLA) is lifelong . Duration of anticoagulation for DVT and venous thromboembolism:Clinical Scenario Duration of Anticoagulation DVT isolated to an upper ext remity or calf that has been p rovoked by surgery, trauma, estrogen , or an indwelling ce ntral venous catheter or pace maker 3 months Provoked proximal leg DVT o r PE 3 to 6 months For patients with cancer and VTE Prescribe LMW heparinConti nue anticoagulation indefinit ely unless the patient is rend ered cancer-free Idiopathic unprovoked VTE Indefinite Antiphospholipid antibody sy ndrome Indefinite

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drug was recently approved by FDA for the extended prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism in hospitalized medically ill patients ?
mcqs.explanation: Betrixaban is a new oral, once-daily factor Xa inhibitor approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for extended -duration prophylaxis of VTE in acute medically ill patients . In patients with no obvious risk factors for VTE , early ambulation with or without mechanical methods (pneumatic compression stockings or venous foot pump ) should be advised. In patients with one risk factor for VTE with no risk of bleeding , LMWH is preferred . In presence of renal failure/cost issues , unfractionated heparin is used . In the case of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia , fondaparinux is preferred . In patients with multiple risk factors, increasing the dose of anticoagulants or using a mechanical device is advised. For patients with risk factors and a high risk of bleeding or contraindication for anticoagulation , mechanical methods are recommended .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is May-Thurner syndrome?

options.a: Compression of right iliac vein by right iliac artery
options.b: Compression of right iliac vein by left iliac artery
options.c: Compression of left iliac vein by right iliac artery
options.d: Compression of left iliac vein by left iliac artery

mcqs.explanation: May-Thurner syndrome (MTS) is caused when the left iliac vein is compressed by the right iliac artery against the fifth lumbar vertebra. It is also called iliocaval venous compression syndrome, iliac vein compression syndrome, Cockett's syndrome, and venous spur.1048 Most patients have a partial obstruction and are asymptomatic . It can however progress to symptomatic extensive deep vein thrombosis (DVT ). It is a cause of recurrent DVT affecting the left leg .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a patient with a cardio-respiratory compromise. Chest X-ray shows a focal area of oligemia . The ECG of the patient is shown below . Choose the false statement regarding this condition.

options.c: Most common ECG abnormality is sinus tachycardia
options.d: Most preferred preliminary investigation is D-dimer

mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of pulmonary embolism. ECG shows the S1Q3T3 sign (i.e, an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III , and an inverted T wave in lead III ) that is relatively specific but insensitive. The most common sign of pulmonary embolism is tachypnea . Most common symptom of pulmonary embolism is dyspnea . Most common ECG abnormality in pulmonary embolism is sinus tachycardia.Most common preliminary investigation used is D-dimer.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman underwent bariatric surgery. On postoperative day 4, she developed pulmonary embolism as confirmed by a CT pulmonary angiography. Her blood pressure was 70/44 mmHg with poor urine output . IV fluids were administered with dobutamine after which the blood pressure increased to 82/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step to manage this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Surgical pulmonary embolectomy is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient. This patient is suffering from a massive pulmonary embolism. In such cases , thrombolytic therapy is given once diagnosis is made using CT pulmonary angiography or bedside ECHO. But, since this patient underwent a large open abdominal operation (bariatric surgery), thrombolysis is contraindicated due to the increased risk of life -threatening bleeding . Therefore, surgical embolectomy must be done. The main pulmonary arteries are incised , and fresh clots are removed. Contraindications for thrombolysis: • Haemorrhagic stroke • Ischemic stroke in the last 6 months1049 • CNS tumours • Major surgery/trauma in the last 3 weeks • Active bleeding • Bleeding diathesis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old lady was admitted with unprovoked pulmonary embolism from left distal leg DVT . On admission, her coagulation studies were normal . She was started on unfractionated heparin with the first dose of warfarin on the same day.

options.a: Discontinue warfarin and start long term low molecular weight heparin
options.c: Send HIT tests and start argatroban or lepirudin

mcqs.explanation: This patient had suboptimal anticoagulation management. The best approach would be to reinstitute heparin and continue warfarin . The patient had unprovoked PE from lower limb DVT . She was started on warfarin bridged with heparin initially. Warfarin & parenteral anticoagulation need to be overlapped for at least 5 days, independent of the INR achieved during these 5 days in patients with acute venous thromboembolism. Warfarin inhibits protein C, protein S (which is part of the fibrinolytic pathway ) in addition to factors II , VII , IX, X. Protein C has a short half-life (4-6 hours) and thus decreases early. Since protein C is antithrombotic, decreased levels of protein C by warfarin renders the patient hypercoagulable during the first few days of treatment before factor II with a long half-life (36 hours) decreases and protects the patient from thrombosis. Thus warfarin creates a prothrombotic state in the first 5 days putting the patient at risk of progression of thrombosis unless a parenteral anticoagulant is given overlapping warfarin for these days.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old lady is admitted with unprovoked pulmonary embolism. On admission, her PT was 13 .6 seconds (normal 9.6-13 .4 seconds ) and aPTT was 62 seconds (normal 28.2-34.6 seconds ). She has no history of bleeding . Thrombophilia work up was done and she was found to have a strong lupus anticoagulant. How will you manage the patient 's initial anticoagulation ?

options.a: Start intravenous unfractionated heparin with aPTT goal in the upper therapeutic range
options.b: Start intravenous unfractionated heparin and monitor with anti Xa tests
options.c: Start warfarin without heparin bridge because aPTT is already in the therapeutic range
options.d: Start intravenous argatroban and monitor by aPTT

mcqs.explanation: This patient is most probably suffering from antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) as her lupus anticoagulant is strongly positive . In such patients , the initial anticoagulation is with unfractionated heparin and is monitored by anti-Xa tests . Due to the presence of lupus anticoagulant, the lab measurement of aPTT will show erroneously prolonged aPTT . Therefore, even though there is an apparently prolonged aPTT , the patient is at increased risk of thrombosis and not bleeding , and hence patients with APS should be anticoagulated . Anti Xa tests are not influenced by APS. So, the patient can be monitored for the adequacy of anticoagulation with UFH by monitoring anti-Xa. Option A: The patient 's aPTT is already prolonged due to lupus anticoagulant, so we cannot monitor the patient with aPTT after starting unfractionated heparin. Option C: Warfarin in the first few days of therapy , causes a decrease in Protein C & S levels , c ausing a prothrombotic state . Hence , a heparin bridge is necessary for APS which is already a pro-thrombotic state .1050 Option D: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor used in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT ) to prevent thrombosis and also to increase platelet levels . Therapy is monitored with aPTT . Note : Lupus anticoagulant may function as an inhibitor in vitro by binding to the reagent phospholipid and blocking the phospholipid -dependent reactions of the intrinsic pathway . The net effect is a prolongation of the aPTT .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 53-year-old woman underwent hip replacement surgery. A week after the surgery, the patient developed swelling of the legs associated with pain on palpation . Her heart rate is 70 beats per min. There is no history of hemoptysis or significant weight loss. There is no previous history of pulmonary embolism. What is the risk of developing pulmonary embolism in the patient based on Well's score?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of developing pulmonary embolism in this patient is high (Option B) according to the three-tiered Well's clinical risk assessment score. Calculation of Well's score: • Clinical signs of DVT = 3; - swelling of legs , pain on palpation (Moses sign) • No alternative diagnosis = 3 • Heart rate is <100 BPM = 0; - 70 BPM • Surgery in previous 4 weeks = 1.5; - hip replacement surgery 1 week ago • No previous pulmonary embolism = 0 • No Hemoptysis = 0 • No malignancy = 0; - no significant weight loss Total score = 7.5 Risk stratification: • High risk = > 6.0 • Moderate risk = 2.0 to 6.0 • Low risk = <2.0 (in patients with low risk , to further confirm the risk - pulmonary embolism rule -out criteria (PERC) may be referred ) Note : There is no other alternative diagnosis which is more likely in this condition, where there is a clear clinical presentation of a deep vein thrombosis, with the associated risk factors of a recent surgery and immobilization. Hence , 3 points can be added to the score.1051

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man with hemiplegia is brought to the OPD for a follow -up visit. He suffered from a stroke 2 months ago. On examination, he was found to have slurred speech and a positive Babinski sign. Which other examination findings are expected to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given patient has slurred speech and a positive Babinski sign, which is suggestive of an upper motor neuron lesion (UMN lesion). Exaggerated deep tendon reflexes are a feature of UMN lesions . The distal muscle groups are affected more than the proximal muscles and the axial muscles are spared (as the anterior corticospinal tracts supplying the axial muscles have bilateral representation ) in UMN lesions . Axial muscles are involved when the lesion is severe or bilateral. Hypertonia in the form of spasticity is seen in the upper motor neuron lesions . Fasciculations and hypotonia are features of lower motor neuron lesions .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about hypertonia is false ?

options.b: Rigidity is present throughout the range of motion
options.c: Spasticity predominantly affects the extensors of upper limb
options.d: Rigidity affects flexors and extensors equally

mcqs.explanation: Spasticity predominantly affects the antigravity muscles - flexors in the upper limb and extensors in the lower limb.Spasticity Rigidity Seen in lesions of pyramidal t racts Seen in lesions of the extrapy ramidal tracts such as rubros pinal and vestibulospinal trac ts Velocity dependent - More no ticeable with fast movements Present throughout range of motion without change in int ensity Clasp -knife phenomenon - su dden release after reaching m aximum Lead pipe or plastic stiffness Predominantly affects antigra vity muscles Affects flexors and extensors equally

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with pseudobulbar palsy?
mcqs.explanation: Jaw jerk is brisk in pseudobulbar palsy . Bilateral corticobulbar lesions produce pseudobulbar palsy . This condition is characterized by dysarthria, dysphagia , dysphonia , emotional lability , bilateral facial weakness , and brisk jaw jerk. Damage to lower motor neurons of the cranial nerves in the brainstem is called bulbar palsy . Depressed jaw jerk is seen in bulbar palsy . Pseudobulbar palsy is analogous to UMN lesions exhibiting hyperreflexia . Bulbar palsy is analogous to LMN lesions exhibiting hyporeflexia .1058

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Match the following pairs of reflexes and their root values:
mcqs.explanation: The correct match is:Reflex Root val ue Biceps C5, C6 Cremaste ric L1 , L2 Knee L3 , L4 Plantar L5 - S2 Ankle S1, S2

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: All of the following drugs have to be stopped before a lumbar puncture , except :
mcqs.explanation: Aspirin and other NSAIDs can be continued in a patient who is scheduled to undergo a lumbar puncture (LP). These drugs have not shown an increased risk of developing spinal hematomas. Hence an LP can be performed in patients receiving these drugs. Options A and B: Abciximab and eptifibatide are Gp IIb / IIIa inhibitors. Platelet aggregation remains abnormal following the discontinuation of these drugs. LP , spinal and epidural procedures must be avoided until the platelet function is normal . Option D: Rivaroxaban is an oral factor Xa inhibitor. LP should be avoided in patients receiving this drug due to the risk of developing epidural or spinal hematomas. Other factor Xa inhibitors, namely, fondaparinux and apixaban must also be held prior to LP , spinal and epidural procedures .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A pathologist received a blood-tinged CSF sample for evaluation. The sample was subjected to centrifugation and the following finding was observed. What is the least likely differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows xanthochromatic CSF on centrifugation . This is unlikely with a traumatic tap. A traumatic tap has clear supernatant following CSF centrifugation . Xanthochromia refers to the yellowish appearance of CSF. In a lumbar puncture , a traumatic tap can be confused with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) as both show blood in the drawn CSF sample . In such situations , centrifugation of the sample distinguishes the two . • Clear supernatant following CSF centrifugation supports a traumatic tap. • Xanthochromatic supernatant suggests SAH. Xanthochromatic supernatant may be present in the following conditions: • In Liver disease , due to elevated bilirubin levels .1059 • When CSF protein concentration is elevated . • In subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), RBCs are present in the CSF long enough for them to undergo lysis . This releases hemoglobin which is converted to bilirubin, thus staining the CSF yellow .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old woman presents with nausea, fever, and neck rigidity. A lumbar puncture is ordered . All of the following are effective strategies to prevent post -lumbar puncture headache in this patient , except :

options.b: Insertion of a needle with bevel pointed upwards
options.c: Replacement of stylet prior to removal of the needle

mcqs.explanation: The use of a 22 gauge needle (or smaller) can reduce the incidence of post -dural headache after lumbar puncture . Effective strategies that reduce the incidence of PDPH include : • Use of small-diameter needle (22 -gauge or smaller) • Use of atraumatic needle (Sprotte and others) • Replacement of stylet prior to removal of the needle • Insertion of a needle with bevel oriented in a cephalad to caudad direction (when using a stranded needle ) Ineffective strategies : • Bed rest (up to 4h) following LP • Supplemental fluids • Minimizing the volume of spinal fluid removed • Immediate mobilization following LP The customary practice of remaining in a recumbent position post -LP is unnecessary . Studies have shown no benefit in terms of reducing the incidence of headaches .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents to the OPD with sudden onset speech difficulty , tremors, and difficulty in walking. He is noted to have a wide stepping gait. He is a known hypertensive but is not adherent to treatment . Where is the lesion most likely to be seen on neuroimaging?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical features are suggestive of cerebellar ataxia, hence the lesion is most likely to be seen in the cerebellum . Cerebellar ataxia can be caused due to an acute vascular event such as infarction or hemorrhage. Wide stepping gait, a broad-based unstable gait is indicative of cerebellar dysfunction . Few other notable gait abnormalities are: • Short stepped gait- parkinsonism • Scissoring gait- spasticity i.e. UMN lesion • High-stepped , slapping gait- posterior column or peripheral nerve disease • Waddling gait- proximal muscle weakness A few of the cerebellar signs include : • Dysdiadokinesia / dysmetria1060 • Ataxia • Nystagmus • Intention tremor • Speech - slurred or scanning • Hypotonia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man is brought to the emergency ward following an acute episode of inability to move his lower limbs. Examination findings are given below . Which of the following investigations is most appropriate for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute paraparesis. This is caused most commonly by an intraspinal lesion. A negative Babinski reflex and flaccidity are suggestive of a lower motor neuron lesion. Hence , the most appropriate among the given investigations for acute paraparesis with LMN signs is a spinal MRI. Spinal causes of acute onset paraparesis include : • Injury to the spinal cord • Thrombosis of anterior vertebral artery • Hematomyelia • Prolapsed intervertebral disc

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: An elderly diabetic and hypertensive patient was carried to the emergency room in a comatose state . On examination, the blood pressure was 170/100 mmHg and pulse rate was >100/min. Plantar reflex was bilateral extensor . What is the next step to do?
mcqs.explanation: Ruling out glycemic extremes is the first step in the evaluation of this patient who is in a coma as most of the causes of coma are metabolic in origin and with appropriate treatment are completely reversible. In this elderly patient , with no other relevant history, the most likely cause of coma is diabetic ketoacidosis , hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state , or even hypoglycemia (which may present with hypertension ). Other options : The patient presents with tachycardia which is not a sign of raised intracranial pressure (bradycardia, altered respiratory pattern, raised systolic blood pressure ) and hence starting iv mannitol (option 3) to reduce intracranial pressure or doing a CT (option 4) to rule out intracranial space -occupying lesion is not required. The patient is a known case of hypertension which may cause hypertensive encephalopathy due to cerebral edema and would present with a similar history and signs of raised intracranial pressure giving antihypertensive (option 2) medications would treat the condition but it is not the first step as metabolic causes are more common and have to be addressed first. Coma is defined as a deep sleep -like state from which the patient cannot be aroused .Coma could be due to: • Metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, where brain imaging will be normal1061 • Meningitis syndromes • Diseases with prominent focal signs like stroke, or hemorrhage Urgent intervention is needed to prevent further brain damage . It is done by providing supplemental oxygen , intravenous thiamine (at least 100 mg), and intravenous 50% dextrose in water (25 g) empirically . It is crucial to measure baseline serum glucose levels before administering glucose . The initial examination includes evaluating the general appearance ,vitals, breath sounds , response to stimulation, pupil size and responsiveness , and any abnormal posturing or movements. In trauma cases , the neck should be stabilized until ruling out cervical spine fracture. Airway protection and intravenous access is necessary . Immediate therapeutic intervention should be done for hypotension , significant hypertension , bradycardia, arrhythmias affecting blood pressure or marked hyperthermia . Signs of meningeal irritation or fever indicate the need for urgent lumbar puncture . Fundus examination for papilledema and a CT scan of the brain should be performed prior to lumbar puncture in comatose patients .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of autonomic storm?
mcqs.explanation: Brain injury is the most common cause of autonomic storm and typically follows severe head trauma and postresuscitation anoxic-ischemic brain injury. An autonomic storm is an acute state of sustained sympathetic surge which can cause alterations in BP and heart rate, body temperature , respiration, and sweating . Other causes include : • Spinal cord injury • Drugs and toxins (phenylpropanolamine , cocaine, amphetamines , and TCA's; tetanus ; and less often , botulinum toxin) • Autonomic neuropathy • Chemodectomas (e.g., pheochromocytoma ). • Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome can produce a moderate autonomic storm.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: What is the minimum Glasgow coma scale -pupils score for a head injury?
mcqs.explanation: The GCS-P score allows a minimum score of 1. The Glasgow coma scale – pupils score (GCS-P) was described in response to the wish for a single index combining the coma scale with pupillary reactivity as a reflection of brainstem function. Its possible values range from 1 to 15, reflecting an extended range of severity , and may be particularly useful in relating to prognosis. The GCS-P is calculated by subtracting the pupil reactivity score (PRS) from the Glasgow coma scale (GCS) total score :1062 GCS-P = GCS - PRS The minimum score in GCS is 3.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident while driving a motorcycle . During the evaluation, the patient opens his eyes in response to voice and says inappropriate words. He is unable to move his right arm but extends his left arm when a painful stimulus is applied to his right arm . What is the GCS score of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The GCS score of the patient described is 8 (E3 V3 M2). In the case elaborated above, the score allotted is : • Eye -opening to speech —3 • Inappropriate words—3 • Extensor response of the upper limb in response to painful stimuli—2 Patients scoring a GCS of 3 or 4 have an 85% chance of dying or remaining vegetative . However, scores >11 indicate only a 5–10% likelihood of death or vegetative state and an 85% chance of moderate disability or good recovery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a patient post a neurosurgical procedure . The patient opens her eyes in response to a loud voice, localizes pain, and is confused and disoriented . What is the GCS score of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In this patient , GCS is E3M5V4 • Eye -opening to loud voice - 3 • Motor response localizes pain - 5 • Verbal response is confused and disoriented - 4

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Calculate the GCS Score in an intubated patient , with findings of eye movements to pain and abnormal flexion?
mcqs.explanation: The GCS score is E2VNTM3 . In this case: • Eye -opening to pain: E2 • In case of endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy , the verbal component of the score is denoted as 'not testable /NT'. Earlier in intubated patients , the V score was denoted as VT . According to the current update , the V score should be VNT . • Abnormal flexion: M3

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: A patient is brought to the emergency room after he was brutally beaten during a mugging incident. He is unresponsive even to painful stimuli and is apneic; however, he does have a pulse . Which of the following clinical findings would exclude a diagnosis of brain death ?
mcqs.explanation: Constricted pupils would rule out brain death . Brain death is the irreversible cessation of all cerebral function with the preservation of cardiac activity and maintenance of respiratory and somatic function by artificial means.1063 In brain death , the pupils are usually midsized or maybe dilated . However, constricted pupils are not seen . The diagnosis of brain death should be confirmed with the following clinical findings: • Absent brain -originating motor response , including response to pain stimulus above the neck or other brain -originating movements (eg , seizures , decerebrate or decorticate posturing ) • Unresponsiveness to any stimuli • Brainstem damage , as evidenced by dilated or mid-sized pupils without light reaction • Absent corneal, gag, and oculovestibular reflexes • Absent sucking or rooting reflexes • Absent cough with tracheal suctioning • Apnea, indicating medullary destruction • The heart rate should be invariant and does not accelerate to atropine

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: The family of an ICU patient who is in a coma has given consent for organ donation. An apnea test is performed . Lack of respiratory effort at what arterial pCO2 level will aid in confirming brain death ?
mcqs.explanation: To declare brain death , apnea is confirmed if no respiratory effort has been observed in the presence of arterial pCO2 levels of \03760 mmHg (apnea test is positive ). Destruction of the medulla leads to complete and irreversible apnea. Demonstration that apnea is due to medullary damage requires that the PCO2 be high enough to stimulate respiration during a test of spontaneous breathing. An apnea test is conducted to confirm that there is no respiratory effort in the presence of a sufficiently elevated arterial PCO2. Apnea testing can be done safely by the use of preoxygenation with 100 % oxygen prior to and following removal of the ventilator. CO2 tension increases ~0.3–0.4 kPa /min (2–3 mmHg/min) during apnea.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: General Neurology, Brain Death, and GCS
mcqs.question: Clinical criteria for brain death include all except :
mcqs.explanation: Clinical criteria for brain death does not include absent spinal cord reflexes . Deep tendon reflexes /spinal cord reflexes may be present in brain death as the spinal cord is intact. Criteria for brain death : • Coma - Deep , unresponsiveness to noxious stimuli • Absence of brainstem reflexes - Pupillary, oculocephalic , corneal, gag reflex , etc . • Apnea - Absence of spontaneous respiration at arterial pCO2 tension of at least 50–60mm Hg1064

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old patient is undergoing EEG with his eyes open . What is the expected frequency of the waves being recorded ?
mcqs.explanation: Beta waves are seen on the EEG of an adult recorded with eyes open . The frequency of these waves on an EEG is >13 Hz.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged obese man is being evaluated at the sleep clinic. During his EEG recording, he is awake with his eyes closed . Which of the following waves will be predominantly seen ?

options.a: Predominant alpha waves with intermixed beta activity
options.b: Predominant beta waves with intermixed alpha activity
options.c: Predominant theta waves with intermixed delta activity
options.d: Predominant delta waves with intermixed theta activity

mcqs.explanation: In a normal adult awake patient lying quietly with his eyes closed , alpha waves are predominantly seen intermixed with a variable generalized beta activity. This alpha rhythm is attenuated when the eyes are opened .1075

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a type of generalized epilepsy ?
mcqs.explanation: Jacksonian march is a feature seen in focal seizures , not generalized epilepsy . In Jacksonian march, the abnormal motor movements begin in a very restricted region such as the fingers and gradually progress to include a larger portion of the extremity . It represents the spread of the seizure activity over a progressively larger region of the motor cortex.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 13 -year-old boy presents with involuntary, sudden jerking movements of both upper limbs. They occur most frequently in the morning after awakening and are provoked by lack of sleep . This type of seizure is classified as ________.
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME). Myoclonic seizures are the predominant feature of JME and are now classified under both focal onset and generalized onset seizures . Generalized seizures arise at some point in the brain but immediately and rapidly engage neuronal networks in both cerebral hemispheres . Focal seizures arise from a neuronal network either discretely localized within one brain region or more broadly distributed but still within a cerebral hemisphere . Myoclonic seizures are characterized by: • Preserved consciousness • Preserved postural control • Lack of postictal confusion JME is an epilepsy syndrome that has familial inheritance and begins in adolescence . It most commonly occurs in the morning and is provoked by sleep deprivation. JME is usually associated with GTCS and sometimes with absence seizures . EEG shows a typical 4-6 Hz polyspike and wave pattern. Treatment includes administration of sodium valproate.1076 2017 ILAE -International League Against Epilepsy Classification :

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in focal seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: The ictal cry is seen in generalized , tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS). Jacksonian march, Todd's paralysis, and Epilepsia partialis continua are features of focal seizures . Jacksonian march is a feature seen in focal seizures wherein the abnormal motor movements begin in a very restricted region such as the fingers and gradually progress to include a larger portion of the extremity . It represents the spread of seizure activity over a progressively larger region of the motor cortex. Todd's paralysis is a transient focal temporary paralysis usually persisting for a few minutes to hours (maximum up to 48 hours) in the postictal phase . Epilepsia partialis continua refer to continued focal seizures for hours or days. It is often refractory to medical therapy . Tonic contraction of the muscles of expiration and the larynx at the onset of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure will produce a loud moan or ictal cry.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old girl is brought to the OPD with complaints of frequent fainting and sudden falls while playing . She sometimes falls off while sitting in the classroom hitting her head to the desk. She regains consciousness immediately and resumes her activity, and has normal behavior after such episodes . The girl is otherwise healthy . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given history is most consistent with atonic seizures . Atonic seizures are characterized by a sudden loss of postural control and there is no postictal confusion. Options A and D: Absence seizures usually present as blank stares or unresponsiveness for a few seconds . Postural control is not lost during absence seizures . Option C: The girl regains consciousness immediately and has no associated complaints like sweating , fatigue , or tachycardia. She also resumes her activity after the episodes . Also, there is no precipitating factor that points towards syncope . Hence it is unlikely to be syncope .1077

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the hospital . He is found to have a sudden brief lapse of consciousness with preserved postural control. No confusion is reported after regaining consciousness . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Sudden , brief lapse of consciousness with preserved postural control and no post -ictal confusion is seen in absence seizures . Usually , the seizure lasts only a few seconds . EEG shows generalized symmetric 3 Hz spike and wave pattern (as shown below ). Hyperventilation provokes these EEG discharges and seizures .Option A: Atonic seizures are characterized by a sudden loss of postural control. Option B: Myoclonic seizures have preserved consciousness . They involve a sudden brief jerking movement involving the entire body or a part of it. Option D: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures are characterized by post -ictal confusion.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An unconscious patient with a history of seizures is brought to the ED. He then develops muscular flaccidity and excessive salivation. After a few minutes , he begins to regain consciousness and is in a confused state . This phenomenon is associated with which of the following types of seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: The scenario is suggestive of post -ictal confusion which is seen in generalized tonic-clonic seizures . It is not seen in absence seizures , atonic seizures or myoclonic seizures .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the clinic with involuntary, sudden jerking movements of both upper limbs. They occur most frequently in the morning after awakening and are provoked by a lack of sleep . EEG demonstrates bilaterally synchronous spike-and-slow - wave discharges . Which of the following features is not seen in this type of seizure ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myoclonic seizures . Post-ictal paralysis is not seen in these seizures . Myoclonic seizures are characterized by preserved consciousness (rarely very short loss of consciousness ), preserved postural control, Lack of postictal confusion.1078 Myoclonic seizures usually coexist with other forms of generalized seizures but are the predominant feature of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME). The EEG shows bilaterally synchronous spike-and-slow wave discharges. JME or Janz 's syndrome is an epilepsy syndrome that has familial inheritance and begins in adolescence. It most commonly occurs in the morning and is provoked by sleep deprivation. JME is usually associated with GTCS and sometimes with absence seizures . EEG shows a typical 4-6 Hz polyspike and wave pattern. Treatment includes administration of sodium valproate.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The following EEG is that of a 6-year-old girl who is easily distracted in class and exhibits poor scholastic performance. Seizures are precipitated by hyperventilation . What is the diagnosis ?
mcqs.explanation: EEG shows generalized symmetric 3 Hz spike and wave pattern. This is seen in absence seizures . Absence seizures are characterized by a sudden brief lapse of consciousness with preserved postural control that lasts only a few seconds . However, there is no post -ictal confusion. Hyperventilation provokes these EEG discharges and also the seizures . Ethosuximide is the drug of choice in typical absence seizures .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the first-line agent for treating a patient with generalized tonic-clonic seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: The first-line agents in the treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) are Valproate, levetiracetam , and lamotrigine.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy developed abnormal jerking movements that started in his left hand and gradually involved the entire arm . Following this, the patient experienced weakness and difficulty in moving the left arm for about an hour. Two similar episodes have also occurred in the past. Which of the following is the first-line drug for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario describes Jacksonian march followed by Todd's palsy . These are characteristics of a focal seizure . Among the given drugs, the first-line drug for focal seizures is1079 carbamazepine.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following can be used as first-line agents in patients with typical absence seizures , except :
mcqs.explanation: Levetiracetam is not the first-line agent for the treatment of typical absence seizures . First-line drugs for: • Typical absence seizures : Ethosuximide (drug of choice ), valproate, and lamotrigine • Atypical absence seizures : Valproate

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used as the first-line antiepileptic drug in the treatment of both generalized as well as focal seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: Lamotrigine is a first-line drug in the treatment of both generalized tonic-clonic and focal seizures .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the drug of choice for a patient with generalized epilepsy syndrome having mixed seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: Valproate is the drug of choice in generalized epilepsy syndrome having mixed seizures . It is particularly effective in absence , myoclonic and atonic seizures . Valproate is usually first given alone (monotherapy) and if ineffective , another drug such as lamotrigine may be added . In generalized epilepsy , drugs such as phenytoin , carbamazepine, and oxcarbazepine can increase the number of seizures . They can also provoke new seizure types - myoclonic or absence seizures . Hence , they are avoided. Ethosuximide is the drug of choice in typical absence seizures and is not used for GTCS.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with violent shaking of arms and legs for the past 1 hour. He is a chronic alcoholic whose last intake was 2 days ago. IV lorazepam and phenytoin are administered to this patient . After 5 minutes , the seizures have not stopped . What is the next best step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: With seizures occurring for 1 hour, this patient is suffering from status epilepticus . A second dose of lorazepam can be given to control this patient 's seizures if there is no response after 5 minutes of administration of the first dose . Status epilepticus refers to continuous seizures or repetitive , discrete seizures with impaired consciousness in the inter-ictal period . For practical purposes , it is defined as any one of the following : • Continuing seizures >5 minutes or • No regaining of consciousness between 2 seizures . Management of status epilepticus :1080

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old girl, who is taking antiepileptics , has had a seizure -free period of 6 months. She has no family history of epilepsy . Her EEG is now normal and she has a normal neurological exam and intelligence . What would your advice be?

options.a: Stop the treatment and follow up
options.b: Gradually taper the drug and stop treatment

mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario of a girl on antiepileptics for 6 months with no further seizures , no family history, normal EEG , neurological examination, and intelligence , antiepileptics should be continued for another 18 months since she 's already taken for 6 months (minimum 2 years) to prevent seizure recurrence. Anti-epileptic drugs withdrawal is considered only when an adult patient has been seizure -free for \0372 years along with the following criteria: • Normal CNS examination including intelligence • Normal EEG and normal MRI • Single seizure type • No family history of epilepsy . It is preferable to reduce the dose of the drug gradually over 2–3 months. Other options : Option A: Sudden cessation of drug therapy may cause recurrence of seizure hence not advised. Option B: The patient has a seizure -free interval of only 6 months and therefore , is not yet eligible for considering medication withdrawal . Option D: Life-long treatment is not necessary in this case as the patient meets all the above-mentioned criteria for drug withdrawal after 2 years. Note : Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), the most common idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndrome is known to have a high risk of seizure recurrence, and hence antiepileptics are continued lifelong in a majority of patients .1081

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man on antiepileptic therapy for GTCS presents with weight gain, alopecia and thrombocytopenia . Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is the most likely cause for this presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: Weight gain, alopecia , and thrombocytopenia are the side effects of valproate use . Adverse effects of Sodium Valproate (mnemonic: VALPROATE ) • Vomiting • Alopecia • Liver toxicity • Pancreatitis • Rash • Obesity • Anorexia • Teratogenicity (most common: spina bifida), thrombocytopenia , tremors • Edema The first-line agents for treating GTCS are valproate, leviteracetam , and lamotrigine.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with West syndrome?
