mcqs.explanation: Caf\351 au lait is a neurocutaneous marker seen in neurofibromatosis, not a component of West syndrome. The triad of West syndrome is: • Infantile spasms (also called Salaam spells ) • Developmental regression • Hypsarrhythmia (abnormal EEG ) West syndrome is treated with: • ACTH injections • Vigabatrin if associated with tuberous sclerosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old child was brought with repeated epileptic spasms. The child had reached his normal milestone at the age of 2 months. But the parents noticed that he lost the ability to hold his head steadily and he recently couldn't track light or sound. The EEG findings are shown below . What is the drug of choice for the treatment of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is of infantile spasms, developmental regression and the EEG showing hypsarrhythmia is suggestive of West syndrome. The drug of choice for this condition is ACTH. West syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in infancy. It is characterized by a triad of • Infantile spasm (also called salaam spells ) is a convulsive disease characterized by brief, symmetric axial muscle contraction (neck, trunk, and/or extremities ). • Developmental regression1082 • Hypsarrhythmia (Himalayan wave pattern) on EEG : Characterized by a high-voltage , slow, chaotic background with multifocal spikes Treatment of West syndrome includes : • ACTH • Vigabatrin if associated with tuberous sclerosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is effective in controlling infantile spasms in a patient who has the neurocutaneous marker as shown in image?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a Shagreen patch, which is a typical feature of tuberous sclerosis . Vigabatrin is effective in the control of seizures in patients with tuberous sclerosis . Tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease) is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in either the TSC1 or the TSC2 gene . The clinical features seen are as follows : • Seizures • Intellectual disability • Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) • Shagreen patch • Hypomelanotic macules • Periungual fibromas • Renal angiomyolipomas • Cardiac rhabdomyomas. A Shagreen patch is an irregularly thickened , slightly elevated , soft , skin-colored plaque, usually in the lumbosacral region.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy develops an episode of involuntary jerky movements of the left hand accompanied by a repetitive chewing movement. He had a blank look on his face and was unresponsive during this episode . He also has no memory of the episode . EEG was normal and MRI showed hippocampal sclerosis . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of focal seizure with impaired consciousness which along with hippocampal sclerosis is suggestive of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy . The following image shows left hippocampal sclerosis :1083

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding mesial temporal lobe epilepsy ?

options.a: It results in focal seizures with dyscognitive features
options.b: The person experiences an aura before the seizure
options.c: It is associated with a family history of epilepsy
options.d: Seizures can be controlled with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine

mcqs.explanation: Seizures of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy are not controlled with carbamazepine. The condition is refractory to anticonvulsant therapy but responds well to surgical intervention.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs must be avoided in myoclonic seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: Oxcarbazepine is known to worsen myoclonic seizures and is therefore contraindicated in it. Drugs like carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin can worsen the myoclonic, absence , tonic and atonic seizures and are therefore avoided.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is seen in patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?

options.c: EEG showing less than 3Hz Spike and wave discharge

mcqs.explanation: EEG showing <3Hz spike and wave discharge is a characteristic feature of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in childhood . It may occur due to various reasons such as developmental anomalies, mutations, trauma, infections , etc . It is characterized by a typical triad of • Multiple seizure types • Intellectual disability • Typical <3 Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG Treatment includes administration of anti-epileptic drugs such as lamotrigine and sodium valproate . It is frequently refractory to medical therapy and usually has a poor prognosis.1084 Note : EEG with symmetric 3 Hz spike and wave pattern is seen in typical absence seizure .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding Lafora 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Glucocerebrosidase infusions are not the treatment for Lafora 's disease . There is no approved treatment for Lafora body disease . The mainstay of management is anti-epileptic drugs, valproate in particular; however, other AEDs such as topiramate, ethosuximide , and phenobarbital can be used to control seizures . Most recently , perampanel , a new AMPA receptor antagonist AED, is shown to be effective . Lafora body disease is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease and has an adolescent onset . It is associated with polyglucosan intracellular inclusion bodies . It is characterized by: • Progressive myoclonus • Epileptic seizures • Dementia • Ataxia. Diagnosis is by DNA sequencing . Death usually occurs within 10 years of the onset of the disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: You are at a criminal court to provide medical testimony . The trial ends with the accused being sentenced to life imprisonment. Abruptly , the convict breaks into uncontrollable laughter . Within minutes , he collapses and starts to have a seizure . His lawyer reports that he has a childhood seizure disorder. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of a gelastic seizure . This condition is also known as gelastic epilepsy , and is a rare type of seizure that involves a sudden burst of energy , usually in the form of laughing or crying. It is seen when the seizure focus is within the left prefrontal cortex. Gelastic seizures have been associated classically with hypothalamic hamartomas. Option A: Kluver Bucy syndrome is characterized by hypersexuality , placidity , a tendency to explore the environment with the mouth, inability to recognize the emotional significance of visual stimuli, and constantly shifting attention , called hypermetamorphosis . Option B: Witzelsucht is a tendency to joke and make puns. Option C: Pseudobulbar affect is defined by involuntary, sudden , and frequent episodes of laughing or crying that are generally out of proportion or inappropriate to the situation.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old girl is brought to the OPD following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure . She had previous episodes of sudden falls at school and also sometimes stares with a blank face . She is also found to be having poor scholastic performance. Her EEG reveals a slow spike and wave pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.a: Focal seizures progressing to generalized seizures
options.b: Myoclonic epilepsy progressing to generalized seizures

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario reveals multiple types of seizures such as atonic seizures (sudden falls), absence seizures (blank stares and unresponsive), and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in this patient . This is a characteristic feature of Lenox-Gastaut syndrome. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in childhood . It may occur due to various reasons such as developmental anomalies, mutations, trauma, infections , etc .1085 It is characterized by a typical triad of • Multiple seizure types • Intellectual disability • Typical <3 Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG Treatment includes administration of anti-epileptic drugs such as lamotrigine and sodium valproate . It is frequently refractory to medical therapy and usually has a poor prognosis.1086

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Ischemia occurs in the brain when the cerebral blood flow falls below _____.
mcqs.explanation: A decrease in the cerebral blood flow below 20 mL /100 g/min causes reversible ischemia. If this state is prolonged for several hours to days, it can lead to infarction. A decrease in CBF to 0 causes the death of the brain tissue within 4–10 min. Normal cerebral blood flow (CBF) in an adult brain at rest is 50–55 mL /100 g/min.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with acute onset of weakness of the left arm which resolved completely in 10 days. He is known to have mitral stenosis , hypertension and dyslipidemia . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This patient with mitral stenosis and acute onset weakness of the left arm is most likely to have had an embolic stroke, which is a type of ischemic stroke. Embolic strokes tend to occur suddenly with maximum neurologic deficit present at onset . Mitral stenosis is known to cause atrial fibrillation and is a common cause of cardioembolic stroke. Transient ischemic attack (TIA ) is a temporary, focal neurological deficit of sudden onset (stroke-like symptoms ) lasting for less than 24 hours. This occurs due to focal ischemia of the brain , retina or cochlea . Most TIAs last for less than 1 hour to a few minutes . There is a high risk of developing an ischemic stroke after a TIA , especially for the first 3 months following a TIA .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with right-sided hemiparesis that completely resolved in 4-6 hours. What score will you use to determine the risk of a future stroke in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This patient 's clinical features are suggestive of a transient ischemic attack. The risk of stroke following TIAs is determined by the ABCD2 score. CHADS2-VASc score is used to determine the risk of stroke in a patient with atrial fibrillation. CURB-65 is a scoring system used to predict mortality in patients with community-acquired pneumonia.1096 APACHE II is a scoring system used to predict ICU mortality.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old patient with hypertension , diabetes , and asthma is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse during a routine physical examination. ECG findings are shown below . How is the risk of stroke determined in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario along with the ECG findings are suggestive of atrial fibrillation. The risk of stroke in this condition is determined by CHA2DS2 -VASC score. The ECG show irregular QRS complexes of normal morphology and absent P waves.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 73-year-old woman who was brought to the ER with hemiparesis was found to have a lacunar infarction. What causes this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Lacunar infarcts, also called small vessel stroke, refer to infarction following atherothrombotic or lipohyalinotic occlusion of small penetrating arteries in the brain . These penetrating arteries arise from the stem of the middle cerebral artery, circle of Willis, and basilar and vertebral arteries. The principal risk factors are hypertension and old age . The image below shows two lacunar infarctions on a CT.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not caused by a lacunar stroke?
mcqs.explanation: Crural monoplegia with urinary incontinence is not caused by a lacunar stroke. It is caused by the occlusion of A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery. Crural monoplegia refers to a monoplegia of the lower limbs. The types of lacunar syndromes are as follows : • Pure motor hemiparesis - infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule1097 • Pure sensory stroke - infarct in the thalamus • Ataxic hemiparesis - infarct in the pons or internal capsule • Dysarthria and clumsy hand syndrome - infarction in the pons or internal capsule .The ACA is divided into two segments : • The pre-communal (A1) circle of Willis, or stem , which connects the internal carotid artery to the anterior communicating artery • The post -communal (A2 ) segment distal to the anterior communicating artery

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed with an ischaemic stroke. His son says that he holds the comb incorrectly while combing his hair. During the evaluation, he was unable to button his shirt when requested . The lesion is most likely to be in which lobe ?
mcqs.explanation: 1098 The given scenario where the patient is unable to perform learned skilled movements is suggestive of apraxia. The lesion is likely to be in the dominant parietal lobe as apraxia is a feature of a lesion in this area. The features of dominant parietal lobe lesions are as follows : • Apraxia - inability to perform learned skilled movements • Acalculia - difficulty performing simple mathematical tasks • Alexia - inability to recognize or read written words or letters • Agnosia - inability to recognize and identify objects , persons, or sounds • Dysphasia - language disorder marked by deficiency in the generation of speech and its comprehension • Contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia • Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, dysgraphia, finger agnosia, right-left confusion) Features of non-dominant parietal lobe lesions include : • Spatial disorientation • Constructional apraxia • Contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia • Contralateral hemineglect .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features is not likely to be seen in a patient with a temporal lobe lesion?
mcqs.explanation: Neglect is not a feature of temporal lobe lesion. It is a feature of a non-dominant parietal lobe lesion. Features of dominant temporal lobe lesions: • Complex hallucinations - visual, auditory or olfactory • Memory impairment • Complex partial seizures • Wernicke's aphasia • Contralateral superior quadrantanopia Features of non-dominant temporal lobe lesions : • Poor non-verbal memory • Loss of musical skills • Complex hallucinations • Contralateral superior quadrantanopia .1099

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 43-year-old man is brought to the hospital due to extremely aggressive behaviour towards his family. His family members also say that he has become forgetful and has developed urinary incontinence. Which of the following lobes is likely to be involved in his disease process ?
mcqs.explanation: Antisocial behavior, urinary incontinence, and impaired memory in this patient are suggestive of frontal lobe involvement. Features of frontal lobe lesions : • Disinhibition • Lack of initiative • Antisocial behavior • Impaired memory • Incontinence • Grasp reflexes • Anosmia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In the sagittal section of the brain given below if the coloured area is affected , which of the following is not seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Paracentral lobule (PCL ) is the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri of the superolateral surface into the medial surface of cerebral hemisphere . It controls the motor and sensory innervations of the contralateral lower extremity . It is also responsible for cortical control of micturition and defecation . The anterior two -thirds of PCL belong to Brodmann area 4, it reflects the primary motor cortex for the muscles of contralateral leg , foot, and perineum ,it is functionally important in control of bladder and anal sphincters . Therefore, it's called the cortical center of defecation and micturition. The posterior third of the PCL contains 3,2 and 1, it reflects the primary somatosensory representation of the leg and foot. The A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery supplies the paracentral lobule . Lesions in the paracentral lobule lead to: • Weakness and loss of sensation in contralateral lower limb • Urinary incontinence • Fecal incontinence.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which type of aphasia is seen in the lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus?
mcqs.explanation: Lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus cause Wernicke's or Fluent aphasia due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense (area no 22 ). Broca's (Option B) or motor/non-fluent aphasia is seen in lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus which contains the motor speech area. Speech is non-fluent and interrupted , with a paucity of functional words.1100 Comprehension of written language and the ability to name objects are compromised in anomic aphasia (Option C). This aphasia is caused by damage to the angular gyrus that disrupts visual information processing and transmission to the Wernicke area. Conduction aphasia (Option D) is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus , the bundle of nerve fibers connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation complains of sudden onset weakness of the right lower limb, with urinary and faecal incontinence. MRI shows an ischaemic stroke involving the left anterior cerebral artery. Which of the following features would you not expect to see in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Prosopagnosia, also called face blindness , is the inability to recognize faces including one's own image. This occurs due to occipitotemporal lobe damage , seen in posterior cerebral artery (PCA) strokes involving cortical branch occlusion . It is not seen in anterior cerebral artery strokes. The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies parts of the frontal lobe , corpus callosum, paracentral lobule , and other deeper structures . Signs and symptoms of ACA occlusion and structures involved: • Urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence • Paratonic rigidity • Abulia (Akinetic mutism), lack of spontaneity , slowness • Gait impairment • Paralysis of contralateral foot and leg • Paresis of the contralateral arm • Cortical sensory loss over the contralateral lower limb • Dyspraxia of left limbs, tactile aphasia in left limbs.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Infarction of area of distribution of which of the following arteries is most likely to be seen in a patient with hemiplegia ?
mcqs.explanation: Hemiplegia is most commonly associated with infarction of the area of distribution of middle cerebral artery. Middle cerebral artery supplies the motor cortex responsible for sending the output to the motor neurons. Infarction in this territory leads to hemiplegia . Infarction of area of distribution of vertebral, anterior spinal and posterior cerebral arteries can also lead to hemiplegia .1101

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features is not expected to be seen in a patient with a right middle cerebral artery infarct?
mcqs.explanation: Aphasia is not a feature of right middle cerebral artery infarct (MCA). Aphasia occurs when there is damage to the dominant hemisphere , i.e., left hemisphere . The dominant hemisphere contains the language network which includes Broca's area, Wernicke's area, their interconnections and connections with frontal, parietal and temporal areas. The MCA originates from the internal carotid artery. The stem of the MCA is referred to as the M1 segment . It gives rise to cortical and penetrating /lenticulostriate branches. MCA stem occlusion leads to : • Contralateral hemiplegia • Hemianesthesia1102 • Homonymous hemianopia • Global aphasia (dominant hemisphere ) • Anosognosia, constructional apraxia, neglect (non-dominant hemisphere ) Occlusion of the lenticulostriate branches of MCA (lacunar stroke) may affect the genu of the internal capsule . This can lead to dysarthria with contralateral clumsy hand (fine motor weakness ).

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Visual field examination of a 52-year-old stroke patient reveals the finding shown in the image. During examination, you notice that he is not able to comprehend your instructions and sometimes gives irrelevant replies . What is the likely site of arterial occlusion ?

options.c: Left M2 segment of MCA – inferior division
options.d: Right M2 segment of MCA – superior division

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of homonymous right superior quadrantanopia (pie in the sky appearance ) and sensory aphasia. These are seen in occlusion of the inferior division of the opposite side middle cerebral artery (MCA). Parts of the middle cerebral artery: • The MCA originates from the internal carotid artery. The stem of the MCA is referred to as the M1 segment. • In the Sylvian fissure , the MCA divides into superior and inferior divisions. These branches are referred to as the M2 segments of the MCA. Occlusion of the following sites and their effects are given below : • MCA stem (M1) - leads to contralateral hemiplegia , hemianesthesia and homonymous hemianopia amongst other features • Superior division of MCA (M2) on the dominant side - leads to motor aphasia (Broca's) and facio-brachial weakness • Inferior division of MCA (M2) on the dominant side - leads to sensory aphasia (Wernicke's) and contralateral superior quadrantanopia The following image of coronal section of cerebral hemisphere shows the segments of MCA:1103

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient is found to have Wernicke's aphasia without motor involvement. Where is the infarct likely to be?

options.a: ACA territory of the right hemisphere
options.b: ACA territory of the left hemisphere
options.c: MCA territory of the right hemisphere
options.d: MCA territory of the left hemisphere

mcqs.explanation: The presence of Wernicke's aphasia without motor involvement suggests an infarct in the MCA territory of the left (dominant) hemisphere . Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (mostly the left side ). This area is supplied by the inferior division of MCA. MCA divides into superior and inferior divisions in the Sylvian fissure . These branches are referred to as the M2 segments of MCA. • The superior division - supplies the frontal and the superior parietal cortex. • The inferior division - supplies the inferior parietal and temporal cortex. An infarct in the territory of the inferior division of MCA in the dominant hemisphere causes Wernicke's aphasia without weakness . As the frontal cortex (containing the motor area) is supplied by the superior division and is not affected , weakness is not observed. An infarct in the inferior division of MCA of the non-dominant hemisphere (mostly the right side ) causes hemineglect without weakness .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of an anterior choroidal artery lesion?
mcqs.explanation: Aphasia (dominant hemisphere ), constructional apraxia and neglect (non-dominant hemisphere ) are seen in MCA stem occlusion . These features are absent in anterior choroidal artery occlusion . Features common to both MCA and anterior choroidal artery occlusion include : • Contralateral hemiplegia • Hemianaesthesia • Homonymous hemianopia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A man is rushed to the ER after losing control of his car and crashing into a tree . Examination findings are given below . What is the most likely cause for his presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of pontine haemorrhage. Clinical features of pontine haemorrhage are: • Deep coma • Quadriparesis and multiple cranial nerve dysfunction • Decerebrate rigidity • Pin-point pupils • Hyperpnea , hyperpyrexia , severe hypertension , and hyperhidrosis1104 Option A: The presence of hyperpyrexia and pin-point pupils rule out the possibility of spinal cord trauma. Option B: Morphine poisoning is a differential diagnosis for pin-point pupils . But it leads to slower respiratory rate, not tachypnea . Option D: In ponto-medullary laceration, medullary involvement would cause respiratory depression , leading to apnea. But here tachypnea is noted .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with left -sided facial paralysis and left -sided limb weakness for the past 1 hour. Her blood pressure is 160 /100 mm Hg and her CT appears normal . What would be the next step of management?
mcqs.explanation: Sudden onset hemiparesis with apparently normal CT indicates ischemic stroke in this patient . Intravenous thrombolysis(alteplase 0.9 mg/kg ) should be immediately administered to patients with ischemic stroke who arrive in the window period i.e., within 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset . Aspirin + clopidogrel (Option B) is used in secondary prevention of stroke and also to prevent stroke following TIA . Transient ischemic attacks (TIAs ) refer to episodes of stroke symptoms that have a brief duration, the standard definition of duration is <24 h, but most TIAs last <1 hr. TIAs may arise from emboli to the brain or from in situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel . With a TIA , the occluded blood vessel reopens and neurologic function is restored . If a relevant brain infarction is identified on brain imaging, the clinical entity is now classified as stroke regardless of the duration of symptoms . The risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA ) is approximately 10 -15% in the first three months, majorly in the first two days. A reliable estimation of this risk can be obtained using the ABCD2 score. Other options : Option A: If CT is normal it only rules out hemorrhagic stroke and changes of ischemic stroke usually take time to appear on NCCT. Option D: BP control is done when BP exceeds 220 /120 mmHg, if there is malignant hypertension or concomitant myocardial ischemia, or if blood pressure is >185/110 mmHg and thrombolytic therapy is anticipated .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in which of the following patients with ischaemic stroke?
mcqs.explanation: A sustained blood pressure > 185/110 mmHg and recent myocardial infarction are contraindications for initiating thrombolysis in ischemic stroke .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with acute ischemic stroke requires IV thrombolysis. His symptoms had begun at 6:30 PM and he was brought to the hospital by 7:00 PM. For this treatment to be beneficial for the patient , it should be administered within what time?
mcqs.explanation: IV thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke has been proven to be beneficial up to 4.5 hours after the onset of symptoms according to European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study (ECASS) III .1105 According to MoHFW (India), thrombolysis is to be carried out within 4.5 hours of symptom onset . IV tPA should be administered to all eligible acute stroke patients within 3 hours of last known normal and to a more selective group of eligible acute stroke patients (based on ECASS III exclusion criteria) within 4.5 hours of last known normal .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features of stroke need not be treated ?
mcqs.explanation: Neglect is a feature of stroke that need not be treated . Although neglect indicates a poor prognosis, most patients recover without any treatment in 1-6 months. Dysphagia (Option A) poses a high risk of aspiration and hence can't be left untreated . Spasticity (Option B) can be treated with baclofen , tizanidine. Untreated , it creates a psychosocial impact on the patient . Fever(Option C) is deleterious in stroke patients and must be treated . Neglect can arise from injury to cortical-limbic-reticular network, that directs attention and integrates the localization and identification of a stimulus . Neglect is associated with poor scores and slower recovery, but severe neglect is rare beyond 6 months. Recovery is rapid in the first 2 weeks , regardless of the side of stroke. By 3 months, patients might have some residual visual neglect . The choice of an intervention depends on the mechanism of neglect , the patient can be treated for an underaroused right hemisphere which has difficulty processing sensory inputs . Neurogenic dysphagia is an important cause of pulmonary infection in any patient with stroke, motor neuron disease , even transient dysphagia can lead to malnutrition, dehydration , aspiration pneumonia, and airway obstruction with asphyxia, it increases the risk of death and institutionalization. Early placement of nasogastric tube to feed patients after stroke has improved nutrition and reduced deaths . Spasticity is seen in less than 20 % of stroke patients . Patients with bilateral weakness from hypoxic injury are likely to have signs of spasticity . Exaggerated cutaneous and autonomic reflexes and involuntary spasms are disabling problems associated with spasticity . Physical modalities like slow stretching movements and daily passive exercises will reduce symptoms of spasticity and risk of contractures. Baclofen, tizanidine, and clonidine are used in reducing clonus and extensor spasms .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A woman on oral contraceptive pills presents with a headache for 2 days and paraparesis. What could be the most likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of headache and paraparesis in this patient with a history of oral contraceptive use is suggestive of cerebral venous thrombosis. Cerebral venous thrombosis is commonly seen in hypercoagulable states such as: • Oral contraceptive pill use • Pregnancy and puerperium • Inflammatory bowel disease • Dehydration1106 • Intracranial infections . It presents with: • Headache (most common) • Seizures • Intracranial Hypertension • Focal neurological Deficits • Altered Mental status MR venography is used for diagnosis. The below image shows the empty delta sign seen on CECT or MRI with contrast in patients with sagittal sinus thrombosis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice for a patient diagnosed with sagittal sinus thrombosis?
mcqs.explanation: IV heparin is the drug of choice in cerebral venous thrombosis. It prevents further thrombosis and reduces venous hypertension and ischemia. Anticoagulation is often continued indefinitely if thrombophilia is diagnosed . If there is no underlying hypercoagulable state , treatment with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) for 3–6 months may be initiated and then converted to aspirin, depending on the degree of resolution of the venous sinus thrombus. Treatment of CVT : • Acute treatment - IV Heparin or LMWH • Maintenance therapy : • Warfarin for at least 3 months1107 • In pregnant women with a history of CVT - anticoagulation with LMWH throughout pregnancy and till 8 weeks postpartum .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old patient presents with headache and weakness of the right side of the body. He has difficulty in speaking also. Angiography shows a puff of smoke appearance . Which of the following statements regarding this disease is false ?

options.a: It is an occlusive disease involving large intracranial arteries
options.c: Dawson's fingers are the characteristic imaging finding

mcqs.explanation: This patient 's clinical features are suggestive of Moyamoya disease and Dawson's fingers is not a finding in this condition. Dawson fingers are a radiographic feature typically seen in multiple sclerosis (MS) The picture below demonstrates Dawson fingers.Moyamoya disease is an occlusive disease involving large intracranial arteries. It has a bimodal age distribution and is seen in the first and fourth decades : • Childhood moyamoya is characterized by ischemic manifestations • Adult moyamoya is characterized by hemorrhagic manifestations The first symptom is a stroke or recurrent TIA . Treatment is by surgical bypass of extracranial carotid arteries to the dura or middle cerebral artery. This may prevent stroke and haemorrhage. The below image shows the MR angiography findings in a patient with Moyamoya disease .1108 Note : As this is a chronic condition, the lenticulostriate arteries develop a rich collateral circulation around the occlusive lesion. This is seen as a 'puff of smoke' (moyamoya in Japanese) on X-ray angiography.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a component of CHA2DS2 -VASc score?
mcqs.explanation: Age > 60 years is not a component of the CHADS2-VASc score. Age > 75years and age group 65-75 yrs are the two age criteria considered in the score. The CHA2DS2 -VASc score is used to assess the risk of stroke in patients who have atrial fibrillation. Anticoagulation therapy is given when the score is \0372. Patients with a score of 1 may also be considered for anticoagulation therapy . Anticoagulation therapy is given for all the patients of AF having mitral stenosis , hypertrophic cardiomyopathy , or a history of stroke.1109

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient has developed confusion and keeps bumping into objects . He can speak fluently . But on examination, he cannot differentiate between fingers and cannot write . He also gets confused with the examiner's right and left sides . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Gerstmann syndrome. It is commonly associated with damage to the left (dominant) inferior parietal lobule . Gerstmann syndrome consists of: • Acalculia - impairment of simple arithmetic • Dysgraphia - impaired writing • Finger anomia - an inability to name individual fingers • Right-left confusion - an inability to tell whether a hand, foot, or arm of the patient or examiner is on the right or left side of the body Option B: Anton syndrome also known as visual anosognosia occurs due to bilateral infarction in the distal PCAs. It produces cortical blindness and the patients are unaware of the blindness or may even deny it. Option C: Millard-Gubler syndrome occurs due to ventral pontine injury. It causes functional loss of the 6th and 7th cranial nerves and corticospinal tract. This presents as diplopia , ipsilateral facial palsy , ipsilateral loss of corneal reflex , contralateral hemiparesis . Option D: Dejerine -Roussy syndrome is associated with hemisensory loss and severe burning pain in the affected region. It is also known as thalamic pain syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 78 -year-old woman presents with right hemisensory loss followed by agonizing, burning pain in the affected regions. The pain responds poorly to analgesics . These features are classically seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: 1120 Hemisensory loss and severe burning pain in the affected regions is classically seen in Dejerine -Roussy syndrome, also known as thalamic pain syndrome. Dejerine - Roussy syndrome occurs due to occlusion of the thalamic and thalamogeniculate branches arising from the P1 segment resulting in contralateral hemisensory loss and severe burning pain in the affected regions. The P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery extends from the basilar bifurcation to the junction with the posterior communicating artery. This pain responds poorly to analgesics. Anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or gabapentin or tricyclic antidepressants may be beneficial.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 73-year-old woman was brought to the OPD since she has been tripping over things at home. On entering, she complimented the doctor's tie even though he was not wearing one and continued to insist that she could see normally. On examination, bilateral blindness was present but pupillary light reflex was normal . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Anton's syndrome. It occurs due to bilateral infarction in the distal posterior cerebral artery (P2 segment ) and is associated with the following features : • Cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction • Visual anosognosia - denial of loss of vision • Confabulation in the setting of obvious visual loss Option D: Riddoch phenomenon is a condition where cortical blindness is associated with the perception of only moving targets .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of ischemic heart disease now comes to the hospital due to problems with vision. She complains that while turning her head , the image of the previous target still persists for a few seconds before she can see the new target . This phenomenon is seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: The persistence of visual image even after shifting gaze is called palinopsia. It is seen in Balint's syndrome. Balint's syndrome results due to low flow in the watershed areas between distal PCA and MCA territories. It is characterized by the following : • Palinopsia - persistence of a visual image despite gazing at another scene • Asimultagnosia - difficulty to focus on more than one item in the visual field • Optic ataxia - Inability to reach accurately under visual guidance • Ocular apraxia - Inability to direct gaze accurately to a new target Claude 's syndrome is a distinctive brainstem syndrome characterized by ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiataxia. It is due to an intrinsic or extrinsic lesion in the midbrain . Note : While some authors use the term simultanagnosia, others use asimultanagnosia instead . A few authors also use these two terminologies interchangeably .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features do you not expect to see in a patient with Balint's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: 1121 Opsoclonus is not seen in Balint's syndrome. The features of Balint's syndrome are: • Optic ataxia - the inability to guide the arm to reach a certain object in the visual field • Simultanagnosia - the inability to perceive more than one object at a time. In other words, it is the inability to recognize multiple elements in a visual presentation , one object or some elements of a scene can be appreciated but not the display as a whole . • Ocular apraxia - the inability to control voluntary purposeful eye movements • Palinopsia - the persistence of a visual image even after the stimulus has been removed Note : While some authors use the term simultanagnosia, others use asimultanagnosia instead . A few authors also use these two terminologies interchangeably .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia is seen in Weber's syndrome. Weber's syndrome occurs due to infarction in the distribution of the penetrating branches of the PCA. It affects the cerebral peduncle , especially medially , and damages III cranial nerve and the pyramidal fibers. It results in contralateral hemiplegia and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy . Claude 's syndrome is a distinctive brainstem syndrome characterized by ipsilateral third cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiataxia. This is due to an intrinsic or extrinsic lesion in the midbrain .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following is wrong regarding Weber's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Ipsilateral paralysis of the lower face is not seen in Weber's syndrome. However, there is contralateral paralysis of the lower face . Weber syndrome is caused by infarction in the distribution of the penetrating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). It affects the cerebral peduncle , especially medially , with damage to the fascicle of cranial nerve III and the pyramidal fibers. The resultant clinical findings are contralateral hemiplegia of the face , arm , and leg secondary to corticospinal and corticobulbar tract involvement, and ipsilateral oculomotor paresis including a dilated pupil .Structure damaged Effect Cranial nerve III fibres Ipsilateral ptosisIpsilateral di vergent squintLoss of accom modation reflexLoss of light r eflex Corticobulbar tract UMN lesion leading to contra lateral paralysis of the lower f ace1122 Structure damaged Effect Corticospinal tract Contralateral hemiplegia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with loss of upgaze and convergence -retraction nystagmus . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of convergence -retraction nystagmus and loss of upgaze is seen in Parinaud's syndrome. It is caused by a lesion in the dorsal midbrain . The following tetrad of symptoms are seen : • Loss of upgaze • Light-near dissociation • Convergence -retraction nystagmus • Lid retraction Convergence \037retraction nystagmus is irregular, jerky nystagmus in which both eyeballs rhythmically converge and retract into the orbit, particularly on attempting an upward gaze. Nothnagel syndrome is associated with oculomotor palsy and contralateral limb ataxia. Underlying structures involved are the superior cerebellar peduncle and tectum of the midbrain .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with left -sided hemiplegia and examination revealed right-sided abducens nerve palsy and facial nerve palsy . Further investigation revealed a right-sided pontine haemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Ipsilateral abducens and facial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia are seen in Millard–Gubler syndrome. In this syndrome, there is a ventral pontine injury (lesion in abducens fascicle ) that causes lateral rectus palsy.1123 CNS lesion Effects Millard–Gubler Syndrome Ipsilateral abducens nerve we aknessIpsilateral facial nerve palsyContralateral hemiplegi a Raymond's Syndrome Ipsilateral abducens nerve pa lsyContralateral hemiplegia Foville's Syndrome Lateral gaze palsyIpsilateral f acial nerve palsyContralateral hemiplegia Balint's syndrome Optic ataxiaOcular apraxiaVi suospatial disorientation Lateral pontine syndrome (M arie-Foix syndrome) Contralateral hemiparesisCo ntralateral loss of propriocep tion & vibrationIpsilateral li mb ataxiaIpsilateral facial pal syLateral hearing lossVertigo Nystagmus

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following differentiates Foville's syndrome from Millard-Gubler syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Lateral gaze palsy is a feature of Foville's Syndrome which is a result of dorsal pontine injury. Millard-Gubler syndrome occurs due to ventral pontine injury. Lateral gaze palsy does not occur in this condition because the abducens fascicle is injured rather than the nucleus .CNS lesion Effects Millard–Gubler Syndrome Ipsilateral abducens nerve we aknessIpsilateral facial nerve palsyContralateral hemiplegi a Raymond's Syndrome Ipsilateral abducens nerve pa lsyContralateral hemiplegia Foville's Syndrome Lateral gaze palsyIpsilateral f acial nerve palsyContralateral hemiplegia Balint's syndrome Optic ataxiaOcular apraxiaVi suospatial disorientation Lateral pontine syndrome (M arie-Foix syndrome) Contralateral hemiparesisCo ntralateral loss of propriocep tion & vibrationIpsilateral li mb ataxiaIpsilateral facial pal syLateral hearing lossVertigo NystagmusContralateral loss of pain and temperature1124

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Thrombosis of posterior inferior cerebellar artery causes _______.
mcqs.explanation: Thrombosis of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) causes lateral medullary syndrome or Wallenberg syndrome. PICA is a branch of the fourth part of the vertebral artery, which is a branch of the first part of subclavian artery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Wallenberg syndrome is most commonly caused by thrombosis of which of the following arteries?
mcqs.explanation: Thrombosis of the vertebral artery is most commonly implicated in Wallenberg syndrome. Wallenberg syndrome, also called lateral medullary syndrome, is due to occlusion of the ipsilateral vertebral artery in most cases . In the remainder, posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion is responsible . Wallenberg / lateral medullary syndrome affects the following structures : • Descending tract and nucleus of cranial nerve V - Ipsilateral impaired sensation over half of the face • IX and X cranial nerves - Ipsilateral paralysis of palate , vocal cord, diminished gag reflex • Nucleus of tractus solitarius - Ipsilateral loss of taste • Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus , diplopia , vertigo, nausea • Spinocerebellar tract - Ipsilateral ataxia • Descending sympathetic tract - Ipsilateral Horner's syndrome • Lateral spinothalamic tract - Contralateral impaired pain and thermal sensation over half of the body.1125

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features do you not expect to see in a patient with Wallenberg syndrome?

options.d: Impaired sensation on ipsilateral half of face

mcqs.explanation: The pyramidal tracts are not affected in Wallenberg syndrome and therefore hemiplegia is not seen . Wallenberg / lateral medullary syndrome affects the following structures : • Descending tract and nucleus of CN V - I/L impaired sensation over half of face • IX and X CN - I/L paralysis of palate , vocal cord, diminished gag reflex • Nucleus of Tractus Solitarius – I/L loss of taste • Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus , diplopia , vertigo, nausea • Spinocerebellar tract – I/L ataxia • Descending sympathetic tract – I/L Horner's syndrome • Lateral spinothalamic tract – C/L impaired pain and thermal sensation over half of the body.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with medial medullary syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Horner's syndrome is not a feature of medial medullary syndrome. Medial medullary syndrome occurs due to the occlusion of the vertebral artery or a branch of the vertebral or basilar artery. The features of medial medullary syndrome are • CN XII - Ipsilateral paralysis of the tongue • Pyramidal tract - Contralateral hemiplegia • Medial lemniscus - Impaired tactile and proprioception over the contralateral half of the body Horner's syndrome occurs due to a lesion involving the sympathetic fibres. It is seen in lateral medullary syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which is the most common site of bleed in patients with intracerebral hypertensive haemorrhage?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site for intracerebral hypertensive hemorrhage is the putamen . The most common type of intracranial haemorrhage is an intraparenchymal i.e., intracerebral haemorrhage. It is most often caused by a hypertensive bleed . Most common sites of intracerebral hypertensive bleed : • Putamen (basal ganglia) • Thalamus • Cerebellum • Pons.1126

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Raised intracranial tension is not associated with which of the following manifestations ?
mcqs.explanation: Raised ICT is not associated with paraparesis. Manifestations of raised ICT include : • Hypertension • Bradycardia • Respiratory depression • Headache , visual blurring due to papilloedema and abducent nerve palsy • Seizures Paraparesis is usually caused by a spinal lesion such as thoracic myelopathy and neoplasms causing compression of the spinal cord. Rare intracranial causes of paraparesis are: • Parasagittal meningioma • Occlusion of unpaired anterior cerebral artery • Cerebral venous thrombosis affecting the sagittal sinus.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a component of Cushing's triad?
mcqs.explanation: Bradycardia is a component of Cushing's triad. Cushing's triad is characteristically seen in raised ICT . Its components are as follows : • Hypertension • Bradycardia • Respiratory depression .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the casualty with a severe headache , fever, and vomiting for the past 5 hours. There is no history of trauma. CT head is shown below . What is the most common cause for his presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage. The most common cause for this condition is the rupture of a berry aneurysm, also known as a saccular aneurysm. CT shows hyperattenuating material filling the subarachnoid space , which is suggestive of SAH. Most commonly, it occurs around the circle of Willis due to the rupture of a berry aneurysm at this location. Most unruptured intracranial aneurysms are completely asymptomatic . Prodromal symptoms occasionally suggest the site of the enlarging unruptured aneurysm. For example , cranial nerve III palsy with loss of ipsilateral light reflex and focal pain above or behind the eye suggests an expanding aneurysm at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and internal carotid1127 artery. Ruptured aneurysms cause an excruciating thunderclap headache followed by a transient loss of consciousness . Non-contrast CT scan is the investigation of choice for SAH. LP shows xanthochromatic CSF. Treatment involves clipping or coiling the aneurysm to eliminate the risk of rebleeding .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following structures is most likely to be compressed by an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery?
mcqs.explanation: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery will most likely compress the oculomotor nerve. This is because the posterior communicating artery is anatomically located very close to the oculomotor nerve. Patients with an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery can present with symptoms of oculomotor nerve palsy such as: • Unilateral ptosis (LPS ) • Outward eye deviation (MR) • Dilated pupil . The nerves controlling the pupils are located very superficially and these are always affected due to the mass effect of the aneurysm. Therefore the pupil sparing third nerve palsies are unlikely to be due to an aneurysm. Pupil-sparing oculomotor nerve palsy is often assumed to be caused by ischemic injuries such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus . Expanding unruptured aneurysms can occasionally lead to prodromal symptoms which suggest the location of the aneurysm.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: At which of the following locations does a Berry aneurysm have the highest risk of rupture ?
mcqs.explanation: The size and site of aneurysm are important in predicting the risk of rupture . Aneurysms with the following features have a greater risk of rupture : • Size >7 mm in diameter • Located at the top of the basilar artery (i.e origin of the posterior cerebral artery) • Located near the origin of the posterior communicating artery. The most common location of Berry aneurysm is the anterior communicating artery.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The CT finding of a patient is shown below . What is the most common cause for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given image is suggestive of a subdural hematoma and it most commonly results from injury to the bridging dural veins.1128 Subdural hematoma refers to the haemorrhage between the dura and arachnoid mater. The image of the CT scan reveals a hyperdense crescentic lesion. Mass effect with midline displacement can also be seen . Causes of SDH are: • Trauma • Anticoagulants • Antiplatelets • Alcohol abuse • Shaken baby syndrome. Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice . Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhage are: • Typically unilateral • Crescent -like distribution (concavo-convex) around the periphery of the brain • Not limited by sutures and can fill dural reflections • Chronic subdural hemorrhage: Crescent -shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT • Acute subdural hemorrhage: Hyperdense collections on CT

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The CT scan of a patient who was brought to the casualty after a road traffic accident is shown below . Between what structures does blood accumulate in this condition?

options.a: Outer table and inner table of the skull
options.d: Periosteum and aponeurotic layer of scalp

mcqs.explanation: The given CT image is suggestive of extradural haemorrhage (EDH). In this condition, blood accumulates between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. The typical presentation is an initial loss of consciousness following trauma, a complete transient recovery (lucid interval), and a rapid progression of neurological deterioration . This condition is treated by rapid surgical evacuation and ligation or cautery of the damaged vessel .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding extradural hemorrhage?

options.c: Middle meningeal artery bleed is the most common source

mcqs.explanation: In extradural hemorrhage (EDH), CT brain does not show a crescentric opacity . It shows a lentiform opacity .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old hypertensive man presented with an acute -onset headache for the past 2 hours, neck stiffness , nausea, and vomiting. He claims it is the worst headache of his life . There are no focal neurological deficits and his CT scan shows blood in the Sylvian fissure . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This patient 's clinical features of sudden-onset headache with neck stiffness , nausea, and vomiting with no neurological deficits is suggestive of a diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. The presence of blood in the Sylvian fissure confirms this diagnosis.1129 Trauma is the most common cause . However, spontaneous sub-arachnoid bleeding occurs most often due to the rupture of a berry aneurysm. Most of them are found in the anterior circulation, mostly on the circle of Willis. The three most common locations are: • Terminal ICA • MCA bifurcation • Top of the basilar artery. A non-contrast CT scan is the investigation of choice . LP shows xanthochromatic CSF. Treatment involves clipping or coiling the aneurysm to eliminate the risk of rebleeding .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 53-year-old man was admitted with a history of a cerebrovascular accident . On the second day, he becomes drowsy with minimal response . CT finding is shown in the image below . What will be your next line of management?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario describes a 53 year old patient admitted in view of a cerebrovascular accident developing neurologic deterioration (drowsy with minimal response ) on the second day, and CT brain showing significant edema of MCA territory with midline shift. The next line of management is decompressive surgery. Cerebral edema is a potential complication in 5-10% of patients with strokes, leading to obtundation and brain herniation. The severity of edema is highest on the second or third day after the stroke and can last for around 10 days. Medical management may not be successful in case of significant edema or infarcts involving the cerebellum . Decompressive surgery is recommended for patients who are less than 60 years old and experience deterioration \026 48 hours, despite receiving medical therapy . Hypodensity on head CT within the first 6 hours of stroke onset, involving \037 one-third of the MCA territory, early midline shift, and a diffusion -weighted imaging volume on MRI within 6 hours \037 80 mL are predictors of severe cerebral edema .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old man presents to the ER with headache , fever, and vomiting for the past 5 hours. A CT image is shown below . Physical examination shows positive Kernig's and Brudzinski 's signs. Vitals: Temp - 101 F, BP - 120 /88 mmHg, PR - 110 beats /min, pupils reactive. What is the next best step ?
mcqs.explanation: The scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and the treatment of choice for this condition is surgical clipping . CT shows hyperattenuating material filling the subarachnoid space , which is suggestive of SAH. Most commonly, it occurs around the circle of Willis due to the rupture of a berry aneurysm at this location. SAH can present with fever, positive Kernig's sign, and Brudzinski 's sign, as well as mimic meningitis or encephalitis . Treatment with the calcium channel antagonist nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 h) improves outcome , by preventing ischemic injury . Option A: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone is the recommended therapy for bacterial meningitis. Meningitis does not show hyper -attenuated subarachnoid space .1130 Option B: IV Tenecteplase is used for ischemic stroke without bleeding complications .1131

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following functions are likely to be impaired in patients with peripheral neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Peripheral neuropathies can impair sensory, motor, or autonomic function, either singly or in combination. Peripheral nerves are composed of sensory, motor, and autonomic elements . Peripheral neuropathies are classified into those that primarily affect the • Cell body - neuronopathy or ganglionopathy • Myelin - myelinopathy • Axon - axonopathy

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Disorders of autonomic function should be considered in patients with:
mcqs.explanation: Disorders of autonomic function (dysautonomia) is usually considered in patients with: • Unexplained orthostatic hypotension (OH) • Syncope • Sleep dysfunction • Altered sweating (hyperhidrosis or hypohidrosis ) • Impotence • Constipation or other GI symptoms like bloating, nausea, vomiting of old food, diarrhea. • Bladder disorders such as urinary frequency , hesitancy , or incontinence.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman complains of numbness of her hands, generalized weakness , and easy fatiguability . She is a vegetarian. She looks very pale and her peripheral smear reveals macrocytic hypochromic anemia. If untreated , she is at risk of developing which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: 1137 The given clinical scenario of macrocytic anemia and a vegetarian diet is suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency . This typically leads to large fiber neuropathy which presents with loss of proprioception and vibration . Smaller-diameter myelinated and unmyelinated fibers transmit pain and temperature sensation. Hence , small fiber neuropathies present as temperature loss or burning or stabbing pain.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Small fiber neuropathies can be seen in patients with all of the following conditions, except :
mcqs.explanation: Sjogren's syndrome does not cause small fiber neuropathy . It causes preferential large fiber sensory neuropathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presents with weakness of both the lower limbs. On examination, there is a sensory loss in the lower limbs and both the proximal and distal leg muscles have reduced power . This presentation is characteristic of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss. This pattern is characteristic of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathies . It consists of: • Acute form - Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy [AIDP ] also known as Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome [GBS] • Chronic form - Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy [CIDP] Option B: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ) is a multiple degenerative motor neuron disease . It leads to muscle weakness and disability in the absence of sensory symptoms and signs. Option C: Mononeuropathy multiplex refers to multiple compressive mononeuropathies . It presents as asymmetric subacute or acute sensory and motor symptoms and signs. Option D: Polyradiculopathy or plexopathy due to diabetes mellitus presents with asymmetric weakness.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented with peripheral neuropathy with asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss. The differential diagnosis for this condition would include all except :
mcqs.explanation: Hereditary motor neuropathy does not present with asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss. It presents with symmetric distal weakness without sensory loss.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy . Other examples of rare hereditary neuropathies are Friedreich's ataxia, familial amyloid polyneuropathy and Tangier disease .1138

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following are associated with autonomic neuropathies , except :
mcqs.explanation: In hyperthyroidism , excessive thyroxine causes sympathetic autonomic overactivity, not neuropathy . Hypothyroidism can be associated with peripheral neuropathy , most typically carpal tunnel syndrome. Treatment is the correction of hypothyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A young woman presents with complaints of insomnia due to her feet becoming very hot and painful at night. On examination, she has multiple superficial foot ulcers , and she is unable to feel light touch and crude touch . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of burning feet syndrome, seen in HSAN 1. There are five types of hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies (HSAN I–V ), of which the most important are HSAN I and HSAN III . HSAN I has an autosomal dominant inheritance. It presents in adolescence or adulthood as a distal small-fiber neuropathy . It causes burning feet syndrome in which patients present with: • Burning sensation of feet , especially at night • Sensory loss • Foot ulcers . Option B: Dejerine Roussy syndrome, also known as thalamic pain syndrome usually occurs after a stroke. The patient experiences burning pain over affected areas of the body. Option C: HSAN III or Riley Day syndrome presents in childhood . It presents with labile BP, decreased tearing, hyperhidrosis , reduced sensitivity to pain, and areflexia. Option D: Charcot Marie Tooth disease is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy . It is a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN) which presents with motor weakness and skeletal deformities .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of neuropathy seen in diabetes ?

options.d: Distal Symmetric Sensory and Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy

mcqs.explanation: Distal symmetric sensory and sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy and is seen in approximately one-third of patients with DM. Other neuropathies seen in diabetes mellitus are: • The most common mononeuropathies are median neuropathy at the wrist and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow • Diabetic autonomic neuropathy is typically seen in combination with DSPN • Cranial neuropathy (third nerve palsy is the most common) and diabetic neuropathic cachexia The Michigan diabetic neuropathy score is a screening tool used to assess diabetic neuropathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be prescribed as a first-line drug for a patient with painful diabetic neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: 1139 Duloxetine is a selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SSNRI ) and is one of the first-line drugs used in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy . Treatment of painful sensory neuropathies : • First-line: • Lidoderm 5% patch • Tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline , nortriptyline) • Gabapentin, Pregabalin • Duloxetine • Second -line: • Carbamazepine • Phenytoin • Venlafaxine • Tramadol • Third-line: • Mexiletine Optimal glucose control is considered the cornerstone for the treatment of diabetes and its complications. Intensive glucose control has been shown to prevent the development of peripheral neuropathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Sensorimotor neuropathy may be caused by all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Lead poisoning does not cause sensorimotor neuropathy . It causes symptoms and signs of primarily motor neuropathy . The most common presentation of lead poisoning is encephalopathy . The sensation is generally preserved but the autonomic nervous system can be affected in lead poisoning.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following vitamins will you prescribe for a patient on antitubercular therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: Isoniazid (INH), which is a first-line anti-tuberculosis drug, inhibits pyridoxal phosphokinase , resulting in pyridoxine deficiency and neuropathy . Prophylactic administration of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day can prevent neuropathy from developing . 10 mg daily suffices for prophylaxis but patients with evidence of vitamin B6 deficiency may require up to 50 mg daily. Current WHO guidelines recommend routine substitution of pyridoxine to patients who are at risk of peripheral neuropathy , e.g., malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence , diabetics , HIV . However, pyridoxine excess (acute intoxication or long-term use of large doses ) is also found to cause peripheral neuropathy .1140

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: During a regular health checkup , you notice the following nail finding in a 64-year-old man. He lives near a smelting industry on the banks of a river . Which of the following conditions can be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Mee 's lines, transverse white striae of the fingernails. This along with history is suggestive of chronic arsenic poisoning probably due to a contaminated water source . Arsenic poisoning causes toxic sensorimotor polyneuropathy . The neuropathy manifests 5–10 days after ingestion of arsenic and progresses for several weeks , mimicking Guillain–Barre's Syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Identify the diagnosis.
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing thickening of tissues in the temporal and orbital regions with coarse overlying skin suggests a diagnosis of plexiform neurofibroma. Plexiform neurofibroma represents an uncommon variant (30%) of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1). Plexiform neurofibromas are usually evident at birth and result from a diffuse thickening of nerve trunks and surrounding tissues that are usually located in the orbital or temporal region of the face . The skin overlying it may be coarse and associated with hyperpigmentation . Plexiform neurofibromas may produce an overgrowth of an extremity and a deformity of the corresponding bone. NF1 is clinically diagnosed when any 2 of the following 7 features are present : • Six or more caf\351-au-lait macules >5mm in prepubertal and >15mm in postpubertal • Axillary or inguinal freckling • Two or more iris lisch nodules • Two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma • A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or cortical thinning of long bones with or without pseudoarthrosis. • Optic gliomas • A first-degree relative with NF-11141

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common antecedent infectious cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Campylobacter jejuni is one of the most common risk factors for GBS. Infections that may trigger GBS are: • Campylobacter jejuni • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) • Epstein Barr virus • Mycoplasma • Varicella zoster virus • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ), dengue , or influenza, Zika , hepatitis Less commonly vaccinations, surgical procedures , and trauma have been reported to trigger the development of GBS.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following autoantibody isotype is involved in the pathogenesis of Guillian-Barre syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: IgG isotype of autoantibody is involved in the pathogenesis of GBS. IgM isotype autoantibodies are known to play a role in some types of chronic immune neuropathies.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In Guillain-Barre syndrome due to antecedent infection with Campylobacter jejuni, the autoantibodies are most commonly directed against which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Autoantibodies in GBS due to Campylobacter jejuni infection are directed most commonly against GM1 gangliosidase .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of Guillian-Barre syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP ) is the most common type of GBS. There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome, which are recognized by electrodiagnostic studies and pathological distinctions . These include : A. Demyelinating • Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP ) - most common B. Axonal • Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) • Acute motor–sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN) C. Regional GBS syndromes • Miller –Fisher syndrome (MFS)1149 • Pure sensory forms • Ophthalmoplegia with anti-GQ1b antibodies as part of severe motor-sensory GBS • GBS with severe bulbar and facial paralysis • Acute pandysautonomia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which type of Guillain-Barre syndrome most commonly affects patients in the pediatric age group?
mcqs.explanation: The acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is more common in pediatric age groups .Type Age group affected Acute inflammatory demyeli nating polyneuropathy (AIDP) Adults Acute motor axonal neuropat hy (AMAN) ChildrenYoung adu lts Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN) Mostly adults Miller –Fisher syndrome AdultsChildren

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy differs from acute motor axonal neuropathy , in that, in the latter, the complement deposition along with IgG antibodies occurs at:
mcqs.explanation: In AMAN, the complement along with IgG is deposited at the nodes of Ranvier of large motor axons. In AIDP , complement deposits along the outer surface of the Schwann cell .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with Guillian-Barre syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Bladder dysfunction is not usually severe and does not appear early in the course of Guillain-Barre Syndrome(GBS). If bladder dysfunction is a prominent feature and comes early in the course , diagnostic possibilities other than GBS should be considered . GBS is an acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy . It is an autoimmune disorder triggered by infections like: • Campylobacter jejuni • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) • Epstein Barr virus • Mycoplasma • Varicella zoster virus1150 • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ), dengue , or influenza It manifests as a rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis, with or without sensory disturbance . The usual pattern is ascending paralysis. Proximal and distal muscles are equally involved. The lower cranial nerves are frequently affected , causing bulbar weakness .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following sensory deficits is severely affected in a patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Loss of proprioception is severe in Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). GBS affects the large sensory fibers, leading to attenuation or loss of deep tendon reflexes and loss of proprioception . Cutaneous sensory deficits (e.g., loss of pain and temperature sensation) are usually relatively mild.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presents with complaints of lower extremity weakness . He initially noticed difficulty climbing the stairs and now he is unable to stand. He gives a history of bloody diarrhea a few weeks ago. Which of the following parameters are expected to be elevated in the CSF of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). Protein levels are elevated (100 -1000mg/dl) in the CSF of a patient with this condition. The CSF cell counts are usually normal . Albuminocytologic dissociation , which is an elevation in CSF protein without an elevation in white blood cells , is characteristic in GBS. Causes of albuminocytologic dissociation are: • Guillain-Barre Syndrome • Spinal cord tumours

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions does not present with autonomic dysfunction ?
mcqs.explanation: Subclavian steal syndrome does not present with autonomic dysfunction . Option A: Polyneuropathy is seen in sporadic and familial amyloidosis . In some cases , autonomic insufficiency presents before distal painful polyneuropathy accompanied by sensory loss Option B: Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome is associated with autonomic instability . This can present with BP fluctuations , arrhythmias, and GI disturbances . Option C: Botulinum toxin binds presynaptically to cholinergic nerve terminals. After uptake into the cytoplasm , it blocks ACh release . Thus, patients with botulism present with motor paralysis and autonomic disturbances .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old patient presents with rapidly progressing symmetric ascending paralysis since 2 days. Nerve conduction studies are consistent with demyelination . He is found to have an elevated protein level in his CSF. Which of the following autonomic disturbance is likely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 1151 The given scenario is suggestive of Guillian-Barre syndrome (GBS). Postural hypotension is a common autonomic disturbance seen in this condition. Autonomic involvement is common and may occur even in patients whose GBS is otherwise mild. The usual autonomic manifestations are: • Loss of vasomotor control with wide fluctuation in blood pressure , postural hypotension • Cardiac dysrhythmias

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The triad of Miller-Fisher syndrome includes all of the following , except :
mcqs.explanation: Weakness is not seen in the triad of Miller -Fisher syndrome (MFS). Miller Fisher syndrome is a variant of Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome(GBS). Like Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome, symptoms may be preceded by a viral illness . It classically presents as a triad of: • Ataxia • Areflexia • Ophthalmoplegia The condition is usually not associated with weakness , and even if present , is very mild. It is strongly associated with antibodies to the ganglioside GQ1b. The prognosis in Miller Fisher syndrome is usually good with recovery beginning within 2 to 4 weeks of the symptom onset , and completing by 6 months. Some individuals are left with residual deficits . Relapses are rare. Treatment for Miller Fisher syndrome is identical to treatment for Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome: intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg ) or plasmapheresis and supportive care.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the ER with tingling, numbness, and weakness in all four limbs. She says that the weakness started in the lower limbs and progressed to the upper limbs within a day. History is significant for a recent COVID -19 infection and surgery for cervical spondylosis and disc herniation 3 years ago. CT brain was normal and an MRI of the lumbar spine showed foraminal narrowing at L2 -L3 . CSF analysis showed increased protein levels . Which of the following is recommended for the initial therapy of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome(GBS) probably as a result of COVID -19. IV Immunoglobulin is the recommended initial therapy for patients with GBS. High-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIg ) and plasmapheresis are both equally effective in GBS and can be used as the initial therapy . However, IVIg is often the initial therapy chosen because of its ease of administration and good safety record. It is administered as five daily infusions for a total dose of 2 g/kg body weight . Glucocorticoids have not been found to be effective in GBS.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In a patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is suspected when _______

options.a: GBS deteriorates >5 weeks after onset or relapses at least three times
options.b: GBS deteriorates >5 weeks after onset or relapses at least two times
options.c: GBS deteriorates >9 weeks after onset or relapses at least three times
options.d: GBS deteriorates >8 weeks after onset or relapses at least two times

mcqs.explanation: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) should be suspected when GBS deteriorates >9 weeks after onset or relapses at least three times .1152 Onset is usually gradual over a few months or longer, but in a few cases , the initial attack is indistinguishable from that of GBS. CIDP is distinguished from GBS by its chronic course . In other respects , this neuropathy shares many features with the common demyelinating form of GBS, including elevated CSF protein levels and the electrodiagnostic studies findings of acquired demyelination .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions are not associated with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis A infection is not associated with CIDP. Diseases associated with CIDP are: • Hepatitis B • Hepatitis C • Lymphoma • HIV • Diabetic mellitus • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) • Pregnancy • Paraneoplastic syndrome • Inflammatory bowel disease • Amyloidosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All are true about chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy , except :

options.b: Relapse at least 3 times in a patient with Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome
options.d: Small nerve fibers are affected more than large fibers

mcqs.explanation: Large nerve fibers are affected more than small fibers in CIDP. Difference between CIDP and Guillain-barr\351 syndrome(GBS):GBS CIDP Duration <4 we eks >8 weeks Motor symptoms Affect ed Affected Sensory symptoms Mild More significantLargefiber > small fiber Autonomic nervous syst em Affect ed Rare Antecedent event Prese nt Rare1153 GBS CIDP Deep tendon reflex Absen t Absent Steroid No ro le 2nd line of treatment

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is undergoing nerve conduction study . Which of the following findings is least likely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In CIDP, the amplitude is normal since the axons are intact. Nerve conduction study (NCS) in axonal injury and demyelinating diseases :Axonal injury Demyelination Amplitude Decreased Normal Distal latency Normal Prolonged Conduction veloci ty Normal Slow Conduction block Absent Present Temporal dispersi on Absent Present H wave Normal or abs ent Prolonged or abse nt F wave Normal or abs ent Prolonged or abse nt

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In which of the following situations is nerve biopsy not indicated in patients with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy ?

options.b: When other causes of polyneuropathy cannot be ruled out
options.d: When there is no clinical or electrophysiological evidence of nerve functionality

mcqs.explanation: Nerve biopsy should not be done if there is no clinical or electrophysiological evidence of nerve functionality of that nerve in CIDP patients . This is because completely degenerated nerves usually convey limited information. In CIDP, nerve biopsy is indicated when: • Diagnosis is not clear • Other causes of polyneuropathy cannot be ruled out • Electromyography (EMG ) shows axonal involvement

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following can be used for the treatment of a patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy , except :
mcqs.explanation: NSAIDs are not used in the treatment of CIDP.1154 The treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) includes high-dose IV immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis , and glucocorticoids . Initial therapy is usually with IV immunoglobulin. If all the first-line agents fail, immunosuppressants are attempted either alone or as an adjunctive treatment .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
