mcqs.explanation: Levodopa-induced motor complications are more likely to occur in females .1225 The complications include transient, stereotypic , rhythmic movements that predominantly involve the lower extremities . It is seen in younger individuals with severe disease and also with higher doses of levodopa .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old woman on treatment for Parkinson 's disease is brought to the OPD. Her husband is concerned because she has been shopping a lot and reached the maximum spending limit on 2 credit cards in the past week . She has also impulsively been buying several rabbits and raising them in their home. She admits feeling guilty after her purchases . Which of the following drugs is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of compulsive shopping . Pathological gambling, hypersexuality , and compulsive eating and shopping are the adverse effects of dopamine agonists. Levodopa can also cause these effects , but to a lesser extent than dopamine agonists.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with Parkinson 's disease has been scheduled to undergo deep brain stimulation. What is the target site for this procedure ?

options.a: Subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus internus
options.b: Subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus externus
options.c: Substantia nigra pars compacta and globus pallidus externus
options.d: Substantia nigra pars reticulata and globus pallidus internus

mcqs.explanation: The target site for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson 's disease is the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus internus (GPi). It helps improve tremors and reduce both 'off' time and dyskinesia. It does not improve features that fail to respond to levodopa . It does not prevent the development or progression of non-dopaminergic features such as freezing , falling, and dementia .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of Parkinson 's plus syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy is an example of Parkinson 's plus syndrome. Parkinson 's plus syndrome or atypical parkinsonism refers to a group of conditions that present with parkinsonism (rigidity and bradykinesia) but are different from PD due to underlying differences in clinical manifestations and pathology . They may have degeneration of the striatum, globus pallidus , cerebellum , and brainstem as well as the SNc. These include multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and corticobasal syndrome (CBS). PSP is often misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease (PD). The substantia nigra is damaged in both diseases and this accounts for the overlapping symptoms which are observed. In PSP, impairment of cognitive functions occurs before the motor or ocular signs and this serves as an important distinguishing feature . Immunohistochemistry broadly classifies them into two subtypes : synucleopathies and tauopathies .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which among the following features is not expected in a patient with atypical parkinsonism ?

options.c: Poor or no response to levodopa

mcqs.explanation: Early speech and gait impairment are seen in atypical parkinsonism . Features of atypical parkinsonism include : • Early speech and gait impairment1226 • Absence of rest tremor • No motor asymmetry • Poor or no response to levodopa • Aggressive clinical course • Symptoms of severe early autonomic involvement • Early severe dementia also points towards atypical parkinsonism

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presented with Parkinsonism and cerebellar features . MRI showed the finding as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Parkinsonism , cerebellar features , and the 'hot cross bun' sign on MRI suggest multiple system atrophy (MSA). MSA manifests as a combination of parkinsonian , cerebellar , and autonomic features . Based on predominant clinical features it is further divided into : • MSA-P: • Predominantly parkinsonian features are seen • T2 weighted MRI demonstrates hyperintense putaminal rim • MSA-C: • Predominantly cerebellar features are seen • MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy causing pontine hot cross bun sign

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following are the core clinical features for the diagnosis of Lewy body dementia except :
mcqs.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is not a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD ) as per DSM-5. LBD also known as dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most type of progressive dementia after Alzheimer's disease . Protein deposits , called Lewy bodies , deposit in nerve cells in the brain region involved in thinking, memory, and movement (motor control) Core features of LBD as per DSM-5 are fluctuating cognition, attention , alertness , recurrent visual hallucination, and Parkinsonian symptoms . Suggestive features are REM sleep behavior disorder and severe neuroleptic sensitivity . Orthostatic hypotension , erectile dysfunction , and constipation are other features of LBD . Treatment of LBD includes rivastigmine and donepezil which may improve cognition, and reduce hallucinosis and delusion . Pimavanserin may be used to treat psychosis .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presented with Parkinsonian features which is unresponsive to levodopa . MRI image is given below . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 1227 An elderly male with a history of features of Parkinsonism nonresponsive to levodopa should raise suspicion for Parkinson plus syndromes which include progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), also known as the Steele -Richardson-Olszewski syndrome, is a tauopathy and is considered a neurodegenerative disease with no current efficacious treatment . It is characterized by decreased cognition, abnormal eye movements (supranuclear vertical gaze palsy ), postural instability and falls, as well as parkinsonian features and speech disturbances . The atrophy of the midbrain results in hummingbird sign of the brainstem (in the sagittal plane ). The preserved pons form the body of the bird, and the atrophic midbrain , the head , with beak extending anteriorly towards the optic chiasm. Midbrain atrophy is best confirmed with the reduction in the midbrain to pons ratio. Mickey mouse appearance , which is the reduction of anteroposterior midline midbrain diameter , at the level of the superior colliculi is seen on axial imaging. The following image shows the hummingbird sign:According to a recent imaging study data, the insula and frontal cortex seem to be involved in the development of anxiety in adults with Parkinson 's disease .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old girl exhibits rapid, semi-purposeful , graceful , dance-like, involuntary movements. What is this finding?
mcqs.explanation: Rapid, semi-purposeful , graceful , dance-like, involuntary movements are seen in chorea. Sydenham's chorea (also called St. Vitus's dance) is a type of chorea that is typically seen in childhood (5-15 years) with prior exposure to group A streptococcal infection and is thought to be autoimmune in nature. It is characterized by the acute onset of choreiform movements and behavioral disturbances and is self -limiting.1228 Hyperkinetic movement diso rders: Tremor Rhythmic oscillation of a bod y part due to intermittent mu scle contractions Dystonia Involuntary , sustained or rep eated muscle contractions oft en associated with twisting m ovements and abnormal post ure Athetosis Slow, distal , writhing, involu ntary movements with a prop ensity to affect arms and han ds Chorea Rapid, semi-purposeful , grac eful , dance-like, non patterne d, involuntary movements in volving distal or proximal mu scle groups Myoclonus Sudden , brief (<100ms ), jerk- like arrhythmic muscle twitc hes Tics Brief, repeated , stereotyped muscle contractions that can often be suppressed for a sho rt time

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: During rounds, you see that a patient diagnosed with stroke exhibits wild , flinging movements on his right side . Where is the lesion likely to be?
mcqs.explanation: Unilateral wild , flinging movements are called hemiballismus and is seen due to a lesion in the subthalamic nucleus . The most common cause of hemiballismus is stroke.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common acute drug-induced movement disorder?
mcqs.explanation: The most common acute drug-induced movement disorder is dystonia. Drug-induced movement disorders are primarily associated with drugs that block dopamine receptors (neuroleptics ) or central dopaminergic transmission. Neuroleptics are the commonest cause of this condition. Drug-induced movement disorders are classified as: • Acute : Dystonia is the most common acute hyperkinetic drug reaction; generalized in children, focal in adults . • Subacute : Akathisia is the commonest reaction in this category • Tardive syndromes: Develop after months to years of initiation of the drug.1229 • Tardive dyskinesia is the most common. Choreiform movements affecting the mouth, lips, and tongue are seen . In severe cases , trunks, limbs, and respiratory muscles may also be affected . • In one third, TD remits within 3 months of stopping the drug and improvement occur over several years.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common movement disorder?
mcqs.explanation: The most common movement disorder is essential tremor. It can present in childhood but dramatically increases in prevalence over the age of 70 years. Essential tremor is characterized by a high-frequency tremor 6-10 Hz that predominantly affects the upper extremities . The tremor is characteristically improved by alcohol and worsened by stress .Essential trem or Parkinson 's diseas e Bradykinesia\037rigidity\037 micr ographia Absent Present Tremor Usually postur al Usually resting Tone Normal Cogwheel rigidity

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presents with a tremor in both hands that worsens when he is trying to eat or write something . He says that it gets worse when he is stressed and reduces when he drinks wine. His father also had similar symptoms . On examination, there are no resting tremors. Which of the following drugs can be used to control this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of essential tremor. It can be controlled by primidone. The drugs used to treat essential tremors are: • Beta-blockers: propranolol, atenolol • Anticonvulsants: • Primidone • Gabapentine • Topiramate In severe and drug-resistant cases , surgical treatment involves targeting the ventral intermediate (VIM ) nucleus of the thalamus.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old male patient is scheduled to undergo deep brain stimulation for essential tremor. What is the target site for the procedure ?

options.a: Subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus internus

mcqs.explanation: The target for deep brain stimulation in essential tremor is ventral intermediate (VIM ) nucleus of the thalamus.1230 Disease Target sites for deep brain sti mulation Parkinson 's disease Subthalamic nucleus (STN)Gl obus pallidus internus (GPi) Dystonia Globus pallidus internus (GPi) Depression Anterior limb of internal cap sule and cingulum Obsessive -Compulsive Disord er (OCD) Anterior limb of the internal capsule Essential tremor Ventral intermediate (VIM ) n ucleus

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient with a family history of Huntington's disease has come for genetic counselling . All of the following are true about this condition, except :

options.c: Westphal akinetic variant has good prognosis

mcqs.explanation: Westphal akinetic variant has the worst prognosis. Huntington's disease shows an autosomal dominant inheritance. It is a trinucleotide repeat expansion disease with multiple CAG repeats (>40 repeats ) in the coding region of the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p. It demonstrates genetic anticipation with earlier onset if inherited from the father. It presents in the second to third decade of life with cognitive impairment as an early feature . The dominant cognitive feature of HD is executive dysfunction . Additionally , dementia is seen later as the disease progresses . Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia . Decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea. Treatment consists of haloperidol , tetrabenazine (Dopamine depletor ). The following image shows MRI showing dilated ventricles (ex vacuo ventriculomegaly )- due to atrophy of caudate and putamen :1231 MRI showing atrophy of caudate and putamen

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: St. Vitus' dance is the other name for which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Sydenham's chorea was originally called St. Vitus's dance. Sydenham's chorea is more common in females . It is typically seen in childhood (5-1 5 years) with prior exposure to group A streptococcal infection and is thought to be autoimmune in nature. It is characterized by the acute onset of choreiform movements and behavioral disturbances . It is self limited .Treatment is generally restricted to those with severe chorea.The chorea generally responds to dopamine-blocking agents, valproic acid, and carbamazepine.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: All of the following features can be seen in patients with restless leg syndrome, except :

options.a: Symptoms worsen during the evening or night
options.b: Accompanied by an unpleasant sensation in the legs
options.c: Symptoms that begin or worsen with activity
options.d: Partial or complete relief by movement

mcqs.explanation: In restless leg syndrome (RLS), symptoms begin or worsen with rest. It is also called as Willis-Ekbom disease . The four core symptoms required for the diagnosis of RLS are: • An urge to move the legs • Usually caused or accompanied by an unpleasant sensation in the legs (creepy -crawly feeling , paresthesia , or burning) • Symptoms that begin or worsen with rest and partial or complete relief by movement • Worsening during the evening or night Restless leg syndrome is a typical sensory-motor disorder that generally affects the legs during rest periods, especially sleep . There is an irresistible urge to shake the legs associated with burning sensation, itching, and cramps of the legs . In idiopathic cases , dopaminergic1232 hypofunction is postulated . In patients with restless legs syndrome, iron stores are initially repleted , and the aggravating factors are eliminated . If RLS still persists , initial therapy with a gabapentinoid (pregabalin, gabapentin , gabapentin enacarbil) is preferred , rather than a dopamine agonist (pramipexole , ropinirole, rotigotine ). This is due to the high frequency of intermediate and long-term augmentation with dopamine agonists, as well as their risk of impulse control disorders. FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of restless leg syndrome: • Gabapentin • Ropinirole • Pramipexole • Rotigotine A dopamine agonist is used as an alternative in patients with increased risk for side effects from gabapentinoids , such as those with obesity and its complications , a past or present history of moderate to severe depression , a disorder causing gait instability or respiratory failure, and a history of substance use disorder. Non-pharmacological treatments that can be used in restless leg syndrome are: • Avoiding alcohol at bedtime • Massaging affected legs • Hot baths • Applying hot or cold to the affected area • Engaging in moderate exercises1233

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which of the following features are lower motor neuron lesions associated with?
mcqs.explanation: Lower motor neuron lesions are associated with fasciculations .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which of the following is referred to as bulbar paralysis?

options.a: UMN palsy of cranial nerves 1 to
options.b: LMN palsy of cranial nerves 1 to
options.c: UMN palsy of cranial nerves 9 to
options.d: LMN palsy of cranial nerves 9 to

mcqs.explanation: Bulbar paralysis refers to LMN palsy of cranial nerves 9 to 12 . It is seen due to disease processes affecting primarily the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves. The manifestations of bulbar palsy include paralysis of tongue , muscles of swallowing , and facial muscles . There is difficulty handling secretions and maintaining an airway. Causes of bulbar palsy include : • GBS • Polio • Syringobulbia

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which type of disorder is primary lateral sclerosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Primary lateral sclerosis is a progressive isolated upper motor neuron disorder. The spectrum of motor neuron disease includes :1237 • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ): • It is the most common form of motor neuron disease • Includes upper and lower motor neuron pathology (UMN +LMN) • Primary lateral sclerosis : • It is a progressive isolated upper motor neuron disorder (UMN ) • Some patients develop lower motor neuron signs later in their clinical course , at which point the disease is called upper motor neuron-onset ALS • Progressive muscular atrophy: • It is a progressive isolated lower motor neuron disorder (LMN) • Some patients develop upper motor neuron signs later in their clinical course , at which point the disease is called lower motor neuron-onset ALS • Progressive bulbar palsy : • It is a progressive upper and lower motor neuron (UMN +LMN) disorder of cranial muscles • This condition may occasionally stay isolated to the bulbar segment , but more commonly, upper and lower motor neuron signs and symptoms spread to involve other segments . This is then referred to as bulbar-onset ALS

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which of the following is involved in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ) involves the anterior horn cells and corticospinal tract. ALS is the most common form of progressive motor neuron disease . The pathologic hallmark of motor neuron degenerative disorders is the death of lower motor neurons and upper , or corticospinal, motor neurons. LMN consist of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and their brainstem homologs innervating bulbar muscles . UMN originate in layer five of the motor cortex and descend via the pyramidal tract to synapse with lower motor neurons, either directly or indirectly via interneurons. Although at its onset , ALS may cause selective loss of function of only upper or lower motor neurons, it ultimately causes progressive loss of both categories of motor neurons.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man presents with progressive atrophy and weakness of his hands and forearms. On examination, he is found to have spasticity of the legs and brisk jaw jerk. Neuroimaging revealed increased signal in the corticospinal tracts on T2 weighted MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ). The clinical hallmark of ALS is the presence of signs and symptoms of both upper and lower motor neuron (UMN + LMN) dysfunction. The signs of UMN dysfunction include spasticity and brisk jaw jerk, while the signs of LMN dysfunction include atrophy and weakness of limbs. Conventional MRI is usually normal in ALS and is used to exclude other possible causes although i ncreased signal in the corticospinal tracts on T2 -weighted MRI is supportive of the diagnosis of ALS .1238

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: A young college student presents with multiple episodes of falls while climbing stairs. He stated he had been feeling clumsy and weak for the past few months. On examination, he was found to have bilateral positive Babinski 's sign and atrophy of muscles of lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario with both UMN (positive Babinski sign) and LMN (absent reflexes and wasting of muscles ) signs are suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ). It is also known as Lou Gehrig's disease , after the famous New York Yankee baseball player who was affected with the disorder. ALS was first described by Charcot in the 19th century and is also referred to as Charcot's disease . Option A: Kennedy disease is a gradually progressive neuromuscular disorder characterised by wasting of proximal and bulbar muscles . It is caused by a mutation in the androgen receptor gene . Option C: Pelizaeus –Merzbacher disease is an inherited leukodystrophy characterized by problems with coordination, motor skills, and learning. Option D: Charcot-Marie-tooth disease encompasses a group of hereditary sensory and motor neuropathies.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man who presented with progressive weakness was found to have a mix of upper and lower motor neuron findings on examination. His father and his cousin had passed away in their 40s due to similar symptoms . A mutation of the gene encoding which of the following enzymes is likely implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis . This condition is linked to mutations of the gene encoding copper -zinc (Cu, Zn ) superoxide dismutase type 1 (SOD1). Familial ALS accounts for about 10 % of all ALS cases . Option B: Mutations in the NADPH oxidase genes cause chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Option C: Hereditary deficiency of myeloperoxidase (MPO) predisposes to immune deficiency . Option D: Glutathione peroxidase deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: All of the following features can be seen in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis , except :
mcqs.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is not a feature seen in classical ALS . Autonomic symptoms are not classically seen in ALS , although a few cases with autonomic insufficiency have been reported and these are classified separately as ALS -plus syndromes. Option A: The split -hand syndrome describes a frequent pattern of weakness and atrophy in ALS that predominantly involves the median and ulnar-innervated lateral (thenar) hand intrinsic muscles with relative sparing of the medial (hypothenar ) muscles . Option C: There is a well -established link between ALS and frontotemporal executive dysfunction (dementia ) that may precede or follow the onset of upper and/or lower motor neuron dysfunction Option D: Dropped head syndrome is an important clinical sign in ALS caused by severe neck extensor weakness (LMN), which leads to an inability to maintain level head position .1239

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients is unlikely to have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ?

options.a: A patient with difficulty in swallowing
options.b: A patient who has spastic dysarthria
options.c: A patient who starts laughing or crying inappropriately
options.d: A patient with bowel and bladder dysfunction

mcqs.explanation: The patient with bowel and bladder dysfunction is unlikely to have ALS as these findings are not seen in ALS . Even in the late stages of the ALS , sensory & bowel & bladder functions are preserved . Fasciculations , muscle cramps, weakness , atrophy, and bulbar palsy are LMN features seen in ALS. Spasticity , increased reflexes , flexor spasms, and pseudobulbar palsy are UMN features in ALS . A frequent bulbar UMN symptom seen in ALS is the pseudobulbar affect . This is manifested as inappropriate laughing , crying, or yawning. The observed affect is often mood incongruent or may be triggered by stimuli that would not have elicited such a response prior to the development of pseudobulbar affect .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: What is the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis predominantly based on?
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis of ALS is based on clinical criteria that include the presence of upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron signs, the progression of the disease , and the absence of an alternative explanation. There is no single diagnostic test that can confirm or entirely exclude the diagnosis of motor neuron disease in general and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS ) in particular. The revised El Escorial criteria and, more recently , the newer Awaji criteria are being used for the diagnosis of ALS . Practically, the diagnosis is made when it is suggested by the history and physical examination, supported by electrodiagnostic studies (EMG & NCS), and not excluded by neuroimaging (MRI) and laboratory studies (CSF, blood, and urine analysis). Increased signal in the corticospinal tracts on T2 -weighted MRI, if seen , is supportive of the diagnosis of ALS Muscle biopsy is not a routine part of the diagnostic evaluation of ALS but should be performed if there is clinical suspicion of inflammatory myopathy . Genetic testing is not a routine part of the diagnostic evaluation in ALS except in cases where familial ALS (10 %) is suspected .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.chapter: ALS and Other Motor Neuron Diseases
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the only drug known to improve survival in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , riluzole is the only known drug to have any impact on survival in ALS . It can slow ALS progression to a modest degree . It is a neuroprotective drug that blocks glutamatergic neurotransmission in the CNS . Edaravone is a newer drug that is a free radical scavenger . It is thought to reduce oxidative stress , which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of ALS . Edaravone was found to slow functional deterioration in some patients with ALS . It is recommended as an adjunct to riluzole for all patients with ALS .1240

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient walks with a stomping gait. When asked to close his eyes and walk, he is unable to do so. Which of the following tracts is probably affected ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of the posterior column. Posterior column carries proprioception which is essential for coordination of motor movements. Loss of this leads to the development of a stomping gait. This is seen in cases of vitamin B12 deficiency leading to subacute combined degeneration , tabes dorsalis or diabetic neuropathy .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following features would you not expect to find in a patient with cerebellar ataxia?
mcqs.explanation: Intention tremor is a feature of cerebellar ataxia, not resting tremor. Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by the following symptoms :1245 • Gait impairment • Unclear speech or scanning speech • Blurred vision due to nystagmus • Dysdiadochokinesis • Intention tremors - tremor on goal-oriented movements Bilateral and symmetric involvement suggests the following etiologies : • Genetic - SCA gene mutations • Metabolic - Vitamin B1 or B12 deficiency • Immune - Antigliadin antibody syndrome • Toxic - Phenytoin, amiodarone, alcohol Focal, unilateral symptoms with headache, impaired level of consciousness , ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies and contralateral weakness suggest a space -occupying cerebellar lesion.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man presented with gait instability , slurring of speech , and intention tremors, for a few months. He was a former smoker who quit 10 years back. After extensive workup, a paraneoplastic cause was suspected , and chest CT was ordered . It showed a 3cm wide mass near the right hilum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia, which is most likely to be caused by small cell lung cancer here. Paraneoplastic syndromes causing cerebellar ataxia are associated with various antibodies : Sometimes , paraneoplastic ataxias may be the only presenting symptom of the underlying cancer. In paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxias, serum anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies may be elevated , affecting speech and gait.Cancer Antibody seen Breast and ovarian cancer s Anti-Yo antibody Small-cell lung cancer Anti-PQ-type voltage -gated c alcium channel autoantibody Hodgkin's disease Anti-Tr antibodies

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: What is the most common inherited ataxia?
mcqs.explanation: Friedreich's ataxia is the most common form of inherited ataxia (autosomal recessive ), comprising one-half of all hereditary ataxias. Friedrich's ataxia has autosomal recessive inheritance and presents before 25 years of age . The median age of death is 35 years. Women have a significantly better prognosis than men. Friedrich's ataxia presents with clinical features such as dysarthria, progressive staggering gait, frequent falls and titubation . Other neurological symptoms include nystagmus , loss of fast1246 saccadic movements, loss of vibratory and proprioceptive sensation, and ataxia or trunk and limb movements. The lower extremities are more severely involved than the upper ones. Cardiac involvement occurs in 90% of patients . It presents with cardiomegaly , symmetric hypertrophy, and conduction defects . Musculoskeletal deformities are common and include progressive scoliosis , pes cavus, and pes equinovarus .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old man presents with complaints of swaying while walking, frequent falls and slurring of speech. He also gives a history of involuntary nodding movements of the head . On examination, you note the following findings. Which of the following regions of the spinal cord is involved first in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of Friedrich's ataxia, in which the dorsal root ganglion cells are involved first. The primary sites of pathology are the spinal cord, dorsal root ganglion cells , and the peripheral nerves. Spinal cord tracts are involved, and degeneration occurs predominantly in the spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, and posterior columns. Degeneration of cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal , vagus, hypoglossal) and deep cerebellar nuclei can occur. Peripheral nerves are also involved, and there 's a loss of large myelinated fibers. Cerebellar atrophy is also seen . Cardiac changes occur due to myocyte hypertrophy , fibrosis, and degeneration of cardiac ganglia. Note : Friedrich's ataxia may also be associated with vitamin E deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A middle -aged vegan woman presented with tingling and numbness over the limbs and progressive fatigue . Her peripheral smear is given below . Which of the following neurological manifestation would you not expect to see in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario and smear showing macroovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils , is suggestive of megaloblastic anemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency . Myopathy is not a feature of vitamin B12 deficiency . Vitamin B12 deficiency may produce the following neurological manifestations : • Loss of vibration sense and proprioception • Paresthesia - upper limb paresthesias occur before lower limbs are affected . • Unsteady gait - due to sensory ataxia • Peripheral neuropathy • Optic neuropathy • Psychiatric manifestations such as: • Irritated behavior • Severe dementia • Frank psychosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presented with swaying while walking, tingling in palms and feet , and blurring of vision. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent, proprioception and vibration sense are absent over the lower limbs. MRI spine reveals diffuse demyelination . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 1247 The given case scenario is suggestive of subacute combined degeneration (SACD) due to vitamin B12 deficiency . SACD presents with the following features : • Loss of vibration sense and proprioception • Paresthesia - upper limb paresthesias occur before lower limbs are affected . • Unsteady gait - due to sensory ataxia • Loss of deep tendon reflexes • Peripheral neuropathy • Optic neuropathy - can present as blurring of vision • Psychiatric manifestations such as: • Irritated behavior • Severe dementia • Frank psychosis MRI spine shows myelopathy and areas of demyelination . Myelopathy of SACD tends to be diffuse rather than focal. Treatment is replacement therapy is with 1000 �Mg of intramuscular vitamin B12 repeated at regular intervals or by oral vitamin B12 .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The investigations of a male truck driver are given below . Which of the following is he unlikely to present with?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of tabes dorsalis. It presents with loss of reflexes in lower limbs, not hyperreflexia . Tabes dorsalis (or syphilitic myelopathy) is a slow degeneration and demyelination of the neural tracts. It is seen in tertiary syphilis . It primarily involves the dorsal columns of the spinal cord and dorsal roots. It presents with the following clinical features : • Loss of reflexes in lower limbs • Romberg's sign • Bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils - accommodation reflex present , pupillary reflex absent • Loss of position sense and vibration • Stabbing/pricking pain in the legs - this is fleeting or repetitive • Ataxia of the legs and gait disturbances • Paresthesias • Bladder disturbances • Acute abdominal pain with vomiting - visceral crisis Note : Diabetic polyradiculopathy may simulate tabes .1248

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding ataxia telangiectasia ?

options.a: Presents in 4th to 5th decade of life.
options.d: Increased incidence of lymphomas is seen

mcqs.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive condition presenting in the first decade of life . It is associated with a high incidence of recurrent pulmonary infections , lymphomas, Hodgkin's disease , breast cancer, and acute T cell leukemias . Histology shows loss of Purkinje cells , granules, and basket cells in the cerebellar cortex. There is a loss of neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei , inferior olives of the medulla , and anterior horn and dorsal root of the spinal cord. Clinical features of ataxia-telangiectasia include : • Progressive telangiectatic lesions • Oculomotor apraxia • Truncal and limb ataxia • Dysarthria • Extensor plantar reflexes • Myoclonic jerks • Areflexia • Distal sensory deficits • Nystagmus • Cellular and humoral immunodeficiency (absent/ill-developed thymus )

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: An elderly woman is brought to the OPD with complaints of behavioral change, a history of multiple falls, urinary incontinence, and dementia . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario describes an elderly woman with urinary incontinence, dementia (cognitive decline ), and a history of multiple falls (suggestive of a gait abnormality or ataxia). These form the classical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). Both frontotemporal dementia (Option B) and Parkinson 's disease (Option C) are common causes of dementia associated with falls, but urinary incontinence is not commonly appreciated . NPH is, therefore , the most likely diagnosis. Normal pressure hydrocephalus refers to a disproportionate enlargement of the ventricles compared to the degree of cortical atrophy. It is a communicating hydrocephalus caused by delayed resorption of cerebrospinal fluid . Out of the classical triad of symptoms , most patients present with one or two . Hence , neuroimaging showing dilated ventricles is essential , as well as an L- dopa challenge test to rule out parkinson 's disease is recommended . A characteristic MRI of NPH is given below , showing dilated lateral ventricles which are out of proportion to sulcal deepening :1249

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following cranial nerves are affected in cavernous sinus syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The cranial nerves III , IV , V , and VI are affected by cavernous sinus syndrome. The cavernous sinus syndrome is a condition caused by any pathology involving the cavernous sinus. The oculomotor (III ), trochlear (IV ) and trigeminal (V) nerves pass in relation to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. The abducent (VI) nerve passes through the cavernous sinus. Patients with this condition usually present with the following features : • Orbital or facial pain • Orbital swelling and chemosis due to occlusion of the ophthalmic veins • Fever • Oculomotor neuropathy (III , IV , and VI ) • Trigeminal neuropathy (V ) Causes of cavernous sinus syndrome include : • Cavernous sinus thrombosis - most common • Carotid artery aneurysm • Carotid-cavernous fistula • Tumors such as meningioma.1256

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding trigeminal neuralgia?

options.a: The region of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve is always spared
options.b: The pain usually last for a few hours
options.c: The condition is also known as tic douloureux
options.d: It is more common in men

mcqs.explanation: Tic douloureux is another term for trigeminal neuralgia. Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by frequent paroxysms of severe pain in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin. It is sometimes seen in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Middle -aged and elderly females are primarily affected . The pain usually lasts for a short time (seconds to minutes ) but be may intense enough that the patient winces , hence the term 'tic'. A characteristic feature is the presence of trigger zones, typically on the face , lips, or tongue . Patients usually report excruciating pain during activities such as washing the face or brushing the teeth . However, no signs of sensory loss can be demonstrated .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: The high frequency of trigeminal neuralgia in patients with multiple sclerosis is mainly attributed to the involvement of ______.

options.a: Oligodendrocyte -derived myelin covering the beginning of the nerve
options.b: Oligodendrocyte -derived myelin covering the terminal part of the nerve
options.c: Schwann cell –derived myelin sheath covering the beginning of the nerve
options.d: Schwann cell –derived myelin sheath covering the terminal part of the nerve

mcqs.explanation: The high frequency of trigeminal neuralgia in patients with multiple sclerosis occurs due to the involvement of oligodendrocyte -derived myelin covering the beginning of the nerve. Multiple sclerosis is a disorder of oligodendrocyte myelin. It should be ruled out when trigeminal neuralgia is bilateral or develops in a young adult . In such cases , the cause is a demyelinating plaque near the root entry zone of the fifth cranial nerve in the pons. In these patients , a facial sensory loss is also often found in association.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: In patients with trigeminal neuralgia, the nerve is most commonly compressed by ______.
mcqs.explanation: 1257 The superior cerebellar artery most often compresses the trigeminal nerve as it emerges from the brainstem. This causes lancinating pain in the distribution of the nerve which is known as trigeminal neuralgia. Though trigeminal neuralgia can be diagnosed by the clinical features , MRI is recommended to define the underlying cause . In cases refractory to medical management, it also helps to plan for surgical decompression .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A food vlogger presents with complaints of episodes of piercing electric -shock like pain on the left side of her face . The episodes are triggered by chewing food and last for a few minutes . She is further distressed as it interferes with her work. She has tried over the counter analgesics to no avail. What is the drug of choice for her?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia and the drug of choice is carbamazepine . Oxcarbazepine is an alternative to carbamazepine that has less bone marrow toxicity and is equally efficacious . Other drugs used are lamotrigine, gabapentin and baclofen .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about Bell's palsy ?

options.c: MRI shows enhancement of geniculate ganglion

mcqs.explanation: Maximal weakness occurs within 48 hours as a rule in Bells ' palsy . Bell's palsy is an idiopathic , peripheral facial paralysis or paresis of acute onset due to a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve. Clinical presentation of Bell's palsy : • Pain behind the ear (may precede paralysis and last for 1-2 days) • Bell's phenomenon • Asymmetrical face • Hyperacusis (due to stapedial paralysis) • Loss of taste (involvement of chorda tympani). MRI may reveal swelling and uniform enhancement of the geniculate ganglion and facial nerve. Approximately 80% of patients recover within a few weeks or months. The presence of incomplete paralysis in the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign. Recurrence may be seen in some cases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses is most commonly implicated in Bell's palsy ?
mcqs.explanation: Herpes simplex virus is most commonly implicated in causing Bell's palsy . Varicella-zoster virus is the second most common cause .1258

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about Bell's phenomenon ?

options.a: Eyeballs roll upwards on attempting to open the eyes
options.b: Eyeballs roll downwards on attempting to close the eyes
options.c: It is a normal phenomenon evident in facial paralysis
options.d: It is an abnormal phenomenon evident in facial paralysis

mcqs.explanation: Bell's phenomenon refers to a normal phenomenon that becomes evident in facial paralysis. The eyeballs roll up and outwards on attempting to close the eyes . It is also known as the palpebral oculogyric reflex . It is a normal protective reflex resulting in the elevation of globes while blinking to protect the eyes from injury. It also serves to provide a wiper blade -like cleansing function of the cornea by the eyelid . However, it occurs behind the closed eyelids in healthy individuals. It becomes noticeable in Bell's palsy as the eyelids fail to close completely . The image below shows a patient with evident Bell's phenomenon .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: On returning from work, a man noticed that his mother had developed mild right-sided facial drooping. Believing it to be due to a stroke, he immediately took her to the hospital . After extensive evaluation, the doctor ruled out stroke and diagnosed her with Bell's palsy . Which of the following would not be a part of the management of her condition?

options.a: Paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep
options.b: Prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days

mcqs.explanation: Acyclovir may be considered as add-on therapy for patients with severe Bell's palsy as 400mg five times daily for 10 days. Monotherapy is not recommended . Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. Randomized trials found no added benefit of the antiviral agents valacyclovir and acyclovir when compared to glucocorticoids alone. The use of paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep prevents corneal drying. For patients with permanent paralysis, cosmetic surgical procedures have been used to restore a relatively symmetric appearance to the face .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old patient presents with facial weakness and pain for the past 2 days. The following signs are seen on examination. What is the cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The features are suggestive of lower motor neuron (LMN) type of facial palsy .1259 In the image, the absence of wrinkling over the right side of the forehead and incomplete closure of the right eyelid is characteristic of LMN type of facial palsy . In upper motor neuron (UMN ) lesion, the upper part of the face is spared due to bilateral UMN innervation . Features of facial nerve palsy :Feature UMN LMN Side affected Contralater al Ipsilateral Facial muscles involved Lower Both upper and low er Forehead wrinkling Present Absent Emotional incontinence Present Absent Corneal reflex Normal Absent Taste Intact Affected Atrophy of facial muscles Absent PresentNote : Deviation of the angle of mouth should not be confused with drooping of the angle of mouth. Deviation of the angle of the mouth occurs on the normal side due to the action of unaffected facial muscles , while drooping occurs on the affected side .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Identify the correct type of facial nerve palsy in the following patients based on their clinical features :
mcqs.explanation: Patient 1 has left UMN facial nerve palsy and patient 2 has right LMN facial nerve palsy . In an upper motor neuron (UMN ) lesion, wrinkling on the forehead and eyelid closure remains intact. In this lesion, the contralateral side of the face is affected . The first-order neurons from1260 the left cerebral hemisphere cross over (left to right) at the cortical level and relay in the right facial nerve nucleus in the pons. From here the second -order neurons (right facial nerve) descend and supply the right side of the face . Hence , a left UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the right side . In facial palsy, the angle of the mouth deviates towards the normal side . In this patient , since the mouth deviates towards the left , the right facial nerve is affected . In lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions , there is an absence of wrinkling on the forehead and incomplete closure of the eyelid on the ipsilateral side of the face .Feature UMN LMN Side affected Contralater al Ipsilateral Facial muscles involve d Lower Both upper and low er Forehead wrinkling Present Absent Emotional incontinenc e Present Absent Corneal reflex Normal Absent Taste Intact Affected Atrophy Absent Present

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: During the neurological examination of a patient , you note that he has bilateral lower motor neuron palsy of the facial nerve. Which of the following is least likely to cause this?
mcqs.explanation: Diabetes is associated with unilateral LMN palsy . mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a woman with unilateral facial weakness . However, you notice forehead wrinkling is intact. On examination, which of the following findings would you not expect ?
mcqs.explanation: The given features are suggestive of an upper motor neuron (UMN ) lesion of the facial nerve in which the emotional response is affected . Patients with UMN lesions of the facial nerve have emotional incontinence i.e. involuntary, uncontrollable laughter , or crying with a paradoxical deficit of facial expression . Normally cerebellum modulates motor outputs in response to sensory inputs . UMN facial palsy (type of pseudobulbar palsy ) is associated with disruption of cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathways leading to loss of cerebellar modulation resulting in: • Emotional dysmetria (difficulty in fine-tuning emotional responses ) • Emotional disinhibition (excessive emotional output ) Difference between UMN and LMN facial palsy :Feature UMN LMN Side affected Contralater al Ipsilateral Facial muscles involve d Lower Both upper and low er Forehead wrinkling Present Absent Emotional incontinenc e Present Absent Corneal reflex Normal Absent Taste Intact Affected Atrophy Absent Present

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about facial synkinesis?

options.a: Refers to simultaneous bilateral facial nerve palsy
options.b: Refers to facial nerve palsy associated with trigeminal neuralgia
options.c: Occurs due to anomalous regeneration of the facial nerve fibers
options.d: Loss of emotional response is seen in this condition

mcqs.explanation: Facial synkinesis occurs due to anomalous regeneration of facial nerve fibers. Following facial nerve injury , the recovering nerve fibers may aberrantly regenerate and supply other muscles . This results in involuntary muscular movements in the face during voluntary facial movements.1262 Some examples include : • Retraction of the mouth on closure of the eyelids : • Seen when fibers originally connected with the orbicularis oculi aberrantly innervate the orbicularis oris • 'Crocodile tears' also known as Bogorad syndrome: • It refers to anomalous tearing occurring with activity of the facial muscles , such as eating . • Due to aberrant innervation of the lacrimal gland. Note : Frey's syndrome is an aberrant connection between the auriculotemporal nerve and the great auricular nerve, resulting in gustatory sweating .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding hemifacial spasm?

options.a: The contractions are painful and irregular
options.b: It is a complication of Bell's palsy
options.d: Local injection of botulinum toxin is effective

mcqs.explanation: Hemifacial spasms are painless irregular contractions occurring on one side of the face . They commonly occur as sequelae to Bell's palsy . It can also be seen in irritative lesions of the facial nerve such as acoustic neuroma and basilar aneurysm. Treatment is with carbamazepine or gabapentin . In resistant cases , baclofen may be tried. Local injection of botulinum toxin and surgical decompression are alternative options .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following are features of Melkerrson-Rosenthal syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Melkersson -Rosenthal syndrome is a rare disease characterised by the following triad: • Recurrent facial nerve palsy • Facial edema (particularly labial) • Plication of tongue or fissured tongue1263 Facial paralysis along with vesicular rash in the external auditory canal and pinna is seen in Ramsay-Hunt syndrome. It occurs due to herpes zoster infection and is also called herpes zoster oticus . Congenital facial weakness combined with abnormal ocular abduction is seen in Moebius syndrome. Patients may present with bilateral concurrent facial nerve paralysis.

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man presented with complaints of sudden stabs of pain in the throat on yawning. Each episode only lasted for a few seconds and was exacerbated on trying to clear the throat. Which of the following findings can you see on examination?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features are suggestive of glossopharyngeal neuralgia which is associated with cardiac symptoms such as bradycardia, asystole , hypotension , and fainting. It involves the glossopharyngeal (IX) and sometimes portions of the vagus (X) nerve. The condition resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is less common. There is no demonstrable sensory or motor deficit . It can result from vascular compression, multiple sclerosis or tumors. The drug of choice is carbamazepine. If unsuccessful , surgical procedures are indicated : • Microvascular decompression (if vascular compression is evident ) • Rhizotomy of glossopharyngeal and vagal fibers in the jugular bulb1264

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 25-day-old baby is brought to the hospital with complaints of poor feeding and lethargy. On examination , he is found to have bulging fontanelles and hypothermia . Which of the following is the most common cause of his condition?
mcqs.explanation: Home quarantine for 14 days is advised when a person comes in contact with a COVID -19 positive patient. The home quarantined person: • Should stay in a well ventilated single room and stay away from high-risk individuals • Should not attend any religious or social gatherings • Must wash hands often • Must change mask every 6-8 hrs • Their surroundings must be disinfected with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution In case the person being quarantined becomes symptomatic , all his contacts should be home quarantined for 14 days and followed up for another 14 days or till the report turns out negative on lab testing .1552 Isolation is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are sick, to prevent the transmission of disease . Quarantine is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are not ill but are believed to have been exposed to infection , for the purpose of preventing transmission of diseases .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of meningitis in a 30-year-old patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of COVID toes . The image shows pernio-like lesions caused due to COVID -19. Pernio / chilblains are skin lesions on the acral surfaces of the body characterised by the development of erythematous -violaceous or purpuric macules . They may be accompanied by edema and pruritus. It is usually due to cold exposure or underlying hematological disorders but has also been reported in patients with COVID -19 disease . The underlying mechanism is thought to be an inflammatory process . The lesions appear late (postviral phase ) with the patients exhibiting positive IgM/ IgG antibodies for SARS-CoV-2 and negative RT -PCR. However, pernio like lesions can also be seen in early stages of the disease when the patients are still infective . There are no treatment guidelines but high-potency topical corticosteroids may be helpful if the lesions are causing discomfort. Other cutaneous manifestations include exanthematous rash, livedo reticularis, urticaria, MIS-C etc .

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old patient presents with fever, neck rigidity, and headache for the past 3 days. He has a history of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer for which he had received intrathecal chemotherapy via an Ommaya reservoir 10 days ago. On examination, Kernig and Brudzinski 's signs are positive . Which organism is most likely implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: The correct sequence of donning a PPE is first pair of gloves \032 coverall \032 Shoe cover \032 N-95 mask. Preparation for donning the PPE: • To be performed only in the designated area • The health care worker must be prepared for the shift duty by • Taking a meal • Using the washroom • Drinking water prior to entering the donning area • Remove all accessories , jewelry • Change into clean hospital scrubs and closed washable footwear • Perform hand hygiene with soap and water Steps of donning/putting on the PPE: • Hand hygiene • Wear the first pair of gloves • Sterile or unsterile1553 • Make sure the cuff of the gloves goes as far as possible • Examine and wear coverall • Examine the coverall for any damage • Start by wearing the leg sleeves and then the arm sleeves • Zip up and cover the zip with the flap attached • Wear shoe cover • Sit on the clean chair and wear shoe cover • Pull them up till your calves • Wear N-95 mask and wear hood • Hold the mask like a cup in the hand with both the straps hanging out in the front • Place the mask on the face , pull and wear the lower strap first placing it below the ears • Then pull and wear the upper strap placing above the ears • The air leakage should be minimum around the mask when forcibly exhaling • Wear the hood covering the forehead and the cheeks • Wear face shield /eye goggles over the hood and ensure the fit • Wear the second pair of gloves - pull the gloves to cover the sleeve cuff and forearm as much as possible

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, headache , photophobia and neck rigidity since the last 2 days. He had undergone a heart transplant one year back and is on immunomodulatory drugs. During examination, the following sign is elicited . What is the therapy of choice for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The component of the PPE kit to be removed first is the shoe covers. Preparation for doffing the PPE: • To be performed only in the designated area • Check for any leak or soiling • Doffing room should have two chairs, dirty and clean • All the PPE must be discarded in the red bin • Hand hygiene must be performed after every step Steps of doffing the PPE: • Engage the observer and ask him to check the PPE - observer should check for any leak, tear, or contamination of PPE. If contaminated, then it should be disinfected with alcohol-based wipes . • Disinfect the gloves • Remove and discard shoe covers • Sit on the dirty chair with legs apart • Remove the shoe covers by slowly pulling the outer surface starting from the top and then pull from the toes end. Discard them1554 • Disinfect and remove outer pair of gloves • While removing the outer gloves , inner gloves should not be torn or contaminated • Pinch the first glove on the outer surface at the wrist and pull it inside out • Hold this glove in the other hand like a ball • Slide the thumb inside the other glove and remove inside out balling around the previous glove, making it into a single bag. Then discard it. • Disinfect inner gloves • Remove face shield /eye goggle - loosen the screw and remove the face shield by holding it from the back handle. Discard it. • Disinfect inner gloves again • Remove hood and coverall • Slide back the hood by holding it from the top • Separate the zip flap and unzip the coverall suit • Holding the suit at the arms, slide it off the shoulder slightly , then pull the suit from the side of the waist • Roll the arms out one by one • By touching the inner surface of the suit carefully roll out each leg . Discard it • Disinfect and remove inner gloves as previously described • Perform hand hygiene and wear a new pair of gloves • Remove and discard N-95 mask • Do not touch the exposed surface of the mask • Stoop forward and first remove the lower strap • Then pull out the upper strap and remove the mask • Disinfect gloves • Sit on the clean chair and disinfect shoes using alcohol wipes • Disinfect and remove gloves • Perform hand hygiene • Wipe the shoes on sodium hypochlorite soaked doormat at exit • Exit the doffing area and take a shower

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A 21 -year-old female complains of fever, headache and vomiting from the past 3 days. She has been living in the army recruitment camp for the last three weeks . On examination, she has neck stiffness and a maculopapular rash was noted over the trunk and extremities . Which of the following is false about the disease she 's likely suffering from?

options.a: Carriers of this disease can be treated with Rifampicin
options.b: It can lead to adrenal hemorrhage
options.c: Terminal complement deficiency increases the risk of this disease
options.d: Metronidazole is the drug of choice

mcqs.explanation: The front of the face shield is considered to be a contaminated area of the personal protective equipment (PPE). Hence , it should not be touched while doffing . The areas that are considered clean are the parts that will be touched while removing a PPE:1555 • Inside the gloves • Inside and back of the gown including the ties • Ties or earpieces of the mask, goggles , and face shields The areas that are considered contaminated are: • Outside front and sleeves of the isolation gown • Front of goggles , mask, respirator, and face shield • Outside of the gloves

mcqs.question: Which drug is used for mass chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal meningitis?

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A patient comes to ED with fever and headache . On examination he has neck stiffness . CSF analysis was done and it shows the following findings. Most likely diagnosis is:
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis. Intravenous administration of amphotericin B is the first line treatment . Other drugs which are approved for its management include isavuconazole and posaconazole . Surgical debridement is the last line management. Immunocompromised states are important risk factors including diabetes mellitus and glucocorticoid treatment as well as patients on ventilation.1557 Diagnosis can be made by culturing the organisms from sterile sites like needle aspirate, pleural fluid, or a tissue biopsy specimen . The biopsy is most sensitive . It reveals characteristic wide , thick-walled , ribbon-like, aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles . It can present as: • Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis - (most common) the initial symptoms are nonspecific and include eye or facial pain and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and blurry vision. If untreated it can spread from the sinuses to the orbit, and then to the frontal lobe . • Pulmonary mucormycosis - (second most common) • Cutaneous mucormycosis - usually results after trauma • Gastrointestinal mucormycosis - primarily occurs in premature neonates who have disseminated disease or necrotizing enterocolitis • Disseminated mucormycosis

mcqs.subject: Medicine
mcqs.question: A college student presents with fever, headache , and confusion. Lumbar puncture was positive for HSV DNA, detected by PCR. An MRI brain is done to localize the lesions . Which area on the brain is most likely to show lesions ?
mcqs.explanation: This is a case of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), associated with COVID -19 infection . Diagnostic criteria for MIS-C: Children and adolescents 0–18 years of age with fever \0373 days AND two of these : • Rash or bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis or mucocutaneous inflammation signs (palmoplantar erythema , lip hyperemia , periorbital erythema and edema , strawberry tongue , and malar erythema ) • Hypotension or shock. • Features of myocardial dysfunction , pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities (including ECHO findings or elevated Troponin /NT-proBNP) • Evidence of coagulopathy (PT, PTT , elevated D-Dimers) • Acute gastrointestinal problems (diarrhoea, vomiting, or abdominal pain) AND Elevated ESR(>40 mm), C-reactive protein (>5 mg/L), or procalcitonin. AND No other obvious microbial cause of inflammation including bacterial sepsis , staphylococcal or streptococcal shock syndromes. AND Evidence of COVID -19 (RT -PCR, antigen test , or serology positive ), or likely contact with patients with COVID -19. Types of MIS-C:1558 • MIS-C with shock/multi-organ dysfunction • Kawasaki phenotype • MIS-C without shock MIS-C is treated with IV methylprednisolone . The dose can be increased in patients with shock. If the condition does not improve for 48-72 hours, specialists can be consulted for the addition of biologicals to the treatment regimen.

mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, headache , seizures and aphasia. MRI shows hyperintensity in the left frontotemporal region. Which of the following would likely be seen in the CSF analysis?

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Identify the condenser in the following image.
mcqs.explanation: This is a modern compound microscope , and the condenser is located below the stage .The purpose of the condenser lens is to focus the light from the illuminator onto the specimen . Microscopes with a stage condenser lens render a sharper image than those with no condenser lens. The simple microscope was invented first by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek , the father of microscopy and microbiology. It uses 1 lens for magnification. The compound microscope , introduced by Hans and Zacharias Janssen uses 2 lenses , an objective lens and an eyepiece , to provide better magnification power than the simple microscope .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old sex worker presented with a painless ulcer on her vulva . On examination, inguinal lymphadenopathy is present . Which of the following methods has been used to demonstrate the causative agent as per the given image?
mcqs.explanation: 15 A painless genital ulcer with inguinal lymphadenopathy with the presence of spiral organisms on microscopy is suggestive of syphilis . It is caused by Treponema pallidum , demonstrated by dark -field microscopy. Dark -field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies . It uses reflected light and has a higher resolving power than the light microscope . Dark -field microscopy is the the most specific and sensitive technique to visualize Treponema pallidum when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present . Other options : Option B: Phase contrast microscopy improves the contrast to delineate structures within cells . A dark image is formed on a light background. Option C: Fluorescent microscopy uses fluorescent dyes like auramine-rhodamine to appreciate Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites . Option D: The electron microscope , invented by Ernst Ruska, helps in appreciating viral structures . It has a very high resolving power .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which among the following statements is false ?

options.a: Muramic acid is present in prokaryotes
options.b: Mitotic division is present in eukaryotes
options.d: Multiple linear chromosomes present in eukaryotes

mcqs.explanation: 80S ribosome is present in eukaryotes, while 70S ribosome is present in prokaryotes. 80S ribosome has subunits 60S and 40S, while 70S has subunits 50S and 30S.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods will not help you visualize the bacterial cell wall?
mcqs.explanation: The cell wall of bacteria cannot be seen with simple stains or direct light microscopy.16 The bacterial cell wall is present outside the plasma membrane and confers strength and shape to the cell . It is composed of peptidoglycans. The cell wall can be demonstrated by the following methods : • Plasmolysis • Microdissection • Reaction with specific antibodies • Mechanical rupture of the cell • Differential staining procedures (E.g. Chance's method ) • Electron microscopy • Fluorescence microscopy

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following phases of the bacterial growth curve does sporulation occur?
mcqs.explanation: Sporulation occurs in the stationary phase of the bacterial growth curve, which is marked as C in the image. The bacterial growth curve is obtained when a batch of bacteria is seeded in a liquid medium and incubated . It consists of 4 distinct phases : • Lag phase (A) - The bacteria adapt to a new environment. They synthesize and accumulate enzymes and metabolic intermediates required for multiplication . Thus, there is no increase in cell number but cell size increases. Maximum cell size is obtained towards the end of this phase . • Log or exponential phase (B) - The bacteria start dividing and their numbers increase exponentially with time. Cells are smaller and stain uniformly. The growth rate is constant. • Stationary phase (C) - There is depletion of nutrients and accumulation of toxic products . Thus, cell division reduces and a state of equilibrium is attained , where the number of new cells formed equals the number that die . Growth rate is zero. Sporulation occurs during this phase . Many bacteria produce secondary metabolic products such as exotoxins and antibiotics. • Death phase or the phase of decline (D) - Growth rate is negative . The population decreases due to cell death from nutritional exhaustion, toxin accumulation and the action of autolytic enzymes . Involution forms are common.17

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following helps in bacterial adhesion?
mcqs.explanation: Fimbriae help in bacterial adhesion. Fimbriae, also called pili, are hair-like surface appendage that projects from the cell surface as straight filaments . They are primarily seen in Gram-negative bacteria. They are polymers of pilin. Fimbriae are classified based on the function as ordinary pili - for adhesion - and sex pili - involved in bacterial conjugation. The functions of pili are given below : • Bacterial conjugation through sex pili, which transfer of genetic material occurs. • Bacterial adhesion of symbiotic and pathogenic bacteria to host cells using adhesins . • Resistance to phagocytosis . • Antigenic pilin proteins are responsible for the immune response . • Twitching motility to bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Pasteurization is done at ______.
mcqs.explanation: Pasteurization is done at 63 degree Celsius for 30 minutes . Pasteurization is the process of applying heat to milk to kill or stunt the growth of pathogenic bacteria. It was developed by Louis Pasteur. There are two methods for pasteurization : • Holder method : Milk is heated at 63\260C for 30 minutes19 • Flash process : Milk is heated to 72\260C for 15–20 seconds Once heated appropriately , the milk is cooled quickly to 13 \260C or lower . All the non-sporing pathogens (mycobacteria, brucellae , salmonellae ) are killed in pasteurization . In the Holder method , heat resistant Coxiella burnetti may survive. Note : Louis Pasteur pioneered the techniques of pasteurization and sterilization. He also first advanced the germ theory of disease which states that most diseases were caused by microorganisms . Furthermore, he disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and developed vaccines for rabies and fowl cholera. He is thus known as the father of modern microbiology.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods of sterilization involves exposure to 100 \260C for 20 minutes on 3 successive days?
mcqs.explanation: The method of sterilization that involves exposure at 100 \260C for 20 minutes for 3 successive days is called tyndallization or intermittent sterilization. Tyndallization, which utilizes steam, was used for sterilization of media containing gelatin , egg , serum, or sugar. This method may not kill spores of certain anaerobes and thermophiles . Autoclaving has replaced this method now. Other options : Option A: Autoclaving involves heating at 121 \260C for 15 minutes at a pressure of 15psi. This is the used for intruments, linen, laboratory ware. Option C: In pasteurization , milk is heated at either 63\260C for 30 minutes (the holder method ) or at 72\260C for 15–20 seconds (the flash process ), followed by cooling quickly to 13 \260C or lower . Option D: Heating an article at 80–85 \260C for 30 minutes on 3 consecutive days is called inspissation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following works by disrupting the cell membrane?
mcqs.explanation: Lysol works by disrupting the cell membrane. Lysol is a phenol compound , which is obtained by distillation of coal tar. Phenols cause cell membrane damage and inactivate membrane-bound oxidases and dehydrogenases . This causes lysis and release of cell contents . Low concentrations of phenol can precipitate proteins . They are not inactivated by organic matter and are thus useful disinfectants . The mechnisms of action of other disinfecting agents are: • DNA damage • Ionizing radiation • Ultraviolet light • Hydrogen peroxide • DNA reactive chemicals like acriflavin. • Protein modification20 • Alcohol • Chlorine • Iodine • Heavy metals (e.g. thiomersal) • Hydrogen peroxide • Formaldehyde • Glutaraldehyde • Ethylene oxide • Acids and alkalis

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods is used in the test shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows antibiotic sensitivity testing which uses the lawn culture method . Lawn or carpet culture is the method in which a uniform surface growth of bacterium is present on the medium. It is used for antibiotic sensitivity testing (disc method ) and bacteriophage typing . Stab culture (option D) is used for demonstration of gelatin liquefaction and oxygen requirements of bacterium, for maintenance of stock cultures . Streak culture (option A) is routinely used for the isolation of bacteria in pure culture from clinical specimens . Stroke culture (option C) is used for providing pure growth of bacterium for slide agglutination and other diagnostic tests . Other methods of culture include : • Liquid culture - These are preferred for inocula containing antibiotics and other inhibitory substances . • Pour plate culture - It gives an estimate of viable bacterial count in a suspension .21

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following organisms will the following phenomenon not be observed in?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Quellung reaction (halo around the bacteria) and is seen in capsulated bacteria. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not capsulated , therefore Quellung reaction will not be observed in it. In Quellung reaction, a suspension of a capsulated bacterium is mixed with its specific anticapsular serum and examined under the microscope . The anticapsular antibodies bind to the capsule and thus the capsule becomes very prominent and appears swollen . Capsulated organisms can be remembered with the following mnemonic: Some - Streptococcus pneumoniae Killers - Klebsiella pneumoniae Have - Haemophilus influenzae Nice - Neisseria meningitidis Capsules - Cryptococcus neoformans

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old laborer working at a construction site presented with fever and hemoptysis . The sputum sample collected for examination showed the following . The smear will be stained by which of the following sequences ?

options.b: Methylene blue - malachite green - acetic acid-water

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette of fever and hemoptysis in a labourer with the sputum smear showing acid-fast bacilli is suggestive of tuberculosis . Mycobacterium tuberculosis , detected on sputum smear, is appreciated by Ziehl-Neelsen staining, which would includes carbol fuschin - acid - alcohol - methylene blue . Acid-fast bacteria (like MTB) in a stained Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) smear appear bright red against a blue background. Steps involved in ZN staining are: • Place the sample on slide evenly spread it with rotational movement • Air-dry the slide and fix it by passing it over a flame • Apply carbol fuschin stain and heat to fix it. • Wash with water to remove excess stain • Decolourise with alcohol • Apply Methylene blue /Malachite green stain • Wash with water to remove excess stain • View under the microscope Kinyoun modified the classical ZN staining such that heat fixing is not required. It is called the cold method . It involves increasing the concentration of phenol acid and the duration of staining. The slide is then washed with water and decolourized with acid alcohol. Counterstaining with Loeffler 's methylene blue or malachite green is done for a minute and viewed under a microscope . Acid-fast bacteria in a stained smear appear bright red against a blue background. The image attached below summarizes the steps .22 Option A: It depicts the order of Gram staining, which was discovered by Hans Christian Gram in 1884. • Primary staining with para-rosaniline dye (crystal violet, methyl violet or gentian violet). • Application of dilute solution of iodine. • Decolorisation with an organic solvent (ethanol , acetone , aniline). • Counterstaining with the dye of contrasting colour (carbol fuchsin, safranine, neutral red). Option B: It includes the steps for performing Albert's stain which is used for detected Corynebacterium diphtheriae . • A heavy smear of the bacterial isolate is prepared on a glass slide and allowed to dry without fixing. • Albert's stain is applied for (3-4) minutes . Then it is washed with water and Albert's iodine is applied for one minute. • Wash with water and let dry with blotting paper . • Examine the slide under oil immersion. Corynebacterium diphtheriae are slender bacilli with an arrangement resembling the letters V or L. They have metachromatic granules at the poles of bacilli which are also called polar bodies , volutin, or Babes-Ernst granules. Albert staining is useful in the demonstration of metachromatic granules. The presence of metachromatic granules helps to distinguish C.diphtheriae from diphtheroids which lack them. The images below show Corynebacterium diphtheriae .23

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Given are a few case scenarios. The etiological agents of which of the following are microaerophilic?
mcqs.explanation: The aetiological agents of 1 and 2 are microaerophilic. The given case scenarios are: 1. A businessman with epigastric pain and positive urease test has peptic ulcer disease , caused by Helicobacter pylori. It is microaerophilic. 2. Diarrhea caused by Gram-negative , small, spirally curved rod-like, motile bacilli describes Campylobacter jejuni. It is microaerophilic. 3. Rice-water diarrhea and Gram-negative curved bacilli with 'fish-in-stream' appearance describes cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae . It is a facultative anaerobe. 4. Nasopharyngeal swab from a child with paroxysmal cough showing 'mercury drops' colonies describes Bordetella pertussis . It is an obligate aerobe. 5. Dry, rough, raised, irregular colonies on LJ medium describes Mycobacerium tuberculosis . It is an obligate aerobe. Microaerophilic organisms grow best in low oxygen tension (2-10 % oxygen ). Note : Mycobacteria , such as M. bovis, can grow at oxygen tensions ranging from atmospheric to microaerophilic conditions. However, M. tuberculosis is an obligate aerobe.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The given image shows a culture medium with lactose fermenting and non-lactose fermenting bacteria. Which of the following is not a component of the culture medium?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows MacConkey agar. Cysteine is not a constituent of MacConkey agar. MacConkey agar is a differential or indicator medium. Lactose-fermenting organisms (Eg: E. coli) produce a pink color, and non-lactose fermenting organisms (Shigella sp., Salmonella sp.) do not change the color. Contents of MacConkey agar include peptone , lactose , agar, neutral red and24 sodium taurocholate (Mnemonic- PLANT ). MacConkey agar is also a selective medium i.e. the bile salts (sodium taurocholate ) and dyes (neutral red) inhibit the growth of Gram-positive organisms and Gram-negative cocci.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an enrichment medium?
mcqs.explanation: The image 'A' represents alkaline peptone water, which is an enrichment medium used for Vibrio cholerae . The other images represent : Image B- Blood agar with P. aeruginosa colonies Image C- Loeffler 's serum slope , which is used to isolate C. diphtheriae Image D- Chocolate agar with F. tularensis colonies Enrichment media suppress the growth of commensal bacteria and allow for the growth of certain organisms. These media are used for samples with mixed flora e.g. stool . They are always liquid media, like alkaline peptone water. Other examples include tetrathionate broth and selenite -F broth for Salmonella sp. and Shigella sp. Enriched medium are those media to which additional nutrients such as blood, serum, or egg are added . They're used to grow bacteria with specific nutritional requirements. Examples include blood agar to test the hemolytic property of bacteria, chocolate agar for isolation of H. influenzae and Loeffler 's serum slope for isolation of C. diphtheriae .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
