mcqs.question: A microbiologist observes the following growth on a blood agar plate . Which of the following will not be the etiological agent ?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a swarming type of growth on the agar plate . It will not be caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae . Swarming is the growth of motile bacteria in the form of a thin film on solid culture media. It is exhibited by the following : • Gram-positive bacilli - Clostridium tetani (option A), Bacillus cereus (option D) • Gram-negative bacilli - Proteus mirabilis (option C), Proteus vulgaris • Gram-negative halophilic bacteria- Vibrio parahaemolyticus Swarming can be inhibited by increasing the concentration of agar (6%), alcohol, sodium azide, boric acid, chloral hydrate , sulfonamide, and surface -active agents .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Bacterial transduction occurs by

options.d: Uptake of genetic material by other bacteria.

mcqs.explanation: Bacterial transduction occurs by bacteriophages . Transduction is a process of acquiring bacterial DNA from a bacteriophage (virus) that has incorporated bacterial DNA from previous host bacteria.25 Other methods of exchange of genetic material are transformation and conjugation. Transformation involves the uptake of genetic material from the environment, which is released by other bacteria. Conjugation is the direct transfer of DNA from one bacterial cell to another bacterial cell through a sex pilus or bridge . The transferred DNA is a plasmid, a circle of DNA that is distinct from the main bacterial chromosome.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following principles is primarily used in polymerase chain reaction?

options.b: It can amplify small amounts of DNA
options.c: It can amplify small amounts of RNA

mcqs.explanation: The primary principle used in polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the amplification of small amounts of DNA. PCR is an automated process in which a single or a few copies of a DNA piece is amplified to generate of thousands to millions of copies of that particular DNA sequence . There are 3 basic steps are involved in PCR: • DNA extraction from microorganism • Amplification of extracted DNA - Denaturation (95\260C), Primer annealing (55 \260C), Extension (72\260C) • Gel electrophoresis of the amplified product PCR is used in rapid diagnostic tests for infections (e.g. HIV DNA), forensic investigations etc . The founder of PCR is Karry B Mullis .26

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes the reverse transcriptase enzyme used in RT -PCR correctly?
mcqs.explanation: The enzyme involved in RT -PCR is reverse transcriptase (RT) which has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity. In reverse transcription-polymerase chain reation (RT -PCR), reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from the RNA template . RT -PCR can be used for the demonstration of poliovirus RNA, causing paralytic poliomyelitis , in CSF. It can also be used for the detection of viruses from nasopharyngeal swabs (SARS-CoV2 , H1N1 ). In real-time RT -PCR, fluorescent dyes or DNA probes are used to quantify the pathogen DNA load in the specimen . So, it can be used to quantify viral loads in HIV , hepatitis B, etc ., and is also called quantitative PCR (qPCR ).27

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What are jumping genes known as?
mcqs.explanation: Jumping genes are also called transposons. Transposons are genetic elements that can move between chromosomal and extra-chromosomal DNA molecules. Insertion of a transposon leads to acquisition of new characteristics by the recipient DNA. Transposons contain several genes , including those necessary for their migration from one genetic locus to another. They may contain genes for specialised functions like antibiotic resistance . However, they do not contain genes for their replication. Jumping genes were discovered by Barbara McClintock and she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1983 for the same. Other options: Options A and B: The cytoplasmic carriers of genetic information are termed plasmids or episomes . Option D: A cosmid is a type of hybrid plasmid that contains a Lambda phage cos sequence . (Cos sites + plasmid = cosmids).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following situations will you use a sanitizer?
mcqs.explanation: You should use a sanitiser before and after examining the patient and after touching the patients ' surroundings. The hands should be washed with soap and water thoroughly in case they are visibly soiled . Sanitization is the process through which pathogenic organisms are reduced to safe levels on inanimate objects to reduce the likelihood of cross-infections . It is a component of hand-hygiene , which is demonstrated by the image below .28 Note : Disinfectants like chlorhexidine and alexidine have a biguanide functional group. They are mostly used as oral disinfectants and hand products . They are bactericidal but not sporicidal. Mycobacteria are also resistant to these compounds .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An orthopedician is performing the following procedure to visualize the anterior cruciate ligament in a patient . Which of the following will be used to sterilise the instrument used ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows arthroscopy being performed . Arthroscopes are sterilized using plasma sterilization which utilises hydrogen peroxide . In plasma sterilisation , radiofrequency energy is applied to create an electromagnetic field through which hydrogen peroxide vapours are passed . This generates plasma which contains free radicals of hydrogen and oxygen . Plasma denatures all organisms and is used sterilize arthroscopes and ureteroscopes . Sterilization control is monitored by Geobacillus stearothermophilus and Bacillus atrophaeus . Option A: Ethylene oxide has both microbicidal and sporicidal activity. It is used for sterilisation heat -sensitive equipment like heart-lung machines, respirators, suture materials etc . Sterilization control is monitored by Bacillius atrophaeus and Bacillus subtilus . Option B: Gamma rays cause breakage of DNA. It destroys spores and vegetative cells , but is not effective against viruses. It is referred to as cold sterilisation and is used in commercial plants to sterilize plastics , syringes , swabs. Sterilization control is monitored by Bacillus pumilius . Option D: Ultraviolet rays are used to sterilise biosafety cabinets , entryways , operation theatres and laboratories.29

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What type of immunity is being conferred to a neonate receiving the BCG vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: The immunity conferred to a neonate receiving the BCG vaccine is artificial active immunity, as it involves administering a live attenuated vaccine form of Mycobacterium bovis to stimulate an adaptive immune response and develop antibodies , establishing long-term immunity. Types of adaptive immunity: • Natural active immunity: It results from either a clinical or an inapparent infection by a microbe. • Artificial active immunity: It is the resistance induced by vaccines which are preparations of killed or attenuated microorganisms or their products . • Natural passive immunity: It is the immunity passively transferred from mother to baby. In human infants, maternal antibodies are transmitted predominantly through the placenta , while in animals such as pigs , the transfer of antibodies occurs mainly through the colostrum. • Artificial passive immunity: It is the resistance passively transferred to a recipient by the administration of antibodies . Hyperimmune sera of animal or human origin, convalescent sera, and pooled human immunoglobulin are used for this purpose . • Combined immunization : A combination of the active and passive methods of immunization is used . Examples of the above types of immunity: Note : Adoptive immunity is immunity in which immunologically competent lymphocytes are injected . The transfer factor is composed of these immunologically competent lymphocytes . It can passively transfer cell -mediated immunity against those antigens to which the donor is sensitive .Immunity Description Natural active Clinical or subclinicalinfectio n Artificial active Vaccination39 Immunity Description Natural passive Transplacentaltransfer of ant ibody,colostrum Artificial passive Anti-tetanus serum, anti-dip htherial serum Combined immuniz ation Antisera and vaccine are give n at thesame time,e.g- post -e xposure prophylaxis for rabie s

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old with a large dirty wound on his knee and abrasions on his palms presents to the casualty . He does not remember the last time he received a TT injection and was thus given tetanus immunoglobulin. Which of the following is false about this type of immunity?
mcqs.explanation: Giving pre-formed immunoglobulin (e.g. Tetanus immunoglobulin) directly is an example of passive immunity, which is not long-lasting. The differentiating features between active and passive immunity: Negative phase : It is the time period during which the level of measurable immunity is lower than it was before the antigenic stimulus . This is because the antigen combines with any pre-existing antibody and lowers its level in circulation. It is seen at the beginning of the active immune response . Secondary type response : If an individual who has been actively immunized against an antigen experiences the same antigen subsequently , the immune response occurs more quickly and abundantly than during the first encounter.Active Immunity Passive Immunity Actively produced by the host 's immune system Passively received by the host Induced by infection or imm unogens Readymade antibody is trans ferred Immunological memory pres ent No memory Immunity is effective after a l ag period or latent period Immediate immunity Broad specificity Narrow specificity A negative phase may occur No negative phase . Booster effect on subsequent dose The subsequent dose is less e ffective Secondary type response see n No secondary type of respons e More effective Less effective Long-lasting (Years) Short-lasting (Days to weeks ) Example : Vaccines Example : Antisera40

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis was administered transfer factor as treatment. What type of immunity does this result in?
mcqs.explanation: Adoptive immunity occurs when transfer factor is given. Transfer factor is composed of an extract of immunologically competent lymphocytes such as T lymphocytes , NK cells , macrophages , or B cells . It has the ability to passively transfer cell -mediated immunity against antigens to which the donor is sensitive . It has been attempted in the treatment of lepromatous leprosy and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a pattern recognition receptor ?
mcqs.explanation: Bone morphogenetic protein-like receptors are not pattern-recognition receptors . Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs ) are essential for the innate immune system . They identify pathogen -associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) common to classes of microbes and trigger immune responses . These receptors can be found on the cell surface , detecting extracellular pathogens , or within the endosomes and cellular matrix, detecting intracellular invading viruses. PRRs activate pro-inflammatory pathways , promote phagocytosis in cells like macrophages , neutrophils and dendritic cells , and may act as secreted proteins binding directly to pathogens . Based on the localization and functional characteristics, PRRs are classified as: • Membrane-bound PRRs : • Toll-like receptors (TLR )- detect microbial carbohydrates and lipoproteins (Option B) • C-type lectin receptors (CLR )- detect mannose residues • Cytoplasmic (intracellular) PRRs :41 • Nucleotide oligomerization (NOD)-like receptors (NLR ) - NOD1 and NOD2 - Detects bacterial cell wall peptidoglycans (Option A) • RIG -I-like receptors (RLRs ) - detect viral RNA (Option C) • Secreted PRRs On the contrary, BMP receptors are multifunctional transmembrane serine-threonine kinase receptors that belong to the transforming growth factor \037 (TGF-\037) superfamily , regulating cell growth , differentiation , and apoptosis with no role in pattern recognition. Also, there are no receptors termed "BMP-like receptors ". Note : A mutation in the Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2 ) gene enhances the proliferation and reduces the apoptosis of pulmonary vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells , leading to hereditary pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old presents with diarrhea, fever, and vomiting. The given bacteria is implicated . Which toll-like receptor binds to the structure of the bacteria marked A?
mcqs.explanation: The given image and clinical history suggest a typhoid infection . The structure marked A is the flagella of bacteria. Toll-like receptor (TLR ) 5 binds to the flagella of bacteria. Toll-like receptors (TLRs ) are transmembrane receptors that have an extracellular domain, that detect infecting pathogens . • TLR 1 - Mycobacteria and Gram-negative bacteria • TLR 2 - Mycobacteria and Gram-positive bacteria • TLR 3 - Viral RNA • TLR 4 - Gram-negative bacteria • TLR 5 - Flagella • TLR 9 - Bacterial DNA, some herpes viruses, malarial parasite TLRs act through the NF-KB pathway and initiate inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about T cell dependent antigens?

options.a: Their response doesn 't show immunological memory
options.b: They activate only mature B cells

mcqs.explanation: T cell -dependent antigens activate only mature B cells . Depending on their ability to induce the formation of antibodies , antigens are classified as T-cell dependent and T-cell independent antigens.T cell -dependent antigens (T D) T cell -independent antigens ( TI ) Require helper T cell particip ation for the production of i mmune response Directly stimulate antibody p roduction by B cells Structurally complex Structurally simple42 T cell -dependent antigens (T D) T cell -independent antigens ( TI ) Activate only mature B cells monoclonally Activate both mature and im mature B cells polyclonally B cells undergo affinity matu ration and class switch over B cells do not undergo affinit y maturation and class switc h over All classes of antibodies are a ctivated Antibody response is restrict ed to IgM and IgG3 Rapidly metabolized Slowly metabolized Immunological memory pres ent No immunological memory

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a fever of 103 \260F, hypotension , confusion, and a diffuse rash as shown below . 3 days back, she had uncontrollable epistaxis for which a nasal pack was placed . What is the likely mechanism of action of the microbial toxin that has caused her current illness ?
mcqs.explanation: This woman presented with fever, hypotension , and a diffuse erythematous rash, three days after a nasal packing was done. This is characteristic of toxic shock syndrome - commonly caused by staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST -1), which is a superantigen . Superantigens act by causing polyclonal activation of T cells . They activate a large number of T cells irrespective of their antigen specificity . In contrast to regular antigens which bind to the binding groove on T cells , superantigens bind outside the groove directly to the lateral aspect of the TCR \037 chain. This leads to a massive release of cytokines and polyclonal activation of T cells . Clinically, this manifests as fever, hypotension, and skin exfoliation .Examples of organisms that produce superantigens : • Bacterial43 • Staphylococcus aureus- Enterotoxins • Group A streptococci - Pyrogenic exotoxin • Mycoplasma arthritidis- mitogen 1 • Yersinia enterocolitica • Yersinia pseudotuberculosis • Viral • Epstein –Barr virus (EBV) • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) • Rabies nucleocapsid • HIV -encoded negative regulatory factor. • Fungal- Malassezia furfur

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What are the changes in the variable regions of an immunoglobulin known as?
mcqs.explanation: Changes in the variable regions of heavy and light chains of an immunoglobulin are called an idiotype . Other options : Option B: Isotypes are the changes in the constant regions of the heavy chain of the immunoglobulin. Option C: Allotypes refer to multiple alleles that exist for some genes . This leads to subtle amino acid differences that occur in some but not all members of the same species . Option D: An epitope is the smallest unit of antigenicity and it is an antigenic determinant.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about immunoglobulins is false ?

options.a: IgG is used to diagnose fetal infection

mcqs.explanation: IgG cannot detect fetal infections because it is not produced by the fetus in significant amounts. IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following immunoglobulins acts as surface immunoglobulin on B cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Monomeric IgM is the major antibody receptor on the surface of B lymphocytes for antigen recognition . IgD is the other class of antibodies which acts as the B cell receptors .44

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child presents with a history of repeated sinopulmonary infections caused by encapsulated organisms. Which of the following is most likely to be deficient in this case?
mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of IgG2 results in recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated organisms. IgG is the only maternal immunoglobulin that is normally transported across the placenta and provides natural passive immunity to the newborn. IgG1 is the antibody maximally transported across the placenta , whereas IgG2 has the least transplacental movement. Deficiencies of other IgG: • IgG1- bacterial infections (diphtheria, tetanus )(Option A) • IgG3- viral infections (Option C) • IgG4- parasitic infections (Option D)

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Identify the class of immunoglobulin\037 shown in the image below .
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a dimeric structure , characteristic of secretory IgA. IgA immunoglobulin is the major antibody responsible for mucosal immunity. Its serum levels are usually low. It is predominantly present in the extravascular secretions . It is present in secretions such as milk, saliva, and tears, and in secretions of the respiratory, intestinal , and genital tracts. When present in the serum, it exists as a monomer similar to IgG. However, when it is secreted , it exists as a dimer. The dimeric structure consists of two monomers, which are stabilized by two additional polypeptides : • J chain, which stabilizes the molecule . • Secretory component , which is incorporated into the IgA when transported through the epithelial cell .45

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which immunoglobulin is majorly responsible for the reaction demonstrated below ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows blood typing , which works on the principle of agglutination . IgM is mainly responsible for agglutination . It is the most efficient immunoglobulin in agglutination , complement fixation, and other antigen –antibody reactions and is important also in defense against bacteria and viruses. It is a pentamer , and hence is more effective than IgG in opsonization (C3b mediated ), bactericidal action and bacterial agglutination but less effective in neutralization of toxins and viruses.Reaction IgG IgM Precipitation Stron g Wea k Agglutination Weak Stro ng Complement fixati on Mode rate Stro ng Lysis Weak Stro ng

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are counseling a new mother about the importance of breastfeeding . What forms the secretory component of the antibody that is maximally present in breast milk?

options.b: Epithelial cells of lining mucosa only

mcqs.explanation: The antibody maximally present in breast milk is IgA. The secretory component of IgA is formed by epithelial cells of lining mucosa. IgA occurs in two forms- serum IgA (monomer) and secretory IgA. Secretory IgA is a dimer formed by two monomer units joined together by a J-chain and a secretory component (secretory piece ). Secretory IgA along with the J chain is synthesized by the plasma cells situated near the mucosal or glandular epithelium . The secretory component is synthesized by epithelial cells , not by plasma cells . It is believed to protect IgA from denaturation by bacterial proteases .46

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, which of the following are the end products ?
mcqs.explanation: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments. Enzymatic digestion of antibody: • Papain- 2 Fab fragments and one Fc fragment • Pepsin- One F(ab')2 fragment and many smaller fragments • Mercaptoethanol - 2 H and 2 L chains47

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Affinity maturation is due to:
mcqs.explanation: Affinity maturation is due to somatic hypermutation . Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity. It is a result of somatic hypermutation (SHM) of immunoglobulin genes in B cells , coupled to selection for antigen binding. This process occurs in the germinal centers and proceeds for weeks after acute infection or vaccination, or for many cycles during chronic infection . The resulting antibodies can be highly mutated from their germline-encoded counterparts , with increases of several orders of magnitude in affinity for antigen compared to the corresponding na\357ve B cell receptors (BCRs). Other options : Option A: Isotype switching , also known as class switch recombination, is a process where the constant region of the antibody heavy chain is changed , leading to a switch in the antibody isotype (e.g., from IgM to IgG). This process is crucial for the functional properties of antibodies but is not directly involved in affinity maturation. Option C: mRNA splicing is a cellular process that involves the removal of introns and the joining of exons to generate mature mRNA. While this process is essential for the production of functional antibodies , it is not specifically associated with affinity maturation. Affinity maturation primarily occurs through somatic hypermutation . Option D: VDJ rearrangement is the process by which the variable regions of immunoglobulin genes are assembled from gene segments (V , D, and J segments ). This process contributes to the diversity of antibodies but is distinct from affinity maturation. Affinity maturation occurs after VDJ rearrangement and is driven by somatic hypermutation in the variable regions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An immunologist is conducting an experiment to understand precipitation reactions. He notes that on adding excessive amount of antigen to a serum sample containing small amount of antibodies , the amount of precipitate formed is less , compared to adding smaller amount of antigen to the same sample . What is this phenomenon called ?
mcqs.explanation: 48 This phenomenon is called post –zone phenomenon because it has excessive antigen in the test system , leading to weak or even absent precipitation . Lattice hypothesis explains precipitation reactions. The amount of precipitate formed is greatly influenced by the relative proportions of antigens and antibodies . • Prozone phenomenon is caused by excessive antibodies in the test system . (weak/absent precipitation - false -negative test ) • Zone of equivalence- antigen, and antibody are in optimum proportions and maximum precipitation occurs. • Post–zone phenomenon is due to the presence of excessive antigen in the test system . (weaker/absent precipitation )Flocculation : Instead of sedimenting , precipitate remains suspended as floculus .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Double diffusion in two dimensions is called as ___________.
mcqs.explanation: Double diffusion in two dimensions is called the Ouchterlony procedure . Ex: Elek's test for testing toxigenicity in diphtheria bacilli. The images below show the different types of immunodiffusion.49

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the casualty with the following finding. A positive Nagler's reaction confirmed the presence of lecithinase -producing organisms. What is the principle behind this test ?
mcqs.explanation: Nagler's reaction is an example of a neutralization test . It is done for the detection of lecithinase toxin produced by C. perfringens. The alpha-toxin of C. perfringens has phospholipase activity. When grown on a medium containing egg yolk phospholipid , an area of opacity around the bacterial colonies is seen (Nagler's positive ). The presence of antitoxin can inhibit this. Other examples of neutralization tests are: • Plaque inhibition test - neutralization of bacteriophages • Schick test - neutralization of diphtheria toxin by antitoxin • Anti-streptolysin O test - for beta -hemolytic Streptococci .51

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with a painless ulcer on his penis . A Wasserman test is done and is reactive . What is the principle of this test ?
mcqs.explanation: Wassermann 's reaction is an example of a complement fixation test . It is a non-specific test for the diagnosis of syphilis . An antigen combines with its (specific ) antibody in the presence of complement , and the antigen -antibody complex adsorbs the complement . This reaction is not visible and requires the use of an indicator (sheep erythrocytes and the specific anti-erythrocyte antibody).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following activates the classical complement pathway ?
mcqs.explanation: The classical pathway of complement is activated by immune complexes or antigen-antibody complexes . (antigen bound to IgM or IgG). Lipopolysaccharide of gram-negative bacteria activates the alternative complement pathway . The binding of mannose-binding lectin to mannose residues (on the surfaces of Salmonella, Neisseria , and Listeria) activates the lectin complement pathway .52

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In the alternate complement pathway , which of the following functions as C3 convertase?
mcqs.explanation: C3 convertase in the alternate pathway is C3bBb. In the classical pathway and lectin pathway , the C3 convertase is C4b2a.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old girl presents with the finding shown below . She has a history of multiple similar episodes in the past and reports that some of her family members have similar complaints. She has no itching. Which of the following is deficient in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This girl presents with features of hereditary angioneurotic edema , which is due to a deficiency of C1 inhibitor. Hereditary angioneurotic edema is an autosomal dominant disorder that is more common than complement deficiency states . A deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads53 to unregulated activation of kallikrein . This increases the production of vasoactive peptides such as bradykinin. It causes episodes of edema affecting the skin and mucosal surfaces such as the larynx and the gastrointestinal tract. This may result in life -threatening asphyxia or nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea after minor trauma or emotional stress . Note - • C1, C2, C4 deficiency - collagen vascular disorders. • C5-C8 deficiency - recurrent bacteremia with Neisseria54

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: In which of the following areas do B lymphocytes reside ?
mcqs.explanation: B lymphocytes reside in the splenic follicles . Lymphocytes are part of the adaptive immune system . They include B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes . B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow and then migrate to secondary lymphoid organs - follicles of spleen and in follicles of lymph nodes . T lymphocytes are produced in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus . They are also present in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS ) of spleen and paracortex of lymph node.61 In a lymph node, follicles may contain a central region called germinal centre . This contains B cells that have been stimulated by an antigen.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A mother brings her 1-year-old child to the hospital with complaints that he turns blue while breastfeeding . It resolves when he assumes a squatting position. On examination, a cleft palate is seen . Labs show hypocalcemia . Which of the following abnormalities is expected to be seen in the lymphoid organs?

options.a: Decreased size of germinal centres of lymph nodes
options.b: Decreased size of paracortical areas of lymph nodes
options.d: Increased size of the peri arteriolar lymphoid sheath of spleen

mcqs.explanation: Turning blue on breastfeeding with resolution on squatting describes a tet -spell or a cyanotic spell , indicating a congenital cardiac defect . Cleft palate , cardiac defects and hypocalcemia (parathyroid hypoplasia /aplasia) suggest a diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome. In this disorder, a decreased size of paracortical areas of lymph nodes is noted . DiGeorge syndrome is characterised by thymic aplasia, causing a deficiency of T cells and absent cell -mediated immunity. Thus, paracortical areas of lymph nodes and periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen , where T cells reside , are reduced in size. B cells are usually not affected .62

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Match the following specialized macrophages with the tissues they are found in.
mcqs.explanation: The correct answer is I-B; II -C; III -D; IV -E; V-A. Macrophages can be divided into: 1. Blood macrophages (monocytes ) are the largest of the myeloid cells found in the peripheral blood. They survive for 3 days. 2. Tissue macrophages present in different organs. They survive for months. The main functions of macrophages are phagocytosis and antigen presentation . The specialised (tissue -specific ) macrophages present in different tissues are listed below : • Peripheral blood: Monocytes • Placenta: Hofbauer cells • Liver : Kupffer cells • Brain : Microglial cells • Kidney : Mesangial cells • Lungs: Alveolar macrophages • Bone: Osteoclasts • Connective tissue : HistiocytesCell Tissue I. Hofbauer cells B. Placenta II . Histiocytes C. Connective tissu e III . Kupffer cells D. Liver IV . Microglia E. Brain V . Mesangial cell s A. Kidney

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most potent stimulator of naive T-cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Mature dendritic cells are the most potent stimulator of naive T cells . Naive CD4+ T cells are activated when they come in contact with two ligands - MHC class II and a costimulary membrane protein (eg : CD28). Both of these are present in antigen-presenting cells , the most potent of which is the mature dendritic cell . Other professional antigen-presenting cells include macrophages and B lymphocytes (option C). Other options :63 Option B: Follicular dendritic cells are functionally different from dendritic cells . They are not antigen -presenting -cells and do not activate naive T cells . Option D: NK cells do not stimulate naive T cells .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Nude mice are not resistant to xenograft due to the absence of _______
mcqs.explanation: Nude mice are not resistant to xenograft due to absence of T cell . A xenograft is a tissue graft or organ transplant from a donor of a different species . Nude mice lack body hair, hence the name. They lack a thymus and thus cannot generate mature T lymphocytes . The absence of T-lymphocytes makes them unable to mount adaptive immune responses requiring helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells . The absence of functioning T cells also prevents the rejection of allografts & xenografts .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about T-cell receptors is false ?

options.a: In 95% of T cells , the TCR consists of �o and \037 polypeptide chains.
options.b: \035\034 TCR recognize peptide antigens presented by MHC molecules .
options.c: Each TCR is non-covalently linked to six polypeptide chains, which form CD3 complex .
options.d: The linked CD3 complex and \033 chains initiate activating signals.

mcqs.explanation: \035\034 TCR recognize different type of antigens without the requirement of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) Each T cell recognizes a specific bound antigen by means of an antigen-specific T-cell receptor (TCR ). The TCR is a heterodimer and is of two types : • \036\037 TCR (95%) recognize peptide antigens that are presented by MHC molecules on the surfaces of antigen-presenting cells . • \035\034 TCR (5%) recognize peptides , lipids , and small molecules , without a requirement for display by MHC proteins . They have particular localization patterns in the mucosal tissues , which protect against microbes that try to enter through epithelia .64 TCRs are non-covalently bound to six polypeptide chains or three dimers (a \034\032 pair, a \035\032 pair, and a \033\033 or \033\031 pair), forming the CD3 complex and the \033 dimer. The CD3 complex and \033 dimer convey signals received by the receptor to the interior of the cell .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old requires a kidney transplant due to chronic kidney disease . Her 2 children match her HLA type 4/6 and 5/6 respectively. On what chromosome is this match protein sequence located ?
mcqs.explanation: HLA complex of genes is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (chromosome 6p21 ). The human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system or complex is a gene complex encoding the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins . In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens (HLA) because they were initially detected on leukocytes by the binding of antibodies . The combination of HLA alleles in each individual is called the HLA haplotype . The function of MHC molecules is to display peptide fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells . The HLA system is highly polymorphic. Each individual's HLA alleles differ from the other. It has to be checked before organ transplantation. The HLA complex consists of 3 separate clusters of genes : • Class I– A, B and C loci • Class II – DR, DQ and DP loci • Class III – Complement C2 and C4 of classical pathway and properdin factor B of the alternate pathway , heat shock proteins (HSP), TNF �o and \037.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding MHC molecules ?

options.a: MHC class II presents peptide antigen to CD4 T cells
options.b: The action of MHC II occurs via endocytic pathway
options.c: MHC Class II presents endogenous antigens
options.d: MHC II is present on antigen presenting cells

mcqs.explanation: MHC class II presents exogenous antigens while MHC class I presents endogenous antigens.65

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: You are observing flow cytometry being performed at a laboratory for MHC class 1 antigen. Identify the cells that lack this antigen.
mcqs.explanation: Red blood cells are anucleated cells that lack MHC class I antigens. MHC class I antigens are present on platelets and all nucleated cells , except sperm cells . They are responsible for the presentation of peptide antigen to CD8 T cells . The human major histocompatibility complex (MHC), or the HLA complex , is a cluster of genes whose products are responsible for antigen presentation to T cells , transplant rejection , etc. HLA complex of genes is present on the short arm of chromosome 6. The genes are clustered in three regions named MHC region-I, II and III . MHC class II antigens are present only on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages , dendritic cells , B cells ). They present the peptide antigen to CD4 T cells . APCs also contain MHC class I antigens. MHC region III comprises of genes that code for complement factors like C2, C4, C3 convertase, factor B and properdin, heat shock protein, tumor necrosis factor and steroid 21 -hydroxylases .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A patient newly diagnosed with HIV is found to have a CD4+ count of 78cells /\265 L. Which of the following is not a function of these cells ?
mcqs.explanation: CD4+ is a marker of T helper and memory cells . They do not produce immunoglobulins. CD4+ T cells are activated when an antigen-presenting cell expressing MHC-II binds to them. The activated CD4+ T cell differentiates into T helper (TH) cells and regulatory T cells . The TH cells are further differentiated into TH1 , TH2 and TH17 cells . Helper T cells have the following functions: • Activation and proliferation of cytotoxic T cells • Regulation of monocyte -macrophage system • Activation of B cell to produce plasma cells • Production of interleukins Memory cells (Tm) have both CD4+ and CD8+ markers . They provide anamestic immune response and are thus responsible for immunogenic memory. Immunoglobulins are produced by the plasma cells .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the surface markers of T and B cells ?
mcqs.explanation: T cells do not express CD10. CD10 is a marker of pre-B cell and germinal center B cells . Given below is a list of cell surface markers and the cells they are expressed on: • CD3: All T cells • CD4: Helper T cells • CD8: Cytotoxic T cells • CD4, CD25: Regulatory T cells66 • Ig, CD19, CD20 , CD21 : B Cells • CD10: Pre-B Cells , germinal center B cells • CD40, MHC-II: Macrophages • CD16, CD56: NK Cells • CD34: Hematopoietic stem cells Note : Pan T antigens are antigens found on all T cells and include CD2, CD3, CD5 and CD7 .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following markers is used for the identification of memory T cells ?
mcqs.explanation: CD45RO is used as a marker for the identification of memory T cells . CD45RA is a marker for virgin or nai\037ve T helper cells .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: In a patient with influenza, there is decreased expression of MHC proteins on the surface of the virus-infected cells . Which component of the immune system acts on such cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Natural killer cells (NK cells ) act on virus-infected cells with reduced MHC expression . NK cells are a subtype of lymphocytes that kill damaged or infected cells . NK cells express CD16 and CD56. Their action is inhibited when MHC I is expressed on normal cells . This prevents NK Cells from killing normal cells . In the presence of a viral infection or malignancy, MHC expression of a cell is reduced . Thus, NK cells get activated and kill virus-infected /tumor cells . NK cells also secrete cytokines (IFN-\035) which activate macrophages (option B) for destruction of ingested microbes. Other options : Option A: Cytotoxic T cells act when cells expressing MHC I present endogenous antigens. Option D: Helper T cells act when cells expressing MHC II (antigen-presenting cells ) present exogenous antigens.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A 9- year-old boy was brought with colicky pain, nausea, vomiting. Lab investigations revealed eosinophilia and stool examination shows the following egg . Which interleukin is secreted in this scenario?
mcqs.explanation: A child with colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting with eosinophilia likely has a parasitic infection with Ascaris lumbricoides (egg shown in the image). Parasitic infections trigger the release of IL -5. In a parasitic infection , Th2 cells are stimulated and they produce IL -4 and IL -5. IL -4 stimulates the differentiation of B-cells into IgE-secreting plasma cells , while IL -5 stimulates the maturation and release of eosinophils from the bone marrow . The secreted IgE coats the parasite. The activated eosinophils bind to the IgE-coated parasite and kill them through the release of major basic protein.67

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Macrophages are the major source of ______.
mcqs.explanation: Macrophages are the major source of IL -1. Macrophages are phagocytic cells that secrete the following molecules : • Enzymes - Lysozyme, proteases , elastases , collagenases , plasminogen activator. • Cytokines - Interleukins 1, 6, 8, , ; TNF-�o ; TGF-\037; prostaglandins. • Platelet -derived growth factor (PDGF), Platelet activated factor (PAF). • Colony-stimulating factor (CSF), Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) • Complements - C2, C4. • Reactive O2 species (ROS)- H2O2 , NO, OH. Interferon-gamma (IFN-\035) is secreted by T-cells . It is one of the most potent macrophage activators.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following mediators of inflammation is an example of a C-X-C chemokine?
mcqs.explanation: Interleukin-8 is an example of a C-X-C chemokine. Chemokines are chemotactic (chemoattractant ) cytokines. They recruit leukocytes to sites of inflammation. The C-X-C or alpha chemokines have a total of four cysteines , of which the first two separated by one amino acid. represented by 'X'.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an antigen-presenting cell ?
mcqs.explanation: T cell is not an antigen-presenting cell . Antigen presenting cells contain MHC class II molecules on their surface . They digest pathogens at the site of infection and display those exogenous antigens to T lymphopcytes , thus leading to T lymphocyte activation. Examples of antigen-presenting cells include dendritic cells , macrophages , B cells , glial cells (brain ), fibroblasts (skin), thymic epithelial cells and vascular endothelial cells .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A surgeon takes the following 2 images of a patient 's arm 6 weeks apart. Which of the following mediators promote the process shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows wound healing. TGF-\037 (transforming growth factor-\037) is responsible for wound healing . TGF-\037 is produced by B and T cells and it inhibits their proliferation. It acts as a growth factor for fibroblasts and promotes wound healing. It stimulates the production of collagen , fibronectin and proteoglycans . It also promotes class switching of B cells to IgA. IL -10 is also involved in wound healing and suppression of inflammation.68 Option B: IFN-�o inhibits viral replication, activates NK cells , and regulates the activity of macrophages and T cells . Option C: TNF-�o is involved in tumour cytotoxicity , phagocytic cell activation, and antiviral and antiparasitic effects . It is an acute phase protein. Option D: IFN-\037 has antiviral activity.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A patient 's plasma has high levels of interferon beta . He most likely has an infection due to _____
mcqs.explanation: Interferon-beta is secreted during infection due to viruses. Interferons are classified as cytokines. Interferons are non-toxic, non-antigenic and species -specific molecules . They are inactivated by proteases . They are stable at pH over 2-10 , except INF-\035 (labile at pH 2) and are non-dialysable and non-sedimentable . There are three types of interferons - �o , \037 and \035. IFN-�o or leukocyte interferon is produced by leucocytes . It has antiviral activity, is immunoregulaotry and antiproliferative. IFN-\037 or fibroblast interferon is produced by fibroblasts and epithelial cells . It has antiviral activity and is thus increased in viral infections . It enhances MHC class 1 and NK cell activity. IFN-\035 or immune interferon is produced by T-lymphocytes, NK cells . It activates macrophages , increases neutrophil function, enhances both MHC class 1 and class II expression and has anti-proliferative (anti-tumour) functions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.chapter: Structure and Functions of the Immune System & ...
mcqs.question: A newborn diagnosed with a hepatoblastoma is planned for liver transplantation. Her father is found to be an HLA match, and he donates part of his liver. What type of transplantation is described here?
mcqs.explanation: The transplant of an organ/tissue from a father to child is an example of an allograft.69

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What route of administration of the shocking dose of an antigen is most effective in causing an anaphylactic reaction?
mcqs.explanation: The intravenous route of administration is the most effective route of administration for shocking dose in causing anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity syndrome. There are 2 clinical syndromes which are characterised as: • Anaphylaxis - acute , potentially fatal systemic form • Atopy - chronic, recurrent, non-fatal, localized form Priming dose: For induction of hypersensitivity reactions, the host should have contact with the antigen , leading to priming of the appropriate B or T lymphocytes . Shocking dose : Subsequent contact with allergen causing manifestations of hypersensitivity .75 Effectiveness : intravenous > intraperitoneally ~subcutaneously > intradermally (least )

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which type of reaction is the Schultz -Dale phenomenon ?
mcqs.explanation: The Schultz –Dale phenomenon is a type I hypersensitivity reaction. It describes in-vitro contraction of smooth muscles that have been exposed to antigens, demonstrating immediate hypersensitivity reaction in some human and animal tissues . Other type I hypersensitivity reactions are the Prausnitz-Kustner reaction and the Theobald Smith phenomenon .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The presence of which of the following antibodies is demonstrated by the Prausnitz-Kustner reaction?
mcqs.explanation: The presence and activity of IgE antibodies are demonstrated by the Prausnitz–K\374stner (P–K) reaction. In this method , the serum is injected from an allergic person into the skin of a nonallergic individual. Then a suspected antigen is later injected into the same site . A positive P-K reaction is a wheal and flare reaction seen in the non-allergic individual. This indicates that the suspected antigen is causing hypersensitivity . Because of the danger of transmitting viral hepatitis and AIDS, this test is no longer used .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A child, upon ingestion of shellfish , developed a tingling sensation in the mouth, swelling of the face , lips, and tongue , and also complained of abdominal pain and dizziness. What type of reaction is this?
mcqs.explanation: This child who developed tingling in the mouth, and swelling of the lips and face after eating shelf life is an example of an IgE mediated type of hypersensitivity reaction.76 Anaphylaxis is a severe , potentially life -threatening allergic reaction that occurs rapidly and affects the whole body. It is characterized by a sudden release of histamines and other chemicals from the immune system in response to an allergen , such as certain foods , medications , insect stings, or latex. The onset of symptoms can occur within minutes to a few hours after exposure to the allergen .The primary mediators are histamine and serotonin. The secondary mediators are prostaglandins and leukotrienes . Clinically, anaphylaxis can present with a combination of symptoms that typically include : • Respiratory Symptoms : Patients often experience wheezing and respiratory distress due to bronchoconstriction. Other signs may include shortness of breath, coughing , and a feeling of tightness in the chest . • Skin Symptoms : Urticaria (hives) and angioedema (swelling of the skin and mucous membranes) are common. These skin reactions usually develop rapidly, often within minutes to two hours of exposure to the allergen . • Cardiovascular Symptoms : Hypotension (low blood pressure ) is a key indicator of anaphylaxis. Patients may also experience tachycardia (increased heart rate) and, in severe cases , shock. • Gastrointestinal Symptoms : Abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and cramps can occur, particularly if the anaphylaxis is triggered by food allergens . • Neurological Symptoms : Dizziness, lightheadedness , or loss of consciousness can occur due to the sudden drop in blood pressure and reduced oxygen supply to the brain .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Two days after penicillin administration, a patient developed antibodies that resulted in hemolysis . Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
mcqs.explanation: Development of antibodies resulting in hemolysis after penicillin administration is an example of a type II reaction. This is a drug-induced type II hypersensitivity reaction. Penicillin in high doses can result in immune-mediated hemolysis via the hapten mechanism. In this, the drug attaches to surface of RBC membrane. Antibodies are produced that are targeted against this combination of penicillin and RBCs.77 Complement is activated by the attached antibody leading to the removal of red blood cells by the spleen .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A skin transplant was done from a sister to her brother. After a few years, a brother-to-sister skin transplant was done, but rejection occurred. What is this phenomenon known as?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario describes an Eichwald -Silmser effect , which is a unilateral sex-linked histo-incompatibility . While transplants between same-sex siblings are successful , grafts from female to male are also successful , but an exception is seen when the donor is a male and the recipient is a female . Such grafts are rejected as the grafted male tissue (XY ) will have antigens determined by the Y chromosome which will be absent in the female (XX ) recipient .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old girl is brought with complaints of sensitivity to light and profuse lacrimation. On inspection , the given finding is seen on her upper tarsal conjunctiva. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
mcqs.explanation: Spring catarrh or vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction. It is a bilateral, seasonally recurrent, chronic conjunctivitis due to type I hypersensitivity allergic reaction to an external antigen. The antigen reacts with IgE, this stimulates mast cell degranulation leading to the release of histamine and other mediators of the allergic response . Spring catarrh is one of the several forms of allergic conjunctivitis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is involved in the hyperacute rejection of renal transplants?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperacute graft rejection is an example of type II hypersensitivity reaction. It is mediated by preformed antibodies. It is a rare event that occurs in kidney transplantation.78 Graft rejectio n Time taken for rejection Immune mechanisms involve d Type of hypersensitivity Hyperacute Minutes to hours Preformed antibodies II Acute Weeks to months Cytotoxic T-cell mediated IV Chronic Months to years Chronic DTH mediated and Ab mediated IV

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about anaphylaxis?

options.a: It is a type I hypersensitivity reaction
options.c: Primary mediators like IL 4, IL 5 and GM-CSF are released

mcqs.explanation: IL4 , IL5 , GM-CSF are secondary mediators and not primary mediators. Anaphylaxis is a type I reaction and is mediated through IgE. Primary mediators are preformed contents of mast cells and basophil granules such as histamine, serotonin. They cause vasodilation and bronchoconstriction. Secondary mediators are newly formed upon stimulation by mast cells, basophils , and other leucocytes (such as leukotrienes IL3 , IL4 , IL5 , IL6 ; GM-CSF, and prostaglandins) which lead to inflammatory cell infiltrates .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: While studying the patient data on hypersensitivity reactions over the last 2 months, you are tasked with classifying the cases by type . Who among the following patients falls under type II hypersensitivity ?

options.b: Eczematous reaction on the hand of an HCW wearing powdered gloves
options.c: A patient with heat intolerance, sinus tachycardia, and proptosis
options.d: Glomerulonephritis in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus

mcqs.explanation: Heat intolerance, sinus tachycardia, and proptosis of the eye suggest a diagnosis of Grave's disease . It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction that results in the binding of anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone (anti-TSH) antibodies to TSH receptors and stimulates the thyroid cells to produce thyroid hormones. Type II hypersensitivity reactions involve combining the of IgG antibodies with the antigenic determinants on the surface of cells leading to cytotoxic effects .79 Other options : Option A: Berylliosis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Option B: Eczematous reaction on the hand of an HCW wearing powdered gloves (contact dermatitis) is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. Option D: Glomerulonephritis in a patient with SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus ) is a type III hypersensitivity reaction.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old hiker presents with an itchy rash on her wrist. She gives a history of getting brushed with poison ivy on a trek the previous day. What cells are involved in this reaction?
mcqs.explanation: The history and image suggest a diagnosis of contact dermatitis , a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells . These are delayed hypersensitivity reactions and are induced by sensitized T cells , which on contact with the specific antigen releases cytokines that produce biological effects on leucocytes , macrophages , and tissue cells . Two types of delayed hypersensitivity are: • Tuberculin type • Contact dermatitis type

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old hypertensive man complains of fever, migraine, loss of appetite , and myalgia. On examination, splinter hemorrhages and palpable purpura are noted . On CT angiography, aneurysm and stenosis of medium-sized vessels are observed. What is the type of hypersensitivity reaction associated with this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa. It is an example of a type III hypersensitivity reaction. In type III hypersensitivity , immune complexes may deposit in tissues or blood vessels , and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating the complement system . The inflammatory reaction causes tissue injury.80 The pathogenesis of systemic immune complex disease can be divided into three phases : • Formation of immune complexes • Deposition of immune complexes • Inflammation and tissue injury. Examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions: • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis • SLE • Polyarteritis nodosa • Reactive arthritis • Serum sickness • Arthus reaction • Farmer's lung • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis • Type II lepra reaction • Henoch Schonlein purpura

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is implicated in the autoimmune disease shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The disease shown in the image is myasthenia gravis. It is an example of type II hypersensitivity . Type II hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by antibodies directed towards self -antigens- cell surface or extracellular matrix.81

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old patient comes with recurrent episodes of sneezing , rhinorrhea , and watering of the eyes . She says she has these symptoms throughout the year. Which of the following immunoglobulins will be elevated in her case?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette describes a case of chronic allergic rhinits. IgE is elevated in these cases . Perennial allergic rhinitis, a type of chronic rhinitis is a year-round problem and is often caused by indoor allergens such as dust and animal dander in addition to pollens that may exist at the time. Symptoms tend to occur regardless of the time of the year.82

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old child has a history of recurrent skin and respiratory tract infections . Investigations are carried out and a disorder of phagocytosis is suspected . Which of the following will not be a differential diagnosis in this case?
mcqs.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is not a disorder of phagocytosis . It is due to a developmental defect involving the endodermal derivatives of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches . Cell -mediated immunity is defective due to decreased T-cells . Affected individuals also have depressed graft rejection , hypocalcemia , and cardiac defects .87 Disorders of phagocytosis : • Leukocyte adhesion deficiency • Chediak–Higashi syndrome • Chronic granulomatous disease • Tuftsin deficiency • Cyclic neutropenia Other options : Option B: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency leads to defective neutrophil migration to sites of infection , peripheral neutrophilia , and recurrent infections without pus . Option C: Chediak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder due to defects in lysosomal transport protein (LYST), leading to defective microtubule polymerization and defective phagolysosome formation. There is neutropenia and recurrent infections . Option D: Chronic granulomatous disease is due to a defect in NADPH oxidase resulting in the absence of respiratory burst. It presents with recurrent infections with catalase -positive microbes.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old boy presents with meningococcal meningitis. He has a history of recurrent bacterial chest and ear infections . Family history reveals that he has a male cousin (maternal side ) who died in infancy from infection . The physician suspects X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Which of the following is false regarding his condition?

options.a: It is caused by a mutation of the BTK gene
options.b: Both humoral and cell mediated immunity are affected
options.c: All classes of immunoglobulin levels are reduced
options.d: Lymph node biopsy shows depletion of follicles

mcqs.explanation: X-linked or Bruton's agammaglobulinemia is primarily a disease of humoral immunity. Cell -mediated immunity is not affected . It is an inherited immunodeficiency disease caused by mutations in the gene coding for Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK). B cells do not differentiate and mature. They are arrested in the pre-B cell stage . There are extremely low IgG levels (below 100 mg/dL) and an absence of other immunoglobulin classes . The tonsils and lymph nodes are usually atrophic. Lymph node biopsy reveals depletion of cells of B cell -dependent areas (follicles). Babies born with this disorder have virtually no peripheral B cells (<1%) and suffer from recurrent bacterial infections .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An immunologist orders a nitroblue tetrazolium test on a child suspected to have a primary immunodeficiency disease . What condition is she screening the child for?
mcqs.explanation: The Nitroblue Tetrazolium Test (NBT) is used as a screening test for chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) by assessing the reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in phagocytes . This principle relies on the color change of nitroblue tetrazolium, which transforms from colorless /yellow to deep blue when it encounters ROS. A higher nitroblue test score indicates that the cell is more efficient in producing ROS. In chronic granulomatous disease , there is an NADPH oxidase defect . Hence , the phagocyte cannot produce reactive oxygen species or radicals required for bacterial killing, which results in recurrent infections . Here, the leukocytes fail to reduce nitroblue tetrazolium during phagocytosis . Hence , a negative test (NBT remains colourless to yellow ) is seen in CGD. A positive test result means neutroph ils turn blue , as shown below :88 A negative test means nitroblue tetrazolium remains colourless /yellow , as shown below :

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old boy is brought with a history of recurrent pneumonia. He also has eczema and a history of prolonged bleeding after circumcision. Peripheral smear shows thrombocytopenia with small platelets . Which of the following is most likely to be deficient ?
mcqs.explanation: The history here is highly suggestive of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS), a condition characterized by decreased IgM levels . Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder. It is caused by mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) that primarily affects the T lymphocytes . Normally, WASp regulates the actin cytoskeleton and thus helps in cell adhesion, migration, and the formation of synapses between antigen-presenting and target cells . In WAS, there is a progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood resulting in defects in cellular immunity.89 The clinical features of WAS are a triad of recurrent bacterial infections , eczema, and bleeding due to thrombocytopenia (with small platelets ). Diagnosis is based on intracellular immunofluorescence analysis of WAS protein (WASp) expression in blood cells . IgM levels in the serum are low, but levels of IgG are usually normal . IgA and IgE levels are normal or elevated . Reduced -sized platelet is a typical feature of WAS. The image below shows an 18-month-old child with WAS, showing multiple petechiae and hematoma.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric OPD with multiple cold abscess lesions as shown below on his face , chest , and back. The child has a history of recurrent\037 respiratory infections . On examination, he has atopic excoriations over the skin folds . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A child with multiple abscesses (as shown in the image above) with a history of atopy and recurrent respiratory infections suggests immunodeficiency , and the most probable diagnosis is Hyper IgE syndrome. The hyper -IgE syndromes are rare primary immunodeficiency syndromes characterized by recurrent severe staphylococcal abscesses of the skin, lungs , and other sites , eczema, eosinophilia , and marked elevation of serum IgE levels . They occur in 2 forms: • Autosomal dominant - involves mutations in the gene encoding STAT -3 (also known as Job syndrome) • Autosomal recessive - involves mutations in DOCK8 . In Job syndrome, mutation of the STAT3 gene leads to IgE overproduction without modulation. Loss of modulation is due to the absence of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL -6, IL -10 , and IFN-gamma. Lack of IL -6 leads to deficiency of CD4 + Th17 cells , making them susceptible to various infections . It usually presents as a triad of atopic dermatitis, recurrent skin staphylococcal infections , and recurrent pulmonary infections that occur early in childhood . The eczematoid rash affects the scalp and face , gets superinfected with Staphylococcus aureus and forms cold abscesses . Candida infections are common. Recurrent staphylococcal pneumonia with pneumatocoeles is also90 commonly seen . Other non-immunological features are: • Dysmorphic facial features that appear in early adolescence and are absent in the autosomal recessive form • Craniosynostosis • Arnold-Chiari type 1 • Hyperextensible joints • Scoliosis • Pathological fractures • Retention of primary teeth • Vascular complications • Ocular complications Diagnosis is based on measurements of serum IgE levels >2000U/mL where IgA, IgG and IgM concentrations are generally normal , in adjunct with the clinical features seen in Job syndrome. It is associated with peripheral blood eosinophilia . The treatment primarily focuses on preventing infections through the use of antimicrobials, including antibiotics and antifungals , along with immunoglobulin replacement therapy .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a combined immunodeficiency disorder associated with both B-cell and T-cell defects ?
mcqs.explanation: Louis–Bar syndrome or ataxia-telangiectasia is a combined immunodeficiency disorder. Ataxia-telangiectasia is a syndrome complex that comprises neurologic , immunologic, endocrinologic, and cutaneous disorders. The gene involved in this condition is the mutation in the ATM gene mapped to the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q22 -23 ). The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive . There is defective DNA repair and increased sensitivity to ionizing radiation. Clinical features : • Progressive cerebellar ataxia • Oculocutaneous telangiectasias • Chronic sinopulmonary disease • High incidence of malignancy - adenocarcinomas and lymphoreticular tumors (lymphoma, leukemia, and Hodgkin's disease ) • Humoral and cellular immunodeficiency • Ovarian dysgenesis and chromosomal abnormalities • Hypoplastic thymus • Ataxia and chorioathetoid movements start in infancy. The onset of telangiectasia is around 3 to 6 years and involves the face , conjunctiva and other parts of the body. By 12 years of age , affected children are usually confined to wheelchairs due to progressive ataxia.91 Death occurs due to sinopulmonary infection in early life or due to malignancy in the second or third decade . They lack IgA and IgE. Cell -mediated immunity is also defective . The image below shows ocular telangiectasia in a patient with A-T.Other options : Option B: DiGeorge syndrome is a cellular immunodeficiency disorder associated with T-cell deficiency . Options C and D: Chediak-Higashi syndrome and tuftsin deficiency are disorders of phagocytosis .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old boy presents with reports showing fungal pneumonia, the causative organism is shown below . Parents give a history of recurrent bacterial infections . Laboratory analysis show markedly elevated IgM and low levels of IgG. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his illness ?

options.a: Defective cytokine signaling in T-cell precursors
options.b: Autosomal-dominant mutation in the STAT3 gene
options.c: Deficiency in CD40 ligand or CD
options.d: Defect in the NADPH oxidative pathway

mcqs.explanation: The given history of recurrent bacterial infections and fungal pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (as shown in the image above), along with elevated IgM and low IgG levels , are suggestive of hyper -IgM syndrome, an inherited deficiency in the CD40 ligand or CD40. Hyper-IgM syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency disorder that is inherited as: • X-linked form (most common): CD40 ligand (CD40L) defect on T-helper cells , preventing B-cell activation, class switching and memory cells formation. • Autosomal recessive form: Affect CD40 on B-cells or enzymes like activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), a DNA-editing enzyme expressed in B cells . The B-cell response to T-independent antigen is unaffected . CD40–CD40L interactions are also required for IL -12 secretion . So, defects in this pathway result in increased susceptibility to intracellular pathogens . In normal immune response , B-cells expressing CD40 on their surface interact with CD40L on T-cells to undergo class switching from IgM to various other classes (IgG, IgA, IgE) depending on the type of antigen. Thus, failure of this class switching leads to an increase in IgM with extremely low levels of IgG and no IgA or IgE.92 Clinical features include recurrent pyogenic infections caused by low levels of opsonizing IgG antibodies . Patients are highly susceptible to pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. The illustration below depicts the defects in components of T-cell & B-cell interactions that give rise to primary immunodeficiency .Other options : Option A: Defective cytokine signalling in T-cell precursors is seen in X-linked Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). It is caused by a mutation in the common \035-chain (\035c) subunit of cytokine receptors . This defect disrupts Interleukins (IL -2, IL -4, IL -7, IL -9, IL -15 and IL -21 ) signalling, leading to low T-cell and NK-cell numbers. Although B-cell numbers are normal , these are non-functional due to the absence of T-cell help , resulting in impaired antibody synthesis . Option B: Mutation in the STAT3 gene is seen in an autosomal dominant form of Hyper IgE syndrome (also known as Job syndrome), characterized by recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses , recurrent pulmonary infections often with pneumatoceles and atopic dermatitis . Here, serum IgE levels are markedly elevated (due to IgE overproduction without modulation), and IgA, IgG and IgM concentrations are generally normal . Option D: A defect in NADPH oxidative pathway is seen in chronic granulomatous disease , leading to failure of the oxidative burst in phagocytes , predisposing individuals to catalase -positive microbial infections .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought with complaints as shown below . The parents report that these complaints have been present for the last 2 years. Which of the following is found to be the most effective treatment for this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: This 5-year-old boy presenting with a 2-year history of thick, white -coated tongue and dystrophic nail changes , as shown in the above image, suggests chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, for which transfer factor therapy and amphotericin B have been reported to be the effective treatments . Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) is characterized by deficient cell -mediated immunity to candida, usually due to defects in IL -17. Mutations affecting the IL -17 signalling pathway lead to93 impaired IL -17 production and defective TH17 function, compromising mucosal and skin defence mechanisms and increasing susceptibility to fungal infections . Patients develop persistent fungal infections of the skin, nails, oral cavity, and genitals , primarily caused by Candida species . Despite chronic mucocutaneous involvement, these patients typically do not develop invasive candidiasis. A key feature of CMC is the absence of delayed hypersensitivity to candida antigens. However, circulating antibodies to them are present in high titres . They do not show increased susceptibility to other infections but may develop endocrinopathies , autoimmune disorders, and vascular abnormalities. Transfer factor therapy and Amphotericin B have been reported to be effective for the treatment of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An infant with a history of delayed separation of the umbilical cord now presents with recurrent pneumonia. The total leukocyte count is 20 ,000 /microlitre. Which of the following genetic defects is most likely present ?

options.a: Mutation of Bruton tyrosine kinase gene
options.b: Low levels of NADPH oxidase and negative DHR test
options.c: Reduced phagocyte surface expression of sialyl-Lewis x
options.d: Excessive IgM with reduced IgG and IgA

mcqs.explanation: This history of delayed separation of the umbilical cord with recurrent pneumonia and peripheral leucocytosis is highly suggestive of leucocyte adhesion defect (LAD ). In this defect , there is reduced phagocyte surface expression of sialyl-Lewis X. LAD is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting leukocyte function. Neutrophils have reduced adhesion , mobility, and phagocytic ability. There are three main types of LAD : • LAD 1- Defective \0372 integrin common chain (CD18), leading to abnormal neutrophil chemotaxis and defective tight adhesion. • LAD 2- Reduced phagocyte surface expression of sialyl-Lewis X (fucosylated protein), leading to abnormal neutrophil rolling and tethering. • LAD 3- Defect in regulatory protein (kindlin 3, also known as Fermt 3) involved in activating the ligand affinity for \0372 integrins, leading to abnormal neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion (milder than type 1). LAD is characterised by recurrent bacterial and fungal infections , reduced inflammatory responses despite elevated blood neutrophilia, and delayed wound healing and delayed umbilical cord loss. in patients with LAD type 3, there may be bleeding as \0372 integrin on platelets is non-functional. Typical signs of inflammation may be absent, pus does not form with few neutrophils on biopsy of infected tissues along with massive hyperleukocytosis (>30,000 /�ML) in the blood. Early allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used in the treatment of severe LAD .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about severe combined immunodeficiency disorders?

options.a: Reticular dysgenesis of de Vaal is a mild form of combined immunodeficiency
options.b: They are inherited as autosomal dominant disorders
options.c: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is associated with chondrocyte abnormalities
options.d: The defect in Swiss type agammaglobulinemia is at the level of multipotent hemopoeitic stem cell

mcqs.explanation: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is associated with chondrocyte abnormalities. Severe combined immunodeficiency disorders are associated with severe deficiency of both humoral and CMI. They are inherited in both X-linked and autosomal recessive modes . There are different forms of this disorder:94 • Reticular dysgenesis is the most serious form of combined immunodeficiency . Here the defect is at the level of the multipotent hemopoietic stem cell . • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is associated with enzyme deficiency . The condition is associated with chondrocyte abnormalities which can be discerned radiologically . • Swiss -type agammaglobulinemia is associated with lymphocytopenia and severe defect in CMI. The basic defect is at the level of the lymphoid stem cell .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an immunologically privileged site ?
mcqs.explanation: The seminiferous tubules are an immunologically privileged site . Immunologically privileged sites can tolerate the introduction of antigens without eliciting an immune response . This allows a higher likelihood of graft survival , even without perfect HLA matching. As a result , an allograft can be placed in these sites without endangering a rejection reaction. The unique immune tolerance in these regions is primarily due to the lack of effective lymphatic drainage, which prevents antigen presentation to the immune system , and the presence of blood-tissue barriers that restrict immune cell infiltration. Low vascularity contributes to immune privilege by minimising antigen exposure and immune cell recruitment. Examples of immune-privileged sites are the anterior chamber of the eye , cornea, testes , and brain . Note : Although part of the brain , the blood-brain barrier is absent at the area postrema, therefore it is not an immune-privileged site .95

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the Lancefield grouping of \037-hemolytic -streptococci based on?
mcqs.explanation: Lancefield grouping of \037-hemolytic -streptococci is based on group-specific carbohydrate C antigen present on the cell wall. He classified them into 20 serological types from Group-A to Group V except for I and J. Group A \037-hemolytic streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes ) are further classified by Griffith typing based on protein antigens (M, T, R) present on the cell surface .103

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An elderly diabetic lady presented with swelling and pain of her right leg following a skin biopsy . She was febrile at the time of examination and hemorrhagic bullae with necrosis of the surrounding skin were noted on her leg . Gram staining of the pus collected from the bullae is shown below . Which of the following is the most likely organism causing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of necrotizing fasciitis which is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A \037-hemolytic streptococcus ). Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive inflammatory infection of the fascia, with secondary necrosis of the subcutaneous tissues . It has also been referred to as Meleney ulcer, acute dermal gangrene , hospital gangrene , suppurative fasciitis , and synergistic necrotizing cellulitis . The source of the infection is either the skin, with organisms introduced into the tissue through trauma, or the bowel flora, with organisms released during abdominal surgery. The onset of symptoms is usually quite acute and is marked by severe pain at the site of involvement, malaise, fever, chills, and a toxic appearance . The affected limb is edematous with the overlying skin turning dusky with mottled erythema and the development of hemorrhagic bullae . This is a surgical emergency as the condition is rapidly fatal. Treatment of the condition includes : • Surgical intervention is the major therapeutic modality in cases of necrotizing fasciitis . • Antibiotics- penicillin (1-4 million U IV q4h) plus clindamycin (600-900 mg IV q8h). The following image shows surgical debridement being done for a case of necrotising fasciitis .104

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old child was brought in by her mother to the OPD with complaints of fever, sore throat, and a scarlatiniform rash. A throat swab was taken and sent to the lab for culture on blood agar. Which of the following factors is responsible for the zones of hemolysis seen in the culture below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario o a patient with fever, sore throat, and a scarlatiniform rash is suggestive of scarlet fever caused by Streptococcus pyogenes . Streptolysin S is the factor responsible for the zones of hemolysis seen around streptococcal colonies on blood agar. Streptococci produces two hemolysins: • Streptolysin O is called so because it is oxygen -labile . It is also heat -labile and it has specific cardiotoxic and leucotoxic activity. • Streptolysin S is called so because it is soluble in serum. It is also oxygen -stable hemolysin . It is a protein but is not antigenic. The following image shows blood agar with colonies of streptococci with hemolytic zones around them:105

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms produces superantigen ?
mcqs.explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes produces streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin (SPE), which is a superantigen .
