Mycobacteria can be identified based on their biochemical reactions as follows : The first four tests are used to distinguish between M. tb complex and atypical mycobacteria while the last four tests are used to distinguish between M. tb and M. bovis.Biochemical tes t M. tb M. bov is NTM Catalase Weak + Weak + +++ Peroxidase ++_ Arylsulfatse --+ Niacin +- - Nitrate reductio n +- N/A Pyrazinamidase +- N/A TCH sensitivity Resista nt Sensiti ve N/A

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 54-year-old male presents with an ulcer on his hand. On swab culture , growth of M. ulcerans is seen. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 184 Mycobacterium ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer. M. ulcerans produces a toxin called mycolactone which leads to formation of Buruli ulcer. This is a chronic, debilitating , necrotizing disease of the skin and soft tissue which is characterized by the formation of ulcers that progressively enlarge over time if left untreated . The ulcers heal with disfiguring scars. The image below shows a Buruli ulcer.Option A: Hunner's ulcers are seen in a subset of patients with interstitial cystitis . These are areas of inflammation on the bladder wall. The image below shows a cystoscopic image of a Hunner's ulcer.Option B: Meleney 's ulcer or post -operative synergistic bacterial gangrene occurs in immuno-compromised individuals following abdominal surgery. It is caused by a synergistic interaction between microaerophilic nonhemolytic Streptococcus and hemolytic aerobic Staphylococcus aureus.185 Option D: Marjolin ulcer is a rare and aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma that grows from burns, scars, or poorly healing wounds. The image below shows a Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man who works at an aquarium and handles the fish without protective equipment presents to the OPD with the following finding. Infection with which of the following bacteria led to his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a fish tank granuloma that is caused by M. marinum . The typical clinical presentation is as a single , small violet papule or nodule confined to one extremity, developing 2-3 weeks after trauma. The nodule may break down to form an indolent ulcer. M. marinarum is a natural pathogen of fish and amphibians, which spreads to humans who come in contact with contaminated swimming pools or fish tanks. Other non-tuberculous mycobacteria causing disease in humans include : • M. kansasii : Disease resembles pulmonary TB • M. scrofulaceum : Cervical lymphadenitis • M. avium complex : Pulmonary, disseminated TB , especially in AIDS patients • M. fortuitum : Nail salon furunculosis M. paratuberculosis (aka Johne's bacillus ) causes Johne's disease in cattle . It is associated with Crohn's disease in humans.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about the microbiological diagnosis of the disease afflicting the patient shown below ?

options.a: Acid fast staining is done by Ziehl-Neelsen technique , using 25% sulphuric acid
options.b: Sample should be collected from the centre of the lesion
options.c: The number of samples to be collected is 3-
options.d: It is cultivated in nine banded armadillos and foot pads of mice

mcqs.explanation: The image depicts leonine facies in a patient suffering from leprosy or Hansen's disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae . It is cultivated in nine-banded armadillos and footpads of mice.186 M. leprae is a Gram-positive , weakly acid fast bacillus . Thus, 5% sulphuric acid (option A) is used for decolourisation to demonstrate M.leprae 's acid-fastness . On microscopy, the bacilli appear bound together in masses called globi, within which they are arranged in a 'cigar bundle ' appearance . For leprosy diagnosis, specimens are collected from the nasal mucosa, skin lesions and earlobes . Nasal smears are collected from the internal septum of the nose. Skin smears are collected from the edges of the lesions (option B) rather than from the centre . Slit skin smears are taken as well . The skin is pinched up tight to minimise bleeding and a cut is made with a scalpel , deep enough to get into the infiltrated layers. This is done over the buttocks , forehead , chin, cheek , and ears (at least 5-6 different areas) (option C).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the generation time of lepra bacilli?
mcqs.explanation: The generation time of lepra bacilli is 12 -13 days. Generation time, also known as doubling time, is the time it takes for the bacterial population to double . It can also be measured as the time between two cell divisions under optimum conditions. The generation time of different bacilli are given below : • Lepra bacilli- -13 days average (may vary from 8-42 days) • Tubercle bacilli- 15-20 hours • Coliform bacilli- 20 minutes

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What are the bacteria present in Virchow's cells ?
mcqs.explanation: The bacteria present in Virchow's cells is M. leprae . Lepromatous leprosy lesions contain large aggregates of lipid laden macrophages (lepra cells /Virchow cells ) which are often filled with globi (masses) of acid fast bacilli. The image below shows a high-power Fite -Faraco stain of a skin lesion showing globi of M.leprae .187

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You counsel a patient with leprosy about lepra reactions before starting her on multidrug therapy. Which among these is correct regarding these reactions?
mcqs.explanation: Statements 2, 4, and 5 regarding lepra reactions are correct. Type 2 lepra reactions are unrelated to drug therapy , whereas type 1 reactions may occur within a year of starting treatment . New lesions typically appear in type 2 lepra reactions. They are tender and erythematous subcutaneous and dermal nodules . Existing lesions show no changes .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient diagnosed with leprosy was undergoing further evaluation for classification of type and immune response . Which of the following statements is false regarding the intradermal test used in such evaluation?

options.b: It has no value in prognostication of leprosy
options.d: BCG vaccine may convert a negative test to positive

mcqs.explanation: The lepromin test has value as a prognostic test for leprosy . The lepromin, or Mitsuda test , is a method to measure cellular immunity in leprosy . It is a skin test for delayed hypersensitivity to lepra antigens. A bacillary suspension of inactivated M. leprae is injected just under the skin and the induration reaction is measured 3–4 weeks after. It is used to classify leprosy . A negative lepromin test is seen in lepromatous and borderline leprosy . It is negative in children <6 months of age , it may be positive at the end of 1st year. BCG vaccine is capable of converting a negative lepromin test to a positive .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are performing the test shown in the image on a patient . How many days later do you ask the patient to return so that you get an accurate read on the Mitsuda reaction?
mcqs.explanation: Mitsuda 's reaction is read in the 3rd week , i.e., on the 21st day or 20 days after the day of injection. Lepromin test is a skin test for delayed hypersensitivity to lepra antigens. It is the only method for studying immunity in leprosy . A bacillary suspension of inactivated M. leprae is injected just188 under the skin. The first reaction to occur is the early reaction of Fernandez, which consists of erythema and induration developing in 24-48 hours. It usually remains for 3-5 days; it is usually poorly defined and carries less significance . The second and more meaningful result is the late reaction of Mitsuda , starting at 1-2 weeks (7-10 days), reaching a peak in three or four weeks , and gradually subsiding over the next few weeks . On the 21st day, if there is a nodule more than 5 mm in diameter , the reaction is said to be positive . Note : The 21st day is 20 days after the day of injection which is counted as the 1st day.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A leprosy vaccine is being introduced on a pilot basis in India. Which of the following mycobacterial species is the basis for its development ?
mcqs.explanation: Mycobacterium indicus pranii is the basis for the development of a leprosy vaccine. The leprosy vaccine species was originally called Mycobacterium W (M.w) but was later renamed Mycobacterium indicus pranii. The vaccine is administered via intradermal route. The dose is 0.1 ml. It is divided into two equal doses and given on both arms. Booster doses will be given to maintain the immunity level . These are given only in one arm .189

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An old woman presented to the OPD with dysuria and frequent micturition. Urinalysis showed pus cells , and culture on MacConkey agar showed the following . Which organism is involved here?
mcqs.explanation: This patient who presented with dysuria and frequent micturition with urinalysis showing pus cells , and growth of lactose -fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar suggests a diagnosis of urinary tract infection by Escherichia coli. Enterobacteriaceae family is classified based on their action on lactose present in MacConkey's medium as: • Lactose fermenters - Escherichia , Klebsiella • Late lactose fermenters - Shigella sonnei • Non-lactose fermenters - Salmonella species , Shigella species The image below shows lactose fermenting and non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar.Mnemonic to remember non-lactose fermenters : (SPY PSM) • Salmonella • Proteus • Yersinia • Providencia- late fermenter • Shigella (except S.sonnei which is a late lactose fermenter )198 • Morganella

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The stool culture of a patient with suspected food poisoning produced hemolytic colonies on blood agar. The isolated organism gave a positive indole test and a positive MUG test . You observe the following colonies on eosin methylene blue agar. Identify the organism.
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario of a patient with suspected food poisoning with stool culture growing hemolytic colony on blood agar with a positive indole test and MUG test with a iridescent green colony growth on eosin methylene blue agar is characteristic of Escherichia coli. E. coli produces the enzyme \037-glucuronidase which is tested using the MUG test . In it, the substrate MUG (4-methylumbelliferyl -\037-glucuronide ) is reduced by the enzyme to produce a fluorescent color which indicates a positive MUG test .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the cut-off for bacteriuria beyond which a diagnosis of catheter -associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) can be made?
mcqs.explanation: The cut-off value for bacteriuria to diagnose catheter -associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) is >103 CFU /mL . The minimum criterion for catheter -associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (CA-ASB) is >102 CFU/mL.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A tourist came to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and watery diarrhea. Which of the following strains of E. coli is most commonly implicated in this case?
mcqs.explanation: This patient with watery diarrhea most likely has traveller's diarrhea caused by Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC). Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common organism that causes diarrhea in travelers. It produces the following toxins: • LT (heat-labile toxin) - acts by \026cAMP • ST (heat-stable toxin) - two types of ST are known, ST-A (ST-I) and ST-B (ST-II ) • ST-A is soluble in methanol and acts by \026 cGMP in the intestine . • ST-B is insoluble in methanol, and the mode of action is not known. Other options : Option A: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC ) causes infantile diarrhea in developing countries . It adheres to the mucosal surface of the small intestine using E. coli adherent factor (EAF) and locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) and causes effacement of microvilli . Option B: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC ) produces verocytotoxin, which targets vascular endothelium . It causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome. Option D: Enteroinvasive E.coli (EIEC) invades interstitial epithelial cells in the intestine and causes a condition resembling shigellosis . This ability is determined by a plasmid, which can be detected as a diagnostic test .199

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Identify the organism below that causes effacement and attachment of intestinal cells .
mcqs.explanation: Attachment and effacement lesions on intestinal cells are caused by enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC ). E. coli is the second most common cause of diarrhea in the pediatric age group. Rotavirus is the most common cause . EPEC causes watery diarrhea which is self -limiting. EPEC adheres to the mucosal cells of the small bowel and causes loss of microvilli (effacement). This leads to the formation of filamentous actin pedestals or cuplike structures and occasionally may cause entry of the EPEC into the mucosal cells . Pathogenicity requires the presence of two important factors: • Bundle -forming pilus encoded by plasmid containing EPEC adherence factor (EAF). • Chromosomal locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) pathogenicity island.The image below shows an electron microscopy image of E Coli.200

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are investigating an outbreak of diarrhea. You find out that the etiological agent causes stacked-brick formation on hep -2 cells as shown below . What is the likely organism?
mcqs.explanation: The stacked -brick pattern of adherence on hep -2 cells is caused by enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC ). Enteroaggregative E. coli has been associated with persistent diarrhea. Intestinal colonization of EAEC is mediated by aggregative adherence fimbriae (AAF). EAST-1 toxin (enteroaggregative heat -stable toxin) is considered to be a major virulence factor for EAEC . The given image shows the stacked -brick pattern of adherence on microscopy at 600x magnification.201

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 29-year-old woman presented with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia , and acute renal failure. She was diagnosed with hemolytic uremic syndrome and treated with plasmapheresis and dialysis . What is false about the infectious causative agent?

options.b: It does not produce a Shiga like toxin
options.d: There is person to person transmission.

mcqs.explanation: Hemolytic -uremic syndrome (HUS) is caused by enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC ) serotype O157:H7. It produces a Shiga like toxin, therefore EHEC is also known as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). Other options : Option A - Strains of E. coli producing verocytotoxin or Shiga toxin (stx2a-g) can cause diarrheal disease ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal hemorrhagic colitis and HUS. The most common EHEC belongs to serotype O157:H7. Option C - In EHEC diarrhea, fecal leukocytes are commonly seen (70%) but although it is an infectious condition, fever is not seen . The absence of fever can lead to its misdiagnosis as a non-infectious condition such as intussusception or ischemic bowel disease . Option D - The disease is transmitted through contaminated feces . Person-to-person transmission can occur if infected persons do not wash their hands after using the toilet or after changing diapers . Note : Shiga toxin produced by S. dysenteriae is referred to as Stx.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Sereny test was employed for laboratory diagnosis of which of the following organisms?
mcqs.explanation: The Sereny test is an animal pathogenicity test that used to be employed for laboratory diagnosis of enteroinvasive E. coli and Shigella . Freshly isolated suspension of bacteria is instilled into the eyes of guinea pigs which leads to mucopurulent conjunctivitis and severe keratitis. It is not in use anymore as we have better methods of detecting toxigenicity now like molecular methods .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the culture media used to differentiate E. coli O157 :H7 from other E. coli?

options.d: Thiosulphate citrate Bile salt sucrose medium

mcqs.explanation: Sorbitol-MacConkey agar is used to differentiate E. coli O157 :H7 from other E. coli. E. coli O157 :H7 does not ferment sorbitol and produces pale colonies on Sorbitol-MacConkey agar. All other strains of E. coli ferment sorbitol. Thus they produce pink colonies on Sorbitol-MacConkey agar. O157 :H7 strains do not contain \037-glucuronidase and so are unable to use the substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl -\037-glucuronide (MUG ). Thus, they give a negative MUG test .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Match the following E.coli with their respective pathogenesis .
mcqs.explanation: The correctly matched pairs are as follows : The various strains of Escherichia coli are:202 • Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common organism that causes diarrhea in travelers. It produces the following toxins: • LT (heat-labile toxin)- acts by \026cAMP • ST (heat-stable toxin)- two types of ST are known, ST-A (ST-I) and ST-B (ST-II ) • ST-A is soluble in methanol and acts by \026cGMP in the intestine . • ST-B is insoluble in methanol, and the mode of action is not known. • Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) invade interstitial epithelial cells in the intestine and cause a condition resembling shigellosis . This ability is determined by a plasmid, detection of which can also be a diagnostic test . Sereny's test was employed to diagnose EIEC but it is not in use anymore. • Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC ) produces verocytotoxin, which targets vascular endothelium . It causes hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic uremic syndrome. • Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC ) causes infantile diarrhea in developing countries . It adheres to the mucosal surface of small intestine using EAF and LEE and causes effacement of microvilli . This leads to attachment and effacement lesions of intestinal cells . • Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC ) produces the stacked brick pattern of adherence on hep -2 cells . EAEC has been associated with persistent diarrhea. Intestinal colonization of EAEC is mediated by AAF (aggregative adherence fimbriae). EAEC produces EAST-1 toxin (enteroaggregative heat -stable toxin) which is considered to be a major virulence factor.E. co li Mechanism of action 1. ET EC A. Produce a heat -stable toxi n and cause activation of gua nylyl cyclase 2. EI EC B. Invades intestinal mucosal cells 3. E HEC C. Produces a toxin against v ascular endothelium cells 4. EP EC D. Adhere to the mucosal sur face and cause effacement of microvilli

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: E.coli is an aerobe and facultative anaerobe.
options.b: Proteus infection increases risk of uric acid stones .
options.c: E.coli is motile by peritrichous flagella .
options.d: Proteus can metabolise phenylalanine to phenylpyruvic acid.

mcqs.explanation: Proteus increases the risk of struvite stones in the bladder as it leads to the alkalinisation of urine. Struvite stones are magnesium-ammonium phosphate stones that appear as rectangular/coffin-lid crystals shaped on urine microscopy. Uric acid stones are precipitated in acidic urine. Proteus produces enzyme phenylalanine deaminase which converts phenylalanine to phenyl pyruvic acid. This property is the basis for the phenylalanine deaminase test .203 The test is performed by inoculating the organism in phenylalanine agar. After incubation, % ferric chloride is added to the media. If phenyl pyruvic acid was produced , it will react with the ferric chloride and turn dark green . If the medium remains a straw colour, the organism is negative for phenylalanine deaminase production . E. coli is an aerobe and facultative anaerobe. Its motility is due to the presence of peritrichous flagella . It is the most common cause of urinary tract infections .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following shows Dienes phenomenon ?
mcqs.explanation: Dienes phenomenon is exhibited by Proteus mirabilis. When two identical strains of Proteus are inoculated at different places of the same culture plate , the resulting swarms of growth coalesce and no line is formed between swarming cultures of the same strain. However, if they are from two different strains, the spreading films of growth fail to coalesce and remain separated by a narrow but easily visible furrow (known as Dienes line). This is known as Dienes phenomenon . The image below shows Dienes phenomenon.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Blood culture of the sputum sample taken from a patient diagnosed with hospital -acquired pneumonia, showed a characteristic phenomenon as shown in the image. Identify the bacteria that exhibit this phenomenon .
mcqs.explanation: The given image of the blood culture finding shows the characteristic bull's eye swarming pattern exhibited by Proteus. Proteus species move very actively with the help of peritrichous flagella , resulting in swarming on solid media. It can be suppressed by the addition of: • phenyl ethyl alcohol • chloral hydrate204 • sulphonamides • sodium azide • boric acid • increasing the concentration of agar to 6%. Swarming does not occur on MacConkey medium and cystine -lactose -electrolyte -deficient (CLED) medium . Proteus is a gram-negative bacillus seen as a normal gastrointestinal flora. The two most common species causing infection in humans are P. mirabilis and P. vulgaris, which can be differentiated by spot indole test . P. mirabilis is indole negative while P. vulgaris is indole positive . Production of urease enzyme by Proteus, which hydrolyses urea to ammonia causes alkalinization of urine. Alkalinization of urine leads to the precipitation of organic and inorganic compounds which contributes to the formation of Struvite stones . P. mirabilis is associated with urinary tract infections while P. vulgaris is usually associated with wound and soft tissue infections . Other organisms that show swarming include : • Clostridium tetani • Vibrio parahaemolyticus • Serratia

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man from north India presents with a deformity as shown in the image below . He gives a history of foul -smelling purulent nasal discharge before this nodule appeared . Which of the following organisms is responsible for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The above image and clinical scenario are suggestive of rhinoscleroma and it is caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. K. rhinoscleromatis is a gram-negative bacillus also known as Frisch bacillus . It is endemic in north India. Rhinoscleroma is characterized by chronic granulomatous hypertrophy of the nose. Biopsy of the lesion shows : • Mikulicz cells - large foamy cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated , cytoplasm containing causative bacilli. • Russell bodies - eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in the plasma cells . These are also observed in multiple myeloma. Other options : Option A: Rhinosporidium seeberi causes rhinosporidiosis. Option C: K. ozaenae causes atrophic rhinitis. Option D: K. oxytoca is associated with hemorrhagic colitis .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You notice a sputum sample of a patient suspected of having ventilator-associated pneumonia turns progressively redder over time. Microscopic examination of the sample reveals an absence of red blood cells . Which of the following organisms could have caused this?
mcqs.explanation: The given condition of sputum sample turning redder over time can be caused by Serratia marcescens .205 Serratia marcescens are pleomorphic coccobacilli that can grow in sputum after collection and can mimic hemoptysis because they produce a red pigment called prodigiosin. S. macescens mainly cause healthcare -associated infections such as ventilator-associated pneumonia, meningitis, endocarditis , septicemia and peritonitis . They can contaminate IV fluids , surgical instruments, and antiseptic solutions .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old boy presented with a single painless papule on his penis with no enlarged lymph nodes . A smear was made from the lesion and stained with Wright- Giemsa stain which showed the finding as shown in the following picture . Identify the organism.
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette and the image showing Donovan bodies in Wright/Giemsa-stained impression smears indicate a diagnosis of donovanosis caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. They appear as rounded coccobacilli within cystic spaces in large mononuclear cells (called Pund cells ). Klebsiella granulomatis shows bipolar condensation of chromatin giving a safety pin appearance . Bipolar staining (safety pin appearance) is shown by: • H. ducreyi • Vibrio parahaemolyticus • Klebsiella granulomatis • Yersinia pestis • Burkholderia pseudomallei • Burkholderia mallei206

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A child presents with a high fever, acute abdominal pain, and malaise. The child passes small amounts of bloody mucopurulent stools with increasing tenesmus and cramps. What is the most likely causative organism?
mcqs.explanation: Acute onset of symptoms (fever, abdominal cramps) with dysentery (bloody mucopurulent stools ) and tenesmus is most likely due to Shigella dysenteriae . Shigella dysenteriae is a Gram-negative bacillus causing bacillary dysentery in humans. It is spread through faeco -oral transmission. Other options : Option A: Vibrio cholerae results in watery diarrhea with characteristic rice watery stools . Option B: Viruses such as rotavirus and norovirus causes watery diarrhea through mucosal irritation . Option D: Entamoeba histolytica results in gradual onset of symptoms usually 1-3 weeks with dysentery .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following toxins acts by inhibiting protein synthesis ?
mcqs.explanation: Shiga toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis . Shiga toxin or verotoxin is an exotoxin produced by Shigella species . It consists of two subunits A and B. The B subunit binds to globotriaosylceramide receptors on the target cell , and then, the A subunit gets internalized. The A subunit leads to inhibition of 60S ribosome, leading to shut down of protein synthesis . Its site of action is in the endothelial cells of small blood vessels of GIT .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy developed bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen did not ferment lactose or mannitol. Which of the following organisms is implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: Shigella dysenteriae does not ferment mannitol and lactose . Shigella species cause bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramps). They do not ferment lactose , except S.sonnei which is a late lactose fermenter . To differentiate between the various Shigella species , mannitol fermentation is noted . Classification of pathogenic Shigella species :Designation Grou p Mannitol Fermentati on Ornithine decarboxyla se LactoseFermentation S. dysenteria e A - - - S. flexneri B + - - S. boydii C + - - S. sonnei D + + Late lactose fermente r212

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following salmonellae is non-motile?
mcqs.explanation: S. gallinarum is non-motile. Salmonellae are aerobic or facultatively anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli. They are motile due to the presence of peritrichous flagella , except S. gallinarum and S. pullorum.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A Greek patient with travel history to India is diagnosed with enteric fever. What is the minimum amount of pathogen required to cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Enteric fever is caused by S. typhi or S. paratyphi. The minimum amount of S. typhi required to cause enteric fever is 103 to 106 organisms. Enteric fever spreads through the feco-oral route. It presents with step -ladder fever and abdominal pain after an incubation period of 10 –20 days. Over the next week , the patient can develop abdominal distension , diarrhea, splenomegaly and characteristic rose spots on the abdomen due to vasculitis. The amount of pathogen required to cause an infection in the host is known as the infectious dose . The infectious doses of few bacteria are given below : • Escherichia coli - 106 – 108 organisms • Shigella - 10 – 100 organisms • Escherichia coli O157 :H7 - <10 organisms

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the incubation period of Salmonella typhi ?
mcqs.explanation: The incubation period for Salmonella typhi is from 5 to 21 days. The incubation period for Salmonella typhi typically averages 10 –14 days, but can range from 5 to 21 days. The duration is likely dependant on the inoculum size and the host's health and immune status .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man presented to the ER with fever, splenomegaly , and a rash as shown in the image below . After admission, he developed intestinal perforation and an exploratory laparotomy revealed several longitudinal ulcers in the small bowel . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Rose spots . The combination of this with fever, splenomegaly , presence of longitudinal ulcers in the intestine and intestinal perforation is suggestive of enteric fever. The term enteric fever includes typhoid fever caused by Salmonella typhi and paratyphoid fever caused by Salmonella paratyphi A, B and C. Enteric fever presents with step ladder pyrexia. The fever is accompanied by relative bradycardia which is known as the Faget sign. Hepatosplenomegaly is a common finding on examination. Rose spots that fade on pressure appear on the skin during the second or third week . Since bile is a good culture medium for the bacilli, they multiply abundantly in the gallbladder and are discharged continuously into the intestine . In the intestine , it causes inflammation and213 necrosis leaving behind the characteristic typhoid ulcers which are oriented along the axis of the intestine (longitudinal ulcers ). Ulceration of the bowel leads to two major complications - intestinal perforation and hemorrhage. Option B: In intestinal tuberculosis , ulcers are perpendicular to the axis of the intestine (transverse ulcers ). Option C: Flask shaped ulcers are characteristic of amoebiasis. Option D: Hemorrhagic colitis is caused by Shigella dysenteriae and some strains of E. coli. It is characterised by bloody diarrhea with tenesmus .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: While evaluating a patient suspected to have enteric fever, you order a widely used tube agglutination test in the second week of his illness . Which of the following statements regarding this test is false ?

options.a: H agglutinin titer > 160 and O agglutinin titer > 80 is considered significant
options.b: O antibody cannot differentiate between Salmonella types .
options.c: O antibody lasts longer and hence is not indicative of recent infection .
options.d: High titer value in a single test is not confirmative.

mcqs.explanation: The tube agglutination test which is widely used for the diagnosis of enteric fever is the Widal test . The O antibodies detected via this test disappear within a few weeks of disease resolution and so are indicative of recent infection . Widal test is a serological test for the measurement of O and H antigens of Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi present in the patient 's serum. Four antigens are used - O antigens of S. typhi (TO), H antigens of S. typhi (TH), H antigens of S. paratyphi A (AH) and H antigens of S. paratyphi B (BH). Paratyphoid O antigens cross-reacts with the typhoid O antigen due to the sharing of factor 12 . It is not used in the test and thus , O antibody cannot differentiate between Salmonella types . H agglutinin titer > 160 and O agglutinin titer > 80 is considered significant. However, a 4-fold rise in titers between 1st and 3rd week is more significant compared to a single high titer because of the possibility of an anamnestic reaction - a transient rise of titer due to unrelated infections (malaria , dengue ) in persons who had a prior enteric fever. After one week interval, if the titer increases, it indicates true infection . If the titer decreases , it indicates an anamnestic reaction.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young man with fever for 2 weeks has the following serology findings. Which of the given statements is true about the disease he has?

options.a: Intestinal perforation following infection with S.typhi occurs in the 1st week .
options.b: Faget 's sign is seen in enteric fever.
options.c: In Widal test , Felix tube is used to detect H antigen.
options.d: Blood culture is the gold standard of diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Widal results showing titers for O antibody >80 and H antibody for S.typhi to be >160 is suggestive of enteric fever. Faget 's sign is seen in enteric fever. Enteric fever, caused by Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi A, B and C , presents with step ladder pyrexia. The fever rises one day and falls the subsequent morning . It continues to form peaks and troughs . Hepatosplenomegaly is a common finding on examination. Rose spots that fade on pressure appear on the skin during the second or third week . Faget 's sign is the unusual pairing of fever with bradycardia (relative bradycardia) instead of tachycardia. It is also observed in yellow fever, brucellosis , and tularemia. Intestinal perforation (option A) is a complication of enteric fever caused by Salmonella typhi. It occurs in the 3rd week following infection . Widal test is a serological test used for the diagnosis of enteric fever during the 2nd week . It measures the levels of H and O antigens in the patient 's serum.214 Bone marrow culture is the gold standard (option D) for diagnosis of enteric fever. Blood culture is most commonly performed to confirm the diagnosis, however, bone marrow is more sensitive .H antigen O antigen Flagellar antigen Somatic antigen Fluffy /woolly agglutination se en Granular agglutination seen Appear late and persist for lo nger duration Appear early and persist for s horter duration Dreyer's tube (conical bottom) used Felix tube (round bottom) us ed

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient , suspected to have enteric fever, has been started on ceftriaxone by his local village healer 2 days ago. Which investigation will confirm his diagnosis at this stage ?
mcqs.explanation: Bone marrow culture is preferred at this stage . Bone marrow culture is the most sensitive test (>80% sensitivity ) for diagnosis of enteric fever. It remains positive for upto 5 days after starting antibiotics, unlike blood culture . Hence , it is preferred in the patient above who has been on antibiotics for 2 days. Blood culture has a sensitivity of about 60% for diagnosis of enteric fever. Its sensitivity drops with duration of illness , and is thus useful onlyduring the 1st week of enteric fever. It rapidly becomes negative on treatment with antibiotics. Stool culture has a sensitivity of 30% and only yields positive results from the 2nd or 3rd week onwards. Urine culture has low sensitivity and may be positive only after the 2nd week. Note : The sensitivity of diagnostic methods for enteric fever is duodenal content culture > bone marrow culture > blood culture . However, duodenal content culture is rarely done in clinical practice .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are administering a Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine to a child in Germany before his trip to India. Which of the following is false about the antigen used in this vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: Vi capsule polysaccharide antigen is a heat -labile antigen used in the Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (ViCPS ) for typhoid . Vi antigen is found in Salmonella typhi , S. paratyphi C and S. dublin. It is a capsular antigen and is a polysaccharide. It acts as a virulence factor by inhibiting phagocytosis and resisting complement activation and bacterial lysis . It envelopes the O antigen, and thus , many S. typhi strains fail to agglutinate with O antiserum. However, it can be destroyed by heat . It is alcohol stable . This antigen is poorly immunogenic. The Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine (Vi CPS) contains purified Vi polysaccharide . It is given as a single dose of 0.5ml intramuscularly to children over 2 years of age . It is recommended for travellers to areas endemic for Salmonella infections .215

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A man living in the UK is planning to travel to India. His doctor prescribes the necessary vaccines prior to travel including an oral typhoid vaccine. What is the schedule for this vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: The oral typhoid vaccine is given on days 1, 3, 5, and 7. Typhoral or Ty21a is a live attenuated oral typhoid vaccine. It is given in 4 doses given on days 1, 3, 5, and 7. No antibiotics should be given during this period . lt is indicated only in individuals over 6 years of age . Protective immunity starts after 7 days of the last dose and lasts for 4 years. Ty21a can also be administered to HIV -positive , asymptomatic individuals as long as their CD4 count is above 200 /mm3 . It is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is not used for typhoid fever in adults ?
mcqs.explanation: Amikacin is not used in the treatment of typhoid fever. Amikacin is an aminoglycoside . Despite showing efficient in vitro killing of Salmonella, first- and second -generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides have proven to be ineffective in actual clinical cases .Antibiotic therapy for enteric fever in adults Indication Agent Dosage (Route) Duration, D ays Empirical Treatment Ceftriaxone 2 g/d (IV) -14 Azithromycin 1 g/d (PO) Fully Susceptible Optimal treatment Ciprofloxacin 500 mg bid (PO) or 400 mg q12 h (IV ) 5-7 Azithromycin 1 g/d (PO) Alternative treatment Amoxicillin 1 g tid (PO) or 2 g q6h (IV ) Chloramphenicol 25 mg/kg tid (PO or IV ) 14-21 Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxaz ole /800 mg bid (PO) 7-14 Multidrug -resistant, fluroqui nolone-susceptible Optimal treatment Ceftriaxone 2 g/d (IV) -14 Azithromycin 1 g/d (PO) Alternative treatment Ciprofloxacin 500 mg bid (PO) or 400 mg q12h (IV ) 5-14 Quinolone -resistant Optimal treatment Ceftriaxone 2 g/d (IV) -14 Azithromycin 1 g/d (PO) Antibiotic therapy for enteric fever in adults Alternative treatment High dose ciprofloxaci n 750 mg bid (PO) or 400 mg q 12h (IV ) -14 Ceftriaxone -resistant Optimal treatment Meropenem 1 g q8h (IV ) -14 Azithromycin 1 g/d (PO) 5

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient developed fever and diarrhoea after consumption of undercooked eggs . Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

options.a: Gastroenteritis due to non-typhoidal salmonellosis is usually self limited .
options.b: Stool cultures remain positive for 4-5 weeks after infection .
options.c: Most common isolate from stool culture is Salmonella enteritidis .
options.d: Non-typhoidal salmonellosis can be acquired from multiple animal reservoirs.

mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of non-typhoidal salmonellosis (NTS). The most common organism isolated in NTS from stool culture is Salmonella typhimurium. Nontyphoidal salmonellosis refers to illnesses caused by all serotypes of Salmonella except for Salmonella typhi , Salmonella paratyphi A, B, and C. Transmission of nontyphoidal salmonellosis occurs usually through the consumption of food or water contaminated with animal feces . Transmission may also occur through food products , especially eggs , poultry , undercooked ground meat, and hence multiple animals act as reservoirs for non-typhoidal salmonella. Gastroenteritis is the most common clinical presentation of NTS. The illness usually lasts 4–7 days, and most people recover without treatment . Culturing organisms continues to be the mainstay of clinical diagnostic testing for nontyphoidal salmonella infection . Approximately 90% of isolates are obtained from routine stool culture until 4-5 weeks after infection .217

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A child presents with profuse , painless diarrhea. Stool microscopy shows the following finding. What is this characteristic appearance called ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae . The image shows the characteristic fish in stream appearance of Vibrio . Other options : Options A and B: School of fish appearance and railroad appearance are shown by Haemophilus ducreyi . Option D: Drumstick appearance is shown by Clostridium tetani due to its spherical and terminal spores .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: While studying the microscopic features of Vibrio cholerae , you observe the following finding. What type of motility can you see here?
mcqs.explanation: The given microscopic finding shows the darting motility characteristic of Vibrio cholerae . Vibrio cholerae is actively motile with a polar flagellum . The actively motile vibrios appear like a 'swarm of gnats'.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: On the basis of which antigen is Vibrio cholerae classified under the Sakazaki typing scheme ?
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholerae are classified based on O antigen, under Sakazaki typing scheme . Based on the presence or absence of O antigen, V . cholerae is classified as O1 which agglutinate with antisera to O1 group (agglutinable vibrios ) and non-O1, which do not agglutinate with antisera to O1 group (non-agglutinable vibrios ). As per the Gardner and Venkatraman classification , Vibrios are classified into Group A (V . cholerae ) and Group B (others) based on H antigen or flagellar antigen. Gardner and Venkatraman classification:228

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding non-agglutinable vibrios ?

options.a: They belong to serogroup O2 – O
options.c: They are not agglutinated by O-1 antiserum
options.d: These are similar to V . cholera in most cultural and biochemical reactions

mcqs.explanation: Non-agglutinable vibrios are non-pathogenic (except O139) and hence , they are called non-cholera vibrios. The vibrios which are not agglutinated by O-1 antiserum are called non-agglutinable (NAG) vibrios. They belong to the serogroups O2–O200 of which only serogroup O-139 is known to cause epidemics of cholera. They are similar to Vibrio cholerae in most biochemical reactions and culture characteristics, except that they are hemolytic to sheep erythrocytes and give a positive Voges-Proskauer reaction.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A microbiologist studying Vibrio cholera added sulphuric acid to a 24-hour peptone culture of the organism and a reddish -pink color developed . Which of the following is true about the test he performed ?

options.a: It is known as methyl red test
options.b: A nitrosoindole compound is formed giving it the red colour
options.c: The red colour is obtained due to pigment production by the bacteria
options.d: The red colour is obtained due to acid & gas production by Vibrio

mcqs.explanation: The test described here is the 'cholera red reaction' given by Vibrio cholera. When few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid are added to a 24-hour peptone water culture , a reddish -pink colour develops due to the formation of nitrosoindole . Vibrio cholerae reduce nitrates to nitrites and convert tryptophan to indole . These two properties contribute to the cholera red reaction.229 Other options : Option A: The methyl red (MR) test is used to detect the production of sufficient acid during the fermentation of glucose by bacteria. It is used to classify Enterobacteriacae . Option C: Vibrio cholera does not produce any colored pigment . Option D: Vibrio ferments carbohydrates leading to production of acid but no gas.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman presents with complaints of passing profuse loose stools which looked like rice water for the past 3 days. There's a history of similar symptoms in the family. Stool samples were sent to the lab for analysis and the test given in the image is performed . Identify this test .
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario of passing profuse rice-water stools with similar complaints in the family suggests a probable diagnosis of cholera. The test shown in the above image is the string test and it is performed to identify Vibrio cholerae . To perform the string test , a loopful of the bacterial culture is mixed with a drop of 0.5% sodium deoxycholate in saline on a slide . The bacterial cells of Vibrio cholerae are lysed by sodium deoxycholate , causing the suspension to lose its turbidity and become mucoid. A string is formed when the loop is drawn away from the suspension . Note : The duodenal string test refers to the Entero test performed for the diagnosis of giardiasis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bacteria is not microaerophilic?
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholera is a facultative anaerobe and is not microaerophilic.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The disruption of which of the following is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio ?
mcqs.explanation: 230 The disruption of zonula occludens is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae . Zonula occludens toxin (Zot) is an enterotoxin elaborated by Vibrio cholerae that increases intestinal permeability by interacting with a mammalian cell receptor with subsequent activation of intracellular signaling leading to the disassembly of the intercellular tight junctions. Mechanism of action of cholera toxin: • The cholera toxin molecule consists of 1 A and 5 B subunits . The B (binding) units attach to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on the surface of jejunal epithelial cells . The A (active) subunit , on being transported into the enterocyte, dissociates into A1 and A2 . A2 fragment only links biologically active A1 to the B subunit . • A1 causes prolonged activation of cellular adenylate cyclase and accumulation of cAMP, leading to outpouring into the small intestinal lumen, of large quantities of water and electrolytes . This leads to watery diarrhea which is isotonic with plasma but contains much more potassium and bicarbonate. • The toxin also inhibits the intestinal absorption of sodium and chloride . • All clinical manifestations and complications in cholera result from the massive water and electrolyte depletion thus caused .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young child was brought to the ER with a history of loose stools . On examination, she is tachycardic, appears lethargic and skin goes back slowly after the skin pinch test . She was admitted and started on IV fluids and input-output charting was done. The given image shows stool output from the patient . Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the toxin responsible for the same?

options.b: Toxin causes Increased guanyl cyclase activity
options.c: The toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of dehydration, profuse diarrhea, and rice water stools is suggestive of cholera. Cholera toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase . Mechanism of action of cholera toxin: • The cholera toxin molecule consists of 1 A and 5 B subunits . The B (binding) units attach to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on the surface of jejunal epithelial cells . The A (active) subunit , on being transported into the enterocyte, dissociates into A1 and A2 . A2 fragment only links biologically active A1 to the B subunit .231 • A1 causes prolonged activation of cellular adenylate cyclase and accumulation of cAMP, leading to outpouring into the small intestinal lumen, of large quantities of water and electrolytes and the consequent watery diarrhea, that is isotonic with plasma but contains much more of potassium and bicarbonate. • The toxin also inhibits the intestinal absorption of sodium and chloride . • All clinical manifestations and complications in cholera result from the massive water and electrolyte depletion thus caused .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not play a role in the virulence of Vibrio cholerae ?
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio cholerae possesses lipopolysaccharide (LPS) O antigen but it plays no role in the pathogenesis of cholera. It is responsible for the immunity induced by killed vaccines. Factors involved in virulence of Vibrio cholerae : • In the small intestine , vibrios can cross the protective layer of mucus and reach the epithelial cells by using mucinase and other proteolytic enzymes . • Toxin co-regulated pilus (TCP), is essential for the adhesion to the epithelial surface and colonization of the bacteria in small intestine . • Cholera toxin (also known as choleragen and cholera enterotoxin) causes watery diarrhea through cAMP-mediated pathway .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An El Tor vibrio was identified to be the causative agent of a diarrhea epidemic . Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of this organism?

options.a: Resistant to El Tor phage V
options.d: Not susceptible to group IV phage

mcqs.explanation: El Tor vibrios are susceptible to El Tor phage V.232

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are a medical officer at a district hospital and receive 13 patients with rice-water diarrhea and dehydration . You suspect cholera and want to send the stool samples to the hospital lab. Which of the following media will you not use ?
mcqs.explanation: Nutrient agar is not used to transport Vibrio cholerae . It is a simple media used to grow non-fastidious organisms, but not to transport them. Transport media for Vibrio cholerae : • Venkatraman -Ramakrishnan (VR ) medium • Cary-Blair medium If the specimen can reach the laboratory in a few hours, it may also be transported in enrichment media. Examples include : • Alkaline peptone water • Monsur's medium. If transport media are not available, strips of blotting paper may be soaked in the watery stool and sent to the laboratory packed in plastic envelopes .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bacteria shows Kanagawa phenomenon ?
mcqs.explanation: Kanagawa phenomenon is shown by Vibrio parahaemolyticus . It refers to hemolysis occuring when the bacteria are inoculated on Wagatsuma agar. Pathogenic strains of V . parahaemolyticus are hemolytic , while non-pathogenic strains are non-hemolytic . This phenomenon occurs due to a heat -stable hemolysin .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An outbreak of food poisoning in a coastal city is determined to be due to contaminated seafood . The causative bacteria formed the following colonies on TCBS agar and showed hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar. Which of the following statements regarding the organism implicated here is false ?

options.c: It produces peritrichous flagella on solid medium
options.d: It gives a positive string test

mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario of an organism that caused food poisoning due to contaminated seafood in addition to the cultural characteristics is suggestive of food contamination by Vibrio parahaemolyticus . It is a capsulated organism. V . parahaemolyticus is an enteropathogenic halophilic vibrio that is an important cause of food poisoning throughout the world. It inhabits the coastal seas , where it is found in shrimps, crabs, and oysters . It forms opaque green colonies with a raised centre and flat translucent periphery on TCBS agar unlike V . cholera which forms yellow colonies . Pathogenic strains show hemolysis on Wagatsuma agar which is known as Kanagawa phenomenon . This can be used as a test for pathogenecity . Other options : Option B: It shows bipolar staining and has a tendency for pleomorphism , especially when grown on 3% salt agar. Option C: Unlike other vibrios , it produces peritrichous flagella when grown on solid media. Polar flagella are formed in liquid cultures . Option D: String test is positive like with V. cholera.233

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following vibrios has the highest salt tolerance ?
mcqs.explanation: Vibrio with the highest salt tolerance of up to 10 % NaCl is Vibrio alginolyticus . The salt tolerances of vibrio species are as follows : • V . cholerae optimally grows at 0.5–1% NaCl concentration. Its growth is inhibited by high concentration of >6% NaCl. • V . mimicus grows best at low salt concentrations of 0.5-1% like V . cholerae . • V . parahaemolyticus grows optimally salt concentration of 2-4 %. It has a salt tolerance up to 8%. • V . vulnificus has a salt tolerance similar to V . parahaemolyticus . • V . alginolyticus has the highest salt tolerance of up to 10 % NaCl.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A fisherman presented to the ER with a wound on his left leg . He tells you he had got a small cut a week back that got worse after his recent fishing trip. On examination, you note vesicles and bullae around the wound . Specimen taken from the bullae revealed lactose -fermenting colonies . What is the causative agent ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario of contact with seawater of an existing wound leading to cellulitis by a lactose -fermenting bacteria suggests infection with Vibrio vulnificus. V . vulnificus ferments lactose but not sucrose . It has a salt tolerance of up to 8%. Infection with V . vulnificus can manifest in 2 ways: • Soft-tissue infections can occur after contact with seawater and progress to cellulitis . • Primary septicemia can occur in patients, typically with underlying liver disease , who have acquired the organism through the gastrointestinal tract after recent consumption of raw shellfish . Note : V . cholerae , V . parahaemolyticus, and V. alginolyticus do not ferment lactose although lactose may be split very slowly by V. cholerae .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are correctly matched except :

options.b: Vibrio alginolyticus - Infections of the eyes , ears and wounds

mcqs.explanation: Vibrio vulnificus causes wound infection following contact of open wounds with sea water. In immunocompromised hosts , and particularly those with liver disease , it penetrates the gut mucosa following ingestion . It may not cause any gastrointestinal manifestations and directly enters the bloodstream , leading to the rapid development of septicemia with high mortality. Other options : Option A: V. parahaemolyticus causes food poisoning associated with marine food. It also causes acute diarrhea, unassociated with food poisoning. Option B: V. alginolyticus has been associated with infections of the eyes , ears, and wounds in human beings exposed to seawater .234 Option D: Cholera is caused by V . cholerae via its toxin but it does not cause dysentery which is characterized by bloody diarrhea. It is mainly associated with watery diarrhea.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 17-year-old presents to you with complaints of passing loose stools . Given below are the findings of his stool microscopy. Infection with which of the following bacteria would you consider in your differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clip shows darting motility which is seen in Vibrio cholerae and Campylobacter jejuni. Thus, among the given options, infection with C. jejuni should be considered as a differential diagnosis in this case. Campylobacter jejuni possesses a single polar flagellum , hence it exhibits darting motility . Shigella dysenteriae is a non-motile organism.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young man presented with complaints of a tingling sensation in his hands and feet . He also complains of weakness in his legs that is slowly spreading to his upper body. He had an episode of bloody diarrhea 10 days ago. Which of the following organisms is the likely cause of this patient 's condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario with ascending paralysis is suggestive of the development Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome (GBS) following diarrhea. The organism that likely caused this patients condition is Campylobacter jejuni, which can cause diarrhea and trigger GBS. Campylobacter is a slender , spirally curved, gram-negative bacillus . Growth occurs under microaerophilic conditions. The organism also shows darting motility . Asymptomatic campylobacter infection also may trigger Guillain-Barr \351 syndrome.Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute , fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy that is autoimmune in nature. In C. jejuni infection , bacterial lipopolysaccharide triggers an autoimmune response against axons via molecular mimicry, hence causing GBS. Other organisms associated with GBS include cytomegalovirus , M. pneumonia, and Epstein -Barr virus.235

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young man presented with bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and fever. Lab investigations showed leucocytosis and stool microscopy revealed RBCs and leucocytes . Darkfield microscopy showed a bacteria having darting motility . Which of the following is a selective culture medium for this organism?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of fever, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain and leucocytosis alongwith microscopy findings of RBCs and WBCs in fecal smear, and organism having darting motility are suggestive of infection with Campylobacter jejuni. The selective culture medium used for Campylobacter is Skirrow 's media. Other selective media for Campylobacter include : • Butzler's medium • Campy-BAP media The transport medium used for Campylobacter is the Cary-Blair medium.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Identify the organism & the stain seen in the image given below .
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Helicobacter pylori stained using Warthin -Starry stain. H.pylori is a Gram-negative spiral rod that is motile by a unipolar tuft of lophotrichous flagella . The bacteria are present only in the mucus overlying the gastric mucosa and do not actually invade into the mucosa. The given image shows Helicobacter pylori on gastric mucosa stained with Warthin -Starry silver stain.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms produce urease ?
mcqs.explanation: Helicobacter pylori produces urease . Urease -producing organisms: (Mnemonic-PUNCH) • Proteus236 • Ureaplasma urealyticum • Nocardia • Cryptococcus , Corynebacterium urealyticum • H. pylori

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are a surgery resident evaluating a 45-year-old female patient with complaints of burning abdominal pain for the past 2 months that is relieved on taking food. You determine the disease to have a bacterial etiology . Which of the following is the most sensitive test to detect the causative organism here?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is suggestive of a duodenal ulcer caused by Helicobacter pylori. The urea breath test is the most sensitive test for the diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori infection . To perform this test , the patient drinks a urea solution labelled with radioactive carbon-14. The patient then blows into a tube . If H. pylori urease is present , the urea is hydrolyzed , and labelled carbon dioxide is detected in breath samples . The sensitivity of the urea breath test is >90%.237

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 20 year old male presents with acute onset cough and thick sticky sputum . There is a history of repeated lung infections since childhood . Chest Xray shows evidence of bilateral upper lobe bronchiectasis . On evaluation, the chloride concentration in his sweat is >60 mEq/L. What is the organism majorly associated with this patient 's respiratory disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Bilateral upper lobe bronchiectasis with a history of repeated lung infections since childhood and evelated sweat chloride concentration suggests a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF). Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common etiological agent associated with chronic airway infection in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF).242 In cystic fibrosis, there is thick inspissated mucus and impaired mucociliary clearance. Due to these factors, lungs are often colonized in infancy and early childhood with Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae . In adulthood , they are replaced by P. aeruginosa. This results in chronic inflammation, which leads to airway modelling and bronchiectasis . Note : Burkholderia cepacia complex is an opportunistic environmental pathogen . It causes fatal respiratory distress and septicemia in CF patients . This is termed as 'cepacia syndrome'.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms causes scombroid fish poisoning?
mcqs.explanation: Scombroid fish poisoning is associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It follows the consumption of both scombroid (mackerel-like) fish and nonscombroid fish that have not been refrigerated properly . The musculature of these dark - or red-fleshed fish undergoes decomposition by Morganella morganii, Escherichia coli, Proteus species , Klebsiella species , and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. There is consequent decarboxylation of the amino acid L-histidine to form histamine. A second compound is thought to play a causative role in this intoxication because large doses of oral histamine do not reproduce the affliction . The toxin or toxins involved are heat stable and are not destroyed by cooking or freezing . Symptoms develop within 15–90 min of ingestion . Most cases are mild, with tingling of lips and mouth , mild abdominal discomfort, and nausea. The more severe and commonly described presentation includes flushing , conjunctival hyperemia , pruritus, urticaria, and angioedema . Without treatment , the symptoms generally resolve within 8–12 h.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient comes to the dermatology OPD complaining of greenish discoloration of her nails. You diagnose her with green nail syndrome. Production of which of the following helps differentiate the organism implicated here from other members of its genus ?
mcqs.explanation: Green nail syndrome is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Production of pyocyanin helps differentiate it implicated here from other Pseudomonas species . Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the only member of the Pseudomonas species that produces pyocyanin which is a bluish-green pigment . Other species of Pseudomonas also produce pigments but they cannot produce pyocyanin. Some of the other pigments produced by Pseudomonas species including P. aeruginosa are pyoverdin/flourescein (greenish -yellow pigment ), pyorubin (red pigment ) and pyomelanin (brown pigment ).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The mechanism of action of exotoxin A of Pseudomonas resembles that of _________.
mcqs.explanation: The action of exotoxin A of Pseudomonas aeruginosa is similar to that of the diphtheria toxin. Both exotoxin A and diphtheria toxin cause ADP ribosylation of EF-2 and inhibit protein synthesis . Exotoxin A is a single - chain polypeptide with A and B fragments. The B fragment binds the toxin while the A fragment inactivates EF-2 in the presence of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD). This leads to the inhibition of polypeptide chain elongation and thus , protein243 synthesis .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient with acute onset fever, cough and hemoptysis is diagnosed to have Whitmore's disease . Which of the following organisms causes this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Burkholderia pseudomallei causes Whitmore's disease . Melioidosis was first described by Whitmore and Krishnaswami. Whitmore isolated the bacillus , and hence , it is known as Whitmore bacillus and melioidosis is called Whitmore's disease . Melioidosis is similar in presentation to glanders disease (caused by Burkholderia mallei). Humans are infected tby contact with contaminated soil via skin abrasions. Types of melioidosis : • Acute - It causes acute pneumonia with upper lobe infiltrates or severe necrotizing disease . It can also mimic tuberculosis with fever, cough , hemoptysis . It may lead to septicemia . • Chronic - It can lead to the development of multiple caseous or suppurative foci, with skin and subcutaneous abscesses . These can lead to lymphangitis and lymphadenopathy . It may involve bones and other internal organs. The bacillus has a safety -pin appearance on methylene blue staining. Treatment is divided into two stages : an intensive 2 week phase of ceftazidime or a carbapenem followed by at least 12 weeks of oral cotrimoxazole to eradicate the organism and prevent relapse .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A horse-groomer was diagnosed with ulcerative tracheobronchitis. Upon enquiry, it was discovered that one of his horses had recently died of pneumonia after developing a fever and subcutaneous nodules . Which of the following statements is false about the likely causative agent?

options.c: It is the causative agent for Glanders disease .
options.d: It induces Strauss reaction on inoculation into guinea pigs .

mcqs.explanation: The development of ulcerative tracheobronchitis after contact with an infected horse is suggestive of glanders which is caused by Burkholderia mallei. It is an oxidase variable organism. In this case, the horse likely had glanders , which presents with fever, pneumonia, and subcutaneous nodules called Farcy buds. Discharges from the respiratory tract and skin are highly infectious and can be transmitted to humans through close contact (occupational route). The244 horse-groomer likely contracted the infection by the inhalational route and developed acute glanders, which is characterised by fever, mucopurulent nasal discharge and ulcerative necrosis of upper respiratory tract (ulcerative tracheobronchitis). It may lead to septicemia and has a high fatality rate. Percutaneous exposure causes local suppurative skin lesions with associated regional lymphadenopathy . B. mallei is a non-motile Gram-negative bacillus causing Glanders disease . It is an aerobe and a facultative anaerobe. It is oxidase variable i.e. it is usually oxidase negative but may occasionally show a positive reaction. It is a biosafety level 3 pathogen and so must be handled only in specialised laboratories. When male guinea pigs are inoculated intraperitoneally with suspected infectious material, it causes Strauss reaction. B. mallei sets up a necrotizing inflammation in the scrotal sac within a few days and can be confirmed bacteriologically .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is Burkholderia cepacia resistant to?
mcqs.explanation: Burkholderia cepacia is resistant to cefotetan . B. cepacia complex strains are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides , polymixin, first and second -generation cephalosporins (e.g. cefotetan ) and carboxypenicillins . This antimicrobial resistance is mediated by efflux pumps, antimicrobial degradation , modifying enzymes or altered membrane functions. B. cepacia is a Gram-negative bacillus which can cause severe necrotizing pneumonia in patients with chronic granulomatous disease . It can lead to fatal septicemia in patients with cystic fibrosis. Antimicrobial agents that are effective against B. cepacia complex include meropenem , ceftazidime , trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, piperacillin and temocillin .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An organism cultured in Bordet–Gengou medium shows smooth, refractile , glistening colonies resembling 'bisected pearls' or 'mercury drops'. The organism is most likely ______.
mcqs.explanation: The organism showing colonies resembling 'bisected pearls' or 'mercury drops' on Bordet-Gengou medium most likely is Bordetella pertussis . Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative coccobacillus . It causes whooping cough or pertussis in children. It can be isolated on the enriched medium Bordet-Genou medium (potato -blood-glycerol agar). After incubation for 48 to 72 hours, B. pertussis colonies are small, dome-shaped , smooth, opaque, viscid, greyish white , refractile , and glistening resembling 'bisected pearls' or 'mercury drops' and are surrounded by a hazy zone of hemolysis . If growth is confluent , an 'aluminium paint' appearance is seen . In culture films , Bordetella pertussis bacilli tend to be arranged in loose clumps , with clear spaces in between , giving a 'thumbprint' appearance . B. parapertussis (option A) grows on nutrient agar with the production of a brown, diffusible pigment after two days. It also grows more rapidly than B.pertussis on charcoal blood agar.245

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy with incomplete vaccination history comes with vomiting after bouts of severe, violent cough . What is the mechanism of action of the toxin responsible for this child's disease ?

options.a: Activation of phospholipase and degrades cell membrane

mcqs.explanation: Post-tussive vomiting and bouts of cough in an unimmunized child points to a diagnosis of pertussis , caused by Bordetella pertussis . It secretes pertussis toxin (PT), which acts by ADP ribosylation and disrupts signal transduction of many cell types . This promotes lymphocytosis . The pertussis toxin disrupts protein synthesis and causes necrosis of parts of the epithelium , leading to pseudomembrane formation. Pertussis toxin also promotes sensitization to histamine and enhances insulin secretion but these effects have not been demonstrable in patients . They are only seen in experimental animals. B. pertussis also produces other toxins like: • Adenylate cyclase toxin (ACT)- It acts by catalysing the production of cAMP by various types of cells and inhibiting phagocytosis . • Heat labile toxin (HLT )- It is a cytoplasmic protein present in all bordetellae . It is dermonecrotic and lethal in mice. Its pathogenic role is not known. • Tracheal cytotoxin (TCT)- It is low molecular weight peptidoglycan which induces ciliary damage in hamster trachea.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about pertussis toxin?

options.a: It is expressed on the surface of the bacillus .
options.c: "A" portion of A-B structure is the enzymatically active moiety .
options.d: It is similar to cholera toxin in its structure and function.

mcqs.explanation: Pertussis toxin (PT) can be toxoided . PT is one of the toxins produced by Bordetella pertussis . It is expressed on the surface of the bacillus and secreted into the surrounding medium. It has an A-B structure , the A portion being the enzymatically active moiety and B, the binding component . PT is similar to cholera toxin in its structure and function. PT has ADP-ribosylating activity and acts on inhibitory Gi �o subunit of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR), whereas cholera toxin acts on stimulatory Gs �o subunit of246 GPCR. Pertussis toxoid is the major component of the acellular pertussis vaccine. A toxoid is a toxin that has lost its toxicity but retains its antigenicity .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old unimmunized child presents with whooping cough . Which of the following constituents of the causative organism is responsible for facilitating its adhesion to the respiratory epithelium ?
mcqs.explanation: Whooping cough is caused by Bordetella pertussis . Filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) is responsible for facilitating the adhesion of Bordetella pertussis to the respiratory epithelium . Bordetella pertussis produces 3 hemagglutinins : Pertussis toxin (PT ), lipid factor and FHA. FHA is a surface protein and is readily shed . Along with fimbrae, it helps in the adhesion of B. pertussis to the cilia of the respiratory epithelium and to erythrocytes . FHA and PT also promote secondary infection by coating other bacteria such as Haemophilus influenzae and Pneumococci. They then assists their binding to respiratory epithelium. This phenomenon has been termed 'piracy of adhesins '.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the incubation period of pertussis in humans?
mcqs.explanation: The incubation period of pertussis in humans is 7-14 days. Pertussis is caused by Bordetella pertussis. After the incubation period , the disease takes a protracted course comprising three stages : • Catarrhal: It lasts 1-2 weeks and is characterized by coryza, lacrimation, mild cough , low-grade fever, and malaise. • Paroxysmal: It lasts 2-4 weeks with the cough becoming more frequent and spasmodic . The cough comes in repetitive bursts of 5–10 in number, often within a single expiration. Post-tussive vomiting is frequent. The episode may be terminated by an audible whoop , which occurs upon rapid inspiration against a closed glottis at the end of a paroxysm. • Convalescent : It lasts 1–3 months and is characterized by gradual resolution of coughing episodes . Whooping cough is also known as '100-day cough '. For 6–12 months following the illness , intercurrent viral infections may be associated with a recrudescence of paroxysmal cough .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a 6-year-old unimmunised girl with cough and abdominal pain. Her mother informs you that her daughter has bouts of violent coughing which frequently ends with a loud whoop and is accompanied by vomiting. She gives history of similar complaints in a classmate 2-3 weeks back. Which of the following drugs will you prescribe for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario of whooping cough , post -tussive vomiting, and abdominal pain, along with positive history of exposure in an unimmunised child is suggestive of pertussis . Erythromycin or one of the newer macrolides such as azithromycin or clarithromycin is the drug of choice for the treatment of this condition. Antibiotic therapy in pertussis is used to eradicate the bacteria from the nasopharynx . The treatment is beneficial if it is started within 10 days of the disease . Macrolides are the drugs of247 choice . Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Cotrimoxazole) is recommended as an alternative for individuals allergic to macrolides. Macrolides may also be used in the chemoprophylaxis of pertussis . Post-exposure prophylaxis is given to household close contacts , and high-risk contacts (infants, immunocompromised, pregnancy).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young child with unknown immunization history is suspected to have whooping cough . Which of the following methods will you prefer to use to collect a specimen for culture ?
mcqs.explanation: Whooping cough is caused by Bordotella pertussis . The most effective method for collecting a specimen for the culture of this organism is the per-nasal or nasopharyngeal swab method . Respiratory specimens may be collected for the culture (gold standard) of Bordetella pertussis by three different methods : • Per-nasal swab: A Dacron or rayon tipped swab on a flexible nichrome wire is passed along the floor of the nasal cavity and material is collected from the pharyngeal wall. This specimen is the most effective and best suited for diagnostic procedures . • Cough plate method : A culture plate is held about 10 to 15 cms in front of the patient 's mouth during a bout of cough . • Post-nasal (peroral) method : Secretions from the posterior pharyngeal wall are collected with a cotton swab on a bent wire passed through the mouth. Other diagnostic tests for pertussis include direct fluorescent aantibody test and PCR on nasopharyngeal specimens . Enzyme immunoassays of antibodies after exposure to B. pertussis can also be used for patients between 2-4 weeks of illness .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A pregnant woman comes to the ANC clinic for her 2nd dose of the Tdap vaccine. Which of the following constitutes the acellular component of this vaccine?

options.d: Pertussis toxoid, filamentous hemaglutinin , and fimbrial protein

mcqs.explanation: Tdap vaccine is the tetanus , diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine. The component of the acellular pertussis vaccine is inactivated pertussis toxin (PT) and it may contain one or more bacterial components such as pertactin , filamentous hemagglutinin , and fimbrial protein. Pertussis vaccine is usually administered in combination with the toxoids of diphtheria and tetanus (DTaP ). Five doses of pertussis vaccine are recommended - at 2, 4, 6 and 15–18 months of age followed by a booster dose at 4–6 years of age . Tdap is now also recommended for pregnant women in between 27 weeks and 36 weeks of gestation by the ACOG. This is because infants between the age of 0-2 months are vulnerable to pertussis as they do not begin their vaccine schedule before 6 weeks of age . Thus to protect these infants , placental transfer of maternal pertussis antibodies has proven to be the most effective approach. Children under 4 years who are contacts of patients should receive a booster even if they had been previously immunized. Non-immunized contacts should receive full series of vaccination and also chemoprophylaxis with erythromycin for 10 days after contact with the patient has ceased .248

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A woman presents with fever with chills and a productive cough . Chest X-ray is suggestive of lobar pneumonia. She had undergone splenectomy 2 years back. Sputum culture on blood agar shows the following . What is the causative agent ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario of bacterial pneumonia in a splenectomised individual along with the image showing satellitism on blood agar points towards an infection due to Hemophilus influenzae . Pneumonia can occur as a part of overwhelming post -splenectomy infection (OPSI). This is a fatal post-splenectomy complication occuring due to infections with encapsulated organisms such as S. pneumoniae , H. influenzae , and N. meningitidis . It can be prevented by vaccinating against these organisms within 2 weeks of undergoing splenectomy . Satellitism is seen when S. aureus is streaked across a plate of blood agar on which H. influenzae has been inoculated . After overnight incubation, the colonies of H. influenzae will be large and well developed alongside the streak of Staphylococcus and smaller when they are farther away from the streak. This is due to the release of factor V by lysis of RBCs mediated by S. aureus. Factor V is required for the growth of H. influenzae . The given image shows satellitism on blood agar254

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with fever, seizures , and altered sensorium. Gram stain of the CSF is given below . Satellitism was seen on blood agar. Which of the following statements is false about this disease ?

options.a: This is the most serious disease produced by this organism.
options.b: The disease is more common in young adults .
options.c: The bacilli reach the meninges from the nasopharynx through the bloodstream .
options.d: Cefotaxime is the drug of choice

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and the image showing gram-negative coccobacilli in the CSF are suggestive of hemophilus meningitis caused by H.influenzae . Hemophilus meningitis is more common in children between 3 months and 3 years of age and not common in young adults . Other options: Option A: Meningitis is the most serious disease caused by H. influenzae . The case fatality rate is 90% if untreated . Option C: H. influenze is transmitted via respiratory droplets . Thus, it is introduced into the nasopharynx of the contacts of an infected individual. It has to enter the bloodstream to reach the meninges .
