All neonates born to mothers who have reactive nontreponemal and treponemal test results should be evaluated with a quantitative nontreponemal serologic test (RPR or VDRL ) performed329 on the neonate 's serum, because umbilical cord blood can become contaminated with maternal blood and yield a false -positive result . FTA-ABS or TPHA is used for confirmation of syphilis in a patient with reactive RPR or VDRL test . T. pallidum cannot be detected by culture .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the causative agent of yaws ?
mcqs.explanation: Causative agent of yaws is Treponema pertenue . It is one of the endemic treponematoses that spreads by direct contact. The image shows ulcerative skin lesions seen in yaws.Causative age nt Disease T. pertenue Yaws T. pallidum Venereal syphili s T. carateum Pinta T. endemicu m Endemic syphili s

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the causative organism and the corresponding vector for epidemic relapsing fever?
mcqs.explanation: Epidemic relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia recurrentis and is transmitted by louse .330 Endemic relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia duttoni , Borrelia hermsii, Borrelia parkeri, etc , and is transmitted by ticks.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: During a louse outbreak among jail inmates, a few of them developed fevers that subsided after 3-5 days. The fever relapsed after a week and subsided again. Many patients had tender splenomegaly on examination. Which culture medium is used to isolate the organism implicated here?

options.d: Mannitol, egg -yolk, phenol red, polymyxin agar

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of louse -born relapsing fever (LBRF ) caused by Borrelia recurrentis . Barbour -Stoenner-Kelly broth medium is used to isolate all Borrelia species except for B.miyaotoi. Tender splenomegaly and relapsing fever in the background of a louse outbreak point towards the diagnosis of LBRF . It was very common during wars and in the jails of former days but with improvements in hygiene and the discovery of insecticides , it has now become rare.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which one of the following micro-organisms uses antigenic variation as a major means of evading the host immune system ?
mcqs.explanation: Borrelia recurrentis uses antigenic variation as a major means of evading the host immune system . It causes relapsing fever. Borrelia readily undergoes antigenic variations in vivo and this is believed to be the reason for the occurrence of relapses in the disease . Antigenic variations occur because of DNA rearrangements in linear plasmids present in borrelia.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 23 year old presented with fever, myalgia, and skin lesion as shown in the image. What is the causative organism for the above condition?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows erythema migrans, seen in Lyme disease . It is caused by Borrelia Burgdoferi. The lesion has a target center with partial central clearing and a bright red outer border. It usually begins as a red macule or papule at the site of the tick bite . The tick implicated is the black-legged tick, Ixodes scapularis, shown in the image below .331 The most severe manifestation of Lyme disease is Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), reported in 10–15% of individuals with localized erythema migrans. The activation of the inflammatory response in LNB contributes to the pathogenesis of a broad spectrum of neurologic disorders.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Following a flood , there is an outbreak of fever. Water samples from various sources are being studied for pathogens . The bacteria shown in the given image was isolated as a potential cause of disease . Which of the following animals is the most important reservoir of these organisms?
mcqs.explanation: The electron micrograph shows the spirochete , Leptospira interrogans, which causes the water-borne disease , leptospirosis . Rats are the most important reservoir. Transmission of leptospires may follow direct contact with urine, blood, or tissue from an infected animal or exposure to environmental contamination.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A farmer who works in paddy fields presented with fever, intense myalgia, and hematochezia . Lab investigations showed sharply elevated creatinine levels and high liver enzymes . What is the causative organism?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of Weil's disease which is caused by leptospira . Long hours of working in a field with water (paddy field ), is a high-risk factor for the development of leptospirosis . Weil's syndrome is the severe form of leptospirosis that encompasses the triad of hemorrhage, jaundice , and acute kidney injury. The treatment of choice is IV penicillin or IV ceftriaxone .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: At a relief camp in Karnataka , a few people developed fever, myalgia, and conjunctival suffusion . Rapid diagnostic IgM ELISA tests performed in the field showed leptospirosis. Which of the following culture media can be used to confirm this diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Ellinghausen , McCullough , Johnson, Harris (EMJH) media is the culture medium used for leptospira .332 Other culture media that can be used are Korthof 's, Stuart's, and Fletcher 's media. The image below shows EMJH medium, with Dinger's ring/zone. The growth of the leptospires is at a maximum density at this zone. It is identified as an area of increased turbidity , beneath the surface of the semi-solid medium. It is the zone of optimum oxygen tension for the growth of the bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy is admitted with fever, icterus , conjunctival suffusion , and hematuria for 15 days. Which serological test should be done for diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: History of fever with liver and kidney involvement should arouse suspicion for leptospirosis (Weil's disease). A microscopic agglutination test is used for the diagnosis of leptospirosis . Serotype -specific tests : • Microscopic agglutination test • Macroscopic agglutination test Option A: Widal test is used to screen for typhoid fever Option C: Weil-Felix reaction is used to diagnose rickettsial fevers Option D: Paul-Bunnell test is the investigation of choice for infectious mononucleosis .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presents with right upper quadrant pain, calf pain, conjunctival suffusion , icterus , and fever. Examination shows tender hepatomegaly . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette is leptospirosis . Leptospirosis is a zoonosis caused by spirochetes of the genus Leptospira. Patients with mild disease may present with flu-like symptoms of sudden onset , fever with chills, headache , abdominal pain, conjunctival suffusion , and myalgia. The muscle pain usually affects the calves, abdomen, and back. Mild cases can be treated with oral doxycycline , ampicillin, or amoxicillin.333 Severe leptospirosis is rapidly progressive and is associated with high fatality . The classic presentation of the severe disease called Weil's syndrome includes the triad of hemorrhage, jaundice , and acute kidney injury. Jaundice when present can be profound and physical examination may reveal an enlarged , tender liver. Temperature -pulse dissociation /relative bradycardia can be seen . Moderate to severe cases are treated with intravenous penicillin , ampicillin, or ceftriaxone . The image below shows icterus and conjunctival suffusion in a patient with leptospirosis .Leptospira are actively motile organisms and are best seen using a dark -field microscope . They are thin, tightly coiled , and flexible spirochetes with one end forming a hook. Diagnosis is by microscopic agglutination test . Transmission occurs through cuts or breaks in the skin and mucous membranes (conjunctival and oral mucosa). Several outbreaks have been reported that resulted from exposure to floodwaters contaminated by urine from infected animals. The organism enters the bloodstream and lodges in the parenchymatous organs (liver and kidneys) leading to hemorrhage and necrosis of the tissue334 causing dysfunction of the organs. The lifecycle of Leptospira is shown below .Illness is classically biphasic after an incubation period of up to 1 month. The stages are: • Acute leptospiremic phase - the organism can be cultured from blood. • Resolving immune phase - the organism can be cultured from urine. The stages may not be clinically distinguishable . Other options : Option A - Chikungunya is a viral disease that presents with saddle -back fever, conjunctival suffusion , and photophobia . Migratory arthralgia, especially involving small joints may also be seen . A maculopapular or petechial rash is frequently seen on the trunk. Option C - Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a form of severe dengue with bleeding manifestations . Evidence of plasma leakage and thrombocytopenia is also generally seen . Option D - Encephalitis due to Hepatitis A is seen in fulminant hepatitis , a rare complication. Patients present with confusion, disorientation, ascites , and edema .335

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the protein coat covering the nucleic acid in a virion known as?
mcqs.explanation: The protein coat covering the nucleic acid in a virion is called capsid . The parts of a virus include : • Nucleocapsid - capsid with enclosed nucleic acid • Tegument - proteinaceous structure present between the envelope and capsid . • Envelope - lipid -containing membrane that surrounds some virus particles . It is acquired during viral maturation by a budding process through a cellular membrane. • Peplomers - virus-encoded glycoproteins , on the outer surface of the envelope as projections .Characteristics of viruses: • Do not have a cellular organization • Have either DNA or RNA but never both • Obligate intracellular parasites • Lack enzymes necessary for protein and nucleic acid synthesis • Filterable • Cannot be grown on artificial media • Unaffected by antibiotics. Note : Martinus beijerinck proposed the theory of contagium vivum fluidum (living infectious fluid ) while studying the cause of mosaic disease of tobacco plant. He is known as the father of virology.342

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses has a single -stranded DNA?
mcqs.explanation: Parvovirus has single -stranded DNA. All DNA viruses are double -stranded , except parvovirus . (only single -stranded DNA virus) All RNA viruses have only one copy of single -stranded RNA except : • Reovirus- double -stranded RNA virus. • Retroviruses- Two copies of single -stranded RNA. Parvovirus is the smallest DNA virus that infect human beings .DNA RNA Largest virus Poxviru s Filovirus Smallest vir us Parvovir us Picornavir us

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding enveloped viruses?
mcqs.explanation: The lipid of enveloped viruses is largely of host-cell origin, whereas protein is virus coded . The following are the differences between enveloped and non-enveloped viruses.Enveloped viruses Non-enveloped viruses Ether sensitive Ether resistant Heat labile Heat stable Pleomorphic Non-pleomorphic Susceptible to bile salts Resistant to bile salts

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an enveloped virus?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis C virus is an enveloped virus. It has a linear, single -stranded RNA genome , enclosed within a core and surrounded by an envelope .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient in the ICU requires fresh frozen plasma (FFP). The FFP that arrives from the blood bank is labeled as Solvent/Detergent plasma, which destroys lipid -enveloped viruses. Which of the following viral infections is the patient still susceptible to?
mcqs.explanation: The patient is still susceptible to hepatitis A infection . It is a non-enveloped virus, and hence it's not affected by SD plasma.343 Solvent/Detergent plasma (SD plasma) is a form of blood plasma made from plasma collected from many people which is then processed with solvents in an attempt to remove viruses. Only the viruses with an envelope are susceptible to SD plasma destruction . Hepatitis B, C, and Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ) are enveloped .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following viruses is a segmented genome found?
mcqs.explanation: Segmented genome is found in orthomyxovirus. Segmentation of viral genomes allows for the exchange of intact genes between related viruses during coinfection . This recombination is known as reassortment. There is a rearrangement and joining of nucleic acid sequences to form a unique chimeric genome . The new genome is usually less fit than the parent viruses, but occasionally, it results in an evolved virus with increased fitness . Examples of segmented viruses (ARBO): • Arenavirus (2 segments ) • Rotavirus (11 segments ) • Bunyavirus (3 segments ) • Orthomyxovirus (8 segments ) The image below shows the segmented genome seen in the influenza virus (Orthomyxoviridae)

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old with HIV is brought with complaints of the rash shown below . Where does DNA replication occur in the viruses falling in the same family as the microbe causing this rash?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows pink, fleshy umbilicated papules suggesting molluscum contagiosum . It is caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus belonging to Poxviridae. DNA replication in these viruses occurs in the host cytoplasm .344 DNA viruses RNA viruses Replicati on Nucleus Cytoplasm Exceptio n Poxvirus - cytoplas m Orthomyxovirus, retrovirus- nucleus

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An epidemic involving an ss-RNA virus with 3'-5' RNA has broken out in West Africa. Which of the following enzymes do such viruses use in genome replication?
mcqs.explanation: An ss-RNA with a 3'-5' strand is a negative -stranded RNA. These viruses use RNA replicase or RNA-dependent RNA polymerase during genome replication. In positive -stranded RNA viruses, the viral RNA itself acts as mRNA. In negative -stranded RNA viruses, the polarity is opposite that of mRNA. So the genome requires RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to synthesize their mRNA. Examples of negative -stranded RNA viruses (Mnemonic: Always bring da polymerase or fail to replicate ): • Arenaviruses • Bunyaviruses • Deltaviruses • Paramyxoviruses • Orthomyxoviruses • Filoviruses • Rhabdoviruses

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The virus shown below was suspected to be the cause of a deadly hemorrhagic fever outbreak in Guinea in March 2021 . How is it transmitted ?

options.a: Direct contact with infected body fluids

mcqs.explanation: The image shown above is the Ebola virus. It is spread by direct contact with infected body fluids . Ebola is a filamentous virus with a single -stranded RNA genome . The shapes of some viruses are shown below .345 Rotavirus : Wheel-shaped virus346

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An elderly diabetic man presents with a complaints of fever, cough and difficulty in breathing for the past 3 days. He gives a history of international travel 10 days back. Laboratory reports show positive for COVID -19. What is the symmetry of the causative virus?
mcqs.explanation: The patient is suffering from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID -19). The coronavirus implicated shows an enveloped helical symmetry. Properties of Coronaviridae family: • They are enveloped RNA viruses. • They contain a genome of unsegmented single -stranded and positive -sense RNA • They have helical nucleocapsid

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding symmetry of viruses ?

options.a: Viral symmetry is studied by heavy metals stains.
options.b: The most efficient closed shell sub-unit arrangement is icosahedral.
options.c: Icosahedral symmetry involves 12 faces and 20 vertices .
options.d: It is not possible for 'empty ' helical particles to form

mcqs.explanation: Icosahedron has 20 faces (each an equilateral triangle) and 12 vertices. Option A: Study of viral symmetry by standard electron microscopy requires the use of heavy metal stains (e.g., potassium phosphotungstate ) to emphasize surface structure . It is a form of negative staining. Option B: Symmetry observed with animal viruses is of the icosahedral pattern. It is the most efficient arrangement for subunits in a closed shell . Option D: A regular, periodic interaction between capsid protein and nucleic acid is required to maintain a stable helical symmetry. Therefore, it is not possible for empty helical particles to form. Given below is Icosahedron:347

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses shows an enveloped icosahedral symmetry?
mcqs.explanation: Enveloped icosahedral symmetry is seen in the rubella virus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An immunologist is working on growing the influenza virus for vaccine production at the National Institute of Virology, Pune. Which of the following sites is used for the given purpose in a fertilized egg ?
mcqs.explanation: Allantoic cavity inoculation (1) is used for the growth and replication of the influenza virus for vaccine production . Embryonated eggs are used for the cultivation of viruses.348 Note : Both allantoic and amniotic cavity inoculation are recommended for initial isolation of the influenza virus. However, it is simpler to inoculate the virus into the allantoic cavity, as compared to the amniotic cavity, thus allantoic inoculation is the best answer.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Quantitative infectivity assay of viruses is done by _______.
mcqs.explanation: Quantitative infectivity assay of viruses is done by plaque assay. Assay of infectivity of virusesPhysical methods Biological methods Can estimate total viral count Can estimate total viral count Cannot differentiate between infectious and noninfectious virus particles Can detect infectious virus Examples :Real-time PCRAnti gen detection assayElectron microscopy Examples :Qualitative - endpoi nt biological assayQuantitativ e- plaque and pock assayThe image below shows a plaque assay.The image below shows pock assay.349

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which virus causes the cytopathic effect of syncytium formation?
mcqs.explanation: The cytopathic effect of syncytium formation is caused by the measles virus.350

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old lady presents with the lesions shown below . What is the causative organism?
mcqs.explanation: The lesions shown are cold sores, also known as herpes labialis caused by Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV -1). Herpes labialis primarily affects the lip and typically present as thin-walled , umbilicated vesicles , the roof of which breaks down with superficial ulcers . They generally heal without scarring. HSV -1 can be isolated from lesions in and around the mouth and is transmitted by direct contact or droplet spread from cases or carriers. HSV -2 is responsible for the majority of genital herpes infections and is commonly transmitted venereally . The images below show lesions of herpes labialis.360

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Cowdry Type A inclusions are seen in:
mcqs.explanation: Cowdry type A inclusions are seen in the vesicles of Herpes Simplex infection The classic Cowdry type A inclusion appears as a light purple , homogeneous intranuclear structure surrounded by a clear halo. The inclusions stain with antibodies to HSV , permitting a rapid, specific diagnosis of HSV infection .361

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 13 -year-old girl has had 4 episodes of meningitis over the last 4 years, with the disease lasting a few days at a time, leaving slowly resolving neurological symptoms such as visual and memory loss. A CSF cytology shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and a diagnosis of Mollaret 's meningitis is made. Which organism is implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: Mollaret 's meningitis or benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis is most commonly caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV ). Demonstration of HSV antibodies in CSF or persistence of HSV DNA in CSF can establish the diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A dentist presents to the surgery OPD with the findings shown below . He is febrile . Microscopic examination of the tissue reveals Tzanck cells . What is the causative agent?
mcqs.explanation: The image suggests herpetic whitlow , confirmed by the presence of Tzanck cells on microscopy. It is caused by HSV -1. It is often contracted by health care workers that come in contact with the virus when exposed to oral secretions . On Tzanck smear, which is a rapid, diagnostic method , Tzanck cells are seen . These are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Tzanck smear is also used in the diagnosis of Hailey-Hailey disease , Darier's disease , hand-foot-and-mouth disease , etc .362 Diagnosis of herpes simplex virus: • Most sensitive test - HSV DNA- PCR (can differentiate between HSV 1 and 2) • Most definitive test - virus isolation using human diploid fibroblast in which cytopathic changes can be observed as early as 24 - 48 hours. • Microscopy - Tzanck smear is prepared by Wright or Giemsa stain. Intranuclear type A inclusion bodies may be seen in Giemsa-stained smears.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A young male presents to the STD clinic with painful lesions as shown in the image. What is the most likely microscopic finding of the lesion?
mcqs.explanation: Clusters of vesicles are seen on an erythematous base along with painful and pruritic lymphadenopathy suggest a diagnosis of genital herpes . Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are present on microscopy. The Tzanck smear is a rapid, sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic method . Smears are prepared from the lesions , from the base of vesicles , and stained with a 1% aqueous solution of O-toluidine blue for 15 seconds . Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained ground glass chromatin - Tzanck cells are seen . The typical herpes lesions are thin-walled , umbilicated vesicles , the roof of which breaks down, leaving tiny superficial ulcers . They heal without scarring. The most common site of cutaneous lesions in the face - on the cheeks , chin, around the mouth, or on the forehead .363

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Your neighbor's child complains of fever and develops a rash. On examination, the rashes are present all over the body, and look like 'dewdrops lying on the skin'. The child says that his friend in school had similar complaints a few days ago. Which of the given statements is true about this rash?

options.b: The rash usually starts on the distal parts of limbs
options.c: All the lesions are of same age
options.d: Scabs are also infectious in chicken pox

mcqs.explanation: The condition described here is chickenpox. It is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. The following are the characteristics of rash seen in chicken pox : • The rash is centripetal in distribution. • It evolves rapidly, progressing through macule , papule , vesicle , pustule , and finally scab. • It is a pleomorphic rash and appears in crops, hence varying stages of lesions can be noticed at a given time. • The lesions resemble a dewdrop lying on the skin, as they are superficial and do not involve the deeper layers of the skin.364

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: While on rounds in the NICU, you notice a newborn baby with a zig-zag dermatomal cicatrix on the forehead and left side of the face . The limbs are small and atrophied . Microcephaly is noted . Which maternal infection are these findings characteristically associated with?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital varicella syndrome. Hence , an antenatal history of varicella zoster virus (VZV ) infection would be significant in the mother of this baby. Fetal varicella infection occurs if the mother gets infected during the first half of pregnancy. Clinical features include : • Cicatrix, a zigzag scarring in a dermatomal distribution • Microphthalmia • Cataracts • Optic atrophy • Chorioretinitis • Microcephaly • Limb hypoplasia • Motor and sensory deficits

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the predominant pathogen to infect renal transplant recipients one to four months following transplantation?
mcqs.explanation: The predominant pathogen to infect renal transplant recipients in the period around 1 to 4 months following the transplantation is cytomegalovirus (CMV). The most common CMV presentation in kidney transplant patients are fever (common), leukopenia , hepatosplenomegaly , myalgia, and arthralgia. JC virus and BK virus are common infections after solid organ transplantation based on the site of infection . This means BK and JC viruses are the most common organisms to infect the kidney after any solid organ transplant. But CMV is the predominant organism to cause infection in a person who has undergone a renal transplant. (Not the most common organism to affect the kidney after any solid organ transplant). Because of the frequency and severity of CMV disease , antiviral prophylaxis with ganciclovir or valganciclovir is being used in renal transplant recipients whenever indicated to prevent CMV disease .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An infant is brought by his worried parents with a rash and yellowish discoloration of the skin . On examination, the baby has petechiae , jaundice , hepatosplenomegaly , and microcephaly . The developmental assessment shows global developmental delay . An axial cut of the non-contrast CT of the brain is given below . What is the causative organism?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features and imaging suggest a diagnosis of congenital CMV infection . The non-contrast CT head shows periventricular calcifications and ventriculomegaly . Features of congenital CMV infection : • Petechial rash • Jaundice365 • Hepatosplenomegaly • Microcephaly • Deafness • Chorioretinitis • IUGR • Periventricular calcification and ventriculomegalyOption A: Congenital rubella syndrome is a triad of cardiac defects , cataracts, and congenital hearing loss. Option B: Neonatal herpes presents as skin lesions with eye involvement, encephalitis , and disseminated disease . Option D: Fetal varicella syndrome is manifested as cicatrizing/scarring skin lesions , chorioretinitis, hypoplastic limbs, low birth weight , and CNS defects due to cerebral atrophy. Note : In 15-20 % of infants with congenital CMV infection , microcephaly is not detected at birth. It may develop as the child grows and is detected at follow -up visits for other complaints.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Choose the correct statement regarding CMV.

options.a: Ganciclovir resistance is due to mutation in UL97 phosphotransferase gene
options.b: CMV can be cultured in vitro in any mammalian cell
options.c: Commonest manifestation of CMV associated disease is watery diarrhea
options.d: UL54 mutated CMV strains do not show cross resistance to Foscarnet

mcqs.explanation: Resistance to ganciclovir most commonly occurs due to mutations in the UL97 phosphotransferase gene . Option B: Human CMV replicates in vitro only in human fibroblasts, although the virus is often isolated from epithelial cells of the host. Option C: CMV infection is mostly subclinical. Option D: UL54 mutations can confer resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir, and foscarnet.366

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Where are owl's eye inclusion bodies seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Owl 's eye inclusion bodies are intranuclear basophilic inclusion bodies seen in CMV infection .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What does the Paul-Bunnell test diagnose ?
mcqs.explanation: Paul-Bunnell test is used to diagnose kissing disease (infectious mononucleosis ) caused by Epstein –Barr virus (EBV). It is a heterophile agglutination test used to identify the heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep erythrocytes . Patients suffering from infectious mononucleosis due to Epstein –Barr virus (EBV) will produce antibodies that will react and agglutinate sheep erythrocytes .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are studying the association of human herpesvirus-4 with other diseases . Which of the following patients have diseases associated with this virus?
mcqs.explanation: Human herpesvirus-4 or Epstein -Barr virus causes infectious mononucleosis , Burkitt's lymphoma, and is associated with oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV patients . EBV may cause the following malignancies: • Burkitt's lymphoma • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (in people of Chinese origin), • Lymphomas in immunodeficient persons such as AIDS or transplant recipients . Endemic or African Burkitt's lymphoma has got nearly 100 % association with EBV, as compared to non-endemic and HIV -associated Burkitt's lymphoma. Oral hairy leukoplakia is triggered by EBV in patients with poor immune status , most commonly with HIV . Oral submucous fibrosis is associated with the human papillomavirus (HPV ).367 Adult T cell leukemia is associated with the human T-cell leukemia virus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses is known to cause hemorrhagic cystitis , diarrhea, and conjunctivitis?
mcqs.explanation: Adenovirus is known to cause hemorrhagic cystitis , diarrhea, and conjunctivitis. Acute hemorrhagic cystitis in children is caused by adenoviruses types 11 and 21 . The following table shows various syndromes caused by adenoviruses and associated serotypes :Syndrome Adenovirus serotyp es Respiratory disease in childre n 1, 2, 5, Sore throat, febrile cold, pne umonia 3, 4, 7, 14, ARD in military recruits 4, 7, Follicular (swimming pool ) c onjunctivitis/ Pharyngoconju nctival fever 3, Epidemic keratoconjunctiviti s (shipyard eye ) 8, 19, Diarrhea 40, 41

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Viral infection mimicking erythroblastosis fetalis is:
mcqs.explanation: Parvovirus B19 infection mimics erythroblastosis fetalis . Parvovirus B19 is associated with: • Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease ) • Transient aplastic crisis • Pure red cell aplasia • Erythroblastosis fetalis (most commonly in early pregnancy) Picornavirus , Epstein -Barr virus, HSV infection do not mimic erythroblastosis fetalis .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which organism causes the disease shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The image showed a rash on the cheeks and face , with a slapped cheek appearance , characteristic of erythema infectiosum / fifth disease . It is caused by Parvovirus B19 .368 Parvovirus B19 usually presents as a respiratory infection , with an erythematous maculopapular rash and arthralgia. The rash starts as prominent erythema of the cheek , popularly known as slapped -cheek appearance . The rash further spreads to the trunk and limbs followed by lymphadenopathy and arthralgia. It induces aplastic crisis in sickle cell anemia patients . Infection during pregnancy leads to non-immune fetal hydrops (highest risk in the first half of gestational period ).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old child presents with skin lesions , suspected to be molluscum contagiosum . How is the diagnosis of this condition typically made?
mcqs.explanation: Diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum is based on clinical appearance . Molluscum contagiosum manifests as pink pearly wart-like lesions with a characteristic dimple at the center (umbilicated ), not associated with inflammation and necrosis.Option B: Skin biopsy or smear of expressed material shows characteristic inclusion bodies but is necessary only when the diagnosis is uncertain. Options A and C: Viral culture and PCR for viral DNA are not used for diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the causative organism of the condition shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows condyloma acuminata. It is most commonly caused by Human papillomavirus (HPV ) 6 and 11 . Condyloma acuminata is a benign, genital wart which is a moist, soft , pedunculated wart found on the external genitalia . Microscopically , the characteristic features include :369 • A branching villous structure with connective tissue stroma • Epidermis showing hyperkeratosis and acanthosis (thickening) • Cytoplasmic vacuolization of the squamous cells (koilocytosis ) is characteristic of HPV infection . • No evident dysplasiaOption A: Treponema pallidum can cause condylomata lata in secondary syphilis . It is smoother and flatter and may be associated with induration and ulceration. (image below )Option C: Human papillomavirus 16 and 18 are associated with carcinoma of the cervix and anogenital region. Option D: Hemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid. Given below is the image of chancroid.370

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with plantar warts as shown below . Which type of human papillomavirus is responsible for causing these ?
mcqs.explanation: HPV types 1a, , and 27 accounts for most plantar warts. HPV 7 causes hand warts in butchers (butcher 's warts). HPV 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminata, sinonasal papilloma , and squamous papilloma of the larynx .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: As a CHC medical officer , you organize an outreach program for HPV vaccination and the prevention of cervical cancer. Which protein is used for antigenic response in this vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: The HPV vaccines use virus-like particles (VLPs ) that consist of the HPV L1 major capsid protein. The L1 protein self -assembles into VLPs when expressed in eukaryotic cells . These VLPs contain the same epitopes as the HPV virion . But they do not contain genetic material and cannot transmit infection . The immunogenicity of the HPV vaccines relies on the development of conformational neutralizing antibodies to epitopes displayed on viral capsids . The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6, , 16, 18, , 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil-9. It has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers.HPV Vaccine Types Quadrivalent (Gardasil) 6, , 16, Bivalent (Cervarix ) 16, Nonavalent (Gardasil- 9) 6, , 16, 18, , 33, 45, 52, 8371

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Nonavalent HPV vaccine works against which of the following strains of the virus?
mcqs.explanation: The nonavalent HPV vaccine works against strains 6, , 16, 18, , 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is usually commercialized in the name of Gardasil-9. It has received expanded indication which now includes the prevention of oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers.HPV Vaccine Types Quadrivalent (Gardasil) 6, , 16, Bivalent (Cervarix ) 16, Nonavalent (Gardasil- 9) 6, , 16, 18, , 33, 45, 52, 8

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An HIV -positive patient presents with the following skin lesions . Which of the following diseases is associated with the virus implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: The above image showing red-purple macules and plaques in an HIV -positive patient is suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma, caused by human herpesvirus 8. It also causes primary effusion lymphoma. It is one of seven currently known human cancer viruses or oncoviruses. HHV -8 or Kaposi 's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is known to cause Kaposi 's sarcoma, in immunocompromised persons. Cancer patients receiving chemotherapy , AIDS patients , and organ transplant recipients are all at a high risk of showing signs of infection . KSHV is a known causative agent of four diseases : • Kaposi 's sarcoma • KSHV-associated multicentric Castleman's disease (MCD) • Primary effusion lymphoma • KSHV inflammatory cytokine syndrome

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following viruses is implicated in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by the JC virus. JC virus-induced progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is one of the neurologic diseases associated with HIV infection . Option B: BK virus is associated with nephropathy in transplant recipients . Option C: The long-term sequelae associated with measles infection is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis . Option D: Herpes simplex virus causes temporal lobe encephalitis .372

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a non-enveloped virus that causes hepatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis A and E are non-enveloped viruses, while Hepatitis B, C, and D are enveloped viruses.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man hailing from Mumbai presents to you with complaints of abdominal pain and malaise. On examination, he is icteric and the liver is palpable 6 cm below the costal margin. On further questioning, he informs you that a few weeks back the drains surrounding his house were overflowing due to the monsoon flooding . Which of the following is the most likely etiology ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario with icterus , hepatomegaly , and environmental history is suggestive of acute viral hepatitis , likely to be caused by hepatitis A or E viruses. Hepatitis A and E are transmitted by feco -oral route. Overcrowding, poor hygiene , and fecal contamination of water supplies such as after monsoon flooding can lead to spreading of the disease . Hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted by parenteral routes , e.g. blood transfusions.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 18-year-old man presents with fever, diarrhea, and jaundice . He gives a history of consuming food at a roadside stall. Which of the following statements is incorrect about the etiological agent ?

options.c: It is transmitted by feco -oral route
options.d: A formalin inactivated vaccine is used for prevention

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of viral hepatitis which is most likely to be Hepatitis A. Hepatitis A virus belongs to the family Picornaviridae . It is transmitted by feco -oral route and most of the infections are symptomatic.380 There is no definitive treatment , thus , only supportive therapy is given.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: What is the average incubation period for Hepatitis A virus?
mcqs.explanation: The average incubation period of the Hepatitis A virus (HAV ) is around 30 days. It ranges from 15-50 days. The clinical disease has a prodromal stage and an icteric stage .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is called as Australia antigen?
mcqs.explanation: HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is also known as the Australia antigen. It is called so because it was first isolated from the serum of an Australian person. Sera from hepatitis B patients when observed under an electron microscope show three types of particles : • A spherical particle : 22nm , most abundant, contains only HBsAg. • Filamentous or tubular particle : 22nm, contains only HBsAg. • A double -walled spherical structure : 42nm diameter , is the complete Hepatitis B virus. It was described by Dane and is called Dane particle .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is also referred to as Dane particle ?
mcqs.explanation: Dane particle refers to Hepatitis B. Sera from hepatitis B patients when observed under an electron microscope show three types of particles : • Spherical particle : 22nm , most abundant, contains only HBsAg.381 • Filamentous or tubular particle : 22nm, contains only HBsAg. • A double -walled spherical structure : 42nm diameter , is the complete Hepatitis B virus. It was described by Dane and is called Dane particle .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old male patient with chronic hepatitis B has high levels of serum HBeAg. Which of the following viral genes is involved in coding the same?
mcqs.explanation: HBeAg is coded by the C gene . The presence of high levels of HBeAg (and HBV DNA) suggests high infectivity. HBV Genome has four overlapping genes. They code for: • S gene -It codes for surface antigen. • C gene - • When the C region alone is translated : HBcAg is formed. • When translation begins from Pre C region, HBeAg is formed. • P gene - Codes for DNA polymerase . • X gene - Codes for a non-particulate protein HBxAg.382

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: While drawing blood from a patient with hepatitis B, it splashes into the eyes of a nurse. Which of the following markers will appear first in her blood if she gets infected ?
mcqs.explanation: HBsAg is the first marker to appear in the blood after infection . It can be detected even before the elevation of serum transaminases and onset of clinical illness . Usually, it disappears within 2 months of onset of clinical disease but may last for even 6 months and beyond . If it persists beyond 6 months, it indicates chronic hepatitis . Anti-HBs is the protective antibody, which appears soon after HBsAg, disappears and remains in serum for a long time.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient with hepatitis B presents to OPD for follow -up. Which of the following serological markers will not be detected in his blood?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) is not present in blood because it is enclosed within the HBsAg coat. However, antibodies against HBc (Anti-HBc) are the earliest antibody markers to be seen in the blood after 1-2 weeks . Note : • HBsAg: Earliest marker to be detected in the serum of Hepatitis B-infected persons. • Anti HBc: Earliest antibody to be detected in the serum of Hepatitis B-infected persons. The given image shows hepatitis B virus and its antigens383

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: There are 3 to 5% healthy hepatitis B carriers in India who are asymptomatic . They are at the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma in the future because _________

options.a: They are unable to mount inflammation against the virus
options.b: Virus can integrate with host DNA and form complementary DNA
options.c: There is a risk of elevation of transaminases
options.d: Liver parenchymal cells are in a state of high proliferation

mcqs.explanation: In most tumors, HBV DNA is integrated into the cell genome , and in most cases , the virus DNA has undergone rearrangements, including deletions . After integration, it promotes the overexpression of cell genes that can also contribute to oncogenesis . The only viral gene product that is consistently present in the tumor cells is the X protein.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The given life cycle is suggestive of which of the following viruses?
mcqs.explanation: The given life cycle is of the hepatitis B virus. Steps : • The infectious virion attaches to cells and uncoating occurs. • Cell enzymes in the hepatocytes convert dsDNA to covalently closed circular double -stranded DNA (cccDNA) • HBV mRNA and pre-genome RNA is synthesized using cccDNA as a template . • pre-genome RNA is encapsidated by packaging signal into new core particles . • These new core particles are templates for HBV reverse transcriptase. • Negative -strand DNA is synthesized by viral polymerase by reverse transcription. • The cores bud from the pre-Golgi membranes, acquiring HBsAg-containing envelopes . • Once viral particles are assembled , they either exit the cell or cause reinfection of the same cell .384

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed with Hepatitis B infection . Which of the following markers will always be present in his serum, even during recurrences , or if he develops chronic hepatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: A patient who has had exposure to HBV will have anti-HBc antibody even when he has moved into the chronic or recurrent stages . IgM anti-HBc reappears during acute recurrences while IgG anti-HBc is found in chronic states. The HBsAg antigen is present in chronic hepatitis B, while the antibody anti-HBs is not.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not synthesized by pre-core mutants of hepatitis B virus?
mcqs.explanation: Pre-core mutants of hepatitis B virus are unable to synthesize HBeAg. In the HBV genome , the C gene consists of 2 regions: • Pre-C region- When translation begins from the Pre-C region, HBeAg is synthesized . • C-region- When it begins from the C-region, HBcAg is synthesized . In the HBeAg sequence of pre-core mutants, there is a G to A switch at the 28th amino acid, causing a stop codon. Hence , pre-core mutants are unable to synthesize HBeAg. The image below shows the HBV genome :

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: The serological profile of a patient is given below . What is your diagnosis?

options.a: Acute HBV infection with high infectivity
options.c: Chronic HBV infection with high infectivity
options.d: Acute HBV infection with low infectivity

mcqs.explanation: HBsAg and IgM Anti-HBc are positive , indicating an acute hepatitis B infection . HBeAg positive indicates that the patient is highly infectious .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An HBsAg positive primigravida presents to you for routine antenatal care. She asks you about the risk of transmission of HBV to her baby. Which of the following is not related to the same?
mcqs.explanation: 385 Breastfeeding is not related to the vertical transmission of hepatitis B virus. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in HBsAg-positive mothers. Mother -to-child transmission of HBV can occur via three modalities : • Intrauterine transmission- Transplacental transmission is uncommon. Another route is via a breach in the placental barrier exposing maternal blood to fetal blood e.g. - threatened preterm labor. • Transmission during delivery - It is the most frequent method of vertical transmission. It is mostly due to newborn contact with the mother's infected secretions or blood at the time of delivery (normal /instrumental). • Postpartum transmission- Though HBV DNA is present in breast milk, it is not transmitted to the fetus . However, cracked nipples expose the infant to maternal blood, and can transmit the virus to the infant. Immunoprophylaxis with HBIg is indicated for babies born to HBsAg-positive mothers followed by a three -dose hepatitis B recombinant vaccine.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An intern takes a hepatitis B vaccine booster dose before his ward postings begin. Which of the following serological markers will indicate immunity against HBV in this case?
mcqs.explanation: Presence of anti-HBs with the absence of all other serological virus markers indicates immunity following HBV vaccination .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding HBV vaccination ?

options.a: The current vaccine is prepared by cloning 'S gene ' of HBV in Baker 's yeast
options.b: A single dose of HBV vaccine is recommended for high-risk groups for pre-exposure prophylaxis
options.c: For high-risk mothers who are seronegative, hepatitis B vaccine can be given during pregnancy.
options.d: Hepatitis B vaccine should be administered intramuscularly in the deltoid muscle .

mcqs.explanation: Pre-exposure prophylaxis consists of administration of a 3–4 dose series of hepatitis B vaccine given over a 6-month period . The pre-exposure prophylaxis of Hepatitis B vaccine schedule is as follows : The vaccine is genetically engineered by cloning 'S gene ' in baker's yeast . It has non-glycosylated HBsAg particles given along with an alum adjuvant. Pregnancy is not a contraindication for hepatitis B vaccination . The efficacy has been shown to be similar to that for non-pregnant adults, with overall seroconversion rates approaching 95 percent after three doses which can be taken during routine prenatal care. The vaccine is given intramuscularly, in the deltoid muscle and can be co-administered with other vaccines.Group Vaccine dose in mL (Active in gredient in \265 g/mL) Schedule Newborn 0.5 mL (10 \265 g) <24 hours, 6 weeks , 14 weeks (if administration of the first dose within 24 hours of birt h is not possible , then 6, , and 14 weeks )386 Group Vaccine dose in mL (Active in gredient in \265 g/mL) Schedule Healthy persons aged \02319 yea rs 0.5 mL (10 \265 g) 0, 1, 2 / 6 months Healthy persons aged \02420 ye ars 1.0 mL (20 \265 g) 0, 1, 2 / 6 months Persons on hemodialysis or i mmunocompromised person s 2.0 mL (40 \265 g) 0, 1, 2, 6 months

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A known case of hepatitis B going into hepatic failure is found to have a high viral load. Which of the following serological markers will not contribute to the viral load?
mcqs.explanation: Anti-HBs will not contribute to the high viral load, as it is not a marker of active viral replication. HBeAg, HBV DNA, and HBV DNA polymerase are markers of active viral replication and will contribute to the high viral load. HBeAg is a qualitative marker while HBV DNA is a quantitative marker of the replicative phase .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man with heroin addiction presents with fatigue , palpable purpura, joint pains, and abdominal pain. Urine analysis shows massive proteinuria. Which of the following viruses should be tested for in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mixed cryoglobulinemia , which is strongly associated with hepatitis C. Hence , the patient should be tested for hepatitis C.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which hepatitis virus shows maximum chronicity in adults ?
mcqs.explanation: Maximum chronicity is seen in HCV infection , followed by HBV infection .387 5-10% of adults infected with HBV develop chronic infection . The majority of neonates affected with hepatitis B develop chronic hepatitis . HEV is associated with chronic infection only in immunocompromised individuals. HAV is not associated with chronicity. Note : The most common cause of post-transfusion hepatitis in developed countries is hepatitis C

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient with fulminant hepatitis is found to have coinfection with hepatitis B and hepatitis D viruses. Which of the following structures of HBV aid in the survival of HDV ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis D virus (HDV ) is an incomplete /defective virus. It requires HBV , to provide the envelope protein (HbsAg) to aid in its survival . Hepatitis D is called the delta virus. Two types of infection may occur: • Co-infection - acute HDV and HBV infections occur simultaneously • Super -infection - Delta viral infection occurs in a person already harboring HBV . This most often leads to chronic hepatitis Coinfection and superinfection can cause fulminant hepatitis . HBV vaccination is protective against HDV .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: In the year 1955, following sewage contamination of drinking water in New Delhi , an outbreak of jaundice ensued . Electron microscopy of fecal samples from the affected population revealed a virus resembling caliciviruses. Which of the following was the etiological agent ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) resembles caliciviruses in morphology and physical characteristics. Hepatitis E is a non-enveloped virus with ssRNA genome Note : The largest HEV epidemic occurred in New Delhi in 1955-1956.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about viral hepatitis ?

options.a: Anti LKM-3 antibody is associated with hepatitis B infection
options.b: Anti-LKM1 antibodies are associated with hepatitis C infection
options.c: IgM anti-HAV antibody appears during the late incubation period
options.d: Enterically transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis is caused by hepatitis E virus

mcqs.explanation: The anti-LKM-3 antibody is associated with hepatitis D infection , not hepatitis B. Anti–liver-kidney microsomal antibodies (anti-LKM) are many of several autoantibodies that are detected in the serum of patients with different types of acute or chronic liver disease . These antibodies are targeted against antigens of the cytochrome P450 system . They are also associated with chronic hepatitis C and autoimmune hepatitis . Option C: IgM anti-HAV antibody indicates current/recent infection . It appears during the late incubation period , peaks in 2-3 weeks, and disappears after 3-4 months. IgG denotes remote infection or immunity. It appears around the same time, peaks at 3-4 months, and persists for a long time. Option D: Hepatitis E infection was previously known as an epidemic or enterically transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis . It is transmitted by feco -oral route.388

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following subtypes of HIV is most common in India?
mcqs.explanation: Subtype C of HIV is the most common in India. It causes more than 95% of HIV infections . Subtypes A and C are more readily transmitted by heterosexual contact than subtype B, which is mainly transmitted by homosexual contact and injections.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about HIV ?
mcqs.explanation: HIV is a thermolabile virus. It is readily inactivated by heating to 60 \260C for 10 minutes and at 100 \260C in seconds. At room temperature (20 –25 \260C) in the dried blood, it may survive for 1 week . Option A: HIV crosses the blood-brain barrier . It may cause encephalopathy leading to loss of higher functions, progressing to dementia . Option B: HIV is a spherical , enveloped virus. Its genome is composed of two copies of identical single -stranded positive -sense RNA. Option C: HIV is inactivated by treatment with 0.3% hydrogen peroxide , 50% ethanol , 35% isopropanol or 10 % household bleach . A 2% solution of glutaraldehyde is effective for the disinfection of medical instruments.393

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a nonstructural gene of HIV ?
mcqs.explanation: The tat gene (trans-activating gene ) is a non-structural gene . HIV has structural and non-structural genes : • Structural genes - Genes coding for structural protiens : • gag- Codes for core and shell protein p55 , which is cleaved to p15, p18 and p24 • env- Codes for envelope glycoprotein gp160 which is cleaved to gp120 and gp41 • pol- Codes for enzymes : Polymerase , reverse transcriptase, protease and endonuclease • Non-structural and regulatory genes : • tat- Trans -activating gene • nef- Negative factor gene • rev- Regulator of virus gene • vif- Viral infectivity factor gene • vpu- (only in HIV -1) and vpx (only in HIV -2) • vpr- Stimulates only the promoter region of the virus • LTR - Long terminal repeat sequences

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of HIV replication?
mcqs.explanation: HIV replicates by the sequence RNA-DNA-RNA. The provirus initiates viral replication by directing the synthesis of viral RNA and other components . Hence , the sequence is RNA–ssDNA–dsDNA–RNA. HIV genome is composed of 2 single -stranded positive -sense RNA. When a virus infects a cell , the viral RNA is transcribed by the enzyme reverse transcriptase, first into single -stranded DNA and then to double -stranded DNA which is integrated into the host chromosome. Note : If the options include RNA-DNA-RNA and RNA-DNA-DNA-RNA then the latter would be the choice . The given image represents HIV replication394

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: As part of developing the public health policy on HIV in India, which of the following modes of transmission would you focus on the most?
mcqs.explanation: Heterosexual transmission is the most common mode of transmission of HIV infection in developing countries such as India and African countries . In many Western countries , male-to-male sexual transmission is the dominant mode of transmission. Blood transfusion carries the highest risk per 10000 exposures of getting HIV from an infected person. However, it is not the most common mode of transmission.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old bisexual man goes to an ICTC centre for counselling about HIV . Which of the following is false about HIV transmission?

options.a: Male -to-female HIV transmission has more risk of causing infection than female -to-male transmission
options.b: The risk of acquiring HIV with unprotected receptive anal intercourse is lower than that with penile -vaginal intercourse
options.c: The quantity of HIV -1 in plasma is a primary determinant of the risk of HIV -1 transmission
options.d: Male circumcision is associated with a lower risk of HIV acquisition for heterosexual men

mcqs.explanation: The risk of HIV acquisition associated with unprotected receptive anal intercourse is relatively higher than that seen in penile -vaginal intercourse . This is because the rectal mucosal membrane is thin and fragile and anal intercourse is associated with microtrauma (rectal tears). The differences in transmission rates between men and women are because the vagina and cervix are exposed to semen for a longer duration, increasing the risk of transmission. However, the penis and urethral orifice are exposed relatively briefly to infected vaginal fluid , lowering the risk .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Specific binding of the HIV to the CD4 receptor occurs via which of these ?
mcqs.explanation: The specific binding of the HIV to the CD4 receptor is by the envelope glycoprotein gp120. Option B - Cell fusion occurs via binding to gp41. Cell fusion is essential for infection to take place . Option C, D - Binding to CD4 receptor requires the participation of a co-receptor CXCR 4 for T cell tropic HIV strains and CCR 5 for macrophage-tropic strains.395

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A patient presents to you with a history of sharing needles during IV drug abuse with an HIV -positive partner. HIV -antibody spot test was negative , however p24 antigen assay was positive. You explain to him that he is currently in the window period for HIV . Which of the following statements would you use to explain the concept to him?

options.a: It is the time period between infection and onset of first symptoms
options.b: It is the time period between infection and detection of antibodies
options.c: It is the time period between exposure and onset of viral multiplication
options.d: It is the time period between exposure and appearance of symptoms

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the patient has experienced a high-risk exposure to HIV due to sharing needles during IV drug abuse with an HIV -positive partner. The period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV is known as the window period. The window period may last anywhere between 2–8 weeks to a few months. During this period , the individual may be highly infectious . HIV infection can be detected during this period by p24 antigen assay and PCR.396

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 41-year-old man was admitted for hernioplasty and initial investigations revealed that he is HIV -positive . He gives no history of contact and has no HIV -associated symptoms . Which of the following statements is incorrect about this phase of HIV infection ?

options.d: Rapid decline of CD4 count is common

mcqs.explanation: The given patient is in the latent period of HIV infection . During the latent phase of HIV infection , the CD4+ T cell count declines steadily and not rapidly. All patients infected with HIV pass through a phase of clinical latency during which they are asymptomatic . This can last for years. During the latent phase , patients show positive HIV antibody tests and they are infectious . There will be varying degrees of viral multiplication . Throughout the course of untreated infection and even during the stage of clinical latency , HIV is actively replicating or is sequestered in lymphoid tissues .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the clinic requesting an HIV test . He had unprotected sexual contact with another man 3 weeks ago. Antibodies against which of the following will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot?
mcqs.explanation: Antibodies against gp41 will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot. Antibodies to HIV usually appear within 3–6 weeks of primary infection . The appearance of HIV -binding antibodies occurs prior to the appearance of neutralizing antibodies . The only viral proteins that elicit neutralizing antibodies are the envelope proteins gp120 and gp41. The order of appearance of antibodies is as follows : Antibody to envelope gp41 > Antibodies to gag protein (p24 and p55 ) > Antibodies to envelope gp120 > Antibodies to gag protein p17 > Antibodies to pol gene products (p31 and p66). Note : The earliest antigen to appear in the blood following HIV infection is p24.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You are an officer with the Center for Disease Control and are screening a high-risk population for HIV . Which of the following methods will you use as a screening tool?
mcqs.explanation: ELISA is most commonly used as a screening test for HIV .397 Screening tests possess high sensitivity but are not highly specific . ELISA is a simple , relatively inexpensive screening test . The most commonly used confirmatory test is Western blot. Western blot demonstrating antibodies to products of all three of the major genes of HIV (gag, pol, and env) is conclusive evidence of infection with HIV . It is considered positive if it shows antibodies against at least two of the following gene products : p24, gp41, gp120/160 .398

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following RNA viruses has an 8 segmented genome with its site of replication being the nucleus ?
mcqs.explanation: Influenza virus has an 8 segmented genome . Its site of replication is the nucleus , unlike other RNA viruses. Influenza virus belongs to the Orthomyxoviridae family. Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus , except pox. Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm , except retroviruses and orthomyxoviruses. Examples of segmented viruses (ARBO): • Arenavirus (2 segments ) • Rotavirus (11 segments ) • Bunyavirus (3 segments ) • Orthomyxovirus (8 segments ) The image below shows the segmented genome seen in the influenza virus (Orthomyxoviridae)

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A microbiologist working on influenza virus in a lab, observes reversal of hemagglutination . What is this phenomenon known as?
mcqs.explanation: 406 Elution is the process of reversal of hemagglutination and the release of the virus from the red cell surface. Influenza virus contains two surface antigens : • Hemagglutinin (HA) - causes RBC agglutination ; facilitates viral entry into cells • Neuraminidase (NA) - an enzyme that destroys the receptor HA uses to bind to RBCs causing elution/reversal of hemagglutination . Hence , it is also called a receptor destroying enzyme (RDE).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding antigenic drift?

options.a: There is a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure
options.b: It doesn 't account for the periodic epidemics of influenza
options.c: The new antigens thus formed are totally unrelated to the previous antigens
options.d: Antibodies to the predecessor viruses do not neutralise the new variants

mcqs.explanation: Antigenic drift causes a gradual sequential change in antigenic structure . It accounts for periodic epidemics . This property forms the basis for the development of annual influenza vaccines. Antigenic variation is a property of influenza viruses by which it alters the antigenic structure on its surface and thus avoids a host immune response . It is of two types - Antigenic shift and antigenic drift.Antigenic shift Antigenic drift Antigenic structure Abrupt, drastic change Gradual, sequential change Periodicity - 20 years 2 - 3 years Epidemiological effect Pandemics and major epide mics Periodic epidemic and spora dic cases Genetic cause Large genetic re-assortment Point mutation Antibodies to predecessor str ains Do not neutralize the new va riant Neutralizes the new variant t o varying degrees407 Antigenic shift Antigenic drift Clinical relevance Animal-origin viruses infecti ng humans e.g. Swine flu, CO VID -19 Annual influenza vaccine dev elopmentCommon cold - Peo ple can get flu more than onc e

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is represented by the given form of replication?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the replication of influenza virus. Stages of replication: • Attachment , penetration , uncoating- the virus is internalized by receptor -mediated endocytosis • Transcription and translation- Viral transcription occurs in the nucleus . The mRNAs are produced from viral nucleocapsids . • Viral RNA replication- Viral genome replication is accomplished by the same virus-encoded polymerase proteins involved in transcription. • Maturation- The virus matures by budding from the surface of the cell .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: You receive multiple patients from a poultry farm presenting with fever, dyspnea , cold, and cough . You suspect an outbreak of Avian flu. Which of the following virus strains causes the same?
mcqs.explanation: H5N1 is a strain of avian influenza. Transmission occurs only from birds (e.g. poultry ). Recombination occurs in pigs . Human-to-human transmission is very rare. It causes flu-like symptoms and can cause severe respiratory illness . Option A: H1N1 causes swine flu Option C: H3N2 causes Hong Kong flu Option D: H2N2 caused a pandemic in 1957

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old girl with a history of fever, rhinorrhea , sore throat, and myalgia presented with multiple episodes of vomiting and seizures . She was diagnosed with Reye 's syndrome. Which of the following is incorrect about the most likely etiological agent ?

options.a: Virus shedding is present before symptoms begins
options.b: 5-12 years is a high risk group

mcqs.explanation: The most likely etiological agent in the given case of Reye 's syndrome is the influenza virus. Children <5-years, especially those <2-years of age are at the highest risk of serious complications related to influenza infection . Other high-risk groups for influenza include adults \02460 years of age , persons with chronic diseases , persons who are immunocompromised. Option A: The virus is shed in respiratory secretions a day before the onset of illness and for 3-4 days thereafter . Option C: Birds, especially aquatic birds act as reservoirs of influenza viruses. Option D: Secondary attack rate is 5-15%.408 Note : Reye 's syndrome is precipitated by the interaction of a viral infection (such as influenza) with salicylates . Therefore, aspirin is not given to pediatric patients with influenza and influenza-like illness .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of headache and drowsiness since 2 days. He had a history of fever, ear pain, and difficulty in swallowing for 1 week . On examination, you see the following . Brudzinki 's sign is positive . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with fever, parotitis, headache , drowsiness , and positive Brudzinki 's sign is suggestive of meningitis secondary to mumps. Mumps is caused by the mumps virus and is characterized by fever, bilateral or unilateral parotid swelling which may be tender . Parotitis can present with ear pain and difficulty in swallowing . It usually resolves in a week . Meningoencephalitis /aseptic meningitis can occur before , along with, or after parotitis. Most commonly, it manifests 5 days after parotitis. It can present with headache , neck stiffness , and drowsiness . Complications of mumps: • Aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis • Epididymo -orchitis- Usually unilateral. Seen in post -pubertal males • Oophoritis • Other complications include pancreatitis and myocarditis Note : Non-mumps parotitis can be caused by: • Epstein -Barr virus - causes infectious mononucleosis • Coxsackievirus - causes herpangina • Parainfluenza virus - causes croup

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 9-month-old child is brought to the OPD for MMR vaccine. Which strain of mumps virus is used in the same?
mcqs.explanation: The strain of mumps virus used in the MMR vaccine (Measles , Mumps , Rubella) is the Jeryl-Lynn strain. The virus is attenuated by serial passage in embryonated eggs and grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture . Note : The schedule of MMR vaccine as per the National Immunisation Schedule is from 9 completed months to 12 months. (can be given till 5 years of age ).

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A mother brings her 5-month-old baby to the casualty with complaints of fast breathing and poor feeding . She also gives a history of fever, cold, and cough for 3 days. On examination, nasal flaring and expiratory wheeze are present . Which of the following statements is false about the viral etiology of the same?

options.a: The cytopathic effect is syncytium formation
options.b: Ribavirin is the drug of choice
options.d: It is the most important cause of bronchiolitis

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiolitis caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV ). Palivizumab is given for RSV prophylaxis in high-risk infants such as premature babies,409 immunocompromised infants, etc . Option A - The characteristic cytopathic effect is syncytium formation (multinucleated giant cell ). Option B - Inhaled ribavirin is the drug of choice . Option D - RSV causes upper and lower respiratory tract infections in infants, and is the most common cause of bronchiolitis from ages 6 weeks to 6 months. It can cause pneumonia and tracheobronchitis and is common during winters and monsoon.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An unimmunized man presents with fever, malaise, and an erythematous rash starting from behind the ears and progressing to the face and trunk. Given below is an image of lymphoid tissue taken from this patient . What pathological finding do you see here?
mcqs.explanation: Warthin -Finkeldey cells are seen here. These are multinucleate giant cells , which are found in the lymphoid tissues of patients with measles . The cytopathic effect of measles consists of multinucleate syncytium formation with numerous acidophilic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions, as shown in the image below . Option B: Warthin -Starry stain is used to detect spirochetes and to stain H. pylori and B. henselae Option C: Langhans giant cells are seen in tuberculosis Option D: Aschoff giant cells are seen in rheumatic fever

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy with no prior immunization history presents with fever, cough , and coryza. On examination of the buccal mucosa, you see the following . Which stage of the disease is this finding seen in?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Koplik's spots present in measles . They are seen during the prodromal phase of the illness . Koplik's spots are small bluish-white ulcerations on the buccal mucosa opposite to the first and second lower molars and are pathognomonic of measles . They contain giant cells , cytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions, and virion components . They can involve the entire buccal mucosa and fade as the maculopapular rash develops.410 Stages of measles : The natural history of measles has 3 stages as follows : • Prodromal stage - It begins 10 days after infection and lasts until day 14. It consists of cough , coryza, redness of eyes , lacrimation, photophobia , vomiting, and diarrhea. Koplik's spots appear in this stage . • Eruptive stage - A dusky, red maculopapular rash appears . It starts behind the ears spreads downwards to the trunk and lower extremities . Antibodies appear in this stage and are detectable by IgM ELISA . The symptoms such as fever and rash usually resolve spontaneously or go on to develop complications . • Post-measles stage - Weakness and weight loss may persist . The infection may become chronic and cause secondary infections such as cancrum oris, candidiasis etc . The image below shows Koplik's spotsThe image below shows the characteristic maculopapular rash in measles411

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following disease has the highest mortality once clinically manifested ?
mcqs.explanation: Rabies is a vaccine-preventable , zoonotic, viral disease . Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. Spread of rabies: • Centripetal spread - • The virus enters the peripheral neurons, it moves via retrograde fast axonal transport towards the spinal cord or brainstem a.k.a the central nervous system (CNS) at a speed of up to 250 mm/day. • Once within CNS, it spreads quickly to other regions in the CNS through fast axonal transport. It infects neurons primarily, but may rarely infect astrocytes . • Centrifugal spread - After CNS infection is established , it spreads along the sensory and autonomic nerves to: • Salivary glands • Adrenal glands • Skin Rabies virus replicates in acinar cells of the salivary glands and is secreted in the saliva of rabid animals that serve as vectors.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old pet -groomer was brought to the casualty with a history of breathlessness , excessive agitation, and restlessness . His bystanders give a history of progressive behavioral change and he had a fever, sore throat, and generalized weakness 1 month back. On examination, pulse was 100 bpm, SpO2 was 98% on room air. Which of the following samples will not be preferred to detect the etiological agent ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario is highly suggestive of rabies. Corneal impression smears are not performed, as they are of low diagnostic yield . Laboratory diagnosis of rabies is performed by the following methods : • Antigen detection - Direct immunofluorescence (IF) from specimens of : • Skin biopsy from the nape of the neck including hair follicles . Rabies antigen is present in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles . It is the most sensitive and specific test . • Corneal smears were previously used . They are not used anymore as they are of low diagnostic yield . • Viral isolation- Intracerebral inoculation in mice can be attempted from the brain , CSF, and saliva . • Antibody demonstration from serum and CSF. • Viral RNA detection by RT -PCR . • Postmortem examination of brain tissue samples - demonstration of Negri bodies .412

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: An officer of the Indian Forest Services is bitten by a rabid fox while on duty . Which of the following statements is true about the etiological agent ?

options.a: The incubation period is 4 to 5 days

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of infection with the street form of rabies virus. Street rabies causes disease. All mammals are susceptible to rabies. Cattle , cats and foxes are highly susceptible , whereas dogs and humans have intermediate susceptibility . Differences between street rabies and fixed rabies:Street rabies Fixed rabies (produced by re peated passages ) Causes disease Doesn't cause disease Produces Negri body Doesn't produce Negri body Affects salivary glands Doesn't affect salivary glands Incubation period - 3 mont hs Incubation period - 4-5 days

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old man was brought to you with a history of fever, behavioral changes , and seizures . He is foaming at the mouth and is unable to ingest liquids. The patient was admitted to the ICU, however he died soon after. Post mortem brain samples showed the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing Negri bodies and the case scenario of fever, neurological symptoms like seizures and altered sensorium, hydrophobia (due to painful muscle contractions during swallowing liquids), and hypersalivation are suggestive of encephalitic rabies. Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons that are composed of rabies virus proteins and viral RNA. These are commonly observed in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and in pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus . Their presence is a characteristic pathologic finding in rabies. The image below shows Negri bodies :413

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Babes nodules are seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Babes nodules are seen in rabies. Mononuclear inflammatory infiltration in the leptomeninges , including microglial nodules are called Babes nodules .The most characteristic pathologic finding in rabies is the Negri body. These are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in brain neurons that are composed of rabies virus proteins and viral RNA. The image given below shows Negri bodies .

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding rabies vaccination ?

options.a: Bitten dog should be observed for a minimum of 10 days.
options.b: Four-dose regimen is given as 0.1ml intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 28.
options.c: Pre-exposure prophylaxis regimen consists of 3 doses .
options.d: The dose of human anti rabies immunoglobulin is 20 IU/kg.

mcqs.explanation: 414 According to the Updated Thai Red Cross Regimen (2-2-2 -0-2) for post exposure prophylaxis , reconstituted rabies vaccine is given as follows : • 0.1 ml intradermally • Sites - two sites at the same visit. It is given in both the deltoids • Schedule - Days 0, 3, 7, and 28 Healthy dogs, cats, or ferrets may be confined and observed for 10 days. The dosage of equine rabies immunoglobulin (eRIG) is 40 IU/kg while that of human anti-rabies immunoglobulin (hRIG ) is 20 IU/kg body weight . PrEP regimens for individuals of all ages are as follows : • Three intramuscular or intradermal vaccine doses on days 0, 7, and 21 or 28.415

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: Which family does yellow fever virus belong to?
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever virus belongs to the family flaviviridae , which contains the genus Flavivirus . The important species under genus Flavivirus include : • Yellow fever virus • Dengue virus • Japanese encephalitis virus • Kyasanur forest disease virus • West Nile encephalitis • Zikavirus Note : Arbovirus is a term used to refer to any viruses that are transmitted by arthropod vectors. There is no family or order by the name arbovirus . The word arbovirus stands for ARthropod-BOrne virus.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old boy from Uttar Pradesh was rushed to the emergency department with a headache , fever, and blurred vision followed shortly by unresponsiveness to verbal commands. He is suspected to have viral encephalitis . Which of the following transmits this endemic disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Endemic viral encephalitis is suggestive of Japanese encephalitis . It is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnuii. It is the leading cause of childhood neurological viral infection in India. In endemic areas such as North India, it typically affects children <15 years of age as by early adulthood , the majority of the population has protective immunity following natural exposure to the virus. Ardeid birds like herons and egrets are reservoir hosts , while the amplifier hosts are pigs . It is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes , and human infection is a tangential dead end.

mcqs.subject: Microbiology
