Option C: Papilledema is a passive disc swelling seen with raised intracranial pressure . The blind spot is enlarged due to the edema of the optic disc. Option D: Medullated or opaque nerve fibers are the abnormal myelination of nerve fibers of the retina. Normally, optic nerve myelination stops at the level of lamina cribrosa. If the myelination continues beyond the optic disc it leads to the expansion of the blind spot . On ophthalmoscopic examination, these are seen as a whitish patch with feathery margins.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Which statement regarding M\374ller cells is false ?

options.b: Their nuclei lie in the outer nuclear layer
options.c: Their foot processes form the inner & outer limiting membranes
options.d: They contribute to inner blood retinal barrier

mcqs.explanation: The nuclei of M\374ller cells lie in the inner nuclear layer. M\374ller cells are a type of macroglial cells of the retina. The human retina contains 8–10 million M\374ller cells. Their nuclei lie in the inner nuclear layer and their processes extend across the retinal layers to form the inner and outer limiting membranes. Their functions include : 1. Providing structural stability to the retina 2. Interacting with other neurons and their functional and metabolic support 3. Providing neurons with trophic substances and removing metabolic waste 4. Playing a critical role in regulating the extracellular space volume as well as ion and water homeostasis and in maintaining the inner blood - retinal barrier Astrocytes are another type of macroglial cells of the retina. They play a crucial role in retinal vascularization. In the mature retina, they are restricted to the nerve fiber and ganglion cell layers.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the development of retinal vasculature?

options.a: Grow to temporal ora by 34 weeks of gestation
options.b: Grow to nasal ora by 36 weeks of gestation
options.c: Originate from mesenchymal tissue during week 16 of gestation

mcqs.explanation: 202 Retinal vessels reach temporal ora at approximately 40 weeks of gestation . Retinal vessels develop de novo from mesenchymal tissue , beginning during the 4th month of gestation . They radiate outward (centrifugally ) from the optic nerve, reaching the nasal ora by 36 weeks .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A preterm baby treated for respiratory distress syndrome is found to have white pupillary reflex on opthalmologic examination. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A preterm baby, treated for respiratory distress syndrome, with leucocoria (white pupillary reflex ) most likely has retrolental fibroplasia. Retrolental fibroplasia, also known as retinopathy of prematurity , is a proliferative retinopathy . Risk factors include prematurity , very low birth weight and supplemental oxygen therapy (given for respiratory distress syndrome). ROP can be mild and may resolve spontaneously , but may lead to blindness in serious cases .203

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Which of the following is included under threshold disease when screening neonates for retinopathy of prematurity ?

options.a: ROP stage 1 extending from 6'o clock to 11 '0 clock in zone 1 with plus disease
options.b: ROP stage 3 extending from 2'o clock to 7'o clock in zone 2 with plus disease
options.c: ROP stage 3 extending from 1'o clock to 4'o clock in zone 1 without plus disease
options.d: ROP stage 2 extending from 3'o clock to 6'o clock in zone 2 with plus disease

mcqs.explanation: ROP stage 3 extending from 2'0 clock to 7'o clock (6 clock hours) in zone 2 with plus disease fits into the definition of threshold disease. Threshold disease of retinopathy of prematurity is defined by the CRYO-ROP study as: • Stage 3 disease : Ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous • Involvement of zones 1 or 2 • Involvement of either at least 5 contiguous (continuous ) clock hours or 8 non-contiguous clock hours • Associated with "plus disease ": Dilatation and tortuosity of posterior pole vessels in at least two quadrants at the posterior pole . Treatment of threshold disease is laser photocoagulation of the involved part within 72 hours of diagnosis.Treatment of the various stages of ROP includes : • Pre-threshold type 1 disease - Treatment is now recommended within 48 hours and is done by laser photocoagulation of avascular retina. • Pre-threshold type 2 disease (Any ROP not following under type 1)- Observation for progression • Threshold disease - Laser photocoagulation of avascular retina • Aggresive posterior-ROP- Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents , eg ., bevacizumab • Tractional retinal detachment (stage 4A) - Pars plana vitrectomy204

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: All of the following are true statements regarding retinopathy of prematurity except :

options.a: First screening should be done 32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks PNA, whichever is later
options.b: For infants less than 28 week , screen at 3 week of postnatal age to detect APROP
options.c: Neonates are best examined at ophthalmology OPD and hence should be transported
options.d: Screening is done using indirect ophthalmoscopy by an expert ophthalmologist

mcqs.explanation: Neonates are best examined in the neonatal unit itself under the supervision of the attending neonatologist. It is not recommended to transport infants to the ophthalmic outpatient department for examination. The first screening examination should be carried out by indirect ophthalmoscopy at 32 weeks PMA or 4 weeks PNA, whichever is later. For infants born at less than 28 weeks , screening is done at 3 weeks PNA to detect APROP . Aggressive posterior ROP ("rush" disease , AP-ROP), if untreated , usually progresses to total retinal detachment (stage 5) within a few days. It is characterized by its posterior location, prominence of plus disease and ill-defined nature of the retinopathy .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A preterm neonate admitted to NICU who received supplemental oxygen is being screened for retinopathy of prematurity . Fundus examination reveals a subtotal retinal detachment. How will you stage the disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Subtotal retinal detachment is considered to be stage 4 of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The clinical staging of ROP is as follows: • Stage 1 - Formation of a demarcation line at the edge of vessels , dividing the vascular from the avascular retina. • Stage 2- Formation of an intraretinal ridge • Stage 3- Ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous • Stage 4- Subtotal retinal detachment • Stage 5- Total retinal detachment205

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 14-day-old neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation had developed respiratory distress syndrome at birth. You want to screen for retinopathy of prematurity . How many weeks from now would you schedule the screening ?
mcqs.explanation: In the scenario above, the postnatal age of the premature infant is 2 weeks , and therefore , the infant must be screened in 2 weeks i.e., 4 weeks of postnatal age , as per the guidelines for the management of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). ROP guidelines state that the first examination should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of postnatal age (after birth) or between 31 –33 weeks of post -conceptional age (calculated as gestational age + postnatal age ), whichever is later. Ideally , 2 examinations must be performed ; however, 1 may suffice if it shows complete retinal vascularisation.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important factor for the development of diabetic retinopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: 206 The most important factor for the development of diabetic retinopathy is the duration of diabetes . Diabetic retinopathy constitutes the retinal changes seen in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus . The most important factor for its development is duration of diabetes after the onset of puberty , followed by glycemic control. It is more common in type 1 diabetes mellitus . The presence of hypertension increases the risk of diabetic retinopathy . First fundus examination for type 1 diabetes is done after 5 years after diagnosis and for type 2 is done at the time of diagnosis. The frequency of follow -up for types 1 and 2 diabetes mellitus is every year. Diabetes in pregnancy is followed up every 3 months. The earliest feature of diabetic retinopathy is microaneurysms, which are present in the inner nuclear layer of the retina.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings on a fundus examination would suggest severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy ?

options.a: Significant venous beading in any of the 4 quadrants

mcqs.explanation: Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants is a feature of severe NPDR. Note : Macular star is a feature of malignant hypertensive retinopathy .

mcqs.question: A person is diagnosed to have diabetes on his 45th birthday. When will you recommend a dilated fundus examination for him?

options.d: When he complains of decrease in vision

mcqs.explanation: A 45 year old diagnosed with diabetes mellitus is likely to have type 2 diabetes and thus , he should undergo screening for diabetic retinopathy immediately . Duration of diabetes is the most important risk factor for developing diabetic retinopathy , especially proliferative diabetic retinopathy . The recommendations for first fundus examination in diabetic retinopathy is: • Within 3-5 years of diagnosis in type 1 diabetes • Immediately in type 2 diabetes .207 Later, the screening is continued once every year in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes . In the event proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops , screening is done more frequently - once every 2 months.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology

mcqs.question: ETDRS study was related to?
mcqs.explanation: Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) was a randomized clinical trial that studied the effect of photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema . The results of the study demonstrated the beneficial effects of focal photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema. The study resulted in the recommendation that all eyes with clinically significant diabetic macular edema should be considered for focal photocoagulation .

mcqs.question: A patient with a history of diabetes and hypertension underwent fundus fluorescent angiography (FFA) to evaluate his decreasing vision. The FFA yields an image as shown below , which is characteristic of:
mcqs.explanation: The fundus fluorescent angiography (FFA) image shows enlarged foveal avascular zone, seen as a hypofluorescent patch in the macula (white arrow), with surrounding capillary non perfused areas (blue arrow). Both of these are suggestive of macular ischemia.The above mentioned findings when combined with the history of diabetes in this patient points towards the diagnosis of diabetic macular ischemia. FFA images in a case of diabetic retinopathy are given below : • Non proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) • Punctate or pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence - microaneurysms • Abnormal branching of arteriovenous shunt - intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) • Patchy filling defects of ischemia due to capillary atrophy or non perfusion208 • Increase in the size of hypoperfusion in foveal avascular zone in macular ischemia 2. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy(PDR) • Fluorescein leakage - in retinal neovascularization. • Leakage in the disc region suggests neovascularization of the disc (NVD) and leakage in other regions suggests neovascularization elsewhere (NVE). The image below shows pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence and areas of fluorescein leakage in the fundus .Option B: Macular edema also known as cystoid macular edema (CME ) is a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer of the retina following a break in the blood-retina barrier . On fundoscopy , a honeycomb appearance is seen , and on FFA, flower petal pattern can be seen . The below image shows the flower petal pattern on FFA as seen in CME .209 Option C: Submacular hemorrhage also known as subretinal hemorrhage will obscure the choroidal dye visualization and appaers as ill defined areas of hypoperfusion in the corresponding area. The retinal vessels overlying the area would , however will be visualized. There are no assosciated features of pinpoint hyperfluorescence and vascular leakage that are usually seen with diabetic macular ischemia. The below given images show fluorescein angiography which reveal blocked fluorescence in the maculae of both eyes due to subretinal hemorrhages.Option D: Premacular hemorrhage is a term used to define vitreous hemorrhage that occurs in the subhyaloid space . It is seen as a region of hypofluorescence with no overlying retinal vasculature visualization on FFA.

mcqs.question: A 69-year-old patient with hypertension has silver wiring, papilledema , and arteriovenous nipping visible on fundoscopy , but no other changes . How would you grade his disease ?
mcqs.explanation: 210 A patient with hypertension having "silver wiring," papilledema , and arteriovenous nipping visible on fundoscopy has Grade IV retinopathy .

mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male, newly diagnosed with systolic hypertension , presents with a three -week history of bilateral blurry vision. His visual acuity is 20 /30 and 20 /120 in the right and left eye , respectively . The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Which of the following findings is least likely to be seen on his fundoscopy ?
mcqs.explanation: Systolic hypertension (systolic blood pressure over 200 mm Hg) with bilateral blurry vision and unremarkable examination findings point to a diagnosis of hypertensive retinopathy . Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) are not seen in hypertensive retinopathy . IRMA is a feature of diabetic retinopathy . Arteriolar narrowing occurs due to vasoconstriction and sclerosis of retinal vessels due to hypertension. Cotton wool spots are areas of nerve fibre layer infarcts. They occur due to capillary obliteration in hypertension .211

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: The following image shows the picture of the fundus in a patient taken 48 hours after sustaining severe head trauma. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows multiple cotton wool spots around the disc. This is Purtschers' retinopathy , which is classically associated with severe head injury. It is also seen in pancreatitis and chest trauma due to fat/air embolism. Ophthalmoscopy reveals multiple , variably sized cotton-wool spots and intraretinal hemorrhages around the optic nerve. There is no effective treatment .

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true regarding sickle cell retinopathy ?

options.a: Sea-fan appearance is seen in supero -temporal quadrant .
options.b: HbSS has more severe ocular manifestations than HbSC.
options.d: Central retinal vein occlusion may be seen .

mcqs.explanation: Hemoglobin SC and S-Thal disease have the most severe ocular manifestations , although sickle SS disease has the most severe systemic manifestations . The incidence of proliferative retinopathy in SC disease (Hb SC) is 33%, sickle cell thalassemia (Hb S-Thal) is 14%, SS disease (Hb SS) is 3%. In sickle cell retinopathy , elevated blood viscosity may occlude venules and arterioles, as well as capillaries . The following fundus findings can be noted as a result : • Retinal vascular peripheral non-perfusion • Retinal hemorrhages: "salmon patches ," "iridescent spots ," and "black sunbursts" are hallmarks of nonproliferative sickle cell retinopathy. • Peripheral retinal neovascularization in a "sea fan" configuration is the hallmark of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy . They are also described as "parachute " lesions . They are most commonly found in the supero -temporal vascular arcades. • Angioid streaks (Rupture of Bruch's membrane) Conjunctival "comma-shaped " capillaries and iris atrophy are other ocular findings seen . Complications of sickle cell retinopathy include central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO ) (occurs due to retinal hypoxia), vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment . The image below shows 'sea fans' as seen on fluorescein angiography.212

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Roth spots are seen in ________.
mcqs.explanation: Roth's spots are seen in acute leukemia. Roth's spots are retinal hemorrhages with white or pale center . The white centre due to coagulated fibrin -platelet plug is surrounded by red rim that is caused by hemorrhage. Roth's spots may be seen in: • Subacute bacterial endocarditis • Leukemia • Diabetes • Sickle cell retinopathy • Hypertensive retinopathy • HIV retinopathy • Systemic lupus erythematosus The fundus image below shows Roth's spots .213 Option B: Uveal melanoma devolps due to malignant transformation of the normal melanocytes present in the uveal tissue . Primary posterior uveal melanoma (choroidal melanoma) which forms the majority of uveal melanoma manifests as: • A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown dome shaped mass • "Collar stud " appearance on B-scan - when the tumor breaks through the Bruchs membrane and protrudes into subretinal space • "Double circulation" sign Primary anterior uveal melanoma frequently involves the iris and presents as nodular melanocytic mass on the iris. The below given fundus image shows the "double circulation sign" of choroidal melanoma.Option C: Uveal lymphoma is characterized by localized or diffuse uveal infiltrates of malignant lymphoma cells . Fundus examination in these patients show diffuse creamy thickening of posterior uvea with nodular accentuation .214

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with 6/6 vision in the right eye and vision for only hand movements in the left eye . On fundoscopy , the right eye appears normal . The left eye shows retinal detachment , subretinal yellowish exudates , and telangiectatic vessels . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Unilateral decreased vision with retinal detachment , subretinal yellowish exudates and telangiectatic vessels in a young boy points to the diagnosis of Coats' disease . Coats' disease , described by Coats in 1908, affects boys three times more often than girls, has no reported racial or ethnic predilection , and is usually unilateral. The average age at diagnosis is 8–16 years. The clinical course is generally progressive . It is characterized by discrete zones of retinal vascular abnormalities like aneurysmal dilatation and leakage. It is associated with localized lipid deposition (hard exudates ) and varying degrees of subretinal exudates . Vessels may appear telangiectatic , and they may have aneurysms that are grape-like, clustered , or light bulb-shaped . The image below depicts the typical vascular abnormalities with aneurysmal dilatation, telangiectasia , exudation , and severe lipid deposition in the macula which are seen in Coat's disease .

mcqs.question: A 64-year-old female presented with complaints of blurring of vision and pain in her left eye . She also gave a history of redness in her left eye about 3 months back, which she passed off as normal conjunctivitis. On tonometry, the IOP is 55 mm Hg. The slit-lamp revealed rubeosis iridis in all four quadrants. The fundus picture of the patient is given below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Monocular blurring of vision and pain with "splashed sauce " appearance on fundoscopy points towards a diagnosis of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO ). Ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO ) is characterised by sudden visual loss. There is splashed sauce appearance on fundoscopy due to retinal hemorrhages. Risk factors include high intraocular pressure (IOP), hypertension and blood viscosity syndromes. Its complications include neovascularisation of the iris (rubeosis iridis) and neovascular glaucoma (NVG). NVG typically occurs 3 months after the occlusive event. Up to 50% of eyes develop NVG following ischaemic CRVO . Pan-retinal photocoagulation is the treatment of choice .215 CRVO is classified into two types : • Ischemic CRVO : Characterized by relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD ), markedly reduced visual acuity, and many cotton-wool spots • Non-ischemic CRVO : Characterized by normal pupillary reaction, reduced visual acuity , and few cotton-wool spots Treatment usually involves treating the underlying cause and complications .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A man with history of hypertension and loss of vision in the left eye has the following fundoscopy findings. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image above demonstrates characteristic flame-shaped hemorrhages, localized to the superotemporal sector of the retina. The image, along with loss of vision and history of hypertension , points to a diagnosis of branched retinal vein occlusion (BRVO ), specifically affecting the superotemporal branch of the retinal vein. Occlusion of a single branch of the retinal vein leads to branched retinal vein occlusion . This occlusion leads to impaired venous drainage, resulting in the accumulation of blood within the retina. The visual defect in BRVO tends to be partial. Note : The different types of retinal vascular obstructions are branched retinal vein obstruction (BRVO ), central retinal vein obstruction (CRVO ), branched retinal artery obstruction (BRAO) and central retinal artery obstruction (CRAO). Retinal vein occlusion (RVO ) is the second most common retinal vascular disorder after diabetic retinopathy . In CRVO , tortuosity and engorgement of all branches of the central retinal vein are seen , affecting all quadrants of the retina.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden painless vision loss in his left eye . He has had a similar episode before but his vision was quickly restored . On physical exam, a carotid bruit is heard and a relative afferent pupillary defect is noted on ocular examination. His fundus appears as shown below . Which of the following is the best immediate step in the management of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Sudden painless unilateral vision loss with carotid bruit (carotid artery disease ) and the fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The best immediate step in management is ocular massage among the given options . Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) occurs due to obstruction of the retinal artery at the level of lamina cribrosa. Risk factors include heart disease , carotid artery disease , mucormycosis, varicella infection , radiation exposure and trauma. It may be caused by the following : • Emboli of carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli • Atherosclerosis -related thrombosis • Retinal arteritis with obliteration • Angiospasm • Raised intraocular pressure • Thrombophilic disorders216 Patients often present with sudden painless monocular loss of vision with history of a similar episode that resolved spontaneously (amaurosis fugax). On examination, direct pupillary reflex is absent and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD ) is positive . Fundus examination shows marked attenuation of arteries (thread like arteries), interrupted blood flow in vein (cattle track appearance ), cherry red spot , severe edema and retinal pallor. A cherry-red spot of the macula is typical and arises in this area because of the absence of ganglion cells at the foveola resulting in the transmission of the normal choroidal color. This in contrast to the surrounding area where intense retinal whitening blocks the transmission of the normal choroidal color. Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by IV acetazolamide or ocular massage . Ocular massage is considered the most effective method . Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy , or laser photodisruption in some cases . In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial .

mcqs.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with complaints of sudden painless loss of vision in the left eye since yesterday. She also gives a history of temporal headaches , myalgias, and pain in the jaw while chewing . Examination of the left eye reveals a visual acuity of HM+ and an RAPD . Fundus examination of the left eye shows cattle trucking of blood within the retinal veins on applying gentle pressure . Which of the following is the likely cause of fundal findings?

options.c: Non- ischemic central retinal venous occlusion

mcqs.explanation: A 52-year-old woman temporal headaches , myalgias and pain in the jaw while chewing likely has giant cell arteritis (GCA). Given that she has sudden painless monocular loss of vision with RAPD and points to a diagnosis of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). GCA is the most common primary vasculitis in adults . It is a risk factor for the development of CRAO. CRAO occurs due to obstruction of the retinal artery at the level of lamina cribrosa. When obstruction to the blood flow is not complete , the flow may be partially restored . Thus, gentle pressure upon the globe may break the column of venous blood into red beads separated by clear interspaces . This gives the characteristic 'cattle truck' appearance . Option A: Ischemic CRVO shows a characteristic "splashed tomato sauce " appearance on fundoscopy . Option C: Non-Ischemic CRVO does not present with such a severe loss of visual acuity . Option D: Branched retinal artery occlusion presents with hemifield visual defects .

mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden painless loss of vision. Fundoscopy findings are shown below . Which of the following findings do you expect in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Sudden painless monocular loss of vision with fundoscopy showing Hollehorst plaque is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion ( CRAO ). Relative afferent pupillary defect is seen in these cases . Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli that are seen in retinal arterioles . On fundus examination , it gives an appearance of a refractile yellow -white color substance in the retinal vessels . Note : Although elevated intraocular pressure has been implicated as a cause of central retinal artery obstruction, it is unlikely that intraocular pressure can be raised high enough to block arterial inflow to the eye217

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye . He describes the sensation that a curtain was coming up over his affected eye . In addition, 7 days ago the patient noticed what he described as flashing lights and floaters . He gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. A B-scan image of his left eye is shown below . Which of the following statements best describes the pathology ?

options.b: Fibrovascular membranes in the vitreous causing traction
options.c: Fluid accumulation between NSR and RPE due to retinal tear
options.d: Fluid accumulation between NSR and RPE due to choroidal exudation

mcqs.explanation: The prodromal symptoms of flashing lights , floaters followed by loss of monocular vision (curtain over the eye ) and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment . Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the result of the accumulation of fluid between NSR and RPE due to a retinal tear. Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium . Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is the most common type of retinal detachment . It occurs due to fluid accumulation after a retinal break (tear). High myopia, trauma, pseudophakia , aphakia are predisposing factors. Patients present with photopsia (flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break), floaters and visual field defect (black curtain/veil in front of the eye ). Signs include hypotony , as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE and Shafers sign or tobacco dusting (pigments in the anterior vitreous). The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations . The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear and the most dangerous location of retinal break is the supero -temporal retina. Treatment is by prophylactic laser barrage, scleral buckling, pneumatic retinopexy and pars plana vitrectomy . Other types of retinal detachment are tractional and exudative type : Tractional retinal detachment occurs when fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina. It is seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, central retinal venous occlusion , Eales disease and ROP. The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen . Treatment is with pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation . Exudative retinal detachment is seen when exudative fluid from the choroid collects in the subretinal space . Patients present with visual field defects , floaters due to vitritis but no218 photopsia . The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen . Shifting fluid is seen . The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with tear at 3:30 .

mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Pneumatic retinopexy is an outpatient procedure where retinal detachment is sealed with air insufflation . Which of the following gases would you use while performing the said procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: Sulphur hexafluoride is the gas used in pneumatic retinopexy for the treatment of retinal detachments Pneumatic retinopexy is used for the treatment of fresh retinal detachments with a single retinal break in the superior two -thirds of the fundus . In this procedure , a bubble is injected intravitreally through the conjunctiva and postoperatively the patient is positioned so that the bubble tamponades the retinal break against the retinal pigment epithelium .219

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman who is 8 months pregnant, myopic, and diabetic presents to you with sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye . She is a known case of Eales ' disease . Her blood pressure is 170/110 mmHg. Which of her conditions is responsible for a fundus finding of retinal detachment with a positive shifting fluid sign?
mcqs.explanation: Exudative retinal detachment is characterized by positive shifting fluid sign. Among her conditions, toxemia of pregnancy is one of the causes of exudative retinal detachment . Exudative retinal detachment occurs due to the presence of subretinal fluid in the absence of tear or traction. It is caused by: • Malignant melanoma of the choroid • Retinoblastoma • Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) syndrome • Uveal effusion syndrome • Posterior scleritis • Coat's disease • Malignant hypertension • Pregnancy-induced hypertensive retinopathy • Sympathetic ophthalmitis Patients present with sudden and painless diminution of vision, visual field defects and grey reflex (detached retina looks grey). Indirect ophthalmoscopy is the investigation of choice . The image depicts retinal detachment showing a smooth, detached convex retina with subretinal fluid.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Shifting fluid sign is seen in?
mcqs.explanation: 220 The presence of shifting fluid is a hallmark feature of serous or exudative retinal detachment . In serous retinal detachment , there is a subretinal accumulation of the serous fluid mostly due to the breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier . When the position of the head is altered , the fluid shifts to the dependent portion. Serous retinal detachment has a smooth convex configuration. A retinal tear or preretinal traction is absent. Other options : Option B: Traction RD has a concave configuration and breaks are absent. Retinal mobility is severely reduced and shifting fluid is absent. Option C: Rhegmatogenous RD presents with tobacco dust in anterior vitreous with substantial vitreous blood or inflammatory cells . Retinal breaks are also seen .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Hollenhorst plaques are seen in _______.
mcqs.explanation: Hollenhorst plaques are seen in central retinal arterial occlusion (CRAO). They are cholesterol emboli seen in retinal arterioles . They originate from atherosclerotis plaques in larger arteries. The image below shows Hollenhorst plaques (arrow).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: Identify the condition.
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a loss of foveal reflex and central serous retinopathy , therefore showing focal foveal detachment . There is oedema at the fovea signifying foveal detachment from underlying retinal pigment epithelium . Macular oedema is also present (grey dull retina with a ring reflex around the site of oedema ). Thus, the most appropriate choice would be foveal detachment .221 Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of neurosensory retina in the macular region. It occurs due to increased permeability of choriocapillaris, leading to fluid accumulation in the subretinal space . Therefore, it is now known as central serous choriopathy (CSC). If there is serous retinal detachment at macula, there is sudden painless loss of vision. Patients also have relative positive scotoma, micropsia and metamorphopsia . On ophthalmoscopy , a circular ring reflex present . The foveal reflex is absent. On fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), an enlarging ink -blot pattern or smoke-stack pattern is seen . Treatment is generally not required. It is usually self -limiting, but often recurrent. Steroids are contraindicated.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is the given sign seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The image depicts fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showing an enlarging ink -blot pattern/enlarging dot sign, which is seen in central serous retinopathy (CSR). Smokestack appearance is another pattern of fundus seen in CSR and is a characteristic sign of this condition. Amsler grid is used for: • Assess macular function and detecting maculopathy . • Evaluate the visual field of 10 \260 • Good for follow -up in CSR222

mcqs.chapter: Retinal vascular disorders and Retinal detachment
mcqs.question: The ETDRS chart is used for visual evaluation in diabetic patients . What does ETDRS stand for?

options.a: Extended treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
options.b: Early treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
options.c: Emergency treatment for diabetic retinopathy study
options.d: Emerging treatment for diabetic retinopathy study

mcqs.explanation: ETDRS stands for Early Treatment for Diabetic Retinopathy Study . ETDRS was a clinical trial designed to evaluate if argon laser photocoagulation or aspirin treatment can reduce the risk of visual loss or slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy in patients with mild-to-severe nonproliferative or early proliferative diabetic retinopathy . During the study , three new visual acuity charts were created in place of Snellen 's visual chart.223

mcqs.question: A 25-year-old artist visits an art gallery . A painting of checkered squares appears distorted only to him, as shown below . He decides to go see an ophthalmologist who after initial evaluation, suggests an FFA. The FFA shows a characteristic smoke stack appearance . Breakdown of which of the following barriers is responsible for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a characteristic smoke stack pattern on FFA is suggestive of a diagnosis of central serous retinopathy. In CSR, the outer blood-retinal barrier is disrupted . CSR is the serous detachment of the neurosensory retina with focal and multifocal areas of leakage at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), mainly affecting the macular area. That is why the patient who is usually a young male presents with macular symptoms such as blurring of central vision, metamorphopsia. The blood-retina barrier (BRB ) is composed of inner and outer barriers . The outer BRB refers to the barrier formed at the retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cell layer and regulates the movement of solutes and nutrients from the choroid to the sub-retinal space . By contrast, the inner BRB , similar to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is located in the inner retinal microvasculature and comprises the microvascular endothelium, which lines these vessels . The image given below shows the smoke-stack pattern seen in CSR.Amsler grid is used in detecting maculopathy . Uses : • Assess macular function • Evaluate the visual field of 10 \260 • Good for follow -up in CSR The image below shows Amsler's grid.237

mcqs.question: Where does fluid accumulate in central serous retinopathy ?

options.a: Between the Bruch membrane and retinal pigment epithelium
options.c: Between the outer plexiform layer and inner nuclear layer

mcqs.explanation: Fluid accumulation in central serous retinopathy (CSR) is in the subretinal space due to abnormal permeability of the choriocapillaris. The image depicts optical coherence tomography showing fluid accumulation in the subretinal space , with shallow retinal detachment .

mcqs.question: A 60-year-old female presented with acute loss of vision and metamorphopsia . There is a history of the positive scotoma. Fundal changes are given below . What will be the fundus fluorescein angiography finding?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario and the fundal image depicting focal fundal detachment are suggestive of central serous retinopathy . An enlarging inkblot pattern or smoke stack pattern is seen in FFA.238 Central serous retinopathy refers to the spontaneous serous detachment of the neurosensory retina in the macular region. Recent studies implicate an abnormal choroidal circulation as the cause of CSR. Clinical features : • Retinal detachment - Sudden painless loss of vision • Relative positive scotoma • Micropsia • Metamorphopsia Investigations: • Ophthalmoscopy - circular ring reflex present and foveal reflex absent • FFA - enlarging inkblot pattern or smoke stack pattern Spontaneous resolution is seen in most cases and hence observation is enough. Steroids are contraindicated . The disease is usually self -limiting but may recur. The image depicts fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), showing an enlarging ink -blot pattern/enlarging dot sign, which is seen in central serous retinopathy (CSR).Other options : Option B- Petaloid appearance is seen in cystoid macular edema Option C- Stars in the sky appearance is suggestive of drusen Option D- Dual circulation is a pathognomonic feature of choroidal melanoma

mcqs.question: A 69-year-old man who is a chronic smoker, hypertensive , and has a BMI of 35 kg/m2 complains of diminished vision in the right eye . His visual acuity is 6/36 BE and the anterior segment appears normal . His fundus is as shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario along with the image which shows drusen (druplets ) are a feature of dry or non-exudative age -related macular degeneration (ARMD).239 Drusen are the earliest visible clinical signs of ARMD. They are composed of lipid , amyloid, complement factors, and associated cellular components . There are two types of ARMD: • Dry (non-exudative, non-neovascular) ARMD is the most common form, comprising around 90% of the diagnosed cases . Initially characterized by macular Drusens, which later progress to geographical atrophy. Geographic atrophy (GA) is the advanced stage of dry ARMD. Antioxidants like the AREDS2 supplements have proven effective . • Wet (exudative , neovascular) ARMD is much less common than the dry type , but it is associated with more rapid progression to advanced sight loss. mcqs.question: Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is primarily indicated in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is primarily indicated in an occult choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM). ICGA is used to visualize the choroidal vasculature. Its main use is to differentiate between classic and occult CNVM when the clinical picture is not clear.

mcqs.question: Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF is used in the treatment of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is used as the treatment of wet age -related macular degeneration (ARMD).240 Wet ARMD is characterized by retinal pigment epithelial detachment and choroidal/subretinal neovascularization. Treatment of ARMD depends on the location of the choroidal neovascularization membrane: • For extrafoveal membrane - Laser photocoagulation • For subfoveal and juxta foveal membranes, treatment options are as follows : • Intravitreal injection of anti -VEGF agents • Photodynamic therapy - the dye used is verteporfin followed by exposure to light from a diode • Transpupillary thermotherapy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: An old cab driver whose livelihood depends on his driving is distressed . He complains that everything appears distorted and he perceives objects to smaller than their usual size. His anterior segment appears normal . Examination of the fundus reveals a honeycomb appearance of the macula. FFA is shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image is that of fluorescein angiography showing the "flower petal pattern," which is seen in cystoid macular edema (CME ). The characteristic flower -petal appearance is due to the accumulation of dye in the outer plexiform layer and inner nuclear layer at the macula The accumulation of fluid in the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer leads to retinal thickening at macula and loss of foveal depression , formation of cystic spaces (honey-comb macula). Risk factors include retinitis pigmentosa , uveitis, niacin, PGE2 analogues , epinephrine in aphakia, diabetic retinopathy , retinal venous occlusion and Irvin -Gass syndrome (CME post -cataract surgery). Symptoms may include blurring of vision, distortion, and micropsia. Therapeutic approaches for treating CME depend on the underlying etiology . This includes steroids , carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, anti-VEGF agents , PPV for associated vitreomacular traction.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the emergency department and is found to have a corneal abrasion, corneal ulcer, corneal perforation, and foreign body. Which of the following will not cause hypotonic maculopathy in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Suprachoroidal hemorrhage will not cause hypotonic maculopathy in this patient . Maculopathy is common in eyes developing hypotony , which is defined as IOP <6 mmHg. The most common cause is excessive drainage following glaucoma filtration surgery (Option D). Other causes include trauma such as cyclodialysis of the uvea (Option B), penetrating injury (Option C), chronic uveitis, retinal detachment , and other systemic causes such as dehydration , uncontrolled diabetes , uremia, and treatment with hyperosmotic agents . They usually cause bilateral hypotonic maculopathy . Suprachoroidal hemorrhage is a bleed into the suprachoroidal space that results from the rupture of the posterior ciliary artery. When the bleed is severe it causes extrusion of intraocular contents that is termed as expulsive hemorrhage. It is a rare but dreaded complication of the phacoemulsification procedure . Signs seen in suprachoroidal hemorrhage are: • Progressive increase in intraocular pressure • Prolapse of iris241 • Loss or partial obscuration of the red reflex • In severe cases there can be extrusion of the posterior segment contents into the anterior chamber and through the incision such as vitreous extrusion Immediate treatment involves rapid closure of the incision followed by administration of IOP-lowering medications such as oral acetazolamide and topical or systemic steroids to reduce inflammation. Standard post -operative antibiotics can be added in these patients .

mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A 45-year old patient on systemic treatment for rheumatoid arthritis develops bilateral painless decrease in vision. What does the image show?

options.a: Fluorescein angiography showing bull's eye maculopathy
options.b: Autofluorescence showing changes of bull's eye maculopathy

mcqs.explanation: The investigation shown in the image is an autofluorescence showing bull's eye maculopathy . Hydroxychloroquine, which is generally used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, toxicity causes bull's eye maculopathy . Chloroquine binds to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium , causing cytotoxic effects . RPE atrophy occurs in the macula, resulting in dark areas on the autofluorescence image. Other causes of Bull's eye maculopathy include chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, congenital cone dystrophy , juvenile X-linked retinoschisis, and juvenile Batten's disease . Fundus autofluorescence is a non-invasive imaging modality . It reflects the morphological changes associated with the metabolism of lipofuscin and does not require the injection of any fluorescent dye . A fundus image of bull's eye maculopathy is shown below :The following image shows the difference between fundus autofluorescence and fluorescence angiography242 Other ocular effects of chloroquine include : • Chloroquine keratopathy—vortex keratopathy • Ocular palsy , ptosis • Electroretinographic depression • Optic neuritis • Posterior subcapsular cataract

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A study used electroretinography (ERG) in military conscripts whose visual abnormalities could not be explained by the findings of ophthalmologic , neurological , and psychiatric examinations. The ERG of pure malingerers was found to be, as shown below . The activity of which cells of the retina is depicted by the a-wave?
mcqs.explanation: "a" wave in an electroretinogram (ERG) represents rods and cones. Electroretinography is used to evaluate retinal functions by examining the electrical response to a light stimulus . Electroretinograms (ERGs) show the amplitudes of currents that flow within the eye following exposure to a point of light . The amplitudes are analyzed into waves, which are composed of the responses of neuronal, glial, and retinal pigment epithelial cells . ERG: • The a-wave originates from photoreceptors (rods and cones) • The b-wave originates from Muller and bipolar cells , but is directly dependant on photoreceptors • The c-wave originates from retinal pigment epithelial cells and retinal glial cells • Oscillatory potentials (OPs) originate in the inner retina Scotopic ERGs are used to evaluate responses starting from rod photoreceptors exposed to flash-light in darkness, and photopic ERGs are used to evaluate responses starting from cone photoreceptors exposed to flash-light under constant light exposure .243

mcqs.question: Which area of the retina has the highest concentration of rods?
mcqs.explanation: Mid-periphery of the retina has the highest concentration of rods. mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A researcher is studying mutations in the rhodopsin gene which are responsible for some forms of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa . On which chromosome is this gene located ?
mcqs.explanation: The gene for rhodopsin is located at 3q22 .1 Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected . It is a genetic disease . The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary types , it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis. The presenting feature is night blindness . Investigations: • Perimetry - the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision. • Electroretinography - reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves. Retinitis pigmentosa is a condition with no cure. There are drugs used to slow down the progression such as acetazolamide for concomitant cystoid macular edema . Recently , vitamin A has been recommended , although the efficacy has not been established .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?

options.a: RPE forms the inner blood retinal barrier
options.b: Electroculogram is an assessment of RPE health
options.d: Bruch's membrane is the basement membrane of RPE

mcqs.explanation: Tight junctions between retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) form the outer blood-retinal barrier . The inner blood-retinal barrier is formed by the tight junctions between the endothelial cells of retinal capillaries . RPE serves many functions, like • Development of photoreceptors during embryogenesis244 • Tight junctions between RPE form the outer blood-retinal barrier • Absorption of fluid from the subretinal space and adhesion of the underlying neurosensory retina • Selective transport of metabolites to and from the retina • Uptake , transport, storage , metabolism , and isomerization of vitamin A • Regeneration of the visual pigment rhodopsin • Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segment tips • Absorption of stray light by melanin If the RPE is damaged , this is seen as a loss of autofluorescence (RPE-deficient areas appear darker on autofluorescence images). Bruch's membrane is the basement membrane of RPE.

mcqs.question: Which of the following disorders is not associated with retinitis pigmentosa ?
mcqs.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is associated with abetalipoprotenemia (Bassen–Kornzweig syndrome) and not with abetaglobulinemia .Syndromes associated with R P (Atypical RP) Usher syndrome Sensory neuraldeafness + RP Bardet–Biedl syndrome(Previ ously called Lawrence–Moon –Biedl–Bartum Syndrome) Polydactyly , obesity , mental handicap, and kidney disease + RP Kearn–Sayre syndrome Ocular myopathy and heart d isease + RP Refsum Syndrome Varied skin as well as neurol ogical and visceral features + RP Bassen–Kornzweig syndrome Abetalipoprotenemia and aca nthocytosis + RP Neuropathy , ataxia, and retin itis pigmentosa (NARP) Neuropathy and Ataxia + RP

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about retinitis pigmentosa ?
mcqs.explanation: Electroretinogram (ERG) is abnormal in retinitis pigmentosa (RP). ERG is a sensitive diagnostic test in retinitis pigmentosa that shows reduced scotopic , subnormal responses in early disease and becomes completely extinguished in advanced disease . Electroocoulogram (EOG ) is also abnormal in retinitis pigmentosa .245 Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited or acquired pigmentatory retinal dystrophy affecting the rods more than the cones. The earliest manifestation is worsening of night blindness and delayed adaptation which gradually progresses to tunnel vision and ultimately loss of central vision. The classic triad of findings in RP comprises : • Bone-spicule retinal pigmentation • Arteriolar attenuation • 'Waxy' disc pallor The image below shows the classical triad findings of retinitis pigmentosa .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: What is the diagnosis from the image given below ?
mcqs.explanation: The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules , which implies retinitis pigmentosa (RP). Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected . It is a genetic disease . The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary type , it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis. The presenting feature is night blindness . Investigations: • Perimetry - the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision. • Electroretinography - reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves. Atypical types of RP are as follows : • Sectoral RP • Pericentric/Inverse RP246 • RP sine pigmento • RP punctata albescens There is no effective treatment for RP.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is the Mizuo phenomenon seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Mizuo phenomenon is seen in Oguchi's disease . Oguchi 's disease is a type of congenital stationary night blindness with abnormal fundus . Congenital stationary night blindness refers to a group of disorders characterized by infantile-onset nyctalopia but non-progressive retinal dysfunction . The fundus has an unusual golden yellow color in the light -adapted state , which becomes normal after prolonged dark adaptation (Mizuo or Mizuo–Nakamura phenomenon ). The following image shows a comparison in the fundus appearances ("A" shows the golden yellow color of the fundus in a light -adapted state ; "B" shows normal -appearing funds after prolonged dark adaptation of 3 to 4 hours)Rod function is absent even after 30 minutes of dark adaptation (normal dark adaptation time is 20–30 mins) but recovers to a near-normal level after a long period of dark adaptation (4 hours).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Flat electrooculogram (EOG ) is an Arden ratio of _______.
mcqs.explanation: A flat electrooculogram (EOG ) is an Arden ratio of less than 1.25. An EOG measures the standing potential of the eye . It reflects the activity of the RPE and the photoreceptors. This means that an eye blinded by disease proximal to the photoreceptors will have a normal EOG . Arden ratio is the ratio between the light peak and the dark trough in an EOG .247 The normal Arden ratio is 1.85 and above. A flat EOG occurs when the Arden ratio is less than 1.25. Best disease is an autosomal-dominant childhood disease characterized by the dystrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium . In Best disease , the Arden ratio is less than 1.50.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A young patient presents with loss of central vision. ERG is normal , but EOG is abnormal . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis based on the above scenario is Best 's disease . Best 's disease/Vitelliform macular dystrophy is an inherited macular dystrophy in which lipofuscin accumulates in the central macula causing progressive central vision loss. It is autosomal-dominant and linked to the mutation in the bestrophin (VMD2 ) gene . It is characterized by bilateral yellow , yolk-like (vitelliform) macular lesions . The stages of evolution of the macular lesions are described as progressing from: • Pre-vitelliform stage • Vitelliform stage - scrambled egg stage with or without hypopyon • Vitelliruptive - the lesion breaks and visual acuity drops • The atrophic stage Patients with Best 's disease usually have good visual acuity when the "yolk" remains intact. Diagnosis: This is the only disease with relatively normal ERG results associated with an abnormal EOG. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) reveals that the vitelliform material appears as a dome-shaped , hyperreflective , and homogenous lesion, located below the hyperreflective photoreceptor layer. The image below shows Best 's disease - the typical vitelliform lesion in an 11 -year-old girl.248

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A young patient presents with loss of central vision. There is a family history of a similar condition. Both EOG and ERG are normal . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis based on the given scenario is Stargardt's disease . Stargardt's disease also known as Stargardt macular dystrophy or fundus flavimaculatus is the most common macular dystrophy . It most commonly is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner caused by a mutation on an adenosine triphosphate -binding cassette (ABCA4) gene . Characterized by macular "pisciform" flecks that accumulate at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), sometimes resulting in central macular atrophy early in life . Patients develop a macula with a "beaten bronze" appearance caused by atrophic changes in the RPE. In addition, a "dark " or "silent" choroid is seen on the fluorescein angiography that appears as a prominent retinal circulation against hypofluorescent choroid. The electroretinogram (ERG) and electro -oculography (EOG ) are normal early in the disease but may be reduced in more advanced cases . Of note, the ERG findings do not directly correlate with clinical findings. There is no known proven treatment for this disease . Because ABCA4 plays a role in vitamin A processing in the visual cycle , additional vitamin A is suspected to make the disease worse .The image below shows macular pisciform flecks .249 Other options : Option A: Retinitis pigmentosa : abnormal electroretinogram (ERG). Option B: Rod–cone dystrophy : abnormal ERG. Option D: Best 's disease : Normal ERG with abnormal electrooculogram (EOG ).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Silent choroid on FFA is a feature of which of the following disorders?
mcqs.explanation: Silent /Dark choroid on FFA is a feature of Stargardt's disease . The classic feature of 'silent choroid' is due to the masking of background choroidal fluorescence by lipofuscin deposits in the subretinal space . Stargardt disease constitutes the most common type of macular dystrophy . It has mutations in a photoreceptor cell -specific ATP -binding cassette gene (ABC4) that is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive manner . The disease usually starts in the juvenile group with progressive central vision loss and color vision loss that occurs due to the atrophy of the macular retinal pigment epithelium with an accumulation of discrete pisciform flecks of lipofuscin . Signs of Stargardt's disease : • Beaten bronze appearance of the macula that is caused by the atrophic changes in the RPE. • Silent /Dark choroid on FFA. • Visual field testing shows central vision loss. • The electroretinogram (ERG) is normal early in the disease but may be reduced in more advanced cases . Fundus flavimaculatus is genetically considered to be a part of the same spectrum as Stargardt's disease with late onset i.e. usually after 40 years of age .250 Other options : Option B: Best 's disease also known as vitelliform macular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant macular dystrophy in which lipofuscin accumulates in the central macula, causing progressive central vision loss. This disease is linked to mutations in the bestrophin (VMD2 ) gene and they do not exhibit silent choroid on FFA. Findings seen in Best 's disease are: • Vitelliform(yolk like) appearance of the fundus • Relatively normal ERG results associated with abnormal EOG The given below is the fundus picture of Best 's disease showing an egg yolk lesion in the macula.Option C: Age related Macular degeneration (ARMD) also known as senile macular degeneration is a chronic and progressive bilateral degenerative disorder of the macula that affects older individuals >50 yrs. ARMD is classified as dry and wet ARMD where the hallmarks are the presence of drusen and choroidal neovascularization respectively . Drusen are extracellular eosinophilic deposits between RPE and Bruch's membrane.251 Clinical features include loss of central vision, distorted vision (lines seen as wavy), and sudden painless loss of vision as seen in wet ARMD. The image below shows Drusens in the macular area in dry macular degeneration .Option D: Cystoid Macular edema (CME ) is a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform layer and the inner nuclear layer of the retina following a break in the blood-retinal barrier . In CME on fundoscopy , a honeycomb appearance and on FFA flower petal pattern can be seen . The below image shows the flower petal pattern on FFA as seen in CME .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A neonate with leukocoria and strabismus is diagnosed to have persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV ). Which of the following congenital disorders is it associated with?
mcqs.explanation: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV ) is associated with Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13 ).252 PHPV is a developmental disorder of the vitreous humor. In this condition, there is persistence of the embryonic hyaloid vessel . • Anterior PHPV - Here, the remnant vessel is attached to the back of the lens but does not reach the optic nerve. • Posterior PHPV - In this form of the disease , the vessel arises from the optic nerve. Clinically, PHPV presents with leucocoria and microphthalmia, and there can be complications such as tractional retinal detachments. This condition has a poor prognosis regardless of the time of intervention.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: When compared to blood, vitreous humor has a high concentration of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: When compared to blood, vitreous humor has a high concentration of ascorbate. The vitreous: plasma ratio of ascorbic acid concentration is 9:1. This high concentration of ascorbic acid is maintained by the active transport by the ciliary body epithelium , and it is attributed to the ability of the ascorbate to absorb ultraviolet rays and act as a free radical scavenger.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman complains of discomfort in her left eye . There is a past history of blunt trauma in her childhood which made her left eye blind. Slit-lamp examination of her left eye is shown below . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: These are synchysis scintillans, which are floaters composed of cholesterol bodies , found in the vitreous (extending into the anterior chamber in this picture ). Synchysis scintillans are vitreous opacities that occur as a consequence of chronic vitreous haemorrhage, often in a blind eye . This condition is usually discovered , when frank haemorrhage is no longer present . They are composed of cholesterol derived from plasma cells or degraded products of erythrocytes . Vitreous opacities can be caused by a variety of pathological processes and the following are few examples of vitreous opacities : • Vitreous haemorrhage • Asteroid hyalosis • Synchysis scintillans • Amyloidosis • Vitreous cyst • Persistent fetal vasculature.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A slit-lamp examination reveals the following finding. It is also noted that these yellow -white vitreous opacities do not settle down when the eye is immobile. All of the following statements about this condition are true except :
mcqs.explanation: The examination findings are suggestive of asteroid bodies /hyalosis. It is not common in myopes .253 Asteroid hyalosis is a common degenerative process in which calcium pyrophosphate particles collect within the vitreous gel . It is seen clinically as numerous tiny round yellow -white opacities of varying size and density . These move with the vitreous during eye movements but do not sediment inferiorly when the eye is immobile. Only one eye is affected in 75 % of patients ; it rarely causes visual problems and the majority of patients are asymptomatic . The cause of asteroid hyalosis is unknown, but it has been associated with diabetes mellitus , hypertension , and hypercholesterolemia . The prevalence of asteroid hyalosis increases with age and affects 3% of those aged 75 –86 years. It is more common in men than in women. While treatment of asteroid hyalosis is usually unnecessary , vitrectomy may occasionally be indicated .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: A young male presents with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage. What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: For a young male presenting with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage, the diagnosis is Eale 's disease . Eales disease is an idiopathic occlusive peripheral periphlebitis . It is characterized by three overlapping stages : inflammatory, occlusive , and retinal neovascular. Visual prognosis is good in the majority of cases . It is an important cause of visual morbidity in young males from the Indian subcontinent . Diagnosis: • Symptoms - Floaters or sudden visual reduction due to vitreous hemorrhage. There can be neurological deficits as well . • Mild anterior uveitis • Fundus - The condition is typically bilateral, although often asymmetrical. • Peripheral periphlebitis • Branch retinal vein occlusion • Peripheral capillary non-perfusion; microaneurysms, tortuosity , vascular shunts, and neovascularization with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage Treatment: • Steroids : Periocular, systemic , topical , and intravitreal steroids seem to be helpful in the inflammatory stage . • Antitubercular treatment

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is characteristic of Eale 's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Eale 's disease is an idiopathic inflammatory venous occlusion (phlebitis ) that primarily affects the peripheral retina that is periphlebitis and is characterized by recurrent bilateral vitreous hemorrhage. Superficial retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots can be sometimes seen , but they are not characteristic of Eales disease .254

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: What is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of a vitreous hemorrhage?
mcqs.explanation: The investigation of choice for vitreous hemorrhage is ultrasonography (USG) B-scan. Mild hemorrhage causes sudden onset floaters and diffuse blurring of vision, but may not affect visual acuity , whilst a dense bleed may result in sudden painless loss of vision. B-mode ultrasonography (B-scan) in unclotted vitreous hemorrhage generally shows a uniform appearance , and once cellular aggregates develop , small particulate echoes become visible. Causes of vitreous hemorrhage: • Acute posterior vitreous detachment associated either with a retinal tear or avulsion of a peripheral vessel • Proliferative retinopathy • Diabetic • Retinal vein occlusion • Sickle cell disease • Eales disease • Vasculitis • Miscellaneous retinal disorders • Macroaneurysm • Telangiectasia • Capillary hemangioma • Trauma • Systemic • Bleeding disorders • Terson syndrome- refers to the combination of intraocular and subarachnoid hemorrhage secondary to aneurysmal rupture , most commonly arising from the anterior communicating artery. Treatment is dictated by severity and cause , but an increasingly low threshold is being adopted for early vitrectomy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Sub-hyaloid hemorrhage is _______.
mcqs.explanation: Sub-hyaloid hemorrhage is dome-shaped or boat-shaped . Subhyaloid hemorrhage is the collection of blood in the potential space between the posterior vitreous and internal limiting membrane of the retina. The image depicts a sub-hyaloid hemorrhage which is boat-shaped .255

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: What is a reverse hypopyon ?

options.a: Collection of pus in the vitreous
options.b: Collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber

mcqs.explanation: Reverse hypopyon is the collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. Silicone oil is the vitreous substitute that is injected into the vitreous cavity after vitrectomy . When it gets emulsified , it enters the anterior chamber and collects in the upper part. Complications of silicone oil in the anterior chamber: • Glaucoma • Band-shaped keratopathy The image below shows reverse hypopyon.256

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Macular disorders, Retinal dystrophies, and Vit...
mcqs.question: Which anti-fungal can be administered intravitreally?
mcqs.explanation: Voriconazole and amphotericin-B can be given intravitreally. Vancomycin and ceftazidime is the preferred combination for endophthalmitis (intravitreous). Amikacin (0.4 mg in 0.1 ml) or gentamicin (0.4 mg in 0.1 ml) are used less frequently in endophthalmitis owing to the risk of macular infarction.257

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: What is the embryonic origin of the lens?
mcqs.explanation: The lens of the eye originates embryonically from the surface ectoderm . Surface ectoderm gives rise to lens, conjunctival and corneal epithelium and epithelial lining of lacrimal glands and tarsal glands.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Where are the youngest fibers of the lens present ?
mcqs.explanation: The youngest fibers of the lens are the peripheral part, the cortex. The nucleus of the lens is the central part containing the oldest fibers. The lens fibers are produced by mitosis of the epithelial cells in the pre-equatorial zone. As the lens fibers elongate and the new ones are formed, the older ones are pushed towards the depth of the lens so that the youngest fibers are the most superficially located .268

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: At a routine ophthalmological check-up, a patient was found to have bilateral, Y-shaped lens opacities as shown below . He was diagnosed with suture cataracts. Which zone of the lens nucleus is not involved here?
mcqs.explanation: The primary fibers in the embryonic nucleus of the lens do not form Y-shaped sutures . The image shows bilateral cataracts in the Y-shaped sutures of the lens. These are very slowly progressive congenital cataracts and do not require any surgical intervention. Types of lens nucleus and their age of development : • Embryonic nucleus : Innermost nucleus formed at around 1–3 months of gestation • Fetal nucleus : From 3 months of gestation till birth • Infantile nucleus : From birth to puberty • Adult nucleus As lens fibers grow anteriorly and posteriorly , a pattern emerges where the ends of the fibers meet . These patterns of cell association are known as sutures . Y-shaped sutures are recognizable at about 8 weeks of gestation .269

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: What is the ligament of Weigert?

options.a: Attachment of the vitreous to the posterior capsule of the lens
options.d: Attachment of the lens to the ciliary muscles

mcqs.explanation: The hyaloideo -capsular ligament of Weigert is the attachment of the vitreous to the posterior capsule of the lens. It is the annular region (1–2 mm in width and 8–9 mm in diameter ) where the vitreous is attached to the posterior aspect of the lens. Erggelet 's or Berger's space is at the centre of the hyaloideo -capsular ligament , a potential space between the vitreous and the lens. The canal of Cloquet arises from this space and courses posteriorly through the central vitreous, which is the former site of the hyaloid artery in the embryonic vitreous. Posteriorly, Cloquet 's canal opens into a funnel -shaped region anterior to the optic disc, whch is known as the area of Martegiani.270

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Where does the crystalline lens derive its nutrition from?
mcqs.explanation: The crystalline lens derives its nutrition from the aqueous humor. The lens is an avascular structure . It receives nutrition mostly from the aqueous humor and, to some extent , from the vitreous humor as well . Glucose is the main energy source . Major intrinsic protein 26 (MIP 26)/Aquaporin 0 in the lens is responsible for maintaining transparency by transporting water and glycerol across the lens. Anti-oxidant mechanisms in the lens: • Reduced glutathione (most important) • Glutathione peroxidase • Superoxide dismutase • Catalase • Vitamin C, Vitamin E, carotenoids .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: While studying the histological anatomy of the lens, you are measuring the thickness of the lens capsule in various areas. At which of the following zones would you get the lowest measurement ?
mcqs.explanation: The lens capsule is the thinnest at the posterior pole , measuring 4 \265 m. Other options : Option A: At the anterior pole , the thickness of lens capsule is 14 \265 m. Option C: In the pre-equator region, lens capsule is the thickest , measuring 23 \265 m. Option D: At the equator, as shown in the illustration below , the thickness is 17 \265 m.271

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: You are observing the given slide in a histology examination. Where is the marked structure absent?
mcqs.explanation: The slide shows the histology of the lens and the structure marked in the subcapsular epithelium . The epithelium of the lens is absent on its posterior surface . The lens epithelium is a single layer of cells on the anterior surface of the lens. There is no epithelium on the posterior surface , as these cells are used up in filling the central cavity of the lens vesicle during the development of the lens. The anterior epithelial lining creates new lens fibers throughout a person's life .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Ascorbate and alpha-tocopherol are maintained in the lens in the reduced state by _______.
mcqs.explanation: Ascorbate and alpha-tocopherol are maintained in the lens in the reduced , functional state by glutathione . Glutathione is present in high concentrations in the lens, particularly in the epithelial layer. One of its key functions is to maintain protein thiols in their reduced state , which preserves the lens transparency by preventing the formation of high molecular weight crystalline aggregates and protects the lens from oxidative stress. The lens is highly prone to photochemical reactions from continuous exposure to ultraviolet rays (295–400 nm), leading to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Its defence relies heavily on superoxide dismutase , ascorbate, catalase and glutathione peroxidase . With ageing or cataracts, levels of glutathione and ascorbic acid (in reduced form) significantly decrease .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: As part of a public health initiative, screening for cataract is being carried out. What is the most common cause of this healthcare issue in the population ?
mcqs.explanation: 272 The most common cause of cataracts is ageing , specifically senile (age -related ) cataract. Important causes of cataract: • Aging (Most common) • Congenital cataract (crystallin gene - CRYAA, CRYAB, CRYGC, CRYGS) (Option A) • Diabetes mellitus (Option B) • Syndermatotic - atopic dermatitis is the most common skin condition associated with cataract • Galactosemia - reversible cataract • Radiation- UV rays, X-rays, gamma rays, infrared • Toxic agents - Corticosteroids , miotics (long-acting anticholinesterases , e.g., echothiophate ) (Option C) • Obesity Senile cataract is the most common type of acquired cataract and is also known as age -related cataract. The two types of senile cataracts are cortical (soft cataract)-75 % and nuclear (hard cataract)-25%. In cortical cataract, the cuneiform type (70%) is the most common, and the cupuliform type is the most visually handicapping .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: You are compiling a literature review on congenital cataracts diagnosed in the last few years. Which of the following is the most common type ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common type of congenital cataract is the blue -dot cataract. Cataracta-punctata -caerulea , commonly known as blue dot cataract, is a prevalent type of congenital cataract. It typically develops during the first two decades of life . This condition is characterized by distinctive rounded bluish opacities located in the peripheral region of the adolescent nucleus and the deeper cortical layers of the lens. While these opacities are generally stationary and do not impair vision, larger ones may cause slight visual disturbance .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: The parents of a child have been informed at a PTA meeting that he has a lot of incomplete classwork. On being questioned , the child complains that he is unable to see things clearly and is having difficulty in reading and writing. On ophthalmic examination, he is found to have a cataract. Which type of congenital cataract most commonly presents with these findings?
