mcqs.explanation: Lamellar or zonular cataract is the most common type of congenital cataract presenting with visual impairment. The etiology may be either genetic or environmental in origin. • Genetic - familial autosomal-dominant • Environmental form is associated with: • Vitamin D deficiency • Hypocalcemia • Sometimes , maternal rubella infection contracted between the 7th and 8th week of gestation may also cause lamellar cataract. The main mass of the lens internal and external to the zone of cataract is clear.273 Small linear opacities like spokes of a wheel (riders) may be seen towards the equator.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old woman delivers a baby girl with a congenital rash, as shown below , and patent ductus arteriosus. What type of cataract is commonly associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario showing blueberry muffin rash, combined with patent ductus arteriosus in a baby girl, suggests a diagnosis of congenital rubella syndrome, which is typically associated with a progressive , pearly white nuclear cataract. Ocular effects of rubella: • Microphthalmia • Rubella keratitis • Angle-closure glaucoma • Nuclear pearly cataract • Salt and pepper fundus (a most common ocular feature of rubella) due to diffuse chorioretinitis.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: The following finding is found on the ophthalmologic examination of an 18-year-old girl. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image above characteristically depicts a Christmas tree cataract, featuring multiple refractile colors commonly observed in myotonic dystrophy . Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by difficulty relaxing skeletal muscles after contraction. The initial symptoms typically manifest during adolescence or early adulthood . Cataracts are an early and prominent feature in 90% of patients with myotonic dystrophy . They typically present as fine, dust -like opacities interspersed with iridescent , polychromatic spots in the cortical layer beneath the anterior and posterior lens capsule , resembling a Christmas tree . These cataracts may remain stable or progress .274 Surgical outcomes are generally favourable.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology OPD with the findings shown below . She has been diagnosed with a right-sided senile cataract. Identify the stage of the cataract.
mcqs.explanation: The above image represents an advanced stage of cataract progression characteristic of a Morgagnian hyper -mature cataract. Morgagnian hyper -mature cataracts are characterized by liquefaction of the entire cortex. The lens is converted into a bag of milky fluid . The small, brownish nucleus settles at the bottom, its position altering with a change in the position of the head . Senile cataract is the most common type of acquired cataract and is also known as age -related cataract. The two types of senile cataracts are cortical (soft cataract)-75 % and nuclear (hard cataract)-25%. Cortical cataract is further divided into the cuneiform and cupuliform types . Nuclear cataracts: These may be pigmented due to the deposition of urochrome pigments . These are cataracta brunescens (brown), cataracta nigra (black), cataracta rubra (red).Cuneiform(70%) Posterior subcapsular /Cupulif orm(5%) Radial spoke-like opacity star ting in the periphery and ext ending centrally Central saucer-shaped opacit y in the posterior cortex just below the capsule Late visual loss Early loss of visual acuity ; m ost visually handicapping sen ile cataract

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Where is polychromatic luster noted ?
mcqs.explanation: Polychromatic luster is seen in complicated cataracts. Due to disturbances in nutrition of the lens due to inflammatory/degenerative disease of other parts of the eye like iridocyclitis and ciliary body tumors. In inflammations/degenerations affecting the posterior segment , a characteristic opacification is seen in the posterior part of the cortex in the axial region (posterior subcapsular cataract). These cataracts present with a breadcrumb appearance and polychromatic luster . Even in the early stages , vision is impaired.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Who among the following patients can potentially develop drug-induced cataracts?
mcqs.explanation: Patients taking dexamethasone (corticosteroid ) are prone to drug-induced cataracts, predominantly presenting as discoid posterior subcapsular cataracts.275 Drugs causing cataracts: Other options : Option A: Zoledronate, a bisphosphonate drug can cause orbital inflammation, uveitis, and scleritis . Option B: Hydroxychloroquine, a drug used in malaria and rheumatoid arthritis, does not cause cataracts, chloroquine does . It can rarely cause retinal toxicity . Option D: Ethambutol is used in anti-tubercular therapy and its use has been shown to cause optic neuritis.Drugs Type of cataract Corticosteroids Discoid, posterior subcapsula r Anticholinesterase s Anterior subcapsular Chlorpromazine Yellow -brown anterior capsul ar granules/stellate /anterior p olar Busulfan Posterior subcapsular Chloroquine White, flaky, posterior subca psular Amiodarone Anterior subcapsular

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: The ophthalmologic examination on a 23 -year-old college student revealed the following image. What disease is commonly associated with this ocular finding?
mcqs.explanation: The given picture of a slit-lamp biomicroscope examination depicts the anterior lenticonus , which is associated with Alport syndrome. In Alport's syndrome, both anterior and posterior lenticonus are seen , but anterior lenticonus is more common. The diagnosis of lenticonus is typically confirmed through slit-lamp examination. Note : Lowe's syndrome is an oculo -cerebro-renal syndrome characterized by congenital cataract, glaucoma, and posterior lenticonus

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man, diagnosed with bilateral cataracts two months ago, reports being able to read better without prescription glasses. However, he complains that his distant vision has become blurrier. Which type of cataract typically causes this phenomenon ?
mcqs.explanation: The phenomenon described is the second sight of old age , seen in nuclear cataracts. Due to nuclear sclerosis , there is an increase in the refractive index, causing progressive myopia. A patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles . This improvement in vision is termed second sight .276

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old lady is a known case of diabetes and is on insulin for the last 8 years. Her sugars are poorly controlled and now she complains of hazy vision. What type of cataract will be characteristically noted in her eyes ?
mcqs.explanation: The typical appearance of a diabetic cataract is a snowflake cataract. Hyperglycemia is reflected in a high level of glucose in the aqueous humor, which diffuses into the lens. Here, glucose is metabolized into sorbitol, which accumulates within the lens, resulting in secondary osmotic overhydration.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old woman presents with an inability to see objects in bright light . On examination, she is diagnosed with a cataract. In which of the following cataract is this characteristic finding not seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The inability to see objects in bright light is not a feature of cuneiform cataract, as the lens opacity is peripheral, allowing visibility in bright light during miosis. The loss of the ability to see objects in bright light is a feature of posterior subcapsular cataract (visually handicapping ), cupuliform cataract and nuclear cataract as these present with central opacities . When a person is exposed to bright light, the pupil undergoes miosis (constriction). These central opacities come to lie directly in the path of axial rays, allowing no transmission of rays. Therefore, there is an inability to see objects in bright light . However, in dim light , when there is mydriasis (dilatation of the pupil ), some rays may pass around the opacity , leading to an improvement in dim-light vision. Furthermore, the complicated cataract, steroid -induced cataract, radiation-induced mainly present with a posterior subcapsular cataract and therefore have a similar clinical picture .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: You are counseling the parents of Nisha, a 1-month-old child diagnosed with a congenital lamellar cataract in both eyes . What is the course of treatment you would advise?

options.c: Cataract surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) implant
options.d: Pars plana lensectomy with no IOL implant

mcqs.explanation: Cataract surgery with an intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is the treatment of choice in congenital cataracts.277 It involves an extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE ) with primary posterior capsulorhexis and anterior vitrectomy. After removal of the cataractous lens, a posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL ) is implanted . The critical period for the development of the fixation reflex in both unilateral and bilateral visual deprivation disorders is 2–4 months of age . Thus, any cataract dense enough to impair vision must be dealt with before this age , and the earliest possible time is preferred . • Bilateral dense cataract- early surgery by 4-6 weeks of age • Unilateral dense cataract or involving visual axis- urgent surgery within days Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is contraindicated in children.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old girl is being evaluated for an aortic root aneurysm. She says her mother died of an aortic dissection at the age of 43. She is tall and slim. A musculoskeletal system finding is shown below . What is the most common lens subluxation noted in the genetic disease she is suffering from?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette of a girl with tall, slim stature , an aortic arch aneurysm, Steinberg sign (positive thumb sign), and similar family history suggest a diagnosis of Marfan's syndrome. It is most commonly associated with a superotemporal subluxation of the lens. The image below shows a subluxated lens in a patient with Marfan's syndrome.Congenital subluxation of the lens is called ectopia lentis . Types of ectopia lentis are as follows : • Simple type • Ectopia lentis et pupillae (pupil also displaced in opposite direction) • Ectopia lentis associated with syndromes • Marfan's syndrome- superotemporal subluxation of lens • Homocystinuria- inferonasal subluxation of the lens • Weill–Marchesani- downward, forward subluxation of the lens.278 • Ehler –Danlos syndrome

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Introduction, Types of Cataract and Clin...
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases does not show a specific pattern of cataract?
mcqs.explanation: A specific pattern of cataract is not seen in leprosy . A specific pattern of cararact is seen in the following : • Juvenile diabetes : Snowflake cataract • Myotonic dystrophy : Christmas tree cataract • Wilson's disease : Sunflower cataract279

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: A child has congenital cataract involving the visual axis, which was detected at birth. When should the child be operated up on?

options.c: At 1 year of age , when the globe attains normal size
options.d: At 4 years, when ocular and orbital growth is complete

mcqs.explanation: The child should be operated at 4-6 weeks of age .288 When a child has unilateral or bilateral cataract impairing vision (involving the visual axis), the cataract surgery must be performed before 2-4 months of age . This is because 2-4 months is the critical period for visual maturation and development of the fixation reflex in children. A unilateral cataract is more dangerous than a bilateral cataract because the risk of amblyopia is greater. Under-correction of intraocular lens (IOL) power is needed in children. In children < 2 years of age : • In unilateral cases , primary implantation is indicated as soon as the patient is fit for anesthesia , ideally between 2 and 3 months of age . The power is undercorrected by 20 %. • The earlier the surgery is done, the better the chance that deep amblyopia can be overcome. • After the cataract has been aspirated , an elective posterior capsulectomy –anterior vitrectomy is performed. The posterior chamber IOL is inserted through a scleral tunnel , which is prepared in advance. • Sulcus implantation is indicated in neonates and infants less than 1 year of age . In children between 2 and 8 years of age : • An IOL is implanted but power is undercorrected by 10 %. • An in-the-bag IOL is chosen for children above 1 year of age because they are less likely to need an IOL exchange. Beyond 8 years, IOL power is the same as the calculated value.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: In which of the following cataract surgeries is a self -sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision used ?
mcqs.explanation: The self -sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision is made in small-incision cataract surgery (SICS). SICS is a type of extracapsular cataract extraction techniques (ECCE ). In these techniques , the major portion of the anterior capsule with the epithelium , nucleus , and cortex are removed, leaving behind the intact posterior capsule . Note : Newer cataract surgeries include femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS), micro-incision cataract surgery (MICS) and Phaconit. FLACS is a microincision cataract surgery or a micro-phacoemulsification where a femtosecond laser is used to make the corneal incisions, perform capsulorhexis and fragment the lens. MICS refers to the phacoemulsification techniques that can be performed through a microincision (& lt ;2 mm). Phaconit is the term for the bimanual micro-phacoemulsification done with the needle incision technique through an incision of <1mm.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: In which of the following patients is an intracapsular cataract extraction indicated ?
mcqs.explanation: At present , the only indication of intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is markedly subluxated and dislocated lens. In ICCE, the entire cataractous lens along with the intact capsule is removed by rupturing the zonules . Therefore, weak and degenerated zonules are a prerequisite for this method . Methods of289 lens delivery include cryoextraction (best method ), forceps extraction (Arruga forceps ), wire vectis method and Indian Smith method . ICCE is no longer used for cataract treatment due to the large incision required, inability to implant an IOL and a high rate of complications like vitreous loss, retinal detachment and cystoid macular edema .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is the length of the incision used in phacoemulsification ?
mcqs.explanation: The length of the incision in phacoemulsification varies from 1.5 to 2.4 mm. The option closest to this answer is B, i.e., 2 to 2.5 mm. In phacoemulsification , the nucleus of the lens is emulsified and aspired . This is done by the phacoemulsifier. It acts through a hollow 1-mm titanium needle , which vibrates by at an ultrasonic speed of 40000 times a second . The steps of phacoemulsification are given below : • Step 1 - Small clear corneal incision • Step 2 - Continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis • Step 3 - Hydro dissection • Step 4 - Hydro delineation is done in some cases . • Steps 5 and 6 - Emulsification and aspiration of the nucleus • Step 7 - Removal of the cortical lens matter using an irrigation-aspiration technique • Step 8 - Implantation of a foldable lens Length of the incision in various cataract surgeries : • Phacoemulsification - 1.5–2.4 mm. • Micro-phacoemulsification - 1–1.5 mm. • Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE)- –14 mm. • Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE )- 8–12 mm.290

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is the most common late complication following cataract surgery?
mcqs.explanation: The most common late complication following cataract surgery is posterior capsule opacification . Posterior capsule opacification , known as after or secondary cataract, is the most common late postoperative complication. It may be caused by residual opaque lens matter or proliferation of left out anterior epithelial cells .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: In a patient undergoing cataract surgery, which of the following is the most important strategy in the prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis ?

options.b: One week antibiotic therapy prior to surgery

mcqs.explanation: The most important factor in the prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis is preoperative preparation with povidone-iodine. Postoperative endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis . Flora of the eyelids and conjunctiva are the most frequent source . Other potential sources include contaminated solutions and instruments, environmental air, and the surgeon and other operating room personnel . Prophylaxis for postoperative endophthalmitis includes : • Instillation of 5% povidone-iodine into the conjunctival fornices and leaving this undisturbed for at least 3 minutes prior to surgery. This is the most important factor. • Scrupulous preparation of the surgical site • Treatment of pre-existing infections such as blepharitis • Antibiotic prophylaxis • Intracameral cefuroxime (1 mg in 0.1 mL ) injected into the anterior chamber (AC) at the end of surgery.291 • Post-operative subconjunctival injection can achieve bactericidal levels in the AC for at least 1–2 hours. • Preoperative topical fluoroquinolone antibiotics are frequently given in regimens from 1 hour to 3 days before surgery Patients present with ocular pain, diminished vision, circumciliary congestion and hypopyon . The differential diagnosis for postoperative endophthalmitis includes retained lens material in the AC, vitreous hemorrhage, postoperative uveitis and toxic reaction to the use of inappropriate or contaminated irrigating fluid or viscoelastic .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: A patient , 36 hours after cataract surgery, presents with complaints of pain and visual disturbance. His eye is as shown below . What is the management of this condition?

options.c: Bandage and padding of the eye

mcqs.explanation: A post cataract surgery patient presenting within 36 hours of surgery with inflammation, congestion and hypopyon as seen in the image, is suggestive of acute bacterial endophthalmitis . The treatment of acute bacterial endophthalmitis is intravitreal antibiotics. Endophthalmitis is an intraocular inflammation affecting the inner structures of the eyeball . Acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis occurs within 1-7 days after cataract surgery and the most important factor to prevent it is preoperative administration of 5% povidone iodine. The cardinal features of endophthalmitis are pain, swelling of the lid, and a decrease in vision. The patient classically shows inflammation of the eye , corneal edema and a hypopyon due to the pouring of exudates in the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber. Once the endophthalmitis sets in it is important to treat all the cases empirically with a combination of antibiotics and steroids from the beginning. The various drugs, routes and surgical management used to treat endophthalmitis are as follows : • The mainstay of treatment is intravitreal injections of antibiotics. • First choice : Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus ceftazidime 2.25mg in 0.1ml. • Second choice :Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus amikacin 0.4mg in 0.1ml. • If there is no improvement, a repeat intravitreal injection should be given after 48 hours • Topical antibiotics are started immediately and used frequently . • Vancomycin (50mg/ml) or cefazolin (50mg/ml) • Amikacin (20mg /ml) or tobramycin • Systemic antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice . • Steroid therapy includes : • Intravitreal injection of dexamethasone (0.4mg in 0 . 1ml) which is started along with antibiotics. • Topical dexamethasone (0.1%) • Oral steroids such as prednisolone are started after 24 hours of intensive antibiotic therapy . • Supportive therapy includes : • Cycloplegics such as atropine 1%292 • Anti-glaucoma drugs such as oral acetazolamide or timolol in patients with raised intraocular pressure • Pars plana vitrectomy is done if the patient does not improve with the above therapy in 48-72 hours or when the visual acuity is reduced to hand movements near the eye Other options : Option A: Steroids are given in endophthalmitis to reduce the inflammation of the tissues . The preferred route of administration is either by intravitreal injections, topical concentrations or oral route. Intravenous route (option A) of administration of steroids is not used in endophthalmitis . Option B: Systemic administration (intravenous) of antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice as an add on.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: A 62-year-old presented with diminished vision 1 year after cataract surgery. The findings are shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Diminished vision 1 year after cataract surgery, supported with the image of vacoulated clusters seen behind IOL is suggestive of Elschnig's pearls. It is a type of after cataract. After cataract, or secondary cataract or posterior capsular opacification , is a late postoperative complication that follows extracapsular extraction of the lens. It is the most common late postoperative complication. It may be caused by residual opaque lens matter or proliferation of left out anterior epithelial cells . Different types of after cataract include : • Elschnig 's pearls: The subcapsular epithelial cells proliferate and develop into vacuolated soap bubble like clusters along the posterior capsule . • Soemmering's ring: A peripheral dense ring is formed behind the iris and is enclosed between layers of the capsule . • Dense membranous after-cataract: It is formed in the pupillary area impairing the vision. • Thin membranous after-cataract: It is thickened posterior capsule .293 Treatment of after cataract is by Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy of the posterior capsule , which works on the principle of photodisruption , or surgical posterior capsulotomy . Option B: Irvine –Gass syndrome is cystoid macular edema (CME ) that develops in post -cataract surgery patients . Though it is mostly clinically insignificant, some cases can present with blurring of vision, one to three months after surgery. In CME , on fundoscopy a honeycomb appearance and on fundus fluorescein angiography(FFA) flower petal pattern can be seen . The below image depicts the flower petal pattern seen on FFA.Option C: Post operative endophthalmitis presents as ocular pain, diminished vision and hypopyon within months to years after the surgery. Fungal endophthalmitis can rarely occur with puff ball exudates in the vitreous cavity. Option D: UGH syndrome is where uveitis, glaucoma and hyphema occurs simultaneously . It is seen commonly with rigid anterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice for after cataract?
mcqs.explanation: Nd:YAG laser is the treatment of choice for after cataract. Thin membranous after-cataract, thickened posterior capsule and Elschnig 's pearls are treated with Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy . Dense membranous after-cataract requires capsulotomy using a vitreous cutter . Sommering's ring, if the central posterior capsule is clear, requires no treatment . Other options : Option A: Intra -capsular cataract extraction (ICCE) is currently used for the treatment of markedly subluxated and dislocated lens. Option B: Intravitreal steroids may be used for the treatment of acute endophthalmitis , an early postoperative complication of cataract surgery. Option C: Anterior vitrectomy is performed for the treatment of cystoid macular edema with vitreous incarceration. This is a late post -cataract surgery complication.294

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is the cause of late -onset endophthalmitis after cataract surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Late-onset endophthalmitis after cataract surgery is caused by Propionibacterium acnes. Late or delayed -onset endophthalmitis following cataract surgery develops when an organism of low virulence such as P. acnes, becomes trapped within the capsular bag (saccular endophthalmitis ). Organisms can become sequestered within macrophages , protected from eradication but with continued expression of bacterial antigens. Patients present with symptoms between 4 weeks to years (mean 9 months) postoperatively following an uneventful cataract surgery.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: An elderly male residing in an old-age home is brought to the hospital with senile cataracts in both eyes . He says he had difficulty in seeing objects for a few years, but never went to the clinic. He is posted for surgery in 3 weeks . Which of the following is a complication is he unlikely to develop in the 3 weeks until his surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Hypopyon is not a complication of senile cataracts. Hypermature , or senile cataracts, can lead to the following complications . • Phacoanaphylactic uveitis: The lens proteins may leak into the anterior chamber. They may act as an antigen and induce antigen–antibody reaction, leading to phacoanaphylactic uveitis. • Lens-induced glaucoma: • Phacomorphic glaucoma: Most common, seen in intumescent cataract. The lens swells and causes secondary angle closure glaucoma. • Phacolytic glaucoma: Seen in hypermature cataract. The leaked lens proteins are engulfed by macrophages , which clog the trabecular meshwork and cause secondary open -angle glaucoma. • Phacotopic glaucoma: Seen in hypermature cataract. The lens may subluxate or dislocate and block the angle of the anterior chamber. • Subluxation or dislocation of the lens: It may occur due to degeneration of zonules in the hypermature stage .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is the best irrigating fluid for cataract surgery?
mcqs.explanation: The best irrigating fluid for cataract surgery is balanced salt solution plus glutathione (BSS plus ). In the early days of phacoemulsification, the only irrigating solutions available were normal saline, plasmalyte , and lactated Ringer's solution . Their main adverse effects were endothelial cell toxicity . The buffer in BSS Plus is bicarbonate, which is an improvement over the sodium acetate and citrate buffers in BSS.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: How many weeks following surgery are spectacles prescribed ?
mcqs.explanation: 295 Spectacles are prescribed 6 weeks after cataract surgery after the course of steroids is over. It is the time required for the incison to heal. Then visual acuity is checked and glasses are prescribed .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: A 72-year-old diabetic who underwent uncomplicated cataract extraction with PCIOL implant 15 days back presents with painless , decreased vision in the operated eye . His visual acuity is 6/12 and does not improve with a pinhole . On examination, the anterior chamber is deep , and PCIOL is well -centered in the capsular bag. Dilated fundus exam reveals clear media, and optic nerve with a cup -to-disc ratio of 0.4, a few peripheral microaneurysms, and a dull foveal reflex . The rest of the fundus exam is unremarkable. Which test would be of least benefit ?
mcqs.explanation: In the above case scenario, gonioscopy would be the least helpful . A painless decrease in vision after cataract surgery could be due to: • Posterior capsular opacification (most commonly, after 1-3 months) • Cystoid macular edema (early) • Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (delayed ) In the given question, the media is clear (rules out posterior capsular opacification ). Also, there are no symptoms nor signs of retinal detachment (RD), hence it is ruled out. Decreased vision not improving with a pinhole in the presence of clear media is attributable to macular pathology . Also, there is a dull foveal reflex . The diagnosis in this patient is cystoid macular edema (CME ). The incidence of clinical CME is about 1% to 2% following uncomplicated cataract surgeries . The incidence of angiographic evidence of CME is 10 times greater at around 10 % to 20 %. Optical coherence tomography (option A) is useful in identifying cystoid macular edema and evaluating the vitreomacular interface . It is also useful in the measurement of retinal thickening, thus allowing the assessment of the therapeutic response . On fluorescein angiography (option B), the classic petaloid leakage in the fovea is seen in the case of CME . Amsler's grid (option D) is a macular function test . Hence , the least useful in this scenario is gonioscopy .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: Two months after undergoing cataract surgery, a 45-year-old man is found to have after cataract. He is planned for an Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy . What is the principle behind the use of this laser?
mcqs.explanation: The principle of the Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm) is photodisruption . Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy is used for treatment of thin membranous after-cataract, posterior capsular opacification and Elschnig 's pearls. The plasma produced at the laser target expands and disrupts the tissues , creating an opening . Double frequency Nd:YAG laser is used in posterior segment photocoagulation .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: Which of the following complaints in a patient presenting to your OPD would prompt you to perform a Fincham's test ?
mcqs.explanation: Fincham's test is used to distinguish whether the colored halos are due to cataract or glaucoma. Colored halos are rainbow-colored rings seen around lights at nighttime . It may be caused by c ataracts , acute congestive glaucoma and mucopurulent conjunctivitis. These conditions lead to prismatic disruption of light .296

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: As part of the pre-operative evaluation of a patient posted for cataract surgery, you are asked to calculate the power of the IOL to be implanted . What investigation do you perform?
mcqs.explanation: The power of the intraocular lens (IOL) to be implanted after cataract surgery is calculated by a biometer and the procedure is termed as biometry. Biometry consists of keratometry and axial length measurement . The most common method of determining IOL power uses a regression formula called modified Sanders–Retzlaff– Kraff (SRK) formula, which is given below : E = A - 2.5L - 0.9K Where, • E is the emmetropic power designated for the eye • A is a predetermined constant, which is specific for each intraocular lens type • L is the axial length of the eyeball in millimeter , determined by using the "A" scan ultrasonography • K is the average corneal curvature, which is determined by keratometry. The image given below shows a biometer .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: In the SRK formula for intraocular lens power calculation 'E=A-2.5L-0.9K', the value of L is estimated using__________
mcqs.explanation: In the SRK formula, the value of L is calculated using the A-scan ultrasonographic biometry. The most widely used formula for intraocular lens power calculation is the modified Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff (SRK) formula, given by: E = A - 2.5L - 0.9K Where, • E: Emmetropic power designated for the eye • A: Predetermine constant which is specific for each intraocular lens type .297 • L: Axial length of eyeball in millimeters, determined using the A scan ultrasonography . • K: Average corneal curvature determined by keratometry. Given below is an image of A scan ultrasonography .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: What is a rigid intraocular lens made of?
mcqs.explanation: Rigid IOLs are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). Depending on the type of material of manufacturing, 3 types of posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOLs ) are available: • Rigid IOLs are made entirely from polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). • Foldable IOLs are made of silicone , hydrogel , acrylic, and Collamer. These are implanted through a small incision. • Rollable IOLs are ultra-thin IOLs made of acyrlic or hydrogel . These are implanted through a 1-mm incision after micro-incision cataract surgery technique .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: A patient , on follow -up after cataract surgery, has the lens shown below . What is the type of lens implanted in the patient ?

options.b: Modified C loop posterior chamber IOL

mcqs.explanation: The image depicts Singh and Worst's iris claw lens. This lens is an iris-supported lens, which is fixed with the help of sutures , loops or claws . They are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications and are thus only used if posterior chamber IOLs cannot be implanted .298 Note : Kelman multiflex type of anterior chamber intraocular lens (ACIOL) is the most commonly used ACIOL . Anterior chamber IOLs lie entirely in front of the iris and are supported in the angle of the anterior chamber. These are associated with a higher incidence of bullous keratopathy. Thus, they are currently used only for correction of aphakia in cases where posterior chamber IOLs cannot be used (eg : rupture of posterior capsule ).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: An 80-year-old man is posted for cataract surgery. The given lens is chosen to be used for implantation. Identify the lens.

options.b: Modified C loop posterior chamber IOL
options.c: Singh and Worst's iris claw lens

mcqs.explanation: The above image depicts a modified C-loop type of posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL). A PCIOL rests entirely behind the iris. They may be supported and fixed by capsular bag fixation of PCIOL (most ideal method ), ciliary sulcus fixation or scleral fixation. The PCIOL consists of a central part overlying the optic axis is called the optic and the peripheral arms used for placement and stabilization called the haptics .299

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Lens - Cataract Surgery, Complications and IOLs
mcqs.question: Identify the intraocular lens shown below .
mcqs.explanation: The given image is of a toric IOL used to correct pre-existing astigmatism. The dotted markings on the optic of the IOL indicate the axis of IOL , and it is aligned to coincide with the steep axis of the patient 's eye . For every, one degree of misalignment, about 3 percent of the lens cylinder power is lost.300

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the normal aqueous production rate?
mcqs.explanation: The rate of formation of aqueous humor is 2-3 �ML/min. Formation of aqueous humor involves the following : • Ultrafiltration • Secretion - Na/K ATPase of non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary process • Diffusion313

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the critical angle of the air-cornea interface ?
mcqs.explanation: The critical angle of the air–cornea interface is 46 degrees . Gonioscopy is a method of evaluating the anterior chamber (AC) angle. Direct goniolenses include the Koeppe , Medical Workshop , Barkan , and Swan–Jacob. Indirect goniolenses include Goldmann, Zeiss, and Posner. Structures seen on gonioscopy from anterior to posterior are: • Schwalbe line: represents the posterior limit of Descemet 's membrane • Trabecular meshwork • Scleral spur • Ciliary body and root of the iris Shaffers grading of angle width : Grade 4 (35–45\260) is the widest angle, characteristic of myopia and pseudophakia ; the ciliary body can be visualized without tilting the lens. Grade 3 (25–35\260) is an open -angle in which the scleral spur is visible. Grade 2 (20 \260) is an angle in which the trabeculum but not the scleral spur can be seen . Grade 1 (10 \260) is a very narrow -angle in which only the Schwalbe line, and perhaps the top of the trabeculum, can be identified . A slit angle is one in which there is no obvious iridocorneal contact but no angle structures can be identified . Grade 0 (0\260) is closed due to iridocorneal contact.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which statement regarding the depth of the anterior chamber is false ?

options.a: Depth is less in women than men

mcqs.explanation: The depth of the anterior chamber decreases with age .314 Anterior chamber depth • The anterior chamber is shallow in very young and in old age . • At other periods of life , it is normally about 2.5 mm deep . • Depth is less in women than in men. • Depth is more in myopes . • Depth is less in hypermetropia and in angle-closure glaucoma

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The child in the picture has large corneas, photophobia , and lacrimation. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of an infant with large corneas, lacrimation and photophobia supported with the image is suggestive of congenital glaucoma. Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) also known as developmental glaucoma refers to abnormally high intraocular pressure (IOP) which results from the developmental anomaly of the angle of the anterior chamber. It can be classified as: • True congenital or newborn glaucoma in which IOP is elevated during intrauterine life and the baby is born with ocular enlargement . • Infantile glaucoma: which manifests prior to age 3 years. • Juvenile glaucoma: IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age . Clinical findings include : • Blepharospasm • Buphthalmos : Large eyeball due to stretching of the globe from elevated IOP prior to the age of 3 years. • Corneal enlargement : • Corneal haze is due to corneal edema . • Blue sclera - due to the shining of the underlying uveal tissue through the thinned-out sclera • Haab striae are healed breaks in Descemet 's membrane Treatment: • Goniotomy - when the angle of the anterior chamber is visible through the clear cornea. • Trabeculectomy when the corneal clouding prevents visualization of the angle. • Filtration procedures such as Trabeculectomy or combined trabeculectomy with trabeculectomy if the above procedures fail. • Glaucoma drainage devices in unresponsive cases . Other options : Option A: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood that is seen between 1-2 years.315 Findings of Retinoblastoma include : • Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex )- the most common manifestation • Strabismus • Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma • An endophytic tumor grows into the vitreous as a white mass that may 'seed ' into the gel . If calcification is present it gives a "cottage cheese appearance ". An exophytic tumor grows outwards and causes overlying exudative retinal detachment . The image below shows the leucocoria of the left eye .Option C: Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) is an inherited corneal dystrophy that manifests since birth with endothelial degeneration . It appears as diffuse bilateral corneal edema in the absence of elevated IOP. The clinical features of the disease include corneal clouding , visual impairment, and nystagmus . Option D: Megalocornea is a bilateral non-progressive X-linked condition that most commonly affects males. In this condition, the horizontal corneal diameter is \03112mm (<2 years) and is \03113 mm(>2 years). It is characterized by a clear cornea, normal corneal thickness, and no breaks in the descemet 's membrane. Systemic associations of Megalocornea include Marfan's syndrome, Apert syndrome, Ehlers -Danlos, and Down syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A neonate is brought with complaints of photophobia and watering . Clinical examination shows normal tear passages and clear but large cornea. Investigation reveals Haab's striae seen in the eye . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This neonate with complaints of photophobia and watering with large cornea and Haab's striae is suggestive of buphthalmos . Haab's striae are horizontal/circumferential breaks in Descemet 's membrane seen in buphthalmos . Buphthalmos (Bull-like eyes ) is an enlargement of the eyeball seen in true congenital and infantile glaucoma, usually when the disease onset is before 3 years.316 The image given below shows Haab's striae and a child having buphthalmos in congenital glaucoma.Note : Vogt's striae are vertical, fine, whitish lines (folds /tears) in Descemet 's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus. The image given below shows Vogt's striae.317

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the clinic for a change of her presbyopic glasses . This is the third time that she is coming in 2 months. What is the likely underlying diagnosis in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Frequent changes in presbyopic glasses in this patient is a symptom of open -angle glaucoma (OAG). This is due to increasing accommodative failure as a result of constant pressure on the ciliary muscle and nerve supply . In intumescent cataracts, patients report difficulty with distance vision and frequent change of spectacle prescription . However, it is not associated with frequent changes of presbyopic glasses .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Normal cup -to-disc ratio is up to_______.
mcqs.explanation: Normal cup -to-disc ratio is up to 0.6. Although the average cup -to-disc ratio is around 0.3 to 0.4, a ratio of up to 0.6 may be found in healthy individuals. This larger ratio is frequently seen in cases of large discs , myopic discs or physiological cupping . A cup -to-disc ratio of > 0.6 is suggestive of glaucoma.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 61-year-old man, who is a known case of diabetes mellitus , presents with headache and eye pain. He also reports difficulty with driving at night. Examination showed a laminar dot sign. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a patient with headache and eye pain along with the finding of a laminar dot sign is suggestive of glaucoma. The laminar dot sign is an advanced glaucomatous change in the optic disc. This occurs because the pores in the lamina cribrosa are slit-shaped and are visible up to the margin of the disc. Glaucomatous changes in the optic disc Early glaucomatous changes :318 • Slit defects of the retinal nerve fiber layer • Splinter hemorrhages on disc margin • Large cup - 0.7 or more • Asymmetry of the cups : A difference equal to or more than 0.2 between two eyes is significant • Vertically oval cup Advanced glaucomatous changes : • Marked cupping (Beanpot cupping ) • Thinning of neuroretinal rim • Bayonetting sign - Sharp angulation of vessel at the margin of the excavated cup • Laminar dot sign

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the last visual field to be affected in glaucoma?
mcqs.explanation: The temporal visual field is the last field to be affected in glaucoma. The pattern of visual field progression in glaucoma from early to severe is predictable in light of the pattern of thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer, which usually begins with the superior and inferior arcuate fibers, then the papillomacular bundle and finally, the nasal fibers. Since the nasal fibers are the last to be involved, the temporal field is the last to be affected in glaucoma.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a late visual field defect in open -angle glaucoma?
mcqs.explanation: Bjerrum scotoma (arcuate) is a late and clinically significant visual field defect . Progression of visual field changes seen in glaucoma:Early non-specific changes Isopter contractionBaringof a blind spot :Exclusion of blind spot from the central field Early significant changes Peripheral nasal step (may be early or late )Paracentral scot omain Bjerrum's area.Siedel ' s scotoma:Paracentral scoto ma joins the blind spot Late significant changes ArcuateorBjerrum scotomaRi ngorDoublearcuate scotoma: When 2 arcuate scotomas joi n togetherRoenne 's central n asal step319 Early non-specific changes Isopter contractionBaringof a blind spot :Exclusion of blind spot from the central field Advanced glaucomatous field defects Tubular visionNo light perce ption: Complete visual field d efect .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old patient presents with progressive deterioration of vision. The pupillary reaction is sluggish and the IOP is elevated . Fundoscopy shows a large and deep cup and the visual field reveals paracentral scotoma. What is the first line of treatment for this diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of deterioration of vision, sluggish pupils , elevated IOP and paracentral scotoma is suggestive of primary open -angle glaucoma (POAG). Timolol is one of the first-line agents used in the treatment of primary open -angle glaucoma. First-line agents for the treatment of glaucoma are: • Prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost and bimatoprost • Topical beta -blockers such as timolol, betaxolol , and levobunolol • Selective alpha 2 adrenergic agonist brimonidine Adjunctive therapy : Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors Laser trabeculoplasty : In cases where intraocular pressure (IOP) is uncontrolled despite maximal tolerated medical therapy . Note : Since prostaglandin (PG) analogs are not included in the options , the next best option to choose is timolol. Historically, beta -blockers were the most common first-line agents used in the medical treatment of POAG. However, with an increase in our experience with newer agents , specifically the prostaglandin analogues that facilitate outflow , they were recognized as being more efficacious in lowering IOP and systemically safer than beta -blockers. As a result , now they are the first-line agents in glaucoma treatment .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient with a known case of MI on aspirin comes with shortness of breath. She has an active history of asthma and uses inhalational bronchodilators, her last attack was 7 months ago. She was recently prescribed medications for increased intraocular pressure . What is the likely cause of her current symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: This patient with a history of asthma now presenting with shortness of breath after starting medications for increased intraocular pressure was most likely diagnosed with glaucoma. The drug she was likely prescribed was timolol, a non-selective beta blocker. Timolol is a non-selective beta -blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta -blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta -2 block on bronchi). They cause bronchospasms and are therefore contraindicated in patients with asthma (e.g. timolol, levobunolol ). Ocular beta -blockers reduce intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous formation by blockade of \0302 receptors . Timolol is specifically associated with allergic blepharoconjunctivitis and punctal stenosis Side effects : Systemic : Bronchospasm, bradycardia, decreased cardiac output , hypotension , depression , impotence , and altered lipid profile .320 Contraindications: Asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease , congestive heart failure, sinus bradycardia, and atrioventricular blocks Other options : Option A: The patient has been stable on aspirin for the past three years which is unlikely to be the cause of her current symptoms . Option B: Betaxolol is a beta 1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma. Option C: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin (PGF2 alpha) analog and does not precipitate bronchial asthma.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: As a first-year ophthalmology resident , you have been referred a case of glaucoma. He complaints that his current medication is causing excessive drowsiness and is interfering with his work. Which of the following anti-glaucoma medications can cause drowsiness ?
mcqs.explanation: Brimonidine is an anti-glaucoma medication that can cause drowsiness . It is a selective alpha-2 agonist. It can cross the blood-brain barrier and, hence , causes drowsiness and CNS depression ; it is contraindicated in infants and children. A new class of glaucoma drugs, Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitors, promises to act specifically on the trabecular meshwork, a main outflow and blockage site in glaucoma. ROCK inhibitors are not yet approved and available for glaucoma patients . Two US companies, Aerie and Altheos , are currently in early clinical research development with topical ROCK inhibitors to lower IOP.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old female , who is a known case of sickle cell anemia, comes to the casualty with a history of severe eye pain, redness , and diminution of vision. On examination, the visual acuity is 6/60, and there is circumcorneal congestion , corneal edema , and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the drug of choice from the given options ?
mcqs.explanation: This patient with complaints of severe headache , corneal congestion , and edema with a shallow anterior chamber most likely has acute angle closure glaucoma. Since this patient has a past history of sickle cell disease , intravenous mannitol is the drug of choice for this patient Acetazolamide is contraindicated in cases of sickle-cell anemia since these drugs tend to increase sickling of erythrocytes .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old female presents with an acute painful red-eye . An image of her eye is shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario, supported with the image of the mid-dilated and vertically oval pupil is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The pupil is non-reactive to both light and accommodation. Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to the occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris (iridotrabecular contact [ITC]), obstructing aqueous outflow . Angle closure can be primary, when it occurs in an anatomically predisposed eye or secondary to another ocular or systemic factor. Classification :321 Symptoms : Pain, redness , photophobia , impaired vision, watering Signs: • Corneal edema - colored halos • Conjunctiva- congestion , chemosis • IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg • AC very shallow • Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated • Angle- completely closed , Grade 0 Treatment: • Immediate- Intravenous mannitol, intravenous acetazolamide followed by oral dose , topical beta-blockers, brimonidine, latanoprost • Definitive- Laser peripheral iridotomy, filtration surgeryPrimary angle-closure suspec t (PACS) Gonioscopy shows posterior meshwork ITC in three or mo re quadrants but no peripher al anterior synechiae (PAS).I ntraocular pressure (IOP), op tic disc, and visual field are n ormal.No PAS are seenThe ri sk of PACG at 5 years may be around 30%. Primary angle closure (PAC) Gonioscopy shows three or m ore quadrants of ITC with rai sed IOP and/or PAS or excess ive pigment smudging on the TM.Normal optic disc and fi eld . Primary angle-closure glauco ma (PACG) ITC in three or more quadra nts, with glaucomatous optic neuropathy .Optic nerve dam age from an episode of severe IOP elevation, such as acute angle closure , may not appea r as typical glaucomatous cup ping.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 36-year-old woman develops pain in the eye after dark -room/prone-provocative test . Which of the following drugs should be avoided?
mcqs.explanation: Pain after dark -room prone-provocative test indicates occludable angles . Hence , atropine is contraindicated as it is a long-acting mydriatic and can precipitate angle closure . Dark -room/prone-provocative test (DRPPT )- The patient sits in a dark room, face down for one hour without sleeping (sleep induces miosis). The intraocular pressure (IOP) is checked322 (immediately after the test , as IOP can normalize very rapidly), and an IOP rise of 8 mmHg or more is frequently considered significant.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A young female presents with sudden onset severe pain in the left eye after watching a movie. She rushes to the hospital as there is a progressive loss of vision. She has ciliary injection and a shallow anterior chamber. The pupil is semi dilated and the cornea appears oedematous . What is the procedure of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of sudden onset severe pain in the eye , progressive loss of vision, shallow anterior chamber, semi-dilated pupil , and edematous cornea is suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Laser iridotomy is the procedure of choice especially in emergency situations . The attack may have been precipitated by pupillary dilation, which may result from activities such as going to a movie theater . Laser iridotomy re-establishes the communication between the posterior and anterior chamber, bypassing the pupillary block; hence , it immediately relieves crowding of the angle. Various surgical and laser modalities used in glaucoma: Angle-closure glaucoma: • Laser iridotomy by Nd:Yag along with prophylactic iridotomy of the other eye \033 Treatment of choice . • Trabeculectomy \033 Filtration surgery Congenital glaucoma: • Goniotomy • Trabeculotomy Primary open -angle glaucoma: • Laser trabeculoplasty : Argon or diode (if not controlled medications ) • Trabeculectomy : Filtration surgery (if not controlled medications ) Absolute glaucoma: • Cyclocryotherapy • Nd:Yag lasercyclo destruction

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old male presented with progressive blurred vision, photophobia , and eye pain. On examination , there was conjunctival redness , a mid-dilated pupil , and a shallow anterior chamber in the right eye . He has been treated both medically and surgically for the condition but showed no improvement. The following procedure incorporates a device to aid drainage. Identify the device .
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of glaucoma not responsive to medical treatment and trabeculectomy and the device used is an ex-Press\231 glaucoma implant (mini shunt). It is a form of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) to increase aqueous drainage. Ex-PRESS glaucoma implant is a small stainless steel device . It is inserted under a scleral flap during a modified trabeculectomy . Complications such as hypotony are lower than with standard trabeculectomy .323 Glaucoma drainage devices are devices that allow aqueous outflow by establishing communication between the anterior chamber and sub-Tennon's space /sub-conjunctival space . While these devices were traditionally reserved for high-risk patients , or after trabeculectomy had failed , they are becoming increasingly popular. The commonly used devices are as follows : 1. Shunts using episcleral explants • Ahmed glaucoma valve: Silicone • Molteno implant - Polypropylene plate and silicone plate • Baerveldt implant - Silicone 2. Mini-shunts • Ex-Press\231 Mini-Shunt: Stainless steel • iStent \256 - Titanium

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is Glaukomflecken ?
mcqs.explanation: Glaukomflecken is anterior subcapsular lenticular opacity and a component of Vogt's triad seen in patients after an acute angle closure glaucoma attack. The Vogt's triad comprises of: • Glaukomflecken • Patches of iris atrophy • Slightly dilated nonreactive pupil

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old patient presents with painless white eye with an intraocular pressure of 60 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario fits the description of glaucomatocyclitic crisis. Glaucomatocyclitic crisis/Posner–Schlossman Syndrome [PSS]) describes recurrent attacks of unilateral acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) associated with mild anterior uveitis. The mechanism is thought to be acute trabeculitis , and there is evidence that infection , possibly cytomegalovirus (CMV) or Helicobacter pylori, may play a role. PSS typically affects young to middle -aged adults . Males are affected more frequently than females . Signs: • Slit-lamp biomicroscopy typically shows a few anterior chamber cells and one to several fine white central keratic precipitates . • Mydriasis is common; posterior synechiae are not a feature . • IOP is typically raised to over 40 mmHg, out of proportion to iritis severity . • Gonioscopy shows an open -angle.324 Treatment: • Topical steroids are used to control inflammation, with aqueous suppressants to lower the IOP. • Topical or oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents may also be beneficial . Note : In PSS, the rise in IOP is out of proportion to the pain felt . There is often a mild discomfort and pain may even be absent.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: An ophthalmologist evaluating a patient with glaucoma identifies the following finding on slit-lamp examination. What is the finding?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a pattern of the deposition of pigments on the back of the cornea in pigmentary glaucoma. They are called Krukenberg spindles . Pigmentary glaucoma is an open -angle glaucoma having the following features : • Krukenberg spindles • Gonioscopy shows pigment accumulation along the Schwalbe line inferiorly, and this accumulation is called the Sampaolesi line. • Radial transillumination defect in the iris is a pathognomonic feature . • Pigment granules may be deposited on the anterior surface . There may be a Scheie line or Zentmayer ring of pigment on the peripheral /equatorial surface around the zonular insertions. Other options : Option A: Ferry line: Corneal epithelial iron line at the edge of filtering blebs of glaucoma surgery Option B: Fleischer line/ring: Epithelial iron deposits at the base of the cone in keratoconus Option C: Hudson–Stahli line: Iron deposition line in the corneal epithelium , which is commonly seen in the junction between middle and lower third cornea. This finding is mainly age -related .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Malignant glaucoma is seen in __________.
mcqs.explanation: Malignant glaucoma is seen after intra-ocular surgery (usually after trabeculectomy ). Ciliary block glaucoma is also called malignant glaucoma/inverse glaucoma. It can be seen after any intraocular surgery. Forward flow of the aqueous is blocked as tips of ciliary processes rotate forward and press against the lens/intraocular lens (IOL)/anterior hyaloid of the vitreous. Hence , aqueous humor starts collecting in the vitreous cavity. Signs: • High intraocular pressure (IOP) and absent bleb . • Negative Seidel test . • Shallow anterior chamber (AC) Treatment:325 • Initial treatment is with cycloplegics (atropine 1%) to dilate the ciliary ring and push the vitreous -lens-iris posteriorly . • Subsequent treatment if medical therapy fails is with Nd:YAG laser hyaloidotomy . • Pars plana vitrectomy can be considered in conditions that don't respond to the above treatment modalities .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is iridocorneal endothelial syndrome associated with?

options.a: Progressive atrophy of the iris stroma
options.b: Bilateral stromal edema of the iris
options.d: Deposition of glycosaminoglycans in Descemet 's membrane

mcqs.explanation: Progressive atrophy of iris stroma is a clinical entity of iridocorneal endothelial syndrome (ICE). ICE syndrome is a proliferative endotheliopathy , which leads to secondary angle-closure glaucoma. It includes three clinical entities : • Progressive iris atrophy • Chandler's syndrome - corneal edema • Cogan–Reese syndrome - nodules and nevus on the iris; hence , it is known as iris nevus syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is seen in hypersecretory glaucoma?
mcqs.explanation: Hypersecretory glaucoma is associated with epidemic dropsy . Epidemic dropsy occurs due to Argemone mexicana poisoning. Here, glaucoma is due to excessive production of aqueous humor.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: 100 -day glaucoma is seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: 100 -day glaucoma is a neovascular glaucoma that occurs in ischemic type of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). It is known as 100 -day glaucoma because it occurs 3 months after the episode of CRVO . Although neovascular glaucoma occurs as a complication in Eale 's disease (Option B) and central retinal artery occlusion (Option C) and long-term use of topical steroid therapy causes steroid -induced glaucoma (Option D) none of them are termed as 100 -day glaucoma. CRVO is further classified into two types : • Non-ischemic CRVO : occurs secondary to venous stasis.It is the most common type of CRVO of the two . • Ischemic CRVO : occurs due to acute occlusion of the central retinal vein. It is also termed as hemorrhagic retinopathy . Ischemic CRVO presents with sudden loss of vision and Relative afferent pupil defect (RAPD ).326 Fundus examination shows massive enlargement of retinal veins and massive retinal hemorrhages giving a "splashed tomato appearance ". Other findings include cotton wool spots , optic disc edema and neovascularization at the disc and in the periphery . Pathagnomic features of ischemic CRVO that differentiates it from non-ischemic CRVO are: • RAPD • Reduced amplitude of B-wave on electroretinogram • Visual field defects Complications of the disease : • Neovascular Glaucoma known as 100 day glaucoma • Neovascularisation of iris known as Rubeosis iridis • Vitreous hemorrhage • Proliferative retinopathy The below -given fundus image is of the "splashed tomato" appearance of CRVO .Option B: Eales disease is an idiopathic inflammatory disease of the peripheral retinal veins.It is considered to be a hypersensitivity reaction to the tubercular proteins and it is commonly seen in young males. It is characterized by recurrent vitreous hemorrhage. Complications include : • Neovascular glaucoma • Proliferative vitreoretinopathy • Tractional retinal detachment , • Rubeosis iridis Option C: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is most often caused due to an embolus from an atherosclerotic plaque. It presents as sudden painless loss of vision and amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness that is due to ischemia). Fundus examination shows an opaque,327 milky-white retina with a cherry-red spot . Neovascular glaucoma may occur as a delayed complication of CRAO but it is not termed as 100 day glaucoma. The below image depicts the fundus image seen in CRAO with the cherry red spot .Option D:Steroid induced glaucoma is a type of secondary open angle glaucoma that usually follows weeks -months of topical steroid therapy .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the progression of ocular hypertension to primary open -angle glaucoma?

options.a: Reducing IOP is effective in delaying the onset of POAG
options.b: Thin cornea is a risk factor for POAG development
options.c: Family history is not a risk factor for POAG development
options.d: Increased cup disc ratio is a risk factor for POAG development

mcqs.explanation: Family history is a risk factor for the development of primary open -angle glaucoma. Ocular hypertension (OHT) is characterized by only raised intraocular pressure (IOP). Optic disc and normal visual field are normal , with no evidence of angle closure . Risk factors for the progression of ocular hypertension to primary open -angle glaucoma include the following : • African American race • Thin cornea • Increasing age • Increased cup -disc ratio • Increased IOP • Family history of POAG

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument given in the image below .
mcqs.explanation: 328 The given image shows Baerveldt implant which is a glaucoma drainage device (GDD)/seton/aqueous shunt. It consists of a scleral plate that is sutured to the sclera and a tube connecting it into the anterior chamber. It is valveless, and hence , it carries the risk of postoperative hypotony due to excessive aqueous drainage. Glaucoma drainage devices are devices that allow aqueous outflow by establishing a communication between the anterior chamber and sub-Tennon's space /sub-conjunctival space . The glaucoma valve implant is also known as a seton . The commonly used devices are as follows : 1. Shunts using episcleral explants • Ahmed glaucoma valve: Silicone • Molteno implant- Polypropelene plate and silicone plate • Baerveldt implant- Silicone 2. Mini-shunts • Ex-Press\231 Mini-Shunt: Stainless steel • iStent \256- Titanium

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the drug of choice for inverse glaucoma?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for inverse glaucoma is atropine. Inverse glaucoma is a type of secondary angle-closure glaucoma caused by the flow of aqueous humour posteriorly to the posterior segment instead of the posterior chamber. The increased pressure in the posterior segment pushes the lens forward leading to the shallowing of the anterior chamber. Miotics are contraindicated as they can cause the ciliary zonules to slack, the lens to move forward and further shallowing of the anterior chamber. So mydriatic and cycloplegic agents such as atropine are administered . Inverse glaucoma is also called : • Malignant glaucoma • Ciliary block glaucoma • Aqueous misdirection. Note : Pilocarpine is the drug of choice in angle -closure glaucoma but is contraindicated in inverse glaucoma. Whereas, atropine is the drug of choice in inverse glaucoma but is contraindicated in angle -closure glaucoma.329

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: An elderly male who is a known case of diabetes presents with blurry vision near the center of his field of vision. He also informs that colours appear washed out or faded . His IOP was found to be elevated . Which of the following drugs should not be used to control IOP in this diabetic patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This diabetic patient with new onset central loss of vision and reports of colors appearing faded or washed out most likely has macular edema. Prostaglandin analogs have a high propensity to cause and further exacerbate cystoid macular edema and hence are not preferred in this patient . Drugs associated with cystoid macular edema (CME ): • Prostaglandin analogues • Epinephrine • Dipivefrine (only the non-selective alpha agonists, in aphakic eyes ) • Tamoxifen • Timolol • Docetaxel • Interferons • Fingolimod • Thiazolinediones • Niacin (pseudo -CME )

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In a 55 -year-old patient presenting with secondary open -angle glaucoma, what is the most likely etiology ?
mcqs.explanation: Pseudoexfoliation (PEX ) syndrome is the most likely cause of secondary open -angle glaucoma. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an ocular manifestation of an age -related systemic disorder of the extracellular matrix, characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of fibrillar extracellular material in many ocular and systemic tissues . The clinical hallmark of PEX syndrome is the deposition of whitish abnormal pseudoexfoliative debris on the anterior lens capsule . A deposition is also noted on: • Zonules (causing zonulolysis and phacodonesis , lens subluxation ) • Pupillary margin • Trabecular meshwork (causing the secondary open -angle glaucoma)

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs increases the uveoscleral outflow ?
mcqs.explanation: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin drug, which acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure . Mechanism of action: Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles . This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases , which increases the uveoscleral outflow .330

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: True regarding POAG:
mcqs.explanation: In primary open -angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E). Statement A: Gonioscopy cannot visualize the specific abnormalities that occur in the trabecular meshwork in POAG. Gonioscopy diagnoses POAG because of the visibility of all the structures of the angle of the anterior chamber in contrast to the non-visibility of different structures in angle closure glaucoma. Statement C: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is associated with exacerbation of IOP with pupillary dilatation and not POAG. Statement D: There is a 10 % increased risk of POAG in siblings and a 4% increased risk in children of patients with POAG. POAG also known as chronic simple glaucoma of adult -onset is characterized by the presence of any 2 of the following 3 categories of changes : • Increased intraocular pressure : • IOP >21mmHg on more than one occasion, and/or • Circadian variation in IOP of >8 mmHg, or • Asymmetry in IOP > 5 mmHg between both eyes • Optic nerve head changes suggestive of glaucomatous damage . These may include one or more of the following changes : • Vertically oval cup • Cup -disc (C:D) ratio > 0.6 (average cup : disc ratio 0.3-0.4) • Asymmetry in C:D ratio > 0.2 between both eyes . • Narrowing, notching, or pallor of the neuroretinal rim . • Disc haemorrhages • Nasal shifting of retinal vessels -Bayonetting sign • Lamellar dot sign • Visual field changes - isopter contraction, barring of blind spot , paracentral scotoma, Seidel 's scotoma, Bjerrum's scotoma, double arcuate scotoma, and Roenne's central nasal step . A patient presenting with just raised IOP and visual field defects with normal optic nerve head findings such as a normal C:D ratio can still be diagnosed as POAG (statement E).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old lady was started on an ocular medication that she was instructed to take daily. She develops redness of the eye . Examination reveals a colour change of the iris and orbital fat atrophy. Which of the following medications was she likely prescribed ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history of a patient that has iris pigmentation and redness of the eye , was most likely started on latanoprost.331 Drug Side Effects Latanopr ost Allergic conjunctival hypere mia, permanent increase in ir is pigmentation , orbital fat at rophy. Timolol Exacerbation of asthma and c hronic obstructive pulmonar y disease , bradycardia, depre ssion, impotence Scopola mine Photosensitivity , blurred visi on Pilocarpi ne Corneal edema , miosis, induc ed myopia, decreased vision, brow ache, retinal detachmen t

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: First drug to be given in acute angle-closure glaucoma is _________.
mcqs.explanation: The first drug to be given in acute angle-closure glaucoma is oral acetazolamide or intravenous mannitol. Acetazolamide reduces IOP by decreasing the production of aqueous. The definitive drug is pilocarpine as it constricts the pupil and breaks the attack. Finally, when the corneal edema resolves, the patient has to undergo laser iridotomy to prevent such attacks in the future . So, laser iridotomy is the definitive management for acute angle-closure glaucoma.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The normal extent of the visual field superiorly is ________.
mcqs.explanation: The extent of visual field superiorly is 50\260 Normal extent of the visual field : • Temporal: 90\260/100 \260 • Inferiorly: 70\260 • Nasal: 60\260 • Superiorly : 50\260 Note : According to Parson 's 22nd Ed., Page no. , the visual field extends 60o superiorly . However, most journals and other standard textbooks consider the answer to be 50o. Hence, we choose 50o as the most appropriate answer.332

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are false about the ciliary body?

options.a: It consists of the pars plana and pars plicata.
options.b: Contraction of the ciliary body helps in accommodation.
options.d: It derives its blood supply from short posterior ciliary arteries.

mcqs.explanation: The ciliary body derives its blood supply from the long posterior ciliary artery and anterior ciliary arteries, which form the major arterial circle at the root of the iris. The ciliary body is a triangular structure that begins at the base of the iris and becomes continuous with the choroid at the ora serrata. It is approximately 6–6.5 mm in an anteroposterior dimension. It consists of an anterior portion called the pars plicata and a posterior portion called the pars plana (option A). The pars plicata contains approximately 70 finger-like projections called ciliary processes , which are covered by the ciliary body epithelium . These processes secrete aqueous humor (option C). The pars plana is the flat part of the ciliary body and ends at the ora serrata. The smooth muscle of the ciliary body is divided into three groups of fibers: • Outer longitudinal portion that attaches anteriorly to the scleral spur and trabecular meshwork fibers339 • Middle oblique portion • Inner circular portion (responsible for accommodation) (option B)

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child with the following finding has high myopia. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows corectopia , an abnormal eccentrically placed pupil . It can be a congenital anomaly or an acquired defect with essential iris atrophy. It may be associated with high myopia or ectopia lentis , among other conditions.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the casualty after ocular trauma with a D-shaped pupil . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A D-shaped pupil is seen in iridodialysis. Iridodialysis is the dis-insertion of the iris root from the ciliary body attachment . It may occur following ocular trauma. A red reflex can be obtained from the peripheral gap in the iris. The given image depicts iridodialysis and a D-shaped pupil .340

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the pathognomonic sign of acute anterior uveitis?
mcqs.explanation: The pathognomonic sign of acute anterior uveitis is keratic precipitates (KP). Keratic precipitates are proteinaceous cellular deposits at the back of cornea. The composition of KPs varies with the type of uveitis. Anterior uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue from the iris to the pars plicata of the ciliary body. Slit-lamp examination shows the following signs in anterior uveitis: • Corneal signs • Corneal edema • Keratic precipitates (Pathognomonic) • Posterior corneal opacity • Anterior chamber signs • Aqueous cells • Aqueous flare (earliest sign) • Hypopyon • Deep and irregular anterior chamber due to posterior synechiae • Iris signs • Loss of normal pattern • Change in color • Iris nodules (Koeppe , Busacca) • Posterior synechiae • Neovascularization341 • Pupillary signs • Constricted pupil • Irregular pupil shape • Ectropion of pupillary margin • Occlusion pupillae

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the first sign a patient with anterior uveitis may show?
mcqs.explanation: Aqueous flare is the earliest sign of acute anterior uveitis. Aqueous flare is due to the leakage of protein particles into the aqueous humor from damaged blood vessels . It is demonstrated on the slit-lamp examination. It is based on the principle of Brownian movement or Tyndall phenomenon. Aqueous flare is usually marked in non-granulomatous uveitis and minimal in granulomatous uveitis. The presence of cells in the anterior chamber denotes an active inflammatory process . The image below is a high magnification slit-beam photograph 3\3271 mm in size in a darkroom showing the presence of cells and flare.342

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old lady presents with eye pain, photophobia , and red-eye . The slit-lamp examination finding is shown below . On which layer of the cornea are these present ?
mcqs.explanation: Eye pain, photophobia and red-eye along with the slit lamp finding of keratic precipitates suggests a diagnosis of acute anterior uveitis. Keratic precipitates are proteinaceous cellular deposits occurring at the back of the corneal endothelium . Keratuc precipitates are arranged in a triangular fashion, occupying the center and inferior parts of the cornea (Arlt's triangle).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a 45-year-old man admitted for acute anterior uveitis. What is the pupillary shape you expect to find in his eyes ?
mcqs.explanation: The pupil in acute anterior uveitis is constricted (pupillary sphincter spasm), irregular and sluggishly reactive to light In an acute attack of uveitis, the pupil is irregular and narrow due to irritation of sphinchter pupillae . Pupillary signs in chronic anterior uveitis is as follows : • Festooned pupil results from the application of mydriatics in segmental posterior synechiae . • Occlusio pupillae results when the pupil is completely occluded due to the organization of the exudates across the pupillary area. • Seclusio pupillae due to ring synechiae, that prevent the circulation of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber. The image below shows a festooned pupil .343

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient with sarcoidosis shows Koeppe 's nodules on ophthalmologic examination. Where are these seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Koeppe 's nodules and Bussaca's nodules develop on the iris in granulomatous uveitis. Granulomatous uveitis is a chronic proliferative inflammation seen in reponse to tuberculosis , leprosy , syphilis and sarcoidosis.
