Infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells , with proliferation of mononuclear cells leads to the formation of iris nodule . Koeppe 's nodules are seen at the pupillary margin. Bussaca's nodules are seen on the peripheral part of the anterior surface of iris.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the type of synechiae formed in iris bombe?
mcqs.explanation: 344 Iris bombe formation is due to the development of annular or ring synechiae . Annular posterior/ring synechiae are 360 \260 adhesions of the pupillary margin to the anterior capsule of the lens. They prevent the circulation of aqueous humor from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber (seclusio pupillae). Thus, the aqueous collects behind the iris and pushes it anteriorly leading to iris bombe. This is usually followed by a rise in intraocular pressure . The anterior chamber is funnel -shaped when ring synechiae are present . The image below shows iris bombe on slit lamp examination.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old woman has been having repeated episodes of red-eye , eye pain, and blurred vision. She is diagnosed with chronic granulomatous uveitis. Which of the following is not a cause ?
mcqs.explanation: Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a type of non-granulomatous uveitis.345 Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is an insidious progressive anterior uveitis. It is mostly unilateral and associated with early cataract formation. Stellate keratic precipitates are seen and there is a notable absence of posterior synechiae . Causes for chronic granulomatous uveitis include sarcoidosis, tuberculosis , herpes simplex , herpes zoster, syphilis , leprosy , brucellosis and phacoanaphylactic .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Intermediate uveitis is also called as ________.
mcqs.explanation: Intermediate uveitis refers to pars planitis. It involves inflammation of the pars plana. The uvea consists of the iris, ciliary body and choroid. Inflammation of uveal tissue is called uveitis. It can be classified anatomically as follows : • Anterior uveitis: Inflammation of iris and pars plicata, consisting of iritis, iridocyclitis and anterior cyclitis • Intermediate uveitis: Inflammation of pars plana (pars planitis) • Posterior uveitis: Inflammation of the retina with or without involvement of the retina. It includes choroiditis, chorioretinitis, retinochoroiditis and neuroretinitis. • Panuveitis Pathological classification divides uveitis into suppurative and nonsuppurative uveitis. Nonsuppurative uveitis is further classified into nongranulomatous and granulomatous uveitis. The image is a schematic representation of the anatomical classification of uveitis.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In a patient with intermediate uveitis, which of the following is a pathognomonic examination finding?
mcqs.explanation: Snow banking is the hallmark of intermediate uveitis.346 Snow banking refers to greyish white fibrovascular plaques over the pars plana, with or without peripheral retinal periphlebitis . Intermediate uveitis is the inflammation of the pars plana and presents with retrolental flare, few keratic precipitates , vitreous cells and snow-ball opacities (Ant's egg opacities ). These are typical exudates present near the ora serrata in the inferior quadrant . Treatment of intermediate uveitis is by the Kaplan 4-step protocol : • Periocular steroid : Sub tenon injection of triamcinolone acetate • Systemic steroid • Cryotherapy over snow banking • Pars plana vitrectomy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: While studying a cohort of patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, you are evaluating the risk of iridocyclitis among the different subtypes of JIA . Which subtype has the highest risk of iridocyclitis associated ?
mcqs.explanation: ANA-positive oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA ) is associated with the highest risk for iridocyclitis (uveitis). A positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test result confers increased risk for uveitis in children with JIA and requires periodic slit-lamp examination. Uveitis in JIA is characteristically chronic, non-granulomatous, and bilateral. It presents as a white eye without congestion - white uveitis. Complications include complicated cataracts, secondary glaucoma, and band-shaped keratopathy . Note : Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation can be considered in most pediatric patients with well -controlled uveitis, but JIA -associated uveitis should be considered as a relative contraindication.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Where is Amsler's sign seen ?
mcqs.explanation: 347 Amsler sign is seen in Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI). Amsler sign is the hemorrhage caused by cataract surgery in FHI. During cataract surgery, fine filiform hemorrhages from the opposite angle are seen to occur as soon as the anterior chamber is opened . This is due to neovascularization. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is an insidiously progressive , non- granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral. Stellate KPs are seen and tiny crystals (Russell bodies ) may be present on the iris surface . There are no posterior synechiae . Rubeosis iridis may be present . The 1st image shows Fuchs heterochromic uveitis. The right eye is normal . The left hypochromic eye is affected . The 2nd image shows stellate keratic precipiates .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is Posner-Schlossman syndrome?

options.a: Ipsilateral optic atrophy with contralateral papilloedemac
options.b: Unilateral glaucomatous changes with mild anterior uveitis

mcqs.explanation: 348 Posner–Schlossman syndrome is characterized by unilateral glaucomatous changes with mild anterior uveitis. This syndrome, also known as glaucomatocyclitic crisis or hypertensive uveitis, presents with recurrent unilateral attachs of acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) (>40 mmHg) changes , fine white central keratic precipitates (KPs) and mydriasis. Treatment includes topical corticosteroids , cycloplegics , and aqueous suppressants .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 44-year-old patient with AIDS and opportunistic infections was started on treatment . He develops a sterile hypopyon anterior uveitis that is suspected to be drug-induced . Which of the following drugs may be implicated here?
mcqs.explanation: Rifabutin causes uveitis in AIDS patients. Causes of drug-induced uveitis include: • Cidofovir • Rifabutin • Bisphosphonates • Oral moxifloxacin

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is associated with transient hypopyon syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Behcet 's disease presents with recurrent iridocyclitis associated with transient hypopyon . Behcet 's disease is a systemic vascular disease . It is associated with HLA B5 >> B51. Patients have obliterative vasculitis due to circulating immune complexes , leading to a recurrent, bilateral non-granulomatous uveitis. There is acute recurrent iridocyclitis , transient hypopyon , periphlebitis , retinitis, vitritis and cystoid macular edema (CME ).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with photophobia and blurring of vision. On examination, the eye appears as shown below . What is the mainstay of treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario of photophobia and blurring of vision along with red-eye and irregularly shaped pupil suggests a diagnosis of anterior uveitis. Steroids and cycloplegics are the mainstay of the treatment of uveitis. Steroids are the drug of choice in anterior uveitis. They reduce inflammation by their anti-inflammatory effect . Cycloplegics like 1% atropine relieve spasm of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscles . They prevent the formation of synechiae and reduce exudation . Systemic therapy includes steroids , NSAIDs, and immunosuppressants . Immunosuppressants like voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) are used in severe cases . They are being studied under a program called LUMINATE.349

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient describes the image below on the Amsler grid test . In which of the given conditions is this phenomenon noted ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows metamorphopsia seen in posterior uveitis. Metamorphopsia is a condition in which patients perceive distorted images of the object . It is measured using the Amsler grid, which tests the central 10 degrees of vision. In posterior uveitis, metamorphopsia occurs due to macular edema . Posterior uveitis is a painless inflammation of the choroid. Patients present with various visual symptoms like defective vision, black spots floating in front of the eye , micropsia/macropsia and positive scotomas.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following features is unlikely to be noted in a patient with Vogt -Koyanagi-Harada syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Iris heterochromia is not a feature of Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome. Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome is an idiopathic , multi-system disorder characterised by autoimmunity against melanocytes . It is associated with HLA -DR1 and HLA -DR4 across different racial groups .356 Patients may present with cutaneous , neurological and ocular features . Cutaneous features include alopecia , poliosis and vitiligo (option A). Neurological features include meningism, encephalopathy , tinnitus, deafness and vertigo (option B). Ocular features include bilateral chronic granulomatous panuveitis (option C), posterior uveitis, exudative retinal detachment , perilimbal vitiligo (Suguiura's sign) and sunset glow appearance of the fundus . The modified diagnostic criteria for Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome are as follows : • Absence of a history of penetrating ocular trauma • Absence of other ocular disease entities • Bilateral uveitis • Neurological and auditory manifestations • Integumentary findings, not preceding the onset of the central nervous system or ocular diseases , such as alopecia , poliosis , and vitiligo. The treatment is high-dose (1–2 mg/kg/day) oral prednisolone , tapered over 3–6 months. This may be preceded by intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (500–1000 mg/day).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A middle aged male presents with recurrent oral ulcers and ulcers over his scrotum. He also has pain and redness of both his eyes . A positive pathergy test is noted . What is the HLA association of the disease this patient is most likely to be suffering from?
mcqs.explanation: Recurrent oral ulcers , ulcers over his scrotum with binocular pain and redness and a positive pathergy test point to a diagnosis of Behcet 's disease . HLA B5 (HLA B51) is associated with Behcet 's disease . Behcet 's disease is a systemic vasculitis that can cause recurrent oral ulcers , genital ulcers , skin lesions and ocular inflammation. Pathergy test is usually positive . Ocular inflammation occurs in about 70% of patients and tends to be more severe in men. A classical presentation is relapsing /remitting acute onset panuveitis with retinal vasculitis which resolves spontaneously even without treatment . It is usually bilateral and non-granulomatous. Patients present with a transient mobile hypopyon in a relatively white eye . They may develop visual impairment if retinal vascular disease (vasculitis and occlusion) occurs. Other options : Option A: HLA -B27 is associated with Reiter's syndrome. Option B: HLA DR1 and HLA -DR4 are associated with Vogt–Koyanagi–Haradas disease . Option D: HLA Bw54 is associated with Possner–Scholssman syndrome. Note : The association between HLA -A29 and birdshot retinochoroidopathy is the most consistent of any medical disorder . Approximately 95% of patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are HLA -A29 –positive .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 28 year old man presents to the medicine OPD with cough with hemoptysis of 1 month duration. A sputum culture done is shown below . What is the most common ocular manifestation associated with this infection ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) colonies on the Lowenstein -Jensen medium. In tuberculosis (TB ), granulomatous panuveitis is the most common357 ocular feature . Ocular TB commonly occurs due to hematogenous spread from pulmonary TB . It can have multiple presentations like lupus vulgaris of eyelid , tubercular conjunctivitis, interstitial keratitis, granulomatous uveitis and endophthalmitis. Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to the MTB antigen. Treatment of granulomatous panuveitis is anti-tubercular therapy (ATT ) plus steroids .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In a patient showing salt and pepper appearance of the fundus , which of the following is not a differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Salt and pepper fundus is not seen in tuberculosis . Salt and pepper fundus is seen when there are multiple small black and white spots present on the retina. It is also known as pseudo -retinitis pigmentosa . Its causes include congenital syphilis , rubella, Refsum's disease , carriers of albinism, Leber's congenital amaurosis and retinitis pigmentosa sine pigmentosa .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old lady presented with dry, itchy eyes , blurred vision, and sensitivity to light . She says there are black dots floating around in her visual field . She denies wearing any spectacles or contact lenses . On fundoscopy , the following image is obtained . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Dry, itchy eyes , blurred vision, sensitivity to light with candle wax dripping on fundus examination points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a chronic granulomatous multi-system disease . Ocular inflammation occurs in 25–70% of sarcoid patients , which includes uveitis, conjuctival and lacrimal gland involvement. Chronic granulomatous panuveitis may be seen . Anterior uveitis is the most common manifestation. In anterior uveitis due to sarcoidosis, "mutton fat" keratic precipitates (KPs) and/or small granulomatous KPs with iris nodules (Koeppe and/or Busacca) are seen . Trabecular meshwork (TM) nodules and/or tent -shaped peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) is also seen .358 In intermediate uveitis, vitreous cells with snowbanking and snowball opacities /string of pearl appearance are seen . Posterior uveitis presents with candle -wax dripping (thick venous sheathing and periphlebitis ), pre-retinal nodules (Lander's sign), choroidal granulomata and sarcoid infiltration. Other ocular features seen are interstitial keratitis and band-shaped keratopathy. Steroids are the mainstay of treatment in sarcoidosis.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common ocular manifestation in patients infected by the human immunodeficiency virus?
mcqs.explanation: Microangiopathy is the most common ocular feature of HIV infection . Microangiopathy of the retina in HIV consists of the hemorrhages, micro-aneurysms and cotton-wool spots or soft exudates (axonal debris). Cotton wool spots are the most common finding of HIV retinopathy . HIV leads to multiple opportunistic infections of the eye like cytomegalovirus (CMV) - most common cause of posterior uveitis in HIV - toxoplasmosis , Pneumocystis carinii and herpes zoster. These infections present as keratitis, choroiditis, retinitis and endophthalmitis . The most common ocular adverse effect in patients receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART ) is immune recovery uveitis (IRU). It is a non-granulomatous uveitis (usually anterior uveitis and vitritis) associated with a paradoxical or exaggerated reactivation of the immune system and an increase in intraocular inflammation. It occurs after receiving HAART for CMV chorioretinitis. Visual complications of IRU include cataract, cystoid macular edema (CME), glaucoma, and epiretinal membrane formation.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: An HIV positive patient presented to OPD with painless blurring of vision. On fundus examination , the following findings were seen . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Painless blurring of vision in an HIV positive patient with "sauce and cheese " or "pizza pie " retinopathy (shown in the image) is characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.359 CMV retinitis is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in patients with HIV . It is often asymptomatic and can be classified as central or peripheral CMV retinitis. Central CMV retinitis is characterised by dense , white areas of retinal necrosis and retinal hemorrhage in the areas of necrosis - pizza pie or sauce and cheese appearance . Peripheral CMV retinitis is less demarcated. The infection spreads along the vascular arcades in a brush fire-like fashion.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A newly diagnosed HIV -positive lady with CD4+ count of 35/�ML presented with decreased visual acuity and floaters . On fundus examination, there were dense , white areas of retinal necrosis with interspersed areas of retinal hemorrhage. What is the most rapid and accurate method to confirm the diagnosis?

options.c: Viral nucleic acid detection in intraocular fluid
options.d: Viral antibody detection in blood by ELISA

mcqs.explanation: An HIV -positive patient with CD4+ count of 35/�ML presenting with decreased visual acuity , floaters and pizza pie retinitis (dense , white areas of retinal necrosis with interspersed areas of retinal hemorrhage) likely has CMV retinitis. The most rapid and accurate method to diagnose cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is viral nucleic acid detection in the intraocular fluid . CMV retinitis is an opportunistic infection seen in HIV patients with a CD4+ count less than 50/�ML . Patients present with reduced vision due to macular involvement and floaters due to vitritis. One eye is usually affected initially. Retinitis is seen . Frosted branch angiitis (FBA), which is marked vascular sheathing that occurs in about 6% patients , may be seen . Cataract is common late -stage manifestation of CMV retinitis. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART ) is the mainstay of management, restoring the patient's innate ability to suppress CMV activity. Valganciclovir is a prodrug of ganciclovir that is taken orally. Ganciclovir slow -release intravitreal implant can also be used . Screening of patients with low CD4+ counts: • 3-monthly, if <50/�Ml • 6-monthly, if 50–100 /�Ml • Yearly, if >100/�Ml

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old man presented with blurring of vision in the right eye . Examination reveals mild iritis, severe vitritis, and a focal necrotic lesion on the macula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Monocular iritis, severe vitritis with a focal necrotic lesion on the macula is a classical description of ocular toxoplasmosis . Ocular toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan. It causes severe recurrent attacks of posterior uveitis in adults , due to reactivation at previously inactive cyst -containing scars. A single inflammatory focus of fluffy white retinitis or retinochoroiditis associated with a pigmented scar (" satellite lesion") is typical . "Headlight in the fog" is the classic description of a white retinal inflammatory nidus viewed through vitritis. "Spill-over" anterior uveitis is common. Treatment: • Prednisolone (1 mg/kg) is given initially and tapered according to clinical response . • Pyrimethamine is administered as a loading dose of 75 –100 mg for 1–2 days followed by 25–50 mg daily for 4 weeks in combination with oral folinic (not folic) acid 5 mg three times a week to360 retard thrombocytopenia , leukopenia , and folate deficiency . • Sulfadiazine 1 g four times daily for 3–4 weeks is usually given in combination with pyrimethamine. • Intravitreal therapy with clindamycin (1 mg) and dexamethasone (400 �Mg) may be as effective as triple therapy in reactivated infection . The image shows the characteristic "headlight in the fog" appearance :

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In which disease is the "headlight in fog" appearance seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The "headlight in fog" appearance is seen in toxoplasmosis . Ocular toxoplasmosis presents with iridocyclitis , which can be granulomatous or non-granulomatous. There is focal superficial necrotizing retinochoroiditis along with vitritis, which gives the "headlight in fog" appearance (image). Fundoscopy shows deep retinitis and papillitis with granulomas. Old choroid lesions of toxoplasmosis are punched -out lesions with pigmented borders. The treatment of choice for ocular toxoplasmosis is triple therapy with systemic steroids , pyrimethamine, and sulfadiazine . Clindamycin is also used .361

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presented with red-eye , ocular pain, and acute loss of vision to the casualty . On fundoscopy , areas of retinal ischemia and necrosis were seen , leading to a diagnosis of acute retinal necrosis. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.b: It is seen in immunocompetent individuals.
options.c: Posterior pole is involved initially with centrifugal spread .
options.d: It may lead to retinal detachment .

mcqs.explanation: In acute retinal necrosis, the posterior pole is typically spared until late . Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) occurs in immunocompetent individuals. It is a severe posterior uveitis causing retinal necrosis. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is the most common cause of acute retinal necrosis in adults . Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV ) are the commonest causes of acute retinal necrosis in children. Patients present with confluent peripheral necrotizing retinitis, retinal arteritis with vaso-occlusion, and vitritis. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are common due to retinal thinning from large areas of necrosis. The posterior pole is involved only in the later stages . Aciclovir is administered intravenously (10 mg/kg, every 8 hours) for 10 –14 days, and then orally (800 mg, five times daily) for 6–12 weeks . Oral valaciclovir or famciclovir may be substituted for oral aciclovir , with similar outcomes but better tolerability . Intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet may enhance the prognosis. Systemic steroids may be started 24 hours after the initiation of antiviral therapy , especially in severe cases . Laser retinopexy is performed around necrotic areas. Progressive outer retinal necrosis is a manifestation of HSV or varicella zoster virus (VZV ) that occurs in immunocompromised individuals. It may begin at the posterior pole or the periphery . It has a rapid course and is not generally associated with vasculitis.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old male presents with a painful decrease in vision of his right eye for the past 3 days. He underwent right phacoemulsification with PC-IOL insertion 6 months ago. Examination revealed a mild granulomatous anterior uveitis with minimal hypopyon and mild vitritis. There is a white plaque seen on the posterior lens capsule . Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy for this condition?

options.a: Vitrectomy and intravitreal injection of amphotericin B
options.c: Vitrectomy, removal of the IOL , and intravitreal injection of gentamicin
options.d: Vitrectomy, posterior capsulotomy , and intravitreal injection of vancomycin

mcqs.explanation: Painful decrease in vision following cataract surgery 6 months ago with granulomatous anterior uveitis, hypopyon , vitritis and a white plaque on the posterior lens capsule suggests a diagnosis of delayed -onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by Propionibacterium acnes. The best management for the above clinical scenario would be vitrectomy and posterior capsulotomy , followed by intravitreal injection of vancomycin.362 Delayed -onset endophthalmitis , a complication of cataract surgery, has a slow course and panuveitis like picture . There is low grade anterior chamber inflammation and vitritis. When caused by P. acnes, it typically presents from 3 months to 2 years after surgery with a characteristic white retro-lenticular plaque on the posterior capsule of lens. Endophthalmitis caused by Candida occurs within 3 months of surgery. Management includes anterior vitrectomy, IOL explantation , posterior capsulectomy , intravitreal vancomycin, and a scleral-fixated intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after ____________.
mcqs.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is seen after a penetrating trauma. Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis seen after a penetrating trauma or less frequently , following intraocular surgery, usually multiple vitreoretinal procedures . Patients present between 2 weeks and 3 months after initial injury. The earliest symptom is blurred near vision in the sympathizing (uninjured) eye . The earliest sign is a retrolental flare in the sympathizing eye . Anterior uveitis develops in both eyes . The fundus shows multifocal choroidal infiltrates in the mid-periphery . Sub-retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) infiltrates corresponding to Dalen–Fuchs nodules (image)(a granuloma situated between Bruch membrane and the RPE) are also present. Steroids are the basis of treatment . High-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months. Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclosporine , and methotrexate can be used in resistant cases or as steroid -sparing agents . Enucleation of a severely injured eye with no visual potential within 2 weeks of injury prevents the occurrence of sympathetic ophthalmia.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of endophthalmitis in a patient following eye trauma?
mcqs.explanation: 363 Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of post -traumatic endophthalmitis , followed by Bacillus cereus . However, if the trauma involves soil contamination, Bacillus cereus is the most common cause of post-traumatic endophthalmitis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs should not be used in a patient with uveitis and raised IOP?
mcqs.explanation: Pilocarpine should not be used in cases of uveitis with raised intraocular pressure . Hypertensive uveitis or inflammatory glaucoma occurs when uveitis is associated with raised IOP. It is treated with topical cycloplegics (atropine), topical steroids and IOP-lowering drugs like topical timolol or systemic acetazolamide . Pilocarpine is contraindicated since it causes miosis and ciliary spasm. It also increases intraocular inflammation.364

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is defined as loss of eyelashes ?
mcqs.explanation: Madarosis is the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows . • Loss of eyebrows is seen in leprosy and myxedema . • Loss of eyelashes is seen in chronic blepharitis .Other options : Option A: Tylosis is a thickening of the tarsal border of the eyelid . Option C: Trichiasis is an inward misdirection of cilia, with the normal position of the lid margin.374 Option D: Distichiasis is the presence of a double row of eyelashes .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the term used to describe an extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line?
mcqs.explanation: The extra row of eyelashes behind the grey line is called distichiasis . Distichiasis can occur due to congenital or acquired causes . These lashes may irritate the cornea. Management is by lid splitting with cryotherapy to the base of the hair follicles . Other options : Option A: Trichiasis is inward misdirection of cilia, with the normal position of the lid margin. Option C: Tylosis is the thickening of the tarsal plate . Option D: Madarosis is the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows .375

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A term neonate is referred to the district hospital for an ophthalmic exam. Partial fusion of her right upper and lower eyelids by a central narrow band of tissue is noted as shown below . The left eye examination is normal . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows an adhesion between the margins of the upper and lower eyelids , which suggests ankyloblepharon. It may occur as a congenital anomaly or as acquired adhesions after healing of chemical burns, ulcers, or traumatic wounds of the lid margins. Treatment is the excision of the adhesions between lid margins. In severe cases where the adhesions involve the angle of the eyes , epithelial grafts can be used . Other options : Option A: Symblepharon is the adhesion between the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, whereby the eyelids become adherent to the eyeball.Option C: Blepharophimosis is a congenital anomaly in which the extent of the palpebral fissure is decreased . It appears contracted at the outer canthus.376 Option D: Lagophthalmos is characterized by the inability to close the eyelids voluntarily. It may be due to a malfunction of the facial nerve. The image below shows nocturnal lagophthalmos (inability to close eyelids during sleep ).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A male patient complains of a foreign body sensation, irritation , and lacrimation in the right eye. During the evaluation, you notice the following findings with normal lid margins. What is this condition known as?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the above image is suggestive of trichiasis. Trichiasis refers to the inward misdirection of cilia, which usually rub against the eyeball with the normal position of the lid margin. These patients present with foreign body sensations and photophobia . They experience troublesome irritation , pain, and lacrimation. On examination, one or more misdirected cilia touching the cornea are seen . The conjunctiva may be congested . Treatment includes :377 • Epilation : Mechanical removal with forceps • Electrolysis : Method of destroying the lash follicle by electric current. • Cryoepilation • Surgical correction.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What defines telecanthus ?

options.d: Widened root of the nose with normal inter-pupillary distance

mcqs.explanation: Telecanthus means an increased distance between medial canthi (widened root of the nose) with normal inter-pupillary distance . In hypertelorism , there is a wide bony separation of the orbits. In epicanthus , there are bilateral vertical folds of skin that extend from the upper or lower lids towards the medial canthi. They may give rise to pseudoesotropia .378

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Weiss operation is done in which of the following condition?
mcqs.explanation: Weiss operation is done in senile entropion. In this operation, the transverse lid split , and everything sutures are placed . Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe . It is more common in the lower lid. Causes include : • Horizontal lid laxity • Vertical lid instability • Over-riding of the pretarsal by the preseptal orbicularis during lid closure • Orbital septum laxity

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: For which of the following is medial conjunctivoplasty the surgical modality of treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: Medial conjunctivoplasty is done in involutional ectropion . Ectropion is the eversion of the lid margin and eyelashes away from the globe . Types : • Involutional/senile - affects the lower lid of elderly patients . • Cicatricial - caused by the scarring or contracture of the skin and underlying tissues • Paralytic - caused by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy • Mechanical - caused by tumors on or near the lid margin that mechanically evert the lid379 • Congenital

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a feature of blepharophimosis syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Entropion is not a feature of blepharophimosis syndrome. Blepharophimosis , ptosis , and epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES) consists of the following : • Narrow palpebral fissure • Ptosis • Congenital ectropion of the lower lid • Telecanthus • Epicanthus inversus: an extra fold of skin arising from the lower lid The image below shows blepharophimosis .380

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The physician noticed the following finding in a patient that came to the OPD for an eye exam. Which of the following pair of muscles are likely to be affected in this patient ?

options.b: Levator palpebrae superioris and superior oblique
options.d: Levator palpebrae superioris and Muller 's muscle

mcqs.explanation: The patient has mild right eye ptosis . Injury or weakness of levator palpebrae superioris and Muller's muscle leads to ptosis . Levator palpebrae superioris is the important upper eyelid retractor. Frontalis and Muller 's muscle assist in the elevation of the upper eyelid .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is a cause of pseudoptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Brow ptosis is a type of pseudoptosis , not ptosis . Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid to a level that covers more than 2mm of the superior cornea. Types of ptosis : • Mechanical ptosis - Can be due to lid tumors, multiple /big chalazions, and conjunctival scarring • Aponeurotic ptosis - Due to dehiscence of the aponeurosis and in postoperative patients • Involutional ptosis seen in old age • Neurogenic ptosis due to a 3rd nerve palsy , Horner syndrome and synkinetic ptosis/Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking ptosis • Myogenic ptosis • Congenital : most common myogenic ptosis • Simple • Blepharophimosis syndrome • Congenital synkinetic ptosis381 • Acquired • Myasthenia gravis • Lambert–Eaton syndrome • Ocular myopathy Causes of pseudoptosis (apparent ptosis): • Lack of support of the lids by the globe e.g. artificial eye , microphthalmos, phthisis bulbi, or enophthalmos. • Contralateral lid retraction • Ipsilateral hypotropia • Brow ptosis occurs due to excessive skin on the brow, or seventh nerve palsy , which is diagnosed by manually elevating the eyebrow • Dermatochalasis

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses . He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors . Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis and ptosis is the most common ocular feature of the disease . Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction most commonly caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies . The disorder is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles where the weakness increases during repeated use and may improve following rest. Ptosis and diplopia are common initial complaints due to early involvement of the lids and extraocular muscles (EOMs ). Of them, Ptosis is a more common manifestation than diplopia . Ptosis in myasthenia gravis is insidious, bilateral, and frequently asymmetrical. Investigations of myasthenia gravis include : • Ice pack test -This tests for a transient improvement of the ptotic eyelid on placing an ice pack for 2 minutes , as the cold inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase . • Tensilon (Edrophonium) test - This tests for a transient improvement in the weakness on administration of a short-acting anticholinesterase such as edrophonium . • Antibody testing - for Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies , MuSK protein antibodies helps support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions will not have a finding of bilateral ptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Bilateral ptosis is not seen in Marfan's syndrome. Causes of unilateral ptosis :382 • Horner's syndrome • Oculomotor nerve palsy Causes of bilateral ptosis : • Congenital • Senile /involutional/aponeurotic • Blepharophimosis syndrome • Myasthenia gravis • Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) - seen in Kearns-Sayre syndrome • Myotonic dystrophy • Ocular myopathies The image below shows a case of botulinum toxicity with bilateral ptosis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: During OPD hours, a patient came with the finding shown below . On examination, the upper 4 mm of the cornea is covered by the upper eyelid . What is the grade of ptosis in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In this question, 4 mm of the cornea is covered by the upper eyelid . Subtracting 2 mm from this implies that there is 2 mm of ptosis , which is classified as mild grade. In bilateral cases , the grade of ptosis can be determined by measuring the amount of cornea covered by the upper lid and then subtracting 2 mm. Depending upon this value, the ptosis is graded as follows : • Mild : 2 mm • Moderate : 3 mm • Severe: 4 mm383

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A child with a high risk of amblyopia is planned for surgical correction of unilateral simple congenital ptosis . He has poor levator function. What is the treatment of choice in this case?
mcqs.explanation: Frontalis sling procedure is the treatment of choice for congenital ptosis with poor levator function.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents to you with anhidrosis and enophthalmos . Examination reveals miosis along with mild ptosis . You decide to correct the ptosis by performing a Fasanella-Servat operation, by resecting which of the following muscles ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Horner's syndrome and the associated mild ptosis in this condition can be corrected by resecting Muller 's muscle . Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the paralysis of Muller 's muscle . Fasanella-Servat operation is indicated in cases having mild ptosis (< 2 mm) and good levator function. In this surgery, the upper tarsal border along with its attached Muller 's muscle and conjunctiva are resected .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A couple brought their 11 -month-old child for an eye exam when they noticed that his left upper eyelid was in a lower position than his right one. The mother also noticed that his left upper eyelid goes "up and down" when she breastfeeds him. His delivery was unremarkable. When the baby opens his mouth or sucks his thumb, the left eyelid ptosis disappears . What is the pathology behind this condition?

options.a: Superior division of the third cranial nerve is misdirected
options.b: Sympathetic nerves to Muller 's muscles are misdirected
options.c: Ophthalmic division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected
options.d: Mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon . In this condition, the mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected to the levator muscle . Some cases of congenital ptosis are associated with the Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon . The vast majority are unilateral. Signs include retraction of the ptotic lid in conjunction with stimulation of the ipsilateral pterygoid muscles by chewing , sucking, opening the mouth, or contralateral jaw movement. Less common stimuli to winking include jaw protrusion, smiling, swallowing , and clenching of teeth . Jaw-winking does not improve with age although patients may learn to mask it. The following image shows a woman with Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon . See how her right eyelid ptosis retracts with the opening of the mouth.384

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the causative agent for blepharitis acarica?
mcqs.explanation: Blepharitis acarica is caused by Demodex folliculorum . Blepharitis is a chronic inflammation of the margins of the lids. The two types are • Anterior • Seborrheic and ulcerative types • Caused by staphylococci , mainly • Posterior – Mebomianitis Occasionally caused by • Demodex folliculorum – Blepharitis acarica • Crab louse – Phthiriasis palpebrarum The following image shows swollen and inflamed eyelid suggestive of blepharitis .385

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common malignant tumor of the eyelid ?
mcqs.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma constitutes 85–90% of all malignant epithelial eyelid tumors. It is locally malignant and most commonly involves the lower lid, followed by the medial canthus, upper lid, and outer canthus.Type Common location Clinical features Spread Basal cell carcinoma Lower lid/Medial canthus NoduleCentral ulceration withpearlysurface ,telangie ctasia local Squamous cell carcin oma Lower lid, from previous a ctinic keratosis Ulcerwith thickened margi ns,keratosispapillomatous Local, lymph nodes Sebaceous cell carcin oma Upperlid Nodule -likechalazionMulti focalFemales >malesRecur rencescommon Local intraepithelial lymp h nodes Malignant melanoma Previous nevi >6 mmpigmented ,Vascula rizationinflammation Local, vascular lymph nod es

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following systemic drugs is used specifically in the management of periocular basal cell carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Vismodegib is the systemic drug used for the management of periocular basal cell carcinoma (BCC). Vismodegib is an eye -sparing adjuvant therapy of periocular and orbital BCC for patients : • Who cannot tolerate surgery or radiotherapy , or • With relapsed locally advanced disease after surgery or386 • With metastatic disease . Vismodegib is a Hedgehog pathway inhibitor, given 150 mg orally twice a day. Treatment options for BCC consist of surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy . Surgical excision using Mohs micrographic surgery or wide surgical excision with frozen section margin control is the first-line treatment of periocular BCC. Other options : Option A: Imiquimod 5% topical cream can also be used in patients with BCC. But, it is not a systemic drug. Option C: Siponimod is the drug approved for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis . Option D: Interferons are generally not used in periocular BCC.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old girl was brought by her worried parents due to a swelling on the eyelid as shown below . They were told by a local village doctor that the swelling will disappear on its own but recently it has been increasing rapidly. What would be the most likely management of this baby's condition?

options.b: Treatment with intralesional steroids at 2 years of age

mcqs.explanation: The history and image are suggestive of capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular region causing severe mechanical ptosis . Immediate management with oral propranolol is the treatment of choice in this case. The ptosis is so severe that it obstructs the pupillary area (visual axis) with the risk of sensory deprivation amblyopia. This warrants immediate treatment to reduce the bulk of the tumor. Capillary hemangioma regresses spontaneously very often . It may be managed by oral propranolol, oral prednisolone , or intralesional steroid . Indications for treatment of patients with capillary hemangioma with pharmacologic therapy are: • Visual symptoms (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion , strabismus) • Cosmesis • Optic nerve compression • Exposure keratopathy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Identify the clinical condition.
mcqs.explanation: The image shows plexiform neurofibroma of the upper lid causing an S-shaped deformity of the upper lid and mechanical ptosis . This is seen particularly in neurofibromatosis type 1. NF1 is caused by the autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. It is a tumor suppressor gene that encodes neurofibromin, a negative RAS regulator. The disease is clinically diagnosed when any two of the following seven features are present : • Six or more caf\351-au-lait macules (CALMs) - They are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis and are present in almost 100 % of patients . They are present at birth but increase in size, number, and pigmentation , especially during the first few years of life , and are scattered over the entire body. • Axillary or inguinal freckling387 • Two or more iris Lisch nodules - They are iris hamartomas that are best identified by a slit-lamp examination . They are present in the majority of patients with NF1. • Two or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma • A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or cortical thinning of long bones such as the tibia • Optic gliomas (most frequently observed CNS tumor in NF1) • A first-degree relative with NF-1

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following sign is used to describe the fullness of eyelids seen in Grave's ophthalmopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: The fullness of the eyelids is described as the Enroth's sign in Graves ophthalmopathy .388

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: Moll glands are examples of _______
mcqs.explanation: Moll glands are examples of apocrine sweat gland. Moll glands are present in the eyelid . They are a type of modified apocrine sweat glands opening either into a lash follicle or directly onto the anterior lid margin between the lashes . Zeis glands are a type of modified sebaceous glands associated with lash follicles . Meibomian glands are modified sebaceous glands found in the tarsal plates .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A patient presented with a painless swelling and watering in his left eye . Examination revealed the following finding. Which of the following statements is false regarding his diagnosis?

options.a: It needs to be surgically treated .
options.c: It does not have malignant potential.
options.d: It is a chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation.

mcqs.explanation: A painless swelling on the lower lid is suggestive of a chalazion (tarsal cyst /meibomian cyst ). It has the malignant potential to become an adenocarcinoma of the meibomian gland. Chalazion is the chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation (option D) of the meibomian gland (option B). It presents as painless swelling of the eyelid . It is more common in adults than children. Treatment includes incision and curettage (option B) and intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetate .396

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A recurrent chalazion should be subjected to histopathological evaluation to exclude the possibility of _____.
mcqs.explanation: A recurrent chalazion should be subjected to histopathological evaluation to exclude the possibility of sebaceous gland carcinoma. Note : A chalazion can undergo malignant change into sebaceous gland carcinoma (adenocarcinoma of meibomian gland). Recurrences of chalazia are not uncommon. However, the physician should entertain the possibility of malignancy in such cases and should biopsy a lesion that recurs or appears atypical . The pathologist should be alerted to the suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma and frozen sections and lipid stains should be requested .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the clinic with severe left eye pain, watering , and swelling of the lid for 2 days. He says it's difficult to see the laptop screen while working and he is unable to complete his daily targets . On examination, tender swelling is noted as shown below . What is the cause of this finding?
mcqs.explanation: The patient has acute presentation and painful swelling in the palpebral conjunctiva as shown in the image, suggestive of internal hordeolum . It is an acute suppurative inflammation of the meibomian gland associated with blockage of the duct . Other options : Options A and B: Hordeolum externum or stye is the acute staphylococcal infection of the hair follicle /Zeis gland/Moll gland.Option D: Chalazion is a chronic non-suppurative lipogranulomatous inflammation of the Meibomian gland.397

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: What is the length of the nasolacrimal duct ?
mcqs.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct is 12 –18 mm long. The lacrimal drainage system consists of the lacrimal sac, which is 10 –12 mm long. It lies in the lacrimal fossa, between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests . The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity. The nasolacrimal duct is the inferior continuation of the lacrimal sac. It is 12 –18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally . The opening of the duct into the inferior meatus is partially covered by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner). The puncta are openings on the lid margin. There are two canaliculi from the puncta. Each canaliculus (superior and inferior) has two parts: Vertical (2 mm) and horizontal (8 mm). The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite to form the common canaliculus , which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac. A small flap of mucosa (Rosenm\374ller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac and prevents the reflux of tears into the canaliculi. The image below shows structures of the lacrimal apparatus.398

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: Where does the nasolacrimal duct open ?
mcqs.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus . The nasolacrimal duct is the inferior continuation of the lacrimal sac. It is 12 –18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally . The opening of the duct into the inferior meatus is partially covered by a mucosal fold , called the valve of Hasner. The valve of Hasner prevents reflux from the nose.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old woman came for an eye exam due to a gritty sensation that has been causing her a lot of discomfort. On examination, Rose Bengal staining is positive . She is diagnosed with keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Which of the following layer of the tear film is deficient in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is due to the deficiency of the aqueous layer of the tear film. In keratoconjunctivitis sicca, patients present with irritation and foreign body sensation. Marginal tear strip is reduced . The conjunctiva become dry and lustreless with positive Rose Bengal staining. Causes of keratoconjunctivitis sicca: • Sjogren's syndrome (primary keratoconjunctivitis sicca) • Non-Sjogren's keratoconjunctivitis sicca • Primary age -related hyposecretion (most common) • Lacrimal gland deficiencies - congenital, infiltration by tumors or sarcoidosis, surgical removal • Lacrimal gland duct obstruction - old trachoma, burns, SJS • Reflex hyposecretion (neurogenic causes ) - Parkinson disease , 7th nerve palsy , reflex sensory block399

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the phenol red test for dry eye ?

options.b: It measures tear production based on the length of colour change in the thread
options.c: If color changes to blue , it depicts mucin deficiency .

mcqs.explanation: Phenol red test measures the tear production according to the length of colour change in the thread. In phenol red test , the alkalinity of tears changes its colour to bright orange on contact. It doesn 't require anaesthesia (unlike Schirmer's test ). Three millimetres of a fine dye -impregnated 75 -mm cotton thread is placed under the lateral one-fifth of the inferior palpebral lid margin for 15 seconds . Based on length of colour change, • >20 mm - normal tear production • 10 to 19 mm - borderline dry eye • <10 mm - severe dry eye

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: Identify the test shown below .
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a tear strip placed in the lower lid of the eye . This is the Schirmer test which is used to check for dry eye . Dry eye is a multifactorial disease of the eye characterised by loss of homeostasis of the tear film. Patients present with irritation , foreign body sensation and dryness . Treatment of dry eye includes medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops , most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs ). Other tests for dry eye include : • Tear film break-up test is used to determine the interval between a complete blink and appearance of first randomly distributed dry spot on the cornea. A drop of fluorescein is instilled in the eye , following by examination in the cobalt-blue light of a slit-lamp. • Rose Bengal staining is used for the detection of dry, dead epithelium in dry eye . • Tear osmolarity test is performed with an osmometer . Other options : Option B: Ishihara plates are used to test colour vision. They help detect red-green colour blindness . Option C: Jones test is used in watering eye . It uses fluorescein dye . Option D: Goldmann's tonometry is used to measure intra-ocular pressure . It consists of a double prism mounted on a slit-lamp.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: You are conducting retrospective research on factors responsible for dry eye disorder. As a part of your study , you are looking through the files in the clinic of dry eye patients . Which among the following patients would not be included in your study ?

options.a: A 26 year old patient showing decreased levels of lactoferrin in tear samples
options.b: A 20 year old patient showing tear film break up at 18-20 seconds
options.c: A 24 year old patient showing A pattern stain in Rose bengal staining
options.d: A 22 year old patient showing Schirmer test tear strip wet upto 9 mm

mcqs.explanation: A patient with tear film break up at 18-20 seconds is considered to be normal . All the other patients have dry eye .400 Tear film break-up (BUT) time is the interval between a complete blink and the appearance of a first randomly distributed dry spot on the cornea. It is an indicator of the adequacy of the mucin component of tears. Inference: • 15-35 seconds - normal • < 10 seconds - unstable tear film Other options : Option A: Tear samples can be assayed for the presence of markers known to be decreased (e.g. lactoferrin) or elevated (e.g. matrix metalloproteinase -9) in dry eye . This is known as tear constituent measurement . Option C: A patient with A pattern on Rose Bengal staining has severe dry eye . Option D: A patient with 9mm wet Schirmer strip has moderate dry eye .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: The findings of a test done in a patient under evaluation for dry eye are shown below . Identify the test .
mcqs.explanation: The image above depicts lacrimal scintigraphy . Lacrimal scintigraphy (dacryoscintigraphy) is used to assess the lacrimal drainage function. A radioactive tracer (technetium -99m) is instilled into the conjunctival sac. Its path is then visualised with an Anger gamma camera. It is useful for the evaulation of watering eye . Other tests for evaluation of watering eye include regurgitation test , syringing, fluorescein dye disappearance test (FDDT), Jones dye test and dacryocystography . Other options : Option A: In regurgitation test , steady pressure with the index finger is applied above the medial palpebral ligament. Option B: In dacryocystography , a radioopaque material is inserted into the lacrimal sac, following which X-rays are taken. Option C: The image shows the Jones dye test .401

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: What is the site of blockage in congenital dacryocystitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The site of blockage in congenital dacryocystitis is the nasolacrimal duct . Congenital dacryocystitis occurs due to the stasis of secretions in the lacrimal sac due to congenital blockage in the nasolacrimal duct . Membranous occlusion at its lower end near the valve of Hasner is the commonest cause . The image below shows a neonate with congenital dacryocystitis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A mother noticed the following finding in her 3-month-old child. There is a history of watering and discharge from his right eye since birth. Which of the following is the best next step in the treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: 402 The image showing right-sided swelling in the lacrimal sac area along with watering of the eye is suggestive of congenital dacryocystitis . Treatment for a 3-month-old child includes sac massage with topical antibiotics. Congenital dacryocystitis is chronic inflammation of the lacrimal sac in newborn infants. It occurs due to congenital blockage of the nasolacrimal duct . More than 90% of patients with undergo spontaneous resolution by 1 year of age . Treatment of congenital dacryocystitis depends on the age of the child: • Less than 9 months: Massaging (Crigler's massage which increases the hydrostatic pressure within the sac) and antibiotic eye drops • 9 months to 4 years: Probing • Older children (> 4 years): Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) gives the best result . In DCR, an opening is made into the nasal cavity from the lacrimal sac.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with watering from the right eye for 1 year. Syringing revealed a patent drainage system . Rest of the ocular examination was normal . A provisional diagnosis of lacrimal pump failure was made. Which of the following test will help in the confirmation of the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Lacrimal pump failure can be confirmed with dacryoscintigraphy . Lacrimal pump failure means an inability of the lid muscles to push tears towards the punctum for drainage. It is also called functional obstruction and may be secondary to lower lid laxity or orbicularis muscle weakness (eg . facial nerve palsy . It is confirmed by dacryoscintigraphy , in which a radioactive tracer (technetium -99m) is instilled into the conjunctival sac and its path visualised with an Anger gamma camera. An atonic lacrimal sac is seen . Note : In cases of partial obstruction of the lacrimal apparatus, forced injection of fluid into the canalicular system (dacryocystography ) can overcome the obstruction sites and point to a diagnosis of lacrimal pump failure. Thus, dacryoscintigraphy is better for the confirmation of lacrimal pump failure.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis . Which of the following is the surgery of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) DCR involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. It re-establishes the lacrimal drainage and is hence the preferred surgery for chronic darcyocystectomy . Chronic dacryocystitis is a long-standing inflammation of the lacrimal sac. Streptococcus hemolyticus and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common etiological agents . Initial treatment is with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents . Sequelae include lacrimal fistula formation and mucocele formation , which when infected , leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy . Treatment of lacrimal fistula is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).403

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic dacryocystitis , refractory to the medical treatment , has been scheduled for dacryocystorhinostomy. Following the surgery, the sac would be draining into the _______.
mcqs.explanation: After dacryocystorhinostomy , the lacrimal sac drains into the middle meatus . Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: What is the most common ocular manifestation in mumps?
mcqs.explanation: The most common ocular manifestation in mumps is dacryocystadenitis . Dacryocystadenitis , or inflammation of the lacrimal gland, is seen in mumps. It presents as a painful swelling in the lateral part of the upper lid.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Lacrimal Apparatus and Glands of t...
mcqs.question: Which is the most common lacrimal gland tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common lacrimal gland tumor. It is also the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. Pleomorphic adenoma, or benign mixed tumor, presents commonly in middle age as a slowly progressive painless swelling in the upper outer quadrant of the eyelid . The bone is usually not invaded in these tumors. They are treated by surgical removal along with their intact pseudo -capsule . Malignant tumors of the lacrimal gland such as adenoid cystic carcinoma (option A), mucoepidermoid carcinoma (option C) and malignant mixed tumor (option D) generally occur in the elderly with a short history of appearance, rapid progression and pain. These tumors also present in the upper eyelid and are known to invade the adjacent bones. Radical surgical procedures and high dose radiotherapy are necessary for the removal of the tumor. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. Both malignant and benign tumors are known to push the eyeball downwards and inwards while restricting the upwards and outwards movement of the eyeball . The most common epithelial tumors, in order of frequency, are as follows : • Benign mixed tumor (BMT), also known as a pleomorphic adenoma (PA) • Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) • Pleomorphic adenocarcinoma (ACA) • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma404

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following structures does not pass through the superior orbital fissure ?
mcqs.explanation: The optic nerve (2nd cranial nerve) passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure . Anatomy of the orbit Orbit is a pear-shaped cavity, the stalk of which is the optic canal. The volume of the orbit is 30 cc. The image below shows the bones forming the orbit.Wallsof the orbit Bonesforming them Roof Lesser wing of the sphenoidT he orbital plate of the frontal bone Lateralwall (strongest wall) Greater wing of the sphenoid Zygomatic bone Floor(most frequently fractur ed wall) Zygomatic boneMaxillary bo nePalatine bone Medialwall (thinnest wall) Maxillary boneLacrimal bone Ethmoid boneSphenoid boneThe inferior orbital fissure lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the maxilla, connecting the orbit to the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae . Through it run the maxillary nerve, the zygomatic nerve, and branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion, as well as the inferior ophthalmic vein.411

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: You are volunteering in a medical camp held in an orphanage. You see a kid with hypoplasia of the zygoma and mandible along with antimongoloid slant of palpebral fissures as shown below . These findings correspond to which of the following syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The given findings correspond to Treacher–Collins syndrome. Treacher–Collins syndrome/Mandibulofacial dysostosis refers to a condition resulting from the hypoplasia of the zygoma and mandible. Ocular features : • Indistinct inferior orbital margin • Coloboma of the lower eyelid • Anti-mongoloid slant of palpebral fissures Systemic features • Macrostomia with a high-arched palate • External ear deformity • Bird-like face The image below shows features of Treacher–Collins syndrome.Craniofacial dysostosis /Crouzon syndrome refers to the premature closure of the coronal and sagittal sutures (brachycephaly —clover-leaf skull) associated with maxillary hypoplasia . Ocular associations include the following : • Blue sclera • Megalocornea • Aniridia • Glaucoma • Cataract • Ectopia lentis • Optic nerve hypoplasia412 The image below shows a baby with Crouzon syndrome.Apert syndrome is the most severe form of craniosynostosis, involving premature closure of multiple cranial sutures (acrocephaly ), along with syndactyly of the fingers and toes . The image below shows the hands of a patient with Apert syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of trauma, presented with diplopia , epistaxis , and restricted eye movements. Looking at the CT image given below , what will be your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario plus the supportive CT image showing the "hanging drop sign" is suggestive of a blowout fracture of the orbital wall. Blow-out fractures are isolated comminunited fractures caused from direct trauma to the orbit that results in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure . This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall which is usually the posteromedial413 portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fracture is the medial wall of the orbit. The patient with blow out fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paresthesia along the infraorbital nerve are also very common. Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called as the "hanging drop sign" or "tear drop sign". Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10 -14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics. Le fort fracture- Is the term used to describe different types of maxillary fractures.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of an orbital blowout fracture?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of an orbital blowout fracture is the floor of the orbit. Blow-out fractures are isolated comminunited fractures caused from direct trauma to the orbit that results in a backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in the intraorbital pressure . This causes a fracture at the weakest point of the orbital wall which is usually the posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone in the orbital floor. The second most common site for orbital blowout fracture is the medial wall of the orbit (Option A). The fractures of the roof(Option C) are relatively rare and most often do not require any treatment.The lateral wall(Option B) of the orbit is the most solid orbital wall and a fracture here is usually seen in injuries with extensive facial damage . The patient with blow out fracture usually presents with immediate periorbital edema and blood extravasation in and around the orbit. Proptosis of the eyeball secondary to orbital edema or hemorrhage with paresthesia along the infraorbital nerve are also very common. Imaging by a plain x-ray in water's view or by CT demonstrates depression of bony fragments and orbital contents herniating through the orbital floor into the maxillary antrum. This is called as the "hanging drop sign" or "tear drop sign". Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10 - days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotics. The below given CT image shows hanging drop sign.414 The below given X-ray image in water's view shows "hanging drop sign".

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding the clinical sequelae expected in a patient with orbital blowout fracture is false ?

options.a: Anesthesia of the cheek is very common.
options.b: Emphysema of eyelids is more common with medial wall fracture.
options.c: Enophthalmos develops about 10 days after the injury.
options.d: Severe ocular damage is seen in most cases .

mcqs.explanation: Severe ocular damage associated with a "blowout " fracture is rare. This is because a "blowout fracture" is nature's way of protecting the globe from injury. Clinical features of blow out fracture are as follows : • Periorbital edema • Paresthesia and anesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve (lower lid, cheek , side of the nose, upper lip, and upper teeth ) • Emphysema of the eyelids -more frequent with medial wall fractures415 • Proptosis-seen initially due to orbital edema and hemorrhage. • After about 10 days, as the edema decreases , the eyeball sinks backward and somewhat inferiorly, resulting in enophthalmos and mechanical ptosis . • Double diplopia - diplopia in upward as well as downward gaze

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Two people who got in a brawl are brought to the emergency department because of severe facial injuries. In one of those patients , there is periorbital ecchymosis and anesthesia over the cheek . Orbital blowout fracture is suspected . What X-ray finding will confirm this diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The X-ray finding seen in an orbital blowout fracture is hanging drop/tear-drop sign. Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow -out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water's view.The optimal time for surgery following a blowout fracture is 10 –14 days. Indications for surgery in a blowout fracture are as follows : • Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma • A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum • Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze • Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: All of the following are characteristic clinical findings that are associated with a history of blunt trauma to the eye , except :
mcqs.explanation: Vossius ring, not Soemmering's, is seen after blunt trauma to the eye Soemmering's ring refers to a thick ring of after cataract, also known as "secondary cataract." It is the opacity that persists or develops after extracapsular lens extraction.416 Blunt trauma to the eye produces : • Vossius ring - It is a circular ring of brown pigment seen on the anterior capsule . It occurs due to the striking of the contracted pupillary margin against the crystalline lens. • Rosette cataract - It is the most typical form of concussion cataract. • Commotio retinae (Berlin's edema ) - It manifests as milky white cloudiness involving a considerable area of the posterior pole with a "cherry-red spot " at foveola.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of globe rupture following trauma?
mcqs.explanation: The superonasal limbus is the most common site of globe rupture . This occurs due to the contrecoup effect —the lower temporal quadrant is the most exposed to trauma; hence , the effect is seen in the superonasal limbus, which lies on the opposite side .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is the following clinical finding seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses , which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in bilateral anterior cranial fossa fracture. It is also known as panda eyes /raccoon eyes . The pooling of blood surrounding the eyes is most commonly associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This finding is typically not present during the initial evaluation and is delayed by 1 to 3 days. If bilateral, this finding is highly predictive of a basilar skull fracture.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Clinical examination patients with which of the following conditions would show Dalen Fuchs Nodules ?
mcqs.explanation: Dalen Fuchs nodules are seen in sympathetic ophthalmitis and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease (VKH) syndrome. These are local granulomas due to the proliferation of lymphocytes and epithelioid cells and are located between RPE and Bruch's membrane. The image below shows Dalen Fuchs nodules .417

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following views would you advise, so as to visualize the optic foramina ?
mcqs.explanation: The Rhese view in an X-ray scan helps in the visualization of the optic foramina . The optic foramen/optic canal transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery. Rhese view: for optic foramenOther X-ray views of the orbit: 1. Caldwell 's view: Occipitofrontal Structures seen : • Superior orbital fissure • Greater and lesser wing of the sphenoid418 • Ethmoid and frontal sinus • Floor of the sella 2. Water's view: • Occipitomeatal : floor of the orbit is seen (important in "blow-out" fractures) • Occipitomental : maxillary sinus and floor of the orbit 3. Towne' s view: Structures seen • Dorsum sellae of the sphenoid bone • Inferior orbital fissure

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Heterochromia iridis may be caused by which of the following intraocular foreign bodies ?
mcqs.explanation: Heterochromia iridis may be caused by iron deposition . Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. In siderosis bulbi, the iris is first stained greenish and later turns reddish brown, causing heterochromia iridis. Chalcosis refers to the specific changes produced by the alloy of copper in the eye . Clinical features include the following : • Kayser –Fleischer ring- a golden brown ring that occurs due to the deposition of copper in the Descemet 's membrane of the cornea. • Sunflower cataract- produced by the deposition of copper under the anterior capsule of the lens. It is brilliant golden green in color and arranged like the petals of a sunflower . The image below shows siderosis bulbi.419

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is most likely to produce this finding on CT?
mcqs.explanation: The CT image shows hyperostosis of the lateral wall of the left orbit. Hyperostosis causing lesions are: • Sphenoid wing meningioma • Fibrous dysplasia • Metastasis from cancer prostate

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old construction worker presented to the emergency department with complaints of pain and decreased vision over his right eye . He gives a history of accidental exposure with a cleaning agent that contains ammonia . Ocular examination finding is given below . According to the Roper-Hall system , what is the grade of chemical injury?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a grade II chemical injury. There is limbal ischaemia in the lower left quadrant involving <1/3 of the limbus and a hazy cornea with visible iris details . The Roper–Hall system is used for the classification of chemical injuries to the eye . Chemical injuries to the eye : • Alkali burns are twice as common as acid burns. • Alkalis tend to penetrate more deeply than acids, as the latter coagulate surface proteins , forming a protective barrier . • Most commonly involved alkalis are ammonia , sodium hydroxide , and lime.Grad e Limbal ischemia Corn ea Iris Progno sis I Absent Clear Visibl e Excelle nt420 Grad e Limbal ischemia Corn ea Iris Progno sis II <1/3 of limbus Hazy Visibl e Good III 1/3 - 1/2 of limbus Hazy Obscu red Guarde d IV >1/2 limbus Opaq ue Obscu red Poor421

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of bilateral proptosis in children?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of bilateral proptosis in children is neuroblastoma. Most common cause : The image below shows the bilateral proptosis .Unilateral proptosis Bilateral proptosis In children: Orbital cellulitis In children: Neuroblastoma a nd leukemia (chloroma) In adults : Thyroid ophthalmo pathy In adults : Thyroid ophthalmo pathy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions does not presents as pulsatile proptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , hemangioma will not present with pulsatile proptosis . Causes of pulsatile proptosis : • Pulsating vascular lesions : • Caroticocavernous fistula - most common • Saccular aneurysm of ophthalmic artery • Transmitted cerebral pulsations in conditions with a deficient orbital roof:430 • Congenital meningocele /meningoencephalocele • Neurofibromatosis • Traumatic or operative hiatus Causes of intermittent proptosis : • Orbital varix - most common • Periodic orbital edema Causes of reducible proptosis : • Orbital varix • Hemangioma • Caroticocavernous fistula

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with unilateral non-pulsatile proptosis , which is compressible and increases on bending forward. No thrill or bruit is present . MRI shows a retrobulbar mass with enhancement . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The likely diagnosis from the above clinical scenario is orbital varix . The type of proptosis seen in orbital varix is non-pulsatile , intermittent , and reducible proptosis . On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head , turning the head forcefully , hyperextension of the neck, and coughing , the varices fill up, causing proptosis , and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position. All the other conditions listed , namely, carotid cavernous fistula , orbital encephalocele , and neurofibromatosis, present with pulsatile proptosis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old man with a history of blunt trauma to the head 2 months earlier presented with rapidly progressive swelling , pain, and diminishing vision in the left eye . The physical examination of the left eye revealed chemosis and pulsating proptosis . A bruit could be heard with a stethoscope placed on the left temple . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of carotid–cavernous fistula . All the given options are causes of proptosis following trauma, but among these , only a carotid-cavernous fistula presents with the classic triad: • Pulsatile proptosis • Chemosis • Bruit Selective carotid angiography is the investigation of choice . A carotid-cavernous fistula requires a definitive treatment , which currently involves the endovascular technique . The fistula can usually be occluded with a balloon or coil, without the sacrifice of the carotid artery.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions will present with pseudoproptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: 431 Buphthalmos causes pseudoproptosis . The other listed conditions, namely, pseudotumors , orbital hemorrhage, and cavernous sinus thrombosis, produce actual proptosis . Pseudoproptosis is a condition in which the eyeball appears to be proptosed , but there is no actual forward displacement .
