mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: The casualty intern noticed that a patient had unequal pupils . The anisocoria was greater under light . Which of the following drugs would be helpful in quickly differentiating between the potential causes ?
mcqs.explanation: Anisocoria greater in the light indicates the large pupil to be abnormal due to poor pupillary contraction from a parasympathetic abnormality. Among the given options, 1% pilocarpine and 0.1% pilocarpine can be used to differentiate fixed dilated pupil . Mydriasis due to neurologic origin (3rd nerve palsy ) responds readily to 1% pilocarpine , whereas there will be no response if the dilation is due to anticholinergic causes . Pupillary constriction to 0.1% pilocarpine diagnoses Adie's pupil (due to denervation hypersensitivity ). Application of 0.1% pilocarpine shows no response in other conditions or in the normal eye . Example : A person presenting with dilated pupil following accidental application or inadvertent rubbing of atropine or antimuscarinic alkaloids from wild plants into the eye will not constrict in response to topical application of 1% Pilocarpine. But the patient showing dilation due to 3rd nerve palsy shows pupillary constriction in response to pupillary instillation of 1% pilocarpine . Note : Cocaine and phenylephrine are used in anisocoria that is greater in the dark to diagnose Horner's syndrome. In these patients , the small pupil fails to dilate even after the instillation of cocaine.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old lady with advanced spondylosis underwent cervical vertebral fusion surgery. In the post -operative room, the resident noted that her pupils were unequal. Which of the following features would rule out the possibility of Horner's syndrome in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Horner's syndrome causes all the following except mydriasis. It causes miosis. Horner's syndrome (oculosympathetic palsy ) The majority of the cases are unilateral. Causes of bilateral involvement include cervical spine injuries and autonomic diabetic neuropathy . Painful Horner syndrome, especially of acute onset , should raise the possibility of carotid dissection . Clinical features • Mild ptosis (usually 1–2 mm) as a result of weakness of M\374ller muscle • Anisocoria is accentuated in dim light • Pupillary constriction to light and near stimuli is normal . • Hypochromic heterochromia ( lighter color iris on affected side ); in congenital cases .505 • Mild ptosis (Mullers muscle is affected ) • Reduced ipsilateral sweating (only if the lesion is below the superior cervical ganglion) Pharmacological tests • Hydroxyamphetamine and adrenaline may be used to differentiate a preganglionic from a postganglionic lesion. • Phenylepherine (1%) • Result : In an established (10 days) postganglionic lesion, the Horner pupil will dilate and ptosis may be temporarily relieved . A central or preganglionic Horner pupil and a normal pupil will not dilate or will dilate minimally. • Explanation: In postganglionic Horner's syndrome, the dilator pupillae muscle develops denervation hypersensitivity to adrenergic neurotransmitters due to its dysfunctional local motor nerve. • Apraclonidine (0.5% or 1.0%) • Result : A Horner pupil will dilate , but a normal pupil is essentially unaffected . • Explanation: Alpha-1 receptors are upregulated in the denervated dilator pupillae . • Cocaine (4%) is instilled into both eyes • Result : The normal pupil will dilate , but the Horner pupil will not. • Explanation: Cocaine blocks the re-uptake of noradrenaline secreted at the postganglionic nerve ending, which accumulates and causes dilatation of a normal pupil . In Horner's syndrome, there is no noradrenaline being secreted , so cocaine has no effect .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: Where is the cell body of the second -order neuron in the sympathetic pathway for the pupil ?
mcqs.explanation: The cell body of the second -order neuron in the sympathetic pathway for the pupil lies at the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8–T1). The sympathetic pathway to the iris muscles consists of a chain of three neurons: • The first neuron arises from the hypothalamus along the brain stem to synapse in the intermediolateral column of the spinal cord—the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T1). • From here (C8-T1), the second -order neuron arises. This joins the cervical sympathetic chain and synapses at the superior cervical ganglion. • The third-order neuron arises from the superior cervical ganglion and travels through the cavernous sinus along with the internal carotid artery. • Sympathetic fibers join the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and pass through the ciliary ganglion to the nasociliary and short ciliary nerves.506

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: A simultaneous lesion in both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply of the eye leads to which of the following ?

options.a: Mydriatic pupil that reacts to light
options.b: Constricted pupil that reacts to light
options.c: Mid-sized pupil that doesn 't react to light
options.d: Mid-sized pupil that reacts to light

mcqs.explanation: Simultaneous lesion in both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply of the eye leads to mid-sized pupil that doesn't react to light . Pupillary dilation is achieved by sympathetic innervation of dilator pupillae . Therefore, any lesion of the sympathetic supply of the pupil leads to constricted pupil . Pupillary constriction is a parasympathetic function. Lesions in this pathway leads to dilated pupil and failure to constrict. A mid-sized unreactive pupil due to a lesion of both parasympathetic and sympathetic supplies is seen in aneurysms of the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: During the neurological examination of a patient , on shining light in his left eye , the left pupil does not constrict but the right pupil does . On shining light in his right eye , the right pupil constricts and left doesn 't. The defect is in:
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of left eye efferent (oculomotor nerve) defect . The loss of pupillary light reflex (both direct and consensual ) in the left eye associated with a preserved direct pupillary response in the right eye is characteristic of an efferent pupillary defect .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common feature of third nerve palsy , in a case of long-standing, uncontrolled diabetes ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common feature seen in diabetic oculomotor palsy among the given options is ptosis . In the anatomical arrangement of the nerve fibers of the 3rd cranial nerve, the fibers controlling the pupillary reflex are present superficially and are thus spared from diabetic ischemia-induced injury which starts from the central nerve fibres. Thus, pupil sparing is commonly seen in diabetic patients .507 The etiology of diabetic neuropathy is hyperglycemia -induced damage to nerve cells and neuronal ischemic change due to microvascular angiopathy . Involvement of the third cranial nerve is most common and it often presents with early features of ptosis and diplopia with pupil sparing. The involvement of levator palpebrae superioris muscle of the eyelid manifests as ptosis and the involvement of extraocular muscles such as medial rectus ,inferior rectus and inferior oblique presents as opthalmoplegia with diplopia . All the muscles mentioned above are supplied by the Occulomotor nerve. Note : Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery is an important cause of isolated third nerve palsy with involvement of the pupil . This is because the aneurysm impinges on the superficial pupil nerve fibres of the 3rd cranial nerve.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man was brought to the OPD by his daughter with complaints of drooping of his left eyelid and double vision. The pupillary examination was normal . What is the likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: Ptosis and double vision with no other features suggest an acquired, isolated 3rd nerve palsy with pupillary sparing. This is seen in ischemic conditions such as diabetes . The vasoneurium supplies the nerve from outside to inside. As the somatic fibres are located in the inner part of the nerve, these fibres are affected more in the setting of ischemia. The parasympathetic pupillary fibres which run on the outside can remain unaffected (resulting in pupillary sparing). In compressive lesions , the parasympathetic fibres are affected before any disruption of the motor fibres. So pupillary sparing is not seen . Isolated 3rd nerve palsy Causes • Microvascular disease associated with systemic risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes is the most common cause of third nerve palsy . • Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery at its junction with the internal carotid, both direct and secondary to subdural hematoma with uncal herniation. • Episodic - migraine, compression, ischemia, and alterations in intracranial pressure • Miscellaneous - tumour and inflammatory diseases such as syphilis , Lyme disease , and sarcoidosis; giant cell arteritis; and vasculitis associated with collagen vascular disorders. Signs • Profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle • Abduction and depression in the primary position ("down and out") • Normal abduction as the lateral rectus is intact • Limited adduction due to medial rectus weakness • Limited elevation due to the weakness of the superior rectus and inferior oblique508

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Visual Pathway and Pupillary Reflexes
mcqs.question: The patient presented with the following appearance when asked to look straight. What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows adduction of the right eye due to paralysis of the right lateral rectus , indicating right abducens (6th) nerve palsy . The nucleus of the sixth (abducens or abducent ) nerve lies at the mid-level of the pons. Nuclear lesion: A nuclear sixth nerve lesion also causes the failure of horizontal gaze towards the side of the damage due to the involvement of the adjacent horizontal gaze center (paramedian pontine reticular formation). Foville (inferior medial pontine ) syndrome is most frequently caused by vascular disease or tumors involving the dorsal pons. It is characterized by the following : • Ipsilateral involvement of the fifth to eighth cranial nerves • Central sympathetic fibers (Horner syndrome) • Horizontal gaze palsy Millard–Gubler (ventral pontine ) syndrome involves the fasciculus as it passes through the pyramidal tract. As well as ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy , there is contralateral hemiplegia and often an ipsilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy . Clinical features : • Esotropia in the primary position due to relatively unopposed action of the medial rectus • Limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion • Normal adduction of the affected eye • A compensatory face turn is towards the side of the paralyzed muscle in unilateral palsy509

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: The longest part of the optic nerve measures _____.
mcqs.explanation: Intraorbital part is the longest part of the optic nerve. It measures from 25 mm to 30 mm. Length of the optic nerve ranges from 3.5 cm to 5.5 cm.519 80% of the fibers originate from the macular region. Parts of optic nerve:Parts Lengt h Intraocular part 1 mm Intraorbital part 25–3 0 mm Intracanalicular part 5–9m m Intracranial part 10 –16 mm

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of papilledema ?
mcqs.explanation: Disruption of neurofilaments is not a feature of papilledema . Papilledema is the swelling of the optic nerve head secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP). "Disc swelling " and "disc edema " are non-specific terms that include papilledema but also indicate a disc swollen from other causes . All patients with papilledema should be suspected of harboring an intracranial mass. Features of papilledema : • Raised ICP • Edema of the optic nerve head • Blockage of axoplasmic flow • Axonal swelling • Collection of extracellular fluid • Painless progressive loss of vision • Enlargement of the blind spot • Color vision, visual acuity , and pupillary reaction are normal , until optic atrophy sets in.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A resident notes the following fundus picture in a patient referred to the ophthalmology OPD with visual complaints. What does it suggest ?
mcqs.explanation: The fundoscopic image shows dilated veins with a blurred disc margin which is suggestive of papilledema. Ophthalmoscopic features of papilledema: • Early-stage :520 • Obscuration of the disc margins (nasal margins first) • Absence of spontaneous venous pulsation at the disc • Mild hyperemia of the disc • The blurring of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer • Established papilledema : • The disc appears to be enlarged and elevated (mushroom or dome-shaped ) • Macular fan appears • Paton's lines- circumferential greyish white folds may develop due to the separation of nerve fibers • Visual fields show enlargement of the blind spot • Veins become tortuous and engorged • Multiple cotton-wool spots and superficial hemorrhages • Chronic or long-standing (vintage) papilledema : • The optic disc gives the appearance of the dome of a champagne cork • Small drusen-like crystalline deposits (corpora amylacea) may appear on the disc surface • Atrophic stage : • Secondary optic atrophy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions show ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema ?
mcqs.explanation: Ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema are seen in Foster –Kennedy syndrome. Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia ) is a form of stroke characterized by the presence of an ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis or hemiplegia . Millard–Gubler syndrome is a lesion of the pons. It is also called ventral pontine syndrome. Benedikt syndrome, also known as paramedian midbrain syndrome, involves the fasciculus of oculomotor nerve as it passes through the red nucleus and is characterized by ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral extrapyramidal signs such as hemitremor.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. On examination, the eye is white and there are no obvious signs on ophthalmoscopy . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a sudden painful loss of vision in the absence of fundoscopic changes is suggestive of retrobulbar neuritis. There are 3 types of optic neuritis: papillitis , neuroretinitis, and retrobulbar neuritis. The common causes of retrobulbar neuritis include demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO or Devic's disease ).521 Clinically, optic neuritis is characterized by sudden , progressive visual loss. Ocular movements are painful in retrobulbar neuritis and painless in papillitis and neuroretinitis. Glowing sensations known as phosphenes may be induced with sound or movement. Color vision may also be impaired. On examination, Marcus Gunn pupil or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD ) is usually noted due to asymmetric involvement. The most common visual field defect is a central or centrocecal scotoma. The image below shows papillitis .Type Retrobulbar neuritis Papillitis Neuroretinitis Pathology Inflammation of the optic n erve behind the disc Inflammation of the optic n erve head Inflammation of the optic n erve head and the macula Fundus appearanc e Optic disc appears normal Hyperemia and oedema of the optic disc with or witho ut peri-papillary flame-sha ped hemorrhages Macular star (due to exudat es that form around macul a) Prevalence Most common in adults Most common in children Least common type Associated conditio ns Strong association with de myelinating disorders like MS, NMO Weak association with dem yelinating disorders Cat-scratch disease , Lyme disease , Syphilis etc.The image below shows macular star appearance in neuroretinitis.522

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old patient has come to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints that her vision becomes temporarily blurry after a hot bath in the evening. This resolves by itself after a few hours. She has a past history of an episode of painful unilateral optic neuritis, 3 months back which resolved with steroids . What is being described here?
mcqs.explanation: Episodic , transient obscuration of vision on exertion or on exposure to heat , which recovers on resting or moving away from the heat in an isolated optic neuritis patient is called Uhthoff phenomenon . It is commonly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS). Option A: Pulfrich's phenomenon is an illusion of depth perception . It is seen in MS. Option C: Lhermitte's sign refers to passive neck flexion causing an electric shock-like sensation radiating to the spine and shoulders . This is a result of the increased sensitivity of the myelin to stretch or traction; it is also seen in MS. Option D: Riddoch phenomenon refers to ability to perceive kinetic but not static targets . It is seen in cortical blindness .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: In a patient with multiple sclerosis , which of the following visual field defects is most likely?
mcqs.explanation: Central scotoma is more likely to occur with multiple sclerosis . It is also seen with retrobulbar neuritis and macular pathology . Option A: Optic chiasma compression causes bitemporal hemianopia Option C: Enlarged blind spot occurs with papilloedema Option D: Tunnel vision occurs in glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa and Retinal pan photocoagulation

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Optic neuritis is a common presentation in which of the following diseases ?
mcqs.explanation: 523 One of the common presentations of MS is optic neuritis. Multiple sclerosis (MS) results from demyelinating plaques in the central nervous system . Option A: Myasthenia gravis is the autoimmune destruction of the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Option B: Guillain–Barr \351 syndrome is the postinfectious autoimmune-induced destruction of peripheral nerves, resulting in an ascending paralysis. Option D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease of the motor nerve fibers of the lateral columns and anterior horns of the spinal cord that results in progressive muscular atrophy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old female patient presents with 6/60 visual acuity in one eye and 6/18 in the other eye. She has recurrent episodes of diminution of vision which recovers on treatment with steroids . She also has a history of transverse myelitis . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette of a patient presenting with decreased visual acuity and a history of transverse myelitis which is treated with steroids is indicative of Neuromyelitis optica (NMO). Neuromyelitis optica also known as Devic's disease is an autoimmune demyelinating disease in which antibodies are formed against Aquaporin 4 present in the cell membranes of Astrocytes . It is characterized by the findings of unilateral or bilateral optic neuritis developing within a few weeks of transverse myelitis (demyelination of the spinal cord). The disease may be monophasic or recurrent. Diagnostic Criteria for Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD ): Diagnostic Criteria for NMOSD associated with AQP4-IgG • At least 1 core clinical characteristic • A positive test for AQP4-IgG using the best available detection method (cell -based assay) • Exclusion of alternative diagnoses Core Clinical Characteristics: • Optic neuritis is usually bilateral and causes severe visual loss. • Acute myelitis - may be severe , transverse and typically longitudinally extensive involving three or more contiguous vertebral segments. • Area postrema syndrome: episodes of otherwise unexplained hiccups or nausea or vomiting • Acute brainstem syndrome • Symptomatic narcolepsy associated with NMOSD-typical diencephalic MRI lesions For acute cases of NMO, high-dose glucocorticoids or plasma exchange is used . Mycophenolate mofetil , rituximab, and glucocorticoids with azathioprine are used for prophylaxis against relapses . The FDA has approved satralizumab, a humanized IgG2 monoclonal antibody, for the treatment of NMO spectrum disorder with AQP4 antibody positivity . Eculizumab , a complement inhibitor, and inebilizumab, a B-cell depletion agent , are two more n ew drugs that have recently been approved for use in NMO attack prevention.524 A history of transverse myelitis with optic neuritis(decreased visual acuity ) rules out Multiple sclerosis (option D). It is an autoimmune inflammatory and demyelinating disease of the CNS that affects both upper motor neurons (UMN ) and lower motor neurons (LMN) with involvement of sensory system , ocular system and bowel and bladder function. Ocular manifestations of MS include Optic neuritis(usually retrobulbar)- decreased visual acuity , internuclear ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man with suspected optic neuropathy is being evaluated for visual field defects . Goldman perimetry reveals bilateral centrocecal scotomas. Which of the following is most likely to be the causative agent ?
mcqs.explanation: Centrocecal scotoma is most commonly seen in tobacco-induced amblyopia. It is also seen in vitamin B12 deficiency . Tobacco amblyopia is caused by excessive smoking and chewing of tobacco. The toxic agent involved is cyanide found in tobacco. It is characterized by bilateral and gradually progressive impairment of central vision. The classic visual field defect is a centrocecal scotoma, often involving both the blind spot and the macula. Option B: Ethanol amblyopia is similar to tobacco amblyopia but often presents with peripheral neuritis and a "central scotoma". Option C: Methanol amblyopia often results in complete blindness . Option D: Quinine amblyopia results in near-complete blindness with associated deafness and tinnitus.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: An anxious, young man came to the ER with complaints of having sudden trouble seeing with his left eye and a recent history of tripping over things. There was no associated pain or difficulty moving the eyes . An ophthalmology consultation was requested . On perimetry , the following visual field defect was picked up. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The perimetry result depicts altitudinal hemianopia, which is most commonly seen in anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION). Altitudinal hemianopia can also be seen in suprasellar tumors and occipital lobe lesions , but the frequency is very low compared to that of AION. Hence , AION is the single best answer. The two types of AION are as follows : • Arteritic AION- caused by giant-cell arteritis • Non-arteritic AION (NAAION)- more common Clinical features : Note : Corticosteroids are not proven to be effective in NAAION. The image given below shows pale disc edema of Arteritic AION.Features AAION NAAION Age >70 years <70 years Sex F > M F = M HeadacheJaw claudicati on Present Absent525 Features AAION NAAION Visual loss Marked Less marked Optic disc Pale disc edema Hyperemic disc edema C reactive protein Raised Normal ESR Highly raised Raised FFA Disc delay and choroidal dela y Only disc delay Treatment Corticosteroids Levodopa–carbidopa combin ation for 3 weeks and then d ouble dose for 1 month

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: What does the given fundoscopic picture suggest ?
mcqs.explanation: The given fundoscopic image clearly depicts cupping , thinning of the neuroretinal rim , and nasal shifting of vessels . This are characteristic of glaucomatous optic atrophy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with optic atrophy?
mcqs.explanation: Leprosy is not associated with optic atrophy. All the other given conditions can cause optic atrophy. Causes of optic atrophy: • Primary optic atrophy • Optic neuritis • Compression by tumors and aneurysms526 • Hereditary optic neuropathies • Toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies • Trauma • Secondary optic atrophy • Chronic papilledema • Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy • Papillitis • Consecutive optic atrophy • Extensive retinal photocoagulation • Retinitis pigmentosa • Prior central retinal artery occlusion • Glaucomatous optic atrophy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old man with a history of pernicious anemia was referred to ophthalmology for complaints of gradually progressing visual disturbances . On perimetry , which of the following defects is most likely to be seen in him?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario of pernicious anemia with gradually progressive visual disturbances is suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency . B12 deficiency is known to cause centrocecal scotoma and it is an important cause of nutritional optic atrophy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy has bilateral optic atrophy with diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests Wolfram syndrome. It is due to WFS1 gene mutation. The presentation is usually between the ages of 5 and 21 years; diabetes mellitus is typically the first manifestation, followed by visual problems . It has a poor prognosis. Clinical features are: (DIDMOAD) • Diabetes insipidus • Diabetes mellitus • Optic atrophy • Deafness (sensorineural type ) Option A: Kjer's optic neuropathy is an autosomal dominant condition. It presents with vision loss in early childhood and no significant systemic features . Option B: Behr syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. Clinical features include optic atrophy, pyramidal tract signs, ataxia, intellectual disability , urinary incontinence, and pes cavus Option D: Leber's congenital amaurosis is an autosomal recessive condition. It usually presents with significant vision loss in infancy and nystagmus .527

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of amaurosis fugax ?
mcqs.explanation: Amaurosis fugax is a sudden and transient monocular blindness , which is reversible. It is a marker of advanced carotid artery atherosclerosis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Champagne cork disc is seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Champagne cork disc is seen in chronic papilledema . The optic disc gives the appearance of the dome of a champagne cork . Small drusen-like crystalline deposits (corpora amylacea) may appear on the disc surface . The most reliable sign to differentiate between papillitis and papilledema is pupillary reaction. Pupillary light reflex is normal in papilledema whereas it is sluggish in papillitis .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following defects is implicated in Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: In Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), the defect is a mutation of maternal mitochondrial DNA. Therefore the condition has a maternal inheritance. LHON causes bilateral, subacute painless loss of vision. The characteristic visual field defect is a centrocaecal scotoma. Pupillary light reflex is relatively preserved until the late stage of the disease . Optic neuritis and optic atrophy start in one eye and goes on to involve the other eye subsequently . It typically affects males between the ages of 15 and 35 years. The diagnosis of LHON should be considered in any patient with bilateral optic neuropathy , irrespective of age . Prognosis is poor, although some visual recovery may occur in a minority of cases even years later. Note : LHON plus refers to rare variants with additional manifestations such as neuromuscular dysfunction .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man developed a painless diminution of vision in his right eye 6 months ago but did not seek medical attention . Two weeks ago, he started to notice mild blurring in his left eye and has now come for evaluation. According to him, his elder brother and maternal uncle also had similar vision problems . Which fundus finding would point towards Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy in this patient ?

options.c: Hyperemic optic disc with telangiectatic capillaries

mcqs.explanation: Hyperemic optic disc with telangiectatic capillaries would be suggestive of LHON. LHON is related to a mitochondrial DNA mutation. This results in impaired mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate production , which affects the highly energy -dependent optic nerve. In the acute phase , the optic disc is hyperemic and swollen with telangiectatic capillaries . However, the optic disc does not leak on fluorescein angiography. Later stages may show primary optic atrophy.528

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: In order to diagnose a case as idiopathic intracranial hypertension , which of the following features is not necessary ?

options.b: Elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture

mcqs.explanation: Papilledema is not a mandatory criterion for the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH ). Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a diagnosis of exclusion . Obstructive, compressive , and infiltrative CNS lesions must be excluded by neuroimaging studies . Papilledema , although present in 90% of the patients , is not necessary for diagnosis. Elevated CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture is the hallmark of IIH . Risk factors of IIH include : • Female sex • Obesity • Nalidixic acid • Tetracycline • Vitamin A • Oral contraceptives • Use of or withdrawal from corticosteroids

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most reliable sign to clinically differentiate between a case of papillitis and papilledema ?
mcqs.explanation: The most reliable sign to differentiate between papillitis and papilledema is pupillary reaction. Pupillary light reflex is normal in papilledema whereas it is sluggish in papillitis . Visual acuity and colour vision are also relatively more preserved in papilledema compared to papillitis . The other three disc signs seen on ophthalmoscopy are present in both papillitis and papilledema .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A patient evaluated for dizziness and visual disturbances was found to have down-beating nystagmus . A brain lesion was suspected and the patient was referred for an MRI. What is the most likely site of the lesion?

options.b: Pineal region and the dorsal midbrain

mcqs.explanation: Down-beat nystagmus is usually due to a lesion at the cervico-medullary junction (e.g. Arnold-Chiari malformation, syringobulbia) or as a manifestation of cerebellar degeneration . Other causes of down-beat nystagmus: • Drugs (phenytoin , lithium, barbiturates, carbamazepine) • Wernicke's encephalopathy • Demyelinating disorders Acquired nystagmus can be attributed to disturbances of the three mechanisms that normally ensure steady gaze—visual fixation, the vestibulo -ocular reflex , and the mechanism that makes it possible to hold the eyes at an eccentric eye position (e.g. far-right gaze). Other types of nystagmus :529 Type of Nystagmus Etiology Slow-horizontal Largeposterior cerebrallesion s (e.g. stroke) Mixed horizontal (Torsional ) Usually associated with verti go and seen investibular syst emlesions Up -beat Medulla ,the ventral tegment um and the anterior vermis o f the cerebellum Periodic alternating Cerebellar disease (In PAN, th e horizontal jerk nystagmus s pontaneously reverses the dir ection of the quick phase eve ry few seconds ) See -saw Lesion involvingparasellar re gion and optic chiasm(e.g. pit uitary tumours, third ventricl e) Gaze-evoked Side -effect ofdrugs , including sedatives , anticonvulsants a nd alcohol, as well ascerebell ardisease

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: An RTA patient with severe head trauma is admitted to the surgical ICU for observation. On examination , nystagmus was noted . His CT scan reveals a transverse fracture of his left temporal bone. Which of the following statements is true regarding the nystagmus ?

options.a: Slow phase is towards the left and fast phase towards the right
options.b: Slow phase is towards the right and fast phase towards the left
options.c: It is an up-beating type of nystagmus
options.d: It is a down-beating type of nystagmus

mcqs.explanation: Fracture of the temporal bone causes vestibular injury resulting in a horizontal nystagmus with slow phase towards the affected side and fast phase towards the opposite side . Peripheral vestibular nystagmus occurs in lesions of the labyrinth or vestibular nerve. Normally, there is tonic input to the brainstem vestibular nuclei from the periphery . Loss of the tonic input from the left vestibular nerve leads to deviation of the eyes towards the left side , which is the slow phase of the nystagmus . The cortical correction brings the eyes back to the centre in the primary gaze which is the fast-phase directed towards the right side .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the site of lesion in internuclear ophthalmoplegia ?
mcqs.explanation: In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) the lesion is at the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). In INO, there is impaired adduction on the ipsilateral side of the lesion, and nystagmus on abduction on the contralateral side . When the gaze is initiated in the motor cortex, the horizontal gaze center or the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF ) generates the eye movements. The PPRF has two outputs . The first is to the ipsilateral 6th cranial nerve nucleus which causes abduction of the ipsilateral eye . The second output is to the contralateral MLF which sends an impulse to the contralateral 3rd cranial nerve nucleus causing contralateral adduction . These two outputs from PPRF lead to conjugate movement of the eyes to the same side .530 Therefore, a lesion in the right MLF leads to failure of the right eye adduction . The left eye , however, abducts normally. This is called internuclear ophthalmoplegia . The following image shows the pathway for horizontal eye movements as described above.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: You are evaluating an elderly patient in the stroke ICU, who was admitted three days back with a history of sudden onset nausea, vomiting, and gait abnormalities. The visual examination showed conjugate horizontal left gaze palsy . He could maintain gaze near mid-position but could not cross the midline to the left side . His MRI is likely to show involvement of which of the following brain areas?
mcqs.explanation: Horizontal gaze palsy can occur due to a lesion in parapontine reticular formation (PPRF ). Horizontal gaze: • It involves 2 muscles - the ipsilateral lateral rectus and the contralateral medial rectus . • Center for this pathway is parapontine reticular formation (PPRF ). • From here, they move to the ipsilateral 6th nerve nucleus .531 • Next , they pass through the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus . Lesions affecting the abducens nuclei will also cause ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy , because of damage to motor neurons and internuclear neurons originating from the nuclei . Lesions involving the PPRF will lead to horizontal gaze palsy , as PPRF acts as a relay centre that connects the frontal eye fields in the cerebral cortex to the abducens nuclei . Conjugate horizontal gaze palsy can also be caused by lesion(s) involving both the abducens motor fibres and the MLFs preceding the abducens nucleus . Bilateral horizontal gaze palsy will be caused if lesion(s) involve both abducens nuclei or bilateral PPRF. Isolated damage to the MLFs will cause the classic INO where eye abduction is preserved , however, the ipsilateral eye will not be able to be adducted on conjugate horizontal gaze. Conjugate eye movements • Binocular movements in which the eyes move synchronously and symmetrically in the same direction. • Main types • Saccades : They are fast movements controlled by the contralateral frontal lobe . • Pursuits: They are slow following movements controlled by the ipsilateral occipital lobe . Image: The Horizontal gaze pathwayLesions in this pathway • Horizontal gaze palsy : Due to lesion in the PPRF of the same side • Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): Caused by lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) • One and a half syndrome: Caused by lesions in both MLF and PPRF of the same side Vertical gaze palsy Center is located in the rostral interstitial nucleus of the dorsal midbrain (riMLF).532 The important types of vertical gaze palsy are as follows : • Parinaud's syndrome: Upgaze palsy • Steel –Richardsons syndrome: Downgaze palsy

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: A patient has normal vertical saccades . On attempted left gaze as shown in the image below , the patient develops left jerk nystagmus. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely location of the lesion according to the given clinical scenario and the image is the right medial longitudinal fasciculus. The image depicts an attempted left gaze and concludes that there is an adduction deficit in the right eye . This causes jerk nystagmus in the abducting left eye . This is most likely due to a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) ipsilateral to the side of the adduction deficit . Hence , this is a case of a right MLF lesion or Right Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO).

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.chapter: Disorders of Optic Nerve and Gaze Palsies
mcqs.question: Ophthalmoplegic migraine clinically presents as ___________.

options.a: Headache with irreversible loss of optic nerve function
options.b: Headache associated with recurrent third nerve palsy
options.c: Headache associated with third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsy

mcqs.explanation: Ophthalmoplegic migraine refers to headache associated with third, fourth, and sixth nerve palsy . Ophthalmoplegic migraine almost always involves the third nerve. Rare cases of sixth nerve involvement, and even rarer cases that involve the fourth nerve, have also been reported . Clinical criteria for the diagnosis of ophthalmoplegic migraine include : • A prior history of typical common or classic migraine headaches • Ophthalmoplegia that occurs during (or, rarely, just before ) an established migraine attack • Exclusion of other reasonable causes by clinical and radiological studies533

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults ?
mcqs.explanation: Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults . Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which is the most common primary malignant tumor of the lid?
mcqs.explanation: The most common primary malignant tumor of the lid is basal cell carcinoma . The second most common tumor of the lid is squamous cell carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common lid malignancy in HIV patients ?
mcqs.explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is the commonest malignancy of the lid and conjunctiva in HIV patients . It appears as a violaceous non-tender nodule on the eyelid or conjunctiva. It is a rapidly growing acquired neoplasm composed of malignant stromal cells densely vascularized by blood vessels of capillary size. The typical lesion appears as an expanding , bright red subepithelial mass that projects through and replaces the overlying conjunctival epithelium . Spontaneous bleeding leading to bloody tears or a subconjunctival hematoma is relatively common. Conjunctival Kaposi 's sarcoma can be treated by excision, cryotherapy , radiation therapy (external beam or contact therapy ), chemotherapy , or topical or intralesional interferon-\037.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cannot be used in the management of the clinical condition shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular area. Interferon beta is not used in the management of capillary hemangioma. However, note that interferon alfa-2a is used in resistant cases . A capillary haemangioma is the most common tumor of the orbit and periorbital area in childhood . It may present as small isolated lesions or large masses that can cause visual impairment (due to mechanical ptosis and the resulting sensory deprivation amblyopia), systemic effects (severe thrombocytopenia ), or exist as part of PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial lesions , Cardiac abnormalities, Eye or Endocrine abnormalities) 30% of lesions resolve by the age of 3 years and about 75 % by the age of 7. Indications for treatment are: • Visual (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion , strabismus)542 • Cosmesis • Optic nerve compression • Exposure keratopathy Treatment options include : • Beta blockers- oral propranolol, topical timolol. • Steroids - intralesional triamcinolone or betamethasone , topical clobetasol , systemic steroids . • Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine- for steroid -resistant sight -threatening lesions • Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: An 8-year old child presented with right-sided proptosis . Biopsy of the orbital mass was done and histopathological examination revealed this picture . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS). Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood . 40% of rhabdomyosarcomas develop in the head and neck, and they are the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but are still a rare condition. The older age of the child presenting with proptosis suggests rhabdomyosarcoma (average age 7 to 8 years) than retinoblastoma (average age at presentation is 18 months). The histopathology shows elongated to round spindle cells with features of skeletal muscle at different stages of maturation with highly eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei – the embryonal type of rhabdomyosarcoma Immunohistochemistry is useful in identifying skeletal muscle proteins , such as alpha-actin, myosin, desmin, and myoglobin Rhabdomyosarcoma shows a strong tendency for local invasion , local recurrence, and hematogenous and lymphatic metastases. Decision-making for management is based on histopathologic confirmation as well as the staging of orbital RMS, which includes imaging (MRI of primary tumor, chest -CT, Tc bone scan), pathology , and work-up for metastases (bone marrow biopsy ). Treatment options include chemotherapy (vincristine, cyclophosphamide , and actinomycin D) and radiotherapy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with painless decrease in vision and metamorphopsia . Fundus examination revealed the lesion shown in the image. What is the expected finding on angiography?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vigenette is of a patient presenting with painless dimunition of vision and metamorphopsia with the right fundus showing choroidal melanoma superotemporal to the optic disc and involving the macula. In this patient a "Double circulation" pattern consisting of an internal circulation within the lesion and the normal vascularity of the overlying retina will be seen on angiography.543 Although collar stud (Option C) appearance is pathagnomic for choroidal melanoma, it can be seen on B-scan and not on angiography. Choroidal melanoma is a primary intraocular malignancy in adults that peaks around 60 years of age . Symptoms include a range of visual disturbances such as painless decrease in vision and metamorphosia when macula is involved. Other features of Choroidal melanoma includes : • A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown dome shaped mass • Clumps of orange pigment are common over the mass • Collar stud appearance on B-scan (option C): It is pathagnomic of choridal melanoma. It is seen if the tumour breaks through the Bruch's membrane into the subretinal space . • Associated haemorrhage Smoke stack pattern (option A) and ink blot (option B) pattern is seen on FFA in central serous retinopathy (CSR). CSR is the spontaneous serous detachment of the sensory neuroretina in the foveal region with or without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) detachment . This occurs due Choroidal vascular hyperpermeability . On FFA it is initially seen as an ink -blot pattern or smoke stack pattern of hyperfluorescence which then spreads to take the configuration of mushroom or umbrella pattern. The below given images depict the smoke stack pattern and mushroom pattern respectively544

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 68-year-old man presents with jaundice . He was recently diagnosed with malignant melanoma of the uvea but did not receive proper treatment due to the prevalent pandemic situation. Investigations reveal liver secondaries . What would be the ideal line of management?
mcqs.explanation: The spread of malignant melanoma of the uvea outside the orbit is treated with enucleation + chemotherapy + immunotherapy. Orbital spread of the malignant melanoma necessitates exenteration but metastasis elsewhere can be treated by enucleation , chemotherapy, and immunotherapy.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A father has noticed that his child's left pupil appears white as shown below . Worried about this, the father consults an ophthalmologist. All of the following should be included in the differential diagnosis except :
mcqs.explanation: The child has leukocoria and congenital glaucoma is not to be included in the differential diagnosis. Various conditions, other than retinoblastoma, which present as leukocoria are collectively called pseudoglioma. Differential diagnosis of leukocoria: • Retinoblastoma • Congenital cataract • Coloboma of the choroid • Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous • Toxocara infestation • Norrie disease • Coat's exudative retinopathy Intraocular pressure (IOP) is usually raised in retinoblastoma and lowered in pseudoglioma .545

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Retinoblastoma arises from which of the following structures ?
mcqs.explanation: Retinoblastoma (also called glioma retinae) arises from the neurosensory retina. It is a proliferation of neural cells that have failed to evolve normally. Tumours are composed of small basophilic cells (retinoblasts ), with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm . It is of 4 types : • Endophytic (into the vitreous) with seeding of tumor cells throughout the eye • Exophytic (into the subretinal space ) leading to retinal detachment • Mixed type • Retinocytoma: retina may be diffusely infiltrated

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common clinical presentation of retinoblastoma?
mcqs.explanation: The most common clinical presentation of retinoblastoma is leukocoria plus strabismus. Clinical features of retinoblastoma: • Present within the first two years of life • Leukocoria • Strabismus • Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma • Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis . • Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases . • Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare. Signs: • An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous , dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification. • An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed " into the gel . • An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment. Investigations: • Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria. • Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope • MRI of the orbit + brain546

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy was brought by his parents with concern about being increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye . As further workup reveals a tumor, the eye is enucleated and the microscopic appearance is as shown in the image. Molecular analysis of the tumor indicates loss of cell cycle control in the tumor cells . Where is the responsible gene located ?
mcqs.explanation: The histology showing Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes and clinical history of white reflex point towards a diagnosis of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is due to mutation in Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14 . Retinoblastoma was first cancer known to be directly associated with a genetic abnormality. The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes , the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Knudson 's two -hit hypothesis describes the occurrence of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Knudson 's two -hit hypothesis describes the occurrence of retinoblastoma. Knudson 's hypothesis can be stated as follows : • Two mutations (hits), involving both alleles of RB are required to produce retinoblastoma. • In familial retinoblastoma, one of the pair of alleles of RB1 is mutated in all the cells of the body. When a further mutagenic event ("second hit" according to the "two -hit" hypothesis proposed by Knudson ) affects the second allele , the cell may then undergo malignant transformation . A large majority of these children develop bilateral and multifocal tumors. • In sporadic cases , both RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast (two hits). Familial retinoblastoma patients also have a predisposition to non-ocular cancers because of the presence of the mutation in all cells , such as pinealoblastoma (usually before the age of 5 years), osteosarcomas , soft tissue sarcomas, and melanomas. Note :547 Trilateral retinoblastoma = Pinealoblastoma + Bilateral retinoblastoma

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Why would an ophthalmologist use the Reese -Ellsworth classification for retinoblastoma?

options.a: For the management of the tumor
options.b: For the staging of the tumor
options.c: For the assessment of the survival of the eye after local therapy
options.d: For the assessment of the survival of the patient after surgery

mcqs.explanation: Reese –Ellsworth classification is used in predicting which eye would survive the local therapy (cryotherapy, photocoagulation , plaque radiation therapy ) and retain useful vision. Cryotherapy is used for retinoblastoma lesions anterior to the equator and photocoagulation for lesions posterior to the equator.Grou p Prognosis for maintenance of sight Features 1 Very favorable Solitary tumor, <4DD, at or b ehind the equatorMultiple tu mors, all <4DD, all at or behi nd the equator 2 Favorable Solitary tumor, 4–10 DD, at o r behind the equatorMultiple tumors, all 4–10DD all behin d the equator 3 Possible Any lesion anterior to the eq uatorSolitary tumor, >10DD behind the equator 4 Unfavorable Multiple tumors, some >10 D DAny lesion extending anteri orly to ora serrata 5 Highly unfavorable Massive tumors involving mo re than one half of the retina Vitreous seeding

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old boy who presented with strabismus and leukocoria is suspected to have retinoblastoma . A B-scan detects multiple endophytic masses with calcifications , the largest measuring 6DD, and the smallest measuring 4 DD. CT scan reveals intraocular foci of calcifications and no other anomaly. The ophthalmologist decides to use chemo-reduction and local therapy to treat this child. According to Reese -Ellsworth classification , this belongs to which group?
mcqs.explanation: Multiple tumors of 4-10 DD in size behind the equator belong to group 2.Grou p Prognosis for maintenance of sight Features 1 Very favorable Solitary tumor, <4DD, at or b ehind the equatorMultiple tu mors, all <4DD, all at or behi nd the equator 2 Favorable Solitary tumor, 4–10 DD, at o r behind the equatorMultiple tumors, all 4–10DD all behin d the equator548 Grou p Prognosis for maintenance of sight Features 3 Possible Any lesion anterior to equato rSolitary tumor, >10DD behi nd equator 4 Unfavorable Multiple tumors, some >10 D DAny lesion extending anteri orly to ora serrata 5 Highly unfavorable Massive tumors involving mo re than one half of the retina Vitreous seeding

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice when retinoblastoma involves the optic nerve?
mcqs.explanation: Optic nerve involvement is treated by enucleation + adjuvant chemotherapy + radiotherapy Indications for enucleation [Group E tumor - according to the International Classification of Retinoblastoma (ICRB )]: • Tumor involves more than half of the retina • Optic nerve involved • Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved Chemotherapy commonly used is a three-drug regimen containing vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following regimen is commonly used \037 in the treatment of retinoblastoma?
mcqs.explanation: Chemotherapy commonly used is a three-drug regimen containing vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice for anterior lesions of retinoblastoma?
mcqs.explanation: Cryotherapy is used for anterior lesions of retinoblastoma. Photocoagulation for posterior lesions of retinoblastoma.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The most common secondaries in choroid are from _____.
mcqs.explanation: The most common secondaries in choroid originate from the breast (overall and in females ), and lungs (in males).549 Examination shows the elevation of the retina, usually at the posterior pole . It is usually bilateral. Metastases are usually treated with systemic chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Radiotherapy may also be given.550

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: For a patient presenting with gradual, painless diminution of vision, the differential diagnosis would not include _________.
mcqs.explanation: Methyl alcohol amblyopia causes sudden painless diminution of vision. It is a toxic neuropathy of the optic nerve.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: What is the angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellen 's chart at 60m distance ?
mcqs.explanation: 563 The angle subtended by the largest alphabet on the Snellens chart at 60m distance is 5 minutes . Visual acuity is a measure of the spatial resolution of the eye or an estimation of its ability to discriminate between two points. Snellens chart is used for Visual acuity assesment . In snellens chart the alphabets decrease in size as we move from above-downwards and these lines, from above-downwards should be read at 60, 36, 24, 18, , 9, 6, 5 and 4 m respectively . At these distances , the respective letters subtend a visual angle of 5 minutes . Hence , the largest alphabet that should be read at 60 m subtends a visual angle of 5 minutes in the eye .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man comes to the OPD for an eye exam. He is having difficulty reading newspapers but has no problem watching television . At what distance would you ask him to read a Jaeger's chart from?
mcqs.explanation: Jaeger's chart is held at a distance of 35 cm away from the patient .564 It is used to measure near vision. The smallest letter is designated as N5 or J1 and the largest as N48. Snellen 's near vision chart can also be used . The image below shows a Jaeger's chart.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 61-year-old man, known case of diabetes mellitus , presented with headache and eye pain. He also reports difficulty with driving at night. Visual field -testing indicates peripheral vision loss. The ophthalmologist uses the following instrument during his examination of this patient . What is he measuring by using the following instrument?
mcqs.explanation: The instrument shown is the Schiotz tonometer , which is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). This patient 's complaints of headache , eye pain, difficulty in adapting to darkness, and examination findings of peripheral vision loss with increased intraocular pressure , is suggestive of glaucoma. Schiotz tonometer is a type of indentation tonometer . The principle behind its use is that the plunger will indent a soft eye more than a hard eye .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the procedure shown in the image?

options.a: The concept of the procedure was introduced by Goldmann.
options.b: It is used to treat after cataract
options.c: It is based on the Imbert-Fick law
options.d: It is used to investigate glaucoma

mcqs.explanation: The instrument shown is an applanation tonometer , which is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann. It is based on Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere (P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A). P = W /A The different types are Goldmann tonometer , Perkin 's tonometer , pneumatic tonometer , pulse air tonometer, tono-pen.566

mcqs.explanation: The above image is of the dynamic contour tonometer such as the Pascal tonometer . The dynamic contour tonometer (Pascal) offers a non-invasive and direct method of intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement with an additional measurement of the ocular pulse amplitude . This type of tonometer is unaffected by the corneal thickness and it is the tonometer of choice in post -Lasik patients . Option A: Pachymetry is used to measure the corneal thickness. The below image is of pachymetry .Option C: Auto Refractotemetry is a computerized refractometer that is used to find out the error of refraction. The report of the A scan is displayed as a unidimensional display of spikes along a baseline where the distance between the spikes gives the indirect measurement of the tissues . mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which among the following phases indicate complete filling of the retinal arterioles and capillaries on fundus fluorescein angiography?
mcqs.explanation: Complete filling of retinal arterioles and capillaries is seen in the arterio-venous phase . In FFA, sodium fluorescein dye is injected into the antecubital vein. A fundus camera is then used to take photographs : • 1st picture - after 5 seconds , then every second for 20 seconds , every 3–5 seconds for the next 1 minute • Last picture - after 10 minutes • Pre-arterial phase - choroidal circulation is filling569 • Arterial phase - start filling of retinal arteriole till its completely filled • Arterio-venous phase - complete filling of retinal arterioles and capillaries followed by laminar filling of veins • Venous filling- arterioles are emptying and veins are fillingIndications for fundus fluorescein angiography: • Diabetic retinopathy • Vascular occlusion • Eale 's disease • Central serous retinopathy • Cystoid macular edema

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A woman came to the OPD due to blurring of vision while working on her laptop . Retinoscopy was performed at 1 m without cycloplegia . The red reflex moves in the same direction as the retinoscope . Which of the following refractive errors is not possible in this patient ?

mcqs.explanation: The given dye in the strip is lissamine green . It is used as 1% concentration. Lissamine green stains dead and degenerate cells , but does not stain healthy epithelial cells . mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: The following image indicates :
mcqs.explanation: The given image is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy . The central image shows the primary position of gaze where the patient 's left eye is deviated down and out with ptosis of the left eyelid . From the eye movements in other positions , it can be seen that adduction and elevation are absent and depression is reduced in the left eye . All of these findings are indicative of oculomotor nerve palsy . 3rd Cranial nerve(oculomotor nerve) palsy presents with: • Ptosis due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle (LPS ) • Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus (6th nerve supply ) and superior oblique muscles (4th nerve supply ) • Dilated pupil and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy (involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply ) • Limited adduction , elevation and depression due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus , inferior oblique and inferior rectus .Option A: Trochlear(4th cranial) nerve palsy presents with superior oblique muscle paralysis. Clinical findings of trochlear nerve palsy include :581 • Hypertropia (elevation) in the primary position • Extorsion that is greatest in abduction • Compensatory head posture with contralateral face turn and head tilt with chin slightly depressed . This position is assumed to avoid Diplopia . • Limitation of depression • Normal abduction and elevation. The below given image depicts 4th cranial nerve palsy .Option B: Lateral rectus palsy is seen in cases of isolated Abducens nerve palsy . These patients present with esotropia /convergent squint in primary position with limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion. This is due to unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle in the affected eye . There is also a compensatory head turn towards the side of the lesion to reduce the symptom of Diplopia . The adduction is normal in lateral rectus palsy .582 Option C: Internuclear opthalmoplegia occurs following an injury to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). A unilateral lesion to the MLF leads to the failure of adduction in the ipsilateral eye with a normal abduction of the contralateral eye . The below given image depicts the pathogenesis of Inter nuclear opthalmoplegia in detail .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Photostress test is used to differentiate between :
mcqs.explanation: Photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve. This test is of particular use in early macular diseases such as central serous retinopathy . In this test , one eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line on the near chart. A bright light is then shone into the eye for 15 seconds , and the patient is asked to read the line again, and the time taken to recover is noted . The test is repeated with the other eye .583 In normal people and in patients with optic nerve disease , the recovery time is not affected . Whereas, in patients with macular disease the recovery time is prolonged and is usually more than one-third of the normal recovery time. This is because , in macular disease , the photoreceptors are damaged , and there is a delay in the visual pigment regeneration process .584

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following deficiencies would you suspect in a patient with acute retrobulbar neuritis?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin B1 deficiency can cause acute retrobulbar neuritis. Nutritional optic neuropathy is characterized by bilateral, symmetric, cecocentral scotomas and disturbance of color vision. Fundus morphology is usually normal . Deficiencies in the following vitamins are primarily responsible for the damage caused to the optic nerve: B1 (thiamine), B6 (pyridoxine), B9 (folic acid), and B12 (cobalamin). These vitamins are cofactors for many metabolic reactions and their deficiency leads to toxic byproduct accumulation within cells , which inhibits the electron transport chain and depresses mitochondrial function. Depletion of ATP leads to nerve dysfunction and eventual nerve death . Chronic alcohol abuse is a commonly associated risk factor and a cause of malnourishment.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: During a community outreach program in a rural area, you come across a girl with a conjunctival lesion as shown in the image. According to the WHO grading, which grade does this child falls under?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Bitot's spot , which is seen in the X1B stage of vitamin A deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions will Koplik's spots and conjunctivitis be seen together ?
mcqs.explanation: Koplik's spots are seen in measles .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presented to the emergency department with an extremely painful right foot. He stated that he had an alcohol binge the previous night. On examination, the right first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, swollen , and extremely tender to palpation . Which of the following ocular conditions is not associated with his underlying condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute gout . Glaucoma is not a known association of acute gout . Ocular manifestations seen in acute gout are episcleritis , scleritis , and uveitis. Ocular structures have a relatively poor solvent ability, in addition to lower temperatures . Therefore, they are predisposed to tophi deposition . As a result of urate deposits , crystal-induced inflammation of the affected tissue is responsible for causing episcleritis , scleritis , and uveitis.592

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Where is snow flake cataract seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Snowflake cataract is seen in diabetes mellitus . Ocular manifestations in diabetes mellitus • Xanthelasma • Telangiectasia • Subconjunctival hemorrhage • Punctuate keratopathy • Descemet 's folds • Rubeosis iridis • Snow-flake cataract • Vitreous hemorrhage • Diabetic retinopathy • Neovascular glaucoma • Recurrent hordeola • Dry eye • Tractional retinal detachment • Diabetic maculopathy • Papillopathy • Central retinal vein occlusion

mcqs.question: You would expect to see oil drop cataract in a patient with ________
mcqs.explanation: Oil droplet cataract is seen in galactosemia . Characteristic associations are: • Diabetes - Snowflake cataract • Wilson's disease - Sunflower cataract • Homocystinuria - Bilateral inferonasal subluxation of the lens

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old girl with neurological manifestations was referred from the pediatric OPD. Her ocular examination findings is as given below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows the Kayser –Fleisher (KF) ring, which is a characteristic finding of Wilson's disease . KF ring consists of the deposition of copper in the Descemet membrane of the cornea. The rings are usually golden -brown and are visible only under the slit-lamp. They do not impair vision. They593 disappear on treatment with anti-copper drugs and reappear with disease progression. They are a characteristic sign of Wilson's disease but are not pathognomonic. They can also be seen in: • Primary biliary cholangitis • Primary sclerosing cholangitis • Cholestasis . Sunflower cataract is a rare finding of Wilson's disease . It occurs due to the deposition of copper in the centre of the lens. It consists of a greenish central opacity with spoke-like radial opacities and is visible only under the slit-lamp. It is also seen in chalcosis (deposition of intraocular copper -containing foreign body). The image given below shows a sunflower cataract:

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions can occur as an ocular manifestation in a patient with dengue ?
mcqs.explanation: Cataract is not an ocular manifestation of dengue . Dengue has varied manifestations , in different organ systems , mainly of inflammation and bleeding . Until recently , apart from retro-orbital pain, eye involvement was not recognized as a common feature of dengue infection . Potential pathogenic mechanisms include a direct viral effect on the eye , an immune-mediated vasculitis, and/or a variety of secondary effects related to dengue -induced vascular leakage and hemostatic derangements . Ocular manifestations of dengue : • Typically , patients complain of painless visual impairment within 1 week from illness onset , often around the time of the platelet nadir. • Conjunctival injection and subconjunctival hemorrhage. • Complications such as retinal hemorrhage, retinal edema , macular ischemia, macular edema , vitreous hemorrhage, vitritis, and optic neuritis or papillitis595 • Depending on the severity of the ocular lesion, gradual improvement in vision occurs over several weeks , although in rare cases permanent visual impairment may result .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation for recurrent seizures . She has a large port-wine stain on the right side of her face as shown below . The MRI of the head shows a leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most common ocular manifestation of the underlying condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge -Webber syndrome (SWS). Glaucoma is the most common ocular manifestation of SWS. Sturge weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder(phakomatoses ) that is characterized by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus , ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis , which causes seizures and mental retardation. Ocular manifestation of SWS include : • Glaucoma - most common ocular manifestation. It develops anywhere between infancy to adulthood . When developed in infancy it presents as buphthalmos . • Diffuse choroidal hemangioma • Serous retinal detachment • Visual field defects - homonymous hemianopia due to the leptomeningeal hemangiomas affecting the optic tract or occipital lobe . • Heterochromia of the iris • Episcleral and conjunctival lesions Option A: Uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue of the eyes . It can be associated with a number of systemic conditions such as sarcoidosis, behcet 's disease , ankylosing spondylitis , reiter's syndrome,Toxoplasmosis and Posner–Schlossman syndrome (PSS). Option B: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited or acquired pigmentatory retinal dystrophy affecting the rods more. The earliest manifestation is worsening of night blindness which gradually progresses to tunnel vision and ultimately loss of central vision. The classic triad of findings in RP comprises bone-spicule retinal pigmentation , arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor. Systemic Associations of RP include : • Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome • Cockayne's syndrome • Refsum's syndrome • Usher 's syndrome • Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome The below given image shows the classical triad findings of Retinitis pigmentosa .596 Option C:Keratitis is the inflammation of cornea which is characterised by corneal edema , cellular infiltration and ciliary congestion . It can be either infectious or non-infectious in nature which includes allergic keratitis, neurotrophic keratitis, exposure keratitis and peripheral ulcerative keratopathies such as Rosacea keratitis and Mooren's ulcer.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man presented with complaints of diminution of vision in both eyes for the last 6 - 8 months. On examination, bilateral cataracts were seen . Incidentally , you also note iris pearls. Which of the following conditions should you suspect in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Iris pearls are pearly -white nodules seen on the iris in leprosy . They are asymptomatic , 0.3 to 1.0 mm in diameter , dull yellowish -white in colour, and are seen at an early stage of the disease . It is not associated with any inflammatory changes in the anterior chamber. Histologically , it consists of lepromatous bacilli packed within mononuclear cells or acid-fast material with accompanying foreign body reaction. Inside the eye , leprosy bacilli preferentially lodge in the iris and ciliary body, due to the relatively cooler temperatures and high vascularity.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with areas of yellowish papular skin lesions and redundant and inelastic folds of skin on the neck and thighs . Which of the following ocular findings is not seen in this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case suggests a diagnosis of pseudoxanthoma elasticum . Arterial macroaneurysm is not a feature of this disease . Ocular findings in pseudoxanthoma elasticum : • Blue sclera • Angioid streaks • Optic nerve head drusen • "Peau-d'orange" appearance of the retina • Choroidal neovascularization597

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: An elderly patient admitted with multiple comorbidities in the ICU, developed exposure keratitis and ulceration. An ophthalmology opinion was sought . Incidentally , on fundoscopy , the resident found the following picture . What is this most likely due to?
mcqs.explanation: The given image suggests a diagnosis of proliferative diabetic retinopathy . The hallmark of Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is neovascularization. Abnormal new vessel formation, which occurs on the inner (vitreous) surface of the retina and may extend into the vitreous cavity, can cause vitreous haemorrhage. Neovascularization is often accompanied by pre-retinal fibrous tissue , which, along with the vitreous, can contract, resulting in traction retinal detachment . In addition, tiny microaneurysms can also be seen .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: In patients with a long-standing history of Crohn's disease , which of the following ocular complications is the most likely to develop ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common ocular manifestation of Crohn's disease is episcleritis . Uveitis is associated with both Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease .

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of decreased vision was evaluated with fundus fluorescein angiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image depicts neovascularization, which is the hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy . Dye can be seen leaking through abnormal neovascular fronds. Both neovascularization of the disc (NVD), as well as neovascularization elsewhere (NVE i.e., 2 DD away from the optic disc margin), are seen . The treatment available for proliferative diabetic retinopathy is photocoagulation of the ischaemic areas to reduce the metabolic demand and decrease or prevent the release of vasoproliferative factors.598

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: As part of a public outreach initiative under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment, you are screening the population of a neighboring village. While preparing your report, what definition of blindness would you use ?

options.a: Presenting distance visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye
options.b: Presenting distance visual acuity less than 1/60 in the better eye
options.c: Presenting distance visual acuity less than 6/60 in the better eye
options.d: Presenting distance visual acuity less than 2/60 in the better eye

mcqs.explanation: The definition of blindness under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI ) is presenting distance visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye and limitation of the field of vision to less than 10 degrees from the center of fixation.

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: Which is the most common cause of preventable childhood blindness ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency . The most common cause of blindness (including adults ), is however, cataract.603

mcqs.subject: Ophthalmology
mcqs.question: You have examined five patients (i-v) in the OPD this morning . Their visual acuity test results are as given below . Who amongst them would be described as blind as per the WHO Vision 2020 definition ?
mcqs.explanation: Patients iii and iv would be classified as blind. In the Vision 2020 initiative, the WHO has revised its definition of blindness . As per the new definition, "Blindness is defined as a presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10 \260 in the better eye ." Note : Blindness is defined for the better eye , hence option (i) is insufficient information to classify as blind, as information about the better eye is not given.
