These are community trials and centre around comparing the incidence of disease before and after the introduction of a preventive measure. They are of two distinct types: • Before and after comparison studies without control. • Before and after comparison studies with control. Non-randomized trials include: • Before and after comparison studies. • Uncontrolled trials. • Natural experiments.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the suspected cause preceding the observed effect an example of?
mcqs.explanation: Temporality refers to the condition when the suspected cause precedes the observed effect. It is a part of Hill's criteria for causal association.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: While investigating a new disease, you are trying to establish the aetiological agent. Which of the following criterion is the most difficult to establish?
mcqs.explanation: Specificity is the most difficult criterion to establish in both chronic and acute diseases. This is because a single factor or cause can give rise to more than one disease. Also, most diseases are multifactorial in origin with no possibility of demonstrating a one-to-one relationship which would indicate specificity.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What does evidence-based medicine refer to?

options.a: Use of experiments to prove the cause of a disease
options.b: Use of clinical trials to prove safety of drugs
options.c: Use of research findings for taking decisions about patient care
options.d: Use of behavioral modification to prevent diseas e

mcqs.explanation: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) refers to the use of modern research findings to guide decision-making about the treatment of individual patients. EBM integrates clinical experience and patient values with the best available research information. Research and studies are given high importance in EBM, while opinions and conventional wisdom of experts are not taken into consideration in the practice of EBM.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In the hierarchy of evidence, which of the following rankings is correct?
mcqs.explanation: The correct order of ranking of the hierarchy of evidence is:120 Meta-analysis and systemic review > Randomised control trial > Cohort study > Case-control study > Case reports.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about systematic reviews?
mcqs.explanation: Meta-analysis is not always performed in systematic reviews. A systematic review is the process of locating and synthesizing the research on a particular question using organized, transparent, and replicable procedures. It ranks high in the hierarchy of evidence in medicine. Steps of a systematic review: • The research question is formulated. It is always focused. • The literature on studies is always found and appraised after criteria of eligibility are established. • Meta-analysis is usually done in a systematic review for quantification but it is not compulsory. These steps are depicted in the diagram below.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A meta-analysis is being performed to evaluate the relationship between obesity and endometrial carcinoma. Which among the following is false regarding this technique?

options.a: File drawer effect can be seen here
options.b: It increases the statistical power by increasing sample size
options.c: Apples and oranges effect can be seen here
options.d: Its validity does not depend on the quality of the systematic review

mcqs.explanation: The validity of the meta-analysis depends on the quality of the systematic review.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a use of epidemiology?
mcqs.explanation: Ensuring community participation is not the use of epidemiology. Community participation is a principle of primary health care.121 Uses of epidemiology: • To study the rise and fall of disease in populations • Community diagnosis • Planning and evaluation • Evaluation of individual's risks and chances • Syndrome identification • Completing the natural history of disease • Searching for causes and risk factors

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: For what purpose were knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) studies first used in India?
mcqs.explanation: Knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) studies were first used in India to study family planning. These studies help in evaluating the knowledge, attitude, and practices of a community. It also g ives an educational diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following quantitative methods is the best to study previous research studies?
mcqs.explanation: The quantitative method which is the best to study previous research studies of a selected topic/research question is meta-analysis. A systematic review is a process of collecting, reviewing, and presenting information from earlier research to answer a question. It is a qualitative technique. It may or may not involve a meta-analysis.122

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: What is the host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stages of maturity called?
mcqs.explanation: A host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stage of maturity is called the definitive host or primary host. A host in which a parasite exists in the larval or asexual form is called an intermediate host or secondary host. A host which acts as the only source of development for a parasite is called the obligate host. Note: A host in which the organism remains alive but no development occurs is called a transport host.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: For which of the following diseases is man the dead-end host?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options, man is the dead-end host for tetanus and rabies. A dead-end host is a host from which the infectious agent lacks a portal of exit to continue its propagation. Humans are dead-end hosts for :127 • Rabies • Tetanus • Bubonic Plague • Trichinosis

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: While studying a disease, you find that it affects both humans and lower vertebrates and can be transmitted in either direction. How would you classify this disease?
mcqs.explanation: A disease that affects both humans and lower vertebrates and which can be transmitted in either direction is classified as amphixenosis. E.g, Trypanosoma cruzi and Schistosoma japonicum. It is a type of zoonoses. Zoonoses are diseases that are transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans. Other types of zoonoses include: • Anthropozoonoses - infections that are transmitted to man from vertebrates. E.g., Rabies , plague etc . • Zooanthroponoses - infections that are transmitted to vertebrates from humans. E.g., Human tuberculosis in cattle. Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak or epidemic of a disease in an animal population, often with the implication that it may also affect human populations. Enzootic disease is an endemic occurring in animals. Note: Epornithic diseases are those diseases which are epidemic in bird populations. E.g., Psittacosis.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: What is a disease imported to an area from another called?
mcqs.explanation: Exotic diseases are those imported into a country where they do not occur usually. E .g, rabies in the United Kingdom. Enzootic diseases are those which are endemic in animals. E.g, anthrax, brucellosis. Epornithic disease refers to an epidemic in birds. E.g, psittacosis. Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak of a disease or an epidemic in animals with the implication that it may affect humans. E.g, Q fever, influenza.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes a disease that has a haphazard occurrence?
mcqs.explanation: Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time. Endemic refers to the constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.128 Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area. Pandemic is an epidemic occurring over a wide area, crossing international boundaries, and usually affecting a large number of people. Note: Opportunistic infections are those that occur in the presence of immune suppression or deficiency like cytomegalovirus.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: In a community, there are usually 40-50 reported cases of dengue every week. This week, there were 48 reported cases. This would classify as:
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease. Endemic diseases a re those that have a constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area. Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area. Outbreak carries the same definition of an epidemic, but is often used for a more limited geographic area. Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: The following are the disease frequencies in a population. Based on the number of cases which of the following i s t he correct match?
mcqs.explanation: Disease 1- the cases have been almost the same so it has to be endemic. Disease 2- there is an alarming increase in the number of cases. It has to be an epidemic. Disease 3- the number of cases has decreased without any explanation so it has to be sporadic. Epidemic refers to the occurrence of a disease in excess of expected frequency. A pandemic is an epidemic affecting a large population over a large geographical area crossing international boundaries. An endemic disease is a r egularly o ccurring disease in a population in expected frequency without any importation from outside. Sporadic diseases present as scattered cases of infection without relation temporally/spatially.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: Surveillance data of an endemic disease reveals that most of the children in the area had been affected and had to be hospitalised. However, most of the adults remained asymptomatic carriers. Which category does this disease belong to?
mcqs.explanation: The disease in question belongs to the category of holoendemic diseases. In such diseases, a higher prevalence and pathogenic response are seen among the children in an area. The adults tend to be either asymptomatic carriers or show reduced damage by the disease pro cess. E . g, malaria.129 An endemic disease is a disease that is present constantly in a population or in a given area without importation from outside. E.g, kala-azar in Bihar. A hyperendemic disease is a disease that is constantly present at high incidence and prevalence among all groups in a population. E.g, dengue in India. A syndemic is the aggregation of two or more concurrent or sequential epidemics or disease clusters in a population with biological interactions, which exacerbate the prognosis a nd burden of disease. It is also known as a synergistic epidemic. Note: Quasiendemic is not a term used in infectious disease epidemiology.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: In which of the following diseases is subclinical infection not seen?
mcqs.explanation: Subclinical infection is not seen in measles. It always causes the development of overt signs and symptoms. Subclinical infection refers to an inapparent, covert, missed or abortive case. The host harbours and sheds the infectious agent but does not develop signs and symptoms of the disease. Subclinical infections are seen in d iseases like: • Hepatitis A • Diphtheria • Japanese encephalitis • Rubella Subclinical infections can only be detected by laboratory tests. They frequently occur during a person's lifetime and are responsible for the immunity shown by humans to a variety of disease-producing microbes. Note: Subclinical cases should be differentiated from latent infections. In a latent infection, the host does not shed the organism but it lies dormant without signs and symptoms.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: In which of the following states will the host not shed the infectious organism?
mcqs.explanation: The host does not shed the infectious organism in case of a latent infection. This is defined as a state in which the host does not show signs and symptoms of the disease and does not shed the organism. It can be seen in conditions like herpes simplex, ancylostomiasis, infections due to slow viruses, Brill-Zinsser disease, etc. Subclinical infection is a state where the host harbours the infectious agent without developing signs and symptoms but sheds the infectious agent. Th is s tate is seen in conditions like hepatitis A , rubella, mumps, etc. Healthy carriers are those who had subclinical infections and later developed a carrier state without suffering from the overt disease. This state is seen in: (mnemonic: CM - DPT)130 • Cholera • Meningitis • Diphtheria • Polio • Typhoid Convalescent carriers are those which shed the infectious agent during the convalescent phase/recovery phase. Such carriers are seen in diphtheria, typhoid, cholera, pertussis, etc.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: While in a health camp, you notice a child with fever and r ash. On subsequent history, you find out that similar symptoms occurred in her friend 6 days back. How will you epidemiologically categorise the child you examined?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the child is categorised as the index case. It is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician. The primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit. A s econdary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case. A suspect case refers to a patient who has all the features of the disease but has not been diagnosed with it yet. Note: There is no such term as tertiary case.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: You are part of a research programme for COVID-19 and are asked to define the median incubation period. How will you define it?

options.a: Interval between onset of symptoms in primary and secondary cases
options.b: Time required for 50% of cases to occur following exposure
options.c: Interval between exposure and the occurrence of the first symptom
options.d: Time required for the start of pathogenesis following exposure

mcqs.explanation: The median incubation period is the time required for 50% of the cases to occur following exposure. The median incubation period of COVID-19 of approximately 5 days. Incubation period is the time interval between invasion of the infectious agent a nd the appearance of the first symptom or sign in the body. It is termed as the latent period in non-infectious diseases. Incubation period depends upon: • Generation time of pathogen • Portal of entry • Infective dose • Individual susceptibility Incubation period is useful for : • Tracing the source of infection and contacts. • Determining the period of surveillance or quarantine. • Planning immunization. • Identification of point source or propagated epidemics. • De termining t he prognosis.131

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: In a school of 100 children, a child developed measles. Four days later, 3 of her classmates d eveloped measles. What do these intervening four days correspond to?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the first child is the primary case and her classmates are the secondary cases. Hence, the interval between them developing the disease i.e., the intervening four days, is called the serial interval. The time interval between the onset of the primary case and the secondary case is called serial interval. By collecting information about a whole series of such disease onsets, the distribution of the secondary cases can be made. From this information , a n approximation of the incubation period can be done. Lead time/lead interval refers to the period between the first possible time of detection and the usual time of diagnosis. Incubatory interval/ incubation period refers to the time period between invasion of a pathogen to appearance of the first sign or symptom. Latent interval/ latent period refers to the period between disease initiation to detection of the disease. It is usually used for non-infectious diseases and i s equivalent to the incubation period . Note : • Primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit. • Secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case. • Index case is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: The time interval between which of the following is called generation time?

options.a: Development of primary case and secondary case
options.b: Receipt of infection by host and maximum infectivity of the same host
options.c: Infection and first sign or symptom
options.d: Infection and initiation of pathogenesis inside the host

mcqs.explanation: Generation time is the time interval between receipt of infectious agent by the host and the point of maximum infectivity of the same host.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.chapter: Basic Definitions in Infectious Disease Epidemi...
mcqs.question: For which of the following diseases i s soil not a reservoir?
mcqs.explanation: The main reservoir of the coccobacilli belonging to the genus Brucella that cause brucellosis are animals like sheep, cattle, horses, goats, whales, and dogs. A reservoir is the environment (e.g. soil, humans, animals, water, etc.) where the infectious agent grows and multiplies (natural habitat) and from where it can be transmitted to a susceptible host. A source is an animal, object, human or substance which acts as an immediate mode of transmission and may or may not be a part of the reservoir. Option A: Coccidiomycosis i s also called Valley fever and the causative fungi belong to the Coccidiodes. The main reservoir of this organism is soil.132 Option B: Bacillus anthracis is a soil commensal and is also found on the hides and dried skins of infected animals. Option C: The natural reservoir for the fungi causing mycetoma is soil.133

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not communicable during the later part of the period marked 3 in the below image?
mcqs.explanation: The period marked 3 in the figure is the incubation period while the later part of the period represents subclinical infection. Rabies is not communicable during its incubation period as it is transmitted from the saliva of a rabid animal through bite or scratch. An incubatory carrier state is one in which carriers shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it. Examples of diseases showing incubatory carrier state are: • M easles • Polio • Mumps • Whooping cough • Diphtheria • Influenza • Hepatitis A Carriers of a disease are classified by the following: • Type: Incubatory, convalescent or healthy. • Duration: Temporary or chronic. • Portal of exit: Urinary, respiratory, intestinal or others.140

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following carriers shed the organism for indefinite periods?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic carriers are those who shed or excrete the organism for indefinite periods. Carriers are classified into chronic carriers and temporary carriers based on the duration. Organisms may be shed continuously or intermittently in chronic carriers. The duration of the carrier state also depends on the disease. Chronic carrier state is seen in typhoid, hepatitis B, gonorrhea, malaria, etc. Temporary carriers are classified into: • Incubatory carriers - Those that shed t he organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it. It is seen in measles, mumps, polio, etc. • Healthy carriers - Those who suffer from subclinical infections and develop a carrier state without developing the overt disease. It is seen in polio, meningococcal meningitis, cholera, diphtheria, etc. • Convalescent carriers - Those that shed the organism during recovery or convalescence. It is seen in typhoid. Paradoxical carrier r efers to a carrier who acquires the pathogen from another carrier. Note : Pseudo-carriers are carriers of avirulent organisms.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases does not show vertical transmission?
mcqs.explanation: Tetanus does not show vertical or transplacental transmission. Transmission of diseases or non-infectious agents transplacentally is called vertical transmission. Diseases that show this type of transmission include:141 • Herpes • HIV • Rubella • Varicella Apart from diseases, non-infectious agents like lithium, thalidomide, stilbestrol, etc. can cross the placenta and lead to the development of congenital anomalies in a foetus. Note: Neonatal tetanus occurs as a result of the failure to use aseptic techniques in managing the umbilical stump, unclean hands, and instruments or contamination by dirt, straw, or other nonsterile materials in the delivery field. Immunisation of pregnant women c an prevent this disease via the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which among the following is false about droplet transmission?

options.a: All droplets can travel only as far as 3 feet
options.b: Droplets are usually larger than 5 microns
options.c: It is a type of direct transmission
options.d: Basic ventilation decreases the potential for this type of transmission

mcqs.explanation: Droplet nuclei can travel as far as 6 feet, whereas a droplet (particle > 5�Mm) travels <30-60cm, as recent studies have shown. Droplets are a mode of direct transmission of infectious agents. They are formed from saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions released during coughing, sneezing, or speaking into the surrounding atmosphere. The expelled droplets may impinge directly up on t he conjunctiva, oro -respiratory mucosa or skin of close contact. This mode of transmission is seen in common cold, diphtheria, etc. Proper basic ventilation and prevention of overcrowding reduce the potential for this type of transmission.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the maximum size of airborne droplet nuclei?
mcqs.explanation: Droplet nuclei are sized less than or equal to 5 microns. They may be formed by evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or be generated purposefully by a variety of atomizing devices (aerosols). They are capable of indirect a irborne transmission of diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, etc. The droplet nuclei may remain airborne for long periods of time, some retaining and others losing infectivity or virulence. These small particles when inhaled are capable of reaching the alveoli and getting retained there.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which o f the following is not a method of direct transmission of communicable diseases?
mcqs.explanation: Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases. It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.142 Droplet nuclei are tiny particles of size 1-5 microns range that may be formed by either due to evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or are formed from aerosols. These droplet nuclei remain airborne for long periods of time and can transmit diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, Q fever and other respiratory infections. Droplet transmission, vertical transmission, and contact with soil are methods of direct transmission of diseases. D ifferences between droplet and droplet nuclei are summarised below:DROPLET NUCLEI DROPLET Indirect transmission Direct transmission It is the residue from evapora ted droplets It is produced while coughing , sneezing , talking <5microns in diameter \0345 microns in diameter No need for close contact for transmission Requires closeness and direct contact for transmission Diseases transmitted : chicke npox, measles etc . Diseases transmitted : diphth eria, meningococcal meningit is etc .

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Spread of disease via which of the following is an example of an indirect mode of transmission?
mcqs.explanation: The spread of a disease through contaminated food is an example of vehicle-borne transmission. It is an indirect mode of transmission. Vehicle-borne transmission is the transmission of infectious agents through food, water and biological products (blood, plasma etc.). Of these, food and water are more frequent vehicles of transmission because they are used by everyone. Mother to child transmission, droplet infection and transmission via dog bite are examples of di rect m odes of transmission.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about fomite-borne transmission is false?

options.a: It is an indirect mode of transmission
options.b: Transmission via contaminated food is an example of this
options.c: Hepatitis A is transmitted in this way
options.d: Routine disinfection can prevent such transmission

mcqs.explanation: Fomites are objects other than water or food that can be contaminated by infectious agents and help in transmitting the disease. They include clothes, towels, linen, cups, plates, spoons, etc. Fomites are an example of an indirect mode of transmission. Some diseases transmitted by fomites include diphtheria, typhoid, hepatitis A, etc. Good public and personal hygiene can prevent this type of transmission.143

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the lodgement and development of an a rthropod on the body surface called?
mcqs.explanation: The lodgement and development of an arthropod on the body surface is called infestation. Infection is the entry and development or multiplication of an infectious agent in a host's body. Contamination is the presence of a disease agent on a body surface like clothes, toys, etc. and also in substances like food or water. Colonization is the presence of a disease agent in or on a host, with growth and multiplication but without any overt clinical expression or detected immune response in the host at the time it is isolated .

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: An entomologist was studying a vector and the pathogen it transmits. He found that the pathogen underwent changes in number and morphology in the vector. What is this type of biological transmission called?
mcqs.explanation: This type of biological transmission where a pathogen undergoes a change in number and morphology in a vector is called cyclo-propagative transmission. Malaria is a disease whose causative organism (Plasmodium sp.) undergoes cyclo-propagative transmission. In malaria, the parasite undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the Anopheles mosquito (vector).

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A patient with chronic lymphedema was found to have a positive DEC provocation test. Which type of biological transmission does the pathogen implicated here undergo?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the patient most likely has lymphatic filariasis. The causative organism of this disease (Wuchereria bancrofti) undergoes cyclo-developmental transmission. Cyclo-developmental transmission is a transmission where the agent undergoes only developmental changes and not multiplication within the vector. DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are a rural medical health officer investigating an epidemic. What is the correct sequence of steps you must follow?
mcqs.explanation: Steps for the investigation of an epidemic are: • V erification of diagnosis • Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic • Defining the population at risk - • Obtaining a map of the area • Counting the population • Rapid search for all the cases - • Medical survey144 • Epidemiological case sheets • Searching for more cases • Data analysis on the basis of time, place and person • Formulation of hypothesis • Testing of hypothesis • Evaluation of ecological factors • Further investigation of the population at risk • Writing the report

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You have been asked to write the final report following the investigation o f a cholera epidemic. Which of the following will you not include in this report?

options.b: Usual number of cases that existed before the epidemic

mcqs.explanation: The final report of an epidemic does not include the incubation period of the disease. The final report following the investigation of an epidemic should include: • Background information - Geography, climate, d emography, socio -economic groups, health service organization, surveillance data and normal disease prevalence. • Historical data - Previous occurrences of the epidemic, the occurrence of any related diseases and discovery of the primary case in the present outbreak. • Methodology of investigations - Case definition, epidemiological questionnaires, collection and laboratory techniques. • Analysis of data - Clinical and epidemiological data, modes of transmission, l aboratory data and all their interpretations. • Control measures - Strategy definitions, methodology of implementation, evaluation methods and preventive measures.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You have been sent to an area to study the ongoing typhoid epidemic. When will you declare the area to be free of the epidemic?
mcqs.explanation: The area will be declared free of the typhoid epidemic when no new cases are reported for 28 days. An area is declared free of an epidemic when there are no cases reported for twice the incubation period of the disease since the last case. The incubation period of typhoid is 14 days. So, in the given s cenario, the area will be declared free of the epidemic when no new cases are reported for twice the incubation period i.e., 14 x 2 = 28 days.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is known as the_______.
mcqs.explanation: 145 The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate. It is calculated by the following formula: Secondary attack rate (SAR\ = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible) Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and d enominator. Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Following an outbreak of a disease, you are asked to calculate the secondary attack rate (SAR). What is the denominator you would use?

options.a: All people having history of contact with a case
options.b: All people s usceptible in the entire area
options.c: All the people in contact with the primary case
options.d: All the close or exposed contacts those are susceptible

mcqs.explanation: The denominator used for calculating SAR is all the close or exposed contacts that are susceptible. The secondary attack rate is defined as the probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period. It is calculated by the formula: Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing t he disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible) Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator. Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A village has 100 children under the age of 5. The coverage of measles vaccination is 60%. Following a case of measles, 26 children developed measles. What is the secondary attack rate?
mcqs.explanation: The secondary attack rate for the given scenario is 66%. The secondary attack rate (SAR) is given by: (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total n umber of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible) Here , number who developed the disease after exposure= Susceptible population= 100 - 60 (vaccinated) - 1 (primary case) = 39 Therefore, SAR = 26 /39 x 100 = 66%. SAR is a measure of communicability.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old man is found to be positive for SARS-CoV -2. On contact tracing, 30 people have been identified as close contacts but non e o f them shows any symptoms or signs. What is the time duration for which they must be quarantined?
mcqs.explanation: Quarantine is the limitation in freedom of movement of healthy contacts of cases, who have been exposed for a period that lasts as long as the maximal incubation period of the disease.146 It is a primary level of prevention and falls under specific protection measures. The various types of quarantine are: • Absolute - Complete limitation of movement • Modified - Selective partial limitation of movement • Segregation - Observation of a group of persons in a population after separation

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following pairs of diseases and their periods of isolation is wrongly matched?

options.a: Rubella – 3 days after onset of rash
options.b: Chickenpox – 6 days after onset of rash
options.c: Herpes zoster – 6 days after onset of rash
options.d: Measles – Up to 5 days after onset of rash

mcqs.explanation: Patients with rubella should be isolated for 7 days after they develop the rash. Isolation is defined as separation, for the period of communicability of infected persons from o thers to prevent or limit transmission of the infectious agent. In settings where women who are in their 1st trimester or sexually active or non-immune without contraception usage may be exposed, outbreak control measures should begin as soon as rubella is suspected and should not be postponed until laboratory confirmation of cases. Note: Multiple sources have confimed the period of infectivity of measles which is from 4 days before the onset of rash to 5 days after th e o nset of rash.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A paradoxical carrier is defined as:

options.a: A person who sheds pathogens during incubation period
options.b: A carrier who acquired pathogen from another carrier
options.c: A person who acquired pathogen from patient
options.d: A patient who became a carrier

mcqs.explanation: A paradoxical carrier is a carrier that acquired a pathogen from another carrier. Incubatory carriers are those who shed the infectious agents during the incubation period of the disease. Convalescent carriers are those who continue to shed the disease agent during the period of convalescence. Healthy carriers are those who had a subclinical infection and developed a carrier state without suffering from overt disease.147

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about herd immunity?

options.a: It refers to group protection beyond what is afforded by the protection of immunized individuals
options.b: Vaccination allows the possibility of 100% herd immunity against a disease
options.c: It is affected by presence and distribution of alternative animal hosts
options.d: It doesn't protect the individual in the case of tetanus

mcqs.explanation: It is not possible to achieve 100% herd immunity against a certain disease but studies have shown this is not necessary for disease control.154 Herd structure is never constant. It is subject to constant variation because of new births, deaths and population mobility. An ongoing immunization programme will keep up the herd immunity at a very high level.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with which of the following?

options.b: Efficacy of the vaccine f or the disease
options.c: Number of vaccines for the disease

mcqs.explanation: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with the number of vaccines for the disease. It varies only due to the virulence of the disease, efficacy of the vaccine and contact parameter for the population.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG)?

options.a: All live vaccines can be given simultaneously with NHIG.
options.b: They are used against measles and hepatitis A.
options.c: There should be a low IgA concentration in NHIG preparations.
options.d: Each NHIG fraction is obtained from at least 1,000 donors.

mcqs.explanation: Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks. NHIG is an antibody-rich fraction that is usually obtained from a pool of at least 1,000 donors. AN NHIG preparation must contain at least 90% intact IgG and minimal IgG aggregates with low IgA concentration. NHIG is commonly used to prevent measles and hepatitis A infections. Specific human immunoglobulins a re m ade from the plasma of patients who have recently recovered from an infection or are obtained from individuals who have been immunized against a specific infection. These preparations have a high antibody content against an individual infection and provide immediate protection.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about specific human immunoglobulins?
mcqs.explanation: Specific human immunoglobulins or hyperimmune human Igs are obtained from selected donors that have high titres of the antibodies to the disease like those who have recovered from the dis ease. I t is commonly used in prophylaxis of chickenpox in highly susceptible individuals and in post-exposure prophylaxis of hepatitis B.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about secondary booster immune response in comparison with primary response?

options.a: Antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity to bind to the antigen
options.b: Antibody response is at a higher level
options.c: Antibody response is maintained for a longer period of time

mcqs.explanation: Production of antibodies is faster in secondary booster response. Primary response is the immune response developed when an antigen is administered for the first time to a person who has never been exposed to it. There is a latent period of 3-10 days before antibodies appear in the blood. Secondary booster response is the immune response e licited by a booster dose. In comparison to a primary immune response, it has a shorter latent period, faster production of antibodies, and155 an abundance of antibodies. The antibody response is maintained at higher levels for a longer period of time, and the antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity or capacity to bind to the antigen.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about live vaccines?

options.a: Simultaneous administration of two live vaccines should be done in the same syringe
options.b: Two live vaccines can be administered simultaneously
options.c: Immuno-compromised state poses a contraindication to live vaccines
options.d: Live vaccines contain both major and minor antigens

mcqs.explanation: Simultaneous administration of vaccines is defined as administering more than one vaccine on the same clinic day, at different anatomic sites. They are not combined in the same syringe. Simultaneous administration of the most widely used live and inactivated vaccines does n ot result in decreased antibody responses or increased rates of adverse reaction. However, in children with functional or anatomic asplenia pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and Menactra brand meningococcal conjugate vaccines should not be administered at the same visit; separate these vaccines by at least 4 weeks. Advantages of simultaneous administration of vaccines: • The organisms multiply in the host and thus, the antigenic dose is larger than what i s i njected. • They have all the major and minor antigenic components. Live vaccines should not be administered to those with an immunocompromised state, since they may cause severe systemic disease by way of viremia/bacteriemia. Note: If live vaccines are not given simultaneously, they must be spaced as follows- • The administration of two live parenteral vaccines or live intranasal influenza vaccines must be separated by at least 4 weeks (28 days). • If two live vaccines are g iven less than 4 weeks apart, the second vaccine should be repeated in four weeks. This is because the live vaccine given first can interfere with the second vaccine, and the person may not develop active immunity to the second vaccine.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a killed vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine. Injectable polio vaccine (Salk vaccine), pertussis vaccine, and rabies vaccine are killed vaccines.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to administration of inactivated or killed vaccines?
mcqs.explanation: The only absolute contraindication to administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine is severe local or general reaction to a previous dose of the vaccine. Inactivated or killed vaccines are made from growing cultures of the organism and then inactivating them with heat or chemicals.They activate the channels of active immunity after injection and are less efficacious than live vaccines. Multiple doses or booster doses are usually required to produce an adequate antibody response.156 Killed vaccines can be given to immune-compromised individuals and in pregnancy as the infective agent is inactivated and cannot grow. Egg allergy is not an absolute contraindication to the administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following are live vaccines?
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever vaccine and Sabin vaccine (oral polio vaccine) are live vaccines. HBV and HPV vaccines are recombinant vaccines. Tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What should be the minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines?
mcqs.explanation: The minimum interval between the administration of two live vaccines is 4 weeks. This is because decreasing the interval between two doses may interfere with the antibody response and protection. Thus, live vaccines can either be given on the same day according to the schedule or 4 weeks apart. Note: In Park 27th ed. the minimum interval between two live vaccines is given as 3 weeks. However, several other standard sources including CDC and UNDP suggested an interval of 4 weeks. When both are given in options, it is recommended to mark 4 we eks a s the correct answer.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In which of the following diseases should active and passive immunisation not be done together?
mcqs.explanation: Active and passive immunization should not be done together for measles as the vaccine used is a live vaccine. Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks. Note: In the case of measles alone, the recommended interval between administration of Measles immunoglobuli ns a nd Live measles vaccine is about 6 months in a non-immunocompromised individual and 8 months in an immunocompromised individual.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the main drawback of polysaccharide-based vaccines?

options.a: They cause severe pain at the injection site
options.b: The immune responses elicited are serotype specific
options.c: It cannot be conjugated with proteins to enhance immunogenicity
options.d: The rate of adverse reactions is very high

mcqs.explanation: Polysaccharide-based vaccines stimulate an antibody response against the surface polysaccharide of the pathogenic-capsulated bacteria. The polysaccharide structure varies not only between bacteria of different species but also between different strains within a single species. Thus, a limitation of these vaccines is that the im mune r esponses are serotype-specific.157 If these vaccines are conjugated with proteins, they are given the capability of eliciting a stronger immune response. Multivalent formulations of both polysaccharide-based vaccines and conjugated vaccines are required to achieve protection against multiple serotypes.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a subunit vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccine is an example of a subunit vaccine made using HBsAg. Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of organisms by recombinant DNA technology. E . g., HPV vaccine (uses L1 major capsid protein) and hepatitis B vaccine (uses HBsAg). BCG is a live attenuated vaccine, IPV is an inactivated vaccine and DPT has diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and a killed pertussis component.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are a medical officer conducting an ANC camp in a rural village near Hubli, Karnataka. Which of the following vaccines would you not administer to a pregnant woman?
mcqs.explanation: Yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy in non-endemic areas. It is a live vaccine and most live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy unless the risk of infection is much greater than the risk of harm to the fetus. Note: Y ellow fever vaccine is not an absolute contraindication as it is administered in certain endemic areas and in outbreaks

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed to have an allergy to e ggs. Administration of which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in this patient?
mcqs.explanation: Influenza and yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in patients having an allergy to eggs.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A newborn baby is HIV + and symptomatic. Which of the following vaccines must not be given to her?
mcqs.explanation: BCG vaccine must not be administrated to HIV -infected infants who are symptomatic despite the presence of high TB prevalence. Since BCG is a live vaccine, it significantly increases the risk of disseminated TB in a symptomatic HIV + infant. However, asymptomatic i nfants who are HIV + can be given BCG, provided the risk of contracting TB is high in that region. In areas of low TB prevalence or risk, the BCG vaccine is avoided.158 WHO recommendations for administering live vaccines in symptomatic HIV + patients: • Measles vaccine (or MMR) is allowed even in the symptomatic stage of HIV infection (except in the terminal phase), so as to prevent serious and life-threatening wild measles virus disease. Avoid MMR only if CD4+ < 15% (severely immunocompromised). • IPV is an inactivated vaccine and must be used as an alternative to OPV.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following side effects is most likely to develop in a newborn, following BCG vaccination?
mcqs.explanation: Ulceration is the most common side effect post BCG vaccination. Following v accination, the local tissue response begins in 2-3 weeks and results in scar formation and healing within 3 months. Side effects most commonly seen include ulceration at the vaccination site and regional lymphadenitis. Some vaccine strains may also rarely cause osteomyelitis. In immunocompromised states, disseminated BCG infection can occur. The image below shows the typical adverse effcts seen following BCG vaccination: • Regional lymphadenopathy • Suppurative l ymphadenopathy with fistula • Ulcer at injection site • Cold abscess at inject site159

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child who had recently received the BCG vaccine comes to you with complaints of fever, pain and swelling at the injection site. You suspect a localised abscess formation. Which of the following steps should be avoided in the treatment of this child?

options.b: Incision and a pplication of INH powder
options.d: Incision and application of PAS powder

mcqs.explanation: There is no need for systemic treatment with INH in case of a local abscess formation after BCG vaccination. If there is a local abscess formation following BCG vaccination, it should be treated by aspiration. If it does not clear, then it should be incised and INH or PAS powder should be applied daily to the site. The patient should be assured of the harmless nature of the lesion.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A complete blood count was obtained for a patient after they were administered vaccine X. The report is shown below. Which of the following options is most likely to be vaccine X?
mcqs.explanation: The lab report shows a low platelet count or thrombocytopenia. This is a possible adverse effect of the MMR vaccine.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Persistent inconsolable crying can be a result of administration of which of the following vaccines?
mcqs.explanation: Persistent inconsolable crying is usually seen after DPT vaccine. It is mostly attributed to the pertussis fraction of the vaccine. It usually lasts for 3 hours and settles after a day or so. Other adverse effects of the DTP vaccine include neurologic effects like encephalitis and encephalopathies.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about the DPT vaccine?

options.a: Adult preparation contains a lower dose of diphtheria than the pediatric version
options.b: Whole killed bacteria of Bordetella pertussis has an adjuvant effect
options.c: The whole-cell killed B. pertussis component is encephalogenic
options.d: Presence of H. influenzae type b component inc reases i ts immunogenicity

mcqs.explanation: 160 H. influenzae type b (Hib) is not a component of the DPT vaccine and hence cannot affect its immunogenicity. It is a component of the pentavalent vaccine. The DPT vaccine is made up of diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus vaccines. The pertussis component in DPT vaccine enhances the potency of the diphtheria toxoid. Both whole-cell killed B. pertussis and acellular pertussis component have this adjuvant effect. The only difference is that whole-cell killed B. pertussis is encephalitogenic a nd immunity is short-lasting, while the acellular pertussis component (DTaP) is devoid of neurological complications. There are two types of DPT vaccines - plain and adsorbed. Adsorption is usually carried out on a mineral carrier like aluminium phosphate or hydroxide. Adsorbed vaccines are more immunogenic and recommended by WHO for national vaccination programmes.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A worried mother brings her baby to your PHC saying her child has gone limp. She mentions the child had recently been given some oral drops as part of a mass vaccination campaign. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the baby's symptoms?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of paralysis and the likely cause is vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis following OPV administration. This is a rare side effect of OPV. Acute-onset flaccid paralysis occurs within 4 to 30 days of receipt of the vaccine in these cases or within 4 to 75 days after contact with a vaccine recipient.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A patient presents with complaints of severe aching pain and weakness in his left arm and shoulder. He mentions he ha d r ecently been administered a vaccine in his left arm, but he does not remember the name of the vaccine. Which of the following could be the most common cause of his symptoms?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of brachial neuritis which is a known complication of the tetanus vaccine. Brachial neuritis is a dysfunction of nerves supplying the arm and shoulder without the involvement of the rest o f the nervous system. It presents with a deep, steady, severe aching pain in the shoulder and arm followed by weakness and wasting in arm and shoulder muscles. Sensory loss may also be present. It is treated symptomatically by analgesics.161

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Select the wrongly matched pair of excipients and vaccines.
mcqs.explanation: Formaldehyde is not used in the BCG vaccine. It is used in IPV and diphtheria and tetanus vaccines. Excipients (other vaccine constituents) include: Adjuvants: serve to enhance the immune reaction to the vaccine , Stabilizers : stabilize and prolong the shelf-life of the vaccine and Preservatives : preserve the components. Some examples are listed below: • As stabilizing agents- • MgCl2 - OPV • MgSO4 - measles • Lactose-sorbitol and sorbitol-gelatine168 • To prevent microbial growth and contamination- • Thiomersal- DPT, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), rabies, influenza, and meningococcal diseases. It contains very small amounts of organic mercury. • Neomycin- MMR and IPV • Other preservatives- • 2-phenoxyethanol - IPV • Phenol - Typhoid vaccine

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about adjuvants in vaccines?

options.a: Immune response is increased by degree or duration by their use
options.b: They are used in HPV vaccines
options.c: There is a high incidence of side effects with their use
options.d: They help in the reduction of amount of immunogens in vaccines

mcqs.explanation: Side effects are rare with the use of adjuvants in vaccines. Adjuvants are substances that are added to vaccines to enhance their immunogenicity by degree and/or d uration. They help in the reduction of the amount of immunogen in vaccines or in the number of doses required to achieve immunity. Aluminium salts are the most commonly used adjuvants. Adjuvants are used in many vaccines like: • Anthrax vaccine • Hep A vaccine • Hep B vaccine • Japanese encephalitis vaccine • DT and DTaP • HPV vaccine • Pneumococcal vaccine

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which adjuvant is used in the DPT vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: Aluminium is the adjuvant used in DPT vaccines. The table below lists adjuvants used in human vaccines:Name Class Components Vaccine Alum Mineral salts Aluminium phosphate , alumi nium hydroxide Diphtheria, tetanus , pneumo coccus , HAV , HBV , anthrax , tick-borne encephalitis , Men C, HPV MF59 Oil-in-water emulsion Squalene, Tween 80, Span 85 Seasonal and pandemic influ enza169 Name Class Components Vaccine AS03 Oil-in-water emulsion Squalene, Tween 80, alpha to copherol Pandemic influenza AF03 Oil-in-water emulsion Squalene, Montane 80, Eum ulgin B1PH Pandemic influenza Viroso mes Liposomes Phospholipids , cholesterol , h aemagglutinin Seasonal influenza, HAV AS04 Alum-adsorbed TLR4 ago nist Alumnium hydroxide , monop hosphoryl lipid A (MPL) HBV , HPV RC-52 Alum-adsorbed TLR4 ago nist Aluminium hydroxide , synth etic MPL HBV

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child has come to you for the administration of the IPV vaccine, as part of his routine immunisation schedule. Which of the following antibiotics may be found in this vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: IPV may contain trace amounts of streptomycin, neomycin or polymyxin B. MMR contain small amount of neomycin. Antibiotics are used during vaccine manufacture to prevent bacterial contamination of tissue culture cells.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following are the most and least heat-sensitive vaccines respectively?

options.a: Sabin vaccine and hep B vaccine
options.c: Japanese encaphalitis vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine
options.d: Salk vaccine and hep B vaccine

mcqs.explanation: Oral polio (Sabin) vaccine is the most heat-sensitive vaccine. Hepatitis B vaccines are the least heat-sensitive alongside meningococcal A vaccine, freeze-dried Hib vaccine and pneumococcal vaccines.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following vaccines should be protected from sub-zero temperatures?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccine is sensitive to freezing and should be protected from sub-zero temperatures. V accines to be protected from freezing are as follows: • Hepatitis B • Cholera • DTaP-hepB-Hib-IPV (hexavalent) • DTwP-hepB-Hib (pentavalent) • Liquid Hib • IPV • Influenza, pneumococcal vaccines • Tetanus, DT, Td170 • Rotavirus (freeze-dried, least sensitive), the liquid form is resistant to freezing • HPV

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What vaccines are supplied in the type of bottle given below?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows an amber-colored vial. Vaccines like BCG and measles vaccine are sensitive to light and thus are supplied in such vials.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a non-electrical cold-chain equipment?
mcqs.explanation: Cold boxes, vaccine carriers, and ice packs are some of the non-electrical components of the cold-chain system. Cold boxes are insulated containers used for transportation and temporary storage of vaccines and ice packs. Vaccine carriers are u sually not used for the storage of vaccines but for their transportation . Ice packs generally have two holes in them for placing vaccines. They are filled with water. The below image shows a cold box containing vaccines and ice packs.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the temperature maintained in the freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive?
mcqs.explanation: The freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive is maintained at – 7 \260C, and it is used to store mainly ice packs. The vaccine storage compartment of this solar cold chain equipment is maintained at 2 to 8 \260C. The other solar cold-chain equipment commonly used is the solar refrigerators direct drive, which uses the sun's energy to freeze phase-change materials like water and then uses this formed171 ice bank to keep the refrigerator cold.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about the device shown in the image below?

options.a: Smaller ones are given to PHCs and the larger ones to district vaccine stores
options.b: They have temperature zones for different vaccines
options.c: Kata thermometer is used to record temperature inside this device
options.d: These devices are provided with baskets to store vaccines

mcqs.explanation: The image shown in the question is of an ice-lined refrigerator (ILR). Dial or digital thermometers are used to record temperatures inside an ice-lined refrigerator. ILRs are the main method of vaccine storage in primary health centers. They are an important part of the cold chain and they maintain a temperature of 2 to 8 \260C for the storage of vaccines. They have different temperature zones for different vaccines. The upper zone is for f reeze -sensitive vaccines like cholera, hep B, rotavirus(liquid), etc while the lower zone is for heat-sensitive vaccines like OPV, measles, etc. All vaccines are kept in the basket provided with ILR. Vaccines like OPV, BCG, measles, and JE can be kept at the bottom of the basket while, DPT, TT, Hep B, IPV , and pentavalent vaccines and diluents are kept in the upper part of the basket.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: While working as a medical officer in a CHC, you experience a sudden power cut in your area due to which the ice-lined refrigerator loses power. What is the time taken for the temperature inside this equipment to rise to t he maximum recommended temperature limit?
mcqs.explanation: Hold-over time is the time taken by cold-chain equipment to raise the temperature inside it, during loss of power, to the maximum temperature limit in its recommended range. For an ice-lined refrigerator(ILR), this time depends on: • Ambient temperature • Frequency of opening the equipment • Quantity of vaccines kept inside with spacing • Condition of ice-pack lining The below image shows an ILR.172

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: At what level is the risk of cold-chain failure the highest?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of cold chain failure is highest at the sub-centre and village levels. Thus, vaccines are not stored at the sub-centre and are supplied on the day of use.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Open vial policy is not applicable to which of the following vaccines?
mcqs.explanation: Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG and measles vaccines. It is applicable for: • DPT • TT • Hepatitis B vaccine • OPV • Pentavalent vaccine • Rotavirus vaccine (New version with the VVM on the side)

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What are the devices given below used to measure?

options.d: Disintegration of vaccine constituents due to temperature

mcqs.explanation: The image shown is of vaccine vial monitors (VVM), which measure the cumulative heat exposure of the vaccine. VVMs a re heat-sensitive indicators that are routinely used to monitor vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain. They record cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color. If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and should be discarded.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are preparing to administer the BCG vaccine to a newborn at a PHC. Before administering the vaccine, you check the vaccine vial monitor. In which of the following observations on the VVM, will you discard the vaccine?

options.b: Inner square has the same color as the outer circle
options.c: Inner circle has the same color as the outer square
options.d: Inner circle is lighter than the outer square

mcqs.explanation: A vaccine must be discarded if the VVM shows the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following vaccine vials can be used based on the vaccine vial monitor (VVM) color changes shown?
mcqs.explanation: From the above image, only vials 1 and 2 can be used as the inner squares of the VVMs are lighter than the outer circles.173 Vial 3 has crossed the discard point as the inner square and outer circle are the same color and thus cannot be used. Vial 4 cannot be used as the VVM shows a darker inner square compared to the outer circle.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are volunteering in a vaccination camp. You perform a shake test before administering a particular vaccine. Which of the following is checked by this test?
mcqs.explanation: The shake test is done to check for damage to vaccines that are sensitive to freezing temperatures. Steps to perform the shake test: • A frozen vaccine is used as a control vial and the vial suspected to be damaged by freezing is taken as the test vial. • Both are shaken after thawing a nd the rate of sedimentation is compared. • If the rate of sedimentation in the test vial is slower than that in the control vial, then it is usable and has not been damaged.Some of the most widely used vaccines are freeze-sensitive. These include vaccines against: • Diphtheria • Tetanus • Pertussis • Haemophilus influenza type b (Liquid ) • Hepatitis B174

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment?
mcqs.explanation: Asepsis is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment. Sterilization is a process of killing or removal of all living microorganisms either in the vegetative or spore state from an area or surface or a medium. Decontamination is the process of rendering an article or area free of contaminants, including microbial, chemical, radioactive and other hazardous materials. Disinfection is the process by which the destruction of microorganisms i s achieved with the use of physical or chemical agents. Microbial forms like spores and some viruses may be resistant to certain disinfectants.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: All of the following are methods of dry heat sterilisation except:
mcqs.explanation: Autoclaving is a method of moist heat sterilization.Dry heat sterilization Moist heat sterilization FlamingIncinerationHot air o ven BoilingPasteurizationAutocla ving

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the temperature that has to be maintained for sterilization in the device shown below?
mcqs.explanation: The image shown is a sterilizing hot air oven. The temperature to be maintained is 160\260 C for 2 hours. Exposure to dry heat in a sterilizing hot air oven ensures the carbonization of organic material and the destruction of microorganisms and spores. The following combinations of temperature and duration of sterilization can be applied in hot air ovens: • 180\260C for 30 mins • 170\260C for 60 mins • 160\037C for 2 hours

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: An OT technician is sterilizing surgical instruments in the following device. What temperature should be maintained?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows an autoclave. Surgical instruments are sterilized at 121\260 C for 10-15 minutes.183 Autoclaving is a form of moist heat sterilization which creates an increased temperature of steam under pressure. This method of sterilization is effective against spores also. Autoclaving is done for instruments that cannot withstand high temperatures of hot air oven or dry heat.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following materials are sterilized by a hot air oven?
mcqs.explanation: Glasswares, oils and powders, swabs, and dressings are sterilized by a hot air oven. Surgical instruments and culture media are sterilized by autoclave.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You have performed an upper GI endoscopy on a HbsAg positive patient. Which of the following should be used to sterilize the scope?
mcqs.explanation: 2% glutaraldehyde is used to sterilize endoscopes and fibreoptic scopes. Aldehydes in 2% solutions (like glutaraldehyde and formaldehyde) have sporicidal activities. Glutaraldehyde is usually efficacious against tubercle bacteria, fungi & viruses.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding the use of ethylene oxide in sterilisation and disi nfection?

options.a: It is an inflammable and explosive gas
options.b: It is used for heat-sensitive objects
options.c: It is mixed with nitrogen for sterilization

mcqs.explanation: A mixture of ethylene oxide with carbon dioxide is used for sterilization, not with nitrogen. Ethylene oxide is an alkylating agent and has inflammable and explosive properties. It is often mixed with the following prior to use: • Carbon dioxide - decreases i ts explosive nature • Water vapor - increases the efficiency of the gas Sterilization using this gas is usually done at 50-60 \260C. and is suitable for heat-sensitive items like plastics, heart valves, dental equipment. It is effective against bacteria, spores, and some viruses.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The following machine was used during a cardiac bypass surgery. How is it best sterilized?
mcqs.explanation: The image shown is a heart-lung machine. It is best sterilized using ethylene oxide. Ethylene oxide gas diffuses through many types of porous materials and readily penetrates some plastics a nd is used for sterilizing machines.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Povidone - iodine is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: Povidone - iodine is an iodophor.184 Iodophors are iodine-based disinfectants in which iodine is combined with solubilizing agents or carriers. This results in the formation of a complex that provides a sustained release reservoir of iodine and releases small amounts of free iodine in an aqueous solution.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of precurrent disinfection?

options.a: Chlorination of a well by village public health authorities
options.b: Disinfection of kidney tray used during delivery of placenta
options.c: Disinfection of bed linen after the death of a patient
options.d: Disinfection of artery forceps following a sur gery

mcqs.explanation: Chlorination of water in a well is an example of precurrent disinfection. Precurrent disinfection refers to prophylactic disinfection prior to discharge of infectious material. This includes pasteurization o f milk, chlorination of water and hand washing. Concurrent disinfection is the application of disinfection methods after discharge of infectious material from a person or soiling. This includes disinfection of urine, faeces, vomit, contaminated linen, clothes, hands. Terminal disinfection is done after the death of a patient or transfer or after cessation of isolation.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Chlorine is the main disinfectant element in all of the following except:
mcqs.explanation: Cetrimide (trade name - Cetavlon) is a quaternary ammonia compound (QAC) that does not contain chlorine. QACs are low-level disinfectants and are sporostatic but not sporicidal. It is a bactericidal agent against vegetative gram-positive organisms. Other QACs include cetrimide (cetavlon) and benzalkonium chloride. Savlon contains cetrimide and chlorhexidine and is mainly used for plastic items. Clinical thermometers may be best disinfected in Savlon mixed with spirit in a 1:6 ratio. Chlorine compounds are potent disinfectants that are bactericidal, f ungicidal, sporicidal , tuberculocidal, and virucidal.Chlorine compounds Mechanism of action and use s 1. Bleaching powder (chlorin ated lime) Disinfection of water, feces , a nd urine 2. Chloramine - T Has a prolonged bactericidal effect , used in a health care s etting 3. Hypochlorites Disinfect infectious waste an d surfaces 4. Halazone tablets Disinfect small quantities of water 5. Superoxidized water Saline is electrolyzed to relea se hypochlorous acid and chl orine, which act as disinfecta nts185

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Hydrogen peroxide is:
mcqs.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is effective against bacteria, fungi, spores and viruses. It is used in the hospital setting to disinfect surfaces. Sporicidal activities require higher concentrations and longer contact times. A 3% solution is also used as an antiseptic and for cleaning wounds and discharging ulcers.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which among the following is a low-level disinfectant?
mcqs.explanation: Benzalkonium chloride is a quaternary ammonium compound that is used as a low-level disinfectant. There are 3 types of disinfectants: • Low-level disinfectant - kills o nly vegetative bacteria, fungi and lipid enveloped viruses (e.g. quaternary ammonium compounds) • Intermediate level disinfectant: kills all microbes including mycobacteria and non-enveloped viruses, but not spores (e.g. alcohol, iodophors) • High-level disinfectant - This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens and some spores if the contact time is increased (e.g. glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide)

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which among t he following is not a sporicidal agent?
mcqs.explanation: Cresol a phenolic compound is not sporicidal. Disinfectants that are not sporicidal are: • Biguanides • Alcohols • Heavy metal disinfectants • Organic acids • QACs • Phenolic compounds Sporicidal disinfectants include: • Aldehydes • Chlorine disinfectants • Hydrogen peroxide • Ethylene oxide186 • Peracetic acids

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following disinfectants has anti-viral action?
mcqs.explanation: Hypochlorite is an antiviral disinfectant. Antiviral disinfectants include: • Chlorine compounds • Phenol (at high concentrations) • Aldehydes • Hydrogen peroxide

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A nurse in a PHC is using bleaching powder to disinfect bed linen contaminated with stool. What is the amount that she should use?
mcqs.explanation: Bleaching powder of 50 g/L of water is required for disinfecting feces and urine. The agents commonly used for disinfecting faeces and urine are:Disinfectant Amount per lit re Per ce nt Bleaching pow der 50 g Crude phenol 100 ml 10 Cresol 50 ml Formalin 100 ml 10

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following methods of disinfection is not effective against prions?
mcqs.explanation: Benzalkonium chloride is not effective against prions. Prions can be inactivated by following the given steps: • Immersing the instruments in 1N NaOH or sodium hypochlorite for 1 hour • Then they are transferred to water • Then they are heated in a gravity displacement autoclave at 121\260C for 1 hour • After this, they are cleaned and subjected to routine sterilization

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the f ollowing methods is not effective for disinfection of sputum of patients?
mcqs.explanation: 187 Chlorhexidine is not used to disinfect sputum. Sputum can be disinfected by: • Autoclaving or boiling - if a considerable amount of sputum is present (e.g. in TB hospitals) • 5% cresol - patients are asked to spit in a sputum cup half-filled with cresol • Burning - for samples received in gauze or paper handkerchiefs
