mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Rideal-Walker co-efficient is employed for the assessment of which of the following?
mcqs.explanation: The Rideal-Walker coefficient helps in assessing the power of a disinfectant relative to phenol. It assesses this by determining the phenol coefficient (PC). A PC value of > 1 indicates that it is more effective than phenol. The higher the number, the greater its effectiveness in comparison to phenol and vice versa. Traditional organisms used to test the power of the disinfectant include S. aureus and Salmonella enteric subtype typhi. Phenol coefficient = The dilution o f test disinfectant which kills microorganisms in a given time \367 The dilution of phenol which kills the microorganism in the same time under identical conditions.188 Other tests that are used for disinfectants are as follows: • Chick Martin test - modification of the Rideal-Walker test where disinfectants act in the presence of organic matter like feces or yeast to simulate natural conditions • Kelsey-Skyes test (capacity test) - tests the capacity of a disinfectant to retain its activity when used repeatedly. • In-use test - determines whether the chosen disinfectant is effective in actual hospital use Joseph Lister first introduced p henol (carbolic acid) as an antiseptic to sterilize surgical instruments and clean wounds. Lister's work led to a reduction in postoperative infections and made surgery safer for patients, distinguishing him as the 'Father of Modern Surgery' and 'Father of Antiseptic Surgery'.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding the Spaulding classification?

options.a: Semi-critical items require high level disinfection
options.b: Non-critical items do not require disinfection
options.c: C ardiac catheters are classified as critical items
options.d: Critical items are associated with a high risk of infection

mcqs.explanation: Under the Spaulding classification, non-critical items require intermediate or low-level disinfection.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: While collecting blood for samples, you have spilled some on the floor. What would be the immediate next step?

options.a: Call the infection control team of the hospital

mcqs.explanation: The immediate next step in this scenario is to clean the spilled blood with absorbable material. This absorbable material is then discarded in the yellow bin. Following this, sodium hypochlorite solution is used to decontaminate the surface. The concentrations of sodium hypochlorite used are: • < 10 mL blood spill - 1:100 dilution to decontaminate non-porous surfaces • > 10 mL blood spill or culture spill - 1:10 dilution for the first application, followed by 1:100 dilution

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A blood spill in the operation theatre must be cleaned with _____.
mcqs.explanation: Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%. If the spill contains large amounts of blood or body fluids, clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard the contaminated materials in appropriate, labelled containment. A 1:10–1:100 dilution of 5.25%–6.15% sodium hypochlorite (i.e., household bleach) or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant has been recommended for decontaminating blood spills.189

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following are true for a screening test?
mcqs.explanation: Screening tests are done on apparently healthy individuals, the results of the test are relatively inaccurate, the tests are based on one criterion. The difference between screening and diagnostic tests is given below: Screening tests are recommended in the following conditions: • Early diagnosis changes the disease course201 • In a disease with an asymptomatic stage • In a disease with a test for diagnosis and treatment • The natural history of the disease is well knownScreening test Diagnostic test Done on apparently healthy Done on patients with signs a nd symptoms Applied to groups Applied to single patients Based on one criterion or cut -off point Based on evaluation of a num ber of symptoms , signs, and l aboratory findings Less accurate More accurate Less expensive More expensive Not a basis for treatment Used as a basis for treatment The initiative comes from the investigator or agency provi ding care The initiative comes from a p atient with a complaint

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Below is a diagram depicting the natural history of the disease. Which point marks the onset of symptoms?
mcqs.explanation: Point C represents a point where signs and symptoms appear. Various points marked in the image represent the following: Point A: Entry of infectious agent into the host. Point B: Pathological and physiological changes occur in the stage of the subclinical phase. These changes are induced by the causative agent but are not sufficient enough to cause clinical signs and symptoms. Point C: Marks onset of clinical signs and symptoms. Point D: Usual time of diagnosis at which clinical s igns and symptoms are well evident.202

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In the following natural history of disease flowchart, point A to C is called as?
mcqs.explanation: Lead time is the period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the usual time of diagnosis (point C). Screening time is the time difference between the first point of diagnosis and the critical point of diagnosis. Diagnosis of a disease before the critical point has a good outcome and reduces the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred. S creening m ust be done in conditions where there is a considerable time lag between the onset of disease and the usual time of diagnosis. That is conditions with a long lead time. Generation time is defined as the interval of time between the onset of infection by a host and the maximal infectivity of that host.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In which of the following diseases, screening procedure increases the overall survival to the maximum?
mcqs.explanation: Screening of colon cancer increases the overall survival to the maximum. Colon cancer has a long lead time and can be detected early before pathological changes occur. It c an be curable if treated early, otherwise fatal in half the cases. Early diagnosis and treatment before the critical point have a good outcome and reduce the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred. Other diseases that can be screened are: • Cervical cancer203 • Breast cancer • Prostate cancer

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of prospective screening?

options.a: Cervical Pap smear in a 40 year old patient
options.b: Neonatal screening of a new-born baby for hypothyroidism

options.d: Urine for sugar screening in a 40 year old man

mcqs.explanation: Screening of immigrants to a country is an example of prospective screening. mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of prescriptive screening?

mcqs.explanation: Screening of infants for phenylketonuria is an example of prescriptive screening. mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of multiphasic screening?

options.a: Chest X-ray for TB in large populations
options.c: Pap smear in women above 40 years
options.d: Random blood sugar during antenatal visits

mcqs.explanation: Annual health checkups are an example of multiphasic screening. Types of screening: • Multiphasic screening is the application of two or more screening tests in combination with a large number of people at one time. Example- Annual health checkups. • High-risk or selective screening is done on high-risk groups. Example- MRI screening of breast done annually in 25-year old women with BRCA 1, BRCA 2 mutations in a first-degree relative. • Mass screening is a screening of a whole o r large population like using a chest X-ray for TB screening in large populations. It is done for diseases with high prevalence.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A large number of tests were done in series. Which o f the following will be true?

options.b: Sensitivity will decrease, specificity will increase
options.d: Sensitivity will increase, specificity will decrease

mcqs.explanation: When a large number of tests are done in series, net sensitivity is decreased and net specificity is increased. Screening tests are done in series when the result of the first test determines whether to run the second test or not. e.g., HIV screening is done using consecutive ELISA. Screening tests are done in parallel when the second test is independently p erformed regardless of what the first test result is. Both the tests are done at the same time. For e.g., In LFT, multiple tests are done together like SGOT, SGPT, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, etc. Following are the trends that are observed while evaluating screening tests:Tests in Serie s Tests in parallel Combined sensitivi ty Decreases Increases Combined specificit y Increases Decreases Combined PPV Increases Decreases Combined NPV Decreases Increases205

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Colon cancer screening is being done by a hemoccult stool test in a healthcare center. Patients who test positive, undergo a repeat stool hemoccult test. If the second test comes out positive, the individual is referred for more extensiv e evaluation. How is this method of screening affecting sensitivity and specificity?

options.a: Net sensitivity and net specificity are both increasing
options.b: Net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity is increasing
options.c: Net sensitivity is increasing and net specificity is decreasing
options.d: Net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity remains the same

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, tests are being performed in series. Here, the net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity is increasing. Screening tests are done in series, where the result of the first test determines whether to run the second test or not. e.g. HIV screening is done using consecutive ELISA. Screening tests are done in parallel, where the second test is independently performed regardless of what the first test result is. Both the tests are done at the same time. F or e.g. In LFT, multiple tests are done together like SGOT, SGPT, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, etc. Following are the trends that are observed while evaluating screening tests:Tests in Serie s Tests in parallel Combined sensitivi ty Decreases Increases Combined specificit y Increases Decreases Combined PPV Increases Decreases Combined NPV Decreases Increases

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Blood pressure is measured in an individual 5 times a day under the same conditions by a new screening test. All 5 readings obtained are the almost same. What is the attribute of a new screening test being described?
mcqs.explanation: The attribute of a new screening test to yield the same reading when repeated under the same conditions is called reliability. Reliability is also called precision or reproducibility.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Ten successive readings of hemoglobin level of a single sample measured by a new method are given below. The hemoglobin level meas ured b y the previous standard test was 10.2 . What is true regarding the new method?
mcqs.explanation: The new method for measuring hemoglobin has high validity and low reliability. The new test doesn't give the same values on repeat testing, thus it has low reliability. The mean value of all the readings is 10. The mean is close to the value of 10.2 , which is obtained from the standard test, making t he validity high. The validity of a test implies that the test must give correct and accurate results. It represents the closeness to a true/ actual value. The reliability of a test implies that the test must give consistent results when repeated on the same individual or material, under the same conditions.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Out of 100 people having lung cancer, 60 tested positive by a new screening test. Out of 900 people who don't have lung cancer, 300 tested positive. What will be the numerator while calculating sensitivity and its value?
mcqs.explanation: 206 The numerator of sensitivity in a screening test is true positive and its value is 60. True positives are those people who tested positive and actually have the disease. Out of 100 people with lung cancer, 60 are tested positive i.e. true positive. The given data is represented below: TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative Sensitivity is the ability of a screening test to detect true positive(TP) out of the total number of people who have the d isease (TP+FN). Sensitivity = TP/ TP+FN = 60/60+40 = 60%Diseas e + Diseas e - Total Test + 60(TP ) (F P) Test - 40(FN) (T N) Total 100 900 1000

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A screening test was carried out among 114 people out of which 15 have a disease. The test showed 22 people tested positive for the disease among which 14 actually had the disease. What is the sensitivity of the test?
mcqs.explanation: The sensitivity of the above screening test is 93%. The given data is represented below TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative Sensitivity is given as TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 14/15 = 93%.Diseas e + Diseas e - Total Test + 14(TP ) 8(FP) Test - 1(FN) 91(TN) Total 15(TP+ FN) 99(FP+ TN) 114

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A researcher finds out a sensitive test to be positive for a person. For diagnosis, which of the following will hold true?

options.a: It confirms that the person does not have the disease
options.b: It suggests that if the disease is rare, the person surely has the disease
options.c: I t confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common
options.d: It is an expected finding in case the disease is prevalent

mcqs.explanation: A sensitive test, if it is positive it confirms that the person has the disease if the disease is common.207 The sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease. In other words, Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect true positives (TP) out of total disease (TP+FN). Sensitivity = TP/ TP+FN

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: 1000 patients from a healthcare setup were screened for disease 'X' with a new test (biopsy). The test showed positive results in 90 patients out of the 100 who actually had the disease. What is the sensitivity of the new test?
mcqs.explanation: The sensitivity of new test is 90/100. Biopsy gives the definitive number of cases for Disease X. Hence, the given data is represented below: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN\ = 90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 90% True positive is defined as a positive t est result in a person who has the disease.Diseas e + Diseas e - Test + 90(TP ) unkno wn Test - (FN) unkno wn Total 100

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Specificity of a screening test is the ability of a test to detect:
mcqs.explanation: Specificity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who do not have the disease, i.e. true negative. Sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease, i.e. true positive. False-positive are those who don't have the disease but tested positive. False-negative are those who have the disease but tested negative.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: 5000 persons underwent screening for a disease. Out of 500 diseased, 350 tested positive, and out of healthy people, 3000 tested negative. Which of the following is true?
mcqs.explanation: The sensitivity of the above screening test is 70% and Specificity is 66.6%. The given data is represented below: Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 350/500 = 0.7 = 70%. Specificity = TN/(FP + TN) x 100 = 3000/4500 = 0.6666 = 66.6%.208 Disease + Disease - Total Test + 350(TP) 1500(FP) Test - 150(FN) (TN) Total 500(TP +FN) 4500(TN +FP) 5000

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: If a patient tests positive for a disease, which of the following represents the probability of her actually having the dise ase?
mcqs.explanation: Positive predictive value implies the probability of a person with a positive test, actually having the disease. It is the ability of a test to detect true positive(TP) out of total positive(TP+FP) and it is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease. PPV = TP/TP+FP

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: To calculate the positive predictive value of a new screening test for breast carcinoma, what will you use for the denominator?
mcqs.explanation: The denominator for the calculation of the positive predictive value of a screening test is true positives + false positives. Positive predictive value (PPV ) of a test is TP/(TP + FP) x 100. It indicates t he probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. It is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease. Predictive value is affected by sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence. However, it is affected the most by prevalence.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following maximally affect the positive predictive value of a test?
mcqs.explanation: Positive predictive value (PPV ) is maximally affected by the prevalence of the disease. If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the high will be the positive predictive value of a screening test, and t he more accurate will be the test. If the prevalence declines, the PPV will be low. PPV is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease. It is affected the most by prevalence. However, both sensitivity and specificity can change the predictive value.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following reflects the diagnostic power of a screening test?
mcqs.explanation: 209 The predictive accuracy of a screening test reflects its performance and diagnostic power. Predictive accuracy is given by: • Positive predictive value (PPV ): the probability of a person with a positive test, actually having the disease. • Negative predictive value (NPV): the probability of a person with a negative test, definitely not having the disease. Sensitivity is the ability of a screening test to detect true positive out of total disease. Specificity is the ability o f a screening test to detect true negative out of total nondiseased. The reliability of a test implies that the test must give consistent results when repeated on the same individual or material, under the same conditions.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Screening of 100 immigrants for COVID-19 with a new test showed 48 positive and 52 people negative. Those who tested negative underwent RTPCR out of which 25 came positive. Which of the following is lowest for the new test compared to RTPCR?
mcqs.explanation: The sensitivity of the new screening test is low compared to RTPCR. The new screening test showed 52 people negative, out of which 25 are detected positive by RTPCR. i.e. 25 are false negative. The false-negative rate is the number of false-negative out o f total people having the disease. False -negative rate = 1 - Sensitivity The false-negative rate increases as sensitivity decreases. In this scenario, because the new test has more false negatives, it would have low sensitivity as compared to RTPCR.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: While screening a disease with a new screening test, the test is positive in many patients who actually don't have the disease. Which of the following is true?
mcqs.explanation: The given new screening test has low specificity. The test is positive in many patients who actually don't have the disease, i.e. high false positives. The false-positive rate is the number of false positives out of total n on-diseased. False -positive rate = 1-Specificity The false-positive rate is inversely proportional to specificity. Hence, the given test with high false positives will have low specificity. Positive predictive value (PPV )= TP/TP+FP. It shows the positive predictive value(PPV ) of the test decreases with an increase in false positives. An increase in the false-positive does not affect the prevalence of the disease. The prevalence of a disease depends on the incidence(I) a nd duration(D) of the disease. Prevalance= I x D210

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: ECG findings detecting the myocardial infarction obtained from the department of cardiology are given in the table below. Which of the following is true with regard to the below table?

options.b: Sensitivity is the same as specificity
options.d: PPV is the same as NPV

mcqs.explanation: In the above scenario, PPV is the same as NPV. Predictive value of a positive test (PPV) = TP/(TP + FP) x 100 = 300/(300+100) x 100= 75 % Predictive value of a negative test (NPV) = TN/(FN + TN) x 100 = 75/(25+75) x 100 = 75 % Hence PPV = NPV In this scenario, sensitivity is 92% and the specificity is 43% as per the following calculation, Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 300/(300+25) x100 = 92% Specificity = TN/(FP + TN) x 100 = 75/(100+75) x100 = 43%MI Pres ent MI Abs ent Positive E CG (TP) (FP) Negative ECG 25(FN) (TN)

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A new test for hepatitis C is performed on 200 patients with the biopsy-proven disease and 200 patients who are free of the disease. The test shows positive results on 180 of the patients with the disease and negative results on 150 of the patients without the disease. Which of the following is true?
mcqs.explanation: The specificity of the above screening test is 75%. The given data is represented below: TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative Specificity = TN/(FP + TN) x 100 = 150/200 = 75% Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 180/200 = 90% PPV = TP/(TP + FP) x 100 = 180/230 = 78% NPV=TN/(FN + TN) x 100 = 150/170 = 88%Hep C + Hep C - Total Test + 180(TP) 50(FP) Test - (FN) 150(TN) Total 200 (TP +FN) (FP +TN)

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Due to an effective prevention program, the prevalence of a disease in a community has been reduced by 90%. However, the physicians continue to use the same screening test for that disease. Which of the following changes is expected to be seen?
mcqs.explanation: If the prevalence of the disease falls, the negative predictive value(NPV) increases. The NPV of the test is inversely proportional to the prevalence of a disease. The PPV of the test is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease. Sensitivity and specificity are independent of the prevalence of the disease in the area. They do not change with the change in prevalence.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In a population of 10000, the prevalence of a disease is 20%. The sensitivity of a screening test is 95% and specificity is 80%. What is the positive predictive value of the test?
mcqs.explanation: The positive predictive value (PPV ) of the test is 54.3%. The prevalence of the disease is 20% in 1 0000, i .e., 2000 people have the disease(TP + FN) and 8000 are disease-free (FP + TN). The sensitivity of the test is 95%, i.e. TP/(TP + FN) = 95%. Thus, the true positives (TP)= 95/100 x (TP + FN) = 95/100 x 2000 = 1900. The specificity of the test is 80%, i.e. TN/(FP + TN) = 80%. Thus, the true negatives (TN)= 80/100 x (FP + TN) = 80/100 x 8000 = 6400. The given data is represented below: TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative From the above table, PPV is calculated as TP/(TP + FP) x 100 = 1900/3500 = 54.3%. An alternate formula(Bayes theorem) that can be used is PPV = (Sn x P) / (Sn x P)+[(1-Sp)(1-P)] Sn- Sensitivity, P- Prevalence, Sp- SpecificityDisease + Disease - Total Test + (TP) (FP) 3500(TP +FP) Test - (FN) (TN) 6500(FN +TN) Total 2000 (TP +FN) 8000(FP +TN) 10000

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The prevalence of the disease 'X' in a population is 30%. The diagnostic test for this disease has a specificity of 0.80 and a sensitivity of 0.90. What is the negative predictive value of the test?
mcqs.explanation: The negative predictive value of the above test is 95%. For convenience, let us assume that the total population in this scenario is 100. The prevalence of the disease is 30%. So the total number of people with the disease is 30(TP+FN) and disease-free(FP+TN) is 70.212 Since sensitivity is 0.90, i.e. TP/(TP + FN) = 90%. The total true positives (TP) = 90/100 x (TP+FN) = 90/100 x 30 = 27 False-negative(FN) = 30-27 = Since specificity is 0.80, i.e. TN/(FP+TN) = 80%. Total true negatives (TN\ =(FP+TN) x 80/100 = 70 x 80/100 = 56 False-positive(FP) = 70-56 = 14 The given data is represented below: Negative predictive value (NPV) = TN/(FN + TN) x 100 = 56/59 = 0.949 = 95%. An alternate formula(Bayes theorem) that can be used is NPV = (1-P) x Sp /[P x (1-Sn)] +[(1-P) x S p] Sn - Sensitivity, P- Prevalence, Sp- SpecificityDiseas e + Diseas e - Total Test + 27 (TP) 14 (FP) Test - 3 (FN) 56 (TN) Total 30(TP +FN) 70(FP+ TN) 100

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which o f the following is best for determining the threshold for diagnosis of a positive test?
mcqs.explanation: The receiver operator characteristic curve is the best for determining the threshold for the diagnosis of a positive test. It is also used for the comparison of two or more screening/ diagnostic tests of disease with each other. The following is an example of a ROC curve for a screening test.213

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which curve from the given image reflects a better test?
mcqs.explanation: Test A is the best test among the four given, as it has the highest sensitivity and the lowest false positive rate (100-specificity). A receiver operating characteristic curve(ROC) is obtained by plotting a test's true positive rate (sensitivity) against its false-positive rate ( 100- specificity) for different diagnostic cut-off points. The shape of the curve reflects the quality of the test. The better the test, the more it moves to the upper left (more the area under the c urve). For a good test, sensitivity comes close to 100% on the y-axis, and the false positive rate comes close to 0% on the x-axis.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The fasting blood glucose levels of a population from two overlapping distributions are shown in the below graph. A test was done with the cutoff of 120mg/ dl for diagnosing diabetes. What does the shaded area represent?
mcqs.explanation: The shaded area represents the false positives (Non-diabetics incorrectly classified as diabetics).

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Observe the following curves, which of the following is a true statement about sensitivity and specificity when the curve changes from green to pink?
mcqs.explanation: Both sensitivity and specificity are higher in the test represented in pink (Test B) compared to the test represented in green (Test A). Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive. It is the probability of t he test being positive when the disease is present. Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) or Sensitivity = 1 – false-negative rate. Specificity is the proportion of all people without the disease who test negative. It is the probability of the test being negative when the disease is absent.214 Specificity= TN / (TN + FP) or specificity= 1 – false-positive rate. Test B has an increased number of true positives and true negatives and decreased number of false positives and negatives, compared to Test A. Hence leading to increased sensitivity and specificity.215

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: When did the WHO declare that smallpox has been globally eradicated?
mcqs.explanation: The WHO declared the eradication of smallpox on 8th May 1980.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not included in the case definition of smallpox?

options.a: Acute onset fever and malaise 2-4 days before onset of rash
options.b: Development of a maculopapular rash starting on the face and forearms
options.c: Evolution of the rash to umbilicated pustules within 48 hours
options.d: No alternative diagnosis explaining the illness

mcqs.explanation: The rash of smallpox evolves within 48 hours, to first form deep-seated, firm, and well-circumscribed vesicles, which later become umbilicated or confluent pustules. Case definition for notification of smallpox: • An individual of any age with acute onset fever, malaise, severe prostration, headache, and backache 2-4 days before the onset of rash. • Development of a maculopapular rash starting on the face and forearms and then spreading to the trunk and legs. Rash evolves within 48 hours to deep-seated, firm, and well-circumscribed vesicles, which later become umbilicated or confluent pustules. • Lesions that appear at the same stage of development (i.e. all are vesicles or all are pustules) on any given part of the body. • No alternative diagnosis explaining the illness. • Laboratory confirmation: Identification of variola (smallpox) DNA with PCR or isolation of the vi rus f rom a clinical specimen

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old b oy presents to you with complaints of fever and malaise. He also complains of an itchy rash which first appeared on the trunk as shown below. When is this disease the most contagious?

options.b: 2 days before and 5 days after the onset of rash
options.c: 7 days before to 7 days after the onset of rash
options.d: 4 days before to 4 days after the onset of rash

mcqs.explanation: The rash (different stages at one time) in the image and the clinical history are suggestive of chickenpox. The period of communicability for chickenpox is 2 days before and 5 days after the onset of rash.222

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not characteristic of the rash of chicken pox?
mcqs.explanation: The rash of chickenpox is superficial and the rash of smallpox is deep-seated. Difference between the rash of chickenpox and smallpox:Chickenpox Smallpox Centripetal Centrifugal Spares palmsandsoles ,rash m ostly on flexor surfaces Palms and soles involved, ras h predominant on extensor s urfaces Superficial Deep -seated Vesicles are unilocular and gi vedewdroponrose petal appe arance Vesicles are multilocular and umbilicated Rash ispleomorphicand sym metrical Rash ismonomorphic Rapid evolution Slow evolution

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are true about chickenpox?
mcqs.explanation: Chickenpox is caused by the human herpes virus-3 (varicella-zoster virus). It remains latent in the sensory ganglion. Reactivation of the virus can cause shingles. The secondary attack rate of chickenpox is very high, 85% (range 61%–100%). The characteristic infective vesicle, surrounded by an erythematous halo, is described as a dewdrop on a rose petal. The scab of chickenpox is not infective. The vaccine given for chickenpox prophylaxis is live attenuated vaccine.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The varicella vaccine can be safely administered to which of the following individuals?

options.c: A HIV infected patient with CD4+ T cell levels > 15%
options.d: A patient on long term corticosteroid therapy

mcqs.explanation: Varicella vaccine can be considered for clinically stable HIV infected children or adults with CD4+ T cell level \03415%, including those receiving active antiretroviral therapy. Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in: • Pregnant women • Immunocompromised patients • Patients allergic to neomycin Following vaccination, salicylates should be avoided for 6 weeks to prevent Reye's syndrome.223

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child with a fever and rash was brought to your OPD. Oral findings as shown in the image were observed. During which period can this disease spread to others?

options.a: 4 days before and 2 days after the appearance of rash
options.b: 2 days before and 2 days after the appearance of rash
options.c: 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash
options.d: 2 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows koplik spots, which are a pathognomonic sign of measles. The period of communicability for measles is 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash. The patient is isolated for 7 days from the onset of rash.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about measles?

options.b: Otitis media is a common complication
options.d: Large number of carriers are present

mcqs.explanation: The most common complication of measles is otitis media, occurring in about 10–15 % of patients. Measles is caused by an RNA virus of the Paramyxovirus family. The incubation period of measles is 10 to 14 days. The only source of infection is a case o f measles. Carriers are not known to occur. The complications of measles include: • Otitis media (most common) • Measles-associated diarrhea • Pneumonia • Conjunctivitis • Febrile seizures • Subacute sclerosing pan encephalitis (rare but is fatal) - occurs several years after primary infection

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: During a measles epidemic in the community, an eight-and-a-half-month-old child was vaccinated for measles. What is the correct immunisation schedule to be followed for her, regarding measles?

options.a: The child should be given a second dose after 4 weeks.
options.b: The child should be given a second dose as soon as she reaches 9 months of age.
options.c: The child should directly be given the second dose of measles at 16 months.
options.d: The c hild should be given the second dose of measles at 12 months of age.

mcqs.explanation: In this child, the next dose of measles vaccine should be given after 4 weeks. While the scheduled age of receiving a measles vaccine is 9 months, it can be lowered up to 6 months during a m easles epidemic in the community. For infants immunized between 6 to 9 months of age, a second dose should be administered as soon as the child reaches the age of 9 months. It is to ensure adequate immunity has developed, provided that 4 weeks have elapsed since the last dose. In this child, the first dose was given at the age of 8 and a half months, and there must be a gap of 4 weeks between the two doses. If the child were to be vaccinated as soon as she turns 9 months old, only tw o w eeks would have been elapsed.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child was brought to you with complaints of fever, malaise and a rash. You diagnose the child with measles. What is the recommended period of isolation for this disease?

options.a: From onset of rash to 3 days after rash
options.b: 2 weeks before rash to 1 week after rash
options.c: From onset of rash to 5 days after rash
options.d: From catarrhal stage to 5 days after rash

mcqs.explanation: 224 The isolation period for measles is from the catarrhal (prodromal) stage to 5 days after the onset of the rash. The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 5 days after the appearance of the rash. Isolation of the patient for a week from the onset of rash adequately covers the period of communicability.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is correct about the criteria for elimination of measles?

options.a: There should be an absence of transmission of epidemic measles
options.b: The duration of absence of transmission should be \034 6 months
options.c: A well-performing surveillance system should be present
options.d: Absence of transmission should be seen in multiple geographical areas

mcqs.explanation: Measles elimination is operationally defined as the absence of endemic measles transmission in a defined geographical area (region or country) for \03412 m onths in the presence of a well-performing surveillance system.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about the Measles-Rubella campaign?

options.a: It is a mass vaccination campaign organised to introduce MR vaccine
options.b: Follow-up campaign is organised every 3-5 years
options.c: It covers children from 9 months to 15 years of age
options.d: Mop-up strategy is a part of the campaign

mcqs.explanation: Mop-up strategy is not a part of the Measles-Rubella campaign. Measles-Rubella vaccine introduction campaign: • A mass vaccination campaign to introduce an MR vaccine • Targets a wide age group of children: 9 months to < 15 years • All children in the target age group receive an additional dose of the vaccine • Regardless of previous vaccination status or history of illness. Measles-Rubella follow-up campaign: • A m ass vaccination campaign as a periodic event every 3–5 years guided by country-specific surveillance data • Target age group for immunization: all children aged > 9 months, who were born after the previous MR vaccination campaign

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to the WHO, what percentage of immunization coverage is needed for eradication of measles?
mcqs.explanation: According to the WHO, eradication of measles requires achieving an immunization coverage of at least 96% of children under 1 year of age.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about Rubella infection?

options.a: It is a type of droplet infection
options.c: Infection in early pregnancy causes a milder form of disease in the fetus
options.d: Fetus a ffected i n late pregnancy may have only deafness

mcqs.explanation: Earlier the rubella infection occurs in pregnancy, greater is the damage to the foetus. The m ajor determinant of the extent of fetal infection in congenital rubella syndrome is the gestational age at which fetal transmission occurs.225 Rubella infection in 1st trimester can cause: • Abortions • Still birth • Skin lesions - blueberry muffin rash • Congenital rubella syndrome

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to the WHO, which of the following tests cannot be used to confirm a case of swine flu?

options.c: 4-fold rise in virus specific neutralizing antibodies

mcqs.explanation: ELISA is not included in the criteria for confirming a case of H1N1. The ELISA is an easy to perform, highly specific, and fairly sensitive diagnostic tool for the 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) virus infections. However, it is not included in the WHO 's list of confirmation tests. According to WHO, 2009 pandemic (H1N1) virus infection i s confirmed by one or more of the following tests: • Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) • Viral culture • 4\037fold rise in H1N1 virus\037specific neutralizing antibodies

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the route of administration of avian influenza vaccine?
mcqs.explanation: The avian influenza H5N1 vaccine is administered intramuscularly. H5N1 avian influenza vaccine was approved in 2017 for the age group of 18 to 64 years of age who are at increased risk of exposure to the H5N1 influenza virus subtype contained in the vaccine. It is administered intramuscularly in the upper arm and g iven in 2 doses, days apart. Note: The live attenuated H1N1 influenza vaccine is given intranasally.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Vaccine that requires strain change due to evolving organism is?
mcqs.explanation: Influenza vaccine requires periodic strain change due to antigenic change in the surface glycoprotein of the virus. The change may be gradual (antigenic drift) or drastic (antigenic shift).

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Pandemic that occurred in 2009 was due to which influenza virus?
mcqs.explanation: 226 Recent influenza pandemic occurred in 2009 due to the emergence of a novel H1N1 influenza A virus. Past influenza pandemics: • 1968 pandemic due to H3N2 virus • 1957-58 pandemic due to H2N2 virus • 1918 pandemic due to H1N1 virus227

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important factor in reduction of diphtheria cases?
mcqs.explanation: Vaccination is the most important factor responsible for the reduction of diphtheria cases over the past decade.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about pertussis?

options.a: Most of the infections are subclinical
options.c: Secondary attack rate is 90 % in unimmunized individuals
options.d: Cerebellar ataxia is a common chronic complication

mcqs.explanation: The secondary attack rate in pertussis is about 90% in unimmunized individuals. The source of infection in pertussis is a case of pertussis. There is no evidence of subclinical infections. The patients are most infectious during the catarrhal stage. The chief complications of pertussis are: • Bronchopneumonia • Bronchitis • Bronchiectasis235

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Droplet precaution and isolation i s to be done for all of the following conditions except:
mcqs.explanation: Droplet precaution and isolation is not done for localized varicella zoster, as it is only transmitted through direct contact. Varicella-zoster localized in the patient with an intact immune system with a lesion that can be contained/covered do not require droplet precaution. Disseminated varicella in any patient requires airborne and contact precautions. Diphtheria, pertussis, and mycoplasma are transmitted by droplets and hence require droplet precaution a nd i solation. Although patients are not contagious starting 48 hours after antibiotic therapy, droplet precautions are typically maintained until the completion of the antibiotic course and are culture-negative on two cultures taken 24 hours apart. Droplet precautions include the use of masks, gowns, gloves and protective eye gear when providing direct patient care.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to IMNCI, which of the following is a key clinical sign for pneumonia classification?
mcqs.explanation: According to the IMNCI, three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with suspected pneumonia: • R espiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified under pneumonia if: • > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months • > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years of age • Lower chest wall indrawing indicates pneumonia • Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission. The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.236 Signs of severe pneumonia are : • Not able to drink • Persistent vomiting • Convulsions • Lethargic or unconscious • Stridor in a calm child • Severe malnutrition

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to IMNCI, a 6-month-old child is said to have pneumonia if the child has fast breathing with a respiratory rate more than:
mcqs.explanation: Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing: • Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified as pneumonia if: • > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months • > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years o f age • Lower chest wall indrawing indicates severe pneumonia • Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission. The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.Signs of severe pneumonia are : • Not able to drink • Persistent vomiting • Convulsions237 • Lethargic or unconscious • Stridor in a calm child • Severe malnutrition

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A one-and-half-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. On examination, respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?

options.b: Give IV antibiotics and refer t o higher centre
options.c: Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
options.d: No need of treatment only home remedies

mcqs.explanation: From the given clinical scenario, it can be easily inferred that the child has pneumonia. The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care advice. The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae has 23 serotypes. In which of the following patients is this vaccine most beneficial?

options.b: A patient with sickle cell disease
options.d: A patient with recurrent otitis media

mcqs.explanation: The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease. S. pneumoniae is an encapsulated organism that is detected by the spleen and is removed. However, in sickle cell disease, the sickled cells block the vessels in the spleen which results in splenic infarction. This hyposplenism results in an increased risk of pneumococcal infection. Hence, pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV -23) is given to these patients a s a prophylactic measure to reduce this risk.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following tests is used to determine the prevalence of TB infection?
mcqs.explanation: Mantoux or tuberculin testing is used to detect the prevalence of TB infection.238 Infection of tuberculosis does not always lead to disease. In latent infections, the Mantoux test can be positive without any clinical symptoms. Therefore, the prevalence of TB infection is detected by the Mantoux test. However, the prevalence of TB disease is confirmed by a sputum smear.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old patient has been given an intradermal injection of 0.1ml PPD (5 tuberculin units) over the forearm. After 72 hrs, the site is examined as shown in the image below. What is the interpretation of the result obtained?

options.a: Tuberculin test negative, suggesting immunity from TB
options.b: Tuberculin test positive, suggesting an active infection
options.c: Tuberculin test negative, suggesting a recent or past infection
options.d: Tuberculin test positive, suggesting a recent or past infection

mcqs.explanation: The above image shows an induration of >10 mm after 72 hrs of intradermal PPD injection suggesting a positive tuberculin test(TST), indicating recent or past infection. In TST, 0. 1 m l of PPD (purified protein derivative) containing 5 TU (tuberculosis unit) is injected intradermally and induration is read after 48-72 hours. An induration of 10 mm or more is considered positive in patients from countries with a high prevalence of tuberculosis. Surrounding erythema is not considered. A positive tuberculin test indicates hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein, denoting either latent infection with tubercle bacilli, or BCG immunization, or rece nt o r past infection with or without clinical disease. False positives may be seen in infections with related mycobacteria and false negatives in miliary tuberculosis, severely immunosuppressed states, etc.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate method to assess the incidence of tuberculosis in the community?

options.a: Identify all positives to tuberculin test
options.c: Identify new converter t o tuberculin test
options.d: Screen all under 5 years children with tuberculin test

mcqs.explanation: Identification of new converters to the tuberculin test is a marker of the incidence of tuberculosis. Identification of all positives to the tuberculin test is a marker of the prevalence of tuberculosis. Tuberculin conversion refers to the situation where an individual's t uberculin skin test (TST) results in changes from negative (0–4 mm diameter induration) to positive (equal to or >10 mm diameter induration) within a 24-month period. TST conversion is considered presumptive evidence of acquired latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and potential risk for progression to active tuberculosis disease.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Tuberculin testing is done at which anatomical site?
mcqs.explanation: Mantoux/ Tuberculin testing is carried out by injecting 1 TU of PPD in 0.1 ml intradermally on the flexor (ventral) surface o f the left forearm, midway between elbow and wrist. The result of the test is usually read after 48-96 hours, but reading it after 72 hours is ideal. The horizontal transverse diameter of induration is measured, based on which the following diagnosis can be inferred: • < 6 mm – Negative • 6–9 mm – Doubtful239 • \034 10 mm – Positive

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The approach shown in the image is a part of which of the following?
mcqs.explanation: Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build approach for eliminating TB in India is part of the National Strategic Plan for TB (2017-2025). The components of this approach are: • Detect - Early identification of presumptive TB cases, at the first point of care, be it private or public sectors, and prompt diagnosis using high sensitivity diagnostic tests. • Treat - Provide sustained, equitable access to high quality TB treatment, care and support services. • Prevent - P revent the emergence of TB in susceptible populations. • Build - Undertake critical management reforms, restructuring of HR and financial norms, pathways for private sector participation, in order to improve efficiency, effectiveness.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most rapid diagnostic test for pulmonary TB?
mcqs.explanation: The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by sputum microscopy, with results in 30 minutes. It has the least sensitivity and specificity. Smears are stained by Ziel Neelson acid-fast stain. CBNAAT gives results within 90 minutes. C artridge-based nucleic acid amplification test is a Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific automated, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification assay, having fully integrated and automated amplification and detection using real-time PCR. Quantiferon TB gold plus takes 24 hours to give the result. The radiometric BACTEC method takes approximately 2-3 weeks. Sputum culture takes approximately 2 to 8 weeks.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: BCG vaccine provides protection against which of the following?
mcqs.explanation: BCG vaccine provides protection against CNS and disseminated TB. It does not prevent primary infection. More importantly, it does not prevent reactivation of latent pulmonary infection, the principal source of bacillary spread in the community. The impact of BCG vaccination on transmission of mycobacterium tuberculosis is therefore limited.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the next step in management of a TB smear positive patient with no significant findings on a chest X ray?
mcqs.explanation: The next best step in a smear-positive patient with no findings on chest-xray is to perform a CB-NAAT. This patient is a microscopically confirmed case of tuberculosis (TB).240 According to the TB annual report, CBNAAT has been tried to be established in all centres. Ideally, drug sensitivity status via NAAT is to be done following a sputum smear before initiation of treatment. This helps in the early detection and treatment of drug-resistant TB. This has been integrated into the regular TB services to detect rifampicin resistance at the time of diagnosis. Depending on the sensitivity of the tubercle bacilli, appropriate ATT is started. If NAAT is n ot done and sputum is positive, patient is considered as Microbiologically positive with sensitivity status unknown.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are posted in a TB clinic. You need to start an intensive phase (HRZE 75/ 150/400/275) r egimen for a patient weighing 70 kgs. How many tablets of the FDCs are to be taken by him on a daily basis?
mcqs.explanation: An adult weighing 65-75kg needs to take 5 tablets of FDC (fixed-dose combinations) containing HRZE 75/150/400/275 in the intensive phase. The new WHO guidelines suggest the number of FDC tablets to be taken daily according to five weight band categories. Note: A TB patient kit contains the full course of treatment for a single patient and thus assures t he TB patient that his or her medications will be available throughout treatment. The kit provides health workers with a container that has all the required drugs in the necessary strengths and quantities. This helps limit confusion and wastage and makes it easier to monitor the regularity of treatment; avoiding stock-outs also helps to maintain patient confidence in the health system.Weight category Number of tablets (FDCs) Intensive phaseHRZE75 /150/ /275 Continuation phaseHRE75 /15 0/275 25-34 kg 2 35-49 kg 3 50-64 kg 4 65-75 kg 5 >75 kg 6

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to NTEP, how will you classify a TB patient who had taken antitubercular drugs for only 3 weeks in the past?
mcqs.explanation: Under NTEP, a new case is defined as a TB patient who had never taken ATT previously or taken ATT for <1 month.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the appropriate schedule for the treatment of multi-drug resistant tuberculosis?

options.a: 6 drugs for 4-6 months followed by 4 drugs for 12 months
options.b: 7 drugs for 4-6 months followed by 4 drugs for 5 months
options.c: 4 drugs for 4 months followed by 6 drugs for 10-12 months
options.d: 5 d rugs for 6 months followed by 4 drugs for 12 months

mcqs.explanation: The appropriate schedule for the treatment of multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is 7 drugs for 4-6 months followed by 4 drugs for 5 months.241 Note: Pearl 1720 has been updated according to NTEP 2021 guidelines.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs is not used in the management of a patient with MDR-TB under NTEP?
mcqs.explanation: PAS (para-aminosalicylic acid) is not included under the MDR-TB regimen.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding the duration for treatment of XDR TB?

options.a: Intensive phase is for 6 to 9 months
options.d: A combination of oral and injection drugs are used

mcqs.explanation: All oral longer MDR-TB regimen is used for the treatment of XDR-TB patients for a duration of 20 months.Regimen class Drugs All oral longer MDR TB regi men Bdq(6 months) Lfx Lzd Cfz C s for 18-20 months

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a criteria for the bedaquiline conditional access programme under RNTCP?

options.a: Patient below 5 years can be included
options.b: Post menopausal females can be included
options.c: Patients with stable controlled arrhythmia can be included

mcqs.explanation: Patients under 5 years are excluded from the bedaquiline conditional access programme. The criteria to be met under the bedaquiline conditional access programme are as follows: • Children aged 5 to <18 years of age and weighing at least 15 kg (in consultation with a paediatrician) • Females on non-hormone-based contraceptive or post-menopausal females can be included. • Patients with controlled stable cardiac arrhythmia can be considered after cardiac consultation. • P regnant women to be excluded

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding TB is false?

options.a: The Index TB guidelines are used for extra pulmonary TB.
options.b: X-pert MTB/RIF assay is an adjunct for diagnosis of lymph node TB.
options.c: Steroids may b e used in patients with pleural TB without HIV for 4 weeks.
options.d: Duration of ATT for TB meningitis is 9 months.

mcqs.explanation: Steroids may be used in HIV -negative patients with TB meningitis and pericarditis for 4 weeks, but not for pleural TB. The Index TB guidelines for extrapulmonary TB are as follows: • Duration of ATT in TB meningitis is for 9 months and lymph node and abdominal TB is 6 months. • X-pert MTB/RIF assay may be used as an adjunct in the diagnosis of lymph node TB and TB meningitis. • Steroids may be used in HIV -negative patients with TB meningitis and pericarditis f or 4 weeks.242

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Where is the National Tuberculosis Institute located?
mcqs.explanation: National Tuberculosis Institute is located in Bangalore. Important national centers for tuberculosis in India: • Tuberculosis Research Center: Chennai • National Tuberculosis Institute: Bangalore • National Institute of Tuberculosis and Respiratory Diseases: Delhi • JALMA Institute for Leprosy and Other Mycobacterial Diseases: Agra.243

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation for polio?

options.a: Polio immunization drives for infants to reduce the occurence.
options.b: Arranging for schooling for a child suffering from residual polio paralysis.
options.c: Resting the limbs affected by polio in neutral position.
options.d: Providing calipers for walking to patients affected by polio.

mcqs.explanation: Resting the limbs affected by polio in a neutral position is an example of disability limitation. It is an intervention done to either halt or prevent the transition of the disease process from impairment to handicap. Rehabilitation has been defined as the use of medical, social, educational, and vocational measures for training the individual to the highest possible level of functional ability. Like providing calipers for walking to patients and arranging schoolin g a fter being affected by polio. Immunization drives are examples of specific protection.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A person is involved in unsafe sexual practices. Which of the following viruses is least likely to get transmitted via this route?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatitis E has feco-oral or waterborne transmission. It does not transmit sexually. Transmission of Hepatitis A, C, and D can occur sexually. Transmission of the hepatitis A virus can occur from any sexual activity with an infected person and is not limited to fecal-oral contact. People who are sexually active are considered at risk for hepatitis A if they are MSM, live with or are h aving s ex with an infected person, or inject drugs.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: For how long is Hepatitis A excreted in the feces?

options.a: One week before the symptoms appear
options.b: Two weeks after the symptoms appear
options.c: Two weeks before the symptoms and two weeks thereafter
options.d: One week before the symptoms and one week thereafter

mcqs.explanation: HAV is excreted in the feces for about 2 weeks before the onset of jaundice and for up to 2 weeks thereafter. The risk of transmitting is greatest at 2 weeks before to 1 week after the onset of jaundice.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: An intern sustains a needlestick injury while drawing blood from a Hepatitis B positive patient. Assuming he has been infected, which among the following will be the first to rise?
mcqs.explanation: 253 HbsAg is the first serological marker to be detected in Hepatitis B infection.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old pregnant woman is rushed to the hospital with labor pains at 34 weeks of gestation. She did not attend any prior antenatal visits. On further evaluation, she is found to be positive for HbsAg. Which of the following should be administered to the newborn after delivery?

options.d: Immunoglobulin, followed by vaccine 1 month later

mcqs.explanation: The simultaneous administration of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and hepatitis B vaccine is more efficacious than HBIG alone for the prevention of the carrier state in newborn babies of HBV-positive mothers. HBIG does not interfere with the antibody response to the hepatitis B vaccine. This combined procedure is ideal both for postexposure prophylaxis of persons accidentally expose d t o blood known to contain hepatitis B virus and for the prevention of the carrier state in the newborn babies of carrier mothers. HBIG (0.05–0.07 mL /kg) IM • As early as possible, preferably within 24 hours of exposure Hepatitis B vaccine (20 mcg/1.0 mL ), IM • 1st dose: within 7 days of exposure • 2nd and 3rd dose: at one and six months, respectively

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: HCV screening is done for which of the following p eople?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with a history of IV drug abuse, HIV , and a history of blood transfusion 32 years ago are screened for HCV. Since the screening o f blood for Hepatitis C was started after 1992, hence people who have received a blood transfusion before 1992 (in this MCQ, the year is 1992 in point 3) have to be screened. HCV screening is done for people who may be at risk for infection. These include: • People who received blood, blood products, or organs before screening for hepatitis C virus was implemented • Current or former injecting drug users • People on long-term hemodialysis • Health-care workers • People living w ith HIV • People with abnormal liver tests or liver disease • Infants born to infected mothers.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Rotavirus?

options.a: Severe rotavirus infections are limited to children aged 5-7 years.
options.b: Rotavirus is shed in high concentrations for several days in the stools and vomit of infected children.
options.c: Rotavirus diarrhoea increases in frequency during drier, cooler months.
options.d: Clean water supplies and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on viral transmission.

mcqs.explanation: 254 Severe rotavirus gastroenteritis is largely limited to children aged 6-24 months, not 5-7 years. Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhea in children aged <5 years globally. In developing countries, 75% of the children acquire their first rotavirus infection in the first 12 months. The universal occurrence of rotavirus infections shows that clean water supply and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on virus transmission. In t ropical areas, rotavirus diarrhea occurs throughout the year, increasing in frequency in drier, cooler climates. Transmission is through the feco-oral route, person-to-person contact, or indirectly through fomites. Infected individuals shed very high concentrations of the virus for many days in their stool and vomit.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A mother brought a 2 month old child with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting. As a part of management, you advise her regarding vaccination for rotavirus. Which is the false statement regarding the same?

options.a: Rotarix is administered in 2 oral doses.
options.b: It cannot be given in an immunocompromised child.
options.c: The first dose of Rotarix is contraindicated for infants <12 weeks.
options.d: It is not a part of catchup vaccination programmes due to its risk of intussusception.

mcqs.explanation: The first dose of the Rotarix vaccine is contraindicated for infants > 12 weeks of age due to the potential risk of intussusception. Hence, it is n ot a part of catch-up immunization programs as the age is difficult to ascertain in such programs. Rotavirus vaccines are live, attenuated, and are administered orally. So, it is not given to an immunocompromised child. Given below are the different Rotavirus vaccines available along with their schedule:Vacci nes Number of do ses Interval between dose s Maximum age li mit Rotari x 6 weeks10 weeks 12 weeks24 wee ks RotaT eq 8, 16, 24 weeks 32 weeks Rotav ac 6, , 14 weeks 32 weeks Rotas il 6, , 14 weeks 1 year

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following s tatements is false for carriers of cholera?

options.a: A convalescent carrier may continue to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks.
options.c: The gall bladder is infected in chronic carriers.
options.d: The antibody titres of a contact carrier is normal while the stool culture is positive.

mcqs.explanation: The antibody titers of all carriers are risen and positive till the person harbors the organism. A cholera carrier is defined as an apparently healthy person excreting V.cholerae O1 in stools. Selective media and enrichment is needed for their diagnosis. In cholera, 4 types of carriers are described. • Incubatory/Pre-Clinical carriers: The duration of carrier state is 1-5 days (incubation period). They present with symptoms later.255 • Convalescent carriers: Recovered from an attack of cholera, continues to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks, due to ineffective antibiotic treatment. • Contact/Health carrier: Due to subclinical infection contracted through a case or an infected environment, may excrete for 10 days. • Chronic carriers: Gallbladder is infected, duration may be as long as 10 years.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for how many days after recovery?
mcqs.explanation: A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for 14-21 days after recovery. This type of carrier c ontinues to excrete vibrios after being recovered from an attack of cholera. It is seen due to ineffective antibiotic treatment. These carriers can often become chronic or long-term carriers.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child is brought to the PHC with a cute diarrhea. The doctor based on the history suspects that the child may be suffering from an infection due to shigella over cholera. Which of the following points on the history, apart from bloody stools, favors the doctor's suspicion?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options, the presence of fever favors the suspicion towards Shigella as the infectious agent. The absence of rectal pain and the presence of vomiting favors cholera while abdominal cramps are present in both of these conditions. Symptomatic differential diagnosis o f shigella and cholera:Symptoms Cholera Shigella Diarrhea Acute watery Acute bloody Fever No Yes Abdominal cra mps Yes Yes Vomiting Yes No Rectal pain No Yes Stool >3 loose stools per day, water y like rice water > 3 stools /day, with blood or pus .

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following guidelines will you follow to treat a child diagnosed with cholera?

options.b: A cardiotonic should be added if shock persists even after treating with iv fluids.
options.c: If the diarrhoea persists after 48 hours of treatment, suspect resistance.
options.d: Antidiarrheals and antiemetics should be started.

mcqs.explanation: In patients with cholera, if diarrhea persists after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, resistance to the antibiotic should be suspected. Treatment for cholera: • Rehydration therapy - is started immediately, either oral or intravenous.256 • Antibiotic therapy - As soon as vomiting has stopped (usually after 3-4 hours of rehydration). Fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used. • Shock in diarrhea must be corrected by intravenous fluids only. Antidiarrhoeals, cardiotonics, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and corticosteroids are not used.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 36-year-old man is diagnosed with cholera. Which of the following drug would you prescribe to his family member s t o prevent the spread of the disease?
mcqs.explanation: Tetracycline is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of cholera. It should be given for: • A dults - a 3-day period in a twice-daily dose of 500mg • Children (4-13 years) - 125mg • Children (0-3 years) - 50mg Alternatively, the long-acting tetracycline (doxycycline) may be used for chemoprophylaxis, if the prevailing strains are not resistant. A single oral dose of doxycycline (300 mg for adults and 6 mg/kg for children under 15 years) has proved to be effective. Chemoprophylaxis is advised only for household contacts or a closed community in which cholera has occurred.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera?
mcqs.explanation: The most important effective measure against cholera is health education. The prophylactic measures against cholera include: • Health education • Food hygiene practices • Hand washing practices after defecation • Drinking safe water • Knowledge about ORS

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: You are a medical officer posted in a village 'X'. The village has been affected by the epidemic of cholera. What is the first step that should be taken to decrease the incidence of the disease?

options.b: Cholera vaccination to all uninfected individuals
options.d: Treat everyone in the village with tetracycline

mcqs.explanation: Safe water supply and sanitation is the first step to be taken to decrease the incidence of cholera. Steps taken to decrease the incidence of cholera include: • Safe water supply • Excreta disposal257 • Food sanitation • Disinfection • Early case detection Cholera Vaccines: available in oral forms • Dukoral • Sanchol and mORCVAX • Euvichol • Vaxchora • CVD103-HgR - no longer produced Sanchol and Euvichol are available for mass vaccination campaigns. The campaigns have been implemented in areas experiencing an outbreak, in areas at heightened vulnerability during humanitarian crises, and among populations living in highly endemic areas, known as hotspots. Vaxcho ra i s given for adults (18 – 64 years) who are traveling to an area of active cholera transmission, at least 10 days before the trip. Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for the control of cholera. This is because the drug's effect is only short-lived (a few days). Moreover, for preventing 1 case of cholera, around 10,000 individuals must be given the drug. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for only household contacts of confirmed cases with tetracycline.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: In the ward, a patient with cholera soils the bed with stools. Which chemical should be used to disinfect the bed?
mcqs.explanation: The most effective disinfectant for cholera stool is a coal tar disinfectant with Riedel-Walker (RW) coefficient of >10 such as cresol. Bleaching powder, if used, should be of good quality. For disinfection, attention should be paid to the following: patient's stools and vomit; clothes and other contaminated personal items; the latrine, the patient's house, and neighborhood.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Cholera is a notifiable disease locally and nationally. Which of the following statements is true regarding the international health regulations for the notification of Cholera?

options.a: Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 72 hours of its occurence.
options.b: The number of cases and deaths a re to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
options.c: An area is declared free of cholera when 1 month has elapsed since the last case.
options.d: Mass chemoprophylaxis must be initiated immediately.

mcqs.explanation: The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared f ree of cholera. International health regulations for the notification of Cholera: • Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence. • The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera. • When twice the incubation period (5 days) i.e. 10 days has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case, an area is declared free of cholera.258 • Mass prophylaxis is not advised in cholera, as it fails to stop the spread of the disease. Chemoprophylaxis is only advised for household contacts or a closed community.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy has had 15 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomited twice in the last 4 hours. The child is restless and has sunken eyes. On examination, he is irritable but is drinking fluids. What is the optimal therapy for the child?

options.c: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids

mcqs.explanation: Oral rehydration therapy is the optimal therapy to treat acute diarrheas in some dehydration patients. Recommended formulation: Reduced osmolarity ORS solution, which has a reduced concentration of sodium (75 mmol/liter) and glucose (75 mmol/liter). It helps in reducing the adverse effect of hype rtonicity o n net fluid absorption. According to IMNCI guidelines, irritable child who is able to drink fluids come under some dehydration category.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A mother brings her child with complaints of acute diarrhea. After an initial assessment, you diagnose that the child has some dehydration. You counsel the mother to give ORS. After how many hours shall she be advised to discard the old solution and prepare a new one?
mcqs.explanation: The freshly prepared ORS should not be used after 24 hours. Guidelines for administering ORS: • After each loose stool, give: • Children <2 years of age - 50-100 ml (a quarter to half a large cup) of fluid • Children 2 to 10 years - 100-200 ml (a half to one large cup) • Older children and adults - as much fluid as they want • For children <2 years, give a teaspoon every 1 to 2 minutes and offer frequent sips out of a cup for older children. Try to give the estimated required amount wi thin a 4 - hour period. • If the child vomits, wait for 10 minutes, then give a spoonful every 2 to 3 minutes.259 • If the child wants to drink more ORS solution than the estimated amount and does not vomit, there is no harm in feeding him/her more. • If the child is breastfeeding, continue breastfeeding with ORS solution.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A baby is brought with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting. The weight of the baby is 12 kgs. What is the estimated amount of fluid to be replaced in 4 hours?
mcqs.explanation: According to the guidelines of ORS by WHO, a child with a weight of 11-15.9 kg has to be treated with 800-1200 ml of ORS solution within the first 4 hours. Guidelines for oral rehydration therapy (for all ages) during the first four hours by WHO: The patient's age should be used i f weight is not known. The approximate amount of ORS required in ml may also be calculated by 75 x body weight (kg).Age Under 4 mo nths 4-11 mon ths 1-2 y rs 2-4yrs 5-14 yr s 15 yrs or ove r Weight (kg) under 5 5-7.9 8-10. 11 -15. 16-29 .9 30 or over ORS solution ( ml) -400 400 -600 600 - 800-1 1200 -2 2200 -4000

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 9-month-old baby with diarrhea is feeding well and is thirsty. Skin pinch when done returns in 2 seconds. What is the treatment?

options.a: 200-400 ml of ORS to be given in the first four hours.
options.b: 400-700 ml of ORS to be given in the first four hours.
options.c: 700-900 m l of ORS to be given in the first 4 hours.
options.d: In addition to the usual fluid intake, 100-200 ml should be given after each loose stool.

mcqs.explanation: According to the IMNCI classification, the baby has some dehydration and comes under Plan B. The amount of ORS given is 75ml/kg body weight. Here, the weight of the child is not specified. Hence, 400-700 ml of ORS at home is to be given in the first four hours according to the age of the child. The below table shows the amount of ORS to be given according to the age of the child. In addition to this, 50-100 ml extra fluid is given after each loose stool. After four hours, the baby is reas sessed a nd the appropriate plan is selected again for the continuation of the treatment. The four rules of home treatment are: • Give extra fluid • Give zinc supplements (1 tablet per day for 14 days, dissolved in a small amount of ORS or breast milk or clean water) • Continue breastfeeding • Counsel the mother to return if there is blood in stools and if the child is feeding poorlyAge under 4 mon ths 4-11 mon ths 1-2 yea rs 2-4 yea rs 5-14 yea rs 15 years and ov er Weight(kg) under 5 5-7.9 8-10.9 11 -15.9 16-29 .9 30 or over260 Age under 4 mon ths 4-11 mon ths 1-2 yea rs 2-4 yea rs 5-14 yea rs 15 years and ov er ORS solution ( ml) -400 400 -600 600 -8 800-12 1200 -22 2200 -4000

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which among the following home remedies are not advised for a child with diarrhea?

options.a: A mixture of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar in 1 L of drinking water
options.b: Unsalted water in which a cereal has been cooked
options.d: Soup with 3g/litre salt added to it

mcqs.explanation: Salted water in which cereal has been cooked can be given to a child with diarrhoea. If the WHO ORS mixture is not available, a simple mixture of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar must be dissolved in 1 L of drinking water and given to the child. Fluids that do not contain salt in water, for eg: rice water, unsalted soup, yoghurt drinks, green coconut water, etc, must not be given. 3g/litre of salt must be added to such drinks before giving it to the child with diarrhoea. The infant's u sual diet of cereals, vegetables and other foods should be continued and never be diluted. The child should be given as much nutrient-rich food as acceptable. Avoid the following: • Sweetened drinks with sugar, like commercial fruit juices and sweetened tea, as they lead to osmotic diarrhoea and hypernatremia. • Fluids with a stimulant and purgative effect like coffee and medicinal tea infusions.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A child with severe dehydration is being treated with intravenous fluids for the past 2 hours. Which of the following will be used as an early indicator for adequate rehydration?
mcqs.explanation: Skin elasticity and pulse strength are the most helpful indicators for adequate intravenous rehydration .261 The urine output may be unchanged even after 3-4 hours of adequate rehydration. Hence, it cannot be a criterion for continuous examination. The initial rehydration must be fast until an easily palpable pulse is present. Reassess the patient every 1-2 hours. After 1-2 liters of fluid have been infused, the drip should be slowed down till the blood pressure and pulse return to normal. Rehydration must be continued otherwise till all signs of dehydration have disappeared. O RS s hould be given when the patient can drink oral fluids. Puffy eyelids are a sign of excess rehydration and intravenous fluids must be stopped when it occurs.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy is referred from a sub-center due to a feeble pulse and low BP. The patient has had diarrhea for 2 days. He has sunken eyes and is lethargic. On examination, BP is 90/60 mmHg. Which of the following fluids cann ot be used for resuscitation in this patient?
mcqs.explanation: This patient has severe dehydration which is treated by giving IV fluids. Plain glucose and dextrose solutions should not be used as they worsen the hyperosmolar state. Intravenous rehydration: Used for initial rehydration for patients in shock or those who are unable to drink. • Ringer's lactate solution/Hartmann's s olution - Used for injection. Best commercially available solution. • Diarrhea treatment solution- Recommended as an ideal polyelectrolyte solution for intravenous infusion. • Normal saline- Used if nothing else is available. It is the poorest fluid, as it does not correct the acidosis and will not replace the potassium losses.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the recommended dosage for zinc supplements in children with diarrhea?

options.a: 20 mg of zinc daily for infants < 12 months of age for 10-14 days
options.b: 20 mg of zinc for children > 6 months of age for 7 days
options.c: 10 mg of zinc for children > 12 months of age for 20 days
options.d: 10 mg of zinc for children < 6 months of age for 10-14 days

mcqs.explanation: According to WHO and UNICEF, 10 mg of zinc is given to infants < 6 months of age for 10-14 days. 20 mg of Zinc is given to infants > 6 months o f age for 10-14 days during an episode of acute diarrhoea . This is done to reduce the duration and severity of the episode and prevent recurrence in the following months. Intensified Diarrhea Control Fortnight : The goal is to attain zero child deaths due to childhood diarrhea.
