mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about mental health?

options.a: Mental disorders are universal, not specific to any group
options.b: Mental health is the mere absence of mental illness
options.c: Heredity can contribute to mental illnesses
options.d: Substance abuse is a type of mental illness

mcqs.explanation: Mental health is a state of well-being in which an individual realizes his or her own abilities and not merely the absence of mental illness. It is the ability to cope with stress, be productive, and contribute to the community. Mental disorders are universal and are not specific to any particular group. They are associated with hereditary (family history of psychiatric disorders) and environmental factors. Substance abuse and alcohol addiction are considered types o f m ental illness.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following are sociopathological factors associated with mental health?
mcqs.explanation: Economic insecurity, anxiety, and frustration are the sociopathological factors associated with mental health. The factors leading to mental health illnesses include: • Organic - cerebral arteriosclerosis, neoplasms, endocrine, metabolic and chronic diseases • Hereditary - schizophrenia • Socio-pathological factors - worries, anxiety, frustration, emotional stress, tension, unhappy marriages, broken homes, poverty, industrialization, u rbanization, changing family structure,900 population mobility, economic insecurity, cruelty, rejection, neglect. • Environmental - environmental toxins, substance abuse, radiation, nutritional factors, mineral deficiencies, infectious diseases during prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal periods (like rubella), road traffic accidents.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The incidence of mental illness is higher in individuals who are exposed to causal f actors during which period of life?
mcqs.explanation: Exposure to causal factors during the initial 5 years of life leads to an increased incidence of mental illness. This period is critical for lifelong mental health behavior a nd learning, even more crucial than adolescence. During early childhood, the growth and development of children are most vulnerable to external environmental stressors. A continuous, intimate, and warm relationship with the child's parents during infancy and childhood is very important.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: All of the following can be used for the secondary prevention of mental illness in patients except:
mcqs.explanation: Improving the social environment is a method of primary prevention of mental illness, not secondary prevention. The levels of prevention of mental illness and measures are g iven below: • Primary prevention - improving the social environment and the promotion of mental health awareness • Secondary prevention - early diagnosis and family-based health services like casework and family counseling • Tertiary prevention - measures to reduce the duration of mental illness as well family and community stresses to prevent further breakdown and disruption

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are considered to have a major mental illness?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with manic depressive psychosis are considered to have a major mental illness. Mental health disorders are classified as: • Major (psychotic or not in touch with reality) - include schizophrenia, manic depressive psychosis, and paranoia • Minor (non-psychotic, remain in touch with reality) - include neuroses (like OCD), personality and character disorders Dementia occurs secondary to organic causes.901

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a service offered to patients with mental health disorders?
mcqs.explanation: Employment services are not included under mental health services. Mental health services include: • Early diagnosis and treatment • Group and individual psychotherapy • Mental health education • Use of modern psychoactive drugs • Rehabilitation • After-care services - help drug-dependent persons to adapt to regular life following treatment and rehabilitation

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old man is brought to the casualty with a suspected drug overdose. H is sister tells you that he has recently started taking a 'superman drug' after hearing about it from his friends. What drug is she referring to?
mcqs.explanation: Amphetamines are also known as the superman drug. This is because their effects include increased self-confidence a nd endurance. However, its usage leads to tolerance and dependence.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is currently the most widely used illicit substance in the world?
mcqs.explanation: Cannabis is the most widely used illicit substance in the world. Cannabis is obtained from Cannabis sativa, C. indica, and C. americana. It is colloquially called marijuana. Other forms of this drug are charas or hashish and bhang. The image given below shows the cannabis plant.902

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the most widely used legal addictive substance in India?
mcqs.explanation: Tobacco is the most widely used legal addictive substance in India, followed closely by alcohol as the second most widely consumed substance.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an objective of the National Mental Health Programme of 1982?

options.a: Ensure equal human rights to mentally ill
options.b: Promote community participation in mental health services
options.c: Promote application of mental health knowledge
options.d: Provide accessibility of mental health care

mcqs.explanation: Ensuring equal rights to mentally ill people is not an objective of the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP). It was launched in 1982 with the following objectives: • Ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental health care • Encourage the application of mental health knowledge in general care • Promote community p articipation in mental health services development The National Mental Health Programme was relaunched as The Mental Health Care Act, which includes provisions for equal rights for those with mental illness.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component o f the District Mental Health Programme?
mcqs.explanation: Screening is not a component of the District Mental Health Programme. It includes the following components: • Training of all mental health workers at the nodal institute in the state • Increasing public awareness by education to reduce stigma • Early detection a nd treatment • Providing data for future planning, improvement in service and research Activities by the DMHP for positive mental health include: • School mental health services • College counseling services • Workplace stress management • Suicide prevention services

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not included in the Mental Healthcare Act of 2017?

options.a: Advance directive rights of the mentally ill
options.d: Procedure for admission, treatment and discharge of the mentally ill

mcqs.explanation: Establishing mobile mental health camps for the benefit of mentally ill patients is not included under the Mental Healthcare Act of 2017.903 This act encourages the mobilization of resources to improve mental health care across the country as well as reduce stigma and improve social inclusion/support for those with mental illness. It also has provisions to improve outcomes and protect their rights. The provisions of this act include: • Rights of persons with mental illness to access health care, live without discrimination and enjoy confidentiality. • Advance directives to allow mentally ill people to make d ecisions about their treatment • Procedures for admission, treatment (behavioral and interpersonal therapy, medications), and discharge • Decriminalizing suicide and prohibiting electroconvulsive therapy unless anesthesia is used The act also has clear instructions for the central and state mental health authorities and other mental health establishments on their endeavors.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: According to the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme, which of the following is not included in the Mental Health Care Act, 2017?
mcqs.explanation: According to the WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP), screening of family members is not included in the Mental Health Care Act, 2017. The Mental Healthcare Act of 2017 has provisions that include: • Rights of persons with mental illness to access health care, live without discrimination and enjoy confidentiality. • Advance directives to allow mentally ill people to make decisions about their treatment • Procedures for admission, treatment (behavioral and interpersonal therapy, medications), and discharge • Decriminalizing suicide and p rohibiting electroconvulsive therapy unless anesthesia is used These are achieved through the mobilization of resources to required areas, and by providing social support.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The National Suicide Prevention Strategy aims to reduce suicide mortality by _______ in the country by 2030.
mcqs.explanation: The National Suicide Prevention Strategy (NSPS) aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% in India by 2030. It is a multisectoral approach that will involve national and international government ministries, families, communities, and educational institutes to help prevent suicide. India has a h igh burden of suicide. It is the leading cause of death among individuals between 15-29 years of age. Epidemiology • Young and middle-aged adults between 18-45 years • Males more than females904 • Daily wage earners and people who earn <1,00,000 per annum • Individuals with family issues and illnesses Hanging and poisoning were the most common methods of suicide. It accounts for >3/4th of all suicides. Risk factors for suicide • Psychiatric illnesses- Depression, BPD, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders • Alcohol and other substance abuse disorders • Major physical illness • Job or financial loss • Relationship or social loss • Domestic violence or abu se • La ck of social support • The stigma associated with help-seeking behavior of mental disorders • Lack of social support and sense of isolation.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of the REDS path in the National suicide prevention strategy?

options.a: Reduce suicidal deaths by 2% in the next 5 years
options.b: Enhance health services to provide suicide prevention strategies
options.c: Develop community resilience, and societal support for suicide prevention

mcqs.explanation: The National Suicide Prevention Strategy (NSPS) is a multisectoral approach that will involve national and international government ministries, families and communities, and educational institutes. It aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% in India by 2030. It recommends REDS path for suicide prevention. • Reinforce leadership, p artnership, and institutional capacity in the country • Enhance the health services capacity to provide suicide prevention services • Develop community resilience, societal support for suicide prevention and reduce stigma against suicidal behaviours • Strengthen surveillance and evidence generation. Objectives • To establish effective surveillance mechanism for suicide prevention in next 3 years • To establish psychiatric OPDs that provide suicid e p revention services through District Mental Health Programme, within next 5 years • To integrate mental well-being curriculum in all educational institutes within next 8 years.905

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old male prisoner is being evaluated for aggressive tendencies and antisocial behavior. Which of the following genotypes is associated with these symptoms?
mcqs.explanation: XYY genotype is often associated with aggressive tendencies, antisocial, and often, criminal behavior. It is called Jacob's syndrome. Option A: XXY genotype is associated with Klinefelter's syndrome. Option B: XO genotype is associated with Turner's syndrome. Option C: Triple X syndrome is associated with genotype XXX. It is also called super female.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is the risk of developing Down's syndrome in a baby born to a 45-year-old woman?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of developing Down's syndrome in a baby born to a 45-year-old woman is 1 in 50. The risk of developing of Down 's s yndrome in a baby born to a 20-year-old woman is around 1 in and it increases with rising maternal age. It is an autosomal disorder caused by trisomy of chromosome 21.910

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not autosomal dominant?
mcqs.explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia or Louis-Bar syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. Autosomal dominant conditions include: • Neurofibromatosis • Marfan's syndrome • Retinoblastoma • Huntington's chorea • Polycystic kidney disease

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Which of the following i s incorrect regarding autosomal recessive disorders?

options.a: Both male and female offspring are affected
options.c: Most inborn errors of metabolism have this form of inheritance
options.d: It affects more people at a later age than in childhood

mcqs.explanation: Autosomal recessive disorders usually manifest in childhood or earlier. Heterozygotes are unaffected by the disease. When both parents are heterozygous, each offspring (both male and female) has a 1:4 chance of being affected. Examples o f autosomal recessive disorders include several inborn errors of metabolism like phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, and galactosemia.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy with recurrent hemarthrosis was found to have deficiency of factor VIII. He was adopted and his family history is unknown. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemophilia A. It is an X-linked recessive disorder. Hemophilia is of two types: • Hemophilia A - due to mutations in the F8 gene leading to factor VIII deficiency • Hemophilia B - due to mutations in the F9 gene leading to factor IX deficiency Affected children often present with prolong ed b leeding after procedures like circumcision or major bleeds like intracranial hemorrhages. When the child begins to walk, bleeding into the joint (hemarthrosis) may occur, causing painful swellings and reddening. Laboratory investigations show elevated aPTT, with normal PT and platelet count. It is treated by the administration of factor VIII or factor IX concentrates.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A pathologist is examining the peripheral smear of a patient with anemia. Which o f the following is incorrect about the epidemiology of this disease?

options.a: It is prevalent in areas with high frequency of malaria
options.b: It is an autosomal dominant disorder
options.c: Couples at risk can undergo prenatal testing and diagnosis
options.d: It manifests during the first year of life

mcqs.explanation: The given peripheral smear shows sickling of RBCs, suggestive of sickle cell anemia. It is an autosomal r ecessive disorder. The prevalence is high among Africans. This disorder usually has its onset during the first year of life. Couples at risk can opt for prenatal testing and diagnosis as well.911

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What was the primary goal of the Human Genome Project?

options.a: To introduce a gene sequence into a cell
options.b: To develop new diagnostic techniques for genetic disorders
options.c: To determine the sequence of nucleotide base pairs in human DNA
options.d: To study the precise genetic composition of specific populations

mcqs.explanation: The primary goal of the Human Genome Project was to determine the sequence of nucleotide base pairs that make up human DNA and to map all genes from the human genome (20,500 genes). The project was launched in 1990 and deemed complete in 2003.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is Hardy-Weinberg law related to?
mcqs.explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg law is related to population genetics. Population genetics is the study of the precise genetic composition of a population and various factors determining the incidence of inherited traits in them. Founder effect i s a violation to this law. It is due to difference in expression of the genes in founding population. This is responsible for the difference in the distribution of disease in population.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The Hardy-Weinberg law is applicable in populations w ith which of the following?
mcqs.explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg law is applicable for infinitely large, static populations with random mating.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: Match the following.
mcqs.explanation: Positive eugenics encourages the breeding of those with desirable phenotypes. Negative eugenics discourages the breeding of those with undesirable phenotypes. Euthenics is the environmental m anipulation to enable genes to express themselves. Euphenics is the science of making phenotypic improvements in humans after birth, generally to affect a problematic genetic condition.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A young woman with a family history of beta-thalassemia is planning to marry her first cousin. Which of the following will you recommend for this woman?
mcqs.explanation: This young woman must be advised to undergo prospective counseling. It refers to the process explaining to heterozygous individuals the risk of having affected children if they marry another heterozygous individual. It is performed prior to conception. Retrospective c ounseling is performed after the genetic disorder has already occurred in the first child .912

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old pregnant woman is planned for amniocentesis. What is the gestational age at which it can be done at the earliest?
mcqs.explanation: Amniocentesis can be done as early as 14 weeks of gestation. It refers to the examination of a sample of amniotic fluid to diagnose chromosomal disorders and some metabolic errors. It is indicated in the following cases: • Pregnant women aged 35 years or above • Family history of: • Chromosomal abnormalities • Metabolic errors • Chromosomal translocation • Sex-linked genetic disease

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: What is a Punnett square used for?
mcqs.explanation: A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict the probability of a particular genotype in an offspring . It is a standard tool for genetic counselors. The image given below shows a Punnett square.

mcqs.subject: PSM
mcqs.question: The risk of genetic diseases in consanguineous marriage between first cousins is?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of genetic diseases in consanguineous marriage between first cousins is 4-8%. The risk of genetic diseases in non-consanguineous marriage is 2-4%.913

Pathology.desc: General & systemic pathology, haematology, clinical pathology

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: How many base pairs the human genome is made of?
mcqs.explanation: The human genome is the complete set of nucleic acid sequences for humans and is made up of 3.2 billion base pairs. It is encoded as DNA within the 23 chromosomes (haploid ). In 2007, a multinational project called Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE ) concluded that about 80% of the human genome does not code for the proteins . However, they allow for the binding of proteins or are involved in the regulation of gene expression , in a cell type -specific fashion. They are known as functional non-protein-coding genes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes the non-coding regulatory RNAs?

options.a: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.b: Transcribed from protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated
options.c: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA and translated to regulatory proteins
options.d: Transcribed from non-protein-coding regions of DNA but never translated

mcqs.explanation: The non-coding regulatory RNAs are the functional non-protein-coding regions of the DNA, which are transcribed to RNA but are never translated into proteins . The two important types of non-coding regulatory RNAs are the micro RNA (miRNA ) and the long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). These RNAs play an important role in the regulation of gene expression .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alterations in DNA sequence?
mcqs.explanation: Epigenetics is the branch of molecular biology that deals with the study of heritable changes in gene function not involving changes in the DNA sequence . These heritable changes involve factors that mediate processes such as: • Histone organization • DNA methylation • Chromatin organization These in turn regulate the genomic organization and gene expression in a cell -type -specific fashion. The dysregulation of these epigenomic factors plays a major role in the development of malignancy. Green tea catechins have been reported to modulate epigenetic processes . They can reverse DNA methylation of tumor suppressor genes and increase the transcription of these genes .13

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Micro-RNA are involved during which of the following stages ?
mcqs.explanation: Micro-RNAs (miRNA ) act during the post -transcriptional stage . It is a type of non-coding RNA. The primary function of miRNA is to modulate the translation of target mRNAs into their corresponding proteins . After the target RNA is transcribed from its gene (post -transcriptional), the miRNA may either induce mRNA cleavage or repress its translation. This is referred to as gene silencing . Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) are short RNA sequences that can be introduced experimentally into cells . They have functions similar to endogenous miRNA (serve as substrates for the Dicer enzyme and interact with the RNA-induced silencing complex ). They may have a therapeutic role in silencing certain oncogenes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about microRNAs ?

options.b: They are involved in cell differentiation and carcinogenesis
options.c: Mature forms of microRNAs are single stranded
options.d: They can suppress tumor suppressor genes

mcqs.explanation: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small noncoding, single -stranded RNAs. They are approximately 22 nucleotides in length . MicroRNAs mediate inhibition of messenger RNA (mRNA ) translation through the action of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC ). They control normal cell growth , differentiation , and cell survival . miRNA can be of 2 types : • Tumour-suppressive miRNAs - decrease the translation of oncogenic mRNAs • Onco-miRNAs - suppress tumor-suppressor genes Other noncoding RNAs include : • piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) - involved in post -transcriptional gene silencing • snoRNAs - involved in maturation of rRNA , assembly of ribosomes and noncoding RNAs • lncRNAs - regulate the activity of chromatin 'writers', which modify histones and control gene expression

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of cell injury?
mcqs.explanation: Hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury. Causes of cell injury include : • Hypoxia • Physical agents • Chemical agents and drugs • Infectious agents • Immunologic reactions • Genetic abnormalities14 • Nutritional imbalances The mechanism of hypoxic cell injury is reduced oxidative respiration. The most common cause of hypoxia is ischemia. Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) is a transcription factor with protective effects against hypoxic injury such as: • Promotion of blood vessel formation • Stimulation of cell -survival pathways • Enhancement of anaerobic glycolysis The cells most sensitive to hypoxia are neurons. The most sensitive neurons include : • Pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus (especially , area CA1, also known as Sommer's sector ) • Cerebellar Purkinje cells • Pyramidal neurons in the cerebral cortex The cells most resistant to hypoxia are fibroblasts.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: Atrophy is a type of reversible cell injury
options.b: Plasma membrane blebbing occurs in reversible cell injury
options.c: On removal of stimulus , necrosis can be reversed
options.d: Chronic sublethal stimulus can cause cellular aging

mcqs.explanation: On removal of stimulus , necrosis cannot be reversed. It is an irreversible cell injury. Cellular adaptations are the reversible responses where the cells achieve an altered steady state in response to physiologic or some pathologic stimuli. They can be reversed if the stimulus causing stress or injury is removed. These cellular adaptations include : • Hypertrophy • Hyperplasia • Atrophy • Metaplasia Chronic sublethal stimuli are unable to cause cell death but may lead to certain changes in cells , such as: • Intracellular accumulations • Pathological calcifications • Cellular aging15

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a feature of reversible cell injury?

options.a: Large amorphous densities in the mitochondria
options.d: Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER

mcqs.explanation: Small amorphous densities are seen in the mitochondria in reversible cell injury. The following changes occur in reversible cell injury: • Cellular swelling - earliest change • ATP depletion leads to sodium-potassium pump failure • Na and water accumulate within the cell causing cellular swelling • Fatty change - • Seen in cells involved in or dependent on fat metabolism (liver hepatocytes and myocardial cells ) • Light microscopy - no noticeable changes • Ultrastructural findings - • Mitochondrial swelling and small amorphous densities • Plasma membrane blebs • Swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) • Detachment of ribosomes from granular ER • Nuclear changes like disaggregation of granular and fibrillar filaments Note : The formation of large amorphous densities in the mitochondria is a feature of irreversible injury.16

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most important light microscopic feature of irreversible cell injury?

options.b: Cell membrane blebs and loss of microvilli
options.d: Nuclear changes like pyknosis and karyolysis

mcqs.explanation: Nuclear changes like pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis are features of irreversible cell injury visible on light microscopy. The ultrastructural findings visible on electron microscopy include : • Large amorphous floccular densities in mitochondria • Cell membrane blebs and loss of microvilli • Ribosomal detachment from endoplasmic reticulum

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Thrombosis is initiated by:
mcqs.explanation: Thrombosis is initiated by endothelial injury. Thrombosis is is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel , obstructing the flow of blood through the circulatory system . Three primary abnormalities, often referred to as Virchow triad, are known to induce thrombosis. They include: • Endothelial injury - most important factor • Stasis or turbulent blood flow • Hypercoagulability of the blood

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about cellular adaptations is correct?

options.a: Hyperplasia involves synthesis of intracellular components
options.b: Atrophy is defined as decrease in cell size
options.c: Atrophy is the decrease in number and size of cells
options.d: Metaplasia is an irreversible replacement of a cell by another cell type

mcqs.explanation: 17 Atrophy is a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue due to a decrease in cell size and number. Cellular adaptations are reversible changes in the size, number, phenotype , metabolic activity, or functions of cells in response to changes in their environment. There are 4 types : • Hypertrophy - • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the size of cells • Involves synthesis and assembly of intracellular structural components • Hyperplasia - • Increase in organ size due to an increase in the number of cells • It is due to division and proliferation of stem cells • Atrophy - reduction in organ size due to a decrease in cell size and number. • Metaplasia - one differentiated cell type (epithelial or mesenchymal ) is replaced by another cell type

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with long-standing hypertension develops left ventricular hypertrophy . Which of the following transcription factors do not play a role in this?
mcqs.explanation: HNF is a transcription factor involved in the development of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY ), not the development of cardiac hypertrophy . The transcription factors involved in cardiac muscle hypertrophy are: • GATA4 – hypertrophic stimuli result in enhanced DNA-binding activity of GATA-4 • MEF2- increases due to pressure and volume overload • NFAT (Nuclear Factor for Activated T-cells )18

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: How does myosin change during muscle hypertrophy ?
mcqs.explanation: During muscle hypertrophy , the \037-isoform of the myosin heavy chain is replaced by the �o -isoform. It produces slower and more energetically economic contraction. During hypertrophy , there may occur a switch of contractile proteins from the adult isoforms to the fetal or infantile isoforms.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Both physiological hyperplasia and hypertrophy are simultaneously seen in which of the following individuals?

options.a: A 24-year-old man vigorously training for an athletic race
options.b: A 35-year-old woman regularly taking combined oral contraceptive pills
options.c: A 50-year-old man with proliferation of liver cells following transplantation
options.d: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation

mcqs.explanation: Physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia can be simultaneously seen in the uterus during pregnancy. In early pregnancy, uterine growth is due to hyperplasia of uterine smooth muscle cells ; however, the predominant growth of the uterus during pregnancy occurs after mid-gestation , by way of stretch \037induced myometrial hypertrophy . Simultaneous physiological hypertrophy and hyperplasia also occur in the female breast during puberty and pregnancy. Option A: Enlargement of skeletal muscles in athletes is an example of physiological hypertrophy . Option B: Combined oral contraceptive pills causing endometrial hyperplasia is an example of pathological hyperplasia . Option C: Following transplantation of a liver lobe , the remaining liver cells proliferate so that the organ grows back to its original size (compensatory hyperplasia ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following do not usually undergo hyperplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: Skeletal muscle and heart muscle usually undergo hypertrophy , not hyperplasia . Examples of physiologic hyperplasia : • Female breast during puberty and pregnancy (hormonal hyperplasia ) • Uterine smooth muscle during early pregnancy • Compensatory hyperplasia of liver cells after partial resection Examples of pathologic hyperplasia : • Endometrial hyperplasia • Benign prostatic hyperplasia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of physiological atrophy?

options.a: Atrophy of the legs of a bedridden patient
options.b: Atrophy of the arm muscles following a nerve injury
options.c: Muscle wasting in a child suffering from marasmus
options.d: Uterine atrophy after delivery by Cesarean-section

mcqs.explanation: Uterine atrophy following delivery is an example of physiological atrophy.19 Atrophy is defined as a reduction in the size of an organ or tissue due to a decrease in cell size and number. The following mechanisms are involved in atrophy: • Decreased protein synthesis due to decreased metabolic activity • Increased destruction of proteins by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway The various types of atrophy are:Stimulus /type of atrophy Example Physiologic atrophy Loss of hormonal stimulation Atrophy of the uterus after p arturitionAtrophy of the end ometrium, vaginal epitheliu m, and breast after menopau se During embryonic developme nt Certain structures , like notoc hord and thyroglossal duct Pathologic atrophy Disuse atrophy (decreased w orkload) Atrophy in a limb that has be en immobilized following a fr acture Denervation atrophy (loss of nerve supply ) Skeletal muscle atrophy follo wing nerve injury Ischemic atrophy Senile atrophy of the brain a nd heart due to atheroscleros is Inadequate nutrition Severe muscle wasting in ma rasmus Pressure atrophy Atrophy of surrounding unin volved tissues caused by an e nlarging benign tumor

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The cross-section of the brain of an 84-year-old man with dyslipidemia is given below , in comparison with a normal brain . Which of the following is the most likely pathological change?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows narrowing of gyri and widening of sulci in a senile brain , which is suggestive of senile atrophy. It is due to a gradual decrease in blood supply as a result of atherosclerosis , known as ischemic atrophy. The various types of pathological atrophy are:Pathologic atrophy Disuse atrophy (decreased w orkload) Atrophy in a limb that has be en immobilized following a fr acture20 Pathologic atrophy Denervation atrophy (loss of nerve supply ) Skeletal muscle atrophy follo wing nerve injury Ischemic atrophy Senile atrophy of the brain a nd heart due to atheroscleros is Inadequate nutrition Severe muscle wasting in ma rasmus Pressure atrophy Atrophy of surrounding unin volved tissues caused by an e nlarging benign tumor

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of metaplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common type of metaplasia is squamous metaplasia , in which the normal columnar cells are replaced by squamous epithelial cells . The table below shows various types of metaplasia : GERD: Gastroesophageal reflux diseaseTissue Metaplasia Cause Airways Squamous metaplasia : Norm al pseudostratified epitheliu m is replaced by the squamo us epithelium . Bladder stones Esophagus Columnar metaplasia :Normal squamous epithelium is repl aced by the glandular column ar epithelium (Barrett's esoph agus) Chronic GERD Cervix Squamous metaplasia : Norm al glandular epithelium may be replaced by the squamous epithelium Low pH of the cervix Muscle Connective tissue metaplasia : Formation of bone in the mu scle tissue ; (myositis ossifica ns) Following intramuscular hem orrhage21

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The lining epithelium of the respiratory tract of a middle -aged man who is a chronic smoker shows a change from columnar to stratified squamous epithelium , as depicted in the image below . The change is called :
mcqs.explanation: The change described in the question is called metaplasia . It is defined as a reversible change in which one type of differentiated cell is replaced by another type . The table below shows various types of metaplasia : GERD: Gastroesophageal reflux diseaseTissue Metaplasia Cause Airways Squamous metaplasia : Norm al pseudostratified epitheliu m is replaced by the squamo us epithelium . Chronic smoking,Deficiency of retinoic acid Urinary bladd er Squamous metaplasia : Norm al transitional epithelium is r eplaced by squamous epitheli um. Bladder stones Esophagus Columnar metaplasia : Norma l squamous epithelium is repl aced by the glandular column ar epithelium (Barret's esoph agus) Chronic GERD Cervix Squamous metaplasia : Norm al glandular epithelium may be replaced by the squamous epithelium . Low pH of the cervix Muscle Connective tissue metaplasia : Formation of bone in the mu scle tissue ; (myositis ossifica ns). After intramuscular hemorrh age22

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is an example of connective tissue metaplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: Myositis ossificans is an example of connective tissue metaplasia . It refers to the formation of cartilage , bone, or adipose tissue (mesenchymal tissues ) in tissues that normally do not contain these elements . Myositis ossificans is characterised by bone formation within muscle tissue following traumatic injury to the area. However, this type of metaplasia is less clearly seen as an adaptive response .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Deficiency in which of the following vitamins can lead to metaplastic transformation in the lung?
mcqs.explanation: The deficiency of vitamin A (retinoic acid) induces squamous metaplasia in the respiratory epithelium .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Anaplasia refers to:

options.b: Variation in cell size and shape
options.c: Replacement of one type of cell by other

mcqs.explanation: Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation . The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level. The extent to which neoplastic cells resemble normal cells , both morphologically and functionally , is called differentiation. Anaplasia is an important morphological feature of malignant transformation . The morphological features of malignancy include : • Anaplasia • Pleomorphism - variation in the size and shape of cells • Increased N: C ratio (nucleus : cytoplasmic ratio) - around 1:4 in normal cells , increases to 1:1 in malignant cells • Hyperchromasia - coarsely clumped and darkly stained chromatin within irregular nuclei • Increased mitosis - atypical , bizarre mitotic figures • Loss of polarity - sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion23

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is false regarding necrosis?

options.a: It is due to denaturation of protein
options.b: It is due to enzymatic digestion

mcqs.explanation: Necrosis is a passive process , not active. It is due to denaturation of protein and enzymatic digestion .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the correct sequence of events that occur during necrosis?
mcqs.explanation: 33 The sequence of events in necrosis is: cellular swelling \035 pyknosis \035 karyorrhexis \035 karyolysis Necrosis is defined as the spectrum of morphological changes that follow cell death due to the progressive degradative action of enzymes . Morphological changes that occur in necrosis are as follows : Cytoplasmic changes - • Increased eosinophilic staining on H&E specimens • Moth -eaten appearance of the cytoplasm - due vacuolated cytoplasmic organelles formed by enzymatic degradation • Glassy and homogenous cytoplasm - due to loss of glycogen in the cytoplasm Nuclear changes - • Pyknosis - nucleus first shrinks and becomes more condensed • Karyorrhexis - fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus • Karyolysis - nucleus fades away leaving behind only the cell membrane or empty cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 58-year-old man was admitted with sudden , substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm . On examination, he was diaphoretic and dyspneic with an irregular pulse . Despite resuscitative measures , he died within an hour of admission. Autopsy revealed the following gross appearance of the interventricular myocardium. Which of the following microscopic changes is most likely to be present ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and image showing dead tissue are suggestive of myocardial infarction. It is characterized by coagulative necrosis. In coagulative necrosis, despite cell death , the outline and architecture of the cells are preserved for a few days. This is because the cell injury is mainly due to the denaturation of all proteins , including the enzymatic proteins . This prevents the proteolysis of the dead cells . Ultimately, these necrotized cells are removed by phagocytosis and the lysosomal action of the enzymes of the leukocytes . Examples of coagulative necrosis: • Ischemic injury in all organs, except the brain • Dry gangrene

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of the following pathological change seen in the spleen ?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a pale , wedge -shaped area of infarction in the spleen . An infarct is a region of ischaemic necrosis resulting from the obstruction of blood flow , typically due to occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage. The most common cause of solid organ infarts is thromboembolism. The pattern of ischemic necrosis seen in solid organ infarction is coagulative necrosis. However, CNS infarctions are an exception . They cause liquefactive necrosis.34

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old woman died in the hospital 3 days after she was admitted with a sudden onset of right-sided weakness of her body, along with slurring of speech . An autopsy showed the following finding in the brain . What is this pathological change in this lesion?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a stroke, which results in ischemic injury to the brain . This results in liquefactive necrosis. Liquefactive necrosis refers to cell death by enzymatic degradation . The brain contains microglial cells , which contain many enzymes . When these cells are broken down, they release these enzymes , resulting in liquefactive necrosis. The various types of necrosis are as follows :Type Example Coagulative necrosis Infarcts in all organs except t he brain Caseous necrosis Tuberculosis Liquefactive necrosi s AbscessesBrain infarctWet ga ngrene Fat necrosis Pancreatitis, Breast Fibrinoid necrosis VasculitisAschoff bodiesMali gnant hypertension

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The gross specimen of the pancreas from a patient who died of acute pancreatitis is shown below . What is it suggestive of?
mcqs.explanation: The given specimen shows yellow nodules with areas of chalky-white deposits , which are suggestive of fat necrosis. Fat necrosis results from the release of activated pancreatic lipases into the substance of the pancreas and the peritoneal cavity. These enzymes act on surrounding tissue to release fatty acids, which then combine with calcium to produce grossly visible chalky-white areas (fat saponification). Histologic examination reveals foci of shadowy outlines of necrotic fat cells , with basophilic calcium deposits , surrounded by an inflammatory reaction. The various types of necrosis include :Type Example Coagulative necrosis Infarcts in all organs except t he brain Caseous necrosis Tuberculosis Liquefactive necrosi s AbscessesBrain infarctWet ga ngrene Fat necrosis Pancreatitis, Breast Fibrinoid necrosis VasculitisAschoff bodiesMali gnant hypertension35

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the type of necrosis seen in the vessel wall of a patient with polyarteritis nodosa?
mcqs.explanation: Immune reactions involving blood vessels , as seen in the case of polyarteritis nodosa, usually show fibrinoid necrosis. Fibrinoid means fibrin-like. In some immune disorders, the antigen-antibody complexes get deposited in the blood vessels . These complexes result in complement activation (type III hypersensitivity ) leading to cell injury. This leads to leakage of fibrin out of the blood vessel , giving a pinkish appearance around the blood vessels . Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in the following conditions: • SLE • Libman -sacks endocarditis • Arthus reaction • Serum sickness • Polyarteritis nodosa • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis • Malignant hypertension36

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is involved in recognition and clearance of necrotic cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Inflammasomes are involved in the recognition and clearance of necrotic cells . Inflammasomes are involved in pyroptosis , a process of programmed cell death distinct from apoptosis and necrosis. This process is dependent on caspases 1, 4, and 5 and is responsible for killing of infected cells . It occurs in the following sequence : • Activation of inflammasome complex by infected cells • This causes activation of caspase -1 • This results in generation of IL -1, which is responsible for fever, inflammation, leukocyte recruitment Option B: Toll-like receptors (TLR )- recognizes molecules shared by pathogens Option C: P-selectins - an important role in the initial recruitment of WBCs at the site of inflammation & in platelet recruitment and aggregation at the site of injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In cases of cell injury, all of the following are responsible for the increased eosinophilic staining and glassy homogenous cytoplasm except :
mcqs.explanation: In cell injury, there is a loss of glycogen, which leads to a change in cytoplasmic appearance . An increase in glycogen particles is not a feature of cell injury. In cell injury, the following changes are seen in the cytoplasm : • Increased eosinophilic staining due to - • Increase in denatured proteins (which bind to acidic dyes like eosin) • Loss of cytoplasmic RNA (nucleic acids bind to basic dyes like hematoxylin) • Glassy , homogeneous appearance - due to loss of glycogen particles37 • Moth -eaten appearance - vacuolated appearance due to enzymatic digestion of cytoplasmic organelles

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a true statement about apoptosis ?

options.a: There is enzymatic digestion of cellular contents
options.b: It is associated with adjacent inflammation

mcqs.explanation: The plasma membrane remains intact in apoptosis . Apoptosis literally means falling-off in Greek. It is a pathway of programmed cell death . Apoptotic cells break up into fragments called apoptotic bodies . These apoptotic bodies have intact plasma membrane but altered structures . Hence , they are subjected to phagocytosis without eliciting inflammation. Necrosis is an unprogrammed form of cell death that includes : • Enzymatic digestion • Adjacent inflammation • Karyolysis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an example of physiological apoptosis ?

options.a: Endometrial cell break-down during menstrual cycle
options.b: Apoptosis of M\374llerian structures in male fetuses
options.c: Elimination of neutrophils after an acute inflammatory response
options.d: Atrophy in parenchymal organs following duct obstruction

mcqs.explanation: Atrophy in parenchymal organs after duct obstruction is a pathological cause of apoptosis . Physiological causes of apoptosis : • During embryogenesis - M\374llerian inhibiting factor causing apoptosis of the Mullerian structures in the male fetus • Hormone-dependent apoptosis - • Endometrial cell breakdown during the menstrual cycle • Regression of the lactating breast after weaning. • Cell loss in proliferating cell populations - turnover of cells of intestinal crypt epithelium • Elimination of neutrophils after an acute inflammatory response and lymphocytes at the end of an immune response Pathological causes of apoptosis : • DNA damage beyond repair • Accumulation of misfolded proteins leads to endoplasmic reticulum stress • Cell injury in certain viral infections (e.g., Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis ) • Pathologic atrophy after duct obstruction in parenchymal organs like pancreas, parotid gland, and kidneys

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an anti-apoptotic protein?
mcqs.explanation: 38 BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic proteins . They get inserted into the mitochondrial membrane and result in the formation of channels. This allows proteins from the inner mitochondrial membrane to leak out into the cytoplasm . On the other hand, antiapoptotic proteins of the BCL2 family, like BCL -2 and BCL -XL limit the escape of proapoptotic mitochondrial proteins .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a stress sensor of apoptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Smac, also known as Diablo is not a stress sensor of apoptosis . It is a proapoptotic protein that initiates the caspase cascade by neutralizing IAPs (physiological inhibitors of apoptosis ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What are apoptotic bodies made up of?
mcqs.explanation: Apoptotic bodies are made up of cytoplasm with tightly packed organelles , and nuclear fragments. During apoptosis , extensive plasma membrane blebbing occurs, followed by cell fragmentation into apoptotic bodies by a process called budding . In apoptotic cells , phosphatidylserine , which is normally present on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane, flips to the outer leaflet . Hence , it gets recognized by tissue macrophages and leads to phagocytosis of the apoptotic bodies . Annexin V is a marker of apoptosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Caspase cleaves proteins at:
mcqs.explanation: Caspases are cysteine proteases that cleave proteins at the aspartic acid residue . Hence , the activation of caspases plays a key role in the process of apoptosis .39 The activation of caspases depends on a finely tuned balance between production of pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins . Two distinct pathways converge on caspase activation: • The mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway • The death receptor (extrinsic) pathway

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the function of FLIP protein in the pathway of apoptosis ?
mcqs.explanation: FLIP is a cellular protein that inhibits the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis . It is a caspase antagonist that inhibits the activation of caspases involved in the extrinsic or death receptor pathway . Some viruses produce homologs of this protein. This may play a role in keeping infected cells alive. There are two pathways that can lead to caspase activation and cause apoptosis of the cell . APAF-1 - Apoptotic peptidase activating factor-1 TNF - Tumor necrosis factorMitochondrialorintrinsicpath way Death receptororextrinsicpat hway Activation inside the cell Activation outside the cell Occurs in response to:DNA d amageRadiationInfection Involved in:Elimination of sel f-reactive lymphocytesKilling of target cells by cytotoxic T- cells Involves release of pro-apopt otic proteins (BAX, BAK)The y form aBAX-BAKchannel in the mitochondrial membrane Involves death receptors on c ell surfaces (have a death do main)These includeTNF -1and Fas(CD95) of the TNF family Leakage ofcytochrome -cresul ts in the formation of Cyt.c-A PAF1 complex , followed byap optosomeformation FasLon T-cells binds to Fas b ind adapter proteins via deat h domain Activation ofcaspase 9 Activation ofcaspases 8and10 Both pathways converge into a common pathway that invo lves the activation of caspase s 3, 6, 7 (executioner caspase s)40

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways are seen in:
mcqs.explanation: Intrinsic and extrinsic pathways are both seen in apoptosis . Apoptosis has two pathways : APAF-1 - Apoptosis activating factor-1 TNF - Tumor necrosis factorMitochondrialorintrinsicpath way Death receptororextrinsicpat hway Activation inside the cell Activation outside the cell Occurs in response to:DNA d amageRadiationInfection Involved in:Elimination of sel f-reactive lymphocytesKilling of target cells by cytotoxic T- cells Involves release of pro-apopt otic proteins (BAX, BAK)The y form aBAX-BAKchannel in the mitochondrial membrane Involves death receptors on c ell surfaces (have a death do main)These includeTNF -1and Fas(CD95) of the TNF family Leakage ofcytochrome -cresul ts in the formation of Cyt.c-A PAF1 complex , followed byap optosomeformation FasLon T-cells binds to Fas b ind adapter proteins via deat h domain Activation ofcaspase 9 Activation ofcaspases 8and10 Both pathways converge into a common pathway that invo lves the activation of caspase s 3, 6, 7 (executioner caspase s)41

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following pathological changes is represented by the marked structure seen on histopathology of a liver specimen ?
mcqs.explanation: The above histopathological image shows Councilman or acidophil bodies . They represent hepatocytes undergoing apoptosis . Councilman bodies are commonly seen in acute viral hepatitis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following features is not true about necroptosis ?

options.a: It is a form of programmed cell death

mcqs.explanation: Caspase activation does not occur in necroptosis . It is a caspase -independent form of programmed cell death .42 Necroptosis is a programmed form of necrosis (which is normally an unprogrammed process ). Though the activation of this pathway is similar to apoptosis , there is no activation of caspases , which is an important part of apoptosis . Necroptosis is triggered by the activation of TNFR1 by TNF-\037. This induces the recruitment of RIP1 and RIP3 kinase and the formation of a necrosome. The necrosome reduces cellular ATP levels . Necroptosis occurs in the following conditions: • Pathological - ischemic brain injury, neurodegenerative diseases , viral infections • Physiological - formation of the mammalian bone growth plate The following table lists the differences between apoptosis and necroptosis :Feature Apoptosis Necroptosis Induction stimuli Oxidative stress , death recept or ligands, chemotherapy Viral or chemical exposure , r adiation, endogenous or path ological factors Morphological chan ges Nuclear pyknosis, membrane blebbing , generation ofapopt oticbodies Swelling of cellsand organelle s, loss of membrane integrity Molecular changes Cleavage of caspases , DNA fr agmentation Acidosis, random DNA degra dation, release of cellular pro teins Clearance Apoptotic bodies phagocytos ed by neighboring cells and macrophages Necrotic cells ingested by ma crophages , significant inflam mation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true about pyroptosis except :

options.b: There is loss of membrane integrity
options.c: It is a form of programmed cell death

mcqs.explanation: Caspases 1, 4, and 5 are involved in pyroptosis , not caspase 8. Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death that is different from apoptosis and necrosis. It is involved in the clearance of necrotic and microbe-infected cells . It occurs in the following sequence : • Activation of the inflammasome complex • Activation of caspase -1 • Generation of IL -1 - results in fever, inflammation, leukocyte recruitment Pyroptosis differs from apoptosis by the following features : • There is cellular swelling • There is loss of cell membrane integrity • It is associated with inflammation • Caspases 1, 4, and 5 are involved43

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: During the autopsy of a 90-year-old woman, a normal -looking liver was noted . The following microscopic appearance of hepatocytes was noted . Which of the following cellular mechanisms is likely responsible for this finding?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows brownish lipofuscin granules within the liver cells . It is composed of lipid-containing residues of lysosomal digestion that are formed due to autophagocytosis . Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment that is due to free radical injury to the tissue . It is prominent in the liver and heart of aging patients or patients with severe malnutrition and cancer cachexia. Autophagy is a process by which the cell consumes itself . It involves the sequestration of cellular organelles into cytoplasmic autophagic vacuoles (autophagosomes ) that fuse with lysosomes , resulting in the digestion of the enclosed material. It occurs in the following conditions: • As a survival mechanism during nutrient deprivation and stress conditions • Cancers, inflammatory bowel diseases , neurodegenerative disorders - due to dysregulation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most reliable marker for cellular autophagy ?
mcqs.explanation: Microtubule -associated protein light chain 3 (LC3 ) is a reliable marker for cellular autophagy . There is increased synthesis of this molecule during autophagy . LC3 plays a role in elongation and closure of the autophagosomal membrane. Autophagy (self -eating ) is the process in which the starved cell eats its own components in an attempt to reduce nutrient demand to match the supply . Option A: Atg5 protein, although associated with autophagy , is not a reliable marker as there is no differential expression during autophagy initiation. Option B: RIP3 (receptor associated kinase 3) is a unique kinase involved in necroptosis . Option D: Annexin V is a marker for cellular apoptosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following forms of cell death is induced by lipid peroxidation?
mcqs.explanation: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent pathway of cell death that is induced by lipid peroxidation. It is triggered by an increase in membrane lipid peroxidation in response to the following signals: • Excessive intracellular levels of iron • Reactive oxygen species (ROS) This leads to a loss of selective permeability of the plasma membrane, which ultimately leads to cell death . Unlike necrosis, the process is regulated by specific signals and can, therefore , be prevented by reducing iron levels . Ferroptosis has been linked to cell death in a variety of human pathologies including: • Cancer44 • Neurodegenerative diseases • Stroke Other forms of cell death that are not dependent on lipid peroxidation include : • Necroptosis or programmed necrosis - programmed cell death without caspase activation • Pyroptosis - programmed cell death that is dependent on caspases 1, 4, and 5

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not involved in efferocytosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Efferocytosis is a specialized type of phagocytosis , where apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed with the help of macrophages , epithelial cells, and fibroblast cells . During this process , ligands bind to the apoptotic bodies and send 'eat me' signals. These signals are recognized by receptors present on phagocytes that bind and engulf these cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases is not caused by an abnormal folded protein?
mcqs.explanation: Pompe disease is a glycogen storage disorder caused by the deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha glucosidase enzyme. It is not due to abnormal folded proteins . During normal protein synthesis , chaperones in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) control the proper folding of newly synthesized proteins . Misfolded polypeptides are ubiquitinated and targeted for proteolysis . Sometimes , unfolded or misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER as a result of inherited mutations or environmental stress . This induces a protective response called the unfolded protein response that increases the production of chaperones . This reduces the levels of misfolded proteins in the cell . However, when the accumulation of misfolded proteins overwhelms these adaptations , it results in ER stress which leads to the activation of caspases and, ultimately , apoptosis . Some diseases that occur due to the accumulation of abnormal folded proteins are: • Alzheimer's disease • Huntington's disease • Parkinson 's disease • Prion diseases • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis • Tay-Sachs disease45

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The following finding was noted on the cardiac tissue specimen of an 82-year-old man. Which of the following is false about the given finding?

options.a: It is a tell -tale sign of free radical injury
options.b: It is injurious to the cell and its function
options.c: It is derived through lipid peroxidation
options.d: It can also be seen in liver of aging patients

mcqs.explanation: The given histopathological image shows yellow -brown lipochrome or lipofuscin pigment . It is not injurious to the cell or its functions.53 Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment derived from the peroxidation of lipids of subcellular membranes. It is an indicator of free radical injury to the cells . It is an insoluble , brownish yellow , granular intracellular material that is seen in the liver, brain , and heart due to normal aging. The brown pigment in large amounts can give a characteristic appearance to the tissue called brown atrophy. It can also be seen in patients with severe malnutrition and cancer cachexia.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is examining a liver biopsy specimen from a patient with liver disease . The following finding is noted . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding?
mcqs.explanation: The given histopathological image shows hepatic macro-vesicular steatosis along with intraparenchymal cholestasis , which is suggestive of fatty liver. This condition can occur due to alcoholism. The lipid accumulates in the hepatocytes as vacuoles. These vacuoles have a clear appearance on hematoxylin and eosin staining.54 A few causes of fatty liver are as follows : • Alcoholism - most common cause in developed countries • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) - associated with diabetes and obesity • Toxins • Malnutrition • Dyslipidemia • Anoxia Fatty change is mostly seen in the liver because it is the major organ involved in fat metabolism. It may also occur in the heart, muscles , and kidneys. The most common form of lipid accumulation is triglycerides . Other forms of lipid that can be accumulated include cholesterol , cholesterol esters , and phospholipids .55

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions are associated with the intracellular accumulation of cholesterol and cholesterol esters ?
mcqs.explanation: Fabry disease and abetalipoproteinemia are not associated with intracellular accumulations of cholesterol and/or cholesterol esters . The following conditions are associated with the intracellular accumulation of cholesterol and/or cholesterol esters : • Xanthomas - accumulation of lipid -laden macrophages in the subepithelial connective tissue of the skin and in tendons • Strawberry gallbladder (cholesterolosis) - accumulation of cholesterol -laden macrophages in the lamina propria of the gallbladder • Niemann–Pick disease type C - mutations in NPC1 or NPC2 gene results in impaired cholesterol transport inside the cells • Atherosclerosis - foamy macrophages in the tunica intima of smooth muscles

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old male patient presented with backache. Urine examination revealed nephrotic range proteinuria with Bence-Jones proteins. Laboratory reports showed hypercalcemia . Histopathological examination of the bone marrow aspirate showed the findings as given below . The findings seen on histopathology are due to the accumulation of:
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the histopathological image showing Russell bodies are suggestive of multiple myeloma. These are globular, eosinophilic intracellular accumulations of immunoglobulins.56

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 36-year-old man with a history of chronic alcoholism presented with increasing abdominal girth and malaise. On examination, shifting dullness was present and the liver span was 6 cm. Histopathological examination revealed the presence of intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in hepatocytes . What is the content of these inclusions?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease . In this condition, there are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions called Mallory Denk bodies . They are composed of intermediate keratin filaments . Mallory bodies are also seen in the following conditions: • Morbid obesity • Indian childhood cirrhosis • Wilson's disease • Primary biliary cirrhosis57 There are several types of cytoskeletal proteins such as microtubules , thin actin filaments , thick myosin filaments, and intermediate filaments (10 nm). The intermediate filaments provide a flexible intracellular scaffold that organizes the cytoplasm and resists the forces applied to the cell . They are divided into five classes : • Keratin filaments - characteristic of epithelial cells (forms Mallory Denk bodies ) • Neurofilaments - neurons (forms neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease ) • Desmin filaments - muscle cells • Vimentin filaments - connective tissue cells • Glial filaments - astrocytes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An elderly man diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung underwent surgical resection . Histopathological examination of the resected hilar lymph nodes revealed the following finding as given below . Which of the following is the most likely cause for this?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and histopathological image of the lymph node showing abundant black-colored pigment within the macrophages are characteristic of pulmonary anthracosis. The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles . The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes , which causes the blackening of the tissues . The carbon dust may also induce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker's pneumoconiosis . It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles , such as coal mines.58 The following images show the accumulation of various types of pigments within cells .59

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 58-year-old man died 24 hours after the onset of substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm. On autopsy , an atheromatous plaque was seen obstructing the left anterior descending artery. Which type of calcification is most likely to be seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Atheromatous plaques are associated with dystrophic calcification. This is seen in the presence of normal calcium levels in the serum. The deposition of calcium in dead or dying tissues is called dystrophic calcification. Although it occurs in the presence of normal serum calcium, it can be worsened by hypercalcemia . Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type . Some examples include atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis and areas of caseous necrosis in tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following patients would you not expect metastatic calcification?

options.b: A 75 -year-old woman suffering from multiple myeloma

mcqs.explanation: Tuberculosis is associated with dystrophic calcification in the areas of caseous necrosis, not metastatic calcification. Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues in the presence of hypercalcemia . Causes of hypercalcemia include Paget 's disease , malignancy, and sarcoidosis. Metastatic calcification can occur throughout the body, but it mainly affects : • Interstitial tissues of the vasculature • Kidneys • Lungs • Gastric mucosa The calcium deposits morphologically resemble those described in dystrophic calcification. Although they generally do not cause clinical dysfunction , extensive calcifications in the lungs may be evident on radiographs and may produce respiratory distress . Massive deposits in the kidney (nephrocalcinosis ) can lead to renal damage.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following stains is not used in the detection of calcium in tissues ?
mcqs.explanation: The Congo red stain is used for staining amyloid bodies , not calcium. The following staining techniques are used for calcium: • Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) - • Calcium forms a blue -black lake with hematoxylin • Azan stain - • Used to distinguish osteoid from the mineralized bone • Alizarin red S stain -61 • Forms an orange-red lake with calcium • Works best with small amounts of calcium • An example is Michaelis –Gutmann (MG) bodies , seen in malakoplakia • Von Kossa method - • Useful for tissues containing large amounts of phosphates and carbonates, such as bone • Silver ions react with phosphate in the presence of acidic material • Silver phosphate gets degraded to silver in presence of light , giving black color • MG bodies also stain with von kossa stain. The image given below demonstrates MG bodies which are seen in malakoplakia using the Von Kossa stain.62

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following stains is used for staining melanin?
mcqs.explanation: Masson–Fontana stain is used to stain melanin, a brown-black endogenous pigment . The following different staining techniques are used for melanin: • Dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA)-oxidase method - • Most specific method • DOPA-oxidase acts on DOPA in the melanin-producing cells to produce a brownish-black deposit as shown below• Masson Fontana stain - • Used to stain melanin and argentaffin granules in neuroendocrine cells (e.g. carcinoid syndrome) • It stains melanin black, as shown below63 • Schmorl's method - stains melanin blue -green , as shown below

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is responsible for an increased incidence of cancer in old age ?
mcqs.explanation: Increased incidence of cancer in old age is due to telomerase reactivation. Normally, with every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell -cycle arrest or apoptosis . This is called replicative senescence . Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres . This enzyme is usually present in germ cells but is absent in most somatic cells . Abnormal reactivation of telomerase in somatic cells leads to evasion of senescence and apoptosis . It enables the cells to divide several times than normal .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding sirtuins?
mcqs.explanation: Sirtuins are responsible for an increase in insulin sensitivity . Hence , it can play an important role in the treatment of diabetes . Sirtuins are a class of proteins that possess either mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase or deacylase activity. They have been shown to slow down the aging process . Calorie restriction and intake of red wine are associated with an increase in sirtuin levels . Sirtuins act by the following mechanisms: • Inhibition of the metabolic activity • Reduction in apoptosis • Stimulation of protein folding64 • Inhibition of free radical damage • Increased insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism • Ensure that damaged DNA is not propagated , preventing the accumulation of mutations • Promotes replicative senescence under chronic stress

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
mcqs.explanation: A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing , which can remove lipids . When the tissue sample goes through rapid freezing , it becomes firmer. The ice acts as an embedding media allowing the tissue to be sectioned . The temperature range in the cryostat machine usually ranges from 0\037C to -35\037C. The majority of the tissue can be appropriately sectioned between -15\037C to -25\037C. Tissue samples that contain water can be sectioned at a higher temperature . The tissues that contain more fat will need to be cut at a lower temperature . The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues . It is used in the following conditions: • Fat emboli in lung tissue • Renal cell carcinoma • Sebaceous gland tumors of the skin • Lipid-rich carcinomas Fixatives containing alcohols , or routine processing with clearing, will remove lipids . Fixation can be achieved by the following methods : • Physical methods - heating , microwaving, cryopreservation • Chemical methods - immersion of specimen in fixative, perfusing vascular system with a fixative Given below are a few fixatives with their uses : The most commonly used fixative is 10 % neutral buffered formalin.Technique/Tissue Fixative Electron microscopy Glutaraldehyde Trephine biopsy -bone marr ow Zenker 's fluid (AZF fixative) GI biopsies Bouin's fixative Brain Formalin ammonium chlorid e Adrenal biopsy Orth's fluid Pap smear Ethanol65

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old diabetic male presented with arthralgia and skin pigmentation . On examination , he was found to have hepatomegaly , arthropathy involving small joints, excessive skin pigmentation with a characteristic slate -grey hue , and hypogonadism . As a part of the work-up, liver biopsy was done. Which of the following stains should be used for staining the biopsy specimen ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemochromatosis in which there is iron overload. The excess iron gets deposited in tissues as hemosiderin which can be detected using Perl's Prussian blue stain. It is based on the principle of the formation of ferric ferrocyanide , which is blue in color. Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin -derived granular pigment that is golden yellow to brown. It accumulates in the tissues when there is a local or systemic excess of iron. Iron is normally stored within cells in association with the protein apoferritin, forming ferritin micelles . Large aggregates of these micelles are hemosiderin deposits seen both in light and electron microscopy.66

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old woman is undergoing evaluation for premature cataracts, thinning of skin, alopecia , osteoporosis , and atherosclerosis . She is found to have a hereditary genetic mutation in the WRN gene . This gene encodes which of the following proteins ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical features are suggestive of Werner syndrome, a premature aging disorder. The mutated gene encodes a DNA helicase . Werner syndrome is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the WRN gene . This gene encodes a protein with multiple DNA-dependent enzymatic functions including: • ATPase • Helicase • Exonuclease DNA helicase is involved in DNA replication and repair. A defect in this enzyme causes rapid accumulation of damaged chromosomes that may mimic the injury that normally accumulates during cellular aging. Affected persons show various manifestations of premature aging including: • Atherosclerosis • Senile cataract • Skin atrophy • Alopecia • Osteoporosis They are also at risk for the development of a variety of cancers. Patients typically die in the 5th decade from either cancer or cardiovascular disease .67

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Who listed the four cardinal signs of inflammation?
mcqs.explanation: The four cardinal signs of inflammation were first listed by Aulus Celsus . He was a Roman medical writer of the first century AD. These are: • Rubor - redness • Tumour - swelling • Calor - heat • Dolor - pain These signs are the hallmarks of acute inflammation. Rudolf Virchow added the fifth clinical sign of inflammation, loss of function, functio laesa.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following stimuli can trigger an inflammatory response ?
mcqs.explanation: The complement system does not trigger an inflammatory response . It reacts against microbes and results in the production of mediators of inflammation. The major triggers of inflammation include : • Infections - bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites , toxins • Tissue necrosis - due to ischemia, trauma, physical or chemical injuries • Foreign bodies - • Endogenous - DNA breakdown products (uric acid), cholesterol crystals, lipids • Exogenous - splinters , dirt, sutures , etc • Trauma • Immune reactions - against microbes, self -antigens, or environmental substances76

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors ?
mcqs.explanation: NOD-like receptors and RIG -like receptors are cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors . Pattern-recognition receptors are the cellular receptors that recognize microbes and damaged cells . Types of pattern-recognition receptors : • Cellular receptors for microbes - • Toll-like receptors on the plasma membrane and endosomal vesicles • C-type lectin receptors on the plasma membrane of macrophages and dendritic cells • Cytosolic receptors - • NOD-like receptors detect bacterial peptidoglycan • RIG -like receptors detect viral RNA • Circulating proteins : Mannose-binding lectin and collectins

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about the acute inflammatory process ?

options.a: It is a mechanism of innate immunity
options.b: Monocytes and macrophages are mainly involved
options.c: Tissue injury is usually mild and self -limited
options.d: Local and systemic signs are prominent

mcqs.explanation: The prominent cells in acute inflammation are neutrophils . The initial, rapid response to infections agents and tissue damage is called acute inflammation. It is a mechanism of innate immunity that occurs in response to mild and self -limited tissue injury. It is associated with prominent local and systemic signs. The major components of acute inflammation are: • Vasodilation and increased permeability of small blood vessels • Changes in the leukocytes - • Migration from the microcirculation • Accumulation at the site of inflammation • Activation to eliminate the offending agent Chronic inflammation is a mechanism of adaptive immunity and is of longer duration. It is associated with • Presence of lymphocytes and macrophages • Proliferation of blood vessels • Deposition of connective tissue

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common mechanism of vascular leakage in acute inflammation?
mcqs.explanation: The most common mechanism of vascular leakage in acute inflammation is the contraction of endothelial cells .77 This is an immediate , transient response mediated by histamine, bradykinin , and leukotrienes . The contraction of the endothelial cells results in an increase in the interendothelial spaces . Other mechanisms of vascular leakage include : • Endothelial injury - results in endothelial cell necrosis and detachment • Transcytosis - increased transport of fluids and proteins

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A man is brought to the casualty with swelling after sustaining a bee sting over his face . Which of the following vascular changes is not observed in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Bee stings result in acute inflammation at the site of the sting. In this condition, there is decreased oncotic pressure due to protein leakage . There is a release of inflammatory mediators like histamine which result in the following vascular changes : • Vasodilation - results in erythema and stasis of blood flow • Increased vascular permeability - • Due to mediators like histamine, kinins , or endothelial injury (direct or leukocyte -induced ), or transcytosis • Results in leakage of proteins (reduced vascular oncotic pressure ) and leukocyte migration • Increased hydrostatic pressure - results in fluid leakage from blood vessels resulting in edema The image below shows the changes seen during acute inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: During normal blood flow in venules , which cells occupy the central axial column?
mcqs.explanation: Blood flows in blood vessels as central axial/laminar column and peripheral chaotic columns. During normal blood flow in venules , the central axial column is occupied by the red blood cells78 (RBCs). These RBCs displace the leukocytes toward the wall of the vessel (chaotic column). During inflammation, stasis leads to slow blood flow and reduced wall shear stress . This further pushes the WBCs towards a peripheral position along the endothelial surface .
