This is called margination . Subsequently , leukocytes adhere to the endothelium , then detach and bind again. This is referred to as rolling on the vessel wall. The cells finally come to rest and adhere firmly to the endothelial wall.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true with regard to selectins ?

options.b: There are L, E and P types of selectins
options.c: P-selectins are expressed on the endothelium

mcqs.explanation: Selectins are a group of molecules that mediate low-affinity interactions between the leukocytes and the endothelium . Due to the low-affinity nature of these interactions, they are easily disrupted by the flowing blood. They play a major role in the initial rolling interactions of leukocytes with the vascular endothelium . The expression of selectins and their ligands is regulated by cytokines produced in response to infection and injury. There are 3 types of selectins : • L-selectin - expressed on leukocytes • E-selectin - expressed on endothelium • P-selectin - expressed on activated platelets and endothelium

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an integrin molecule ?
mcqs.explanation: CD 31 or platelet endothelial cell -adhesion molecule 1 (PECAM-1) is a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily . It is not an integrin molecule . The various endothelial and leukocyte adhesion molecules include : • Selectin family - mediates initial rolling interactions between leukocytes and endothelium • Integrin family - • Involved in migration and firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium • Includes LFA-1, MAC-1, and VLA -4 • Immunoglobulin family - • PECAM (CD31) - most important adhesion molecule for diapedesis • ICAM-1 - binds to �o 2 integrins on leukocytes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a ligand for integrins?
mcqs.explanation: 79 The ligands for integrins include : • ICAM-1 (CD54) • ICAM-2 (CD102 ) • VCAM-1 (CD106 )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Sialyl-Lewis X is linked to which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Sialyl-Lewis X refers to sialylated oligosaccharides bound to mucin-like glycoprotein . These molecules function as ligands for selectins . The expression of selectins and their ligands is regulated by cytokines produced in response to infection and injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which molecule plays a major role in the following phenomenon seen in leukocytes ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows diapedesis by leukocytes . CD31 or platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule (PECAM-1) plays a major role in diapedesis . Diapedesis or transmigration refers to the migration of the leukocytes through the endothelium . It mainly occurs in postcapillary venules.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, which of the following cells are the major cause of tissue injury?
mcqs.explanation: In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute tissue injury is caused mainly by neutrophils . ARDS is a clinical syndrome manifested as a result of severe lung injury. The initiating event is alveolar epithelial cell damage . It is characterized by acute inflammation, causing increased pulmonary vascular permeability and edema . Neutrophils adhere to the activated endothelium and migrate into the interstitium and the alveoli. Here, they degranulate and release inflammatory mediators. These include : • Proteases • Reactive oxygen species • Cytokines Macrophages are involved in the stage of resolution .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Infection with which of the following organisms would produce an inflammatory infiltrate with neutrophilic predominance beyond 48 hours?
mcqs.explanation: 80 In Pseudomonas infection , the inflammatory infiltrate has a neutrophilic predominance for several days. Normally, in acute inflammation, neutrophils predominate the inflammatory infiltrate during the first 6 to 24 hours. However, they are short-lived, and disappear within 24 to 48 hours, following which they are replaced by monocytes. Monocytes survive longer and also proliferate in the tissues . Thus, they become the dominant population in prolonged inflammatory reactions. The exceptions to this pattern include : • Pseudomonas infections - neutrophilic dominance in the infiltrate for several days • Viral infections - lymphocytes are the initial cells • Allergic reactions - eosinophils are the main cell type • Some types of hypersensitivity - dominated by activated lymphocytes , macrophages , and plasma cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is involved in inducing the migration of leukocytes to sites of injury?
mcqs.explanation: C5a induces the migration of leukocytes to the site of injury. It functions as an endogenous chemoattractant. Both exogenous and endogenous substances can act as chemoattractants . The most common exogenous agents include bacterial products like peptides with N-formylmethionine terminal amino acids and certain lipids . Endogenous chemoattractants include several chemical mediators: • Cytokines - particularly those of the chemokine family (IL -8) • Complement system components - particularly C5a • Arachidonic acid metabolites - mainly leukotriene B4

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an opsonin?
mcqs.explanation: C3b functions as an opsonin. Opsonization is the process of coating a foreign particle and preparing it for phagocytosis . The substances involved in this process are called opsonins and include : • Mannose-binding lectin • C3b, C4b, C5b • IgM and Fc receptor of IgG • CRP • Fibrinogen81 Elie Metchnikoff was the first person to describe the process of phagocytosis , and is hence known as the Father of Innate Immunity.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not have antioxidant action?
mcqs.explanation: Myeloperoxidase is an oxidative enzyme, not an antioxidant. Antioxidants provide protection against potentially harmful oxygen -derived radicals. Serum, tissue fluids , and host cells possess antioxidant mechanisms. These include : • Catalase • Superoxide dismutase • Glutathione peroxidase • Iron -free fraction of transferrin • Carotenoids • Ceruloplasmin Myeloperoxidase is an oxidative enzyme with antimicrobial activity. It is seen in azurophil (primary) granules of neutrophils . It is involved in the production of hypochlorous acid and destroys microbes by means of halogenation and lipid peroxidation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Oxygen -dependent killing is done through which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: NADPH oxidase is involved in the oxygen -dependent killing of microbes. It results in generation of reactive oxygen intermediates . This process is called the oxidative burst. It involves the generation of H2O2 , and eventually hypochlorous acid. This H2O2 -MPO-halide system is the most efficient bactericidal system of neutrophils .82 Carotenoids, glutathione peroxidase , and the iron-free fraction of transferrin are antioxidants or free radical scavengers that prevent oxygen -mediated injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 7-month-old male infant was brought with a 2-day history of fever and abscess over the neck. The mother reveals that the child has had similar recurrent infections in the past. The result of the nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction test was found to be abnormal . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and abnormal nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction test are suggestive of chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). CGD is a rare primary immunodeficiency of phagocytes . It is an X-linked recessive disorder due to the deficiency in the NADPH oxidase enzyme. This is important in the respiratory or oxidative burst. It usually manifests in the first year of life with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase -positive organisms, including: • Staphylococcus aureus • Escherichia coli • Aspergillus species

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A nitroblue tetrazolium test is performed in a child with recurrent infections . Functions of which of the following are assessed by this test ?
mcqs.explanation: Nitroblue tetrazolium test (NBT) is done to assess the function of phagocytes . The principle is based on the color change of the colorless nitroblue tetrazolium compound to a deep blue when exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS). The higher the nitroblue test score, the better the cell is at producing ROS. In chronic granulomatous disease , there is an NADPH oxidase defect . Hence , the phagocyte is unable to produce reactive oxygen species or radicals required for bacterial killing, which results in recurrent infections . Hence , there is a reduced color change with the NBT test .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions have defective phagolysosome formation?
mcqs.explanation: Defective phagolysosome formation is seen in patients with Chediak–Higashi syndrome (CHS). It is a rare autosomal recessive defect . There is an abnormal fusion of azurophilic lysosomes of neutrophils and cytoplasmic granules of monocytes and lymphocytes , which leads to the presence of giant lysosomal granules. Hence, there is abnormal post -phagocytic phagolysosomal fusion, degranulation , and impaired microbicidal activity. There is rapid neutrophil turnover leading to low counts. Clinical features include : • Recurrent infections - • Commonly affect the skin, upper and lower respiratory tract83 • Common organisms - Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae , Group A Streptococcus, Gram-negative enteric (Klebsiella , Proteus, Shigella , Pseudomonas ) • Accelerated phase in some patients - • Hemophagocytic syndrome and aggressive lymphoma • These patients require bone marrow transplantation • Albinism with neurological defects

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is frustrated phagocytosis ?

options.a: Release of lysosomal contents due to damaged membrane
options.b: Engulfment of infectious pathogens and degradation by phagolysosome
options.c: Release of lysosomal enzymes when phagocytes cannot engulf targets

mcqs.explanation: The term frustrated phagocytosis refers to the release of large amounts of lysosomal contents into the external environment due the inability of the phagocytes to engulf . When immune complexes are deposited on relatively flat immovable surfaces , the phagocytes are unable to surround and ingest them. In this case, the activation signals lead to an uncontrolled release of the lysosomal contents , despite lack of phagocytosis . This is known as frustrated phagocytosis . Other processes may lead to the release of lysosomal contents into the external environment: • Controlled secretion of granule contents - normal response of activated leukocytes • Damage to the phagolysosome membrane by certain phagocytosed substances like urate crystals

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What does the following image show?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows the phenomenon of emperipolesis . Here, intact hematopoietic cells are seen within the cytoplasm of the host cell without any damage . The cells frequently involved are neutrophils, lymphocytes , and plasma cells . Both the cells are viable and there are no physiological and morphological consequences to either of them.84

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not present in the primary granules of neutrophils ?
mcqs.explanation: Lactoferrin is present in the secondary granules of neutrophils , not primary. The types of granules present in neutrophils are: Primary and secondary granules can fuse with phagocytic vacuoles containing engulfed material. Otherwise , the granule contents can be released into the extracellular space .Azurophil (Primary ) granules Specific (Secondary) granules Small storage granules Antimicrobial molecules LysozymeMyeloperoxidase ,d efensins , BPI LysozymeLactoferrin --- Neutral proteinases ElastaseCathepsin GProteina se 3 Collagenase complement acti vator GelatinasePlasminogen activ ator Acid hydrolases Cathepsins B, D�o -D-Glucuro nidase\037-MannosidasePhosph olipase A2 Phospholipase A2 Cathepsins B, D�o -D-Glucuro nidase\037-Mannosidase Cytoplasmic membrane recep tors --- CR3, CR4FMLP receptorsLa minin receptors --- Other molecules85 Azurophil (Primary ) granules Specific (Secondary) granules Small storage granules Chondroitin-4-sulfate Cytochrome B558Monocyte -c hemotactic factorHistaminas eVitamin B12 -binding protei n Cytochrome B558 BPI : bactericidal permeabilit y-increasing proteinFMLP: N -formyl methionyl -leucyl -phe nylalanine

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following is major basic protein seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The major basic protein is the predominant constituent of the crystalline core of the eosinophil granule. It is also called proteoglycan -2 and is encoded by the PRG2 gene . This protein is involved in: • Antiparasitic defense mechanisms - functions as a cytotoxin and helminthotoxin • Immune hypersensitivity reactions • Lysis of epithelial cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)?

options.a: They prevent the spread of the microbes by trapping them in the fibrils
options.b: Nuclear chromatin in the NETs are the source of nuclear antigens in SLE
options.c: In sepsis , platelet activation is involved in NET formation
options.d: NETs play a major role in phagocytosis

mcqs.explanation: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are not involved in phagocytosis . This is because the nuclei of the neutrophils are lost during NET formation, leading to their death . Hence , they cannot phagocytose pathogens . NETs are networks of extracellular fibers that consist of a viscous meshwork of nuclear chromatin. They trap microbes at sites of infection , preventing their further spread . They also contain a high concentration of antimicrobial proteins like neutrophil elastase , cathepsin G, and histones that have a high affinity for DNA. They are produced by neutrophils in response to the following triggers : • Pathogens - Mainly bacteria and fungi • Inflammatory mediators - • Chemokines • Cytokines (mainly interferons) • Complement proteins • Reactive oxygen species NETs have also been detected in the blood during sepsis . In this condition, platelet activation is involved in NET formation86 The nuclear chromatin in the NETs is a source of nuclear antigens (histones and associated DNA) in systemic autoimmune diseases , particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). This triggers autoantibody production and further clinical manifestations .87

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the first mediator to be released during inflammation?
mcqs.explanation: Serotonin and histamine are among the first mediators to be released during inflammation. They are stored as preformed molecules in cells . Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine ) is a preformed vasoactive mediator that is present in platelets and certain neuroendocrine cells , such as in the gastrointestinal tract. Its functions include vasoconstriction and neurotransmitter action in the gastrointestinal tract.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following may serve as a source of histamine production ?
mcqs.explanation: The sources of histamine include platelets , basophils , and mast cells (major source ). Preformed histamine is stored in the granules of mast cells and other cells . It is released by degranulation in response to a variety of stimuli, including: • Physical injuries - trauma, cold, or heat • Binding of antibodies to mast cells • Products of complement called anaphylatoxins (C3a and C5a) Its vasoactive effects are mediated mainly via binding to H1 receptors on microvascular endothelial cells . The functions of histamine include : • Vasodilation • Increased vascular permeability • Endothelial activation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The release of arachidonic acid from the membrane phospholipids is mainly mediated by which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The release of arachidonic acid (AA) from the membrane phospholipids is mainly mediated by phospholipase A2 and C. AA is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that may be derived from the following sources : • Dietary sources96 • From the conversion of the essential fatty acid linoleic acid • From membrane phospholipids via phospholipase A2 and C (in response to mechanical, chemical, or physical stimuli) • From diacylglycerol by the action of diacylglycerol lipase AA-derived mediators are also called eicosanoids (20 -carbon fatty acids). They are synthesized by two major classes of enzymes : • Cyclooxygenases - produces prostaglandins • Lipoxygenases - produces leukotrienes and lipoxins These mediators bind to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) on many cell types . They stimulate vascular and cellular reactions in acute inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about prostaglandins is false ?

options.a: TxA2 is the major product in platelets
options.b: Prostacyclin is a vasodilator and inhibits platelet aggregation
options.c: PGD2 is the major prostaglandin produced by mast cells

mcqs.explanation: Prostacyclin synthase is present in the vascular endothelium . It is responsible for the formation of prostacyclin (PGI2 ) and PGF1a (its stable end product). Prostacyclin is a vasodilator and a potent inhibitor of platelet aggregation . Thromboxane synthase is present in platelets , and hence , TxA2 is the major product in these cells . PGD2 is the major prostaglandin produced by mast cells and is a chemoattractant for neutrophils .97

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding leukotrienes ?

options.a: They are produced by leukocytes and mast cells by action of lipoxygenase
options.b: 5-lipoxygenase is the predominant enzyme in neutrophils
options.c: LTB4 is a potent chemotactic agent and activator of neutrophils
options.d: Leukotrienes are less potent mediators of bronchospasm

mcqs.explanation: Leukotrienes are more potent than histamine in increasing vascular permeability and causing bronchospasm. They are produced by leukocytes and mast cells from arachidonic acid by the action of lipoxygenase . They are involved in vascular and smooth muscle reactions. There are three different lipoxygenases (5, , 15). 5-lipoxygenase is predominant in neutrophils . The principal actions of various arachidonic acid metabolites in inflammation are as follows :Eicosanoid Action PGI2 (prostacyclin )PGE1,PGE 2,PGD2 Vasodilation Thromboxane A2 Vasoconstriction LeukotrienesC4,D4,E4 Increased vascular permeabil ityIntense vasoconstrictionBr onchospasm LeukotrienesB4 Chemotaxis,neutrophilactivat ionLeukocyte adhesionGener ation of reactive oxygen speci esRelease of lysosomal enzy mes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the principal action of leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4?
mcqs.explanation: The principal action of leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 is increased vascular permeability .98 Eicosanoid Action PGI2 (prostacyclin )PGE1,PGE 2,PGD2 Vasodilation Thromboxane A2 Vasoconstriction LeukotrienesC4,D4,E4 Increasedvascularpermeabilit yIntensevasoconstrictionBro nchospasm LeukotrienesB4 Chemotaxis,neutrophilactivat ionLeukocyte adhesionGener ation of reactive oxygen speci esRelease of lysosomal enzy mes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an anti-inflammatory cytokine?
mcqs.explanation: IL -4 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine. It induces alternatively activated macrophages . This results in tissue repair and the resolution of inflammation. The following are anti-inflammatory cytokines: • IL -4 • IL -10 • IL -13 • TGF-�o • Lipoxins Lipoxins suppress inflammation by inhibiting leukocyte recruitment. They inhibit neutrophil chemotaxis and adhesion to endothelium.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a CXC chemokine?
mcqs.explanation: IL -8 is a typical example of a CXC chemokine. Chemokines are a family of small (8 to 10 kD) proteins . They act primarily as chemoattractants for specific types of leukocytes . They are classified into 4 groups , according to the arrangement of cysteine (C) residues in the proteins. This is given in the image and the table below .99 Type of chemok ine Structure Action and example C-X-C 1 amino acid residue separati ng the first 2 of the 4 conserv ed cysteine residues Involved inneutrophil activat ionandchemotaxisExample -I L-8 C-C The first 2 conserved cysteine residues remain adjacent Attract monocytes , eosinophi ls, basophils , lymphocytesEx amples :Monocyte chemoattra ctant protein (MCP-1)Eotaxin Macrophage inflammatory pr otein- 1\037 (MIP-1\037)Regulated and normal T--cell expressed and secreted (RANTES) C chemokines Lack the 1st and 3rd of the 4 conserved cysteines Specific forlymphocytesExam ple - lymphotactin CX3C Contain 3 amino acids betwe en the 2 cysteines The only known member of t his class is calledfractalkine .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Fractalkine belongs to which chemokine family?
mcqs.explanation: Fractalkine is the only known member of the CX3C chemokine group. CX3C chemokines contain 3 amino acids between the 2 cysteines . This chemokine exists in two forms: • Cell surface -bound protein - • Induced on endothelial cells by inflammatory cytokines • Promotes the strong adhesion of monocytes and T cells100 • Soluble form - • Derived by proteolysis of the membrane-bound protein • Potent chemoattractant activity for the same cell . The image below shows the structure of CX3C chemokine.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What type of chemokine is MCP-1?
mcqs.explanation: MCP-1 belongs to the CC type of chemokine. Here, the first two conserved cysteine residues remain adjacent to each other. The CC chemokines include : • Monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP1) • Eotaxin • Macrophage inflammatory protein1\037 (MIP1\037) • Regulated and normal T-cell expressed and secreted (RANTES) The image below shows the structure of C-C chemokine:101

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Serum concentrations of which of the following decrease during inflammation?
mcqs.explanation: During inflammation, there are reduced levels of albumin. This occurs in order to allow an increase in the liver's capacity to synthesize acute phase reactants. Hence , albumin is called a negative phase reactant. Negative acute -phase proteins concentration decreases during inflammation. These are: • Albumin • Transferrin • Retinol-binding protein • Antithrombin • Transcortin • Alpha 2-HS glycoprotein • Alpha-fetoprotein • Thyroxin -binding protein • Insulin-like growth factor 1 • Factor 12 Acute -phase proteins are plasma proteins synthesized by the liver in response to inflammation. These include C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A (SAA) protein. The synthesis of these molecules in hepatocytes is stimulated by cytokines. IL -6 stimulates the synthesis of CRP and fibrinogen and IL -1 or TNF for SAA.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 39-year-old woman is being evaluated for anemia. She is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis. Increased levels of which of the following is responsible for her anemia?
mcqs.explanation: 102 In this scenario, the woman has a chronic illness , rheumatoid arthritis. In chronic disease states , elevated plasma concentrations of hepcidin cause anemia. Increased hepcidin reduces the availability of iron. Fibrinogen binds to red cells and causes rouleaux formation. They sediment more rapidly at unit gravity than do individual red cells . This is the basis for measuring the erythrocyte sedimentation rate in inflammation. C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid A (SAA) bind to microbial cell walls . They act as opsonins and fix complement . They also bind chromatin.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true for platelet -activating factor?

options.a: It is secreted by mast cells
options.d: It is involved in leukocyte adhesion

mcqs.explanation: Platelet -activating factor (PAF) primarily causes vasoconstriction. PAF is a phospholipid -derived mediator known to have multiple inflammatory effects . It may be secreted by the following : • Platelets • Basophils • Mast cells • Neutrophils • Macrophages • Endothelial cells . Its functions include : • Platelet aggregation • Vasoconstriction • Bronchoconstriction • Leukocyte adhesion • Vascular permeability and vasodilation at low doses

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The critical step in complement activation involves the proteolysis of the which component ?
mcqs.explanation: The critical step in complement activation is the proteolysis of the third (and most abundant) component, C3. The complement system can be activated by one of three pathways : • Classical pathway - antibody-mediated and triggered by fixation of C1 to antibody (IgM or IgG) that has combined with antigen • Alternative pathway - triggered by microbial surface molecules in the absence of antibody103 • Lectin pathway - plasma mannose-binding lectin binds to carbohydrates on microbes and directly activates C1. All three pathways of complement activation lead to the formation of an active enzyme called the C3 convertase. It splits C3 into two functionally distinct fragments, C3a and C3b.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with an inherited deficiency of C1 inhibitor will have which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The deficiency of C1 INH causes hereditary angioedema . C1-inhibitor (C1 INH)is the largest member of the serpin superfamily of proteins . It normally inhibits the following : • Complement system • Kallikrein system • Factor XII or Hageman factor Deficiency of C1 INH is associated with hereditary angioedema (hereditary angioneurotic edema). It leads to decreased C4 and C2 levels and bradykinin accumulation. There is swelling due to leakage of fluid from blood vessels into connective tissue . It is an autosomal dominant disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not caused by bradykinin ?

options.c: Pain at the site of injection

mcqs.explanation: Bradykinin results in vasodilation. Kinins are vasoactive peptides derived from plasma proteins called kininogens, by the action of specific proteases called kallikreins . The enzyme kallikrein cleaves high molecular weight kininogen, to produce bradykinin . Actions of bradykinin : • Increases vascular permeability • Potent vasodilator • Contraction of smooth muscle • Dilation of blood vessels • Pain when injected into the skin

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: During an inflammatory response , which of the following does not increase vascular permeability?
mcqs.explanation: IL -4 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine and does not have any effect on vascular permeability .104 Inflammatory change Principal Mediators Vasodilation HistamineProstaglandins Increased vascular permeabil ity HistamineandserotoninC3aa ndC5a(by the release of vasoa ctive amines from mast cells , other cells )LeukotrienesC4,D 4, E4, Chemotaxis, leukocyte recrui tment , activation TNF, IL -1ChemokinesC3aand C5aLeukotriene B4 Fever IL -1, TNFProstaglandins Pain ProstaglandinsBradykinin Tissue damage Lysosomal enzymes of leukoc ytesReactive oxygen species

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Fever occurs during inflammation due to all except :
mcqs.explanation: Histamine is involved in the mediation of vascular events of inflammation, not fever. Fever is characterized by an elevation of body temperature , usually by 1\260 to 4\260C. It is one of the most prominent manifestations of the acute -phase response , especially if associated with infection . Substances that induce fever are called pyrogens . They may be exogenous or endogenous . • Endogenous pyrogens - IL -1, TNF, prostaglandins • Exogenous pyrogens - • Lipopolysaccharides of bacterial walls • They stimulate leukocytes to release endogenous pyrogens (IL -1 and TNF) Cytokines result in an increase in cyclooxygenases that convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandins. These prostaglandins are produced in the vascular and perivascular cells of the hypothalamus . In the hypothalamus , they stimulate the production of neurotransmitters that reset the temperature setpoint to a higher level . This is especially by PGE2.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about fever?

options.a: Aspirin increases fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis
options.b: PGD2 is responsible for resetting the temperature to a higher level
options.d: Fever occurs during inflammation due to release of histamine

mcqs.explanation: IL -1 is an endogenous pyrogen Substances that induce fever are called pyrogens . They may be exogenous or endogenous . • Endogenous pyrogens - IL -1, TNF, prostaglandins • Exogenous pyrogens - • Lipopolysaccharides of bacterial walls • They stimulate leukocytes to release endogenous pyrogens (IL -1 and TNF)105 In the hypothalamus , prostaglandins such as PGE2 stimulate the production of neurotransmitters that reset the temperature setpoint at a higher level . Aspirin decreases fever by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: IL -1 is activated by :
mcqs.explanation: Caspase - 1 activates the biologically active form of IL -1. IL -1 is involved in pyroptosis , a form of programmed cell death that is different from apoptosis and necrosis. It is involved in the clearance of necrotic and microbe-infected cells . It occurs in the following sequence : • Activation of the inflammasome complex • Activation of caspase -1 • Generation of IL -1 - results in fever, inflammation, leukocyte recruitment

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not secreted by T-helper type 2 cells ?
mcqs.explanation: TH2 cells secrete IL4 , IL5 , and IL13 . Three subsets of CD4+ T cells secrete different types of cytokines and elicit different types of inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with which of the following conditions would you observe tertiary lymphoid organs?
mcqs.explanation: Tertiary lymphoid organs are seen in autoimmune conditions such as: • Hashimoto thyroiditis - in the thyroid • Rheumatoid arthritis - in the synovium • SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus ) - in the kidneys Tertiary lymphoid organs are a feature of chronic inflammatory conditions. Here, the accumulated lymphocytes , antigen-presenting cells , and plasma cells cluster together to form lymphoid tissues resembling lymph nodes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Lymph node biopsy of a patient with tuberculosis demonstrated the following findings. From which of the following are these cells derived?
mcqs.explanation: The given histopathological findings in a patient with tuberculosis are suggestive of granulomatous inflammation, with epithelioid and multinucleated giant cells . These cells are derived from the monocyte -macrophage lineage .106 Macrophages activated by IFN-\034 develop into cells with abundant cytoplasm . They resemble epithelial cells and are thus called epithelioid cells . Some activated macrophages may fuse , forming multinucleated giant cells . Collections of activated macrophages , often with T lymphocytes are seen in granulomatous inflammation. Sometimes it is associated with central caseating necrosis. Granulomas may be formed in response to various stimuli: • Immune granulomas - due to T-cell mediated response ; macrophages activate T cells to produce cytokines, such as IL -2 and IFN-\034 • Foreign body granulomas - due to inert foreign bodies in the absence of a T-cell mediated response

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Epithelioid granulomas are not seen in which of the following diseases ?
mcqs.explanation: 107 Kikuchi's lymphadenitis is associated with histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis . It does not show epithelioid granulomatous lesions . Common conditions characterized by epithelioid granuloma formation: • Tuberculosis • Sarcoidosis (non-caseating granuloma) • Brucellosis • Cat scratch disease (stellate shaped or round granuloma) • Syphilis (gumma ) • Lymphogranuloma inguinale • Leprosy • Inflammatory bowel disease • Toxoplasmosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist observes the given findings during the examination of a lymph node sample . Which of the following is the least likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given histopathological image of a lymph node shows a non-caseating granuloma. Tuberculosis is least likely as it is commonly associated with caseating granulomas. Non-caseating granulomas can be seen in the following conditions: • Leprosy • Cat-scratch disease • Sarcoidosis • Berylliosis • Crohn's disease • Hypersenitive pneumonitis • Foreign body granuloma • Q fever • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's). • Hodgkin's lymphoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Stellate granuloma is seen in :
mcqs.explanation: Stellate granuloma is seen in cat-scratch disease . It is also known as subacute regional lymphadenitis . It is a bacterial infection caused by Bartonella henselae . It is acquired following contact with infected animals (commonly cats).108 Regional lymph nodes demonstrate : • Follicular hyperplasia with circumscribed central stellate necrosis with neutrophils • Surrounded by palisading histiocytes (suppurative granulomas) • Sinuses packed with monocytoid B cells • Usually , there are no perifollicular and intrafollicular epithelioid cells109

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following structures lack labile cells ?
mcqs.explanation: 114 The liver contains stable cells , not labile cells . Based on the regenerative capacity of cells , tissues are classified into 3 types : • Labile tissues • Stable tissues • Permanent tissues Labile cells refer to continuously proliferating cells that are lost and replaced by the maturation of stem cells and the proliferation of these mature cells . Tissues containing these cells can readily regenerate after an injury as long as the pool of stem cells is preserved . Some examples of labile cells include : • Hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow • Majority of surface epithelia - • Stratified squamous epithelia of the skin, oral cavity, vagina , and cervix • Cuboidal epithelia of the ducts draining exocrine organs (salivary glands, biliary tract) • Columnar epithelium of the GIT , uterus , and fallopian tubes • Transitional epithelium of the urinary tract

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following tissues does not consist of stable cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac muscle does not contain stable cells . It contains permanent cells which are terminally differentiated and non-proliferative. Based on the regenerative capacity of cells , tissues are classified into 3 types : • Labile tissues • Stable tissues • Permanent tissues Stable cells are quiescent (in the G0 stage of the cell cycle ) and have only minimal proliferative activity in their normal state . However, they can divide in response to injury or loss of tissue mass. They include the following : • Parenchyma of solid tissues (liver, kidney, and pancreas) • Endothelial cells • Fibroblasts • Smooth muscle cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not contain permanent cells ?
mcqs.explanation: 115 Smooth muscle does not contain permanent cells . It consists of stable cells that are capable of dividing in response to injury or loss of tissue mass. Based on the regenerative capacity of cells , tissues are classified into 3 types : • Labile tissues • Stable tissues • Permanent tissues Permanent cells are those which are considered to be terminally differentiated and non-proliferative in postnatal life . In permanent tissues , the repair is typically dominated by scar formation. These cells include : • Neurons • Cardiac muscle • Skeletal muscle - contains satellite cells attached to the endomysial sheath which have some regenerative capacity

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Oval cells are seen in which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Oval cells refer to stem cells in the liver. They are located in the canals of Hering. Regeneration of the liver occurs by two major mechanisms: • Proliferation of remaining hepatocytes - occurs following partial hepatectomy (resection of up to 90% of the liver can be corrected by this mechanism) • Repopulation from progenitor cells (oval cells ) - occurs following chronic liver injury or inflammation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding TGF-�o ?

options.a: It increases the synthesis of collagen
options.b: It increases the degradation of the extracellular matrix
options.c: It is involved in the development of fibrosis in solid organs

mcqs.explanation: TGF-�o (transforming growth factor-�o ) decreases the degradation of the extracellular matrix by inhibiting metalloproteinases . It is produced by most cells in granulation tissue , including alternatively activated macrophages . The functions of TGF-�o include : • Stimulates fibroblast migration and proliferation • Increases synthesis of collagen and fibronectin (connective tissue proteins ) • Decreased degradation of ECM by inhibiting metalloproteinases • Involved in scar formation after injury • Development of fibrosis in lung, liver, and kidneys following chronic inflammation • Anti-inflammatory action by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation and activity116

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following delay healing except :
mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoid excess results in delayed healing, not glucocorticoid deficiency . Various factors affect wound healing including mechanical factors (pressure and torsion and site of injury) and location and extent of the injury. Vitamin C helps in the activation of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases which help in the hydroxylation of procollagen . As inadequately hydroxylated procollagen is vulnerable to enzymatic degradation , vitamin C plays an essential role in wound healing.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In healing by primary intention, by when do macrophages replace neutrophils at the site of injury?
mcqs.explanation: By day 3 of healing by primary intention, macrophages replace the neutrophils at the site of injury. The sequence of events in wound healing is as follows :Time after injury Events Within 24 hours Neutrophils :Migratefrom the incision margin towards the f ibrin clotReleaseproteolytic e nzymesthat begin to clear the debrisBasal cells :Located at t he cut edge of the epidermisS howincreased mitotic activity 24 to 48 hours Epithelial cells :Migrate andpr oliferatefrom the wound edge s towards the centerDeposit basement membrane compo nentsForm acontinuousepith elial layerthat closes the wou nd Day 3 Macrophagesbecome predom inant, with very few neutroph ilsGranulation tissueprogress ively invades the incision spa ceCollagen fibersat the incisi on marginsIncreased thickne ss of the epithelial layer thro ugh continuedepithelialprolif eration Day 5 Neovascularizationreaches its peakas granulation tissue fills the incisional spaceAs new v essels areleaky, new granulati on tissue is oftenedematous 2nd week Continued collagen accumula tionFibroblast proliferation.117 Time after injury Events End of the 1stmon th Scar contains cellular connec tive tissueLargely devoid of i nflammatory cellsCovered by an essentiallynormal epider mis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man underwent excision of a lipoma. The swelling had been excised with a clear linear incision and was sutured cleanly . In this wound , when would you expect peak neovascularization?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a clean surgical incision that is sutured is an example of healing by primary intention. In this type of healing, neovascularization reaches its peak by day 5, as granulation tissue fills the incisional space . These new vessels are leaky, allowing the passage of plasma proteins and fluid into the extravascular space . Hence , new granulation tissue is often edematous .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with an abscess on his back. Septic precautions were taken and the abscess was drained. On follow up, a healthy scar was visible. What is the type of collagen seen in the provisional matrix in this type of healing?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is an example of wound healing by secondary intention. The initial provisional matrix in this type of healing is composed of type III collagen , fibrin, and plasma fibronectin. It is later replaced by a matrix composed primarily of type I collagen . This type of healing occurs when cell or tissue loss is more extensive , such as in large wounds , abscesses , ulceration, and ischemic necrosis in parenchymal organs. The repair process involves a combination of regeneration and scarring.118

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair may give rise to which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair leads to the formation of hypertrophic scar. When this scar tissue grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound , it is known as a keloid. Collagen plays a role in the normal adherence of tissue edges at the site of injury. Contraction in the size of a wound is an important part of the normal healing process . An exaggeration of this process gives rise to contractures. They are particularly prone to develop on the palms, soles , anterior thorax and are commonly seen after serious burns. Inadequate formation of granulation tissue or formation of a scar leads to wound dehiscence and ulceration. The following image shows a hypertrophic scar.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old man comes with the following findings. He says that he cut himself while shaving 3 months back. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The history of a shaving cut and the image showing a large area of scar tissue are suggestive of a keloid . A keloid refers to excess accumulation of collagen at the scar site with growth of the scar tissue beyond the boundaries of the original wound . It does not regress . Option A: Exuberant granulation or proud flesh refers to the protrusion of excessive amounts of granulation tissue above the level of the surrounding skin. This blocks re-epithelialization . Option B: The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen may give rise to a raised scar known as a hypertrophic scar. However, it remains within the boundaries of the original scar. Option D: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, vascular tumor.119

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the OPD with the following finding on her finger. She says that she cut her finger while chopping vegetables 2 weeks ago. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and clinical findings are suggestive of exuberant granulation. It is a deviation in wound healing where excessive amounts of granulation tissue protrude above the level of the surrounding skin and blocks re-epithelialization . It is also known as proud flesh .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In postoperative patients , what is the strength of the incision site in comparison with normal skin following suture removal at the end of 1 week ?
mcqs.explanation: When sutures are removed, usually at 1 week , the wound strength is approximately 10 % of that of normal skin. This increases rapidly over the next 4 weeks . Wound strength reaches approximately 70 to 80% of normal by 3 months. Beyond this, there is not much improvement.120

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with the following finding. Which of the following can cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The finding seen in the given image is pitting edema . Edema can be caused by elevated hydrostatic pressure and reduced colloid osmotic pressure . Under normal circumstances , there is little net movement of fluid out of vessels due to the balance of: • Vascular hydrostatic pressure which has the tendency to push water and salts out of capillaries into the interstitial space • Plasma osmotic pressure or colloid oncotic pressure which has a tendency to pull water and salts back into vessels . The pressure dynamics seen inside a capillary is given below .Atarterial end Atvenous end Capillary hydrostatic pressur e = 30-35 mmHg Capillary hydrostatic pressur e = 15-20 mmHg Osmotic Pressure = 25 mmH g Osmotic Pressure = 25 mmH g Hydrostatic Pressure > Osmo tic Pressure \035Fluid moves o utof the capillary Hydrostatic Pressure < Osmo tic Pressure \035Fluid moves in to the capillary128 Many pathologic disorders are associated with an increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure or a decrease in plasma osmotic pressure , which lead to edema .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about transudate ?

options.a: It is a non-inflammatory edema or effusion
options.b: It is a protein-poor and cell -poor fluid
options.c: It has a specific gravity of less than 1.
options.d: It is caused by increased vascular permeability

mcqs.explanation: Transudate results from increased fluid pressures or diminished oncotic forces in the plasma and is not due to increased vascular permeability . There are 2 types of extravascular fluid - transudate and exudate These differences are depicted in the image below .Transudate Exudate Non-inflammatory edema Inflammatory edema Ultrafiltrate of plasma Increasedvascular permeabili tycaused by inflammatory me diators Low protein content (<3g/dl) , mainly albumin High (>3g/dl) protein content No tendency to coagulate Coagulates readily due to hig h content of fibrinogen Low specific gravity (<1.012 ) High specific gravity (>1.018) Low LDH levels High LDH levels Low cell count (< 500-1000 / \265 L) High cell count Eg . Edema in congestive card iac failure Eg . Pus129

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions does edema result from decreased colloidal osmotic pressure ?
mcqs.explanation: In nephrotic syndrome, edema occurs due to massive proteinuria that leads to a decrease in plasma colloid osmotic pressure . The common causes of reduced plasma osmotic pressure are conditions that cause inadequate synthesis or increased loss of albumin (mainly) and other plasma proteins from circulation. These conditions include : • Protein-losing glomerulopathies (nephrotic syndrome) • Liver cirrhosis (ascites ) • Malnutrition • Protein-losing gastroenteropathy Edema can also occur due to increased hydrostatic pressure as a result of impaired venous return. This is seen in conditions like: • Congestive heart failure • Deep venous thrombosis • Renal artery stenosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true?

options.a: Periorbital edema is seen in severe renal disease
options.b: Pitting edema occurs due to edema in subcutaneous tissues
options.c: Exudative effusions are typically protein-rich and cloudy
options.d: Chylous peritoneal effusion is an example of an exudate

mcqs.explanation: Chylous peritoneal effusion caused by the lymphatic blockage is an example of a transudate . Transudative effusions are typically protein-poor, translucent , and straw-colored . However, there may be certain exceptions like chylous peritoneal effusions which may be milky due to the presence of lipids absorbed from the gut .130 Exudative effusions are protein-rich and often cloudy due to the presence of WBCs. Subcutaneous edema has the following features : • Dependent edema - dependent areas (towards gravity) have high hydrostatic pressures i.e., in the legs when standing and the sacrum when recumbent • Pitting edema - finger pressure over markedly edematous subcutaneous tissue displaces the interstitial fluid and leaves a depression . Edema resulting from renal dysfunction often appears initially in parts of the body containing loose connective tissue , such as the eyelids . Thus, periorbital edema is a characteristic finding in severe renal disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false ?

options.c: Arteriolar dilation is seen in hyperemia.

mcqs.explanation: Hyperemia is seen in inflammation, not congestion . The differences between hyperemia and congestion are summarised below :Hyperemia Congestion Active process due to arteriol ar dilation Passive process due to impair ed venous outflow Edema is absent Edema is present Red color of the tissues Blue-red color of the tissue (d ue to deoxyhemoglobin ) Seen in inflammation Seen in right heart failure an d portal venous obstruction i n cirrhosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 82-year-old man presents to the ER with fever and tachycardia since last night. On examination , he is drowsy , his BP is 92/54 mmHg and his temperature is 103 \260F. His wife tells you he had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection 5 days ago for which he had been prescribed antibiotics. He is a known case of colon cancer and also has a history of myocardial infarction 6 months ago. What type of shock is he likely suffering from?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of septic shock as a result of gram-negative sepsis originating from a urinary tract infection . Gram-negative organisms contain lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane, which triggers the release of cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF). These cytokines cause a cascade of events culminating in increased capillary permeability and redistribution of circulatory volume into the interstitium . It is also known as warm shock, due to fever and increased perfusion . Other types of shock are: • Anaphylactic shock - sudden circulatory collapse due to type I hypersensitivity reaction • Cardiogenic shock - ventricular failure, often following myocardial infarction; is a form of cold shock • Hypovolemic shock - due to blood or fluid loss131

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the first step of hemostasis ?

options.d: Binding of platelets to exposed vWF

mcqs.explanation: The first step of hemostasis is arteriolar vasoconstriction. The normal process of hemostasis is as follows : • Arteriolar vasoconstriction - After vascular injury, local neurohumoral factors induce transient vasoconstriction. • Primary hemostasis - The various steps involved in this process are: • Platelets bind via glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptors to von Willebrand factor (vWF ) on exposed extracellular matrix (ECM ) • Activation of platelets which undergo a change in shape and release their granules • Released adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and thromboxane A2 (TxA2 ) induce additional platelet aggregation through platelet GpIIb-IIIa receptor binding to fibrinogen • Formation of the primary platelet plug • Secondary hemostasis - Local activation of the coagulation cascade involving tissue factor and platelet phospholipids results in fibrin polymerization, cementing the platelets into a definitive secondary hemostatic plug . • Clot stabilization and resorption - Counter-regulatory mechanisms, mediated by tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, a fibrinolytic product ) and thrombomodulin, confine the hemostatic process to the site of injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following coagulation factors is bound and activated by tissue factor?
mcqs.explanation: The tissue factor binds and activates factor VII . Tissue factor is produced by the subendothelial cells in the vessel wall such as vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. It is a membrane-bound procoagulant glycoprotein . Secondary hemostasis involves a sequence of events , which results in the polymerization of fibrin. This is achieved by cross-linking fibrin monomers into insoluble strands that serve to stabilize the loose platelet clot formed in primary hemostasis .132

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not found in \037-granules of platelets ?
mcqs.explanation: Serotonin is present in the dense or delta (\033) granules of the platelets , not alpha(\037) granules. Platelets are disc-shaped , anucleate cell fragments that are released from the megakaryocytes in the bone marrow into the bloodstream . The functions of these platelets depend on their glycoprotein receptors , contractile cytoskeleton , and cytoplasmic granules. There are two types of cytoplasmic granules present in platelets : • Alpha granules • Dense or delta granules \037-granules contain: • Adhesion molecule P-selectin on their membranes133 • Proteins involved in coagulation like - • Fibrinogen • Coagulation factor V • vWF • Protein factors involved in wound healing like - • Fibronectin • Platelet factor 4 (a heparin-binding chemokine) • Platelet -derived growth factor (PDGF) • Transforming growth factor �o (TGF �o ) \033-granules contain: • Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP ) • Ionized calcium • Serotonin • Epinephrine

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with prolonged bleeding is found to have vitamin K deficiency . The function of which of the following clotting factors would be unaffected in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: A deficiency of vitamin K does not alter the function of factor V. Vitamin K is required as a cofactor for the \034-carboxylation of factors II , VII , IX, and X. Calcium binds to \034-carboxylated glutamic acid residues that are present in these factors during clotting . This action of vitamin K is antagonized by drugs such as warfarin , which is widely used as an anticoagulant.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The function of which of the following factors is not screened by the partial thromboplastin time assay?
mcqs.explanation: The partial thromboplastin time (PTT) assay screens the function of the proteins in the intrinsic pathway . As factor VII is only a part of the extrinsic pathway , it cannot be assessed by this test . The factors assessed by the PTT assay are XII, XI, IX, VIII , X, V, and II and fibrinogen. In this assay, clotting of plasma is initiated by the addition of negatively charged particles (e.g., ground glass ) that activate factor XII (Hageman factor) together with phospholipids and calcium, and the time to fibrin clot formation is recorded .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the function of thrombomodulin?
mcqs.explanation: Thrombomodulin is an anticoagulant.134 It is produced by all endothelial cells except those in cerebral microcirculation. It binds to thrombin on the endothelial cell surface . When bound in this complex , thrombin loses its ability to activate coagulation factors and platelets , and instead cleaves and activates protein C. Activated protein C/protein S complex is a potent inhibitor of coagulation factors Va and VIIIa . This action results in an anticoagulant effect . The effect of recombinant thrombomodulin administration in sepsis -induced coagulopathy and DIC is being studied currently. Other important anticoagulant substances are: • Antithrombin III - It inhibits the activity of thrombin and other factors like XIIa, XIa, Xa, and IXa. It is activated by binding to heparin-like molecules . • Proteins C and S - These proteins are vitamin K–dependent proteins that inactivate factors Va and VIIIa . • Endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2 ) and nitric oxide (NO) - These are potent vasodilators and inhibitors of platelet aggregation . • Tissue factor pathway inhibitor - This is derived from the endothelium and inhibits tissue factor VIIa and Xa molecules .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Leiden mutation is of factor:
mcqs.explanation: Leiden mutation is a single nucleotide mutation that occurs in factor V . This is named after the city in The Netherlands where it was discovered . Of the inherited causes of hypercoagulability , point mutations in the factor V gene and prothrombin gene are the most common.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a part of Virchow's triad?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperviscosity is not part of Virchow's triad. However, hyperviscosity states as in polycythemia vera may, in turn, cause small vessel stasis that may cause thrombosis. Virchow's triad in thrombosis: • Injury to endothelial cells can alter local blood flow and affect coagulability . • Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence ), in turn, can cause endothelial injury. • Hypercoagulability of blood These factors may promote thrombosis independently or in combination.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following structures are lines of Zahn seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Thrombi often have grossly and microscopically apparent laminations called lines of Zahn . These are formed by pale platelet and fibrin deposits alternating with darker red cell -rich layers.135 They signify that a thrombus has formed in flowing blood. Their presence can therefore distinguish antemortem clots from the nonlaminated postmortem clots . The below histopathological image of a thrombus shows these alternating bands called lines of Zahn.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following do chicken fat clots refer to?
mcqs.explanation: Chicken fat clots refer to post -mortem clots i.e., clots that are formed after death . Postmortem clots are gelatinous and have a dark red (currant jelly ) dependent portion where red cells have settled by gravity and a yellow (chicken fat) upper portion due to coagulation of plasma. Antemortem clots can be differentiated from postmortem clots by: • Presence of lines of Zahn136 • Attachment to the underlying vessel wall

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Saddle embolus is seen in which of the following vessels ?
mcqs.explanation: An embolus in the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery is referred to as a saddle embolus . Pulmonary emboli (PE) originate from deep venous thromboses and are the most common form of thromboembolic disease . In more than 95% of cases , PE originates from leg deep vein thrombi (DVTs ). Fragmented thrombi from DVTs are carried through progressively larger veins and the right side of the heart, before slamming into the pulmonary arterial vasculature. Depending on the size of the embolus , it can have 3 fates : • It can occlude the main pulmonary artery • It can straddle the pulmonary artery bifurcation (saddle embolus ) • It can pass out into the smaller, branching arteries The CT image given below shows a saddle embolus lodged in the main pulmonary artery extending into both its limbs as indicated by the red arrows.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Following autopsy , an H&E stained specimen of the lung was obtained which is given below . What could be the likely cause of death ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the presence of laminated swirls of squamous cells in the pulmonary arteriole which is characteristically seen in amniotic fluid embolism(AFE).137 AFE is a life -threatening obstetric emergency characterized by sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The underlying cause is the infusion of amniotic fluid or fetal tissue into the maternal circulation via a tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins. Findings at autopsy include : • Presence in the maternal pulmonary micro-vasculature of- • Squamous cells shed from fetal skin • Lanugo hair • Fat from vernix caseosa • Mucin derived from the fetal respiratory or gastrointestinal tract • Marked pulmonary edema • Diffuse alveolar damage • Presence of fibrin thrombi in many vascular beds due to DIC

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in patients with DIC?
mcqs.explanation: Increased prothrombin time (PT) is a feature of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acute , subacute , or chronic thrombohemorrhagic disorder occurring as a secondary complication in a variety of diseases . It is characterized by the activation of the coagulation sequence , which leads to the formation of microthrombi throughout the microcirculation of the body. As a consequence of the thrombotic diathesis , there is a consumption of platelets , fibrin, and coagulation factors and, secondarily, activation of fibrinolytic mechanisms. Laboratory investigations in DIC reveal the following :138 • Thrombocytopenia • Prolonged prothrombin time (PT)/thrombin time (TT) • Decreased fibrinogen level • Elevated levels of fibrin-split products (D-dimers)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Red infarcts do not occur in which of the following organs?
mcqs.explanation: White infarcts occur in the spleen , not red infarcts. Red infarcts occur in the following conditions: • Venous occlusions (e.g., testicular torsion) • Loose, spongy tissues (e.g., lung), where blood can collect in the infarcted zone • Tissues with dual circulations (e.g., lung and small intestine ), which allows blood to flow from an unobstructed parallel supply into a necrotic zone • Tissues previously congested by sluggish venous outflow • When flow is re-established at a site of previous arterial occlusion and necrosis (e.g., following angioplasty of an arterial obstruction) The below image shows a hemorrhagic, roughly wedge -shaped pulmonary red infarct.White infarcts occur with arterial occlusions in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (e.g., heart, spleen, and kidney), and where tissue density limits the seepage of blood from adjoining capillary beds into the necrotic area. The below image shows a sharply demarcated white infarct in the spleen .139 Septic infarctions occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize or when microbes seed necrotic tissue . In these cases , the infarct is converted into an abscess , with a correspondingly greater inflammatory response .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A bridge construction worker presents with generalized bone pain. He is found to have ischemic necrosis of bilateral femoral heads , left tibia, and right humerus. Caisson disease is suspected . What is this condition related to?
mcqs.explanation: Caisson disease is a chronic form of decompression sickness which occurs when individuals experience a sudden decrease in atmospheric pressure . It is named after the pressurized vessels that are used in bridge construction as workers in these vessels are known to suffer from both acute and chronic forms of decompression sickness. When air is breathed at high pressure , increased amounts of gas, particularly nitrogen, are dissolved in the blood and tissues . If there is a sudden fall in pressure , the nitrogen comes out of the solution in the tissues and the blood and forms gas emboli. In Caisson disease , the persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system leads to the development of multiple foci of ischemic necrosis. The more common sites are the femoral heads , tibia, and humeri.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Chest X-ray of a 60-year-old woman with dyspnoea at rest revealed right-sided pleural effusion. A pleural fluid analysis was done. Which of the following findings would rule out a transudative cause ?
mcqs.explanation: High plasma protein content in the pleural fluid would rule out a transudative cause . In a transudative effusion , the fluid has low protein content , little or no cellular material, and low specific gravity. It is essentially an ultrafiltrate of the blood plasma. It is produced as a result of osmotic or hydrostatic imbalance across the vessel wall. There is no increase in vascular permeability . The table below gives the differences between transudative and exudative effusion .140 Features Transudate Exudate Process Passive (increased pressure ) Active (inflammation) Vascular permeability Normal Increased Plasma protein leak Absent Present Protein content of fluid Low S.G<1.012Low protein High S.G>1.020High prot ein Fibrin Absent Present Inflammatory cells Absent Present141

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are caused by single -gene mutations?
mcqs.explanation: Mendelian disorders are caused by single -gene mutations. A mutation is defined as a permanent change in the genetic material that can result in altered protein function and phenotypic changes . Mutations that affect germ cells are transmitted to the progeny and can give rise to inherited diseases . Human genetic disorders can be broadly classified into three categories : • Single -gene mutations - these diseases usually follow the classic Mendelian pattern of inheritance. • Chromosomal disorders - These arise from the structural or numerical alteration in the autosomes and sex chromosomes. Like a monogenic disease , they are uncommon but associated with high penetrance . • Complex multigenic disorders - They are more common and are caused by interactions between multiple variant forms of genes and environmental factors. Such variations in genes are common within the population and are also called polymorphisms .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases is associated with non-sense mutation?
mcqs.explanation: A non-sense mutation is seen in �o 0 thalassemia. A point mutation is a change in which a single base is substituted with a different base. The point mutations within the coding sequences of the DNA are of two types :153 • Missense mutations: These involve alteration of a single base in a triplet of bases . It leads to the replacement of one amino acid by another in the gene product . These mutations alter the meaning of the sequence of the encoded protein. Based on the substituted amino acid coded , the missense mutations are again of two types : • Conservative missense mutation: The substituted amino acid is biochemically similar to the original. It typically causes little change in the function of the protein. • Non-conservative missense mutation: This type of mutation replaces the normal amino acid with a biochemically different one. • Nonsense mutations: It is a point mutation in a sequence of DNA that results in a premature stop codon. For example , a point mutation affecting the codon for glutamine (CAG) creates a stop codon (UAG) if U is substituted for C. This change leads to premature termination of �o -globin gene translation, and the short peptide that is produced is rapidly degraded . The resulting deficiency of �o -globin chains can give rise to a severe form of anemia called �o 0 thalassemia . Option B: \037-thalassemias are caused by inherited deletions that result in the reduced or absent synthesis of \037-globin chains. Option C: Sickle-cell anemia is an example of non-conservative missense mutation. It occurs due to the replacement of the 6th glutamic acid by valine in the beta -globin gene on chromosome 11 . Option D: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder caused by intrinsic defects in the red cell membrane skeleton that render red cells spheroid less deformable and vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following traits are examples of co-dominance inheritance?
mcqs.explanation: ABO blood group and HLA are both examples of codominant inheritance. In a codominant phenotype , alleles of a gene pair in a heterozygote are fully expressed . Thereby resulting in an offspring with a phenotype that is neither dominant nor recessive and both the alleles of a gene pair contributes to the phenotype . Mendelian traits are usually described as dominant or recessive : • A dominant allele produces a dominant phenotype in individuals who have one copy of the allele , which can come from just one parent. • A recessive allele produces a recessive phenotype , in individuals who have two copies of the allele , one from each parent. The illustration below shows the codominant inheritance pattern of the blood group.154 Hair colour, height , and skin color are polygenic traits.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the term for the phenomenon where a single mutant gene leads to many end-effects ?
mcqs.explanation: Pleiotropism is characterized by a single mutant gene , which may lead to many end effects . For example , in sickle-cell anemia, the point mutation in the gene not only predisposes the red blood cells to hemolysis but can also block the vessels . This leads to splenic fibrosis, organ infarcts, and bone changes . The numerous differing end-organ derangements are all related to the primary defect in hemoglobin synthesis . Option B: In variable expressivity , a trait is seen in all individuals carrying the mutant gene but is expressed differently among them. Option C: Polymorphisms are caused by interactions between multiple variant forms of genes and environmental factors. Option D: Genetic heterogeneity refers to mutations at several genetic loci that may produce the same trait. An example of this is profound childhood deafness - an apparently homogeneous clinical entity that results from many different types of autosomal recessive mutations.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is autosomal dominant?
mcqs.explanation: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder. It is caused by a mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor -3 (FGFR-3) gene . The primary defect is abnormal chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate that causes development of short and thick bones. Clinical features :155 • Short limbs • Normal trunk • Large head • Saddle nose • Exaggerated lumbar lordosis • Severe spinal deformity may lead to cord compression

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old woman presents with sudden onset chorea and behavioral changes . Genetic investigation reveals CAG repeats . What is the mode of inheritance of this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Huntington's disease . It is an autosomal-dominant inherited disorder. Huntington disease (HD) also known as Huntington chorea is associated with CAG repeats and anticipation. It has an adult -onset and cell loss within a specific subset of neurons in the basal ganglia and cortex is seen . The characteristic features of HD include involuntary movements, dementia , and behavioral changes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old man is being evaluated for weakness and atrophy of distal limb musculature . Physical examination showing characteristic facies is given below . What is the mode of inheritance of this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and image showing the characteristic hatchet facies are suggestive of myotonic dystrophy (dystonia myotrophica). It is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder affecting muscle function. There are mainly two types : • DM1 - In this type , the affected gene is DMPK, which codes for myotonic dystrophy protein kinase, a protein expressed predominantly in skeletal muscle . The gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 19.156 • DM2 - It is caused by a defect of the CNBP gene on chromosome 3.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: After evaluation, a patient with the given finding is diagnosed with Bourneville disease . What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)/ Bourneville disease is an autosomal-dominant genetic disorder. TSC affects the differentiation , proliferation, and migration of cells early in development . This results in a variety of hamartomatous lesions that may affect virtually every organ system of the body. Two distinct genetic loci have been identified which are on chromosome 9 (TSC1 ) and on chromosome 16 (TSC2 ). The most common cutaneous manifestation of TSC is hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf macules ) and is observed in most children with tuberous sclerosis . It presents at birth or appears within the first few years of life and may fade or disappear in adulthood . The following image shows an ash-leaf macule .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases have autosomal recessive inheritance?
mcqs.explanation: Albinism is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man presents with a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure . He was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus . Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly . His liver microscopy on Prussian blue staining is given below . What is the mode of inheritance of his disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of hereditary hemochromatosis. It is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder that involves the HFE gene . Hemochromatosis is characterized by excessive iron accumulation that results in tissue damage . It consists of a triad of:157 • Micronodular cirrhosis • Bronzing of the skin • Diabetes mellitus Diagnosis is by elevated levels of serum ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation, and confirmation by a gene assay. Note : Autosomal recessive disorders include almost all inborn errors of metabolism .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients has a disease showing the given mode of inheritance?

options.a: A 16-year-old boy with hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon
options.b: A 15-year-old boy with ataxia, cardiomegaly , scoliosis , and pes cavus
options.d: A 1-year-old boy with micro-thrombocytopenia , eczema and recurrent infections

mcqs.explanation: The given pedigree chart is pointing towards an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. A boy with cardiomegaly , scoliosis , and pes cavus is suggestive of Friedreich's ataxia. This is an autosomal recessive inherited disease , resulting from a mutation of a gene locus on chromosome 9. The condition causes nervous system damage and movement problems . It usually begins in childhood and leads to impaired muscle coordination (ataxia) that worsens over time. Scoliosis, cardiomegaly , and foot problems may also develop . Option A: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon are suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) which is an autosomal-dominant inherited disorder. Option C: Vitamin D–resistant rickets is an X-linked dominant inherited disorder. Option D: A child with a triad of micro-thrombocytopenia , eczema, and recurrent infections points towards Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. It is an X-linked recessive inherited disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A newborn on routine head -to-toe examination was found to have ambiguous genitalia . Further investigations confirmed a deficiency of the 21 -hydroxylase enzyme. What is the mode of inheritance of the given condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia . It includes a group of autosomal recessive disorders, each of which involves a deficiency of an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone , or both. The most common form is known to occur due to the deficiency of 21 -hydroxylase , resulting from mutations or deletion of CYP21A .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A baby is brought to the OPD with a history of vomiting and poor feeding . Examination reveals a musty odor in the baby's sweat and urine. Guthrie 's test is found to be positive . Which of the following is false about this condition?

options.a: The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive
options.b: It is due to mutations in the PKU gene
options.c: It is an inborn error of amino acid metabolism

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of phenylketonuria (PKU). It is caused by mutations in the PAH gene which encodes for phenylalanine hydroxylase . Phenylketonuria is the most common inborn error of amino acid metabolism . It is less commonly known as phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency . The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive .158

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year old man presents to the clinic with complaints of lower back pain and passing dark red -colored urine. He was diagnosed with malaria and is on antimalarials for the past 3 days. The peripheral smear of the patient is shown below . What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of glucose -6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency . It is the most common enzyme deficiency in humans, inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder. The gene that codes for G6PD is located in the distal long arm of the X chromosome at the Xq28 locus . The inheritance pattern is similar to that of hemophilia and color blindness , where males usually manifest the abnormality and females are carriers. Females may be symptomatic if they are homozygous or if inactivation of their normal X chromosome occurs.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with delayed developmental milestones . On examination , multiple lip lacerations and the given nail findings are noted . Laboratory reports reveal hyperuricemia . What is the mode of inheritance in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome. It is an X-linked recessive inherited disorder characterized by the deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine -guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT). Lesch–Nyhan syndrome and its variants are caused by mutations in the HPRT gene on the X chromosome. The disorder is associated with 3 major clinical elements : • Overproduction of uric acid (hyperuricemia) • Neurologic disability - intellectual disability and delayed milestones • Behavioral problems - self -mutilation (excessive biting of lips and nails)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 6-foot-5-inch man undergoing a routine physical examination was found to have an early diastolic murmur . His family pedigree chart is given below . Identify the mode of inheritance of this condition.
mcqs.explanation: The patient 's height and the presence of early diastolic murmur in the given clinical scenario are suggestive of Marfan syndrome. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant disorder. The family pedigree confirms the mode of inheritance. The following flow chart helps in making out the pattern of inheritance from a given pedigree chart.159 Patients with Marfan syndrome have pleiotropic manifestations : • Skeletal systems - Tall and decreased upper to lower segment ratio with long arms, hands, and fingers • Deformities of the chest wall, vertebral column, and foot arches • Cardiovascular abnormalities - mitral valve prolapse leading to mitral regurgitation and dilatation of aortic root leading to aortic regurgitation , aortic dissection , and rupture . • Ocular - superio -temporal lens dislocation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old girl with the given physical findings develops mitral regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse . Eye examination reveals bilateral dislocation of the lens. This condition most commonly results from an inherited defect in which of the following proteins ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marfan's syndrome. It is due to the inherited defect of the protein fibrillin 1. Fibrillin is a major building block of microfibrils. This constitutes the structural components of the suspensory ligament of the ocular lens and serves as substrates for elastin in the aorta and other connective tissues . It occurs in two homologous forms: • Fibrillin-1: encoded by FBN1, mapped on chromosomes 15q21 .1. Mutations cause Marfan's syndrome. • Fibrillin-2: encoded by FBN2, mapped on chromosomes 5q23 .31 .
