Mutations cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The most striking abnormalities of the Marfan syndrome are seen in which of the following systems ?
mcqs.explanation: 160 Skeletal abnormalities are the most striking feature of Marfan syndrome. Skeletal abnormalities include : • Unusually tall, with exceptionally long extremities and long, tapering fingers and toes • The joint ligaments in the hands and feet are lax, suggesting that the patient is double -jointed . Typically , the thumb can be hyper -extended back to the wrist • The head is commonly dolichocephalic (long-headed ) with bossing of the frontal eminences and prominent supraorbital ridges Spinal deformities include : • Kyphosis • Scoliosis • Rotation/slipping of the dorsal or lumbar vertebrae • Pectus excavatum (deeply depressed sternum) • Pigeon-breast deformity Ocular changes include bilateral subluxation or dislocation (outward and upward ) of the lens, referred to as ectopia lentis . Cardiovascular lesions are the most life -threatening features of this disorder. The two most common lesions are: • Mitral valve prolapse • Dilation of the ascending aorta due to cystic medionecrosis The images given below show features seen in patients with Marfan's syndrome.161

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiovascular lesions , like rupture of aortic dissections , are the most life -threatening features of the Marfan syndrome. The weakening of the media predisposes the aorta to an intimal tear. It may initiate an intramural hematoma that cleaves the layers of the media to produce aortic dissection . After causing the cleavage of the aortic layers for a considerable length , sometimes extending to the root of the aorta or down to the iliac arteries, the hemorrhage often ruptures through the aortic wall. Although mitral valve lesions are more frequent, they are clinically less important than aortic lesions. Loss of connective tissue support in the mitral valve leaflets makes them soft and billowy , creating a so-called floppy valve.162 Valvular lesions , along with the lengthening of the chordae tendineae , frequently give rise to mitral regurgitation. Similar changes may affect the tricuspid and, rarely, the aortic valves.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following mode of inheritances is seen in Ehler –Danlos syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The mode of inheritance of Ehler –Danlos syndrome (EDS) encompasses two Mendelian patterns , namely: • Autosomal dominant • Autosomal recessive The biosynthesis of collagen can be disturbed by genetic errors that may affect any one of the numerous structural collagen genes or enzymes necessary for posttranscriptional modifications of collagen . Such molecular heterogeneity results in the expression of EDS as a clinically variable disorder, with varied patterns of inheritance.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman presents with back pain and weakness . On examination, she is found to have lax skin. X-ray findings are shown below . Lab reports show a deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of the kyphoscoliotic form of Ehlers -Danlos syndrome (EDS). This was previously known as Type VI EDS. The kyphoscoliotic form of EDS is caused by the deficient activity of the enzyme procollagen -lysine , 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1 (PLOD1 , or lysyl hydroxylase 1). It is a generalized connective tissue disorder characterized by: • Friable hyperextensible skin • Thin scars • Easy bruising • Generalized joint laxity • Severe muscular hypotonia at birth • Progressive scoliosis may be present at birth or may develop within the first year of life

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What type of collagen is involved in the classic Ehlers -Danlos syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Classic Ehlers -Danlos syndromes (EDS) type involves type V collagen (defects in genes COL5A1 and COL5A2). Types I and II of EDS are termed as classic forms. Type I is severe , while type II is milder. It has an autosomal-dominant type of inheritance. Clinically, this type is characterized by skin and joint hypermobility, atrophic scars, and easy bruising.163

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers -Danlos syndrome is classified as:
mcqs.explanation: Dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers -Danlos syndrome (EDS) is type VIIc .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following pair is incorrectly matched ?
mcqs.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy has an autosomal recessive inheritance, not autosomal dominant.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 1-month-old infant diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis , and hepatosplenomegaly . Bilateral adrenal calcification was noted radiologically . Which of the following enzyme is deficient in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Wolman disease . It is due to a deficiency of the lysosomal acid lipase enzyme. It is an autosomal recessive disease . It leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides . It presents in the first few weeks of life with: • Failure to thrive • Vomiting • Abdominal distention • Steatorrhea • Hepatosplenomegaly • Hyperlipidemia • Extensive bilateral calcifications of the adrenal glands No specific therapy is available and death usually occurs within 6 months of life .164

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of these is not a form of sphingolipidoses ?
mcqs.explanation: Hurler disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis . Sphingolipidoses are a group of lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of sphingolipids . It includes : • Niemann–Pick disease • Fabry disease • Krabbe disease • Gaucher disease • Tay–Sachs disease • Metachromatic leukodystrophy

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common lysosomal storage disorder?
mcqs.explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.170 It is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from mutations in the gene encoding glucocerebrosidase .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 8-month-old child presents with mental retardation, blindness , and muscle weakness . On evaluation, deficiency of hexosaminidase \037-subunit is found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and hexosaminidase \037-subunit deficiency are seen in Tay–Sachs disease . Sphingolipidoses with their deficient enzyme: • GM1 Gangliosidoses - GM1 Ganglioside �o - galactosidase deficiency • Type 1- infantile, generalizsed • Type 2- juvenile • GM2 Gangliosidosis : • Tay–Sachs disease - Hexosaminidase \037-subunit • Sandhoff disease - Hexosaminidase �o -subunit • GM2 Gangliosidosis variant AB - Ganglioside activator protein Note : Tay–Sachs disease is the most common form of GM2 gangliosidosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Tay–Sachs Disease ?

options.a: Affected infants are normal at birth
options.b: Neurons in the CNS, ANS, and retina are affected
options.c: Accumulations stain positive for oil red O and Sudan black B
options.d: Whorled configurations within mitochondria are seen

mcqs.explanation: In Tay–Sachs disease , an electron microscope shows whorled configurations within lysosomes composed of onion-skin layers of membranes. Affected infants appear normal at birth but begin to manifest signs and symptoms at about 6 months of age . The involvement of neurons in the central and autonomic nervous systems and retina dominates the clinical picture . There is a severe motor and mental deterioration, beginning with motor incoordination and mental obtundation. This leads to muscular flaccidity , blindness , and increasing dementia . Over the span of 1 or 2 years, a completely vegetative state is reached , followed by death at age 2 to 3 years On histologic examination, the neurons are ballooned with cytoplasmic vacuoles, each representing a markedly distended lysosome filled with gangliosides . A cherry-red spot appears in the macula, representing the accentuation of the normal color of the macular choroid. This is in contrast with the pallor produced by the swollen ganglion cells in the remainder of the retina. This finding is characteristic of Tay-Sachs disease and other storage disorders affecting the neurons. The image given below shows a cherry-red spot on retina.171

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with metachromatic leukodystrophy will have which of the following enzyme deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive condition caused by the deficiency of arylsulfatase A. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of cerebroside sulfate . These sulfatides can contribute to white matter injury, demyelination , and gliosis . Macrophages with vacuolated cytoplasm are scattered throughout the white matter. They contain metachromatic material, which can be detected in the urine and peripheral nerves when stained with toluidine blue .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following enzyme is deficient in patients with Krabbe disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Krabbe disease is due to the deficiency of galactosylceramidase . The onset of symptoms is between 3 and 6 months of age , dominated by motor signs such as stiffness and weakness . They often don't survive beyond the age of 2 years. The brain shows loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes with a similar process affecting the peripheral nerves. The aggregation of engorged macrophages called globoid cells in the brain parenchyma and around blood vessels is the characteristic and diagnostic feature of Krabbe disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following diseases will have ceramide trihexoside accumulation?
mcqs.explanation: Ceramide trihexoside (also known as globotriaosylceramide ) is accumulated in Fabry disease . The enzyme defect seen in this disease is \037-galactosidase A.172 Clinical features : • Painful acroparaesthesia • Hypohidrosis • Abdominal cramping • Diarrhea • Small petechiae around the umbilicus • Lenticular opacities • Corneal dystrophy

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Niemann–Pick disease ?

options.a: Inherited deficiency of aryl sulfatase is present

mcqs.explanation: Niemann–Pick disease types A and B are two related disorders that are characterized by lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase . The disease is typically inherited as an autosomal recessive condition on chromosome 11 . Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive neurologic involvement, marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin , progressive wasting , and early death within the first 3 years of life . Type B disease patients have organomegaly , but generally no central nervous system involvement. They usually survive into adulthood .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Given below is an electron microscopy picture of lysosomes . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Electron microscopy showing zebra bodies is suggestive of Niemann–Pick disease . Zebra bodies are engorged secondary lysosomes that contain membranous cytoplasmic bodies resembling concentric lamellated myelin figures . Similar zebra bodies can also be seen in mucopolysaccharidoses .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding I-cell disease ?

options.a: It is characterised by defective phosphorylating enzymes
options.b: It is a glycogen storage disorder
options.c: It is associated with gingival hyperplasia
options.d: High levels of hydrolytic enzymes in plasma are seen

mcqs.explanation: Inclusion-cell (I-cell) disease , also referred to as mucolipidosis II , is a part of the lysosomal storage disease family. It is characterized by the deficiency of phosphorylating enzymes essential for the formation of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker . Acid hydrolases lacking the recognition marker cannot be targeted to the lysosomes but are secreted extracellularly . It is characterized by:173 • Coarse facial features • Gingival hyperplasia • Clouded corneas • Restricted joint movements • Claw hand deformities • Kyphoscoliosis • High plasma levels of lysosomal enzymes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about mucopolysaccharidosis ?

options.a: Hunter syndrome is due to a deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase
options.b: Hurler syndrome is due to a deficiency of \037-L-iduronidase
options.c: They are inherited as autosomal recessive traits, except Hunter syndrome
options.d: Hunter syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant disease

mcqs.explanation: All the mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited as autosomal-recessive traits except Hunter syndrome. It is inherited as an X-linked recessive disease . The mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs) are a group of closely related syndromes that result from genetically determined deficiencies of enzymes involved in the degradation of mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans ). Mucopolysaccharides are abundant in the ground substance of connective tissues . In the absence of enzymes involved in their degradation, they accumulate within lysosomes in various tissues and organs of the body. Two among these are: • Hurler syndrome - deficiency of \037-L -iduronidase • Hunter syndrome - deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which glycogen storage disorder is a lysosomal storage disease ?
mcqs.explanation: 174 Glycogen storage disorder type II , also called Pompe disease , is the only glycogen storage disease with a defect in lysosomal metabolism. It is an autosomal-recessive metabolic disorder. It is caused by the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome due to deficiency of the lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy presented with severe pain in his left leg which worsened over the last few months. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly and developmental delays were noticed . Labs revealed the following findings on light and oil immersion respectively of the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is deficient in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and bone marrow aspiration images showing necrotic bone with lack of osteocytes in the lacunae (Image A) and Gaucher cells (Image B)are suggestive of Gaucher's disease . This condition has a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase . Gaucher cells are plump macrophages that characteristically have a crumpled tissue paper appearance (Image B) of the cytoplasm. It is due to the accumulation of glucocerebrosides . They can be seen in Virchow–Robin spaces (perivascular fluid -filled cavities that surround perforating arteries and veins in the brain parenchyma) in patients with cerebral involvement.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Gaucher's disease ?

options.b: Type 1 has splenic and skeletal involvement
options.c: Type 1 has no detectable enzyme activity

mcqs.explanation: In type 1, enzyme activity is reduced but detectable . Gaucher disease is of two types :Type 1:Chronicnon -neuropat hic form Type 2:Acute neuronopathic f orm Most common Less common Spleen and skeletal system ar e mainly involved Hepatosplenomegaly is seen Spares the central nervous sy stem The central nervous system is involved Enzyme activity is reduced b ut detectable No detectable enzyme activit y Principally in Jews of Europe an stock Has no predilection for Jews Longevity is shortened Death at an early age

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old child presents with growth retardation and abdominal distension . On examination , the child has characteristic doll -like facies with thin extremities . Blood investigations reveal hypoglycemia , lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia , and hyperuricemia . USG abdomen shows hepatomegaly and renomegaly . What deficiency causes the given clinical condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Gierke disease . It is due to the deficiency of glucose 6 phosphatase enzyme. The condition usually manifests as:175 • Failure to thrive • Stunted growth • Hepatomegaly • Renomegaly Hypoglycemia is due to the failure of glucose mobilization which often leads to convulsions. Lactic acidosis , hyperlipidemia , and hyperuricemia result from deranged glucose metabolism . Many patients also develop gout , skin xanthomas, and bleeding tendency (due to platelet dysfunction ). With treatment , most patients survive and develop late complications (e.g., hepatic adenomas).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which enzyme is deficient in McArdle 's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: McArdle 's syndrome is caused due to the deficiency of muscle phosphorylase . In the skeletal muscles , as opposed to the liver, glycogen is used predominantly as a source of energy during physical activity. If enzymes hydrolyzing glucose are deficient , there will be an accumulation of glycogen in the muscles . This will cause muscle weakness due to impaired energy production . Enzyme deficiencies leading to muscle glycogen storage include : • McArdle disease /type V glycogenosis - deficiency of muscle phosphorylase • Type VII glycogen storage disease - deficiency of muscle phosphofructokinase Typically , individuals with myopathic forms present with muscle cramps after exercise . This is because lactate levels in the blood fail to rise after exercise due to a block in glycolysis .176

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: At what stage of mitosis is standard karyotyping performed ?
mcqs.explanation: Standard karyotyping refers to an arrangement of chromosomes from a cell that is undergoing mitosis at metaphase . At other mitotic stages , the chromosomes are not sufficiently condensed or are too dispersed to allow for the counting and comparison of pairs under the microscope . In a metaphase spread , the individual chromosomes take the form of two chromatids connected to the centromere . A variety of staining methods are available to identify the individual chromosomes on the basis of a distinctive and reliable pattern of alternating light and dark bands. The most common method used involves a Giemsa stain and is hence called G-banding. Standard G-banding can detect approximately 400 to 800 bands per haploid set . The image below shows G-banding (karyogram of human male using Giemsa staining):185

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: In cytogenetic terminology , how are the following marked structures designated ?
mcqs.explanation: The short arm of a chromosome (marked as 1) is designated p (for petite ), and the long arm (marked as 2) is referred to as q (the next alphabet ).In a banded karyotype , each arm of the chromosome is divided into two or more regions bordered by prominent bands. The regions are numbered (e.g., 1, 2, 3) from the centromere outward . Each region is further subdivided into bands and sub-bands, and these are ordered numerically as well .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: What aberration occurs when a break occurs at both ends of a chromosome with the fusion of the damaged ends ?
mcqs.explanation: A ring chromosome is an aberrant chromosome whose broken ends fuse together to form a ring. Ring chromosomes behave abnormally in meiosis or mitosis and usually result in serious consequences . In rare cases , the telomeres at the ends of a chromosome fuse without any loss of186 genetic material, which results in a normal phenotype . A ring chromosome is denoted by the symbol r in human genetics .The following image shows a representative karyotype from a well -differentiated transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder . The chromosome indicated by 'r' represents a ring chromosome. Also evident are monosomy 9, 18, and X and trisomy 7.Option A: In a translocation, a segment of one chromosome is transferred to another. Option C: Inversion refers to a rearrangement that involves two breaks within a single chromosome, with reincorporation of the inverted, intervening segment . Option D: Isochromosome formation results when one arm of a chromosome is lost and the remaining arm is duplicated . It results in a chromosome consisting of two short arms only or of two long arms.187

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not associated with the change in genetic material?
mcqs.explanation: Inversion involves only a rearrangement of the genetic material. There is no change in the genetic material. It occurs as a result of two breaks within a single chromosome. The intervening segment between the breaks gets inverted and reincorporated. It is of two types : • Paracentric - inversion involving only one arm of the chromosome • Pericentric - inversion involving opposite sides of the centromere Inversions are often fully compatible with normal development . Transversions are mutations where a purine base pair is replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about Down's syndrome?

options.a: Leukemia is the major cause of death in early childhood
options.b: It is the most common chromosomal disorder
options.c: Robertsonian translocations of chromosome 21 are less common
options.d: These children are prone to develop autoimmune diseases

mcqs.explanation: In Down's syndrome, the major cause of death in infancy and early childhood is cardiac disease , not leukemia. Down's syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder and is a major cause of mental retardation. Maternal age is a strong risk factor. This condition can occur by the following mechanisms: • Majority of cases - meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in the ovum • Rarely - Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14) The clinical features of Down's syndrome include : • Mental retardation • Facial dysmorphism - flat facial profile , oblique palpebral fissures , and epicanthic folds • Congenital heart disease - endocardial cushion defects (ASD, VSD, AV valve malformations)188 • Atresias of the esophagus and small bowel • Neuropathologic changes characteristic of Alzheimer's disease - in patients > 40 years • Increased risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7 ) • Predisposition to autoimmune diseases and serious lung infections

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old child was brought by the mother with complaints of delay in reaching motor milestones . Examination revealed oblique palpebral fissures , epicanthal folds , and the following finding. Auscultation revealed a pan-systolic murmur in the left sternal border. This child is at risk of developing which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing a single palmar crease (simian crease ) are suggestive of Down's syndrome. It is associated with an increased risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7 ) in affected children < 2 years old. Children with trisomy 21 have a 10 to 20 -fold increased risk of developing acute leukemia. • In children < 2 years of age - acute megakaryoblastic leukemia(AML-M7 ) is the most common • In children > 3 years of age - acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) is the most predominant

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A 7-month-old infant is being evaluated for failure to thrive. Examination reveals low-set ears, a short neck, and the following findings. Auscultation reveals a holosystolic murmur over the pulmonic area. Which of the following statements about this condition is false ?

options.b: Karyotype of this child is 47, XY +
options.c: It may be associated with horseshoe kidney
options.d: There is increased risk of leukemia

mcqs.explanation: The images show the index finger overlapping other fingers and rocker bottom feet . This along with the clinical features is suggestive of Edward 's syndrome. Leukemia is not a feature of this condition. It is due to the inheritance of a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 as a result of meiotic nondisjunction (47, XY +18). The incidence is 1 in 8000 births. The clinical features of Edward 's syndrome include : • Low-set ears • Short neck189 • Overlapping fingers • Congenital heart defects • Renal malformations • Limited hip abduction • Rocker-bottom feet • Prominent occiput • Mental retardation • Micrognathia Note : Although , rocker bottom feet are seen in both Edward 's syndrome and Patau's syndrome, overlapping of fingers is characteristic of Edward 's syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in children with Patau syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Low set ears are a feature of Patau syndrome, not high set ears. Patau syndrome occurs due to trisomy 13 and is characterized by: • Microphthalmia • Polydactyly • Microcephaly and mental retardation • Cleft lip and palate • Cardiac defects • Umbilical hernia • Renal defects • Rocker-bottom feet (commonly seen in Edwards syndrome also)190

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: What hypothesis states that one X chromosome, maternal or paternal, is randomly inactivated during development ?
mcqs.explanation: Lyon's hypothesis states the idea of the inactivation of the X chromosome. It states the following : • Only one of the X chromosomes is genetically active • The other X undergoes heteropyknosis and is rendered inactive (known as Barr body) • Inactivation of either the maternal or paternal X occurs at random among all the cells of the blastocyst on or about day 5.5 of embryonic life • Inactivation of the same X chromosome persists in all the cells derived from each precursor cell . The molecular basis of X inactivation involves the XIST gene .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man was referred for infertility evaluation. On examination, he was tall with a lack of body hair. Gynecomastia and micropenis were also noted . Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype . Which of the following statements is not true about the condition?

options.a: Levels of follicle -stimulating hormone are reduced

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter 's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle -stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated . The clinical features include : • Eunuchoid body habitus - elongated body and long legs (increased length between the soles and the pubic bone) • Absence of secondary sexual characteristics - lack of body and facial hair, deep voice • Small atrophic testes • Micropenis • Gynecomastia • Lower IQ, but no mental retardation The following hormonal variations are seen in these patients : • Elevated FSH • Elevated estradiol • Low testosterone • Insulin resistance - increased incidence of type 2 diabetes Patients with Klinefelter syndrome are at a higher risk for: • Male breast cancer (20x more common than in normal males) • Extragonadal germ cell tumors • Autoimmune diseases - systemic lupus erythematosus191

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and short stature . Examination shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples , and absent secondary sexual characteristics. USG abdomen shows a small uterus and streak ovaries. What is the most common karyotypic abnormality seen in individuals with this condition?

options.b: Isochromosome of the long arm of X chromosome
options.c: Deletion of portions of long arm of X chromosome
options.d: Deletion of ends of long and short arm of X chromosome

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of Turner 's syndrome. In this condition, the most common karyotypic abnormality seen is a missing entire X chromosome, seen in more than half the cases . Less commonly, structural abnormalities of the X chromosome and mosaicism can also occur. The common feature of the structural abnormalities is to produce partial monosomy of the X chromosome. In order of frequency, the structural abnormalities of the X chromosome include the following : • An isochromosome of the long arm , 46,X,i(X)(q10), resulting in the loss of the short arm • Deletion of portions of both long and short arms, resulting in the formation of a ring chromosome - 46, X,r(X) • Deletion of portions of the short or long arm - 46X,del (Xq) or 46X,del (Xp ). The mosaic patients have a 45,XO cell population along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal cell types . Few patients with this condition also have Y-chromosome sequences , either as a complete Y chromosome or as fragments of Y chromosomes translocated on other chromosomes. These patients are at a higher risk for the development of a gonadal tumor (gonadoblastoma ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is not caused by trinucleotide -repeat mutations involving non-coding regions?
mcqs.explanation: Huntington's disease is due to CAG (trinucleotide ) repeat mutation in the coding region of the gene , not the non-coding region. Expansion of trinucleotide repeats is an important genetic cause of human disease , particularly neurodegenerative disorders. The causative mutations are associated with the expansion of a stretch of trinucleotides that usually share the nucleotides G and C. In all cases , the DNA is unstable , and an expansion of the repeats above a certain threshold impairs gene function. Expansions affecting noncoding regions will cause a loss of function mutation. They include : • Fragile X syndrome • Myotonic dystrophy • Friedreich ataxia Expansions affecting coding regions cause a gain of function mutation. They include : • Spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease ) • Huntington disease • Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (Haw–River syndrome) • Spinocerebellar ataxia types 1, , , ,

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: All of the following are features of fragile X syndrome except :
mcqs.explanation: Macro-orchidism (large testicles ) are seen in fragile X syndrome, not micro-orchidism. Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common). It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation, characterised by multiple tandem repeats of the CGG sequence in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene . It is associated with the phenomenon of anticipation, where the disease phenotype worsens over generations within a family. The affected males are mentally retarded , with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60. The characteristic phenotypic features include the following : • Long face with a large mandible • Large everted ears • Macro-orchidism • Hyperextensible joints • High arched palate • Mitral valve prolapse The given image shows a child suffering from fragile X syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: 70 CGG premutations in the FMR1 gene are characteristic of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: CGG premutations in the FMR1 gene are characteristic of fragile X ataxia. It is also known as fragile X tremor and fragile X-associated primary ovarian failure. Normally, the FMR1 gene is methylated and silenced , and the number of CGG repeats remains < .193 However, abnormalities in this gene lead to the accumulation of CGG-containing FMR1 mRNAs, which are toxic to the cell . Depending on the type of mutation, there are 2 distinct syndromes: • Fragile X ataxia syndrome (FXTAS): -200 repeats (premutation ) which causes gain of function • Fragile X syndrome (FXs ): - 4000 repeats (full mutation) leading to loss of function More than half the individuals with FXTAS develop a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome starting in their 6th decade . It is characterized by intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia and may progress to Parkinsonism . Option B: Prader-Willi syndrome is associated with deletion of paternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the maternal allele . Option D: Friedreich ataxia is due to GAA repeat sequences in the noncoding regions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: What is the mode of inheritance of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is an example of mitochondrial inheritance. It is inherited along the maternal line, as shown in image 4.In diseases following the mitochondrial pattern of inheritance, all children of an affected mother and normal father develop the disease . However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother do not inherit the disease . Hence, only the daughters of the affected mother will transmit the disease . This is because this condition is due to a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria. The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa have very few mitochondria if present . Hence , the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum. LHON is a neurodegenerative disease that manifests as progressive bilateral loss of central vision. Visual impairment starts between ages 15 and 35, leading eventually to blindness . Other features include cardiac conduction defects and minor neurologic manifestations .194

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which chromosome is involved in myotonic dystrophy ?
mcqs.explanation: Chromosome 19 is involved in myotonic dystrophy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Maltese cross crystals in the urine are seen in which of the following diseases other than nephrotic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Maltese cross crystals in the urine are seen in Fabry's disease . Urine analysis in Fabry's disease may reveal oval fat bodies and birefringent glycolipid globules under polarized light showing a Maltese cross appearance . It can also be seen in nephrotic syndrome. The following image shows Maltese cross casts:Note : Maltese cross appearance is also seen in short-range shotgun wounds and babesiosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A young male patient as shown below presents with complaints of infertility . On examination, he lacked pubic and facial hair. The genital examination was consistent for a micropenis. Further investigations reveal elevated LH and FSH levels . What is the most common cardiac lesion associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture most likely suggests Klinefelter 's syndrome. The most common cardiac lesion in this condition is mitral valve prolapse which is seen in nearly half the adults . Systemic manifestations associated with Klinefelter 's syndrome: • Gynecomastia • Type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome • Mitral valve prolapse • Osteoporosis and fractures195 • Male infertility • Higher risk for breast cancer, extragonadal germ-cell tumors • Systemic lupus erythematosus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Huntington's chorea?

options.a: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder
options.b: There is loss of function type of mutation
options.c: There are abnormal repeats of CUG
options.d: Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome

mcqs.explanation: Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide repeat disorder. It is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats (>40). It occurs due to a gain-of-function (expansion) mutation in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p. The disease shows genetic anticipation and has an early-onset (2-3 decades ) if inherited from the father. Cognitive impairment is an early feature. Pathologically , atrophy of caudate and putamen with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly is seen . Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia and decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea. Treatment consists of haloperidol and tetrabenazine . Trinucleotide repeat disorders:Disease Repe ats Clinical features Fragile X- syndrome CGG Mental retardation, large ear s, and jaws, macroorchidism in males Myotonic Dystrophy (chromo some 19) CTG Muscle loss, cardiac arrhyth mia,cataracts, frontal balding Huntington's disease CAG Affective disorder Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 CAG Progressive ataxia, dysarthria, dysmetria . Friedreich's ataxia GAA Progressive ataxia,dysarthria, hypertrophiccardiomyopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: Which amongst the following is true about Turner 's syndrome?

options.a: Webbing of hands and toes are associated with risk of visceral anomalies
options.b: Noonan syndrome is more associated with cardiac defects
options.c: Absence of neck webbing is associated with higher risk of co-arctation of aorta
options.d: Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies

mcqs.explanation: In Turner 's syndrome, webbing of the neck is associated with a higher risk of cardiac anomalies. The image below summarises the clinical features of Turner 's syndrome.196 The image given below shows the webbing of neck.Noonan syndrome is characterised by mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway . The most common of these is the PTPN11 which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase on chromosome 12 . Clinical features include : • Short stature • Short webbed neck • Cystic hygroma • Tall forehead • Low posterior hairline • Dental malocclusion197 Although it shares many clinical features with Turner 's syndrome, Noonan syndrome affects both sexes . It follows an autosomal dominant pattern and it also has a different pattern of congenital heart disease , typically involving right-sided lesions .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders and Other Genetic Disorders
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of intellectual disability . She also has difficulty in walking and balancing, and her speech is delayed for her age . The parents also say that she frequently has sudden bouts of laughter . She is a known case of seizure disorder since the age of 3. This condition is associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Angelman syndrome. It can occur due to one of the following genetic abnormalities: • Deletion (most common) - band q12 on the long arm of maternal chromosome 15 • Paternal uniparental disomy - inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from the paternal pair of chromosomes • Defective imprinting - defect in the resetting /maintaining of imprints during gametogenesis or after fertilization Chromosome 15 diseases (mnemonic - MAP): • M: Marfan syndrome • A: Angelman syndrome • P: Prader Willi syndrome The following images show children suffering from Prader-Willi syndrome.Prader-Willi syndrome AngelMan syndrome Deletion (most common) Paternal chromosome 15 Maternal chromosome 15 Uniparental disomy(less com mon) Maternal disomy(duplication ) Paternal disomy(duplication ) Clinical features Elevated ghrelin levels - hype rphagiaTruncal obesitySevere hypotoniaShort statureSmall hands and feet with hypoton iaHypogonadotropic hypogon adismCognitive impairment Short statureSeveremental re tardationwith lack of speechS tiff arm movementsSpastic , u ncoordinated walk (ataxia)Sei zuresInappropriate outbursts of laughter (happy puppets )198 The following image shows a child suffering from Angelman syndrome.199

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a hallmark of malignancy?
mcqs.explanation: Cancer cells are insensitive to growth -inhibitory signals. All cancer cells are known to show around 8 fundamental physiological changes in the cell , which are considered as the hallmarks of cancer. These changes include the following : • Self -sufficiency in growth signals - once activated, tumors can proliferate without external stimuli • Insensitivity to growth -inhibitory signals - tumors do not respond to inhibitors of cell growth . This is attributed to the inactivation of the tumor-suppressor genes in cancer cells • Altered cellular metabolism - tumor cells switch to aerobic glycolysis , called the Warburg effect • Evasion of apoptosis • Limitless replicative potential • Sustained angiogenesis • Ability to invade and metastasis • Ability to evade the host immune response

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the Warburg effect ?

options.a: Cancer cells are characterized by high levels of glucose uptake
options.b: Cancer cells convert glucose to lactic acid even in the presence of ample oxygen
options.c: Conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the HMP pathway
options.d: Aerobic glycolysis provides cancer cells with metabolic intermediates

mcqs.explanation: Increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the glycolytic pathway (not HMP). Even in the presence of ample oxygen , cancer cells demonstrate a distinctive form of cellular metabolism . This is characterized by high levels of glucose uptake and increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid via the glycolytic pathway . This phenomenon is called the Warburg effect . Aerobic glycolysis provides rapidly dividing tumor cells with metabolic intermediates that are required for the synthesis of cellular components , whereas mitochondrial oxidative phosphor - ylation? does not.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about adenomas?

options.d: They can be of non-glandular origin

mcqs.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is an example of a mixed tumor consisting of epithelial and myoepithelial cells with or without stromal components . Adenomas are benign epithelial tumors. They can arise from: • Glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example , follicular adenomas of the thyroid, which arise from the thyroid gland and forms glandular structures • Glandular cells but form non-glandular structures - for example , heterogeneous mass of adrenal cortical cells growing as a solid sheet • Non-glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example , benign epithelial neoplasm that arises from renal tubular cells growing in the form of numerous tightly clustered small glands207

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All are small round blue cell tumors except :
mcqs.explanation: Hemangioblastoma is not a small round blue cell tumor. Hemangioblastomas are tumors of central nervous system that originate from vascular tissues . They demonstrate the proliferation of capillaries with variable sized , closely packed , and thin walled vessels as seen in the image below.Small round blue cell tumors consist of small round cells that stain blue on routine H&E staining sections . They include : • Neuroblastoma • Retinoblastoma • Ewing 's sarcoma • Wilms tumor • Rhabdomyosarcomas • Acute leukemia The following is the image of neuroblastoma showing Homer-Wright pseudorosettes .208

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a disorganized but benign mass composed of cells indigenous to the involved site ?
mcqs.explanation: Hamartomas are disorganized but benign, masses composed of cells indigenous to the involved site . Examples of hamartoma include : • Mammary hamartoma • Pulmonary chondromatous hamartoma • Splenic hamartoma • Neurocristic hamartoma • Fibrous hamartoma of infancy Option A: Choristomas are heterotopic rests of cells . Option D: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells . They contain recognizable mature or immature cells or tissues belonging to more than one germ cell layer, and sometimes all three germ layers. Option C: Papillomas are benign epithelial neoplasms . They are characterized by microscopically or macroscopically visible finger-like or warty projections from epithelial surfaces .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: While examining an excision biopsy sample , the pathologist notices anaplastic cells . Which of the following tumors will show this characteristic finding?
mcqs.explanation: Anaplasia or lack of differentiation is a characteristic feature of malignant neoplasm like sarcoma. Differentiation refers to the extent to which neoplastic parenchymal cells resemble the corresponding normal parenchymal cells , both morphologically and functionally .209 The image below shows a hepatocellular carcinoma characterized by large anaplastic carcinoma cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm , large hyperchromatic nuclei , and prominent nucleoli . The normal trabecular structure of the liver is distorted .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio?
mcqs.explanation: The normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio is 1:4 to 1:6. Normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio implies that the volume occupied by the cytoplasm is 4 to 6 times greater than the volume occupied by the nucleus . Abnormal nuclear morphologies that are seen in malignant cells : • Nuclei disproportionately large for the cell • Nuclear shape is variable and often irregular • Chromatin • Coarsely clumped • Hyperchromatic • Nucleoli are abnormally large

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer. Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in the microscopic examination of the resected tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Loss of polarity is a microscopic finding in malignant neoplasm , like metastatic breast cancer. In malignancy, the orientation of cells is markedly disturbed , and polarity is lost. Sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion. Morphological changes in cancer cells : • Anaplasia210 • Pleomorphism • Nuclear changes • Nuclei disproportionately large for the cell • Nuclear shape is variable and often irregular • Chromatin - coarsely clumped and hyperchromatic • Nucleoli are abnormally large • Atypical mitosis • Loss of polarity

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of post -coital bleeding . On per speculum examination , a friable mass is seen and a punch biopsy is done. The presence of which of the following features in microscopic examination of biopsy specimen differentiates invasive carcinoma from carcinoma in situ?
mcqs.explanation: Once the tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the tumor is said to be invasive . Progression of cancer occurs in the following stages : dysplasia \035carcinoma in situ\035invasive carcinoma In situ carcinoma is when dysplastic changes are marked and involve the full thickness of the epithelium , but the lesion does not penetrate the basement membrane. It is a pre-invasive neoplasm . The tumor is said to be invasive when the basement membrane is breached by the tumor cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Choose the correct statement (s):

options.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.b: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.c: A is true; R is false
options.d: A is false ; R is true

mcqs.explanation: All tumors with invasive property (malignant tumors) may not necessarily metastasize . Examples of tumors with invasive properties but do not metastasize are: • Gliomas • Basal cell carcinomas of the skin Both of these cancers invade early in their course , but rarely metastasize . Thus, it is evident then that the properties of invasion and metastasis are separable .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a breast lump. On clinical examination, nodes are not palpable . Mammography is suggestive of a malignant tumor. Which of the following nodes is often biopsied to assess the presence of metastasis microscopically ?

options.a: Largest lymph node in the region of the primary tumor
options.b: Smallest lymph node in the region of the primary tumor
options.c: First lymph node that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor
options.d: Last lymph node that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor

mcqs.explanation: The sentinel lymph node, which is the first node in a regional lymphatic basin that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor, is often used to assess the presence or absence of metastatic lesions in the lymph nodes microscopically . Sentinel node mapping can be done by the injection of radiolabeled tracers or colored dyes . Examination of frozen sections of the sentinel lymph node is often performed during surgery. It can guide the surgeon to the appropriate therapy .211 Sentinel node examination has also been used for detecting the spread of: • Melanomas • Colon cancers

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an angiogenesis promoter in tumor cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Thrombospondin is an anti-angiogenic factor. Angiogenic and antiangiogenic factors are produced by tumor and stromal cells and are essential for the vascularization of tumors. Angiogenic activators include : • Angiogenin • Interleukin-8 • Growth factors: • Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) • Basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) • Transforming growth factor (TGF)-\037 and �o • Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-\037 • Platelet -derived endothelial growth factor • Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor • Placental growth factor • Hepatocyte growth factor • Epidermal growth factor Anti-angiogenic factors include :212 • Angiostatin • Endostatin • Interferon • Platelet factor 4 • Thrombospondin • Prolactin 16 KD fragment • Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1, 2, and 3

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following malignancies is least likely to occur in those with only alcohol abuse and without any additional risk factors?
mcqs.explanation: Alcohol abuse alone increases the risk of carcinomas of the oropharynx (excluding lip), larynx, and esophagus . Alcohol and tobacco together synergistically increase the risk of cancers in the upper airway and digestive tract.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A textile factory worker who is repeatedly exposed to benzene is at increased risk of developing which of the following tumors?
mcqs.explanation: Repeated exposure to benzene is associated with increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) Malignancies associated with repeated exposure to benzene : • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) • Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL ). • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). • Multiple myeloma. Note : While studies have shown that benzene has a propensity to cause bladder carcinoma , it is most commonly associated with AMLs.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old patient employed in plastic industry for 30 years is diagnosed with a tumor in the liver. On resection , the gross specimen shows greyish white lesions with multiple reddish -brown hemorrhagic foci and several blood-filled spaces shown by arrows in the image given below . Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history and findings of the gross specimen are suggestive of angiosarcoma of the liver and beryllium is not a risk factor for the development of this tumor. Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to: • Vinyl chloride • Androgenic steroids • Arsenic • Thorotrast213 Histological specimen of angiosarcoma of the liver is given below .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with lung carcinoma . Which of the following is implicated in the causation of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Radon is implicated in the causation of lung carcinoma . Carcinogens implicated in lung carcinoma are: • Asbestos • Arsenic • Beryllium • Chromium • Nickel • Radon.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old patient who is a known case of cholangiocarcinoma presents with intermittent fever and jaundice . Which of the following organisms is commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Opisthorchis viverrini (liver fluke ) is implicated in the pathogenesis of cholangiocarcinoma. Apart from Opisthorchis viverrini , Clonorchis sinensis is also known to cause cholangiocarcinoma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the least radiosensitive cell in blood?
mcqs.explanation: The least radiosensitive cell in the blood is the platelet . The most radiosensitive cell in the blood is the lymphocyte .214 The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is G2M. The least radiosensitive is the S phase .215

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is overexpressed in patients diagnosed with glioma?
mcqs.explanation: Gliomas show overexpression of PDGF-�o and TGF-\037. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild -type glioblastomas are associated with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) amplification and homozygous CDKN2A deletion .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is associated with loss of function mutation in RET proto-oncogene ?
mcqs.explanation: Loss of function mutation in RET proto-oncogene is associated with Hirschsprung's disease . Hirschsprung's disease is caused by mutations in other genes encoding proteins involved in enteric neurodevelopment . These include : • RET ligand glial-derived neurotrophic factor • Endothelin • Endothelin receptor Note : Medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasias , types 2A and 2B are usually due to gain of function mutations in RET proto-oncogene .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors is associated with mutation of the ALK receptor ?
mcqs.explanation: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is a membrane-bound receptor tyrosine kinase. When aberrantly expressed , it is associated with neuroblastoma pathogenesis . It serves as a therapeutic target . Neuroblastoma is one of the most common solid cancers among children.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a painless loss of vision. Fundus examination reveals the lesion shown in the image. Which of the following GTP-binding proteins show point mutations in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and fundus examination are suggestive of uveal melanoma which is associated with a point mutation of GNAQ protein or GNA11 genes . Uveal melanomas (UM ) originate from melanocytes in the interior wall of the eye . This includes the iris, ciliary body, and the choroid with marked differences in light exposure (from dark anterior to illuminated posterior). GNAS mutation causes pituitary adenoma and other endocrine tumors.225 The 3 RAS genes in humans (H-RAS, K-RAS, and N-RAS) are the most common oncogenes in human cancer. They code for a family of proteins called GTP-binding (G) proteins , which are involved in transmitting signals within cells (cellular signal transduction). When RAS is 'switched on' by incoming signals, it subsequently switches on other proteins , which ultimately results in cell growth , differentiation , and survival . Mutations in RAS genes can lead to the production of permanently activated RAS proteins . As a result , this can cause unintended and overactive signaling inside the cell , even in the absence of incoming signals. Because these signals result in cell growth and division, overactive RAS signaling can ultimately lead to cancer.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following are coded by the MYC genes ?
mcqs.explanation: MYC oncogene codes for nuclear regulatory proteins . It is the most commonly involved transcription factor in tumors. The MYC proto-oncogene MYC activates the expression of many genes that are involved in cell growth. It upregulates the expression of telomerase and reprograms somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is associated with the translocation of cyclin D1?
mcqs.explanation: Translocation of cyclin D1 is seen in mantle cell lymphoma. Mantle cell lymphoma is an uncommon lymphoid neoplasm that is characterized by overexpression of cyclin D1. It is a type of non Hodgkins lymphoma that involves (11 ;14) translocation i.e. between IgH locus on chromosome 14 and the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about Knudson 's two -hit hypothesis theory on retinoblastoma?

options.a: Familial type is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
options.b: It involves both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q
options.c: In sporadic cases , both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast
options.d: In familial cases , children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene and the other copy is normal

mcqs.explanation: Retinoblastoma is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Knudson 's hypothesis , also known as the two -hit hypothesis or multiple -hit hypothesis states that cancer is the result of accumulated mutations in a cell 's DNA. Two mutations (hits), involving both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q14 , are required to produce retinoblastoma. In familial cases , children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene in the germline (the first hit), and the other copy is normal . Retinoblastoma develops when the normal RB allele is mutated in retinoblasts as a result of a spontaneous somatic mutation (the second hit). Most individuals inheriting a germline defect in one RB allele develop unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma as it is an autosomal dominant disease . Sporadic cases are comparitively rare. In sporadic cases , both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast (two hits). The image given below shows the Knudson 's two -hit hypothesis .226

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: If the RB gene is hypophosphorylated , which of the following will happen ?

options.a: Cell cycle will stop at G
options.b: Cell cycle will stop at G
options.c: There will be no effect on cell cycle as RB gene phosphorylation is not needed
options.d: The cell cycle progresses and cell divides

mcqs.explanation: If the retinoblastoma (RB) gene is hypophosphorylated , it is active and the cell cycle will stop at G1. RB is a cell -cycle regulator because it binds to and inactivates a transcription factor (E2F). This is necessary for the transcription of certain genes necessary for the progression from the G1 to S phase . The phosphorylation of RB results in the release of E2F. This activates gene transcription and cell -cycle progression occurs. The image given below shows the cell cycle regulation by RB gene .227

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about p53?

options.b: P53 inactivation causes cell cycle arrest at G2-M
options.c: Cancers demonstrate biallelic loss of function mutations in TP
options.d: p53 can be inactivated by E6 protein of HPV

mcqs.explanation: P53 is the tumor suppressor gene and activation (not inactivation) causes cell cycle arrest at the G1-S and G2-M phase of the cell cycle . P53 regulates : • Cell cycle progression • DNA repair • Cellular senescence • Apoptosis It is activated by: • Anoxia • Inappropriate signaling by mutated oncoproteins • DNA damage It is the most frequently mutated gene in cancers. It upregulates the expression of proteins such as the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, thereby causing cell -cycle arrest at the G1-S. It also transactivates and transrepresses target gene to induce G2/M arrest. Mutation in the p53 gene causes resistance in tumors to radiation and chemotherapy . The E6 protein of human papillomavirus (HPV ) binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase , thereby helping in the longevity of the cells . E6 from high-risk HPV types has a higher affinity for p53 than E6 from low-risk types . Li -Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder due to a defect in the tumor suppressor gene P53 located on chromosome 17.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia ?
mcqs.explanation: p63 is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia . p53 is ubiquitously expressed , while p63 and p73 show more tissue specificity . p73 has strong pro-apoptotic effects after DNA damage induced by chemotherapeutic agents .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old man was found to have multiple GI polyps . He was operated on for thyroid cancer 2 years back. His family history is significant for breast cancer in his mother and endometrial cancer in his aunt. Germline loss-of-function mutations of which gene is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Cowden syndrome. This condition is caused due to germline loss of function mutation in PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) gene . PTEN is a membrane-associated phosphatase encoded by a gene on chromosome 10q23 that is mutated . Cowden syndrome is characterized by skin appendage tumors and an increased incidence of epithelial cancers, particularly of the breast, endometrium , and thyroid.228

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman presented with hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI was done and showed the presence of bilateral acoustic schwannomas . Which protein involved in cytoskeletal stability is mutated in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and MRI findings are suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2). Merlin protein is mutated in NF-2, sporadic schwannomas, and meningiomas. Cells lacking Merlin do not establish stable cell -to-cell junctions. They are insensitive to normal growth arrest signals generated by cell-to-cell contact.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Germline loss-of-function mutation of which gene causes Gorlin syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Germline loss-of-function mutations of the PTCH1 gene cause Gorlin syndrome. Gorlin syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. Clinical features include : • Multiple basal cell carcinomas • Highly characteristic facies - large forehead • Bifid or misshapen ribs • Vertebral and other skeletal anomalies • Pits of the skin of the palms and soles • Dysgenesis of the corpus callosum • Calcification of the falx cerebri - at an earlier age than is seen in non\037affected individuals • Macrocephaly Acquired biallelic loss-of-function mutations of PTCH1 cause sporadic basal cell carcinomas and medulloblastoma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man patient presents with anemia and abdominal pain. On examination, he has pigmented macules over the palms, soles , and oral mucosa. Further investigations reveal loss-of-function mutations of the STK11 gene . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Loss-of-function mutations of STK11 cause the Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. The STK22 gene , also known as LKB1 , encodes a serine/threonine kinase that is an important regulator of cellular metabolism . Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. It is associated with arborizing polyps of the gastrointestinal tract (small intestine > colon > stomach). It increases the risk of multiple epithelial cancers, particularly of colon, breast, lung, pancreas, and thyroid.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with complaints of a palpable mass in both breasts. Histopathology examination shows the following finding. Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positivity . Which protein that maintains cell adhesion, and thereby inhibits cell motility , is mutated in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: 229 The given scenario is suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast which involves mutated E-cadherin protein. In this condition, the histopathological examination shows infiltrating small monomorphic discohesive tumor cells arranged in an Indian -file or single -file pattern. The image below shows the single file pattern seen in lobular carcinoma of the breast.Reduced cell surface expression of E-cadherin is seen in carcinomas of: • Breast • Esophagus • Colon • Ovary • Prostate E-cadherin is a cell -surface protein that maintains intercellular adhesiveness . Loss of E-cadherin causes disaggregation of cells , which can then invade locally or metastasize . Germline loss-of-function mutations of the E-cadherin gene lead to familial gastric carcinoma . Sporadic gastric carcinomas are also associated with the loss of E-cadherin expression.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the BRCA genes ?

options.a: BRCA1 is located on the long arm of chromosome
options.d: BRCA 2 mutation is associated with male breast carcinoma

mcqs.explanation: BRCA2 (not BRCA 1) mutation causes well -differentiated cancer.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding apoptosis ?

options.a: p53 induces apoptosis in cells with DNA damage
options.b: Extrinsic apoptotic pathway is more frequently disabled in cancer cells
options.c: Chemoradiation induces apoptosis in cancer cells
options.d: BCL2 is over-expressed in follicular lymphomas

mcqs.explanation: The intrinsic apoptotic pathway is most frequently disabled in cancer cells to evade cell death .230 p53 is an important pro-apoptotic protein that induces apoptosis in cells that are unable to repair DNA damage . Chemotherapy and radiation therapy kills cancer cells mainly by inducing apoptosis via the intrinsic pathway . In greater than 85% of follicular B-cell lymphomas, the anti-apoptotic gene BCL2 is overexpressed due to a (14;18) translocation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following genes promote epithelial -mesenchymal transition in epithelial tumors?
mcqs.explanation: SNAIL and TWIST , which encode transcription factors, promote epithelial -to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). In EMT, carcinoma cells downregulate certain epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and upregulate certain mesenchymal markers (e.g. vimentin and smooth muscle actin). This favors the development of a promigratory phenotype that is essential for metastasis . EMT has been documented mainly in breast carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase?
mcqs.explanation: ABL is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase. Tyrosine kinases may be receptors and non-receptors . Nonreceptor tyrosine kinases normally localize to the cytoplasm or the nucleus . These are: • ABL - translocation causes CML and point mutation causes ALL • JAK mutation - seen in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia , and myelofibrosis as well as other myeloproliferative disorders Receptor tyrosine kinases: • VEGFR • PDGFR • EGFR In chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and some acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ), the ABL gene is translocated from its normal abode on chromosome 9 to chromosome 22 where it fuses with the BCR gene forming the Philadelphia chromosome. The resultant chimeric gene encodes a constitutively active, oncogenic BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: The mutations/changes that convert proto-oncogene to oncogene include all except :
mcqs.explanation: Enhancer deletion does not convert a proto-oncogene to an oncogene . Mechanisms of activating oncogenes :231 Mechanism Activation of oncogenes Mutation Mutation activates the gene . A classic example is the point mutation of the RAS oncoge ne. Promoter insertion Insertion of a viral promoter region near a gene activates i t. Enhancer insertion Insertion of a viral enhancer region near a gene activates i t. Chromosomal translocati on One chromosome is split off and joined to another. An ex ample is the Philadelphia chr omosome. Gene amplification Abnormal multiplication of a gene resulting in many copie s. This can occur with oncoge nes and genes involved in tu mor drug resistance .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Mutation in which of the following oncogenes can serve as a tumor antigen?
mcqs.explanation: RAS is an oncogene that undergoes mutation and serves as a tumor antigen. Tumor cells express antigenic molecules on their surface that elicit an immune response . These are called tumor antigens. Some tumor cells evade immune response which results in growth of the tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following mechanisms does not lead to immune evasion by the tumor cells ?

options.a: Inhibition of PD-1 receptor on T-cells

mcqs.explanation: Inhibition of PD-1 receptor (programmed death -1 receptor ) on T cells causes activation of immunity against the tumor cells , not evasion. PD-1 receptors present on T cells inhibit T-cell activation. This allows tumors to evade the host immunity by the upregulation of the expression of factors like PD-L1 and PD-L2 , which act on PD-1 receptors .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old girl is referred with recurrent blistering rashes over the face and upper limbs which worsened following exposure to sunlight . There is a history of similar skin lesions in her family and 2 of her uncles were diagnosed with skin cancers at young ages . Examination reveals the presence of multiple lentigos and xerosis. What is the likely pathological mechanism of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum . It is caused by a defect in the DNA nucleotide excision repair pathway resulting in inability to repair pyrimidine dimers.232 Clinical features of xeroderma pigmentosum : • Actinic keratosis • Hyperkeratotic lesions • Multiple lentigos • Xerosis • Corneal scarring The image of a child with xeroderma pigmentosum is given below .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which of the following disorders is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism?
mcqs.explanation: Fanconi syndrome is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism. It is a rare disorder of kidney tubule function. Diseases with defects in DNA repair by homologous recombination: • Bloom syndrome and ataxia–telangiectasia triggered by DNA-damaging agents such as ionizing radiation • Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in multiple genes responsible for coding for proteins that participate in DNA repair pathways and are triggered by DNA-crosslinking agents like chemotherapeutic drugs. • Familial breast cancer is due to inherited gene defects in BRCA1 and BRCA 2 genes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old patient presents with right iliac fossa pain. Imaging shows the presence of an ileocaecal mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a starry sky pattern. What is the translocation involved in this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history and biopsy findings are suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma and the translocation involved is t(8;14).233 Burkitt lymphoma, also known as small non-cleaved-cell lymphoma, is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation and deregulation of the c-myc gene on chromosome 8. The classic t(8;14)(q24 ;q32 ) reciprocal translocation results in the transposition of the c-myc proto-oncogene on chromosome 8 with one of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) genes on chromosome 14. This results in activation of the c-myc gene and is considered responsible for tumor proliferation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Which epigenomic regulatory gene is mutated in most of the follicular lymphomas?
mcqs.explanation: MLL2 is an epigenomic regulatory gene that is mutated in most follicular lymphomas. It results in histone methylation. Epigenetics refers to factors other than the sequence of DNA that regulate gene expression . These factors involved in epigenetics are: • Histone modifications • DNA methylation • Nucleosome positioning / chromatin remodeling

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: The loss of which of the following micro RNAs leads to upregulation of BCL -2?
mcqs.explanation: The loss of miR -15 leads to upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL -2. miR -15 and miR -16 are tumor-suppressive miRNAs involved in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL ). Onco-miRNAs include :234 • miR200 - promotes epithelial -mesenchymal transitions that promote tumor invasion and metastasis • miR155 - involved in human B-cell lymphomas

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Molecular Basis of Cancer and Tumor Immunity
mcqs.question: Identify the correct statement regarding immune surveillance.

options.a: Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers
options.b: Mutation of tumor supressor genes decreases antigen toxicity
options.c: PD1/ PDL1 activation leading to tumor supression
options.d: Binding of CD28 leads to immune tolerance

mcqs.explanation: Anti-CTLA -4 antibody ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA -4) plays an important inhibitory role in the control of T-cell activation. Ipilimumab is a fully -humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4). It has been postulated that anti-CTLA -4 antibodies act by blocking inhibitory signals from effector T-cells , allowing costimulatory signaling and generation of antitumor T-cell responses . In vitro studies demonstrated also that the antitumor activity of CTLA -4 blockade is mediated by Fc gamma receptor -expressing macrophage and hypothesized a possible role of regulatory T-cell depletion in the tumor microenvironment . Option B - Mutation of tumor supressor genes is associated with increased risk of cancer. Antigen toxicity is when the immune response to an antigen is excessive or misdirected , causing damage to tissues or organs. Option C - PD1/PDL1 is an immune checkpoint whose activation inhibits T-cell function and helps with immune tolerance . Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction using immune checkpoint inhibitors reactivates T cells and enhances immune responses against tumors. Option D - CD28 is primarily involved in providing the second signal required for T cell activation. The first signal comes from the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR ) and the antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Without CD28-mediated costimulation, T cells that only receive the TCR signal (without the second signal) can become anergic.235

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors is best suited to study the mechanism of multi-step carcinogenesis ?
mcqs.explanation: Multi -step carcinogenesis is best studied in colon carcinoma . The molecular model for the evolution of colorectal cancers is described as Fearon-Vogelstein adenoma-carcinoma sequence .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following procarcinogens does not require metabolic activation?
mcqs.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is a directly -acting carcinogen that does not require metabolic activation. Carcinogens can be direct -acting or indirect-acting based on their activation. Direct-acting carcinogens require no metabolic conversion to become carcinogenic. Most are weak carcinogens, but some are important because they are cancer chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g.,245 alkylating agents ). The direct -acting carcinogens include : • Alkylating Agents : • �o -Propiolactone • Dimethyl sulfate • Diepoxybutane • Anticancer drugs (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nitrosoureas, and others) • Acylating Agents : • 1-Acetyl -imidazole • Dimethylcarbamyl chloride Indirect-acting carcinogens (procarcinogens) are chemicals that require metabolic conversion to become active carcinogens. The carcinogenic product of metabolism is called an ultimate carcinogen. The indirect-acting carcinogens include : • Polycyclic and heterocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons: • Benz[a]anthracene • Benzo[a]pyrene • Dibenz[a,h]anthracene • 3-Methylcholanthrene • 7,12-Dimethylbenz [a]anthracene • Aromatic amines, amides, azo dyes : • 2-Naphthylamine (�o -naphthylamine) • Benzidine • 2-Acetylaminofluorene • Dimethylaminoazobenzene (butter yellow ) • Natural plant and microbial products : • Aflatoxin B1 • Griseofulvin • Cycasin • Safrole • Betel nuts • Others • Nitrosamine and amides • Vinyl chloride , nickel, chromium • Insecticides , fungicides • Polychlorinated biphenyls246

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents with a hyperpigmented lesion on his face . He is a farmer by occupation and works for long hours with sun exposure . He is at increased risk for all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Seborrheic keratosis is not associated with exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from sun exposure .
