UV rays derived from sun exposure are associated with the increased incidence of: • Squamous cell carcinoma • Basal cell carcinoma • Melanoma of the skin Actinic keratosis is a precancerous skin condition that can cause squamous cell cancer if untreated .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which form of radiation is responsible for cutaneous cancer?
mcqs.explanation: UVB (ultraviolet B) causes cutaneous cancers due to the formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA. When DNA absorbs energy from UVB, there is a covalent crosslinking of pyrimidine bases and distortion of the DNA helix. This prevents proper pairing of the dimer with bases in the opposite DNA strand. Normally, these defects are repaired by nucleotide excision repair pathway . Defects in nucleotide excision repair pathway result in xeroderma pigmentosum . UV portion of the solar spectrum is divided into three wavelength ranges: Note : UVC is the most potent mutagen but is not considered significant as it is filtered out by the ozone layer.Spect rum Wavele ngth UVA 320 -40 0 nm UVB 280-32 0 nm UVC 200 -28 0 nm

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of which of the following malignancies?
mcqs.explanation: Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of myeloid leukemia. Carcinogenic radiations include : • Electromagnetic radiation -247 • X-rays • \034 rays • Particulate radiation - • \037 particles • �o particles • Protons • Neutrons Cancers due to ionizing radiation: • Most frequent - myeloid leukemia and thyroid cancer • Intermediate frequency - cancers of breast, lungs , and salivary glands • Relatively resistant cancers - cancers of skin, bone, and gastrointestinal tract

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors is not caused by microbes?
mcqs.explanation: Adenocarcinoma carcinoma of the lung is not associated with microbial etiopathogenesis . It is associated with smoking and genetic predispositions .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following malignancies is caused by HTLV -1?
mcqs.explanation: Human T-cell leukemia-lymphoma virus (HTLV -1) causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL ). HTLV -1 encodes the viral protein Tax , which leads to polyclonal expansion of T cells . It exhibits tropism for CD4+ T cells . Human infection requires transmission of infected T cells through sexual intercourse , blood products or breast feeding . Leukemia develops only in 3-5% of infected individuals, typically after a long latent period of 40-60 years.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following pairs of HPV oncoproteins and target genes are correctly matched ?
mcqs.explanation: The target genes for viral oncoproteins of human papilloma virus (HPV ) are as follows : • E6 - p53 • E7 - RB The image given below shows the functions of the E6 and E7 oncoproteins of HPV .248

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 13 -year-old child presents to the OPD with fever, pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Peripheral smear showed a predominance of lymphocytes . The heterophile agglutination test is positive . The causative organism of this condition is not implicated in which of the following tumors?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein -Barr virus. This virus is not implicated in follicular lymphoma. Epstein –Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpesvirus family, has been implicated in: • African form of Burkitt lymphoma • B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed • A subset of Hodgkin lymphoma • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma • Gastric carcinoma - most common EBV associated malignancy • T-cell lymphoma and natural killer (NK) cell lymphoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about Epstein -Barr virus is incorrect?

options.a: EBV infection always results in Burkitt lymphoma
options.b: It uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach and infect B cells
options.c: It is implicated in B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed people
options.d: It is a potent inducer of B-cell growth and transformation

mcqs.explanation: Epstein -Barr virus (EBV) infection does not always result in Burkitt lymphoma. EBV infection is highly prevalent even in areas where Burkitt lymphoma is not found. It commonly causes infectious mononucleosis . EBV uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach to and infect B cells . EBV genome triggers B-cell signaling pathways inducing B-cell growth and transformation . The infection of B cells is latent as there is no viral replication and the cells are not killed . However, B cells latently infected with EBV express viral proteins that result in the ability to propagate indefinitely in vitro. In the absence of T-cell immunity, EBV-infected B cells can rapidly grow out as aggressive B-cell tumors.249

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following pathogens is implicated in the causation of primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) is a gamma-herpesvirus associated with Kaposi sarcoma, multicentric Castleman disease , and primary effusion lymphoma. They are lymphoproliferative diseases that are most commonly observed in immunocompromised individuals. The viral genome expresses genes responsible for inhibition of apoptosis , cell cycle entry, and angiogenesis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with abdominal distension and intermittent fever. Peripheral smear findings are normal. A tumor is resected and the histopathology image of the resected lymph node is shown below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and histopathological image showing follicular hyperplasia of lymph nodes are suggestive of Castleman disease . Castleman disease (angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia ) is a lymphoproliferative disorder that can be associated with HHV -8 (multicentric Castleman disease or MCD) or idiopathic (unicentric Castleman disease or UCD) There are 3 major histological subtypes: • Hypervascular (UCD) - • Lollipop appearance - atrophic germinal centers with radially penetrating blood vessels • Onion skin appearance of mantle zone around germinal centers • Plasma cell subtype (UCD or MCD) - hypertrophic germinal centers , increased vascularity • Mixed variant (MCD) - mix of hypervascular and plasma cell subtype features in the same lymph node The clinical features include : • Multiple enlarged lymph nodes • Night sweats • Weight loss • Weakness and fatigue • Hepatosplenomegaly As this condition is associated with elevated levels of IL -6, the treatment involves IL -6 inhibitors like siltuximab and tocilizumab. Note : Hodgkin's lymphoma has characteristic Reed -Sternberg cells in the histopathological section of lymph nodes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an EBV oncogene behaving like a constitutively active CD40 receptor ?
mcqs.explanation: 250 LMP-1 is an EBV oncogene that behaves like a constitutively active CD40 receptor . The CD40 receptor -like activity stimulates B-cell growth . LMP-1 activates the NF-\032B and JAK / STAT signaling pathways and promotes B-cell survival . It also prevents apoptosis by activating BCL2 .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of development of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is implicated in the following conditions: • Peptic ulcer • Gastric adenocarcinoma - preceded by chronic gastritis, gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia , and dysplasia • MALT lymphoma of the stomach - through polyclonal B cell proliferation Helicobacter pylori is protective for: • Barrett's esophagus • Adenocarcinoma of esophagus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common endocrinopathy caused by tumors?
mcqs.explanation: Cushing syndrome is the most common endocrinopathy caused by tumors. Endocrinopathy refers to ectopic hormone production by non-endocrine tumors. Approximately , 50% of the individuals with Cushing syndrome as endocrinopathy have carcinoma of the lung, chiefly the small-cell type . Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome. Cancer-associated hypercalcemia occurs due to: • Osteolysis induced by cancer - due to primary or secondary involvement of the skeleton by tumor • Production of calcemic humoral substances by extraosseous neoplasms - for example , parathyroid hormone-related protein. Only this mechanism is considered to be paraneoplastic .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following tumors present with pure red cell aplasia as a paraneoplastic manifestation?
mcqs.explanation: Thymoma often presents with pure red cell aplasia as a paraneoplastic manifestation. Thymomas are unusual neoplasms of thymic epithelial tissue , ranging from small indolent tumors to aggressive thymic carcinomas. Pure red cell aplasia is a rare cause of anemia, caused by the absence of RBC precursors in the bone marrow . Causes of pure red cell aplasia include : • Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia251 • Drug exposure - phenytoin , azathioprine, and isoniazid • Auto-immune disorders - neutralizing antibodies against erythropoietin • Parvovirus infection • Hereditary - Diamond Blackfan syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which subtype of acute myeloid leukemia presents with disseminated intravascular coagulation as a paraneoplastic manifestation?
mcqs.explanation: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as a paraneoplastic syndrome is most commonly associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and prostatic adenocarcinoma. Major determinants of coagulopathy in APL are endogenous factors of the malignant leukemic cells and their interaction with host defense mechanisms. Factors that cause coagulopathy include : • Increased expression of procoagulant activity (PCA) • Expression of fibrinolytic and proteolytic properties • Secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines - interleukin-1b (IL-1b) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old patient presents with loss of weight and appetite . On clinical examination, grade IV clubbing is evident . Imaging shows periosteal new bone formation and synovial effusion . Which of the following tumors is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history is suggestive of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy . It is commonly associated with bronchiogenic carcinoma . Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterised by the following : • Periosteal new bone formation, primarily at the distal ends of long bones, metatarsals, metacarpals, and proximal phalanges • Arthritis of the adjacent joints • Clubbing of the digits

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old patient presents with generalized tiredness , malaise, muscle weakness , and bone pain. Laboratory investigations reveal serum calcium to be 13 mg/dL. Which of the following is lung cancers is implicated in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history and laboratory investigations are suggestive of hypercalcemia . It is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Tumors associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia : • Breast carcinoma • Lung carcinoma • Renal cell carcinoma • Ovarian carcinoma252

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following paraneoplastic manifestations is likely to occur in a patient with a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor presents with osteomalacia as a paraneoplastic manifestation. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor is caused due to mutation of the FGF-23 gene .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old obese female presents with skin changes in her axilla and neck as shown in the image. Which of the following tumors is not associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture is suggestive of acanthosis nigricans. It is not associated with thymoma. Acanthosis nigricans is a disorder characterized by gray-black patches of thickened , hyperkeratotic skin with a velvety appearance. The causal mechanism is immunologic due to secretion of epidermal growth factor. Acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with: • Gastric carcinoma • Lung carcinoma • Gynecological cancers • Breast carcinoma • Bladder carcinoma • Gallbladder and bile -duct carcinoma • Acromegaly and gigantism • Dermatomyositis • Diabetes • Hashimoto thyroiditis • Lupus erythematosus • Phenylketonuria • Polycystic ovary syndrome • Systemic sclerosis • Wilson syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with headache , vertigo, tinnitus, and visual disturbance . On further evaluation, blood hemoglobin and hematocrit levels are found to be 18 g/dL and 62% respectively . Which of the following tumors does not present with these paraneoplastic manifestations ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history and laboratory investigations are suggestive of polycythemia which is not seen in melanoma as a paraneoplastic manifestation. Polycythemia , as a paraneoplastic syndrome, is mediated by erythropoietin (EPO). EPO is a glycoprotein that induces differentiation of erythrocyte colony-forming units in the bone marrow253 to promote red blood cell production . Under normal physiological conditions, EPO is produced by peritubular renal interstitial cells in response to local tissue hypoxia. However, in tumors, EPO production occurs in the neoplastic cells themselves .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of these paraneoplastic syndromes is associated with small-cell carcinoma lung?
mcqs.explanation: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH ) is associated with small cell carcinoma of lung.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old patient notices spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules in different parts of the body. Which of the following malignancies is not associated with this clinical presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation is suggestive of migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and it is not associated with bladder carcinoma . Trousseau syndrome may be encountered in association with deep -seated cancers, most often carcinomas of the pancreas or lung. It is caused by hypercoagulability leading to multiple repeated venous thromboembolism. Malignant brain tumors, hematological malignancies, and adenocarcinomas of the pancreas, stomach, ovary , uterus , lungs , and kidneys are at the highest risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE ) development . Advanced, metastatic cancer has been shown to be associated with an increased risk of VTE compared with localized tumors.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old patient with paroxysmal hypertension is suspected to have malignant pheochromocytoma . Which of the following tumor markers will help you confirm your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The serum levels of catecholamines are elevated in malignant pheochromocytoma . Extra-adrenal location is the only criteria for malignancy in pheochromocytoma . Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine -secreting tumor that may precipitate life -threatening hypertension. It is classically associated with three syndromes: • von Hippel -Lindau (VHL ) syndrome • Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) • Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) Catecholamines produced by pheochromocytomas are metabolized within chromaffin cells . Norepinephrine is metabolized to normetanephrine, and epinephrine is metabolized to metanephrine . Because this process occurs within the tumor, independent of catecholamine release , pheochromocytomas are best diagnosed by the measurement of these metabolites , rather than by measurement of the parent catecholamines .254

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are oncofetal antigens?
mcqs.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) are oncofetal antigens. Alpha-fetoprotein is a valuable clinical aid in diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of the following tumors: • Primary hepatocellular carcinoma • Hepatoblastoma • Non-seminomatous testicular germ cell tumors • Embryonal carcinoma • Teratomas • Choriocarcinoma • Yolk sac carcinoma • Germ cell tumors of the ovary and extragonadal germ cell tumors Regenerated hepatic tissue following liver damage due to viral hepatitis , chemically induced necrosis, and liver surgery are associated with moderately raised serum AFP levels . Carcinoembryonic antigen is normally detected in glycocalyx of fetal epithelial cells . It is useful in detection , assessing recurrence, and prognosis of the following tumors: • Adenocarcinoma of lung • Colorectal carcinoma CEA levels >5 ng/dL are noted in ascites fluid associated with malignancy. Canalicular pattern for polyclonal CEA more sensitive for hepatocellular carcinoma , metastases in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and not sensitive for metastasis in bile duct adenoma. Elevated levels are also present in the following non-neoplastic conditions: • Cirrhosis • Biliary obstruction • Hepatitis • Inflammatory bowel disease • Smokers • Post-surgical bowel sequestration • Mucocele • Benign cysts may be positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old patient is diagnosed with breast cancer. Which of the following glycoproteins is expected to be elevated in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The level of cancer antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3) is elevated in patients with breast cancer.255 The reference range of serum CA 15-3 is less than 30 U/mL. It is used to monitor response to breast cancer treatment and disease recurrence.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 51-year-old male patient who is a chronic smoker presents with dry persistent cough and progressive dyspnea . You are suspecting small cell carcinoma of lung. Which of the following tumor markers is likely to be elevated in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of small cell carcinoma of the lung (SCLC) in which levels of neuron-specific enolase (NSE) are elevated . NSE is also called gamma enolase or enolase 2 (ENO2) and is encoded by ENO2 gene . It is a phosphopyruvate hydratase that is produced by small-cell lung carcinomas, which are neuroendocrine in origin. Their levels have been implicated as a prognostic factor for patients with small-cell lung cancer.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors?
mcqs.explanation: NRG-1 (Neuregulin -1) is not a marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). GIST are the most common mesenchymal tumor of the abdomen, the stomach being the most common site . They arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the GIT . GIST is seen in the 5th to 6th decade of life and has an equal preponderance among males and females . Most patients present with haematemesis , melena, or vague abdominal pain. The most common indications for surgery include bleeding and obstruction. The GIST may occur in a sporadic form or as part of familial syndromes. In sporadic GIST , the most common mutations seen are gain-of-function mutation in KIT (75-80%) and PDGFRA mutation (8%). Microscopically , GIST has elongated spindle cells or plumper epithelioid cells , or a mixed pattern. The below image shows the microscopy of GIST composed of bundles , or fascicles , of spindle -shaped tumor cells .256 Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient GIST is a subset of wild -type GIST seen with Carney triad or Carney-Stratakis syndrome. Imatinib can be used to treat GIST with mutations in KIT or PDGFRA. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) - deficient GIST is imatinib-resistant, so sunitinib, sorafenib, or regorafenib can be used instead . During surgical resection of GIST , care must be taken to prevent capsule rupture , which causes seeding of nearby tissues leading to relapse in 100 % of the cases . If capsule rupture occurs, adjuvant therapy with imatinib is indicated regardless of tumor extent . Other options : Option A: KIT (CD117): This is the most well -known marker for GISTs. About 85% of GISTs show mutations in the KIT gene , leading to the expression of the KIT protein on the cell surface . KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and its activation is a key driver in the pathogenesis of GISTs. Option B: SDH (Succinate Dehydrogenase ): SDH mutations are associated with a subset of GISTs, particularly those that are KIT and PDGFRA wild -type . Loss of SDH function is characteristic of this subgroup , and SDH deficiency can be demonstrated through immunohistochemistry . Option C: PDGFRA (Platelet -Derived Growth Factor Receptor Alpha): Mutations in the PDGFRA gene account for approximately 5-10% of GISTs. Similar to KIT, PDGFRA is a receptor tyrosine kinase, and mutations in this gene can lead to the development of GISTs.257

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of innate immunity?
mcqs.explanation: B cell is not a component of innate immunity. It is a component of adaptive immunity. Innate immunity refers to the body's natural immunity. It is a built -in defence system that is present since birth. It differs from adaptive immunity in that it does not require any prior sensitization to an antigen. The major components of innate immunity are as follows : • Epithelial barriers that block the entry of microbes263 • Phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages ) • Natural killer (NK) cells • Dendritic cell • Cells that can sense and react to microbes - mast cells , epithelial and endothelial cells • Plasma proteins - complement system factors, mannose-binding lectin , and C-reactive protein • Innate lymphoid cells • Lung surfactant

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the mechanism by which toll-like receptors stimulate immune response against bacterial products ?

options.c: NF\032B mediated transcription of nuclear factor

mcqs.explanation: Toll-like receptors (TLRs ) stimulate immune response by NF\032B mediated transcription of nuclear factors. TLRs are pattern recognition receptors which activate two sets of transcription factors: • NF-\032B - stimulates the synthesis and secretion of cytokines and the expression of adhesion molecules . Both are critical for the recruitment and activation of leukocytes • Interferon regulatory factors - stimulate the production of the antiviral cytokines like type I interferons The image given below shows a toll-like receptor .264 The various classes of innate immune receptors are as follows : Mannose receptor is a soluble pattern-recognition receptor . mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is seen with:
mcqs.explanation: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is mediated by NK cells , neutrophils and eosinophils (killing certain parasitic worms like helminths via IgE antibodies ). In ADCC, cells / antigens are coated with IgG antibodies . These are killed by effector cells like NK cells and macrophages . These effector cells bind to the target by their receptors for the Fc fragment of IgG and cell lysis proceeds without phagocytosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following occurs due to gain-of-function mutations in NOD-Like receptors ?
mcqs.explanation: The gain of function mutations in NOD-Like receptors (NLRs ) result in periodic fever syndromes called autoinflammatory syndromes. They are a group of clinical conditions characterised by recurrent inflammatory episodes . This disorder is marked by abnormally increased inflammation, mediated predominantly by cells and molecules of the innate immune system, with a significant host predisposition . NOD-like receptors are cytosolic receptors that signal via a cytosolic multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. This activates caspase -1 that generates biologically active form of interleukin-1 (IL -1). IL -1 is a mediator of inflammation that recruits leukocytes and induces fever. The autoinflammatory syndromes respond very well to treatment with IL -1 antagonists. Note : Autoimmune diseases result from T and B-lymphocyte reactions against self -antigens.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio?
mcqs.explanation: Normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio is 2:1. Approximately 60% of mature T cells are CD4+ and about 30% are CD8+. T-lymphocytes (thymus -derived cells ) constitute 60–70% of peripheral blood lymphocytes . T-cell progenitors are derived from the bone marrow , but travel to the thymus , where they mature. T cells can be divided into three main subtypes : They are located in the paracortical areas of lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen . They have an antigen-specific T-cell receptors (TCR ) which have alpha/beta polypeptide chains components . Demonstration of TCR gene rearrangement by southern blot is a molecular marker of T-cell lineage . The CD molecules present on T cells are CD1, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7 , CD8 and CD28. CD3 is involved in signal transduction and is also called a pan T - cell marker . CD40 ligand on the surface is required for B-cell activation and induction of immunoglobulin.266 Type of T cell Function Helper T cell (CD4+) Helps B lymphocytes to mak e antibodies and activate oth er leukocytes to destroy micr obes Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CT Ls or CD8+) Kill infected cells Regulatory T cells Limit immune responses and prevent reactions against sel f-antigens.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not expressed in the B-cell receptor complex ?
mcqs.explanation: CD86 is a protein expressed on antigen-presenting cells , and not B-cell receptor complex . This protein provides costimulatory signals necessary for T-cell activation and survival . B-cell receptor complex expresses the following : • CD79a and CD79b - essential for signal transduction through the antigen receptor • CD21 or CR2 - complement receptor (recognize complement products during innate immune response ) and Epstein –Barr virus (EBV) receptor • CD40 - receives signals from helper T cells Other B cell -associated markers are CD10 (CALLA ), CD19, CD20 , CD22 , CD23 .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are the most important antigen-presenting cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Dendritic cells or interdigitating dendritic cells are the most important antigen-presenting cells . They initiate T-cell responses against protein antigens. They are located in the epithelium and interstitium . They express many receptors for capturing and responding to microbes (and other antigens), including toll -like receptors (TLRs ) and lectins . They also express high levels of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) for presenting antigens to and activating T cells . In response to microbes, dendritic cells are recruited to the T-cell zones of lymphoid organs. Here, they present antigens to T cells with help of MHC. Similar cells with dendritic morphology in the germinal centers of lymphoid follicles in the spleen and lymph nodes are follicular dendritic cells . They bear Fc receptors for IgG and receptors for C3b. Immature dendritic cells within the epidermis are called Langerhans cells . Note : • Aggretope - part of the antigen associated with the MHC molecule on the antigen-presenting cell • Epitope - antigenic part of contact with the T-cell receptor267

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about macrophages ?

options.a: It acts as an antigen presenting cell
options.b: It plays a role in humoral immunity
options.c: It plays a role in cell -mediated immunity
options.d: It is a component of innate immunity only

mcqs.explanation: Macrophages are components of both innate and acquired immunity. They phagocytose microbes and protein antigens. They process the antigens and present the peptide fragments to T cells . Thus, macrophages function as antigen-presenting cells in T-cell activation. They also participate in the effector phase of humoral immunity. Macrophages efficiently phagocytose and destroy microbes that are opsonized (coated ) with IgG or C3b. They are key effector cells in certain forms of cell -mediated immunity to eliminate intracellular microbes. In this type of response , T cells activate macrophages and enhance their ability to kill ingested microbes.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about natural killer cells ?

options.a: CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules
options.b: They are involved in antibody-dependant cytotoxic killing
options.c: IL -12 stimulates the proliferation of NK cells
options.d: They activate macrophages by secreting IFN-\

mcqs.explanation: IL -2 and IL -15 stimulate the proliferation of NK cells . On the other hand, IL -12 activates the killing of target cells and secretion of IFN-\034. NK cells are large granular lymphocytes , which constitutes 5% to 10 % of peripheral blood lymphocytes . CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules . Functions of NK cells : • Killing of a variety of virus-infected cells and tumor cells , without prior exposure to or activation by these microbes or tumors • Secretion of interferon-\034 (IFN-\034), which activates macrophages to destroy ingested microbes • Antibody-dependent cell -mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) - NK cells express CD16 which is a receptor for IgG Fc tails. Hence , these cells have the ability to lyse IgG-coated target cells . ADCC is also seen in immune responses involving neutrophils , eosinophils , macrophages , etc . The image given below shows activating and inhibitory receptors of natural killer (NK) cells .268 Note : A new group of T cells has been discovered called NK-T cells . These are T cells that contain markers of NK cells . These are important defence mechanisms against microorganisms like Listeria monocytogenes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of these is common to both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells ?

options.a: They are MHC l restricted cells
options.b: Require antibodies to be present for action

mcqs.explanation: Both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells are effective against virus-infected cells . The NK cells have different mechanisms of action while killing target cells . NK cells can lyse IgG-coated target cells by binding to the Fc tail of IgG, through the CD16 receptor expressed on NK cells . This phenomenon is known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). NK cells secrete various cytokines such as interferon-\034 (IFN-\034), which activate macrophages to destroy ingested microbes. Target cell destruction by NK cells is also mediated through two others receptors - activating receptors and inhibitory receptors . The activating receptors enable NK cells to recognize infected and stressed cells . The inhibitory receptors recognize self class-I MHC molecules , that are expressed on all healthy cells thereby preventing NK cells from killing normal cells . Virus infection / neoplastic transformation overexpresses the activating receptors and simultaneously reduces the expression of class-I MHC molecules . As a result , NK cells are activated and the infected cells are killed. CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes directly kill damaged cells . The differences between NK cells and cytotoxic T-cells are:Natural killer (NK) cell Cytotoxic T-cells Does not requirepriming -rap id response in hours requirepriming -takes days to respond269 Natural killer (NK) cell Cytotoxic T-cells MHC unrestricted MHC restricted Antibody-mediated and non- antibody-mediated killing Non-antibody mediated killin g / direct cytotoxicity Kills virus-infected and neopl astic cells by apoptosis Kills virus-infected , neoplasti c, and donor graft cells by ap optosis Antigen non-specific Antigen-specific Memory is absent Memory is present

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following markers on antigen-presenting cells function as costimulatory molecules for T cells ?
mcqs.explanation: CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) are the costimulatory molecules present on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). They bind to CD28 protein present on T cells . This promotes the expansion of antigen-stimulated T cells and their differentiation into effector and memory cells . T-cell activation requires two signals that are delivered by APCs. They include : • Antigens displayed by APCs in the form of peptides bound to MHC molecules , that are recognised by T-cell receptors • Costimulatory signal (as it stimulates T cells in conjunction with antigen) provided by molecules on APCs that engage particular costimulatory receptors on T cells In the absence of costimulation , T cells that recognize antigen either fail to respond and die or enter a state of unresponsiveness known as anergy. Thus, costimulation is a key determinant of the outcome of a T-cell encounter with an antigen.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cytokines induces T-helper type 2 cells ?
mcqs.explanation: 270 IL -4 induces T helper 2 cells . Mechanism of cell -mediated immunity: • Antigen-presenting cells \035 recognized by naive CD4+ T cells \035 IL -2 secretion \035 T-cell proliferation and differentiation \035 activated CD4+ T helper cells • Activated CD4+ T cells further differentiate into effector cells that secrete different sets of cytokines and perform different functions

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: B-cells are induced to produce IgE by which of the following :
mcqs.explanation: IL -4 stimulates B-cells to differentiate into IgE secreting plasma cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Production of which of the following antibodies is induced by polysaccharides and lipids ?
mcqs.explanation: Polysaccharides and lipids stimulate the secretion of mainly IgM antibodies . B lymphocytes use their antigen receptors to recognize various types of antigens: • Proteins (through CD40L and cytokine-mediated helper T-cell actions) - induce production of IgG, IgA, IgE • Polysaccharides and lipids - induce production of IgM mainly Helper T cells also help in antibodies by the mechanisms: • Stimulate formation of germinal centers which consist of proliferating B cells • Induce isotype switching through cytokines IFN-\034 and IL -4 • Affinity maturation - stimulate the production of antigen-specific antibodies Isotype switching and affinity maturation occur mainly in germinal centers .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, which of the following are the end products ?
mcqs.explanation: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments. If an antibody molecule is digested with papain, cleavage occurs above the disulfide bonds that hold the heavy chains together . This generates 3 separate fragments, two of which are called Fab (fragment antigen binding), and one of which is called Fc (fragment crystallizable ). The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by papain.271 Cleavage of the antibody molecule with pepsin generates one large fragment called F(ab\264)2 and a digested Fc fragment. The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by pepsin .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following cells is recirculation seen ?

options.c: Both plasma cells and T lymphocytes
options.d: Both B lymphocytes and plasma cells

mcqs.explanation: Lymphocyte recirculation is seen in T lymphocytes . Migration of the lymphocytes between blood and lymphoid organs is called recirculation. Naive lymphocytes traverse the peripheral lymphoid organs, where immune responses are initiated . When antigen-presenting cells activate them, the effector lymphocytes migrate to sites of infection and inflammation.272 In contrast, plasma cells remain in lymphoid organs and the bone marrow . They do not need to migrate to sites of infection because they secrete antibodies that are carried to distant tissues .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following about \034\037 T-cells is incorrect:

options.a: Kills extracellular bacteria by granulysin and perforin
options.b: Need antigen processing and presentation for it recognition

mcqs.explanation: \034\037 T-cells do not need antigen processing and presentation for its recognition. There are two types of T cells : \034\037 T-cells and \037\036 T-cells . The functions of \034\037 T-cells : • Provide protection against mycobacteria by direct killing of infected macrophages • Kills extracellular bacteria by granulysin and perforin • Plays a role in maintaining self -tolerance • Capable of recognising and lysing diverse cancers in an MHC-unrestricted manner \037\036 T-cells have MHC restricted action.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Basophils are activated by:
mcqs.explanation: Basophils are activated by IL -5 and IL -3. Note : IL -5 primarily activates eosinophils .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Among the following , which cells have MHC class II ?

options.c: B cells , dendritic cells , mononuclear phagocytes

mcqs.explanation: Class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules are mainly expressed on macrophages , B lymphocytes , and dendritic cells . These cells present ingested antigens to T-cells . The function of MHC molecules is to display peptide fragments of protein antigens for recognition by antigen-specific T cells . In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens (HLA ) because they were initially detected on leukocytes by the binding of antibodies . The combination of HLA alleles in each individual is called the HLA haplotype . The genes encoding HLA molecules are clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6. Uses of MHC/ HLA typing include : • Anthropology • Transfusion • Paternity testing • Forensic science • Transplantation273 • Disease correlation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not encoded by MHC class III genes ?
mcqs.explanation: �o 2 microglobulin associated cell surface molecules are encoded by MHC class I and not class III . Class III MHC molecules include : • Complement proteins (such as C2, C4, and B factor) • Cytokines (such as TNF-\037, LTA , and LTB ) • Properdin factor BQ of alternate pathway • Enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase • Heat-shock proteins Class III molecules are encoded by genes located between those that encode class I and class II molecules .274

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child, upon disturbing a beehive , had several stings. After a few minutes , he developed shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse . What is the pathogenesis of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of anaphylaxis following a bee sting. This is an example of IgE -mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity. Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions. There are four types of hypersensitivity reactions. Immediate (Type 1) hypersensitivity is also called allergic reactions. They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens ) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals. IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fc\031g receptors . Reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and Fc\031RI, activation of mast cells , and release of mediators. The principal mediators are histamine, proteases , and other granule contents like prostaglandins and leukotrienes and cytokines. It occurs in two phases : immediate phase and late phase . The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late -phase reaction (inflammation). The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis. The image given below shows the sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity .280

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Arthus reaction is caused by which of the following process ?
mcqs.explanation: Arthus reaction is characterized by a localized area of tissue necrosis due to immune-complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity reaction) vasculitis in the skin. This reaction can be produced experimentally by intracutaneous injection of antigen in a previously immunised animal that contains circulating antibodies against the antigen. As the antigen diffuses into the vessel wall, it binds with the preformed antibody, and immune complexes are formed locally . These complexes precipitate in the vessel walls and cause fibrinoid necrosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old female patient presents with ptosis , diplopia , and progressive muscular weakness towards the end of the day. She has improvements in symptoms after administering edrophonium . The given clinical condition is an example of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis. It is an example of a type II hypersensitivity reaction. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that is usually associated with autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors . In Type II hypersensitivity , antibodies react with antigens present on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix cause . These antibodies destroy cells , trigger inflammation, or interfering with normal functions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and smoky, cola-colored urine 2 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. He is found to have periorbital edema and mild hypertension . Urine examination shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts in the urine with mild proteinuria. Which type of hypersensitivity is responsible for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephritic syndrome due to post -streptococcal glomerulonephritis . This is an example of a type III hypersensitivity reaction. In type III hypersensitivity , immune complexes may deposit in tissues or blood vessels , and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement . The pathogenesis of systemic immune281 complex disease can be divided into three phases : • Formation of immune complexes • Deposition of immune complexes • Inflammation and tissue injury This results in various manifestations like vasculitis, glomerulonephritis and arthritis. Examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions: • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Reactive arthritis • Polyarteritis nodosa • Serum sickness • Arthus reaction • Farmer's lung • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis • Type II lepra reaction • Henoch–Schonlein purpura The image given below shows the mechanism of type III hypersensitivity reactions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man with a fever and chronic cough is administered 0.1 mL of purified protein derivative intradermally over the forearm. After a few hours, the injection site appears as follows . Which of the following does this represent ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario shows a positive tuberculin test . It is a classical example of type IV or delayed or cell -mediated hypersensitivity reaction.282 Tuberculin test involves intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD, also called tuberculin), a protein-containing antigen of the tubercle bacillus . In a previously sensitized individual, reddening and induration of the site appear in 8 to 12 hours, reach a peak in 24 to 72 hours, and thereafter slowly subside . Morphologically , delayed -type hypersensitivity is characterized by the accumulation of mononuclear cells , mainly CD4+ T cells and macrophages , around venules . The cell -mediated type of hypersensitivity is caused by inflammation resulting from cytokines produced by CD4+ T cells and cell killing by CD8+ T cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: True about anaphylactoid reaction are all except :
mcqs.explanation: Anaphylactoid reactions are those reactions that are similar to the anaphylactic reactions but are not IgE mediated . These reactions are caused by direct degranulation of the mast cells or basophils , which causes the release of mediators. Unlike the classic anaphylaxis which occurs on re-exposure to the allergen , the anaphylactoid reaction can occur even on the first exposure . The most common agents that can cause an anaphylactoid reaction include NSAIDs and radiocontrast media. In 2014 , World Allergy Organisation has introduced two new terms: • Immunologic anaphylaxis - It includes anaphylactic reactions mediated by IgE, IgG (in animals), and immune complex / complement -mediated reactions. • Non-immunologic anaphylaxis (previously called anaphylactoid reaction) - It includes reactions caused by agents which cause massive degranulation of mast cells or basophils in the absence of immunoglobulin. The image given below shows the sequence of events in type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.283

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following autoimmune diseases are not mediated by antibodies ?
mcqs.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is mediated by T cells , not antibodies . Antibody-mediated diseases : • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia • Autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura • Pemphigus vulgaris • Vasculitis caused by ANCA • Goodpasture syndrome • Myasthenia gravis • Acute rheumatic fever • Graves disease • Pernicious anemia • Insulin resistant diabetes T cell -mediated diseases : • Rheumatoid arthritis • Multiple sclerosis • Psoriasis • Type 1 diabetes mellitus • Inflammatory bowel disease • Contact sensitivity Note : In T cell mediated diseases , although the role of T cells have been demonstrated , antibodies may also be involved in tissue injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which gene is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity?
mcqs.explanation: PTPN22 gene is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity. PTPN22 , which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase , is associated with the following conditions: • Rheumatoid arthritis • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD ) • Type 1 diabetes Because these disorders have a fairly high prevalence , PTPN22 is said to be the gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity. Option A: Mutations in FOXP3 cause a systemic autoimmune disease called IPEX (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy , enteropathy , X-linked).284 Option C: Polymorphisms in the gene encoding for NOD2 are associated with Crohn's disease . Option D: AIRE mutation is associated with the autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: During development , thymic cells recognizing self -antigens are removed to prevent autoimmunity. Which gene among the following is involved in the process ?
mcqs.explanation: The above process is called central tolerance and the AIRE (AutoImmune REgulator) protein is necessary for this process . Immature self -reactive T and B lymphocyte clones recognize self -antigens during their maturation in the central lymphoid organs (thymus for T cells , bone marrow for B cells ). They are killed or rendered harmless. The removal of self reacting T lymphocytes in the thymus is called negative selection / deletion. For this process , AIRE protein is needed . Mutations in the AIRE gene results in autoimmune disorders (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy). B cells undergo a process called receptor editing . When developing B cells encounter an antigen, it formulates a change in the receptor that makes the antigen unrecognizable . Self -reacting B cells can also undergo apoptosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is responsible for autoimmunity in Epstein -Barr virus infection ?
mcqs.explanation: Autoimmunity in Epstein –Barr virus (EBV) infection is the result of polyclonal B cell activation. Microbes may induce other abnormalities that promote autoimmune reactions. Some viruses, such as EBV and HIV , cause polyclonal B-cell activation, which may result in the production of autoantibodies . The role of infections in autoimmunity is exemplified by the following : • Molecular mimicry of antigenic cross-reactivity: The structural similarity of the microbial antigens and self -antigens. Rheumatic heart disease is an example in which streptococcal proteins cross-react with myocardial proteins causing myocarditis. • Upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules by infectious organisms. • Polyclonal B cell activation: Caused by EBV and HIV , resulting in the production of autoantibodies . • Alteration of tissue antigens: Infections may alter tissue self -antigens so that they activate T cells and lose the property of self -tolerance .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Homogeneous or diffuse nuclear staining pattern may reflect antibodies to all the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Homogeneous or diffuse nuclear staining does not reflect antibodies to RNA. The nucleolar pattern of staining represents antibodies to RNA.285 Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are directed against antibodies to: • DNA • Histones • Nonhistone proteins bound to RNA • Nucleolar antigens The most widely used method for detecting ANAs is indirect immunofluorescence . The pattern of nuclear fluorescence suggests the type of antibody present in the patient 's serum.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What type of cell is the lupus erythematosus cell ?
mcqs.explanation: The lupus erythematosus (LE) cell is a phagocytic neutrophil or macrophage. Nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous to produce LE bodies or hematoxylin bodies . Phagocytic neutrophils or macrophages engulf the denatured nucleus of an injured cell . Demonstration of LE cells in vitro was used in the past for the diagnosis of SLE. The image below shows a lupus erythematosus (LE) cell .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old lady presents with the following finding. On further investigations, anti-ds DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are found to be positive . Which of the following is not seen in the given clinical condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In this condition, lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary gland is not seen . However, this finding is seen in Sjogren's syndrome. If cell nuclei are exposed to anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs), they can bind to them. The nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous . They are called lupus erythematosus (LE) bodies or hematoxylin bodies .286 An acute necrotizing vasculitis involving capillaries , small arteries, and arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis is seen in SLE. Central penicilliary arteries in the spleen may show concentric intimal and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia , producing so-called onion-skin lesions .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a part of the IgG4 spectrum ?
mcqs.explanation: Celiac disease is not an IgG4-Related disease . IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a newly recognized constellation of disorders characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibody-producing plasma cells and lymphocytes , particularly T cells , storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis , and usually increased serum IgG4. IgG4-RD spectrum includes : • Mikulicz syndrome - enlargement and fibrosis of salivary and lacrimal glands • Riedel thyroiditis • Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis • Autoimmune pancreatitis • Inflammatory pseudotumors of the orbit, lungs , and kidney287

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Leukocyte -adhesion deficiency type 2 is due to the absence of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Leukocyte -adhesion deficiency (LAD ) type 2 is due to the absence of Sialyl-Lewis X. Physiologically Sialyl-Lewis X has the necessary ligand for the selectins which bind to leukocytes . Inherited defects in leukocyte adhesion: • Type 1 - defect in the biosynthesis of the �o 2 chain shared by the LFA-1 and Mac-1 integrins • Type 2 - absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose containing ligand for E- and P-selectins . It is due to a defect in the fucosyltransferase , the enzyme that attaches fucose moieties to protein backbones. The major clinical problem in both conditions is recurrent bacterial infections due to inadequate granulocyte function.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Ch\351diak-Higashi syndrome?

options.b: It has an autosomal recessive inheritance
options.d: Granules are absent in white blood cells

mcqs.explanation: 297 Leukocytes contain giant granules in Ch\351diak–Higashi syndrome as seen in peripheral blood smears. They are due to aberrant phagolysosome fusion. The image shows giant granules in a neutrophil in Ch\351diak–Higashi syndrome.Ch\351diak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. The defective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes results in defective phagocytes function and susceptibility to infections . The abnormalities are neutropenia , defective degranulation , and delayed microbial killing, causing: • Albinism - melanocytes • Nerve defects - nervous system cells • Bleeding disorders - platelets298 The gene associated with this disorder encodes a large cytosolic protein called LYST , which is believed to regulate lysosomal trafficking.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 2-month-old baby was brought with complaints of fever and fast breathing for 5 days, and was diagnosed with pneumonia. Further history revealed baby had recurrent infections . Blood culture revealed infection from Nocardia spp . Nitroblue tetrazolium test turned out to be negative . Which of the following statement is false regarding this condition?

options.b: It is due to oxidase deficiency

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests chronic granulomatous disease . It is due to a macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction, not lymphocytic . Chronic granulomatous disease is a defect in bacterial killing and renders patients susceptible to recurrent bacterial infections . The name of this disease comes from the macrophage-rich chronic inflammatory reaction that tries to control the infection when the initial neutrophil defense is inadequate . This often leads to collections of activated macrophages that wall off the microbes, forming granulomas.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Match the following complement deficiencies with the disorders.
mcqs.explanation: The disorders caused due to complement deficiency are: The deficiency of C2 is the most common complement protein deficiency .Complement Disease /syndrome C1 esterase inhibitor Hereditary angioneurotic ede ma C1, C2, C4 Pyogenic infections , systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) C1q , C1r , C1s Pyogenic infections , SLE C3 Pyogenic infections ,Glomerul onephritis , SLE Factor H Hemolytic uremic syndrome( HUS), Pyogenic infections , Gl omerulonephritis , SLE C5 to C8 Recurrent infections withNei sseriaspp . Properdin Meningococcal meningitis Factor D Meningitis , sepsis -Neisseria Factors H and I Recurrent pyogenic infection s DAFF and CD59 Paroxysmal nocturnal hemog lobinuria (PNH) Mannan-binding lect in Respiratory tract infections MASP-2 Respiratory tract infections299

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presents with recurrent swelling of the face and lips as shown with vomiting and diarrhea when emotionally stressed . What is the most likely deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hereditary angioneurotic edema . It is due to the deficiency of C1 inhibitors. Hereditary angioneurotic edema is an autosomal dominant disorder, which is more common than complement deficiency states . Targets of C1 inhibitors are proteases , specifically C1r and C1s of the complement cascade , factor XII of the coagulation pathway , and the kallikrein system . Deficiency of C1 inhibitor leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein . This increases the production of vasoactive peptides such as bradykinin . It causes episodes of edema affecting the skin and mucosal surfaces such as the larynx and the gastrointestinal tract. This may result in life -threatening asphyxia or nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea after minor trauma or emotional stress .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old baby was brought with severe diaper rash. The parents gave a history of recurrent infections in the past 4 months which required frequent hospitalization. On examination white patches were present in oral mucosa which could be scraped easily . The biopsy of the thymus showed remnants of Hassall's corpuscles . Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

options.c: It is due to defect only in cell mediated immune response
options.d: B cell count can be normal

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The biopsy of the thymus showing remnants of Hassall's corpuscles indicates it is due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency . SCID is a defect in both humoral and cell -mediated immune responses . Usually the defect lies in the T-cell compartment with secondary impairment in humoral immunity. Affected infants present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive. Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus , causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens , including: • Candida albicans • Pneumocystis jiroveci • Pseudomonas • Cytomegalovirus • Varicella There are 2 types of SCID based on inheritance: 1. X-linked SCID is the most common form and hence it is more common in boys than in girls. The genetic defect is the mutation in the common \034-chain (\034c) subunit of cytokine receptors . T-cell numbers are greatly reduced , and although B cells may be normal in number, antibody synthesis is impaired because of the lack of T-cell help . The thymus contains lobules of undifferentiated epithelial cells resembling fetal thymus .300 2. Autosomal recessive is most commonly caused due to deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). The deficiency of ADA leads to the accumulation of deoxyadenosine and its derivatives (e.g., deoxy -ATP ). They are toxic to rapidly dividing immature lymphocytes , especially those of the T-cell lineage . Hence , there may be a greater reduction in the number of T lymphocytes . In the two most common forms (\034c mutation and ADA deficiency ), the thymus is small and devoid of lymphoid cells . In SCID caused by ADA deficiency , remnants of Hassall's corpuscles can be found. Note : X-linked SCID is the first human disease in which gene therapy has been successful .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which gene is not involved in SCID?
mcqs.explanation: BTK mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia and not SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency ). Severe combined immunodeficiency is a defect in both humoral and cell -mediated immune responses . In this condition, the following genes are involved: • JAK3 • RAG1 • IL -7R Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens , including: • Candida albicans • Pneumocystis jiroveci • Pseudomonas • Cytomegalovirus • Varicella

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 9-month-old baby was brought with a cough and difficulty in breathing. The baby was admitted with similar complaints in the past. On auscultation , coarse crepitations were heard. Quantitative serum immunoglobulin analysis was done and serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were low. His cellular immunity was found to be normal . Which of the following is false about his condition?

options.b: Germinal centres of lymph nodes are underdeveloped
options.c: Manifestation is seen usually after 6 months of age

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Bruton agammaglobulinemia/ X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA). Even though it is an immunodeficiency disease , it is paradoxically associated with autoimmune diseases such as arthritis and dermatomyositis in 35% of individuals. The classic form of this disease has the following characteristics: • B cells are absent or markedly decreased and the serum levels of all classes of immunoglobulins are decreased • T-cell mediated reactions are normal • Germinal centers of lymph nodes , Peyer's patches , the appendix , and tonsils are underdeveloped301 • Plasma cells are absent throughout the body XLA is characterized by the failure of B-cell precursors (pro-B cells and pre-B cells ) to develop into mature B cells . It is associated with mutations in a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase called Bruton tyrosine kinase (Btk). The related gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome. This X-linked disease is seen almost entirely in males. The disease usually does not become apparent until about 6 months of age , when maternal immunoglobulins are depleted . Affected individuals are susceptible to infections with: • Bacteria that are normally opsonized by antibodies and cleared by phagocytosis • Haemophilus influenzae • Streptococcus pneumonia • Staphylococcus aureus • Giardia lamblia - intestinal protozoan that is normally resisted by secreted IgA, causes persistent infections • Enteroviruses • Echovirus • Poliovirus • Coxsackievirus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old boy was brought to the OPD with delayed development . On examination, he had the following appearance . Further workup revealed hypocalcemia and an atrial septal defect . Chromosomal studies showed deletion of 22q11 . All are true about this syndrome except :

options.a: It is associated with T cell deficiency
options.b: Thymic aplasia is a prominent feature
options.d: Failure of development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal arches

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with the image suggests DiGeorge syndrome. It results from the failure of the development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches . They give rise to the thymus , the parathyroids, some of the C cells of the thyroid, and the ultimobranchial body. The absence of cell -mediated immunity causes poor defense against certain fungal and viral infections . The T-cell zones of lymphoid organs, i.e. paracortical areas of the lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen , are depleted . Ig levels may be normal or reduced , depending on the severity of the T-cell deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is least likely to be a feature in a patient with Hyper-IgM syndrome?

options.a: It has X-linked mode of inheritance
options.b: They have normal serum IgG levels
options.c: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia can be seen
options.d: They have normal B-cell and T-cell numbers

mcqs.explanation: The serum of patients with Hyper-IgM syndrome contains extremely low levels of IgG. In Hyper-IgM syndrome production of IgM antibodies is normal but the ability to produce IgG, IgA, and IgE antibodies is deficient . There are normal or elevated levels of IgM, no IgA or IgE, and extremely low levels of IgG. It affects the ability of helper T cells to deliver activating signals to B cells and macrophages . However, B cells and T cells counts are normal . It is mostly an X-linked disease , that has mutations in the gene encoding CD40L located on Xq26. If the disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern , then there are loss-of-function302 mutations involving either CD40 or the enzyme called activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID). Those with CD40L mutations are also susceptible to pneumonia caused by the intracellular organism Pneumocystis jiroveci. This is due to CD40L -mediated macrophage activation, a key reaction of cell -mediated immunity being defective . Recurrent pyogenic infection occurs because the level of opsonizing IgG antibodies is low. Occasionally , the IgM antibodies react with blood cells , giving rise to autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia , and neutropenia . In older patients , the proliferation of IgM-producing plasma cells that infiltrate the mucosa of the gastrointestinal tract is seen .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial infections and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. The flow cytometry analysis of the boy (Boxes 3& 4) is shown below (Boxes 1 & 2 are normal ). What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells . The B-cell response to antigens, is unaffected , accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies . Hence , the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome. The given clinical scenario and the flow cytometry is suggestive of Hyper IgM syndrome. The flow cytometry shows the following findings: • In comparison of image 3 to 1, where side scatter is plotted against CD 19: B-cell gating is present . Gating of B cells means selecting a cell during a flow cytometry experiment for further analysis or data presentation.CD 19 is widely expressed on B cells . Hence the graph shows B cell gating. Side scatter measurement provides information about the granularity of a cell . • In comparison of image 4 to 2, where CD 40 is plotted against CD 19: B cells are present only in quadrant 4, which means that there is CD 40 deficiency . The deficiency of the CD40 and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching and the production of memory cells . The B-cell response to antigens is unaffected , accounting for the presence of increased IgM antibodies . Hence , the condition is known as Hyper IgM syndrome. Given below is the explanation of how to interpret flow cytometry results :303 Interpretation of results : Quadrant 1- Cells marked in green : -VE for A antigen, +VE for B antigen Quadrant 2- Cells marked in purple : -VE for both the antigens. Quadrant 3- Cells marked in yellow : +VE for both the antigens Quadrant 4- Cells marked in red: +VE for A antigen, -VE for B antigen

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with isolated Ig A deficiency would have associated deficiency of which of the following IgG subtypes ?
mcqs.explanation: Isolated IgA deficiency is associated with deficiency of IgG subtypes IgG2 and IgG4. IgA deficiency -affected individuals have extremely low levels of both serum and secretory IgA. It may be familial or acquired in association with toxoplasmosis , measles , or some other viral infection . Because IgA is the major antibody in external secretions , mucosal defenses are weakened , and infections occur in the respiratory, gastrointestinal , and urogenital tracts. Symptomatic patients commonly have recurrent sinopulmonary infections and diarrhea. IgA-deficient patients have a high frequency of respiratory tract allergy and a variety of autoimmune diseases , particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are mutated in X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome is due to mutations in the gene encoding an adaptor molecule called SLAM-associated protein (SAP). It is characterized by an inability to eliminate Epstein -Barr virus (EBV), eventually leading to fulminant infectious mononucleosis and the development of B-cell tumors.304 In about 80% of cases , the disease is due to mutations in the gene encoding the adaptor molecule SAP. Defects in SAP contribute to attenuated NK cell and T-cell activation, resulting in increased susceptibility to viral infections . Option B: LYST gene is associated with Chediak-Higashi syndrome. Option C: BTK gene is associated with Isolated growth hormone deficiency type III . Option D: TBX1 gene is associated with 22q11 .2 deletion syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following lymphoid tissue findings is seen most commonly in patients with common variable hypogammaglobulinemia ?
mcqs.explanation: Normal B-cell count is most commonly seen in lymphoid tissues of individuals with the common variable hypogammaglobulinemia . It is a heterogeneous group of disorders in which the common feature is hypogammaglobulinemia , generally affecting all the antibody classes , but sometimes only IgG. In contrast to X-linked agammaglobulinemia, most individuals with common variable immunodeficiency have normal or near-normal numbers of B-cells in the blood and lymphoid tissues . These B cells , however, are not able to differentiate into plasma cells . FDA approved XEMBIFY in 2019 , % immunoglobulin solution for subcutaneous injection. It is indicated for the use of primary humoral immunodeficiency disorders in patients 2years of age and older.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought with complaints of red rashes over his skin. His mother says that the child will be constantly scratching the rashes. On asking any previous history she says the child keeps getting recurrent infections which mostly require hospitalization. Blood investigations showed a low platelet count. Which of the following is false regarding this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The given history with eczema, recurrent infections , and thrombocytopenia points towards Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. In this condition, IgM levels in the serum are low. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP), which is located on Xp11.23 . The X-linked disease is characterized by thrombocytopenia , eczema, and a marked vulnerability to recurrent infection , resulting in early death . Platelets are small in size. The thymus is morphologically normal , at least early in the course of the disease , but there is the progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood and in the T-cell zones (paracortical areas) of the lymph nodes , with variable defects in cellular immunity. Patients do not make antibodies to polysaccharide antigens, and the response to protein antigens is poor. IgM levels are low, IgG is usually normal , while the levels of IgA and IgE are often elevated . Patients are prone to developing B - cell lymphomas.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the OPD with complaints of repeated falls while walking for the past 1 year. She had difficulty in eating, gripping , or holding things. On examination, hand mouth incoordination and slurring of speech were noted . On ocular examination, the following finding was seen . All are true about this condition except :

options.a: There is defective production of IgA and IgG
options.b: Affected gene is located on chromosome
options.d: There is increased risk of malignancy

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario and image showing telangiectasia are diagnostic of ataxia-telangiectasia . It is an autosomal-recessive disorder, not autosomal dominant.305 The most prominent humoral immune abnormalities are defective production of IgA and IgG2. The gene responsible for this disorder is located on chromosome 11 and encodes a protein called ATM. The ATM protein is a sensor of DNA damage (double -strand breaks), and it activates p53 by phosphorylation . Ataxia-telangiectasia is characterized by abnormal gait (ataxia), vascular malformations (telangiectases ), neurologic deficits , increased incidence of tumors, and immunodeficiency . It may affect both B and T cells . There is a high incidence of lymphomas and leukemias .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Human immunodeficiency virus affects CD4 cells due to their interaction with which protein?
mcqs.explanation: The CD4 cells are affected by HIV due to their interaction with gp120. HIV -1 virion is spherical and contains an electron -dense , cone-shaped core surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from the host cell membrane. Target cells of HIV include CD4+ helper T cells (worst affected ), monocyte -macrophages , and dendritic cells . The virus core contains: • Major capsid protein p24 • Nucleocapsid protein p7 /p9 • Two copies of viral genomic RNA • The three viral enzymes (protease , reverse transcriptase, and integrase ) The viral core is surrounded by a matrix protein called p17, which lies underneath the virion envelope . The viral envelope is studded by two viral glycoproteins , gp120 and gp41, which are critical for HIV infection of cells . Viral glycoprotein gp120 binds to CD4+ cells in the host. CXCR4 and CCR5 function as coreceptors for HIV -1 entry into CD4+ cells . This binding leads to a conformational change in gp41 causing exposure of a hydrophobic region called the fusion peptide at the tip of gp41. This peptide inserts into the cell membrane of the target cells (e.g., T cells or macrophages ), leading to the fusion of the virus with the host cell . The image below shows the pathogenesis of HIV infection .306

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cell types is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of HIV infection ?
mcqs.explanation: The neutrophil is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ) infection . HIV enters the body and affects T cells, dendritic cells , and macrophages . Particularly, memory and activated T cells are infected , but it is inefficient at productively infecting naive (unactivated) T cells . Completion of the viral life cycle in latently infected cells occurs only after cell activation, and in the case of most CD4+ T cells , virus activation results in cell lysis . The image below shows the pathogenesis of HIV infection .307

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most common CNS neoplasm in HIV patients ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common central nervous system (CNS) neoplasm in patients with HIV infection is primary CNS lymphoma. Lymphomas are the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppressed individuals, including those with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and immunosuppression after transplantation. They are associated with latent infection with Epstein –Barr virus (EBV). The vast majority of primary brain lymphomas are of B-cell origin. At least two mechanisms appear to underlie the increased risk of B-cell tumors in HIV -infected individuals. They are: • The unchecked proliferation of B cells infected with oncogenic herpes viruses in the setting of profound T-cell depletion (AIDS). • Germinal center B-cell hyperplasia in the setting of early HIV infection . The most common site for lymphoma in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) is the central nervous system (CNS).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man, who is HIV -positive , presents with generalized lymphadenopathy . Which of the histopathological features is least likely to be seen on lymph node biopsy ?

options.d: Collection of monocytoid B Cells in sinuses

mcqs.explanation: Hematoxylin bodies are seen in lymph nodes in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Features of AIDS-related lymphadenopathy : Early stages of HIV infection : • Florid hyperplasia of B cell follicles • Follicle lysis • Monocytoid B cells in sinuses • Neutrophils and dermatopathic lymphadenopathy • The interfollicular zone shows vascular proliferation, which may progress to Kaposi sarcoma Late stages of HIV infection : • Severe lymphoid involution • Possible hyalinization of the germinal centers • Burnt-out lymph nodes , which become atrophic and may harbor numerous opportunistic pathogens , often within macrophages

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old HIV -seropositive man presents with raised violaceous plaques over the legs . Microscopy shows a lesion in the dermis with dilated , jagged vascular channels lined and surrounded by plump spindle cells . It contains red cells with marked hemorrhage, hemosiderin pigment , and mononuclear inflammation. Mitotic figures are also seen . Which organism is associated with this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is Kaposi sarcoma, caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8). Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm, that is highly associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It is the most common cancer seen in patients having AIDS. Though the308 incidence of Kaposi carcinoma reduced , it still occurs in 2-3% of HIV -infected individuals. The pathogenesis of Kaposi sarcoma that is caused by HHV8 includes : • A virally encoded G protein that induces VEGF production , stimulating endothelial growth • The lytic infection caused by HHV8 increases the pro-inflammatory cytokines • HHV8 encoded proteins inhibit the p53 induced apoptosis The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin and the histologic appearance of Kaposi sarcoma, demonstrating sheets of proliferating spindle cells :

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45 -year-old HIV -positive patient has patchy pneumonia. Smears of induced sputum and sedimented cells from lavage fluid stained with methenamine silver are as seen below . Which is the most likely organism implicated ?
mcqs.explanation: The smears stained with methenamine silver show black-colored stained cysts resembling the crushed ping pong balls of Pneumocystis jirovecii.309 Approximately 15% to 30% of untreated HIV -infected people develop pneumonia during the course of the disease . It is mainly caused by the fungus P. jirovecii (reactivation of prior latent infection ).310

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following best describes an amyloid?
mcqs.explanation: Amyloid can be best described as a proteoglycan . Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of fibrillar proteins . Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins . The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans (heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate ), and plasma proteins (serum amyloid P component ). The abundant charged sugar groups in these adsorbed proteins give the deposits staining characteristics that resemble starch (amylose ). Therefore, these deposits are called amyloid. Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic , hyaline, extracellular substance .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a patient with reactive systemic amyloidosis , which of the following proteins are likely to get deposited in the tissues ?
mcqs.explanation: There is the deposition of AA proteins in reactive systemic amyloidosis (secondary amyloidosis ). In inflammatory states , there is a release of IL -1 and IL -6, which act on the liver cells . The liver increases the production of SAA (serum amyloid-associated ) proteins which circulate bound to high-density lipoproteins . This gives rise to AA proteins , which get deposited in tissues causing reactive systemic amyloidosis or secondary amyloidosis . The most common sites are the kidney and heart. It is usually seen secondary to: • Rheumatoid arthritis (most common) • Tuberculosis • Bronchiectasis • Chronic osteomyelitis317 • Inflammatory bowel disease • Ankylosing spondylitis • Malignancies - renal cell cancer, Hodgkin's lymphoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of reactive amyloidosis worldwide ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of reactive amyloidosis worldwide is rheumatoid arthritis.
