Bite cells are trapped in splenic cords and removed by phagocytes leading to extravascular hemolysis . The images given below show Heinz bodies and bite cells seen in G6PD deficiency .404

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: A patient with G6PD deficiency was suspected to have acute hemolytic episode . Which of the following features would you expect to see in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Acute hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is intravascular . This is marked by anaemia, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria. These episodes are self -limited and intermittent . Reticulocytosis occurs during the recovery phase . Hence , features related to chronic hemolysis (e.g., splenomegaly , cholelithiasis ) are absent.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old food blogger presents with complaints of icterus and abdominal fullness . She returned yesterday from a vacation in Egypt where she tried fava beans. Her peripheral smear is given below . This condition is protective against which of the following malarial parasites ?
mcqs.explanation: The peripheral smear shows RBCs with anisopoikilocytosis with polychromasia and many bite cells (arrows) suggestive of G6PD deficiency . This condition is protective against Plasmodium405 falciparum malaria . Malarial parasites preferentially invade RBCs which are rich in G6PD. G6PD deficiency causes oxidative stress and hemolysis , preferably in the older RBCs. Reticulocytes and young erythrocytes have much higher G6PD activities and are less susceptible to oxidant damage . P. falciparum can invade erythrocytes of all ages . P. vivax , and P. ovale invade reticulocytes (immature erythrocytes ) preferentially . Hence , a low G6PD level in older RBC is protective against P. falciparum malaria . Episodic hemolysis in this condition can be triggered by fava beans which is a staple in Egyptian cuisine. The images given below show Heinz bodies and bite cells seen in G6PD deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about G6PD-deficiency anemia?

options.a: Hemolytic episodes occur both intravascularly and extravascularly
options.b: G6PD Mediterranean deficiency is the most severe form.
options.c: Older RBCs are more prone to hemolysis than younger ones
options.d: Hemolysis continues as long as there is exposure to oxidant drugs

mcqs.explanation: 406 Hemolysis in G6PD-deficiency anemia does not continue for the entire period that the patient takes the offending drug. It stops after a few days. Two variants of G6PD, designated as G6PD– and G6PD Mediterranean , cause most of the clinically significant hemolytic anemias. The half-life of G6PD- is moderately reduced , whereas that of G6PD Mediterranean is markedly reduced ; hence , the severity of deficiency is greater with the Mediterranean variant . The most common normal variant is G6PD B. The hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis . The damaged red cells are sequestered in the spleen and killed by macrophages , causing extravascular hemolysis . The oxidative stresses can denature hemoglobin , resulting in intravascular hemolysis . In individuals with G6PD deficiency , acute intravascular hemolysis begins 2 to 3 days after exposure to oxidants. Only older RBCs are at risk for lysis. The hemolytic episode is self -limited because hemolysis stops when only younger G6PD-replete red cells remain, even if the patient continues to take the offending drug.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: What class of antibodies are involved in the most common form of immunohemolytic anaemia?
mcqs.explanation: Warm antibody type is the most common form of immunohemolytic anaemia. Most of the causative antibodies in this condition belong to the IgG class. Immunohemolytic anaemia is caused by antibodies that cause premature destruction of the red cells . Based on the temperature at which the different types of antibodies bind to the RBCs stably , they are classified as: • Warm antibody type - most common • Cold agglutinin type • Cold hemolysin type

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: Match the immunohemolytic anaemia with the type of hemolysis .
mcqs.explanation: The type of hemolysis seen in the different immunohemolytic anemia are: Autoimmune hemolytic anemias (AIHA ) cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis . In warm antibody type , hemolysis is extravascular. IgG-coated red cells are phagocytosed and destroyed in the spleen . In cold agglutinin type , hemolysis is extravascular and intravascular . In the peripheral vascular bed (low temperature ), IgM binds to the red cells . This causes agglutination and complement -fixing. They are unbound when they reach the general circulation. However, the IgM interaction causes deposition of sublytic quantities of C3b. It is an excellent opsonin, which leads to the removal of RBCs by phagocytes in the spleen , liver , and bone marrow . Cold hemolysin type is a rare subtype of AIHA . Hemolysis is intravascular . IgG binds to the P blood group antigen on the red cells , which leads to complement -mediated lysis .407 Type Hemolysis Warm antibo dy Extravascular Cold agglutini n Extravascular and intravascul ar Cold hemolys in Intravascular

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman was brought to the casualty with loss of consciousness . On examination , pallor, icterus and splenomegaly were noted . Her past history was significant for meningitis 2 weeks ago which was treated with iv antibiotics. Lab investigations showed anemia and increased osmotic fragility. Which of the following statements is false regarding the probable diagnosis?

options.a: Rh blood group complex are involved in the pathogenesis
options.c: Direct Coombs agglutination test is diagnostic

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of drug-induced warm antibody type of immunohemolytic anemia. In this condition, primarily extravascular hemolysis is present . LDH may be increased when there is hemolysis . Two different mechanisms for drug-induced immune hemolytic anemias are: Antigenic drugs: • Anemia occurs 1-2 weeks after initiation of large IV dose of the offending drug • These drugs bind to red cell membrane and are recognised by anti-drug antibodies • They can cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis • E.g. penicillin , cephalosporins , quinidine Tolerance-breaking drugs: • Antibodies are produced against red cell antigens, particularly Rh antigens • E.g. alpha-methyl dopa

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria?

options.a: IgG class of antibodies are involved
options.b: Antibodies are directed against Rh antigen
options.d: It mostly occurs in children following a viral infection

mcqs.explanation: In paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), antibodies are directed against the P blood group antigen. PCH is a cold hemolysin type of hemolysis caused by IgG autoantibodies classically . They are also called Donath Landsteiner antibodies and are produced often in response to a viral infection . This antibody is a biphasic hemolysin . i.e., the antibody binds to RBC at colder temperature but hemolysis occurs at core temperature 37\260C. This can cause substantial , sometimes fatal, intravascular hemolysis , and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children following viral infections and usually recover within 1 month. Immuno -hemolytic anaemias are of 3 types :408 Antibody ty pe Antigen on the RBC surface Temperature for hemolys is Warm aggluti nin IgG Rh antigen 37\260C or higher Cold agglutini n IgM I antigen (adults )i antigen (in fants) 30\260C, usually 0-10 \260C Cold hemolys in IgG P antigen Biphasic hemolysis (37\260C)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: G6PD deficiency and Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia most commonly seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia is most commonly seen with disseminated intravascular coagulation. It occurs in the following conditions: • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) • Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ) • Hemolytic -uremic syndrome (HUS) • Malignant hypertension • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Disseminated cancer A common pathogenic feature in these disorders is a microvascular lesion. Deposition of fibrin and platelets result in luminal narrowing . These vascular changes produce shear stresses . These changes mechanically injure the passing red cells producing schistocytes or helmet cells on the peripheral smear. The image given below shows schistocytes or helmet cells .409

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most potent vasoconstrictor?
mcqs.explanation: The most potent vasoconstrictor is urotensin2 followed by endothelin and angiotensin.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a component of \033 granules of platelets ?
mcqs.explanation: Epinephrine is a component of \033 granules of platelets . The different components of platelet granules are: • \037 granules • Fibrinogen • Fibronectin • PF4 • Factor V, VIII • PDGF • TGF • \033 granules • ADP • Calcium • Serotonin • Histamine • Epinephrine

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Rees and Ecker diluting fluid is used in ______
mcqs.explanation: Rees and Ecker's solution is used as a diluting fluid in the RBC pipette for performing platelet counts. Its composition is: The steps involved in platelet count are: I - Filling the pipette • Diluting fluid is drawn to mark 1 of the RBC pipette and expelled419 • Blood is aspirated to 0.5 mark of the RBCs diluting pipette • Diluting fluid is aspirated to 101 mark • Blood and diluting fluid are mixed mechanically for 5 min II - Filling the counting chamber • Allow the counting chamber to stand for 20 -30 minutes to allow the platelets to settle . • To prevent drying out of the preparation, it should be kept in a moist atmosphere , this is most easily arranged by placing the filled counting chamber in the bottom of a clean Petri dish, alongside which arrange a small piece of cotton wool which has been soaked in water and squeezed out. Petri dish lid is additionally put over the dish. • After 20 -30minutes, the counting chamber can be removed and carefully transferred to the microscope stage . III - Counting the number of platelets • Focus on the surface of the hemocytometer chamber with a high power dry objective . Dim the light to make the thrombocytes visible, and count all of the thrombocytes in the entire center 1 mm\262 (erythrocyte counting area) of both sides of the hemocytometer . This gives the number of thrombocytes in 0.2 l of 1: 200 dilution of blood. • The number of thrombocytes counted X 1000 = number of thrombocytes /l of undiluted blood.Components Valu e Sodium citrate 3.8 g Formaldehyde (40 %) 0.2 ml Brilliant cresyl blue 0.1 g Distilled water 100 ml

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old girl with dengue hemorrhagic fever is being monitored by measuring platelet count. Spontaneous bleeding is associated with platelet values below _______ /\265 L.
mcqs.explanation: Spontaneous bleeding (non-traumatic) is associated with platelet values below 20 ,000 platelets /\265 L. It most often involves small vessels . The common sites for such hemorrhages are: • Skin • Mucosa of gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts • Intracranial bleeding - most feared site of bleeding The production of the platelets is regulated by the hormone thrombopoietin produced in the liver. The platelet synthesis is also specifically increased by interleukin 6. The average lifespan of the platelets is 7–10 days. The normal platelet count is 1,50,000 - 4,00,000 /\265 L.420

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding functional platelet disorders?

options.a: Normal platelet count and normal bleeding time
options.b: Normal platelet count and increased bleeding time
options.c: Decreased platelet count and increased bleeding time
options.d: Decreased platelet count and decreased bleeding time

mcqs.explanation: Functional platelet disorders have normal platelet count and increased bleeding time. Classification of platelet functional disorders: • Defect in platelet -vessel wall interaction (disorders of adhesion) • Von Willebrand disease - deficiency or defect in plasma vWF • Bernard –Soulier syndrome - deficiency or defect in GP Ib IX • Defects in platelet -platelet interaction (disorders of aggregation ) • Congenital afibrinogenemia - deficiency of plasma fibrinogen • Glanzmann thrombasthenia - deficiency or defect in GPIIb -IIIa • Disorders of platelet secretion and signal transduction • Storage pool deficiency - \037-Granule deficiency and gamma-Granule deficiency • Quebec platelet disorder • Chediak–Higashi syndrome • Gray platelet syndrome • Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome • Disorders of platelet coagulation -protein interaction • Scott syndrome - defect in factor Va -Xa interaction on platelets

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about vonWillebrand factor?

options.b: Its deficiency can also cause factor VIII defect
options.c: Its deficiency may cause defective platelet adhesion
options.d: It serves as a carrier for factor VIII

mcqs.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (vWF ) is not synthesized by hepatocytes . They are produced by endothelial cells of liver and megakaryocytes . It is also found in: • Platelet granules - lesser compared to endothelial cells • Endothelial cells within cytoplasmic vesicles called Weibel-Palade bodies • Subendothelium - binds to collagen It mediates the adhesion of platelets to sites of vascular injury (subendothelium ). It links the exposed collagen to platelets . It facilitates platelet to platelet interaction and also stabilizes the hemostatic plug against shear forces . It is a carrier protein for factor VIII and also protects it from proteolytic degradation and stabilizes it. The half-life of factor VIII is about 2.4 hours when free and 12 hours when bound to vWF in the circulation. Since vWF stabilizes factor VIII , a deficiency of vWF gives rise to a secondary decrease in factor VIII levels . This may be reflected by a prolongation of the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) in von Willebrand disease types 1 and 3.421

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman is found to have uncontrolled bleeding after a minor cut injury. Her lab investigations are given below . Which of the following statements are false about her condition?

options.c: Type 3 is inherited as autosomal dominant

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand disease (vWD ). Type 3 vWD is inherited as an autosomal recessive disease . The characteristics of different subtypes of vWD are: Type 1 is the most common subtype of vWD . In Type 2, vWF is expressed in normal amounts, but missense mutations are present that lead to defective multimer assembly . This type has several subtypes , of which type 2A is the most common. Laboratory findings in vWD : • Prolonged bleeding time • Normal platelet count • Hess test - positive tourniquet test due to defective platelet adhesion • Ristocetin-induced aggregation - defective and diagnostic of this disease • Platelet aggregation with ADP, collagen, and thrombin - normal • Increased aPTT Though the synthesis of factor VIII remains normal , the half-life of VIII in plasma decreases due to reduced vWF (carrier ) levels . This leads to secondary VIIIC deficiency in plasma. So, the intrinsic pathway of coagulation is affected . Hence , aPTT is increased in these patients .Subt ype Description Inheritance Lab findings Type Quantitative deficiency of vW F Autosomal domin ant Reduced vWF antigen, activit y and Factor VIII422 Subt ype Description Inheritance Lab findings Type Qualitative defect in vWF Autosomal domin ant Reduced vWF activity to anti gen ration<0.6 Type Near-complete (quantitative) deficiency of Factor VIII Autosomal recessi ve Marked reduction or absence in Factor VIII levels

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following occurs due to a defect in \033 granules of the platelets ?
mcqs.explanation: Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome occurs due to a defect in platelet \033 granules. Platelet granules disorders include : • Gray platelet syndrome - involves \037 granules and characterized by thrombocytopenia with large platelets that appear pale on the peripheral smear (due to deficiency of the \037 granules) • Quebec platelet syndrome - defect in \037 granules • Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome - defect in \033 granules and characterized by hypopigmentation and bleeding manifestation • Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome - mutations in the WASp gene expressed in the X chromosome and characterized by microthrombocytopenia, eczema, recurrent infections

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with large platelets on peripheral smear is diagnosed to have Bernard -Soulier disease . Deficiency of which of the following causes this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Bernard –Soulier disease is due to deficiency of Gp Ib/ IX. Bernard –Soulier syndrome is characterized by large platelets . Ristocetin aggregation is abnormal . Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia .Deficiency Defect Disease Gp Ib/IX Adhesion of platelets Bernard –Soulier syndro me Gp IIb /IIIa Aggregation of platelets Glanzmann thrombasth enia von Willebrand fact or Adhesion>Aggregation Von Willebrand disease423

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Bernard -Soulier syndrome?

options.a: There is defective adhesion of platelets to sub-endothelial matrix
options.b: Deficiency of the platelet membrane glycoprotein complex Ib-IX is seen
options.c: Platelet aggregation by ristocetin is normal
options.d: It has an autosomal recessive inheritance

mcqs.explanation: In Bernard –Soulier syndrome, platelet aggregation by ristocetin is abnormal . The receptor for vWF i.e. Ib-IX is essential for normal platelet adhesion to the subendothelial extracellular matrix. In this condition, there is deficiency of Gp Ib/ IX. Clinical manifestations include epistaxis , ecchymoses , menorrhagia, gingival bleeding , and gastrointestinal bleeding . Laboratory findings seen in Bernard -Soulier syndrome: • Prolonged bleeding time • Moderate thrombocytopenia • Platelet aggregation by ristocetin is deficient (but ADP, arachidonic acid, epinephrine , collagen - normal). • Clot retraction - normal • Abnormally large platelets The image given below shows the abnormally large platelets on peripheral smear seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome.424

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old girl with a history of easy bruising was referred for further evaluation. Her previous lab reports showed that platelet count and morphology were normal . Platelet aggregations tests are given below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Glanzmann thrombasthenia. It is an abnormality of platelet GPIIb -IIIa (fibrinogen receptor ). Platelets are unable to adhere to each other and to the underlying tissue of the damaged blood vessels . It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner . The symptoms include mucocutaneous bleeding in the neonatal period , menorrhagia, ecchymoses , epistaxis , and gingival hemorrhage. Types of Glanzmann thrombasthenia include : • Type 1: Absence of GPIIb -IIIa • Type 2: Reduced surface expression of GPIIb -IIIa / Essentialis athrombia - clot retraction is normal425 • Type 3: Dysfunction of GPIIb -IIIa Laboratory features of Glanzmann thrombasthenia: • Normal platelet count and morphology • Platelet aggregation occurs in response to ristocetin, but not to other agonists (such as ADP, thrombin , collagen or epinephrine ) • Clot retraction is absent

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old boy is brought with a history of recurrent impetigo . Physical examination findings are given below . Platelet counts are low and peripheral smear shows abnormally small-sized platelets . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (WAS). The given image shows (A) multiple petechiae over face and hematoma under the right eye and (B) eczema of the foot. This syndrome is an X-linked recessive , primary immunodeficiency disorder involving the WAS gene . It is characterised by the triad of: • Severe eczema • Thrombocytopenia • Recurrent infections Small platelets are seen in: • Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome • X-linked thrombocytopenia Large platelets are seen in: • Bernard -Soulier syndrome • Myeloproliferative syndrome • Myelodysplastic syndrome • May–Hegglin anomaly • Gray platelet syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with epistaxis , easy bruising and menorrhagia. There is no history of drug intake. Physical examination shows scattered petechiae and a normal -sized spleen . Her lab investigations are given below . Antibodies against which of the following can lead to this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Autoantibodies seen in ITP are most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb -IIIa or Ib-IX. It is a diagnosis of exclusion due to the following findings: • Bleeding tendency - petechiae • Low platelet count, elevated bleeding time • Presence of megathrombocytes in the peripheral smear - a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis • Female preponderance426 • Absence of splenomegaly Note : Prothrombin time (PT) is normal in ITP .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which class of antiplatelet antibodies are seen in patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura?
mcqs.explanation: Antiplatelet antibodies in chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP ) are mainly IgG class. Autoantibodies most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins are IIb -IIIa or Ib-IX. It can be demonstrated in the plasma and bound to the platelet surface in about 80% of patients .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed to have idiopathic ITP . Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in her?
mcqs.explanation: Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are uncommon in idiopathic (primary) ITP . They are seen in secondary ITP . Chronic ITP occurs most commonly in adult women younger than 40 years of age . The female -to-male ratio is 3: 1. It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction. It is of 2 types : • Primary or idiopathic - without any risk factors • Secondary - presence of predisposing conditions like SLE, HIV , CLL Signs of accelerated thrombopoiesis that are seen in this condition are: • Megakaryocytes in bone marrow • Megathrombocytes (abnormally large platelets ) in peripheral blood The image given below shows 2 megakaryocytes seen in bone marrow aspirate (Wrights stain).Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood. It occurs with equal frequency in both sexes , mostly after a viral illness . It is self -limited condition, resolves within 6 months.427

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following predisposing conditions are likely to develop chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura?
mcqs.explanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus , HIV infection , chronic lymphocytic leukemia, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome can predispose to the development of secondary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP ). The predisposing conditions of secondary chronic ITP include : • Autoimmune conditions • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) • Immune thyroid disease • Evans syndrome • Lymphoproliferative diseases • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia • Large granular T-lymphocyte lymphocytic leukemia • Chronic infection • Helicobacter pylori • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ) • Hepatitis C virus (HCV)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 63-year-old man with moderate COVID pneumonia developed DVT . Therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin was started . His lab investigations are given below . Which of the following is false about this condition?

options.b: Lesser incidence with use of LMWH

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). It is not self -resolving. Thrombocytopenia occurs in about 5% of persons receiving heparin and is of two types :Feature Type I Type II Incidence More common Less common Occurrenc e Rapidly after onset of therap y 5 to 14 days after therapy Pathogene sis Direct platelet -aggregating ef fect of heparin Antibodies against heparin-pl atelet factor 4 complexes Severity Less severe Often leads to life -threatenin g venous and arterial thromb osis Treatment Self -resolving Immediate discontinuation o f heparinAlternate non-hepar in anticoagulant to be used428

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following commonly cause drug-induced thrombocytopenia except _____
mcqs.explanation: Terlipressin does not cause drug-induced thrombocytopenia . Drug-induced thrombocytopenia can be caused by: • Vancomycin • Quinine • Rifampin They cause thrombocytopenia through direct effects on platelets or secondary to immunologically mediated platelet destructions . Quinine, quinidine, and vancomycin bind to platelet glycoprotein and create antigenic determinants that are recognized by antibodies .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A post -operative patient was started on prophylactic unfractionated heparin for DVT . Which of the following is false regarding this drug?

options.a: It is an indirect thrombin-factor Xa inhibitor
options.b: It is safe in patients with renal impairment
options.d: On development of HIT , LMWH can be started alternately

mcqs.explanation: The risk of severe heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is lowered with LMWH but not eliminated . Hence , once severe HIT develops even LMWH exacerbates the thrombotic tendency and must be avoided. Management of HIT includes the immediate withdrawal of heparin therapy and instituting an alternative non-heparin anticoagulant.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions is associated with ADAMTS13 deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: ADAMTS13 deficiency is associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ). ADAMTS13 is also called vWF metalloprotease which degrades very high-molecular-weight multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Its deficiency causes accumulation of these multimers in the plasma and promotes platelet activation and aggregation . TTP is a part of a spectrum of clinical syndromes called thrombotic microangiopathy. They are caused by insults that lead to excessive activation of platelets , which deposit as thrombi in small blood vessels . Features of TTP include : • Fever • Thrombocytopenia • Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia • Transient neurologic deficits • Renal failure429

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of hematuria and melena for 10 days. Laboratory investigations reveal mild thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation tests . Peripheral smear is given below . Which organism is most frequently involved in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and peripheral smear showing helmet cells or schistocytes are suggestive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). This condition is most commonly associated with enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli strain O157 : H7 worldwide . This strain releases Shiga-like toxin. This toxin is absorbed from the inflamed gastrointestinal mucosa into the circulation and causes endothelial dysfunction . It leads to platelet activation and aggregation . Children and older adults are at the highest risk . The image given below shows schistocytes or helmet cells seen in HUS.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Deficiency of which of the following complement components is not associated with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome is not associated with deficiency of CD59. It is associated with deficiency of the following components : • Complement factor H • Membrane cofactor protein (CD46) • Complement factor I These three proteins prevent excessive activation of the alternative complement pathway . Deficiencies of these proteins can be caused by inherited defects or acquired inhibitory autoantibodies . The disease may be associated with a remitting, relapsing course .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Coombs test is found to be positive in a patient with thrombocytopenia . Which of the following conditions could be a likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: 430 Coombs test is positive in immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) as it is an immunogenic cause of thrombocytopenia . Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) are nonimmunogenic causes . Hence , Coombs test is negative in these conditions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is affected in patients with Weber-Osler-Rendu syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Weber–Osler–Rendu syndrome is a disorder of the blood vessels . It is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations that modulate TGF-�o signalling. It is also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia . This condition is characterized by dilated , tortuous blood vessels with thin walls that bleed readily . Bleeding is most common in the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis ), tongue , mouth, and eyes , and throughout the gastrointestinal tract. Platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) are normal. Clinical conditions in which abnormalities of vessel wall cause bleeding include : • Infections - meningococcemia , infective endocarditis , rickettsioses • Collagen defects - Ehlers –Danlos syndrome, scurvy, and Cushing's syndrome • Perivascular amyloidosis - most common with amyloid light -chain (AL ) amyloidosis • Henoch–Sch\366nlein purpura • Drug reactions431

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common hereditary disease associated with life -threatening bleeding ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common hereditary disease associated with life -threatening bleeding is hemophilia A. It is caused by mutations in factor VIII , an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade . Note : von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presents with the following finding after a trivial fall. His lab investigations are given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario showing hemarthrosis and elevated aPTT is suggestive of hemophilia . Specific tests for measuring levels of factor VIII and factor IX can determine whether it is hemophilia A or hemophilia B respectively. Clinical features of hemophilia : • Hemarthroses - joint hemorrhages, later causing progressive deformities • Recurrent bleeding • Pseudotumour syndrome - fascial hemorrhages that occur as blood-filled cysts with calcification and proliferation of fibroblasts, giving the appearance of the tumor It is associated with elevated aPTT and normal platelet count, bleeding time, and PT. Option A: In ITP , the platelet count is low and bleeding time is prolonged . Option B: In functional platelet disorders, like Bernard Soulier syndrome, the platelet count is normal and bleeding time is prolonged . Option D: In vitamin K deficiency , both PT and aPTT are prolonged . PT is relatively more prolonged than is the aPTT .437

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy was found to have excessive bleeding following tooth extraction. Lab investigations revealed prolonged aPTT , decreased serum factor VIII levels and normal VwF activity. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency ). It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. Hence , it affects mainly males and homozygous females . Hemophilia B is also inherited as X-linked recessive trait. Hemophilia C is inherited as an autosomal-recessive trait.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about hemophilia ?

options.c: Hemophilia A in female may indicate unfavourable lyonization
options.d: Hemophilia A can occur without any family history

mcqs.explanation: Hemophilia A and B mostly affect males, but rarely can affect females also. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, affecting mainly males and homozygous females . Rarely, excessive bleeding occurs in heterozygous females . It is due to the inactivation of the X chromosome bearing the normal factor VIII allele by chance in most cells (unfavourable lyonization). About 30% of patients have no family history and the disorder is caused due to new mutations. Hemophilia B is inherited as X-linked recessive trait. There is a deficiency of factor IX. Hemophilia C is an autosomal-recessive condition and hence can occur in females . There is a deficiency of factor XI.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old child with easy bruising was diagnosed to have moderate hemophilia A. What will be the percentage of normal factor VIII in her?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with moderate hemophilia A have 2% - 5% of normal levels of factor VIII . The clinical manifestations of Hemophilia A vary in severity , corresponding to the level of factor VIII present. They can be classified as:Severi ty Levels of factor VIII Mild 6-50% Mode rate 2-5% Sever e <1%

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following lab findings are seen in patients with hemophilia A?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with hemophilia A have: • Prolonged partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) - intrinsic pathway abnormality • Normal prothrombin time (PT)438 • Normal bleeding time • Normal platelet count

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A newborn baby develops severe umbilical cord bleeding soon after birth. Lab investigations are given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of factor XIII deficiency . A positive urea lysis test confirms the diagnosis. Factor XIII is also known as clot-stabilizing factor that converts unstable fibrin clot into a stable clot. Its deficiency typically presents as excessive umbilical cord bleeding in the newborn. Laboratory findings in this condition are: • Normal levels of bleeding time (BT), platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and thrombin time (TT) • Positive urea lysis test - confirmatory test which demonstrates lysis of clot by hyperosmolar urea in affected individuals The parameters for the given diseases :Condition PT aPTT BT TT Platelet count Urea lysis te st Vitamin K deficiency increa sed increased increa sed normal /incre ased normal /decre ased negative Von Willebrand disease norma l normal /incre ased increa sed normal normal negative Hemorrhagic disease of ne wborn increa sed increased increa sed normal /incre ased normal /decre ased negative Factor XIII deficiency norma l normal norma l normal normal positive

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A Hemogram of a 23 -year-old patient with a bleeding disorder is given below . Which of the following would you use to differentiate between heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and afibrinogenemia in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Reptilase is a thrombin agonist which is used to differentiate heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT ) and afibrinogenemia. It is resistant to the action of heparin. The differential diagnosis for normal platelet count with elevated PT, aPTT and TT are HIT and afibrinogenemia. After adding reptilase , if the TT is corrected , it points to HIT . In afibrinogenemia, since there is an absence of fibrin, there is no change in the TT .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old child was diagnosed to have Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. What is this condition associated with?
mcqs.explanation: 439 Kasabach–Merritt syndrome is associated with DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation ). This syndrome is characterised by the following features : • Rapidly growing vascular tumour • Thrombocytopenia • Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia • Consumptive coagulopathy An unusual form of DIC occurs in association with giant hemangiomas. In this type , stasis and recurrent trauma to the fragile blood vessels cause thrombi to form within the neoplasm . The image given below shows a reddish -blue lesion covering the lower part of the abdomen. It is a caverno-capillary haemangioma seen in Kasabach–Merritt syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following clotting factor deficiency will not affect clotting in vivo ?
mcqs.explanation: Factor XII deficiency will not affect the clotting in vivo . Unlike the clotting cascade in the lab (in vitro), the cascade in the body (in vivo ) differs slightly - as tissue factor (TF) is the major initiator of the cascade . The TF/VIIa complex is the most important activator of factor IX and factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X. Factor V is involved in both the pathways as shown in the image below . The coagulation cascade in the laboratory: • Extrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube ): Tissue factor \035 Factor VII \035 Factor X. • Intrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube ): Factor XII \035 Factor XI \035 Factor IX \035 Factor X Laboratory methods to initiate clotting include : • Intrinsic pathway - adding phospholipids , calcium, and either a negatively charged substance such as glass beads440 • Extrinsic pathway - a source of tissue factor

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which test evaluates the extrinsic pathway ?
mcqs.explanation: Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation . PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin). This indicates the overall efficiency of the extrinsic clotting system . Causes of prolonged PT: • Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs - vitamin K antagonists • Liver disease - obstructive jaundice • Vitamin K deficiency • Disseminated intravascular coagulation • Previously undiagnosed factor VII , X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect (rare) Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT ) measures the clotting time of plasma after the activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and CaCl2, but without added tissue thromboplastin. It indicates the overall efficiency of the intrinsic pathway . Causes of prolonged APTT : • Disseminated intravascular coagulation • Liver disease • Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells • Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants • A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor) • Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII441 • Intake of oral anticoagulant drugs • Vitamin K deficiency

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: You are collecting a blood sample to send for prothrombin time in a patient in the ward. Which of the following is true about this investigation?

options.c: Test must be done within 2 hours of sample collection

mcqs.explanation: The test for prothrombin time is done within 2 hours. The differences between PT and aPTT are:Feature PT aPTT Coagulation pathway teste d Extrinsic and com mon Intrinsic and common Normal value -13 seconds 25-35 seconds Sample Platelet -poor plasm a Platelet -poor plasma Activating agent Thomboplastin KaolinSilicaEllagic acid

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: At what temperature should you store the sample for antiphospholipid antibody factor assays?
mcqs.explanation: The sample for antiphospholipid antibody assay must be stored at <4\260. Samples for coagulation studies should be stored always at room temperature (20 to 25 degrees ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old male patient presents to the casualty with severe bleeding following a road traffic accident . He is a known cardiac disease patient on anticoagulant therapy . As an intern, you were asked to collect blood for coagulation studies . Which colour vacutainer will you pick?
mcqs.explanation: The most commonly used vacutainer for coagulation studies is a blue vacutainer containing trisodium citrate. The benefits of trisodium citrate are that the calcium ion is neutralized more rapidly in citrate. Other anticoagulants are unacceptable for coagulation studies . The labile factors (factors V and VIII ) are unstable in oxalate (grey), whereas heparin (green) and EDTA (lavender) directly inhibit the coagulation process and interfere with end-point determinations . Also, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests are more sensitive to the presence of heparin (green ). The image given below shows colour coding of vacutainers with the anticoagulant used and their practical uses .442 Note : Heparin is used for blood sample collection for electrolyte estimation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the color of vacutainer containing sodium fluoride as a content ?
mcqs.explanation: Sodium fluoride is present in the grey coloured tube . Sodium fluoride inhibits glycolysis . Hence , is used for the estimation of blood glucose and alcohol.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child was brought to the emergency department with a big lesion on his forearm. As a surgery resident you decide to excise the lesion in the emergency operation theatre . Which of the following investigations will test the entire coagulation pathway ?
mcqs.explanation: Thromboelastography (TEG) tests the entire coagulation pathway . It measures coagulation cascade , platelet function, and fibrinolysis. It is a test that quantitatively measures the ability of whole blood to form a clot. The advantages are: • Global assessment of blood coagulability , including coagulation cascade , platelet function, and fibrinolysis • Rapid real-time bedside test with a simple methodology (point-of-care testing ) • Diagnosis of coagulopathic bleeding • Guide transfusion therapy and decrease the use of blood products • 443 Detect dynamic changes in blood coagulation during resuscitation • Predict the clinical efficacy of therapeutic agents affecting blood coagulability444

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Choose the correct option regarding the storage temperatures of blood components .
mcqs.explanation: The recommended storage temperatures of different blood components is as follows :Blood component Storage temperatu re Whole blood and red blood c ells 2–6\260C Fresh frozen plasma -30\260C or lower Cryoprecipitate Below -30\260C AlbuminFreeze -dried factor VIII 2–8\260C Platelet –24\260C

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be used to store blood for up to 35 days?
mcqs.explanation: Citrate dextrose phosphate adenine-1 (CDPA-1) can be used to store blood for up to 35 days. It helps in improving ATP synthesis during storage . Hence , it increases the shelf life .449 The disadvantage of using CDPA-1 is that it increases uric acid stone formation. The shelf life of storage with other components are: • Acid Citrate dextrose – 21 days • Citrate-phosphate dextrose – 21 days

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is correct regarding transfusion of the blood received from blood bank ?

options.a: It should be started within 4 hours of receiving it from the blood bank .
options.b: It should be completed within 4 hours of receiving from the blood bank .
options.c: No such time restraint and can be done anytime.
options.d: It should be completed within 6 hours of receiving from the blood bank .

mcqs.explanation: Blood received from blood bank should be completely transfused within 4 hours of receiving. Principles of blood administration: • All blood products should be given through an appropriate blood administration set containing a filter. • A careful aseptic technique should be practised at all times . • Vital signs should be documented before and after transfusion and as clinically required. For the first 15 minutes after the infusion has begun , the patient should be kept under close observation to detect any signs of a serious transfusion reaction. If none is observed, the infusion rate may be increased . • One unit of red cells is often given in 1 to 4 hours, depending on the amount to be transfused and on the patient 's cardiovascular status. Infusion of a unit for longer than 4 hours is not recommended , as there is a risk of bacterial proliferation because the opened unit is at room temperature . • No other solution and no medication should be added to or infused through the same tubing as a blood product . • Ringer's lactate or other solutions containing calcium must never be added to a blood product because the calcium present leads to coagulation . • After the transfusion has been completed , the transfusion tag or record should become part of the patient 's chart.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients receiving blood transfusions are more prone to develop bacterial sepsis ?

options.a: A young women with severe anaemia

mcqs.explanation: Patients with thrombocytopenia receiving blood transfusions (platelets ) are more prone to develop bacterial sepsis . Sepsis is mostly due to significant bacterial contamination of the blood products . Platelets have the maximum risk of causing this condition when compared to red cell preparations. Since patients with thrombocytopenia receive platelet transfusion, they are at an increased risk of infections . Platelets (unlike red cells ) must be stored at room temperature . This is a condition that is favourable for bacterial proliferation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started while waiting for the culture reports. The blood components that are preferred for the other conditions are :450 • Anaemia - RBCs • Hemophilia - FFP • vonWillebrand disease - cryoprecipitate

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient has been brought with severe bleeding to your ER. His blood group is unknown. Fresh frozen plasma from which of the following blood groups can be given?
mcqs.explanation: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) from AB blood group can be given to this patient as it is the universal plasma donor. AB plasma does not contain antibodies against antigens on RBCs of AB blood group. O Rh-negative blood is the universal blood donor. It is used during emergency packed cell blood transfusion with an unknown blood group. It is preferred because it lacks the A and B and Rh antigens. Hence , it cannot be hemolyzed by anti-A, anti-B or anti-D antibodies in the recipient 's blood.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common reaction occurring in patients undergoing blood transfusions?
mcqs.explanation: The most common blood transfusion reaction is the febrile nonhemolytic reaction.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Blood transfusion was started in a patient with severe anaemia. Within a few minutes she developed generalised pruritis, swelling of the tongue and stridor. Which antibody deficiency in the recipient most commonly causes this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe , potentially fatal, allergic reactions. These are most likely to occur in patients with IgA deficiency . Such reactions may occur when blood products containing certain antigens are given to previously sensitized recipients . It is triggered by recipient IgG antibodies that recognize IgA in the infused blood product .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Following blood transfusion in a post -operative patient , the following finding was noted . Which of the following is responsible for this reaction?
mcqs.explanation: The given image, showing a raised and erythematous lesion, is suggestive of urticaria. Such reactions may be triggered by the presence of an allergen in the donated blood product that is recognized by IgE antibodies in the recipient . These are mild reactions occurring more commonly in 1% to 3% of transfusions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with thalassemia developed pallor and dizziness 1 week following blood transfusion. His lab reports are given below . Which of the following is seen in this condition?

options.a: Direct coombs test negative , IgG mediated
options.b: Direct Coombs test positive , IgG mediated
options.c: Direct coombs test negative , IgM mediated
options.d: Direct coombs test positive , IgM mediated

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of delayed hemolytic reaction following blood transfusion. It is IgG mediated and gives a positive result in direct Coombs test .451 These antibodies recognize foreign protein red cell antigens in a previously sensitized recipient (through a prior blood transfusion). They present with laboratory features of hemolysis like low haptoglobin level and elevated LDH. Acute hemolytic reactions are usually caused by preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells that fix complement . The direct Coombs test is usually positive .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who was admitted for blood transfusion developed transfusion-related acute lung injury. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?

options.a: Pre-existing lung diseases are a risk factor
options.b: Incidence with platelet transfusion is more than that with whole blood
options.c: Symptoms develop after 2 days of transfusion
options.d: Subsequent transfusions from the same donor increases the incidence

mcqs.explanation: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI ) is sudden -onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after the transfusion. It occurs within 6 hours, and not after 2 days following transfusion. TRALI is a severe fatal complication of blood transfusion. The incidence of TRALI is low (1 per 10,000 transfusions). However, it may occur more frequently in patients with preexisting lung disease . The pathogenesis involves a two -hit hypothesis : • Priming event - increased sequestration and sensitization of neutrophils in the microvasculature of the lung • Second hit - the factor (most commonly MHC class I antigens) present in the transfused blood product activates the primed neutrophils TRALI can occur in transfusions with all plasma-containing blood products . However, it is more likely to occur following the transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and platelets . This is because these products contain high levels of donor antibodies . Note : TRALI is important to recognize because donor products that induce complications in one patient are much more likely to do so in a second . Indeed , recent measures to exclude multiparous women from plasma donation have resulted in reduced incidence of TRALI .452

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old man is receiving massive blood transfusion following a fall from height . 4 hours after transfusion, he becomes breathless and oxygen saturation decreases . Chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates . Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.b: Treatment involves discontinuation of blood transfusion
options.d: It is mediated by macrophages in lung vasculature

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury). It is mediated by neutrophils entrapped in the lung vasculature. Features of TRALI are: • Fever • Hypotension • Hypoxemia • Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates - not responsive to diuretics Treatment is mainly supportive and blood transfusions are discontinued . The mortality rate in this condition is 5-10%.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A CKD patient had to undergo dialysis and his Hb was 5.2gm/dL. So two blood transfusions were to be given. The first bag was completed in 2 hours. The second was started and in the midway, he developed shortness of breath and hypertension . Vitals were BP - 180/120 mmHg and pulse rate - 110 /min. What is the cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). TACO is caused by rapid or excess transfusion of red cell preparations or plasma products . This condition is characterized by: • Dyspnea with O2% <90 at room air • Bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray • Systolic hypertension • Elevation of brain natriuretic peptide , 1.5 times that of pre-transfusion levels It can be prevented by administering the transfusion slowly , at the rate of 1 to 2 ml of blood/kg of body weight per hour. Diuretics are also used if necessary .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who receives recurrent transfusions for thalassemia develops fever and chills during this time. There is no evidence of hemolysis . Which of the following measures can decrease the rate of transfusion reactions?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR). Such reactions can be prevented by using leukoreduced RBCs. Removal of leukocytes from the blood is called leukoreduction . It is done before storage to prevent cytokine formation. FNHTR may occur due to the following : • Sensitization to the WBC antigens by previous blood transfusions or pregnancy • Cytokines produced by the donor leukocytes during storage • Bacterial contamination Note : Luspatercept is an erythroid maturation agent , a receptor fusion protein consisting of a modified extracellular domain of human activin receptor type -2B linked to the human Ig-G1 Fc domain. The drug was recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of transfusion-dependent453 thalassemia .454

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of these is not a pre-leukemic condition?
mcqs.explanation: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is not a preleukemic condition. It is an autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to IgG autoantibodies that bind to the P blood group antigen and cause intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children and show recovery within a month. Option A: Few patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) develop acute non-lymphocytic leukemia. This is thought to arise from the injured marrow as a secondary hematopoietic disorder. Option B: Bone marrow aplasia preceding acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) is a rare condition that usually affects children. It generally follows the recovery of normal blood counts and most commonly occurs within 6 months of the onset of aplasia. Option C: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 10 % to 40% of individuals with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). It is usually accompanied by the appearance of additional cytogenetic abnormalities.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of acute leukemia?

options.a: Arrest in differentiation and increased apoptosis
options.d: Arrest in differentiation and decreased apoptosis

mcqs.explanation: In acute leukemia, there is an arrest in differentiation and decreased apoptosis . Genomic aberrations create oncoproteins. They arrest normal maturation, turn on pro-growth signaling pathways , or protect cells from apoptotic death .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: As per WHO classification , what percentage of blast cells in bone marrow biopsy is required to diagnose a patient with acute leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: As per WHO classification , % of blast cells must be present in the bone marrow and / peripheral smear for the diagnosis of acute leukemia. In FAB criteria, the cut-off is more than 30%.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions does not increase the risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: Polycythemia vera increases the risk of developing AML, not ALL . Inherited diseases that are associated with a higher risk of developing leukemias are: • Bloom syndrome • Fanconi anemia • Ataxia–telangiectasia • Down syndrome • Type-1 neurofibromatosis461 Other germline risk factors for the development of ALL : • Li -Fraumeni syndrome • Familial ALL syndrome Note : AML has a higher incidence during the neonatal period than ALL among children with Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, and Down syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: Precursor B-cell or pre B cell (previously classified as L1 ) type is the most common subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a primary T-cell marker ?
mcqs.explanation: CD10 is not a primary marker of T cells . It is a marker of pre-B cells and germinal-center B cells . Note : Although CD10/ Common ALL antigen (CALLA ) can be found in B-ALL and T-ALL , it is primarily expressed by pre-B cells and germinal centre B cells . Lymphoblasts of both B and T cell lineages , express CD10 that is lost upon progression to a mature phenotype . It is variably expressed by a few mature B cell tumours. However, the expression of CD10 by mature T cells has not been well established .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Block-like positivity for PAS on immunohistochemistry of a bone marrow sample is seen . Which of the following cells show this finding?
mcqs.explanation: Lymphoblasts in acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL ) show block-like or dot-like PAS positivity . Erythroblasts in acute myeloid leukemia-M6 (AML-M6) show diffuse periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positivity. The image given below shows dot-like positivity for periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) in lymphoblasts .462

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells does not stain positively with Sudan black?
mcqs.explanation: Lymphocytes do not stain positively with Sudan black dye . Although some positivity may be seen in azurophilic granules of lymphoblasts. Sudan Black B (SBB) is a lipophilic dye that binds irreversibly to an undefined granule component in granulocytes , eosinophils , and some monocytes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most commonly affected gene in patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: The most commonly affected gene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL ) is NOTCH1. B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia is associated with mutations of genes such as PAX5, E2A, and EBF. It may be associated with balanced t(12 ;21 ) involving the genes ETV6 and RUNX1.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is found to have t(9;22 ). What will be the size of BCR-ABL fusion protein produced ?
mcqs.explanation: The size of BCR-ABL protein in t(9;22 ) associated with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is 190 kDa. BCR-ABL fusion transcript protein with t(9;22 ): • Major BCR (M-BCR) 210 kDa size in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with weaker tyrosine kinase activity • Minor BCR (m-BCR ) 190 kDa size in acute lymphoblastic leukemia ( ALL ) with stronger tyrosine kinase activity463 • Micro BCR (�M-BCR) 230 kDa size in myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) with exuberant neutrophilia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: On immunophenotyping of a patient with early pre-B acute leukemia, which of the following marker will be negative ?
mcqs.explanation: Cytoplasmic immunoglobulins and CD10 are negative in early pre-B acute leukemia but become positive in pre-B ALL .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not usually involved in the immunohistochemistry of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: Cytokeratin is not a marker of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). It is an epithelial cell marker for thymoma. Tdt, CD1a, and CD3 are markers of ALL .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old boy with fever, weight loss came to the hospital . On examination, he was pale and had significant lymphadenopathy . The bone marrow histology of the person is as given below . Your diagnosis is?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario with bone marrow histology showing lymphoblasts (condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli , scanty agranular cytoplasm ) is suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. ALL is more common in childhood . Clinical features of ALL include : • Bone marrow failure - anemia, fever, infections , bleeding • Mass effects due to neoplastic infiltration - bone pain, generalized lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly , hepatomegaly , and testicular enlargement • CNS manifestations - headache , vomiting, and nerve palsies • B-ALL - Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement • T-ALL - Mediastinal mass, compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum, lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An adolescent male patient presents with fatigue . His total leucocyte count is 138 x 10 ^9 / L with 80% blasts on the peripheral smear. Chest X-ray shows a large mediastinal mass. The bone marrow aspirate is as shown below . What would the immunophenotyping of this patient 's blasts most likely demonstrate ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and bone marrow aspirate are suggestive of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Thus, immunophenotyping of the blasts would demonstrate an immature T-cell phenotype (Tdt/CD34/CD7 positive ). The bone marrow aspirate shows lymphoblast with condensed nuclear chromatin, small inconspicuous nucleoli , and scanty cytoplasm lacking granules. ALL is usually seen in adolescent boys with thymic involvement in 50% to 70%. It has an abrupt stormy onset , within days to a few weeks of the first symptoms .464 Clinical features of ALL include : • Bone marrow failure - anemia, fever, infections , bleeding • Mass effects due to neoplastic infiltration - bone pain, generalized lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly , hepatomegaly , and testicular enlargement • CNS manifestations - headache , vomiting, and nerve palsies • B-ALL - Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement • T-ALL - Mediastinal mass, compression of large vessels and airways in the mediastinum, lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a patient with acute leukemia, the immunophenotype pattern of the blasts is positive for CD10 , CD13, CD19, and CD33. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) based on immunophenotyping . CD10 and CD19 are markers for B-cell lineage and this patient most probably have B-ALL . Although CD13 and CD33 are myeloid antigens, their expression does not exclude the diagnosis of B- ALL . Option B: The diagnosis of mixed phenotypic acute leukemia (MPAL)/ acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage (ALAL \(previously known as biphenotypic leukemia) requires a demonstration of multiple lineages in blast cells . According to WHO's latest update (2022 ), the requirements for assigning more than one lineage to blast cells are : In the absence of MPO or evidence of monocytic differentiation , expression of CD13 and CD33 is not sufficient for a diagnosis of MPAL. Hence , biphenotypic leukemia is not the answer here.B cell lineage CD19 strong:\0301 expressed CD , CD22 , CD79aCD 19 weak: \030 2 or more strongly expresse d CD10, CD22 , CD79a T cell lineage CD3 positive Myeloid linea ge Myeloperoxidase (MPO)ORM onocyte differentiation (non- specific esterase , CD11c, CD1 4, CD64, lysozyme )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with weight loss and fever is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following is a good prognostic indicator of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of t (12 ;21 ) indicates a good prognosis in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). It involves genes ETV6 and RUNX1. Conversely, a translocation involving the MLL gene , t(9;22 ), and hypodiploidy are associated with a bad prognosis.465

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Bone marrow biopsy of a patient shows > 20 % immature blasts with scanty cytoplasm , no granules, and inconspicuous nucleoli . They also stain positive with PAS. Which of the following are good prognostic markers of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given bone marrow biopsy report is suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). The good prognostic markers of ALL include trisomy 7, hyperdiploidy , and age of 5 years.466

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a myeloid marker ?
mcqs.explanation: CD3 is not a myeloid marker . It is a T-cell lymphoid marker . Cell markers :474 • B-cell : CD10, CD19, CD20 , CD22 , CD23 , CD24, CD79b, CD103 , Pax-5, kappa, lambda, CD200 , cytoplasmic kappa, cytoplasmic lambda • T- cell : CD1, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD6,CD7 , CD8, TCR apha-beta , TCR gamma-delta , cytoplasmic CD3 • Myeloid : CD11b, CD13, CD14, CD15, CD33, CD64, CD 117, myeloperoxidase

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of acute myeloid leukemia?
mcqs.explanation: The most common type of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is AML - M2 or AML with maturation. The least common type of AML is AML M7 or megakaryocytic.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common subtype of acute myeloid leukemia seen in patients with Down's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most common subtype of AML seen in Down's syndrome is acute myeloid leukemia-M7 (AML - M7 ) or acute megakaryocytic leukemia. Myeloid proliferations of Down's syndrome are usually megakaryoblastic. It includes : • Transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM) - occurs at birth or within days of birth and resolves in 1 to 2 months • Myeloid leukemia associated with Down syndrome - occurs later, but usually in the first 3 years of life . Both are characterized by GATA1 mutations and mutations of the JAK-STAT pathway .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-man presents with nosebleeds , bleeding gums, and multiple ecchymoses . Lab investigations show the following findings. The blasts are positive for CD33. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). AML is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation , leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow . It occurs at all ages , but the incidence rises throughout life , peaking after 60 years of age . The peripheral smear shows blasts with abundant cytoplasm , fine azurophilic granules, Auer rods, and delicate nuclear chromatin with 1-4 prominent nucleoli . The blasts are positive for CD33. Occasionally , blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukemic leukemia). Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukemia in pancytopenic patients .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Peripheral smear of a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia shows myeloblasts with the following finding. What are these made of?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Auer rods in myeloblasts . These are needle -shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion of lysosomes .475 Auer rods contain peroxidase and lysosomal enzymes . Myeloblasts with bundles of Auer rods are called faggot cells and are seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions are Auer rods seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Auer rods are seen in: • Acute promyelocytic leukemia • Myelodysplastic syndromes • Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia These are not seen in acute monocytic leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old male patient is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. The peripheral blood smear picture is given in the image. The cell indicated by the arrow is best described as:
mcqs.explanation: The given cell shows multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell resembling a bundle of sticks. Such cells have been termed as faggot cells (faggot in French means bundle of sticks). Since the question specifically asks about the cell , the best answer is faggot cell (not Auer rods). Option A: Auer rods are distinctive needle -like azurophilic granules present in many cases but particularly numerous in AML with the t(15;17) aberration (acute promyelocytic leukemia). Option B: The term flaming promyelocyte refers to cells that appear to be breaking apart, taking on a vibrant reddish -purple hue with the apparent liberation of granules into the surrounding cellular matrix. Option C: Promyelocytes containing fine granules appear dusky or hazy and are referred to as dusky promyelocytes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Increased levels of serum muramidase are seen in patients with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Serum muramidase or lysozyme levels are seen to be increased in patients with acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML - M4). It is also increased in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which type of AML is known as Di Guglielmo disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Acute myeloid leukemia-M6 (AML-M6) or acute erythroid leukemia is known as Di Guglielmo disease . AML-M6 accounts for 1% of AML cases . It has two subtypes :476 • Erythroid/myeloid leukemia (M6a, more common) - Dyserythropoiesis is prominent • Pure erythroid leukemia/ erythemic myelosis / Di Guglielmo disease (M6b, rare) - >80% erythroid precursors. Clinical findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia , and variable neutropenia . Positive stains for erythroid cells are glycophorin A, hemoglobin A, CD36, CD71, CD117, and PAS.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with which of the following conditions, a dry tap may be seen on bone marrow aspiration?
mcqs.explanation: Acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AML M7 ) may yield a dry tap on marrow aspiration. It may be associated with extensive bone marrow fibrosis as a result of the stimulation of the normal fibroblasts by the local secretion of platelet -derived growth factor (PDGF) by the leukemic cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Bone marrow aspirate of a patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia shows the presence of faggot cells . What is the most likely subtype of acute myeloid leukemia, the patient is suffering from?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of faggot cells is highly suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia - M3 (AML - M3) or acute promyelocytic leukemia. A cluster of Auer rods is known as a faggot cell . It is characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) M3. The image given below shows AML M3 with a cluster of Auer rods (faggot cell ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia presents with a one-day history of bleeding gums, subconjunctival bleed , and purpuric rash. Investigations done are given below . Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely to be detected ?
mcqs.explanation: 477 The patient shows features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). It is most likely to be associated with acute myeloid leukemia - M3 or acute promyelocytic leukemia. The pathogenesis behind this is t(15,17) or PML-RARA fusion gene . Option A: Inversion 16 is seen in acute myelomonocytic leukemia or AML - M4. Option B: t(8;21) is seen in AML with differentiation or AML - M2. Option C: Inversion 3 is seen in AML - M7 (megakaryoblastic) which shows normal or increased platelet count. It has a poor prognosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which type of acute myeloid leukemia is myeloperoxidase negative ?
mcqs.explanation: AML M0 is negative for myeloperoxidase (MPO). AML-M5 (monocytic), AML-M6 (erythroid), and AML-M7 (megakaryocytic) are also negative for MPO. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is located in the primary granules of neutrophils and their precursors, in eosinophil granules, and in the azurophilic granules of monocytes . The most primitive myeloblasts are negative , with granular positivity appearing progressively as they mature toward the promyelocyte stage . Promyelocytes and myelocytes are the most strongly staining cells in the granulocyte series. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive . AML-M4 shows both myelocytic and monocytic differentiation . Hence , it shows both MPO and non-specific esterase (marker for monocytes ) positivity .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with fatigue and recurrent infections undergoes bone marrow evaluation. It shows > 20 % myeloblasts , which stain positive for CD61. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with myeloblasts that stain positive for CD61 is suggestive of acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AML-M7 ). AML M7 is the least common type of AML. Blasts of megakaryocytic lineage predominate and are associated with marrow fibrosis. There is also frequent budding of cytoplasmic margins. They are CD41+ and CD61+. They stain negatively with Sudan black B (SBB) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). Blasts are reactive with PAS and acid phosphatase . The prognosis for this type of acute leukemia is poor.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who developed the following lesions over the body was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. Which subtype of AML does this patient most likely have?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows leukemia cutis. It is seen in acute myeloid leukemia - M4 and acute myeloid leukemia - M5. It refers to leukemic cells infiltrating the skin. Signs and symptoms related to the involvement of tissues other than the marrow are usually less striking in AML than in acute lympho cytic leukemia (ALL ). But tumors with monocytic differentiation (AML M4, M5 ) often infiltrate the skin (leukemia cutis ) and the gingiva. This probably reflects the normal tendency of monocytes to extravasate into tissues .478

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for 20 days. He has gingival hyperplasia , hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy . Investigations done are given below . Bone marrow biopsy shows 100 % cellularity with many blasts cells that are peroxidase negative and non-specific esterase positive . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia-M5 (AML-M5) or acute monocytic leukemia. The patients with AML - M5 develop organomegaly , lymphadenopathy , gingival hyperplasia , CNS involvement, and other tissue infiltration. The bone marrow aspirate shows 20 % or more blasts . Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei , lack Auer rods, and are nonspecific esterase positive . Myeloperoxidase is present in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils and their precursors. It is positive in AML M1, M2, M3, M4 and negative in AML M0. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive . When positive , the granules are smaller than in neutrophils and diffusely scattered throughout the cytoplasm . The image given below shows bone marrow aspirate in AML - M5.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child presents with bilateral proptosis . After evaluation, he is diagnosed with chloroma. Which of the following is not a marker for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: CD61 is a marker of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, not chloroma. Lysozyme, CD43, CD45, CD117, and MPO are positive markers of chloroma. Chloroma, also called myeloid sarcoma, granulocytic sarcoma, or myeloblastoma is an extramedullary tumor that occurs in 2% to 14% of patients with AML. Frequent sites of involvement are: • Skin • Lymph nodes • Gastrointestinal tract479 • Bone • Soft tissue , testis • Peritoneum Orbital involvement of myeloid sarcoma is rare without any evidence of systemic involvement. Proptosis is the most common presentation . Other symptoms include lacrimal swelling , conjunctival mass lesion, retinal hemorrhages, ptosis , dystopia . Decreased visual acuity and ocular movement restriction have also been reported .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions are Arbiskov cells seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Arbiskov cells are monocytes seen in myeloblastoma or chloroma. Chloroma, also known as granulocytic sarcoma, is a hematopoietic stem cell tumor, where myeloblasts are located at extramedullary sites . Orbit is one of the most common sites of occurrences in pediatric population . It is seen in AML - M2 most commonly. Other conditions associated are myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative syndromes. The image given below shows Arbiskov cells in chloroma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All-trans retinoic acid is used in the treatment of tumor that is associated with which of the following genetic aberrations?
mcqs.explanation: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA ) is used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML), which is associated with PML-RARA fusion gene . Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) is associated with a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 producing a PML-RARA fusion gene . This fusion gene encodes for a chimeric protein, which consists of a part of the PML protein and a part of the retinoic acid receptor -\037 (RAR \037).480 The normal RAR \037 binds to the DNA and activates the transcription in the presence of retinoids. However, the chimeric protein produced by PML-RARA has reduced affinity for retinoids. This causes inhibition of transcription, thereby preventing gene expression for cellular differentiation . This leads to the accumulation of myeloid progenitor cells . The condition is treated with all-trans retinoic acid. It binds to the PML-RARA chimeric protein. This causes conformational change such that the protein regains its normal function and activates DNA transcription.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cytogenetic changes suggest a favorable prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia?

options.a: t (11q23 ;v) with diverse MLL fusion genes

mcqs.explanation: Normal karyotyping with mutated NPM indicates a favorable prognosis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which among the following patients with acute myeloid leukemia has a good prognosis?

options.a: A 56-year-old patient who developed post -chemotherapy AML
options.b: An infant with AML having complex karyotype
options.c: A 60-year-old patient diagnosed with AML-M0 type
options.d: A patient with AML having Inversion

mcqs.explanation: Inversion 16 is associated with a good prognosis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML).481

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most common subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma?
mcqs.explanation: Nodular sclerosis is the most common type of Hodgkin's lymphoma, while mixed cellularity is most common in India. The incidence of nodular sclerosis is equal in men and women. It commonly involves the lower cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal lymph nodes . It commonly affects adolescents and young adults . It has an excellent prognosis.
