mcqs.explanation: Infections are the most common cause of death in patients with myeloma. Complications of multiple myeloma include : • Infections • Renal failure • Cardiac failure • Hypercalcemia • Anemia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue , pain over the ribs, and confusion. Lab investigations reveal anemia, hypercalcemia , and increased serum creatinine. X-ray shows lytic lesions on the bones. Which of the following is the most powerful prognostic indicator of this condition at the time of diagnosis?

options.a: Number of myeloma cells in the marrow

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of multiple myeloma. The most powerful prognostic indicator of this condition at the time of diagnosis is serum �o 2 microglobulin. Beta-2 microglobulin is a low-molecular-weight protein found on the surface of all nucleated cells . It is the light chain of the HLA histocompatibility complex .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not associated with poor prognosis in a patient with multiple myeloma ?
mcqs.explanation: t(11;14) is associated with a good prognosis in patients with myeloma. t(4;14), high serum beta -2 microglobulin, and low serum albumin are all poor prognostic factors in myeloma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain. On examination, he has pallor and bony tenderness . A skeletal radiographic survey reveals several punched -out lytic lesions. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M band in the gamma globulin region. Which of the following is not associated with a poor prognosis in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma. Translocations involving cyclin D1 are associated with a good outcome in this condition. t(14;16), deletions of 17p, and t(14;20 ) are associated with a more aggressive course .573

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: Which among these is not diagnostic of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance?
mcqs.explanation: Bence–Jones proteinuria is not diagnostic of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS ) because it is seen in multiple myeloma also. MGUS is the most common monoclonal gammopathy . Diagnostic criteria of MGUS according to International Myeloma Working Group guidelines (2014 ): • Serum monoclonal protein <3g/dL • Clonal bone marrow plasma cells < % • Absence of end-organ damage such as hypercalcemia , renal failure, anemia and bone lesions (CRAB ) • No amyloidosis The three distinct clinical types of MGUS are: • Non-IgM MGUS : • Most common subtype of MGUS • Approximately 1% of patients with MGUS develop a symptomatic plasma cell neoplasm , usually multiple myeloma, per year • IgM MGUS : • IgM MGUS accounts for approximately 15% of MGUS cases • It can progress to Waldenstr\366m macroglobulinemia, but progression to multiple myeloma is rare • Bence–Jones proteinuria has been reported in approximately 20 % of these cases • Light chain MGUS (LC-MGUS): • LC-MGUS is a unique subtype of MGUS in which there is no immunoglobulin heavy-chain component • Urinary M protein <500 mg/24 hour • LC-MGUS may progress to light -chain smoldering multiple myeloma (idiopathic Bence–Jones proteinuria) and to light -chain multiple myeloma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: A patient with complaints of blurred vision, bleeding gums, and tingling sensation over the extremities is diagnosed with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Which of the following immunoglobulins is this condition associated with?
mcqs.explanation: High levels of IgM are seen in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. In lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, high levels of IgM lead to symptoms related to hyperviscosity of the blood. This is known as Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia. 'M' or monoclonal spike is seen in this condition. Here, it is caused by IgM; in multiple myeloma, it is caused by IgG. It is characterized by the absence of lytic lesions and normal serum calcium levels .574 IgM greatly increases the viscosity of the blood, giving rise to a hyperviscosity syndrome characterized by the following : • Visual impairment • Neurologic problems • Bleeding • Cryoglobulinemia The normal relative viscosity of the serum is 1.8. Hyperviscosity is seen in: • Multiple myeloma • Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia • Cryoglobulinemia • Myeloproliferative disorders

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Which of the following genes is mutated in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Virtually all cases of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma are associated with acquired mutations in MYD88 . The most common cytogenetic abnormality associated with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is deletion of 6q .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in patients with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia?

options.a: M spike in serum protein electrophoresis
options.d: Absence of lytic lesions on imaging

mcqs.explanation: Serum calcium levels remain normal in Waldenstr\366m macroglobulinemia. Waldenstr\366m macroglobulinemia is a syndrome characterised by the following : • Hyperviscosity syndrome due to high levels of IgM • Most commonly occurs in association with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma • 'M' or monoclonal spike • Absence of lytic lesions • Normal serum calcium levels • Diffuse marrow infiltration by plasma cells , plasmacytoid lymphocytes , and lymphocytes (all from the same clone) • Cells do not form tumor masses or produce lytic lesions • Lymphocytes commonly contain Dutcher bodies (intranuclear inclusions) • Bence–Jones proteins in 20 –30%575

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common site for extramedullary plasmacytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Extramedullary plasmacytomas are seen in the upper respiratory tract. Most of them are seen in the nasopharynx, oropharynx, sinuses , and larynx. Plasmacytoma is a tumor of plasma cells of bony or soft tissue . It can occur anywhere in the body without evidence of systemic disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: What is Seligmann's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: \037- heavy chain disease (HCD) is known as Seligmann's disease . There are three heavy chain diseases : • \037- heavy chain disease - Seligmann's disease • \034- heavy chain disease - Franklin 's disease • �M- heavy chain disease - Associated with light -chain secretion (Bence–Jones proteinuria) in a few cases

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Multiple Myeloma and Plasma Cell Disorders
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a history of bone pain, weakness , and loss of weight for 3 years. On examination, enlarged lymph nodes and organomegaly are noted . Peripheral smear shows 22 % plasma cells , which are \022-chain restricted . Serum IgE level is elevated . X-ray image of the lumbar vertebra shows lytic punched -out lesions . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of plasma cell leukemia. In this case, the peripheral blood smear shows 22 % of plasma cells and presents with organomegaly . Plasma cell leukemia is defined by the observation in blood of more than 20 % clonal plasma cells by differential count of the leucocytes or by counting more than 2 \327 109 per liter circulating clonal plasma cells. Plasma cell leukemia (PCL) is a rare and aggressive form of leukemia and plasma cell dyscrasia. PCL can be divided into primary PCL (PCL ) and secondary PCL (sPCL) following previously diagnosed multiple myeloma (MM); the latter typically occurring at a late and advanced stage of MM. Patients with plasma cell leukemia are more likely to have extramedullary involvement of liver and spleen , causing organomegaly than in multiple myeloma. (Option A)576

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 73-year-old woman presents with chronic fatigue and easy bruising. She has had surgery for ovarian cancer 7 years ago along with chemoradiation. Her lab reports reveal pancytopenia and bone marrow biopsy shows the following finding. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of therapy -related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS). The bone marrow biopsy stained with Perl's Prussian blue shows ringed sideroblasts . They are erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria visible as perinuclear granules as shown in the image below .Myelodysplastic syndrome is a group of clonal stem cell disorders characterized by maturation defects , associated with ineffective hematopoiesis . It is of two types : • Primary MDS - develops slowly , usually after 50 years of age . • Secondary or therapy -related MDS (t-MDS) - develops 2 to 8 years after toxic drug or radiation exposure with poor prognosis Patients usually present with weakness , infections and hemorrhages due to pancytopenia . Both types of MDS have a high risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). However, most frequent and rapid transformation occurs in therapy -related MDS (t-MDS).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cytogenetic change in children with myelodysplastic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: 588 Monosomy 7 is the most common cytogenetic change seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) in children. 5q deletion is the most common cytogenetic change seen in MDS in adults . The del (5q) abnormality is the dominant clone in most cases of MDS. This involves the stem -cell compartment and hence occurs as an early or initiating event in disease pathogenesis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of these histopathological findings would you not expect to see in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Pseudo –Pelger –Huet cells are seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and not Pelger –Huet cells . Pelger –Huet cells are seen in Pelger –Huet syndrome, which is due to mutations in the lamin B-receptor gene . It is a neutrophil differentiation disorder with leukocyte appearance as: • Dumbbell -shaped bilobed nuclei • Reduced number of nuclear segments • Coarse clumping of the nuclear chromatin In MDS, pseudo -Pelger Huet cells are seen due to abnormal nuclear budding i.e. neutrophils with only 2 nuclear lobes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following bone marrow and peripheral blood findings is not seen in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Image 3 showing hypocellular bone marrow is not seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS.) In this condition, bone marrow is hypercellular. However, pancytopenia results from ineffective hematopoiesis . The image given below shows the histopathological findings seen in MDS.589

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue , weight loss, and heaviness in the left hypochondrium for 6 months. His hemogram and peripheral smear are given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). In this condition, the peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells , myelocytes , metamyelocytes , and blasts . Hence , the histological picture is described to have garden party or college girl appearance . The image given below shows the peripheral smear in CML showing garden party or college girl appearance .CML is a myeloproliferative disorder with peak incidence in the 5th to 6th decades of life . It occurs due to the chimeric BCR-ABL gene . Clinical features of CML: • Hypermetabolism • Fatigability • Weakness • Weight loss and anorexia • Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis causing - • Splenomegaly • Mild hepatomegaly • Lymphadenopathy Hematological findings include : • Mild -to-moderate anemia • Leukocytosis590 • Platelets - usually increased • DLC shows predominantly neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes , myelocytes , eosinophils , and basophils and blasts (>10%) Note : Convent girl appearance is seen in CLL .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What mutation results in Philadelphia chromosome?
mcqs.explanation: Philadelphia chromosome results from t(9;22 )(q34 ;q11 ). It is most commonly seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). CML is due to the formation of a chimeric BCR-ABL gene or Philadelphia chromosome. This gene is derived from a reciprocal translocation (9;22 )(q34 ;q11 ). The image given below shows the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome.This translocation can be identified on fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH). The image given below shows (9;22 ) translocation as seen on FISH.591

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Bone marrow biopsy in a patient shows pseudo -Gaucher cells . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Psuedo -Gaucher cells are characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). These cells are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled, green -blue cytoplasm . Their presence indicates a good prognosis. Bone marrow findings in CML: • Markedly hypercellular marrow - increased maturing granulocytic precursors • Elevated eosinophils and basophils • Increased megakaryocytes - include small, dysplastic forms • Erythroid progenitors - normal or mildly decreased • Increased reticulin deposition • Overt marrow fibrosis - rare early in the course • Pseudo -Gaucher cells • Sea blue histiocytes The image given below shows pseudo -Gaucher cells in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).592

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old woman with fever and splenomegaly was diagnosed to have chronic myeloid leukemia. She was started on imatinib therapy . After a few months of therapy , she had persistent progressive splenomegaly and fatigue . Which of the following will not be seen in this phase ?
mcqs.explanation: In a patient with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), progressive splenomegaly , not responsive to therapy is suggestive of an accelerated phase . In this phase , blasts are <20% in blood or marrow . Diagnosis of an accelerated phase of CML requires one of the following criteria: • Persistent or increasing WBC (>10 \327 109 /L), unresponsive to therapy • Persistent or increasing splenomegaly, unresponsive to therapy • Persistent thrombocytosis (>1000 \327 109 /L), unresponsive to therapy • Persistent thrombocytopenia (<100 \327 109 /L) unrelated to therapy • % or more basophils in the peripheral blood • %-19% blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow • Additional clonal chromosomal abnormalities in Ph+ cells at diagnosis that include "major route" abnormalities (second Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, trisomy 19), complex karyotype , or abnormalities of 3q26 .2 • Any new clonal chromosomal abnormality in Ph+ cells that occurs during therapy

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the percentage of blast cells in the blast phase of CML?
mcqs.explanation: In the blast phase of chronic myeloid leukemia, there are >20% blasts in the bone marrow . The 3 phases of CML are: • Chronic phase is the most common presentation . It is characterized by:593 • Leukocytosis - bimodal distribution with higher proportions of mature segmented neutrophils and myelocytes • Blast cells <10% • Increased basophils and eosinophils • Monocytosis <3% • Accelerated phase occurs in 50% of the patients who present with increasing anemia, thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly . It is characterized by: • Blast count 10 -19% • Basophilia >20% • Blast phase in CML occurs in an average of 3 years after the diagnosis. It is characterized by: • Large foci or clusters of blasts on the bone marrow biopsy >20%. • Presence of extramedullary blastic infiltrates (e.g., myeloid sarcoma or chloroma)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in a patient with Myelodysplastic /Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia ?
mcqs.explanation: Myelodysplastic /Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia (previously named as atypical chronic myeloid leukemia) shows minimal absolute basophilia, i.e., <2% of total WBCs. Myelodysplastic /Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia is a leukemic disorder having features of both myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features at the time of diagnosis. It is classified under the WHO 5th edition (2022 ) MDS/MPN category . Characteristics of myelodysplastic /myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia : • Peripheral blood leukocytosis with an increased number of mature and immature neutrophils • Prominent dysgranulopoiesis • Philadelphia chromosome-negative • Neutrophil precursors (promyelocytes, myelocytes , metamyelocytes ) >10% of WBCs • Minimal absolute basophilia <2% of WBCs • Absolute monocytosis <10% of WBCs • Hypercellular bone marrow • <20% blasts in blood and bone marrow • Thrombocytopenia Differences between CML and myelodysplastic /myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia:Feature CML Myelodysplastic /Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia BCR-ABL gene Present Absent594 Feature CML Myelodysplastic /Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia Basophilia Present <2% Myeloblasts in peripheral blo odMyeloblasts in bone marro w <2%<5% <20 %<20 % Granulocytic dysplasia Minimal/ abs ent Prominent

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients will have a decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score?

options.a: A 65-year-old-man with garden party appearance on peripheral smear
options.b: A 50-year-old man with Reed Sternberg cells on LN biopsy
options.c: A 35-year-old woman with Hb level of 23 g/dL
options.d: A 43-year-old woman with smudge cells on peripheral smear

mcqs.explanation: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP ) score is decreased in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) i.e. garden party appearance on peripheral smear.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not cause relative polycythemia ?
mcqs.explanation: High altitude produces absolute polycythemia and not relative polycythemia . Polycythemia denotes an abnormally high red cell count, usually with a corresponding increase in the hemoglobin level (> 16 \261 2 g/dL). It is 2 types : • Relative - hemoconcentration due to decreased plasma volume • Absolute - increase in the total red cell mass Causes of relative polycythemia include : • Dehydration - deprivation of water, prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, excessive use of diuretics • Gaisb\366ck syndrome - stress polycythemia where affected individuals are usually hypertensive , obese , and anxious Causes of absolute polycythemia include : • Primary - intrinsic abnormality of hematopoietic precursors • Polycythemia vera • Inherited erythropoietin receptor mutations • Secondary - red cell progenitors responding to increased levels of erythropoietin • Compensatory due to cyanotic heart and lung disease , high altitude • Paraneoplastic erythropoietin secreting tumours Note : In dengue hemorrhagic fever, increased vascular permeability causes plasma leakage and volume loss. Hence , relative polycythemia is seen .595

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young boy from high altitude came with fever and weakness and had the following reports - Hemoglobin 17 g%, TLC is 21 ,000 with neutrophils 25, lymphocytes 30, eosinophils 5, myelocytes and metamyelocytes 40 in peripheral smear. Next step in the investigation should be:

options.d: Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia (Hb>16 g/dL). Hence , erythropoietin levels (EPO) are estimated next, to differentiate between primary or secondary polycythemia . Based on EPO levels : • Primary polycythemia - normal / decreased • Secondary polycythemia - increased Options A and B: JAK 2 mutation and Philadelphia chromosome analysis is only done as a last resort. Option D: Bone marrow estimation with reticulin is done for myelofibrosis which can be seen in the spent / late stage of the disease . However, peripheral smear findings are not suggestive of primary myelofibrosis . Leukoerythroblastic reaction with dacrocytes is seen in myelofibrosis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman who presented with aquagenic pruritis had a Hb level of 20 g/dL. Her lab investigations are given below . Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia vera. Hepatic failure is not seen in this condition. Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. In this condition, clonal erythrocytosis occurs autonomously i.e. independent of erythropoietin . Clinical features of polycythemia vera: • Headache • Hypertension • Dizziness • Intense pruritis, aquagenic pruritis • Peptic ulcer • Venous thrombosis - Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, stroke, myocardial infarction • Minor hemorrhages - epistaxis , gum bleeding Laboratory findings in polycythemia vera: • Panmyelosis - increased marrow production of red cells , granulocytes , and platelets • Low erythropoietin • Elevated hematocrit • Hyperuricemia Complications of polycythemia vera: • Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis - spent /late phase • Acute myeloid leukemia596

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 63-year-old woman complains about throbbing pain over both palms. Her examination findings and lab reports are given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of essential thrombocythemia (ET). The image showing erythematous hands is suggestive of erythromelalgia . Essential thrombocythemia (essential thrombocytosis ) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm . It is associated with mutations that increase JAK-STAT signaling. WHO criteria for diagnosis of essential thrombocythemia : • Major criteria - • Platelet count \030450 \327 109 /L • Bone marrow biopsy showing proliferation mainly of the megakaryocyte lineage with increased numbers of enlarged , mature megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei • Not meeting WHO criteria for BCR-ABL1 chronic myeloid leukemia, PV , PMF, myelodysplastic syndromes, or other myeloid neoplasms • Presence of JAK2 , CALR , or MPL mutation • Minor criteria - the presence of a clonal marker or absence of evidence for reactive thrombocytosis Diagnosis of ET requires meeting all 4 major criteria or the first 3 major criteria and the minor criterion Option A: Polycythemia vera can also present with erythromelalgia . However, it also presents with increased Hb levels . Option C: Fibrosis (not reticulin fibrils) is seen in bone marrow biopsy of primary myelofibrosis . Option D: WBC counts are increased in leukemoid reactions.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions do not have a leukoerythroblastic picture on peripheral smear?
mcqs.explanation: Leukoerythroblastic picture is not seen in patients with thalassemia as it is a hemoglobinopathy and does not involve myeloid precursors. Abnormal presence of immature precursors of blood in the peripheral blood smear is called leukoerythroblastosis . Findings include : • Nucleated red cells • Dacryocytes (or teardrop RBC) - formed due to damage to red cell membrane caused by fibrous tissue in the marrow • Immature cells of granulocytic series It occurs due to conditions causing marrow replacement like: • Primary myelofibrosis - fibrosis of bone marrow • Myelophthisic anemia - space occupying lesions of bone marrow597 • Gauchers disease • Spent phase of polycythemia vera The image given below shows a leukoerythroblastic blood picture with nucleated RBCs, tear-drop cells , and immature myeloid cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not included under MDS/MPN overlap syndromes?

options.c: MDS/MPN with SF31B mutation and thrombocytosis

mcqs.explanation: Myelodysplastic syndrome/ myeloproliferative neoplasm (MDS/MPN) overlap syndromes are a group of chronic clonal myeloid malignancies in which there are features of both MDS and MPN at the time of presentation . According to the 5th edition WHO classification (2022 ), it includes : • Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia • MDS/MPN with neutrophilia (previously atypical chronic myeloid leukemia) • MDS/MPN with SF31B mutation and thrombocytosis • MDS/MPN not otherwise specified

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not compatible with a diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia?

options.c: More than 20 % blasts in blood or bone marrow
options.d: Absent or minimal dysplasia in myeloid lineages

mcqs.explanation: More than 20 % of blasts in the blood or bone marrow are not compatible with a diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML). In this condition, blasts are less than 20 %. WHO 5th edition diagnostic criteria (2022 _for chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) include : Prerequisite criteria: • 1. Persistent absolute (\0300.5 \327 109 / L) and relative (\03010%) peripheral blood monocytosis . • 2. Blasts constitute <20% of the cells in the peripheral blood and bone marrow .598 • 3. Not meeting diagnostic criteria of chronic myeloid leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN).b • 4. Not meeting diagnostic criteria of myeloid /lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine kinase fusions.c Supporting criteria: • 1. Dysplasia involving \0301 myeloid lineage .d • 2. Acquired clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality. • 3. Abnormal partitioning of peripheral blood monocyte subsets .e Pre-requisite criteria must be present in all cases : • If monocytosis is \030 1 \327 109 / L: one or more supporting criteria must be met. • If monocytosis is \0300.5 and <1 \327 109/ L: supporting criteria 1 and 2 must be met. Subtype criteria: • Myelodysplastic CMML (MD-CMML): WBC < \327 109 /L • Myeloproliferative CMML (MP-CMML): WBC \030 \327 109 /L a. Blasts and blast equivalents include myeloblasts , monoblasts, and promonocytes . b. MPN with monocytosis can mimic CMML. In these instances, a documented history of MPN excludes CMML. The presence of MPN features in the bone marrow and/or a high burden of MPN-associated mutations (JAK2, CALR , or MPL) tends to support MPN with monocytosis rather than CMML. c. Criteria for myeloid /lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine kinase fusions should be specifically excluded in cases with eosinophilia . d. Morphologic dysplasia should be present in \03010 % of cells of a hematopoietic lineage in the bone marrow. e. Based on the detection of increased classical monocytes (>94%) in the absence of known active autoimmune diseases and/or systemic inflammatory syndromes.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old boy with Noonan syndrome presents with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. You are suspecting juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: HbF levels are increased in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), not Hb A2 . JMML is a hematopoietic stem cell -derived myeloproliferative neoplasm of early childhood . It is one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms. It is associated with mutations in the RAS pathway . Neurofibromatosis 1, Noonan syndrome, and trisomy 8 mosaicism can predispose to this condition. Aggressive types include PTPN11 mutation and neurofibromatosis type 1. WHO diagnostic guidelines of JMML: * Germline mutation ( indicating Noonan syndrome) needs to be excluded . It is associated with a poor prognosis and only a few patients undergo spontaneous regression.599 Category I (Mandatory):Clini cal and hematologic features Category II :Genetic (only 1 re quired) Category III : Category I + the se findings: SplenomegalyPeripheral bloo d monocyte count \0301 \327 109 /L Blast percentage in periphera l blood and bone marrow <2 0%No Philadelphia chromos ome (BCR/ABL1 rearrangeme nt)Exclusion of KMT2A muta tion Somatic mutation inPTPN11 * orKRAS* orNRAS *Clinical d iagnosis of Neurofibromatosi s type 1 or NF1 mutationGer mline CBL mutation Hemoglobin F increased for ageMyeloid or erythroid prec ursors on the peripheral bloo d smearHypersensitivity to G M-CSF by colony assay and S TAT5 hyperphosphorylationT hrombocytopenia with hyper cellular bone marrow

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with _____
mcqs.explanation: Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. A mutation in JAK2 , a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway , can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera. It is characterized by : • Increased marrow production of red cells , granulocytes , and platelets (panmyelosis ) • Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit • Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding . • Headache , dizziness, hypertension , dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke. • Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus • Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia • 15% to 20 % of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis , • PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients . Primary myelofibrosis • Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen . • Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL. • Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes , which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet -derived growth factor) and TGF-�o . • Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow . • So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice , which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow , abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids . • Blood shows mild leukocytosis , decreased Hb and hematocrit levels , and elevated LAP scores. • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20 % of cases .600 Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2 , MPL, or CALR mutations. • Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases ) or MPL (5% to 10 % of cases ), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin . • In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR ), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm . Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive , it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown. CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22 ]). PV , PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients is least likely to have leukemoid reaction?

options.d: A patient with acute myocardial infarction

mcqs.explanation: Myocardial infarction does not cause leukemoid reaction. Leukemoid reaction is defined as persistent leukocytosis above 50000 cells /mm3 , where the cause is other than leukemia. Causes of leukemoid reaction include : • Severe infections • Malignancy • Severe hemorrhage • Acute hemolysis • Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) • Asplenia • Diabetic ketoacidosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Electron microscopic picture of which of the following conditions is shown below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given electron microscopy image shows tennis racket shaped Birbeck granules. These granules are characteristic of Langerhans cell histiocytosis . These granules are pentalaminar tubules with dilated terminal ends . This gives a characteristic tennis racket appearance on electron microscopy. They contain the protein langerin (CD207). The image given below shows the Birbeck granules as seen on electron microscopy.601 On peripheral smear, the proliferating Langerhans cells are characterised by: • Abundant vacuolated cytoplasm • Vesicular nuclei containing linear grooves or folds - coffee bean nuclei The image given below shows Langerhans cells with coffee bean nuclei and moderately abundant pale cytoplasm mixed with a few eosinophils.Note : Tennis racket cells in light microscopy seen in sarcoma botryoides .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a histiocytic neoplasm ?
mcqs.explanation: Rosai–Dorfman disease is not a histiocytic neoplasm . It is sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy .602 WHO classification of histiocytic / hematolymphoid neoplasm 2016 includes the following : • Histiocytic sarcoma • Langerhans cell histiocytosis • Langerhans cell sarcoma • Indeterminate dendritic cell tumour • lnterdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma • Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma • Fibroblastic reticular cell tumour • Disseminated juvenile xanthogranuloma • Erdheim–Chester disease

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: You are suspecting Langerhans cell histiocytosis in a child with an enlarging scalp lesion. Which of the following markers will you test to confirm your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: S-100 is a marker for Langerhans cell histiocytosis . Tumour cells in this condition typically express the following : • HLA -DR • S-100 • CD1a

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her father, who states that the girl is drinking a lot of water lately . Physical examination reveals exophthalmos . Further workup shows the presence of multiple lytic bone lesions involving her calvarium and the base of her skull. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hand–Sch\374ller–Christian disease . Langerhans cell histiocytosis presents as multiple clinicopathological entities : 1. Hand–Sch\374ller–Christian disease is a multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis. It usually affects young children. It is characterized by the triad of: • Diabetes insipidus (excessive thirst) - involvement of the posterior pituitary stalk of the hypothalamus • Exophthalmos • Multiple lytic bone lesions It usually undergoes spontaneous regression. It is treated with local excision or irradiation . 2. Letterer–Siwe disease is a multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis . It occurs most frequently before 2 years of age , but occasionally affects adults . It is characterized by the following features : • Cutaneous lesions , resembling a seborrheic eruption - caused by infiltrates of Langerhans cells over the front and back of the trunk and on the scalp603 • Hepatosplenomegaly • Lymphadenopathy • Pulmonary lesions • Destructive osteolytic bone lesions • Due to marrow infiltration - anemia, thrombocytopenia , predisposition to recurrent infections (otitis media and mastoiditis ) Treatment involves intensive chemotherapy. This condition is fatal if left untreated . 3. Eosinophilic granuloma is a unifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis . It is characterized by the proliferation of Langerhans cells admixed with variable numbers of eosinophils , lymphocytes , plasma cells , and neutrophils . These lesions occur in the following sites : • Medullary cavities of bones - most commonly the calvarium , ribs, and femur • Skin • Lungs • Stomach Bone lesions can manifest as: • Asymptomatic • Pain • Tenderness • Pathologic fractures. Treatment is by local excision or irradiation . 4. Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is most often seen in adult smokers. It regresses spontaneously upon cessation of smoking.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The X-ray of a 65-year-old man is given below . Clinical examination, and hematological and urinary tests were normal . Which of the following is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing a solitary punched -out lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim with a beveled edge appearance , along with the age of the patient with history of normal hematological and urinary tests is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis . Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells , called Langerhans cells . Their normal function is to present antigens. It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions . It can also infiltrate the skin (of the scalp ), lungs , liver, spleen , bone marrow , or the central nervous system .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true regarding the procedure done using the instrument given in the image below ?

options.c: Procedure can be done in both lateral & prone position
options.d: Diagnosing an infiltrative or granulomatous disease

mcqs.explanation: 604 The image shows a bone marrow biopsy needle . Thrombocytopenia is not in itself a contraindication for bone marrow biopsy . However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes . Indications of bone marrow biopsy : • Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia , thrombocytopenia , pancytopenia • Evaluation of polycythemia , thrombocytosis , leukocytosis • Diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors • Diagnosis and evaluation of plasma cell disorders and leukemias • Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases • Evaluation of fever of unknown origin, suspected mycobacterial , fungal, or parasitic infections , or granulomatous diseases Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy : • Severe hemophilia • Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy • Severe bleeding disorders Procedure for bone marrow biopsy : Prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure . Posterior superior iliac spine is identified . After disinfection and local anaesthesia, the patient is asked to inhale slowly through the nose and exhale slowly through the mouth to relieve anxiety .The needle is inserted and rotated on its axis. On reaching the desired depth , the stylet is removed and needle is advanced. The needle is rotated in the opposite direction to loosen the specimen . It is then withdrawn using the same rotational movement.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Blood examination shows pancytopenia , which can be correct?
mcqs.explanation: 605 Megaloblastic anemia (hypocellular phase ), hairy cell leukemia, and hypocellular MDS can show pancytopenia. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is not associated with pancytopenia . Causes of pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow : • Acquired aplastic anemia • Hypocellular myelodysplastic syndrome • Rare aleukemic leukemia • Some acute lymphoid leukemia • Rare lymphomas of bone marrow • Copper deficiency Causes of pancytopenia with cellular bone marrow : • Myelodysplastic syndromes • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) • Hypersplenism • B12 , folate deficiency , Copper deficiency • Myelofibrosis • Aleukemic leukemia • HIV , Brucellosis , Leishmaniasis, Tuberculosis Sepsis • Myelophthisis • Bone marrow lymphoma • Sarcoidosis • Hairy cell leukemia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions will have the least chances of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration?
mcqs.explanation: Follicular lymphoma is the least likely cause of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration. Causes of dry tap are: • Metastatic carcinoma infiltration • Chronic myeloid leukemia • Myelofibrosis • Hairy cell leukemia • Acute leukemia • Hodgkin's lymphoma • AML- M7606 Causes of pancytopenia with cellular marrow are: Primary disease of marrow - • Myelodysplastic syndrome • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) • Myelofibrosis • Aleukemic leukemia • Myelophthisis • Bone marrow lymphoma • Hairy cell leukemia Secondary to systemic disease - • SLE, sarcoidosis • B12 , folate deficiency • Copper deficiency • Hypersplenism • Alcohol • HIV infection , TB • Brucellosis , leishmaniasis Note : Although marrow is hypercellular in CML, MDS etc ., extensive marrow fibrosis (rare) has been proposed to account for a dry tap on bone marrow biopsy .607

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: From which period of embryogenesis does the liver become the chief site of hematopoiesis ?
mcqs.explanation: 613 From the 3rd month of embryogenesis, the liver becomes the chief site of hematopoiesis . Development of hematopoietic tissues: • Yolk sac - blood cell progenitors first appear during the 3rd week • Liver - hematopoietic stem cells migrate to the liver during the 3rd month of embryogenesis • Bone marrow - hematopoiesis starts in bone marrow during the 4th month of intrauterine life and becomes the predominant site after birth

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which cells in the bone marrow are referred to as nurse cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Nurse cells are specialized macrophages in the bone marrow that assist in the development of red blood cells (RBCs).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Bone marrow biopsy of a normal adult is given below . What is the ratio of structures marked A and B?
mcqs.explanation: The structures marked A are fat cells and B are hematopoietic elements . The normal ratio of fat cells to hematopoietic elements in a normal adult is 1:1.In hypoplastic states (like aplastic anemia), the proportion of fat cells is greatly increased (increased fat to cell ratio). Conversely, fat cells often disappear in conditions like hematopoietic tumors and in diseases with compensatory hyperplasias (like hemolytic anemias) and neoplastic proliferations such as leukemias (decreased fat-to-cell ratio).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a marker for pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells ?
mcqs.explanation: 614 CD34 is an antigen of pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells and progenitor cells of many lineages .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is called leukocyte common antigen?
mcqs.explanation: CD45 is called leukocyte common antigen because it is found in all leukocytes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Kostmann syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Kostmann syndrome is characterized by neutropenia . It is a rare congenital condition in which inherited defects in specific genes impair granulocytic differentiation. This results in severe congenital neutropenia . It presents in young children as recurrent bacterial infections (such as otitis media, cellulitis) and oral ulcers . It is associated with an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of agranulocytosis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of agranulocytosis is drug toxicity . Causes of agranulocytosis include : • Inadequate or ineffective granulopoiesis - • Suppression of hematopoietic stem cells - aplastic anemia, infiltrative marrow disorders • Suppression of committed granulocytic precursors • Ineffective hematopoiesis - megaloblastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndromes • Congenital conditions - Kostmann syndrome615 • Increased destruction or sequestration of neutrophils - • Immunological injury to neutrophils - idiopathic , systemic lupus erythematosus , drug exposure • Increased peripheral utilization - bacterial, fungal, or rickettsial infections • Splenomegaly

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who was started on chemotherapy 2 weeks ago is found to have a neutrophil count of 2000 /mm3 . Below what neutrophil count is he at risk of developing serious infections ?
mcqs.explanation: Serious infections are most likely when the neutrophil count falls below 500/mm3 .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy is brought with complaints of episodes of severe , violent coughs , followed by a high-pitch intake of breath that sounds like a whoop . These coughing episodes are usually followed by vomiting. He and his family are refugees and his prior vaccination records are not available. Lab investigations of this child will likely reveal which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of whooping cough or pertussis . It is due to Bordetella pertussis infection and results in lymphocytosis . Causes of lymphocytosis include : • Pertussis • Tuberculosis • Brucellosis • Hepatitis A • Cytomegalovirus • Epstein -Barr virus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man admitted to ICU develops sepsis 3 days after insertion of a central venous catheter . A peripheral blood smear reveals the following . What does the structure marked by the arrow indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The given peripheral smear, prepared from an individual with bacterial sepsis , shows reactive changes in neutrophils . The arrow-marked structure is a D\366hle body.616 Reactive changes in neutrophils associated with leukocytosis in severe inflammatory disorders are: • Toxic granules, which are coarser and darker than the normal neutrophilic granules, represent abnormal azurophilic (primary) granules • D\366hle bodies are patches of the dilated endoplasmic reticulum that appear as sky-blue cytoplasmic puddles • Toxic cytoplasmic vacuoles The image given below shows a neutrophil with cytoplasmic vacuoles.617

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not cause follicular hyperplasia of the lymph nodes ?
mcqs.explanation: B-cell lymphoma results in malignant proliferation within the lymph node, not follicular hyperplasia . Follicular hyperplasia is a benign condition caused by stimuli that activate humoral immune responses . It may occur in: • Rheumatoid arthritis • Toxoplasmosis • Early stages of HIV infection It is defined by the presence of large oblong germinal centres (secondary follicles ), which are surrounded by a collar of small, resting naive B cells (mantle zone).618

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia ?

options.c: No variation in shape and size of the follicles

mcqs.explanation: In reactive lymphoid hyperplasia , there is marked variation in the shape and size of follicles . Features favoring reactive lymphoid hyperplasia , which are absent in neoplastic follicles are: • Preservation of the lymph node architecture , including the interfollicular T-cell zones and the sinusoids • Marked variation in the shape and size of the follicles • Presence of frequent mitotic figures and phagocytic macrophages • Recognizable light and dark zones

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which of the following organs are tingible body macrophages found?
mcqs.explanation: Tingible-body macrophages are found in lymph nodes . A tingible -body macrophage is a type of macrophage predominantly found in germinal centers containing many phagocytosed apoptotic cell debris. This debris is referred to as tingible bodies (tingible meaning stainable). The presence of these macrophages suggests non-neoplastic reactive hyperplasia of the lymph node, or can be seen as the stars in the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma.619

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy presented with complaints of fever, sore throat, and enlarged lymph nodes . Paul Bunnell's test was done and found to be positive . What type of lymphoid hyperplasia is seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis . Acute viral infections , like infectious mononucleosis , produce paracortical hyperplasia . There are three types of lymph node hyperplasia . They are: • Follicular hyperplasia • Paracortical hyperplasia • Sinus histiocytosis (reticular hyperplasia ) Paracortical hyperplasia is seen in the T-cell-containing paracortical region of the lymph node. It is caused by stimuli that trigger T-cell–mediated immune responses . The involved regions typically contain:620 • Immunoblasts • Activated T-cells 3-4 times the size of resting lymphocytes t • Round nuclei • Open chromatin • Several prominent nucleoli • Moderate amounts of pale cytoplasm • Hypertrophy of sinusoidal and vascular endothelial cells , with infiltrating macrophages and eosinophils

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with breast cancer with lymph node metastases , which of the following changes is seen in affected lymph nodes ?
mcqs.explanation: In the case of lymph node metastases , there is prominent reticular hyperplasia . Reticular hyperplasia or sinus histiocytosis refers to an increase in the number and size of the cells that line lymphatic sinusoids . Although nonspecific , this form of hyperplasia may be particularly prominent in lymph nodes draining cancers such as carcinoma of the breast. The lining lymphatic endothelial cells are markedly hypertrophied and macrophages are greatly increased in numbers, resulting in the expansion and distension of the sinuses . The image given below shows reticular hyperplasia in the lymph node.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is false ?

options.a: There is systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T cells
options.b: The most common trigger is infection with Epstein -Barr virus
options.c: It presents as an acute febrile illness with hepatosplenomegaly
options.d: Hemophagocytosis seen in bone marrow is sufficient for diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Hemophagocytosis is usually seen on bone marrow examination, but it is neither sufficient nor required to make the diagnosis of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH ).621 HLH is a reactive condition also known as macrophage-activation syndrome. The common feature of all forms of HLH is the systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T-cells . The most common trigger for HLH is an infection , particularly with EBV (Epstein -Barr virus). It is characterized by acute febrile illness associated with splenomegaly , hepatomegaly , and cytopenias .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature in patients with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH ) is associated with very high serum ferritin levels . Laboratory findings in HLH include : • Anemia • Thrombocytopenia • High serum ferritin • High plasma IL2 receptor levels • Elevated liver enzyme levels • High triglyceride levels • Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)622

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Vascular injury causes intimal thickening by which of the following mechanisms?
mcqs.explanation: Vascular injury results in intimal thickening due to smooth muscle proliferation. Vascular injury stimulates the migration of smooth muscle cells of the tunica media to the tunica intima. These smooth muscle cells proliferate and also synthesize extracellular matrix leading to intimal thickening. This is the stereotypical response of the vessel wall to an injury regardless of the cause of injury. The image below shows intimal thickening occurring in response to vascular injury.631

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Endothelial dysfunction is implicated in all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Endothelial dysfunction is not implicated in aneurysm formation. An aneurysm occurs due to the pathology of connective tissue within the vascular wall. Endothelial dysfunction is the pathological alteration of the endothelium such that it becomes pro-inflammatory and prothrombogenic. It is caused by various injuries to endothelial cells : • Hemodynamic stresses - responsible for vascular pathology in hypertension • Lipid products - leading to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis • Advanced glycation end-products (AGE) - responsible for diabetic microangiopathy • Viruses, bacterial products , cytokines, and complement components

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Identify the condition:
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows arteriosclerosis and calcification in the tunica media, that does not encroach on the vessel lumen. This is suggestive of Monckeberg 's medial sclerosis . Monckeberg 's medial sclerosis affects medium-sized muscular arteries and is characterized by calcification of the medial walls of the affected arteries. Adults aged over 50 years are usually affected .632 Arteriosclerosis refers to the thickening of the arterial wall and loss of elasticity . There are four patterns of arteriosclerosis : • Small vessel arteriosclerosis - involves small arteries and arterioles • It has two variants - hyaline arteriosclerosis , and hyperplastic arteriosclerosis • Monckeberg medial sclerosis - involves calcification of the walls of muscular arteries • Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia - usually a healing response to inflammation (eg: arteritis) or mechanical injury (eg: stent insertion) • Atherosclerosis - mainly involves elastic and muscular arteries

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The following incidental finding is seen on a radiograph of a 60-year-old man. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

options.a: It involves the internal elastic lamina
options.b: It involves the external elastic lamina

mcqs.explanation: The given radiograph shows extensive calcification of the femoral arteries which is suggestive of Monckeberg medial sclerosis . It is characterized by the calcification of the walls of muscular arteries, typically starting along the internal elastic lamina and involves the media of the arteries. It occurs in people aged 50 years and above as a part of senile degeneration . It is not associated with hypertension or diabetes . It is usually an incidental finding.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following pathological changes occurs in the small vessels of patients suffering from hypertension?
mcqs.explanation: Hypertension results in hyaline arteriosclerosis of the small vessels . Hypertension leads to a variety of vascular pathologies . In small blood vessels , hypertension may lead to arteriosclerosis which is the thickening of the vessel wall. It has two variants which are hyaline arteriosclerosis and hyperplastic arteriosclerosis .633 In large and medium-sized arteries, hypertension leads to degenerative changes in the vessel walls, leading to: • Dissection • Aneurysm formation • Cerebrovascular hemorrhage • Acceleration of atherosclerosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is responsible for arteriolar wall thickening in hyaline arteriosclerosis?
mcqs.explanation: The arteriolar wall thickening in hyaline arteriosclerosis occurs as a result of plasma protein deposition . Hyaline arteriosclerosis occurs due to injury to the endothelial cells . This allows plasma protein leakage into the arteriolar wall. The endothelial injury also stimulates increased matrix synthesis by the smooth muscle cells . These lead to the deposition of homogenous pink hyaline material causing the thickening of arteriolar walls .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathology resident is studying a vascular biopsy sample . This vascular lesion is less likely seen in which of the following conditions
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows hyaline arteriosclerosis . It occurs in the following conditions: • Elderly patients who are normotensive • Benign hypertension : due to chronic hemodynamic stresses • Diabetes mellitus : due to hyperglycemia-induced endothelial dysfunctionSevere hypertension causes hyperplastic arteriosclerosis with the characteristic onion skin appearance as seen below :634

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The renal biopsy of a 50-year-old chronic hypertensive patient is given below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows hyperplastic arteriosclerosis , as noted by the onion-skin appearance of the arteriole. This is seen in malignant nephrosclerosis . Nephrosclerosis is caused by sclerosis of the small arteries and the arterioles of the kidney leading to diffuse impairment of renal blood supply . It is of 2 types :Benignnephrosclerosis Malignantnephrosclerosis Seen in benign hypertension Seen in malignant hypertensi on Causeshyaline arteriosclerosi s Causeshyperplastic arterioscl erosisandfibrinoid necrosisof the arterioles .635 The characteristic flea -bitten appearance of the kidney is seen in malignant nephrosclerosis (shown below). This is due to small petechial hemorrhages resulting from the rupture of arterioles .636

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presented with chest pain. Past history is significant for dyslipidemia and an ischemic stroke 2 years ago. Coronary angiography was performed and showed the following . What is the correct sequence of events leading to this condition?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing occlusion of the left circumflex coronary artery are suggestive of atherosclerosis . It progresses in the following sequence : • Endothelial injury and dysfunction • Accumulation of lipoproteins in the vessel wall • Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium • Platelet adhesion • Factor release from activated platelets , macrophages , and vascular wall cells • Smooth muscle cell proliferation, extracellular matrix production , and recruitment of T cells • Lipid accumulation both extracellularly and within cells • Calcification of ECM and necrotic debris late in the pathogenesis Hence , atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. The two most important causes of endothelial injury leading to atherosclerosis are hemodynamic disturbances and hypercholesterolemia . The image below shows partial occlusion of the left circumflex coronary artery.637

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most important independent risk factor for atherosclerosis is family history. The familial predisposition to atherosclerosis is usually polygenic . It is related to the familial clustering of other established risk factors, such as hypertension or diabetes . It may also be due to inherited variations in pathophysiologic processes such as inflammation. Hyperlipidemia (specifically hypercholesterolemia ) is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis . Even in the absence of other risk factors, hypercholesterolemia is sufficient to initiate lesion development .638

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common site of atherosclerosis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of atherosclerosis is the lower abdominal aorta. In descending order, the most extensively involved vessels in atherosclerosis are: • Lower abdominal aorta • Coronary arteries • Popliteal arteries • Internal carotid arteries • Arteries of the circle of Willis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The autopsy of a 14-year-old boy who died in a motor vehicle accident showed the following lesions on the inner surface of the aorta. What do these lesions indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows yellow spots on the inner surface of the aorta, which represent fatty streaks. They indicate a collection of foamy macrophages in the intima of the vessel wall. Fatty streaks may be present in the aorta of infants, virtually all adolescents , and even individuals without known risk factors. These lesions are not indicative of atherosclerosis , but some of them may evolve into atheromatous plaques later in life by smooth muscle proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Where are the following cells in an atheromatous plaque derived from?
mcqs.explanation: The cells marked in the image above are the foam cells in atheromatous plaques . They refer to lipid -laden monocytes / macrophages or smooth muscle cells within the plaques . These cells ingest lipoproteins accumulated within the intima of the vessel wall. Since these lipoproteins are modified due to the action of inflammatory mediators, they cannot be degraded further within these cells . This leads to the accumulation of modified lipids within these cells converting them to foam cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In which part of the atheromatous plaque are the T-cells and macrophages in abundance?
mcqs.explanation: T-cells and macrophages are in abundance in the shoulder of an atheromatous plaque. Structure of an atherosclerotic plaque: • Superficial fibrous cap - made up of smooth muscle cells and connective tissue , especially collagen . It also contains macrophages , foam cells , and lymphocytes . It determines the stability of plaque. • Necrotic core - contains lipid (cholesterol and cholesterol esters ), debris from dead cells , calcium, and foam cells . • Shoulder - a more cellular area containing macrophages , T-cells , and smooth muscle cells .639 • Periphery - shows neovascularization/proliferation of small blood vessels . The image below shows the structure of an atherosclerotic plaque.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding a stable atherosclerotic plaque?
mcqs.explanation: A stable atherosclerotic plaque has abundant smooth muscle cells . These cells synthesize collagen which stabilizes the plaque. Both these features contribute to a thick fibrous cap that prevents the easy rupture of a plaque.Stable plaque Vulnerable plaque Dense collagen Less collagen Thick fibrous cap Thin fibrous cap640 Stable plaque Vulnerable plaque Minimal inflammation Increased inflammation Less extracellular lipid Abundant extracellular lipid Abundant smooth muscle ce lls Few smooth muscle cells Few foam cells Abundant foam cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a 50-year-old normotensive patient with a 10 -year history of dyslipidemia , which of the following complications is he at the least risk of developing ?
mcqs.explanation: A 50-year-old patient suffering from dyslipidemia for the past 10 years is likely to have atherosclerosis. Dissection is associated with hypertension , not atherosclerosis . An atherosclerotic plaque may undergo pathological changes such as: • Thrombus formation - due to rupture, ulceration, erosion • Increase in plaque size - due to hemorrhage into the plaque These consequences occlude the lumen of the vessel and impair the blood supply . Impaired blood supply may lead to claudication , ischemic heart disease , myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, or even gangrene . The thrombus may dislodge and cause an embolism. Atherosclerotic debris released due to plaque rupture may produce microemboli, known as atheroembolism . Atherosclerotic plaques also cause ischemic atrophy of the underlying media. This causes weakness of the vessel wall leading to aneurysm formation. The image below depicts the late complications of atherosclerosis .641

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with anginal chest pain is planned for coronary angiography. What level of stenosis would you expect to see in the affected artery?
mcqs.explanation: This symptomatic patient likely has >70% occlusion of his coronary arteries. This is known as critical stenosis . It refers to the stage at which the occlusion is sufficiently severe to produce tissue ischemia. This leads to clinical manifestations of ischemia such as: • Stable angina • Bowel ischemia • Intermittent claudication

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Elevated levels of which of the following is not a predictor for stroke?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated plasminogen levels are not associated with stroke. Elevated levels of the following are predictors for stroke: • C-reactive protein - also indicates risk for MI, PAD and used to monitor effectiveness of risk reduction measures like exercise , weight loss • Homocysteine - also correlates with MI, PAD, venous thrombosis, and premature vascular disease • Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 - marker of hemostatic and/or fibrinolytic function and also predicts risk of MI

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with symptoms of heart failure. He had undergone a coronary bypass procedure with a small-diameter graft 3 weeks ago. What is the likely cause for his presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of an early failure of a small diameter venous graft (\0218 mm). The likely mechanism for graft failure within the 1st month is acute thrombosis. Late vein graft failure (after months to years) is due to: • Neointimal hyperplasia (1 month to 1 year) • Atherosclerotic plaque (> 1 year) • Aneurysm Based on the diameter of the synthetic or autologous vascular graft, it can be: • Large diameter graft (12-18mm) - • Used in high-flow locations such as the aorta • Small diameter graft (\0218 mm) - • Includes saphenous vein or left internal mammary artery • Used in coronary bypass surgeries642

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding the KLF-2 transcription factor?

options.c: Production is induced by laminar blood flow
options.d: Responsible for the atheroprotective role of statins

mcqs.explanation: Kruppel like factor-2 (KLF-2) is responsible for turning off the inflammatory gene transcription. KLF-2 production is induced by laminar blood flow which is seen in normal endothelium . This transcription factor activates the atheroprotective genes and turns off inflammatory gene transcription. Statins up-regulate KLF-2 expression in endothelial cells , and this activity is associated with an anti-inflammatory phenotype . Up -regulation of KLF-2 gene expression may be a novel strategy for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis .643

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Pulsating hematoma is associated with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Pulsating hematoma is associated with a false aneurysm. An aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart. There are 2 types : • True aneurysm • Due to weakened and thinned, but intact arterial wall • False aneurysm • Due to a defect in the vascular wall • Results in an extravascular hematoma that communicates with intravascular space • Causes transmission of arterial pulsations to the hematoma (pulsating hematoma) Dissection occurs when blood enters a defect in the arterial wall and tunnels /dissects between its layers. The image below shows a pseudo /false aneurysm of the left ventricle.False aneurysm Dissection Defect across all the layers of the vessel wall Defect is usually an intimal t ear Hematoma is extravascular ( outside the vessel wall) Hematoma is within the laye rs of the vessel wall Hematoma is lined by extrav ascular connective tissue Hematoma is lined by the lay ers of the vessel wall649

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with a severe headache and transient loss of consciousness . On examination , neck rigidity was present and blood pressure was 160 /110 mmHg. A CT brain was done as shown below . Which type of aneurysm could have been involved in causing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in a hypertensive patient. It may occur due to the rupture of Berry aneurysms, which are saccular aneurysms. Aneurysms are classified as: • Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall. • Fusiform aneurysms are diffuse , circumferential dilations involving long vascular segments . • Both saccular and fusiform aneurysms are true aneurysms because they have an intact vessel wall. • Dissecting aneurysm is produced when a dissection leads to an aneurysm. The image below shows the CT appearance of a SAH.650

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient who is a known case of hypertension was diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is the likely underlying pathophysiology causing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The likely underlying pathophysiology causing this condition is increased metalloproteinase expression that degrades extracellular matrix and weakens the vessel wall. The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are atherosclerosis and hypertension . Aneurysms occuring as a consequence of atherosclerosis occurs most commonly in the abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries. Option A: Obliterative end-arteritis of vasa-vasorum occurs in late stage syphilis and can contribute to aneurysms Option D: Medial hypertrophy of vasa-vasorum occurs in hypertension , which is associated most commonly with ascending aortic aneurysms.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Arterial aneurysms due to underlying cystic medial degeneration are seen in patients with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Cystic medial degeneration leading to aneurysms is a feature of Marfan syndrome. Cystic medial degeneration refers to the degenerative changes in the media of the vessel wall that lead to aneurysm formation. These include : • Loss of smooth muscle cells • Loss of elastic fibers • Inadequate extracellular matrix synthesis • Increased production of glycosaminoglycan It can be caused due to: • Medial ischemia - atherosclerosis , hypertension • Defective connective tissue - Marfan syndrome, scurvy The image below (Movat stain) shows a cross-section of the aortic media from a patient with Marfan's syndrome showing elastin fragmentation (stained black) and loss of smooth muscle cells (cells stained red and nuclei stained violet).651

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following causes aneurysm formation due to defective elastin ?
mcqs.explanation: Loeys–Dietz syndrome leads to aneurysm formation due to defective elastin (due to a defect in TGF-�o signalling pathway ). Aneurysms are caused due to structural or functional defects in the connective tissue of the vascular wall. The following conditions cause intrinsic defects in connective tissue leading to aneurysm formation:Syndrome Defect in Loeys–Dietzsyndrome Synthesis ofelastinandcollage ns IandIII Ehlers –Danlossyndrome Synthesis oftype III collageni n some subtypes Marfansyndrome Synthesis of the proteinfibrill incausing weakening of elasti c tissue Scurvy(vitamin C deficiency ) Collagencross -linking

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of syphilitic aneurysms?
mcqs.explanation: Syphilitic aneurysms most commonly involves the ascending aorta. Late-stage syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum of the aorta. This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media resulting in aneurysmal dilation.652

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old normotensive patient with dyslipidemia is undergoing a regular check-up. He is at an increased risk of developing all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Dyslipidemia is not a direct risk factor for deep vein thrombosis. Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and its complications , including abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). AAA can also be associated with smaller aneurysms of the iliac arteries. Patients with AAA are also likely to have atherosclerotic lesions in other vascular beds that may lead to ischemic heart disease or stroke.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following myocardial infarcts cause aneurysm as a post -MI complication?
mcqs.explanation: Anterior transmural infarcts are involved in causing aneurysm as a post -MI complication. Posterior transmural infarcts are more likely to be complicated by conduction blocks, right ventricular involvement, or both.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient was diagnosed with an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm of a diameter of 3.6cm. On a follow -up visit 1 year later, the diameter was noted to be 3.8cm. What is the risk of rupture of the aneurysm in this patient at present ?
mcqs.explanation: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) of size \021 4 cm with slow growth have no risk of rupture . The risk of rupture for AAA is directly related to the size of the aneurysm: • \0214 cm - nil • 4–5 cm - 1% per year • 5–6 cm - 11 % per year • >6 cm - 25% per year Most aneurysms expand at a rate of 0.2 to 0.3 cm/year. The risk of rupture increases when there is a growth of > 0.5 cm/6 months as well as in active smokers.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man presents with sudden onset chest pain radiating to the back between the scapulae . The CT of this patient is given below . What is the major risk factor for developing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with the CT finding of a second column of blood after an intimal tear is the classic presentation of an aortic dissection . The major risk factor for aortic dissection is hypertension . Dissection occurs when blood enters into the media to form a blood-filled channel between the laminar planes of the media. It usually occurs due to a tear in the intima which allows blood in the lumen to flow into the media. It may also occur due to the rupture of vasa vasorum . It occurs due to: • Hypertension • Connective tissue defects like Marfan syndrome • Iatrogenic trauma during coronary catheterization or cardiopulmonary bypass653

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 2D echocardiography of a patient who presented with chest pain showed the following appearance of the aorta on suprasternal parasagittal view. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.b: It is a severe type of dissection

mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a double -barreled aorta with a superior and inferior lumen. It is a less severe type of dissection because it is less likely to cause hemorrhage.A double -barreled aorta is seen there are two intimal tears. Hence , the hematoma enters the media through an intimal tear but re-enters back into the lumen through another intimal tear present distally . As the blood enters the lumen back, this type of dissection does not progress , thus averting hemorrhage. This creates a false vascular channel in the blood vessel which, over time, can be endothelialized to become chronic dissections .654

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: How would you classify the following according to the DeBakey classification ?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows proximal dissection of only the ascending aorta. This is classified as type II as per DeBakey's classification . Classification of aortic dissection : • Stanford Type A - proximal lesions . These are more common and dangerous . It may involve: • Both the ascending and descending aorta - DeBakey type I • Only the ascending aorta - DeBakey type II • Stanford Type B or DeBakey type III - distal lesions not involving the ascending part and usually beginning distal to the subclavian artery655

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a large vessel vasculitis?
mcqs.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following vasculitides involves veins except ?
mcqs.explanation: Giant cell arteritis does not involve the veins. Vasculitides affecting the veins are as follows : • Leukocytoclastic vasculitis • Behcet disease • Buerger disease (Thrombangiitis obliterans)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset blindness . He gives a history of frequent headaches along the sides of his scalp . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of giant cell arteritis.663 Giant cell / temporal arteritis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of large to small-sized arteries that especially affects the temporal arteries. It is seen in people over 50 years of age . It usually presents with facial pain or headache along the course of the superficial temporal artery. It can also affect : • Ophthalmic arteries- leading to sudden onset diplopia or blindness • Aorta- leading to giant-cell aortitis • Vertebral arteries A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Giant cell arteritis needs to be promptly diagnosed and treated with steroids to prevent permanent blindness .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An elderly patient presented with temporal headache and jaw claudication . She was diagnosed to be a case of Giant cell arteritis. Which of the following statements about giant cell arteritis is incorrect?

options.b: A negative biopsy excludes the diagnosis
options.c: The classic lesions are medial granulomas
options.d: Fragmentation is seen in internal elastic lamina

mcqs.explanation: A negative biopsy cannot exclude the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis. It is because the lesions are focally distributed . A biopsy sample may be taken from the normal part of the artery leading to a false -negative report. An adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment . Biopsy findings: • Giant cell arteritis is primarily medial granulomatous inflammation. • These lesions involve the internal elastic lamina leading to elastic lamina fragmentation. • There is intimal thickening that reduces the luminal diameter . Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells , infiltrate of T cells (CD4+ >CD8+), and macrophages . Note : According to the 21st edition of Harrison 's Medicine , as involvement of the vessel may be segmental , getting a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens would help to increase a positive yield . And Robbin's 10th edition mentions that an adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment. Image: Giant-cell arteritis with intimal thickening and internal elastic lamina fragmentation664

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old lady presents with weakness of the left upper limb. On examination, the blood pressure recorded on the left upper limb was found to be lower than that of the right upper limb. Her aortic arch angiogram showed narrowing of the arch of the aorta and subclavian artery. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and radiological findings are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu's arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis affecting medium and large-sized arteries, in this case, the aortic arch and its branches. Clinical manifestations include vision disturbances and profound weakening of the pulses , especially in the upper extremities . Histopathology : • Irregular thickening of the vessel wall is seen with associated intimal hyperplasia . • Characteristic granulomatous inflammation, with the presence of giant cells and patchy medial necrosis. • Disease progression is associated with collagenous scarring and chronic inflammatory infiltrates across all layers of the vessel wall. Other options - Option A: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, is an inflammation of medium and large-sized vessels . It is more common in women and people aged >50 years. The clinical features include headache associated with scalp pain and jaw claudication , fever, fatigue , malaise, and weight loss.
