Half of the patients have temporal artery abnormalities such as enlargement , tenderness , nodular swelling , and loss of pulse of the temporal artery, either unilateral or bilateral. Gentle pressure on the scalp may elicit focal or generalized tenderness . Though the arch of the aorta may also be involved in giant cell arteritis (known as giant cell aortitis), it is seen in people more than 50 years of age . Whereas, Takayasu arteritis is seen more commonly in adolescents and young women. Option C: Thromboangitis obliterans, also known as Buerger's disease , is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder involving medium- and small-sized vessels in the distal extremities . It is most frequently seen in male smokers less than 40 years of age .665 Option D: Behcet 's disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers , genital ulcers , and uveitis. There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations , with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young girl with bilaterally unequal pulses is diagnosed with Takayasu Arteritis. Which of the following is the most commonly involved site in Takayasu arteritis?
mcqs.explanation: The most commonly involved blood vessel in Takayasu arteritis is sublclavian artery. Takayasu arteritis is an inflammatory and stenotic disease of medium and large-sized arteries characterized by a strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches. It is also known as aortic arch syndrome. The order of arteries affected in Takayasu arteritis is subclavian artery > common carotid artery > abdominal aorta > renal artery > aortic arch = vertebral > coeliac axis > iliac > pulmonary > coronary artery. Takayasu arteritis causes irregular thickening of the vessel wall with intimal hyperplasia leading to narrowing of the lumen and organ ischemia. It may have various clinical presentations depending on the vessel involved: • Arch of aorta and its branches: • Subclavian artery- leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities . Hence it is also known as pulseless disease • Carotid arteries- leads to weak pulses , blindness , neurological deficits • Distal aorta- leads to claudication of the legs • Pulmonary artery- leads to pulmonary hypertension • Coronary arteries- leads to myocardial infarction • Renal arteries- leads to systemic hypertension

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young male presents to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain. The small bowel is found to have a small infarcted area which is surgically removed. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen is given below . Which of the following is the most likely cause of the small bowel infarction?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are suggestive of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN). PAN affects small or medium-sized muscular arteries. It typically affects young adults . The patient may present with rapidly accelerating hypertension due to renal artery involvement (most common) or abdominal pain and bloody stools caused by involvement of gastrointestinal vessels . Option A: Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis is a vascular pathology seen in severe hypertension . Option B: Cystic medial degeneration leads to dissecting aortic aneurysm. Option C: M\366nckeberg's arteriosclerosis does not cause infarction.666

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is characteristically spared in polyarteritis nodosa?
mcqs.explanation: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) characteristically spares the pulmonary circulation. PAN is a systemic vasculitis of small or medium-sized muscular arteries. It typically involves the renal (most commonly involved) and visceral vessels . It has no association with ANCA, but about 30% of patients have chronic hepatitis -B.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child was brought to the hospital with complaints of fever, rash and swelling of her hands and feet since past 5 days. There is desquamative skin rash, oedema of hands and feet , erythema of palms and soles , oral erythema , and cervical lymphadenopathy . What is the likely condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Kawasaki disease or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness associated with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels . It is commonly seen in infants and children <4 years of age . Clinical features include : • Fever • Conjunctival and oral erythema • Blistering, edema of hands and feet • Erythema of palms and soles • Desquamative rash • Cervical lymphadenopathy The disease is usually self -limiting. In some cases , the disease may involve coronary artery leading to thrombosis and acute myocardial infarction. Intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin may be given to reduce the risk of coronary artery disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following antibodies is associated with vasculitis seen in patients with Kawasaki disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Antibodies to endothelial cells are associated with vasculitis in Kawasaki disease . Option A: Immune complex deposition is characteristic of vasculitis due to systemic immunologic disorders such as SLE. Option B: ANCA-associated vasculitis is seen in microscopic polyangiitis , Churg–Strauss syndrome, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis . Option D: Autoreactive T cells are seen in giant cell arteritis. Reports have been described in children with a multisystem inflammatory condition (MIS-C) linked to COVID -19 infection with some features similar to Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome. Although shock is rarely associated with Kawasaki disease , many children with the inflammatory syndrome related to COVID show signs of shock.667

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness occurring in children aged 4 years or younger . It is usually self - limiting. This vasculitis affects large to medium-sized vessels and even small vessels . It is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome because it can present with non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral erythema , edema of the hands and feet , desquamative rash, and cervical lymph node enlargement . It has a predilection for coronary artery involvement and is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children. Untreated patients may develop coronary artery ectasia or aneurysms, leading to rupture or thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and sudden death . Espundia is the muco-cutaneous variant of Leishmaniasis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 27-yr-old woman, presented to OPD with complaints of joint pain and photosensitivity . On examination , you see a butterfly rash on the face and petechial hemorrhages on the lower limbs. On serology ANA, turns out to be positive . Which of the following is the most likely cause of vasculitis in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus . The vasculitis occurring in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus is due to immune complex deposition . Vasculitis is the inflammation of the vessel wall. The various mechanisms that cause vasculitis are: • Immune-mediated inflammation- Vasculitis caused by immune-mediated inflammation may occur due to the following factors: • Immune complex deposition : Seen in systemic immunological disorders like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) • Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA): Seen in Wegener 's granulomatosis, Churg–Strauss disease , etc • Anti endothelial cell antibodies : Implicated in Kawasaki disease • Autoreactive T cells • Infectious pathogens - by direct invasion, generating immune complexes or triggering cross-reactivity. • Physical or chemical injury- from irradiation , trauma, toxins, etc .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 43 year-old-male patient came to the clinic with complaints of occasional hematuria and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Examination revealed tiny petechial hemorrhages over his lower limbs. The patient tests positive for the anti-proteinase -3 antibody . Which of the following is true about this major antibody?

options.a: It is also known as p-ANCA
options.d: It shows perinuclear staining on immunofluorescence

mcqs.explanation: Anti-proteinase -3/PR3 -ANCA / c-ANCA is triggered by certain infections as proteinase 3 shares similarities with many microbial peptides . This is the major antibody responsible for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are a heterogeneous group of autoantibodies directed against the constituents of neutrophils or monocytes . Many patients with vasculitis have circulating antibodies that react with neutrophil cytoplasmic antigens. The two most important ANCAs related to vasculitis are:668 • Anti-proteinase -3/PR3 -ANCA/c-ANCA - Directed against PR3 which is a neutrophil azurophilic granule constituent . • Anti-myeloperoxidase /MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA - Directed against MPO which is a lysosomal granule constituent involved in oxygen free -radical generation. MPO-ANCAs are induced by several therapeutic agents , particularly propylthiouracil .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a pauci-immune rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis ?
mcqs.explanation: Type III or pauci-immune-type of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) may be a component of systemic vasculitis such as Wegener granulomatosis or microscopic polyangiitis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about microscopic polyangiitis is not true?

options.a: It affects capillaries , small arterioles, and venules
options.c: It is also known as leukocytoclastic vasculitis
options.d: Lesions of different stages of activity coexist in the same vessel

mcqs.explanation: All lesions of microscopic polyangiitis tend to be of the same age in any given patient , unlike polyarteritis nodosa where all stages of activity from early to late may coexist in different vessels or even within the same vessel . Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that affects capillaries , small arterioles , and venules . It is associated with MPO-ANCA. It is also called leukocytoclastic vasculitis because of apoptotic neutrophils . It may involve the skin, mucous membranes, lungs , brain , heart, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and muscle . Therefore, the patient may present with hemoptysis , hematuria, proteinuria, bowel pain or bleeding , muscle pain or weakness, and palpable cutaneous purpura. Necrotizing glomerulonephritis (90% of patients ) and pulmonary capillaritis are particularly common.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 21 -year-old boy, who is a known case of asthma, presents with wheezing and rhinitis. Laboratory results show peripheral eosinophilia and antibodies against neutrophil myeloperoxidase . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the lab findings are suggestive of Churg–Strauss syndrome. Churg-Strauss Syndrome / Allergic granulomatosis and angiitis is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically associated with: • asthma • allergic rhinitis • asymmetric mono neuritis multiplex • lung infiltrates • peripheral hypereosinophilia • extravascular necrotizing granulomata. It is a multisystem disease with cutaneous involvement (palpable purpura), gastrointestinal tract bleeding , and renal disease . Eosinophilic infiltrates may also be seen in the myocardium giving rise to cardiomyopathy .669 p- ANCA (MPO-ANCA) is positive in about 50% of cases . Histological features are similar to those observed in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) or microscopic polyangiitis but characteristically accompanied by granulomas and eosinophils . Eosinophilic vasculitis seen in Churg-Strauss syndrome:

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents with hematuria, intermittent hemoptysis and chronic sinusitis. His chest radiograph shows multiple opacities and cavities. Renal biopsy suggests focal necrotizing glomerulonephritis . Which of the following is not seen in this condition?

options.a: Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of Wegener 's granulomatosis. It is associated with PR3 - ANCA (and not MPO- ANCA) in about 95% of cases . Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis/Wegener granulomatosis is a necrotizing vasculitis characterized by a triad of necrotizing inflammation: • Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract or the lung • Necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels , most prominently in the lungs • Focal necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis Males are affected more often than females . The most common clinical features include persistent pneumonitis with bilateral nodular and cavitary infiltrates , chronic sinusitis, mucosal ulcerations of the nasopharynx, and evidence of renal disease . Image: Chest radiograph showing pulmonary granulomatosis670

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 15-year old boy comes to the clinic complaining about recurrent painful oral ulcers . He also experiences repeated episodes of eye redness and pain which subside with medication. On examination, ulcers are seen on his genitals . Which of the following features would you not expect to see in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Beh\347et disease . Nail fold capillary abnormalities are typically seen in systemic sclerosis . Behcet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers , genital ulcers , and uveitis. Other skin findings include erythema nodosa (red tender nodules on legs ) and positive pathergy test (pustular reaction 24-48 hrs after sterile needle puncture or normal saline injection). There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations , with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms. Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation in children. Pulmonary aneurysms are the most severe feature of pediatric BD. It is associated with HLA subtype B51. T helper 17 (Th17) cells play an important contribution in the recruitment of neutrophils , which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child presents with colicky abdominal pain and purpuric skin lesions on the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs . Urine analysis reveals hematuria and mild proteinuria. The most probable diagnosis is:
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Henoch-Sch\366nlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder, commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features : • Skin lesions - characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs , and also the buttocks • Abdominal manifestations - include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding . • Renal manifestations - include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in the adults671 It is strongly associated with atopy in a few patients , and the onset often follows an upper respiratory infection . IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following structures are involved in Buerger's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Arteries, veins and nerves can be involved in thrombangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease ). It is a vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries and secondarily extends into contiguous veins and nerves. With time, all three structures can be encased in fibrous tissue .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old male smoker presents with intermittent claudication and gangrene of the lower extremities . Biopsy of the blood vessels supplying this area shows acute and chronic inflammation, with luminal thrombosis containing small neutrophilic microabscesses . Granulomatous inflammation appears to extend into the contiguous veins and nerves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is thromboangiitis obliterans / Buerger disease . It is the segmental , thrombosing, acute and chronic inflammation of medium-sized and small arteries. It principally involves the tibial and radial arteries. It is seen in heavy cigarette smokers, usually before the age of 35 years. HLA -A-9 and HLA -B-5 associated with a high risk of TAO. The patients present with intermittent claudication , chronic ulcerations of the extremity , and later progress to frank gangrene . The microscopy findings include luminal thrombosis (thrombangiitis), that is, thrombus containing microabscesses that occlude the lumen (obliterans). They contain small microabscesses composed of neutrophils . Berger disease refers to IgA nephropathy. It is seen within 3-5 days of sore throat. It is associated with purpuric rash in the lower limbs.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following histologic findings would be most suggestive of Buerger's disease in a patient ?

options.a: Mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasavasorum

mcqs.explanation: Luminal thrombosis containing small microabscesses composed of neutrophils is seen in thromboangiitis obliterans or Buerger disease . Option A: Adventitial mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasa vasorum has been described in Takayasu arteritis. Option B: Fragmented neutrophils undergoing apoptosis infiltrating blood vessels termed leukocytoclastic vasculitis are seen in small vessel vasculitis. Option D: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels seen in immunologically mediated vasculitis syndromes.672

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes angiosarcoma?
mcqs.explanation: Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm . It is a vascular tumor arising from the endothelial cells . Benign vascular tumors are characterized by well -formed vascular channels lined by normal endothelial cells . Whereas, malignant vascular tumors are characterized by poorly formed vessels with cellular atypia.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following vascular tumors are not derived from endothelial cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Hemangiopericytoma is not derived from endothelial cells . It is a malignant vascular tumor derived from supporting cells of the blood vessels . Vascular tumors derived from endothelial cells are: • Hemangioma • Lymphangioma • Angiosarcoma The endothelial origin of vascular neoplasms can be confirmed using endothelial cell -specific markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.680

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a true neoplasm ?
mcqs.explanation: Cystic hygroma / cavernous lymphangioma is a true neoplasm . It is a benign vascular tumor arising from endothelial cells . Options A and B: Nevus flammeus and port wine stain are vascular ectasias which are not true neoplasms . They are congenital or acquired malformations. Option D: Bacillary angiomatosis is non-neoplastic reactive vascular proliferation in response to opportunistic bacilli.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common form of vascular ectasia ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common form of vascular ectasia is nevus flammeus . Vascular ectasias are the conditions involving the dilatation of blood vessels . They can be congenital or acquired malformations or hamartomas. Telangiectasia is the permanent dilation of small blood vessels . They lead to red lesions in the skin or mucous membranes. Various types of vascular ectasias are as follows : • Nevus flammeus (birthmark ): Pink /purple flat lesions on the head or neck. They regress spontaneously . Image showing nevus flammeus in a newborn:• Port-wine stain: A special form of nevus flammeus . It thickens the skin surface . It grows during childhood and does not fade with time. Image showing port-wine stain in a child:681 • Spider telangiectasias : They are pulsatile and blanch with pressure . These commonly occur on the face , neck, or upper chest . They are associated with hyperestrogenic states , such as pregnancy or liver cirrhosis.• Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu disease ) is caused by mutations in genes related to the TGF-�o signaling pathway . It is characterized by dilated blood vessels with thin walls that bleed easily . There can be bleeding from the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis), tongue , mouth, eyes , and the gastrointestinal tract. The image below shows multiple flat non pulsating telengiectasias in a patient with Osler-Weber-Rendu disease :682

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A young girl presents with recurrent seizures , mental retardation and a skin lesion as shown in the image below . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the facial port-wine stain as seen in the image is characteristic of Sturge -Weber syndrome. This is characterized by a triad of: • Facial port wine nevus - usually found in the distribution of the ophthalmic division (V1 ) of the trigeminal nerve • Glaucoma • Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis (LAM) - can lead to seizures , mental retardation or hemiplegia and are seen as intracranial tram-track calcifications on CT as given below .683

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about hemangioma is true?

options.a: Capillary hemangioma is the most common type of hemangioma
options.b: Cavernous hemangioma usually regresses completely by 7 years of age
options.c: Juvenile hemangioma is infiltrative and does not regress spontaneously
options.d: Pyogenic granuloma is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus

mcqs.explanation: The most common type of hemangioma is capillary hemangioma. Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors of infancy and childhood . They are of the following types : • Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type . They occur in the skin, subcutaneous tissues , and mucous membranes of the oral cavities and lips. • Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels. They are more infiltrative and frequently involve deep structures . They do not spontaneously regress . • Juvenile hemangiomas/strawberry type hemangiomas of the newborn are extremely common. They arise in the skin and grow rapidly for a few months, and usually regress completely by the age of 7 years. • Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that present as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa. They bleed easily and are often ulcerated . It is not caused by bacterial infection .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A child is brought by her parents to the OPD with complaints of a swelling on the right thigh. Further evaluation led to the diagnosis of capillary hemangioma in this patient . What is the most appropriate next best step ?

options.a: Explain about the risk of malignant transformation of the tumor
options.b: Test the child for retrovirus infection
options.c: Enquire about history of exposure to polyvinyl chloride
options.d: Assure the parents about spontaneous regression of the tumor

mcqs.explanation: Capillary hemangiomas are present from birth and initially increase in size, but many eventually regress spontaneously . They are generally benign. Images show the gross and microscopic pictures of capillary hemangioma:684

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma is diagnosed with von Hippel -Lindau disease . This condition is associated with which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: von Hippel –Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas. These vascular lesions are commonly found in the cerebellum , brain stem , retina, pancreas, and liver. Cavernous hemangiomas are large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma. They are infiltrative and involve deep structures . They do not regress spontaneously . The given image shows the microscopic appearance of cavernous hemangioma:

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following vascular lesions are commonly seen in patients with Turner syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: 685 The vascular lesions commonly seen in Turner syndrome are cavernous lymphangiomas of the neck. Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are massively dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells and separated by connective tissue stroma. They are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and rarely in the retroperitoneum . They can be enormous causing gross deformities around the neck. Image shows cavernous lymphangioma of the neck associated with a girl having Turner syndrome:

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A middle aged male patient presents with a swelling on his left thumb as shown in the image below . Which of the following statements about this swelling is false ?

options.a: It is caused by a bacterial infection
options.d: It is a type of capillary hemangioma

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a pyogenic granuloma. It is not caused by bacterial infection . The term pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer as it neither contains pus nor is it a granulomatous lesion. These are capillary hemangiomas that appear as red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa. They are most commonly benign. They tend to grow rapidly, bleed easily and are often ulcerated . Histologic image of pyogenic granuloma:686

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Granuloma gravidarum is a type of ________.
mcqs.explanation: Pregnancy tumor or granuloma gravidarum is a type of pyogenic granuloma that occurs infrequently in gingiva of pregnant women. These lesions may spontaneously regress , especially after pregnancy, or they may undergo fibrosis. Occasionally , they require surgical excision.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following vascular tumors arising from arteriovenous structures is involved in thermoregulation ?
mcqs.explanation: The vascular tumor arising from arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation is glomus tumor. These tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies which are specialized arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation . They are benign but extremely painful due to abundant nerve fibers. Histopathology shows branching vascular channels separated by stroma containing glomus cells in nests :687

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of glomus tumors?
mcqs.explanation: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the distal portion of the digits , especially under the fingernails.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old HIV -positive female patient presents with fever, weight loss, and cutaneous lesions as shown in the image. Microscopic examination reveals capillary proliferation and neutrophilic infiltration. Which of the following is the causative organism?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette and the microscopic findings suggest the diagnosis of bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella henselae . Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family like Bartonella henselae688 and Bartonella quintana . These lesions can involve the skin, bone, brain , and other organs. They contain stromal neutrophils , nuclear dust , and causal bacteria. Histology shows capillary proliferation with endothelial cells exhibiting nuclear atypia and mitosis. Modified silver (Warthin -Starry) stain is used for demonstrating clusters of tangled bacilli. The given image shows histologic appearance of bacillary angiomatosis:

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old HIV seropositive male presents with skin lesions over the distal portion of the lower limbs as shown in the image below . Biopsy shows a lesion composed of proliferating spindle cells along with small vessels and spaces containing red cells . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are most suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma. Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is highly associated with AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). Classic Kaposi sarcoma occurs in older men of Eastern European and Meditteranean descent . It has the following three clinical stages : • Patches - red-purple macules on the distal lower extremities • Plaques- patches progress to large violaceous raised plaques . Lesions spread proximally. • Nodules - Lesions become nodular with more neoplastic features . This stage also progresses to involve nodes and viscera. Diseases caused by HHV -8 infection primarily in patients with HIV infection include : • Kaposi sarcoma • Multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) • Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) The given image shows sheets of proliferating spindle cells :689

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which type of Kaposi sarcoma is most commonly seen in patients with HIV infection ?
mcqs.explanation: AIDS-associated or epidemic Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an AIDS-defining illness , and worldwide , it represents the most common HIV -related malignancy. Four forms of KS are recognized , based on population demographics and risks:Type Classic Endemic African Transplant-associated AIDS- associated epi demic KS Epidemiolo gy Older men of eastern European and Meditt eranean descentNot a ssociated with HIV HIV seronegative indi viduals Solid organ transplan t recipients HIV -infected individ uals Clinical feat ures Skin plaques and nod ules Lymph node and visc eral involvement Cutaneous , mucosal a nd visceral lesions Lymph nodes involve d

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with vague upper abdominal pain is diagnosed with hemangioendothelioma of the liver. What is this classified as?
mcqs.explanation: Hemangioendothelioma is classified as intermediate -grade neoplasm . It encompasses a spectrum of vascular neoplasms with clinical behavior intermediate between benign well -differentiated hemangiomas and anaplastic angiosarcomas.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An elderly male working in a factory manufacturing PVC pipes is at risk of developing which of the following cancers?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with carcinogenic exposures to polyvinyl chloride .690 Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm that primarily affects older adults . The tumor often involves the skin, soft tissue , breast, and liver. Angiosarcomas are locally invasive and can readily metastasize .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common causative agent for lymphangitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Group A beta -hemolytic streptococci are the most common agents responsible for lymphangitis . Lymphangitis represents acute inflammation elicited by the spread of bacterial infections into lymphatics . It is manifested by red, painful subcutaneous streaks (the inflamed lymphatics ) and painful enlargement of the draining lymph nodes (lymphadenitis ). Filariasis causes obstructive lymphedema and chronic lymphadenitis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes Milroy disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Milroy disease refers to heredofamilial congenital lymphedema . Causes of lymphedema : Primary lymphedema : • Simple congenital lymphedema • Heredofamilial congenital lymphedema (Milroy disease ) Secondary or obstructive lymphedema: • Malignant tumors obstructing lymphatic channels • Surgical removal of regional groups of lymph nodes , e.g., radical mastectomy • Postirradiation fibrosis • Filariasis • Post-inflammatory thrombosis and scarring691

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following layers is not present in the cardiac valve?
mcqs.explanation: Adventitia is not a layer of the cardiac valves. It is the outermost layer of a blood vessel . It contains connective tissue , a few cells , macrophages , mast cells , fibroblasts, and the nerves and vessels that supply the vascular wall. Cardiac valves are lined by endothelium and share a tri-layered architecture : • Fibrosa is a dense collagenous core at the outflow surface . It is connected to the valvular supporting structures . • Spongiosa is a central core of loose connective tissue • Ventricularis or atrialis is a layer rich in elastin on the inflow surface .701

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: You are conducting an autopsy of an elderly patient who was found dead in his home. Which of the following changes in the heart will not be suggestive of normal aging?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, an increase in the size of the left ventricle is not normally seen in the heart of an elderly person. The size of the left ventricular cavity is decreased in the aged heart, particularly in the base-to-apex dimension. This change is exacerbated by systemic hypertension . Changes in the aging heart: • Chambers: • Increased left atrial cavity size • Decreased left ventricular cavity size • Valves: • Fibrous thickening of valve leaflets • Aortic and mitral valve calcific deposits • Epicardial coronary arteries: • Diminished compliance • Calcific deposits • Atherosclerotic plaques • Myocardium: • Increased subepicardial fat • Brown atrophy • Lipofuscin deposition • Basophilic degeneration • Amyloid deposits • Aorta: • Dilated with a rightward shift • Elastic fragmentation and collagen accumulation • Atherosclerotic plaque

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What type of cells are heart failure cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages . They are telltale signs of previous episodes of pulmonary edema . In cardiac failure, red cells and plasma proteins extravasate into the edema fluid within the alveolar spaces . These are then phagocytosed and digested by macrophages . The iron recovered from haemoglobin is stored in the form of hemosiderin. The image given below shows heart failure cells within alveolar spaces .702

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of left -sided diastolic heart failure?
mcqs.explanation: Hypertension is the most common cause of left -sided diastolic heart failure. Left-sided heart failure can be divided into systolic and diastolic failure. Diastolic failure predominantly occurs in patients older than age 65 years. Here, the left ventricle is abnormally stiff and cannot relax during diastole . Causes of diastolic heart failure: • Hypertension : most common • Diabetes mellitus • Obesity • Bilateral renal artery stenosis703 Systolic failure is due to insufficient ejection fraction, i.e., pump failure. It occurs when the contractile function of the left ventricle is deranged .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not cause isolated right-sided heart failure?
mcqs.explanation: Isolated right-sided heart failure is not caused by left -sided heart failure. Isolated right-sided heart failure is not common and usually occurs in patients with disorders affecting the lungs . Therefore, it is often referred to as cor pulmonale . It is caused by disorders of the lung parenchyma and pulmonary vasculature. It is also caused by conditions causing pulmonary vasoconstriction like obstructive sleep apnea and altitude sickness. Pulmonary hypertension is the common feature of these disorders, which leads to hypertrophy and dilation of the right side of the heart. Right-sided heart failure is most commonly caused by left -sided heart failure. This is because an increase in pressure in the pulmonary circulation from left -sided failure burdens the right side of the heart.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A massive pulmonary embolism occurs in a patient with acute cor-pulmonale . What pathological changes do you expect in the heart of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the patient has acute cor pulmonale . This causes right ventricular dilation without hypertrophy . On cross-section , the normal crescent shape of the right ventricle is transformed to a dilated ovoid. In chronic cor pulmonale , the right ventricular wall thickens. The hypertrophied right ventricle may compress the left ventricular chamber. It can also cause regurgitation and fibrous thickening of the tricuspid valve.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The liver specimen obtained after the autopsy of a patient is given below . What could be the likely cause of this finding?
mcqs.explanation: In the image, the liver specimen shows a nutmeg liver appearance , which occurs in congestive hepatomegaly. This is secondary to passive congestion due to right heart failure. In right heart failure, there is congestion of hepatic and portal vessels , greatest around the central veins. This leads to increased liver size and weight . The pericentral zones become congested and red-brown. The periportal regions are normal coloured and tan. This leads to a nutmeg liver appearance . With longstanding failure, the central areas can become fibrotic, eventually culminating in cardiac cirrhosis. Pathological changes are also seen in the spleen and the gastrointestinal tract. Portal venous hypertension also causes the enlargement of the spleen , with platelet sequestration . This is known as congestive splenomegaly . This can also contribute to chronic congestion and oedema of the bowel .704

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which hormone reduces the risk of myocardial infarction in women of reproductive age ?
mcqs.explanation: Estrogen reduces the risk of myocardial infarction in women in the reproductive age group. Accelerated coronary artery disease is associated with the postmenopausal decline in estrogen production. However, postmenopausal hormonal replacement therapy (HRT ) has not been shown to be beneficial . The most common cause of death in older women is ischemic heart disease . Through middle age , males have a relatively increased risk of myocardial infarction.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presented to the casualty with severe , sudden -onset chest pain radiating to the left arm . ECG showed ST-segment elevation in precordial leads . The person succumbed after 3 hours. On autopsy , the patient 's heart was immersed in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution . What colour would be imparted to the heart?

options.b: Viable myocardium appears brick red and infarct appears pale
options.c: Viable myocardium appears red and infarct appears dark blue
options.d: Viable myocardium appears unstained and the infarct appears dark red

mcqs.explanation: Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution imparts a brick red colour to the viable non-infarcted myocardium. The infarct appears unstained and pale . Myocardial infarcts < 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to identify the area of necrosis. This is done by immersing the tissue slices in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution . The histochemical stain imparts a brick-red colour to intact, noninfarcted myocardium. Here, lactate dehydrogenase , LDH , activity is preserved . LDH leaks out through the damaged membranes of dead cells , so an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone. The image given below shows an ischemic brain after immersion in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution. The pale unstained region is the infarcted zone.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the approximate time of onset of microvascular injury in ischemic cardiac myocytes ?
mcqs.explanation: Microvascular injury begins >1 hour after the onset of ischemia.705

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction?
mcqs.explanation: Relaxation of myofibrils is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction. Myofibril relaxation, mitochondrial swelling and glycogen loss can be detected by electron microscopy within half an hour of myocardial infarction.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: You are conducting the autopsy of a patient who passed away following myocardial infarction. What would be the earliest light microscopic change that can be observed in the heart of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest light microscopic change that can be observed in the heart of this patient is the waviness of myocardial fibres. This is seen within \275-4 hours at the border of the infarct. These changes are a result of the forceful contractions of viable fibres. The contractions cause stretching and buckling of immediately adjacent , noncontractile dead fibres. Myocyte vacuolization or myocytolysis may also be seen in the infarct margins. It is due to the accumulation of salt and water in the sarcoplasmic reticulum . Such myocytes are viable but poorly contractile . The image below shows microscopic features of myocardial infarction showing wavy myocardial fibres. There are wavy fibres that are elongated and narrow , as compared with normal fibres. The widened spaces between the dead fibres contain edema fluid and scattered neutrophils .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Following myocardial infarction, coagulative necrosis begins at?
mcqs.explanation: Early coagulative necrosis begins in myocardial infarction by 4–12 hours. However, it is prominent between 1 to 3 days after myocardial infarction.706

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The heart of a patient who had suffered a myocardial infarction is subjected to a histopathological examination. The microscopic image is given below . What time following infarction would you observe this?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows neutrophilic infiltration into the myocardium. Early neutrophil infiltration starts by 12 –24 hours following the infarction. It can be visualised by examination with a light microscope . The necrotic myocardium elicits acute inflammation most prominent between 1 and 3 days. During this time, there is a brisk interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils . The image given below shows neutrophilic infiltration into the myocardium following MI.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient was admitted four days back following acute myocardial infarction. What type of cells would you expect to see in the infarcted area in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, 4 days after MI, macrophages are seen in the infarcted area. They phagocytose dead myocytes at the border of the infarct earliest by 72 hours. Removal of the necrotic myocytes is most noticeable by 3 to 7 days. The image below shows a macrophagic infiltrate in the infarcted area.707

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Match the following :
mcqs.explanation: The correct match is: • Well established granulation - 10 - 14 days • Complete scarring - > 2 months • Myocyte hypereosinophilia - 12 - 24 hours • Grey white scar - 2-8 weeks • Loss of nuclei and striations - 1 - 3 days

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old woman is found dead in her home. On autopsy , hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen . How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
mcqs.explanation: The given autopsy finding of hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture occurs most frequently 3-7 days after myocardial infarction (MI). During this time, the lysis of the necrotic myocardium is maximum. Thus most of the infarct has been converted to friable granulation tissue . The risk factors for free -wall rupture are: • Age > 60 years • Female gender • First MI • Large, transmural and anterior MI • Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy • Preexisting hypertension708 It is less frequent in patients with prior MI because associated fibrotic scarring inhibits myocardial tearing. Complications of MI: • Heart failure - • This is due to ventricular dysfunction caused by the infarct and ventricular remodeling • Usually occurs within a day • Cardiogenic shock - • This is usually seen in severe multivessel coronary artery disease due to extensive involvement of myocardium • Usually occurs within a day • Arrhythmias - most common complication, occurring usually 2 days after infarction • Most common arrhythmia within one hour of MI - ventricular fibrillation • Most common arrhythmia after one hour of MI - supraventricular tachycardia • Myocardial rupture - occurs when there is transmural necrosis of a ventricle. It includes the following - • Left ventricular free wall rupture (most common) - leads to cardiac tamponade • Interventricular septal rupture - leads acute ventricular septal defect (VSD) • Papillary muscle rupture - leads to severe mitral regurgitation • Mitral regurgitation (MR) - this can occur due to - • Transient papillary muscle dysfunction - mid-systolic or late -systolic murmur • Rupture of papillary muscle - pansystolic murmur • Dressler syndrome (post -MI syndrome) - • This is an immune-mediated reaction and presents as pericarditis, pleurisy , and fever • It can occur even 48 hrs after MI but usually occurs 1–6 weeks after MI and often subside after a few days • Ventricular aneurysm • Infarct expansion associated with mural thrombus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What causes tigered myocardium?
mcqs.explanation: Tigered myocardium appearance occurs as a result of prolonged moderate hypoxia due to fatty change. It is the gross appearance of the heart with bands of yellow myocardium alternating with normal myocardium.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following causes the maximum damage in reperfusion injury?
mcqs.explanation: 709 In reperfusion injury, the maximum damage is caused by free radicals. Reperfusion is the restoration of blood flow to the ischemic myocardium threatened by infarction. Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. Once the flow is restored , there is bleeding . On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes . These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres. Reperfusion injury may be mediated by: • Oxidative stress • Calcium overload • Inflammatory cells recruited after tissue reperfusion

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What creatine kinase isoenzymes do the heart muscle contain?
mcqs.explanation: Heart muscle contains MM and MB isoenzymes of creatine kinase. Creatine kinase (CK) has three isoenzymes : • CK-1 (BB) - brain , nerve tissue , prostate (small amounts), intestine , lung, bladder , kidney, uterus , thyroid • CK-2 (MB) - heart and skeletal muscle • CK-3 (MM) - skeletal and heart muscle Elevation of the CK-MB isoforms is seen in MI. CK-MB is less sensitive and less specific , therefore , troponins are preferred for the diagnosis of MI. CK-MB begins to rise within 3-12 hours of the onset of MI. It peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal within approximately 48-72 hours.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient comes to the hospital after 3 hours of the onset of chest pain. ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads . Which of the following enzymes would be elevated in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of acute myocardial infarction (MI). Enzymes elevated after 4 to 8 hours of MI are CK-MB (creatine kinase MB) and troponins. When cardiac troponin is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI. If it is the only assay available, it can be used , but it is far less sensitive and less specific .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnoea . His wife reports that he had chest pain 7 days back which had lasted for 2 days. You suspect that the patient 's chest pain was due to myocardial infarction. If so, blood levels of which of the following enzymes would be elevated now?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, on post -MI day 7, troponin and LDH will be raised. Troponins are highly specific for MI and remain elevated for 7 to 10 days.710 Troponins are proteins that regulate calcium-mediated contraction of the cardiac and skeletal muscles . It is the single biomarker preferred for diagnosing MI, late diagnosis of MI, and diagnosis of reinfarction. Troponin I is more important than troponin T. Cardiac troponin increases rapidly in patients with reinfarction. Sometimes , the cardiac troponin concentration is elevated , but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. Then the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20 % or greater increase in the cTn measurement . Myoglobin is the earliest enzyme to increase after MI. It is a protein that is found in the skeletal and cardiac muscles , which binds oxygen. It is a very sensitive indicator of muscle injury. But it is not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle . Myoglobin and SGOT levels come to baseline before day 1.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The blood levels of various cardiac biomarkers are measured in a patient following myocardial infarction. This is represented in the given graph. Which biomarker does the yellow curve depict ?
mcqs.explanation: The yellow curve here shows the levels of CK-MB which starts rising around 4 to 8 hrs post -MI, peaks at 24 hours and becomes normal at 48 to 72 hrs. The post -myocardial infarction blood levels of the different cardiac biomarkers are shown in the image given below .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Loss-of-function mutation in potassium channel gene KCNQ1 results in which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Loss of function mutation in K+ channel genes KCNQ1 and KCNH2 produces the long QT syndrome. The gain-of-function mutation produces the short QT syndrome. Long QT syndrome manifests as arrhythmias associated with excessive prolongation of cardiac repolarization. Stress -induced syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD), are common presentations . Short QT syndrome presents with arrhythmias associated with abbreviated repolarization intervals. They also present with palpitations , syncope , and SCD.711 Brugada syndrome manifests as ECG abnormalities like ST-segment elevations and right bundle -branch block. This occurs in the absence of structural heart disease . Here, patients classically present with syncope or SCD during rest or sleep or after large meals. Familial atrial fibrillation is caused by a gain of function mutation in genes coding potassium channels.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common mechanism behind sudden cardiac death ?
mcqs.explanation: The mechanism behind sudden cardiac death (SCD) is most often a lethal arrhythmia , e.g., asystole or ventricular fibrillation. Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of SCD, responsible for 80% to 90% of cases . But, the mechanism of SCD is most often a lethal arrhythmia . Infarction need not occur. Most of the patients who have SCD but are successfully resuscitated do not show any enzymatic or ECG evidence of myocardial necrosis. Ischemic injury can directly affect the major components of the conduction system . But, most cases of fatal arrhythmia are triggered by electrical irritability of the myocardium.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions have an increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with hyperlipidemia have an increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease (CAD). Hyperlipidemia is considered the second most common risk factor for CAD worldwide after hypertension. Hypercholesterolemia was implicated in 55 % of cases with combined hyperlipidemia in 41% cases .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is lipoprotein a [Lp (
mcqs.explanation: Lipoprotein a [Lp(a)] contains the apolipoprotein B-100 portion of LDL linked to apolipoprotein A (apo A). It is an altered form of low-density lipoprotein (LDL ). Increased Lp(a) levels are associated with coronary and cerebrovascular disease risk . It is independent of total cholesterol or LDL levels .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Histology of reperfused myocardium:
mcqs.explanation: Reperfused myocardium shows eosinophilic contraction bands on light microscopy. They occur in irreversibly injured myocytes with damaged membranes, when blood supply is restored 12 -24 hours after MI. During ischemia, the intracellular levels of calcium are increased due to impaired calcium cycling and sarcolemmal damage . This leads to augmented and uncontrolled contraction of myofibrils712 after reperfusion . On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes . These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres. Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. This leads to bleeding after the flow is restored .713

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: What is the most common type of cardiomyopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common type of cardiomyopathy is dilated cardiomyopathy . Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the least frequent. Cardiomyopathies are a heterogeneous group of diseases of the myocardium associated with mechanical and/or electrical dysfunction . They usually exhibit inappropriate ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation. The causes are frequently genetic . Cardiomyopathies maybe primary predominantly involving the heart or secondary to a systemic or multiorgan disorder. They occur in the absence of any coronary artery disease , valvular heart disease , congenital heart disease , or systemic arterial hypertension . Types of cardiomyopathy : • Dilated cardiomyopathy • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy723 • Restrictive cardiomyopathy • Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy • Left ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Alcohol abuse is strongly associated with the development of:
mcqs.explanation: Alcohol abuse is strongly associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy . Alcohol and its metabolites , especially acetaldehyde have a direct toxic effect on the myocardium which leads to the development of dilated cardiomyopathy . Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy : • Acquired causes : • Infectious and non-infectious myocarditis: most common cause globally • Alcohol is the most common cause in India • Pregnancy: • Pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy (PACM) • Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) • Stress -induced : Takotsubo cardiomyopathy • Drug-induced : • Doxorubicin (anthracycline) • Trastuzumab • Cyclophosphamide • Nutritional deficiency : • Beriberi (thiamine), • Keshan disease (selenium ), • Carnitine deficiency • Endocrine: Hypo and hyperthyroidism , acromegaly, diabetes mellitus • Others : • Cobalt toxicity , • Heavy metals (lead , mercury, arsenic, lithium) • Familial causes (50%): • Mutation in the cardiac myocyte titin gene • Haemochromatosis • Syndromes: Duchenne muscular dystrophy , Becker's muscular dystrophy724

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the largest protein expressed in humans?
mcqs.explanation: Titin is the largest protein expressed in humans. Titin is the third myofilament of cardiac muscle . It has a single giant polypeptide spanning from Z-disk to the M-band region of the sarcomere. Mutation in TTN , the gene encoding titin, is responsible for 20 % of all cases of dilated cardiomyopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Two brothers were arguing over a property dispute when the elder of the two complained of chest pain and collapsed . He was taken to the hospital but was declared brought dead . The condition responsible for the death of the patient is grouped under which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of sudden cardiac death in a previously healthy man, under a stressful situation, is suggestive of takotsubo cardiomyopathy . It is a type of dilated cardiomyopathy . Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is also called broken heart syndrome, apical ballooning syndrome, or stress-induced cardiomyopathy . During extreme psychological stress , there is a catecholamine surge . This causes microcirculation spasms which lead to a transient myocardial stunning. It is usually seen in middle -aged women. It leads to left ventricular contractile dysfunction . The left ventricular apex is most often affected which leads to apical ballooning. This resembles a "takotsubo," which is Japanese for "fishing pot for trapping octopus ". Histologically , acute cases may show microscopic areas of necrosis characterized by myocyte hyper contraction known as contraction band necrosis. Chronic cases may exhibit microscopic foci of granulation tissue . The first image below shows a ventriculogram showing takotsubo cardiomyopathy . The second image shows a 'takotsubo,' or octopus fishing pot .725

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A patient is admitted to the hospital with heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy . Toxicity by which of the following does not cause this?
mcqs.explanation: Selenium deficiency (Keshan 's disease) is known to produce dilated cardiomyopathy and not its toxicity. Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy : Acquired causes : • Infectious and non-infectious myocarditis is the most common cause globally • Alcohol is the most common cause in India • Pregnancy: • Pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy (PACM) • Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) • Stress -induced : Takotsubo cardiomyopathy • Drug-induced : • Doxorubicin: anthracyclines • Trastuzumab • Cyclophosphamide • Nutritional deficiency : • Beriberi (thiamine), • Keshan disease (selenium ) • Carnitine deficiency • Endocrine: Hypo and hyperthyroidism , acromegaly, diabetes mellitus • Others :726 • Cobalt toxicity • Heavy metals (lead , mercury, arsenic, lithium) Familial causes (50%): • Mutation in the cardiac myocyte titin gene • Haemochromatosis • Syndromes: Duchenne muscular dystrophy , Becker's muscular dystrophy

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A 55 yr old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below . Which type of cardiomyopathy is usually seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, stained blue with Perl's Prussian blue stain. The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is the predominant type of cardiomyopathy seen in hemochromatosis. Hemochromatosis can also produce restrictive cardiomyopathy , but it is less common than DCM. The image below shows hemochromatosis. There is hepatocellular iron, stained with Perl's Prussian blue .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: The histological examination of the heart of a patient who died due to heart failure is given below . What underlying condition did the patient most likely have?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the histology image shows ninja-star like nuclei in myocytes . This is suggestive of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). These are non-specific findings but the presence of \030 5% myocytes with ninja star-like nuclei are suggestive of DCM. Here, DCM is due to titin-truncating mutations. Truncating mutations are those which shorten the coding sequence of the genes .727 Histologically they appear as variable myocyte hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis. The nuclei are enlarged, bizarre and hyperchromatic exhibiting a ninja-star like appearance . The image given below explains the ninja star-like nuclei in the myocytes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy who collapsed while playing basketball was brought to the emergency room and was resuscitated . On evaluation, he was found to have sustained ventricular tachycardia secondary to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy . Which syndrome is associated with this?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the patient suffered from sustained ventricular tachycardia secondary to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC ). ARVC is associated with Naxos syndrome. ARVC is autosomal dominant cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement in the myocardium of the ventricles. It most commonly affects the right ventricle. It is due to mutations in the gene encoding desmosome -associated protein plakophilin 2. This leads to defective cell -adhesion proteins in the desmosomes that link adjacent cardiac myocytes . As shown in the image below , Naxos syndrome is characterized by woolly hair and palmoplantar hyperkeratosis .728 Morphology shows severe thinning of the right ventricular wall due to loss of myocytes , accompanied by extensive fatty infiltration and fibrosis. The image given below is a gross photograph of the heart showing dilated right ventricle and near transmural replacement of its free wall with fat and fibrosis.Carvajal syndrome is a variant of Naxos disease but is associated with dilated cardiomyopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: An autopsy was done for a young patient who had a sudden cardiac death . It revealed massive myocardial hypertrophy without ventricular dilation. The image obtained on microscopy is given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and autopsy findings are suggestive of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). The image given is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy as seen in HCM.729 HCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults . It is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of >15mm on ECHO. The left ventricular myocardium is poorly compliant. This leads to abnormal diastolic filling and intermittent ventricular outflow obstruction, i.e., primarily diastolic dysfunction . The gross features of HCM are: • Massive myocardial hypertrophy usually without ventricular dilation • Asymmetric septal hypertrophy - disproportionate thickening of the ventricular septum relative to the left ventricle free wall • Banana -shaped left ventricle- due to bulging of the ventricular septum into the lumen The image given below shows changes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared to a normal heart. HCM shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and thickened left ventricle wall.Histologic features of the HCM are: • Massive myocyte hypertrophy - with transverse myocyte diameters frequently greater than 40 �Mm, normal is approximately 15 �Mm. • Myofiber disarray- haphazard disarray of bundles of myocytes , individual myocytes , and contractile elements in sarcomeres within cells • Interstitial fibrosis and replacement fibrosis The image given below is a histologic section of cardiac muscle showing myocyte disarray and extreme hypertrophy seen in an abnormal HCM septum .730

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are most commonly seen in the gene encoding which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are most commonly seen in the genes encoding �o -myosin heavy chain (�o -MHC). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an autosomal dominant disease . In the majority of cases it is due to missense mutations in the following two sarcolemmal protein genes : • Myosin binding protein C (MYBC) • Beta myosin heavy chain (MYH7 )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which of the following can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy ?
mcqs.explanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is caused by hemochromatosis, ergotamine , amyloidosis and carcinoid syndrome. Trastuzumab causes dilated cardiomyopathy . Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is characterized by increased ventricular stiffness causing impaired diastolic filling of the ventricles. The stiffness is secondary to an underlying disease causing accumulation of intra and intercellular substances in the myocardium. Causes of RCM: • Infiltration disorders • Amyloidosis (most common) • Sarcoidosis • Storage disorders • Fabry's disease • Glycogen storage disease (type II >> III )731 • Hemochromatosis (DCM>RCM) • Fibrotic disorders • Scleroderma • Endomyocardial fibrosis • R-Radiation • E-Ergotamine • S-Serotonin • T-Tropical Endomyocardial fibrosis • C-Carcinoid syndrome • Miscellaneous : post open heart surgery, diabetes . Morphology of RCM: • Ventricles are of almost normal size or slightly enlarged • The myocardium is non-compliant • Biatrial dilation is commonly observed • Patchy or diffuse interstitial fibrosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive dyspnoea on exertion for one week along with a diffuse rash. Blood investigations are significant for an absolute eosinophil count of 4600 / mm\263. Which of the following is caused by the patient 's condition?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the patient has progressive dyspnoea along with hypereosinophilia . This is suggestive of Loeffler 's endocarditis . It leads to restrictive cardiomyopathy . There is peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic infiltrates in multiple organs, including the heart. Major basic protein (MBP) is a toxic product released from eosinophils . This initiates endomyocardial necrosis followed by scarring. It leads to endomyocardial fibrosis, typically with large mural thrombi. Many patients with Loeffler 's endocarditis have a myeloproliferative disorder. This is associated with chromosomal rearrangements involving platelet -derived growth factor receptor (PDGF)-\037 or -�o genes .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old girl was brought to the outpatient department with complaints of difficulty in breathing and fatigue . The child had a history of intrauterine exposure to mumps. The cardiac evaluation showed a decrease in ventricular compliance . Which of the following would be the cause of the child's symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: In this scenario, the decrease in ventricular compliance indicates restrictive cardiomyopathy . Endocardial fibroelastosis is an uncommon restrictive heart condition characterized by fibroelastic thickening that typically involves the left ventricular endocardium. It is most common in the first 2 years of life . It results from several different insults including viral infections (e.g., intrauterine exposure to mumps) or mutations in the gene for tafazzin. These mutations affect mitochondrial inner membrane integrity .732 Endomyocardial fibrosis is a disease of children and young adults in Africa and other tropical areas. It is characterized by fibrosis of the ventricular endocardium and subendocardium that extends from the apex upward . The aetiology is unknown. Loeffler endomyocarditis results in endomyocardial fibrosis, typically with large mural thrombi. The overall morphology is similar to the tropical disease . In addition to the cardiac changes , there is often peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic infiltrates in multiple organs, including the heart.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Myocarditis is most commonly caused by which of the following viral infections ?
mcqs.explanation: Viral infections are the most common cause of myocarditis. Coxsackie viruses A and B and other enteroviruses account for most of the cases . Myocarditis is a diverse group of pathologic entities in which infectious microorganisms and/or a primary inflammatory process cause myocardial injury.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which serum protein is the major component of senile cardiac amyloid deposits ?
mcqs.explanation: Transthyretin is the major component of senile cardiac amyloid deposits . It is a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein. Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or it may be localized . This is particularly seen in the elderly (senile cardiac amyloidosis ). It has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis . Presentation of cardiac amyloidosis : • Restrictive cardiomyopathy - most common • Asymptomatic • Dilation • Arrhythmias • Ischemic disease • Valvular disease . The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls . Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface , particularly on the left . Histologically , hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid are found in: • Interstitium • Conduction tissue • Valves, endocardium • Pericardium • Small intramural coronary arteries.733 The image given shows an endomyocardial biopsy of a patient with cardiac amyloidosis stained as follows : A) Congo red only, B) Apple -green birefringence under polarized light

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: One week following a diagnosis of myocardial infarction, a patient experiences precordial pain and develops a fever of 101 .5\260F. Physical examination is remarkable for a loud friction rub. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario suggests post-myocardial infarction fibrinous pericarditis. It is the most common type of pericarditis. Clinically, there is a loud pericardial friction rub. There is a rubbery fibrin mass loosely glueing the parietal and visceral pericardium together (bread and butter ). It may resolve or become organized to produce adhesive pericarditis. It is usually seen following : • Myocardial infarction • Rheumatic fever • Trauma • Uremia • Radiation • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) • Severe pneumonia Types of acute pericarditis: Serous pericarditis: There is a mild inflammation of epicardial and pericardial surfaces . Both acute and chronic inflammatory cells are present . There is exudative serous fluid , usually 50–200 mL . Thus, it develops slowly and rarely alters cardiac function. It is caused by: • Rheumatic fever734 • SLE • Systemic scleroderma • Tumours • Uremia • Viral infection • Tuberculosis Suppurative /purulent pericarditis: It may be due to bacterial, mycotic, or parasitic invasion . The inflammation may extend into the surrounding mediastinum. It usually , results in organization and, therefore , constrictive pericarditis with clinical sequelae . The entry of the pathogen into the pericardium may be by: • direct extension • seeding from blood • lymphatic spread • seeding by instrumentation Hemorrhagic pericarditis: It can be due to tuberculosis or a malignant neoplasm (from lung or breast). It can also be seen following cardiac surgery. Caseous pericarditis is almost always tubercular in origin.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction 4 weeks back, develops fever, pericardial chest pain and pericardial effusion . What is the aetiology behind the patient 's present condition?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, fever, pericardial pain and effusion 4 weeks after MI, is suggestive of Dressler's syndrome. The aetiology of Dressler 's syndrome is autoimmune. It is also known as post -myocardial infarction (post-MI) cardiac injury syndrome. It occurs one week to as long as two to three months after MI. A fibrinous or fibrinohemorrhagic pericarditis usually develops around the second or third day following a transmural infarct. It is a result of the underlying myocardial inflammation. Dressler 's syndrome is believed to have an autoimmune aetiology . There is an inflammatory reaction to myocardial neo-antigens formed as a result of MI.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: The autopsy of a patient who died due to heart failure revealed concretio cordis. Which of the following is this condition associated with?
mcqs.explanation: Concretio cordis occurs in advanced cases of constrictive pericarditis. In constrictive pericarditis, a thick,0.5 - 1cm, fibrous scar tissue is formed. This can obliterate the pericardial space and sometimes calcify . In extreme cases , it can resemble a plaster mold and is known as concretio cordis. Constrictive pericarditis may be idiopathic or can occur following : • Pericarditis- serous or caseous735 • Cardiac surgery • Heavy irradiation Adhesive mediastinopericarditis occurs when adhesion and fibrosis extends from the parietal pericardium into the mediastinum Soldier's plaque is a focal pearly thickened epicardial plaque. It indicative of healed pericarditis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common primary tumour of the adult heart?
mcqs.explanation: Myxomas are the most common primary tumours of the heart in adults . 90% of myxomas are located in the atria. The left -to-right ratio of the myxoma is approximately 4:1. The region of the fossa ovalis in the atrial septum is the favoured site of origin. Histopathological examination shows stellate or globular myxoma, "lepidic ," cells . Peculiar vessel -like or gland-like structures are characteristic. Major clinical manifestations are fever and malaise (due to IL -6). Valvular "ball-valve" obstruction or embolization can occur. Important points on cardiac tumors: • Most common cardiac tumour: metastasis • Most common benign cardiac tumour: atrial myxoma • Most common primary cardiac tumour in adults : atrial myxoma • Most common primary cardiac tumour in children: rhabdomyoma The image given below shows an abundant amorphous extracellular matrix. It contains scattered multinucleate myxoma cells in various groupings , including abnormal vessel -like formations.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is commonly seen in patients with null mutations of the PRKAR1A gene?
mcqs.explanation: 736 Null mutations in the PRKAR1A gene is seen in Carney's complex . Cardiac myxomas are present in 30–40% of Carney complex patients. Familial syndromes associated with myxomas have activating mutations in the GNAS1 gene or null mutations in PRKAR1A . Mutations in GNAS1 is associated with McCune -Albright syndrome. PRKAR1A gene encodes a regulatory subunit of a cyclic -AMP-dependent protein kinase (Carney complex ). Skin lesions are the most common manifestation of the Carney complex . The most common type of endocrine tumour in the Carney complex is the primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD). It is a form of bilateral adrenal hyperplasia that leads to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-independent Cushing syndrome. NAME syndrome and LAMB syndrome are subsets of the Carney complex . The LAMB acronym refers to lentigines , atrial myxoma, and blue nevi. NAME refers to nevi, atrial myxoma, myxoid neurofibromas, and ephelids . Components of Carney Complex : • Skin pigmented lesions (lentigines , blue nevi, other) • Myxomas (cutaneous , mucosal, cardiac, other) • PPNAD (Cushing Syndrome) • GH-PRL -producing adenomas (acromegaly ) • Leydig or Sertoli cell tumors • Ovarian cystadenoma or carcinoma • Thyroid adenoma or cancer • Psammomatous melanotic schwannoma • Breast ductal adenoma • Osteochondromyxoma • Cancers (liver, pancreas, adrenal) Carney triad: • Extra-adrenal paraganglioma • Gastrointestinal stromal tumor • Pulmonary chondroma Carney–Stratakis Syndrome: Familial paraganglioma and gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of a cardiac myxoma?
mcqs.explanation: Atrial myxomas most commonly occur in the left atrium. Myxoma is usually single , but can rarely be multiple . The region of the fossa ovalis in the atrial septum is the favoured site of origin. Mobile tumours exert a "wrecking-ball" effect , causing damage to the valve leaflets .737 They can be sporadic or familial. The image given below shows a gross picture of an atrial cardiac myxoma arising from the region of the fossa ovalis and extending to mitral valve orifice:Sporadic Type Myxoma Familial Type Myx oma Single Multiple Postoperative recurrance NIL Present Younger age Left atria - Most common sit e

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: The histopathologic findings seen in a resected heart mass is given below . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given histological slide shows abundant spider cells . They are seen in rhabdomyoma. Microscopically , they are composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes . Routine histologic processing often artifactually reduces the abundant cytoplasm to thin strands that stretch from the nucleus to the surface membrane. This appearance is referred to as "spider " cells . Rhabdomyoma is the most frequent primary tumour of the pediatric heart. 50% of cases are associated with tuberous sclerosis , with mutations in the tumour-suppressor genes TSC1 and TSC2 . They are usually multiple and occur in ventricles preferentially . They often regress spontaneously and may, therefore , be considered as hamartomas. Image given shows spider cell in rhabdomyoma:738

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: The single most important long-term limitation of cardiac transplantation is ________
mcqs.explanation: The single most important long-term limitation of cardiac transplantation is allograft arteriopathy. Complications following cardiac transplantation: Allograft rejection : It is the primary concern that requires close surveillance. Both classic cellular rejection and antibody-mediated rejection is recognized . Cellular rejection is characterized by interstitial lymphocytic inflammation, with associated myocyte damage .
