Allograft arteriopathy: It is the single most important long-term limitation for cardiac transplantation. It is a late , progressive , diffusely stenosing intimal proliferation in the coronary arteries, leading to ischemic injury. It can lead to silent myocardial infarction since transplant patients have denervated hearts and do not experience angina. Progressive congestive heart failure and sudden cardiac death can also occur. Other postoperative problems include infection and malignancies, especially Epstein –Barr virus-associated B-cell lymphomas. The image given below shows allograft arteriopathy. There is severe diffuse concentric intimal thickening producing critical stenosis . The internal elastic lamina and media are intact (Movat pentachrome stain, elastin black)739

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of the condition shown in the given image?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a heart with left ventricular hypertrophy . The most common cause of left ventricular hypertrophy is chronic hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases and Cardiac...
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients with cardiac hypertrophy will have an associated increase in capillary density ?

options.b: A patient with an echo finding of an aortic valvular area of 0.6cm\
options.c: A patient with a high pitched holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex
options.d: A patient who is a marathon runner who came for a pre-run evaluation

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, a marathon runner will have cardiac hypertrophy with increased capillary density . Aerobic exercise , e.g., long-distance running, is associated with volume-load hypertrophy accompanied by an increase in capillary density . This is not seen in other forms of hypertrophy . This decreases resting heart rate and blood pressure . In hypertrophy due to pressure or volume overload, there is a sustained increase in mechanical work . This cause myocytes to increase in size thus increasing the size and weight of the heart. The hypertrophied heart has an increased oxygen consumption but decreased supply . This is because hypertrophy is not accompanied by a proportional increase in capillary numbers. This leads to ischemia-related decompensation , which can evolve to cardiac failure and eventually lead to death . The causes and consequences of hypertrophy are summarized in the below image.740 Heart weight , rather than wall thickness, is the best measure of hypertrophy in dilated hearts. A patient with systemic hypertension has pressure -overload hypertrophy . A patient with an echo finding of an aortic valvular area of 0.6cm\262 is suggestive of aortic stenosis . There is pressure -overload hypertrophy . A patient with a high pitched holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex is suggestive of mitral regurgitation. There is volume-overload hypertrophy .741

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Most congenital heart diseases arise between what weeks of embryogenesis ?
mcqs.explanation: Most congenital heart diseases arise from faulty embryogenesis during gestational weeks 3 to 8 when major cardiovascular structures form and begin to function. The most common congenital heart disease is ventricular septal defect (VSD), whereas the 2nd most common is atrial septal defect (ASD).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What congenital heart defect is associated with Char syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Char syndrome is associated with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The clinical presentation of this syndrome includes PDA with facial dysmorphism and abnormal fifth digits . The following images show the facial dysmorphism associated with Char syndrome.745

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cardiac defects is not associated with Down's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta is a feature of Turner 's syndrome, not Down's syndrome. Down's syndrome (trisomy 21 ) is the most common cause of congenital heart disease (CHD). Cardiac defects in Down's syndrome are due to endocardial cushion defects . Cardiac defects in various chromosomal anomalies are as follows :Syndrome Cardiac defects Down's syndrome (Trisomy 2 1) Ventricular septal defectPate nt ductus arteriosusAtrial sep tal defect Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13 ) Ventricular septal defectPate nt ductus arteriosusAtrial sep tal defect Edward 's syndrome (Trisomy 18) Ventricular septal defectPate nt ductus arteriosusAtrial sep tal defectDextroposition Turner syndrome (Monosom y X) Bicuspid aortic valveCoarctat ion of the aortaDilated ascen ding aorta

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common type of atrial septal defect ?
mcqs.explanation: Secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is the most common type of ASD.746 ASDs are abnormal , fixed openings in the atrial septum caused by incomplete tissue formation that allows communication of blood between the left and right atria. It results in a left -to-right shunt. Excess blood flow through the ASD and/or the pulmonary valve results in a murmur . They are generally well -tolerated and usually do not become symptomatic before the age of 30 years. ASDs are classified according to their location: • Secundum ASD (90%) - usually isolated defects , can be of any size, multiple or fenestrated • Primum anomalies (5%) - occur adjacent to the AV valves, often associated with AV valve defects and/or VSD • Sinus venosus defects (5%) - located near SVC entrance and can be associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return to the right atrium

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of tetralogy of Fallot ?
mcqs.explanation: Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH ) is a feature of the tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), not left ventricular hypertrophy . The four cardinal features of tetralogy of Fallot are as follows : • Ventricular septal defect (VSD) • Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonary stenosis ) • An aorta that overrides the VSD • Right ventricular hypertrophy It is the most common type of cyanotic congenital heart disease (CHD). The heart is typically enlarged and is classically boot-shaped due to marked right ventricular hypertrophy .747

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD for evaluation of cognitive impairment. Parents report that the child is overly-friendly with strangers. On examination, elfin facies and hypotonia are noted . Investigations reveal hypercalcemia . Which of the following cardiac defects is associated with this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The given features are suggestive of Williams (Williams–Beuren) syndrome. It is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis . This condition is due to deletions on chromosome 7 which includes the gene for elastin . These mutations may cause supravalvular stenosis by disrupting elastin –smooth muscle cell interactions during aortic morphogenesis . There is thickening of ascending aortic wall and consequent luminal constriction. Other features of the syndrome include : • Elfin facies - wide mouth, chubby cheeks , long philtrum, small nose, and delicate chin (as shown in the image)748 • Cognitive abnormalities • Intellectual disability (usually mild) • Personality changes - over-friendliness to strangers • Hypotonia • Connective tissue abnormalities • Endocrine abnormalities (hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, hypothyroidism , early puberty )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of mitral stenosis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease . Mitral stenosis is the most common lesion in rheumatic heart disease . In rheumatic mitral stenosis , calcification and fibrous bridging across the valvular commissures create fish mouth or buttonhole stenosis . Rheumatic mitral stenosis is associated with loud S1. The most common causes of various valvular diseases are: • Aortic stenosis (AS) - calcification due to normal aging or congenitally bicuspid aortic valves • Aortic regurgitation (AR) - dilatation of the ascending aorta, often secondary to hypertension and/or aging • Mitral regurgitation (MR) - myxomatous degeneration (mitral valve prolapse )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man presented with chest pain and exertional dyspnea for the past 2 months. He has no history of cardiac disease . Examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography was done, which revealed an aortic valve with functional cusps and a valve area of 0.8 sq. cm. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.c: It is due to abnormal fusion of valve commissures
options.d: Midline of larger cusp is major site of calcification

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and echo findings are suggestive of calcific aortic stenosis secondary to bicuspid aortic valve (2 functional cusps ). It is due to incomplete separation of valve commissures during development , not abnormal fusion.749 In a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve, the 2 functional cusps are usually of unequal size. The larger cusp has a midline raphe that results from incomplete commissural separation during development . The raphe is frequently a major site of calcific deposits . This condition is associated with mutations in the following areas: • Chromosomes 18q , 5q, and 13q • Chromosome 9q - loss-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 gene Late complications include : • Aortic stenosis or regurgitation • Infective endocarditis • Aortic dilation and/or dissection . • Predisposed to progressive calcification - Approximately 50% of cases of aortic stenosis in adults . Note : Acquired bicuspid valves result from abnormal fusion of valve commissures because of an acquired deformity (rheumatic valve disease ). It produces a conjoined cusp that is generally twice the size of the nonconjoined cusp .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman who came for a routine check-up was incidentally found to have a late systolic murmur with a mid-systolic click. Echocardiography revealed thickening and redundancy of mitral leaflets with bulging into the left atrium. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features and echocardiography findings are suggestive of mitral valve prolapse (MVP) or Barlow syndrome. It is not associated with degenerative calcified deposits (seen in calcific valvular degeneration , not MVP). Barlow syndrome is more common in females . It may be an isolated condition or less commonly can be associated with connective tissue disorders like Marfan's syndrome. In this condition, there is mitral annular dilatation with floppy mitral valve leaflets . They prolapse or balloon back into the left atrium during systole . The following pathological changes are seen : • Interchordal ballooning (hooding) of the mitral leaflets • Thick , rubbery, redundant leaflets • Thickened mural endocardium The main histologic change is marked thickening of the spongiosa layer with deposition of mucoid called myxomatous degeneration . Most individuals diagnosed with MVP are asymptomatic . On auscultation , a mid-systolic click, sometimes followed by a mid to late systolic murmur is heard. Chest pain mimicking angina and dyspnea occur rarely. The complications include : • Infective endocarditis • Mitral insufficiency • Stroke or other systemic infarcts750 • Arrhythmias • Sudden cardiac death (rarely)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old man presented with dull aching abdominal pain and diarrhea for the past 2 months. On examination, his face and chest appeared flushed . In a 24-hour urine sample , 5HIAA levels were elevated . CT scan of the abdomen revealed a mass in the terminal ileum . Cardiac involvement in this syndrome is characterized by all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. Mitral stenosis is not a feature of cardiac involvement in this condition. Carcinoid heart disease refers to the cardiac manifestations caused by the bioactive compounds released by carcinoid tumors. Classically , the endocardium and valves of the right heart are primarily affected . Findings in carcinoid heart syndrome: • Endocardial plaque-like thickening and fibrosis • Tricuspid insufficiency • Pulmonary stenosis • No valve destruction • Myocardium not involved The left side of the heart is less commonly affected because the pulmonary vascular bed degrades the mediators. However, left heart carcinoid lesions can occur in the setting of ASD or VSD, or in the case of primary pulmonary carcinoid tumors.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most commonly involved valve in carcinoid heart disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Carcinoid heart disease most commonly affects the tricuspid valve. It usually affects right heart structures . The most common features are tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis .751

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy is admitted with fever and polyarthritis. He had a bout of streptococcal sore throat infection two weeks back. His ESR on admission was 80mm/hr and fever 39\260C. What is the mechanism of tissue injury in this condition?

options.c: Type II and type III hypersensitivity
options.d: Type II and type IV hypersensitivity

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with polyarthritis (1 major ) along with fever and ESR elevated (2 minor) is suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. It is an example of type II hypersensitivity . This condition classically occurs a few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis or, less commonly, skin infections . The antibodies to streptococcal cell -wall antigen cross-react with myocardial antigen resulting in macrophage activation and inflammation. Acute rheumatic carditis is a common manifestation of active RF and may progress over time to chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD), mainly manifesting as valvular abnormalities. Damage to heart tissue may be caused by a combination of antibody and T-cell-mediated reactions.758

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the least commonly affected heart valve in acute rheumatic fever?
mcqs.explanation: The least commonly affected valve in acute rheumatic fever is the pulmonary valve. The most commonly affected valve is the mitral valve.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman died due to cardiac failure. On autopsy , on the mitral valve, small warty vegetations were present along the lines of closure . There were also irregular thickenings in the left atrium. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and the gross findings seen are diagnostic of rheumatic heart disease . Inflammation of the endocardium and the left -sided valves results in fibrinoid necrosis within the cusps or tendinous cords. Overlying these necrotic foci and along the lines of closure are small (1 to 2 mm) warty vegetations . Subendocardial lesions , exacerbated by regurgitant jets , can induce irregular thickenings called MacCallum plaques , usually in the left atrium.759

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a town where the prevalence of all-age rheumatic heart disease is 5 per 1000 per year, all of the following are included as major Jones criteria except :
mcqs.explanation: Monoarthralgia is a minor Jones criterion in moderate -high risk population (all-age rheumatic heart disease prevalence of >1 per 1000 population per year). Major criteria for acute rheumatic fever include the following :Criteria Characteristics Carditis Most commonly affected valv e - Mitral valveAcute RHD - MRChronic RHD - MSLeast c ommon - Pulmonary valvePa ncarditis, bread and butter p ericarditis Migratory Polyarthritis Most common manifestation Affects large joints,involves o ne joint after the otherNon-e rosive arthritisNo residual de formityImproves rapidly with aspirin Subcutaneous nodules Painless nodulesOn extensor surfaces of elbows , shin, and occiput Erythema marginatum Red macular rash that spares the faceNo residual scarring Sydenham's chorea Late manifestationInvoluntar y purposeless movementsAss ociated with emotional labilit y and depression

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old male patient presents with severe dyspnoea . Mitral stenosis with left atrial hypertrophy is seen . Vegetations present on the mitral valve were excised . What is the most likely diagnosis based on the given HPE image?
mcqs.explanation: The given image depicts Aschoff 's body, which is suggestive of rheumatic valvular disease . Aschoff 's bodies have the following components : • Anitschkow cells or plump macrophages • Abundant cytoplasm • Caterpillar cells - refer to centrally condensed chromatin into slender , wavy ribbons • Foci of fibrinoid necrosis • Aschoff 's giant cells - multinucleated larger macrophages • T-cells760 • Plasma cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The following finding was observed in a post -mortem specimen taken from a patient with acute rheumatic carditis. All of the following features are present except :
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows Aschoff 's bodies . Bacterial colonies are not a component . Aschoff 's bodies have the following components : • Anitschkow cells or plump macrophages • Abundant cytoplasm • Caterpillar cells - refer to centrally condensed chromatin into slender , wavy ribbons • Foci of fibrinoid necrosis • Aschoff 's giant cells - multinucleated larger macrophages761 • T-cells • Plasma cells

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old female patient with a long-standing history of rheumatic heart disease was admitted to hospital due to severe breathlessness . She died on the 3rd day following admission. The mitral valve shows the following findings on autopsy . What is the cause of these findings?
mcqs.explanation: The given image is of mitral stenosis showing fish mouth or buttonhole appearance in rheumatic heart disease. It is due to calcification and fibrosis. Rheumatic heart disease is also associated with subendocardial irregular thickenings known as McCallum plaques , as shown below .762

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is implicated in acute infective endocarditis ?
mcqs.explanation: Acute infective endocarditis is due to infection by highly virulent organisms like Staphylococcus aureus . It results in rapidly necrotizing and destructive lesions . Infective endocarditis is classified into acute and subacute forms. • Acute - infection of a previously normal heart valve by a highly virulent organism • Subacute - infection in previously deformed valves by organisms of lower virulence (S.viridans, S. epidermidis, HACEK )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis underwent prosthetic mitral valve insertion. In the first 2 months following surgery, he is at the highest risk of infection with which of the following organisms?
mcqs.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase -negative Staphylococci (like S. epidermidis ). The following organisms are implicated in infective endocarditis following prosthetic valve surgery: • Early (< 2 months) - Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis • Intermediate (2-12 months) and late (> 12 months): • Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus - more common • Enterococci and Staphylococcus epidermidis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presented with a high-grade fever, chills, and breathlessness for 4 days. He has no other known medical conditions but has a history of IV drug abuse . On examination, the following painful lesions were noted and a regurgitant murmur was heard on auscultation . All of the following are minor criteria for diagnosis of this condition except :
mcqs.explanation: 763 The given features and the image showing painful Osler nodes are suggestive of infective endocarditis. Echo showing a valve-related mass is a major criterion according to Duke's criteria. Infective endocarditis (IE) is a microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural endocardium. The aorta, aneurysms, other blood vessels , and prosthetic devices can also become infected . Most infections are bacterial. Vegetations on heart valves are the classic hallmark of IE. They are friable, bulky, potentially destructive lesions . They contain fibrin, inflammatory cells , bacteria, or other organisms. The mitral valve is most commonly involved . Complications of infective endocarditis: • Cardiac complications - valvular insufficiency or stenosis , myocardial ring abscess , suppurative pericarditis • Embolic complications - left -sided (brain , spleen , kidney) or right-sided lesion (lung infarct and abscess ) • Renal complications - embolic infarcts, focal (more common) or diffuse glomerulonephritis (less common)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the modified Duke's criteria?

options.a: Single positive blood culture for HACEK group is a major criterion
options.b: Single positive blood culture for Coxiella Burnetti is a major criterion
options.d: Documentation of four minor criterion allows a clinical diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti is considered as one of the major criteria to establish the diagnosis of infective endocarditis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman presented with chest pain and breathlessness for 1 month. Examination revealed a regurgitant murmur . Transesophageal echocardiography revealed vegetations on both sides of mitral valve leaflets . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with vegetations on both sides of valve leaflets is suggestive of Libman –Sacks endocarditis . It is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus . The vegetations in this condition have the following features : • Small - 1 to 4 mm in diameter • Single or multiple • Sterile , pinkish vegetations • May be located on both sides valve leaflets • Associated with intense valvulitis - characterized by fibrinoid necrosis Mitral valve is more frequently involved and regurgitation is the usual functional abnormality.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in which condition?
mcqs.explanation: Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in infective endocarditis .764 Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Aortic and mitral valves are the most commonly affected , however, in some cases , the right heart valves may be involved. Vegetations may be single or multiple and may involve one or more valves. Embolization often occurs and may lead to septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms at the site of lodgement due to the presence of virulent organisms in the emboli.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Match the following morphology of vegetations with the conditions in which they are found.
mcqs.explanation: The rightly matched vegetations with the conditions that they are seen are as follows : 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B Rheumatic heart disease often presents with rheumatic fever phase where small, warty 1- 2 mm vegetations , also called veruccae, extend along the lines of closure of the valve leaflets . The cardinal anatomical changes of the mitral valve in chronic RHD are: • Leaflet thickening • Commissural fusion and shortening • Thickening and fusion of the tendinous chords Infective endocarditis has large, irregular, friable masses on the valve cusps that can extend onto the chordae. These vegetations can be single or multiple and may involve one or more valves. They are potentially destructive lesions and contain fibrin, inflammatory cells , bacteria or other organisms. They can erode into the underlying myocardium and produce a ring abscess . They are prone to embolisations , resulting in abscess formation wherever they lodge due to the presence of virulent organisms. Thus, it may lead to sequelae like septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms. Subacute infective endocarditis contains less destructive vegetations . They contain granulation tissue at their bases indicative of healing. Fibrosis, calcification and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate can develop over the time. Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis is characterised by one or more small, 1-5 mm, sterile vegetations which are usually attached at the line of closure . They are seen associated with hypercoagulable states like chronic DIC or malignancy. They are loosely attached to the underlying valve and are non-destructive in nature. They do not cause any inflammatory reaction but they can be a source of systemic embolisation . Libman -Sack's endocarditis has small - or medium - sized , 1- 4 mm, sterile vegetations associated with systemic lupus erythematosus . They may be present on one or both the sides of the leaflets , on the valve surface , chordae or anywhere on the endocardium. These vegetations develop due to immune complex deposition and complement activation. They cause intense valvulitis resulting in fibrinoid necrosis of the valve substance. Persistent injury to the valves can result in scarring and leaflet fusion.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis ?
mcqs.explanation: 765 Vegetations in non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) are of 1 to 5 mm size. NBTE is seen in patients with debilitating conditions such as cancer and sepsis or systemic hypercoagulable states . Hence it is also called marantic endocarditis . There is the deposition of small sterile thrombi loosely attached to the leaflets of cardiac valves. They form single or multiple vegetations along the lines of closure of the leaflets or cusps . They are non-invasive and do not elicit an inflammatory reaction. It can be a source of systemic emboli.766

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the minimum amount of proteinuria required to diagnose a patient with nephrotic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The minimum amount of proteinuria required to diagnose a patient with nephrotic syndrome is 3.5 g/day.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of generalized swelling of the body and frothy urine. Urinary examination revealed grade 3 proteinuria and the presence of hyaline and fatty casts. There were no red blood cells in the urine. Which of the following statements about her condition is true?

options.a: IgA nephropathy is the likely diagnosis.
options.b: It is associated with low C3 levels .
options.c: No IgG or C3 deposition is seen on renal biopsy .
options.d: Alport syndrome is the likely diagnosis.

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario in this child is strongly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change disease (MCD). It is characterized by the absence of immune deposits on biopsy and histopathological examination. It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peaks between 2–6 years). Biopsy findings of MCD are as follows : • Light microscopy - glomeruli appear normal (hence called 'minimal change') • Immunofluorescence studies - no Ig or complement deposits779 • Electron microscopy - diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells (podocytopathy)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old boy is brought for a follow -up visit. He was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome 3 months ago and had been started on a course of oral prednisolone . During the current visit, no improvement is noted with regards to facial puffiness and urine analysis reveals grade 3 proteinuria. Mutations in all of the following are associated with this condition except :
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of steroid -resistant nephrotic syndrome. It can be caused due to mutations in the following components of the glomerular filtration barrier : • Nephrin, podocin - are molecular components of the slit diaphragm complex • Alpha-actinin 4 - is a component of the foot process cytoskeleton Megalin is not a component of the glomerular filtration barrier . It is present in proximal convoluted tubular cells . Mutations in megalin may lead to some proteinuria but not nephrotic syndrome because glomerular filtration of proteins is not affected .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old man presents with sudden onset flank pain and hematuria. Ultrasound reveals enlargement of both kidneys. He is a known case of membranous nephropathy . What is the likely pathophysiology for his current presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario in a patient suffering from membranous nephropathy , which is a type of nephrotic syndrome, is suggestive of renal vein thrombosis. It is due to the loss of antithrombin III (an endogenous anticoagulant) in urine. Renal vein thrombosis is most often a consequence of a hypercoagulable state . In adults , it is most commonly seen in patients with membranous nephropathy .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, all of the following are decreased except :
mcqs.explanation: In nephrotic syndrome, there is an increase in fibrinogen levels .780 The following proteins are increased in nephrotic syndrome: • Fibrinogen • Lipoproteins - due to increased synthesis The following proteins are decreased in nephrotic syndrome as a consequence of selective proteinuria: • Albumin - the largest proportion of protein lost in nephrotic syndrome. • Transferrin • Cholecalciferol -binding protein • Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) • Ferritin • Coagulation factors • Antithrombin III

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with radiologically confirmed reflux nephropathy develops nephrotic -range proteinuria. What is the most likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome due to a secondary cause (reflux nephropathy). Secondary nephrotic syndrome in adults is most likely due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults . It is a podocytopathy , with degeneration and focal disruption of visceral epithelial cells and effacement of foot processes . Glomerular hyalinosis and sclerosis are seen due to the entrapment of plasma proteins and increased extracellular matrix deposition. FSGS is classified as follows : • Primary • Idiopathic FSGS • Secondary • HIV associated • Heroin addiction • Sickle cell disease • Obesity • Hypertensive nephropathy • Renal conditions • Focal glomerulonephritis (e.g. IgA nephropathy ) • Renal ablation • Unilateral renal agenesis or renal dysplasia • Reflux nephropathy781 • Inherited • Mutated proteins of the slit diaphragm - podocin, alpha-actinin 4, TRPC6Electron microscopy of FSGS shows : • Diffuse effacement of the podocyte foot processes • Focal detachment and degeneration of the epithelial cells • Absence of electron -dense deposits

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients diagnosed with which variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are likely to have the worst prognosis?
mcqs.explanation: The collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is associated with the worst prognosis.782 There are 5 variants of FSGS: • Collapsing variant - poor prognosis • Glomerular tip variant - good prognosis • Cellular variant • Perihilar variant • Not otherwise specified - most common Given below is a histological image of collapsing glomerulopathy showing the involvement of the entire glomerular tuft and proliferation of visceral epithelial cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Given below is an electron microscopy image showing deposits in the kidney. What could be the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 783 The given electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney which is suggestive of membranous nephropathy . The following electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney.Membranous nephropathy is characterized by the diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall. It is due to the accumulation of deposits containing Ig along the subepithelial side of the basement membrane.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents with complaints of facial puffiness and frothy urine. Given below is his renal biopsy findings. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and the histopathological image showing uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall are suggestive of membranous nephropathy .784 Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in the adults /elderly. It is a chronic immune-complex -mediated disease . The following image of the glomerulus shows the characteristic spikes . The spikes are formed due to the presence of basement membrane material (have affinity to silver stain) in between the immune complex deposits (lack affinity to silver stain).785

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Mesangial deposits are seen in which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Mesangial deposits are seen in the following conditions: • IgA nephropathy (Berger disease ) • Henoch–Schonlein purpura • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis • Lupus nephritis classes I and II • Resolving postinfectious glomerulonephritis786

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 29-year-old man presented with complaints of blood in his urine. Urine analysis was positive for proteins and red cell casts. A renal biopsy was done as shown below . Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed granular deposits of C3 on either side of the glomerular basement membrane but was negative for IgG, C1q , and C4. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario, immunofluorescence findings, and the image showing proliferating mesangial cells and capillary endothelial cells are suggestive of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type 2 (MPGN type 2) or dense -deposit disease .The following image shows bright deposits scattered along capillary walls and in the mesangium by immunofluorescence microscopy with antibodies to C3.787 This condition belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies and primarily affects children and young adults . It is associated with a dysregulation in the alternative complement pathway . It is clinically and morphologically similar to MPGN type 1 but pathogenetically distinct from it. In this condition, a circulating autoantibody called C3 nephritic factor is present , which stabilizes the C3 convertase enzyme. The stabilized C3 convertase enhances C3 activation and consumption causing hypocomplementemia . Patients will have consistently decreased serum C3 levels , but normal C1 and C4 levels . The prognosis is poor, with about half of these patients progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the given serum electrophoresis image?
mcqs.explanation: 788 The given electrophoresis shows hypoalbuminemia and increased alpha-2 globulin , which is classically seen in nephrotic syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of primary nephritic syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease ) is the most common cause of primary nephritic syndrome in the world. Nephritic syndrome is characterized by: • Acute onset of hematuria • Urinalysis - red cell casts • Diminished glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (oliguria) • Mild to moderate proteinuria • Hypertension • Azotemia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old man is being evaluated for hematuria after UTI. Histopathology showed mesangial widening and endocapillary proliferation. The following finding is seen on immunofluorescence , which was positive for C3 and negative for IgG. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario, histopathology findings of mesangial widening and endocapillary proliferation, as well as immunofluorescence showing mesangial deposits are suggestive of IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease ). It is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide . It is characterized by recurrent hematuria/ nephritic syndrome and the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangium. Patients generally present with gross hematuria after respiratory, gastrointestinal or urinary tract infection .789 The systemic variant of IgA nephropathy is called Henoch–Sch\366nlein purpura. It is a disorder of children which presents with similar renal manifestations with characteristic IgA deposits in the mesangium in about one-third of the patients .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops fever, oliguria, periorbital edema and smoky cola-colored urine 2-weeks after recovery from sore throat. His renal biopsy image is given below . Which of the following statements is false about the given condition?

options.a: A rapidly progressive form with oliguria develops in 50% of children
options.b: It is a form of proliferative glomerulonephritis
options.c: Granular IgG and C3 deposits are seen on immunofluorescence
options.d: Dome-shaped subepithelial humps are seen on electron microscopy

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and histopathology image showing hypercellular glomeruli are suggestive of post -streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Rapidly progressive disease with oliguria is very rare (< 1% of patients ).Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis . It is usually preceded by an acute streptococcal sore throat or impetigo around 1-4 weeks prior. It usually presents with features of nephritic syndrome including:790 • Hematuria • Red cell casts in the urine • Azotemia, oliguria • Hypertension • Mild to moderate proteinuria • Edema On microscopy, the following findings are seen : • Light microscopy - enlarged , hypercellular glomeruli with influx of leucocytes (endocapillary proliferation) • Electron microscopy - subepithelial humps • Immunofluorescence - granular IgG and C3 deposits on glomerular basement membrane and mesangium Majority (> 95%) of affected children eventually recover renal function with conservative therapy.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is examining the following renal biopsy specimen . What does it show?

options.a: Proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and WBCs in Bowman space
options.b: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall
options.c: Proliferating mesangial cells and increased matrix deposition in the mesangium
options.d: Proliferation of capillaries with fibrin deposition

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a crescent -shaped mass of proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and leukocytes within the Bowman capsule . It is a characteristic feature of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) or crescentic glomerulonephritis .RPGN is a type of nephritic syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury with necrosis and formation of crescents . It is usually immune-mediated and may be associated with circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs), anti-GBM antibodies , and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).791 Injury to the glomerular capillary wall leads to the escape of procoagulant factors and cytokines in the Bowman space . This triggers : • Proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells - mostly parietal, but also some visceral cells • Recruitment of leukocytes and fibroblasts • Pathognomonic crescents - due to the circumferential accumulation of these cells and fibrin The crescents progressively compress the capillary tuft . This results in a rapid decline of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and, consequently , acute kidney injury (AKI). Thus, the degree of crescent formation correlates with the severity and the prognosis of the disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with recurrent hemoptysis and renal failure underwent renal biopsy . It revealed the presence of crescents in most of the glomeruli. Immunofluorescence finding is shown in the image below . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario, histopathology findings, and immunofluorescence showing linear, dense , and smooth deposits are suggestive of Goodpasture 's syndrome.792 Goodpasture 's syndrome is an anti-GBM (glomerular basement membrane) antibody-mediated disease . The antibodies are directed against the non-collagenous portion of the \0373 chain of collagen type IV . As it is present in both the alveoli and GBM, it usually presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure. It makes up about 1/5 of cases of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis . Crescents with linear deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomerular basement membrane are seen on histopathology . Note : Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis ) causes the pauci-immune type of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis . There is an absence of immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 18-year-old otherwise healthy boy presents with complaints of hematuria. His father has also had similar complaints since childhood . Light microscopy of the renal biopsy specimen showed no abnormalities. Diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane was seen on electron microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with normal findings on light microscopy and diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy are highly suggestive of benign familial hematuria (thin basement membrane disease ). It is a type of hereditary nephritis manifested clinically by familial asymptomatic hematuria. The following are the differences between Alport's syndrome and benign familial hematuria.Features Alport's syndrome Benign familial hematuria Inheritance X-linked (most common)Aut osomal inheritance Autosomal inheritance Affected protein \0375 chain of type IV collagen ( Most commonly) \0373 or \0374 chains of type IV co llagen . Hearing Loss Present Absent Ocular abnormalities Present Absent793 Features Alport's syndrome Benign familial hematuria Progress to end-stage renal d isease Yes No Electron microscopy Irregularthickeningandthinni ngof basement membraneSpl itting and lamination of lami na densa -basket-weaveappea rance Diffuse thinningof the glomer ular basement membrane Prognosis Poor Good

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common manifestation of Alport's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The most common manifestation of Alport syndrome is gross or microscopic hematuria, frequently accompanied by red cell casts. Proteinuria and oliguria may develop later in the disease , and rarely, nephrotic syndrome develops . The deafness may be subtle requiring sensitive testing . There are no significant light microscopy changes in Alport syndrome. On electron microscopy, the glomerular basement membrane shows : • Irregular foci of thickening, alternating with attenuation (thinning) • Pronounced splitting and lamination of the lamina densa - basket-weave appearance794

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A middle -aged male patient has proteinuria. Looking at the immunofluorescence image below , what is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given immunofluorescence staining of the kidney biopsy specimen shows positive staining for fibrinogen, IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q , C3, \022 chain, and k light chain. This is known as full -house effect . It is seen in lupus nephritis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Urinary albumin excretion of how much is considered as microalbuminuria ?
mcqs.explanation: Urinary albumin excretion in the range of 30–300 mg/24 hours is called microalbuminuria . It is the hallmark of early diabetic nephropathy .795 The terms microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria are no longer used now. Proteinuria is currently classified as:Type of Proteinuria Total proteinuria (mg/day) Albuminuria(mg/d ay) Normal-range <150Mainly Tamm -Horsfall p rotein (70-75 mg/day) < Moderately increas ed 150-500 30-300 Severely increased > > 300

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presented with the blurring of vision. Urine examination showed proteinuria. Fundus examination showed dot and blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and cotton wool spots . Histopathology of the kidney was as shown below . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and histopathology image showing acellular periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive nodules are suggestive of Kimmelstiel –Wilson disease . It occurs in patients with diabetic nephropathy .796 The following renal lesions are encountered in diabetic nephropathy : • Glomerular lesions - • Capillary basement membrane thickening • Diffuse mesangial sclerosis • Nodular glomerulosclerosis / Kimmelstiel –Wilson disease • Intercapillary glomerulosclerosis • Renal vascular lesions - hyaline arteriolosclerosis • Pyelonephritis - necrotizing papillitis Option A: In amyloidosis , glomerular deposits appear as thickenings of the mesangial matrix, forming interlacing broad ribbons of amyloid. Option B: In focal segmental glomerulosclerosis , there is focal and segmental hyalinosis and sclerosis of the capillary wall with lipid droplets in the sclerosed area. Option D: In lupus nephritis, immune complex deposits are seen in the mesangium or along the entire basement membrane (wire loop lesions ), with mesangial cell proliferation.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 51-year-old male patient came with complaints of hematuria to the clinic. On examination, he was normotensive and had pedal edema . Investigations revealed the patient had no glycosuria and had a creatinine of 9. His renal biopsy is shown below . Which of the following investigations should be done to identify the disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Based on the given clinical history and microscopy showing crescents , rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is suspected . Among the given options , anti- GBM antibody testing should be done, since it is a part of the work-up of RPGN.797 Type 1 RPGN includes renal limited disease and Goodpasture 's disease . In this condition, antibodies are produced against the non-collagenous domain of the \0373 chain of collagen IV of the GBM. Microscopy findings of Goodpasture 's disease are: • Immunofluorescence - linear deposits of Ig and complement along the glomerular basement membrane • Electron microscopy - wrinkling of the glomerular basement membrane with focal disruptions without any immune complex deposition . A variant of Goodpasture 's disease with pulmonary involvement is known as Goodpasture 's syndrome. Option A: ANA testing is done if SLE is suspected . Electron microscopy will show immune complex deposits .798 Option C: HIV RNA testing is done in immunodeficiency syndrome associated with weight loss. Electron microscopy will show diffuse podocyte injury with complete foot process effacement . Tubuloreticular inclusions will be seen in endothelial cells . Option D: Urine electrophoresis is done if nephrotic syndrome is suspected .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is seen in:
mcqs.explanation: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is seen in HIV , SLE, CLL , and Hepatitis B. MPGN is caused due to immune-mediated injury. It often presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture . The causes of MPGN are as follows : • Primary MPGN (Idiopathic) • Secondary MPGN • System lupus erythematosus (SLE) • \0371-antitrypsin deficiency • Infections - hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV , schistosomiasis , endocarditis , infected ventriculoatrial shunts, chronic visceral abscesses • Malignancies - chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) MPGN is characterized by the proliferation of cells predominantly in the mesangium and the capillary loops . Hence it is also called mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis . There are 2 types of MPGN: • Type I - It is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes and mesangiocapillary proliferation. • Type II - It is now known as dense -deposit disease . It belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies . Light microscopy findings of MPGN are as follows : • Lobular glomeruli with proliferating mesangial cells , capillary endothelium , and infiltrating leukocytes (endocapillary proliferation) • Duplication of the basement membrane gives a double contour or tram-track appearance . It is especially evident in silver or PAS stains.799

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man was brought to the ER by his friends after they found him lying unconscious next to an empty antifreeze bottle . Investigations were significant for the following findings. This condition predominantly affects which part of the kidney?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) due to ingestion of ethylene glycol . Toxins usually result in ATN by causing damage to the proximal convoluted tubules (PCTs). Ethylene glycol poisoning produces marked ballooning and hydropic or vacuolar degeneration of PCT. Calcium oxalate crystals are often also found in tubular lumens. Direct toxic injury to the tubules in ATI can be caused by: • Endogenous agents : Myoglobin , hemoglobin, monoclonal light chains, bile /bilirubin • Exogenous agents : Drugs, radiocontrast dyes , heavy metals , and organic solvents

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman presents with urinary frequency, urgency , and burning during urination of two days duration. Presence of which of the following additional findings would make you suspect pyelonephritis in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: White blood cell casts are specific features of pyelonephritis . Neutrophil -rich casts (pus casts) indicate renal involvement because casts are formed only in tubules . The urine contains many leukocytes (pyuria) derived from the inflammatory infiltrate. It is found in both upper and lower UTIs and cannot differentiate between them. Fever is also a non-specific finding. Ascending infection is the most common cause of clinical pyelonephritis . Note : Sterile pyuria is defined as white cells in the urine in the absence of significant bacterial growth. It is seen in renal TB .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common organism causing acute pyelonephritis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common organism causing acute pyelonephritis is Escherichia coli. The organisms that cause acute pyelonephritis include : • E. coli • Proteus • Klebsiella • Enterobacter species • Mycobacteria - caseating granulomatous inflammation • Fungi - non-caseating granulomatous inflammation • Viruses (CMV and adenovirus) - immunocompromised people808

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Periglomerular fibrosis is considered typical of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Periglomerular fibrosis is considered typical of chronic pyelonephritis . Histopathological features of chronic pyelonephritis are: • Dilated tubules with flattened epithelium may be filled with casts resembling thyroid colloid (thyroidization) • Chronic interstitial inflammation and fibrosis in the cortex and medulla • Periglomerular fibrosis • Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), usually several years after the scarring has occurred and often in the absence of continued infection or persistent vesicoureteral reflux

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist noted the following microscopic finding while examining a slide of a kidney. What is the likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows dilated tubules with flattened epithelium , filled with casts, resembling thyroid colloid (thyroidization). This is seen in chronic pyelonephritis .809 Option A: In acute tubular necrosis, there is focal tubular epithelial necrosis, tubulorrhexis. Option C: In acute interstitial nephritis, there is patchy edema and mononuclear cell infiltrates . Option D: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), wire-loop lesions are seen .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following patients are at risk of developing renal papillary necrosis except :

options.a: A 14-year-old girl being treated for thalassemia major
options.b: A 60-year-old man with longstanding diabetes mellitus
options.c: A 46-year-old man with a history of analgesic abuse
options.d: A 24-year-old woman identified to have sickle cell trait

mcqs.explanation: Necrotizing papillitis or acute papillary necrosis is not associated with thalassemia . Major causes of acute papillary necrosis include • Diabetes mellitus • Sickle cell disease or trait • Analgesic abuse nephropathy • Obstruction by calculi • Focally in renal tuberculosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of flank pain and fever with chills. CECT abdomen showed dilated and enlarged left renal pelvis with the multiloculated calyces and resection of the kidney was done. The gross specimen showed large yellowish -orange nodules . Histological examination revealed foamy macrophages . Which of the following is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features and histological findings are suggestive of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. It is associated with Proteus infection and obstructive uropathy . Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a relatively rare form of chronic pyelonephritis characterized by the accumulation of foamy macrophages intermingled with plasma cells , lymphocytes , polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and occasional giant cells . The lesions sometimes produce large, yellowish -orange nodules that may be grossly confused with renal cell carcinoma . CECT abdomen shows dilated and enlarged renal pelvis and calyces showing a multiloculated appearance referred to as the bear paw sign.810

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following do not result in granular contracted kidneys?
mcqs.explanation: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and amyloidosis cause enlarged kidneys. Causes of contracted kidneys: • Symmetric • Chronic glomerulonephritis • Benign nephrosclerosis • Asymmetric • Chronic pyelonephritis Causes of enlarged kidneys:811 • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis • Amyloidosis • Polycystic kidney disease • Hydronephrosis (bilateral obstruction) The following image shows the gross appearance in benign nephrosclerosis illustrating the fine, leathery granularity of the surface .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings is not associated with malignant hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Image 4 shows a leather -grain appearance , which is seen in benign nephrosclerosis . Features of malignant hypertension : • Flea bitten kidney - small petechial hemorrhages on the cortical surface , leading to a mottled appearance • Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles - cytologic detail is lost and the vessel wall takes on a smudgy eosinophilic appearance due to fibrin deposition • Onion-skinning (hyperplastic arterioles ) - intimal thickening with the fine concentric layering of collagen & smooth muscles812 The differential diagnosis for flea -bitten kidney includes : • Polyarteritis nodosa • Subacute bacterial endocarditis (SABE) • Malignant hypertension

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome can be caused by all except :
mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 leads to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ). Two common pathogenetic triggers of thrombotic microangiopathies are: • Endothelial injury - HUS • Excessive platelet activation and aggregation - TTPTypical HUS Atypical HUS 5-10 days afterdiarrhealillnes sE.coliO157 :H7orShigella dys enteriaetype I Mutation in genes encoding c omplement regulatory protei n Shiga-liketoxinsproduced cau seendothelialdamage .This lea ds to platelet activation and t hrombi. Uncontrolledactivationof the complementsystem due to:An tiphospholipid antibodiesPre gnancy complicationsOCPsSc leroderma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought with blood in the urine. His mother says he had bloody diarrhea, fever, and vomiting 10 days ago. His BP is 130 /90 mm Hg, and he is jaundiced . Investigations reveal a platelet count of 50,000 cells /cu mm, BUN of 35mg/dl, and creatinine of 3.5mg/dl. Which of the following cells would you expect to see in the peripheral smear?
mcqs.explanation: 814 The clinical scenario is suggestive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). It is characterized by the presence of schistocytes in peripheral smear. It indicates microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Cholemic nephrosis is associated with which of the following casts?
mcqs.explanation: Cholemic nephrosis is associated with casts of bile. In patients with acute or chronic liver disease with advanced liver failure, renal function may be impaired. This is called hepatorenal syndrome. This can be associated with highly elevated bilirubin levels with bile cast formation (also known as cholemic nephrosis) in distal nephron segments .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man died in a road traffic accident . On autopsy , the following appearance of the kidney was noted . Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

options.a: Cysts in liver, pancreas, and spleen

mcqs.explanation: The gross image suggests that the patient had autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This condition is not associated with hepatic fibrosis. However, patients with autosomal recessive (childhood ) polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) have congenital hepatic fibrosis. ADPKD is associated with mutations in PKD1, encoding polycystin 1, and PKD2, encoding polycystin 2. The multiple expanding cysts of both kidneys ultimately destroy the renal parenchyma and cause renal failure. Cysts arise from the tubules throughout the nephron and, therefore , have variable lining epithelia. The common extrarenal manifestations of ADPKD include : • Hepatic cysts - most common • Seminal vesicle cysts - can result in infertility • Arachnoid membrane cysts - usually asymptomatic , may increase the risk of subdural hematoma • Pancreatic cysts • Splenic cysts • Intracranial berry aneurysms • Subarachnoid hemorrhages • Mitral valve prolapse There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients , but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proved. However, there is a three -fold increase in the incidence of bronchiectasis in ADPKD patients .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about the polycystin gene ?

options.a: Polycystin -1 is most commonly involved in ADPKD
options.b: Polycystin -2 is a calcium ion channel
options.c: Mutation in polycystin -2 causes more severe form of ADPKD
options.d: Polycystin -1 is involved in cell interactions

mcqs.explanation: The polycystin -2 mutation is less commonly involved and less severe .815 Polycystin -1 is encoded by the PKD1 gene located on chromosome 16p13 .3. It is expressed in tubular epithelial cells , particularly those of the distal nephron. It contains domains that are usually involved in cell -cell and cell -matrix interactions. Mutations in PKD1 account for about 85% of cases of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease ) and it causes a more severe form of the disease . Polycystin -2 is an integral membrane protein that is expressed in all segments of the renal tubules and in many extrarenal tissues . It functions as a Ca2+ cation channel. Overall, it causes a less severe form of ADPKD disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common extrarenal site of cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common extrarenal site of cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the liver. 40% of individuals with autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) have one to several cysts in the liver (polycystic liver disease ) that are usually asymptomatic . The cysts are derived from the biliary epithelium . Cysts occur much less frequently in the spleen , pancreas, and lungs . There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients , but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proved.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with ADPKD, the mutated genes are located on which chromosomes?
mcqs.explanation: The genes mutated in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) are located on chromosomes 16 and 4. This condition occurs due to mutations of the PKD1 gene (chromosome 16) and PKD2 gene (on chromosome 4). These genes encode for polycystin 1 and 2 proteins respectively .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Mutations in fibrocystin are seen in which condition?
mcqs.explanation: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is caused by mutations in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21 -p23 which encodes fibrocystin. The gene is highly expressed in adult and fetal kidneys and also in the liver and pancreas. Fibrocystin has been localized to the primary cilium of tubular cells . The serious manifestations of ARPKD are usually present at birth, and may cause death by renal failure. The following gross findings are seen : • Enlarged kidneys with smooth external appearance • Spongelike appearance due to numerous small cysts in the cortex and medulla • Dilated elongated channels at right angles to the cortical surface , completely replacing the m edulla and cortex816 On microscopic examination, there is cylindrical or, less commonly, saccular dilation of all collecting tubules with linning of cuboidal cells . In almost all cases , the liver has cysts associated with portal fibrosis and proliferation of the portal bile ducts , termed congenital hepatic fibrosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Hepatic fibrosis is a feature of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatic fibrosis is a feature of childhood (autosomal recessive ) polycystic kidney disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A routine urine examination of a 46-year-old woman shows thorn-apple crystals. Past history is significant for constipation and longstanding use of laxatives. What is the likely composition of these crystals?
mcqs.explanation: Ammonium biurate crystals appear as spheres with radial or concentric striations and irregular projections or thorns, referred to as thorn apples . They are seen in laxative abuse .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with chronic kidney disease , what type of casts are seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Broad casts are seen in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). They are also known as renal failure casts. Broad casts are defined as those with a diameter 2-6 times that of normal casts. They indicate chronically damaged tubules or collecting ducts . They indicate a poor prognosis.817

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 18-month-old child is brought to OPD with complaints of blood in his urine. Examination reveals a non-tender mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline. Blood pressure is also found to be elevated . Imaging reveals a left renal tumor and surgical resection is planned . The gross appearance of the mass is shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing a well -circumscribed tumor with multiple necrotic, hemorrhagic, and cystic changes in the upper pole of the kidney are suggestive of a nephroblastoma or Wilms' tumor. It is the most common primary renal tumor of childhood (2-5 years of age ). Around 10 % of cases are associated with genetic syndromes and gonadal dysgenesis may be seen . Clinical manifestations of Wilms' tumor include : • Large abdominal mass - usually unilateral and does not cross the midline • Abdominal pain • Hematuria • Hypertension • Intestinal obstruction (in some cases)826 Nephrogenic rests are the precursor lesions of Wilms' tumor and suggest an increased risk of developing a contralateral Wilms' tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Wilms tumor?

options.a: It is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder
options.b: It is associated with MIC-2 gene expression
options.c: It is associated with the deletion of chromosome 11p
options.d: The most common presentation is hematuria

mcqs.explanation: Wilms' tumor is associated with the deletion of chromosome 11p13 . It is an autosomal-dominant disorder. The most common clinical presentation is an abdominal mass. Note : MIC-2 gene expression is seen in neuroblastoma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with Wilms tumors, which of the following microscopic features are indicative of resistance to chemotherapy ?
mcqs.explanation: In Wilms' tumor, the presence of anaplasia is indicative of resistance to chemotherapy . This correlates with the presence of TP53 mutations and, hence , is associated with a poor prognosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important prognostic factor in Wilms' tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Anaplastic histology is the most important prognostic factor in Wilms' tumor. It is seen in about 5% of cases and is characterized by the presence of cells with large, hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei , and abnormal mitoses . It is associated with TP53 mutations and resistance to chemotherapy . Anaplasia is uncommon in children < 2 years. Hence , tumors presenting at an young age have a significantly better prognosis than those presenting in older children. Prognostic factors in Wilms' tumor include :Favorable prognosis Adverse prognosis Histologic type Classic triphasic componen t Anaplastic histology Tumor stage Low High Molecular alteration s ---- 11q deletion16q deletionGain of chromosome 1q Age of onset <2 years >2 years

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not associated with Wilms tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Bilateral polycystic kidneys are not associated with Wilms tumor.827 Wilms' tumor can be associated with: • Aniridia - WAGR syndrome • Gonadal dysgenesis - Denys –Drash syndrome • Hemihypertrophy and omphalocele - Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old girl is being evaluated for a history of recurrent seizures and abdominal discomfort. Examination reveals the following nail findings. Which of the following should she be screened for?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing periungual fibromas are strongly suggestive of tuberous sclerosis . This condition is associated with renal angiomyolipomas (present in 25–50% of cases ). Tuberous sclerosis is a multisystem disorder that has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. The mutations are involved in the TSC1 gene that encodes hamartin on chromosome 9 and the TSC2 gene that encodes a protein tuberin on chromosome 16. The clinical features of tuberous sclerosis include : • Skin lesions - • Hypomelanotic ash leaf –type macules • Periungual fibromas or Koenen tumors (small fibromas or nodules of skin around fingernails or toenails) • Shagreen patch- roughened , raised lesion with an orange-peel consistency , primarily in the lumbosacral region • Facial angiofibromas • Confetti skin lesions • Neurological features - • Epilepsy and intellectual disability (due to cortical tubers ) • Autism spectrum disorder • Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas • Other tumors - • Cardiac rhabdomyoma • Renal angiomyolipomas, renal cysts • Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis Angiomyolipoma is a benign renal neoplasm (hamartoma) originating from perivascular epithelioid cells (PEComa). It consists of vessels , smooth muscle , and fat in variable proportions. They are highly susceptibility to spontaneous hemorrhage. The histological image of renal angiomyolipoma is given below :828

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old diabetic patient is being evaluated for chronic abdominal discomfort. CECT of the abdomen and pelvis shows a heterogeneously enhancing renal mass with a central stellate scar. On resection , the tumor appears mahogany brown. What is the site of origin of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history is suggestive of renal oncocytoma. It arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting ducts . It is a benign epithelial neoplasm . Grossly, these tumors appear tan or mahogany brown and relatively homogeneous . They are usually well encapsulated with a central scar in one-third of cases . Microscopically , they are composed of large eosinophilic cells having small, round, benign-appearing nuclei that have large nucleoli . Ultrastructurally , these eosinophilic cells have numerous mitochondria. The gross and histological appearances of renal oncocytoma are shown in the images given below :829 Oncocytes refer to epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm (due to the accumulation of mitochondria). They can arise in various tissues and are referred to as: • Hurthle cells /Ashkenazy cells in the thyroid gland • Oxyphilic cells in the parotid gland • Apocrine metaplasia in the breast

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important determinant of malignant potential in the papillary type of renal tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The most important determinant of malignant potential in the papillary type of renal tumor is the size of the tumor. The papillary type of renal tumors includes : • Renal papillary adenoma (\021 1.5 cm) • Papillary type of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) - > 1.5 cm Small renal papillary growths are fairly common and incidentally found. Ruling out of malignancy is one of the processes carried out during the evaluation of donor transplant kidneys.Papillary renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the second most common type of renal cell carcinoma and it arises from proximal tubules . It can be multifocal or bilateral. It is typically hemorrhagic and cystic , especially when large. It is often a circumscribed tumor composed of papillae formed by delicate fibrovascular cores that often contain foamy macrophages and Psammoma bodies . It has two histological types : • Type 1 papillary RCC - single layer of cells on the basement membrane and low-grade nuclear features831 • Type 2 papillary RCC - pseudostratification of cells and usually has high-grade nuclear features

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The following image shows a nephrectomy specimen of a patient diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma . What is the likely histopathological finding in this tumor?

options.c: Small cells with high N/C ratio

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a bright yellow variegated mass distorting the renal outline at the lower pole . This is suggestive of the clear cell type of renal cell carcinoma (RCC). The yellow color is due to prominent lipid accumulation. Gross findings of various types of renal tumors:Clear-cell RCC Papillary RCC Chromophobe RC C Oncocytoma Angiomyolipoma Site of origin Proximal tubular epithelium Proximal tubule Intercalated cells of collecting duct s Intercalated cells of collecting duct s Perivascular epit helioid cells (PEC oma) Numb er Solitary, globular, unilateral Multifocal and bil ateral Solitary, unilatera l Usually solitary Mostly solitary, c an be multifocal Color Golden yellow , d ue to the high lipi d content of their cells Grey tan to dark brown,depending on the degree of intratumoral hem orrhage Light tan to brow n Mahogany brown Yellow to pinkish -tan,depending o n the relative pro portions of the va rious components Capsul e Pseudocapsule + Pseudocapsule + Circumscribed bu t unencapsulated Well encapsulate d Circumscribed bu t unencapsulated Appear ance Variegated with c ysts , necrosis, he morrhagic foci Variegated, friabl e Homogenous Homogenous Variable

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The nephrectomy specimen of a tumor of a 40-year-old man shows the following histological presentation . Which of the following familial cancer syndromes is this condition associated with?

options.b: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows eosinophilic cells with prominent cell membranes and perinuclear halo, which is suggestive of chromophobe cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It is associated with Birt–Hogg–Dub\351 syndrome. Other familial cancer syndromes and the common malignancies associated with them are: • Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome - papillary RCC • Large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm , large nuclei , and prominent inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli . • Tuberous sclerosis - clear-cell RCC • Von Hippel –Lindau syndrome (VHL ) - clear-cell RCC The image given below shows the histology of chromophobe cell RCC.832

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following subtypes of renal cell carcinoma is matched incorrectly with its respective cytogenetic patterns ?

options.c: Hereditary papillary RCC - loss of Y
options.d: Sporadic papillary RCC - loss of Y

mcqs.explanation: Loss of Y chromosome is a feature of sporadic papillary carcinoma , not hereditary papillary RCC.833 Various types of renal carcinoma and their cytogenetic abnormalities are given below : • Papillary renal cell carcinoma - • Sporadic type - trisomies 7 and 17, loss of Y chromosome • Familial type - trisomy 7 (mapped to MET gene ) • Clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma (whether familial, sporadic, or associated with VHL syndrome) • Loss of sequences on the short arm of chromosome 3, which harbors the VHL gene

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma is the most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma , accounting for 70% to 80% of renal cell cancers. It is most likely to arise from the proximal tubular epithelium as solitary lesions . It has a characteristic tendency to invade the renal vein. The histological features are: • Rounded or polygonal tumor cells • Abundant clear or granular cytoplasm , which contains glycogen and lipids • Arranged in a solid to trabecular (cordlike) or tubular pattern The histological appearance of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma is shown in the image given below :834 Note : The Furhman nuclear grading system was previously used for histological grading of RCC (except chromophobe RCC). It is now replaced by the WHO/International Society of Urologic Pathology (ISUP) grading system .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors does not have papillary architecture on histopathology ?
mcqs.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-deficient renal cell carcinoma does not show papillary architecture. It is associated with a bubbly appearance of histopathology . It is a malignant epithelial tumor associated with germline mutations in the SDH gene . It is composed of vacuolated , eosinophilic -clear cells arranged in a solid, nested , or tubular pattern. The presence of the vacuoles imparts the characteristic bubbly appearance , as shown below .835 Renal cell carcinoma subtypes with papillary architecture in histology : • Papillary renal cell carcinoma • Hereditary leiomyomatosis renal cell carcinoma • Xp11 translocation renal cell carcinoma • Collecting duct renal cell carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following subtypes of renal cell carcinoma shows large cells having a plant-cell -like appearance with a perinuclear halo on histological examination?
mcqs.explanation: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma shows large cells having plant-cell -like appearance with a perinuclear halo. They are arranged in solid sheets with a concentration of the largest cells around blood vessels .836 Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma can differentiated from oncocytoma and clear cell RCC as follows : • Oncocytoma does not show perinuclear halo whereas chromophobe RCC shows perinuclear halo • CK7 is diffusely positive in chromophobe RCC but it is negative in clear-cell RCC. Chromophobe RCC cannot be histologically graded because of its innate nuclear atypia. The histological image of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is given below :

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is found to have a renal tumor and malignancy is suspected . Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the renal tumor associated with this condition?

options.a: It constitutes 5% of all renal tumors
options.b: Cytogenetic testing of the tumor shows multiple chromosomal losses
options.d: It arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct

mcqs.explanation: The renal tumor commonly associated with Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (RCC). It has an excellent prognosis. It constitutes 5% of all renal carcinomas. It arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Cytogenetic testing of the tumor shows multiple chromosomal losses and extreme hypodiploidy . The histological image of chromophobe RCC is given below :837

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following tumors characteristically shows a hobnail pattern on microscopy?
mcqs.explanation: Collecting duct carcinoma or Bellini duct carcinoma shows a characteristic hobnail pattern and prominent desmoplastic stroma on microscopy. The hobnail pattern refers to the bulbous nuclear projections of epithelial cells that protrude into the lumen as little bumps. It is associated with tubular, tubulopapillary , or tubulocystic pattern. Collecting duct carcinoma arises from the principal cells of the renal collecting ducts of Bellini. The majority of these tumors are associated with poor outcome , due to their highly aggressive clinical course . The histological section showing collecting duct carcinoma with the characteristic hobnail pattern is given below:838 Note : The hobnail pattern is also seen in clear cell carcinoma of the ovary .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Individuals with the sickle cell trait are at a higher risk of developing which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Individuals with the sickle cell trait are at a higher risk of developing medullary renal cell carcinoma . It is a rare, highly aggressive neoplasm and is morphologically similar to collecting duct carcinoma . The hypoxic microenvironment in the renal medulla created by hyperosmolarity , low pH, and stasis enhances red blood sickling and ischemic damage . This leads to chronic regenerative proliferation of medullary epithelium and activation of hypoxia-induced signaling pathways , which in turn promote neoplastic change. The histological section of renal medullary carcinoma showing prominent cytological atypia is shown below :839

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is studying the histopathological slide from a nephrectomy specimen from a patient with renal carcinoma . He observes neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm and papillary architecture . Which of the following subtypes of renal carcinoma is this likely to be?
mcqs.explanation: Xp11 translocation carcinoma contains neoplastic cells with clear cytoplasm with a papillary architecture on histopathology . It is also associated with Psammoma bodies .
