Histopathological findings in chronic viral hepatitis are: • Portal lymphocytic / lymphoplasmacytic inflammation • Interface activity - inflammatory cells cross the limiting plate and cause periportal hepatocyte injury • Portal, periportal , and portoportal bridging fibrosis932 Specific findings in viral hepatitis : • Hepatitis B - ground glass hepatocytes • Hepatitis C - lymphoid aggregates and steatosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with liver failure, which of the following tests is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum alkaline phosphatase is used to evaluate biliary excretory function. It is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes . Serum ammonia , activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and serum albumin are used to evaluate hepatic synthetic function. Prothrombin time (PT), aPTT and serum ammonia levels are increased in liver failure, whereas serum albumin level is decreased .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in the histopathological examination of the liver in patients with malaria ?
mcqs.explanation: Macronodular cirrhosis is not seen in the histopathological examination of patients with malaria . Histopathological changes in the liver in cases of malaria include the following : • Kupffer cell hyperplasia • Hemozoin pigment deposition within Kupffer cells and macrophages • Focal necrosis • Mild mononuclear portal infiltrate • Fatty change and periportal inflammation

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Identify the incorrect match.
mcqs.explanation: Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in acute hepatitis and yellow fever. Option A: Mallory–Denk bodies are eosinophilic materials made of keratin intermediate filaments. They are seen in alcoholic liver disease , non-alcoholic fatty liver disease , Wilson's disease , and chronic biliary tract diseases . Option C: Ground-glass hepatocytes are liver cells that have eosinophilic granular, glassy cytoplasm seen on light microscopy. The appearance is due to the swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum by HBsAg and is a diagnostic hallmark of chronic hepatitis B. Option D: Circumferential onion skin fibrosis around a degenerating bile -duct lumen is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis .933

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with ascites , melena, and splenomegaly is diagnosed with portal hypertension . Which of the following is not an intrahepatic cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Obstructive portal vein thrombosis is the prehepatic cause of portal hypertension . Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease , cirrhosis, and schistosomiasis are intrahepatic causes of portal hypertension. The most dominant cause is cirrhosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of liver histology in patients with non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis?

options.b: Thrombosis of the medium and small portal vein branches

mcqs.explanation: Bridging fibrosis is not seen in non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. In this condition, there is periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis. The fibrous septa end blindly in the lobule and do not bridge with other portal tracts, unlike those seen in cirrhosis. Idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (INCPH) is a rare disease characterized by intrahepatic portal hypertension in the absence of cirrhosis or other causes of liver disease and splanchnic venous thrombosis. A liver biopsy is essential in making a diagnosis of INCPH. The features observed are as follows : • Luminal narrowing or obliteration of portal vein branches • Micronodular transformation • Sinusoidal dilatation with formation of mega sinusoids • Periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Match the histopathological sections of liver and the different conditions.
mcqs.explanation: In the given image, images marked 1 is normal liver, 2 is alcoholic steatosis , 3 is micronodular cirrhosis and 4 is alcoholic hepatitis . Histopathological findings in the following conditions are: • Alcoholic steatosis : • A mix of small and large fat droplets • Ethanol inhibits fatty acid metabolism , leading to lipolysis and increased triglyceride . These triglycerides accumulate and cause steatosis . Liver enzymes are normal at this stage . • Micronodular cirrhosis: • The average nodule size is 3 mm in this close -up view, which is typical of the micronodular cirrhosis of alcoholic liver disease • Alcoholic hepatitis : • Mallory-Denk bodies - clumped , amorphous, eosinophilic material in ballooned hepatocytes . These inclusions are characteristic, but not a specific feature of alcoholic liver disease .934

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Match the following :
mcqs.explanation: The liver findings seen in the hepatotoxic drugs are:Drugs Liver findings Valproat e Microvesicular steatosis Allopurin ol Fibrin ring granuloma Amiodar one Mallory-Denk bodies Isoniazid Noncaseating epitheloid gran ulomas935

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Mutation in which of the following genes causes Wilson's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Wilson's disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene . It an autosomal recessive condition. The ATP7B gene is located on chromosome 13q . The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions: • Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin • Helps excrete free copper in bile .943 The resulting ATP7B deficiency leads to reduced bound copper and impaired free copper excretion. This causes excess deposition of free copper in the tissues , particularly in the liver, brain and eye . Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive condition leading to impaired absorption of copper and subsequent copper deficiency . Here, the mutation is in the ATP7A gene .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man with tremors and chronic hepatitis is found to have the following ophthalmic finding. This patient is also likely to have which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the Kayser -Fleischer ring. This,along with the background of hepatitis and neuropsychiatric features is characteristic of Wilson's disease . The patient is thus likely to have basal ganglia atrophy. In the majority of cases , neuropsychiatric manifestations follow hepatic manifestations . It is due to the deposition of free copper in the basal ganglia and cortex. Free copper deposition in the basal ganglia leads to bilateral degeneration and atrophy.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following would you use to screen an asymptomatic sibling of a patient with Wilson's disease?
mcqs.explanation: Genetic testing for the ATP7B gene is used to screen asymptomatic 1st and 2nd-degree relatives of patients with Wilson's disease . This helps to differentiate the heterozygous from the homozygous individuals. This can be useful in the early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms . Low serum ceruloplasmin , raised 24 hr urinary copper and Kayser -Fleischer rings are diagnostically helpful . Estimation of hepatic tissue copper is the gold standard for diagnosis. It is measured using neutron activation analysis / atomic absorption spectrometry .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old male patient presented with personality changes and jaundice . Slit-lamp examination confirmed the diagnosis of Wilson's disease . Which of the following statements is true regarding the condition?

options.a: Ceruloplasmin in blood increases and urinary copper excretion decreases
options.b: Ceruloplasmin in blood decreases and urinary copper excretion decreases
options.c: Ceruloplasmin in blood increases and urinary copper excretion increases
options.d: Ceruloplasmin in blood decreases and urinary copper excretion increases

mcqs.explanation: The ceruloplasmin level in the blood decreases , and the copper content in urine increases in Wilson's disease .Lab markers Change in Wilson's diseas e Reason Serum ceruloplas min \026\026 ATP7B deficiency results in r educed bound copper 24h urinary coppe r \027\027 Excess free copper excreted i n urine

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following stains can be used to demonstrate excess copper deposition in Wilson's disease?
mcqs.explanation: 944 Excess copper deposition in Wilson's disease is demonstrated by rhodanine stain. Microscopic findings in Wilson's disease include : • Fatty infiltration (macrovesicular) • Glycogen deposition in periportal hepatocytes • Macronodular cirrhosis in decompensated stages . Orcein stain is used to stain copper -associated proteins (eg : ceruloplasmin ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 yr old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below . This patient most likely suffers from ________
mcqs.explanation: The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. In the given scenario, the liver microscopy image shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's Prussian blue stain. Hemochromatosis is an inherited or acquired metabolic disorder caused by excessive iron absorption. Iron overload leads to the accumulation of iron in parenchymal organs such as the liver and pancreas followed by the heart, joints, and endocrine organs. The image below shows the triad of haemochromatosis.The image below is the liver microscopy image showing hepatocellular iron, stained with Perl's Prussian blue .945 The total body iron pool ranges from 2 to 6 gm in normal adults . In hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm, more than one-third of which accumulates in the liver.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis is found to have a mutation in the HFE gene . On which chromosome is it located ?
mcqs.explanation: HFE gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p). It is the most commonly mutated gene in patients with hereditary hemochromatosis. HFE encodes an HLA class I–like molecule that regulates the synthesis of hepcidin in hepatocytes . The most common HFE mutation is a cysteine -to-tyrosine substitution at amino acid 282 (C282Y).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man evaluated for chronic abdominal pain is found to have hepatomegaly and serum ferritin level of 1800 micro g/l. Which of the following complications is he at the greatest risk of developing ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemochromatosis. A patient with hemochromatosis is at risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma . Hepatocellular carcinoma is a significant cause of death in hemochromatosis. The risk is much greater than in the general population . The disease progression of hemochromatosis is as shown below :946

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding hemochromatosis?
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal hemochromatosis is not an inherited disease . It is a disease of unknown origin manifested by severe liver disease and extrahepatic hemosiderin deposition . It might be related to maternal alloimmune injury to the fetal liver. Adult hemochromatosis is generally a milder disease than the juvenile form. With treatment , life expectancy is normal . Bantu siderosis or African iron overload is due to dietary iron overload. Consumption of beer prepared in iron pots or drums is the cause of dietary iron overload. Skin pigmentation in hemochromatosis mostly results from increased melanin synthesis . This is due to iron deposition and not hemosiderin deposition . In severe hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm. More than one-third of this accumulates in the liver. In normal adults , it is in the range of 2 to 6 gms.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organs does not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis?
mcqs.explanation: The testes do not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis. Hypogonadism in hemochromatosis is not due to the deposition of iron in the testis . It is due to a derangement in the hypothalamic -pituitary axis. This results in decreased gonadotrophins and testosterone levels . The testis will appear small and atrophic. Deposition of hemosiderin is seen in the following organs in the decreasing order of severity : • Liver • Pancreas • Myocardium947 • Pituitary gland • Adrenal gland • Thyroid • Parathyroid gland • Joints • Skin

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old male patient with emphysema was found to have elevated liver transaminases. His liver biopsy image is given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario, the most likely diagnosis is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency . The liver biopsy image shows periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase -resistant round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes . These are characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency . It is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding that results in impaired secretion of \0371 antitrypsin into the serum. \0371AT deficiency results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase causing panacinar emphysema . It also causes liver disease as a consequence of an abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes . Cutaneous necrotizing panniculitis also occurs in a minor subset of patients . Hepatocellular carcinoma develops in 2% to 3% of cases . The image given is a photomicrograph of a liver biopsy from a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency . The PAS with diastase stain shows the diastase -resistant pink globules that are characteristic of this disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: On which chromosome is the gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin present ?
mcqs.explanation: 948 The gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin is located on the long arm of chromosome 14. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a plasma glycoprotein synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes . For \0371-antitrypsin genes , the general notation is "Pi" for "protease inhibitor." An alphabetic letter is given for the position on the isoelectric gel . This gene has different alleles that produce different amounts of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT). • M allele - normal levels of the AAT protein • S allele - moderately low levels • Z allele - very low levels The alleles are expressed in a codominant manner .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common clinically significant mutation causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common clinically significant mutation causing \0371-antitrypsin deficiency is PiZ. Homozygous individuals, with PiZZ , have only 10 % of normal circulating \0371-antitrypsin. So, they are at high risk of developing clinical disease . PiMM is the most common genotype seen in normal individuals, present in about 90% of individuals. PiS variant is clinically asymptomatic . Pi-null is a rare variant with no detectable serum alpha-1 antitrypsin.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: An 11 -year-old girl with persistently elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT ) has been diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis . Which of the following pathological features would you not expect in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Bile duct injury and granulomas are uncommon in autoimmune hepatitis except in case of overlap with primary biliary cirrhosis. Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH ) is characterised by extensive inflammation, fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis. The pathologic features include : • Emperipolesis - Lymphocytes and plasma cells within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes . • Interface hepatitis or piecemeal necrosis. • Rosette formation due to necrosis of groups of hepatocytes and resultant regeneration . The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic interface hepatitis .949

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false with regard to autoimmune hepatitis ?

options.a: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows antinuclear antibodies (ANA).
options.c: It can progress to liver failure.
options.d: Inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of plasma cells .

mcqs.explanation: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-liver kidney microsomal autoantibodies (anti-LKM1) and anti–liver cytosol -1 (ACL -1) antibodies not ANA. Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-nuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) and anti–soluble liver antigen / liver pancreas antigen (anti-SLA/LP ) antibodies . It less commonly shows anti-mitochondrial (AMA) antibodies . Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disorder characterized by continuing hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. It can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Histocompatibility haplotypes such as HLA -B1 , HLA -B8, HLA -DR3 , and HLA -DR4 are common in patients with autoimmune hepatitis .950 Histopathological features include : • Plasma cell predominance in inflammatory infiltrates • Extensive interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis) • Hepatocyte rosettes The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis showing characteristic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and interface hepatitis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following antibodies would you not expect to see in a patient with autoimmune hepatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Anti-TIF1 \034 antibodies are not associated with autoimmune hepatitis . Anti-TIF1 \034 antibodies are found in patients with dermatomyositis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Identify the incorrect match.
mcqs.explanation: Chronic hepatitis D is associated with anti-LKM 3 antibodies .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: The histopathological findings obtained after a liver biopsy is given below . What would be the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Onion-skin fibrosis is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis . The smaller ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis show a striking circumferential "onion skin" fibrosis around an increasingly atrophic duct lumen. This eventually leads to the obliteration by a "tombstone " scar. The image shows primary sclerosing cholangitis . There is a degenerating bile duct that is entrapped in the dense concentric onion-skin fibrosis.951

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of primary sclerosing cholangitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts . There is dilation of preserved segments . On histopathologic examination, large ducts show acute neutrophilic inflammation of the epithelium . The inflamed areas develop strictures . Small ducts show onion-skin fibrosis around the atrophic duct lumen. There is an obliteration of ducts by a tombstone scar.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with Sjogren's syndrome. Other associated conditions are: • Thyroiditis • Scleroderma • Rheumatoid arthritis • Raynaud phenomenon • Celiac disease PBC is an autoimmune disease . It is characterized by nonsuppurative, inflammatory destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts . Large intrahepatic ducts and the extrahepatic biliary tree are not involved. It is a disease of middle -aged women, with a female predominance of 9:1. Antimitochondrial antibodies are the most characteristic laboratory finding in PBC. Histopathologic examination shows diagnostic florid duct lesions . These are lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with or without granulomas centred around the bile duct . They also show Mallory–Denk bodies .952 The image given below shows primary biliary cholangitis .953

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver?
mcqs.explanation: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver.958 It appears as a red-blue , soft nodule , usually < 2 cm in diameter . It may be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for a metastatic tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain. She has been taking oral contraceptives for the past 7 years. CECT reveals an isodense lesion in the liver with homogenous enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal venous phase . Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.b: It can be associated with MODY -
options.c: Serum amyloid A may be upregulated
options.d: �o -catenin-activated adenoma has no risk of malignant transformation

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatic adenoma. �o -catenin-activated adenomas have a high risk of malignant transformation . Hepatic adenomas are benign tumors of hepatocytes . Spontaneous rupture of the hepatic adenoma may cause intraabdominal bleeding , which is a surgical emergency . Hepatic adenomas are classified into 3 subtypes : • HNF1-\037-inactivated adenomas - • No risk of malignant transformation • Often associated with oral contraceptive pill use (OCP) and MODY -3 • �o -catenin-activated adenoma - • High risk of malignant transformation • Associated with oral contraceptive pills (OCP) and anabolic steroids usage • Inflammatory adenomas - • Associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) • Upregulation of C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid A • % may have concomitant �o -catenin activating mutations • Moderate risk of malignant transformation The gross specimen of hepatic adenoma is shown below .959

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Patients with cirrhosis of the liver are at a higher risk of developing which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Dysplastic nodules are associated with liver cirrhosis. High grade dysplastic nodules may eventually develop into hepatocellular carcinoma in viral hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought with abdominal swelling . On examination, a mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant . Laboratory evaluation shows serum alpha-fetoprotein level of 1,50,000 ng/mL . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein level are suggestive of hepatoblastoma . Hepatoblastoma is the most common malignant liver tumor of early childhood , usually < years. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the most important clinical marker for hepatoblastoma. It remains the key clinical marker of malignant change, response to the treatment , and relapse . Histological section of hepatoblastoma showing proliferating hepatoblasts consisting of round epithelial type cells is given below .960

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Patients with all of the following are at a higher risk of developing hepatoblastoma except :

options.a: A 6-year-old child diagnosed with new-onset hypertension
options.b: A premature infant with low birth weight
options.c: A 5-year-old child diagnosed with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
options.d: A 9-year-old child with a family history of familial adenatomatous polyposis

mcqs.explanation: Hypertension is not a risk factor for hepatoblastoma . Risk factors for hepatoblastoma include : • Prematurity and low birth weight (LBW ) • Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following parameters indicates a good prognosis in hepatoblastoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Pure fetal histology hepatoblastoma is associated with a very good prognosis. They may be cured by surgical resection without adjuvant chemotherapy . Prognostic factors in hepatoblastoma include : Prematurity and low-birth weight (LBW ) are associated with hepatoblastoma but do not affect its outcome .Good prognosis Bad prognosis Low tumor stagePure fetal hi stology High tumor stageLow AFP le velsSmall cell undifferentiate d histologyRhabdoid features Vascular invasion961

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which one of the following syndromes is associated with a higher incidence of hepatoblastoma?
mcqs.explanation: Gardner syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome is associated with hepatoblastoma. Activation of WNT signaling plays a major role in hepatoblastomas . This occurs by a variety of mechanisms including mutations in APC gene . Hence , patients with FAP syndromes frequently develop hepatoblastomas . The following syndromes are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma : • Hereditary tyrosinemia • Alpha-1 antitrypsin defeciency • Familial hemochromatosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma is chronic hepatitis B virus infection . More than 85% of cases of hepatocellular carcinoma occur in countries with high rates of chronic hepatitis B virus infection . Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma are: • Hepatitis B virus • Hepatitis C virus • Alcohol • Aflatoxin • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency • Hemochromatosis • Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis • Tyrosinemia • Smoking Activation of �o -catenin and inactivation of p53 are the two most common early mutational events seen in hepatocellular carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following are the precursor lesions for hepatocellular carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Focal nodular hyperplasia and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are not precursors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The precursors of HCC inlcude : • Hepatocellular adenoma - especially those with �o -catenin-activating mutations • Small cell and large cell change - cellular dysplasias962 • Dysplastic nodules - low-grade and high-grade

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with chronic abdominal discomfort. Imaging reveals a solitary well -encapsulated hepatic mass with a central fibrous scar and stellate calcification. Further investigations reveal elevated neurotensin levels and negative hepatitis B serology . Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.a: Histology reveals oncocytic hepatocytes separated by collagen bundles
options.b: It is associated with a relatively good prognosis
options.c: Majority of these tumors are resectable
options.d: It is associated with liver cirrhosis

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibrolamellar carcinoma . It is usually not associated with liver cirrhosis. Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a distinctive and rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It usually occurs < 35 years of age . There is no gender predilection and no identifiable predisposing conditions. It has a good prognosis compared to the classical HCC. Majority (50-75 %) of these tumors are resectable. It usually presents as a single large, hard scirrhous tumor with fibrous bands coursing through it. Microscopically, it is composed of oncocytes growing in nests or cords separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagen bundles . The histological section of fibrolamellar carcinoma is given below . It shows malignant-appearing, oncocytic hepatocytes separated by dense bundles of collagen .963

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following agents is not associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to arsenic, thorotrast and vinyl chloride . Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm . There is equal gender predilection . The tumor may occur at any site , but most often involves skin, soft tissue , breast and liver. Various hepatic tumors and associated etiological agents are given below :Tumor Etiological agents Hepatocellular adenom a Oral contraceptives , anabolic steroids Hepatocellular carcino ma Alcohol, thorotrast Cholangiocarcinoma Thorotrast Angiosarcoma Thorotrast, vinyl chloride , ar senic

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common tumor of the liver?
mcqs.explanation: The most common tumors of the liver are metastatic tumors. The common primary sources of liver metastasis are: • Colon carcinoma • Breast carcinoma • Lung carcinoma964 • Pancreatic carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: A 53-year-old patient with anorexia and weight loss is found to have non-tender hepatomegaly on physical examination. CT scan of the abdomen shows multiple nodules in the liver and investigations reveal elevated ALP and AST levels , with no elevations in AFP. Which of the following is the most likely cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a metastatic liver tumor. Metastases are the most common malignant neoplasms of the liver. The most common primary sources are the colon, breast, lung, and pancreas, although any cancer at any site of the body may spread to the liver. Patients with metastases typically have multiple nodules replacing the normal liver parenchyma. There may be no clinical or laboratory evidence of hepatic insufficiency . Often , the only telltale sign of secondaries in the liver will be hepatomegaly .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk for cholangiocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: Typhoid carriers are not at risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma. Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary malignant tumor of the liver after hepatocellular carcinoma . It is a malignancy of the biliary tree , arising from bile ducts within and outside of the liver. The risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma include the following : • Infestation by liver flukes (particularly Opisthorchis and Clonorchis ) • Primary sclerosing cholangitis , and other chronic inflammatory diseases of the large bile ducts • Chronic hepatitis B and C infections • Cirrhosis • Inflammatory bowel disease • Diabetes mellitus , obesity , non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) • Alcohol and tobacco • Precursor lesions - • Biliary intraepithelial neoplasias • Mucinous cystic neoplasms • Intraductal papillary biliary neoplasia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: What does Klatskin tumor refer to?
mcqs.explanation: Klatskin tumors are extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas located in the perihilar region. These tumors are located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts . Distal tumors arise in the common bile duct posterior to the duodenum . Regardless of the site , the prognosis is poor.965

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.chapter: Neoplasms of Liver and Biliary tract
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding gallbladder carcinoma ?

options.b: Gallstones are the most important risk factor
options.c: Her2 overexpression is seen in about 2/3 of the cases
options.d: It usually has a good prognosis

mcqs.explanation: Gallbladder carcinoma carries a poor prognosis because it is typically detected late due to non-specific symptoms . Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. Most carcinomas of the gall bladder are adenocarcinomas. Gallbladder cancer is at least twice as common in women than in men. The most important risk factor for gallbladder cancer (besides gender and ethnicity ) is gallstones , which are present in 95% of cases . Her-2/neu is overexpressed in around 2/3 of the cases , and therefore , they can be targeted for therapy .966

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder is the Phrygian cap. It refers to an inward folding of the fundus of the gallbladder . It is named for its resemblance to a conical hat.970 The other common congenital anomalies of the gallbladder are: • Agenesis - absence of all or any portion of the hepatic or common bile ducts • Biliary atresia - hypoplastic narrowing of biliary channels • Choledochal cysts - congenital dilations of the intra and/or extrahepatic biliary system

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old man presented with severe right upper quadrant pain for 8 hours associated with nausea and vomiting. A diagnosis of acute cholecystitis was made and he underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy . The specimen is shown below . This finding is associated with all the following conditions except :
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows pigmented gallstones , which are not associated with hyperlipidemia syndromes. Pigmented gallstones are made of bilirubin and calcium salts. They can occur in: • Chronic hemolytic syndromes971 • Ileal resection • Biliary infection • Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency Cholesterol stones are made of crystalline cholesterol monohydrates . Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for the development of cholesterol gallstones . The following image shows cholesterol gallstones :

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old man was rushed to the ER with right upper quadrant pain for the last 6 hours. He had been diagnosed with gallstones 10 years ago but had not undergone any treatment. Imaging revealed gallbladder wall thickening. He underwent a cholecystectomy which revealed a shrunken and nodular gallbladder with a thick wall. The following was noted on microscopy. This condition is associated with:

options.a: Dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario of chronic cholecystitis and image showing lipid -laden xanthoma cells are suggestive of xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis . This condition results due to the rupture of Rokitansky –Aschoff sinuses .972 Rokitansky –Aschoff sinuses are bile -filled outpouchings of the gallbladder mucosa through the gallbladder wall. They develop in reaction to chronic inflammation of the gallbladder . Eventually , they may rupture into the wall of the gallbladder . This results in the accumulation of macrophages that have ingested biliary phospholipids , which are called xanthoma cells .Chronic cholecystitis may have other sequelae : • Porcelain gallbladder - dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall • Hyalinizing cholecystitis - replacement of the gallbladder wall by dense fibrosis, with or without calcification (leads to higher incidence of gallbladder carcinoma ) • Hydrops of the gallbladder - atrophic, obstructed , dilated gallbladder containing clear fluid Acute cholecystitis includes the following variants : • Emphysematous cholecystitis - acute infection of the gallbladder by gas-forming organisms • Acalculous cholecystitis - due to gallbladder stasis and ischemia

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas?
mcqs.explanation: Pancreas divisum is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas. The pancreas develops by fusion of the larger dorsal and smaller ventral pancreatic buds . The dorsal duct is the dominant duct during development and it drains into the minor papilla . The ventral duct drains into the major papilla . After fusion, the following ducts are formed: • Main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) - formed by fusion of ducts of dorsal and ventral buds , drains into the major papilla • Accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini ) - formed by the proximal portion of the dorsal duct , drains into the minor papilla In pancreas divisum, the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse . Hence , the majority of the pancreas continues to drain through the dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor973 papilla while the ventral duct , along with the bile duct , drains into the major papilla . These patients are more prone to pancreatitis .The other congenital anomalies of the pancreas are: • Annular pancreas - band-like ring of normal pancreatic tissue encircling 2nd part of duodenum , may cause obstruction • Ectopic pancreas - common in stomach, duodenum , and jejunum (found in about 2% of postmortem exams) • Agenesis - rarely seen , associated with mutations of PDX1 (homeobox gene )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old boy presented with severe abdominal pain for the last 24 hours with radiation to the upper back. He has had multiple similar episodes since his childhood . Family history revealed similar episodes in the father. Investigations revealed elevated serum levels of amylase and lipase . Which of the following statements is not true about the given condition?

options.a: It is commonly associated with mutations in the PRSS1 gene
options.b: This boy has a 40 % lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer
options.c: It may be associated with mutations in the CFTR gene
options.d: Hypocalcemia is an important triggering factor this condition

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario in a young patient with positive family history of similar episodes is suggestive of hereditary pancreatitis . Acute episodes of pancreatitis can be precipitated by hypercalcemia , not hypocalcemia . The following genes are implicated in hereditary pancreatitis : • Gain-of-function mutation in trypsinogen gene (PRSS1 ) - most common • Loss-of-function mutation in trypsin inhibitor gene (SPINK1) • Loss of CFTR - abnormal secretions that promote protein plugging , duct obstruction, leading to pancreatitis Hereditary pancreatitis is associated with a 40% lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presented with vague abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss for the last 6 months. He also reported spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules at different locations on his body. On examination, thrombophlebitis and epigastric tenderness were noted . Investigations revealed elevated serum CEA and CA 19-9. Which of the following genetic mutations is most frequently associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: 974 The presence of the above clinical symptoms with migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and elevated serum levels of CEA and CA 19-9 in an elderly man point to a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. The most frequently associated mutation with this condition is K-RAS. It is attributed to the production of platelet -aggregating factors and procoagulants from the tumor or its necrotic products . Both venous and arterial thrombi can occur. Venous thrombi can embolize to the lungs . Molecular alterations involved in pancreatic carcinogenesis are: Following genes are associated with an inherited predisposition to pancreatic cancer: • BRCA2 mutation - pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and ovarian cancers • PRSS1 mutation - pancreatic carcinoma secondary to hereditary pancreatitisGene Type Chromo some KRAS(most common oncoge ne) Oncogene (activated by point mutation) 12p CDKN2A(most common tum or-suppressor gene ) Tumor suppressor gene 9p TP53 Tumor suppressor gene 17p SMAD4 Tumor suppressor gene 18q

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist was studying a biopsy specimen from a patient with pancreatic cancer. He observed that it resembled ovarian stroma. What is it likely to be?
mcqs.explanation: Mucinous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas have dense stroma, similar to the ovarian stroma. These tumors have large cystic cavities filled with thick, tenacious mucin. They are lined by columnar, mucin-producing epithelium with dense stroma. This results in similarity to ovarian stroma. They usually arise in the tail of the pancreas and can be precursors to invasive carcinomas. They are associated with mutations in the KRAS oncogene , and the tumor-suppressor genes TP53 and RNF43.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of these are characteristic features of pancreatic carcinoma except :

options.a: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor
options.b: Carcinoma of body of pancreas often present with jaundice

mcqs.explanation: Patients with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas develop jaundice due to obstruction of the biliary tract. Cigarette smoking doubles the risk of pancreatic cancer and is the leading preventable cause . The clinical features depend on the location of the tumor. • Head - painless , palpable gallbladder with mild jaundice is suggestive of malignancy (according to Courvoisier's law)975 • Body and tail - may remain asymptomatic until later stages as they do not impinge on the biliary tract and do not cause jaundice Other common pathological features of this condition are: • Desmoplastic reaction - growth of fibrous or connective tissue • Perineural invasion , as well as lymphatic and large vessel invasion

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following have the highest risk of pancreatic cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome have the highest risk of pancreatic cancer. mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of fistulization in GIT ?
mcqs.explanation: The esophagus is the most common site of fistulization in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT ). A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea. The fistula is usually present near the tracheal bifurcation, with or without esophageal atresia. A blind proximal pouch with a distal tracheooesophageal fistula is the most common type of tracheoesophageal fistula (Type C). % of the patients have associated VACTERL anomalies (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal , renal, and limb).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?
mcqs.explanation: 986 The most frequent site of the ectopic gastric mucosa is the upper third of the esophagus , where it is referred to as an inlet patch . It is congenital and mostly asymptomatic. Occasionally , it can release acid, which can result in dysphagia , esophagitis , Barrett esophagus, or, rarely, adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old man came with complaints of difficulty in swallowing and a persistent feeling of something stuck in his throat. He also reports bad breath and regurgitation of food particles . Barium swallow revealed the following . This condition occurs due to a defect in which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and barium swallow image are diagnostic of Zenker 's diverticulum. It occurs due to a defect in the Killian's triangle (Killian's dehiscence ). Killian's triangle is an anatomical triangular area bordered superiorly by the firm oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle and inferiorly by the horizontal fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle . It is located immediately above the upper esophageal sphincter . Although the Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is an anterolateral defect , it is rarely symptomatic .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All of the following may be seen in patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome except :
mcqs.explanation: Paterson–Brown–Kelly or Plummer–Vinson syndrome is associated with non-progressive dysphagia , especially with incompletely chewed food. This syndrome is common in women aged >40 years. The other components of this syndrome are: • Post-cricoid webs in the upper esophagus • Iron -deficiency anemia • Glossitis • Cheilosis Esophageal webs are idiopathic , semi-circumferential lesions composed of fibrovascular connective tissue and overlying epithelium. They are usually limited to the proximal esophagus and may cause obstruction. They are associated with: • Plummer–Vinson syndrome • Gastroesophageal reflux disease • Chronic graft-versus-host disease • Blistering skin diseases The images below show endoscopic and barium swallow appearances of esophageal webs .987

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presented with complaints of difficulty in swallowing solid foods . An upper GI endoscopy revealed the following finding just above the gastroesophageal junction. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows an esophageal ring. Rings located above the gastroesophageal junction are classified as type A esophageal rings. Esophageal rings are circumferential and thick. They include mucosa, submucosa , and occasionally, hypertrophic muscularis propria. There are 3 types : Steakhouse syndrome refers to intermittent food impaction causing complete obstruction due to the presence of Schatzki rings.988 Type A rings Type BorSchatzki rings Type C rings Caused by normal physiologi c smooth muscle contraction s Most common typeAssociate d with hiatus hernia Rare findingsIndentations on radiographic studies due to diaphragmatic crural pressur e Seenabovethe gastroesophag eal junction (GEJ) in the dist al esophagusCovered by squa mous mucosa Located at thesquamocolumn arjunctionCovered by gastric cardia-type mucosa Found in the mostdistalporti on of the esophagus

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old woman is being evaluated for dysphagia and chest pain. She traveled to Brazil on a business trip 5 months ago. Barium swallow reveals the following finding. Which of the following could have caused this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and barium swallow showing the bird-beak appearance are suggestive of achalasia cardia. With respect to this patient 's travel history, Chagas' disease due to infection with Trypanosoma cruzi must be suspected . The infection destroys the myenteric plexus which results in failure of peristalsis and esophageal dilatation. Duodenal , colonic, and ureteric myenteric plexuses can also be affected by Chagas' disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about the pathology of achalasia cardia?

options.c: Decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal part of esophagus
options.d: Decreased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter

mcqs.explanation: Achalasia cardia is characterized by decreased release of NO(nitric oxide) and VIP (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide ) in the distal part of esophagus . Normally, NO and VIP are secreted by the inhibitory neurons of the Auerbach's plexus in the distal esophagus. This leads to relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). In achalasia cardia, these inhibitory neurons degenerate leading to decreased release of NO and VIP . This causes increased LES tone. The triad of achalasia cardia is as follows: • Incomplete relaxation of LES • Increased tone of LES • Absent peristalsis (aperistalisis )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A mother brought her 8-year-old son to the OPD with complaints of refusal to eat and poor weight gain. The child complained that food often gets stuck in his throat. Endoscopy revealed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and image showing multiple stacked esophageal rings are characteristic of eosinophilic esophagitis . mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect about eosinophilic esophagitis ?

options.a: Majority of patients have associated atopic conditions
options.b: Feline esophagus is an endoscopic finding
options.c: Treatment of choice is systemic steroids
options.d: May be associated with food products like cow's milk and soy products

mcqs.explanation: Treatment of choice are proton pump inhibitors, which when started as primary therapy is effective in 30 - 50 % of affected individuals. Additionally , elimination of allergenic proteins from diet as it is is associated with atopy and exposure to food allergens like cow's milk and soy products . Swallowed topical steroids are used as well . mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to you with progressive heartburn and difficulty in swallowing . She also describes episodes of painful blanching and bluish discoloration of her fingers and toes on exposure to cold. The following findings are noted on examination. Antibodies to which of the following are most likely to be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The symptoms of the patient in the above case scenario and the image showing calcinosis are the characteristic findings of the CREST syndrome or limited scleroderma. Patients with this condition characteristically have antibodies directed against centromeric proteins (anti-centromere antibodies ). CREST syndrome is characterized by the following : • Calcinosis • Raynaud phenomenon • Esophageal dysmotility • Sclerodactyly • Telangiectasia In the esophagus , progressive atrophy and fibrous replacement of the muscularis propria leads to hypomotility and dysphagia . The lower 2/3 of the esophagus develops a rubber-hose –like inflexibility . The associated dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter gives rise to gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett metaplasia , and stricture .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presented with blood in his vomitus. He gives a history of binge drinking followed by multiple episodes of vomiting the prior night. He is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?

options.a: It is due to longitudinal mucosal tears
options.b: The gastroesophageal musculature fails to relax
options.c: The tears cross the gastroesophageal junction

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a Mallory–Weiss tear. They require only conservative management and healing tends to be rapid and complete . They are longitudinal mucosal tears that may cross the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ). Forceful retching or vomiting along with failure of reflex relaxation of the gastroesophageal musculature results in tears involving the mucosa and submucosa . It usually occurs secondary to conditions like acute alcohol intoxication or hyperemesis gravidarum . Boerhaave syndrome is a much more serious disorder characterized by transmural rupture of the distal esophagus. This results in acute mediastinitis with severe chest pain, tachypnea , and shock. Such patients generally require urgent surgical intervention.991

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most frequent cause of esophagitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most frequent cause of esophagitis is reflux of gastric acid into the lower esophagus . The most common cause of gastroesophageal reflux is transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Reflux esophagitis leads to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). This can cause Barrett's esophagus and eventually can cause adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which organism can cause esophageal infections in healthy individuals?
mcqs.explanation: Esophagitis in healthy individuals can be caused by the Herpes simplex virus. However, it is relatively uncommon. In immunosuppressed individuals, infections can be caused by: • Herpes simplex virus • Cytomegalovirus • Candida

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Punched -out ulcers in the esophagus are caused by:
mcqs.explanation: Infection with Herpes simplex virus (HSV ) typically results in punched -out ulcers in the esophagus . HSV esophagitis commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients . For diagnosis, the biopsy sample should be taken from the edge of the ulcer. The following microscopic findings are noted : • Ballooning degeneration • Ground-glass changes in nuclei • Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusion bodies992 Note : CMV esophagitis causes shallow ulcerations . The biopsy is taken from the base of the ulcer and shows characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions bodies .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old patient with haematemesis is found to have the following finding on upper GI endoscopy . He has traveled to Zambia several times over the past 3 years. What could be the likely cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing bleeding esophageal varices are suggestive of hepatic schistosomiasis . It is the second most common cause of varices worldwide . Liver cirrhosis, mostly in association with alcoholic liver disease , is the most common cause of varices.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: All are true about Barrett oesophagus except :

options.b: Seen in 10 % of individuals with symptomatic GERD
options.c: Increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma

mcqs.explanation: Barrett's esophagus increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma . Barrett's esophagus is a complication of GERD and it is estimated to occur in as many as 10 % of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Microscopically , it is seen as the replacement of the squamous esophageal epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia ).The following images show endoscopic and microscopic images of Barrett's esophagus :993

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man with chronic dyspepsia underwent upper GI endoscopy . The biopsy findings are shown below . What is the special stain that has been used ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image is of Barrett's esophagus showing intestinal metaplasia . The special stain used here is Alcian blue , which stains the acid mucin present in the goblet cells .
