mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with severe emphysema underwent lung volume reduction surgery. The resected specimen is shown below . What type of emphysema is this?
mcqs.explanation: The given gross image is characteristic of centriacinar emphysema .1094 In paraseptal emphysema subpleural spaces are mainly affected (shown below ).1095 In panacinar emphysema all air spaces within acini are evenly enlarged (shown below ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with COPD, the emphysematous damage is most likely to involve which of the following structures ?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) usually have centriacinar emphysema which involves respiratory bronchioles. Emphysema is classified into four major types : • Centriacinar • Panacinar • Paraseptal • Irregular1096

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea , chronic cough with sputum , and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below . Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?
mcqs.explanation: The above gross specimen shows emphysematous damage involving enlargement of the entire acinus suggestive of panacinar emphysema. It is caused due to alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency . In panacinar (panlobular) emphysema, the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli. It occurs commonly in the lower zones and in the anterior margins of the lung and is most severe at the bases . The image below shows panacinar emphysema .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man is being evaluated for dyspnea and cough for 2 months. He is not a smoker. Workup revealed emphysematous changes at lung bases . He reports that his father and uncles were diagnosed with liver failure and lung disease at relatively young ages . Where is the gene encoding the defective protein located ?
mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of \0371-antitrypsin deficiency . The \0371-antitrypsin is encoded by the proteinase inhibitor (Pi) locus on chromosome 14. \0371-AT is a polymorphic gene located on chromosome 14. It is part of a larger family of structurally unique serine protease inhibitors, referred to as serpins. The most common clinically significant mutation in \0371-antitrypsin deficiency is PiZZ . \0371-antitrypsin, normally present in serum, tissue fluids , and macrophages is a major inhibitor of proteases (particularly elastase ) secreted by neutrophils during inflammation. The absence of \0371- antitrypsin activity results in excessive digestion of elastic tissue by elastase . Patients with \0371-antitrypsin deficiency have a markedly increased tendency to develop panacinar emphysema .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the normal value of y/x in the following representation ?
mcqs.explanation: 1097 In the above image, y/x denotes the ratio of the thickness of the submucosal gland layer to that of the bronchial wall. This is called as Reid index and it is normally 0.4. It is increased in chronic bronchitis.Chronic bronchitis is defined by the presence of a persistent productive cough for at least 3 consecutive months in at least 2 consecutive years. The single most important cause is cigarette smoking. The distinctive features of chronic bronchitis are as follows : • Hypersecretion of mucus • Hypertrophy of submucosal glands • Goblet -cell hyperplasia • Inflammation Difference between clinical presentation of emphysema and chronic bronchitis:Predominant Bronchitis Predominant Emphysema Age (year) 40-45 50-75 Dyspnea Mild ; late Severe; early Cough Early; copious sputum Late; scanty sputum Infections Common Occasional Respiratory insufficiency Repeated Terminal Cor pulmonale Common Rare; terminal Airway resistance Increased Normal or slightly increased Elastic recoil Normal Low Chest radiograph Prominent vessels ; large hear t Hyperinflation ; small heart Appearance Blue bloater Pink puffer1098

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man was brought to the ED with fever, cough with expectoration , and difficulty in breathing for 1 day. He is a chronic smoker and he has had similar progressive symptoms for the last 4 years. Past PFT findings showed reduced FEV1 and increased RV with normal diffusion capacity . Which of the following is the most common organism implicated in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario gives a picture of acute exacerbation of COPD. The most common bacterial cause of acute COPD exacerbation is Haemophilus influenzae . Moraxella is the second most common bacterial cause of acute exacerbation of COPD.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presented with recurrent episodes of breathlessness , wheeze , and chest tightness . Auscultation of the chest revealed bilateral wheeze . Sputum microscopy reveals the following . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the sputum microscopy showing Charcot–Leyden crystals (arrows in below image), lakes of mucus, and numerous eosinophils , are diagnostic of bronchial asthma.Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction caused by airway hyperresponsiveness to a variety of stimuli. Atopic asthma is caused by a TH2 and IgE-mediated immunologic reaction to environmental allergens (type -1 hypersensitivity reaction). Triggers for non-atopic asthma are less clear but include viral infections and inhaled air pollutants . Genetic susceptibility for developing asthma: • Chromosome 5q - site of the susceptibility locus for asthma • IL -13 gene polymorphisms (on 5q chromosome) - most consistent associations with asthma or allergic disease • IL -4 receptor gene variants - associated with atopy , elevated total serum IgE, and asthma The sputum of patients with bronchial asthma shows : • Charcot–Leyden crystals - made of an eosinophilic membrane protein called galectin 10 • Curschmann spirals - spirals of mucus plugs from subepithelial mucous gland ducts or bronchioles1099 • Creola bodies - desquamated epithelial cells • Numerous eosinophils Note : The hygiene hypothesis was previously used to explain the development of asthma and other hypersensitivity disorders.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A resected specimen of a lung is shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image above shows markedly distended bronchi involving the middle and lower lobe of the lung which is seen in bronchiectasis . Bronchiectasis is a suppurative lung disease with abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi. It is an end-stage condition of various diseases that result in destruction of the bronchial wall and its surrounding supporting tissues . The normal clearing mechanisms are impaired, either due to congenital causes or due to bronchial obstruction. This results in pooling of secretions , secondary infection , and inflammation, often with necrosis, fibrosis, and eventually cystic dilation of airways up to four times the normal size. Note : Kartagener syndrome is a primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Transbronchial biopsy from a patient showed the following microscopic finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image above shows alveolar spaces filled with balls of fibroblasts (Masson bodies ). This is characteristically seen in cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP). Masson bodies are polypoid plugs of loose organizing connective tissue within alveolar ducts , alveoli, and bronchioles along with foci of fibrosis.1100 The clinical presentation of COP is the development of nonspecific systemic and respiratory symptoms . It is associated with filling of the lung alveoli that is visible on a chest X-ray as patchy unilateral or bilateral consolidation. COP was previously known as bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world?
mcqs.explanation: Silicosis is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world. Silicosis is caused by the inhalation of crystalline silica (e.g., quartz ). Individuals involved with the concrete work, sandblasting , stone carvers , and jewelers using chalk molds are at high risk . Pneumoconioses encompass a group of chronic fibrosing diseases of the lung resulting from exposure to organic and inorganic particulates , most commonly mineral dust .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common manifestation of asbestosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure . They are well -circumscribed plaques of dense collagen , often containing calcium. They develop most frequently on the parietal pleura and over the domes of the diaphragm. They do not contain asbestos bodies , and only rarely occur in persons without prior asbestos exposure . Asbestos occurs in two distinct forms - serpentine chrysotile (more common) and amphibole (more pathogenic ). Exposure may result in the following conditions: • Localized fibrous plaques or, rarely, diffuse pleural fibrosis • Pleural effusions • Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis ) • Lung carcinoma • Mesotheliomas • Extrapulmonary neoplasms including laryngeal, ovarian , and colon carcinomas The image below shows fibrous pleural plaques seen on the diaphragmatic pleural surface in asbestosis .1101

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient working in a factory presented with lung fibrosis and thickening of pleura . Biopsy was done. Diagnosis from the histopathology picture is:
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing typical asbestos bodies are suggestive of asbestosis . Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis associated with asbestos exposure . The disease -causing capabilities of the different forms of asbestos depend on concentration, size, shape , and solubility . This condition is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis. Asbestos bodies are a typical finding. They are golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods with a translucent center . They consist of asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material and arise when these fibers are phagocytosed by macrophages .1102 Other inorganic particulates may become coated with similar iron-protein complexes and are called ferruginous bodies .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients A, B, and C presented to the OPD with symptoms of progressive dyspnea and cough . Further history and workup revealed the following findings. Who among them is more susceptible to developing tuberculosis ?
mcqs.explanation: Patient B is a worker in the sandblasting industry with eggshell calcification on x-ray. This is suggestive of silicosis . Patients with silicosis have a higher risk of tuberculosis as the crystalline silica impairs the ability of pulmonary macrophages to kill phagocytosed mycobacteria. mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presented with dyspnea and cough . Chest X-ray revealed irregular linear densities , particularly in both lower lobes . Histopathological examination of lung biopsy is shown below . This patient has a higher risk of developing :
mcqs.explanation: The image shows golden -brown, beaded rods with a translucent center called asbestos bodies which are seen in asbestosis . These patients are at risk of developing both lung1103 carcinoma and mesothelioma .Asbestosis is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis and the presence of multiple asbestos bodies . Option A: Centrilobular emphysema may develop in simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis . Option B: Increased susceptibility to tuberculosis is seen in silicosis . Option C: Occupational asthma may be triggered by fumes (epoxy resins, plastics ), organic and chemical dust (wood , cotton, platinum), gases (toluene ), or other chemicals (formaldehyde, penicillin products ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of low-grade fever, dry cough , and progressive dyspnea . Examination reveals the following painless skin lesion. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy . Lung biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

options.d: Anergy to common skin test antigens

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and image showing the lesion of lupus pernio point towards sarcoidosis. It is a multisystemic disease characterized by polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia . Lupus pernio is seen in cutaneous sarcoidosis and presents as infiltrated erythematoviolaceous plaques involving the nose, cheeks , ears, lips, forehead , and fingers. On the cheeks , telangiectasia is characteristic. It is usually painless . As it does not ulcerate , it is not as mutilating as lupus vulgaris. Immunological abnormalities include : • Polyclonal hyperglobulinemia • A CD4/CD8 ratio > 3.5 • T- cell expansion and macrophage activation • Impaired dendritic cell function • Anergy to common skin tests . The hallmarks of sarcoidosis include :1104 • B/L hilar lymphadenopathy • Non-caseating granulomas • Lupus pernio • Erythema nodosum (acute sarcoidosis) Syndromes associated with sarcoidosis are: • Mikulicz syndrome - sarcoidosis combined with uveoparotid involvement • Lofgren's syndrome - acute presentation of sarcoidosis, consisting of arthritis, erythema nodosum, and bilateral hilar adenopathy The image below shows the characteristic non-caseating sarcoid granuloma.The image below shows stellate inclusions known as asteroid bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.1105 The image below shows laminated concretions composed of calcium and proteins known as Schaumann bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.1106

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common gene mutation associated with pulmonary hypertension ?
mcqs.explanation: Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2 ) is the most common gene mutation in pulmonary hypertension . Inactivating mutations in this gene are found in 75 % of the familial cases of pulmonary hypertension , and 25% of sporadic cases . The BMPR2 receptor is a cell surface protein belonging to the TGF-�o receptor superfamily . It is involved in the regulation of growth , differentiation , and apoptosis of pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells . Due to the mutation, there is enhanced proliferation and reduced apoptosis of vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells leading to pulmonary hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old man presented with a persistent dry cough and progressive dyspnea . HRCT showed a crazy-paving pattern. Microscopy of BAL aspirate is shown below . Antibodies against which of the following are seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and microscopy showing alveoli filled with a dense , amorphous, protein-lipid granular precipitate are suggestive of autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP). It is caused by circulating neutralizing antibodies specific for granulocyte -macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).1107 PAP is a condition characterized by the accumulation of surfactants in alveoli and terminal airways. It can be due to impaired clearance or abnormal production of surfactants. PAP can be of three forms: • Primary (most common): There is impaired GM-CSF-dependent surfactant clearance by the alveolar macrophages . It can be due to: • Autoantibodies against GM-CSF (acquired/idiopathic /autoimmune PAP) • Mutation in GM-CSF receptors (hereditary PAP) • Secondary: There is a reduction in the number or ability of alveolar macrophages that causes impaired surfactant clearance. It can be due to: • Silicosis • Immunodeficiency disorders • Hematopoietic disorders and malignancies1108 • Congenital : It affects neonates and children. There is abnormal surfactant production due to mutation in the genes coding for: • Surfactant protein B • Surfactant protein C • ATP binding cassette protein member 3

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old patient presented with cough , fatiguability , and weight loss. He was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on bronchoscopy . The resected specimen had a hilar lymph node that was 1cm in size and showed a black pigment . What is the black pigment likely to be?
mcqs.explanation: 1109 The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment . The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles . The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes . This accumulates and causes the blackening of the lung tissues or anthracosis. It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles , such as coal mines. It is also the most common exogenous pigment found in the human body as a result of air pollution in urban areas. The aggregates of the carbon dust may induce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker's pneumoconiosis . The following image shows anthracosis with deposition of black carbon particles , within the cytoplasm of macrophages .1110 Option B: Melanin is brown-black in color which occurs as a result of oxidation of tyrosine in melanocytes, as shown in the following histopathology of a lymph node.Option C: Lipochrome or lipofuscin (brown lipid ) is seen as a yellow -brown pigment in histopathological sections of the liver and heart of normal aging patients , patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia. It is derived through lipid peroxidation and indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. The following image shows a cardiac myocyte with fine yellow -brown lipofuscin granules in the perinuclear region.1111 Option D: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived golden -yellow colored pigment seen in conditions associated with iron overload such as hemochromatosis. The following image shows extensive intra-alveolar hemosiderin deposition following pulmonary hemorrhage.1112

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.a: The most common cancer worldwide is lung cancer
options.b: The most common malignant tumors of the lung are metastases
options.c: The most common cause of cancer mortality worldwide is lung cancer
options.d: The lung is the most common site of metastatic neoplasms

mcqs.explanation: According to Globocan 2020 , the most common cancer worldwide is breast cancer. However, lung cancer remains the leading overall cause of cancer mortality. Lung cancers: • The most common malignant tumors of the lung are metastases / secondaries . • The most common primary malignant tumor of the lung is bronchogenic cancer. • The most common histology is adenocarcinoma (43.8%), followed by squamous cell (26 .2%).1117

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common symptom seen in patients with lung cancer?
mcqs.explanation: The major presenting complaints of lung cancer patients are cough (75 %), weight loss (40%), chest pain (40%), and dyspnea (20 %). mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Histopathological findings of a lung tumor biopsy are shown below . Which of the following is the most sensitive and specific marker of this tumor?[Image unavailable]
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows keratin pearls and islands of large polygonal malignant cells . These as seen in squamous cell carcinoma of the lungs . P40 is the most sensitive and specific marker for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lungs . Other markers include cytokeratin 5/6 and P63. TTF -1 and napsin-A are the markers for adenocarcinoma. Chromogranin , synaptophysin , and CD56 are the markers for small cell lung carcinoma . Note : The 2015 World Health Organization Classification of Lung Tumors has made a recommendation that at least one antibody each for squamous (P40 or P63) and glandular (e.g. TTF -1) differentiation should be used for an initial workup. Thus a simple panel of TTF -1 and p40 may be able to classify most non-small cell carcinoma -not otherwise specified cases .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which is the most aggressive type of lung cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Small-cell carcinoma of the lung is the most aggressive type of lung cancer. This tumor originates from neuroendocrine progenitor cells (Kulchitsky cells ), which are present in the lining bronchial epithelium . Histopathological examination of small cell lung carcinoma shows : • Clusters of small cells with scant cytoplasm • Ill-defined cell borders • Finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern) • Absent or inconspicuous nucleoli The cells are round, oval, or spindle -shaped , and nuclear molding is prominent. The image below shows the histopathological findings of small cell lung carcinoma .1119

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 53-year-old man who is a chronic smoker is diagnosed with lung carcinoma . Histopathology of the lung tissue is shown in the image below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical features and the histopathology showing the Azzopardi effect are suggestive of a small cell carcinoma of the lung. Azzopardi effect is described as basophilic staining of vascular walls due to encrustation by DNA from necrotic tumor cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Non-smoker patients with lung carcinoma are most likely to have a mutation in which of the following genes?
mcqs.explanation: Non-smoker patients with lung carcinoma are most likely to have a mutation in the EGFR gene . mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of bloody cough , dyspnea , and weight loss. During the evaluation, a CT-guided lung biopsy reveals the following picture . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of adenocarcinoma lung. It is the most common form of lung cancer. It is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation . The tumor cells produce mucin. It is usually located peripherally (it arises from the terminal bronchiole). Molecular genetics show frequent mutations in EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, and RET (Receptor tyrosine kinase genes ) or KRAS mutations. Histologically , lepidic growth patterns are seen . It refers to the pattern of spread of the tumor in which the tumor cells "crawl" along normal -appearing alveolar septae and resembles butterflies resting on a fence . Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns , including acinar , lepidic , papillary, micropapillary, and solid with mucin formation. Tumor cells are positive for mucin and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF -1) Tumors 3 cm or less in diameter characterized by lepidic growth pattern without stromal invasion are now called adenocarcinoma in situ (formerly called bronchoalveolar carcinoma ).1120 The image below shows histopathological findings of adenocarcinoma of the lung.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would be positive in a patient with adenocarcinoma lung?
mcqs.explanation: Thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF -1), mucin, and napsin-A are positive in adenocarcinoma lung. TTF -1 is required for normal lung development . It can be used to distinguish primary adenocarcinoma of the lungs (TTF -1 positive) from other histological types of lung cancers, metastatic adenocarcinoma, and mesothelioma (TTF -1 negative ). P40 and P63 are the markers for squamous cell carcinoma . Chromogranin , synaptophysin , and CD56 are the markers for small cell lung carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 75 -year-old man presents with a cough and shortness of breath. He has been working in a shipping factory for 30 years. On x-ray, a mass is seen in the right apical region of the lung. A biopsy sample is taken from the mass. Which of the following tumor markers is likely to be positive in this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Calretinin is most likely to be positive in this tumour as the given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma . Malignant mesothelioma is a rare malignant tumour of the pleura , associated with heavy asbestos exposure (shipping factory). The lifetime risk of developing mesothelioma in heavily exposed individuals is as high as 7% to 10 %. It has strong male predilection (3:1). There is a long latent period of 25 to 45 years for the development of asbestos -related mesothelioma . The image below shows a lung autopsy sample with mesothelioma .1121 Grossly, it appears as a diffuse lesion arising either from the visceral or parietal pleura . The affected lung becomes ensheathed by a thick layer of soft , gelatinous , grayish pink tumor tissue . Microscopically , they are of three types : epithelioid (60%), sarcomatoid (20 %), and mixed (20%). Electron microscopy in mesothelioma will show numerous long, slender microvilli and abundant monofilaments but absent microvillous rootlets and lamellar bodies . The image below shows the epithelioid type of mesothelioma showing cuboidal , columnar, or flattened cells forming tubular or papillary structures resembling adenocarcinoma. Inset shows strong positivity for Calretinin immunostain.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 59-year old man presented with persistent wheezing , episodes of hemoptysis , and dry cough . Bronchoscopy revealed a mass occluding the left bronchus. Biopsy of the specimen revealed polygonal cells with fine stippled chromatin and eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests . The tumor was positive for CD 56, synaptophysin , and chromogranin . What is the cell of origin of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: 1122 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchial carcinoid. Bronchial neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) arise from Kulchitsky cells . WHO divides neuroendocrine neoplasms into four categories : • Typical carcinoid • Atypical carcinoid • Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma • Small-cell carcinoma Carcinoid tumors are low-grade malignant epithelial neoplasms that represent 1% to 5% of all lung tumors. It is not related to smoking. Carcinoids may occur in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. On gross examination, these tumors grow as fingerlike or spherical polypoid masses that project into the lumen of the bronchus or as collar button lesions , penetrating the bronchial wall to fan out in the peribronchial tissue . Histologically , the tumor is composed of organoid, trabecular, palisading , ribbon, or rosette -like arrangements of cells separated by a delicate fibrovascular stroma. On electron microscopy, the cells exhibit the dense -core neurosecretory granules. Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for serotonin, neuron-specific enolase , bombesin, calcitonin, or other peptides . % of the cases may produce carcinoid syndrome. Most carcinoids follow a relatively benign course and have good prognosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What percentage of patients with bronchial carcinoids present with carcinoid syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Approximately , % of bronchial carcinoids give rise to the carcinoid syndrome. Most bronchial carcinoids follow a relatively benign course , do not have secretory activity and do not metastasize to distant sites . Classic carcinoid syndrome is characterized by intermittent attacks of diarrhea, flushing , bronchospasm and cyanosis. Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialised product of tryptophan metabolism by argentaffin cells (cells in the carcinoid tumor). It is then metabolised and excreted in urine. If urinary levels of 5- HIAA exceed 25 mg/day, a diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome can be made.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A solitary coin lesion was seen on a routine X-ray of a patient . After evaluation, he was diagnosed with lung hamartoma . Which of the following is the most common tissue seen in these lesions ?
mcqs.explanation: Cartilage is the most common connective tissue in lung hamartoma . Pulmonary hamartoma consists of nodules of connective tissue intersected by epithelial clefts . There are islands of cartilage , fat, smooth muscle , and entrapped respiratory epithelium in1123 pulmonary hamartoma . It is a benign clonal neoplasm associated with chromosomal aberrations involving either 6p21 or 12q14 -q15. Lung hamartoma is usually discovered as an incidental coin lesion on a routine chest radiograph. The given below is an image of lung hamartoma .1124

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman is being evaluated for chronic headaches , infertility , and galactorrhea. MRI of the brain shows the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and brain MRI showing a pituitary adenoma are suggestive of a lactotroph adenoma (prolactinoma).1130 Pituitary adenomas are usually found in adults . The most common genetic alterations in this condition are mutations in G proteins (particularly GNAS). Depending on their size, they are classified as: • Microadenomas - diameter < 1 cm • Macroadenomas - diameter > 1 cm They may be functioning or non-functioning. The most common type of functioning pituitary adenomas are prolactinomas. The clinical features of prolactinoma include : • Due to mass effect - • Features of raised intracranial tension • Visual field disturbances (bitemporal hemianopia) - due to compression of optic chiasm • Hypopituitarism - due to compressed hypophyseal stalk • Due to hyperprolactinemia - • Galactorrhoea • Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea • Infertility • Loss of libido • Gynecomastia Serum prolactin concentrations tend to correlate with the size of the adenoma. The normal range of serum prolactin is 5-20 �Mg/L. The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 �Mg/L.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Presence of which of the following features is required to diagnose a patient with pituitary carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: The following features are required for the diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma : • A pituitary tumor that has metastasized to distant sites , either craniospinal or systemic sites (and/or) • Presence of a pituitary tumor that is not contiguous with the primary sellar tumour Pituitary carcinoma is extremely rare (< 1% of total tumors). They are associated with activating mutations of the HRAS oncogene . The diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma cannot be made based on histologic appearance alone. Though pituitary adenomas normally show cellular monomorphism and the absence of a reticulin network, they can have some overlapping features with malignant tumors such as: • Atypical adenomas - show pleomorphism and atypical mitosis • Invasive adenomas - • Non-encapsulated1131 • Show local invasion into cavernous and sphenoid sinuses , dura, brain • However, they remain confined to the primary tumor site

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells secrete parathyroid hormone?
mcqs.explanation: Parathyroid hormone (PTH ) is secreted by the chief cells of the parathyroid glands. The function of the parathyroids is to regulate calcium homeostasis . This gland is composed of two cell types : • Chief cells - • Polygonal cells with uniform nuclei and pink cytoplasm • Water-clear appearance - due to presence of large amounts of cytoplasmic glycogen • Secretory granules containing PTH • Oxyphil cells - Slightly larger cells with acidophilic cytoplasm with no known function. The following image shows the normal histology of the parathyroid gland:1132 C-cells or parafollicular cells are present in the thyroid. They secrete calcitonin.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia (isolated hypercalcemia without signs or symptoms ) is primary hyperparathyroidism. It is also the most common cause of hypercalcemia overall. Primary hyperparathyroidism results in autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH ), resulting in elevated levels . It usually results from an adenoma or hyperplasia of parathyroid tissue . The most common cause of symptomatic hypercalcemia is malignancy. The most common mechanism through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is the secretion of the PTH -related peptide (PTHrP ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman presented with bone pain and abdominal cramps for the past 1 week . She has had multiple prior hospital admissions for management of recurrent renal calculi. Investigations revealed elevated serum calcium and PTH levels with reduced phosphate levels . Which of the following is the most common pathological change responsible for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism . The most common cause is a sporadic, solitary parathyroid adenoma. Parathyroid tumors may be associated with cyclin D1 gene inversions and MEN1 mutations. Hyperparathyroidism refers to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH ). It is classified into: • Primary - autonomous overproduction of PTH • Secondary - compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia • Tertiary - persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after correction of prolonged hypocalcemia . (e.g. after renal transplant)1133 The classical symptoms and signs of primary hyperparathyroidism are due to hypercalcemia as well as increased parathyroid hormone (PTH ) levels . The features of hypercalcemia are as follows : The features of elevated PTH levels are as follows : • Osteitis fibrosa cystica • Osteopenia /osteoporosis • Hyperuricemia and gout • Pseudogout • Increased production of calcitriol • Nephrolithiasis • Hypophosphatemia • Anemia The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic - "bones, stones , groans, moans with fatigue overtones"System Clinical features Musculoskeletal Bone painSkeletal deformitie sPathological fracturesMyalgi a and arthralgia Renal Renal stones (Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate )Nephro calcinosisPolyuria and dehyd rationRenal failure GIT ConstipationNausea , vomitin g, anorexiaAbdominal painPe ptic ulcer diseaseAcute pancr eatitis Neuropsychiatric Anxiety, depressionCognitive dysfunctionIrritabilityHalluc inations Cardiac Short QT intervalBradycardia Hypertension Ectopic calcification Cornea: Band keratopathyExt ravascular tissues : calcinosis Small arteries: calciphylaxis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old woman was evaluated for chronic backache and abdominal pain. Investigations revealed the following . What is the most likely bone finding seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and lab findings point towards a diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism . The bone finding associated with this condition is osteitis fibrosa cystica . This condition is also called brown tumor or von Recklinghausen disease of bone.1134 In hyperparathyroidism , high levels of PTH result in increased osteoclast activity. This results in bone loss which predisposes to microfractures and secondary hemorrhages. This results in the following changes : • An influx of macrophages that form giant cells • Mass of reparative fibrous tissue • Increased vascularity, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin deposition - results in brown color The image given below is showing a brown tumor with numerous giant cells with interstitial hemorrhage, hemosiderin.Option A: Osteoporosis circumscripta is a large, well -defined lytic lesion seen in the skull of patients with Paget 's disease . Option B: Fraying and cupping of the metaphysis of the bones are classically seen in patients suffering from rickets. Option D: Punched out lytic lesions of the bone are seen in patients with multiple myeloma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 46-year-old woman is referred with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia . During the evaluation, she is found to have high serum levels of insulin. Measurement of which of the following can help in reaching the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinemia . As C-peptide is a marker of endogenous insulin secretion , its levels would help in identifying the source of insulin: • High C-peptide - excess insulin production (insulinoma) • Normal/ low C-peptide - exogenous insulin administration (factitious disorder) The precursor molecule of insulin is pre-proinsulin, which gets cleaved to form proinsulin. This proinsulin gets cleaved to form insulin and C-peptide (by-product ). Hence , both are secreted in equimolar quantities during insulin secretion . Hence , the level of C-peptide corresponds to the level of endogenous insulin. The levels of C-peptide decrease with the loss of �o -cell mass in type 1 diabetes .1135

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following chromosomal anomalies are least likely to develop diabetes mellitus ?
mcqs.explanation: Edward 's syndrome or trisomy 18 is not associated with diabetes mellitus . Genetic syndromes associated with diabetes mellitus include : • Down's syndrome (trisomy 21 ) • Klinefelter 's syndrome (XXY karyotype ) • Turner 's syndrome (XO karyotype ) • Prader–Willi syndrome (deletion of paternal chromosome 15) Other causes of diabetes mellitus include : • Genetic defects in insulin action - • Type A insulin resistance • Lipoatrophic diabetes • Exocrine pancreatic defects - • Chronic pancreatitis • Pancreatectomy /trauma • Neoplasia • Cystic fibrosis • Hemochromatosis • Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy • Endocrinopathies - • Acromegaly • Cushing syndrome • Hyperthyroidism • Pheochromocytoma • Glucagonoma • Infections - • Cytomegalovirus • Coxsackie B virus • Congenital rubella

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is studying a Congo red-stained slide of pancreatic tissue . He observes it under polarized light and notes the following finding. This finding is commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: 1136 The image shows a Congo red-stained biopsy specimen with apple -green birefringence under polarized microscopy. It is indicative of amyloid accumulation within the pancreatic islets . This is commonly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus . Amyloid deposition begins in and around capillaries and between cells . In advanced stages , the islets may be virtually obliterated and fibrosis may also be observed.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a detrimental effect of advanced glycation end-products in patients suffering from diabetes mellitus?

options.a: Deposition of excess basement membrane material due to TGF-�o release
options.b: Generation of reactive oxygen species in endothelial cells
options.c: Increased anticoagulant effect on endothelial cells and macrophages
options.d: Increase in vascular smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix

mcqs.explanation: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) result in increased procoagulant effects on endothelial cells and macrophages , not anticoagulant effects . AGEs are formed by nonenzymatic reactions between intracellular glucose -derived dicarbonyl precursors with the amino groups of proteins . They bind to a specific receptor (RAGE) that is expressed on inflammatory cells (macrophages and T cells ), endothelium , and vascular smooth muscle . The detrimental effects of the AGE-RAGE signalling axis within the vascular compartment include : • Release of cytokines and growth factors, including TGF-�o - leads to deposition of excess basement membrane material • Generation of reactive oxygen species in endothelial cells . • Increased procoagulant activity on endothelial cells and macrophages . • Enhanced proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and synthesis of extracellular matrix These effects are responsible for the microvascular and macrovascular complications in diabetes mellitus .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm ?
mcqs.explanation: Insulinoma (�o -cell tumors) is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm . It produces sufficient insulin to induce clinically significant hypoglycemia . The three most common and distinctive clinical syndromes associated with functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasms are as follows : • Hyperinsulinism • Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (hypergastrinemia) • Multiple endocrine neoplasias (MEN )

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 39-year-old man was referred to a higher center for further evaluation of peptic ulcer disease refractory to high doses of proton pump inhibitors. There is a history of pituitary and parathyroid tumors in his family members. Serum gastrin level was found to be 1690 pg /ml (normal < 100 ) and a neuroendocrine tumor is suspected . Which of the following is false about this condition?

options.a: It is associated with intractable jejunal ulcers
options.b: This patient likely has a solitary tumor
options.d: Tumors usually originate in Passaro's triangle

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a gastrin-producing tumor or gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). The family history of pituitary and parathyroid tumors is suggestive1137 of MEN1 syndrome. This syndrome is associated with multifocal gastrinomas. On the other hand, sporadic gastrinomas are usually single . Gastrinomas usually arise in the duodenum, peripancreatic soft tissues , pancreas. The site of origin is the duodenum when ZES is associated with MEN1. Most tumors are locally invasive and metastasize early. Hypergastrinemia gives rise to extreme gastric acid secretion and peptic ulceration, that is refractory to proton pump inhibitors. It results in multiple ulcers in duodenum , stomach, and uncommon areas like jejunum.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with longstanding diabetes mellitus came with complaints of bulky stools . Ultrasound abdomen showed the presence of multiple gallstones . Hypersecretion of which of the following leads to this presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of a \033-cell tumor or somatostatinoma. It results in hypersecretion of somatostatin. Somatostatin inhibits pancreatic and biliary secretions . Patients with somatostatinoma usually present with vague abdominal pain along with the triad of: • Gallstones - due to bile stasis • Diabetes mellitus - due to inhibition of insulin secretion • Steatorrhea - due to inhibition of pancreatic exocrine secretion and bile secretion

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient presented with profuse watery diarrhoea and muscle cramps for the past few weeks . The diarrhoea was intractable to antibiotics and stool culture was negative for organisms. He also complained of indigestion and frequent bloating. On investigation, he was found to have microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Serum potassium was 2.4 mmol/L . Upper GI endoscopy was normal . Excess of which of the following hormones leads to this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of WDHA syndrome. It is due to hypersecretion of VIP (vasoactive-intestinal peptide ). WDHA syndrome includes the following features : • Watery diarrhea • Hypokalemia (Serum K+< 3.5 mmol/L ) • Achlorhydria (bloating, indigestion , iron deficiency ) Neural crest tumors, such as neuroblastomas, ganglioneuroblastoma , ganglioneuromas, and pheochromocytomas can also be associated with VIPoma syndrome.1138

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Graves' disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism . It is an autoimmune disorder due to the production of TSH-receptor stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) which cause hyperthyroidism . It is characterized by the triad of: • Thyrotoxicosis • Infiltrative ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos) • Dermopathy (pretibial myxedema ) Glycosaminoglycan deposition , lymphoid infiltrates , and fatty infiltrates are responsible for ophthalmopathy and dermopathy . Grossly, there is a diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland and a beefy deep red parenchyma. Histology shows tall crowded follicular cells with scalloped margins and lymphoid infiltrates . Laboratory features include elevations in free T3 and T4 and decreased TSH.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old lady presents with loss of weight , tremors of the hand, and irritability for the past 4-5 months. Examination findings and investigations are given below . All of the following contribute to these eye findings except :

options.a: Lymphocytic infiltration in the retroorbital space

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the given image showing exophthalmos is suggestive of Graves' ophthalmopathy . Sympathetic overactivity of Muller 's muscle results in a wide , staring gaze and lid lag, but not exophthalmos. Exophthalmos is characterized by abnormal protrusion of the eyeball . It is due to increased volume of the retroorbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles because of:1148 • Marked lymphocytic infiltration of the retro-orbital space • Inflammation with edema and swelling of extraocular muscles • Accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate • Increased numbers of adipocytes (fatty infiltration)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following disorders does not lead to hyperthyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is not associated with hyperthyroidism . It is associated with transient thyrotoxicosis , followed by chronic hypothyroidism . Thyrotoxicosis is a hypermetabolic state caused by elevated circulating levels of free T3 and T4. On the other hand, hyperfunctioning of the thyroid gland itself is referred to as hyperthyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the finding seen in the following histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen from a patient with an enlarged thyroid?

options.a: Dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centre

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows follicular hyperplasia with a scalloping colloid . The clinical scenario along with the image is suggestive of Graves' disease . In Graves' disease , the thyroid is diffusely hyperplastic . The follicles are lined by tall columnar epithelial cells that project into lumina. The cells actively resorb the colloid in the center of the follicle which results in a scalloped appearance of the edges of the colloid .1149

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman presented with diffuse thyroid swelling for the past 6 months. She says that it has increased in size over the last 1 month. Investigations reveal elevated TSH levels . Histopathological examination is done, as shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture and image showing Hurthle cells are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. In this condition, the following microscopic features are seen : • Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes , plasma cells , and well developed germinal centers • Atrophied thyroid follicles • The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm (oncocytes) • This is called oncocytic metaplasia • These cells are called Hurthle cells1150 • Ultrastructurally , these cells have numerous mitochondriaHashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease , characterized by the gradual destruction of the thyroid gland leading to thyroid failure. It is commonly seen in women between 45 to 65 years of age . It is caused by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase . Morphologically , there is a diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland, with an intact capsule . It is well demarcated from the adjacent structures . Note : Oncocytes can arise in various tissues and are referred to as follows : • Hurthle cells / Ashkenazy cells - thyroid gland • Oxyphilic cells - parotid gland • Apocrine metaplasia - breast1151

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings will you not observe in a thyroid gland biopsy taken from a patient suffering from Hashimoto thyroiditis?
mcqs.explanation: Orphan-Annie eye nuclei are a feature of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, not Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure. It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient . The thyroid gland is often diffusely enlarged , painless , with some degree of hypothyroidism . This may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis (Hashitoxicosis). It is associated with an increased risk of: • Other autoimmune conditions • Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphomas • Papillary carcinoma Histologically , the following findings are seen : • Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes , plasma cells , and well developed germinal centers • Atrophied thyroid follicles • The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm • This is called oncocytic metaplasia • These cells are called Hurthle cells1152

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world?
mcqs.explanation: Autoimmune hypothyroidism is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world. The thyroid gland is typically enlarged. The circulating autoantibodies found in this disorder are: • Antimicrosomal antibodies • Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies • Antithyroglobulin antibodies Note : Wolff-Chaikoff effect refers to iodine-induced hypothyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old woman presented with fever, malaise, and painful enlargement of the thyroid gland after a few days following viral fever. On investigation, thyroid antibodies were normal and serum T4 was slightly raised. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical condition is suggestive of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis . It is the most common cause of a painful thyroid. It is also known as painful subacute thyroiditis , de Quervain thyroiditis , or migratory thyroiditis (this is because the pain can shift to different locations in the thyroid). Option A: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis (postpartum thyroiditis ) is typically painless . It often occurs after pregnancy and is characterized by lymphocytic inflammation in the thyroid. Option B: Riedel 's thyroiditis is a rare disorder characterized by a painless , rapidly growing thyroid mass with extensive fibrosis involving the thyroid and contiguous neck structures . Option C: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that presents as painless enlargement of the thyroid associated with some degree of hypothyroidism in middle -aged women.1153

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about solitary thyroid nodule is incorrect?

options.a: They are more common in women
options.c: Solitary nodules are more likely to be malignant than are multiple nodules
options.d: Nodules in younger patients are less likely to be malignant

mcqs.explanation: Nodules in younger patients are more likely to be malignant than those in older patients . The solitary thyroid nodule is a palpably discrete swelling within an otherwise apparently normal thyroid gland. A higher incidence is seen in areas with endemic iodine deficiency . They are more common in women than in men. Malignant transformation is more common in: • Solitary nodules > Multinodular goiter • Solitary nodules in males > females • Cold nodules > Hot nodules However, benign neoplasms are more common than thyroid carcinomas by a ratio of nearly 10 :1.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common thyroid cancer?
mcqs.explanation: The most common thyroid cancer is papillary carcinoma . Major subtypes of thyroid carcinoma and their relative frequencies are as follows : • Papillary carcinoma - most common • Follicular carcinoma • Medullary carcinoma • Anaplastic carcinoma - least common Thyroid carcinomas are derived from the thyroid follicular epithelium , except medullary carcinoma which is derived from parafollicular C cells .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A patient with a long-standing history of thyroglossal cyst develops a neck swelling . The biopsy of the lesion is given below . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows psammoma bodies , which are seen in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. This type of carcinoma is associated with a history of long-standing unresected thyroglossal cyst .1154 Psammoma bodies are concentrically calcified structures often present within the cores of papillae in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. These structures are almost never found in follicular and medullary carcinomas. They arise from: • Infarction and dystrophic calcification of papillae tips • Calcification of intra-lymphatic tumor thrombi. Psammoma bodies are seen in: • Papillary carcinoma (thyroid, kidney, endometrium , lungs ) • Prolactinoma • Meningioma • Papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a solitary, non-tender, firm nodule on the left side of her neck. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. A fine-needle biopsy revealed malignant cells . The tumor was excised and examined under light microscopy as shown below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of empty appearing nuclei, also called Orphan Annie eye nuclei as seen in the above image is diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma include : • Branching papillae with fibrovascular stalk • Covering epithelium is simple or stratified cuboidal • Orphan Annie eye nuclei - • Empty -appearing nuclei due to dispersed chromatin • They are diagnostic , regardless of papillary architecture • Psammoma bodies - concentric calcified structures • Foci of lymphatic invasion1155 Note : Orphan Annie refers to a comic book character with empty appearing eyes , as shown below .1156

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect?

options.a: It is the most common form of thyroid carcinoma
options.b: Diagnosis can be made based on nuclear features , even in the absence of typical architecture
options.c: It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation

mcqs.explanation: Hematogenous spread is rare in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Metastases to lymph nodes are more commonly associated with this condition. It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation. The presence of nuclear features such as Orphan Annie eye nuclei (empty -appearing nuclei ) are diagnostic , regardless of papillary architecture .1157

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is studying the following FNAC from a patient 's thyroid nodule . Which is the most common site of metastasis for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The FNAC image is suggestive of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Among the given options, the most common site of metastasis is the lungs .The histological features of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid are: • Papillary architecture • Nuclear findings (enough to diagnose the condition even in the absence of papillary architecture ) • Nuclear overlapping, grooving, crowding • Ground-glass appearance (Orphan Annie eye nuclei ) • Dusty and pale chromatin1158 • Intranuclear inclusion bodies The most common mode of spread overall is through the lymphatic route, with lymph node metastases being common at initial presentation .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: In patients with papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, which of the following genes may be involved?
mcqs.explanation: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is associated with gain-of-function mutations in the following genes : • NTRK1 (receptor tyrosine kinase) • RET (receptor tyrosine kinase) • BRAF (serine/threonine kinase)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common variant of papillary thyroid cancer?
mcqs.explanation: The most common variant of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is the follicular variant . It has the following features : • Characteristic nuclear features of papillary carcinoma • Almost entirely follicular architecture • Can be either - • Encapsulated - favorable prognosis (or) • Poorly circumscribed and infiltrative - requires aggressive treatment The variants of papillary carcinoma include :Variant Description Tall-cellvariant 50% of cells withheight 2 tim es the widthSeen inolderindi vidualsHave higher frequenci es of vascular invasionExtrat hyroidal extension , and cervi cal and distant metastases Diffuse sclerosingvariant In younger individuals, inclu ding childrenDiffuse fibrosist hroughout the glandLymph n ode metastasesare present in almost all cases .Lacks BRAF mutations Cribriformvariant Associated withfamilial aden omatous polyposis (FAP)Beta- cateninmutation1159 Variant Description Columnar-cellvariant Elongated nuclei with pseudo stratificationof the nucleiPoo r prognosis Solidvariant More common in childrenAss ociated with Chernobyl nucle ar accidentNote : According to the latest WHO classification of thyroid tumors, the non-invasive encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC ) has been renamed as non-invasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP ) to better reflect the indolent course of this tumor. This was done to prevent potential overtreatment and reduce the burden to patients of a cancer diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients is likely to have the best prognosis?

options.a: A 30-year-old man with papillary carcinoma thyroid
options.b: A 45-year-old woman with follicular carcinoma thyroid
options.c: A 78 -year-old man with anaplastic carcinoma thyroid
options.d: A young man with MEN - II syndrome having medullary carcinoma thyroid

mcqs.explanation: Papillary thyroid cancers have the best prognosis, with a 10 -year survival rate seen in more than 95% of the patients . The prognosis of papillary thyroid cancers is dependent on several factors, including age (being less favorable among patients older than 40 years), the presence of extrathyroidal extension , and presence of distant metastases . The thyroid cancer with the worst prognosis is anaplastic carcinoma .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old woman coming from a hilly area presents with a hard swelling in the neck which moves up with deglutition and does not move with protrusion of the tongue . The biopsy of the frozen section is given below . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the given histopathological image showing uniform sheets of cells with capsular invasion by tumor cells is suggestive of follicular carcinoma thyroid. The following images show follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.1160 Option A: In follicular adenoma, there is no capsular invasion . Option C: Anaplastic carcinoma is associated with rapidly progressive swelling with obstructive features and undifferentiated cells on histopathology . Option D: In medullary carcinoma , amyloid stroma is seen on histopathology .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following mutations may be found in patients with follicular carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: RAS mutations are associated with follicular carcinoma . It is also associated with acquired mutations in the PIK3CA gene (PI3K/AKT arm of the receptor tyrosine kinase signaling pathway ) and the PAX8-PPARG fusion gene .1161

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a proto-oncogene implicated in carcinoma of thyroid?
mcqs.explanation: p53 is is a tumor-suppressor gene and not an oncogene . The following are the proto-oncogenes implicated in carcinoma of the thyroid.Proto-oncog ene Tumor RAS Papillary thyroid carcinomaF ollicular thyroid carcinomaH urthle cell carcinoma RET Papillary thyroid carcinoma Medullary thyroid carcinoma MET Papillary thyroid carcinomaF ollicular thyroid carcinoma BRAF Papillary thyroid carcinomaT all-cell poorly differentiated c ancerAnaplastic carcinoma

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman presents with thyroid swelling . The histology of the swelling is as shown below . Investigations reveal elevated calcitonin levels . Which of the following is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and histological appearance showing amyloid stroma are suggestive of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. This condition can occur in the setting of MEN2A (Sipple syndrome) or MEN2B.1162 Medullary carcinomas of the thyroid are neuroendocrine neoplasms derived from the parafollicular cells or C cells of the thyroid. They may be: • Sporadic (70%) • Familial or associated with MEN2 syndromes (30%) - • More aggressive and metastasize more frequently than sporadic • Usually bilateral and multicentric Both forms can be associated with RET mutations. These tumors may present with: • Mass in the neck • Dysphagia • Hoarseness • Diarrhea due to the secretion of VIP • Cushing's syndrome due to ACTH secretion Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle -shaped cells , which may form nests , trabeculae, and even follicles . Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. These lesions secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen.1163

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the OPD with rapid weight gain and easy bruisability over the past 1 month. She was started on oral prednisolone for dermatomyositis 2 months ago. On examination, moon facies and abdominal striae are noted . Her BP is 160 /110 mm Hg. Which of the following pathological changes is seen in this condition?

options.a: Corticotroph cells with homogenous and pale cytoplasm
options.b: Accumulation of keratin filaments in adrenal cells
options.c: Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells
options.d: Basophilic nuclear inclusion bodies in corticotroph cells

mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. In this condition, the normal basophilic cytoplasm of the corticotrophs of anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and pale . This is termed the Crooke hyaline change and is due to the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm . This change occurs due to high levels of circulating glucocorticoids in Cushing's syndrome.1170 Based on the cause of Cushing's syndrome, the following pathological changes are seen in the adrenals: • Iatrogenic - atrophy of zona fasciculata and zona reticularis (as zona glomerulosa functions independently of ACTH) • ACTH-dependent - diffuse hyperplasia (due to high ACTH levels ) • ACTH-independent - nodular hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma Note : Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells are called spironolactone bodies . They are seen in Conn's syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common clinical feature of Cushing syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Obesity is the most common clinical feature of Cushing's syndrome. Clinical features of Cushing's syndrome are attributed to the glucocorticoid , mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid actions of cortisol. They include :System Clinical features Body fat Centralortruncal obesity (mos t common)Buffalo hump (fat deposition behind the neck) Moon facies Skin Purple striae (over abdomen & flanks)Acne and Hirsutism Easy bruisingFacial plethora Hyperpigmentation Musculoskele tal Proximal myopathyOsteopor osis1171 System Clinical features Metabolic Poorly controlled hyperglyce miaDyslipidemia Reproductive OligomenorrheaAmenorrhea Renal Hypokalemic alkalosis CVS AtherosclerosisDiastolic Hyp ertensionEdema Hematologic Hypercoagulable stateLymph openiaNeutrophiliaEosinope nia CNS DepressionPsychosisAnxiety

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, and dizziness for the past 3 days. On examination, the following findings are noted . Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and blood glucose is 48 mg/dl. Which of the following would you expect in this patient ?

options.a: High ACTH and low renin levels
options.b: High ACTH and high renin levels
options.c: Low ACTH and normal renin levels
options.d: Low ACTH and low renin levels

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and the image showing hyperpigmentation of palmar creases and oral mucosa are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency . It presents with low aldosterone , high renin, and high ACTH levels . In primary adrenal insufficiency , lack of aldosterone production results in compensatory rise in ACTH and renin levels . The high ACTH results in hyperpigmentation . The most common causes are autoimmune in developed countries and tuberculosis in developing countries . In secondary adrenal insufficiency , there is pituitary dysfunction leading to low ACTH levels . Renin and aldosterone levels are normal , as they function independently of ACTH.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy was referred with fever, altered sensorium, and non-blanching rash for the past 2 days. He developed rapidly progressive shock and DIC. Despite resuscitation measures , he died . The following appearance of his adrenals was noted on autopsy . All of the following can cause this condition except :
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing bilateral adrenal hemorrhage are suggestive of Waterhouse -Friderichsen syndrome. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not a cause of this condition. It is caused by highly virulent organisms such as: • Neisseria meningitidis or meningococci (classically ) • Streptococcus pneumoniae or pneumococci • Pseudomonas aeruginosa • Haemophilus influenzae • Staphylococcus species This condition is more common in children. Overwhelming bacterial infection leads to bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, thereby causing acute adrenal insufficiency . This is likely a result of direct bacterial seeding of small vessels and endothelial dysfunction caused by microbial products and inflammatory mediators.1172 It usually presents with rapidly progressive hypotension and shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with widespread purpura. Without prompt recognition and treatment , death occurs within hours to a few days.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism ?
mcqs.explanation: Bilateral nodular hyperplasia of the adrenal glands is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism. Adrenal adenoma is the second most common cause . It is usually solitary, but multiple adenomas may occur occasionally. Other rare causes include : • Ectopic aldosterone -producing tumors • Familial idiopathic hyperaldosteronism - due to germline mutations of KCNJ5 (encodes a potassium channel)

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What is the underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome is adrenal adenoma. Hyperaldosteronism may be primary or secondary. Primary hyperaldosteronism is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone with resultant suppression of RAAS . It can occur due to adrenal hyperplasia , adenoma, or carcinoma . It presents with the following features : • Hypertension (most common) • Hypokalemia • Metabolic alkalosis • Polyuria (due to ANP) • Polydipsia (due to polyuria) • Muscle weakness It is confirmed by elevated ratios of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (PAC / PRA ). When primary hyperaldosteronism is due to an aldosterone -secreting adenoma, it is called Conn syndrome. Patients are usually treated with spironolactone followed by surgical removal of adenoma. In patients treated with spironolactone , the adenomas contain eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions called spironolactone bodies.1173 In secondary hyperaldosteronism , aldosterone release occurs in response to the activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAAS ).

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk of developing adrenocortical carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: MEN2B syndrome is associated with pheochromocytoma and medullary carcinoma of thyroid, not adrenocortical carcinoma . Adrenocortical carcinoma is associated with the following hereditary cancer syndromes: • Li –Fraumeni syndrome - due to germline TP53 mutations • Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome - a disorder of epigenetic imprinting • MEN1 syndrome - due to mutations of MEN1 gene1174

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought for the evaluation of recurrent seizures over the last 3 months. Past history is significant for chronic oral candidiasis for 2 years. On examination, nail dystrophy is noted . Further investigation reveals serum calcium of 6.9 mg/dl and prolonged QT interval. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of autoimmune polyendocrinopathy (APS) type 1. It is also called APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy ). It is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene . This gene usually increases tolerance of central T-cells to peripheral tissue antigens. When this function is lost, the T-cells become more prone to mount immune reactions against tissue antigens, promoting autoimmunity. These patients develop autoantibodies against IL -17 and IL -22 , which are crucial for defense against fungal infections . It presents in childhood with the following features : • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis • Ectodermal dystrophy (abnormalities of the skin, dental enamel, and nails) • Organ-specific autoimmune disorders such as - • Autoimmune adrenalitis • Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism • Idiopathic hypogonadism • Pernicious anemia Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS) type 2 usually presents in early adulthood as a combination of the following : • Adrenal insufficiency • Autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations , headaches , and sweating . Her BP was 155/95 mm Hg and HR was 135/min. Investigations revealed elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines and a right adrenal mass on CT abdomen. She should be examined for the presence of all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma . This patient does not need to be examined for a shagreen patch. It is a feature of tuberous sclerosis syndrome, which is not associated with pheochromocytoma . Familial syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma are: Even patients with no family history must be evaluated for findings of these genetic syndromes, as they may occur sporadically in some cases .Syndrome Clinical manifestations Neurofibromatosis Caf\351-au-lait spotsAxillary and inguinal frecklingOptic nerv e gliomaLisch nodules1175 Syndrome Clinical manifestations von Hippel -Lindau (VHL ) sy ndrome HemangioblastomasRenal cel l carcinomaPancreatic endocr ine neoplasms MEN2A syndrome Medullary thyroid carcinoma Parathyroid hyperplasia MEN 2B syndrome Medullary thyroid carcinoma MarfanoidhabitusMucocutan eous ganglioneuromatosis

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is most commonly involved in Wermer syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common manifestation of Wermer's syndrome or MEN-1 syndrome. MEN1 syndrome is due to germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor-suppressor gene , which encodes a protein called menin. The most commonly secreted products are pancreatic polypeptides .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an indicator of malignant transformation in a patient with pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: The definitive diagnosis of malignancy in pheochromocytomas is based exclusively on the presence of metastases to regional lymph nodes as well as distant sites like liver, lung, and bone. Capsular and vascular invasion may be encountered even in benign lesions . Malignant pheochromocytomas are histologically and biochemically the same as benign ones. Hence , typical histological criteria like cellular atypia, mitotic spindles , and vascular invasion are insufficient to confirm malignancy in pheochromocytomas.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A pathologist is studying the following slide from the biopsy of a patient with an abdominal mass. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given histopathology slide shows nests of cells arranged in an organoid pattern, with fibrovascular septae , and finely granular cytoplasm . This is called the zellballen pattern. It is typically seen in paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas . Paragangliomas are benign neuroendocrine tumors arising from paraganglia in the neck or abdomen. They are composed of chief and sustentacular cells arranged in an organoid pattern.1176

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old woman was being evaluated for persistent hypertension . Workup revealed a tumor located near the bifurcation of the aorta. Surgical excision was done and HPE examination revealed a zellballen pattern of cells . Where did this tumor likely originate from?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a paraganglioma (ectopic pheochromocytoma ) located in the abdomen. They commonly arise from the organ of Zuckerkandl , located at the bifurcation of the aorta. It is part of the vertebral paraganglia (clusters of chromaffin cells along the autonomic nerve chains). Other sites of origin of paragangliomas include : • Urinary bladder - rarely • Carotid and aortic bodies • Ganglion nodosum of the vagus nerve • Jugulotympanic ganglia1177

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What mutation is likely to be seen in patients with familial paraganglioma syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Familial paraganglioma is most likely associated with mutations in the SDH (succinate dehydrogenase) gene . The SDH complex is involved in mitochondrial electron transport and oxygen sensing . It is believed that SDH mutations also lead to the upregulation of HIF-1\037, which is a key oncogenic driver in this type of tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 21 -year-old young man presents with a neck mass. Past history is significant for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma 6 months ago. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the following finding. Which of the following should the patient be screened for?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing mucosal neuromas are suggestive of MEN2B syndrome. This condition is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. The MEN syndromes are a group of inherited diseases of multiple endocrine organs. Tumors occur at a younger age than sporadic tumors, either synchronously (at the same time) or metachronously (at different times ). MEN2 syndrome occurs due to abnormal activation of the RET gene . Medullary carcinoma is seen in both MEN 2A and 2B syndromes. However, it tends to be more aggressive and metastasizes more frequently in MEN2B syndrome. Note : RET gene is deactivated in Hirschsprung disease .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: What gene is mutated in polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome occurs due to germline mutations in the EPAS1 gene . This syndrome presents with neuroendocrine tumors and early-onset polycythemia . RET gene mutation is seen in MEN2A and MEN2B syndromes. SDHD and SDHB mutations are seen in hereditary paraganglioma 1 and hereditary paraganglioma 4 syndromes respectively.1178

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following lesions does not arise from the terminal duct lobular unit of the breast?
mcqs.explanation: Periductal mastitis arises from the large lactiferous ducts . It is also known as squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts , recurrent subareolar abscess , or Zuska disease. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is the basic functional and histopathological unit of the breast. Successive branching of large ducts eventually leads to the TDLU. Sclerosing adenosis , blue dome cyst , and carcinoma breast arise from the TDLU.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following lesions arise from the large ducts of the breast?
mcqs.explanation: Duct ectasia and Paget 's disease arise from the large ducts of the breast. Normal anatomy of the breast includes ducts , lobules , and stroma. Successive branching of the large ducts eventually leads to the terminal duct lobular unit. Atypical hyperplasia arises from the terminal ducts and lobules , whereas , fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumors arise from the intralobular stroma.

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast. On examination, you notice her nipple is erythematous and tender with a purulent exudate . Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute mastitis. The most common cause of acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus. Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess ). It is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples . Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses .1191 Option A: Breast abscess caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is uncommon, only a few cases have been documented in immunocompromised patients . Options B and C: Streptococcal infections tend to spread throughout the breast in the form of cellulitis .

mcqs.subject: Pathology
mcqs.question: Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with a history of smoking?
mcqs.explanation: Periductal mastitis is strongly associated with a history of smoking. More than 90% of the affected individuals are smokers. Periductal mastitis is also called recurrent subareolar abscess or squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts or Zuska disease . In this condition, a relative deficiency of vitamin A associated with smoking or toxic substances in tobacco smoke alters the differentiation of the ductal epithelium . Histologically , there is keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the nipple ducts . Keratin shed from these cells is trapped and plugs (keratin plug ) the ductal system , causing dilation and eventually rupture of the duct . This results in keratin spillage into the surrounding periductal tissue forming a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response .
