options.c: 400 mcg of folic acid after confirmation of pregnancy

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows spina bifida, the most common neural tube defect (NTD). 4000 mcg of folic acid periconceptionally is given to prevent NTDs in subsequent pregnancies . The normal dose of folic acid in pregnancy is 400 mcg (0.4 mg). However, the history of a previous pregnancy with an NTD raises the risk of another NTD in subsequent pregnancies . An increased dose of folic acid is thus prophylactically given during the periconceptional period to prevent NTD in the next child.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old girl presented with the triad of diarrhoea, dermatitis , and delayed mental development . The child had neutral aminoaciduria and a positive Obermeyer test . Which of the following statement is false regarding the vitamin deficient in this child?

options.c: It decreases the levels of lipoprotein (
options.d: Most fatal complication with high dose of this vitamin is fulminant hepatitis

mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of Pellagra secondary to Hartnup's disease . The vitamin deficient in this condition is niacin. The precursor of niacin is tryptophan and not tyrosine. Niacin/vitamin B3 is a constituent of NAD and NADP. Its deficiency occurs in a maize-based diet (maize is deficient in tryptophan ), carcinoid syndrome (all the tryptophan is converted to serotonin), and hartnup disease (defective absorption from intestine and kidney). Niacin is the only lipid -lowering agent that lowers lipoprotein (a) levels significantly . It also results in a decrease in LDL , VLDL , and triglycerides along with an increase in HDL cholesterol . Niacin deficiency causes pellagra (3Ds)- • Diarrhoea • Dermatitis (Cassal's necklace) • Dementia • Finally death . Niacin toxicity manifests as: • Prostaglandin mediated cutaneous flushing163 • Glucose intolerance • Fulminant hepatitis (most fatal complication) Hartnup's disease is due to impaired renal and intestinal absorption of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids. It is characterized by a varied clinical presentation including ataxia (lack of muscle control), delayed mental development , diarrhoea and dermatitis (pellagra -like symptoms as tryptophan is a precursor of niacin). Diagnosis of niacin deficiency secondary to hartnup's disease is based on neutral aminoaciduria and increased excretion of indole compounds detected by the Obermeyer test . Image: Casal's necklace

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: A 7-month-old child was brought by her mother with complaints of diarrhoea and mucocutaneous lesions as shown in the image. The symptoms have been present since weaning was started . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A child with eczematous rash typically in the perioral and perineal region is characteristic of acrodermatitis enteropathica which is due to secondary zinc deficiency . It is an autosomal recessive disorder seen in infants due to a defect in the intestinal zinc-specific transporter gene . Oral zinc therapy is the preferred management. It classically presents while weaning from breast milk to formula, which has lower zinc bioavailability than breast milk. The symptoms are perioral and perineal rashes, periungual dermatitis- Beau's lines on nails, chronic diarrhea, and alopecia . Children commonly present with symmetrical, eczematous plaques that become vesicular, bullous, pustular , or erosive with characteristic crusting at the edges . The perioral eruption usually spares the upper lip, giving it a U\037shaped or horseshoe \037shaped appearance . Investigations would reveal low serum zinc. Oral zinc therapy is the treatment of choice (3 mg/kg/24 hour) Option A: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is the classical triad of thrombocytopenia , eczema and recurrent pyogenic infections . No history of bleeding rules out this option. Option C: Epidermolysis bullosa presents as bullous lesions in pressure handling areas.164 Option D: In atopic dermatitis usually the lesions will be itchy and distributed in extensor aspects (flexural in adults ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: A young school-going girl, a known case of seizure disorder controlled with valproic acid, complaints of constant bullying by her classmates for her patchy hair loss. Local scalp examination reveals scaly dermatitis and hair loss with intermittent constrictions. Which of the following deficiencies is associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Biotin (Vitamin H or Vitamin B7) deficiency can cause alopecia , dermatitis (periorificial), and thinning of hair. It is commonly seen in individuals who are on long term valproate therapy . Scarring alopecia with islands of dense hair referred to as intermittent constrictions is classically seen in biotin deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: A 2-day-old neonate is noted to have multifocal -clonic seizures . These seizures are unresponsive to pharmacologic therapy . Which vitamin dependency is responsible for such seizures ?
mcqs.explanation: Pyridoxine is one of the causes of refractory seizures in the neonatal period and infancy. Pyridoxine and pyridoxal dependency disorders can cause severe seizures . These seizures , which are often multifocal clonic, usually start during the first few hours of life . It involves a mutation in the ALDH7A1 gene causing a deficiency of an enzyme involved in the degradation of I-alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: Cardiac edema and neuropathy are seen in which of the following vitamin deficiencies ?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac edema and neuropathy are associated with the deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1 ). Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy , irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes , and proprioception . As the disease progresses , increased intracranial pressure , meningismus, and coma develop .165 Wet beriberi (cardiac) is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly , cardiac failure, and edema . It is commonly seen in the refugee camps where people consume polished rice based monotonous diets . Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment . Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Deficiency of Water-soluble Vitamins & Trace El...
mcqs.question: During the routine ophthalmic examination of a 6-year- old child as a part of a school health survey, you notice the following finding as shown in the image. This is characteristically associated with deficiency of _______
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows corneal vascularization , which is characteristic of Riboflavin deficiency . Other features include glossitis , cheilosis , and photophobia collectively called ariboflavinosis. The image below shows Cheilosis and glossitis166

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old infant was brought to the OPD by his mother with a history of passing watery stools more than 4 times in the past day. On examination, the baby is alert and on pinching his skin, it goes back quickly. The infant weighs 5.7 Kg . What is the initial fluid of choice for treating diarrhoea in this infant?
mcqs.explanation: In an infant with diarrhoea, the initial fluid of choice is oral rehydration solution (ORS). The glucose -dependent sodium and water absorption is the principle behind replacing glucose and sodium in a 1:1 molar ratio in the WHO oral rehydration solution (ORS). The low osmolarity of the ORS in the lumen as compared to the blood facilitate absorption of fluid and hence the electrolytes due to the solvent drag. Studies have shown that low osmolarity ORS causes reduction of stool output , decrease in vomiting and decrease in the use of unscheduled intravenous fluids without increasing the risk of hyponatremia. Other home available fluids that can be used are salted rice water/salted yoghurt drinks , vegetable /chicken soup with salt. ReSoMal is given to severely malnourished children. In this case, since the infant's weight is appropriate for its age ORS is given.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The amount of total body water(TBW) in a term neonate weighing 3 Kg is approximately _______
mcqs.explanation: The amount of total body water (TBW) in a term neonate is approximately 75 % of the birth weight . So, in this case, % of 3kg is 2.25 litres. Note - TBW is 90% in early fetal life and becomes 60% by the end of the first year and stays the same till puberty .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the clinical procedure being performed ?

options.b: Femoral IV access for fluid transfusion

mcqs.explanation: The above image shows intraosseous cannulation for fluid transfusion in the anterior proximal tibia. The intraosseous route is an alternative to the intravenous (IV ) route in the transfusion of fluids in shock. • The marrow of long bones has a rich network of vessels that drain into a central venous canal, emissary veins, and ultimately the central circulation. • So, the bone marrow functions as a non-collapsible venous access route. Intraosseous cannulation is recommended for patients in whom IV access proves difficult or unattainable. (e.g., in cardiopulmonary arrest). In such a case, if venous access is not available173 within 1 min, an intraosseous needle should be placed in the anterior proximal tibia. Insertion sites for intraosseous infusion: • In the proximal tibia, 1-2 cm anteromedial from the tibial tuberosity • Distal tibia at the junction of the medial malleolus and the shaft of the tibia • Distal one-third of the femur

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old boy who has been operated on for craniopharyngioma presents with polyuria and polydipsia . On investigation, the serum osmolality is 305 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality is 250 mOsm/kg. The atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) level is normal . What could be the cause ?

options.b: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with \026serum osmolality and \027urinary osmolality , after a cranial surgery, suggests a diagnosis of post -surgical central diabetes insipidus (DI). Irreversible central DI follows most cases of complete resections of craniopharyngioma. Serum osmolality of >295 mOsm/L (normal : 280-295 mOsm/L) and the urine osmolality of <300 mOsm/L (normal : 500-850mOsm/L) are suggestive of DI. A water deprivation test is done to further classify the types of DI. Option A: In postoperative patients , because of IV fluids there is an acute expansion of ECF volume . This suppresses high ADH activity and causes diuresis with normal serum osmolality . Option B: In SIADH, serum osmolality is decreased . Option D: In cerebral salt-wasting syndrome there is hypersecretion ANP and their levels are usually elevated .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All the following statements are true regarding zinc supplementation in children with diarrhoea except :

options.a: It leads to reduced duration, severity , and recurrence of diarrhea
options.b: It reduces the inappropriate use of antimicrobials
options.c: Excessive zinc can cause copper deficiency syndrome
options.d: It is given at a dose of 20 mg/day for 4 weeks

mcqs.explanation: Zinc supplementation is usually given for a duration of 10 to 14 days. • Age <6 months: 10 mg/day • Age >6 months: 20 mg/day Zinc administration for diarrhoea management can significantly reduce mortality and hospital admission. In addition, it improves diarrhoea recovery rates and reduces the inappropriate use of antimicrobials. Excessive zinc therapy can lead to copper deficiency syndrome, hence requires the regular monitoring of plasma zinc and copper concentrations.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child brought to the hospital with a history of loose stools . The mother says he is irritable and drinks water hastily when given. On examination, eyes are sunken and during the skin pinch test , the skin retracted within two seconds but not immediately . What is the treatment for the child?

options.a: Administer the first dose of IV antibiotic and immediately refer to a higher center
options.b: Give oral fluids and ask the mother to continue the same and visit again the next day
options.c: Give zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution only and ask mother to come back if some danger signs develop
options.d: Consider severe dehydration , start intravenous (IV ) fluids , IV antibiotics, and refer to a higher center

mcqs.explanation: The child in this scenario has some degree of dehydration , since the child is restless and irritable, drinks water readily, has sunken eyes , and the skin goes back slowly on the skin pinch test (<2 seconds ) with sunken eyes .174 Treatment includes oral rehydration therapy and zinc supplementation according to WHO Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Diseases (IMNCI) Protocol, Plan B. WHO IMNCI PLANS :

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about reduced (low)-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS)?

options.a: It contains 20 mmol of potassium per litre
options.d: Citrate is provided to prevent or correct base deficit acidosis

mcqs.explanation: The total osmolarity of low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution (ORS) is 245 mmol/L , and it is the most commonly used ORS. • Potassium is provided to replace the large potassium losses , thus preventing serious hypokalemia. • Citrate corrects base-deficit acidosis. • Glucose promotes the absorption of sodium and water in the small intestine .175

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The amount of sodium present in ReSoMal is ________
mcqs.explanation: Rehydration solution for malnourished (ReSoMal) contains 45 mmol/L of sodium. Severely malnourished children have excess intracellular sodium (leaky cell membranes and reduced activity of the sodium–potassium pump ). So, sodium intake should be reduced and a low-sodium oral rehydration solution (ReSoMal) is advised. Because severely malnourished children are deficient in potassium , ReSoMal contains extra potassium , as well as extra glucose or sucrose and selected minerals (Mg, Cu, Zn ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old child weighing 7 Kg , presents to the emergency with a history of vomiting and diarrhea for the last 3 days. On examination, the skin pinch over the anterior abdominal wall goes quickly to its original position. What is the interpretation of the skin pinch test in this child?

options.d: Skin pinch cannot be evaluated in this child

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the child is malnourished, so the skin pinch cannot be evaluated . The child is of age 2 years, and the expected weight is 12 Kg . But, the weight of the child here is 7 Kg, which suggests that the child is malnourished. The child may be having edematous malnutrition (kwashiorkor ), where skin may go back to the original position even in the presence of dehydration . Hence , the skin pinch is not reliable for the assessment of dehydration in this child. Reliable indicators of dehydration in the malnourished child include • Eagerness to drink • Cool and moist extremities • Weak radial pulse • Reduced urine flow

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most dangerous type of dehydration ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypernatremic dehydration is the most dangerous type of dehydration . Hypernatremia causes movement of water from brain cells into hypertonic extracellular fluid , causing brain cell shrinkage and shearing of blood vessels within brain . This leads to central nervous system hemorrhages and thrombosis. The fluid deficit is corrected slowly as rapid treatment of hypernatremic dehydration causes movement of water from the extracellular space into brain cells , leading to cerebral edema , seizures , brain herniation, and even death .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the maximum concentration of dextrose that can be given through a peripheral vascular line in a neonate ?
mcqs.explanation: Through a peripheral vascular line, a maximum of 12 .5% dextrose can be infused .176 The dextrose concentration greater than 12 .5% has an acidic pH and can cause irritation to the peripheral veins, which can lead to thrombophlebitis . Note : Central vein lines can be used for 25% D if needed .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 Kgs has been posted for surgical resection of a tumor. What is the daily maintenance fluid required for this child while he's NPO?
mcqs.explanation: The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml. Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday -Segar method ) is used . Calculation: In the question, the weight of the child is given as 30 Kgs . So, the formula for >20 Kg is used . 1500 mL + (20 mL x weight more than 20 Kgs ) Since the child weight is 30 Kgs , he/she is 10 Kgs more. Therefore, fluid required is = 1500 mL + (20 mL x 10 ) = 1500 mL + 200 mL = 1700 mL .Bodywei ght Fluid required per day 0–10 Kg 100 mL /Kg –20 K g 1000 mL + 50 mL /Kg for eac h Kg >10 Kg >20 Kg 1500 mL + 20 mL /Kg for eac h Kg >20 kg

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of shock in children?
mcqs.explanation: Hypovolemic shock is the most common type of shock in children. Cardiogenic shock: cardiac pump failure due to cardiomyopathies , myocarditis or congenital heart diseases . Hypovolemic shock: loss of body fluid due to diarrhea, vomiting or hemorrhage. Obstructive shock: mechanical barrier which obstructs the cardiac outflow like pericardial tamponade, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism.177 Septic shock: It is the combination of hypovolemic (intravascular fluid loss because of capillary leak) and cardiogenic shock (because of myocardial depression by circulating inflammatory mediators) in association with infection.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old baby was brought by his parents to the ER. The parents complained that the child had been lethargic for a few hours and unresponsive for the past 30 mins. They give a history of 4-5 episodes of vomiting in the past one day. On examination, the baby had tachycardia, tachypnea , and very slow capillary refill time. The pediatrician asks you to initiate IV fluid therapy with a 24G IV cannula. Which colour IV cannula would you use ?
mcqs.explanation: The color of the 24 G cannula is yellow . 24 G cannula is usually used for paediatric age group.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All of the following are causes of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, except ______

options.c: Acidosis due to intestinal bacterial overgrowth

mcqs.explanation: Acidosis due to intestinal bacterial overgrowth causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis because of excessive bacterial metabolism of glucose into lactic acid. Anion gap Normally, in the serum, the total number of cations is equal to the total number of anions. But, few of the anions (lactate , phosphate, and sulphate ) cannot be measured and this is called an anion gap. Anion gap = [Na+] � ([Cl-]+[HCO3-]) Metabolic acidosis Metabolic acidosis is of two types : (1) Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) • Diarrhea (Loss of bicarbonate is compensated by chloride reabsorption) • Renal tubular acidosis • Urinary tract diversions (reabsorption of ammonium and hydrogen by the bowel ) (2) High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) • Lactic acidosis (hypoxia, malignancy) • Ketoacidosis (diabetic , starvation ) • Poisoning (ethylene glycol , methanol, salicylate )178

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Rani , a 6-year-old girl, who is known to have thalassemia , presented to the emergency with weakness, chest pain, and palpitations . There is a history of recent blood transfusion. The ECG of the child shows tall and peaked T-waves and flat P-waves as shown below . What could be the cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The given electrocardiograph (ECG) characteristics show tall and peaked T-waves, flat P waves and since the girl has a recent history of massive blood transfusion, the most likely diagnosis is hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia may be due to blood transfusion (stored blood has increased potassium concentration, due to the failure of the Na+-K+ ATPase pump ). Causes of Hyperkalemia: • Spurious laboratory value • Sampling error • Thrombocytosis • Leucocytosis • Increased intake • Oral or intravenous • Blood transfusions • Transcellular shifts • Acidosis • Tumor lysis syndrome • Hemolysis • Decreased excretion • Renal failure • Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism179 • Drugs • ACE inhibitors • ARB (angiotensin receptor blockers) • Potassium-sparing diuretics ECG Changes of Hyperkalemia • Tall and peaked T waves • Increased PR interval • Flattening of the P wave • ST-segment depression • Widening of the QRS complex Note : Tall T waves are also seen in myocardial ischemia.Option A: • There will be history of fever and ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Option B: • Patient presents with features of cardiac failure and ECG shows ventricular arrhythmias. Option C: • Pulmonary hypertension is a known complication of hemolytic diseases (free Hb, angiotrophic factors causing vasoconstriction) and ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH ).180

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pregnant female arrives at your hospital for her antenatal check-up. As an intern, you were required to draw her family pedigree chart while taking history. She has previously delivered full -term healthy dizygotic twins 5 years back. Which of the following symbol will you use to denote dizygotic twins in a pedigree chart?
mcqs.explanation: Pedigree charts are graphical representations of a person's family tree and are useful for identifying the pattern of inheritance of genetic disorders. Thus, they are vital in the history-taking of patients , especially in pregnancy. Option B is the symbol denoting dizygotic twins in a pedigree chart. Option A denotes monozygotic twins in the pedigree chart. Option C denotes offsprings . Option D denotes consanguineous marriage.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which pattern of inheritance does the pedigree chart denote ?
mcqs.explanation: The above pedigree chart denotes an autosomal recessive pattern. In the above pedigree chart, both males and females are carriers (equally affected ) which indicates an autosomal pattern. Parents are unaffected (both are carriers/heterozygotes ), and no affected members in other generations . 25% of the children are normal , 50% are carriers, and only 25% are affected . This indicates a a recessive pattern. Pedigree charts in various modes of inheritance:193

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While volunteering at the blood donation camp, Ananya came across a case of a thalassemic infant who has an AB-positive blood group. Her father is B-positive and her mother is A-positive. In order to understand more about donor eligibility to explain the concerned parents, she wishes to understand the inheritance pattern of ABO blood grouping . Can you help her out by choosing the correct option?
mcqs.explanation: The inheritance pattern of the ABO blood grouping system is codominance. Codominance: Gene expression and mendelian traits are usually described as dominant or recessive ; in some cases , both of the alleles of a gene pair contribute to the phenotype —a condition called codominance. Examples include histocompatibility and ABO blood group antigens. Classification of genetic disorders Mendelian disorders (Classic inheritance) • Autosomal dominant • Autosomal recessive • X-linked dominant • X-linked recessive Non-mendelian disorders ( Non-classic inheritance) • Trinucleotide repeat mutations • Fragile X syndrome • Friedreich ataxia • Huntington's disease • Mutations in mitochondrial genes : MELAS, MERRF • Genomic imprinting • Angelman syndrome • Prader–Willi syndrome • Silver–Russell syndrome • Gonadal mosaicism Chromosomal disorders: • Microdeletions : Cri du chat syndrome • Down's syndrome, Turner 's syndrome, Klinefelter 's syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An MBBS student , after attending a class on genetic disorders, noticed that a particular disorder appears in three consecutive generations of his family without any sex predilection . While drawing his pedigree chart, it also struck him that phenotypically normal family members were having healthy offspring . Based on this information, he concluded the pattern of inheritance of this disorder. What is the correct pattern?
mcqs.explanation: The pattern of inheritance in this genetic disorder is autosomal dominant. Points in favour: • Autosomal dominant disorders have a vertical mode of transmission (individuals of two generations are affected —parent and children affected ).194 • It appears in three consecutive generations of a family without any sex predilection . • An affected individual has a 50% chance of passing on the deleterious gene in each pregnancy. • Males and females are equally affected . • Unaffected individuals do not pass on the disorder to their children.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young boy presented with a history of a genetic disorder. On further enquiry, his father and grandmother had the same disease as well . Prior to his birth, the doctor had counseled the father that there is a 50% chance of passing the deleterious gene to his offspring irrespective of sex. Which of the following diseases is an example of this inheritance pattern?
mcqs.explanation: Autosomal dominance is the inheritance pattern seen in his question due to three -generation of affected family members with a 50% chance of passing the deleterious gene to the next generation irrespective of sex. Tuberous sclerosis is an example of an autosomal dominant (AD) disorder. Note : • All Ehlers –Danlos syndrome types are autosomal dominant, except types V , VI , and VII . • All types of osteogenesis imperfecta are autosomal dominant, except types II , III , and VII .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Aryan is the first child born to parents suffering from achondroplasia. Although he is not suffering from this condition, the parents wish to know the chances of developing achondroplasia in the second child. What is the correct response ?
mcqs.explanation: The chances of having an affected baby when both parents have achondroplasia (autosomal-dominant disorder) is 75 %. • Autosomal dominant (AD) disorders are manifested in the heterozygous state . • If both of the parents are affected , the chances of having an affected baby are 75 % (50% - 'Aa', and 25% - 'AA'). Note : Here, we consider both parents as 'Aa' (heterozygous ) because 'AA' (homozygous ) is usually fatal in the first few months of life . The odds of having an affected baby does not change with195 subsequent pregnancies .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy presented with short stature and delayed motor milestones . An x-ray showed a trident hand as given below . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The x-ray shows short stubby fingers, with a separation between middle and ring fingers. This is called a trident hand and is seen in achondroplasia. Achondroplasia It is an autosomal-dominant chondrodysplasia and the most common condition characterized by disproportionate short stature . It is caused by mutations in the gene coding for fibroblast growth factor receptor type 3 (FGFR3). Clinical features (see image below ): Short stature , extreme joint laxity, bowing of legs , macrocephaly , frontal bossing, midfacial hypoplasia , small chest , redundant skin folds , recurrent infections , cor pulmonale , and restrictive pulmonary disease196 Radiological features • Champagne glass pelvic inlet • Trident hand • Shortening of tubular bones with metaphyseal flaring. • Chevron deformity

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old child presented with multiple hyperpigmented lesions of around size 15-20 mm in the trunk and extremities . Similar lesions of size 2-3 mm were found in his axillary and inguinal regions. A photograph of his eye showing a characteristic lesion is shown below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The features of cafe -au-lait macules , axillary and inguinal freckling along with Lisch nodules points toward a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1). The multiple hyperpigmented lesions of more than 15 in the trunk and extremities are known as cafe-au-lait macules (>5mm in prepubertal , >15mm in postpubertal ) and are present in % of NF1 cases . The lesions of around 2-3mm in the axillary and inguinal regions are known as axillary/inguinal freckling and are pathognomonic of NF1. The given image shows discrete nodules over the iris, which are referred to as Lisch nodules , and are commonly seen in patients with NF-1. Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas. Neurofibromatosis : It is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome with the following types - Axillary freckling is shown in the image below -NF1 (von Recklinghausen dis ease ) NF2 (Central neurofibromato sis) Mutation on chromosome17 Mutation on chromosome22197 NF1 (von Recklinghausen dis ease ) NF2 (Central neurofibromato sis) 2 or more of the following sh ould be present :6 or more caf \351-au-lait spots2 or more neur ofibromas or one plexiform n euromaFreckling in the axilla ry or inguinal region2 or mor e Lisch nodulesDysplasia of t he sphenoidal and tibial bone A first degree relative with N F1Optic gliomas Predisposes to multiple tumo urs of the nervous system .Mo st commonarebilateral vestib ular schwannomas; intracran ial and spinal meningiomas, gliomas, neurofibromas, and posterior subcapsular lenticul ar opacities .Vestibular schwa nnomas are benign tumours t hat arise from the intracanali cular segment of theinferior division of the vestibulocochl ear nerve.Extracanalicular ex tension into the cerebellopon tine angle can lead to an"ice c ream cone"appearance inMR I.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which one of the following is not included in the criteria for neurofibromatosis 1?

options.c: Dysplasia of the sphenoidal and tibial bone

mcqs.explanation: In neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), two or more of the following clinical manifestations are present : • Six or more caf\351-au-lait macules • Axillary or inguinal freckling • Two or more iris Lisch nodules (hamartomas of iris) • Two or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma • A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoidal and tibial bone dysplasia • Optic gliomas198 • A 1st-degree relative with NF-1

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Consider the following statements about caf\351- au- lait macules associated with neurofibromas:

options.a: Statements A, C and E true, B and D false
options.b: Statements B and C true, A, D and E false
options.c: Statements B, D and E true, A and C false
options.d: Statements A and B true, C, D and E false

mcqs.explanation: Statement C: The spots are scattered over the body surface , with a predilection for the trunk and extremities ; sparing the face . Statement D: For diagnosis, the macules should be >5 mm in prepubertal and >15 mm in postpubertal individuals. Statement E: 6 or more spots should be present for the clinical diagnosis of neurofibromatosis Caf\351-au-lait macules : • Hallmark of neurofibromatosis, present in around 100 % of the patients . • 6 or more caf\351-au-lait spots should be present for the clinical diagnosis of neurofibromatosis along with other criteria. • Present at birth, but increase in size, number, and pigmentation , especially during the first few years of life . Note : Other diseases associated with multiple caf\351-au-lait spots : Ataxia telangiectasia , Bloom syndrome, Fanconi's anaemia, McCune –Albright syndrome, tuberous sclerosis , Maffucci syndrome, Hunter syndrome. Other neurocutaneous syndromes: • Sturge –Weber syndrome: port-wine stain over the trigeminal distribution, contralateral hemiparesis, focal seizures contralateral to the side of facial capillary malformations, calcification of the cerebral cortex, mental retardation, and congenital glaucoma • von Hippel –Lindau disease : retinal angiomas; cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas • Ataxia telangiectasia • Tuberous sclerosis Caf\351-au-lait spots are shown in the image given below :199

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-month-old child presents with a history of a condition seen in the image below . On examination , a characteristic raised skin lesion of orange peel consistency known as shagreen patch is present in his lumbosacral region. Which one of the following is not seen in this autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Optic glioma is not seen in tuberous sclerosis . Tuberous sclerosis /Bourneville–Pringle Disease is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which may present during infancy with infantile spasms (as seen in the image), and has the characterisitic skin lesion known as shagreen patch. It is characterized by Vogt's triad (EPILOA ), which includes • Epilepsy • Low intelligence (IQ) • Adenoma sebaceum The most common manifestations are skin lesions such as ashleaf (hypomelanotic ) macules , adenoma sebaceum , shagreen patch, confetti lesions , and periungual fibromas. Koenen 's tumours (periungual fibromas) are small fleshy tumors that grow under the toe nails/finger nails. Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules are the characteristic brain lesions . Other lesions include bilateral renal angiomyolipomas, facial angiofibroma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, and retinal hamartomas. Vigabatrin is the first-line therapy for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis . Note : Drug of choice for infantile spasms: adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) Image below : Adenoma sebaceum200 Image below : Shagreen patchImage below : Periungual fibroma201

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The first child of a normal healthy couple was diagnosed to have cystic fibrosis. The parents are anxious and wish to seek advice for future pregnancies . What is the percentage of chances for the second child to be affected ?
mcqs.explanation: Cystic fibrosis follows autosomal recessive inheritance. Hence , the disease has a 25% chance of affecting the offspring . If parents are unaffected (both are carriers/heterozygotes ): • 25% chance of normal genotype • 50% chance of carriers • 25% chance of homozygous In autosomal recessive disorders, the disease manifests itself when the offspring has a homozygous state , which means each child has a 25% chance of being affected by the disease . Note : There are 2 alleles for this, say for example "A" = normal allele and "a" = abnormal allele . So, if each parent is phenotypically normal and their child is affected , then they are carriers, i.e., "Aa". So, each parent has a 0.5 (50%) probability of passing the affected allele to the next generation. Also, having each child is an independent event, and the chance that the child receives an abnormal allele from the father (0.5), as well as a mother (0.5), is equal to 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 i.e. 25%.202

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 29-year-old woman is homozygous for an autosomal-recessive gene and her husband is heterozygous for the same. They are planning to start a family and wish to know the outcome of their pregnancy. Which out of the following options correctly represent the percentages of the outcome ?

options.b: No child affected , but all are carriers

mcqs.explanation: If the husband is heterozygous and the wife is homozygous for an autosomal recessive gene , 50% of the children will be affected ; the rest will be carriers. This is pseudo -dominant inheritance, which refers to the observation of apparent dominant (parent to child) transmission of a known autosomal-recessive disorder, or it can also mean the inheritance of a recessive trait mimics a dominant pattern. This occurs when a homozygous affected individual has a partner who is a heterozygous carrier , and their children have a 1 in 2 chance to get affected (50%).203

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the mode of inheritance of Menke's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The mode of inheritance of Menke's disease is X-linked recessive . X-linked recessive disorders have the following features : • Males are affected more commonly and more severely than females . • Female carriers have a 25% risk for having an affected son, a 25% risk for a carrier daughter , and a 50% chance of having a child that does not inherit the mutated X-linked gene . • The affected father will have all daughters (100 %) to be carriers and unaffected sons because they pass their X chromosome to all of their daughters and their Y chromosome to all of their sons. X- linked recessive pattern of inheritance is shown in the image given below :Kinky hair disease (Menkes d isease ) Wilson's disease X- linked recessive Autosomal recessive Mutation of copper -transport ing, P-type adenosine triphos phatase 7A leading tocopper deficiency Mutation of adenosine tripho sphatase 7B on chromosome 13q14 leading toexcessivecop per accumulation. Lowserum copper and cerulo plasmin levels Lowceruloplasmin levels ;low serum-free copper levels andi ncreased urinary copper excr etion

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 41-year-old father of two has an X-linked genetic disorder. His daughter is a carrier for the same and his son is unaffected . His wife is healthy with no inherited disease . Which of the following is an example of this disorder?
mcqs.explanation: 204 The mode of inheritance is X- linked recessive and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an example of such a genetic disorder.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an X-linked disorder?
mcqs.explanation: Color blindness is primarily inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. The genes for color vision are located on the X chromosome. Males have a single X chromosome inherited from mothers. If the X chromosome inherited carries a mutation, males exhibit the disease . However, females become carriers of the color blindness gene and have a 50% chance of passing it on to their children. Female carriers usually are protected because of the random inactivation of one X chromosome. But there is a possibility that the mutant X chromosome remains active if the normal alleles are inactivated in some of the cells so the heterozygous female can express the disorder partially. The image shows the pattern of X-linked inheritance:In color blindness , the mechanism to appreciate one or more primary colors is either defective (anomalous) or absent (anopia). It may be congenital or acquired. Congenital color blindness can be dyschromatopsia (defective color vision of any one of the RGB colors) or achromatopsia (complete color blindness of all three RGB colors). RGB colors are red, green , and blue . Tests for color blindness include the Ishihara test , Hardy–Rand–Rittler test , and Farnsworth–Munsell 100 -hue test .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true regarding ataxia-telangiectasia ?

options.b: Follows autosomal dominant mode of inheritance

mcqs.explanation: Ataxia telangiectasia (AT) or Louis–Bar syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.205 The defect in AT is in the ATM gene localized to chromosome 11q22 -23 . The ATM gene is involved in the repair of double -strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to combined immunodeficiency (impaired immunoglobin isotype switching and association with thymic hypoplasia ) and predisposition to an increased risk of lymphoreticular tumors such as lymphoma or leukemia. AT is characterized by progressive ataxia (beginning during infancy), telangiectasia (initially on bulbar conjunctiva), sinopulmonary infections , hypogonadism , sensitivity to ionizing radiation, insulin resistance , and raised alpha-fetoprotein levels .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presented with progressive muscular weakness showing the following finding. It was found that the child is unable to get up from a squatting position. He was diagnosed with a hereditary muscular disorder. What is the mode of inheritance in this disorder?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical vignette includes an image of a child with pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles along with a history of inability to get up from a squatting position. This is characteristically seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy , which is an X-linked recessive disorder. Salient features of Duchenne muscular dystrophy : • Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease . • X-linked recessive mutations of dystrophin gene on chromosome Xp21. Clinical features : • Progressive weakness , developmental delay , and intellectual impairment • In toddlers : delayed walking, falling, toe walking, and trouble running or walking upstairs • Common sites of muscular hypertrophy : calf > tongue > forearm • Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles due to fibrofatty replacement of muscle • Gower's sign: Patients use their arms and hands to walk up their own body from a squatting position due to the reduced strength in the proximal muscles (hip &thigh) of the lower limbs. • Trendelenburg gait/hip waddle • Inability to walk develops by the age of 10 -14 years. • Complications : Contractures, scoliosis , cardiomyopathy , malignant hyperthermia after anaesthesia . • Death occurs by 3rd decade of life due to respiratory failure. Note : Becker's Muscular Dystrophy (BMD) vs. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) Mnemonic- • BMD: Badly makes dystrophin (defective ) • DMD: Does not make dystrophin (absent )206

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Your second cousin, Prakriti , has been recently diagnosed with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Your relatives are worried and keep calling you to confirm the new information that they read on the internet. In an attempt to settle their doubts about the credibility of online resources , you inform them that all of the following are true except :

options.a: X- linked recessive mode of inheritance
options.b: Atopic dermatitis and eczema during infancy

mcqs.explanation: IgM is decreased in Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, not increased . It is a rare genetic immunodeficiency that keeps a child's immune system from functioning properly . It also makes it difficult for a child's bone marrow to produce platelets , making a child prone to bleeding . This syndrome is associated with decreased IgM, increased IgA, and increased IgE levels . Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Mnemonic WAXTIE • WA : Wiskott–Aldrich • X: X-linked recessive • T: Thrombocytopenia • I: Infections • E: Eczema

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old girl has been diagnosed with a genetic disorder that follows a Mendelian pattern of inheritance illustrated by the pedigree chart below . Which of the following can be a likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given pedigree chart illustrates an inheritance pattern that is suggestive of an X-linked dominant disorder. Hence , hypophosphatemic rickets, which is an X-linked dominant disorder, is a likely diagnosis here. X-linked dominant disorders: • Females are affected twice as often as males. • An affected female has a 50% probability of transmitting the disorders to her son or daughter . • An affected male transmits the disorder to all of his daughters and none of his sons.207 • Some X-linked dominant conditions are lethal in a high percentage of males, e.g., incontinentia pigmenti. Other options : • Lesh–Nyhan syndrome: X-linked recessive disorder affects young boys due to the deficiency of HGPRT enzyme in the purine pathway. It is marked by compulsive self -mutilation of the head and hands, together with learning difficulties and involuntary muscular movements. • Fabry disease : X-linked recessive lysosomal storage disease due to the deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. Affected males have angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis , acroparesthesias , and corneal-lenticular opacities . Note : Mnemonic to remember X-linked dominant disorders: Ribbons For All Children • Ribbons - Rett's syndrome/ Hypophosphatemic Rickets • For - Fragile X tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) • All - Alport syndrome • Children - Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old girl presented with poor growth and social interaction as well as midline stereotypical movements of the hands as seen in the image below . All milestones were normal for the first 2 years. After that, the milestones delayed and her development slowed down. On examination, her gait was slightly clumsy , her speech had regressed to mere babbling and her anthropometry was below the 50th percentile . Following a battery of investigations, the diagnosis of a rare inherited disease was made. What is the affected gene for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given features of poor growth & social interaction, gradual loss of speech , clumsy gait along with the characteristic hand movements point towards a likely diagnosis of Rett's syndrome. The gene involved in Rett's syndrome is the MeCP2 gene located on the X chromosome (Xq28 predominantly of paternal origin). Rett's syndrome: • Almost always affects girls (X- linked dominant) • Development may proceed normally until 1 year of age slowing down to the extent of regression. • After 1 year of age , rapid regression in language and hand skills, motor milestones , and acquired microcephaly become apparent. • Clinical features can include repetitive hand wringing movements, ataxia, breathing dysfunction , bruxism, scoliosis , and profound mental retardation. • Autistic behaviour is a typical finding in all patients . Note : • Rb: Retinoblastoma: 13 chromosome • P53: Li –Fraumeni syndrome, Sarcomas: • NF1: Neurofibromatosis 1-17 • NF2: Neurofibromatosis 2-22 • WT1 : Wilms's tumour: • FGFR3: Achondroplasia208

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While reviewing a junior's research manuscript on trinucleotide repeat sequences , you come across the following list of examples and spot an error . Which of the following diseases will you mark for omission?
mcqs.explanation: Hereditary motor-sensory neuropathy, commonly known as Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy , is a type of X-linked dominant disorder. The rest of the options are associated with trinucleotide repeat sequences . Triple-repeat mutations (Allelic expansion disorders). • Due to an increase in the number of nucleotide repeats above a certain threshold . • Length of the nucleotide repeat often correlates with the severity of the disease . • Anticipation: When repeat length increases from one generation to the next, disease manifestations may worsen or be observed at an earlier age .Disease Repe ats Clinical features Fragile X- syndrome CGG Mental retardation, large ear s, and jaws, macroorchidism in males Myotonic Dystrophy (chromo some 19) CTG Muscle loss, cardiac arrhyth mia,cataracts, frontal balding Huntington's disease CAG Affective disorder Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 CAG Progressive ataxia, dysarthria, dysmetria . Friedreich's ataxia GAA Progressive ataxia,dysarthria, hypertrophiccardiomyopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child presents with previously diagnosed fragile X syndrome. As an intern posted in the department, you are asked to follow up on his cytogenetic analysis report. What is the trinucleotide repeat mutation seen in the report?
mcqs.explanation: The trinucleotide repeat mutation associated with fragile X syndrome is CGG in the familial mental retardation -1 (FMR1) gene . Other common trinucleotide repeat mutations and their associated conditions: • GAA- Friedreich ataxia • CAG- Huntington disease • CTG- Myotonic dystrophy

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability . On examination , his IQ was 45 and a previous report in his records show a trinucleotide repeat mutation of CGG. Which of the following is not seen in it?
mcqs.explanation: In fragile -X syndrome, there would be a small nose, not large. • Fragile X syndrome or Martin–Bell syndrome: Trinucleotide repeat mutation of CGG.209 Remember mnemonic Hello Mr. FRAGILE X Syndrome: • Hello : Hyperextensible joint or high-arched palate • Mr: Mitral valve prolapse • F: FMR1 P deficiency (fragile X mental retardation 1 protein) - upregulates the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) 5 pathway and alters the expression of matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9. • R: Repeating the sequence of 3 nucleotides CGG, recurrent otitis media. • A: Autism/Attention deficit –hyperactivity disorder/Anxiety • G: Giant brain (macrocephaly ) and giant testis (macroorchidism) • I: Intellectual disability , i.e., mental retardation • L: Long face with a large mandible • E: Everted ear • X: X-linked disorder (controversial as to whether it is X-linked dominant or recessive ) The most common genetic cause of mental retardation is Down's syndrome > Fragile X Syndrome. Sherman's paradox: Risk of expressing mental retardation in fragile X syndrome increases in later generations (anticipation). Fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia: Intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia, which may progress to parkinsonism . Note : Inhibitors of the mGluR (overexpressed in fragile X) are undergoing clinical trials. Minocycline (lowers MMP9) has resulted in short-term improvements in anxiety, mood, and the Clinical Global Impression Scale . Image: A child with affected fragile X- syndrome; note the everted ears, long face , and large mandible.210

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As a participant in the Indian Academy of Paediatrics quiz, you are asked to mark the type of inheritance in MELAS. The pedigree chart shown in the image below is provided to explain which family members may be affected (coloured in re
mcqs.explanation: The type of inheritance in MELAS is mitochondrial, which manifests as mitochondrial myopathy , encephalopathy , lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes . Mitochondrial inheritance: • Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual's mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization. • Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease . • 80% of mitochondrial DNA codes for mitochondrial RNA, and therefore most mitochondrial DNA mutations lead to functional problems , which may be manifested as muscle disorders. The following pedigree shows the mitochondrial inheritance pattern-

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In order to understand the topic 'Non-Mendelian disorders', you have prepared flashcards. But, while browsing through them before your viva , the order of cards have been jumbled up. Which of the following option will you choose to correctly match the phenomena with their definitions ?
mcqs.explanation: The phenomena are correctly matched with their definitions as follows - • Genomic imprinting: Phenotypic expression of a gene depending on the parent of origin. • Mosaicism: Single organism possessing more than one genetic line as the result of genetic mutation. • Anticipation: Symptoms become more severe and/or appear at an earlier age as the disorder is passed from one generation to the next. • Non-penetrance : A genetic trait that is present in the genome but does not manifest itself in the individual.211 Genomic imprinting: epigenetic process , that selectively inactivates either the maternal or paternal allele . These defects include : • Beckwith- Wiedemann syndrome • Silver Russell syndrome • Angelman syndrome • Prader Willi syndrome Note : Uniparental disomy: This refers to the situation in which two copies of a chromosome come from the same parent, instead of one from each parent. Eg ., Angelman syndrome and Prader Willi syndrome.Prader–Willi syndrome AngelMan syndrome Deletions (70% cases ) DeletionofPaternal genes afte r maternal gene silencing DeletionofMaternal genes aft er paternal gene silencing Uniparental disomy(UPD) (3 0%) UPD of maternal chromosom e 15 UPD of paternal chromosom e 15

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old presented with a genetic disorder attributed to multifactorial inheritance. This type of inheritance is most likely to play a significant role in which of the following disorder?
mcqs.explanation: Multifactorial inheritance plays a significant role in the appearance of cleft lip. Multifactorial inheritance- It refers to traits that are caused by a combination of inherited , environmental , and stochastic factors. These include the following :Children (congenital malform ation) Adults Pyloric stenosisNeural tube d efectsCongenital heart defect sCongenital dislocation of the hipCleft lip and cleft palate Diabetes MellitusHypertensi onCoronary heart diseaseGou tSchizophrenia212

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: On watching the documentary 'The Secret of Our Lives: The Human Genome Project', a student reads up about the international consortium of scientists who fully deciphered the DNA of the most common chromosomal syndrome. What is this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome) is the most common chromosomal syndrome. It is the second human chromosome whose DNA has been fully deciphered by the Human Genome Project. Chromosomal disorders: These may involve autosomal or sex chromosomes. Note : • Most common trisomy leading to miscarriage/incompatibility with life : Trisomy 16. • F body: Y chromosome (quinacrine, a fluorescence dye , binds strongly to the Y chromosome forming a bright fluorescent spot called an F body).Involving autosomes Involving sex chromosomes Down's syndrome (Trisomy 2 1)Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18)Patau syndrome (Trisomy )Cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion ) Klinefelter 's syndrome (47, X XY )Turner syndrome (45, X0)223

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 39-year-old pregnant woman was found to have an abnormal nuchal translucency scan. An amniocentesis done revealed a chromosomal karyotype of 47, XX ,+21 . This result most commonly occurs due to?
mcqs.explanation: The chromosomal karyotype of 47, XX ,+21 is suggestive of Down's syndrome which occurs due to nondisjunction in maternal meiosis. Non-disjunction points to the failure of the homologous chromosome to separate during the meiotic division. Down's syndrome: • Most common chromosomal disorder • Incidence: 1/800 live births • Mechanism: • Trisomy 21 (meiotic maternal nondisjunction) (95%) • Robertsonian translocation: 4% • Mosaic pattern: 1% Note : • Robertsonian translocations: involve 2 acrocentric chromosomes (chromosomes 13 , 14, 15, , and 22 ) that fuse near the centromeric region, with a subsequent loss of the short arms.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Your aunt has sent you an image of her 1-year-old son's palm using an instant messaging app. She read online that it is mostly present in genetic disorders and wishes to get your opinion. You identify it as a simian crease and prepare a list of differentials . All of the following diagnoses are correct except :
mcqs.explanation: Simian crease (single transverse palmar crease ) is not seen in cystic fibrosis. Simian crease is seen in the following disorders: • Down's syndrome • Fetal alcohol syndrome224 • Trisomy 13 • Cri du chat syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A girl is born at term after an uneventful pregnancy and delivery . On examination, she is noted to be hypotonic , has a protruding tongue , low set ears, an upward slant to the eyes with epicanthal folds , and a single palmar crease . On cardiac evaluation, what is the most common lesion expected in this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The girl is suffering from Down's syndrome and the most common cardiovascular lesion is an endocardial cushion defect . Other associated defects are atrial septum defects (ASD), ventricular septum defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), aberrant subclavian artery, and pulmonary hypertension . Clinical features : (Mnemonic: I C A PROBLEM Somewhere ) • Intellectual disability /Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly • Congenital heart disease • Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/Alzheimer's disease /Atlantoaxial instability /Atresia of the duodenum • Protruding tongue • Round face • Occiput flat/Open wide fontanelle /Open mouth • Brachycephalic /Brushfield 's spots • Low (depressed ) nasal bridge • Epicanthal fold /Ears low set and dysplastic • Mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure ) • Simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes Note : • The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double -bubble sign). • Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL ) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). • AML is more common during the first 3 years of life . • The most common AML associated with Down Syndrome is acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. • The most common haematological manifestation in Downs syndrome is transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM). • Brushfield 's spots are whitish speckling on iris seen in light -skinned people . Image: A child having features of Down's syndrome225 Image: Brushfield 's spots

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 41-year-old entrepreneur is excited to start her family. She has been getting a lot of unsolicited advice about the complications of pregnancy in advanced maternal age . On enquiring about such pregnancies , the doctor advised the mother to get prenatal testing done. All are findings associated with the prenatal diagnosis for Down's syndrome except _________

options.d: Ventricular septal defect may be present

mcqs.explanation: Increased umbilical flow is not seen during the prenatal screening for Down's syndrome, instead , the flow is decreased . Reduced blood flow through the umbilical vessels and abnormal blood flow through ductus venosus (DV) in the first trimester are associated with chromosomal abnormalities, especially Down's syndrome. This decrease in blood flow causes IUGR in infants born with Down syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An elderly primigravida underwent a nuchal translucency scan at 14 weeks which was highly suggestive of Down's syndrome. The doctor advised her to undergo a triple test and called her back at week 16. On receiving her receipt for the payment of the test , she realises that she has been billed wrongly for a component that is not included in the triple test . What is this component ?
mcqs.explanation: 226 Inhibin A is not included in the triple test : Note : • AFP: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein • HCG: Beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin • PAPPA : Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A • UE3: Unconjugated estriolTest Components Triple test AFP + hCG + UE3 Quadruple test Triple test + Inhibin A Combined test (first-trimester screening ) PAPPA + hCG + nuchal trans lucency Integrated test (most sensitive ) Combined test + Quadruple t est

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While writing your medical competitive exams, you come across the following image of karyotyping analysis in a question. You recognize this image as being highly suggestive of a particular syndrome. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above karyotype is suggestive of Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13 ). Clinical features of Trisomy 13 /Patau syndrome (Mnemonic CMC DOCToR OPD) • Cardiac defects (ventricular septal defect /atrial septal defect /patent ductus arteriosus) • Microcephaly , Microphthalmia • Cleft lip/palate • Developmental delay • Ocular hypotelorism • Holoprosencephaly • Thin posterior ribs (missing ribs) • Renal abnormalities • Polydactyly with flexed fingers • Polycystic kidneys • Scalp defects (aplasia cutis ) Image: 37-week male with Patau syndrome demonstrating alobar holoprosencephaly with cyclopia . Facial features included a sloping forehead with a nose superior to a single central palpebral fissure .227

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 10 -month-old boy presented with facial dysmorphism as well as two characteristic findings shown in the picture below . What is the condition affecting this newborn?
mcqs.explanation: The newborn with features of facial dysmorphism, index finger overlapping other fingers, and rocker bottom feet are suggestive of Edward's syndrome (Trisomy 18). Clinical features of Edward 's syndrome: (Remember mnemonic: Hi Mr EDWARDS) • Hypertonia • Microcephaly /Micrognathia • Eighteen trisomy/Elongated skull • Digit overlapping with a closed fist • Webbing of 2nd and 3rd toes • Absent intellect (severe developmental delay )/Absent radii/ Arthrogryposis • Rocker bottom feet • Cardiac Disorders (ventricular septal defect , patent ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect ) and kidney , death . • Small lower jaw (Micrognathia), short sternum, small nipples Note : P, Patau syndrome: Trisomy 13 E, Edward 's syndrome: Trisomy 18 D, Down syndrome: Trisomy 21 Alagille syndrome (AS) is an autosomal-dominant disorder associated with abnormalities of the liver (hypoplasia of hepatic duct ), heart (tetralogy of Fallot ), skeleton , eye , and kidneys and a characteristic facial appearance . William's syndrome is a developmental disorder that is characterized by mild to moderate intellectual disability or learning problems , unique personality characteristics, distinctive facial228 features , and cardiovascular problems .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young girl presents to you with learning disabilities . On examination, you notice a characteristic finding as shown in the picture below . Reports of her investigation scans mention horseshoe kidneys and streak gonads. What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The child shows characteristic webbed neck, learning disabilities , horseshoe kidneys, and streak gonads and is diagnosed with Turner 's syndrome. Turner 's syndrome: • Karyotype , 45; XO , phenotypically females • Chromosomal abnormality XO is present in 60% of individuals, mosaic pattern in 40% • Intelligence remains normal Important features associated with Turner 's syndrome: (mnemonic: See A Baby CLOWN Here) • Short stature , Short fourth metacarpal, Sensorineural hearing loss, Shield chest • Amenorrhea (primary), infertility • Barr body absent • Cardiac defects , Cubitus valgus, Congenital lymphedema • L: Learning disabilities • Ovaries underdeveloped (streak ovaries), Gonadoblastoma (increased risk if Y chromosome material is present ) • Webbed neck • Nipples widely spaced • Horseshoe kidneys Note : The most common cardiac defect in Turner 's is bicuspid aortic valve > coarctation of aorta.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Kaveri recently became pregnant following a history of repeated abortions. She was anxious and wanted to undergo karyotyping this time to detect chromosomal disorders pre-natally. Barr body was found to be absent in her report. Which of the following is associated with an absent Barr body?
mcqs.explanation: Barr body is absent in female having 45 X0 genome . Barr body • Densely staining inactivated condensed X chromosome present in each somatic cell of a female is found in the nucleus . • Chromatid body (Barr body or sex chromatin) is derived from one of the two X chromosomes which become inactivated. • The number of Barr bodies is thus one less than the number of X chromosomes. Turner 's syndrome is female without Barr body. Klinefelter 's syndrome is male with Barr body.229 Note : • Lyon hypothesis states that only one of the two X chromosomes in a female is functional, the other becomes inactive during embryogenesis . • Davidson bodies are small nuclear buds of chromatin shaped like a drumstick found in neutrophils of females .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old adolescent presents with an anti-mongoloid slant, pulmonary stenosis , short stature , webbed neck, and undescended testis . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The adolescent presenting with antimongoloid slant, pulmonary stenosis , short stature , webbed neck, and undescended testis is suggestive of Noonan syndrome. Although the webbed neck is a feature of Turner syndrome as well , the likely diagnosis would be Noonan syndrome since the patient is male (undescended testis ). Noonan syndrome: • Autosomal-dominant disorder (12q ) • Male or female with Turner phenotype ; normal karyotype . Clinical features : • Down-slanting palpebral fissure (antimongoloid slant) • Pectus carinatum • Hypertelorism • Cryptorchidism • Low levels of clotting factor 11 and 12 • Leukemia (Juvenile chronic myelogenous leukemia) • Moderate mental retardation in 25% • Cardiac abnormality: Most common is pulmonary valve stenosis . • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy • Atrial Septal Defect • Coarctation of aorta • Short stature , webbed neck, low set ears, cubitus valgus: similarities with Turner syndrome • Ptosis, micrognathia, clinodactyly , delayed puberty . Difference between Noonan syndrome and Turner syndrome:Noonan syndrome Turner syndrome Normal karyotype (46XX /46X Y) 45, X0(60%) Most common heart disease : Valvular pulmonary stenosis Most common heart disease : Bicuspid aortic valve 25% have mental retardation Mental retardation rare230 Noonan syndrome Turner syndrome Genitourinary:Female : Fertil e, delayed pubertyMale: Infer tile due to cryptorchidism Genitourinary:Female : Inferti le , streak ovariesNo males

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A concerned pregnant woman underwent karyotyping which was highly suggestive of a particular syndrome. The image of her results is shown below . Which of the following abnormalities is associated with patients with the given karyotype ?
mcqs.explanation: The above karyotype - 47, XXY , is suggestive of Klinefelter 's syndrome, in which gynecomastia and long thin limbs are seen . Klinefelter 's syndrome: • Most common sex aneuploidy in males • Classically karyotype is 47, XXY . Other variants can have 48 XXXY ; rarely, 49 XXXXY ; or mosaics with some cells containing normal 46, XY and others 47, XXY • Results from meiotic nondisjunction of sex chromosomes (mostly during 1st meiotic division) Clinical features : • Disproportionately long arms and legs • Mitral valve prolapse • Mental retardation; IQ: 60-80 • Minor developmental and learning disabilities • Lack of secondary sexual characteristics (due to a decrease in androgen production ) • Gynecomastia • Higher risk of breast carcinoma • Testicular dysgenesis231 • Infertility/ azoospermia Note : A variant of Klinefelter 's syndrome—49, XXXXY —presents with short stature .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn with previously diagnosed Cri-du-chat syndrome presented to the hospital . Which of the following is not observed in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Hypotonia is seen in cri-du-chat syndrome, not hypertonia . Cri-du-chat syndrome occurs due to the deletion of chromosome 5p . Main features : • • Hypotonia • Characteristic shrill cry (cat-like cry) in the first few weeks of life • Microcephaly • Hypertelorism • Bilateral epicanthic folds • High-arched palate • Wide and flat nasal bridge • Intellectual disability Note : • Cat-bite infection is caused by Pasteurella multocida . • Tomcat urine odor is seen in multiple carboxylase deficiencies .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A senior asks you to read about an autosomal dominant condition known as Treacher- Collins syndrome. While browsing through numerous journals to learn about the topic , you come across a doubt about its features . Which of the following is not associated with this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Intelligence is not affected in Treacher–Collins syndrome (like in Turners syndrome). Treacher–Collins syndrome/Franceschetti syndrome • Autosomal dominant • Facial appearance : downward sloping palpebral fissures , colobomas and drooping of the lower eyelids , sunken cheekbones , deformed pinnae, atypical hair growth extending towards cheeks • Facial clefts , malformed ears, deafness • Hypoplastic mandible Image: Treacher–Collins syndrome; note the sunken cheekbones , abnormality of ears, and hypoplastic mandible232

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All of the following are seen in a 5-month-old child with Pierre- Robin syndrome except ?
mcqs.explanation: Coloboma iris is not a feature of Pierre–Robin syndrome. Features of Pierre–Robin syndrome- • Micrognathia accompanied by a high-arched or cleft palate • Tongue normal size; the floor of the mouth is foreshortened • Retrognathia: retracted mandible • Glossoptosis /Retroglossoptosis : tongue appears to fall into the throat (retraction of the tongue ) Of the children with Pierre–Robin syndrome, 30–50% have Stickler syndrome. Features include prominent joints, arthritis, hypotonia, hypermobile joints, mitral valve prolapse , hearing loss, and ocular problems (myopia, glaucoma, cataracts, retinal detachment ). Pierre–Robin syndrome as shown in the image below :233

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Shantanu, an avid reader, and a first-year resident , recently finished Joseph Heller 's famous novel 'Catch-22'. While discussing the book with his friend, he realized that the title was an acronym of a chromosomal disorder they had studied . Which of the following is the least likely feature of this disorder?
mcqs.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome, also known as Catch-22 syndrome, is associated with cardiac anomalies and not cranial anomalies. DiGeorge /Shprintzen Velocardiofacial syndrome - Remember the mnemonic CATCH 22 • C: Cardiac anomalies • A: Abnormal facies • T: Thymic aplasia and agenesis of parathyroid glands. • C: Cleft palate • H: Hypocalcemia , hypoplasia of auricle • : 22q11 .2 deletion

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Riya was found to have a height of more than 95 percentile for her age and an arm -span to height ratio of more than 1.05. On further examination, she had flat feet , mild scoliosis , and long slender fingers. An image of her hands showing two characteristic signs is provided below . What other complications can be expected in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The given features are suggestive of a diagnosis of Marfan's syndrome. Subluxation of the lens is a known complication. Image (a) shows Walker -Murdoch (wrist) sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist. Image (b) shows Steinberg (thumb) sign - thumb tip extends from the palm of the hand in a closed fist Features of Marfan's syndrome (Mnemonic: MARFAN'S) • Mitral valve prolapse • Myopia due to upward dislocation of the lens (bilateral ectopic lentis )234 • Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation • Retinal detachment • Fibrillin 1 gene defect : Reduced fibrillin 1 production causing joint laxity • Fifteen (Chromosome 15 is involved) • Flat feet • Arachnodactyly, Astigmatism, Air in lungs (Pneumothorax) • Nearsightedness • Subluxation of lens, Scoliosis , Speech disorders, Sleep apnea The image given below shows the Steinberg (thumb) sign:

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Venkatesh decided to present a rare case report of maternal disomy of chromosome 15 at a scientific conference . He collected the following image representing the disorder's features. What is this disorder?
mcqs.explanation: Maternal disomy of chromosome 15 is seen in Prader–Willi syndrome. The image shows the characteristic features of truncal obesity, short stature , and small hands and feet . Uniparental disomy: Offspring receives both copies of a chromosome from 1 parent and no copies from the other parent. Chromosome 15 diseases : Chromosome 15 has its own MAP (mnemonic), • M: Marfan syndrome • A: Angelman syndrome • P: Prader Willi syndromePrader-Willi syndrome AngelMan syndrome Deletion Paternal chromosome 15 Maternal chromosome 15235 Prader-Willi syndrome AngelMan syndrome Uniparental Diso my Maternal disomy(duplication ) seen in 25% of cases Paternal disomy (duplication ) seen in 5% of cases Clinical features Elevated Ghrelinlevels : Loss of appetite control, obesitySe vere hypotoniaShort statureS mall hands and feetHypogon adotropic hypogonadismCog nitive impairment Short statureSevere mental r etardation with lack of speec hStiff arm movementsSpastic , uncoordinated walkSeizures An inappropriate outburst of laughter (Happy puppets )

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Triangular facies is indicative of which of the following diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Triangular facies is indicative of Russell –Silver syndrome. Russell –Silver syndrome: • Clinical features : Short stature , triangular face (small jaw and pointed chin), microcephaly , limb and facial asymmetry, 5th finger clinodactyly . • A few cases are due to genomic imprinting disorder involving chromosome 11 . Note : Triangular facies is also seen in Alagille syndrome. The image given below shows a child with Russell –Silver syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During an intersectoral collaborative event, an award-winning geneticist from the National Human Genome Research Institute is invited for an endowment oration. He presents his lecture on an experimental form of treatment that uses the transfer of genetic material to cure diseases known as 'Gene Therapy'. Which of the following techniques does he mention for this therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: Electroporation is used in gene therapy. Gene therapy is a technique that uses genes to treat or prevent disease through the delivery of DNA into a patient 's cell by using recombinant viruses/naked DNA/DNA complexes . The methods236 used include intranuclear injection, electroporation , gene -gun, sonoporation, and magnetofection . Gene therapy was first used for severe combined immunodeficiency disorder (SCID), which is due to adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The following is the finding noted in a 12 -month-old baby who is growing well and developing normally since birth. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this finding?

options.b: Maternal history of phenytoin intake during pregnancy should be suspected
options.d: Chromosomal analysis should be done to rule out other chromosomal abnormalities

mcqs.explanation: The picture depicts a Simian crease – a single transverse palmar crease . It is a normal finding in about 3% of the population . In a child with simian crease and normal growth and development , reassurance should be provided. • A simian crease is one of the findings of Down's syndrome however presence of only this finding should not lead to a diagnosis of Down's syndrome. • Maternal history of phenytoin intake during pregnancy does not lead to this finding. However, maternal alcohol intake can be associated with this condition. • Chromosomal analysis in an otherwise well child is not indicated .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) is particularly useful in the modern era of diagnosis in clinical genetics . Which of the following statements is not true regarding this test ?

options.b: Evaluates maternal blood for fetal abnormalities
options.d: Positive test need confirmation by invasive testing

mcqs.explanation: Non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) has a high negative predictive value. NIPS: • Useful in screening high-risk pregnancies for aneuploidies . • Done after 10 weeks of gestation . • Evaluates maternal blood for screening . • Positive tests need confirmation by invasive testing (like amniocentesis , chorionic villous sampling).237

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother reports to the OPD with the complaint that her child smells funny. On examination, you notice that the child has a global developmental delay and smells mousy. What is your probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Mousy odor is characteristically seen in phenylketonuria due to excess phenylacetate (phenyl ketone ) formed in the body. In the absence of phenylalanine hydroxylase , phenylalanine enters into alternate metabolic pathways which result in the formation of phenyl lactate , phenylacetate , and phenylacetylglutamine .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A boy who attends school is sent to the principal's office as he often distracts others by rhythmically rocking back and forth on his seat . His mother worried about his behavior brings him to you. She also gives you a history of seizures . On examination, you notice he has blonde hair, fair skin, microcephaly , prominent maxillae with widely spaced teeth , and growth retardation. His urine changes its color transiently to blue -green on the addition of 1ml ferric chloride solution . What is the cause of CNS symptoms in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette describes a case of phenylketonuria . CNS damage in patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by hyperphenylalaninemia in brain tissue . High blood levels of phenylalanine saturate the transport system across the blood-brain barrier causing inhibition of the cerebral uptake of other large neutral amino acids such as tyrosine and tryptophan impairing brain protein synthesis . Microcephaly , prominent maxillae with widely spaced teeth , enamel hypoplasia , and growth retardation are other common findings in untreated children. Low bone mineral density and osteopenia have been reported in affected individuals of all ages . Excess phenylalanine is metabolized to phenyl ketones (phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate ) that are excreted in the urine. However, these metabolites have no role in the pathogenesis of CNS damage ; their presence in body fluids simply signifies the severity of the condition.247 Hypotyrosinemia can be partially responsible for the signs and symptoms but the primary cause is hyperphenylalaninemia. Laboratory diagnoses of phenylketonuria include : • Guthrie 's test : growth of bacillus subtilis is seen • Ferric chloride urine test : transient blue -green color • Blood phenylalanine levels : elevated • Enzyme studies • Genetic mutation studies • Tandem mass spectrometry : Gold standard screening method for all metabolic disorders.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An infant with severe vomiting who was misdiagnosed as a case of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is being screened for metabolic disorders. Screening reveals hyperphenylalaninemia. On ordering an enzyme study , you would include all of the following enzymes except :
mcqs.explanation: Defects of either phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) or tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) can cause hyperphenylalaninemias. PAH deficiency is diagnosed as phenylketonuria. Malignant hyperphenylalaninemias include three enzyme defects , dihydropteridine reductase ,pyruvoyl tetrahydropterin synthase , and GTP cyclohydrolase which help in BH4 synthesis . The deficiency of BH4 impairs three hydroxylase (phenylalanine , tyrosine, and tryptophan ), and severe neurological symptoms develop because of the lack of neurotransmitters. Dihydropteroate synthase is present only in bacteria and this makes it a useful target for sulfonamide antibiotics, which compete with the PABA precursor.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As a physician treating a 2-month-old baby with phenylketonuria what will be your mainstay of treatment ?
