mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old girl presents with a 2-day history of fever and joint pain. Further questioning reveals that she had a sore throat 3 weeks back for which she did not seek medical help. Acute rheumatic fever is suspected . Which of the following is not a component of the criteria used for the diagnosis of this child's condition?
mcqs.explanation: Erythema nodosum is not a component of Jones criteria which is used for acute rheumatic fever (ARF) diagnosis. Erythema marginatum is a major manifestation of the Jones criteria. It is an evanescent , non-pruritic rash over the trunk and extremities seen in rheumatic fever. The image below shows erythema marginatum.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following constitutes Hutchinson's triad?

options.a: Interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness , mulberry molars
options.b: Interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness , Hutchinson molars
options.c: Interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness , mulberry incisors
options.d: Interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness , Hutchinson incisors

mcqs.explanation: Hutchinson's triad refers to interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness , and Hutchinson incisors. It is seen in late congenital syphilis . The image below shows Hutchinson incisors:311 Congenital syphilis is due to Treponema pallidum . Early features include hepato -splenomegaly , jaundice , diffuse lymphadenopathy , maculopapular or vesiculobullous rash involving hands and feet , persistent rhinitis (snuffles ), and condylomatous lesions . Skeletal changes like saber shins, dental abnormalities like Hutchinson's teeth , and saddle nose (depression of the nasal root) are some late findings. Other clinical features of congenital syphilis : • Clutton joint - Due to synovitis, with sterile synovial fluid • Juvenile tabes and paresis • Rhagades - Linear scars radiating from mucocutaneous fissures of the mouth, anus, and genitalia • Mulberry molars - Abnormal 1st lower molars with excessive cusps • Sabre shin - Anterior bowing of the mid-portion of the tibia • Olympian brow - Bony prominence of the forehead312

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old baby is brought to the paediatrician by his mother because of jaundice . On examination , the baby has hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy . He has a saddle nose and persistent rhinitis as seen in the picture . The baby had been 2300g at birth. The delivery was complicated by preterm labour and a single , painless ulcer with a clean base on the mother's labia. Which of the following feature will not be seen in this baby?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital syphilis . Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia is a characteristic feature of congenital syphilis , not coombs-positive hemolytic anemia. Congenital syphilis results from transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum or during birth by contact with infectious lesions of the mother. Clinical features of congenital syphilis : • Hutchinson's triad - Hutchinson teeth , interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness • Clutton joint - Due to synovitis, with sterile synovial fluid • Juvenile tabes and paresis • Rhagades - Linear scars radiating from mucocutaneous fissures of the mouth, anus, and genitalia • Saddle nose - Depression of nasal bridge • Mulberry molars - Abnormal 1st lower molars with excessive cusps • Sabre shin - Anterior bowing of the mid-portion of the tibia • Olympian brow - Bony prominence of the forehead • Snuffles - Persistent rhinitis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A neonate was delivered via normal vaginal delivery . His mother was diagnosed with active tuberculosis infection during pregnancy but she refused treatment in fear of side effects to the baby. If the baby had been infected prenatally , which of the following organs is most likely to be involved?
mcqs.explanation: The liver is the most commonly involved organ in congenital tuberculosis . Primary infection in a female just before or during pregnancy is more likely to cause congenital tuberculosis . Congenital transmission usually occurs from a lesion in the placenta through the umbilical vein. The tuberculous bacilli may pass through the umbilical vein and develop a hepatic focus . Tuberculosis in neonates generally presents with respiratory distress , hepatosplenomegaly , and lymphadenopathy . Note : The most common route of infection for a neonate is the postnatal airborne transmission from an adult with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presented with a persistent cough . There was a contact history with an active tuberculosis case in his neighborhood . His X-ray revealed prominent hilar lymphadenopathy as shown in the image. Which of the following statements is false regarding this patient 's condition?

options.a: Puhl's lesion at the apex of lung is seen in primary infection
options.b: Most cases of pediatric TB are asymptomatic
options.c: Sputum smear-negative TB does not rule out pediatric pulmonary TB
options.d: The most common site of extrapulmonary TB is the lymph node

mcqs.explanation: The patient had exposure to an active tuberculosis case and has hilar lymphadenopathy (image), suggestive of primary tuberculosis . Puhl's lesion is chronic tuberculosis (TB ) of the apex of the lung, not seen in the primary infection.313 The majority of children develop no signs or symptoms at any level . In primary pulmonary disease , the combination of the parenchymal pulmonary lesion and the corresponding lymph node is called Ghon's complex or the primary complex . Asymptomatic pleural effusion is common and forms part of the primary complex . Erosion of a parenchymal focus of tuberculosis into the blood or lymphatic vessel can result in dissemination of the bacilli and a miliary pattern, with small nodules evenly distributed on the chest radiograph. Sputum smear-negative TB does not rule out pediatric pulmonary TB . Chronic pulmonary tuberculosis is common in children above 7 years of age . The commonest site is the apex of the lung—Puhl's lesion. Regional lymph nodes are not involved. The most common site of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in children is the lymph node. NOTE: • Ranke complex : Ghon's complex undergoes fibrosis and calcification. • Simon focus : Hematogenous spread to the apex of the upper lobe , resulting in a post -primary infective lesion, which heals with scarring. • Simmond's focus : Tuberculous focus in the liver. • Weigert focus : Caseating metastatic tuberculous focus in the wall of a pulmonary vein. • Rich focus : Tuberculous granuloma occurring in the cortex of the brain .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A woman with smear-positive tuberculosis is on anti-tubercular therapy (ATT ). She delivered a healthy male baby at term. How is the newborn managed in this case?

options.b: Breastfeeding + INH for 2 months then BCG vaccine
options.c: Breastfeeding + INH for 6 months then BCG vaccine
options.d: BCG + INH for 6 months + withhold Breastfeeding

mcqs.explanation: In a neonate born to a mother with smear-positive tuberculosis , breastfeeding along with INH prophylaxis for 3-6 months is recommended . BCG vaccine is recommended at birth or after completion of prophylaxis (3-6 months) in all neonates . When a child is born to a mother with active TB , the main aim is the TB -free survival of the newborn. It involves detecting active TB lesions (congenital TB ) and treating them or prevention of transmission of tubercular infection to the neonate from the mother. Prophylaxis with isoniazid (3-6 months) is recommended in neonates born to mothers with TB who are infectious (smear-positive ). Breastfeeding should be continued in these neonates and isolation is recommended only till the mother is infectious , has multidrug -resistant tuberculosis , or nonadherent to treatment . BCG vaccine is recommended at birth or after completion of prophylaxis ( -6 months) in all neonates . However, if the Mantoux test is positive and evidence of disease is found, ATT is started .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old lady is detected to have active tuberculosis at 37 weeks of gestation . She delivers a baby girl 2 days later. As per NTEP guidelines , what advice is given immediately after delivery ?

options.a: INH prophylaxis to be given to the neonate for 6 weeks
options.b: Mother is to be started on ATT

mcqs.explanation: The mother with TB is advised to start ATT immediately irrespective of time of delivery . The management guidelines followed in a case of active TB in a mother immediately following delivery include : • Mother has to be started on ATT .314 • Do not separate the baby from the mother. • Do not withhold breastfeeding . • Screening of household contacts . • Screen the neonate for congenital /active TB . In accordance with the NTEP 2020 guidelines , a newborn whose mother has active TB and is on ATT should be managed with prophylactic isoniazid (INH) for 6 months, BCG vaccination at birth, with the continuation of breastfeeding , after ruling out active TB . INH prophylaxis is given irrespective of the BCG or nutritional status . 10 mg/kg is administered daily for a minimum of six months. During monthly tablet collection , the child should be closely monitored for TB symptoms to rule out active TB and also assess for any INH-related adverse effects . BCG vaccination can be given at birth even if INH preventive therapy is planned . In case the newborn is found to have active TB , ATT is to be initiated along with the administration of BCG vaccine.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A worried couple brought their 4-day-old baby to the pediatrician due to difficulty in feeding and abnormal posture . The baby was delivered at home and the mother never had a prenatal checkup . On examination, the baby's body was rigid, with flexed upper limb and extended back. The umbilical cord was covered with cow dung. The mother says it's their tradition, and that the dirt helps with the falling off of the cord. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.a: The toxin responsible affects the excitatory neurons
options.b: Metronidazole is given as a treatment
options.c: It occurs in infants of unimmunized mothers

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of neonatal tetanus . It is caused by a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani, which inhibits inhibitory neurons, not excitatory neurons. Clostridium tetani is a spore -forming obligate anaerobe commonly found in soil, dust , and gastrointestinal tracts of various animals. The baby's umbilical stump covered with cow dung serves as the source of infection . It also occurs in infants of unimmunized mothers. Tetanus typically manifests within 3-12 days of birth as progressive difficulty in feeding , rigidity, or spasms. Tetanus toxin binds at the neuromuscular junction and enters the motor nerve; it is then transported to the alpha-motoneuron via retrograde axonal transport. Subsequently , the toxin enters the adjacent spinal inhibitory interneurons, where it prevents the release of the neurotransmitters glycine and \023-aminobutyric acid. This leads to blockade of normal antagonistic muscle inhibition, while agonist muscles undergo sustained contraction without relaxing. Neonatal tetanus presents with progressive feeding difficulty (sucking and swallowing ), irritability, and crying. Characteristic features include reduced movement or complete muscle paralysis, rigidity, and spasms. These features may or may not be associated with opisthotonos . Treatment includes supportive care in the form of muscle relaxants ( diazepam), along with the administration of human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) and metronidazole , which is the antibiotic of choice . Parenteral penicillin G can serve as an alternate antibiotic. Excising the umbilical stump in a baby with neonatal tetanus is no longer recommended .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with complaints of sore throat and difficulty in swallowing . The patient also has fever and hoarseness of voice and her facial appearance is as shown below . A provisional diagnosis of Diptheria is made. Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient 's condition?

options.a: It can be diagnosed by the demonstration of antibody by ELISA
options.c: Treatment of contacts is not indicated
options.d: Iron has a critical value in the production of toxins

mcqs.explanation: 315 The image shows a bull-neck appearance due to the soft tissue edema , seen in diphtheria . Iron is essential for the production of toxins in diphtheria . It is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae . Carriers are the most common causes of infection . Immunization does not prevent the carrier state . It spreads via droplets through the respiratory tract (most important), cutaneous lesions, and fomites . The regulation of toxin production in the bacterium is partially controlled by iron, thus making it an important prerequisite for toxin production . Clinical features : • Respiratory tract diphtheria (most common): • Thick , adherent pseudomembrane (grey or white ) on one/both tonsils and adjacent pharynx. Dislodging of the membrane may cause bleeding . • Underlying soft tissue edema and enlarged lymph nodes can cause a bull-neck appearance • Patients with laryngeal diphtheria are at risk for suffocation because of local soft -tissue edema and airway obstruction by the diphtheritic membrane.• Cutaneous diphtheria is an indolent , non-progressive infection characterized by a superficial , ecthyma-like, non-healing ulcer with a gray-brown membrane. • Occasionally , it causes mucocutaneous infections at other sites , such as otitis externa, purulent conjunctivitis, and vulvo-vaginitis. Diagnosis: The culture of the organism from the nose and throat swab specimens is the gold standard. Demonstration of the toxin is done by Elek's gel precipitation test . Gram stain and fluorescent antibody tests are unreliable . Complications include obstruction due to pseudomembrane , myocarditis, and polyneuropathy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A diphtheria screening camp is being held at a rural school to find carriers and to provide them adequate treatment . What is the investigation of choice in this scenario?
mcqs.explanation: 316 The investigation of choice for diphtheria carriers is throat swab culture . Specimens for culture should be obtained from the nose and throat and any other mucocutaneous lesion. A portion of the membrane should be removed and sent for culture along with the underlying exudate in those with overt disease . Direct smear using Gram stain or specific fluorescent antibody is unreliable .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Anuj has been \037 diagnosed with diphtheria and is being treated in the ward. His 3-year-old brother, Ajay who lives in the same house has received vaccination against diphtheria about 16 months back. What is the next best step for the management of the younger sibling, Ajay?

options.b: Nothing as the child is already exposed

mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario, a 3-year-old child is likely to have received the 4th dose (1st booster ) of the diphtheria vaccine between 16–24 months of age according to National Immunization Schedule (i.e., 16 months ago). Since he has received a booster dose within 5 years, only erythromycin is indicated in case of close contact with the diphtheria patient . All household contacts with diphtheria patients should be closely monitored for 7 days. Culture should be taken from both the throat and nose. All contacts should receive antibiotic prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G or erythromycin), regardless of immunization status . Children who have not received a booster dose of the diphtheria toxoid vaccine within 5 years should be given the vaccine in an age -appropriate form. Children who have not yet received their 4th dose should be vaccinated accordingly. If fewer than three doses of diphtheria toxoid have been given, or vaccination history is unknown, an immediate dose of diphtheria toxoid should be given and the primary series completed according to the current schedule . Asymptomatic carriers of diphtheria are treated with antimicrobial prophylaxis for a period of 10-14 days. If an individual has not received a booster dose of diphtheria toxoid within 1 year, an age -appropriate preparation of the vaccine should be administered promptly . Droplet precautions (respiratory colonization) or contact precautions (cutaneous colonization) of cases and carriers are maintained until two consecutive negative cultures (collected 24 hours apart) are obtained after cessation of therapy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young boy is brought to the clinic with complaints of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and painful straining for 4 months. The symptoms were accompanied by rectal prolapse . Stool examination showed the following finding. Infection with which of the following helminths is most likely?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a barrel-shaped ovum, which along with rectal prolapse is characteristic of trichuris trichiura. Trichuriasis is caused by T. trichiura (whipworm), which inhabits the cecum and ascending colon. They bury their thin heads into the intestinal lining causing edema , loosening the elastic epithelium , and weakening the surrounding muscles . This leads to loss of supports and rectal prolapse . Other clinical features include chronic dysentery , anemia , poor growth , and developmental defects . Diagnosis is done by fecal smears showing the barrel-shaped ovum of T. trichiura. The image below shows the barrel-shaped ovum of Trichuris trichiura.317 Albendazole is the drug of choice (400 mg, orally, for 3 days; for all ages ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An anxious mother brought her 4-year-old daughter to the pediatrician. The girl was passing loose , bulky stools for the past 4 days. This was often associated with pain in the abdomen. The pediatrician ordered stool examination, which showed the following organisms. Which vitamin deficiency is the child at the greatest risk for?
mcqs.explanation: The stool examination (image) shows pear-shaped trophozoites having two nuclei and a flagellum , typical of Giardia lamblia. Giardiasis is associated with a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin A. Giardia lamblia is transmitted via contaminated drinking water. Clinical features include acute infectious diarrhea or chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and abdominal pain. Stools initially may be profuse and watery and later become greasy and foul -smelling . Stools do not contain blood, mucus, or leukocytes . It is associated with fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies , iron deficiency , and growth stunting . Diagnosis is done by stool enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or direct fluorescent antibody tests for Giardia antigens ; EIA is superior to microscopy. Treatment includes tinidazole and nitazoxanide.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In a child, the amoebic liver abscess can be diagnosed by demonstrating which of the following ?

options.c: Cysts in the hepatic venous sample

mcqs.explanation: The amoebic liver abscess can be diagnosed by demonstrating Trophozoites in the pus Amebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica . Trophozoites are responsible for tissue invasion and destruction. Amoebic Colitis will present as colicky abdominal pains and frequent bowel movements (6–8/day). Diarrhea is associated with tenesmus , heme -positive stool . Trophozoites invade the intestinal mucosa and produce flask-shaped ulcers.318 Amoebic liver abscess occurs in <1% infected individuals. Fever is the hallmark of amoebic liver abscess . It is associated with abdominal pain, abdominal distention and enlargement , and tenderness of the liver. Changes at the base of the right lung, such as elevation of the diaphragm and atelectasis or effusion , can also occur. The most common finding is a single abscess in the right hepatic lobe , detected on USG, CT, or MRI. The image below shows a CT scan of a right lobe liver abscess .Invasive amebiasis is treated with nitroimidazoles such as metronidazole or tinidazole. This is followed by a luminal amebicide such as paromomycin.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common route of acquiring Ancylostoma duodenale infection ?
mcqs.explanation: Skin penetration is the most common route by which the larva of Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) enters the human body. Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) larvae enter the human host by skin penetration and undergo extraintestinal migration through the venous circulation to the lungs . They enter alveoli and climb up to the bronchial tree and pharynx, and are swallowed . Larvae reach the small intestine and become adult worms. Clinical manifestations include iron deficiency anemia, resulting from chronic occult intestinal blood loss. Dermatitis, sometimes referred to as ground itch, may occur when they penetrate human skin. Eosinophilic pneumonia can also be seen . Infection with a zoonotic hookworm, especially Ancylostoma braziliense, can result in the lateral migration of the larvae causing cutaneous tracts of cutaneous larva migrans. The image below shows the lifecycle of the intestinal hookworm.319 The image given below shows cutaneous larva migrans.Treatment: • Mebendazole 100 mg bid, orally, for 3 days or single dose of 500 mg • Albendazole 400 mg, orally, once

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child from Bihar comes with a fever. Blood examination shows sheathed microfilaria as shown in the image. Identify the organism.
mcqs.explanation: The incidence of Brugia malayi is more in children from Bihar and the image showing microfilaria with two nuclei at the tail. Hence the organism is Brugia malayi, which causes lymphatic filariasis. Brugia malayi (Malayan filariasis), Brugia timori, and Wuchereria bancrofti (bancroftian filariasis) are thread-like nematodes that cause a similar infection called Filariasis. Infective larvae are320 introduced into humans during sucking of blood by the mosquito vector (commonly, culex ). Clinical manifestations include episodic fever, lymphangitis of an extremity , lymphadenitis (especially the inguinal and axillary areas), headaches , and myalgias. Hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy are often seen in children. These symptoms are caused by an acute inflammatory response triggered by the death of adult worms. Diagnosis is done by demonstration of microfilariae in the blood. Blood samples should be obtained between 10 pm and 2 am because microfilaremia is nocturnal. Treatment: • Diethylcarbamazine 1 mg/kg PO as a single dose on day 1 • 1 mg/kg tid on day 2 • 1-2mg/kg tid on day 3 • 6 mg/kg/day divided tid on days 4-14 The image below shows the difference between microfilaria of various filarial nematodes .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A boy is brought to the emergency with repeated episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures . History is significant for a dietary intake of pork. MRI reveals multiple ring-enhancing lesions as shown below . Which of the following organism is the likely cause for seizures in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The likely cause of seizures in a child who has multiple ring-enhancing lesions and dietary history of pork intake is an infection with Taenia solium. Children acquire the adult form of the parasite by ingestion of undercooked pork containing larvae cysts . In the intestines , the cyst converts into adult form. The adult form releases eggs in the stool . If the eggs are ingested (shed by tapeworm carriers or by unhygienic practices ), the larvae are released from the eggs . The larva then invades through the intestines and migrate through the bloodstream to the muscles (and other organs), where they form tissue cysts called cysticercosis . When these larvae find their way to the brain , it is termed as neurocysticercosis .321 Neurocysticercosis typically presents with seizures (focal or generalized ). It can be associated with basilar arachnoiditis that can present with signs of meningeal irritation . Cysticerci in the tissues may present with focal findings from the mass effect . Ocular neurocysticercosis causes decreased visual acuity because of cysticerci in the retina or vitreous, retinal detachment , or iridocyclitis . Treatment includes management of seizures . albendazole therapy (treatment of choice ). Praziquantel can also be used .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding congenital toxoplasmosis ?

options.a: It occurs through hematogenous dissemination to the placenta
options.b: Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation
options.d: It can manifests as hydrops fetalis

mcqs.explanation: IgG is not diagnostic for congenital toxoplasmosis . The presence of IgG antibodies in a newborn can be due to an old infection in the mother, as IgG can cross the placenta . IgM cannot cross the placenta , hence the presence of IgM in newborns confirms the diagnosis of congenital toxoplasmosis . IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests . Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondi. Toxoplasma can be transmitted to humans by three principal routes : • Ingestion of raw or inadequately cooked infected meat • Ingestion of oocysts through exposure to cat litter or soil • Newly infected pregnant woman passing the infection to her unborn fetus It can be acquired orally, transplacentally or rarely, parenterally or by transfusion. Congenital toxoplasmosis : When a mother acquires the infection during gestation , organisms may disseminate hematogenously to the placenta . Infection may be transmitted to the fetus transplacentally or during vaginal delivery . The characteristic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus , and cerebral calcifications may be present . Other clinical features include small size for gestational age , prematurity , persistent jaundice , mild thrombocytopenia , hydrops fetalis , and perinatal death .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis is ______
mcqs.explanation: Chorioretinitis is the most common manifestation of congenital toxoplasmosis . The characteristic triad of congenital toxoplasmosis is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus , and diffuse intracranial calcifications . Clinical manifestations apart from the triad include hydrops fetalis , intrauterine growth retardation, prematurity , peripheral retinal scars, persistent jaundice , and mild thrombocytopenia . Congenital toxoplasmosis occurs when a pregnant woman acquires the infection during gestation . The organism may cross to the fetus transplacentally or at the time of vaginal delivery . The severity of the disease in the neonate is greater if the woman gets infected early in her pregnancy. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii , an obligate intracellular protozoan.322 The diagnosis is made by the detection of IgM anti-toxoplasma antibodies . IgG can cross the placenta is hence , cannot confirm infection in the infant. IgM immunosorbent agglutination assay (ISAGA) and IgA ELISA are the most useful diagnostic tests . Spiramycin can be administered for cases of acute infection in early pregnancy to reduce vertical transmission . It does not cross the placenta and therefore cannot be used to treat an infected fetus . Pyrimethamine-sulfonamide (to be avoided in the first trimester) is used when a fetal infection is confirmed or in maternal infections after 18 weeks .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Maternal antibodies that do not provide significant immunity in a neonate :
mcqs.explanation: Maternal antibodies do not provide significant immunity to polio infection in a neonate . Administering an oral polio vaccine (OPV ) dose at birth can provide early mucosal protection , safeguarding against enteric pathogens before they can hinder the intestinal mucosal immune response . Furthermore, administering OPV during the period when infants are protected by maternal antibodies may help prevent vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP). All pregnant women should receive a tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine during each pregnancy, as early in the 27–36-week-of-gestation window as possible . The maternal antibodies formed from Tdap will provide immunity against tetanus , diphtheria , and pertussis in the newborn. Administering the Tdap vaccine earlier, between the 27th and 36th week of gestation , maximizes the transfer of passive antibodies to the infant (options A and C). Infants less than 6 months are generally protected from measles by maternal antibodies (option D).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the daily dosage of ethambutol for an adolescent of age 14 years?
mcqs.explanation: The daily dosage of ethambutol is 20 mg/kg body weight . First-line antitubercular drugs: Note : • All first-line antitubercular drugs are hepatotoxic except ethambutol . • All first-line antitubercular drugs are bactericidal except ethambutol , which is bacteriostatic .Drug Daily dosage (mg/k g) Adverse effects Isoniazid 10 -15 Peripheral neuritis, hepatic e nzyme elevation Rifampin 15-20 Orange discoloration of secre tions andurine Ethambut ol Optic neuritis,decreased red- green color discrimination323 Drug Daily dosage (mg/k g) Adverse effects Pyrazinam ide 30-40 Hepatotoxicity , hyperuricemi a

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of Hutchinson's triad in congenital syphilis ?
mcqs.explanation: Saber shin is not a component of Hutchinson's triad. Saber shin is the anterior bowing of the midportion of the tibia. Note : Peg-shaped upper central incisor is called as Hutchinson's teeth (erupts during the 6th year of life ). Hutchinson's triad: It is a triad of stigmata seen characteristically in congenital syphilis . The components are as follows : • Hutchinson's teeth • Interstitial keratitis • Sensorineural deafness Image: Hutchinson teeth (peg -shaped upper incisors)324

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A mother brought her 7-year-old child to the OPD because of fever and facial swelling for the past 2 days. She says that he has been refusing to eat because of the pain near the jaw. He has not been vaccinated since birth because of his parent's fear of side effects . On examination, a tender swelling is noted on the jaw as shown in the picture . Which of the following statement is true regarding this patient 's diagnosis?

options.b: Salivary gland involvement is limited to the parotids
options.c: Patient is not infectious prior to clinical parotid enlargement

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mumps. Meningoencephalitis can occur before , along with, or after parotitis. Most commonly, it manifests 5 days after parotitis. Mumps is caused by RNA paramyxovirus. It is spread from person to person via droplets from clinical and subclinical cases . The incubation period is 12 -21 days. The virus appears in the saliva from up to 7 days before to as long as 7 days after the onset of parotid swelling . The patient presents with prodrome lasting 1-2 days consisting of fever, headache , and vomiting. After the prodrome, unilateral or bilateral parotitis develops , which is tender . It may be associated with ipsilateral ear pain. Ingestion of sour or acidic foods may enhance pain. It can be prevented by administering live attenuated , MMR vaccine at 9 months, 15 months and 4-6 years. Option B: Mumps can affect all the salivary glands, but most commonly affects parotid glands. Option C: The patient is infectious from 7 days before to 7 days after the onset of parotid swelling . Option D: Orchitis or oophoritis is a common finding in mumps, along with parotitis. But, mumps leading to infertility is very rare.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: An outbreak of mumps infection was reported from a local school a few days ago. A boy studying in the 2nd standard of that school presented with painful bilateral swelling near his jaw and cheek for 3 days. His mother is anxious about the possible complications of the disease . Which of the following is the most common complication that can occur in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Meningoencephalitis is the most common complication that can occur in mumps in children. Most common complications in mumps: • Children - Meningoencephalitis • Adolescents and adult males - Orchitis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: On your pediatrics rotation, you notice a 2-day-old baby with the rash shown in the image below . Which among the following is the most likely cause for this baby's rash?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows purple papulonodular lesions , which are suggestive of blueberry muffin rash. It is seen in congenital rubella. Blueberry muffin rash represents dermal erythropoiesis . In addition to congenital rubella, it can be seen in: • Congenital viral infections such as cytomegalovirus and parvovirus • Neoplasms such as neuroblastoma and acute myeloid leukemia • Rh hemolytic disease337

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A woman who came with complaints of fever, myalgia, and rash at 12 weeks of gestation is found to have positive IgM titers for rubella. She is advised MTP. If the pregnancy is taken to full term, which of the following triad of complications would you expect to see in the child?

options.b: Sensorineural hearing loss, blueberry muffin rash, microcephaly
options.c: Cataracts, cicatricial skin lesions , limb defects
options.d: Sensorineural hearing loss, cataract, congenital heart defects

mcqs.explanation: The patient has an increased risk of congenital rubella if the pregnancy is taken full term. The triad of complications that would be expected in the child include : • Sensorineural hearing loss: Nerve deafness is the single most common finding among infants with congenital rubella syndrome • Congenital cataract • Congenital heart disease : The most common cardiac defect is patent ductus arteriosus Option A: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications - congenital toxoplasmosis . Option B: Sensorineural hearing loss, blueberry muffin rash, microcephaly - congenital CMV infection . Option C: Cataracts, cicatricial skin lesions, limb defects - congenital varicella syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Palak , a neonate is being evaluated for the finding shown in the image. The mother's prenatal history is significant for viral exanthem in early pregnancy. On examination, a grade 3 murmur is heard on auscultation . Which of the following is the most likely cause for this patient 's murmur ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a bilateral cataract, which along with the antenatal history of viral exanthem is suggestive of congenital rubella syndrome. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common congenital heart disease associated with rubella, followed by pulmonary artery stenosis (PS). Frequency of heart disease in congenital rubella: PDA > PS > VSD > ASD.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a baby in NICU with diffuse petechiae . On examination, mild hepatosplenomegaly, bilateral cataract, and a continuous murmur suggestive of patent ductus arteriosus are noted . Which of the following investigations would you do to diagnose this baby's condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital rubella syndrome. IgM antibody detection in infant blood are done to diagnose congenital rubella syndrome in a newborn. Congenital rubella syndrome is diagnosed by: • Presence of IgM rubella antibodies in the infant shortly after birth (since IgM does not cross the placenta), or • Persistence of IgG antibodies for >6 months (maternally derived antibody would have disappeared)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a high fever, cough , red eyes , and rash. The child's parents say that the rash started on the forehead and behind the ears, then subsequently spread to the neck and body. On examination, a confluent maculopapular rash is noted as shown below . Which of the following is false regarding this child's condition?

options.a: The period of infectivity is 4 days before and 5 days after the appearance of rash
options.b: The most common complication is pneumonia

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of measles . The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media. The most common cause of death is pneumonia (Hecht 's giant cell pneumonia).338 Measles (rubeola) is caused by RNA paramyxovirus . The infection is spread via droplets , with a secondary attack rate \034of 90%. The patients are infectious from 4 days before upto 5 days after the appearance of the rash. The rash appears on the 4th day of fever. It starts from the retro auricular region. Koplik spots are pathognomonic. The most common cause of death is pneumonia. Measles can lead to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) as a late complication. Measles can be prevented by administering live attenuated , Edmonston–Zagreb strain or combined MMR given at 9 months of age .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A young child presented with fever and cough in the OPD. He is observed to have the finding shown in the image below on the inner aspect of cheeks . Which of the following statement is false regarding this clinical finding?

options.a: It appears 1 to 4 days before the rash
options.b: It appears as tiny-rose colored lesions
options.c: It is seen at the level of molars
options.d: It may also occur in conjunctiva

mcqs.explanation: The image shows discrete red lesions with white spots in the center on the inner aspect of the cheeks , suggestive of Koplik spots . They do not appear as tiny rose-colored lesions . Koplik spots are pathognomonic of measles . These are the spots present at the level of molars. They appear 1-4 days prior to the rash. They may also occur in conjunctival folds and vaginal mucosa. Forchheimer spots : Tiny red-colored lesions in the oropharynx or petechial hemorrhages on the soft palate , seen in rubella (German measles ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old boy presents with a history of myoclonic jerks, seizures , and rapid decline in cognitive function. The mother gives a history of fever with a rash at 1.5 years of age . The rash had started behind the ears, progressed to involve the whole body, and resolved on its own. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario with a classic history of exanthematous fever suggestive of measles , seizures , myoclonic jerks, and cognitive dysfunction is suggestive of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). SSPE is a chronic, progressive demyelinating disease that develops years after measles infection , most often in patients between 5-15 years of age . Patients have a history of measles infection at <2 years of age . CSF shows elevated measles antibody levels and MRI shows increased T2 intensity in white matter. No definitive treatment is available. Other complications of measles : • Meningoencephalitis • Giant-cell pneumonitis • Pneumonia • Croup • Secondary infections - otitis media • Protracted diarrhea

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Akshay developed a fever, headache , and a diffuse rash as shown below . The rash is most prominent on the face and chest . He says the rash is very itchy bothering his everyday life . He is a football player and has an upcoming tournament in the next few days. He wants to know if he'll be able to play by then. Considering the rash infectivity , until when would you advise him to stay isolated ?

options.a: 4 days after the appearance of lesions
options.b: 7 days after the appearance of lesions
options.c: 14 days after the appearance of lesions
options.d: After crust formation has occurred over lesions

mcqs.explanation: 339 The above scenario is suggestive of chickenpox. You would advise the boy to stay isolated until after crust formation has occurred over lesions . People with chickenpox are contagious 24-48 hours before the rash is evident and until the vesicles have crusted , which is usually 3-7 days after the onset of rash.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: There is an outbreak of chickenpox among the children at a daycare center . What is the most common extracutaneous site of involvement of this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common extracutaneous site of involvement by the varicella-zoster virus in children is the central nervous system . It is a benign complication of VZV infection in children and generally does not require hospitalization. The most common infectious complication of varicella is secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin , which is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. The most common serious complication of varicella is varicella pneumonia.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Seema is brought to the OPD due to the development of a very itchy rash. Her father says he's worried because she has been constantly scratching her body leading to scratch marks . Before the development of the rash, she had a fever and headache for 2 days. On examination, you note a vesicular rash, which is in different stages of evolution. Which of the following is not a possible complication of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chickenpox caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV ). Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is not a complication of Varicella-zoster infection . It occurs due to measles . The characteristic rash of chickenpox is present in different stages of evolution. Complications of VZV occur with disseminated varicella or with reactivation of infection . This more commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients . Complications include : • Bacterial infections of the skin and soft tissues • Pneumonia • Hepatitis • Acute cerebellar ataxia • Encephalitis • Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy • Sepsis • Shingles /Herpes Zoster: vesicular lesions are confined to the unilateral segment of the sensory nerve (dermatome ). In children, the rash is mild, with complete resolution within 1-2 week . Unlike in adults , postherpetic neuralgia is unusual in children.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A child presents with fever, headache , and a diffuse rash as shown below . The rash resolves by crusting and the child recovers in 10 days. Which spinal segments are most commonly involved in a latent reactivation of this infection ?

options.d: It involves all spinal segments equally

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of chickenpox. Latent reactivation of the infection or shingles most commonly occurs in the T3 to L3 spinal segments .340 Herpes zoster/shingles are characterized by a unilateral vesicular dermatomal eruption associated with severe pain.Herpes zoster ophthalmicus affects the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve. It is shown below :Ramsay–Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus ) affects the facial nerve with an eruption on the tympanic membrane, the external auditory canal, and facial palsy .341

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: You are a pediatrics resident posted in the labor room. You are examining a baby which was delivered via C-section a few minutes ago. You notice that the baby has zig-zag hypertrophic cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution on the left side of the limbs and face . He also has a small head and small limbs. Antenatal history of the mother will be significant for which of the following infection ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital varicella syndrome. Hence , antenatal history of varicella infection would be significant in the mother of this baby. Fetal varicella infection occurs if the mother gets infected during the first half of pregnancy. Clinical features include : • Cicatrix, a zigzag scarring in a dermatomal distribution • Microphthalmia • Cataracts • Optic atrophy • Chorioretinitis • Microcephaly • Limb hypoplasia • Motor and sensory deficits .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A baby in the NICU is being evaluated for his features of microcephaly and hepatomegaly . CT scan revealed nodular periventricular calcifications . Congenital CMV infection is suspected . Which of the following samples is the best to detect the organism using PCR?
mcqs.explanation: Among the following options , urine is the best sample to be sent for the diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection . In congenital CMV infections , the investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture . It should be done within the first three weeks of life (after this period , it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection ). Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine is a more reliable sample than blood.342 Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester. 90% of the infected babies are asymptomatic and have lesser chances of having late sequelae . The clinical manifestations include hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice , chorioretinitis, and microcephaly . Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. One of the long-term sequelae is sensorineural hearing loss. There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection . Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness . The image below shows periventricular calcifications :

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A child is brought to the OPD with complaints of a rash and fever. The worried parents say the rash appeared on his cheeks yesterday. However, this morning , they observed it has spread to the trunk as well . The image of the child is given below . Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

options.a: It is also known as sixth disease
options.b: It is caused by an RNA virus
options.c: It is associated with a transient arrest of erythropoiesis
options.d: It is associated with immune fetal hydrops

mcqs.explanation: The image shows a characteristic slapped cheek appearance of a rash, which is classically present in parvovirus B-19 infection or erythema infectiosum . This is associated with transient aplastic crisis and erythropoiesis is mainly affected . Erythema infectiosum is also known as the fifth disease . The rash appears first on the cheeks called the slapped cheek appearance then spreads to the trunk. It is caused by parvovirus B-19, which a single -stranded DNA virus. Clinical features : • Febrile , non-toxic child with a nonspecific prodrome • Transient aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia • Petechial / purpuric skin eruptions : Papular purpuric "gloves and socks" syndrome (PPGSS) • Myocarditis • Primary maternal infection is associated with non-immune fetal hydrops and intrauterine fetal demise343 • Arthritis and arthralgia (adults)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Niki, a 9-month-old baby is brought to the OPD for a rash. The mother says the baby had a high fever of 103 F for 3 days for which she was given paracetamol. This morning , the baby had no fever but the mother noticed a rash on the trunk. On oral examination, ulcers at the uvulopalatoglossal junction are present . Which of the following statements is false regarding this disease ?

options.a: It is also called as erythema subitum
options.c: It is caused by human herpes virus-
options.d: It is a non-pruritic, morbilliform rash on the trunk

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of roseola infantum. It is also called exanthema subitum, not erythema subitum . Roseola infantum is also called as sixth disease or exanthema subitum (exanthema=breaking out, subitum=sudden rash). It is caused by a human herpesvirus (HHV) -6A, 6B, and 7. Clinical features : • Prodrome of high-grade fever • Non-pruritic, morbilliform rash, which appears as the fever comes down. • Leucopenia and relative lymphocytosis • Nagayama spots : ulcers at uvulo-palatoglossal junction Image: Exanthem subitum

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy came to the OPD with the complaint of fever and sore throat. On examination , you noted generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly . A peripheral blood smear revealed the following picture . What is the most probable diagnosis of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The image of the peripheral blood film shows atypical lymphocytes , also known as Downey cells . The given clinical scenario along with characteristic atypical lymphocytes is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis . Infectious mononucleosis , also called , glandular fever is caused by Epstein –Barr virus (EBV). It is transmitted person-to-person through salivary secretions and blood transfusion. The incubation period is 4 to 5 weeks . It presents with a classic triad of • Fever344 • Pharyngitis • Lymphadenopathy Other clinical features include fatigue and hepatosplenomegaly . The patients are advised to avoid contact sports for 3-4 weeks due to the risk of splenic rupture . The screening test of choice is the monospot test . This is a heterophile antibody test . Atypical lymphocytosis of >10 % is a characteristic laboratory finding. These are CD8 T lymphocytes that develop in response to the infected B lymphocytes . Other diseases caused by EBV include: • Hodgkin's lymphoma • Non-Hodgkin lymphoma • Burkitt's lymphoma • Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma Option B: Kimura disease is s a chronic inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that most commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy . Option C: Scrofuloderma is the result of cutaneous infection adjacent to a tuberculous focus , which may correspond to peripheral ganglionar tuberculosis (the most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in HIV -positive patients and in children).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of infantile diarrhea worldwide ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of infantile diarrhea worldwide is rotavirus . Rotavirus causes diarrhea in children of 3-5 years of age , via the fecal -oral route. The incubation period is 1-3 days. Most cases are asymptomatic or with mild symptoms like watery diarrhea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and temporary lactose intolerance. This is presumably because of the protection by maternal antibodies in breast milk. Diagnosis can be made by rapid antigen detection of rotavirus in stool specimens Lactose intolerance is actually not very common in infants and typically only starts showing up after age 3. All babies are born with lactase in their intestines . As they grow older, the lactase enzyme decreases .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a mode of transmission of hepatitis B from the infected mother to the baby?
mcqs.explanation: Breastfeeding is not a mode of transmission of hepatitis B from an infected mother to the baby. Mother -to-child transmission of HBV can occur via the following three routes : • Intrauterine transmission • Transmission during delivery (most frequent method )345 • Postpartum transmission Postpartum transmission: A proportion of babies may acquire the infection after birth due to close contact with the mother. However, breastfeeding is not a risk factor for HBV infection . Transmission following amniocentesis has been described , but the risk appears low. Newborns born to seropositive Hepatitis B mothers are given Hep B immunoglobulin as well as Hep B vaccination at birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Which fungal infection spreads in neonates through the care giver's hand?
mcqs.explanation: Candida parapsilosis is increasingly responsible for hospital outbreaks, and the hands of healthcare workers may be predominant environment sources .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old boy presented with rigidity and difficulty in movement. He has a history of involuntary movements in a single group of muscles of legs suggestive of myoclonic jerks. On examination, choreoathetosis movements and lead pipe rigidity is noted in the limbs. EEG shows suppression -burst episodes which are characteristic for subacute sclerosing panencephalitis . This clinical presentation is a complication of which of the following infection ?
mcqs.explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare complication of measles . Hence , prior infection with measles is most likely. SSPE occurs 3-8 years after a primary measles infection . It is the least common complication of measles but is almost always fatal. The clinical manifestations occur in 4 stages : Stage I: Maybe missed due to mild symptoms like irritability and reduced attention span. Stage II : Hallmark is massive Myoclonus . Involuntary muscle movements and myoclonic jerks start from one group of muscles but gives way to massive spams and jerks. Stage III : Involuntary movements disappear and are replaced by choreoathetosis , immobility, dystonia, and lead -pipe rigidity due to destruction of deeper parts of basal ganglia. Stage IV : Loss of critical centers that lead to coma and then death . Diagnosis of SSPE is by: • Detection of measles antibody in CSF • Characteristic findings on EEG • Typical histological findings or/and isolation of virus or virus antigen from brain tissue obtained by biopsy or after postmortem .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: Most common heart defect in congenital rubella syndrome is:
mcqs.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common congenital heart disease associated with rubella , followed by pulmonary artery stenosis (PS). Cardiac anomalies have been observed in 50% of children infected during the first 8 weeks of gestation . The incidence of heart disease in congenital rubella syndrome is: PDA > PS (right346 >left ) > ventricular septal defect > atrial septal defect .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old male has the following buccal mucosa finding. After three days, he presents to your OPD with a rash. What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows small red lesions with bluish-white spots in the center on the inner aspects of the cheek opposite to the lower premolar, indicating the presence of Koplik spots . The appearance of these spots , along with a rash appearing three days later, strongly suggests a diagnosis of measles . The measles virus is a single -stranded RNA virus. Measles infection has 4 phases : the incubation period, prodromal illness , exanthematous phase (characterized by the rash), and recovery phase . After an incubation period of 8-12 days, the prodromal phase of measles starts with mild fever and is followed by conjunctivitis, photophobia , coryza, cough , and increasing fever. Koplik spots , appearing 1-4 days prior to the rash, are a characteristic sign of measles . Symptoms gradually intensify over a period of 2-4 days until the first day of the rash. The rash typically begins on the forehead (around the hairline), behind the ears, and on the upper neck as a red maculopapular eruption . It then spreads downward to the torso and extremities , often becoming confluent on the face and upper trunk. Complications include acute otitis media (most common), pneumonia (the most common cause of death ), croup, bronchiolitis, reactivation of tuberculosis , diarrhea, appendicitis , febrile seizures , and encephalitis . Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a rare chronic complication of measles . Other options : Option B: Leukoplakia appears as a white patch in the oral cavity that cannot be wiped off. Option C: Scarlet fever is Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis and is characterized by a distinctive sandpaper rash. The rash appears as a diffuse , finely papular, erythematous eruption that turns the skin bright red and blanches on pressure . It starts around the neck and spreads to the trunk and extremities . Option D: Kawasaki disease (KD) is a systemic inflammatory disorder with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels . It presents with fever, rash (maculopapular, erythema multiforme urticarial , or micropustular ), conjunctivitis, and cervical lymph node enlargement .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: What is the secondary attack rate of chickenpox?
mcqs.explanation: The secondary attack rate of chicken pox is 85% (range 61–100 %) Chicken pox: • Causative agent : Varicella–zoster virus • Incubation period : 2 to 3 weeks • Rash: On 1st day, centripetal , pleomorphic, vesiculopapular lesions with erythematous base (dew drops on rose petal ) Treatment: Acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose ; four doses per day; for 5 days347 Complications : • Cutaneous : Secondary bacterial superinfection of the skin • Systemic : Acute cerebella ataxia, Guillain–Barre syndrome, transverse myelitis , optic neuritis, facial nerve palsy , pneumonia, Reye 's syndrome • Aspirin is contraindicated due to risk of Reye 's syndrome. Vaccine: • Oka strain (live attenuated ) • All adults who have never had chickenpox should receive 2 doses 0.5 mL in the deltoid area subcutaneously . • For <13 years of age , the first dose is administered at 12 –15 months and the second dose at age 4–6 years. • For people older than 13 years, the two doses are administered 4–8 weeks apart. • For those already immunized, booster doses are not needed if titers are adequate .348

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young boy came to visit his mother admitted to the antenatal ward for her delivery . You are the paediatrician on rounds in the adjacent post -natal cubical. His speech was very different from a normal child. Out of curiosity, you examine his oral cavity and the following finding is seen . What would be the most likely cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows an abnormally short lingual frenulum called Ankyloglossia. Ankyloglossia is also called "tongue -tie " due to an abnormally short lingual frenulum that can hinder tongue movement. It can interfere with speech or feeding . In such cases , surgical correction is indicated . The image below shows tongue tie and the classic W-shaped appearance of the tongue on protrusion:Fissured tongue (Option C) (scrotal tongue or lingua plicata) is a benign malformation in which numerous small furrows or deep grooves are present on the dorsal surface of the tongue . Food particles and debris may become trapped in the fissures , resulting in irritation , inflammation, and halitosis. Macroglossia (Option D), or an abnormally large tongue , may be seen in disorders like Down's syndrome, Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, Hurler's syndrome, and cretinism.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Sirish, a young talented singer failed to make it through the Music Idol audition. Deeply affected by this, he drank a full bottle of a drain unclogger . He was rushed to the ER with froth in the mouth. Which of the following could be done as the first step in treatment ?

options.d: Gag the child to induce emesis

mcqs.explanation: 358 The recommended first step in the case of alkali ingestion (most commonly seen with drain uncloggers / house hold cleaning agents ) is dilution through the administration of milk or water. Contraindications in a case of caustic (strong acid or alkali) ingestion : • Neutralization • Induced emesis • Gastric lavage

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Mala, a young student of class 9 accidentally pipettes sulphuric acid while performing volumetric analysis in her chemistry lab. Which type of mucosal damage would you expect in her?
mcqs.explanation: Acid ingestion produces coagulative necrosis. Acid ingestion produces coagulative necrosis and a somewhat protective thick eschar. The amount of acidic agents usually ingested is low as they are generally bitter. Alkali ingestion : Most cases (70%) of caustic ingestions are accidental . Drain uncloggers are most common as they are tasteless so more is ingested . Alkali ingestion produces liquefactive necrosis.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 48-hours-old boy baby born at 35 weeks of gestation regurgitates the feeds given to him. Abdominal examination reveals an airless scaphoid abdomen. A contrast study is performed and the findings are as shown below . What is the possible diagnosis?

options.a: Esophageal atresia in TEF type A
options.b: Esophageal atresia in TEF type D
options.c: Esophageal atresia in TEF type C
options.d: Esophageal atresia in TEF type B

mcqs.explanation: The defect demonstrated in the contrast study depicts oesophagal atresia (EA). Isolated oesophagal atresia falls under tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) type A. Oesophagal atresia is the most common congenital anomaly of the oesophagus , >90% have an associated TEF. Plain radiography in the evaluation of respiratory distress might reveal a coiled feeding tube in the oesophagal pouch and/or an air-distended stomach, indicating the presence of a coexisting TEF. Conversely, pure EA can manifest as an airless scaphoid abdomen. The following classification was given by Gross:359

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A full -term infant with a history of polyhydramnios in utero presents with respiratory distress soon after birth. On examination frothing at the mouth is observed. What would be the immediate investigation of choice ?

options.c: Passing a nasogastric tube with subsequent chest radiography

mcqs.explanation: Newborn presenting with the above features is suggestive of a case of TEF with possible esophageal atresia. This can be confirmed with a chest X-ray image showing a coiled nasogastric tube in the esophageal pouch , as shown in the image below .Indicators of esophageal atresia with or without a tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF) are a newborn presenting with: • Early-onset respiratory distress • Frothing at the mouth and nose • History of polyhydramnios Radiological findings: • Passing a nasogastric tube with subsequent chest radiography will reveal a coiled nasogastric tube in the esophageal pouch . • If an air-distended stomach is also present , it indicates the presence of a coexisting TEF. • Pure EA can manifest as an airless scaphoid abdomen.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Milind, a young child is brought to you for recurrent respiratory symptoms and dysphagia . After ruling out other causes , you suspect a vascular anomaly that could be compressing the esophagus to be causing the symptoms . A CECT is done and the findings are as shown below . Which of the following vascular anomalies is most likely to cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario suggests a diagnosis of dysphagia lusoria, which is caused most likely by the aberrant right subclavian artery. The given image suggests the presence of the right aberrant subclavian artery. Dysphagia lusoria is dysphagia produced due to extrinsic compression of the oesophagus by a developmental vascular anomaly, often an aberrant right subclavian artery or right-sided or360 double aortic arch.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are a new intern posted in the department of pediatrics . The lab reports of a newborn baby admitted to the SNCU arrive and the ABG report is as below . Which congenital anomaly would you suspect in such a setting of electrolyte and acid-base imbalance?
mcqs.explanation: Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, an electrolyte and acid-base imbalance characteristically seen in congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS). A pH of 7.55 indicates alkalosis and plasma HCO3- is 30 mmol/L , which is in the higher range. Both these findings indicate metabolic alkalosis. Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality. i.e Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. • Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). • Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone through the RAAS pathway . • The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. • Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. • Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine. CHPS typically presents with the following: • Non-bilious vomiting, which is progressive, maybe projectile , occurring immediately after a feed , usually presents after the 3rd week of age . • As the vomiting continues , a progressive loss of fluid , hydrogen ions, chloride ions, and potassium leads to hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Hyperbilirubinemia is the most common clinical association of pyloric stenosis , which is also known as the icteropyloric syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-week -old infant presented with non-bilious projectile vomiting and lethargy for 2 days. On abdominal examination, an olive-like mass was palpated . Barium study showed an elongated pyloric channel. Which drug is used in the first week of life can cause this presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given case scenario suggests the diagnosis of Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis . Erythromycin, particularly when given in the first few weeks of life , is found to be associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis .Exposur e Drug Malformation Post-nat al Erythrom ycin Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis Pre-nata l Thalidomi de PhocomeliaGrossly underdev eloped or absent limbs361 Exposur e Drug Malformation Pre-nata l Phenytoin Fetal hydantoin syndromeInt rauterine growth restriction, microcephaly , cleft palate , hy poplastic phalanges , etc . Pre-nata l Misoprost ol Moebius syndromeUnderdev eloped VI and VII CNs resulti ng in facial paralysis and late ral rectus palsy

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Savitri , a 3-week -old baby is having bouts of non-bilious projectile vomiting. On examination, the child seems lethargic and dehydrated. Abdominal examination reveals visible gastric peristalsis . What is the investigation of choice for the diagnosis of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of non-bilious vomiting and visible gastric peristalsis is highly suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis . The investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis is ultrasound. CHPS is associated with hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus resulting in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet . It is common between 3-6 weeks of age . First-born male infants are at the highest risk . Infants usually present with projectile , non-bilious vomiting. Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium . When the infant is given a test feed , visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right, followed by projectile vomiting. The characteristic metabolic abnormality is hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis due to recurrent vomiting. Ultrasound features : • Double -layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called 'Nipple sign' • The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the 'cervix sign' • The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of \0344 mm and a pyloric length of \03416 mm If ultrasound is inconclusive, contrast studies (barium) are performed , which demonstrate • An elongated pyloric channel (string sign), • A bulge of the pyloric muscle into the antrum (shoulder sign), and • Parallel streaks of barium seen in the narrowed channel, producing a "double tract sign." The image attached below shows the USG findings in CHPS.362 Signs in Congenital Pyloric stenosis :Sign String sign Passing of small streak of bar ium through pyloric canal Double /triple track sign Crowding of muscle folds in pyloric canal Diamond sign/twining recess Transient triangular tent like cleft in mid portion of pyloric canal with apex pointing infe riorly. Beak sign Mass impression upon antru m with streak of barium poin ting towards pyloric channel Mushroom sign/kirkin sign/u mbrella sign Indentation of base of duode nal bulb by pylorus Caterpillar sign Gastric hyperperistaltic wave s Shoulder sign Round indentation caused by hypertrophied pyloric muscl e363 The treatment of choice is Ramstedt - Frankelstedt pyloromyotomy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ashwini, the mother of a young baby is concerned after she noticed straw yellow -colored stains in her child's clothing while washing them. She brings the child to you for examination. The child has a mildly elevated temperature and the fluid comes out from the umbilicus , whenever the child strains. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The diagnosis in the above case is a urachal fistula . The clinical vigentte suggesting straw -yellow fluid (suggestive of urine) along with secondary infection (mildly elevated temperature ) and presence of fluid only on straining are all suggestive of urahcal fistula . The urachus is an embryologic canal connecting the dome of the fetal bladder with the allantois, a structure that contributes to the formation of the umbilical cord. In this condition, there is continuous urinary drainage from the umbilicus on straining. It usually presents as a tender , swollen mass secondary to infection . Diagnosis is made by ultrasonography or computed tomography (CT). Definitive management is surgical resection of the tract. A patent vitellointestinal duct , patent omphalomesenteric duct and bladder diverticulum will cause umbilical discharge even in the absence of straining. The discharge in such a case is composed of the contents of the intestine (curdy white in colour mostly ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: On observing the following finding in the X-ray of a baby, what is the most likely diagnosis you would suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of a "double -bubble " sign on a plain abdominal radiograph is suggestive of a diagnosis of duodenal atresia. The double bubble is caused by the distension of stomach and proximal duodenum . Duodenal atresia results from failed recanalization of the intestinal lumen during gestation . A history of polyhydramnios is present ; half of the infants seen with duodenal atresia are premature . The hallmark of duodenal obstruction is bilious vomiting without abdominal distention , which is usually noted on the 1st day of life .364 The initial treatment of infants with duodenal atresia includes nasogastric or orogastric decompression and intravenous fluid replacement . The typical surgical repair for duodenal atresia is duodenoduodenostomy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An infant was brought to the paediatrician with complaints of vomiting and abdominal distention . The parents inform that the baby passes stools that look like currant jelly . On ultrasonography , a target sign was observed. Which of the following is not true about this condition?

options.a: Rota virus vaccine is not associated with increased risk
options.c: The most common cause is idiopathic
options.d: The most common location is ileocolic region

mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of intussusception and the rotavirus vaccine is associated with an increased risk , albeit only a slightly increased risk Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment . The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic . Ileoileal location is seen postoperatively and in Henoch–Sch\366nlein Purpura. 90% of cases of intussusception in children are idiopathic in nature. It can be seen in infants during the weaning period following the introduction of new food, vaccination , or upper respiratory tract infection . The currently approved rotavirus vaccines are associated with a slightly increased risk of intussusception . Lead points are more common in children older than 2 years of age and can cause recurrent intussusception. Some recognizable lead points are as follows : enlarged submucosal Peyer's patch, Meckel 's diverticulum, intestinal polyp , neurofibroma, intestinal duplication cysts , leiomyomas , hamartomas, anastomotic suture line, enterostomy tube , hemangioma, or malignant conditions such as lymphoma or Kaposi sarcoma.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old child is admitted to your unit with recurrent pancreatitis . Which of the following developmental anomalies is likely to be associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Pancreas divisum is the most common congenital anomaly associated with recurrent pancreatitis . It is also the most common pancreatic developmental anomaly. It results from the failure of fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds , due to which, the tail, body, and part of the head of the pancreas drain through the small accessory duct of Santorini rather than the main duct of Wirsung. It may be associated with recurrent pancreatitis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy was playing football with his friends during the PET classes . Suddenly he complained of severe abdominal pain and he is rushed to the pediatric ER. An erect X-ray scan of the abdomen showed the following picture . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Sigmoid volvulus is the most likely diagnosis. It occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon . It is a cause of large bowel obstruction.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presents to the emergency department with sudden -onset severe generalised abdominal pain associated with fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. On examination, his abdomen is tense with generalised tenderness , guarding and McBurnys tenderness is present . No bowel sounds are present . What is the best diagnostic investigation in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute appendicitis . Ultrasound is the best diagnostic investigation in the evaluation of acute appendicitis and has demonstrated >90% sensitivity and specificity .365 The advantages of ultrasound include its easy availability, rapid method , low cost, and freedom from ionizing radiation. The ultrasound criteria for appendicitis include the following : • Wall thickness \0346 mm • Luminal distention • Lack of compressibility • A complex mass in the right lower quadrant • Or an appendicolith Image: Ultrasound showing evidence of appendicitis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Aaradhana , a 14-year-old girl is feeling embarrassed as she has to often rush to the restroom during school hours. Her friends also make fun of her as she blushes frequently for no reason. She was later diagnosed with an appendicular tumour. Labs revealed low levels of niacin with the tumour being positive for synaptophysin . Which of the following biochemical moieties can be demonstrated in the patient 's urine sample ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of a carcinoid tumour. Elevated levels of urinary 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) can be seen in this condition. The carcinoid tumours are neuroendocrine tumours arising from enterochromaffin cells that can occur anywhere in the GIT . In children, they are most commonly seen in the appendix . A carcinoid tumour with metastasis to the liver is likely to produce carcinoid syndrome. The tumour elaborates serotonin, 5-HT, and histamine, which produce flushing (frequent blushing ), watery diarrhoea, bronchoconstriction, and right heart failure. Carcinoid syndrome can cause secondary niacin deficiency as they consume and divert the tryptophan NAD+ pathway to cause the overproduction of serotonin. Thus, these patients can also have pellagra like features . The diagnosis can be confirmed by elevated levels of urinary 5-HIAA.366 The image attached above demonstrates islands and nests of uniform cells with scant, pink granular cytoplasm and salt and pepper chromatin. Synaptophysin is typically positive in carcinoid tumors. Treatment: Essentially surgical. Medical management includes the administration of somatostatin analogues (octreotide ). • Small tumours (<1 cm in size) are treated by appendectomy . • Larger tumours (>2 cm in size) require further bowel resection .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with recurrent colicky abdominal pain and melena. On examination , you note the following lesions in the buccal mucosa. You suspect Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and advice for the endoscopic investigation to look for polyps . In which part of the intestine would you expect to find maximum polyps ?
mcqs.explanation: The hamartomatous polyps in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are seen in order of prevalence : Jejunum > ileum > duodenum > colonic or gastric.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A full -term neonate was found to have distention of the abdomen. He also passed his meconium late and based on further workup was later diagnosed with Hirschsprung disease . Which of the following conditions is least likely to be found in association with this?
mcqs.explanation: Hirschsprung disease is not associated with Edward syndrome (trisomy 18).
