It is associated with: • Trisomy 21 / Downs syndrome • Joubert syndrome • Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome • Shah–Waardenburg syndrome • Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2 syndrome • Neurofibromatosis (Von recklinghausen disease )367 • Neuroblastoma • Urogenital or cardiovascular abnormalities .Hirschsprung disease or congenital aganglionic colon is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexus . It is more common in males. Risk factors include Down's syndrome and RET oncogene . The imaging modality of choice in Hirschsprung's disease is a contrast radiograph with barium or gastrograffin enema (image shown above). The most important film is a lateral or oblique view of the rectum during slow filling. It typically shows a low bowel obstruction. The rectum is seen as a narrow tube and a cone-shaped transition zone, seen proximal to the dilated ganglionated bowel . A rectal suction biopsy is a gold standard for the diagnosis and operative intervention is the definitive treatment. Definitive surgeries for Hirschsprung disease are as follows : • Swenson procedure , where aganglionic bowel is removed and a coloanal anastomosis is performed. • Duhamel procedure , where the aganglionic rectal stump is left in place and the ganglionated normal colon is pulled posterior. • Soave procedure : In this procedure , endorectal mucosal dissection is done within the aganglionic distal rectum and then the ganglionated normal colon is pulled through the remnant muscular cuff , and a coloanal anastomosis is performed. NOTE: In the fetus , migration of the neuronal crest tissues to form myenteric plexus and ganglion cells is completed by the 24th week of life . If interrupted in migration, it results in Hirschsprung disease .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A neonate is being evaluated in the nursery for failure to pass meconium in the last 48 hours. Physical examination reveals abdominal distension and an anal dimple . Wangenstein's invertogram shows a low lying defect . Further evaluation reveals the presence of vertebral and renal deformities . Which of the following conditions is least likely to be seen in this child?
mcqs.explanation: 368 The given clinical vignette is suggestive of imperforate anus in a neonate with VACTERL association (presence of vertebral and renal anomalies in addition to the anal atresia). Lymphedema is not a component of VACTERL syndrome. VACTERL association is a disorder that affects many-body systems . People diagnosed with VACTERL association typically have at least three of the following characteristic features . Components of VACTERL association: • Vertebral • Anorectal • Cardiac • Tracheal • Esophageal • Renal • Radial • Limb anomalies Anorectal malformations: • It occurs due to the post -allantoic gut with the proctodaeum . • Newborns classically present with inability to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distention , intestinal obstruction, improper anal dimple , and sometimes with complaints of passing meconium per urethra. Wingspread Classification : • Low - Below the level of the pelvic floor (puborectalis ). • Intermediate - Occurs at the level of the puborectalis with or without fistula . • High - Anorectal agenesis , rectal atresia. Investigations: • Wangenstein's invertogram is done 6-12 hours after birth with a metal coin strapped to the presumed site of the anus. The X-ray taken is used to measure and classify the deformity . • USG abdomen • Imaging to evacuate associated abnormalities Treatment is surgical.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You notice a 5-year-old boy walking very differently in an orphanage. On probing further the guardian informs that he has a history of frequently soiling his pants. On examination, you find a mass protruding through his anus and a diagnosis of rectal prolapse is made. Which of the following would be the most likely cause for this presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: In this case, the most likely cause of rectal prolapse would be Trichuriasis . It is common in poor rural communities with inadequate sanitary facilities and soil contaminated with human or animal feces . The highest infection rate occurs among children between 5-15 years.369 Clinical manifestations include chronic dysentery , anemia, poor growth , and developmental deficits . In heavy infections , adult worms can extend throughout the colon down to the rectum. Over time, inflammation of the rectum causes tenesmus leading to prolapse . Other options : Pertussis would present with cough , low-grade fever, and sneezing . Increased abdominal pressure due to the persistent cough could cause a prolapse . Chronic constipation is unlikely as the child has a history of frequently soiling his pants, suggestive of dysentery . Cystic fibrosis would manifest much earlier in life with respiratory symptoms like recurrent pneumonia. These children have exocrine pancreatic insufficiency , causing protein and fat malabsorption. This leads to bulky, greasy stools and eventually a prolapse if untreated .370

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: If you were to conduct a death audit on all the cases of under-five paediatric deaths secondary to infective diarrhoea, which of the following pathogens would be responsible for the largest fraction of deaths ?
mcqs.explanation: Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of gastroenteritis in children. It accounts for 29% of deaths caused by diarrhoea in children aged < 5 years.376

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child from an urban slum area is admitted to your unit with diarrhea. Given below are five important micronutrients. The deficiency of which of the following factors increases the risk of death due to diarrhea in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The risk of death from diarrhoea is increased in the presence of deficiencies of micronutrients such as vitamin A, and zinc (2 and 4 only). Both these micronutrients are essential for maintaining mucosal immunity. Vitamin A deficiency increases mortality from diarrhoea, measles , and malaria while Zinc deficiency increases mortality from diarrhoea, pneumonia, and malaria . Recent studies also indicate the usefulness of folic acid in the prevention of diarrhoea.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The Nutritionist in your hospital prepares the diet charts for all the children admitted with diarrhoeal disease . One of the advice papers has fallen off from the case file . The advice sheet mentions that the child has to be put on fasting some times of the day. You would attach the sheet back to the case file with the diagnosis of ___________
mcqs.explanation: Osmotic diarrhoea results from the presence of osmotically active, poorly absorbed solutes in the bowel lumen that inhibit normal water and electrolyte absorption. This type of diarrhoea ceases with fasting. Secretory diarrhoea, infective diarrhoea, dysentery and motility diarrhoea occurs independent of dietary intake and do not subside with fasting.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child with chronic malnutrition presents with diarrheal episodes lasting for more than 2 weeks . The stool sample is positive for Aeromonas and entero -adherent Escherichia coli. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Persistent diarrhoea(Chronic diarrhoea) is defined as a diarrhoeal episode that lasts for more than 14 days. Diarrhoea is defined as • stool volume of more than 10 g/kg/day in toddlers /infants (or) • stool volume greater than 200 g/day in older children Persistent diarrhoea is increasingly observed in children with malnutrition. These are due to infections commonly caused due to enteroadherent Escherichia coli and Aeromonas. Acute diarrhoeas generally last less than 7 days while chronic diarrhoea lasts more than 14 days and is usually a non-infectious pathology .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young child had milk-based dessert at his friend's birthday party. Later, the same evening he developed complaints of bloating, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence . His medical history is significant for viral gastroenteritis a couple of weeks back. Stool examination reveals an acidic pH and is positive for reducing substances . Which type of diarrhea is most likely to be seen in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of acquired lactose intolerance which is an example of osmotic diarrhoea. Lactose is present in milk and dairy products . If it is not absorbed in the small intestine , it reaches the colon, where it is fermented to short-chain organic acids. This releases hydrogen that can be detected in the lactose breath test and also generates an osmotic overload.377 The child with lactose intolerance generally has perianal excoriations. The condition is diagnosed by using stool examination which shows acidic stool positive for reducing substances . Treatment is by diet control using a diet devoid of lactose . It can be congenital due to lactase deficiency or acquired after post -viral gastroenteritis . In secretory diarrhoea, the epithelial cells ' ion transport processes are turned into a state of active secretion . The most common cause of acute -onset secretory diarrhoea is a bacterial infection of the gut . Chronic diarrhoea is, in many cases , the result of an intestinal infection that persists longer than expected . Dysentery /Shigellosis is a type of food poisoning caused by infection with the Shigella species . It is spread by means of faeco -oral transmission.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of loose stools . No history of fever or blood in stools . The mother says he is irritable and eagerly drinks water if given. On examination, eyes are sunken and in the skin pinch test , the skin retracted within two seconds but not immediately . What treatment is advised for the child?

options.a: Give oral fluids and zinc supplementation only and ask mother to come back if danger sign develops .
options.b: Give oral fluids and ask mother to continue the same and visit again the next day.
options.c: Consider severe dehydration start IV fluids , IV antibiotics, and refer to higher centre .

mcqs.explanation: In a child with diarrhea, thirst (eagerly drinks water), sunken eyes , restless and irritable behavior, and skin pinch showing slow retraction (<2 seconds ) point towards some dehydration . Treatment includes oral rehydration therapy , zinc supplementation , and continued breastfeeding according to WHO integrated management of neonatal and childhood diseases (IMNCI) plan B. The degree of dehydration is assessed and managed using the WHO IMNCI PLAN given below :378

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ramya, a 6-year-old child with acute diarrhoea is admitted and started on fluid therapy with reduced osmolarity Oral Rehydration Solution . Which of the following statement is false about reduced osmolarity ORS?
mcqs.explanation: The total osmolarity of reduced osmolarity ORS is 245 mOsm/L (not 311 mOsm/L) Reduced osmolarity ORS is now the global standard of care in the management of acute gastroenteritis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Sathish, your gym partner and father of a 12 -month-old child, calls you for a teleconsult . His child has been passing loose watery stools without fever. He wants to know the medications to be given to his child. What dose of oral zinc would you prescribe to this child?
mcqs.explanation: All children older than 6 months of age with acute diarrhoea should receive oral zinc (20 mg/day) for 10 -14 days during and after diarrhoea. Most of the cases of under-five acute diarrhoea are infectious in aetiology with more than 50% due to the Rotavirus , which is self -limiting. Treatment will include fluid and electrolyte correction and zinc supplementation .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In a child admitted with viral enteritis along with signs of dehydration , which type of acid-base imbalance is likely to be seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Isotonic dehydration with acidosis is the most common finding in children with severe viral enteritis. Viruses that cause human diarrhoea selectively infect and destroy the villus tip cells in the small intestine . In the small intestine , the upper villus enterocytes are differentiated cells , which have absorptive functions, such as the transport of water and electrolytes . On the other hand, the crypt enterocytes are undifferentiated cells and are net secretors of water and electrolytes .379 Selective viral infection of intestinal villus tip cells thus leads to decreased absorption of salt and water (proportionate loss of water and salt—isotonic dehydration ) and an imbalance in the ratio of intestinal fluid absorption to secretion. Metabolic acidosis may be a result of stool bicarbonate losses in children with diarrhoea. These can also be seen due to secondary renal insufficiency or lactic acidosis as a sequelae to diarrhoea.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The intestinal biopsy report of a 7-year-old boy evaluated for chronic watery diarrhoea revealed a flat intestinal mucosa. Which of the following conditions would you suspect in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic diarrhoea with a flat intestinal mucosa can be seen in conditions Tropical sprue , giardiasis, and HIV enteropathy . Causes of the flat intestinal mucosa (subtotal or total villous atrophy): • Celiac disease • Tropical sprue • Giardiasis • Bacterial overgrowth • HIV enteropathy • Eosinophilic gastroenteritis • Cow's milk or soy protein enteropathy • Graft versus host disease • Chemo or radiotherapy • Protein-energy malnutrition • Tuberculosis or lymphoma Amoebiasis and neutrophilic gastroenteritis may also rarely have villous atrophy but the presentation is generally acute . Amoebiasis is characteristically associated with dysentery and biopsy would reveal a flask-shaped ulcer.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Suyash, a 10 -year-old boy presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhoea, and poor appetite after having his favourite white sauce pasta. His mother adds that he develops such symptoms only when he takes pasta or roti. The duodenal biopsy revealed crypt hyperplasia and CD8+ cells in lamina propria. Which of the following tests is least likely to be used for the diagnosis of the condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of celiac disease and an anti-nuclear antibody test is not used in the diagnosis of celiac disease . Symptoms are pre-dominantly seen after consuming a diet rich in gluten (Wheat pasta or roti). Diagnosis of celiac disease is made based on lab and histopathological findings. Celiac disease -specific antibodies are as follows : • Anti-tissue transglutaminase (Anti-TG2) IgA antibodies • Anti deaminated - IgG forms of gliadin peptides antibodies • Endomysial antibodies (EMA)380 The duodenal biopsy will show crypt hyperplasia , villous atrophy and CD8+ cells in lamina propria

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old boy presented with vomiting for 5 days. His sister, who has coeliac disease had similar symptoms. IgA-tissue transglutaminase titre is 5 times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following is not an extraintestinal manifestation of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The boy is suffering from coeliac disease . Polycythemia is not an extraintestinal manifestation of coeliac disease . On the contrary, the most common extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease in the paediatric age group is iron-deficiency anaemia that is refractory to iron therapy , and not polycythemia . Celiac disease is an immune-mediated systemic disorder triggered by the ingestion of wheat gluten and related prolamines from rye and barley. The intestinal symptoms are caused by the atrophy of the small bowel mucosa and malabsorption. The symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, failure to thrive, rectal prolapse , and intussusception . The extraintestinal manifestations are caused due to malnutrition and autoimmunity and they include the following :System Manifestation Possible Cause Hematologic Anaemia (Most common extr aintestinal manifestation) Iron malabsorption Skeletal RicketsOsteoporosisEnamel hypoplasia of the teeth Calcium/vitamin D malabsor ption Muscular Atrophy Malnutrition Neurologic Peripheral neuropathyEpilep syIrritabilityCerebral calcifica tionsCerebellar ataxia Thiamine/vitamin B12 deficie ncy Endocrinolo gic Short statureSecondary hype rparathyroidism Malnutrition calcium/vitamin Dmalabsorption Dermatologi c Dermatitis herpetiformisAlop ecia areataErythema nodosu m Autoimmunity Respiratory Idiopathic pulmonary hemosi derosis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in childhood ?
mcqs.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in children, which, if untreated , will lead to malnutrition. Other rare causes include : • Shwachman–Diamond syndrome381 • Isolated enzyme deficiencies • Chronic pancreatitis • Protein-energy malnutrition

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting for 6 hours. He feels comfortable when he bends forward and assumes a knee-chest position. Which of the following tests is not useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Serum elastase is not used for the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis . The measurement of faecal elastase is used as a screening test for pancreatic insufficiency . The criteria for the diagnosis of pancreatitis in children is defined as 2 of 3 of the following : • Epigastric abdominal pain; • Serum amylase and/or lipase activity at least 3 times greater than the upper limit of normal ; and • Imaging findings characteristic of, or compatible with, acute pancreatitis . Serum lipase is now considered the test of choice for acute pancreatitis as it is more specific than amylase . CT scan has a major role in the diagnosis and follow -up of children with pancreatitis . Other useful investigations are USG, ERCP, and MRCP.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Anwesha, an orator preparing for her international debate finale presents to your clinic with lesions on her lower lip as shown below . She is concerned as these lesions are painful, recurrent and hamper the flow of her speech . Which of the following points about this condition is incorrect?

options.d: They are seen in Gluten -sensitive enteropathy

mcqs.explanation: The lesions given in the above image are aphthous ulcers , and they are not contagious . All the other points are true. Aphthous ulcers are painful, recurrent, and non-contagious oral lesions . They are well -circumscribed, ulcerative lesions with a white necrotic base surrounded by a red halo. They heal in 10 –14 days without scarring. Their aetiology is unclear but the following factors have been implicated : • Allergic or immunologic reactions • Emotional stress • Genetics • Injury to soft tissues in the mouth • Inflammatory bowel disease • Gluten -sensitive enteropathy • Behcet disease • Sweet syndrome • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV ) infection • Cyclical neutropenia382 Treatment generally includes local anaesthetic to relieve pain and B-complex supplementation to enhance healing.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The nanny of a 3-year-old boy brings the child to the ER after he had accidentally ingested button batteries from the mobile phone toy that he was playing with. What would be the next best step in the management of this child?

options.b: Observation and follow up in 24 hours
options.c: Observation until the foreign body passes out in faeces

mcqs.explanation: Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal. Button batteries , in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies , which must be expediently removed because they can cause : • Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time • Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge . Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury. Asymptomatic blunt objects and coins lodged in the oesophagus can be observed for up to 24 hr in anticipation of passage into the stomach.383

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother observed unusual redness on the palms of her young child while putting him to sleep . She brings him to your OPD and on examination, you find mild abdominal distension, splenomegaly , and pedal edema . You admit the child for further evaluation, but on the night of admission, he suddenly starts vomiting fresh blood. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding unless proved otherwise . Bleeding from oesophagal varices is the most common presentation of portal hypertension . Palmar erythema (redness of the palms) and ascites (swelling of the abdomen) are features of liver failure seen in this patient . Upper GI endoscopy is the preferred diagnostic test for oesophagal varices. The management of acute variceal bleeding- • Attain hemodynamic stability through blood transfusion/fluids • Vasoactive drugs (e.g., octreotide ) • Endoscopy to perform ligation or sclerotherapy • Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt should be considered for variceal bleeding refractory to medical and endoscopic therapy . Secondary prophylaxis to reduce the recurrence of bleeding includes - • Nonselective \031 blockade (propranolol, nadolol) • Obliteration of varices through serial treatment via ligation or sclerotherapy391

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old boy was brought by his mother to the ER after having a sudden episode of vomiting blood. On examination, splenomegaly is detected with engorged superficial veins around his umbilicus . Which is the investigation of choice in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding and hence , upper GI endoscopy is the investigation of choice . The upper GI endoscopy provides a definitive diagnosis and an option to treat via band ligation or sclerotherapy . Capsule endoscopy , ultrasound, CT, MRI, and elastography are not recommended because of their suboptimal accuracy compared to endoscopy . Capsule endoscopy is used to investigate an occult /obscure gastrointestinal bleed mostly suspected to be in the small intestine .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which did not subside even after 3 weeks of birth, was observed in a neonate . On investigating, liver enzymes , PT/INR and albumin levels were normal . No hemolysis was seen on a peripheral blood smear. A drop in bilirubin level was observed within a week after treating with phenobarbital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Jaundice persisiting 3 weeks after birth is suggestive of pathological jaundice . Among the given options, Crigler Najjar type 2 presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia which responds to phenobarbital therapy . Dubin Johnson (option C) and Rotor (option A) syndromes lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Crigler Najjar type 2 is an autosomal recessive disease with non-hemolytic , unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by homozygous missense mutations in the enzyme UDP UGT1A1 resulting in reduced (partial) enzymatic activity. The differences between Crigler-Najjar type 1 and type 2 are described in the table below :Crigler Najjar Type 1 Crigler Najjar Type 2 Autosomal recessive Autosomal recessive UDPGT isabsent UDPGT isreduced Severe unconjugated hyperbil irubinemia Less severe Pale stools Normal-coloured stools May proceed tokernicterusan ddoes notrespond to phenob arbitone Does not proceed to kernicter us andis responsive to pheno barbitone

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy was brought to the OPD by his father who observed a yellowish tinge to his skin and eyes . He gives a history of recent onset fatigue after playing football for a few minutes and cannot stay active on the playground for a long time like before . Investigations revealed isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but are normal otherwise . Liver histology revealed a black pigment . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of fatigue , conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and black pigment on liver biopsy , termed as "black liver" is suggestive of Dubin–Johnson syndrome. Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive inherited defect in hepatocyte secretion of bilirubin glucuronide . Disease results from absent function of multiple drug-resistant protein 2, an ATP dependent canalicular transporter.392 The most commonly reported symptoms are abdominal pain and fatigue , jaundice , dark urine, and slight enlargement of the liver. Inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinemia-Dubin–Johnson syndrome Rotor syndrome Autosomal recessive Autosomal recessive Absent function ofmultiple dr ug-resistant protein (MRP-2) Defect in anion transport Black liveron biopsy (due to a ccumulation of epinephrine metabolite ) Black liver is not seen Normal levels of coproporph yrin in urine Increased levels of coproporp hyrin in urine Gall bladder is not visualized on oral cholecystography Gall bladder is visualized on oral cholecystography

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are an intern posted in the paediatrics department and a child with Dubin-Johnson syndrome is admitted to your unit. During rounds, the attending paediatrician asks you which molecular defect causes liver disease in this patient . Your answer would be
mcqs.explanation: Molecular defect causing liver disease in Dubin–Johnson syndrome is ABCC2 (codes for canalicular protein with ATP -binding cassette ), it leads to the mutation of multiple drug-resistant protein 2 (MRP2 ) receptor . Hence , there is a defect in the transfer of conjugated bilirubin from the liver to bile in Dubin–Johnson syndrome. Important diseases and their molecular defects :ATP7A Menke's disease ATP7B Wilson disease CFTR Cystic fibrosis SERPINA 1 \032-1 antitrypsin deficiency ABCC2 (MRP2 protein defe ct) Dubin Johnson syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All are true about transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, except :

options.b: Occurs due to maternal antibody against fetal UGT1A
options.c: It is also known as Lucey Driscoll syndrome
options.d: Stop breast feeding when jaundice sets in

mcqs.explanation: Lucey Driscoll syndrome or transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is a self -limiting condition and there is no need to stop breastfeeding . Lucey Driscoll syndrome is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder affecting enzymes involved in bilirubin metabolism . It causes transient familial neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice occurs during the first 4 days of life . It is due to maternal antibodies against fetal UGT1A1 (UDP glucuronosyltransferase family 1 member A1).393

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Lately, a teacher observed that an anxious young girl had started drooling saliva from her mouth while listening in the classroom. She had also developed a deterioration in her handwriting while taking down notes . Her mother was informed and she brought her child to your clinic. On examination, she had tremors and mild hepatomegaly . A slit-lamp examination was done and showed the following picture . The right statement about this disease is -

options.c: Coombs-positive hemolytic anaemia may be present .
options.d: Patient can be treated with triethylenetetramine

mcqs.explanation: The image shows the Kayser -Fleischer ring, which is characteristic of Wilson's disease . It is an autosomal recessive disorder, characterised by low serum ceruloplasmin levels . Coomb's negative hemolytic anemia may be present . The patient can be treated with triethylenetetramine also known as trientine. Wilson's disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene on Chr.13q . The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions: • Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin • Helps excrete free copper in bile . Thus, an ATP7B deficiency leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues . The drugs used in the management of Wilson's disease include : • Chelating agents as first-line drugs • D-penicillamine • Trientine or triethylenetetramine • Elemental zinc as maintenance therapy .Lab markers Change in Wilson's diseas e Reason Serum ceruloplas min \027\027 ATP7B deficiency results in r educed bound copper 24h urinary coppe r \026\026 Excess free copper excreted i n urine Total serum coppe r \027 Due to marked reduction in c eruloplasmin

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother observed deterioration in her young child's academic performance and loss of interest in everyday activities for the last few weeks . She has also lost the ability to play catch with her brother and complains of muscle weakness . There is mild hepatomegaly noted on examination. Her serum ceruloplasmin levels were reduced . All of the following manifestations can occur in a patient with this disease except ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of reduced ceruloplasmin levels , motor incoordination, and hepatomegaly suggest the patient is suffering from Wilson's disease . Sparse depigmented hair is not a feature of Wilson's disease . It is a feature of Menke's disease. Wilson's disease is caused due to a mutation in the ATP7B gene that leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues . It has the following clinical features : Note : Wilson's disease may also present as cirrhosis and hepatic failure, where shrinkage of liver occurs.394 System Clinical features Hepatic (most com mon) JaundiceAbdominal painHep atomegalyFatigueAscitesVari ceal bleedCoagulation defects Neurological DysarthriaDystoniaParkinson ismSubcortical dementiaDep ressionWing beating tremors Decreased scholastic perform ance Ophthalmic Kayser -Fleischer (KF) ringsS unflower cataract Others Hemolytic anemia (Coombs n egative )Acute pancreatitisFan coni's syndromeHyperparath yroidismCardiomyopathySpo ntaneous abortionsInfertility

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In Wilson Disease , hepatic copper content usually exceeds ____ �Mg/g dry weight .
mcqs.explanation: In Wilson disease , hepatic copper content usually exceeds 250 �Mg/g dry weight . Hepatic copper accumulation is the hallmark of Wilson disease . It is measured using neutron activation analysis/atomic absorption spectrometry .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A male infant was born to a mother with chronic hepatitis B infection . The infant is suspected to have been exposed at the time of delivery. At 4 months, which of the following viral markers signifies ongoing viral replication in the infant?
mcqs.explanation: HBeAg signifies the ongoing viral replication in case of hepatitis B infection .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old boy was brought to the OPD by his mother with a history of fatigue and myalgia for a few days, associated with rashes that started a week before it. On examination, coppery -red coloured skin lesions were seen on the face and limbs including palms and soles . His serology was positive for HBsAg. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The coppery -red colored papules along with a positive HBsAg are suggestive of Gianotti-Crosti syndrome, also known as papular acrodermatitis. It is an immunologic reaction to viral infections . The most common associations are Epstein -Barr virus, hepatitis B virus, Coxsackievirus A16 , and parainfluenza virus, as well as with many childhood immunizations. Skin lesions are monomorphic, firm, coppery red papules sized 1-10 mm. They occur in crops and may become profuse and coalesce into plaques , forming a symmetric eruption on the face , ears, buttocks , and limbs, including the palms and soles . The trunk, scalp , and mucous membrane are relatively spared . The image given below shows the coppery red papules seen in Gianotti-Crosti syndrome.395

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs are not used in the treatment of hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: Ribavirin is a drug used in the treatment of hepatitis C, not hepatitis B. Indications for starting antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B are: • Patients without cirrhosis • HBeAg + with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • HBeAg -ve with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL • Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis. Drugs used in the treatment of hepatitis B are: • First-line treatment : Entecavir or tenofovir • Other drugs: • Pegylated interferon-alpha • Telbivudine • Lamivudine • Adefovir

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young child developed sudden bouts of vomiting and was brought to the ER. Her condition rapidly worsened as she developed seizures. She had a history of influenza infection one week ago. The patient 's liver biopsy will show ______.
mcqs.explanation: Severe vomiting in a 5-year-old child, rapidly worsening to seizures , with a history of viral infection (influenza) is suggestive of Reye 's syndrome. Hence , liver biopsy will show marked microvesicular steatosis .396 Reye 's syndrome is a secondary mitochondrial hepatopathy . It is precipitated due to • Viral infection (influenza, adenovirus, herpes , coxsackievirus A, Epstein –Barr virus) • Salicylate or antiemetic use • Inborn error of metabolism such as single enzyme defects of \337 oxidation. • Toxins There is an acute onset of vomiting and encephalopathy , rapidly progressing to seizures , coma, and death . There is no jaundice. Investigations • \026 ALT and AST • \026 Ammonia • normal bilirubin • Hypoglycemia • PT prolonged • INR increased • Liver biopsy : marked microvesicular steatosis . Necrosis is not seen .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year old girl was rushed to the ER by her parents due to hematemesis . They gave a history of weakness and fatigue for the last few weeks . On examination, the patient had spider telangiectasias and mild palmar erythema . Liver function tests showed the following results - AST-1100IU /L, serum bilirubin- 8mg/dl, albumin- decreased , globulin - elevated , PT- prolonged along with Anti-Nuclear Antibody positive . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The symptoms of liver failure and portal hypertension along with a positive anti-nuclear antibody(ANA) is suggestive of Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis . It is associated with- • Elevated serum aminotransaminase concentrations. • Liver -associated serum autoantibodies. • Hypergammaglobulinemia .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 2-week-old low-birth-weight neonate presents with jaundice . Stools are pale /clay coloured . Liver biopsy shows loss of architecture. The most likely diagnosis is_______.
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal jaundice in a low-birth-weight (LBW ) neonate with consistently pale /clay coloured stools with liver biopsy finding of loss of architecture is suggestive of neonatal hepatitis . Wilson disease and hereditary hemochromatosis will not present with jaundice in the neonatal stage . Hence , they can be excluded . Injury to liver cells can present the clinical and histologic picture of "neonatal hepatitis ." Differentiation between Neonatal hepatitis and EHBA397 Neonatal hepatitis Extrahepatic biliary atresia ( EHBA) Definition It implies intrahepatic choles tasis which includesHepatic i njury due to metabolic , viral , or idiopathic causesIntrahep atic bile duct injury Obliteration of the entire extr ahepatic biliary tree at or abo ve the porta hepatis (85% cas es) ORdistal segmental bile d uct obliteration with patentex trahepatic ducts up to the po rta hepatis (uncommon) Clinical features Family history is presentPre mature or LBW babyClay-col oured stools Family history absentNormal appearance , without looking sickPersistent acholic stools Investigations Liver biopsy : Loss of liver arc hitecture HIDA scan: screening testUS G: triangular cord signLiver b iopsy : bile duct proliferation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother is concerned about her 3-week -old baby having yellowish discolouration of skin and eyes. On examination, the baby is chubby and playful . Stools are pale in color. Further evaluation with USG shows triangular cord sign and liver biopsy shows bile duct proliferation. The most likely diagnosis is ______.
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal jaundice in a neonate without a sick-looking appearance and with acholic stools , USG showing triangular cord sign, and liver biopsy showing bile duct proliferation is suggestive of biliary obstruction, which may be seen in biliary atresia. Wilson disease and Hallervorden Spatz disease (neurodegeneration with iron accumulation in the brain ) do not present with jaundice in the neonatal stage . Hence , they can be excluded . Differentiation between neonatal hepatitis and EHBA Liver biospy : • Biliary atresia is characterized by proliferation of the bile ductule , presence of bile plugs , and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact. • In neonatal hepatitis , there is severe , diffuse hepatocellular disease , with distortion of lobular architecture, marked infiltration of inflammatory cells , and focal hepatocellular necrosis.Neonatal hepatitis Extrahepatic biliary atresia ( EHBA) It implies intrahepatic choles tasis which includes :Hepatic injury due to metabolic , viral , or idiopathic causeIntrahepa tic bile duct injury Obliteration of the entire extr ahepatic biliary tree at or abo ve the porta hepatis (85% cas es) ORDistal segmental bile duct obliteration with patent extrahepatic ducts up to the porta hepatis (uncommon) Clinical features Family history is presentPre mature or LBW babyPigment ed stools Family history absentNormal appearance , without looking sickPersistent acholic stools Investigations398 Neonatal hepatitis Extrahepatic biliary atresia ( EHBA) Liver biopsy : Loss of liver arc hitecture USG: triangular cord signHI DA scan: screening testLiver biopsy : bile duct proliferation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother leaves her 3-year-old son unattended for 20 mins and later finds him holding a blue coloured empty strip of tablets with a few tablets scattered on the floor. A few hours later he is rushed to the ER with nausea and vomiting. As an intern taking the history, you suspect accidental ingestion of paracetamol tablets . The pattern of liver injury you would expect in this case is
mcqs.explanation: The pattern of liver injury caused by paracetamol (acetaminophen ) is centrilobular necrosis. Acetaminophen toxicity results from the formation of a highly reactive intermediate metabolite , N -acetyl -p -benzoquinone imine (NAPQI). In therapeutic use , only about 5% is metabolized by the hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which is then immediately joined with glutathione to form a nontoxic mercapturic acid conjugate . In overdose, glutathione stores are overwhelmed , and free NAPQI is able to combine with hepatic macromolecules to produce hepatocellular necrosis. Single acute toxic dose of APAP is generally considered to be >200 mg/kg in children. Patterns of hepatic drug injury:Disease Drug Centrilobular necrosis Acetaminophen ,Halothane Microvesicular steatosis Valproic acid Acute hepatitis Isoniazid Fibrosis Methotrexate Cholestasis Chlorpromazine,Erythromyci n,Estrogen Veno occlusive disease Busulphan, Cyclophosphami de Portal and hepatic vein thro mbosis Estrogen , Androgen Biliary sludge Ceftriaxone Hepatic adenoma/hepatocell ular carcinoma Oral contraceptive pills , Ana bolic steroids

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are examining a young child who presented to the ER with a high fever and abdominal pain. The patient winces on abdominal palpation of the right upper quadrant . USG showed hydrops of the gallbladder . All of the following conditions are associated with hydrops of the gallbladder except __________.
mcqs.explanation: Hydrops of the gallbladder is not associated with cystic fibrosis. Hydrops of gallbladder is the acute acalculous non-inflammatory distension of the gallbladder , which occurs in infants and children. It is characterized by the absence of calculi, bacterial infections or congenital anomalies of the biliary system .399 Hydrops is distinguished from acalculous cholecystitis by the absence of a significant inflammatory process and a generally benign prognosis. Conditions associated with hydrops of GB: • Infections: Streptococcal pharyngitis, staphylococcal infection , ascariasis, leptospirosis , typhoid fever, and viral hepatitis • Kawasaki disease • Total parenteral nutrition, prolonged fasting • Sickle cell crisis, thalassemia • Sepsis • Mesenteric adenitis , necrotizing enterocolitis Note : In cystic fibrosis cholelithiasis , cholecystitis , micro gallbladder is seen .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The commonest indication for liver transplantation in children is ______
mcqs.explanation: Biliary atresia is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children. Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is defined as a partial or total absence of permeable bile duct between the porta hepatis and the duodenum . It is due to inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree . It leads to obstruction to bile flow thereby causing the leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation. Infants have symptoms of jaundice , pale stools , and dark urine right after birth. In advanced disease , infants present with failure to thrive, hepatomegaly , and ascites due to liver cirrhosis. HIDA scan is the investigation of choice for extrahepatic biliary atresia. An intraoperative cholangiogram is a gold standard investigation for diagnosis. Children with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai's procedure ), require liver transplantation within the first year of life .Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia Type I Atresia restricted to the com mon bile duct Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunosto my Type II Atresia of the common hepati c duct Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y h epatoportoenterostomy ) Type III Atresia of the right and left h epatic duct

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young boy was admitted with complaints of fever and abdominal pain for 2 days. ESR and CRP were elevated and CT Abdomen obtained was as shown in the picture . Which of the following is not a common feature in the given condition?
mcqs.explanation: 400 The symptoms of fever and abdominal pain and a hypodense lesion on the CT are suggestive of a Liver abscess in this patient . Signs and symptoms of a liver abscess include fever, chills, night sweats , malaise, nausea, hepatomegaly, as well as pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant . They also show elevated inflammatory markers , hypoalbuminemia and leukocytosis . However, jaundice is uncommon.401

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The following image shows the chest X-ray of a preterm neonate who was admitted to the NICU in view of severe respiratory distress . What does this suggest ?
mcqs.explanation: From the given clinical picture of respiratory distress in a premature neonate and the X-ray findings of diffuse ground-glass (reticulo-granular) opacities with a characteristic white -out appearance , hyaline membrane disease (HMD) is the most likely diagnosis. HMD, also known as neonatal Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is a relatively common condition resulting from insufficient production of surfactant that occurs in preterm neonates . Maternal diabetes , perinatal asphyxia, and multiple gestations are other known risk factors for the condition. Clinical features include tachypnea , chest retractions, expiratory grunting, and nasal flaring. The infant may or may not be cyanosed .410 X-ray features of HMD include : • Air bronchogram sign • Diffuse ground-glass opacities • Obliteration of cardiac and diaphragmatic contours giving rise to 'white -out' lung (indicates severe disease )Chest radiograph (A) shows reticulogranular opacities throughout both lungs with prominent air bronchograms. The cardiac silhouette is preserved and both lungs are hypoaerated . Chest radiograph (B) shows more severe changes . There is obliteration of the cardiac and diaphragmatic contours due to marked opacification , giving a complete 'white out' appearance

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important risk factor for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Respiratory distress syndrome occurs primarily in premature infants. Its incidence is inversely related to gestational age and birthweight. It occurs in 60–80% of infants delivered at <28 wk of gestational age , in 15–30% of those delivered between 32 and 36 weeks of gestational age , and rarely in those delivered at >37 wk of gestational age . Other risk factors include the following: • Maternal diabetes • Multiple births • Cesarean delivery • Asphyxia • History of previously affected siblings411

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A father runs to a PHC with a baby wrapped in a towel . The neonate was delivered a few hours back, at home, by the local dai. On initial examination, the medical officer notes cyanosis and severe tachypnoea . Which of the following features would favor a diagnosis of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in this child?

options.a: Patchy coarse infiltrates on chest X-ray
options.c: Emaciated appearance with palmar and plantar creases
options.d: Onset of distress after 6 hours of birth

mcqs.explanation: Air bronchogram on chest x-ray is suggestive of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Other chest x-ray findings in respiratory distress syndrome (RDS): • Fine reticulogranular pattern • Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities • White-out lung (severe disease ) Option A: Patchy coarse infiltrates are associated with meconium aspiration syndrome. Option C: Reduced fat under the skin resulting in an emaciated appearance as well as prominent creases is a feature of post -term babies. Respiratory distress syndrome is more common among preterm babies Option D: Onset of respiratory distress syndrome is within 6 hours of birth.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding the treatment of RDS with surfactant is false ?

options.a: It is given in neonates with RDS who fail CPAP
options.b: It is given prophylactically to all neonates at < 31 weeks gestation .
options.c: It can be given as rescue treatment when RDS actually develops .
options.d: Repeated dosing is given every 6-12 hr for a total of 2 to 4 doses .

mcqs.explanation: Surfactant is given prophylactically to all neonates < 28 weeks , not 31 weeks . It is given irrespective of the presence or absence of RDS. The route of administration is intratracheal. Surfactant is indicated in all infants with moderate to severe RDS. It is also given as a rescue treatment when CPAP fails.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A first-year resident receives a call from the casualty regarding an unbooked primigravida , at 32 weeks of gestation. She has presented with regular painful uterine contractions. On examination, her cervix is 2cm dilated . What dose of betamethasone injection should the resident give her?
mcqs.explanation: The woman is currently in preterm labour and the dose of antenatal betamethasone given for avoiding complications of prematurity is 12mg IM every 24 hours (total 2 doses ). Dexamethasone is used , the dose is 6mg IM every 12 hours (total 4 doses ). Corticosteroid administration is recommended for all women in preterm labour (<34 weeks of gestation ). Antenatal steroid administration reduces the risk of the following : (RINN ) • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) • Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH ) • Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) • Neurodevelopmental delay

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman with a history of recurrent late -trimester abortions is in preterm labor, presumed to be due to chorioamnionitis. She has received one dose of betamethasone injection. This is a precious pregnancy and the relatives are concerned about prematurity -related complications in the baby. Which of the following is useful for assessing lung maturity in this fetus ?
mcqs.explanation: 412 The lecithin –sphingomyelin ratio (L /S ratio) is an amniotic fluid test used to assess fetal lung maturity. L/S ratio of < 2 in amniotic fluid indicates lung immaturity. Surfactant starts appearing in the fetal lung by 20 weeks of gestation . Levels indicating lung maturity are detected after 35 weeks . Surfactant is a complex mixture of lipids , proteins , and carbohydrates produced by type II pneumocytes in the lung epithelium . The absence of surfactant in the liquid film lining the alveoli causes an increase in surface tension and alveolar collapse . If not treated , such atelectasis leads to increased work of breathing, intrapulmonary shunting, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoxia, and eventually respiratory failure. The relative concentration of the phospholipids lecithin (L) and sphingomyelin (S) is an indicator of lung maturity. The outward flow of pulmonary secretions from the fetal lungs into the amniotic fluid maintains the level of lecithin and sphingomyelin equally until 32 –33 weeks gestation when the lecithin concentration begins to increase significantly while sphingomyelin remains nearly the same. An L–S ratio of 2.5 or more indicates fetal lung maturity while an L/S ratio of less than 1.5 is associated with a high risk of infant respiratory distress syndrome. Other tests done to assess fetal lung maturity are: • Shake test /bubble test • Phosphatidyl glycerol measurement • Surfactant:albumin ratio • Lamellar body counts

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an indicator of fetal lung maturity?

options.d: Nile blue test showing >50% of blue cells

mcqs.explanation: Nile blue test showing >50% orange cells is a sign of fetal lung maturity, not blue cells . Tests for the assessment of fetal lung maturity include : The Nile blue test involves staining desquamated fetal cells from amniotic fluid with 0.1% Nile blue sulfate . The presence of orange cells > 50% suggests lung maturity. Lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio at 31 to 32 weeks is 1, and at 35 weeks ratio is 2. The ratio \0342 indicates lung maturity (option A). The shake test or bubble test (Clement's test ) (option B) involves mixing amniotic fluid with 95% ethanol, shaking it for 15 seconds , and observing it for 15 minutes . A complete ring of bubbles at the meniscus is a positive test and indicates lung maturity . This is a useful bedside test . The presence of phosphatidylglycerol , (option C) saturated phosphatidylcholine and lamellar body count (>50,000/mcL ) indicates lung maturity. Glucocorticoids accelerate lung maturation and lower the incidence of respiratory distress and neonatal mortality in preterms if the birth was delayed for at least 24 hours after initiation of betamethasone . A single course of corticosteroids is recommended for women between 24 and 36 weeks who are at risk of delivery within 7 days. Intramuscular injections of either 2 doses of 12 mg betamethasone are given 24 hourly or 4 doses of 6 mg dexamethasone are given 12 hourly.413

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A female infant was born in a community hospital by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 34 weeks of gestation. 30 minutes later, the baby's breathing became excessively laboured . Despite providing non-invasive ventilation, the baby died . Post-mortem histopathological examination of the lung showed thick pink membranes lining the small, collapsed alveolar spaces and necrotic debris, mainly within the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts , and unopened alveoli. What are these membranes chiefly composed of?
mcqs.explanation: The history of respiratory distress in a premature baby (34 weeks ) and a biopsy showing pink (hyaline) membranes in the alveoli is indicative of hyaline membrane disease (HMD). The hyaline membranes are composed of layers of fibrin-rich edema fluid and necrotic cells of lining alveoli. Diffuse ischemic damage to the alveoli causes the transudation of proteins into the alveoli to form the hyaline membrane. Hyaline membrane disease (HMD), also known as infantile respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) or respiratory distress syndrome of newborns (RDS) is a syndrome in premature infants caused by developmental insufficiency of pulmonary surfactant production and structural immaturity of the lungs .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A primigravida was taken up for emergency cesarean section in view of placental abruption, at 32 weeks of gestation . Immediately after delivery , you dry the baby, clear secretions from the mouth and nose, and provide tactile stimulation. But even after 30 seconds , you note the baby is still gasping for breath and oxygen saturation has not increased more than 92%. Which is the next best step ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of respiratory distress in a preterm infant is neonatal RDS (hyaline membrane disease ). The infant has presented with moderate respiratory distress without any signs of respiratory failure so early continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the appropriate treatment . CPAP started at birth is the choice for the management of a preterm infant at risk for respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). Early nasal CPAP has shown to lower mortality and risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia . Room air is better than oxygen for the resuscitation of preterm infants, and 100 % oxygen is also harmful, causing increased oxidative stress . The intubate -surfactant-extubate (INSURE) on CPAP technique is recommended for surfactant administration when babies showed signs of RDS and needed more than 30% inspired oxygen to maintain saturation in the normal range .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-hour-old neonate with apnea has been on bag and mask ventilation for the last 30 seconds . She has now started taking spontaneous breaths. The heart rate is still between 100 and 110 /min. What is your next step ?
mcqs.explanation: As per the NRP algorithm, at any time during resuscitation , if the HR > 100 and spontaneous breathing resumes then discontinue ventilation. The components of NRP resuscitation include : (TABCD ) • Temperature - maintain between 36.5 and 37.5 C • Airway- "sniffing" position, clear secretions if needed • Breathing- free flow O2 (maintain sats 91–95%), PPV (40–60 breaths /min), ETT • Circulation- chest compressions :ventilation ratio (3:1 = 90:30; lower 1/3rd sternum; two thumb technique preferred ) • Drugs- Epinephrine , volume expanders Algorithm states : • HR & lt; /min + no respirations \022 Positive pressure ventilation (PPV ) • No response with PPV \022 Endotracheal intubation (ET)414 • HR < 60/min \022 Chest compressions • No response to chest compressions \022 epinephrine

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A preterm infant in the NICU was observed to have marked nasal flare, distinct xiphoid retractions, minimal intercostal retractions, and inspiratory lag with an audible grunt. What would be the Silverman Anderson score?
mcqs.explanation: The Silverman -Anderson score of the child would be 8. Calculation of the Silverman -Anderson score of this child: Total score: A score of more than 7 indicates respiratory failure. The Silverman -Anderson score is a commonly used score to assess respiratory distress . It helps to assess the progression of distress over time and initiate treatment . It is more suited for preterms with respiratory distress syndrome. Scoring is to be done every half an hour and charting is carried out to monitor progress . The image below shows Silverman Anderson retraction score:Criteria Finding Scor e Expiratory grunt Audible with the naked ea r Nasal flaring Marked Xiphoid retraction Marked Intercostal retraction (lower chest ) Minimal Chest movement (upper ches t) Lag Downes ' Score is also used for assessing the severity of respiratory distress . It is more comprehensive and can be applied to any gestational age and condition. Downe 's score of >7 means impending respiratory failure.Score 0 1 Respiratory rat e <60/ min 60–80/min >80/min Air entry Nor mal Mild decrease Marked decrease Cyanosis Nil In -room air On >40% O2 Grunting None Only on auscultatio n Audible with the naked ea r Retraction Nil Mild Moderate

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As part of calculating Downe 's score for a baby, you would assess all of the following except :
mcqs.explanation: Downe 's score does not consider nasal flaring. The severity of respiratory distress is assessed by Downe 's score and Silverman –Anderson score. Downe 's score can be applied for any gestational age . Downe 's score of >7 means impending respiratory failure. Silverman –Anderson score is more suited for preterms with hyaline membrane disease (HMD). Downe 's scoringScore 0 1 Respiratory rat e <60/ min 60–80/min >80/min Air entry Nor mal Mild decrease Marked decrease Cyanosis Nil In room air On >40% O2 Grunting None Only on auscultatio n Audible with naked e ar Retraction Nil Mild Moderate

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Your brother-in-law calls you during one of your night duties and tells you that your sister just delivered a baby girl and that both the mother and the child are doing well following the cesarean delivery . The next morning , however, you get a call that the baby started having trouble breathing and has been shifted to the NICU. He also sends you a photo of her chest X-ray via WhatsApp. On the radiograph, you note streaky, perihilar linear densities and fluid in the horizontal fissure . Which of the following is true regarding the given clinical condition?

options.a: Only observation and supportive therapy is needed
options.b: It can predispose to bronchopulmonary dysplasia

mcqs.explanation: Benign respiratory distress in a newborn with a chest X-ray showing fluid in the interlobar fissure is indicative of transient tachypnoea of newborn (TTN), also known as retained fetal lung liquid syndrome. The management of TTN is supportive oxygen therapy and observation.416 It is more common after a term, cesarean delivery and is due to the delayed clearance of the lung fluid from the interstitium into the pulmonary lymphatics . Other findings of chest x-ray imaging are prominent (perihilar) pulmonary vascular markings , increased interstitial markings , and a "wet silhouette " around the heart.Chest radiograph (A) on day 1 at 6 hours shows a bilateral diffuse ground-glass appearance and fine granularity due to interstitial opacities . Chest radiograph (B) of the same patient at the age of 2 days (B) shows that the pulmonary parenchymal opacities have decreased, though perihilar streaky markings are still present . Treatment is supportive and minimal oxygen treatment (< 40%) is often adequate ; infants usually recover within 3 days.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A preterm, extremely low birth weight baby, delivered by emergency caesarian section was admitted to the NICU and treated for respiratory distress syndrome. She responded to treatment and was discharged . At 6 months of age , she is still having recurrent respiratory distress and requires supplemental oxygen at home. The baby was diagnosed with bronchopulmonary dysplasia . Which of the following does not cause this clinical complication?
mcqs.explanation: Inhalation of nitrous oxide (N2O) is not associated with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Inhaled NO is a pulmonary vasodilator approved for the treatment of hypoxic respiratory failure in term and near-term infants with pulmonary hypertension . It may have a role in preventing BPD. BPD is a pathologic process leading to clinical features of chronic lung disease that originates in the neonatal period and is defined by an oxygen requirement for 28 days postnatally . Inflammatory injury to the developing lungs due to barotrauma and oxygen toxicity resulting from prolonged mechanical ventilation is the key factor driving the pathogenesis of BPD. Together with other antenatal and postnatal factors, it results in aberrant tissue repair, dysregulated vascular and arrested alveolar development , which is the basis of the pathology seen in BPD.417

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A female newborn was delivered at 40 weeks of gestation by emergency C-section , following signs of severe fetal distress . Greenish amniotic fluid was noted . Immediately following delivery , the baby was shifted to the NICU and had to be intubated . Her chest X-Ray is as below . What does it show?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows patchy infiltrates and coarse streaking, which are characteristic findings in the chest X-ray image of infants with meconium aspiration syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn infant, delivered at home, at 42 weeks of gestation , became cyanotic and started breathing rapidly. The child was immediately taken to the nearby primary health centre. As the medical officer prepares to intubate , she notes greenish staining on the vocal cords. Which of the following is this baby likely to develop ?
mcqs.explanation: Respiratory distress in a post -term neonate with a history of greenish (meconium-stained ) amniotic fluid during delivery is suggestive of meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). The aspirated meconium can block the large and small airways, causing patchy atelectasis and emphysema . This produces a ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Severe overinflation can lead to air leak syndromes such as pneumothorax. Meconium consists of water, desquamated GIT cells , skin, lanugo hair, vernix , bile salts, pancreatic enzymes , lipids , and mucopolysaccharides . The bile salts and pancreatic enzymes can cause chemical pneumonitis . Meconium can also cause surfactant inactivation by displacing it from the alveolar surface and inhibiting its surface tension-lowering ability. Severe MAS is associated with remodelling and thickening of the muscular walls , resulting in pulmonary hypertension . Infants who develop MAS typically present in the first 12 hours after birth with varying degrees of respiratory distress . On inspection , many affected infants have 'barrel chests '; crackles (rales) and rhonchi often can be heard on auscultation . In severe cases , the entire lungs can be involved resulting in a total "whiteout " of the lungs on the radiograph. Listeriosis is an infection that is acquired from the mother and is reported to be rarely associated with meconium-stained amniotic fluid.418

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about apnea of prematurity (AOP)?

options.a: Usually resolves by 37 weeks post conceptional age
options.b: Gentle tactile stimulation is often adequate for mild to moderate episodes
options.c: Recurrent AOP can be treated with caffeine or theophylline
options.d: AOP is a risk factor for Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)

mcqs.explanation: Apnea of prematurity (AOP) is not a risk factor for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). It is defined as cessation of breathing for longer than 20 seconds or for any duration if accompanied by cyanosis or bradycardia. It is a diagnosis of exclusion . It is seen in preterm infants and usually resolves by the 37th week of gestation . Recurrent apnea of prematurity may be treated with caffeine or theophylline . It does not predict the future occurrence of SIDS. Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is the sudden death of an infant under one year of age , which remains unexplained after a thorough case investigation, including the performance of a complete autopsy , examination of the death scene , and review of the clinical history.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While monitoring the respiratory rate of the infants in the NICU, you notice one baby which suddenly stops breathing. Which of the following statements is true in this regard?

options.a: Primary apnea is characterized by labile BP and tachycardia
options.b: Caffeine therapy should be given in primary apnea
options.c: Secondary apnea responds to stimulation by establishing normal breathing.
options.d: Central asphyxia can cause secondary apnea

mcqs.explanation: Secondary apnea can occur as a central CNS meditated asphyxia or due to neuromuscular disorders. Apnea is the cessation of breathing for >20 seconds or for any duration if accompanied by bradycardia and cyanosis.Primary Apnea Secondary Apnea Failure to initiate respiratory effort at birth Apnea developing in an infan t who has initiated a respirat ory effort There may be bradycardia an d decreased tone. BP remains normal Can originate in CNS due to asphyxia or peripherally due to neuromuscular disorders419 Primary Apnea Secondary Apnea Respond to tactile stimulatio n Require ventilatory assistanc e and drugs- caffeine or theo phylline

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 15-day-old infant had conjunctivitis, which later developed into respiratory distress and pneumonia. Chest X-ray examination revealed bilateral lung infiltrates . Peripheral smear count showed 14,300 /dL (N 43, L 54, E3). Which of the following is the most likely pathogenic organism?
mcqs.explanation: The organism most likely to cause the mentioned infections is Chlamydia trachomatis. Pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis can develop in 10 –20 % of infants born to women with active, untreated chlamydial infection . Only approximately 25% of infants with nasopharyngeal chlamydial infection develop pneumonia. C. trachomatis pneumonia of infancy has a very characteristic presentation . It usually occurs between 1-3 months of age and is insidious, with a persistent cough , tachypnea , and absence of fever. Auscultation reveals rales; wheezing is uncommon. The absence of fever and wheezing helps to distinguish C. trachomatis pneumonia from respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia. A distinctive laboratory finding is the presence of peripheral eosinophilia (>400 cells /\265 L). The most consistent finding on chest radiograph is hyperinflation accompanied by minimal interstitial or alveolar infiltrates .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The radiologist calls and confirms a Bochdalek hernia in a baby born with multiple congenital anomalies. The baby had been placed under an oxygen hood in the NICU, in view of postnatal respiratory distress . On repeat evaluation, he continues to have sternal retractions and is not maintaining saturation. Which of the following would be your initial clinical intervention in this case?

options.a: Intubate and insert a nasogastric tube
options.c: Insert a central venous pressure line

mcqs.explanation: Once the diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is made or suspected , all patients are intubated . Also a nasogastric tube , connected to continuous suction, is placed in the stomach to reduce lung compression. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect of the diaphragm. The most common type of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia (postero-lateral diaphragmatic hernia); other types include Morgagni hernia (anterior-parasternal), diaphragm eventration, and central tendon defects of the diaphragm. Malformation of the diaphragm allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity, hindering proper lung formation and expansion. Immediate steps of management: Endotracheal intubation \022 Placement of a nasogastric tube \022 Administration of fluids and inotropic agents \022 Administration of surfactant therapy to only preterm infants with findings suggestive of respiratory distress syndrome.Other options: Option B: Bag and mask ventilation is to be avoided as they lead to gastric/abdominal distension and compression of the lung. Option C: Both arterial and central venous lines are inserted ; however, this is not the first line of intervention.420 Option D: To support respiratory failure, the first modality to be used is conventional ventilation, and if there is no improvement, then high-frequency ventilation is used .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn delivered vaginally, at term, was diagnosed with congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The most important limiting factor for survival in this condition is ________.
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary hypoplasia is a very poor prognostic factor in congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Poor prognostic indicators in CDH: • The presence of liver in the thoracic cavity • Pulmonary hypoplasia , pulmonary hypertension • Early respiratory distress , within 24 h after birth • Need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation • Herniation to the contralateral lung (right-sided hernia)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are doing a quick pre-op evaluation of a 2-day-old baby shifted for emergency pediatric surgery. Parents had brought him with a history of sudden , noisy breathing. He appeared cyanotic with decreased breath sounds on the left side of the chest . Chest X-ray taken in the casualty is given below . Which of the following is not true about the underlying condition?

options.b: Most commonly seen on the left side
options.c: Mortality is usually associated with pulmonary hypoplasia
options.d: Pulmonary dilators markedly improve the survival

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical picture of neonatal respiratory distress , absent breath sounds in the left side of the chest , and an X-ray image showing bowel loops in the thoracic cavity is diagnostic of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Though less commonly documented , dextrocardia is seen in association with CDH. A diaphragmatic hernia is defined as a communication between the abdominal and thoracic cavities with or without abdominal contents in the thorax. It is mostly congenital , with a defective formation of the pleuroperitoneal membrane. Females are affected twice as often as males. Bochdalek hernia accounts for up to 90% of the hernias seen in the newborn period , with 80-90% occurring on the left side . So, the heart will be pushed to the right side (dextroposition ). Predictors of a poor prognosis include an associated major anomaly, symptoms before completion of 24 hours since birth, severe pulmonary hypoplasia , herniation to the contralateral lung, and the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO ). Nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator. It reduces ductal shunting and pulmonary pressures , resulting in improved oxygenation.421

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother brought a healthy -looking, 3-month-old infant for routine immunization . As you were giving the shot, you noticed some noisy breathing in the baby, which became worse once he started crying. However, it decreased , as you held him in a prone position. There were no clear signs of distress . According to his mother, he had been feeding well at home and has not had any episodes of apnea or cyanosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A clinical picture of inspiratory stridor that worsens on crying and relieves in a prone position in a newborn without respiratory distress is suggestive of laryngomalacia. Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital laryngeal anomaly and the most common cause of stridor in infants and children. Stridor is exacerbated by any exertion: crying, agitation, or feeding . In the prone position, the stridor disappears .On laryngoscopy , an omega-shaped epiglottis is visualized. In most children, only expectant observation is required as the condition resolves secondary to nervous system maturation, within 18 to 24 months of birth. However, neonates with severe laryngomalacia may develop marked upper airway obstruction resulting in cor pulmonale , life -threatening apneic episodes , feeding difficulties , obstructive sleep apnea, and failure to thrive. In such cases , surgical resection of supraglottic tissues and supraglottoplasty has been the favoured approach.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A senior casualty nurse informs you that a 5-year-old girl with severe respiratory distress might require intubation. You just finished stabilising and placing an ET tube in Mohan, a 57 -year-old man with head trauma and a GCS of 7. Which of the following is not a feature of child's airway?

options.a: The larynx being located higher in the neck at the level of C3-C
options.b: The narrowest part being the subglottic region

mcqs.explanation: The pediatric airway is funnel shaped . In comparison, the adult airway is cylindrical.433 In newborns, the larynx is situated at the level of C3-C4, where it facilitates simultaneous respiration and swallowing during feeding .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During a night shift, you get a call from the ER to come and see a toddler , who presented with complaints of fever, drooling, and a muffled voice since evening. On examination, the child has a stridor and you pick up a "thumb sign" on the lateral x-ray of his neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Thumb sign on lateral x-ray of neck is pathognomonic for acute epiglottitis (AE). It is seen due to epiglottic enlargement . AE is an inflammation of the epiglottis . The arytenoids , false cords, and posterior tongue may also be involved. In children, Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) is the most common cause . This has decreased dramatically since the widespread availability of immunization (pentavalent ). Streptococcus pyogenes , S. pneumoniae , and S. aureus have also been implicated . Non-infectious causes can be foreign body ingestion and trauma from thermal or caustic agents . It has a progressive and potentially fulminating course , characterised by high fever, sore throat, dyspnea , and rapidly progressing respiratory obstruction. AE is a clinical diagnosis and a true emergency , X-ray soft tissue neck is not necessary to confirm it. It may be used to rule out differentials such as laryngotracheobronchitis, foreign body obstruction, retropharyngeal abscess or congenital anomalies. The time taken for X-rays should be avoided in a critically ill child due to the risk of sudden complete airway obstruction. The definitive diagnosis of AE is made during direct laryngoscopy . However, since manipulation can induce a laryngospasm, it is generally avoided. The image below shows thumb sign:

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common etiological agent associated with epiglottitis in children, overall in the world?
mcqs.explanation: 434 The most common etiological agent , overall in the world, of acute epiglottitis in the pediatric age group, now is Streptococcus . In the past, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) used to be the most commonly identified cause of acute epiglottitis . But, since the widespread use of the H. influenzae type b vaccine, invasive disease caused by H. influenzae type b in pediatric patients has been reduced by 99%. Therefore, other organisms, such as Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS), Streptococcus penumoniae , non-typeable H. influenzae , and Staphylococcus aureus, have become the common causes of acute epiglottitis in pediatric age group, overall in the world. Lateral X-ray of the neck shows the thumb sign in acute epiglottitis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5 year old boy was suffering from low grade fever, inspiratory stridor and barking cough for past 5 days. His chest X-ray is given below . What is the cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Barking cough is a feature of laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The X-ray finding is the 'Steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing . The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months-6 years. The clinical features include barking cough , inspiratory stridor, hoarseness , low-grade fever. Management : • Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to the rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure , leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema . • Dexamethasone -by the least invasive route (Oral>IV>IM ). It is indicated in all the grades of croup. • Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %) Antibiotics are not indicated in laryngotracheobronchitis.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: 2-year-old Neha has been having fever since yesterday and is refusing food. Parents became alarmed when she developed an abnormal barking cough today morning and have brought her to the casualty . On examination, the child looked exhausted and had visible chest retractions and stridor. The temperature was 39.6 degrees and SpO2 was 93% on room air. Chest X-ray reveals a 'steeple ' sign. What is the treatment of choice in this child?

options.c: Send a throat swab and start IV antibiotics

mcqs.explanation: Fever, barking cough , inspiratory stridor and a steeple sign on chest radiograph are suggestive of acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup). The treatment of choice in this child is nebulization with racemic epinephrine . Epinephrine acts rapidly and provides immediate relief . It constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure . This increases fluid resorption and reduces airway edema . Westley Croup Severity Score: Overall score and severity • 0 to 2- mild • 3 to 7- moderate • 8 to 11 - severe435 • 12 to 17- impending respiratory failure Treatment of moderate to severe croup : • Racemic epinephrine nebulization • Dexamethasone is indicated in all grades of croup and is given by the least invasive route (Oral>IM>IV) • Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %) • Antibiotics are not indicated in croupFeature 1 3 4 Stridor None With agitatio n At rest Air Entry Normal Decreased Markedly decreas ed Retractions None Mild Moderate Sever e Cyanosis None With agitatio n At Rest Level of Consciousnes s Normal,including slee p Disorient ed

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child in your unit is admitted with acute bronchiolitis. Which of the following is the most common etiological agent responsible for this condition during infancy?
mcqs.explanation: Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV ) is the most likely etiological agent and is responsible for more than 50% of cases . Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract. Clinical features of bronchiolitis include fever, cough , fine inspiratory crackles, expiratory wheezes , and breathing difficulty . Cyanosis may be seen in severe cases . Radiographs may be normal in some patients . In the majority of them, there will be interstitial infiltrates , hyper -expansion of the chest , and peribronchial thickening. Management is mainly conservative. Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen . Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalization and invasive ventilation.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
