mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ask-Upmark kidney refers to ________
mcqs.explanation: The Ask-Upmark kidney is also termed segmental hypoplasia . Renal segmental hypoplasia : • Severe segmental renal atrophy with loss of parenchymal elements in small kidneys is commonly known as segmental hypoplasia . • It refers to small kidneys, usually weighing not more than 35 g. • The scars are seen as cortical depressions overlying shrunken medullary pyramids and their dilated calyces , and they are characterized histologically by colloid -filled tubular microcysts and a paucity or absence of glomeruli . • Most patients are 10 years or older at diagnosis and have severe hypertension . • Nephrectomy usually controls the hypertension .537

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old primigravida was rushed to the OT for an emergency caesarean section . Her pregnancy was unplanned and she did not take folic acid supplementation prior to conception . Moreover, owing to the pandemic led lockdown and her remote residence , she could not adhere to regular antenatal care. The newborn was born with a neural tube defect and immediately shifted to the NICU. What is the least likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 550 Holoprosencephaly is not a neural tube defect (NTD) and hence , it is the least likely diagnosis. Folic acid deficiency , especially in a young primigravida , is a risk factor for the development of NTDs in children, as seen in the given clinical vignette . NTDs result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development . These can be detected in antenatal ultrasound scans and subsequently managed for a better prognosis. The major NTDs include the following : • Spina bifida occulta • Meningocele • Myelomeningocele • Encephalocele • Anencephaly • Syringomyelia • Diastematomyelia (split spinal cord) • Iniencephaly In holoprosencephaly , the forebrain fails to develop into two hemispheres due to mutations in the sonic hedgehog gene at the long arm of chromosome 7. It is a developmental disorder of the brain that results from the defective formation of the prosencephalon and the inadequate induction of the forebrain structures . The three types include , alobar, semilobar, and lobar, apart from the middle interhemispheric fusion variant or syntelencephaly . The image given below shows alobar holoprosencephaly -

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn presented with a tuft of hair over the lumbosacral region. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A tuft of hair over the lumbosacral region in a newborn is suggestive of occult spinal dysraphism or neural tube defect . It comprises a range of conditions, including spina bifida occulta , intradural551 lipoma, and dorsal dermal sinus. Spinal dysraphism is due to the defective fusion of the midline embryonic neural, vertebral, and mesenchymal structures . Associated clinical features are high-arched feet , muscle size and strength differences between legs , and abnormal walking patterns . In newborns and young infants, the neurological examination is usually normal , but older children may experience a lack of sensation in the perineal area and back pain. Most of the patients will have a cutaneous abnormality overlying the lower spine , including a small dimple , a tuft of hair, or a subcutaneous lipoma. The image shows a tuft of hair in a case of spinal dysraphism:Spinal dysraphism also includes meningocele , myelomeningocele , lipomeningocele , diastematomyelia (split spinal cord), thickened filum terminale, and cauda equina tumour. The initial investigation is usually ultrasound in the neonate and the best investigation is MRI. Spina bifida is the most common type of spinal dysraphism, in which the spinal column does not close completely , leaving the spinal cord and its protective covering exposed .552 Myelomeningocele is the most severe form of spina bifida, where the spinal cord and nerve roots are exposed and may be damaged . A sac-like protrusion, containing spinal cord tissue , meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid , is visible outside the body, often leading to significant neurological impairments and disabilities .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman underwent second -trimester screening and had an abnormal presence of a biochemical marker . Following this, she went to a tertiary care referral centre for further investigations. An anomaly scan revealed cranial lemon and cerebellar banana signs. What is the abnormal marker present in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: In the given clinical scenario, the presence of abnormal sonographic markers , like the lemon and banana sign, is highly suggestive of neural tube defects (NTDs). Acetylcholinesterase is used as a biochemical marker of neural tube defects during the screening tests . NTDs account for the largest proportion of congenital anomalies of the CNS. The failure of closure of neural tube allows excretion of fetal substances such as \032-fetoprotein (AFP) and acetylcholinesterase into the amniotic fluid thereby serving as biochemical markers for NTDs. The lemon and banana sign, noted on antenatal imaging, are one of the many notable fruits' inspired signs. The banana sign refers to the shape of the cerebellum owing to caudal displacement while the lemon sign refers to the lemon-shaped head resulting from scalloping of the frontal bones. It is seen in fetuses with open neural tube defects . The image below shows the characteristic lemon sign on ultrasound-553 The image below shows the characteristic banana sign on ultrasound-Note : Pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPPA), inhibin A, and human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) are the biochemical markers of trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child is scheduled for myelomeningocele surgery. Until the patient is waiting for surgery, the covering of the sac will be protected by a gauze soaked in______.
mcqs.explanation: Until the time of surgery, the sac of myelomeningocele has to be covered with a sterile gauze soaked in normal saline. This is to prevent drying and trauma to the sac. As the normal saline is less irritant to the sac, it is preferred . Note :554 Surgery is done as early as possible (within a day of birth).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman was rushed to the casualty of a maternity hospital due to imminent delivery. It resulted in a stillborn baby as shown in the picture below . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows an occipital bone defect with retroflexion of the neck and trunk, which is typical of iniencephaly . Inion is the tip of the external occipital protuberance and this defect comes under the spectrum of neural tube defects . Diastematomyelia (Option A) is a congenital disorder in which a part of the spinal cord is split , usually at the level of the upper lumbar vertebra. Craniorachischisis (Option B) is the anencephaly associated with a continuous bony defect of the spine and exposure of neural tissue. Holoprosencephaly (Option D) occurs when the procencephalon fails to develop into two hemispheres.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly in newborns?
mcqs.explanation: Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus in newborns. Ventriculomegaly is the dilation of the ventricles. When ventriculomegaly occurs in association with raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure , it is called hydrocephalus . Pathologic etiologies can be congenital or acquired. Congenital causes include structural abnormalities such as aqueductal stenosis , agenesis of the corpus callosum, Dandy-Walker malformations, Chiari malformations, and neural tube defects . Acquired causes are intracranial infections (cytomegalovirus , toxoplasmosis), intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic injury, and brain parenchymal tumors. Aqueductal stenosis is the narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct , a narrow channel that connects the third and fourth ventricles in the brain . As a result , the fluid accumulates within the ventricles, causing them to enlarge . Treatment for aqueductal stenosis includes ventriculostomy , diuretics , serial lumbar punctures in specific cases , and CSF diversion. In severe cases , CSF diversion procedures (shunting), may be necessary to redirect the flow of CSF and relieve pressure on the brain .555

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An infant is brought to the OPD with complaints of multiple episodes of vomiting that is more in the morning and relieved when sitting . She has an unusually large head with bulging fontanelles . The image of the child showing a characteristic sign is given below . Which of the following is not a cause of the communicating variant of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical features of frequent vomiting, large head , bulging fontanelles , and a positive sunset sign (as seen in the image) point to a likely diagnosis of hydrocephalus . A vein of Galen malformation can expand to become large and, because of its midline position, obstruct the flow of CSF, thereby causing an obstructive or non-communicating hydrocephalus . Vomiting is more in the morning and becomes better when sitting due to poor absorption of CSF in a lying down position. Hydrocephalus is not a specific disease; it represents a diverse group of conditions that result from impaired circulation or absorption of CSF. Causes of hydrocephalus :Communicating(external/non -obstructive ) Non-communicating(internal /obstructive ) Achondroplasia (raised ICP d ue to jugular foramen stenosi s)Choroid plexus papillomaM eningeal malignancyMeningit isPosthemorrhagicSarcoidosi s Aqueductal stenosisArnold -C hiari malformationDandy–W alker malformationKlippel –F eil syndromeTumours and ne urocutaneous disorders (astr ocytoma)Vein of Galen malfo rmation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Shreya, a 2-year-old girl, presented with irritability for 2 days. On examination, macrocephaly , hypotonia and spasticity were present with a positive head transillumination test . She started walking independently at 18 months and became dry by day a month before her 2nd birthday. An MRI-brain revealed cystic expansion of the fourth ventricle and midline cerebellar hypoplasia . What is the most likely diagnosis explaining her obstructive hydrocephalus ?
mcqs.explanation: The features of hydrocephalus like irritability along with macrocephaly , hypotonia and spasticity indicate a likely diagnosis of Dandy-Walker syndrome. A positive transillumination test is present in this syndrome. The child has developmental delay especially in motor and cognitive milestones556 because normally children walk independently at 12 -13 months and become dry by day around 18 months. The Dandy-Walker malformation consists of a cystic expansion of the fourth ventricle in the posterior fossa and midline cerebellar hypoplasia . It results from a developmental failure of the roof of the fourth ventricle during embryogenesis . Most of the affected patients have hydrocephalus , agenesis of the posterior cerebellar vermis, and corpus callosum. Brisk tendon reflexes , spasticity , clonus, Babinski sign, cerebellar ataxia, and delayed motor and cognitive milestones are seen in this. Management is by shunting if hydrocephalus is present . The image below shows a sagittal section of the magnetic resonance tomography scan of a patient with Dandy-Walker syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old baby presented with fever, poor feeding , and frequent vomiting. On examination , the head circumference was 46.5cm with a positive sunset and Macewen sign. Which of the following infections is associated with the most common cause of the underlying neurological disease in this child?
mcqs.explanation: 557 Symptoms of poor feeding and frequent vomiting with signs of enlarged head circumference and a positive sunset and Macewen sign(crack-pot resonance) points toward a diagnosis of hydrocephalus . Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of hydrocephalus . Out of the above options , mumps infection can cause stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct . Mumps is associated in a child with aqueductal stenosis because - • Mumps virus is neurotropic and is thought to enter the CNS via the choroid plexus and infect the choroidal epithelium and ependymal cells . • CNS complications of mumps include meningitis, meningoencephalitis (most commonly manifests 5 days after the parotitis), transverse myelitis , aqueductal stenosis , and facial palsy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-month-old baby presented with seizures , developmental delay and failure to thrive. Following an MRI, a diagnosis of a neuronal migration disorder was made. What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , schizencephaly is a neuronal migration defect . MRI is the study of choice for elucidating schizencephaly and associated malformations. Neuronal migration is the process during brain development , where the neuronal cells migrate to their proper designated site by various mechanisms, to form the 6-layered cerebral cortex. Any abnormality in the above process leads to neuronal migration defects . Neuronal migration defect includes the following : • Schizencephaly : (schiz = split or cleavage ) It is the presence of unilateral or bilateral clefts within the cerebral hemispheres . The patient can be severely intellectually challenged , with microcephaly , seizures , and spastic quadriparesis. The image below shows schizencephaly :• Lissencephaly (agyria): It is the absence of cerebral convolutions. Rather than the normal 6 layers of the cortex, there may be fewer layers. The child will have developmental delay , microcephaly , and seizures . The image below shows lissencephaly :558 Myelomeningocele (Option B) is a neural tube defect that occurs due to defective closure of the neural tube . Lhermitte–Duclos disease (Option C) is the cerebellar dysplasia leading to focal enlargement of cerebellum and macrocephaly , cerebellar signs, and seizures . Plagiocephaly (Option D) is the asymmetry and flattening of the skull of the child, due to extrinsic moulding forces (consistent sleeping on the same side of the head ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding the given image?

options.c: It is associated with facial angiofibroma
options.d: They are diagnostic of a neurocutaneous syndrome

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows discrete tan-colored nodules over the iris called Lisch nodules (pigmented melanocytic hamartomas). They are seen in neurofibromatosis-1 (NF-1). Facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum ) is a feature of tuberous sclerosis (TS) and not neurofibromatosis. The image below shows facial angiofibroma seen in tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease ).559 Lisch nodules are specifically associated with NF-1 and are usually multiple and bilateral. They are best visualized with a slit lamp examination and don't cause any visual disturbances . Other important ocular manifestations in NF-1 include eyelid plexiform neurofibroma, which causes S-shaped deformity of the upper lid, with a 'bag of worms' like texture , optic nerve glioma, and spheno -orbital encephalocele due to dysplasia of greater wing of the sphenoid . NF-1 (von Recklinghausen's disease ) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a loss-of-function mutation of the NF-1 gene located on chromosome 17q11 .2. NF-1 produces neurofibromin, which acts as a tumor suppressor and a negative regulator of RAS-MAP kinase signaling. Clinical features of NF-1 include caf\351-au-lait macules , axillary freckling, Lisch nodules , neurofibromas, and optic gliomas. NF-1 is more common than NF2 and typically diagnosed in childhood . NF-2 is rarer but often presents with bilateral acoustic neuroma, juvenile cataract and schwannoma. mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During a telemedicine consultation , you come across a case of a 9-year-old child with a previously diagnosed autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome known as tuberous sclerosis . Which one of the following is not seen in it?
mcqs.explanation: Ependymomas are not seen in tuberous sclerosis . Neurocutaneous syndromes like tuberous sclerosis are a group of disorders with abnormalities in both the integumentary system and the CNS (defect of primitive ectoderm ). They include the following : • Neurofibromatosis • Tuberous sclerosis • Sturge –Weber syndrome • von Hippel –Lindau disease • Ataxia telangiectasia Tuberous sclerosis is caused due to mutation of genes coding for hamartin (chromosome 9) and tuberin (chromosome 16), which leads to the formation of hamartomas. Clinical features : • CNS • CNS involvement is the hallmark of tuberous sclerosis . • Glioneuronal hamartomas (cortical tubers ). • Subependymal nodules are lesions found along the wall of the lateral ventricles, where they undergo calcification. • Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs) are the characteristic brain tumours. These benign, slow -growing tumours arise in the periventricular area. • White matter lesions are common and include nodules , cysts , and areas of gliosis and hypomyelination. • Skin • Facial angiofibroma (adenoma sebaceum ) • Periungual fibroma • Shagreen patch • Confetti skin lesions561 • Others • Renal angiomyolipoma • Cardiac rhabdomyoma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During rounds in the neurology ward, an 11 -year-old child is observed with the following lesion on his back. Which of the following characteristic skin manifestation of tuberous sclerosis is depicted in this picture ?
mcqs.explanation: The lesion seen in the picture depicts a shagreen patch . This is a characteristic skin lesion found in patients with tuberous sclerosis . It consists of a roughened , raised lesion with an orange-peel consistency , located primarily in the lumbosacral region. Shagreen is shark skin used as a decorative material present in the image of the question. Skin lesions in tuberous sclerosis : • The typical hypomelanotic ash leaf –type macules on the trunk and extremities are seen in 90% of the patients . It is visualized by the use of a wood ultraviolet lamp. • Facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum ) develop between 4 and 6 years of age ; they appear as tiny red nodules over the nose and cheeks and are sometimes confused with acne. Later, they enlarge , coalesce , and assume a fleshy appearance . • Periungual fibroma are small fibromas or nodules of skin, which form around fingernails or toenails in some adolescent patients . • Confetti skin lesions are seen less commonly as a minor feature of tuberous sclerosis . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child is rushed to the emergency department because of an episode of fits associated with uprolling of eyes and high fever. Kernig's sign is negative and there are no post -ictal neurological deficits . There is a history of a similar episode when the child had a fever due to gastroenteritis . Which of the following is false regarding this type of seizures ?

options.a: Likelihood of developing epilepsy is low
options.b: Associated with temperature of 38\260C or higher
options.c: Antipyretics reduce the risk of recurrent febrile convulsions
options.d: Absence of having a developmental delay

mcqs.explanation: This is a probable case of febrile seizures due to the presence of high fever, no post -ictal deficits and a negative Kernig's sign ruling out meningitis. Antipyretics do not reduce the risk of recurrent febrile seizure , as the seizure often occurs as the temperature is rising or falling abruptly . Febrile seizures are seizures that- • Occur between the age of 6 months and 5 years • Occur at a temperature of 38\260C (100 .4\260F) or higher • Are not due to any CNS infection or any metabolic imbalance • Occur without a history of prior afebrile seizures • Occur with no post -ictal neurological deficit .565 Types of febrile seizures : Investigations: • Lumbar puncture should be performed in the first episode of seizures with fever, for all infants <6 months age (to exclude meningitis). • EEG and neuroimaging are advised for children with atypical febrile seizures . Treatment: Antipyretics and proper hydration. Midazolam or diazepam (rectal) can be used if seizures present . Prophylaxis: • Intermittent prophylaxis : If the febrile seizures are 3 or more in 6 months, or 4 or more seizures in 1 year, oral clobazam (1mg/kg/day) for 3 days during the fever episode . • Continuous prophylaxis : If intermittent prophylaxis fails or in recurrent atypical febrile seizures , sodium valproate and phenobarbitone can be used .Simple febrile seizures Complex (atypical ) febrile sei zures Occurs within 24 hours of th e onset of fever Can occur at any time during a fever Generalized seizures Focal seizures Duration is <15 min Prolonged No recurrence within 24 hrs of seizures Recurrent Chances of going into epileps y 1% Chances of going into epileps y 6%

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Your neighbour, Sheila, frantically knocks on your door to seek help as her toddler had suddenly started convulsing with uprolling of eyes . The child had a high fever and this was his third episode of seizures in 6 months. Post-recovery, Sheila is still anxious and wishes to know the risk factors for such recurrences of febrile seizures . You would explain all of the following except -
mcqs.explanation: Early age of onset (age <1 year) is a risk factor for recurrence of febrile seizures . The other risk factors for such recurrences are as follows : Major: • Age <1 yr • Duration of fever <24 hr • Fever 38-39\260C Minor: • Family history of febrile seizures • Family history of epilepsy • Complex febrile seizure566 • Male gender • Lower serum sodium at the time of presentation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child presents with developmental delay and multiple seizure types . The seizures could not be controlled by an array of drugs. Electroencephalogram (EEG ) shows 1-2 Hz spike and slow waves with polyspike bursts in sleep . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A child with features of developmental delay , intractable seizures and an electroencephalogram (EEG ) showing 1-2 Hz spike and polyspike bursts in sleep has a likely diagnosis of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome- Typically starts between the age of 2 and 10 years. Consists of a triad of: • Developmental delay • Multiple seizure types (includes atypical absences , myoclonic, astatic, and tonic seizures ) • EEG findings 1-2 Hz spike and slow waves, polyspike bursts in sleep , and a slow background in wakefulness Patients will have long-term cognitive impairment and intractable seizures despite multiple therapies . The drug of choice for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is valproate. Other drugs used for this condition are clobazam, lamotrigine, rufinamide and topiramate. Other options : Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome)- Typically , it starts in early adolescence (not in childhood ) and the EEG usually shows generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow -wave discharges Landau–Kleffner syndrome- A rare condition characterized by loss of language skills in a previously normal child (not a child with developmental delay ) West syndrome- Starts between the ages of 2 and 12 months and typical EEG picture is called hypsarrhythmia (high-voltage , slow with chaotic background)Disease Typical EEG features Drug of choice Lennox–Gastaut syndrome 1-2 Hz spike and polyspike b ursts in sleep Valproate Absence seizures 3 Hz spike and slow -wave (sp ike and dome pattern) Ethosuximide Juvenile myoclonic epileps y 4-5 Hz spike polyspike and sl ow-wave discharges Valproate West syndrome Hypsarrhythmia (high-voltag e waves with chaotic backgro und Adrenocorticotropic hormon e (ACTH)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?

options.a: Constitutes of a single seizure type
options.b: Good prognosis and adequate controlled epilepsy
options.d: EEG showing slow (<3Hz) spike and wave discharge

mcqs.explanation: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is associated with 1-2 Hz spike and slow -wave discharges .567 • Typically starts between the ages of 2 and 10 years • Consists of a triad of developmental delay , multiple seizure types (that as a rule includes atypical absence seizures, myoclonic, astatic, and tonic seizures ) and specific EEG abnormalities. • Most are left with long-term cognitive impairment and intractable seizures despite multiple therapies . • Lennox–Gastaut syndrome has a poor prognosis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A concerned kindergarten teacher calls up the mother of one of her students who was having transient lapses of consciousness . The teacher elaborated that the child was having multiple episodes of staring blankly into space for a few seconds before quickly returning to alertness . Following investigations including an EEG , a diagnosis of atypical absence seizures was made. Which of the following is a feature of it?

options.a: Associated with head drop during seizure
options.c: EEG shows 3Hz spike and slow wave pattern

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Harish had a panic attack when he was called to recite a poem on the stage . This was followed by a sudden lapse in consciousness and manifested as a blank stare along with fluttering of eyes . He appeared frozen without any change in the body tone. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of this condition on electroencephalography (EEG )?

options.d: Waves at the rate of 10 / sec

mcqs.explanation: The features of a lapse of consciousness precipitated by hyperventilation (panic attack), without any change in the tone of the body (head drop), point towards a likely diagnosis of petit mal or typical absence seizures . The electroencephalogram (EEG ) in petit mal seizure is associated with a 3 Hz spike and slow -wave discharges . Features of petit mal seizures (typical absence seizures ): • Starts abruptly in childhood (6 to 8 years) • Approximately 25% of patients also develop generalized tonic-clonic seizures . • Characterized by brief lapses of consciousness and sudden discontinuation of activity with staring spell , eye fluttering , or rhythmic movements • No loss of postural control or incontinence • No post -ictal confusion. Hyperventilation for 3-5 min can precipitate the seizures . The drug of choice is ethosuximide . mcqs.question: An 8-year-old boy was playing at his cr\350che centre when he suddenly developed rapid jerky movements of both the upper and lower limbs and was rushed to the emergency department. It had been ongoing for the past 10 minutes and the boy had been unresponsive throughout . Which of the following is not useful in the management of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is that of status epilepticus . This is due to rapid jerky movements causing continuous seizure activity for more than 5 minutes . Carbamazepine is not commonly used in the treatment of status epilepticus . Status epilepticus is defined as continuous or recurrent seizure activity lasting for more than 5 minutes without regaining consciousness . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old girl presented with episodes of brief involuntary muscular twitching that causes her to drop her toothbrush or teacup in the morning . Following investigations including an EEG , a diagnosis of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy was made. Which of the following is not a feature of it?
mcqs.explanation: In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy , EEG characteristically shows 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow -wave discharges . Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome): • It is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults ( 12 -18 years). • They are benign generalized myoclonic seizures with a good prognosis. • They commonly affect the upper limbs more than the lower limbs and sometimes cause the dropping of objects . • Typically , it starts in early adolescence (12 -18 years), with 1 or more of the following manifestations: • Myoclonic jerks in the morning ("shock-like" contraction of a muscle , that is often repeated ), generalized tonic-clonic or clonic seizures upon awakening; and juvenile absences . • Sleep deprivation, alcohol (in older patients ), and photic stimulation provoke seizures . • The EEG usually shows generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow -wave discharges . • The drug of choice for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is valproate. Lamotrigine is also useful .Disease Typical EEG features Drug of choice Lennox–Gastaut syndrome 1-2 Hz spike and polyspike b ursts in sleep Valproate Absence seizures 3 Hz spike and slow -wave (sp ike and dome pattern) Ethosuximide Juvenile myoclonic epileps y 4-5 Hz spike polyspike and sl ow-wave discharges Valproate570 Disease Typical EEG features Drug of choice West syndrome Hypsarrhythmia (high-voltag e waves with chaotic backgro und Adrenocorticotropic hormon e (ACTH)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An adolescent girl complaints of dropping objects from hands precipitated during morning hours and exams. There is no history of loss of consciousness . One of her cousins has been diagnosed with epilepsy . EEG was suggestive of epileptic spikes . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario describes an adolescent girl with myoclonic jerks (a history of dropping objects ) with preserved consciousness. This, along with abnormal EEG findings strongly suggests juvenile myoclonic epilepsy . Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Janz syndrome) is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults . It starts in early adolescence with one or more of the following features : bilateral myoclonic jerks in the morning , causing patients to drop things, generalized tonic-clonic or clonic-tonic-clonic seizures upon awakening, and juvenile absence seizure . Consciousness is usually preserved . Precipitating factors include sleep deprivation, alcohol, and photic stimulation. EEG shows 4 to 5Hz polyspike and slow wave discharges . A family history of epilepsy is often present . The treatment options for JME include sodium valproate, levetiracetam , and topiramate. Benzodiazepine , lamotrigine, perampanel , phenobarbital, primidone, and zonisamide can be considered as add-on drugs. Complete remission is uncommon and has a high risk of seizure recurrence, hence antiepileptics are continued lifelong in a majority of the patients . Other options : Option B: Atypical absence seizures have been associated with myoclonic components and head drop. They are precipitated by drowsiness and EEG shows 1 to 2 Hz spike and slow wave discharges . Option D: In benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes , the child typically wakes at night due to a focal seizure with preserved awareness . Buccal and throat tingling and tonic or clonic contractions on one side of the face are seen , with drooling and preserved consciousness . EEG shows typical wide -based centrotemporal spikes .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 7-month-old boy presents with brief episodes of head drops and flexion of the body, followed by tonic extension of arms and legs . These movements last 1 to 2 seconds and occur in several clusters per day, with 15 to 30 spasms per cluster . EEG is given below and is suggestive of infantile spasms. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for infantile spasms is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The EEG shows a specific type of abnormal chaotic brainwave pattern called hypsarrhythmia. It is characterized by continuous , high-amplitude , asynchronous delta activities with interspersed independent , multiple spikes . Hypsarrhythmia on EEG can occur even between attacks.Excessive corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) production is hypothesized to cause infantile spasms. ACTH administration suppresses CRH secretion and hence controls the seizures . Infantile spasms (West syndrome) • Age of onset is 3–8 months of life571 • Characterized by salaam spells (sudden dropping of the head or flexion of arms, followed by tonic extension of arms and legs ) and hypsarrhythmia on EEG . • Causes include hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy , neurocutaneous syndromes, and idiopathic . • Drug of choice : Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), Vigabatrin . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 8-month old male child presented with delayed motor milestones . He was born at 28 weeks of gestation with a birth weight of 1200 grams. A diagnosis of cerebral palsy is made following investigations. An MRI scan of the brain revealed periventricular leukomalacia. Which of the following subtypes of cerebral palsy is most likely in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely subtype in this child with delayed motor milestones and a history of prematurity and low birth weight is spastic diplegia . This is because the most common sequelae of periventricular leukomalacia (PVL ) is spastic diplegia . PVL is the ischemia of white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles of the brain . Cerebral palsy It is a group of disorders, affecting movement or posture , due to non-progressive disturbances occurring in the developing fetal brain . These could be due to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy .572 The most common subtype of cerebral palsy is spastic diplegia .Cerebral palsy subtype Pathology Spastic diplegia Periventricular leukomalacia Spastic quadriplegia Parasagittal brain injury Spastic hemiplegia Middle cerebral artery territo ry infarction Dyskinetic cerebral palsy Basal ganglia

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which one of the following is not a feature in cerebral palsy ?
mcqs.explanation: Flaccid paralysis is not a feature of cerebral palsy (CP). CP is an upper motor neuron disease characterized by rigidity and scissoring gait. Flaccid paralysis would be seen in lower motor neuron disease . Other options : Option A: Hypotonia is a characteristic feature of athetoid CP. These infants generally have poor head control. Option B: Microcephaly can be seen in CP due to perinatal insults to the developing brain . Option C: Ataxia is a common feature of extrapyramidal CP. mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn presented with high-grade fever, poor feeding and incessant cry for the last 2 days. Multiple episodes of vomiting are present as well . On examination, hypotonia is present along with weak reflexes . The patient is admitted and during rounds, subtle lip-smacking seizures are also observed along with a vacant stare. CSF examination shows reduced glucose , increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils . Which of the following organism is unlikely to cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The acute features of fever, poor feeding, incessant cry, vomiting and seizures points toward a likely diagnosis of neonatal meningitis. The CSF findings correlate with that of bacterial meningitis due to purulent appearance , increased proteins , decreased glucose and a predominance of polymorphs . Neonatal meningitis is not caused by Neisseria meningitidis because , in neonates , bacteria are often acquired from the maternal vaginal flora. mcqs.question: During your PICU rotation, you are assigned a bedside case of a child with fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation . On browsing through his file , you find a lumbar puncture report mentioning the following findings. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's signs) in a child, with CSF showing reduced glucose , increased protein, and increased leukocytes levels is a typical presentation of bacterial meningitis. mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Asif, a young child with previously diagnosed tuberculosis , is brought to your hospital for further management. Examination reveals a characteristic finding as present in the image. What do you expect in the cranial CT of this child?

options.b: Focal involvement of the temporal lobe

mcqs.explanation: A history of tuberculosis along with a positive Kernig's sign (as seen in the image) is suggestive of tubercular meningitis. Cranial computed tomography (CT) in a case of tubercular meningitis shows basal exudates and hydrocephalus . Intracranial tuberculosis can also manifest as ring-enhancing lesions (tuberculoma ), but the basal exudates are the most common and characteristic feature of tubercular meningitis. Tubercular meningitis575 It is common between 6 months and 4 years of age and usually spread by the hematogenous route . The gelatinous exudate infiltrates the corticomeningeal blood vessels leading to hydrocephalus . The three stages are- • Prodromal stage • Stage of meningitis • Stage of coma CSF study shows reduced sugar level , increased protein level , and lymphocytosis . Treatment includes antitubercular drugs for 12 months and corticosteroids (to reduce neurologic sequelae ). TB meningitis is the only indication of steroids in TB . Other options : Ring-enhancing lesions are seen in cerebral abscess , neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma (rich focus). Focal involvement of the temporal lobe is seen in herpes simplex encephalitis . Subependymal calcifications are seen in tuberous sclerosis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Two girls in the same class are diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their 12 -year old friend from the same school is afraid of contracting the disease . What advice should be given to the exposed students ?
mcqs.explanation: Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease . Close contacts of individuals with confirmed meningococcal disease are at an increased risk of developing the illness . Prophylaxis is also offered to individuals with direct and prolonged contact with a case of meningococcal disease . Antibiotics are effective in preventing additional cases by eradicating the carriage of the invasive strain. Treatment is provided to the contacts within 24 hours of identification of the index case. The antibiotics effective include rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone , and azithromycin. Prophylaxis is not generally recommended for medical personnel , except in cases where there is exposure to aerosols of respiratory secretions , such as during mouth-to-mouth resuscitation , intubation, or suctioning . This recommendation applies within 24 hours before or after the initiation of antibiotic therapy in the index case. For the treatment of cases , penicillin is the preferred drug, but ceftriaxone or other third-generation cephalosporins are recommended for patients with penicillin allergy . Droplet infection control precautions should be followed for hospitalized patients for 24 hours after effective therapy has been initiated . Offering quadrivalent meningococcal A, C, W, Y conjugate vaccines in addition to antimicrobial prophylaxis can further reduce the risk of disease among close contacts of cases caused by vaccine capsular groups . Meningococcal vaccines are available in two forms: polysaccharide vaccines and polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines. Polysaccharide vaccines can be given as a single dose to individuals aged 2 years and older . They are offered in bivalent (A, C), trivalent (A, C, W135), and quadrivalent (A, C, W135 , Y) formulations.576 Meningococcal conjugate vaccines are available as monovalent (A or C) or quadrivalent (A, C, W135, Y) formulations. Conjugate vaccines, which offer increased immunogenicity and potential for herd protection , are preferred over polysaccharide vaccines, especially in children under 2 years of age . Both types of vaccines are safe to use during pregnancy.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: How long should a child be isolated after being diagnosed with bacterial meningitis to prevent further transmission?
mcqs.explanation: Isolation of the child is recommended until 24 hrs after the initiation of effective therapy after being diagnosed with acute bacterial meningitis to prevent further transmission. Droplet precautions are recommended for patients with Neisseria meningitides and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis until they have received 24 hours of effective therapy . Patients should be in private rooms, and hospital personnel should wear a face mask when they are within 3 feet (1 meter) of the patient . The child with meningitis shows nonspecific symptoms like fever, anorexia, poor feeding , headache , myalgia, hypotension , petechia , purpura, or a rash. Meningial irritation is indicated by nuchal rigidity, back pain, and Kernig, and Brudzinski signs (usually not seen in infants). Seizures and altered mental status may be present . The recommended empirical antibiotic regimen in a suspected case of meningitis outside the neonatal period is vancomycin combined with a third-generation cephalosporin . Patients allergic to penicillin or cephalosporin can be treated with meropenem , fluoroquinolones, or chloramphenicol . Chemoprophylaxis with rifampicin/ceftriaxone/ciprofloxacin is recommended for all close contacts with meningococcal meningitis regardless of age or immunization status . Rifampicin prophylaxis should be given to all household contacts of patients with invasive disease caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, if an immunocompromised child of any age resides in the household or close family member younger than 48 months has not been fully immunized.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old child with a history of fall 1 year back with parietal bone fracture, has now presented with a painful and growing parietal swelling . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical presentation of a child with a painful and growing parietal swelling , coupled with a history of a prior parietal bone fracture one year ago, strongly suggests the diagnosis of a growing fracture, also known as traumatic encephalocele or leptomeningeal cysts . Skull fractures associated with a dural tear may fail to heal properly . The herniated brain , dilated ventricles , or a leptomeningeal cyst may cause an enlargement of this tear . These fractures are called growing skull fractures. They are usually seen in children < 3 years of age . They present as a localized swelling or palpable skull defect that increases in size, most commonly seen in the parietal region. However, they may go undetected for years and present with delayed onset of neurologic symptoms (headache , seizure , or neurologic deficit ). Other options : Option A: The extended duration of one year makes scalp hematoma unlikely, as it usually resolves within a few months.577 Option C: Subdural hygromas are characterized by fluid accumulation in the subdural space . Most patients with subdural hygromas are asymptomatic , but uncommon symptoms may include headaches , changes in mental status , nausea and vomiting, focal neurological deficits , and seizures . They don't present with scalp swelling . Option D: Chronic abscess may show inflammatory changes like erythema , pus , sinus, and systemic features like fever.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You have been called to declare the brain death of a 12 -year-old child in the ICU. Which of the following is not seen in brain death ?
mcqs.explanation: Decerebrate or decorticate posturing is not seen in brain death as they are motor responses to noxious stimuli that originate from the midbrain and cortex. Brain death , also known as death by neurologic criteria refers to the irreversible and total cessation of all functions of the entire brain , including the brainstem. The three components for diagnosing brain death are a demonstration of coexisting irreversible coma with a known cause , absence of brain stem reflexes , and apnea. Coma requires the patient to be unresponsive, even to noxious stimuli. The diagnosis of brain death can still be made despite positive spinal reflexes . (option B) Brainstem reflexes (pupillary responses , oculocephalic reflex , oculovestibular responses , corneal reflex , jaw reflex , facial grimacing, pharyngeal gag reflex , coughing ) are absent. Apnea is the absence of respiratory drive at PaCO2 of \03460mmHg and > 20mmHg above baseline , which is consistent with brain death . The following manifestations are occasionally seen and should not be misinterpreted as evidence of brainstem function: • Normal systolic blood pressure - SBP >100 mmHg (option A) • Movements originating from the spinal cord or peripheral nerve may occur • Sweating , flushing , tachycardia (option C) • Deep tendon reflexes ; superficial abdominal reflexes ; triple flexion response • Babinski reflex • Spontaneous movements of limbs other than pathologic flexion or extension response • Respiratory-like movements (shoulder elevation and adduction , back-arching, intercostal expansion without significant tidal volumes)578

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common, preventable cause of mental retardation?
mcqs.explanation: Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of mental retardation which results from a deficient production of thyroid hormone. It is more common among girls and the prevalence is about 1:3000 to 1:4000 births. Down's syndrome is the most common overall cause of mental retardation, followed by Fragile X syndrome, which mainly affects boys.585 Causes of mental retardation: Prenat al Congenital hypothyroidismIn fection (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV )Genetic abnormal itiesTrisomy 21Fragile X syn dromeother point mutations and chromosomal abnormalit iesToxins and teratogensAlco holDrugsRadiationInborn err ors of metabolism Perinat al HypoxiaPrematurityIntracra nial haemorrhagePerinatal C NS infection Postna tal Acquired brain injuryCNS inf ection , haemorrhage, malign ancySevere malnutrition and deprivationEnvironmental to xins (lead, mercury)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In a 4-month old, term infant with open posterior fontanelle and hypotonia, you suspect congenital hypothyroidism and send thyroid studies . Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause of permanent congenital hypothyroidism (80–85% of cases ) > dyshormonogenesis (15%). Dysgenesis may involve ectopy , agenesis (absence ) or hypoplasia (underdevelopment ) of the thyroid gland. Dyshormonogenesis results from a defect in any of the steps in thyroid hormone biosynthesis . *TSH - thyroid-stimulating hormone; TRH - thyroid-releasing hormone Acquired hypothyroidism can be caused by iodine deficiency , thyroiditis , radiation, histiocytosis , and drugs. The most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism is autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's). mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are called to see a 3-day-old, term neonate , who has not passed meconium yet . On clinical examination, there is generalized hypotonia and the abdomen is slightly distended without any evidence of ascites or hepatosplenomegaly . Incidentally , you also note a palpable goitre in this baby. Laboratory investigations reveal low T4 and elevated TSH levels . Which of the following is the most likely cause for this child's condition?
mcqs.explanation: A history of decreased activity and late passage of meconium, associated with low T4 and high TSH is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism. In an infant with a palpable goitre , the likely diagnosis is congenital hypothyroidism secondary to thyroid dyshormonogenesis . The most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism is thyroid dysgenesis but it is not associated with goitre . Thyroid dyshormonogenesis results from the deficiency of one or more enzymes involved in thyroid hormone synthesis /secretion . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: At how many weeks of gestation does thyroxine secretion begin in a fetus ?
mcqs.explanation: Thyroxine secretion begins in the fetus at 12 weeks of gestation .587 The fetal thyroid arises from an outpouching of the foregut at the base of the tongue (foramen cecum ). It migrates to its normal location over the thyroid cartilage by 8-10 wk of gestation . The bilobed shape of the thyroid is recognized by 7 weeks of gestation .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An anxious mother has brought a 4-month-old baby with complaints that the baby is not feeding well and is excessively sleepy all the time. Clinical examination reveals jaundice and hypotonia. His picture is provided below . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above picture shows a child with a protuberant abdomen, umbilical hernia, macroglossia, and edematous facies . Also, the infant is sluggish , has jaundice , feeding difficulties , and hypotonia, all of which suggests a diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism . Clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism : • Prolongation of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia- early sign (it is due to delayed maturation of glucuronide conjugation) • Constipation - usually does not respond to treatment • Wide open anterior and posterior fontanelles (>0.5 cm) and cranial sutures • Developmental delay , delayed bone growth , delayed dentition • Cardiovascular- slow pulse rate, cardiomegaly , asymptomatic pericardial effusion , edema • Respiratory- macroglossia, feeding difficulties , choking spells , respiratory difficulties • Haematological - macrocytic anaemia refractory to treatment with haematinics • Nervous system - hypothermia , hypotonia, slow relaxation of deep tendon reflexes , sluggishness , and somnolence

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn with abnormal neonatal screening tests was diagnosed with Pendred syndrome. Which of the following is not a feature of this syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss is present in Pendred syndrome; not conductive hearing loss. Pendred syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder, caused by a mutation in the gene SLC26A4 on chromosome 7, which codes for pendrin, a chloride –iodide transport protein common to the thyroid gland and the cochlea . Clinical features include sensorineural hearing loss and goitre with hypothyroidism . It is the most common cause of syndromic deafness. The biochemical reason for hypothyroidism in patients with Pendred syndrome is impaired iodide organification (resulting from a mutation in the Pendrin gene ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-day-old infant has elevated TSH level and low T4 level on newborn screening . If this condition is left untreated , which of the following is most likely to be seen in this infant in the first few months of life ?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated TSH levels and low T4 levels in a 9-day-old infant are suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism. Prolongation of physiologic hyperbilirubinemia is an early sign of congenital hypothyroidism . It is due to delayed maturation of the hepatic glucuronide conjugation system . Hyperreflexia , hyperirritability and diarrhoea are seen in hyperthyroidism ; not hypothyroidism .588 Note : Kocher –Debr\351–S\351m\351laigne syndrome: The muscles are usually hypotonic in congenital hypothyroidism. Rarely, hypothyroidism in infancy can be characterized by generalized muscular pseudohypertrophy , myxoedema , short stature and cretinism. Affected older children can have an athletic appearance . Boys are more prone to the development of the syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During a rural health camp, a father brings a dull -looking baby with macroglossia and an umbilical hernia. On enquiry, you find out that the parents were told about a thyroid problem in the child at birth, for which they did not pursue any treatment . Which of the following is least likely to be found in children with the given condition?
mcqs.explanation: A dull -looking face with macroglossia, and umbilical hernia in a child with a thyroid disorder are all indicative of congenital hypothyroidism. Craniosynostosis is not seen in neonatal hypothyroidism . It is seen in hyperthyroidism . Craniosynostosis refers to the premature fusion of sutures and closure of fontanelles and often results in abnormal , triangular facies . In congenital hypothyroidism , there is delayed closure of the fontanelles . Palpable goitre , though not common, can be seen in cases of untreated thyroid dyshormonogenesis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As part of a quality improvement project undertaken by the maternal and child health services, you are evaluating the current practice of newborn screening and detection rates of hypothyroidism in various community health centres . Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: Simultaneous measurement of T4 and TSH levels is the ideal method .
options.b: The sample is obtained by heel -prick between 1-5 days of life using dried blood spot .
options.c: Newborn screening always detects the affected twin in same-sex twins.
options.d: Primary TSH, with back up T4 is the most common strategy used .

mcqs.explanation: Newborn screening can fail to detect the affected twin with hypothyroidism . Discordance for thyroid dysgenesis is the rule in monozygotic twins. The transfusion of euthyroid blood from the unaffected twin normalizes the serum levels of T4 and TSH in the affected twin, resulting in delayed or missed diagnoses . Therefore, a second sample for congenital hypothyroidism screening at 14 days of age should be considered in monozygotic twins. Neonatal thyroid screening strategies : • Primarily TSH, backup T4; T4 is measured if TSH level is >20 mU/L • Primarily T4, backup TSH: TSH is measured only if T4 level is low • Concomitant T4 and TSH; it is the most sensitive method Note : the sample is obtained after 24-48 hours, to minimize the false elevation of TSH values due to normal post -delivery neonatal TSH surge .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As an intern posted in paediatrics , you are asked to interpret the results of a heel prick test that you performed on a newborn. Which of the following results is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism ?

options.a: Low T4 level and low TSH level
options.b: Low T4 level and high TSH level
options.c: High T4 level and low TSH level
options.d: High T4 level and high TSH level

mcqs.explanation: Low T4 and high TSH levels indicate primary hypothyroidism . Blood specimen for neonatal thyroid screening is obtained by heel prick between 1 and 5 days of life . Levothyroxine therapy is started immediately after diagnosis, at 10 to 15 \265 g/kg per day.589 Condition Goitr e T4 TSH Thyroid dysgenesis Abse nt Low Elevate d Thyroid dyshormonogenesis Pres ent Low Elevate d Thyroid receptor blocking an tibodies Abse nt Low Elevate d Central hypothyroidism Abse nt Low Normal/ Low Hyperthyroidism Pres ent High Low

mcqs.question: The image given below depicts an x-ray of the knee in a term baby. Which among the following conditions is associated with it?
mcqs.explanation: The deformity shown in the X-ray image is the absence of distal femoral epiphysis , which is a typical radiological feature of congenital hypothyroidism . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ayesha is a 9th standard girl who presented with a neck swelling , which began more than a year ago. Her mother says she is embarrassed about it and always covers her neck with a shawl when she goes to school. Her menstrual cycles have also become irregular as of late . Blood tests reveal slightly elevated TSH levels and the presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO-Abs) and elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level in a child with a goitre is suggestive of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis . Chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease . Clinical presentation can include goitre, growth retardation, and other features of hypothyroidism . The thyroid is diffusely enlarged , firm, and non-tender.591 TSH is moderately elevated and TPO-Abs and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (anti-Tg Abs) can be detected . The image given below shows goitre due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A lady, with a history of a thyroid disorder and three prior abortions, delivered a female neonate prematurely at 34 weeks of gestation. In the newborn infant, tachycardia, irritability, and prominent eyes were noted and neonatal hyperthyroidism was suspected . Which of the following statements is false about the condition?

options.a: Maternal Graves' disease is the most common cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism
options.b: It results from the transplacental passage of maternal stimulatory TSH receptor antibody
options.c: Microcephaly and frontal bossing with triangular facies are common clinical findings
options.d: Neonatal hyperthyroidism occurs in most infants born to mothers with a history of Graves' disease

mcqs.explanation: Neonatal hyperthyroidism occurs in only about 2% of infants born to mothers with a history of Graves' disease . But maternal Graves' disease is by far the most common cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism . Neonatal hyperthyroidism (due to Grave's) results from the transplacental passage of maternal stimulatory thyrotropin/TSH receptor antibody (TSHR-Ab). Clinical features are as follows : • Low birth weight (IUGR) • Premature birth • Microcephaly • Frontal bossing and triangular facies • Warm , moist skin • Irritability, hyperactivity , restlessness , poor sleep • Tachycardia Note : TSHR -Ab (TSH-R-stimulating antibodies ) is another name for TSH-R-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI).592

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pregnant woman with a past history of Grave's disease has currently completed 36 weeks of gestation . She underwent partial thyroidectomy 10 years back and has remained euthyroid since then. The previous child had craniosynostosis. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be detected , if a cord blood sampling is done at delivery ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a history of Graves' disease in the mother and craniosynostosis (neonatal Graves') in the previous child suggests that the fetus is at increased risk of neonatal Grave's disease . Thus, the antibody likely to be found at birth in the cord blood sampling is the TSH receptor stimulating antibody (TRSAb). Neonatal Graves is caused by the transplacental passage of TRSAbs from a mother with a history of Graves' disease . The mothers can have • Active Graves' disease • Graves' in remission • Prior history of Graves' treated with radioactive ablation or thyroidectomy TSRAbs bind to the receptor for TSH and stimulate cyclic AMP, leading to thyroid hyperplasia and unregulated overproduction of thyroid hormone.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old girl, a known case of celiac disease , presented to the pediatric endocrine clinic with a history of neck swelling , tremor, and weight loss. On evaluation, she was found to have Graves' disease . Other conditions that need to be screened in this patient include all of the following except __________.
mcqs.explanation: Type 2 Diabetes mellitus is not associated with Grave's disease . Conditions associated with Grave's disease (autoimmune diseases ): • Diabetes mellitus type 1 • Pernicious anaemia • Celiac disease • Vitiligo • Addison disease • Alopecia areata • Myasthenia gravis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 11 -year-old girl was brought by her parents with complaints of weight loss, increased appetite , and a decline in scholastic performance. Following investigations, a diagnosis of Grave's disease is made. Which of the following is the drug of choice for initial therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: Methimazole is the initial drug of choice for treating Grave's disease (hyperthyroidism ) in children. Option A: Propylthiouracil is not recommended in children because it is associated with fatal hepatotoxicity. Option C: Radioactive iodine is not preferred as the first-line treatment in hyperthyroidism for children. Option D: Levothyroxine is used to treat hypothyroidism .593

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Your unit chief has asked you to present the case of a teenager , who was admitted for evaluation of mental retardation, deaf -mutism and a gait disturbance . He also has a significant patellar clonus. On general exam, you note a goitre but according to lab reports, he is apparently euthyroid . His pubertal development has also been normal . The most likely diagnosis is _______.
mcqs.explanation: The clinical presentation of a euthyroid patient with goitre as well as mental retardation, deaf-mutism, and normal pubertal development points towards neurological endemic cretinism. Endemic cretinism includes 2 different , but overlapping, syndromes: neurologic type and myxedematous type . It is essentially the same disorder, phenotypically modified by the length and severity of postnatal hypothyroidism . Neurological manifestations are interpreted as reflecting the effects of maternal and fetal hypothyroxinemia, secondary to severe iodine deficiency , on the developing nervous system . Both neurologic and myxedematous type can manifest neurologic symptoms . Although neurological cretins are euthyroid , linear growth arrest lines in the long bones are often demonstrated radiologically , suggesting previous hypothyroidism . Option B: Graves disease includes a triad of hyperthyroidism with goitre , ophthalmopathy , and dermopathy (no mental retardation, deafness , or pyramidal signs). Option C: Pendred Syndrome is caused by a mutation in chloride –iodide transporter in thyroid and cochlea resulting in euthyroid /hypothyroid goitre and sensorineural hearing loss (pyramidal signs like clonus are not seen ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: During a health outreach program in Sikkim , you come across 3 children from the same family, with goiter. Endemic cretinism was suspected . Which of the following can be a manifestation of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Strabismus and spastic diplegias are among the manifestations of the neurological type of endemic cretinism. Cretinism is a condition characterized by irreversible abnormalities in intellectual development. Endemic cretinism occurs due to the nutritional deficiency of iodine. It can be neurological cretinism or myxedematous cretinism. It is associated with severe , irreversible mental retardation.594

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: The parents of a neonate diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia come with queries about the disease . They have been told that it's an inherited condition and ask you how is it possible for the baby to be affected when neither of the parents are. What is the mode of inheritance of the disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia / adrenogenital syndrome follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Depending on the enzyme that is deficient , patients will have : • Mineralocorticoid deficiency (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) or excess (hypernatremia, hypokalemia) • Incomplete virilization or precocious puberty in males • Virilization or sexual infantilism in females603

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A baby delivered at home was born with ambiguous genitalia . The parents could not identify the sex of the child. The baby was diagnosed with congenital adrenal hyperplasia . Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is this child most likely to have?
mcqs.explanation: This child is most likely to have a 21 -hydroxylase deficiency as it is the most common enzyme deficiency implicated in congenital adrenal hyperplasia . The second most common is 11 beta -hydroxylase deficiency .21 -hydroxylase enzyme hydroxylates progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to yield 11-deoxycorticosterone and 11 -deoxycortisol, respectively . They help in the synthesis of aldosterone and cortisol. Therefore, the deficiency of this enzyme leads to the deficiencies of aldosterone and cortisol. Also, the accumulated steroid precursors are diverted into the pathway for androgen (testosterone) production .604 Clinical profile in 21 -hydroxylase deficiency: • Aldosterone deficiency : Salt-wasting crises (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension , and metabolic acidosis) • Cortisol deficiency : Hypoglycemia , hyperpigmentation (due to increased ACTH production ), weight loss, weakness , anorexia, vomiting, and shock • Androgens excess : Virilization of females and precocious puberty in males

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: Which of the following types of congenital adrenal hyperplasia is not due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: Under virilizing type of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is not caused by 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . Depending on the extent of enzyme deficiency , CAH caused by 21 -hydroxylase deficiency is broadly classified into classic and non-classic forms: Classic forms can be of two types - salt-wasting and simple virilizing types . • Salt-wasting type is the severe form in which both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient , with excess androgen production . • In the simple virilizing type , there is an impaired synthesis of cortisol and adequate amounts of aldosterone . Here, clinical features are due to the overproduction of androgens. The non-classic form is characterized by partial 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . Cortisol and aldosterone are produced normally, but at the expense of producing excess androgens.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A concerned mother brings her 15-day old baby to you with complaints of decreased activity and vomiting. On examination, the baby is hypotensive , has depressed fontanelles and reduced skin turgor. The image of the external genitalia of the baby is shown below . Which electrolyte abnormality can you expect to see in this baby?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows ambiguous genitalia . This along with signs of dehydration and hypotension suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia (due to mineralocorticoid deficiency ) can be seen in this condition. These babies present at 10 –14 days of age with progressive weight loss, weakness , anorexia, vomiting, dehydration, hypoglycemia , and hypotension . Without treatment , shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: Investigation of choice to diagnose congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency is estimation of ____________ levels .
mcqs.explanation: 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels estimation is the investigation of choice to diagnose CAH due to 21 hydroxylase deficiency . It will be markedly elevated . Other findings include : • Elevated androstenedione and testosterone (in females ). • Low cortisol and aldosterone .605 • Elevated ACTH levels .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: You see Sanjay who is a known case of congenital adrenal hyperplasia , on steroid therapy in the ER with vomiting and fever. You administer double the regular dose of steroids . Which drug is being referred to here?
mcqs.explanation: Hydrocortisone, which is the mainstay treatment for commonest type of CAH, is the drug referred to in the given clinical scenario. Double or triple doses are indicated during periods of stress , such as infection or surgery. Glucocorticoid replacement therapy with hydrocortisone , 15-20 mg/m\262/24 h, orally, in 3 divided doses is continued lifelong . Mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone is used for patients with the salt-wasting disease . The daily dose of fludrocortisone in infants is higher than that in older children.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: The autopsy image of a baby who died during the neonatal period is shown below . Parents of the child undergo genetic counseling regarding future pregnancies . When should the mother be started on steroids in a future pregnancy?

options.a: As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
options.d: After karyotyping and determination of sex of the baby

mcqs.explanation: The autopsy image shows a bilaterally enlarged adrenal gland (white arrows) with a history of death during the neonatal period (probably due to shock, cardiac arrhythmias) which is suggestive of CAH in the baby. Mothers with a previously affected child of CAH should be started with steroid therapy as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed . Since it is an autosomal recessive disorder, there is a risk of the subsequent children being affected . Dexamethasone at 20 �Mg/kg is started to suppress the secretion of steroids by the fetal adrenals (including adrenal androgens) and prevent the virilization of the external genitals in affected females . Then, chorionic villus biopsy is performed to determine the sex and genotype of the fetus , and therapy is continued only if the fetus is an affected female .606

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: You see Sathya, an adolescent in the endocrinology clinic referred by his family physician. He was told by his parents that he was a boy, but he felt differently . As he grew up, he felt increasingly uncomfortable with his identity and this caused him a great deal of sadness and isolation. On examination, he is hypertensive and has genitalia resembling a female phenotype . After karyotyping, you diagnose him with 46XY DSD. Which of the following enzyme deficiency would be in your differential ?
mcqs.explanation: 46XY DSD - a genotypical male with female phenotype - along with hypertension makes the diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 17-hydroxylase deficiency more likely.Clinical profile in 17-hydroxylase deficiency: Aldosterone excess : Salt retention , hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and hypertension . Sex steroid deficiency : In contrast to 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiency , patients with 17-hydroxylase deficiency are unable to synthesize sex hormones. Affected males are incompletely virilized (male pseudo -hermaphroditism/ ambiguous genitalia 46XY ) and there is a failure of sexual development in affected females . Cortisol deficiency is not manifested , as elevated corticosterone is an active glucocorticoid . Intersex or DSD means a condition in which development of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical . There is a greater incidence of gender dissatisfaction , gender non-conformity, gender fluidity in such individuals.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: An infant with hypospadias , bifid scrotum presents with signs and symptoms of salt wasting . Lab reports reveal elevated levels of 17-hydroxy pregnenolone and dehydroepiandrosterone . Which of the following deficiency would you suspect in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of incomplete virilization (hypospadias with or without bifid scrotum and cryptorchidism), salt wasting due to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency , and elevated dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and 17 hydroxy pregnenolone levels are suggestive of 3 beta -hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency .607 Clinical profile in 3\031-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3\031-HSD): • Aldosterone deficiency - Salt-wasting crises (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension , and acidosis ) • Cortisol deficiency - Hypoglycemia , hyperpigmentation (due to increased ACTH production ), and shock • Androgen deficiency - Males are incompletely virilized (male pseudo -hermaphroditism/ambiguous genitalia 46XY/hypogonadism , cryptorchidism) • Excess DHEA (weak androgen)- Females are mildly virilized (acne, hirsutism).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: The most common enzyme deficiency leading to childhood hypertension among the following is ______.
mcqs.explanation: The most common enzyme deficiency leading to childhood hypertension is 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiency causing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Hypertension in CAH is due to 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiency followed by 17-hydroxylase deficiency . Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency cannot be manifested because some corticosterone is synthesized from progesterone , and hence , there are no signs of adrenal insufficiency . - hydroxylase deficiency causes salt-wasting resulting in hypotension .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A boy presents with precocious puberty and hypertension to your OPD. The estimation of ______ will help in the diagnosis of CAH.
mcqs.explanation: Precocious puberty in a male with hypertension is suggestive of CAH due to 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiency . An increase in 11 -deoxycortisol levels is diagnostic of the enzyme deficiency . \031-hydroxlase catalyzes the convertion of deoxycortisol to cortisol. Therefore, \031-hydroxlase deficiency causes an increase in 11 deoxycortisol levels .608

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: On a vacation trip to Hawaii, a father was helping his 7-year-old son change into swimming trunks . He noticed the presence of pubic and axillary hair. He knew it was abnormal and brought the child to the pediatrician. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of pubic and axillary hair in a seven-year-old boy is suggestive of precocious puberty and 17-Hydroxylase deficiency is least likely to cause it. In 17-hydroxylase deficiency , patients are unable to synthesize sex hormones, and hence the affected males are incompletely virilized and present as phenotypic females (but gonads are usually palpable in the inguinal region or the labia). In both 21 -hydroxylase and 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiencies , the respective precursors to the hormones are shunted to the androgen synthesis pathway , resulting in all the signs and symptoms of androgen excess , including virilization of female and precocious puberty in males.609

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia most commonly presents as _______.
mcqs.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) most commonly presents as female pseudohermaphroditism as the most common enzyme deficiency is 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . A female pseudohermaphrodite is a genotypically normal female (46, XX ), whose external genitalia resembles a male's. The image below shows ambiguous genitalia in a female with CAH:The mechanism underlying the endocrine defects in 21 -hydroxylase deficiency is depicted in the image below:Babies with 21 -hydroxylase deficiency typically present around 10 -14 days of age with the subset of symptoms due to aldosterone deficiency , cortisol deficiency and androgen excess . Aldosterone deficiency leads to salt-wasting crises marked by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis.610 Cortisol deficiency causes manifestations like hypoglycemia , hyperpigmentation , weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and shock. Androgen excess in 21 -hydroxylase deficiency results in virilization of females , leading to female pseudohermaphroditism, and precocious puberty in males. Virilization is usually apparent at birth in females and within 2 to 3 years of life in males. Without treatment , shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks . Other options : Option A: Male pseudohermaphroditism is seen in CAH due to 17\032-hydroxylase deficiency resulting in incomplete virilization . 17\032-hydroxylase deficiency is 2nd most common enzyme affected in CAH. Option C: True hermaphroditism is presently referred to as an ovotesticular disorder of sex development(DSD). Here, both ovarian and testicular tissue is present . It is not due to CAH. Option D: 46 XY intersex (now called 46 XY DSD) has under virilization of genitalia . Adrenal causes include lipoid adrenal hyperplasia, 3\031-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency , 17-hydroxylase /17,20 -lyase deficiency , and not 21 hydroxylase deficiency .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A postgraduate examines a female baby in late infancy with failure to thrive. The genitalia appears normal . Reports reveal serum sodium of 125 MEq/L and serum K+ of 6.5 MEq /L. Estimation of which of the following hormones will be helpful in the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of failure to thrive in late infancy, normal genitalia , hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia suggests aldosterone synthase deficiency . Estimation of aldosterone levels will help in the diagnosis. Normal genitalia in female children rules out congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) caused by 21-hydroxylase and 3\031-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency . Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia rule out CAH due to 17-hydroxylase deficiency and 11 \031-hydroxylase deficiency .Infants with aldosterone synthase deficiency may have severe electrolyte abnormalities with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic611 acidosis. Since cortisol synthesis is unaffected , infants rarely become as ill as untreated infants with salt-losing forms of CAH. So some infants escape diagnosis at birth because of normal cortisol levels . Later in infancy or in early childhood , they may exhibit failure to thrive and poor growth . Adults often are asymptomatic , although they may develop electrolyte abnormalities when depleted of sodium through procedures such as bowel preparation for a barium enema.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presents with obesity and short stature , with signs of abnormal masculinization as shown below . Which statement regarding this condition is false ?

options.a: Most common cause is adrenocortical tumor
options.b: Hypertension seen here can occasionally lead to heart failure
options.d: Generalized obesity is a common finding in younger children.

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the image showing round face (moon facies ), obesity , abnormal masculinization, and purple skin striae are suggestive of Cushing's syndrome. The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome is prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids , not an adrenocortical tumor.
