Cushing's syndrome is characterized excess glucocorticoids that can be due to: • Prolonged exogenous administration of glucocorticoids • Excess endogenous cortisol secretion: • In children <7 years: Most often by a functioning adrenocortical tumor • In children >7 years: Most often by an ACTH–producing pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease ) Important clinical features in children: • Obesity or weight gain (most common) • Moon facies • Purple skin striae612 • Abnormal masculinization (acne, bruising, enlargement of the clitoris in girls) • Pubertal developmental delay and amenorrhea in girls • Proximal muscle weakness • Osteoporosis • Hypertension • Hyperpigmentation • Hypokalemic alkalosis • Hyperglycemia • Sepsis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A high school girl Meenu presents to you with anorexia, vomiting, and muscle weakness for the past few months. On examination, she had the finding shown in the image. Which of the following will not be seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Given clinical scenario is suggestive of Addison's disease and hypertension is not seen here. Addison's disease is a primary adrenal insufficiency due to acquired lesions of the adrenal cortex, which prevent the production of cortisol and, often , aldosterone . Hence , due to mineralocorticoid deficiency , there will be hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension . The deficiency of cortisol stimulates the production of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Increased ACTH leads to diffuse hyperpigmentation , including areas not exposed to the sun, such as buccal mucosa and gums. Addison's disease is characterized by the following : • Hyponatremia • Hyperkalemia • Hypotension • Hypoglycemia • Increased ACTH levels • Metabolic acidosis • Hyperpigmentation ACTH stimulation test (cosyntropin\- Low cortisol levels before and after administration of ACTH are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency , Addison's disease .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: You have been called to see a 10 -year-old child in the emergency room with complaints of fever and vomiting for the past three days. On examination the child had tachycardia and there was significant postural hypotension . Upon investigation, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia were present . You suspect adrenal insufficiency . Which of the following is the most likely organism grown in blood culture ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common infectious etiology for adrenal insufficiency in children is meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis . Waterhouse –Friderichsen syndrome: Adrenal apoplexy due to fulminant bacterial infection (most common Meningococcus ).613 Clinical features : Non-specific like fever, rigors, vomiting, headache , disseminated intravascular coagulation (large petechial rashes in the skin and mucous membrane), hypotension , and septic shock Petechial rashes in meningococcal infection :Most commons in adrenal insufficiency : • The most common infectious cause of Addison's disease in India is tuberculosis . • The most common cause of adrenal insufficiency is the sudden withdrawal of steroids in a patient on long-term steroid therapy . • The most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in children is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). • The most common antigen against which antibodies are found in Addison's disease is CYP 21 (21 -hydroxylase ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: In the pediatric ward, a resident is evaluating a case of primary adrenal insufficiency who has failure to thrive, recurrent emesis , and hepatosplenomegaly . Bilateral adrenal calcification is noted radiologically . The most likely diagnosis is ______.
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wolman 's disease . It is a rare lipid disorder caused by a deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase (chromosome 10 ) that leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides in most of the visceral organs. Patients present in the first few weeks of life with failure to thrive, vomiting, abdominal distention , steatorrhea , hepatosplenomegaly , and hyperlipidemia with extensive bilateral calcifications of the adrenal glands.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a case of hyperpigmentation . The patient reports having undergone bilateral adrenalectomy a few years back for Cushing's disease . MRI shows an enlargement of the pituitary adenoma. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 614 The clinical scenario of hyperpigmentation , history of bilateral adrenalectomy and MRI showing enlarged pituitary adenoma points to the diagnosis of Nelson 's syndrome. Nelson 's syndrome is a rare complication of total bilateral adrenalectomy (TBA ). TBA is a procedure used to control hypercortisolism in Cushing's disease (due to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) when resection of the primary tumor is not possible . The loss of feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic -pituitary -adrenal axis following TBA increases CRH. This leads to stimulation of ACTH-secreting corticotroph cells , causing enlargement of the original pituitary tumor or formation of a new one. Nelson 's syndrome is associated with a clinical triad of: • Hyperpigmentation • Excessive ACTH secretion • Corticotroph adenoma Screening is done with fasting plasma ACTH levels and MRI brain performed at regular intervals. Prophylactic pituitary irradiation may be recommended to prevent its incidence . The primary treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Patients will also require life -long glucocorticoid replacement , as they do not produce cortisol. The use of steroidogenic inhibitors in the treatment of Cushing's disease has decreased the need for bilateral adrenalectomy these days. Option B: Steele -Richardson-Olszewski syndrome, also known as progressive supranuclear palsy is a neurodegenerative disease . It affects the brainstem and basal ganglia. Option C: Hamman -Rich syndrome also known as acute interstitial pneumonia, is a rare and severe form of idiopathic interstitial lung disease . Option D: Job syndrome, also known as hyper -IgE syndrome is an autosomal dominant immunodeficiency disorder. It occurs as a result of STAT3 mutation leading to deficiency in the IL -17 producing T cells . This results in impaired recruitment of neutrophils to sites of infection .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: Using novel chemiluminescence immunoassay techniques , you measure the hormonal profile of the adrenal gland of a normal fetus . Which of the following would be present in higher concentrations?
mcqs.explanation: The fetal adrenal gland produces a maximum amount of DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone ). DHEA and DHEA-S serve as estrogen precursors. The maternal adrenal gland does not produce a sufficient amount of DHEA-S. The fetal adrenal glands are quantitatively the most important source of placental estrogen precursors in pregnancy. During most of gestation , the fetal adrenal gland is almost solely dedicated to the production of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate DHEAS .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: A woman has a previous child with congenital adrenal hyperplasia . In the present pregnancy, steroid therapy should be started _______

options.a: As soon as pregnancy is diagnosed
options.d: After karyotyping and determination of sex of the baby

mcqs.explanation: Mothers with pregnancies at risk (previously affected child) of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) should be started with steroid therapy as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed .615 Dexamethasone 20 �Mg/kg is started to suppress the secretion of steroids by the fetal adrenals (including adrenal androgens) and prevent the virilization of the external genitals in affected females . Then, chorionic villus biopsy is performed to determine the sex and genotype of the fetus and therapy is continued only if the fetus is an affected female .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia and Related Diso...
mcqs.question: You see a newborn with an enlarged clitoris and partially fused labia. You also note features such as frontal bossing, brachycephaly , midface hypoplasia , slender fingers, medial bowing of ulna, and heart abnormalities. Investigation reveals a deficiency of P450 oxidoreductase . What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of P450 oxidoreductase (POR) along with the given findings are suggestive of Antley -Bixler syndrome. Features of Antley –Bixler syndrome: These include deficiencies of 17-hydroxylase and 21 -hydroxylase along with other congenital anomalies. It leads to under virilization of males and virilisation of females via an alternate pathway . Virilization of mother is seen because of decreased placental aromatase activity leading to excess androgens in fetus and mother. Congenital anomalies seen are as follows : • Head and face : Craniosynostosis, brachycephaly , frontal bossing, severe midface hypoplasia , with proptosis and choanal atresia. • Limbs: Humeroradial synostosis ; medial bowing of the ulnas; long, slender fingers, with camptodactyly and anterior bowing of the femurs. • Malformations of the heart and kidneys.616

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common tumor associated with growth hormone deficiency in children?
mcqs.explanation: The most common tumor associated with growth hormone (GH) deficiency in children is craniopharyngioma . Growth hormone deficiency can be caused by congenital CNS malformations, genetic defects or acquired neurological insults . Note : • Most common cause of GH deficiency: Idiopathic • Most common infection causing GH deficiency in India: Tuberculosis > Histoplasmosis • Most common infiltration causing GH deficiency in India: Histiocytosis > Sarcoidosis. • Trophic hormone failure with pituitary compression or destruction : GH> FSH> LH > TSH> ACTH. • Most common tumors associated with central diabetes insipidus : Pinealomas, Germinomas621

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Asha was being bullied about her height in school. The concerned parents bring her to the pediatrician who plots the growth chart as shown below . On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and insulin-like growth factor levels are low. Which among the following could be a cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of high GH levels and low insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the GH receptor mutation. It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features as those seen in pituitary dwarfism. Here, growth hormone is produced but is unable to act on the target tissues . Thus, the resting and stimulated GH levels are high and IGF-1 levels are low. In Turner 's syndrome (Option A), loss of the short arm of the X chromosome is implicated in dwarfism. The short stature occurs due to a state of GH resistance , relative deficiency , and decreased utilization. Pituitary dwarfism (Option B) is a condition with GH deficiency . Maternal deprivation dwarfism (Option D) is due to psychosocial causes such as emotional deprivation and neglect . There is an inadequate response to GH stimulation tests . The mechanism is not fully understood . No history suggestive of disturbed maternal or family relationships rules this out.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common genetic cause for multiple pituitary hormone deficiency ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common genetic cause for multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (MPHD)/panhypopituitarism is the mutation of the PROP1 gene . LHX3 and GLI2 are other genes involved in MPHD. GNAS1 mutations cause McCune Albright Syndrome. c-MYC gene is mutated in Burkitt's lymphoma WT -1 gene is mutated in Wilms tumors.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You come across a child with growth hormone deficiency during your ward rounds. Which of the following features would you not expect in this child?

options.a: History of short stature at birth

mcqs.explanation: Children with growth hormone deficiency usually have normal growth at birth. Growth retardation (decline in growth velocity) becomes apparent around 1 year of age . Growth in-utero is dependant on genetic , environmental, nutrition and growth factors. GH levels peak at mid-gestation , increase at birth, and then reduce by 2 weeks of life . At around 6 months of age , GH levels reach pre-pubertal levels and from there on have a major influence on growth . Thus the deficiency becomes apparent after a significant period of GH-dependent growth has occurred. Characteristic features of growth hormone deficiency (Pituitary Dwarfism): • Normal growth at birth with growth retardation becoming apparent around 1 year of age • Proportionate short stature • Hypoglycemic seizures in newborn622 • Small larynx with a high-pitched voice • Small genitalia (micropenis) • Delayed skeletal maturation • Delayed dentition • Delayed puberty (sexual infantilism) • Doll-like facial appearance : small, round facies , frontal prominence, depressed nasal bridge (saddle nose), eyes may bulge , underdeveloped mandible and chin, normal head circumference but craniofacial disproportion due to small facies • Short neck • Normal intelligence .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are evaluating children with short stature on whether they are eligible to receive growth hormone therapy as per FDA guidelines . In which of the following children would you prescribe it?

options.a: An 8 year old with Laron dwarfism
options.b: A neonate diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism
options.c: A 7 year old with Chronic kidney disease
options.d: A 6 year old diagnosed with Maternal deprivation dwarfism

mcqs.explanation: Chronic kidney disease is an FDA-approved indication for growth hormone (GH) therapy . Renal failure is a state of GH resistance. Moderate -to-severe growth retardation in chronic kidney disease is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. GH therapy with recombinant growth hormone has been shown to improve catch-up growth and to allow the child to achieve normal adult height ; the final adult height is still significantly below the genetic target . FDA-approved indications for growth hormone (GH) treatment - • GH deficiency • Turner 's Syndrome • Chronic Renal Failure before Transplantation • Small for Gestational Age / Short Stature • Idiopathic Short Stature • Noonan Syndrome • Prader-Willi Syndrome • AIDS-related wasting • Malabsorption associated with the short-bowel syndrome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Chotu , a 5-year-old boy is on regular outpatient follow -up for growth hormone deficiency diagnosed 2 weeks back. He is planned for recombinant growth hormone therapy . All of the following are possible side effects except -
mcqs.explanation: The use of recombinant growth hormone is associated with the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (not type 1 diabetes mellitus ). Other adverse effects : • Pseudotumor cerebri • Slipped capital femoral epiphysis623 • Gynecomastia • Worsening of scoliosis Children who have been treated with rhGH have a higher risk of developing hemorrhagic strokes in adulthood. Some studies show an increased risk of new neoplasms in cancer survivors .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The most common pituitary adenoma diagnosed in childhood is _________.
mcqs.explanation: The most commonly diagnosed adenomas during childhood are prolactinoma > corticotropinoma > somatotropinoma. Note : Hypothalamic hamartomas that secrete excess gonadotropin-releasing hormone can cause precocious puberty .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Akash is the tallest kid in his 5th -grade class. While at a routine visit for a booster immunization, his pediatrician plots his height on a growth chart and finds him to be above 3-SD for his age . Which of the following can be an endocrine cause for his height ?
mcqs.explanation: McCune –Albright syndrome (endocrine dysfunction affecting multiple glands) is an endocrine cause of tall stature in childhood . The triad of McCune –Albright syndrome is precocious puberty , polyostotic fibrous dysplasia , and cafe au lait macules Causes of childhood tall stature :Non-endocrine causes Endocrine causes Familial (constitutional ) tall s tature Excess GH secretion (pituitar y gigantism) Cerebral gigantism (Sotos sy ndrome) McCune –Albright syndrome Marfan syndrome Precocious puberty Fragile X syndrome Hyperthyroidism Homocystinuria Klinefelter syndrome(XXY ) XYY syndrome Beckwith–Wiedemann syndr ome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: "Weak giants" are produced by _________.
mcqs.explanation: 624 "Weak giants" are due to hyperpituitarism that is most commonly produced by pituitary adenomas. Hyperpituitarism causes growth hormone (GH) excess , leading to tall stature (giants) with weak muscles . Overproduction of GH results in gigantism in children (before fusion of bone growth plate ) and acromegaly in adults . Clinical features include : • Gigantism, prognathism (protrusion of jaw), hypertrophy of frontal bones • Proximal myopathy (though there is muscle hypertrophy , it is weakened due to atrophy of type II muscle fibers) • Acral enlargement in hands and feet (due to thickening of soft tissues ) • Visceromegaly : Enlargement of most organs especially the tongue , thyroid, salivary gland, liver, spleen , kidney, and prostate • Local effects of the adenoma: Headache , visual field defects , raised ICT Note : Although hypothalamic hamartomas can also produce gigantism, the most common cause of gigantism is pituitary adenomas.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young boy is diagnosed to have central diabetes insipidus . A lesion in which of the following nuclei is likely to cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Lesions in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus can cause central diabetes insipidus . These nuclei synthesize vasopressin, a 9-amino-acid peptide with antidiuretic and vascular pressor activity. It is transported to the posterior pituitary via axonal projections , where it is stored for release into the systemic circulation. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is characterized by pathologic polyuria and polydipsia (>2 L/m\262/24 hr or 5 mL /kg/hr). It can result from either : • Vasopressin deficiency (decreased anti-diuretic hormone production ) causes central DI. • Vasopressin insensitivity at the level of the kidney causes nephrogenic DI.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy was brought by his mother with new-onset nocturnal bedwetting . She also reported , he has been drinking more water for the last 3-4 months. 24-hour urine volume was 4 liters and the urine osmolality was low. ADH assays recorded a value was 0.7 pg /mL . T1 weighted MRI brain indicated an absence of a pituitary bright spot . What is the treatment of choice for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus . The treatment of choice is desmopressin. It is a vasopressin analog (V2 receptor agonist). It can be administered intranasally, or subcutaneously . Option A: Leuprolide is a GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analog used in the treatment of prostate cancer, breast cancer, and endometriosis . Option B: Thiazides paradoxically exert an antidiuretic effect in DI but are not the drug of choice . They are generally used in nephrogenic DI.625 Option D: Terlipressin is a long-acting analog on vasopressin that acts on V1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle . It is used as a vasopressor in shock and acute variceal bleeding .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy diagnosed with Wolfram syndrome is admitted to the pediatric ward of your hospital . Which of the following features would you expect to find in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Optic Atrophy is seen in Wolfram syndrome. The components of the syndrome are represented by the acronym DIDMOAD: • Diabetes Insipidus • Diabetes Mellitus (type 1) • Optic Atrophy • Neural Deafness It is caused by mutations of the WFS1 gene .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While working in a tertiary care center , a 5-year-old girl presents with polyuria, polydipsia , and nocturnal enuresis for the past 1 year. A water deprivation test is done and shows low urine osmolality on stopping the intake of water. On desmopressin administration, there is a 7% rise in urine osmolality . The treatment of this condition uses all of the following except ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus . The treatment includes pharmacological treatment combined with salt restriction and not increased salt intake. Treatment of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus : • Adequate water intake along with a low sodium diet • Thiazide diuretics : Acts by • Volume contraction and increases the responsiveness of other parts of the tubule • Increase the AQP2 channels independent of vasopressin • Potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene and amiloride): Amiloride is the drug of choice for lithium-induced DI • Prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor (indomethacin)626

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are suspecting a case of delayed puberty in a 15-year-old boy. To assess puberty in this patient , what is the first sign you would look for?
mcqs.explanation: The first sign of puberty in males is the increase in testicular volume. In males at 11 to 12 years, the growth of the testis (>4 mL in volume) and thinning of the scrotum occurs, which are the first signs of puberty . This is followed by the pigmentation of the scrotum, growth of the penis , and pubarche . Growth of testis > pubarche > adrenarche > growth spurt (TPAG). In females at 10 to 11 years, the breast bud (thelarche ) appears , which is the first sign of puberty followed by the appearance of pubic hair (pubarche), growth spurt, and menarche.632 Thelarche > pubarche > growth spurt > menarche (TPGM).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As an intern, you are currently posted in the Paediatric endocrinology OPD where you see multiple cases of girls having precocious puberty . The condition is defined by the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before the age of_________.
mcqs.explanation: Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before the age of 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys. Depending on the primary source of hormonal production , precocious puberty can be classified in the following manner : Note : Central Precocious Puberty (more common) >> Peripheral Precocious PubertyCentral Precocious Puberty (G onadotropin-dependent pube rty) Peripheral Precocious Pubert y(Gonadotropin independent ) Due to the excess secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH ) from pituitary Due to excess secretion of tes tosterone or estrogen from th e gonads/adrenals. Always isosexual (appearance of phenotypically appropriat e secondary sexual characteri stics before age 8 years in gir ls and before 9 years in boys) . Can be isosexual or heterosex ual (appearance of secondary sex characters of the opposit e sex). GirlsIdiopathic (most commo n)BoysCNS pathology (most c ommon) GirlsEstrogenic ovarian cysts (isosexual )Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (testoster one increases; heterosexual )B oysCAH (isosexual ; most com mon)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old girl was brought to the OPD by her mother who is concerned about her significant increase in height compared to her classmates in the last 2 years. On examination, the girl shows breast development corresponding to B2 Tanner stage . What is the most common brain lesion causing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Hypothalamic hamartoma , a neuronal migration defect , is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty . The onset of breast development before the age of 8 years in females and onset of testicular development (>4 mL ) before the age of 9 years in males is suggestive of central precocious puberty . It is a congenital malformation that consists of ectopically located neural tissue characterised by- • Early-onset of puberty • Seizures associated with unnatural crying or laughing episodes are known as gelastic seizures . Tuberculous meningitis, tuberous sclerosis , and astrocytomas can also cause central precocious puberty .633

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young girl was referred to the paediatrician with stage IV breast development and growth acceleration seen at the age of 5 years. Her estradiol concentrations were elevated . The sagittal MRI of the brain is as shown below . What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: A pedunculated mass in the floor of the 3rd ventricle as shown in the MRI, with elevated levels of estrogen is suggestive of a Hypothalamic Hamartoma , which is the most common brain lesion causing central precocious puberty and is treated with GnRH agonists. Treatment of Hypothalamic Hamartoma- • GnRH agonists (depot -forms or implant) are the treatment of choice of tumour-induced Central precocious puberty • In patients with hypothalamic hamartoma and associated intractable gelastic or psychomotor seizures , stereotactic radiation therapy (Gamma Knife surgery) is more effective and has fewer risks than neurosurgical intervention. Long-acting formulations of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH ) agonists are the preparations of choice for the treatment of central precocious puberty as they maintain fairly constant serum concentrations of the drug for weeks or months.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A primary school teacher notices bloodstains on the skirt of her second -grade student . She immediately informs her parents and accompanies the child to the doctor on campus. On examination, the 7-year-old girl had blood-stained vaginal discharge , enlarged breasts and areola. Which of the following is not a cause for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Vaginal bleeding with well -developed breasts before the age of 8 years is suggestive of precocious puberty . Prader–Willi syndrome is one of the causes of delayed puberty in girls (not precocious puberty ), where there is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism . Hypothalamic hamartoma , McCune –Albright syndrome and hypothyroidism are causes of precocious puberty . Note : In prolonged hypothyroidism , adolescents typically have delayed puberty . Younger children might present with pseudo -precocious puberty, characterized by breast development and vaginal bleeding in girls and macroorchidism in boys. Elevated levels of TSH appear to interact with the FSH receptor (specificity spillover), thus inducing FSH-like effects in the absence of LH effects on the gonads. The FSH-like effect suffices to induce estradiol secretion by the ovaries, whereas in males, testicular enlargement occurs without substantial testosterone secretion.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An incessantly crying 5-year-old girl is brought to the OPD by her father. You observe that she needs support to walk and her trunk is not symmetrically aligned . There is a history of recurrent fractures in her limbs. She also has blood-stained vaginal discharge from a few days. On examination, the girl appears as shown in the image below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Precocious puberty (vaginal discharge ), bony lesions (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia ), and cafe au lait spots , as shown in the picture , are features of McCune –Albright syndrome. There is pain due to the multiple bony lesions and repeated fractures may result in incessant crying in the children and may require regular visits to the orthopaedics department .634 McCune –Albright syndrome is a classical cause of peripheral precocious puberty caused by a mutation of GNAS1 gene . It affects the bones, skin, and several endocrine tissues . Fibrous dysplasia of multiple bones (polyostotic ) represents a major cause of morbidity in this syndrome. The base of the skull and the proximal femurs are most commonly involved, but any bone can be affected . A CT scan is usually recommended even in absence of deformities . The prognosis is favourable for longevity , but deformities , repeated fractures, pain, and occasional cranial nerve compression may result from the bony lesions . Cardinal features : • Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia • Cafe au lait macules • Endocrine abnormalities: hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, adrenal adenomas, and autonomous ovarian hyperfunction , leading to precocious puberty • Predominantly affects girls

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy on examination is found to have genital development corresponding to Tanner stage 1 and his height is below the 3rd Percentile on growth charting. What is the most common cause for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Failure of development of pubertal features by the age of 14 years in male is suggestive of Delayed Puberty . The most common cause of delayed puberty in males and females is a constitutional delay in growth and puberty . Lack of pubertal changes in boys by the age of 14 years is suggestive of delayed puberty . Delayed puberty is more common in boys than in girls.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Breast and papillae appear as a small mound on examination of a young girl. If you are suspecting a case of delayed puberty , it is defined as a lack of development of secondary sexual characters beyond the age of __________.
mcqs.explanation: Delayed puberty in girls is defined as lack of secondary sexual characteristics by the age of 13 years or absence of menarche by the age of 16 years or within 3 years of pubertal onset .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child presents with features of delayed puberty . On investigating , he has decreased levels of LH, FSH, and testosterone . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This patient has low levels of luteinizing hormone (LH ), follicle -stimulating hormone (FSH), and testosterone pointing towards hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and Kallman's syndrome is the only condition in the given choices causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism . Causes of delayed puberty : Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Secondary/central) Hypogonadism is due to the impaired secretion of gonadotropins (FSH and LH ) by the pituitary gland and the resultant lack of sex steroid production • Malnutrition, systemic diseases • Kallmann (anosmia), Prader–Willi syndrome (mental retardation, obesity , low intelligence )635 Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (Primary gonadal failure) Hypogonadism is due to an impaired response of the gonads to the gonadotropins (FSH and LH ), which in turn leads to a lack of sex steroid production and elevated gonadotropin levels (as an attempt of compensation by the body) • Sex chromosome anomalies (Turner's, Klinefelter 's syndrome) • Androgen insensitivity syndrome • Ovotesticular dysgenesis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All of the following are features of Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome except _________.
mcqs.explanation: Hypertension is seen in Laurence–Moon–Biedl syndrome. Laurence–Moon–Bardet–Biedl is an autosomal-recessive disorder of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Characteristic features : • Polydactyly • Obesity • Retinitis pigmentosa • Male hypogonadism • Hypertension • Mental retardation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A female child presents with bilateral inguinal masses , which were thought to be hernias but were found to be testes in the inguinal canals. Which karyotype would you expect to find in the child?
mcqs.explanation: 636 Here, this baby girl with bilateral inguinal masses (testis ) probably has androgen-insensitivity syndrome, where karyotype is 46,XY . Androgen-insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene that makes XY fetuses insensitive to androgens. The patients phenotypically resemble females because a part of the testosterone is converted to estrogen, which leads to the development of female external genitalia , normal development of breast, and female habitus. Patients with Klienfelter 's syndrome have a karyotype of 47, XXY and can have undescended testis , but they have male external genitalia where the phallus tends to be smaller than average. Characteristic features : • Most common forms of male disorders of sexual differentiation (DSD). • 46 XY male child with female phenotype , present with primary amenorrhoea. • Normal male gonads, mostly undescended ones, can present as inguinal masses or hernia. • Here, as testosterone receptors are defective , they do not act on tissues , leading to the absence of secondary sexual characters (absence of pubic hair and axillary hair).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An infant was found to have elevated levels of LH . The baby has a 46, XY chromosome pattern on karyotyping and the vagina is short and ends blindly in a pouch . Which of the following is false in the condition suffered by the infant?
mcqs.explanation: An infant with a 46, XY chromosome pattern and female external genitalia are suggestive of Androgen-insensitivity syndrome(AIS) where there is absent internal female genitalia . These patients have absent internal female genitalia with normal female external genitalia with the vagina ending blindly, in a pouch and normal male gonads in the form of undescended testis (mostly ) which can present as inguinal masses . In a male child (46, XY ), testicular hormones are resistant to receptors , and a part of the testosterone is converted to estrogen leading to the development of female external genitalia and eventually normal development of breast, and female habitus. Features of Androgen insensitivity syndrome at different age groups - • In infants, elevated LH levels should suggest the diagnosis of AIS • Prepubertal females with this disorder are often detected when inguinal masses which prove to be testes • In older children and adults , amenorrhea is the usual presenting symptom . Note : Reifen-Stein syndrome: Males with various forms of ambiguous genitalia and undervirilization (hypogonadism, severe hypospadias , and gynecomastia ). They are phenotypically normal - appearing males with infertility .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 31 -year-old female delivers a term baby. On examination, it has a micropenis and unpalpable testis. She gives a history of acne from 16 weeks of gestation which worsened throughout pregnancy and was treated after delivery . The baby was diagnosed to have female pseudohermaphroditism . Which of the following statements are right about the given condition?

options.b: Female external genitalia and male internal genitalia

mcqs.explanation: 637 Female pseudohermaphrodites are genectic females (XX genotype ) with male external genitalia . Causes : • Enzyme deficiencies : 21 hydroxylase , 11 hydroxylase , and 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD) deficiencies • Maternal androgen excess Male pseudohermaphrodites are genetic males (XY genotype ) with female external genitalia . Causes : • Enzyme deficiencies : 17 hydroxylase and 3-beta HSD deficiencies • Defect in androgen action True hermaphroditism/ovotesticular dysgenesis : An intersex condition in which an individual is born with ovarian and testicular tissue.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is true about ovotesticular disorders of sex development ?

options.b: Ovotestis is seen in the gonadal biopsy
options.c: The response of testosterone to hCG is increased .

mcqs.explanation: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development (DSD) is characterized by the presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue in the same individual. An ovotestis is present in approximately 2/3 of affected individuals. Most affected individuals have a 46, XX chromosomal karyotype , which normally results in female sexual development . In about 10 % of patients , testicular tissue in an individual with a 46, XX karyotype is present as a result of a translocation of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome to the X chromosome or another chromosome. There is a defect in R-spondin1 protein encoded by the RSPO1 gene , described in 46, XX ovotesticular DSD. An abnormal vagina and an underdeveloped uterus are usually present . The testes are usually undescended , and the penis may present with hypospadias . Upon reaching puberty , breast development , feminization, and menstruation may occur. Most affected individuals are infertile , but ovulation or spermatogenesis is possible . The response of testosterone to hCG is normal or reduced .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old girl was brought by her mother with complaints of enlarged clitoris. Karyotype revealed 46XX . What is the likely cause?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a girl (46XX ) with an enlarged clitoris is highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . Congenital adrenal hyperplasia /adrenogenital syndrome is a family of autosomal-recessive disorders caused by the deficiency of enzymes involved in the synthesis of steroid hormones in the adrenal cortex. The majority of cases of CAH are caused by 21 -hydroxylase deficiency . This deficiency leads to a lack of synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone , resulting in the salt-wasting form of the disease , which is the most severe form. Severe 21 -hydroxylase deficiency presents with symptoms including weight loss , dehydrat ion, weakness, hypotension , and electrolyte imbalances. Accumulated steroid precursors like638 17-hydroxyprogesterone , are shunted into the pathway of androgen synthesis leading to elevated levels of androstenedione and testosterone . This can result in abnormal genital development in affected female fetuses during early gestation . Females may have masculinized external genitalia . This can include enlargement of the clitoris, partial or complete labial fusion, and a shared opening of the vagina and urethra (urogenital sinus). Untreated individuals develop signs of androgen excess after birth. These signs include accelerated skeletal maturation, premature epiphyseal closure leading to stunted adult stature , excessive muscular development , the appearance of pubic and axillary hair, acne, and deepening of the voice. In males, enlargement of the penis , scrotum, and prostate . In females , the clitoris may become further enlarged . Diagnosis of confirmed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels . Glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone is done. In a salt-wasting crisis, fludrocortisone supplementation is given. Vaginoplasty and clitoral recession are done for females with ambiguous genitalia .639

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Cancer-'The emperor of all maladies spares no one'. Which of the following is the most common childhood malignancy?
mcqs.explanation: Leukemias are the most common childhood malignancies. Among these , acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) is the most common, accounting for about 77 % of childhood leukemias . Most commons in childhood malignancies: • Second most common malignancy in childhood : Brain tumor • Third most common malignancy in children: Lymphoma • Most common solid tumor in children: Brain tumor

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are asked to review an article titled , 'Childhood cancers- a menace'. Which of the following statements is wrong and needs to be edited out?

options.a: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common type of leukemia in children with Down syndrome.
options.b: The most common intra-abdominal malignancy is Wilm's tumor.
options.c: The most common extracranial solid malignancy is neuroblastoma.
options.d: The most common brain tumors in children are infratentorial.

mcqs.explanation: The most common intraabdominal malignancy in children is neuroblastoma. • The most common leukemias seen in Down's syndrome: acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) > acute myeloid leukemia (AML) • The most common site of a brain tumor in children: Infratentorium • The most common extra-cranial solid neoplasm in children: Neuroblastoma • The most common intra-abdominal neoplasm in children: Neuroblastoma • The most common primary neoplasm of renal tissue in children: Wilm's tumor649

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common leukemia you would encounter in a child with the following findings?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a typical Down's facies (flattened nose, flat occiput , low set ears, protruding tongue ). The most common leukemia in children with Down syndrome is acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). Children with Down syndrome are at increased risk of both acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). % of neonates with Down's syndrome develop transient leukemia or myeloproliferative disorder. These features usually resolve within the first 3 months of life . However, they require close follow -up, because 20 –30% will develop typical leukemia (often acute megakaryocytic leukemia) by 3 years of life . Note : • Most common leukemia in Down's syndrome: B-cell Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (overall) • The most common leukemia in children <3years of age with Down syndrome is acute myeloid leukemia (AML). • Most common AML in Down's syndrome: M7 /megakaryoblastic

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Jeevit, a 7-year-old boy brought to you by his mother, complains of bone pain so severe that he cannot sleep. Investigations reveal:
mcqs.explanation: B-lymphoblastic leukemia(pre-B-ALL) is the most common immunophenotype with TdT+,HLA DR+, CD10+, CD19+, CD20 +, CD24+, Cy Ig + , with onset at 1-10 years of age . The most common type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) in children is B-lymphoblastic leukemia (previously termed pre-B-ALL ) Based on current WHO classification : The most common subtype of ALL is B lymphoblastic leukemia > T lymphoblastic leukemia > Mature B-cell Leukemia (Burkitt leukemia) The production of symptoms and signs of ALL is a result of the replacement of bone marrow by malignant cells and caused by secondary bone marrow failure. On physical examination, findings of pallor, listlessness , purpuric/petechial skin lesions , or mucous membrane hemorrhage can reflect bone marrow failure. The proliferative nature of the disease may be manifested as lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly , or, less often , hepatomegaly . At presentation 75 % of patients have leukocyte counts of <20,000 /\265 L; thrombocytopenia is seen in 75 % of patients and hepatosplenomegaly in 30–40 % of patients . Patients with joint pain may have evidence of joint swelling and effusion . Deep bone pain may be present with marrow involvement , but tenderness will not be elicited .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are posted in the pediatric hematology department as a first-year postgraduate . All of the following cases you encounter are at an increased risk of developing leukemias except :
mcqs.explanation: 650 Fanconi's anemia (not syndrome) predisposes to the development of childhood leukemias eg : B-ALL due to defective DNA repair. Fanconi syndrome is a syndrome of inadequate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules . Congenital pernicious anemia does not predispose to leukemias . Factors predisposing to childhood leukemias • Genetic conditions: • Fanconi's anemia • Bloom syndrome • Ataxia telangiectasia • Li -Fraumeni syndrome • Down syndrome • Severe combined immunodeficiency • Neurofibromatosis 1 • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria • Diamond-Blackfan anemia • Schwachman diamond syndrome • Kostmann syndrome • Environmental factors: • Ionizing radiation • Alkylating agents • Nitrosoureas • Epipodophyllotoxin • Benzene exposure • Advanced maternal age .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: To diagnose a 5-year-old child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a pathologist has to see at least ____ percentage of blast cells in a bone marrow biopsy .
mcqs.explanation: The lower cut-off percentage for diagnosing acute lymphoblastic leukemia on bone marrow biopsy is 25%. Unlike with myeloid leukemias , there is no agreed -upon lower limit for the proportion of blasts required to establish a diagnosis of lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). In general , the diagnosis should be avoided when there are < % blasts . The image below shows numerous lymphoblasts seen on a peripheral smear.651 Work -up of ALL : It is important that all studies necessary to confirm a diagnosis and adequately classify the type of leukemia be performed , including bone marrow aspiration and biopsy , flow cytometry , cytogenetics , and molecular studies . The initial evaluation should also include a CSF examination. If lymphoblasts are found and the CSF leukocyte count is elevated , overt CNS or meningeal leukemia is present . This finding reflects a poorer stage and indicates the need for additional CNS and systemic therapies .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old child who was being evaluated for pancytopenia is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following findings would indicate a poor prognosis?

options.a: Minimal residual disease >0.01% at the end of induction therapy

mcqs.explanation: MRD(Minimal residual disease ) is a quantitative estimate of the burden of leukemic cells present in marrow . MRD>0.01%at the end of induction suggests a poorer prognosis. Initial WBC count of <50,000cells/mm3, B-cell immunophenotype and t(12 ,21 ) indicate a standard risk (Favourable prognosis) Risk -directed therapy is the standard of current ALL treatment and accounts for: • Age at diagnosis • Initial WBC count • Immunophenotypic and cytogenetic characteristics of blast populations • The rapidity of early treatment response (i.e., how quickly the leukemic cells can be cleared from the marrow or peripheral blood) • Assessment of MRD at the end of induction therapy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy is rushed to the casualty due to difficulty in breathing and swelling of the face and neck. Clinically, he has features suggestive of superior vena cava obstruction. Chest X-ray image shows superior mediastinal widening . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 652 T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL ) is the most likely diagnosis since the chest X-ray shows superior mediastinal widening - indicating an involvement of the thymus gland. T-ALL accounts for about 15% of childhood ALL cases ; it is more common in adolescents - this is the time when the thymus reaches maximum size. 60% of patients with T-ALL present with a mediastinal mass. The mediastinal mass may be asymptomatic and detected only on chest x-ray or may cause cough and dyspnea , particularly on lying flat or with facial swelling and plethora due to vascular compression (superior vena cava syndrome). B-ALL presents usually between 1-10 years of age perhaps because the number of normal bone marrow pre-B-cells (the cell of origin) is greatest very early in life .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 2-month-old infant with seizures and failure to thrive has cutaneous nodules and hepatosplenomegaly. On investigations, CBC reveals hyperleukocytosis with a leukocyte count of 1,10 ,000cells/mm3. Peripheral smear and immunophenotyping studies reveal large, irregular lymphoblasts , with a phenotype negative for the CD10 (common ALL antigen) marker . On a cytogenetic study which of the following is most likely to be seen ?
mcqs.explanation: The above findings are diagnostic of Infantile acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Translocation (4;11 ) involving the MLL gene is most commonly associated with Infantile leukemia accounts for the very high relapse rate. 2% of cases of leukemia during childhood occur before the age of 1 year and are referred to as infantile leukemia. Patients often present with hyperleukocytosis and extensive tissue infiltration producing organomegaly. Subcutaneous nodules , known as leukemia cutis , caused by infiltration by leukemic cells are observed more often in infants than in older children. The leukemic cell morphology is usually that of large, irregular lymphoblasts , with a phenotype negative for the CD10 (common ALL antigen) marker (pro-B), unlike most older children with B-ALL , who are CD10 +. Has a very poor prognosis. Note : Infants with AML present with CNS and skin involvement and most commonly have a subtype known as acute myelomonocytic leukemia.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother has noticed recently that her child refuses to be touched , seems to be in distress , and cries inconsolably. She brings her child to you who was investigated thoroughly and was diagnosed to have acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following drugs can be used to treat her?
mcqs.explanation: L-asparaginase is used in the treatment of acute lymphoid leukaemia (ALL ). ALL can present with hepatosplenomegaly, severe joint and bone pains that the kid refuses to be handled . It is observed that some lymphoid malignancies are unable to synthesize asparagine on their own and must derive it from the bloodstream . L -asparaginase catalyses circulating L- asparagine , thereby inhibiting protein synthesis in the cancer cells . Treatment of ALL • Induction: 4 weeks • L-asparaginase: single dose (side effects : pancreatitis , thrombosis) • Vincristine: weekly (side effects : neuropathy, SIADH)653 • Prednisolone • Anthracycline • CNS prophylaxis- intrathecal methotrexate • Consolidation: • Methotrexate • Epipodophyllotoxin • Cyclophosphamide • Cytosine -Arabinoside • Maintenance : 24-36 months • 6-Mercaptopurine • Methotrexate Other options : • Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat chronic myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia with t(9;22 ) BCR-ABL fusion gene . • Tretinoin is used in acute promyelocytic leukaemia with t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion gene . • Cladribine is used in hairy cell leukaemia.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are posted in the hematology department as a pathologist . You are asked to report the bone marrow biopsy slide given below , which belongs to a 3-year-old child who is being evaluated for pancytopenia . To make a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia, what percentage of such cells should you visualize at the least ?
mcqs.explanation: Diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is confirmed by the presence of more than 20 % myeloblast cells (as shown in the image) in the bone marrow . Flow cytometry and special stains can be used to identify myeloperoxidase -containing cells , which confirms the myelogenous origin of leukemia. Note : The diagnosis of acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL ) requires the presence of more than 25% blasts in the bone marrow .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric OPD with complaints of persistent fever for the past 1 week . His CBC is given below :
mcqs.explanation: Monosomy 7 is associated with a poor prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The production of symptoms and signs of AML is a result of the replacement of bone marrow by malignant cells and caused by secondary bone marrow failure-pallor, fatigue , exercise intolerance, bruising, oral mucosal bleeding , or epistaxis, as well as fever, which may be caused by infection or the disease . In addition, patients with AML present with signs and symptoms that are uncommon in Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including subcutaneous nodules or"blueberry muffin" lesions (especially654 in infants), infiltration of the gingiva (especially in monocytic subtypes ), signs and laboratory findings of disseminated intravascular coagulation (especially indicative of acute promyelocytic leukemia), and discrete masses , known as chloromas or granulocytic sarcomas. Prognostic implications of chromosomal abnormalities in AML are given below :Favorable prognosis t(8;21); RUNX1-RUNX1T1Inv (16) or t(16;16); CBF\031NPM1m utationCEBPAmutation Poor prognosis inv (3)t(6;9)5q-del(7q)comple x karyotype (\0343 abnormalitie s)Monosomy7

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child with a violaceous, raised nodular skin lesion which on biopsy is found to be infiltrated by myeloblasts is likely suffering from which type of Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)?
mcqs.explanation: Nodular, violaceous skin lesion infiltrated with myeloblasts is descriptive of Chloroma otherwise known as extramedullary myeloblastoma or granulocytic (myeloid ) sarcoma. Myeloid sarcomas are seen in AML subtypes M2, M4, M5a, and M5b . "Chloroma" was coined due to the peculiar green color of the tumor caused by myeloperoxidase present in tumor cells . These masses can occur in the absence of apparent bone marrow involvement and typically are associated with t(8;21) translocation. Chloromas also may be seen in the orbit and epidural space .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Erythemic myelosis is ______.
mcqs.explanation: Erythemic myelosis is AML M6. Constitute about 1% of AML cases Two subtypes of AML M6: • Erythroid or myeloid leukemia: M6a (more common) • Pure erythroid leukemia: M6b, also called erythemic myelosis (Di Guglielmo disease ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A neonate with trisomy 21 has anemia, petechiae , hepatosplenomegaly , and no life -threatening complications on examination.CBC reveals high leucocyte count and peripheral smear shows numerous myeloblasts . The genetic makeup of blast cells when studied reveals GATA-1 mutations. At 3 months of age , his CBC counts come back to normal and there are no blast cells in his peripheral smear. As his treating physician, what would you recommend?
mcqs.explanation: This infant has a transient myeloproliferative disease , which usually resolves spontaneously in the first 3 months of life , and they require close -follow up because 20 –30% will develop typical leukemia (acute megakaryocytic leukemia) by 3 years of life .655 Approximately 10 % of neonates with Down syndrome develop transient leukemia or myeloproliferative disorder characterized by high leukocyte counts, blast cells in the peripheral blood, and associated anemia, thrombocytopenia , and hepatosplenomegaly . These features usually resolve within the first 3 months of life . Although these neonates can require temporary transfusion support , they do not require chemotherapy unless there is evidence of life -threatening complications . As only 20 -30% of such children develop acute megakaryocytic leukemia a bone marrow transplant would be a drastic step in our case.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 18-month-old child presents to the pediatric OPD with complaints of fever and rashes for the past 1 week after extensive workup gets diagnosed as Juvenile chronic myeloid leukemia. Which of the following findings is not consistent with this baby's diagnosis?

options.a: The genetic study may reveal NF-1 mutation
options.b: The presence of Philadelphia chromosome on FISH
options.c: The bone marrow shows a myelodysplastic pattern with <20% blasts .
options.d: The peripheral smear reveals nucleated RBCs

mcqs.explanation: Patients with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia do not have the Philadelphia chromosome. Formerly termed juvenile chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), it is a clonal proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells that typically affects children younger than 2 years of age . Patients with JMML present with rashes, lymphadenopathy , splenomegaly , and hemorrhagic manifestations . Patients with this disease do not have the Philadelphia chromosome (the Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML). The peripheral blood smear shows an elevated leukocyte count with increased monocytes , thrombocytopenia , and anemia with the presence of erythroblasts . Bone marrow shows a myelodysplastic pattern, with blasts accounting for <20% of cells . Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome have a predilection for this type of leukemia. JMML in the setting of Noonan syndrome is unique, with most patients having a spontaneous resolution .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The most common non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in children is _____________.
mcqs.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in children under the age of 15 years. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL ) is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in adults and adolescents (15-19) years, worldwide . B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL ) is the most common childhood malignancy and the most common leukemia in children. (It is not a non-Hodgkin's lymphoma).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements best describe the behavior of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma in a 10-year-old child?

options.b: Is of high grade and aggressive

mcqs.explanation: In contrast to adult non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL), which is typically indolent , pediatric NHL is usually high-grade and aggressive . NHL in the pediatric age group has distinct clinical and behavior properties when compared to adults . These include the following :656 NHL in adults NHL in children Low/intermediate grade High grade Dominantly nodal Extra-nodal Variable growth fractio n High growth fractio n Poor long-term outcom e Good outcome

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought with complaints of abdominal distension , fatigue , and night sweats for the past 4 months. He also has a 2-month history of postprandial fullness and recurrent non-bilious vomiting. On examination, he is pale , has hepatosplenomegaly and shifting dullness . A CT scan shows mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement . A biopsy specimen of the mesenteric lymph node reveals tumor cells with high mitotic index and starry sky pattern. The cytogenetic study revealed t(8;14).To stage the disease , which of the following systems would you use ?
mcqs.explanation: Retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly , anemia, and short duration of disease , point towards a diagnosis of lymphoid neoplasms .The classic translocation of t(8;14) and starry sky appearance with a high mitotic index on HPE point toward a diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt's lymphoma is the most common type of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma worldwide . St Jude system of staging is used for staging childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The current revised staging system used for NHL is the International Pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Staging System (IPNHLSS) which reflects our increasing ability to diagnose lower levels of organ involvement with disease. For instance, the older staging system (St. Jude/Murphy classification ) did not account for molecular or flow cytometry involvement of bone marrow , which is now reflected in the new system.Disease System of staging Hodgkin lymphoma Ann–Arbor staging Non-Hodgkin Lymphom a St Jude(Murphy ) stagin g Chronic lymphoid leuke mia Rai stagingBinet staging

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A lymph node biopsy of a 9-year-old child with cervical lymphadenopathy showed the following picture. The diagnosis is_____.
mcqs.explanation: In the picture given above, Reed –Sternberg (RS) cells are seen , which is a pathognomonic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). Reed –Sternberg cells are large and either multinucleated or have a bilobed nucleus (thus resembling an "owl's eye " appearance ) with prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli . The RS cell is clonal in origin and arises from the germinal center B cells but typically has lost most B-cell gene expression and function. Hodgkin lymphoma encompasses a group of lymphoid neoplasms that typically arise in a signal node or chain of nodes and spread first to anatomically contiguous sites . WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma includes 5 subtypes namely;657 • Nodular sclerosis • Mixed cellularity • Lymphocyte -rich • Lymphocyte depletion • Nodular lymphocyte predominance

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 - year-old female comes to you with a flu-like illness and left supraclavicular swelling of uncertain nature. Her chest X-ray shows left mediastinal enlargement . CT scan of the chest and abdomen reveals the presence of enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, mediastinum, and liver, and an FDG-PET/CT scan shows multiple scattered consolidation lesions involving also the bones. The diagnosis of classical Hodgkin's lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype , is made on cervical lymph node biopsy . According to Ann-Arbor 's staging system , how will you stage her disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette describes Hodgkin's lymphoma with the involvement of liver and bone marrow, which is classified as Stage 4 according to Ann-Arbor staging . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The following parameter in ALL indicate a poor prognosis ________.
mcqs.explanation: Age >10 years indicates a poor prognosis in ALL . Leukocyte count <50,000/mm3 , hyperdiploidy , and trisomy of chromosomes 4,10 ,17 indicate a good prognosis.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Sanctuary sites of acute lymphoblastic leukemia are______.
mcqs.explanation: Both CNS and testis are considered as sanctuary sites of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ). • A sanctuary site is an area of the body that is poorly penetrated by pharmacological agents and, therefore , serves as a place in which tumor cells or infectious organisms can escape the effects of drug therapy . • Early institution of CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal methotrexate ) is essential to eradicate these escaped leukemic cells . • Testicular involvement is rarely evident at diagnosis, testicular involvement can present as painless testicular enlargement .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly . Bony tenderness is also present . He is most likely suffering from the following type of ALL _____.
mcqs.explanation: 659 B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia (L1) • This is the most common immunophenotype of acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL ) in a child between the ages of 1-10 years. • They present with features of bone marrow failure and organ infiltration such as pancytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly , respectively , so B-cell ALL is the most likely diagnosis. • Bony tenderness may be present due to sub-periosteal infiltration of lymphoblastic cells . • T-cell ALL (L2 ) typically presents in adolescent boys with a large anterior mediastinal mass (thymus or mediastinal lymph nodes ), causing respiratory distress or superior vena cava obstruction.660

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the second most common malignancy in childhood ?
mcqs.explanation: The second most common malignancy in childhood is a brain tumor. The most common malignancy in childhood is Leukemias. Brain tumors in childhood : • Most common solid tumor in children- Brain tumor • Most common site of a brain tumor in children- Infratentorium • Most common brain tumor in childhood- Pilocytic astrocytoma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The MRI scan of an 11 -year-old girl revealed a brain tumor. In which of the following conditions would you do a lumbar puncture for cytological analysis?
mcqs.explanation: Germ-cell tumor is an indication for lumbar puncture for cytological analysis of CSF. Usually , lumbar punctures are contraindicated in intracranial space -occupying lesions with high intracranial pressure as it can lead to brain herniation and death . They are thus delayed until676 surgery or shunt placement . However, in tumors with a risk of leptomeningeal metastases , lumbar puncture is indicated for cytology .Tumors where LP is indicate d Tumors where LP is contrain dicated Medulloblastoma or primitiv e neuroectodermal tumors Infratentorialtumors Ependymoma Supratentorialtumors withmi dline shift Germ cell tumors Tumors withhydrocephalusse condary toCSF obstruction

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother brought her 10 -month-old baby to the hospital with sudden onset vomiting. She has also been noticing an alarming increase in the head size of the baby. On examination, significant macrocephaly is seen . MRI reveals a supratentorial tumor. Which of the following tumors is the most likely cause of this child's presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: Choroid plexus carcinoma is a pediatric supratentorial tumor presenting with macrocephaly and focal neurologic deficits . Choroid plexus tumors are the most common CNS tumors in children aged less than 1 year. These tumors are intraventricular epithelial neoplasms arising from the choroid plexus . Children present with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), whereas infants may present with macrocephaly and focal neurologic deficits . Medulloblastoma , pilocytic astrocytoma, and ependymoma , are all predominantly infratentorial tumors. The age -related differences in the primary location of the tumor are given below :Age Predominant S ite Examples < 1 year Supratentorial Choroid plexus tumor and te ratoma 1 - 10 year s Infratentorial Juvenile pilocytic astrocytom a and medulloblastoma > 10 years Supratentorial Diffuse astrocytoma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Sanam, a 7-year-old kid is suspected to have an ependymoma . Which of the following features on histopathology would favor this diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Perivascular rosettes will be seen on histopathological examination of ependymoma . Other features include ependymal rosettes and monomorphic nuclear morphology . Ependymomas are tumors derived from the ependymal lining of the ventricular system occurring predominantly in childhood . They are usually non-invasive , extending into the ventricular lumen and/or displacing normal structures , sometimes leading to significant obstructive hydrocephalus .677

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A young child was evaluated for increased ICP. A brain tumor was found on an MRI scan. It was resected and sent for histopathological examination. The slide is shown below . This tumor is found most commonly in the __________.
mcqs.explanation: The slide shows perivascular pseudorosettes and ependymal rosettes , characteristic of ependymoma . The most common site of ependymoma in children is the floor of the 4th ventricle. Monomorphic nuclear morphology can also be noted . Ependymomas are tumors derived from the ependymal lining of the ventricular system , occurring predominantly in childhood . These tumors are usually non-invasive , extending into the ventricular lumen and/or displacing normal structures , sometimes leading to significant obstructive hydrocephalus .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A concerned mother brought her daughter to the clinic for evaluation of symptoms that have worsened in the last few weeks . The daughter frequently wakes up at night with severe headaches and vomiting. She has also been having some difficulty walking. On examination, ataxia and multiple cranial nerve palsies are noted . Imaging is suggestive of a brainstem tumor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The MRI given shows a diffuse , infiltrating pontine lesion. Multiple cranial nerve dysfunctions , cerebellar signs, motor weakness , and features of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) are all strongly suggestive of a pontine glioma. These are not amenable for surgical resection . The standard approach is radiation therapy . The prognosis is very poor.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: On your neurology rotation, you come across Ashu, a 5-year-old child who presented with a 6-month history of ataxia, headaches , and vomiting. He was admitted to the ward for further evaluation. MRI scan showed a brain tumor with a combination of solid and cystic components . Biopsy findings of the tumor are shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given slide shows condensed masses of glial filaments occurring in compact areas suggestive of Rosenthal fibers. The clinical features, MRI findings, and histopathology point towards a diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma. Pilocytic astrocytoma is a low-grade astrocytoma tumor. It is the most common type of astrocytoma in children. These are classically found in the cerebellum (infratentorial) and the optic pathway regions. There is usually a 3-6 month history of limb ataxia, secondary headaches , and vomiting. Mural nodule , a contrast medium enhancing nodule within the wall of a cystic mass is seen on MRI. The tumor has a low metastatic potential and is rarely invasive .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the WHO grading for Pilomyxoid astrocytoma?
mcqs.explanation: Pilomyxiod astrocytoma falls under WHO Grade II . Pilomyxoid astrocytoma: Occurs most commonly in the hypothalamic/optic chiasmic region and carries a high risk of local as well as cerebrospinal spread . This astrocytoma affects young children and infants. It is classified as a WHO grade II tumor.678 WHO Grades of brain tumor:WHO grade Example Grade I Pilocytic astrocytomaMyxopa pillary Ependymoma /subepe ndymoma Grade II Diffuse astrocytomaPilomyxo id astrocytomaPapillary/ cellu lar/Clear-cell ependymoma Grade III Anaplastic astrocytomaAnapl astic ependymoma Grade IV Glioblastoma multiformeMal ignant pineoblastoma and m edulloblastoma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are a pathology resident who is looking at a slide , showing small round blue cells and Homer-Wright rosettes as shown below . The history you received from the pediatric surgery resident was that the specimen was resected from a 5-year-old child with ataxia. The tumor was present in the midline vermis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and slide are suggestive of Medulloblastoma . Medulloblastoma is an embryonal CNS tumor, occurring predominantly in the cerebellar vermis that causes ataxia, poor balance, and dysmetria . It may cause obstructive hydrocephalus and often metastasizes extraneurally. Histopathology shows a tumor composed of small, round, blue cells and is characterized by Homer–Wright rosettes and an immunopositivity for synaptophysin . Standard treatment for medulloblastomas is surgical resection , with adjuvant craniospinal radiotherapy for those over 3 years of age and chemotherapy . Prognosis is strongly influenced by surgical resection , the presence of CSF metastases at the time of diagnosis, and the expression of the c-erbB-2 (HER2 /neu) oncogene . Note : Small, round, blue -cell tumors are malignant neoplasms that have a characteristic appearance under the microscope . It consists of sheets of small round cells that stain blue on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Examples are: • Medulloblastoma • Neuroblastoma • Retinoblastoma • Ewing 's sarcoma • Rhabdomyosarcoma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child is brought to the emergency department by his teacher when he started having abnormal jerking movements during math class. The parents give a history of the child having similar episodes in the past. On the way to the CT room, the child had an episode of seizure and was stabilized with lorazepam. The imaging done is shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 679 Calcified cortical mass with a seizure is suggestive of oligodendroglioma . Oligodendrogliomas are uncommon tumors of childhood . These infiltrating tumors occur predominantly in the cerebral cortex and originate in white matter. Treatment involves surgical resection followed by involved field radiation therapy . The image below shows histology of oligodendroglioma showing characteristic fried egg appearance and chicken wire capillaries .Craniopharyngioma is associated with suprasellar calcification. Also, the child may often present with a history of endocrinological and visual complaints.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An erythropoietin -secreting brain tumor is detected in a child. His father passed away one year back from end-stage renal cell carcinoma . Family history is significant for VHL mutation. On examination, a fiery red retina is seen . Which of the following is the most likely tumor present in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma . Von Hippel -Lindau (VHL ) syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition. The major neurological features of VHL include cerebellar hemangioblastomas and retinal angiomas. Cerebellar hemangioblastomas are erythropoietin -secreting tumors, which can lead to polycythemia. It typically appears as a cystic cerebellar lesion with a vascular mural nodule on CT or MRI scan. Retinal angiomas are small masses of thin-walled capillaries , usually located in the peripheral retina that is fed by large and tortuous arterioles and venules appearing as a fiery red vascular mass. It can lead to retinal detachment and visual loss.680 Associations of VHL syndrome include : • Cystic lesions of kidneys, pancreas, liver, and epididymis • Renal cell carcinoma (most common cause of death ) • Pheochromocytoma • Cerebellar hemangioblastoma • Retinal angioma

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Akhil, a 15-year-old boy with sun-setting eyes , has a tumor in the pineal region as seen in the MRI . Parinaud syndrome is suspected . Which of the following findings will not be seen in this boy?

options.c: Convergence retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze

mcqs.explanation: Parinaud's syndrome refers to supranuclear vertical gaze disorder. Parinaud's syndrome/dorsal midbrain syndrome is caused by damage to the posterior commissure. Classically , signs of hydrocephalus are seen due to aqueductal stenosis . Causes : • Pineal region or midbrain tumors (Most common cause ) • Neurocysticercosis • Stroke • Multiple sclerosis Features include the following : • Loss of up-gaze (downward gaze is usually preserved ) • Convergence –retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze • Downward ocular deviation- Setting -sun sign • Lid retraction- Collier's sign681 • Pseudo -Argyll–Robertson pupil - Accommodative paresis ensues and pupils become mid-dilated and show light-near dissociation • Bilateral papilledema • Skew deviation • Pseudoabducens palsy

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old child is brought to the casualty after a minor accident that occurred when he failed to see a bike coming from sideways . His mother says he is a clumsy child, who sometimes knocks things over accidentally even at home. Visual field examination findings are given below . On imaging, an intracranial mass is seen . The resected specimen shows cholesterol -rich machinery-oil-like fluid . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Patients with adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma present with bitemporal hemianopia (image), and the cystic component of this tumor contains a cholesterol -rich, thick, brownish-yellow fluid that is comparable to "machine oil." Craniopharyngiomas develop from remnants of the Rathke pouch . Adamantinomatous variant of craniopharyngioma predominates in childhood . These tumors are usually large and heterogeneous , displaying both solid and cystic components , and occur in the suprasellar region. Patients usually present with headache and visual field abnormalities. These children also have endocrinological abnormalities such as growth failure and delayed sexual maturation due to hypopituitarism (GH deficiency ). These tumors are minimally invasive , adhere to the adjacent brain parenchyma, and engulf normal brain structures . CT may show calcifications associated with the solid and cystic components .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common extracranial solid tumor in the pediatric age group?
mcqs.explanation: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in infants. It is an embryonal cancer of the peripheral nervous system . The signs and symptoms depend on the location of the tumor and the extent of the disease . Neuroblastomas originating from the superior cervical ganglion can present with Horner syndrome. Metastatic disease can cause a variety of signs and symptoms , including the following • Fever • Irritability • Failure to thrive • Bone pain • Cytopenia • Bluish subcutaneous nodules • Orbital proptosis , and periorbital ecchymoses Rapid dancing eye movements (opsoclonus), rhythmic jerking of limbs/trunk (myoclonus), and ataxia are characteristic of the opsoclonus -myoclonus -ataxia syndrome (OMA). It is682 a paraneoplastic syndrome of autoimmune origin with a strong association with neuroblastomas. Some neuroblastomas may undergo spontaneous regression, whereas some may be unresponsive to therapy and run a very aggressive course .Neuroblastoma Wilm's tumor (nephroblasto ma) Age group <2 years of age Peaks at 3-4 years of age Calcifications Very common (90%) Uncommon (10 -15%) Margins Poorly marginated Well circumscribed Vascular invasion Encases vascular structures b ut does not invade them Extends into the IVC and ren al vein Relation with surrounding st ructures Elevates the aorta away from the vertebral columnCommo nly crosses the midline, espec ially behind the aorta Displaces adjacent structures without insinuating between themForms the claw sign wit h the kidney

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child presents with rapid dancing eye movements, rhythmic jerking of limbs and poor coordination. You suspect a paraneoplastic syndrome. Which of the following conditions should you look for in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Rapid dancing eye movements (opsoclonus), rhythmic jerking of limbs/trunk (myoclonus) and ataxia is characteristic of opsoclonus -myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMA). It is a paraneoplastic syndrome of autoimmune origin with a strong association with neuroblastoma. All children with OMA should undergo investigations for neuroblastoma such as ultrasound followed by CT or MRI of chest and abdomen, bone scans and marrow biopsies . The definitive diagnosis of neuroblastoma is through biopsy which shows small round blue cells . Other small round blue cell tumours are medulloblastoma , retinoblastoma, Ewing 's sarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: In the ophthalmology OPD, you see a 3-year-old child with the following finding. There is no history of trauma. There is no significant family history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: This image shows periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis suggestive of metastases of neuroblastoma (a sign of orbital bone involvement). Neuroblastomas may develop at any site in the sympathetic nervous system . Metastatic spread is common in children who are diagnosed after 1 year of age . It occurs via local invasion , hematogenous , or lymphatic routes . Metastatic disease can cause a variety of signs and symptoms , including the following : • Fever • Irritability • Failure to thrive • Bone pain683 • Cytopenia • Bluish subcutaneous nodules • Orbital proptosis , and periorbital ecchymoses

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 10 -month-old infant is diagnosed with neuroblastoma. Which of the following factors is associated with a good prognosis?
