mcqs.explanation: Hyperdiploidy is associated with a good prognosis in neuroblastoma if the child is younger than 1 year of age at diagnosis. Bad prognosis in neuroblastoma is seen in cases of: • Amplification of N-MYC • Loss of Heterozygosiy of 1p, 11 q ,14q • Gain of 17q • TrkB expression

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 2-month history of an enlarging scalp lesion. There is no history of trauma to the head or scalp . The child is otherwise healthy and investigations are normal . X-ray of the head is given below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with the x-ray image showing a punched -out lytic lesion is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). LCH is a rare histiocytic disorder characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions that can infiltrate nearly every organ, most notably the skin (of the scalp ), lungs , thymus , liver, spleen , bone marrow , or the central nervous system . LCH is so named because of its resemblance to the Langerhan 's cells , which are specialized dendritic cells found in the skin and mucosa.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old child is brought with 4 small, purplish , rubbery lesions on his back and arms. On examination, you note inguinal freckling and nodules on the iris as shown below . Which chromosome is involved in the syndrome described in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 1. The NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11 is involved. It is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome. It is diagnosed when at least 2 of the following 7 criteria are met: • 6 or more cafe -au-lait macules • >5mm prepuberty • >15mm post -puberty • Skin -fold freckling- axillary and inguinal • 2 or more iris lisch nodules (image) • 2 or more neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma (purplish , rubbery lesions )684 • Osseous lesions • Osseous dysplasia • Cortical thinning of long bones without a pseudoarthrosis • Low-grade astrocytomas like optic gliomas • 1st degree relative with diagnosed NF-1

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal cord ependymomas are the CNS manifestations of __________.
mcqs.explanation: Vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal cord ependymomas are the CNS manifestations of neurofibromatosis type 2 It is an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22q12 . von Hippel –Lindau syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p25-26 . The CNS manifestation is usually a hemangioblastoma . Turcot syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome, which occurs due to a mutation in the APC gene on chromosome 5q21 . The CNS manifestation is a medulloblastoma .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presented with focal seizures involving the right side of his body. On investigations, a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is found. Which of the following syndromes is most likely to be associated with this?
mcqs.explanation: Subependymal giant-cell astrocytoma is a characteristic CNS finding in tuberous sclerosis .Syndrome CNS Manifestations Gene Neurofibromatosis type 1(aut osomal dominant) Optic pathway gliomasAstroc ytomaMalignant peripheral n erve sheath tumoursNeurofib romas NF1 Neurofibromatosis type 2(aut osomal dominant) Vestibular schwannomasMen ingiomasSpinal cord ependy momas NF2 Von Hippel –Lindau(autosom al dominant) Cerebellar hemangioblastom a VHL Tuberous Sclerosis (autosoma l dominant) Subependymal giant-cell astr ocytomaCortical tubers TSC1 TSC2 Turcot syndrome(autosomal dominant) MedulloblastomaGlioblastom a APC

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common intraocular tumor diagnosed in the pediatric age group?
mcqs.explanation: 685 Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular tumor of the pediatric age group. It is an embryonal malignancy of the retina.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: James was brought by his mother for evaluation of a squint she noticed . On examination, the given finding was observed. Investigations revealed retinoblastoma with a germline RB1 gene mutation. The secondary malignancy most likely to develop in him is:
mcqs.explanation: Children with germline RB1 mutations are at significant risk for the development of secondary malignancies, especially • Osteosarcoma (Most common) • Soft tissue sarcomas • Malignant melanoma The risk of secondary malignancies is further increased by the use of radiation therapy . A pineoblastoma occurring in a child with bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma is called 'trilateral retinoblastoma'. The image shows leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex . It may be seen in the following conditions: • Congenital cataract • Retinoblastoma • Retinopathy of prematurity (retrolental fibroplasia) • Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous • Coats disease • Toxocara endophthalmitis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old boy presented with an abdominal mass. On examination, the mass is firm, smooth, non-tender, and does not cross the mid-line. The boy is also found to have moderate hypertension . Urinalysis reveals microscopic haematuria. Wilms tumor is suspected . This condition can be associated with all of the following except ___________.
mcqs.explanation: Polycystic kidneys are not associated with Wilm's tumor. Wilms tumor (WT ), also known as nephroblastoma, is the most common primary malignant renal tumor of childhood . Polycystic kidney disease can also present with an abdominal mass, hypertension , and hematuria. However, there will be multiple irregular cysts on ultrasound and is not associated with Wilms tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are assisting on a left partial nephrectomy in a child with Wilms tumor. Intraoperatively, a small mass is noted on the right kidney as well . Frozen section reveals it to be a Wilms tumor. What is the stage of Wilm's tumor in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Wilms tumor with involvement of both kidneys is stage 5. Children's Oncology Group (COG) Staging System686 Stage I Tumor confined to the kidne y and completely resected wit h negative lymph nodes . Stage I I Tumor extends beyond the ki dney but is completely resect ed with negative margins and lymph nodes . Stage I II Residual tumor present follo wing surgery confined to the abdomen, including gross or microscopic tumor. Stage I V Hematogenous metastases (l ung, liver, bone, brain , etc .)o r lymph node metastases out side the abdominopelvic regi on Stage V Metastasis to opposite kidney (bilateral renal involvement)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: While posted in the pediatric oncology ward, you come across a case of metastatic triphasic nephroblastoma in a 4-year-old. What is the most common site for metastasis of this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The most common sites for metastases of nephroblastoma or Wilms tumor are the following : • Lungs (Most common) • Regional lymph nodes • Liver The triphasic components visualized on histopathology are- • Malignant small round (blue ) cells (blastemal component ). • Tubular structures /rosettes (epithelial component ). • Loose pauci-cellular stroma with spindle cells (stromal component )687

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most important determinant of prognosis in a child diagnosed with Wilm's tumor?

options.b: Loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 1 p

mcqs.explanation: Histology is the most important determinant of prognosis in Wilm's Tumor . The absence of anaplasia is considered a favorable histological finding. Other prognostic factors for risk -adapted therapy include • Age • Stage • Tumor weight • Loss of heterozygosity at chromosomes 1p and 16q .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child comes with abdominal distension , a palpable mass, and gross hematuria. A biopsy of the mass shows the following picture . Which of the following paraneoplastic syndromes in not associated with this tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The histopathological image shows the characteristic triphasic components of Wilm's tumor. Hypertrophic primary osteoarthropathy is not a paraneoplastic syndrome of Wilm's tumor. Several distinct paraneoplastic syndromes have been reported in Wilm's tumor. They are as follows : • Hypertension • Erythrocytosis /Polycythemia • Hypercalcemia • Cushing syndrome • Acquired von Willebrand disease688 Bleeding may occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome in Wilm's tumor. It is due to acquired deficiency of von Willebrand factor or factor VII deficiency . The triphasic components visualized on histopathology are- • Malignant small round (blue ) cells (blastemal component ). • Tubular structures /rosettes (epithelial component ). • Loose pauci-cellular stroma with spindle cells (stromal component )

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The most common soft tissue sarcoma in the pediatric age group is______.
mcqs.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma, a tumor of striated skeletal muscle , is the most common pediatric soft tissue sarcoma. The most common sites are- head and neck (25%) > genitourinary tract (24%) > extremities (19%) > orbit (9%).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with the lesion shown in this picture . The diagnosis is_____.
mcqs.explanation: The lesion seen in the picture is sarcoma botryoides Vaginal rhabdomyosarcoma may manifest as a grape-like mass of tumor tissue bulging through the vaginal orifice, known as sarcoma botryoides .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The precursor lesion of Wilm's tumor is _______.
mcqs.explanation: • Wilms tumor is derived from foci of incompletely differentiated /undifferentiated renal mesenchyme called nephrogenic rests.689 • Nephrogenic rests usually regress or differentiate , but those that persist can become malignant. • Nephrogenic rests that persist abnormally in the kidneys into postnatal life are seen in 1% of children in the general population , but are seen in up to 90% of children who develop or have a family history of Wilms tumor.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The term "trilateral retinoblastoma" refers to bilateral retinoblastoma + ___________.
mcqs.explanation: A pineoblastoma occurring in a child with bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma is called "trilateral retinoblastoma." In hereditary retinoblastoma (having spontaneous germline RB1 mutation), second malignancies are a major concern. The most common second malignancy is osteosarcoma; other second neoplasms include rhabdomyosarcoma and melanoma.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Tumor which may undergo spontaneous regression is ______.
mcqs.explanation: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal cancer of the peripheral sympathetic nervous system with heterogeneous presentation and prognosis; some tumors may undergo spontaneous regression, whereas some may be unresponsive to therapy and run a very aggressive course .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following pediatric tumors is called a "triphasic" blastoma?
mcqs.explanation: • The classic nephroblastoma, aka Wilms tumor, is a mixed tumor (more than one neoplastic cell type ) derived from one germ-cell layer (examples : Wilms tumor and pleomorphic adenoma of salivary gland). • Histologically , it is made up of the classic "triphasic" combination (recapitulating stages of normal renal development ) of • Stromal • Epithelial , and • Blast cells690

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic because of walking difficulties . His mother says he has always walked on his toes and walks by tilting side -to-side . He also has progressive muscle weakness . There is no history of trauma, fever, or rash. On examination, calf hypertrophy with atrophied thigh muscles is noted as shown below . There is no tenderness on palpation . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The finding of enlarged calf muscles and atrophied thigh muscles with a history of muscle weakness and waddling gait are suggestive of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disease . It is an X-linked recessive disorder. In DMD, pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles which occurs due to muscle enlargement by the infiltration of fat. It is paradoxically weak, unlike the muscle that enlarges due to hypertrophy . Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles is the characteristic feature of DMD, whereas the other 3 conditions mentioned in the options do not have this feature . Clinical features : • Progressive weakness with developmental delay • Pseudohypertrophy of calves • Wasting of thigh muscles • Characteristic Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle . • Gower's sign • Dilated cardiomyopathy Diagnosis: • Elevated serum creatine kinase levels • Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for dystrophin gene697 • If PCR is normal , but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done. Treatment includes supportive management for cardiac decompensation , nutritional management, physiotherapy , and glucocorticoids. Death usually occurs by 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration. Note - The FDA has approved Vamorolone , a novel corticosteroid for the treatment of DMD. The drug offers enhanced anti-inflammatory properties and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism as well . It is potentially a safer and more effective alternative to glucocorticoids . Other options : Option B: Myotonic dystrophy presents with distal muscle weakness , proximal muscle involvement is very late . Option C: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), type 1 (which is most common) presents in infancy. Death occurs early. Option D: Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy presents with predominant involvement of scapular and humeral muscles . The given question describes the involvement of lower limb muscles . Hence , Emery–Dreifuss dystrophy, in this case, is less likely.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The image below shows the model of a skeletal muscle fiber. Which of the following structures is affected in Duchenne muscular dystrophy ?
mcqs.explanation: The structure marked as B in the image represents dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), which is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene . This gene is located on the short arm of chromosome X near the p21 locus (Xp21). Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability , which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components .698

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Abhi, a young boy is being evaluated in the ward for proximal muscle weakness . Waddling gait and Gowers sign are observed in this child. Genetic analysis confirms the diagnosis as Duchenne muscular dystrophy . Which of the following is false regarding this patient 's condition?

options.a: It is less severe than Becker's dystrophy
options.b: Tendon reflexes are lost after age
options.c: Gene affected is the largest gene in humans

mcqs.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is more severe than Becker's dystrophy . In DMD, tendon reflexes are lost after age 6. Becker's dystrophy is similar to Duchenne muscular dystrophy with a genetic defect at the same locus (Xp21) but clinically less severe . Gene affected in both is dystrophin , which is the largest gene in humans. Important differences between Duchenne and Becker's muscular dystrophy :Duchenne 's dystrophy Becker's dystrophy Onset Age : 2–3 years Age : 5–15 years Weakness Progressive Variable Intellectual impairmen t Common Uncommon Prognosis Wheelchair dependant by ad olescence Ambulatory till early adult lif e Death By the age of 18–20 years By 40s or 50s

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You observe a six-year-old child in the ward and notice the following . Which of the following are true regarding this sign?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows the Gowers sign. Patients use their hands to "climb up" their legs when asked to rise from a prone position to compensate for proximal lower -extremity weakness . An early Gowers sign is often evident by age of 3 years and is fully expressed by age of 5 or 6 years. This maneuver can be seen in patients with: • Duchenne muscular dystrophy • Becker's muscular dystrophy • Limb -girdle muscular dystrophy • Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy • Polymyositis • Dermatomyositis699

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A concerned mother brought her son to the clinic because of difficulty writing in school. She also says that his eyes remain partially open when he sleeps . There is no history of trauma or surgery. On examination, he has asymmetric wrist and finger weakness . The mouth appears puckered and rounded , deltoid muscles are flattened and the following finding is observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows winging of the scapula , which when combined with this patient 's features are suggestive of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy . Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition that generally presents with asymmetric weakness in facial and shoulder girdle muscles . Occasionally , finger and wrist weakness is the first symptom . The mouth is rounded and appears puckered because of the protruding lips. Upper facial weakness will manifest as an inability to close the eyes completely in sleep . Scapular winging is prominent, even in infants. Flattening or even concavity of the deltoid contour is seen , and the biceps and triceps brachii muscles are wasted and weak. Eventually , proximal muscles get involved and undergo atrophy, and Gowers sign & Trendelenburg gait appear. Lumbar lordosis, foot drop, and kyphoscoliosis are common complications . Treatment includes orthopedic measures for scoliosis and foot drop, surgical intervention for scapular deformity . Physiotherapy has no value. Other options : Long thoracic nerve palsy : No history of trauma or surgery rules out this diagnosis. Klippel -Feil syndrome: Classic triad of Klippel –Feil syndrome (congenital musculoskeletal condition) • low posterior hairline • short neck • decreased cervical range of motion Myotonic dystrophy patients have a characteristic V-shaped upper lip, a history of myotonia, and progressive weakness .700

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old child presents with leg pain. She had fever and cough 3 days prior. Currently, there is pain on palpation of the calf muscles . Reflexes and other clinical examinations are normal . Lab test reveals CK levels of 2000 IU. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical picture showing pain in the calves occuring within a week of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI), with elevated creatine kinase levels suggests the diagnosis of viral myositis. The specific history of URI suggests influenza myositis. Infectious myositis has a male predominance and is typically seen in young adults . Childhood form presents with fever, malaise, and rhinorrhea and is usually followed by severe pain, especially in the calves. The muscle pain is usually worse with movement and the symptoms last for about a week . In children, toe walking and wide -based gait may be seen because of the involvement of the gastrocnemius -soleus muscles . Other viral causes of myositis include HIV -1 (one of the most common causes of myositis), group B coxsackievirus (epidemic myalgia), HTLV -1 (Human T-lymphotropic virus), and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Lab features of influenza myositis include elevated CK which may be as high as 500 times normal the value. Urine myoglobin is usually positive . Detection of the virus with PCR testing of nasopharyngeal specimens can be carried out but is not of much clinical significance . The histopathological examination would reveal muscle fiber necrosis without much inflammatory change. Treatment includes bed rest, IV fluids , and symptomatic management with analgesics and antipyretics. Amantadine and other antiviral agents may be considered in adults . Complications include myocarditis and respiratory dysfunction . Rhabdomyolysis is an uncommon complication.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Rekha brought her 5-day-old infant to the clinic because of feeding difficulties . She says he does not latch properly . Her antenatal history is significant for polyhydramnios and decreased fetal movements. On examination, hypotonia and hyporeflexia are noted in the baby. which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , only Spinal muscular atrophy presents in infancy. The rest present in late childhood . Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a degenerative disease of motor neurons, that is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner . It usually starts in infancy with hypotonia, hyporeflexia , and thin muscle mass (atrophy). Polyhydramnios may be present prenatally due to weakness in swallowing . Diagnosis is done by genetic testing for SMN gene mutation. Muscle biopsy is done for cases with negative genetic testing and strong clinical suspicion . The muscle biopsy in infancy shows a characteristic pattern of perinatal denervation that is unlike that of a mature muscle . Groups of giant type I fibers are mixed with fascicles of severely atrophic fibers . Treatment is symptomatic and supportive . Recent updates : • Nusinersen is an antisense oligonucleotide approved by the FDA for treating SMA. It is administered intrathecally . • Risdiplam (first oral drug) has been approved by FDA to treat infants >2 months of age with SMA. It is an oral splicing modifier that corrects the splicing defect of SMN2, which leads to701 increased levels of full -length SMN protein.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Pinky , a high school girl, has difficulty in combing her hair and climbing up stairs since 6 months. On examination, Gower sign is positive and maculopapular rash present over MCP joints. What is the next appropriate investigation to be done?
mcqs.explanation: A maculopapular rash over the metacarpophalangeal joints is indicative of Gottron papules in a child with proximal muscle weakness is suggestive of juvenile dermatomyositis . As it is an inflammatory myopathy , the next investigation is serum creatine kinase. Though the gold standard investigation is a muscle biopsy , it is indicated only when the diagnosis is in doubt or when grading of the disease severity is required. Nerve conduction studies are usually normal unless associated with severe muscle necrosis and atrophy. Electromyography would show the characteristic signs of myopathy and muscle fiber necrosis but is preferably performed in a specialized center .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 1-day-old girl is being evaluated for decreased muscle tone. On examination, thin cheeks , high arched palate , inverted V -shaped upper lip, and a narrow head are observed. Facial muscle wasting is prominent. She has a club foot deformity . Her mother has a history of delayed relaxation of hand muscles after opening doors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The patient 's clinical features along with the history of myotonia in the mother are suggestive of Myotonic dystrophy . Facial weakness , inverted V -shaped upper lip, and loss of muscle mass in the temporal fossae are characteristic of myotonic muscular dystrophy . A severe congenital form of myotonic dystrophy appears in infants born to mothers with symptomatic myotonic dystrophy . It is inherited as an autosomal-dominant trait. Clinical features include : • Skeletal deformities (clubfoot deformities alone or congenital contractures involving many joints and can even include the cervical spine ). • Generalized hypotonia and weakness at birth • Facial wasting and weakness • Inverted V -shaped upper lip • Loss of muscle mass in the temporal fossa Infants can require gavage feeding or ventilator support for respiratory muscle weakness or apnea. Other Options : Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), type 1 (which is most common) presents in infancy with hypotonia but has no facial features that are present in this child. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy , the baby appears normal at birth and the facial features present in this child are not seen . Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy presents with predominant involvement of scapular and humeral muscles . The given scenario makes this diagnosis less likely.702

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A small baby who was being evaluated for multiple bone fractures with minor trauma is found to have brittle bone disease . Which of the following is false regarding this disease?

options.a: It is caused by defects in type 2 collagen .
options.c: Blue sclerae and deafness may be associated .
options.d: Biphosphonates are useful in the treatment.

mcqs.explanation: Brittle bone disease is another name for osteogenesis imperfecta (OI). It is due to defects in type 1 collagen , not type 2 collagen . There are 12 types of OI, with type 1 being the most common. Triad of fragile bones, blue sclera, and deafness is known as van der Hoeve syndrome. Treatment includes bisphosphonate therapy and orthopedic rehabilitation.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All of the following are radiological signs of scurvy except _________.
mcqs.explanation: White line of Frankel, ground-glass appearance , and zone of rarefaction are the radiological signs seen in scurvy. Radiological signs in scurvy includes : • White line of Frankel: calcified cartilage at metaphyses • Trummerfeld zone: lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line • Pelkan spur: lateral prolongation of the white line, which is present at the cortical ends • Wimberger ring sign: circular, opaque radiologic shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with anemia and hepatosplenomegaly . X-ray imaging done as a part of the skeletal survey showed the following image. What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Anemia and hepatosplenomegaly in an infant with the X-ray image showing dense bones, and bone within the bone appearance is suggestive of osteopetrosis . Osteopetrosis /Marble bone disease /Albers–Sch\366nberg disease It is a disorder involving defective bone resorption due to mutation of CLCN7 in osteoclasts .703 Clinical features include macrocephaly, developmental delay , anemia (reduced bone marrow cavity), and hepatosplenomegaly (compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis ). Low serum calcium and phosphorus levels with elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH ) and normal vitamin D levels are observed. Radiological features include diffuse bone sclerosis with clubbing of metaphyses . Bone within the bone appearance and "sandwich" appearance of the vertebral bodies can be seen (image). Treatment is symptomatic . Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be done in severe cases . Achondroplasia usually presents with pulmonary symptoms like dyspnea , obstructive sleep apnea, and recurrent infections . In both scurvy and osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), the child cries on touching . On radiography, certain typical features are seen in scurvy, while multiple fractures are seen in OI.704

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Most common rheumatic disease in children is _______.
mcqs.explanation: The most common rheumatic disease in children is juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA ). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis represents a heterogeneous group of chronic disorders characterized by • Arthritis* in \0341 joint • Age at onset : <16 years • Duration of disease : \0346 weeks *Arthritis clinically defined as swelling or effusion , or the presence of 2 or more of the following signs: • limitation of range of motion • tenderness or pain on motion • increased heat712

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are evaluating JIA patients in a pediatric rheumatology clinic. As per the ILAR criteria, which of the following patients would you not include under JIA ?

options.c: A 18-year-old with RF negative Polyarthritis first diagnosed 3 years back

mcqs.explanation: Reactive arthritis is not a subtype of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis(JIA ) so you would not include this subset of patients under your evaluation. ILAR (International League of Associations for Rheumatology ) defines JIA as arthritis of one or more joints with onset below 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks . The subtypes of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA ):- • Oligoarthritis (4 or lesser joints) (Most common type ) • Polyarthritis (5 or more joints) • RF Positive • RF Negative • Systemic JIA • Psoriatic arthritis • Enthesitis -related arthritis • Undifferentiated

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Mohit is brought to the pediatrician by his mother because of red-eye . He complains of blurring of vision and on examination, the pupil appears as shown in the picture . Which of the following subtype of JIA is associated with the highest risk for the ophthalmic complication noted in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The patient has red-eye and the blurring of vision along with the finding of the irregular pupil , which is suggestive of uveitis. ANA-positive oligoarthritis is associated with the highest risk for uveitis in patients with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis. The presence of a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) confers increased risk for uveitis in children with JIA and requires periodic slit-lamp examination every 3 months.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A worried mother brings her 4-year-old girl who has been complaining about pain in the joints of arms and legs for 2 months. On examination, multiple nodules over the bony prominences suggestive of rheumatoid nodules are noted . On investigation, RA-factor was found positive pointing to the diagnosis of RF-positive polyarthritis. Which of the following complication is not likely to occur in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Ankylosis is not seen in patients with RF-positive Polyarthritis. Polyarthritis is characterized by inflammation of \0345 joints in both upper and lower extremities . Rheumatoid factor (RF)–positive polyarthritis resembles the characteristic symmetric presentation of adult rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid nodules on the extensor surfaces of the elbows , spine , and over the Achilles tendons are associated with a more severe course and almost exclusively occur in RF-positive individuals. Complications may include : • Micrognathia (due to chronic temporomandibular joint disease ) • Cervical spine involvement, manifesting as decreased neck extension , occurs with a risk of atlantoaxial subluxation and neurologic sequelae . • Hip disease may be subtle , with findings of erosion.713

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis?
mcqs.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA ) factor is negative in systemic JIA . It is positive in a subtype of polyarthritic type of JIA . Systemic JIA is characterized by a fever of at least 2 weeks and Arthritis in 1 or more joints + at least one of • Evanescent erythematous rash • Prominent visceral involvement, including hepatosplenomegaly • Generalized lymphadenopathy • Serositis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Anuj, a school-going kid has been brought to the pediatric OPD by his mother with complaints of fever for 3 weeks . She says her son has been skipping school because of the fever but in the evening he gets better and plays with his siblings. She also noticed a rash that appears along with fever and disappears spontaneously . He has a history of joint pain on and off since pre-school . On examination, generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are noted along with an evanescent erythematous rash on the trunk. Which of the following characteristically defines the fever associated with this child's condition?
mcqs.explanation: The patient has clinical features of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA ), which is associated with quotidian fever. Quotidian fever - fever that rises to 39\260C (102 .2\260F) once a day and returns to 37\260C (98.6\260F) between fever peaks Systemic JIA is characterized by a fever of at least 2 weeks and Arthritis in 1 or more joints + at least one of • Evanescent erythematous rash that is non-pruritic and migratory with lesions lasting<1 hr. • Prominent visceral involvement, including hepatosplenomegaly • Generalized lymphadenopathy • Serositis

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Aarav is a known case of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA ). He is referred to a Rheumatology specialist center from a local hospital , when his condition started deteriorating on steroid treatment . On examination, the patient has lymphadenopathy , hepatosplenomegaly , and purpura along with the acute onset of high spiking fevers. Vitals show persistent hypotension (85/45 mmHg), tachycardia (160/min), and oliguria. He was urgently admitted into the PICU. The resident physician is confused between macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and JIA flare-up. Which of the following is best suited to distinguish these two ?
mcqs.explanation: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is characterized by all of the listed features . However, the diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow biopsy demonstrating hemophagocytosis and is the best test to distinguish MAS from a flare-up of JIA . MAS is a rare but potentially fatal complication of systemic JIA . It is characterized by an uncontrolled activation and proliferation of T lymphocytes and macrophages . It is the result of a cytokine storm that leads to a dysregulated inflammatory activation of the immune system , with rapid progression to multiorgan failure if not promptly diagnosed and properly treated . It is characterized by the following : • Macrophage hemophagocytosis in the bone marrow • Hypofibrinogenemia (paradoxical fall in erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]) • Hypertriglyceridemia714 • Extreme hyperferritinemia • Fever >38.5\260C • Splenomegaly • Cytopenia affecting at least two of three cell lineages Treatment usually includes high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents in refractory cases .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A mother brought her 12 -day old baby to the OPD due to the rash shown in the picture for the last 5 days. The mother says the rash gets worse in the sun. The infant was born at home and she never had a prenatal check-up. She herself has a history of joint pains and a facial rash which she says is "no big deal ". On examination, Vitals are normal for the baby. A subsequent ECG shows P wave rate 120 /min and R wave rate at 70/min with no relation between the two . Which of the following antibodies will be used to diagnose this baby's condition?
mcqs.explanation: The baby has raccoon eyes (periorbital rash) with complete heart block (P-R dissociation ) suggestive of neonatal lupus erythematosus (NLE). Anti-Ro antibodies are used to diagnose neonatal lupus . Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus (NLE): NLE is not an autoimmune condition. It occurs when maternal autoantibodies enter the fetal circulation (passive transfer). The antibodies responsible for this condition are anti-Ro antibody (anti-SSA) and anti-La antibody (anti-SSB). The periorbital rash typically appears within 6 weeks of life and lasts 3-4 months. However, it can be present at birth. Infants may also have cytopenias and hepatitis , but the most feared complication is congenital heart block. Cardiomyopathy is seen in the most severe cases . The noncardiac manifestations of neonatal lupus are usually reversible, whereas congenital heart block is permanent. Conduction system abnormalities can be detected in utero by fetal echocardiogram beginning at 16 weeks of gestational age . Fluorinated corticosteroids seem to improve cases of hydrops . Significant conduction system abnormalities after birth are treated with cardiac pacing and occasionally intravenous immunoglobulin and steroids , while severe cardiomyopathy may require cardiac transplantation. Transient, noncardiac manifestations are conservatively managed, with topical steroids used occasionally to treat the rash. Other options : Anti-Jo antibodies are a type of myositis-specific antibodies . These are not related to neonatal lupus . Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for SLE (Systemic Lupus erythematosus ). Anti-histone antibodies are present in Drug-induced SLE. Note : SS in SSA and SSB stands for Sj\366gren's syndrome-related . Anti-SSA and anti SSB are antinuclear antibodies and are mainly found in patients with SLE and Sj\366gren's syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Vikas , a high school student is observed to have an indented 'en coup de sabre' lesion as shown in the image below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: En coup de sabre lesion is seen in juvenile localized scleroderma (morphea).715 It appears as an indented , vertical, colourless , line of skin on the forehead . The indentation looks as though the person may have been struck (coup ) by a sword (sabre). This lesion involves the scalp and/or face and often extend into the central nervous system , resulting in neurologic sequelae such as seizures and headaches.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old boy has swelling of knee joints and non-blanching rashes as seen in the picture . Urine exam reveals haematuria +++ and proteinuria +. Platelet levels are normal . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario showing swelling of knee joints (arthritis), non-blanching rash in the lower limbs (palpable purpura), along with hematuria and proteinuria (renal involvement) in a child is suggestive of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP). HSP (IgA vasculitis) is a small vessel vasculitis most commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. It generally follows an upper respiratory tract infection and there is a history of atopy in one-third of the cases . The pathology of HSP involves leukocytoclastic vasculitis and the deposition of IgA in the affected blood vessels . IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy . Clinical manifestations include palpable purpura, the hallmark feature of HSP, which characteristically involves the extensor surfaces of arms and legs . Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthritis and arthralgia are common. Gastrointestinal symptoms can include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding . Renal involvement may lead to gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic syndrome, or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults . A rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis is seen in some cases . Nephritis usually follows the appearance of the rash. Diagnosis of HSP is primarily based on clinical findings, including the palpable purpura, along with the presence of other symptoms . Laboratory tests are not specific to HSP but may show nonspecific markers of inflammation and sometimes elevated levels of IgA. Imaging studies and biopsies of affected tissues can provide additional diagnostic information Treatment of HSP is generally supportive, focusing on hydration, pain relief , and nutrition. Corticosteroids may be used in severe cases or for significant gastrointestinal involvement. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG ) and plasma exchange are occasionally employed for severe disease . Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine. Complications of HSP can include serious gastrointestinal problems , kidney disease , and recurrences , but overall, the prognosis for childhood HSP is favorable. Regular monitoring of blood pressure and urine is recommended to detect and manage potential complications .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Pinky , a small child with Kawasaki disease is admitted to the ward for treatment . Which of the following feature would you not expect to see in her?
mcqs.explanation: Purulent conjunctivitis is not a feature of Kawasaki disease . Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival infection with limbal sparing is characteristically seen in Kawasaki disease . Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and is commonly seen in children between 3 months to 5 years of age .716

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A worried father brought her 5-year-old son to the pediatrician with a history of fever, rash, irritability, and poor feeding . A few days back, he developed perianal desquamation and non-purulent conjunctivitis with edema of the hands and feet . He has been up to date with his immunization . Tongue findings are shown in the image. Which of the following is not likely to occur in the child?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical features are suggestive of Kawasaki disease . Thrombocytosis is a characteristic finding in Kawasaki disease and commonly occurs in the second week . Important laboratory findings of Kawasaki disease are anemia, elevated ESR, and CRP. Major complications of Kawasaki disease are arteritis and aneurysms of coronary vessels , myocarditis, myocardial infarction, and pericarditis.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Nisha presents to the clinic with clinical features suggestive of Kawasaki disease . She was admitted to the ward for treatment . Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Treatment of choice in Kawaski disease is IV immunoglobulins. IV immunoglobulins along with aspirin have proven beneficial in preventing coronary artery abnormalities.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Who among the following children with Kawasaki's disease is at greatest risk for coronary aneurysms?

options.a: 8 year-old girl with 6 days of high fever and strawberry tongue
options.b: 5-year-old boy with 8 days of fever and CSF pleocytosis
options.c: 2-year-old girl with IVIG treatment at 7th day of fever
options.d: 11 -year-old boy with 15 days of fever and low PCV

mcqs.explanation: An 11 -year-old boy with 15 days of fever and low PCV is at the greatest risk for coronary aneurysms. Risk factors for coronary aneurysms in Kawasaki's disease : • Age younger than 1 year or older than 9 years • Male sex • Fever \03414 days • Hematocrit(PCV) <35 percent • Serum sodium concentration <135 mEq/L • White blood cell count >12,000 /mm3 • Elevated ESR and CRP Administration of IVIG during the first 10 days of illness reduces the prevalence of coronary aneurysms fivefold .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy comes to the clinic complaining about recurrent painful oral ulcers as shown in the picture . He also experiences repeated episodes of eye redness and pain which subsides with medication. On examination, similar ulcers are seen on his genitals . Beh\347et disease is suspected . Which of the following feature would you not expect to see in this patient ?

options.d: Tender red nodules on the legs

mcqs.explanation: Behcet disease is not associated with nail fold capillary abnormalities which is typically seen in systemic sclerosis . Behcet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers , genital ulcers , and uveitis. Other skin findings include erythema nodosa (red tender nodules on legs ) and positive pathergy test (Pustular reaction, 24-48 hrs after sterile needle puncture or normal saline injection).717 There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations , with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms. Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation in children. Pulmonary aneurysms are the most severe feature of pediatric BD. It is associated with HLA subtype B51. T helper 17(Th17) cells play an important contribution in the recruitment of neutrophils , which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.718

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the predominant site of hematopoiesis in a 20 -weeks old fetus ?
mcqs.explanation: The liver is the predominant site of hematopoiesis in the fetus during mid-pregnancy. Sites of hematopoiesis :724 • 2–6 weeks - yolk sac (mesoblastic phase) • 8–24 weeks - liver (hepatic phase ) • 28 weeks onwards- bone marrow (myeloid phase ) Note : There is some overlap between the different phases of hematopoiesis . The ranges given above refer to the predominant site of hematopoiesis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Electrophoresis and globin gene sequencing are performed on a normal embryo's blood sample as a part of hematology research. Which of the following type of hemoglobin is likely to be present ?
mcqs.explanation: Hb Portland is likely to be present as it is embryonic hemoglobin . Gower-I (\0202\0172), Gower-II (\0322\0172), and Hb Portland (\0202\0232) are called embryonic hemoglobins and are seen at 8 weeks of intrauterine life. HbM Iwate (option A) and Hb Auckland (option C) and HbM Boston (option D) result from globin mutations that stabilize iron in the ferric state , leading to congenital methemoglobinemia .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: When does hemoglobin synthesis switch from HbF to HbA?
mcqs.explanation: Hemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA at 38 weeks of intrauterine life . Hemoglobin types at various periods : • Chromosome 16 contains alpha (\032) gene cluster (3 genes ): • zeta (\020) • alpha 1 (\0321) • alpha 2 (\0322) • Chromosome 11contains beta (\031) gene cluster (5 genes ): • epsilon (\017) • 2 gamma(\023) • delta (\025) • beta (\031) Changes in globin subunits from embryo to early infancy:Time Major hemoglobin 8th week of intrauterine life : Embryonic hemoglobins , Go wer-1(\0202 \0172), Gower-2 (\0322\0172), and Portland(\0202\0232) are forme d 9th week to birth Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) (\0322\023 2) is the major hemoglobin725 Time Major hemoglobin 24th week HbF constitutes 90% of the t otal hemoglobin 38 weeks The switch to the nearly excl usive synthesis of adult hemo globin (HbA; \0322\0312) At birth HbF constitutes 70% of the t otal hemoglobin 6 month adult pattern HbA > 95%, Hb A2 < 3.5%, HbF < 2.5%

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Hemoglobin fractions were analyzed in a neonate with a family history of sickle cell disease . The test shows elevated levels of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Which of the following is true about HbF?

options.a: HbF accounts for 100 % of the total hemoglobin at term.
options.b: HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation.
options.c: HbF has lower affinity for oxygen than HbA.
options.d: HbF has higher affinity for 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate than HbA.

mcqs.explanation: HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation. Elevated levels of HbF are seen in sickle cell disease and \031-thalassemia , where there is a mutation of the \031 globin gene . Increased HbF levels persist in childhood and later. Properties of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) • HbF is resistant to alkali denaturation. • This property forms the basis of the alkali denaturation test (or Apt test ) to detect the presence of fetal blood in maternal circulation in suspected feto -maternal hemorrhage. • The Kleihauer –Betke test (or acid elution test ) is used to quantitate the amount of feto -maternal hemorrhage to calculate the dosage of anti-D required in Rh-negative mothers. • HBF accounts for 70% of the hemoglobin at term. • Increased HbF can be seen in hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin , sickle cell anemia, beta-thalassemia , HbC disease , and HbE disease726 • HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen . • This allows for gas exchange from maternal circulation by binding to oxygen at a relatively low oxygen tension in the maternal blood supplying the chorion. • HbF has lower affinity for 2,3 bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) than HbA. • Lack of interaction between HbF and 2,3 BPG increases the affinity of HbF to oxygen .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are measuring the life span of RBCs in a normal neonate using chromium-labeled erythrocyte studies as a part of a research project under the clinical hematology department . What would be the result ?
mcqs.explanation: The lifespan of neonatal RBCs is 60-90 days. The short lifespan of neonatal RBCs is the cause for rapid fall in hematocrit immediately after birth. The highest hematocrit during a person's lifetime occurs at birth, and the lowest occurs about 10 weeks later. The lifespan of RBCs in preterm infants is 35-50 days. The average lifespan of RBCs in adults is 120 days.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A concerned mother brings her preschool child to you. She states that her child was fine until yesterday night and now is covered with bruises and purple dots , which she had noticed while changing his clothes in the morning . She informs you that one month back, her child had a cough and cold. Findings on physical examination are normal , other than petechiae and purpura. Which of the following is most likely to be seen while investigating this child?
mcqs.explanation: An otherwise well -baby with acute onset of petechiae and purpura with a preceding history of viral infection 1 to 4 weeks prior to the onset of thrombocytopenia is a classical presentation of (autoimmune) idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. Prolonged bleeding time is a feature of ITP . The most common cause of acute onset of thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well -child is (autoimmune) idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP ). ITP is a bleeding disorder and has prolonged bleeding time, low platelet count, and normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time [PT] and activated partial thromboplastin time [aPTT]). ITP has an acute presentation with a self -limited course in children. Features of ITP : • Commonly affects children between 1-4 years • Preceded by a viral infection • Mucocutaneous bleeding • Ecchymoses and petechiae • Wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) • Retinal hemorrhages • Bleeding into the CNS, which may be life -threatening • Hepatomegaly , splenomegaly , and lymphadenopathy , fever, jaundice are absent • Resolves spontaneously in 80% of the cases in 4-6 weeks .727 Laboratory features of ITP : • Thrombocytopenia (commonly <20,000 /�ML) • Normal/Increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow • Prolonged bleeding time • Normal tests for coagulation (PT/aPTT /INR ) • Eosinophilia and lymphocytosis common • Peripheral smear is normal • Bone marrow biopsy shows megakaryocytes

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pediatrician sees a child in the OPD. He has bruising, petechiae , and occasional minor epistaxis, which has very little interference with his daily activities. Based on further workup, he diagnoses the child as a case of mild ITP . How will he manage this child?

options.c: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin

mcqs.explanation: Other than education , counseling , and watchful expectancy , no therapy is needed for patients with mild ITP. Classification system for ITP : • No symptoms . • Mild symptoms - bruising and petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis which has very little interference with daily living. • Moderate symptoms - more severe skin and mucosal lesions , more troublesome epistaxis , and menorrhagia. • Severe symptoms - bleeding episodes - menorrhagia, epistaxis , and melena - requiring transfusions or hospitalization, symptoms interfering seriously with quality of life . Treatment of ITP : • Mild to moderate bleeding symptoms - watchful expectancy , education , and counseling . • Platelet count < 30,000 + risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)- oral glucocorticoids / intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG ) or IV anti-D • Severe bleeding symptoms - IV methylprednisolone \261 IVIG or IV anti-D • Life-threatening bleeding (eg . intracranial hemorrhage)- platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or IV anti-D Note : The role of splenectomy in ITP should be reserved for 2 circumstances : • The older child (\0344 yr) with severe ITP that has lasted >1 year (chronic ITP ) and whose symptoms are not easily controlled with therapy • When life -threatening hemorrhage (ICH) complicates acute ITP and the platelet count cannot be corrected rapidly with transfusion of platelets and administration of IVIG and corticosteroids .728

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Veena, an adolescent girl has had recurrent episodes of bleeding from her nose and gums. She also gives a history of heavy menstrual bleeding and repeated blood transfusions. Her bleeding time is deranged and flow cytometry reveals markedly decreased CD41 and CD61 expression . A defect in which of the following is most likely seen in her?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Glanzmann 's thrombasthenia which is characterized by defective platelet aggregation . Decreased CD41 (GPIIb ) and CD61 (GPIIIa ) expression are diagnostic of Glanzmann 's thrombasthenia. Bleeding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia is quite severe and is typically mucocutaneous , including epistaxis , gingival, and GI bleeding . Bernard -Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are severe congenital disorders of platelet function. Patients usually present with petechiae and purpura at birth. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometric analysis of the patient 's platelet glycoproteins .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common congenital bleeding disorder?
mcqs.explanation: Von Willebrand disease (VWD ) is the most common congenital bleeding disorder. VWD is thought to affect approximately 0.1- 1% of the population . It is due to abnormal von Willebrand factor (VWF ). VWF is an adhesive protein that acts as a bridge between subendothelial collagen and platelets . It also binds and protects the circulating factor VIII from rapid clearance in circulation. Von Willebrand disease is mostly inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (rarely autosomal recessive ). The types of disease include quantitatively deficient vWF (partial = type 1 or absolute = type 3) or qualitatively abnormal vWF (type 2 = dysproteinemia ). The majority (~ 80%) have type 1 disease . Hemophilia A (factor 8 deficiency ) occurs in 1 in 5,000 males. Hemophilia B (factor 9 deficiency ) occurs in approximately 1 in 25,000 males.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Shortly after birth through normal vaginal delivery , a neonate develops petechiae and purpura. You suspect bleeding disorder and send samples for further workup. A prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal aPTT is seen along with large platelets in the peripheral smear. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Bernard –Soulier syndrome is the likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario. The presence of petechiae and purpura at birth, especially after vaginal delivery , along with prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal aPTT are seen in qualitative platelet defect disorders like Bernard -Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann 's thrombasthenia. The presence of large platelets rules out Glanzmann 's thrombasthenia. Evans syndrome is an autoimmune hemolytic disorder with thrombocytopenia . Von Willebrand's disease doesn 't usually manifest at birth. Bernard –Soulier syndrome is an autosomal recessive functional/qualitative platelet disorder. It is characterized by the deficiency of Gp Ib-IX receptor causing defective platelet adhesion. It is due to genetic mutations in the genes forming the GPIb complex of glycoproteins Ib \032 , Ib\031, V , and IX. Laboratory parameters: • Normal platelet count (or mild thrombocytopenia ) • Large platelets (megathrombocytes ) with dense granules729 • Bleeding time abnormally prolonged • Platelet aggregation tests are normal (with collagen , adenosine diphosphate [ADP], epinephrine ) • Ristocetin aggregation test is abnormal /no response • von Willebrand factor (vWF ) levels are normal .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A panicked father brings his adopted daughter to your OPD with complaints of bleeding gums. Hematological investigations reveal a normal platelet count and a prolonged bleeding time. The ristocetin -aggregation test was abnormal . Which of the following would you include in your differential diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The ristocetin -aggregation test is abnormal in both von Willebrand disease and Bernard –Soulier syndrome. All of the above diseases are inherited bleeding disorders affecting platelet function. Hence, there is prolonged bleeding time but platelet levels are not significantly affected . Platelet aggregation tests use a panel of platelet agonists (adenosine diphosphate [ADP], epinephrine , collagen , and ristocetin ) to measure platelet activation and aggregation in vitro . Ristocetin induces the binding of VWF to platelets and agglutinates platelets . Bernard -Soulier syndrome, a severe congenital platelet function disorder, is caused by an absence or severe deficiency of the VWF receptor on the platelet membrane. Hence , in Bernard –Soulier syndrome, no response (or no aggregation) is seen with ristocetin . The ristocetin -aggregation test is also abnormal in von Willebrand disease . However, it normalizes after the addition of normal plasma (which contains vWF ) since there is no defect in binding receptors .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An ENT surgeon refers a child who had developed prolonged bleeding post -tonsillectomy to the hematology department for evaluation. Workup revealed a qualitative defect in the von Willebrand factor. Which of the following disease is more likely in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand disease (VWD ) and a qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (VWF ) is seen in type 2 VWD . Features of VWD : • Most common type is Type 1 • Most severe type is Type 3 • Most common inheritance: Autosomal dominant • Type 1- partial quantitative deficiency of VWF • Type 2- qualitative deficiency of VWF • Type 3- complete quantitative deficiency of VWF There is no type 4 VWD . Characteristics of the subtypes of VWD are summarized below : AD: autosomal dominant AR: autosomal recessive730 Type Inheritan ce Mechanism Important characteristics 1 AD Partial, quantitative deficienc y of VWF Most common type 3 AR Complete quantitative deficie ncy Most severe VWD 2A AD Loss of VWF multimers (incr eased cleavage by ADAMS13) Platelet adhesion defect 2B AD Increased binding of VWF to platelets causing VWF -platele t complex destruction Thrombo -cytopenia 2M AD Decreased affinity of VWF to platelets Platelet adhesion defect , very rare 2N AR Decreased affinity of VWF to Factor VIII Autosomal hemophilia

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which type of von Willebrand disease is associated with thrombocytopenia ?
mcqs.explanation: von Willebrand disease associated with thrombocytopenia is Type 2B . Pseudo -VWD : VWF is normal , but platelet has increased affinity to VWF ; it presents in a manner similar to VWD 2B with thrombocytopenia .Type Inhe rit Mechanism Important characteristics 1 AD Partial, quantitative deficienc y of VWF Most common type 3 AR Complete quantitative deficie ncy Most severe VWD 2A AD Loss of VWF multimers (incr eased cleavage by ADAMS13) Platelet adhesion defect 2B AD Increased binding of VWF to platelets causing VWF -platele t complex destruction Thrombocytopenia 2M AD Decreased affinity of VWF to platelets Platelet adhesion defect , very rare 2N AR Decreased affinity of VWF to Factor VIII Autosomal hemophilia

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pediatric resident administers 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione intramuscularly to all newborn infants in the ward. Deficiency of which of the following factors is prevented by this medication?
mcqs.explanation: 731 Intramuscular injection of 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione is given to all newborn infants because it prevents the deficiency of factor VII that occurs transiently after birth. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn is caused by a transient deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors, factors II , VII , IX, and X. Causes include : • Lack of free vitamin K from the mother • Absence of the bacterial intestinal flora normally responsible for the synthesis of vitamin K. It is responsive to and prevented by vitamin K therapy (0.5-1 mg of phytonadione ).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The most common bleeding manifestation seen in severe hemophilia is _____________.
mcqs.explanation: Recurrent hemarthrosis is the most common bleeding manifestation of severe hemophilia . Hemophilia is said to be severe when the residual activity of factor VIII is <1%. Clinical features of hemophilia : • Clinically, hemophilia A and B are indistinguishable . • It presents early in life - bleeding after circumcision or when beginning to walk or crawl. • Most common bleeding manifestation in severe hemophilia is recurrent hemarthrosis and the most common joint affected is the knee. • Acute hemarthrosis- local pain, swelling , and erythema ; muscle contractures due to fixed positioning. • Chronic hemarthrosis- synovial thickening and synovitis in response to intraarticular blood. • Muscle hematomas can lead to compartment syndromes. • Hematuria is common but self -limited . • Life-threatening bleeding - bleeding to oropharyngeal spaces , CNS, and retroperitoneum .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following factor deficiencies are matched to the correct disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The correct match is factor XI deficiency and hemophilia C. Clotting factor deficiencies and associated disorders: Factor V— parahemophilia Factor VIII — classic hemophilia , hemophilia A Factor IX— Christmas disease , hemophilia B Factor X— Stuart-Prower disease Factor XI— hemophilia C732

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Dinesh, a 2-year-old boy presented with a painful left ankle swelling and difficulty walking. In the past, he had presented with significant hematomas at immunization sites . On investigation, he was found to have haemophilia A. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The treatment of choice for hemophilia A is factor replacement therapy with factor VIII concentrate . Cryoprecipitate is used when factor concentrates are not available. Each bag of cryoprecipitate contains 80 IU of factor VIII .Blood components Composition Indications Factor VIII concentrates Factor VIII Hemophilia A Factor IX concentrates Factor IX Hemophilia B Cryoprecipitate FibrinogenFactor XIIIFactor VIIIvon Willebrand factor Fibrinogen deficiency ,Factor XIII deficiency ,von Willebran d disease Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) Coagulation factorsProtein C Protein SAntithrombin Deficiency of prothrombin,Fa ctor V ,Factor VII ,Factor X,Fa ctor XI Prothrombin complex concen trates (PCCs) ProthrombinFactor VIIFactor IXFactor X Deficiency of prothrombin,Fa ctor VII ,Factor X

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A grandmother has noticed that her granddaughter 's umbilical stump hasn't fallen off even after 4 weeks . On examination, the pediatrician notices mild bruising. Which of the following clotting factor deficiencies should he suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: Delayed separation of the umbilical stump beyond 4 weeks is a characteristic finding seen in factor XIII deficiency . However, these findings can also be seen in septicemia or local infections . Factor XIII is responsible for the crosslinking of fibrin to stabilize the fibrin clot, symptoms of delayed hemorrhage are secondary to the instability of the clot. Typically , patients have trauma one day and then have a bruise or hematoma the next day. Results of the usual screening tests for hemostasis are normal in patients with factor XIII deficiency . Screening tests for factor XIII deficiency are based on the observation that there is increased solubility of the clot because of the failure of cross-linking.733

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: As a part of the Anemia Mukt Bharat program, you screen preschool children for anemia. What Hb values would prompt you to diagnose anemia in this age group?
mcqs.explanation: Anaemia in a preschool child is defined as a hemoglobin level of <11 g/dL. Preschool age is defined as 2 to 5 years.742 WHO cut-offs for the diagnosis of anaemia:Age Hemoglobin (g/ dL) 6 months to 5years <11 5 to 11 years <11 .5 12 to14 years <12 Non-pregnant women (\03415 ye ars) <12 Pregnant women <11 Men (\03415 years) <13

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old child is brought to the pediatric OPD by his parents with complaints of excessive sleepiness , and poor scholastic performance. On examination, the child has pallor involving the tongue , conjunctiva, and nail beds . A flow murmur is heard upon auscultation . Which of the following is the most likely cause of the underlying disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical signs and symptoms are suggestive of anemia. Acquired hypoproliferative anemia, is the most common cause of anemia in children among the given options . Iron -deficiency anemia (which is classified as an acquired hypoproliferative anemia) is the most common cause of anemia in children and adults worldwide . Iron deficiency is also the most common nutrient deficiency worldwide.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding iron?

options.a: Breast milk has higher iron content than cow's milk.
options.b: Cow's milk has higher oral bio-availability of iron than breast milk.
options.c: Introduction of cow's milk at 5 months of age decreases the risk of iron deficiency .
options.d: Cow's milk protein can cause chronic intestinal blood loss in infants.

mcqs.explanation: Exposure to whole cow's milk protein can cause chronic intestinal blood loss in infants. Therefore, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends delaying the introduction of cow's milk in infancy and limiting it to <700 mL /day. Both cow's milk and breast milk have the same iron content (\0370.1mg/dL). The bioavailability of breast milk iron is 2-3 times higher than cow's milk iron. Exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months of age and complementary feeding with iron-rich foods thereafter reduces the risk of iron-deficiency anemia in infants.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 8-year-old child who has been recently diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia is started on iron therapy . What is the earliest hematological response that you would expect to see following treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia is the earliest hematological response observed following iron therapy in iron-deficiency anemia. Responses to iron therapy in iron deficiency anemia:743 Time after administration Response 12 to 24 h Subjective improvements - de creased irritability, increased appetite 36 to 48 h Bone marrow response - eryth roid hyperplasia 48 to 72 h (peaks at 5-7 days) Reticulocytosis 4 to 30 days Increase in hemoglobin level 1 to 3 months Repletion of stores (ferritin)

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child who was diagnosed 3 months back with iron deficiency anemia presents with low hemoglobin despite being on oral iron therapy . What is the most likely cause for the non-responsiveness that you should consider in your differential ?

options.c: Occult blood loss from parasitic infestations .

mcqs.explanation: Poor compliance is the most likely cause of non-responsiveness to oral iron therapy . Differential diagnosis of microcytic anemia that fails to respond to oral iron: • Poor compliance (most common cause) • Incorrect dose or formulation • Malabsorption of administered iron • Ongoing blood loss, including gastrointestinal, menstrual, and pulmonary • Concurrent infection or inflammatory disorder • Concurrent vitamin B12 or folate deficiency • Diagnosis other than iron deficiency • Thalassemias • Hemoglobins C and E disorders • Anemia of chronic disease • Lead poisoning • Sickle thalassemias , hemoglobin SC disease • Iron refractory iron-deficiency anemia (IRIDA )

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following tests can be used to screen a newborn with a family history of sickle cell disease ?
mcqs.explanation: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is used to screen a newborn with a family history of sickle cell disease . Option A: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the confirmatory test for sickle cell anemia Option C: Heel -prick Guthrie test is the neonatal screening test for phenylketonuria . Option D: Tandem mass spectrometry is being used for neonatal screening of inherited metabolic disorders.744

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ravi , an adolescent with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency room with chest pain and respiratory distress . Pulse oximeter shows 85% saturation in room air. Chest X-ray shows new radiodensities . Sputum and blood culture showed no growth . Which of the following are used in the management of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute chest syndrome and all of the above are used in the management. Acute chest syndrome (ACS) refers to a life -threatening pulmonary complication of sickle cell disease . It is diagnosed with the presence of a new radiodensity on chest radiography with any 2 of the following : • Fever • Respiratory distress • Hypoxia • Cough • Chest pain In this case, the child with sickle cell anemia satisfies the above criteria. He presented with chest pain and respiratory distress and his chest X-ray image shows new radiodensities . Most patients with ACS do not have a single identifiable cause . Infection is the most well -known etiology , yet only 30% of ACS episodes will have positive sputum or bronchoalveolar culture . The most common bacterial pathogens implicated are S. pneumoniae , Mycoplasma pneumoniae , and Chlamydia spp . Oxygen should be supplemented to all patients who demonstrate hypoxia. Blood transfusion is the only method to abort a rapidly progressing episode of ACS. Because of the clinical overlap between pneumonia and ACS, all episodes should be treated promptly with antimicrobial therapy , including at least a macrolide and possibly a third-generation cephalosporin . Regular use of an incentive spirometer at 10 -12 breaths every 2 hours can significantly reduce the frequency of subsequent acute chest pain episodes .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy who is a known case of sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome. Which of the following is the drug of choice to reduce such painful crises in the future ?
mcqs.explanation: Hydroxyurea is the drug of choice for reducing painful crises in sickle cell anemia. Hydroxyurea is a myelosuppressive agent that is effective in reducing the frequency of painful episodes like dactylitis and acute chest syndrome, decreasing the rate of hospitalization, and requirement for blood transfusion. It is safe and well -tolerated in children and infants. Option A: Hydrocodone (opioid ) is used in the treatment of pain crisis in sickle cell anemia. Option C: Corticosteroids is one of the first-line therapies for acute idiopathic thrombocytic purpura (ITP) with risk factors for bleeding . Option D: Ruxolitinib is the drug of choice for the treatment of polycythemia vera.745

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Kevin and Anita both have sickle cell traits. They are devastated when they find out both their children have sickle cell anemia. Kirti is an active 9-year-old. Kamal is her 3-month-old brother. Which of the following prophylactic measures would you not recommend to them?

options.a: Oral penicillin prophylaxis up to 5 years of age in Kamal
options.b: Annual transcranial Doppler ultrasound for Kirti upto age
options.c: Annual ophthalmology screening from the age of 10 years in both
options.d: Hydroxyurea prophylaxis regardless of disease severity or symptoms in both

mcqs.explanation: Hydroxyurea prophylaxis regardless of disease severity is recommended in children over 9 months of age . Hydroxyurea can be considered for use in infants between six and nine months with symptomatic disease . Oral penicillin VK is recommended until at least 5 years of age . It is continued beyond 5 years of age in children with a history of pneumococcal infection . Erythromycin ethyl succinate is used if the patient is allergic to penicillin . Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations are administered because of the risk of functional asplenia . Transcranial Doppler ultrasound is recommended , starting at age of 2 years. This has lead to a decrease in the prevalence of overt stroke among children with sickle cell anemia. Screening should occur annually from age 2-16. Annual ophthalmology screening should commence from the age of 10 years to screen for retinopathy .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is responsible for the most common cause of congenital hemolytic anemia due to an enzyme deficiency ?

options.a: Deficiency of an enzyme in glycolysis pathway
options.b: Deficiency of an enzyme in Hexose monophosphate pathway
options.c: Deficiency of an enzyme in Kreb's cycle
options.d: Deficiency of an enzymes in fructose metabolism pathway

mcqs.explanation: Deficiency of an enzyme in the hexose monophosphate pathway ie., glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD Deficiency), is the most common cause of congenital hemolytic anemia due to an enzyme deficiency Most common enzymopathies causing hemolytic anemia (in order of most common to least ): • Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD) • Pyruvate kinase deficiency • 5' nucleotidase deficiency

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis ?
mcqs.explanation: Rh incompatibility causes immune hydrops fetalis , whereas alpha-thalassemia, parvovirus B19 infection , and twin-twin transfusion syndrome cause non-immune hydrops fetalis . Hydrops fetalis refers to the abnormal fluid collections in fetal soft tissues and serous cavities. Edema , signs of heart failure, and profound intra-uterine anemia are the presenting features in the fetus . Other clinical features include marked hepatosplenomegaly , retardation in brain growth , hydrocephaly , urogenital and cardiovascular deformities , and extramedullary erythropoiesis . Non-immune hydrops fetalis (NIHF) comprises the subgroup of cases not caused by red cell alloimmunization (e.g., Rh(D), Kell ) Bart's hydrops fetalis (alpha-thalassemia ) is caused by the deletion or inactivation of all four alpha-globin alleles , leading to a severe deficiency in alpha-globin chains of Hb and to the746 production of gamma-4 tetramers (Hb Bart). Hb Bart tetramers have an extremely high oxygen affinity and are incapable of effective tissue oxygen delivery . Parvovirus B19 infection can cause fetal anemia, non-immune fetal hydrops , and fetal death .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about abnormal hemoglobins and their mechanisms is true?

options.a: HbS is due to substitution of lysine for glutamine in the 6th position of the beta -globin gene .
options.b: HbH is the deletion of three alpha-globin genes .
options.c: Hb Bart is the deletion of all four beta -globin genes .
options.d: HbC is due to substitution of valine for lysine in the 6th position of the beta -globin gene .

mcqs.explanation: HbH is the deletion of three alpha globin chains. HbS is due to the substitution of valine for glutamic acid in the 6th position of the beta -globin gene (option A). Hb Bart is the deletion of all four alpha-globin genes . (There are only 2 beta -globin genes ) (option C) HbC is due to the substitution of lysine for glutamic acid in the 6th position of the beta -globin gene (option D).

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child presented with pallor, massive hepatosplenomegaly , and hemolytic facies . Which of the following is the most likely iron profile in this patient ?

options.a: Iron - low, Ferritin - low, TIBC -high, TSAT -low
options.b: Iron - high, Ferritin - normal , TIBC -normal , TSAT -normal
options.c: Iron - low, Ferritin - high, TIBC -low, TSAT -low
options.d: Iron - low, Ferritin - low, TIBC -low, TSAT -low

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thalassemia and the most likely iron profile is iron - normal /high, ferritin - normal , total iron - binding capacity (TIBC ) - normal , and transferrin saturation (TSAT ) - normal . Iron - low, ferritin-low, TIBC -high, TSAT -low is seen in iron-deficiency anemia. Iron -low, ferritin-high, TIBC -low, TSAT-low is seen in anemia of chronic disease .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A toddler presented with progressive pallor and abdominal distention . On investigations, he had low hemoglobin. Which of the following red cell indices can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron deficiency anemia?

options.c: Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count

mcqs.explanation: Mean corpuscular volume/ Red blood cell count (MCV/RBC) also known as Mentzer index can be used to distinguish thalassemia from iron-deficiency anemia (IDA ). MCV (mean corpuscular volume) and MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin ) are low in both IDA and thalassemia. RBC count may be normal in thalassemia , whereas it is reduced in IDA. A lower RBC count in IDA means the denominator is smaller, yielding a greater MCV/RBC ratio. Mentzer index is: • More than 13 in iron-deficiency anemia • Less than 13 in thalassemia

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 14-month-old child with Hb 6.3 was undergoing repeated blood transfusions. The last transfusion was given in the 9th month. Which of the following investigation is used for a definitive diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of repeated transfusion, low hemoglobin level , and target cells in the smear are suggestive of thalassemia . Globin gene sequencing is used for its definitive diagnosis.747 High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is used as a screening test for thalassemia (option A). Thalassemia is a hemoglobinopathy that arises due to deficient synthesis of the globin chains. Depending on the chain affected , it is classified into \032-thalassemia and \031-thalassemia . \031-thalassemia is caused by point mutations of the \031-thalassemia gene on chromosome 11 , which diminish the synthesis of \031-globin chains. Splicing mutations are the most common cause of (\031+) thalassemia . There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in \031-thalassemia . Children with severe thalassemia present with distinctive facial features such as maxilla hyperplasia , a flat nasal bridge , and frontal bossing. Other manifestations include pathologic bone fractures, significant hepatosplenomegaly , and cachexia. Blood smears show marked anisocytosis , poikilocytosis , and microcytic hypochromic anemia. Target cells , basophilic stippling , and fragmented red cells also are common. A radiographic image of the skull shows the classic 'crew cut' appearance . Hb Electrophoresis and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) are used as screening tests for thalassemia . DNA diagnosis to detect \031-thalassemia mutations is used for definitive diagnosis. The Mentzer index is the ratio of MCV to RBC count. It is used to differentiate between iron-deficiency anemia and \031-thalassemia trait. The Mentzer index is <13 in thalassemia minor syndrome.
