Transfusions are administered every 3-4 weeks to maintain a pretransfusion hemoglobin level of 9.5-10.5 g/dL. Transfusion-induced hemosiderosis is a significant complication in transfusion-dependent thalassemia . Iron deposition occurs in the liver, endocrine organs, and heart, resulting in complications including hypothyroidism , hypogonadotropic hypogonadism , growth hormone deficiency , hypoparathyroidism , diabetes mellitus , heart failure, and arrhythmias. The image below shows thalassemic facies and crew cut appearance on X-ray:748

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You see a child in the hematology unit who has developed anemia which is progressive along with cardiac decompensation requiring transfusion. He is in the latter half of infancy. You suspect transfusion-dependent thalassemia . Which of the following electrophoresis pattern is seen here?
mcqs.explanation: HbA=0%, HbA2 =5%, HbF=95% is seen on hemoglobin electrophoresis in transfusion-dependent thalassemia. Given clinical picture where the child becomes symptomatic during the second 6 months of life requiring transfusion is suggestive of beta -thalassemia major or transfusion-dependent thalassemia . • Normal pattern- HbA=95%, HbA2 =3.5%, HbF =1.5% • Beta-thalassemia trait- HbA=90%, HbA2 =5%, HbF=5% • Beta-thalassemia intermedia- HbA=45%, HbA2 =5%, HbF=50% Alpha- and beta -thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta -globin chains, respectively . This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival .Disease severity is inversely correlated with the number of functioning globin chains.Each individual carries 2 beta -chain genes and 4 alpha-chain genes .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are given the following x-ray in the viva session . Which of the following is the likely reason behind this abnormal appearance?
mcqs.explanation: Crew-cut or hair-on-end appearance on X-ray imaging of the skull is due to extramedullary hematopoiesis, which is seen in thalassemia . Ineffective erythropoiesis leads to extramedullary hematopoiesis , which causes the widening of the diploic space , thereby causing the thickening of trabeculae . This results in the classical crew-cut or hair-on-end appearance on x-ray imaging of the skull. Extramedullary hematopoiesis also leads to hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged and distorted bony prominences over the face , leading to the characteristic chipmunk facies in thalassemia .749

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You are evaluating a 4-year-old child with \337-thalassemia major . He has been on chronic transfusion therapy since the age of 1 year. He has developed transfusion-induced iron overload. The child has an increased risk of developing which of the following infections ?
mcqs.explanation: Thalassemic children with transfusion-induced iron overload are at an increased risk of infections with Yersinia enterocolitica . Iron excess immunologically compromises the host and greatly enhances yersinial growth . Streptococcus pneumoniae (option A), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (option B), and Chlamydia species (option D) are the common organisms causing infections that predispose to acute chest syndrome in sickle cell anemia.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about Diamond Blackfan Anemia?

options.a: Short stature , craniofacial abnormalities, and triphalangeal thumb are common features .
options.b: Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic anemia.
options.c: Bone marrow failure includes erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages .

mcqs.explanation: Short stature , craniofacial abnormalities, and triphalangeal thumb are common features is the true statement regarding Diamond–Blackfan anemia (DBA). Features of DBA (congenital hypoplastic anemia): • Autosomal dominant inheritance. • Macrocytosis without hypersegmented neutrophils or other megaloblastic features . • Reticulocytopenia . • Absent RBC precursors in the otherwise normally cellular bone marrow . Other lineages are unaffected . • Craniofacial anomaly is the most common congenital anomaly seeen . • Hypertelorism , snub nose, and high-arched palate seen . • Thumb abnormalities- flattening of the thenar eminence and triphalangeal thumb • Short stature Treatment: Corticosteroids , chronic red cell transfusions, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Image showing triphalangeal thumb:750

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: You see a neonate undergoing phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia. Blood workup revealed the presence of a hemolytic picture along with spherocytes and polychromatophilic reticulocytes . MCV is low normal along with elevated MCHC. There was a similar history of hemolytic anemia in the mother. The pedigree analysis points towards an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. The most likely genetic mutation seen in this case is?
mcqs.explanation: The Ankyrin gene mutation is the most likely genetic mutation seen in the given case of autosomal -dominant hereditary spherocytosis (HS). Hemolytic manifestation causing indirect hyperbilirubinemia requiring phototherapy or blood transfusion in infancy with positive family history and typical laboratory findings is suggestive of HS. History of blood transfusions in later life and not infancy is used to classify the severity of the disease . • Most common mode of inheritance of HS- autosomal dominant • Most common gene mutation in autosomal-dominant HS- ankyrin > Band 3 • Most common gene mutation in autosomal-recessive HS- spectrin • Most severe form of HS- spectrin (recessive ) Classification of the severity of HS is based on the requirement of blood transfusion in later life and not during infancy. mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An 11 -year-old child, born out of consanguineous marriage developed signs and symptoms of hemolytic anemia and progressive ataxia. He is a known case of retinitis pigmentosa and also had symptoms of fat malabsorption. A peripheral smear of the child is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical features along with the peripheral smear showing acanthocytes make the diagnosis of abetalipoproteinemia more likely. Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive hemolytic disorder in which acanthocytosis is associated with fat malabsorption, progressive ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa . Acanthocytes or spur cells are spiculated red cells with a few projections of varying size and surface distribution. The most significant associations include abetalipoproteinemia and severe liver disease . Note : Do not confuse acanthocytes with echinocytes or burr cells . They appear with multiple small projections that are uniformly distributed on the red cell surface . It is a universal feature of uremia.753 Image: The peripheral smear below shows regularly spaced , smoothly rounded crenulations, which are characteristic of a burr cell .Peripheral smear in other options : Hemolytic uremic syndrome (option A); Numerous schistocytes and nucleated RBCs with extremely low platelets :Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (option B); bite cells or degmacytes or blister cells . In G6PD deficiency uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies . Bite cells result from the removal of Heinz bodies by macrophages in the spleen . The image below shows bite cells represented by blue arrows, black arrows represent burr cells :754 Hereditary stomatocytosis (option C); Numerous stomatocytes (Uniconcave cup with mouth-shaped area of central pallor), caused by missense mutation in band 3 or AEP

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old child is receiving iron and folic acid supplements under the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS ) Programme. Which of the following is true about this program?

options.a: It was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
options.b: It is meant exclusively for adolescent school girls between 10 -19 years of age .
options.c: It exclusively covers government schools in rural India.
options.d: It recommends that administration of 50 mg of elemental iron.

mcqs.explanation: Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS ) was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the true statement among the given options . Salient features of Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS ): i. Objective of Weekly Iron Folic acid Supplementation (WIFS ): To reduce the prevalence and severity of anemia in the adolescent population (10 -19 years). ii. Target groups755 • School-going adolescent girls and boys in 6th to 12th class enrolled in government/government-aided /municipal schools • Out -of-school adolescent girls iii. Intervention • Administration of supervised weekly iron-folic acid supplements of 60 mg elemental iron and �Mg folic acid by using a fixed -day approach • Screening of target groups for moderate/severe anemia and referring these cases to an appropriate health facility • Biannual de -worming (albendazole 400 mg), six months apart, for the control of helminthic infestation • Information and counseling for improving dietary intake and for taking actions for prevention of intestinal worm infestation

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A toddler is brought by his mother with complaints of poor feeding , lethargy , and chronic diarrhea for the past 4 months. Upon clinical examination, the child has pale conjunctiva and is tachycardic. Blood workup reveals low hemoglobin and smear shows macrocytosis, anisopoikilocytosis , and large neutrophils with hyper -segmented nuclei . Serum homocysteine levels are elevated and methylmalonate levels are normal . Bone marrow shows erythroid hyperplasia . Which of the following is true about this condition?

options.a: Lactate dehydrogenase levels in serum is low.
options.b: Folate -deficient mother's give birth to infants with folate deficiency .
options.c: Methylenetetrahydrofolate (MTHFR) deficiency is associated with megaloblastic anemia.
options.d: Goat's milk fed infants are more likely to develop this disease

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the megaloblastic picture elevated homocysteine levels , and normal methylmalonate levels are suggestive of folate deficiency anemia. Goat's milk is deficient in folate . So goat milk-fed infants are likely to develop folate deficiency anemia. Human breast milk, infant formulas, and pasteurized cow's milk provide adequate amounts of folic acid. In folate deficiency anemia, lactate dehydrogenase levels in serum are elevated . Folate -deficient mothers do not give birth to infants with folate deficiency because there is a selective transfer of folate to the fetus via the placental folate receptors . Methylenetetrahydrofolate (MTHFR) deficiency is the most common inborn error of folate metabolism , and severe cases can produce neurologic and vascular complications ; there is no associated megaloblastic anemia. Malnutrition is the most common cause of folate deficiency in children. Note : Both homocysteine and methylmalonate levels are elevated in B12 deficiency anemia.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A child presents with megaloblastic anemia that is unresponsive to vitamin C, vitamin B12 , and folic acid, but responsive to uridine. What do you suspect ?
mcqs.explanation: Orotic aciduria is to be suspected in this child. Megaloblastic anemia that is responsive to uridine is consistent with orotic aciduria. Orotic aciduria is a rare inborn error of metabolism in children. A defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway results in the failure of conversion of orotic acid to uridine. Supplementation of vitamin B12 , folate , and vitamin C rules out the more common nutritional causes of megaloblastic anemia. Thiamine deficiency (option A) and anemia due to liver disease (option B) do not respond to uridine.756 Pernicious anemia (Option C) responds to treatment with vitamin B12 .757

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Fundoscopic evaluation in an HIV patient showed CMV retinitis. He was started on intravenous foscarnet, a highly ionized drug. Which of the following statements is true about the drug?

options.b: Can cross the blood brain barrier easily

mcqs.explanation: Highly ionized drugs like foscarnet are mainly excreted by the kidneys. They are not reabsorbed from the renal tubules and are hence excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration. Dose reduction is necessary in renal impairment to avoid the accumulation of the drug and associated toxicity . The non-ionized forms of weak acids and bases undergo tubular reabsorption. Option B: The blood-brain barrier limits the entry of ionized, non-lipid soluble drugs. Option C: A drug is more readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when it is in its unionized, more lipophilic form. Option D: As the ionized form has low lipid solubility , it cannot penetrate cell membranes easily .13

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Alkalinization of the urine is done in case of toxicity with which of the following substances ?
mcqs.explanation: Alkalinization of the urine is done in barbiturate poisoning. When the urine is alkaline, weakly acidic drugs like barbiturates are present in highly ionized form and excreted more rapidly. When the tubular urine is made more alkaline, weak acids like barbiturates become highly ionized and are excreted to a greater extent . Similarly, acidification of urine increases the excretion of weak bases . This property is used in the management of drug overdose.Drug Treatment of overdose Weak acids(e.g., phenobarbit al, aspirin) Alkalinization of urine withso dium bicarbonate Weak bases (e.g., amphetami ne) Acidification of urine witham monium chloride

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: When the pH = pKa of a drug, which of the following statements is true?

options.a: Concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50 % non-ionic
options.b: Concentration of the drug is 90% ionic and 10 % non-ionic
options.c: Concentration of the drug is 75 % ionic and 25 % non-ionic
options.d: Concentration of the drug is 25% ionic and 75 % non-ionic

mcqs.explanation: When the pH = pKa of a drug, the concentration of the drug is 50% ionic and 50% non-ionic. pKa is defined as the pH at which a drug exists as 50% ionized (hydrophilic ) and 50% unionized (lipophilic ). For e.g., phenobarbitone is an acidic drug with a pKa of 7.2. At a pH of 7.2, 50% will be unionized. In a more basic plasma (pH=7.4), a lesser fraction (around 40%) will be unionized. Small changes in pH near pKa of a drug may cause large variations in the degree of ionization.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, drug toxicity is least likely with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, drug toxicity is least likely with morphine. Acidic drugs generally bind to plasma albumin while basic drugs bind to alpha-1 acid glycoprotein . Nephrotic syndrome reduces plasma albumin levels , therefore there is a decrease in the protein-bound drug fraction and an increase in the free form, resulting in drug toxicity . This is less likely with drugs having low plasma protein binding such as morphine (only around 35%). Efavirenz, diazepam, and valproate have a very high plasma protein binding of >90% and predominantly bind to albumin and are associated with toxicity in hypoalbuminemia .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What does time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax ) indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The time for peak plasma concentration (Tmax ) indicates the rate at which the drug is absorbed from the administered site . It depends on both the administered site and the drug formulation.14 This is used to determine the timing of the administration of hypnotics with respect to sleep timings. A hypnotic with a higher rate of absorption might be preferred to induce sleep at a shorter latency as the target concentration can be achieved earlier.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The pharmacokinetics of an experimental drug is being studied . If its apparent volume of distribution is 6L /kg, which of the following is true regarding its distribution?
mcqs.explanation: In the present case, the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L /kg (420 L in a normal adult with reference weight 70kg) which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L . Therefore, it can be implied that the drug is having high sequestration in tissues . The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is an imaginary volume throughout which the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains constant throughout . Vd = Dose administered IV / plasma concentration The difference in the volume of distribution based on drug type : • Low Vd • Restricted to the intravascular compartment • Seen in drugs with high molecular weight (e.g., heparin) or high protein binding (e.g., warfarin - 9.8L) • Medium Vd • Lipid insoluble drugs (e.g., gentamicin - 20L ) do not enter the cells and are distributed in the extracellular fluid volume • Small water-soluble molecules (e.g., ethanol - 42L ) are distributed in the total body water • High Vd • Sequestered and accumulated in the tissues • Small lipophilic molecules (e.g., chloroquine - 13000L )

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following parameters is used to assess the extent of drug absorption in a plasma concentration vs. time graph?
mcqs.explanation: The area under the curve of plasma concentration vs. time curve gives the extent of absorption which is calculated by the trapezoidal rule. The following image shows a plasma concentration vs. time graph:15 Two drugs may have the same rate of absorption but a different extent of absorption or bioavailability. The factors upon which the extent of drug absorption depends are: • Lipophilicity - If too lipophilic (e.g., acyclovir), the drug is not soluble enough to cross the water layer adjacent to the cell . • Hydrophilicity - If too hydrophilic (e.g., atenolol ), the drug cannot cross the lipid cell membrane.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about first-order kinetics?

options.a: A constant amount of drug is eliminated in unit time
options.b: The half life increases with an increase in dose
options.c: The rate of elimination is constant
options.d: The rate of elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration

mcqs.explanation: The rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration in first-order kinetics.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You would consider administering a loading dose for a patient if the drug has
mcqs.explanation: The volume of distribution of the drug determines the loading dose of the drug. Loading dose is a relatively large dose of the drug given initially to rapidly achieve the target plasma concentration. It is given by the formula Loading Dose = Vol. of Distribution x Desired Steady -state plasma Concentration. The bioavailability determines the route of administration. Though bioavailability may affect the dose necessary, it will not be the primary factor considered during the calculation of the loading dose . Option A: Clearance is used to determine the maintenance dose . Maintenance dose = Clearance x Desired Steady -state plasma concentration. Options C and D: Plasma half-life primarily determines the frequency of dosing.16

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs approach zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Phenytoin kinetics changes from first-order to zero-order kinetics at higher therapeutic levels . True zero-order kinetics is shown only by ethanol . Some drugs have first-order kinetics at low plasma concentrations while at higher plasma concentration (within therapeutic range ), the mechanism for elimination gets saturated and they change over to zero-order kinetics. Drugs that show early saturation kinetics include : • Warfarin • Aspirin • Theophylline • Verapamil • Fluoxetine • Phenytoin Some drugs show zero-order kinetics at much higher (non-therapeutic / toxic) levels .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following routes of administration will not bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism ?
mcqs.explanation: Hepatic first-pass metabolism occurs in drugs administered via the oral route. When drugs are given orally, they are absorbed in the intestine and reach the liver through the portal vein. During this process , the drug is acted on by enzymes of the liver and intestine . Additionally , the liver may excrete part of the drug in the bile, further reducing the bioavailability. This is called the first-pass metabolism . In all the other routes , the drug directly enters systemic circulation without reaching the liver. Note : Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose of unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation. Hence , the bioavailability of a drug administered intravenously (I.V ) is 100 %. It is neither subjected to the first-pass metabolism as in the oral route nor does it depend on local factors as in subcutaneous , intramuscular, or transdermal.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: In the metabolism of xenobiotics , all of the following are phase 1 reactions except ?
mcqs.explanation: Acetylation is a phase 2 reaction. Metabolizing enzymes in hepatic cells : • Microsomal enzymes - present in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum • Non-microsomal enzymes - present in mitochondria and cytoplasm17

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Sulphonamides undergo which of the following metabolic reactions?
mcqs.explanation: Sulphonamides undergo acetylation . It is a phase II metabolic reaction where compounds having amino or hydrazine residues are conjugated with the help of acetyl coenzyme -A. Drugs that undergo acetylation are: • Sulphonamides • Hydralazine • Isoniazid • PAS • Dapsone • Clonazepam • Procainamide

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: All of the following can cause lupus -like syndromes except :
mcqs.explanation: Penicillin is not associated with a lupus -like syndrome. Drug-induced lupus is a consequence of genetic polymorphism of N-acetyl transferase 2 (NAT2 ) enzyme which results in slow acetylators and fast acetylators : • Slow acetylators of isoniazid, hydralazine, and sulphonamides can have increased toxicity that includes lupus -like syndrome • Fast acetylators can have decreased efficacy as a result of faster metabolism of the active drug Drugs that may result in lupus -like syndrome (The SHIP MeChaniQ has lupus -like syndrome) are: • Sulphonamides / Sulfasalazine • Hydralazine • Isoniazid • Procainamide, Para -aminosalicylic acid • Methyldopa • Chlorpromazine • Quinidine

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient on long-term anticoagulation therapy with warfarin would need an increased dose when coadministered with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: A patient on long-term anticoagulation therapy with warfarin would need an increased dose when coadministered with rifampicin. This is because rifampicin is a potent microsomal enzyme18 inducer and can decrease the effect of warfarin . Rifampicin induces CYP3A and CYP2D6 enzymes . Enzyme inducers: • CYP3A • Carbamazepine • Phenobarbitone (CYP2B1) • Rifampicin (CYP2D6) • Phenytoin • Glucocorticoids • CYP2E1 • Isoniazid • Chronic alcoholism Note : Isoniazid is an inducer for CYP2E1 but an inhibitor for CYP3A4

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Contraceptive failure while on oral contraceptive pills is unlikely to occur with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: Contraceptive failure in patients on the oral contraceptive pill is unlikely to occur with valproate. It is an enzyme inhibitor that inhibits the degradation of OCPs and increases their duration of action. Rifampicin, phenytoin , and phenobarbitone are enzyme inducers and can cause increased metabolism of OCPs leading to contraceptive failure.Enzyme inducers Enzyme inhibitors Mnemonic: CRAP GPSCarba mezepineRifampicinAlcohol ( chronic)PhenytoinGriseofulvi nPhenobarbitoneSulfonylure as Mnemonic: RED VICKRitona virErythromycinDiltiazemVer apamil, ValproateItraconazol eClarithromycin, Cimetidine Ketoconazole

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following microsomal enzymes is important for the activation of procarcinogens?
mcqs.explanation: CYP1A1 /2 enzymes are important in the activation of procarcinogens. They are involved in the metabolism of few drugs like theophylline , caffeine , paracetamol, and carbamazepine. Inducers of CYP1A1 /2: • Polycyclic hydrocarbons • Cigarette smoking19 • Charbroiled meat • Rifampicin • Carbamazepine

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Cytochrome enzymes are not involved in which of the following processes ?
mcqs.explanation: Cytochrome enzymes are not involved in acetylation . Cytochrome enzymes such as CYP450 are involved in phase 1 reactions such as oxidation. They are also involved in bile acid production from cholesterol ; synthesis of steroids and fatty acid signaling molecules like epoxyeicosatrienoic acids.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient is brought to the emergency in an unresponsive state . There is an alleged history of consumption of multiple prescription tablets in an attempt to commit suicide . After the drug was conclusively identified , the doctor recommends dialysis for definitive management. The drug most likely is:
mcqs.explanation: The drug most likely is lithium as it is the only one amongst the given drugs that can be removed by dialysis . It is the treatment of choice in case of severe lithium toxicity (>4mEq/L). The distribution of lithium is mainly restricted to the vascular compartment and it is not bound to any plasma proteins . Dialysis is effective in removing the drugs if they are sufficiently present in the free form in the plasma. Therefore, lithium can be removed by dialysis during an overdose. Drugs not suitable for dialysis are those with: • High volume of distribution - digoxin, verapamil, and organophosphates • High level of plasma protein binding - diazepam

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a prodrug?
mcqs.explanation: Imipramine is not a prodrug. It is a tricyclic antidepressant and has therapeutic activity. It also forms an active metabolite , desipramine . Prodrugs are inactive precursors of active forms. They require metabolic alteration in the body to become active. Examples of prodrugs: • Prednisone • Levodopa • ACE inhibitors (except lisinopril and captopril ) • Sulfasalazine • Methyldopa • Cyclophosphamide • Clopidogrel20

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about P-glycoprotein ?
mcqs.explanation: P-glycoprotein is also known as multidrug resistance protein 1 or MDR1 (not MDR2). It is also denoted by cluster of differentiation 243 (CD243 ). P-glycoprotein (P-gp) is one of the first members of the ATP -binding cassette (ABC) transporter, which acts as an efflux membrane transporter. It is responsible for limiting cellular uptake and the distribution of xenobiotics and toxic substances . It is associated with multidrug resistance (MDR). • Increased P-gp expression : Reduces the absorption of drugs that are substrates for P-gp • Decreased P-gp expression : Leads to supratherapeutic plasma concentrations and drug toxicity

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: For which of the following drugs, is absorption increased after a fatty meal?
mcqs.explanation: The absorption of griseofulvin is increased after a fatty meal. Note : Fatty meals increase the rate of absorption of efavirenz to such an extent as to cause toxicity. Hence , efavirenz is recommended to be taken on an empty stomach.Drug absorption reduced /del ayed by food Drug absorption increased by food AmpicillinAspirinAtenololAzi thromycinCaptoprilIndinavir IsoniazidRifampinSucralfate TetracyclineDoxycycline AtovaquoneCarbamazepineC hlorothiazideCefuroximeDiaz epamGanciclovirLithiumMet oprololRitonavirHydralazine Lumefantrine

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You prescribe an antibiotic course for a patient following cesarean section . What advice would you give regarding breastfeeding ?

options.a: No advice as most of drug are not present in breast milk
options.b: Avoid breastfeeding during the antibiotic course
options.c: Medications to be taken 3-4 hours before next feeding

mcqs.explanation: If the lactating mother needs to take medications that are deemed safe , the dosing optimally should be 30-60 minutes after nursing and at least 3-4 hours before the next feeding . A minimum interval of 3-4 hours allows time for partial clearance of the drug. This ensures the infants are not exposed to the peak maternal plasma concentration that may translate to higher levels secreted into milk. Option A: Most drugs administered are detected in breast milk but most of them are excreted in very small quantities that do not cause any effect in the infants. Option B: Breastfeeding should not be avoided altogether for all medications . Intake of cytotoxic agents and immunomodulatory agents are contraindications for breastfeeding . Option D: The timing of medication should preferably be at an interval where the infants are not exposed to higher maternal plasma concentrations.21

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old patient is on omeprazole for gastroesophageal reflux disease . She is now to be started on dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel . You decide to switch to pantoprazole because of the action of omeprazole on which enzyme?
mcqs.explanation: Omeprazole is replaced with another proton pump inhibitor (PPI ) during coadministration with clopidogrel because of the action on CYP2C19 . Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is activated to its active metabolite by the liver enzyme CYP2C19 . Apart from CYP2C19 , CYP3A4, and CYP2C9 are also involved to a certain extent . Omeprazole serves as both substrate and inhibitor for CYP2C19 . It may inhibit the activation of clopidogrel and decrease its antiplatelet action. Hence , they are not prescribed together .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Subfamily of CYP3A4 is _______
mcqs.explanation: The sub-family of CYP3A4 is A. In CYP enzymes nomenclature , the root CYP is followed by a number designating the family, a letter denoting the subfamily and another number designating the gene . Therefore, in CYP3A4: • 3 - family • A - subfamily A • 4 - individual gene coding for one specific isoenzyme There are numerous CYP isoenzymes in humans. Among them, CYP3A4 is the most abundant and carries out the metabolism of nearly 50% of clinically used drugs.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: How much drug will remain at the end of 6 hours when a patient is given 200 mg drug, 75 mg excreted in 90 min and if the drug follows first-order kinetics?
mcqs.explanation: In first order kinetics, a constant fraction of the drug is excreted in a given time. 75 mg of 200 mg is excreted in 90 minutes /200 = 37.5/100 = 0.375 is eliminated After 90 minutes ; 200 mg-75 mg = 125 mg remains The next 90 minutes (after 180 minutes ) = 125 x 0.375 = 46.875 mg is eliminated , and 125-46.875 = .125 mg remains The next 90 minutes (after 270 minutes ) = 78 .125 x 0.375 = 29.297 mg is eliminated , and 78.125-29 .297 = 48.828 remains The next 90 minutes (after 360 minutes ) = 48.828 x 0.375 = 18.310 mg is eliminated , 48.828-18.310 = 30.518 mg remains after 6 hours. Simpler way to calculate 3/8 fraction is excreted in 90 minutes \037 5/8 remains after 90 minutes . 6 hours (360 min) is 4 times of 90 minutes .22 So 200 x (5/8)(5/8)(5/8)(5/8) = 30 .518 mg remains after 360 minutes23

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Neurotransmitters like noradrenaline, adrenaline, and dopamine act on:
mcqs.explanation: Noradrenaline, adrenaline, and dopamine act through a bundle of seven alpha-helicase trans-membrane receptors which are the G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about G-protein-coupled receptors ?

options.a: G proteins bind to hormones on the cell surface .
options.b: All the three subunits alpha, beta and gamma should bind to each other for G proteins to act.
options.c: G proteins act as inhibitory and excitatory because of differences in the alpha subunit .
options.d: G protein is bound to GTP in resting state .

mcqs.explanation: G proteins act as inhibitory and excitatory because of differences in the alpha subunit . • Excitatory - Gs and Gq • Inhibitory - Gi In the resting-state : • G protein is a heterotrimer consisting of alpha, beta , and gamma subunits . It forms a complex with G-protein-coupled receptors at the intracellular domain. The extracellular domain of GPCR has the binding domain for hormones. G protein subunits do not directly bind them. • The alpha subunit is bound to GDP. Binding of ligand results in activation of GPCR, following which:35 • Alpha subunit undergoes a conformational change • Release of GDP and binding of GTP occurs • GTP bound alpha subunit dissociates from beta -gamma subunit • Both alpha subunit and beta -gamma subunit bind to and regulate effectors only when they are separated .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following GPCRs does not act via the K+ channel?
mcqs.explanation: Angiotensin 1 receptor acts via Ca2+ channels. It does not act through second messengers via the K+ channel. G-protein coupled receptors activate inwardly rectifying potassium channels and increase the permeability of the potassium ions causing hyperpolarisation of the cell . They are called G protein-coupled inwardly-rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs). These receptors include : • M2 muscarinic • A1 adenosine • �o 2 adrenergic • D2 dopamine • 5HT1 serotonin • Somatostatin receptors .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of a GPCR?
mcqs.explanation: Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors among the given options . M1, M2, M3, M4, and M5 are the muscarinic Ach receptors .36 • M1 and M3 act through Gq protein and activate IP3 /DAG causing increased cytosolic calcium. • M2 and M4 act through Gi protein and inhibit adenylyl cyclase causing increased potassium conductance .Nicotinic receptors and GABA-A are examples of ion channel coupled receptors .Insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase receptor .37

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an ion channel receptor ?
mcqs.explanation: Nicotinic cholinergic receptors (both Nm and Nn) are of ligand-gated ion channel type . The binding of ligand alters the permeability of ion channels directly and brings about biological action.Muscarinic cholinergic, beta -adrenergic, and opioid receptors are G protein-coupled receptors .38

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: All of the following agents act by intracellular receptors except ______
mcqs.explanation: Insulin receptors belong to the class of trans-membrane enzyme-linked receptors . Transmembrane enzyme-linked receptors consist of a large extracellular ligand-binding domain. It is connected to an intracellular subunit having enzymatic property through a single transmembrane helical peptide chain. The enzyme on the cytosolic side is usually a protein kinase (tyrosine) or membrane-bound GC (guanylyl cyclase ). Physiological ligands for transmembrane enzyme-linked receptors are mostly growth factors and chemokines. Other receptors belonging to this class include : • Receptor tyrosine kinases - Growth factors (PDGF, EGF, VEGF); insulin • Membrane-bound GC - Natriuretic peptides • Receptor serine-threonine kinases - TGF-\035 Thyroid hormones, vitamin D, and steroids act via intracellular receptors .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a second messenger ?
mcqs.explanation: Guanylyl cyclase is an enzyme that converts GTP to cGMP. It is not a second messenger . Second messengers are: • Diacylglycerol • Inositol triphosphate • Cyclic AMP • Cyclic GMP • Calcium39 • Nitric oxide

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones act through the receptor shown in the image below ?
mcqs.explanation: The receptor in the given image uses tyrosine kinase signaling. Insulin acts through this receptor to exert its functions. Other hormones acting via tyrosine kinase signaling: • Growth hormone • Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF • Prolactin • Leptin

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient with congestive heart failure is being treated with an intravenous infusion of nesiritide. Which of the following receptors does this drug act through?
mcqs.explanation: Nesiritide is recombinant B-type natriuretic peptide . Natriuretic peptide receptors are transmembrane ligand-gated guanylyl cyclase receptors . Natriuretic peptides : • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): released from atrial storage granules in response to an increase in intravascular volume. It decreases blood pressure . • Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP): released from ventricular tissue in response to volume overload. Along with a decrease in blood pressure, it is known to reduce cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. • C- type natriuretic peptide (CNP): synthesized in the brain and endothelial tissues and functions to stimulate long bone growth . ANP and BNP act on the NPR-A receptor . CNP acts on the NPR-B receptor .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: JAK/STAT is a signal transducer for which of the following receptors ?
mcqs.explanation: JAK/STAT is a signal transducer for transmembrane receptors lacking intrinsic enzymatic activity. Interleukin and other cytokines act through such receptors . On binding of the ligand to such receptors: • Receptor dimerization occurs • Increase in affinity for cytosolic JAK (Janus kinase) • Activation of JAK results in phosphorylation of tyrosine residues of the receptor40 • Binding of signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT ) and subsequent phosphorylation of STAT • STAT dimerizes and translocates to the nucleus to regulate gene expression , resulting in a biological response

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Adrenaline is used to treat histamine-induced bronchoconstriction in a patient with brittle asthma. What is this type of antagonism called ?
mcqs.explanation: Adrenaline and histamine are physiological antagonists. Adrenaline and histamine act on bronchial muscles . Histamine acts on H1 receptors and produces bronchoconstriction. Adrenaline acts on \0352 receptors and produces bronchodilation. Two drugs acting on different receptors and resulting in opposite responses means having pharmacological effects in the opposite direction. This is called physiological antagonism or functional antagonism. Option B: Chemical antagonism refers to a reaction between two chemicals to neutralize their effects , such as is seen with chelation therapy . Option C: Competitive antagonism is a type of receptor antagonism that occurs when the agonist and antagonist compete for the same binding site on the receptor . Option D: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors form a complex with an intermediate complex of the substrate and transporter. This inhibits subsequent translocation.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Diamox is given to a patient with glaucoma. It is a non-competitive inhibitor of the carbonic anhydrase enzyme. Which of the following would be the effect of this drug?

options.c: Decrease in both Km and Vmax

mcqs.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors cause a decrease in Vmax . In non-competitive inhibition: • The inhibitor binds to the adjacent site and not the catalytic site of the enzyme • The catalytic property of the enzyme is reduced and hence Vmax is decreased41 • The affinity of the enzyme is not altered and hence Km is unaltered

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Letrozole, a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme aromatase is prescribed to a patient with breast cancer. Which of the following is true about this type of antagonism?

options.a: Antagonism cannot be completely reversed by increased dose of the agonist
options.b: An agonist cannot displace an antagonist from the receptor
options.c: Agonists and antagonists bind to the same receptor
options.d: Dose response curve shifts to the left in the presence of an antagonist

mcqs.explanation: In competitive antagonism, the drug and the antagonist compete to bind to the same site of the receptor . Agonists if present in high concentration, can displace the antagonists from the active site and overcome the competitive antagonism completely . The dose -response curve in the case of competitive antagonism shifts to the right.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the dose -response curve shown in the image below ?

options.b: C is more potent than A
options.c: B is more potent than A

mcqs.explanation: In the above image, drug B is a competitive antagonist. In competitive antagonism, the DRC is shifted to the right whereas in non-competitive antagonism the DRC is flattened . Thus in the above image Drug B is the Competitive antagonist while drug C is the non-competitive antagonist. Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa. • The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . • Thus, in the above image, the potency is drug A > drug C > drug B. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug.42 • It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug. • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is drug A = drug B > drug C.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a true statement regarding inverse agonists?

options.a: Binds to the receptor and causes maximum action
options.b: Binds to the receptor and causes opposite action to that of agonist
options.c: Binds to the receptor and causes no action
options.d: Binds to the receptor and causes submaximal action

mcqs.explanation: Inverse agonists bind to the receptor and cause an action opposite to that of an agonist. The ability of the drug to bind with a receptor is called affinity. The capacity of a drug to induce a functional change in the receptor is called intrinsic activity or efficacy .Type of drugs Intrinsic activity Agonists Partial agonists 0 to 1 Competitive antagonis ts Inverse agonists 0 to -1

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient with symptoms of psychosis is prescribed aripiprazole. Which of the following best describes this drug?

options.a: No intrinsic activity and high affinity for D2 receptor
options.b: High intrinsic activity and no affinity for D2 receptor
options.c: Low intrinsic activity and high affinity for D2 receptor
options.d: High intrinsic activity and low affinity for D2 receptor

mcqs.explanation: Aripiprazole is a D2 receptor partial agonist. Partial agonists have submaximal or low intrinsic activity and high affinity. Partial agonists can behave as an antagonist in the presence of an agonist. Partial agonists block the binding of the agonist to the receptor thereby inhibiting a complete response . Aripiprazole has lower activity than dopamine at D2 receptors . By occupying and blocking the action of dopamine on D2 receptors , it acts similar to an antagonist. It is used in conditions like schizophrenia where dopamine antagonist activity is required.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What type of antagonism is shown by drugs A and B in the following dose -response curve?
mcqs.explanation: The parallel rightward shift of the agonist dose -response curve (DRC) is seen with competitive antagonism. Increasing the dose of the agonist can result in the same maximal response . In non-competitive antagonism, there will be flattening of the agonist DRC.43

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The graph below shows the relationship between the log(dose ) and the response of three drugs, A, B, and C. Which of these drugs has the highest potency ?
mcqs.explanation: Drug A has the highest potency . Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa. • The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . • Thus, in the above image, the potency is Drug A >Drug B> Drug C. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It reflects the capacity of the drug to activate a receptor and produce the response . • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is Drug A = Drug B > Drug C. • Drugs having a similar pharmacological effect can have different efficacies e.g furosemide and metolazone are both diuretics but furosemide has greater efficacy than metolazone .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about the given dose -response curve?

options.a: Drug B is the most potent .
options.b: Drug B is the most efficacious .
options.c: Drug C is more efficacious than drug D.
options.d: Drug A is more potent than drug B.

mcqs.explanation: The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . Hence , Drug B is the most potent . Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa.44 • In the above image, the potency is Drug B> Drug A > Drug C > Drug D. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It reflects the capacity of the drug to activate a receptor and produce the response . • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is Drug A = Drug C =Drug D > Drug B. • Drugs having a similar pharmacological effect can have different efficacies e.g furosemide and metolazone are both diuretics but furosemide has greater efficacy than metolazone .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding the potency and efficacy of a drug is not true?

options.a: In a clinical setup , efficacy is more important than potency
options.b: In the log dose response curve, the height of the curve corresponds with efficacy
options.c: ED50 of the drug corresponds to the efficacy
options.d: Drugs that produce a similar pharmacological effect can have different levels of efficacy

mcqs.explanation: ED50 is a measure of the drug potency, not efficacy . Potency refers to the amount of the drug required to produce a certain response . The x coordinates (dose axis) on the log dose-response curve (DRC) of a drug represent the potency of the drug. A right shift in the DRC indicates a lower potency and vice versa.Potency • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa. • The efficacy of a drug is a more decisive factor in the choice of a drug in the clinical setting • The more the curve shifts towards the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . • Thus, in the above image, Drug A is more potent . The potency is Drug A > Drug B > Drug C > Drug D.45 Efficacy • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. • It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug. • It is mainly a factor in choosing the dose of a drug. • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, efficacy is Drug A >B > C > D.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following shows a U-shaped dose -response curve?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamins and essential metals show a U-shaped dose -response curve. At a low dose , adverse effects are observed because there is a deficiency of these nutrients to maintain homeostasis . As dose increases, homeostasis is achieved , and the bottom of the U-shaped dose -response curve is reached . As the dose increases to surpass the amount required to maintain homeostasis , toxicity can ensue . Thus, adverse effects are seen at both low and high doses .46 Hockey stick-shaped dose -response curve for toxicants that are also metabolic by-products .Inverted U-shaped dose -response curve for ligands that downregulate their receptors .47

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What does the area between the dotted lines in this graph indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The area between the dotted lines in the graph shows the therapeutic window . It is the range of steady -state concentrations of a drug that provides therapeutic efficacy with minimal toxicity . The therapeutic index (TI) describes a relationship between the doses of a drug that causes lethal or toxic effects with the dose that causes therapeutic effects . It is also called the therapeutic ratio. Mathematically , you can calculate TI by following way: Therapeutic Index = LD50/ED50 (or) Therapeutic Index = TD50/ED50 Where, • LD50 (Median Lethal dose ) is the minimum amount of drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population . LD50 could also be replaced with Toxic dose (TD50). • ED50 (Median Effective dose ) is the quantity of a drug that can produce desired therapeutic effects in 50% of the population .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Therapeutic index is used for assessing which of the following factors?
mcqs.explanation: Therapeutic index is used to assess the safety of the drug administered . Therapeutic index = TD50/ED50 • TD50 (Median toxic dose ) = Dose required to produce a toxic effect in 50% of animals tested . • ED50 (Median effect dose ) = Dose required to produce a therapeutic effect in 50% of the individuals. Option B: Efficacy is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug.48 Option C: Potency refers to the concentration (EC50) or dose (ED50) required to produce 50% of maximum effect where EC50 is the concentration of agonist resulting in a half-maximal response . Option D: Median toxic dose is the dose required to produce a toxic effect in 50% of animals tested . Lethal dose is the dose required to kill 50% of animals tested .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Therapeutic index is calculated with which of the following equations?
mcqs.explanation: Therapeutic index is calculated with the following equation = LD50/ED50. Therapeutic index is used to assess the safety of the drug administered . LD50 (median lethal dose ) refers to the dose of the drug at which 50% of the experimental animals die . Larger the LD50, the safer the drug. In humans, TD50 is considered . TD50 refers to the dose of the drug that causes a toxic response in 50% of the population . ED50 (median effective dose ) refers to the dose of the drug at which 50% of the experimental animals show the specific or desired effect Clinically, the therapeutic range bound by the dose that produces the minimal necessary therapeutic effect and the dose that produces the maximal acceptable adverse effect is more relevant.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Calculate the therapeutic index of a drug whose dose -response curves are plotted as shown below :
mcqs.explanation: The therapeutic index is 4. In the above graph, Median lethal dose (LD50) = 400 Median effective dose (ED50) = 10049 Therapeutic index (TI) = LD50/ED50. Hence , Therapeutic index (TI ) = 400 /100 = 4 Clinically, the therapeutic range bound by the dose that produces the minimal therapeutic effect and the dose that produces the maximal acceptable adverse effect is more relevant.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Therapeutic drug monitoring is required in all except ______.
mcqs.explanation: Metformin does not require therapeutic monitoring because it does not have a narrow therapeutic index and the effect on blood sugar levels can be easily measured . Phenytoin, tacrolimus, and cyclosporine have the narrow therapeutic index and therapeutic monitoring is necessary to avoid adverse effects .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about pharmacogenetics is correct?

options.a: It refers to the effect of drugs on genetic expression
options.b: It refers to the genetic basis of variability in drug response
options.c: It is not synonymous with pharmacogenomics
options.d: Drug metabolism is not a highly heritable trait

mcqs.explanation: Pharmacogenetics is the study of the genetic basis for variability in drug action. Genetic differences cause variability in the dose -response curve (DRC) due to alteration in drug action and disposition in the body. The term is used interchangeably with pharmacogenomics. Drug metabolism is highly heritable , as assessed using drug exposure studies in monozygotic versus fraternal twins and from other related subjects .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old male is diagnosed with G6PD deficiency . Which of the following drugs is not contraindicated in his condition?
mcqs.explanation: Ceftriaxone is not contraindicated in G6PD deficient individuals as it does not possess oxidizing property, hence there is no hemolysis . Drugs having the potential to cause hemolysis in G6PD deficient individuals: • Anti-malarials - Primaquine , chloroquine, quinine, pyrimethamine , proguanil • Sulfonamides - Cotrimoxazole • Fluoroquinolones - Nalidixic acid • Nitro furan antibacterial - Furazolidone, nitrofurantoin • Anti-hypertensives - Methyldopa , hydralazine • Anti-convulsants - Phenytoin • Anti-arrythmics - Procainamide50

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Pharmacovigilance refers to:

options.b: Monitoring of unethical trade of drugs

mcqs.explanation: Pharmacovigilance deals with the monitoring of drug safety . WHO definition of pharmacovigilance: "Science and activities related to the detection , assessment , understanding , and prevention of adverse effects or any other drug-related problems ".

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following organizations regulates the clinical trials and approval of investigational new drugs in India?
mcqs.explanation: Central Drug Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) regulates the clinical trials and approval of investigational new drugs in India. The proposal for initiating trials, review of clinical trial results , and recommendations for marketing authorization is done through a committee called the Investigational New Drug (IND) Committee formed by CDSCO. Preclinical trials are performed on animals, and they are regulated by guidelines prescribed by the Committee for the Purpose of the Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) in India. The Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) is the head of the CDSCO, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in India.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You are working as a research associate on clinical trials of a new drug for migraine. What is the dose of the test drug that is usually not exceeded in phase 0 studies ?
mcqs.explanation: The dose of the test drug in phase 0 studies usually does not exceed 100mcg . Phase 0 studies are also called micro-dosing studies . Very low doses of drugs, usually 1/100th of the estimated human dose or a maximum of 100 mcg is used . They are done to obtain pharmacokinetic data in humans at a very early stage of drug development. The micro-dosing stage is not mandatory and not clearly categorized by regulatory authorities yet .58

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Good clinical practice is not required in which phase of clinical trials?
mcqs.explanation: Good clinical practice is not required in the preclinical phase . Good clinical practice (GCP) is an international ethical and scientific quality standard for the design , conduct , performance, monitoring, auditing , recording, analyses , and reporting of clinical trials. It is primarily for the conduct of clinical trials in humans. Preclinical trials are performed on animals and they are regulated by guidelines prescribed by the CPCSEA (Committee for the Purpose of the Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals) in India. The guidelines are laid down in good laboratory practice (GLP ).

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a primary endpoint in phase 1 studies ?
mcqs.explanation: Efficacy is not a primary endpoint in phase 1 studies . Phase 1 studies are generally done in healthy volunteers . Efficacy can be a secondary endpoint in some studies where patients are recruited . The primary endpoints are: • Safety • Tolerability of single /multiple doses • Pharmacokinetic parameters The primary endpoint denotes the purpose of the study for which it is primarily designed . The secondary endpoint denotes the measure of the valuable outcome of the study design .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following phases of a clinical trial is also referred to as efficacy trial?
mcqs.explanation: Efficacy and appropriate dose range is the main aim of phase 2 of clinical trials. It is evaluated on a small group of patients with the target disease . Phase II of clinical trials involve a small group of patients (50-500). Most of the new drugs will be administered for the first time in patients with the target disease . The study is designed to obtain proof of concept (potential of the drug to treat the disease ) and dose -ranging study (provides input for choosing the most appropriate dose for phase 3 studies ). Phase 3 studies are also known as pivotal studies as they establish treatment benefits .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You read a news alert that mentions a novel drug has received marketing approval for diabetes mellitus and that it has shown positive results in a pivotal trial. This corresponds to which phase of clinical trials?
mcqs.explanation: Phase III trials are usually considered pivotal trials and are necessary for the approval of the majority of drugs. They are also called multi-site trials and are done for 3–5 years.59 When the initial Phase III trials are complete , the sponsor (usually a pharmaceutical company) applies to the FDA for approval to market the drug. This application is called either a New Drug Application (NDA) or a Biologics License Application (BLA ). In some drugs related to rare diseases or malignancies, phase II studies are considered as pivotal, and the drug may be approved on the basis of phase II studies .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A pharmaceutical company has set up a team of physicians to oversee the Phase IV clinical trial of a new drug for SARS-CoV2 infection , to identify possible drug interactions. Which is the most appropriate statement about this phase of the clinical trial?

options.a: Done in a group of 50-500 patients
options.b: Done after a drug is approved and marketed
options.c: Done for drugs used in rare diseases
options.d: Done for formulating guidelines for therapeutic use

mcqs.explanation: Phase IV study is conducted after the drug is approved and marketed by regulatory authorities . It includes post -marketing surveillance and other studies that complement the earlier findings of the drug. After the drug is marketed for general use , practicing physicians are identified through whom data about the efficacy , acceptability , and adverse effects of the drug are collected on a structured proforma. Patients treated in the normal course form the study population . Therefore the study population is much larger. Uncommon adverse effects or those that occur only after long-term use and unsuspected drug interactions are detected at this stage .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are true?
mcqs.explanation: Orphan drugs are for the treatment or prevention of rare diseases with little commercial value for pharmaceutical companies. Orphan receptors are receptors that are discovered yet no known ligands are identified . There are two types of drug development . They are: • Traditional drug development : Initial drug discovery is followed by the characterization of the receptors the drugs are used to act on. • Contemporary drug development : Due to advances in molecular biology and genome sequencing, receptors are identified initially. The drugs are identified later using chemical screening later resulting in the discovery of orphan receptors . Special incentives are given by the government to pharmaceutical companies for the development and marketing of orphan drugs. Few examples of orphan drugs are: • Liposomal amphotericin B • Digoxin antibody (Digibind) • Fomepizole

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A pharmacologically inert substance used along with an active ingredient in a formulation is known as the :
mcqs.explanation: 60 An excipient is a pharmacologically inert substance used along with an active ingredient in a formulation. e.g., starch, lactose , FDKP Role of excipients : • Add bulk to the active drug if used in small quantities • Increase the stability of the formulation • Mask unpleasant taste Inhaled insulin (Afrezza) consists of 2- to 2.5-�Mm crystals of the excipient , fumaryl diketopiperazine (FDKP), that provides a large surface area for adsorption of proteins like insulin. Option A: Placebo is an inert substance given in the form of medication. It is generally not combined with the active ingredient . • Endorphins may play a role in the placebo effect especially for analgesic action. • It is used in the controls of clinical trials to elucidate the actual drug effect . • Not all but only a few patients respond to the placebo . Option B: Nocebo is the opposite of the placebo effect where the patient experiences a negative psychodynamic effect due to their pessimistic attitude towards the medications or healthcare professionals . Option C: Inducers refer to agents that increase the expression of cytochrome enzymes involved in the metabolism of drugs.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which one of the following is a placebo ?

options.a: Herbal medication with no effect known

mcqs.explanation: Sham surgery (placebo surgery) is a faked surgical intervention that omits the step thought to be therapeutically necessary . Note : While option A may be considered a placebo due to there being no known effects , it is not certain as to whether all possible effects (known and unknown) have been considered . Hence, weighing options A and C, the better option among the two would be C as sham surgery is a widely used placebo .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following are not reasons for the alteration of drug dosage in the elderly ?

options.a: They have decreasing renal function with age
options.b: They have loss of lean body mass
options.d: Their total body water is decreased

mcqs.explanation: The reason for the alteration of drug dosage in the elderly is decreased baroreceptor sensitivity due to age -related vascular stiffening . Reasons for the alteration of drug dosage in the elderly are: • Progressive decline of renal function • Loss of lean body mass and an increased ratio of fat to muscle , leading to an increased volume of distribution of lipophilic drugs • Decreased body water - causing volume of distribution (Vd) of hydrophilic drugs decreases .61 • Slower absorption due to reduced gut motility . • Plasma albumin decreases with aging which leads to decreased plasma protein binding.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient started on an anti-epileptic for epilepsy developed toxic epidermal necrolysis . It was documented as a type A adverse drug reaction. Which of the following is not true regarding this adverse effect ?

options.a: These reactions occur due to genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a drug.
options.b: These reactions can be predicted from the drug's known pharmacological or toxicological effects

mcqs.explanation: Type A (augmented ) adverse drug reactions (ADR) are not based upon the qualitatively abnormal responses to the drug. It is based on the pharmacological properties of the drug. Examples of type A ADR: • Side effects • Toxic effects • Consequences of drug withdrawal . They are common, reversible, and preventable . Idiosyncrasy refers to the genetically determined abnormal reactivity to a drug. Adverse drug reactions can be classified into two types : • Type A reactions – sometimes referred to as augmented reactions – are dose -dependent and predictable based on the pharmacology of the drug • Type B reactions – bizarre reactions – which are idiosyncratic and not predictable on the basis of drug pharmacology. They can be based on the characteristics of patients .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs if taken during pregnancy can lead to this adverse effect ?
mcqs.explanation: The baby has features suggestive of phocomelia and it results due to the consumption of thalidomide during pregnancy. Phocomelia is associated with underdeveloped limbs and absent pelvic bones. Both upper and lower limbs are affected and a part of the limbs may be missing. Fused fingers and missing thumbs are also seen . Thalidomide was originally used for the treatment of pregnancy-associated morning sickness but was withdrawn due to this adverse effect . It re-entered the market for the treatment of erythema nodosum leprosum . It also has antiangiogenic and immunomodulatory effects .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs can be used in the first trimester of pregnancy?
mcqs.explanation: 62 Propylthiouracil can be used in the first trimester of pregnancy. It is indicated in the management of hyperthyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs cannot cross the placenta and can safely be used in a pregnant woman?
mcqs.explanation: Heparin is a large molecule and cannot cross the placenta . Hence , heparin can be used safely in a pregnant woman. Unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin is the preferred anticoagulant in pregnancy. Option A: Phenytoin crosses the placenta and can cause fetal hydantoin syndrome. Options B and C: Diazepam and morphine are lipophilic molecules and can cross the placenta .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: 'Me -too drugs' do not differ significantly in which of the following pharmacological features as compared to the prototypical drug?
mcqs.explanation: Me -too drugs are chemically related to the prototype or other chemical compounds that have an identical mechanism of action. Various statins present in the market can be considered as "Me -too drugs". The pharmacokinetic parameters (absorption, distribution, metabolism , and elimination) vary significantly between them (atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have a very long duration of action), but the core mechanism of action remains the same: HMG CoA reductase inhibition and decrease in cholesterol synthesis .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: As a medical officer in a PHC, you anticipate a rise in infections following the worsening flood in your area. You write a letter to the district collector requesting to provide an additional supply of essential medicines . Which of the following best describes these medicines ?

options.a: These are drugs needed to treat emergency conditions
options.b: These are drugs needed to treat serious diseases
options.c: These are drugs that satisfy the priority health needs of the population
options.d: These are drugs that have been in use for a long time

mcqs.explanation: Essential medicines are those medicines that satisfy the priority health care needs of the population . They are selected with due regard to: • Public health relevance • Evidence on efficacy and safety • Comparative cost-effectiveness WHO publishes a model list of essential medicines that provides a framework for individual nations to draw their own national list. The 21st Essential Medicines List, published in April 2019 brings the total to 460 drugs deemed essential for addressing the most important public health needs globally .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The schedule that deals with prescription drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act is ______.
mcqs.explanation: Schedule H deals with prescription drugs. All the drugs listed under schedule H should be provided to the patient only with the prescription from a registered medical practitioner.63 All the drugs under the list must have the warning mentioned below , on their packaging listed prominently. "Schedule H drug. Warning : To be sold by retail on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner only" Schedule H1: To be sold on the production of a valid prescription , but the chemist will maintain a separate register where the identity of the patient , contact details of the prescribing doctor, and the name and dispensed quantity of the drug will be recorded . The dispensing quantity should be strictly according to the valid prescription. It is a recently introduced list with the objective of curtailing indiscriminate use of antimicrobials. Schedule X: To be sold with a valid prescription. Prescription in duplicate , separate license requirements, meticulous storage , and dispensing records must be maintained by the chemist . The drugs that have high abuse liability are included in schedule X.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a schedule X drug?
mcqs.explanation: Ketamine is a schedule X drug. According to The Drugs and Cosmetics Act-1945, Schedule X drugs are those that have high abuse liability and are to be sold with a valid prescription only. A prescription in duplicate , separate license requirement, meticulous storage , and dispensing records must be maintained by the chemist . Option B: Thalidomide is a schedule H drug. Option D: Colistin is a schedule P drug.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A first-year resident administers an intramuscular injection to a patient by the Z track technique. What is the advantage of this technique ?
mcqs.explanation: The advantage of the 'Z-track technique ' for intramuscular administration is that it prevents skin staining. Z-track technique procedure : • Stretch the skin by pulling it laterally away from the intended point of injection. • Insert the needle into the site at a 90\037 angle, aspirate by pulling back to see if the needle has a penetrated vessel . • If blood is aspirated withdraw the needle , and repeat the procedure at another site with new equipment and medication. • If no blood is aspirated administer the injection. • Wait for 10 seconds and then withdraw the needle , and release the skin allowing the displaced tissue to seal the needle track. Advantages:64 • The 'Z-track' prevents leakage of the medication into the subcutaneous tissue and skin staining through the tract to the surface of the skin • Pain intensity is also reduced

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Z track technique is used for?

options.c: Administration of long acting depot antipsychotics

mcqs.explanation: The Z-track technique is used for the intramuscular administration of long-acting depot antipsychotics. Advantages: • The 'Z-track' prevents leakage of the medication into the subcutaneous tissue and skin staining through the tract to the surface of the skin • Pain intensity is also reduced65

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A drug label suggests storage in a 'cool' place . What is the temperature at which this drug is to be stored ?
mcqs.explanation: Storing at a cool place means to store at 8-15 degrees C. Examples for drugs to be stored under cool temperature include insulin, nicorandil.Label instructions Temperat ure Store frozen -20oC Keep cool 8-15oC Store at room temperatu re 15-25oC66

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The elimination after 3 half-lives in first-order kinetics is around:
mcqs.explanation: 70 After each half-life , 50% of the drug is eliminated or the plasma concentration becomes half the original value. Therefore, after, • 1 half-life = 50% drug is eliminated • 2 half-lives = 75 % drug is eliminated • 3 half-lives = 87 .5% is eliminated • 4 half-lives = 93% is eliminated

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You have to give 180 mg of ceftriaxone to a patient in a 2 ml syringe that has 10 divisions per ml. The concentration of the drug in the vial is 500 mg/5 ml. How many divisions should be filled in 2 ml of the syringe to give 180 mg?
mcqs.explanation: The syringe should be filled up to 18 divisions to deliver 180 mg ceftriaxone to the patient . Concentration of drug: 500 mg/5 mL \037 100 mg/1 mL The syringe has 10 divisions per mL . Hence , each division corresponds to 1/10 = 0.1 mL The required dosage for the patient is 180 mg that is present in 1.8 mL . 0.1mL =1 division, 1.8mL = 18 divisions.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: 500mg of a drug was administered to a patient . 100mg was cleared in 1 hour. How much of the drug would be left in his body after 3 hours if the excretion of the drug follows zero-order kinetics?
mcqs.explanation: In zero-order kinetics, a constant amount of drug is eliminated in unit time. In this question, 100 mg of the drug is eliminated in 1 hour. After 3 hours, 3 x 100 = 300 mg would be eliminated. 500-300 = 200 mg will be the remaining drug in the body.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: 200 mg of a drug is administered to a patient , of which 20 mg is excreted in 90 minutes . How much of the drug will remain after 3 hours if it follows first-order kinetics?
mcqs.explanation: After 3 hours, 162mg of the drug will remain. In first-order kinetics, a constant fraction of the drug is excreted in a given time. In the given question, 20mg out of 200mg is excreted in 90 minutes , /200 = 0.1 fraction is eliminated every 90 minutes . After 90 minutes , 200mg - 20 mg = 180 mg remains The next 90 minutes (i.e. after 180 minutes ) = 180 x 0.1 = 18 mg is eliminated .71 Therefore, 180 - 18 = 162 mg remains. Simpler way: 1/10 fraction of the drug is excreted in 90 minutes \037 9/10 remains after 90 minutes . 3 hours (180 min) is 2 times 90 minutes . So 200 x (9/10 )(9/10 ) = 162 mg remains after 180 minutes

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Calculate the half-life of a drug X administered to a patient if it has a volume of distribution of 50 liters and clearance of 0.1 L/min.
mcqs.explanation: The half-life of this drug is 350 minutes . In first-order kinetics:Therefore, t1/2 ~ 0.7 x 50/0.1 = 0.7 x 500 t1/2 ~ 350 minutes Where, • t1/2 - Plasma half-life • Vd - Volume of distribution (50) • CL - Clearance (0.1)

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Calculate hepatic clearance of a drug with hepatic blood flow of 2000 mL /min and hepatic extraction ratio of 0.5.
mcqs.explanation: The hepatic clearance is 1000 mL /min.72 Clearance of a drug by an organ is the difference between the rate of presentation of the drug to the organ and the rate of exit of the drug from the organ. It is calculated by the equation: CLorgan = Q x E Where, • Q - Organ blood flow • E - Extraction ratio (organ-specific ) In the question, it is given that the hepatic blood flow (Q) is 2000 mL /min and the hepatic extraction ratio (E) is 0.5. Substituting the values in the above equation, CLorgan = 2000 X 0.5 = 1000 mL /min Note : The extraction ratio (E) is the fraction of the drug that is removed from the blood by the eliminating organ. Extraction ratio (E) = CA-CV/CA Where, • CA is the concentration of drug presented to the organ • CA-CV is the drug removed by the organ

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient is administered drug X that follows first-order kinetics. 40 mg intravenous dose results in a plasma concentration of 2mg/L initially and 1mg/L , 4 hours later. What is the clearance of drug X?
mcqs.explanation: Time taken for the plasma concentration to drop to half, 2 mg/L to 1mg/L = 4 hours (plasma half life -t1/2)Amount of drug in the body = 40 Initial plasma concentration = 273 Therefore, Vd = 40/2 = 20 L Clearance = 0.693 x Vd / t1/2 Clearance ~ 0.7 x 20 /4 Clearance ~ 3.5 L/hour

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A male patient weighing 50 kg has acute severe asthma, for which theophylline infusion is planned. The target plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. The volume of distribution of theophylline is 0.6 L/kg. What will be the loading dose in this patient for intravenous administration?
mcqs.explanation: The loading dose in this patient for intravenous administration is 300mg . Target plasma concentration (Cp) = 10 mg/L Volume of distribution (Vd) = 0.6 L/kg In the above patient , total Vd = 0.6 x 50 = 30 LFor intravenous route; F=1 Where, • Vd - Volume of distribution (liters) • Cp - target serum level (mcg/L) • F - bioavailability factor Loading dose = 10 mg/L x 30L = 300 mg Note : The loading dose of 300 mg is usually not given as a single intravenous injection; it would be given as an infusion or as divided doses administered over a short period to reduce the toxicity associated with high plasma levels .74

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Calculate maintenance dose for a drug M with 100 % oral bioavailability, which needs a target concentration of 2 mg/L and clearance of 20L /hr and dosed QID.
mcqs.explanation: The maintenance dose of the drug is 240 mg.Target plasma concentration (Cp) = 2 mg/L Clearance (CL) = 20L /hr Assuming dosing interval for QID = every 6th hour = x 6 (since the clearance stated is per hour) Bioavailability (100 %), F= Maintenance dose = 2 x 20 x 6/ 1 = 240 mg Note : QID corresponds to 4 times a day. Hence , the dosing interval is 24/4 = 6 hours.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: You have started an infusion of drug Y in a patient at a rate of 200 mg/hr. Drug Y has Vd of 100 liters and clearance of 100 ml/min. What will be the drug concentration at a steady state ?
mcqs.explanation: Steady state concentration (Css) for this drug is 33.33mg/L. Steady state concentration (Css) = Rate of infusion / clearance. Rate of infusion = 200 mg/h Vd = 100 L Clearance = 100 mL /min Clearance = 100 x 60 mL /hr = 6000 mL /hr = 6L /h (converted to L/h) Css = (200 mg/hr) / (6L /hr) = 100 /3 = 33 .33 mg/L

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The clearance of a drug which follows first-order kinetics (in one compartment model ) is 0.2 L/min and volume of distribution is 40 L. What is the t1/2 of that drug?
mcqs.explanation: The t1/2 of the drug would be 140 minutes .75 t1/2 is the time required for the plasma concentration or the amount of a drug in the body to be reduced by 50%. It depends on its clearance and volume of distribution. t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd/Cl where , • Vd - volume of distribution • Cl - clearance. We can take 0.693 approximately as 0.7 Substituting , t1/2 = 0.7 x 40 /0.2 t1/2 = 0.7 x 200 t1/2 = 140 minutes Clinical implications: Half-life determines the duration of the drug effect . It also indicates whether the accumulation of the drug will occur under multiple dosage regimens thereby making it is essential to decide on the appropriate dosing interval.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
