mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: For Na+-K+ ATPase coupling ratio is _____
mcqs.explanation: Na+-K+ ATPase or Na+-K+ ATP pump is an electrogenic pump in that it moves three positive charges out of the cell for each two that it moves in, and it is therefore said to have a coupling ratio of 3:2 . Note : • Na+-K+ ATP pump is found in almost all parts of the body, and it catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and uses the energy for its activity • It is one of the major energy using process in the body. On an average, it accounts for 24% of the energy utilized by the cells , and in neurons it accounts for 70%. Thus, it accounts for large share in basal metabolism

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old diabetic man has been prescribed empagliflozin . Which of the following processes will most likely be affected by this drug?
mcqs.explanation: Empagliflozin is an SGLT -2 inhibitor. SGLT -2 or sodium-glucose transport protein 2 is an example of a cotransporter that plays a key role in glucose absorption from renal tubule by secondary active transport. This process is blocked by SGLT -2 inhibitors, leading to renal loss of glucose and improved glycemic control. • A special property of the transport protein involved in secondary active transport is that a conformational change to allow Na+ movement to the interior will not occur until a glucose48 molecule also attaches to the transport protein. When they both become attached , the conformational change takes place automatically , and the Na+ and glucose are transported to the inside of the cell at the same time. • The figure shows glucose is transported uphill and Na+ is transported downhill . Energy derived from the downhill movement of Na+ is maintained by the Na+-K+ ATPase pump on the basolateral side .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Glucose is absorbed in intestine by?
mcqs.explanation: Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport (sodium co-transport). The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly , by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell . This maintains the concentration gradient across the luminal border of the cell so that more Na+ and consequently more glucose enter. Though both secondary active transport and facilitated diffusion play a role in glucose absorption, it is the initial active transport of sodium through the basolateral membranes of the intestinal epithelial cells that provide the eventual force for moving glucose through the membranes as well . So, secondary active transport is the single best answer for this question.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old lady is diagnosed with Lambart - Eaton syndrome. Radioimmunoassay reveals the presence of serum antibodies against voltage -gated calcium channels. Which of the following process will be affected as a result of this pathology ?
mcqs.explanation: Exocytosis of neurotransmitters at the nerve terminals will be affected as a result of antibodies against voltage -gated calcium channels. After an action potential reaches the terminal endings of a nerve, the influx of Ca2+ via voltage -gated calcium channels leads to the fusion of intracellular vesicles with cell membranes. This results in the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic space . This process will be impaired in the case of Lambert-eaton syndrome.49 Exocytosis is the extrusion of membrane-bound vesicles . In exocytosis , intracellular vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and then release their contents to the extracellular fluid . Solute and water can be released from the cell via vesicles by the process of exocytosis . Exocytosis can be: Constitutive exocytosis : • Involves prompt transport of proteins to the cell membrane in vesicles , with little or no processing or storage • Examples • Goblet cells in the intestine continuously to release mucus • Fibroblasts in connective tissue release collagen Regulated / Non constitutive exocytosis : • Here the proteins from golgi apparatus initially enter the secretory granules, where the processing of prohormones to mature hormones occurs before exocytosis • Examples • Endocrine cells , hormones are stored in secretory vesicles and released in response to a signal from outside the cell . • To insert proteins into the cell membrane like aquaporin insertion Note : • The term 'regulated exocytosis ' is misleading because even constitutive exocytosis is regulated . • Exocytosis involves two families of proteins: Rabs, which help vesicles dock onto the membrane, and SNAREs, which facilitate membrane fusion. • This is Ca2+ -dependent process • Exocytosis , like endocytosis , requires energy in the form of ATP .50

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which pathway is called regulated pathway ?
mcqs.explanation: The non constitutive pathway of exocytosis is called the regulated pathway . Exocytosis can be either constitutive or non constitutive (regulated ): • Regulated or nonconstitutive pathway: Proteins from the Golgi apparatus initially enter secretory granules, where processing of prohormones to the mature hormones occurs before exocytosis . • Constitutive pathway : Involves the prompt transport of proteins to the cell membrane in vesicles , with little or no processing or storage .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old gentleman is diagnosed with elevated blood cholesterol levels . A defect in a process that involves the protein 'clathrin' is being suspected . Which of the following process will be most likely affected by this defect ?
mcqs.explanation: Receptor -mediated endocytosis takes place in coated pits or indentations where the cytoplasmic side of the membrane has high concentrations of protein. The most common protein found in coated pits is clathrin. A GTP binding protein dynamin is involved in pinching off the vesicle formed in clathrin-mediated endocytosisImportance: • Internalisation of many receptors and ligands bound to them eg . LDL , Nerve Growth Factor. • Receptor -mediated endocytosis transports a variety of substances including protein hormones, growth factors, antibodies , and plasma proteins that serve as carriers for iron and cholesterol . • Synaptic function • Abnormalities in receptor -mediated removal of cholesterol from the blood are associated with elevated plasma cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease .51

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Transcytosis occurs in which of the following cell types ?
mcqs.explanation: Transcytosis is seen in epithelial cells of intestine . Transcytosis is endocytosis across one membrane of the cell followed by exocytosis across the opposite membrane. Transcytosis across epithelia or endothelia : Some molecules , such as proteins , are too large to diffuse through the membrane or cross the membrane transporters of epithelia . Instead they are moved across epithelia by transcytosis. Steps : • The molecule is brought into the epithelial cell via receptor -mediated endocytosis .52 • The resulting vesicle attaches to microtubules in the cells cytoskeleton and is transported across the cell by vesicular transport. • At the opposite side of the epithelium , the contents of the vesicle are expelled into the interstitial fluid by exocytosis . Significance : • Transcytosis makes it possible for large proteins to move across an epithelium and remain intact. • It is the means by which infants absorb maternal antibodies in breast milk. The antibodies are absorbed on the apical surface of the infant's intestinal epithelium and then released into the extracellular fluid .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old diabetic man is started on an insulin secretagogue . Which of the following ions is required for emeiocytosis or reverse pinocytosis during the insulin secretion process ?
mcqs.explanation: Emeiocytosis requires Ca2+ directly . Emeiocytosis is the movement of secretory granules to the plasma membrane of the cell , fusion of the granule surface membrane with the cell membrane, rupture of membranes, and liberation of granular contents into the pericapillary space . Insulin secretion (as shown in the image below ):53 • Glucose enters B cells by GLUT-2 transporters. • It is phosphorylated and metabolized to pyruvate (Pyr) in the cytoplasm . • The Pyr enters the mitochondria and is metabolized via the citric acid cycle . The ATP formed by oxidative phosphorylation inhibits ATP -sensitive K+ channels, reducing K+ efflux . • This depolarizes the B cell , and Ca2+ influx is increased . The Ca2+ stimulates the release of insulin by exocytosis . Glutamate (Glu) is also formed, and this primes secretory granules, preparing them for exocytosis . It is promoted by Ca2+, \031 K+ It is inhibited by Mg2+, K+ depletion . The process of emeiocytosis for insulin secretion is depicted in the image below .54

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following equations is used to calculate the equilibrium potential for an ion?
mcqs.explanation: Equilibrium potential for an ion is calculated using the Nernst equation. When there is a concentration gradient for an ion across the membrane, the ion tends to diffuse down the concentration gradient. The electric potential that exactly opposes this net diffusion is called the equilibrium potential for that ion. This is calculated using the Nernst equation.59 It is expressed as the potential inside the cell (intracellular potential relative to the extracellular potential ). To calculate the value of the equilibrium potential :Note : In this formula, the choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign ( +/- ). Mathematically , log (100/10 ) = 1 and log (10/100 ) = - 1. Hence , changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same. This equation is used only to derive the numerical value of the potential . It is NOT used to derive the sign/charge (+/-). The sign/charge is derived from logic: • In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater outside , then the + ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more + relatively . Hence , the potential will be positive . • In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater inside, then the + ion moves from inside to outside . The intracellular potential becomes more - relatively (as + ion moves outside ). Hence the potential will be negative . • In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater outside , then the - ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more - relatively. Hence the potential will be negative . • In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater inside, then the - ion moves from inside to outside . The intracellular potential becomes more + relatively (as - ion moves outside ). Hence the potential will be positive .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used to calculate the equilibrium potential for diffusion of multiple ions?
mcqs.explanation: 60 The Goldman equation is used to calculate the diffusion potential when the membrane is permeable to several different ions. Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equationHere, • P= permeability of the membrane to each ion, and • C= concentrations of the respective ions on the inside (i) and outside (o) of the membrane. The Na+, K+ and Cl- are the most important ions involved in the development of membrane potentials in nerve fibres and muscle fibres.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium explains the ______

options.a: Effect of one non-diffusible ion on the distribution of other non-diffusible ions
options.b: Effect of one permeant ion on the distribution of other permeant ions
options.c: Effect of a permeant ion on the distribution of nondiffusible ions
options.d: Effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions

mcqs.explanation: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium explains the effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions. Consider the situation depicted below ,61 The membrane is permeable to K+ and Cl-. However, it is impermeable to the proteins . The impermeable protein molecules hinder the movement of K+ (negative charge of the proteins holding back positive charge of the K+) and favor the movement of Cl- (like charges repel ). According to the Gibbs-Donnan equation, at equilibrium, the concentration ratios of diffusible ions are equal across the membrane.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Extracellular concentration of a positive ion (with valency = 1) is 100mmol /L and its intracellular concentration is 10mmol /L, the potential across the membrane using Nernst equation is (mV )_______
mcqs.explanation: The potential of a positive ion across the membrane using Nernst equation is +60mV .62 Where, z is valency in the formula. Deriving the numerical value: EMF = 61/1 *log 10 /100 = 61 The choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign ( +/- ). Mathematically , log (100/10 ) = 1 and log (10/100 ) = - 1. Hence , changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same. Deciding the sign/charge: A positive ion with greater concentration extracellularly will try to diffuse inside the cell . A positive intracellular potential is required to prevent this. Hence the sign/charge (potential ) is positive (+). Hence , the potential across the membrane using the Nernst equation is +60mV (the closest answer chosen).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Extracellular concentration of a negative ion (with valency = 1) is 10mmol /L and its intracellular concentration is 100mmol /L. The equilibrium potential for this ion using Nernst equation is (mV ) _____
mcqs.explanation: The equilibrium potential for this negative ion using the Nernst equation is +60mV .63 Where, z is valency in the formula. Deriving the numerical value: EMF = 61/1 *log 100 /10 = 61 Deciding the sign/charge: A negative ion with greater concentration intracellularly will try to diffuse outside the cell . A positive intracellular potential is required to prevent this. Hence , the potential is positive . Hence , the Nernst potential is +60mV (the closest answer chosen).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the Nernst potential for K+ in milivolt (mV )?
mcqs.explanation: The Nernst potential for K+ is � 90mV . Note : • For K+ ions, the concentration gradient is directed outward and the electrical gradient is directed inward. • In general , all excitable cell membranes at rest are maximally permeable to K+ and thus their RMP is close to equilibrium potential of K+ ion.

mcqs.question: Which of the following ions have the highest positive equilibrium potential ?
mcqs.explanation: The ion with the highest positive equilibrium potential is Na+ that is +60mV .64

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The resting membrane potential of a nerve fibre depends on ______
mcqs.explanation: The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a nerve fibre depends on the diffusion of both K+ and Na+ and the Na+-K+ ATPase pump . The most predominant factor, however, is the diffusion of K+ ions. This is because , at rest, the permeability of the membrane of the nerve fibre to K+ ions is almost 100 times greater than that to Na+.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Resting membrane potential of the nerve fibre is equal to equilibrium potential of ______
mcqs.explanation: Resting membrane potential of a nerve fiber is equal to the equilibrium potential of Cl- and is -70mV.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Driving force of a charged ion is____

options.a: Measured membrane potential - calculated equilibrium potential
options.b: Measured membrane potential + calculated equilibrium potential
options.c: Calculated equilibrium potential - Measured membrane potential

mcqs.explanation: The driving force on a charged ion is measured membrane potential (Em) - calculated equilibrium potential (Ex). Net driving force (mV) = Em - Ex where , Em = Actual membrane potential (mV ) Ex = Equilibrium potential for X (mV) When the driving force is negative (i.e., Em is more negative than the ion's equilibrium potential ), then • A cation will enter the cell • An anion will leave the cell

mcqs.question: If the membrane potential of this cell is -80mV the driving force is greatest for which ion?
mcqs.explanation: The driving force is greatest for Ca2+. Net driving force is the difference between the membrane potential and the equilibrium potential for that particular ion. Hence Em - EX . Where: Em = Actual membrane potential (mV ) = -80mV EX = Equilibrium potential for X (mV) For the respective ions: E Ca2+ = +120 ; Driving force = -80 – (120 ) = -200mV E Na+ = +60 ; Driving force= -80 – (60) =-140mV65 E K+ = -90, Driving force = -80 – (-90) =10mV E Cl-= -70, Driving force = -80 – (-70) =-10mV Thus, Ca2+ will have the largest driving force and it will move inwards or into the cell .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following techniques is used to study the current flow across single ion channel?
mcqs.explanation: The patch-clamp technique is used to record ion current flow through a single protein channel. In the patch -clamp experiment , a small pipette is carefully maneuvered to seal off a portion of a cell membrane. The pipette has an electrode bathed in an appropriate solution that allows for the recording of electrical changes through any pore in the membrane.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the effect on the cellular membrane when the extracellular concentration of K+ is decreased ?
mcqs.explanation: When the extracellular concentration of K+ is decreased (hypokalemia), there is increased negativity of RMP. RMP predominantly depends on the diffusion of K+ from inside to outside the cell . This diffusion depends on the concentration gradient with the inside of the cell having a larger concentration of K+ ions. When the extracellular concentration of K+ decreases , the concentration gradient for K+ rises. Therefore, more K+ ions diffuse out of the cell . This leaves the inside of the cell more negative relative to the extracellular space . This increases the negativity of the RMP, leaving the membrane hyperpolarised .

mcqs.question: What is the volume of blood in ml, in a child per kg body weight ?
mcqs.explanation: The total blood volume of a child is around 75 –80 ml/kg. In the neonatal period , it is 85 ml/kg. It rises to a peak of 105 ml/kg by the end of the first month and then drops progressively over ensuing months.

mcqs.question: 500 mg of mannitol was injected out of which 10 % is excreted . After equilibrium, plasma concentration is 3.2 mg/100 ml. Calculate ECF Volume (L).

mcqs.question: Which of the following is higher in the ECF compared to ICF?
mcqs.explanation: The pH of ECF is 7.4 while the pH of ICF is 7.0. There is continuous generation of H+ ions in the ICF due to the various metabolic processes . So, the pH of ICF is a little lower compared to ECF.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most abundant intracellular anion?
mcqs.explanation: Phosphate is the most abundant intracellular anion. • ICF • Major anion- Phosphate • Major cation- K+ • ECF • Major anion- Cl- • Cation- Na+ • Protein content in ICF is ~8 times greater than plasma (ECF)84

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: How many grams of NaCl make 1 mole of NaCl?
mcqs.explanation: 1 mol of NaCl is 58.5 g • A mole is the gram-molecular weight of a substance (molecular weight of a substance in grams) • In this case, the molecular weight of Na-23 and Cl-35.5. • 1 mol of NaCl = 23 g + 35.5 g = 58.5 g Note • Each mole consists of 6 X 10 23 molecules . • The molecular weight of a substance is the ratio of the mass of 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon-12 . Because molecular weight is a ratio, it is dimensionless . • The Dalton (Da) is a unit of mass equal to the mass of 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon-12 . Thus molecular mass is expressed in units.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: How much is one equivalent of calcium (molecular weight = 40)?
mcqs.explanation: 1 equivalent of calcium is 20 g. One equivalent is 1 mol of an ionized substance divided by its valency. For calcium in solution , 1 mol is going to be 40g and its valency is 2. Therefore, 1 equivalent of calcium is 40/2 = 20g.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The unit expressing the concentration of osmotically active particles is_____
mcqs.explanation: 85 The concentration of osmotically active particles is usually expressed in osmoles . Normal plasma osmolality is 280 to 290 mosmole/kg H2O • Example • NaCl dissociate into 2 particles - Na+ and Cl- in an ideal solution . Hence we can say that for every 1 mole of NaCl, there are 2 osmoles . • If a solute is a non-ionizing compound such as glucose , the osmotic pressure is a function of the number of glucose molecules present . • NOTE: The body fluids are not ideal solutions , and although the dissociation of strong electrolytes is complete , the number of particles free to exert an osmotic effect is reduced owing to the interaction between the ions. Thus, 1mol of NaCl per litre body fluids contribute somewhat less than 2 osmoles . The more concentrated the solution , the greater the deviation from the ideal solution .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A female patient was infused with a solution which leads to rapid lysis of the RBCs. Which solution was most likely infused ?
mcqs.explanation: Urea is a highly permeable solute , 300mMol/L urea solution behaves as a hypotonic solution . Urea diffuses to the inside of RBC's via UTB channels very rapidly, while the rest of the solutes in the ECF cannot enter the cell . So the ECF now becomes hypotonic . So, fluid enters the RBC and causes their lysis . Other Options : • Option A : The solution is iso-osmotic. (150mmol of NaCl contains 150mmol of Na+ and 150mmol of Cl- ions making the total osmolality 300 mOsm/L.This is equivalent to 0.9% NaCl which is isotonic.) • Option B and C: The solutions are hyper -osmotic. This will lead to shrinking of the RBCs. Note : • If a cell is placed into a hypotonic solution that has a lower concentration of impermeant solutes (<282 mOsm/L), water will diffuse into the cell , causing it to swell . • If a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution having a higher concentration of impermeant solutes , water will flow out of the cell leading to cell shrinkage.86

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Normal osmolarity of plasma is mainly due to ________.
mcqs.explanation: Normal plasma osmolarity (~290 mOsm/L) is mainly due to Na+ and its accompanying anions, principally Cl- and HCO3- • Osmolarity (mOsm/L) = 2 [Na+] (mEq /L) + 0.055 [Glucose ] (mg/dL) + 0.36 [BUN] (mg/dL) • Because sodium and its associated anions (Cl- , HCO3- ) account for about 94 per cent of the solute in the extracellular compartment, plasma osmolarity (Posm) can be roughly approximated as • Posm = 2.1 x Plasma sodium concentration • With a plasma sodium concentration of 142 mEq/L , the plasma osmolarity would be estimated from the formula above to be about 298 mOsm/L. • In conditions associated with renal disease , the contribution of two other solutes , glucose and urea, should be included . • Because urea easily permeates most cell membranes, it exerts little effective osmotic pressure under steady -state conditions. (Ineffective osmoles ) • Contribution to plasma osmolarity: • Na+ and associated anions: 270 mOsm/L • Glucose : 5 mOsm/L • Urea: 5 mOsm/L • Plasma proteins : 2 mOsm/L • Other ions: 8 mOsm/L87

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Plasma proteins contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles because _____

options.a: High molar concentration, high molecular weight
options.b: Low molar concentration, low molecular weight
options.c: Low molar concentration, high molecular weight
options.d: High molar concentration, low molecular weight

mcqs.explanation: Proteins actually contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles (\0271 mOsm) because of their low molar concentration and high molecular weight . Protein concentration measured as g/L may be high. However, as their molecular weight is high, the protein concentration in terms of moles per liter ( molar concentration) will be low. Thus, they contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles . Detailed explanation: Terms like high, low are always used for comparison. Here we compare plasma proteins and sodium (sodium is chosen because it contributes the maximum part of osmolarity). Look at the values given below (just for understanding )Plasma proteins (Albumi n) Sodiu m Molar concentration 0.75mosm/L(Low) 270mo sm/L Molecular weight ( 1 mole = ) 67,000 g(High) 23g

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Daily water loss in sweat during normal activities is (ml)_____
mcqs.explanation: The amount of water lost by sweating is highly variable, depending on physical activity and environmental temperature . The volume of sweat normally is about 100 ml/day, but in very hot weather or during heavy exercise fluid loss in sweat occasionally increase to 1 to 2 L/hour.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which type of disturbance of body fluids is observed in sweating ?
mcqs.explanation: Sweating \032 loss of water\032 Hyperosmotic volume contraction • The osmolarity of ECF increases because sweat is hyposmotic (relatively more water than salt is lost). • ECF volume decreases because of the loss of volume in the sweat . • Water shifts out of ICF; as a result of the shift, ICF osmolarity increases until it is equal to ECF osmolarity, and ICF volume decreases . • Plasma protein concentration increases because of the decrease in ECF volume. Although hematocrit might also be expected to increase, it remains unchanged because of the water shifts out of the RBCs, decreasing their volume and offsetting the concentrating effect of the decreased ECF volume. • So,Loss of hypotonic fluid causes hypertonic volume contraction.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 73-year-old diabetic man is brought to the emergency with an altered sensorium. He is dehydrated and his blood glucose is 550mg/dl. A hyperosmolar, hyperglycemic state is suspected . Which of the given formulae can correctly evaluate his serum osmolality ?
mcqs.explanation: 88 Calculated serum osmolality = 2 sodium + (glucose /18) + (BUN/2.8). In the given clinical scenario, the patient with untreated type 2 diabetes mellitus has most likely developed a hyperosmolar, hyperglycemic state . His serum osmolality will be significantly raised. The principal determinants of osmolality of serum are the concentrations of sodium, glucose and urea (blood urea nitrogen or BUN). Osmolality is defined as a measure of the osmoles (Osm) of solute per kilogram of solvent (osmol/kg or Osm/kg). The osmolality of the intracellular and extracellular fluids is maintained between 290 and 310 mOsm in each compartment.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Addition of 500 mL of hypertonic saline to the extracellular fluid leads to _______
mcqs.explanation: The images shown in the figure are called Darrow Yannet Diagrams. They depict the change in plasma osmolality and plasma volume in various conditions. If a hypertonic solution is added to the extracellular fluid , the extracellular osmolarity increases and causes osmosis of water out of the cells into the extracellular compartment • ECF osmolality increases. ECF volume increases. • As, ECF osmolality rises, fluid from ICF moves to ECF till osmotic equilibrium is established . So, • ICF osmolality rises. ICF volume decreases . Therefore, the net effect is an increase in extracellular volume (greater than the volume of fluid added ), a decrease in intracellular volume, and a rise in osmolarity in both compartments. Note : The dotted line in the diagram is the change after either addition or removal of fluid

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following Darrow Yannet diagram is suggestive of which condition? ( dotted line denotes the change caused by the condition)
mcqs.explanation: 89 In the given darrow yannet diagram, there is hypoosmostic volume expansion which is suggestive of SIADH. • In SIADH there is excessive secretion of ADH. So, excess water is retained in the body. • So, ECF volume rises. ECF osmolality decreases . • ECF fluid enters ICF untill osmotic equilibrium is re-established . • So, ICF volume rises. ICF osmolality decreases .The Darrow Yannet diagrams of various conditions are shown above

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following Darrow Yannet diagram is suggestive of which condition? Note : The solid line is the original fluid compartment and the colour shaded compartment within the dotted line denotes the change caused by the condition.
mcqs.explanation: 90 In adrenal insufficiency there is hypo -osmotic volume contraction. Aldosterone deficiency leads to increased sodium loss (loss of hyperosmotic fluid ). • The osmolarity of ECF decreases . • ECF volume decreases because of the loss of volume. • Water shifts into ICF; as a result of the shift, ICF osmolarity decreases until it is equal to ECF osmolarity, and ICF volume increases. • So, loss of hypertonic fluid causes hypotonic volume contraction. Please note that in the diagram, the horizontal axis represents volume and vertical axis represents osmolarity.The Darrow Yannet diagrams of various conditions are shown above.91

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Various safety factors prevent excessive fluid accumulation in the interstitial spaces . Total safety factor against edema is (mmHg)_____
mcqs.explanation: The total safety factor against edema is about 17 mmHg. Summary of safety factors that prevent edema is: • The safety factor caused by low tissue compliance in the negative pressure range is about 3 mm Hg • The safety factor caused by increased lymph flow is about 7 mm Hg • The safety factor caused by washdown of proteins from the interstitial spaces is about 7 mm Hg Therefore, the total safety factor against edema is about 17 mm Hg.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: You are an intern and want to determine the quantity of IV fluids needed for a patient . How much amount of transient loss/insensible loss per day would you account for in your calculations ?
mcqs.explanation: 500-600 ml of transient loss/insensible loss per day would have to be accounted for in the calculation. Although water is lost through sweating especially in hot climates or during physical exertion, we tend to lose water at rest as well . Physiologically , water evaporates from the skin and lungs at a rate of about 600 to 700 ml/day. This is known as insensible water loss.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: I-125 labelled albumin is used for measurement of:
mcqs.explanation: I-125 labelled albumin is the most commonly used substance for the measurement of plasma volume .92

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is embryologically and physiologically unrelated to other neural cells ?
mcqs.explanation: Microglia are physiologically and embryologically unrelated to other neural cell types . They arise from macrophages outside the nervous system .104

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following areas is a pseudo -unipolar type of neuron present ?
mcqs.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion is a classic example of a pseudo -unipolar neuron.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Where does the initiation of nerve impulse occur in a spinal motor neuron?
mcqs.explanation: In a spinal motor neuron, initiation of nerve impulse occurs in the axon hillock and initial segment of the axon because it has a very high density of voltage -gated Na+ and K+ channels. Hence , this region is also known as the trigger zone for the action potential . Parts of a Neuron: • Cell body/perikaryon: contains many Nissl bodies . • Dendritic zone where multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated . • Axon hillock: part of the cell body from which the axon arises. • Initial segment : the first part of the axon where propagated action potentials are generated . • An axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings . The unmyelinated regions of a myelinated axon are termed as nodes of Ranvier . • Synaptic knobs/nerve endings where action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters. Note : Action potentials are generated at the initial segment in spinal motor neurons and the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons.105

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which part of the neuron contains a maximum number of Na+ channels per square micrometer?
mcqs.explanation: The maximum number of Na+ channels per square micrometer in myelinated neurons is present at the nodes of Ranvier . It contains 2000 -12 ,000 channels per square micrometer. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are highly concentrated in the nodes of Ranvier and the initial segment in myelinated neurons. The spatial distribution of ion channels along the axon plays a key role in the initiation and regulation of action potential .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In a cutaneous sensory neuron, at which of the following places is the propagated action potential generated ?
mcqs.explanation: In cutaneous sensory neurons, propagated action potentials are generated in the initial node of Ranvier . From a functional point of view, neurons generally have four important zones : • A receptor , or dendritic zone, where multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated • A site where propagated action potentials are generated (the initial segment in spinal motor neurons, the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons) • An axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings • The nerve endings , where action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters The cell body is often located at the dendritic zone end of the axon, but it can be within the axon (eg , auditory neurons)106

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the relationship between diameter of the nerve and conduction velocity ?
mcqs.explanation: The conduction velocity of a myelinated axon increases linearly with diameter . Conduction velocity is increased by: • Increasing the fiber size: Increasing the diameter of a nerve fiber results in decreased internal resistance ; thus , conduction velocity down the nerve is faster. • Myelination : Myelin acts as an insulator around nerve axons and increases conduction velocity . Myelinated nerves exhibit saltatory conduction . It is a rapid process that allows myelinated axons to conduct up to 50 times faster than the fastest unmyelinated fibers. • Activity of the Na+–K+ pump does not directly affect the formation or conduction of action potentials .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What process is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3?

options.a: Movement of Na+ into the cell
options.b: Movement of Na+ out of the cell
options.c: Movement of K+ into the cell
options.d: Movement of K+ out of the cell

mcqs.explanation: The graph depicts action potential . The movement of Na+ into the cell is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3. Once the membrane is depolarized to the threshold , local potential , the upstroke of the nerve action potential is caused by the opening of the Na+ channels. The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage -gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop . When the Na+ channels open , Na+ moves into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential .The process responsible for repolarization is the opening of K+. The K+ permeability becomes very high and drives the membrane potential toward the K+equilibrium potential by the flow of107 K+ out of the cell .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum at which of the following points in a nerve action potential ?
mcqs.explanation: The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum during repolarization (marked as point 3 in the above image). Most of the increase in K+ conductance comes after the increase in Na+ conductance around the time of repolarization.During the early portion of the action potential , the sodium conductance is 1000 times greater than potassium conductance . Therefore, far more sodium ions flow to the interior of the fiber than do potassium ions to the exterior. This causes the membrane potential to become positive at the action potential onset . When the membrane potential rises from � 90 millivolts toward zero, this voltage change causes a conformational change in the K+ channels which allows increased potassium efflux . Then, the sodium channels begin to close and the potassium channels begin to open , and potassium conductance begins to increase (and sodium conductance decreases ). The increased flow of K+ out of the cell causes membrane repolarization. The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state explains the after-hyperpolarization followed by a return to the resting membrane potential .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding the upstroke of a nerve action potential ?

options.a: There is net outward current and the cell interior becomes more negative
options.b: There is net outward current and the cell interior becomes less negative
options.c: There is net inward current and the cell interior becomes more negative
options.d: There is net inward current and the cell interior becomes less negative

mcqs.explanation: Regarding the upstroke of a nerve action potential , there is a net inward current and the cell interior becomes less negative . The direction of the current is either • same as the direction of positive charge ( eg , Na+ )108 • opposite to the direction of negative charge (eg , Cl- ) • opposite to the direction of electrons Since Na+ moves in, there is a net inward current. Since the RMP increases, the cell interior becomes less negative . In response to a depolarizing stimulus, some of the voltage -gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters the cell and the membrane is brought to its threshold potential . The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage -gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop . The rapid upstroke in the membrane potential ensues . So, there is a net influx of Na+, and the interior of the cell becomes positive during the upstroke of the action potential .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is correctly matched ?
mcqs.explanation: The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state also explains the after-hyperpolarization. In response to a depolarizing stimulus, some of the voltage -gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters the cell . The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage -gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop . The rapid upstroke in the membrane potential ensues . The membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential for Na+ (+60 mV ) but does not reach it during the action potential , primarily because the increase in Na+ conductance is short-lived. The Na+ channels rapidly enter a closed state called the inactivated state and remain in this state for a few milliseconds . In addition, the direction of the electrical gradient for Na+ is reversed during the overshoot because the membrane potential is reversed, and this limits Na+ influx; also the voltage -gated K+ channels open . These factors contribute to repolarization. The opening of voltage -gated K+ channels is slower and more prolonged than the opening of the Na+ channels. The net movement of positive charge out of the cell due to K+ efflux at this time helps complete the process of repolarization.109 The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state also explains the after-hyperpolarization, followed by a return to the resting membrane potential . Thus, voltage -gated K+ channels bring the action potential to an end and cause closure of their gates through a negative feedback process . Note : Na+ channels: Positive feedback loop; K+ channels: Negative feedback loop .110

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is known as the time period in which a second stronger impulse can elicit action potential after the application of one stimulus ?
mcqs.explanation: The refractory period is the time period in which a second stronger impulse can elicit action potential after the application of one stimulus . It can be absolute or relative. During the rising and much of the falling phases of the spike potential , the neuron is refractory to stimulation. This refractory period is divided into an • Absolute refractory period , corresponding to the period from the time the firing level is reached until repolarization is about one-third complete • Relative refractory period , lasting from this point to the start of after-depolarization During the absolute refractory period , no stimulus , no matter how strong, will not excite the nerve. However, during the relative refractory period , stimuli that are stronger than normal can cause excitation. The absolute refractory period for large myelinated nerve fibers is about 1/2500 second .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: From where does the relative refractory period start?
mcqs.explanation: The relative refractory period starts from one-third of repolarization till the start of after-depolarization. The refractory period is a period during which another normal action potential cannot be elicited in an excitable cell .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Rheobase is an indicator of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: 111 The rheobase is an indicator of the magnitude of the current. It is the minimum intensity (strength /magnitude ) of stimulation required to generate an action potential when the stimulation is of infinite duration. Utilization time is the minimum time (duration) for which the rheobase has to be applied for the excitation of tissue . Chronaxie is the minimum time (duration) for which a stimulus double the strength of rheobase has to be applied for excitation of tissue .Strength -duration curve gives the idea of the excitability of a tissue . Strength -duration relationship arises because the same minimum electrical charge necessary to excite an action potential can come from a current that is either brief but large or prolonged but small. It is the product of strength and duration that determines excitability , and thus these two parameters are inversely related in their effectiveness .112 Note : Chronaxie is a better index than rheobase and utilization time for comparing the excitability of a tissue .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A slowly rising stimulus fails to fire a nerve because of a process known as __________.
mcqs.explanation: Slowly rising subthreshold currents fail to fire the nerve due to a process called accommodation, which is a type of adaptation. Accommodation is due to inactivation of voltage -gated Na+ channels. Due to the slow rise of stimulus , only a few voltage -gated Na+ channels are activated at a time. These few channels are inactivated by the time more channels are activated. So, at no moment, are a sufficient number of channels activated to give an action potential . When a membrane is depolarized rapidly, a large number of Na+ channels open at once, and an action potential is produced . In contrast, decreased response to a long-lasting and sustained suprathreshold stimulus , in general, is called adaptation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true?

options.a: Type A�o fibre carry information related to pressure
options.b: Type A\035 fibre has the largest diameter
options.d: Type C fibre has the slowest conduction velocity

mcqs.explanation: Type C fibers are the small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities . Greater the diameter of a given nerve fiber, the greater its speed of conduction . The nerve fibers are divided into types A (myelinated ), B (myelinated ), and C(Unmyelinated ). The type A fibers are further subdivided into �o , \035, \025, and \024 fibers.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: You are performing a CNS examination on a patient with a stroke. With his eyes closed , you move his big toe up or down while holding his toe joint. You ask him to state the position of the digit . Which of the following fibers are responsible for the transmission of the sensation tested here?
mcqs.explanation: The test performed here is used to check the proprioception . The large axons like A�o nerve fibers (12 -20 �Mm) carry information regarding proprioceptive sensation and somatic motor function.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In the Erlanger and Gasser classification of peripheral nerve fibers, which type of signal is transmitted by the type B nerve fibers?
mcqs.explanation: The type B fibers transmit the preganglionic autonomic fibers of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems . Erlanger and Gasser classified the fibers into types A, B, and C, and the type A fibers are further subdivided into �o , \035, \025, and \024 fibers. • Type A fibers are the typical large- and medium-sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves. • Type B fibers are smaller fibers with minimal myelination. They transmit impulses of the ANS including the bladder . (B for Bladder)113 • Type C fibers are the small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities . They constitute more than one-half of the sensory fibers in most peripheral nerves, as well as all the postganglionic autonomic fibers.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A man falls into a deep sleep with one arm under his head . He finds he is not able to move this arm when he awakens. However, it tingles and pain sensation in the arm is still intact. What is the reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm ?

options.a: B fibers are more susceptible to pressure than A fibers
options.b: A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
options.c: C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
options.d: Motor nerves are more affected by sleep than sensory nerves

mcqs.explanation: The reason for the loss of motor function without loss of pain sensation is that in the nerves to his arm, A-fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers. Sleeping for a long period with the arms under the head puts pressure on a nerve. It leads to the loss of conduction in large-diameter motor, touch , and pressure fibers, while pain sensation remains relatively intact. A-fibers (includes the motor fibers) are affected . The susceptibility of the nerve fibers to pressure is A>B>C. This is responsible for Saturday night or Sunday morning paralysis.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Spike duration is maximum in which of the following nerve fiber?
mcqs.explanation: Spike duration is maximum is C fibers. The spike duration in decreasing order: C > B > A Absolute refractory period follows the same order: C > B > AFiber s Spike Duration (m s) Absolute Refractory Period ( ms) A 0.4-0.5 0.4-1 B 1.2 1.2 C 2 2

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Golgi tendon organ, being sensory is classified under which subtype of sensory nerve fibres?
mcqs.explanation: Golgi tendon organ, which contains the receptor for inverse stretch reflex , belongs to Class Ib sensory nerve fibres.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which sensory fibers are least susceptible to hypoxia?
mcqs.explanation: Susceptibility of nerve fibers to hypoxia is B >A>C, and in the general classification , type IV sensory nerves are Type C fibers.114

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true regarding a biphasic action potential except __________.
mcqs.explanation: Biphasic Action Potential • This type of record is obtained when both recording electrodes are placed on the surface of an axon that has been stimulated . • The record shows an upward deflection followed by an isoelectric interval and then a downward deflection which denotes to the time taken for the electric potential to travel from one electrode to another.Compound Action Potential • It is a property of mixed nerves. • The record shows multiple peaks in action potential because a mixed nerve is made up of families of fibres with various speeds of conduction . Therefore, when all the fibres are stimulated , the activity in the fast-conducting fibres arrives at the recording electrode sooner than the activity in slower fibers.115
