mcqs.question: End plate potential follows all of the following except ?
mcqs.explanation: End plate potential is a graded potential with the following characteristics: • Magnitude is related to the magnitude of the initiating event • Amplitude decreases over distance • Can be summatedGraded Potential Action Potential Amplitude proportionate to s trength of stimulus . It is grad ed . Independent of stimulus inte nsity – all or none response Can be depolarising or hyper polarizing Depolarizing Is conducted decrementally - amplitude decreases with dis tance Self -propagated unchanged i n amplitude Generated spontaneously or i n response to stimuli- physic al, chemical Generated only in response t o Membrane Depolarization Can be summated Cannot be summated Has no threshold and refract ory period Has a threshold about 15 mv depolarized relative to the res ting potential .Has a refractor y period Not always followed by some action Always followed by some acti on

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following can be used to measure a synaptic potential ?
mcqs.explanation: Instruments required for recording membrane potential /synaptic potential • Stimulating electrodes : Cathode and anode • Recording electrodes : Glass microelectrode (tip diameter <0.5�M) • Display : Cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) • Squid giant axon: It is a large diameter neuron (up to 0.5 mm) from where the recording of potential is easier.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A man who is fond of exotic cuisine develops perioral numbness after eating the Pufferfish . The given poisoning is due to which of the following toxins?
mcqs.explanation: 116 Pufferfish poisoning is caused by the toxin tetrodotoxin . The sodium channels can be blocked by this toxin when it is applied to the outside of the cell membrane where the sodium activation gates are located .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Conduction in the chemical synapses in CNS is
mcqs.explanation: Conduction in the chemical synapses in CNS is always orthodromic. When an action potential is set up in an axon, two impulses travelling in the opposite direction is set up by depolarization on either side of the initial current. In the natural situation, impulses pass in one direction only- from synaptic junctions to axon terminals. Such conduction is called orthodromic. Conduction in the opposite direction is called antidromic. Under natural conditions, impulse conduction is normally only orthodromic. Antidromic conduction is usually only seen when a nerve fibre is stimulated under artificial conditions. In a chemical synapse , conduction is always orthodromic. As the transmission in a chemical synapse is due to the release of neurotransmitters from the presynaptic membrane which activate receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, antidromic conduction (i.e. from the postsynaptic membrane to presynaptic membrane) is not possible . Any impulse travelling in such direction would die as it encounters the first synapse .117

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Fast axonal transport is by all except ______
mcqs.explanation: Fast axonal transport is by all except neurofilaments . Neurofilaments play no role in axonal transport. Fast axonal transport takes place along microtubules which are tubular polymers of protein tubulin . AXONAL TRANSPORT • Protein synthesis occurs in the cell body of neuron and proteins and polypeptides are transported to axonal endings by the axoplasmic flow . • Axonal transport can be orthograde or retrograde. • Orthograde transport • Can be either fast or slow axonal transport and it occurs along microtubules that run along the length of the axon away from the cell body. • Fast axonal transport occurs at about 400 mm/day, and slow axonal transport occurs at 0.5 to 10 mm/day. • Molecular motor involved in orthograde transport is Kinesin. • Retrograde transport, • In the opposite direction (from the nerve ending to the cell body), occurs along microtubules at about 200 mm/day. Synaptic vesicles , nerve growth factor (NGF) and some viruses are transported back to the cell body. • Molecular motor involed in retrograde transport is Dyenin.118

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding axonal transport?

options.b: Slow orthograde axonal transport occurs at 100 mm/day
options.c: Kinesins are required for orthograde axonal transport
options.d: Viruses exploit retrograde transport for invasion

mcqs.explanation: Slow orthograde transport occurs at a speed of 0.5 to 10 mm/day. AXONAL TRANSPORT • Protein synthesis occurs in the cell body of neuron and proteins and polypeptides are transported to axonal endings by the axoplasmic flow . • Axonal transport can be Orthograde or Retrograde. • Orthograde transport • Can be either fast or slow axonal transport and it occurs along microtubules that run along the length of the axon away from the cell body.119 • Fast axonal transport occurs at about 400 mm/day, and slow axonal transport occurs at 0.5 to 10 mm/day. • Molecular motor involved in orthograde transport is kinesin. • Retrograde transport, • In the opposite direction (from the nerve ending to the cell body), occurs along microtubules at about 200 mm/day. Synaptic vesicles , nerve growth factor (NGF) and some viruses (Eg : herpes simplex , rabies, and polio) are transported back to the cell body. • Molecular motor involed in retrograde transport is dyenin.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: When a nerve is cut, which of the following takes place first?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , myelin degeneration would be the best answer. However, the earliest change in Wallerian degeneration after nerve injury is the degeneration of the axon distal to the site of injury (axonal degeneration ) where there is a disruption of the retrograde and anterograde flow of signals within the axon. Wallerian degeneration • If the axon is cut, the part distal to the cut degenerates ; this process is called as Wallerian degeneration. • Orthograde degeneration (Wallerian degeneration ) occurs from the point of injury to the nerve terminal, interrupting neural transmission. • After the injury, the membrane breaks down and the myelin sheath degenerates . The cell body of the injured neuron swells , the nucleus moves to an eccentric position, and the rough endoplasmic reticulum becomes fragmented (chromatolytic reaction). • The nerve then starts to regrow, with multiple small branches projecting along the path the axon previously followed (regenerative sprouting). • When the motor nerve to skeletal muscle is cut and allowed to degenerate , the muscle gradually becomes extremely sensitive to acetylcholine . This is called denervation hypersensitivity or supersensitivity .120

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding the resting membrane potential (RMP) in a nerve fibre?

options.a: It is equal to the RMP of inner hair cells of cochlea
options.b: It can be measured by surface electrodes
options.c: It becomes more positive as extracellular K+ increases
options.d: It depends on the equilibrium potential of Na+

mcqs.explanation: The resting membrane potential is close to the equilibrium potential for K+. So, changes in the external concentration of this ion can have major effects on the resting membrane potential . • If the extracellular level of K+ is increased (hyperkalemia), the resting potential moves closer to the threshold for eliciting an action potential , thus the neuron becomes more excitable . • If the extracellular level of K+ is decreased (hypokalemia), the membrane potential is reduced and the neuron is hyperpolarized . Option a: The RMP of a nerve fiber is -70 mV , while the RMP of inner hair cells is between -45 and -60 mV relative to the fluid that bathes the basal end of the cell . Option b: The membrane potential can be measured only when one electrode is inserted into the interior of the cell . Option d: It depends on the equilibrium potential of K+.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following about sensory nerve fibers is not true?
mcqs.explanation: Group III fibers carrying temperature , crude touch , and pricking pain sensations are \024-type A fibers, not A-gamma type . Alternative Classification Used in Sensory Nerves • Group Ia. Fibers from the annulospiral endings of muscle spindles are �o -type A fibers in the general classification . • Group Ib. Fibers from the Golgi tendon organs are also �o -type A fibers. • Group II . Fibers from most discrete cutaneous tactile receptors and from the flower -spray endings of the muscle spindles are \035- and \025-type A fibers in the general classification .121 • Group III . Fibers carrying temperature, crude touch , and pricking pain sensations are \024-type A fibers in the general classification . • Group IV . Unmyelinated fibers carrying pain, itch, temperature , and crude touch sensations are type C fibers in the general classification

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Absolute refractory period is due to:

options.c: Closure of active gates of sodium channel
options.d: Closure of inactive gates of sodium channel

mcqs.explanation: Absolute refractory period is due to closure of inactive gates of sodium channel. Voltage-gated sodium channels have 3 states that you can find them in. They can either be closed , open, or inactive. When the stimulus causes activation of the open gates , sodium rushes into the cell causing the membrane potential to become more positive . After 0.5 to 1 millisecond , the inactive gate automatically closes and no stimulus , no matter how strong, can excite the nerve. This is called the absolute refractory period .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below :
mcqs.explanation: Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+ Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential . K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. They are responsible for repolarization phase of action potential . Also, the postassium channels return slowly to their closed state , which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization.122 The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below . 1. Resting state - Both channels are closed 2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus . Sodium enters into the cell . The membrane reaches threshold potential. 3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs. 4. Sodium conductance decreases . 5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open . Repolarization occurs. 6. Sodium channels are reset , and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase , the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization. 7. Both channels are closed . The membrane returns to RMP.123

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle . Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
mcqs.explanation: The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second . Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period . It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction. In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second . Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds . In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period ) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves. Hence , the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds . Substituting the value in the formula, we get : Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100 /5 = 20/sec .Tetanization: The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches . The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously , which is multiple \037ber summations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level , the successive contractions eventually fuse together , and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous ,124 this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.125

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are the connective tissue layers of the skeletal muscle except ______
mcqs.explanation: Sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the muscle cell , while the remaining options are connective tissue layers surrounding the muscle . A muscle is made up of individual muscle fibers. Each muscle fiber is a single cell that is multinucleated , long, cylindrical, and surrounded by a cell membrane, the sarcolemma. Arrangement of the connective tissue is shown below .136

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a regulatory muscle protein?
mcqs.explanation: Tropomyosin is a regulatory muscle protein. It extends over the entire actin filament and covers the myosin-binding sites on the actin molecules thus preventing the attachment of actin to myosin. One molecule covers 7 active sites on actinTroponin is another regulatory protein. Troponin molecules are small globular units located at intervals along the tropomyosin molecules . Each of the three troponin subunits has a unique function: • Troponin T binds the troponin components to tropomyosin. • troponin I inhibits the interaction of myosin with actin.137 • troponin C contains the binding sites for the Ca2+ that helps initiate contraction.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following does not belong to dystrophin -glycoprotein complex ?
mcqs.explanation: Perlecan is a large extracellular matrix proteoglycan that plays a crucial role in tissue development and organogenesis . Dystrophin-glycoprotein complex • The dystrophin -glycoprotein complex provides a structural link between the cytoskeleton of the muscle cell and the extracellular matrix, which appears to stabilize the sarcolemma, adds strength to the muscle by providing a scaffolding for the fibrils and prevents contraction-induced injury (rupture ). • Organisation of DG complex • Dystrophin connects F-actin to the transmembrane protein \035-dystroglycan via smaller proteins called Syntrophins. • This \035-dystroglycan , in turn connects to the merosin subunit of laminin 211 in the extracellular matrix via �o -dystroglycan . • The dystroglycans are also associated with a complex of four transmembrane glycoproteins , �o -, \035-, \025-, and \024-sarcoglycan and sarcospan.APPLIED ASPECT • Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy • X-linked recessive disorder • Deletion of DMD gene which codes for Dystrophin • Becker muscular Dystrophy • Dystrophin is present but altered or reduced in amount138 • Limb Girdle Dystrophy • Sarcoglycan is mutated

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Thin filaments consists of all of the following except _______
mcqs.explanation: Myosin forms the thick filament, while actin, troponin, and tropomyosin form the thin filament. Thin Filaments in Sarcomere • The thin filaments are polymers made up of two chains of actin that form a long double helix. • Tropomyosin molecules are long filaments located in the groove between the two chains in the actin. • Each thin filament contains 300 –400 actin molecules and 40–60 tropomyosin molecules . • Troponin molecules are small globular units located at intervals along the tropomyosin molecules . • Each of the three troponin subunits has a unique function: • Troponin T binds the troponin components to tropomyosin. • Troponin I inhibits the interaction of myosin with actin. • Troponin C contains the binding sites for the Ca 2+ that helps to initiate contraction.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following proteins is present in skeletal muscles , but absent in a smooth muscle ?
mcqs.explanation: Actin, myosin, and tropomyosin are present in both skeletal muscle and smooth muscle . But troponin is absent and calmodulin is present in smooth muscle .139

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Myosin filament has a fixed length of ______.
mcqs.explanation: The total length of each myosin filament is uniform, almost exactly 1.6 micrometers.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The thick filament is made up of ________. 1. Heavy chain of myosin 2. Light chain of myosin 3. Dystrophin 4. Titin
mcqs.explanation: The thick filament or the myosin is made up of the heavy chain of myosin and light chain of myosin. The myosin molecule is composed of six polypeptide chains- Two heavy chains, each with a molecular weight of about 200 ,000 , and four light chains with molecular weights of about 20 ,000 each. The two heavy chains wrap spirally around each other to form a double helix, which is called the tail of the myosin molecule . One end of each of these chains is folded into a globular polypeptide structure called a myosin head. These heads contain an actin-binding site and a catalytic site that hydrolyzes ATP . Thus, there are two free heads at one end of the double -helix myosin molecule . The four light chains are also part of the myosin head , two to each head . These light chains help control the function of the head during muscle contraction.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Pseudo H zone in a sarcomere extends between the ______
mcqs.explanation: Pseudo H-zone is the light area between the two sides of M line due to reversal of polarity of the myosin molecules in each of the thick filaments . Sarcomere • The sarcomere is the contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fibre. • Z line: provides attachment to actin filaments . The area between two adjacent Z lines is called the sarcomere. • It is composed of thick and thin filaments: • Thick filament : Myosin • Thin filaments : Actin, tropomyosin and troponin • I band: • Isotropic to light . • Only thin filaments . • Half lies in one sarcomere and half in the next. • A band: • Anisotropic to light . • Myosin plus overlapped actin.140 • H bands: • lighter area in the centre of A band, when the muscle is relaxed , the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments . • Only Myosin • Pseudo H: light portion on two sides of M line because of absence of cross bridges (no myosin head). • M line: centre of A band. Here there are slender cross-connections that hold the thick filaments in proper array .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A cross-sectional view of a skeletal muscle fiber through the H zone would reveal the presence of _______
mcqs.explanation: H zone is the central region of the A band which is lighter than the outer edges of the A band because the H zone is occupied by thick filaments only (No cross bridges ) In the figure , note the section through various levels and the myofilaments observed. • Section through I band \032 only actin (thin filament) • Section through A band (Exlcuding H zone) \032 Actin and Myosin • Section through H zone \032 only myosin (thick filament) • Section through M line \032 thick filament linked with accessory proteins • Section at AI junction \032 both actin and myosin141

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The titin protein present in the muscle fiber binds ______

options.a: The tail ends of actin filaments to Z disc
options.b: The head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc
options.c: The tail ends of myosin filaments to M disc
options.d: The myofibrils to each other, and also to the cell membrane

mcqs.explanation: The titin protein present in the muscle fiber binds the head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc Several proteins other than actin and myosin are also present in the muscle . Some of them include : 1. Titin: • It is the largest known protein. • It runs between the M line and Z disc and binds the head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc. • It has a tethered portion in the A band, where it is attached to the myosin filament and an elastic portion in the I band. • The elastic property of the titin causes elastic recoil of the sarcomere and prevents it from being overstretched . 2. Nebulin : • It extends from the Z disc and runs along the full length of each actin filament. • It regulates the length of the actin filaments. 3. �o -actinin: • It is a component of the Z discs • It binds the plus ends of actin filaments to this disc. 4. Myomesin • It is present in the region of the M line. • It maintains the regular lattice arrangement of the myosin filaments in this region. 5. Desmin:142 • It is an intermediate filament characteristic of the muscle • It encircles the myofibrils near the Z disc and binds myofibrils to each other and also to the cell membrane. 6. Dystrophin: • It is present in the periphery of the muscle fiber, towards the cytoplasmic face of the sarcolemma. • It binds to the actin filaments and the glycoprotein complex , consisting of dystroglycan and sarcoglycan that spans the sarcolemma.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the constituent of the marked area in the electron microscopic picture of muscle ?
mcqs.explanation: Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area. The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin to Z-lines.The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. The area between two Z-lines is called sarcomere. The thick filaments , which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments , are made up of myosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less dense staining I bands. The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where , when the muscle is relaxed , the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments . The Z lines allow for anchoring of the thin filaments . Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins .Titin connects Z-lines to the M line and provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere. Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connecting Z-line to plasma membrane.143 Note : Some sources say that even titin is a component of Z-disc so if alpha actinin is not given in the options titin is the second best answer.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Muscle myosin and actin filaments are kept in place by ______
mcqs.explanation: The side -by-side relationship between the myosin and actin filaments is maintained by a large number of filamentous molecules of a protein called titin. Titin is a filamentous and springy protein. These springy titin molecules act as a framework that holds the myosin and actin filaments in place so that the contractile machinery of the sarcomere will work. One end of the titin molecule is elastic and is attached to the Z disk, acting as a spring and changing length as the sarcomere contracts and relaxes. The other part of the titin molecule tethers it to the myosin thick filament.144

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Choose the true statement regarding the sarcomere in skeletal muscle .

options.a: Desmin binds Z line to sarcoplasmic reticulum
options.b: Actinin binds M line to actin
options.c: Titin binds M line to z line
options.d: The length of myosin changes with contraction

mcqs.explanation: Titin binds M line to Z line Other options Desmin binds Z line to sarcolemma ( not sarcoplasmic reticulum ) Actinin binds Z line to actin ( not M line; in fact, one of the two attachments of actin, desmin and titin, is always Z line) Titin binds M line to z line, forms scaffolding , is responsible for muscle elasticity , is the largest known protein (Largest protein - titin; Largest gene - Dystrophin; Most abundant protein - Collagen ) The length of myosin or actin does not change with contraction; actually , the length of zones I and H get changed (i.e, gets decreased )

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following occurs during skeletal muscle contraction?

options.b: Both H and I band shorten
options.c: Both A and I band shorten
options.d: Both A and H band shorten

mcqs.explanation: Sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of I and H band. • During contraction, the Z lines come closer to each other reducing the length of the sarcomere. • The A band remains constant and M line becomes prominent.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The cross-bridges of the sarcomere in skeletal muscle are made up of _______.
mcqs.explanation: When the action potential reaches the muscle fiber, there is influx of Ca2+ ions. This Ca2+ binds to troponin C and tropomyosin is moved out of the way. Myosin heads can now bind to actin and form so-called cross-bridges . When a head attaches to an active site, this attachment simultaneously causes profound changes in the intramolecular forces between the head and arm of its cross-bridge . This causes the head to tilt toward the arm and to drag the actin filament along with it. This tilt of the head is called the power stroke. Immediately after tilting , the head then automatically breaks away from the active site . Formation of cross-bridges is associated with hydrolysis of ATP and generation of force.145

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: ATPase activity is present in ______.
mcqs.explanation: A feature of the myosin head that is essential for muscle contraction is that it functions as an adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) enzyme. Chemical Events during Muscle Contraction • Before contraction begins , the heads of the cross-bridges bind with ATP . The ATPase activity of the myosin head immediately cleaves the ATP but leaves the cleavage products , ADP plus phosphate ion, bound to the head . (Point A) • When the troponin-tropomyosin complex binds with calcium ions, active sites on the actin filament are uncovered and the myosin heads then bind with these sites . (Point B) • The bond between the head of the cross-bridge and the active site of the actin filament causes a conformational change in the head and the power stroke occurs. (Point C) • Once the head of the cross-bridge tilts , the ADP and phosphate ion that were previously attached to the head are released and a new ATP moelcule binds in that place . (Point D) • The binding of the new ATP molecule causes detachment of the head of myosin from the actin. (Point D) • This cycle is then repeated .146

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Myosin head detaches from actin by which of the following mechanism?

options.b: Entry of calcium into sarcoplasmic reticulum

mcqs.explanation: Binding of ATP on the free site of myosin leads to the detachment of myosin head from the thin filament.147

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In human skeletal muscles , calcium ions are stored in?
mcqs.explanation: In a skeletal muscle , calcium ions are majorly stored in the terminal cisterns of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum . Terminal cisterns are the lateral sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum . The spread of action potential triggers the release of Ca2+ from the terminal cisterns. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the skeletal muscle . Transverse tubules are the internal extensions of the sarcolemma.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true about excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle except that _____

options.a: Acetylcholine is released at the nerve terminal.
options.b: Ca2+ is released from sarcoplasmic reticulum during contraction.
options.c: Ca2+ is pumped back into sarcoplasmic reticulum during relaxation.
options.d: Ca2+ binds to tropomyosin to initiate muscle contraction.

mcqs.explanation: Ca2+ binds to troponin C (not tropomyosin) to initiate muscle contraction.148

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A skeletal muscle contraction ends when _______.

options.a: Ions move out of the cytoplasm
options.b: Ach is metabolised at the Neuromusclular junction (NMR)
options.c: Decreased calcium outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum

mcqs.explanation: Once the Ca2+ concentration outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum has been lowered sufficiently , chemical interaction between myosin and actin ceases and the muscle relaxes. • The SERCA pump uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to remove Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the terminal cisterns, where it is stored until released by the next action potential . • Thus during relaxation • Ca2+ concentration in cytoplasmic decreases . • Ca2+ concentration in sarcoplasmic reticulum increases. Option a: Calcium ions do not move out of the cytoplasm . They are taken up by the sarcoplasmic reticulum .149

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A bodybuilder is regularly working out in a gym. Which of the following is true regarding total heat production during muscle contraction?

options.a: Activation heat is produced when a muscle is contracting
options.b: Initial heat produced is due to the basal metabolic processes .
options.c: Relaxation heat is present in both isotonic and isometric contractions
options.d: Recovery heat of muscle is greater than the initial heat

mcqs.explanation: Activation heat is the heat that muscle produces whenever it contracts. Heat Production in Muscle • Resting heat : The heat given off at rest due to the basal metabolic processes . • Initial heat : The heat produced in excess of resting heat during contraction. It is made up two subtypes : • Activation heat : The heat that muscle produces whenever it is contracting, and • Shortening heat : The heat which is proportional in amount to the distance the muscle shortens. Shortening heat is apparently due to some change in the structure of the muscle during shortening. • Recovery heat : this is the heat liberated by the metabolic processes that restore the muscle to its precontraction state . The recovery heat of muscle is approximately equal to the initial heat . • Relaxation heat : Heat released in a muscle that has contracted isotonically to restore it to its previous length. This extra heat is in addition to recovery heat .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In a 100 -m dash, most of the energy consumed by skeletal muscles to replenish ATP is derived from _______
mcqs.explanation: In a 100 -m dash that takes 10 s, 85% of the energy consumed is derived anaerobically by phosphocreatine , which is hydrolyzed to creatine and phosphate groups with the release of considerable energy . The ATP concentration in a muscle is low enough (4 millimolar) to sustain contractions for 1-2 seconds after which ATP is dephosphorylated into ADP. The ADP is re-phosphorylated by phosphocreatine for the next 5 to 8 seconds . ADP is re-phosphorylated by 3 sources . • Phosphocreatine after 2 seconds upto 10 seconds . • Glycolysis (anaerobic) after 10 seconds upto a minute • Oxidative metabolism - after a minute upto 2-4 hours.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The length of the muscle fiber at the onset of contraction which is required to attain the maximum active tension is known as
mcqs.explanation: The length of the muscle fiber at the onset of contraction which is required to attain maximum active tension is known as resting length . Resting length is also known as the optimum length . It is about 2�Mm. At this length , there is a maximal overlap between the actin and myosin fibers and therefore , the maximum number of cross-bridge binding sites are formed.150 Passive tension is the tension in a muscle when it is not stimulated . Total tension is the tension developed when a muscle contracts isometrically in response to a maximal stimulus . Active tension = Total tension - Passive tension When the muscle fiber contracts, the active tension developed is proportional to the number of cross-bridges between the actin and myosin fibers. Hence , at the resting length , maximum active tension is produced and the muscle fiber contracts with a maximum force of contraction. In the given image, the purple line represents the passive tension in the muscle (before contraction) and its relation with the muscle length , while the red line represents the total tension present (during contraction) and its relation with the muscle length .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true regarding the resting length of a muscle fiber except ________.

options.a: There are maximum cross-bridges between actin and myosin
options.c: The resting length is around 2�Mm in humans
options.d: The velocity of contraction is maximum for any given load

mcqs.explanation: The passive tension is not maximum at resting length of a muscle fiber. Passive tension is the tension in a muscle when it is not stimulated . Total tension is the tension developed when a muscle contracts isometrically in response to a maximal stimulus . Active tension = Total tension - Passive tension151 The active tension is maximum at the resting length of a muscle fiber. This is because there is a optimal overlap between the actin and myosin fibers at the resting length and therefore the maximum number of cross-bridges are formed. (Option A) This provides for the maximum force of contraction at this length . The active tension decreases as the muscle is stretched beyond its normal length . The resting length is around 2�Mm in humans. (Option C) The velocity of muscle contraction varies inversely with the load on the muscle i.e. as the load on the muscle increases, the velocity of contraction decreases . At a given load, the velocity is maximal at the resting length and declines if the muscle is shorter or longer than this length . (Option D)

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Active tension in a muscle depends upon which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Active tension in a muscle depends upon the number of motor units recruited .152 The greater the number of motor units recruited , the greater will be the active tension. Factors affecting muscle tension Tension developed by each fiber • Action potential frequency • Fiber length (length -tension relationship) • Fiber diameter • Fatigue Number of active fibers • Number of fibers per motor unit • Number of active motor units (recruitment)

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following have the maximum density of white muscle fibers?
mcqs.explanation: Extra-ocular muscles have the maximum density of white muscle fibers (type IIB ), which contract quickly with peak tension attained within 7.5 msec of stimulation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All are true about red muscle fibers except -
mcqs.explanation: The red muscle fibers are Type 1 muscle fibers with low/moderate glycolytic metabolism . Rest of the options are true regarding red muscle fibers.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A motor unit is made up of _______________.

options.a: All the muscle fibers within a given muscle
options.b: A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates
options.c: All the neurons going into an muscle of the body

mcqs.explanation: Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates constitute a motor unit. • The number of muscle fibers in a motor unit varies. • In muscles concerned with fine, graded , precise movement, (eg . extraoccular muscles ) each motor unit innervates very few (three to six) muscle fibers. • On the other hand, in human leg and back muscles , number of muscle fibers per motor unit can be upto 600 . • Each spinal motor neuron innervates only one kind of muscle fiber, so that all the muscle fibers in a motor unit are of the same type . • On the basis of the type of muscle fiber they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of their twitch contraction, motor units are divided into S (slow ), FR (fast, resistant to fatigue ), and FF (fast, fatigable ) units.153

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is correct about the recruitment of fast fatiguable motor unit ?
mcqs.explanation: The fast fatigable motor unit is recruited last. Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates constitute a motor unit. On the basis of the type of muscle fiber they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of their twitch contraction, motor units are divided into • S (slow ) • FR (fast, resistant to fatigue ) • FF (fast, fatigable ) units. S fibers have a low innervation ratio (ie, small units) and FF fibers have a high innervation ratio (i.e., large units). The recruitment of motor units during muscle contraction follows a general scheme , the size principle. • In general , a specific muscle action is developed first by the recruitment of S muscle units that contract relatively slowly to produce controlled contraction. • Next , FR muscle units are recruited , resulting in more powerful response over a shorter period of time. • Lastly, FF muscle units are recruited for the most demanding tasks.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Twitch of a single muscle fiber is called _____
mcqs.explanation: Twitch of a single muscle fiber is called fibrillation.154 Fibrillation Fasciculation Twitch of a single muscle fibe r Jerky , visible contractions of groups of muscle fibers Occurs due to the degenerati on of a single �o motor neuro n or its axon. Occur as a result of a patholo gic discharge of spinal motor neurons (motor unit).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A scientist found that the latent period of muscle twitch is 10 ms and the contraction period is 40 ms. What is the tetanizing frequency (Hz)?
mcqs.explanation: Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1/40 ms = 25 Hz. Tetanizing frequency • As the contractile mechanism does not have a refractory period , on rapid stimulation of a muscle , each new contraction occurs before the preceding one is over. As a result , the second contraction is added partially to the first, and thus the total strength of contraction rises progressively with increasing frequency. Such a response is called a tetanus (tetanic contraction). It is a complete tetanus when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Tetany occurs because enough calcium ions are maintained in the muscle sarcoplasm throughout the period of stimulation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Tetanic contraction is due to the accumulation of _______ ions.
mcqs.explanation: Tetanic contraction occurs due to progressive accumulation of Ca2+ ions with rapidly repeated stimulation of skeletal muscle . • With rapidly repeated stimulation, activation of the contractile mechanism occurs repeatedly before any relaxation has occurred, and the individual contractions fuse into one continuous contraction. Such a response is called a tetanus (tetanic contraction). • A single action potential releases sufficient Ca2+ to cause a twitch contraction. • However, the duration of this contraction is very short because Ca2+ is very rapidly pumped back into the SR. • If the muscle is stimulated a second time before the muscle is fully relaxed , there is progressive accumulation of Ca2+ and the force of contraction increases. Thus, twitch forces are amplified as stimulus frequency increases. • At a high level of stimulation, intracellular Ca2+ increases and is maintained throughout the period of stimulation, and the amount of force developed greatly exceeds that seen during a twitch . The response is termed tetany .155

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The function of the Golgi tendon organ is to _________

options.c: Sense changes in position of the muscle
options.d: Sense changes in length of the muscle

mcqs.explanation: Golgi tendon organ sense changes in muscle tension. Golgi tendon reflex (Inverse myotatic/ Inverse stretch reflex ) is disynaptic , is the opposite of the stretch reflex . When the tension in a contracted muscle is significantly elevated , the inhibitory effect from the Golgi tendon organ leads to instantaneous relaxation of the entire muscle . This effect is called the lengthening reaction. It is a protective mechanism to prevent tearing of the muscle or avulsion of the tendon from its attachments to the bone. Note : Muscle spindles senses changes in muscle length (stretch ).156

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are correct regarding mechanisms of depolarisation , repolarisation, and hyperpolarisation in a skeletal muscle action potential ?
mcqs.explanation: Statements 1, 3, and 5 are correct. Action potential in skeletal muscle : • Motor-neuron discharge causes end-plate potential , which when reaches to a threshold value, causes action potential in the muscle fibre. • The depolarization of the muscle fibre is caused by the activation of the voltage -gated sodium channels, which causes the influx of sodium. • During repolarization, the sodium channels are closed , and voltage -gated potassium channels open, which causes efflux of potassium. • The voltage -gated potassium channels close slowly . As a result , the potassium efflux continues , leading to hyperpolarization of the membrane.157 The steps in an action potential in muscle fibre and the neuron, are similar except for the quantitative differences , such as: • RMP is -80 to -90 mV in skeletal muscle fibres, while it is about -70mV in neurons. • The duration of the action potential in skeletal muscle is 1 to 5 msec, which is about 5 times longer than in the largest myelinated nerve fibre. • The velocity of conduction is about 3-5m/s, which is about 1/13th of the velocity of the nerve fibre.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about skeletal muscle contraction?
mcqs.explanation: During the contraction of the skeletal muscle , the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum . Only statement 3 is correct. Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle . The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows : • Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate , which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. • This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the generation of end-plate potential , which is a local potential . • When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an action potential is generated . • The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules , leading to the spread of depolarisation. • The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments .158 • The calcium released , binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin. • The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle . Steps in relaxation: • The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum , by the action of SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase). • Once the calcium concentration is lowered , the interaction between actin and myosin ceases , and the muscle relaxes. Other options : Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction. When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia , the voltage -gated sodium channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodium concentration causes sustained depolarization , which may lead to tetany . Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum . Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sarcolemma) are activated by a depolarizing stimulus , which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum . The increased calcium concentration will eventually lead to muscle contraction.159

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Human cardiac muscle contains ________.
mcqs.explanation: Human heart contains both alpha and beta isoforms of the myosin heavy chain. \035 isoform has a lower myosin ATPase activity than the �o isoform. • �o isoform predominates in the adult atria. • \035 isoform predominates in the adult ventricles. • The spatial distribution contributes to the well coordinated contraction of the heart.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Intercalated discs are seen in _______.
mcqs.explanation: • Cardiac muscle fibres are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel with one another. • The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another, which always occur at Z lines, are called intercalated discs . • It provides a strong union between fibers, maintaining cell -to-cell cohesion , so that the pull of one contractile cell can be transmitted along its axis to the next. • It contains Desmosomes to prevent pulling apart of the cells when strain • At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gap junction which provide low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber to another permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium .165

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Activation of the sympathetic system increases the myocardial contractility of a patient . Which of the following is responsible for this positive inotropic effect ?
mcqs.explanation: Phosphorylation of phospholamban is responsible for the positive inotropic effect on the myocardium observed after the stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system . Phospholamban is a protein that regulates Ca2+ATPase in the sarcoplasmic reticulum . When phosphorylated, phospholamban stimulates the Ca2+ ATPase, resulting in greater uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum . Increased Ca2+ uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum has two effects : It causes faster relaxation (i.e., briefer contraction). it increases the amount of stored Ca2+ for release on subsequent beats . This positive inotropic effect has three important features : increased peak tension, increased rate of tension development , and faster rate of relaxation. Faster relaxation means that the contraction (twitch ) is shorter, allowing more time for refilling . This effect is mediated via activation of \0351 receptors , which are coupled via a Gs protein to adenylyl cyclase . Activation of adenylyl cyclase leads to the production of cAMP, activation of protein kinases, and phosphorylation of proteins that produce the physiologic effect of increased contractility .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is the function of phospholamban ?

options.c: Regulates calcium entry into sarcoplasmic reticulum

mcqs.explanation: • Phospholamban is a protein that regulates SR Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum . In its dephosphorylated state , phospholamban inhibits the Ca2+ ATPase, resulting in diminished uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum , while in its phosphorylated state , there is disinhibition of the Ca2+ ATPase leading to increased uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum . • Increased Ca2+ uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum has two effects : • It causes faster relaxation (i.e., briefer contraction). • it increases the amount of stored Ca2+ for release on subsequent beats . • Phosphorylation of phospholamban is responsible for the positive inotropic effect effect on the myocardium observed after the stimulation of sympathetic nervous system . • This effect is mediated via activation of \0351 receptors , which are coupled via a Gs protein to adenylyl cyclase . • This positive inotropic effect has three important features : increased peak tension, increased rate of tension development , and faster rate of relaxation. • Faster relaxation means that the contraction ( twitch ) is shorter , allowing more time for refilling .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac muscle ?
mcqs.explanation: 166 Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period . In cardiac myocytes , depolarization proceeds rapidly and an overshoot of the zero potential is present . This is followed by a plateau before the membrane potential reaches the RMP (-90mV ). This plateau phase lasts for 200 msec or more. Repolarization is therefore not complete until contraction is 50% completed . Phases of cardiac action potential • 0\032 Depolarisation and overshoot • Due to opening of voltage -gated Na+ channels • 1\032 Initial rapid repolarization • Due to closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels • 2\032 Plateau phase • Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels • 3\032 late rapid repolarization • 4\032 Baseline (RMP) • Phases 3 and 4 are due closure of Ca2+ channels and a slow , delayed increase of K+ efflux through K+ channels. • During phases 0 to 2 and about half of phase 3 of cardiac action potential , cardiac muscle cannot be excited again, that is, it is in its absolute refractory period . It remains relatively refractory until phase 4. Thus, cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following graph displays which physiological law of the heart?
mcqs.explanation: The diagram displays the Length-Tension relationship for a cardiac muscle explaining the Starling law of the heart.167 In the body, the initial length of the fibers is determined by the degree of diastolic filling of the heart, and the pressure developed in the ventricle is proportional to the volume of the ventricle at the end of the filling phase (Starling law of the heart). • The developed tension increases as the diastolic volume increases until it reaches a maximum, then tends to decrease . • The decrease is due to beginning disruption of the myocardial fibers and not due to a decrease in the number of cross-bridges between actin and myosin as seen in skeletal muscle .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Muscles in hollow viscera behave as ______
mcqs.explanation: Hollow viscera are primarily composed of single -unit smooth muscles .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding excitation-contraction coupling in smooth muscle ?

options.b: Sustained contraction occurs with high calcium concentration
options.c: Phosphorylation of actin is required for contraction
options.d: Cellular calcium concentration is essential to cause contraction

mcqs.explanation: Increased cytosolic Ca2+ is essential for contraction of smooth muscles . Events in Excitation Contraction Coupling in Smooth Muscles .168 A unitary smooth muscle is unique in that it can contract when stretched even in the absence of any extrinsic innervation . Stretch is followed by a decrease in membrane potential and an increase in the tone of the muscle . Other options : Option a: Troponin is absent in smooth muscle . Option b: Sustained contraction of the smooth muscle occurs even when the calcium concentration falls. This is mainly because of the latch-bridge mechanism where the myosin cross-bridges remain attached to the actin. This mechanism allows for maintaining the contraction with less expenditure of energy and is particularly important in the vascular smooth muscle . Option c: Unlike skeletal muscle where troponin binding is essential for contraction, the smooth muscle contraction requires phosphorylation of myosin (not actin).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Calmodulin is mostly both structurally and functionally related to ______
mcqs.explanation: Calmodulin is structurally and functionally related to troponin. In place of troponin, smooth muscle cells contain a large amount of the regulatory protein calmodulin. Calmodulin is similar to troponin; it is different in the manner in which it initiates contraction. Calmodulin initiates contraction by activating the myosin light chain kinase. Troponin , on the other hand, initiates contraction by causing a conformational change in the tropomyosin molecule which then uncovers the active sites on the actin filament.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A sustained contraction with little expenditure of energy is made possible by a latching mechanism in ________.
mcqs.explanation: • Smooth muscles can maintain prolonged full tonic contraction with little use of energy (as little as 1/300 the energy required for comparable sustained skeletal muscle contraction) and with little169 continued excitatory signal due to this mechanism. • This is due to the fact that even after dephosphorylation of myosin, the cross-bridges continue to cling on for some time. • The excitation coupling mechanism occurring in smooth muscle is similar to the skeletal muscles but for a few features : • The process is slow and a low energy mechanism. • There is no fixed length tension relationship as it shows the property of plasticity (smooth muscles behaving like a viscous mass rather than a rigidly structured tissue ). • This mechanism is specially useful in vascular smooth muscles .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The most distinguishing feature between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle is ______
mcqs.explanation: Actin, myosin, and tropomyosin are present in both skeletal muscle and smooth muscle . But, troponin is absent and calmodulin is present in smooth muscle .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following acts to increase the release of calcium ions from the endoplasmic reticulum of a smooth muscle ?
mcqs.explanation: In response to a stimulus , the efflux of calcium from intracellular stores occurs through an Inositol triphosphate receptor (IP3R )- Ca+2 channel. The source of Ca+2 in smooth muscle contraction can be different depending on the activating stimulus . • The influx from the extracellular site through voltage or ligand-gated Ca+2 channels in the plasma membrane • Efflux from intracellular stores (eg , sarcoplasmic reticulum ) through the RyR and the inositol triosephosphate receptor (IP3R ).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding smooth muscle is false ?

options.a: Unitary smooth muscle has an unstable membrane potential
options.b: Dense Bodies are present instead of Z lines
options.c: It can exert a variable tension at any given length
options.d: Sympathetic stimulation produces excitatory membrane potentials

mcqs.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation (norepinephrine) of a smooth muscle produces inhibitory potentials and relaxation. Parasympathetic stimulation (or acetylcholine ) causes depolarization and contraction in the smooth muscle . Smooth muscle can be divided into: • Unitary smooth muscle - has low-resistance gap junctions between individual muscle cells and functions in a syncytial manner • Multiunit smooth muscle - made up of individual units with few or nil gap junctions. Blood vessels have both unitary and multiunit smooth muscle in their walls .170 Option A: Unitary smooth muscle has an unstable membrane potential with continuous irregular contractions independent of its nerve supply . This state of partial contraction is called tonus or tone. Option B: Dense bodies are present instead of Z lines in smooth muscle . These are bound to actin filaments by �o -actinin. Option C: Smooth muscle can exert variable tension at any given length . This property is called plasticity . When a unitary smooth muscle is stretched , it first exerts increased tension. However, if it is held at this length after stretching, the tension gradually decreases . This is referred to as plasticity .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog. Identify the tetanising frequency.
mcqs.explanation: Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz . In the above graph, we know, • The speed of the paper is 1000mm /sec . • The y-axis represents millivolts, the x-axis represents time. • The scale on the x-axis is 10mm . • The area under the graph represents the muscle contraction. Contraction period (latent period to maximum force of contraction) includes 3 scales = 30 mm. As paper speed is 1000mm /sec , Contraction period = 30mm = (30/1000 ) = 30 msec. Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000 /30 = 33Hz . Tetanization The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches . The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously , which is multiple \037ber summations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level , the successive contractions eventually fuse together , and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous , this is called tetanization. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.171

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A synapse is a junction between _______.
mcqs.explanation: Impulses are transmitted from one nerve cell to another cell at junctions called synapse . These are the junctions where the axon or some other portion of one cell (the presynaptic cell ) terminates on the dendrites , soma, or axon of another neuron or, in some cases , a muscle or gland cell (the postsynaptic cell ). There are two major types of synapses : • Chemical • Electrical When a neuron terminates on a muscle , it is called a neuromuscular junction . This is an example of a chemical synapse .181

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are true regarding chemical synapses except _____

options.a: These are the most common type of synapses
options.b: Neurotransmitter is produced by the presynaptic neuron
options.c: Protoplasmic continuity between pre- and post - synaptic membrane ensures faster conduction

mcqs.explanation: Chemical synapses are interneuronal junctions without protoplasmic continuity . Most of the synapses used for signal transmission in the central nervous system of the human being are chemical synapses . In these synapses , the first neuron (presynaptic neuron) secretes neurotransmitters at its nerve ending synapse . This transmitter, in turn, acts on receptor proteins in the membrane of the next neuron (post -synaptic neuron) to excite the neuron, inhibit it, or modify its sensitivity in some other way. As neurotransmitters are released only by the pre-synaptic neuron, the synaptic conduction in the CNS is only orthodromic (unidirectional).182

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In a typical chemical synaptic cleft , the extracellular distance between the presynaptic plasma membrane and the postsynaptic plasma membrane is approximately _____
mcqs.explanation: In a typical chemical synaptic cleft , the extracellular distance between the presynaptic plasma membrane and the postsynaptic plasma membrane is approximately 20 -40nm .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding neurotransmitters?

options.a: All neurotransmitter are derived from amino acids
options.b: Nitric oxide is a neurotransmitter in the CNS
options.c: They do not act on ionotropic receptors
options.d: They are released on repolarization of the nerve

mcqs.explanation: Nitric oxide is a neurotransmitter in the CNS. Neurotransmitters are the substances that mediate chemical signaling between neurons. They can be choline esters , biogenic amines, amino acids, and neuropeptides . Two main classes of chemical substances that serve as neurotransmitters:183 • small-molecule neurotransmitter (acetylcholine ) • large molecule neurotransmitter (enkephalin) They can act on ionotropic receptors (ligand-gated ion channels) and/or metabotropic receptors on the postsynaptic membrane to produce a change in membrane potential to bring about their action. Criteria for the substance to be neurotransmitter: • the substance must be demonstrated to be present in the presynaptic terminal. • the cell must be able to synthesize the substance . • should be released on depolarization of the terminal. • there should be specific receptors for it on the postsynaptic membrane. • if the substance is applied exogenously to the postsynaptic membrane at physiologic concentration, the response of the postsynaptic cell must mimic the in vivo response .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a monoamine neurotransmitter?
mcqs.explanation: GABA is not a monoamine neurotransmitter. It is an amino acid. Biogenic amines are small, charged molecules that are synthesized from amino acids and contain an amino group (R—NH2). Amines known to act as neurotransmitters are dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), epinephrine (adrenaline), serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT]). Amino acids and their derived amines acting as neurotransmitters: • Tyrosine - catecholamines : dopamine, norepinephrine , and epinephrine . • Tryptophan - serotonin • Histidine - histamine

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding metabotropic neurotransmitters?

options.a: They act through second messenger systems
options.b: They bind to cationic channels and increase influx of Na
options.c: They bind to anionic channels and increase influx of Cl
options.d: They inhibit the fusion of synaptic vesicle with the synaptic cleft

mcqs.explanation: Neurotransmitter receptors that act through second messenger systems are called metabotropic receptors . Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the post -synaptic membrane to activate ion channels in one of the two ways: • by gating ion channels directly (ionotropic receptors ). • by activating a second messenger (metabotropic receptor ) for a prolonged postsynaptic neuronal excitation or inhibition. Most commonly activated is a G-protein coupled membrane receptor . The following four changes can occur usually after binding to a G-protein coupled receptor : • Opening specific ion channels through the post -synaptic cell membrane.184 • Activation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) or cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in the neuronal cell . • Activation of one or more intracellular enzymes . • Activation of gene transcription. Activation of gene transcription is one of the most important effects of activation of the second messenger systems because gene transcription can cause formation of new proteins within the neuron, thereby changing its metabolic machinery or its structure .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding the neurotransmitter glutamate in the brain ?

options.a: It is involved in excitatory neurotansmission
options.b: It is a minor neurotransmitter in the brain
options.c: It acts via both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors
options.d: Glycine binding to the NMDA receptor is essential for the receptor to respond to glutamate

mcqs.explanation: Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter responsible for ~75 % excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS. Glutamate is the best -known example of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters. It brings about its action via both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors . Glutamate Receptors :Type Mechanism of Action Ionotropic Glutamate Recept ors AMPA, Kainate receptors Primarily permits influx of N a+ and efflux of K+ \032EPSP ( excitatory postsynaptic poten tial) NMDA receptors Permits \031 influx of Ca2+ alon g with Na+\032EPSP (excitator y postsynaptic potential )(Gly cinebinding to the NMDA rec eptor is essential for the rece ptor to respond to glutamate ) Metabotropic Glutamate Rec eptor (mGluR) Leads to either \031 in IP3 /DAG or \023cAMP

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a well -known inhibitory brain neurotransmitter?
mcqs.explanation: GABA (gamma-amino-butyric acid) is probably the best known inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain , especially in the forebrain regions. GABA mediates both presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition GABA Receptors : Other options : • Glutamate is a good example of an excitatory brain neurotransmitter.185 • Acetylcholine and glycine have been known to play either excitatory or inhibitory neurotransmitter roles depending on the particular brain circuits under study . mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which is not true about neuromodulators ?

options.a: Modify the postsynaptic neuron's response to a specific neurotransmitter
options.b: May change the presynaptic neuron's release of a transmitter
options.c: May be released by the presynaptic neuron along with the neurotransmitter

mcqs.explanation: Neuromodulators typically have actions that are slower than neurotransmitters. Neuromodulators are chemicals released by neurons that have little or no direct effects on their own but can modify the effects of neurotransmitters. They can modify the postsynaptic neuron's response to a neurotransmitter and they can change how much of a neurotransmitter the presynaptic neuron synthesizes or releases . Neuromodulators also can be released by the presynaptic neuron along with the neurotransmitter.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A medical student was doing research in a laboratory that studies the neuromuscular junction. Which of the following events at the junction are listed in correct sequential order?

options.a: Motor neuron action potential , acetylcholine release , Ca2+ entry at the endplate
options.b: Ca2+ entry into the motor nerve terminal , acetylcholine release , Na+ entry at the endplate
options.c: Ca2+ entry into the motor nerve terminal , Na+ entry at the endplate , motor neuron action potential
options.d: Na+ entry at the endplate , acetylcholine release , muscle fiber action potential

mcqs.explanation: Events Occurring at the Chemical Synapse : The action potential arriving at the end of the motor neuron increases the permeability of its endings to Ca2+ \023 Ca2+ enters the endings and triggers a marked increase in exocytosis of the acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles \023 Binding of acetylcholine to nicotinic receptors increases the Na+ and K+ conductance \023 Resultant influx of Na+ produces a local depolarizing potential , the endplate potential \023 The current created by this local potential depolarizes the adjacent muscle membrane to its firing level \023 Action potentials are generated on either side of the endplate and are conducted away from the endplate in both directions along the muscle fiber. This muscle action potential , in turn, initiates muscle contraction. Acetylcholine is then removed from the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase , which is present in high concentration at the neuromuscular junction.187

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is due to the influx of ______.
mcqs.explanation: Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is due to the influx of sodium ions (Na+). At the post -synaptic membrane, neurotransmitters binding to receptors generate responses that can be excitatory or inhibitory. If it generates an excitatory response (makes the membrane more electrically positive / depolarized ), it is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) because it makes the cell more likely to reach an action potential . EPSP may be due to • The opening of sodium channels or calcium channels to allow large numbers of positive electrical charges to flow to the interior of the postsynaptic cell . • Depressed conduction through chloride or potassium channels or both. • Various changes in the internal metabolism of the postsynaptic neuron to increase the number of excitatory membrane receptors or decrease the number of inhibitory membrane receptors .188 As seen in the figure , following the discharge of the sensory neuron, there is positivity in the motor neuron signifying a EPSP.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential (IPSP ) is due to influx of ______
mcqs.explanation: Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential (IPSP ) is due to the influx of chloride ions (Cl-). If, binding of a neurotransmitter causes the postsynaptic membrane to become more negative (hyperpolarized), it is called an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP ) because hyperpolarization moves the membrane potential farther from the threshold and makes the cell less likely to reach an action potential . IPSP may be due to : • Increase in Cl- influx. This action causes diffusion of negatively charged chloride ions from outside the postsynaptic neuron to the inside, thereby carrying negative charges inward and increasing the negativity inside. This leads to hyperpolarization. • Increase in K+ efflux . This action causes positive ions to diffuse to the exterior, which causes increased negativity inside the neuron, which leads to hyperpolarization. • Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors or decrease the number of excitatory receptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following effect in the motor neuron is due to:

options.a: Opening of chloride ion channels through the pre-synaptic neuronal membrane
options.b: Increase in conductance of potassium ions to the inside of the neuron
options.c: Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors
options.d: Increase in conductance of sodium ions inside the neuron

mcqs.explanation: Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors can cause the effect shown, namely, the generation of IPSP . In the figure given, there is an increased negativity in the motor neuron following the action potential in the interneuron. So, the synaptic potential is IPSP . This can be caused at the189 postsynaptic membrane due to Cl- influx, K+ efflux or activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors or decrease the number of excitatory receptors . Other options : • Opening of chloride ion channels through the post -synaptic neuronal membrane. • Increase in conductance of potassium ions to the outside of the postsynaptic neuron. • Increase in conductance of sodium ions inside the neuron causes the generation of an EPSP.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Slow inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP ) is generated by all except _______
mcqs.explanation: Slow EPSPs and IPSPs are not generated by skeletal muscles . Slow excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSPs) are seen in autonomic ganglia, cardiac, and smooth muscle , and cortical neurons. EPSPs and IPSPs occur after a latency of 0.5ms while slow EPSPs and IPSPs occur after a latency of 100 –500 ms and last for several seconds . The slow EPSPs are due to a decrease in K+ efflux , and the slow IPSPs are due to an increase in K+ efflux .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following physiologic processes is not correctly matched ?

options.c: Presynaptic inhibition: GABA-B receptors decrease K+ conductance .
options.d: Presynaptic inhibition: GABA-A receptors increase Cl– conductance .

mcqs.explanation: GABA-B receptors are present in the spinal cord and appear to mediate presynaptic inhibition via a G-protein that produces an increase in K+ conductance . PRE-SYNAPTIC INHIBITION • Presynaptic inhibition is a process mediated by neurons whose terminals are on excitatory endings, forming axoaxonal synapses . • The first transmitter shown to produce presynaptic inhibition was GABA. On the pre-synaptic membrane • Acting via GABA-A receptors , GABA increases Cl– conductance . • GABA-B receptors appear to mediate presynaptic inhibition via a G-protein that produces an increase in K+ conductance . • This leads to hyperpolarization of the pre-synaptic membrane and inhibition of release of the neurotransmittor from the pre-synaptic neuron.190 POST-SYNAPTIC INHIBITION • Postsynaptic inhibition occurs when an inhibitory transmitter such as glycine or GABA is released from a presynaptic nerve terminal onto the postsynaptic neuron to induce an IPSP in the postsynaptic neuron. • In the figure shown below , an inhibitory transmitter such as GABA is released from the nerve terminals of an inhibitory interneuron (dark ) that synapses on a postsynaptic neuron.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Renshaw cell inhibition is ________
mcqs.explanation: Renshaw cell inhibition is an example of feedback inhibition. The axon of a spinal motor neuron has a recurrent collateral that synapses on an inhibitory interneuron that terminates on the cell body of the same and other motor neurons. The inhibitory interneuron is called a Renshaw cell and its neurotransmitter is glycine .191

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Feedforward inhibition is seen in ________
mcqs.explanation: Feedforward inhibition is seen in the cerebellum . In the cerebellum , stimulation of basket cells / stellate cells produces IPSPs in the Purkinje cells (i.e, inhibits Purkinje cells ) In feedforward inhibition, a presynaptic cell excites an inhibitory interneuron which then inhibits the next follower cell . In cerebellum (Refer flow chart):This arrangement is called feed -forward inhibition which presumably limits the duration of excitation produced by any given afferent volley. Note : Renshaw cell carries out the negative feedback inhibition of a spinal motor neuron.192

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Presynaptic facilitation is due to prolonged opening of_____
mcqs.explanation: Presynaptic facilitation is due to prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels . In presynaptic facilitation, the serotonin released at the axoaxonal ending increases the intraneuronal cAMP levels \032 phosphorylation and consequent closure of K+ channels \032 slowing of repolarization and prolonging the depolarization by prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A person with myasthenia gravis notes increased muscle strength when he is treated with an acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor. The basis for his improvement is due to the increase in _______

options.a: The amount of acetylcholine (ACh) released from motor nerves
options.b: The level of ACh at the muscle end plates
options.c: The number of ACh receptors on the motor end plates
options.d: Synthesis of norepinephrine in motor nerves

mcqs.explanation: Treatment with AChE inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine ) prevents the degradation of ACh and prolongs the action of ACh at the muscle end plate . Myasthenia gravis: • It is caused by the presence of antibodies to the ACh receptor . • Is characterized by skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability resulting from a reduced number of ACh receptors on the muscle end plate. • The size of the EPP (end plate potential ) is reduced . • Treatment with AChE inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine ) prevents the degradation of ACh and prolongs the action of ACh at the muscle end plate , partially compensating for the reduced number of receptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old woman had an autonomic neuropathy that disrupted the sympathetic nerve supply to the pupillary dilator muscle of her right eye . While having her eyes examined, the ophthalmologist placed a sympathomimetic drug in both her eyes . The right eye became much more dilated than the left eye . This suggests that:

options.a: The sympathetic nerve to the right eye had regenerated
options.b: The parasympathetic nerve supply to the right eye remained intact and compensated for the loss of the sympathetic nerve
options.d: The left eye also had nerve damage and so was not responding as expected

mcqs.explanation: 193 Denervation supersensitivity develops in the muscle after the nerve supplying it is cut. Since the nerve to her right dilator pupillae is damaged , the right eye becomes excessively sensitive to the sympathomimetic drug. So, the right eye becomes much more dilated than the left . Denervation Supersensitivity : • When the motor nerve to skeletal muscle is degenerated , the muscle gradually becomes extremely sensitive to acetylcholine . This is called denervation hypersensitivity or supersensitivity. • Normally nicotinic receptors are located only in the vicinity of the motor endplate where the axon of the motor nerve terminates . When the motor nerve is severed , there is a marked proliferation of nicotinic receptors over a wide region of the neuromuscular junction. • Denervation supersensitivity also occurs at autonomic junctions. Smooth muscle , unlike skeletal muscle , does not atrophy when denervated , but it becomes hyperresponsive to the chemical mediator that normally activates it. • This hyperresponsiveness can be demonstrated by using pharmacologic tools rather than actual nerve section. Prolonged use of a drug such as reserpine can be used to deplete transmitter stores and prevent the target organ from being exposed to norepinephrine for an extended period . Once the drug usage is stopped , smooth muscle and cardiac muscle will be supersensitive to subsequent release of the neurotransmitter. Option a) If the symapthetic nerve would have regenerated , both right and left eye would have been equally sensitive to the drug and so, would have dilated equally. Option b) Parasympathetic nerves supply the spinchter pupillae muscle . So, if stimulated they would constrict the eye not dilate it. Also, the drug added was a sympathomimetic agent . So, parasympathetic nerves are not stimulated in the first place Option d) If the left eye was damaged , it would also have denervation supersensitivity . Again, both eyes would dilate equally, but more than that of normal .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is not true about neurotransmitters?

options.a: They must be present at the pre-synaptic membrane
options.b: Neurons must be able to synthesize the substance
options.c: They are released on repolarization of the nerve
options.d: Specific receptors must be present on the post -synaptic membrane

mcqs.explanation: Neurotransmitters should be released on depolarization of the terminal. • Neurotransmitters are the substances that mediate chemical signaling between neurons. • The transmission of information at chemical synapses involves the release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic cell , diffusion across the synaptic cleft , and binding of the neurotransmitter to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane to produce a change in membrane potential .
