There are 2 zones: • Conducting zone • Consists of the first 16 generations • Incapable of gas exchange • Respiratory zone • Consists of the last 7 generations (17-23 ) • Capable of gas exchange Terminal bronchiole is the transition point between the conducting and respiratory zone.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which among the following has the highest airway resistance ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , bronchi (medium-sized airway) offer maximum resistance . The best answer here is bronchi, as all the other options suggest smaller airways, while bronchi are the only medium-sized airway. Airflow can be derived from Poiseuille-Hagen formula: Q =\021 \033Pr4 /8\020L Where • Q is the flow rate • \021 is pie symbol • \033P is the pressure difference356 • r is radius • \020 is viscosity • L is length Also, Flow rate (Q) = pressure difference (\033P)/ resistance (R). Therefore, substituting this in Poiseuille- Hagen formula, \033P/ R = \021 \033Pr4 /8\020l 1/R = \021 r4/8\020l R = 8\020l/ \021 r4 Therefore it can be derived that airway resistance is inversely proportional to the radius by the power of four. With Poiseuille - Hagen formula we might feel that the smallest airways are the major site of resistance . However, the contribution by the smallest airways is very little to the overall total resistance . This is because , the airway branches in each generation exist in parallel rather than in series . As the parallel branching increases, the resistance decreases . (Total cross-sectional diameter of small airways put together is high). Thus the overall resistance of the small airways is very small. Also, airflow velocity decreases substantially as the effective cross-sectional area increases (i.e., the flow becomes laminar ). Other factors affecting airway resistance : • Lung volume, as lung volume increases the resistance decreases and vice versa. Lung volume increases the transairway pressure thus increasing the caliber of the airway. • Airway mucus, edema , and contraction of bronchial smooth muscle increase the airway resistance . Its clinical application is seen in asthma, bronchitis, and emphysema • The density and viscosity of inspired gas also contribute to airway resistance . A gas with more density imparts more resistance .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy with shortness of breath was diagnosed with chronic inflammation of conducting airways. Which of the following is not a feature of the affected structure ?

options.a: Includes first 16 generations starting from trachea
options.c: Secrete variety of molecules that aid in lung defence
options.d: Membrane bound organelles namely lamellar bodies are present

mcqs.explanation: Chronic inflammation of conducting airways is suggestive of asthma. Lamellar bodies are storage bodies of surfactant present in the alveoli and not the conducting airway. The conducting airways form the first 16 generations from the trachea to the terminal bronchial. It is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium . It also consists of smooth muscles which are responsible for bronchoconstriction and dilatation. It also consists of other specialized cells such as: • Basal cells - stem cells • Clara/Club cells - specialized epithelial cells (non-ciliated cuboidal cells ) that: • Functions as stem cells • Helps in lung defense .357 The conducting airways secrete several substances that in lung defense such as: • Secretory immunoglobins - IgA • Collectins - surfactant protein(SP)-A and SP-D • Defensins • Reactive oxygen species • Reactive nitrogen species .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Maximal smooth muscle relative to wall thickness is seen in _______.
mcqs.explanation: Smooth muscle is maximum in terminal bronchioles.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: An elderly smoker who presented with an acute exacerbation of COPD is administered salbutamol. Which one of the following substances has a similar mechanism of action?
mcqs.explanation: Salbutamol, a short-acting beta (adrenergic) agonist (SABA) is a bronchodilator. Similarly, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP ) is also a bronchodilator. Along with dynorphin, it is part of the non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) inhibitory system . Bronchial innervation : Other potent bronchoconstrictors are histamine and leukotrienes . Clinical relevance: • Methacholine sensitivity test or Airway hyperresponsiveness test : Methacholine which is similar to acetylcholine causes exaggerated bronchoconstriction in case of bronchial asthma. • 5-Lipoxygenase inhibitor (5-LOX inhibitor-Zileuton), selective CysLT-receptor antagonists (Cys leukotriene receptor antagonist-zafirlukast, pranlukast, and montelukast ), and \0352 receptor agonists are used in the treatment of asthma.Site Type of recept or Effect Sympathetic system Tracheal and bronchial smoo th muscle \0352 Relaxation Bronchial glands �o 1\0352 Reduce secretionIncrease sec retion Parasympathetic system (mor e predominant) Tracheal and bronchial smoo th muscle M2, M3 Contraction Bronchial glands M2, M3 Stimulation358

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells secrete surfactant in lungs ?
mcqs.explanation: Type 2 pneumocytes secrete surfactant in the lungs . Alveolar Lining Epithelial Cells Two types • Type I cells – The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium ); Helps in gas exchange • Type II cells – Granular pneumocytes produce surfactant Type II cells make 60% of epithelial cells in alveoli but type I cells form 95% of the total surface area because of its flat surface . Type II cells are stem cells which help in replenishing damaged Type 1 pneumocytes in conditions like drug-induced pulmonary toxicity by amiodarone, bleomycin etc . Other cells – Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells ), lymphocytes , plasma cells , neuroendocrine cells (APUD cells-Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation ), and mast cells .359

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Surfactant is composed mainly of_____
mcqs.explanation: Major surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine i.e Lecithin. Sphingomyelin is a minor surfactant. The surfactant is a surface -active agent in water, which means that it greatly reduces the surface tension of water. Pulmonary surfactant is produced by type 2 pneumocytes . Most important components are • Phospholipid - dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) also known as Dipalmitoyl Lecithin. Lecithin is the most abundant lipid in surfactant. • Phosphatidylglycerol - minor component • Surfactant apoproteins • Calcium ions. • 4 unique apoproteins of surfactant: surfactant protein (SP)-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D. Clinical relevance: • Tests to assess fetal lung maturity: • L/S ratio i.e. Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio: Ratio \017 2 is considered normal . • Shake test /Bubble test /Clement test : Formation of stable foam in the presence of surfactant. • Phosphatidylglycerol levels in Amniotic fluid • Autosomal dominant familial interstitial lung disease has absent surfactant protein SP-C. • Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis - Autoantibody against GM-CSF which is involved in clearance of surfactant.360

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All are true of surfactant except _____

options.b: Deficiency of surfactant causes Infant Respiratory Distress Syndrome
options.c: Helps prevents alveolar collapse according to Bernoulli's principle
options.d: Decrease in surfactant increases the work of breathing

mcqs.explanation: Surfactant helps to prevent alveolar collapse according to Law of Laplace.(Not Bernoulli's) Physiologic advantages of surfactant • By reducing surface tension it increases lung compliance • Reduces the lung's tendency to recoil • Helps to keep the alveoli dry • Helps to prevent pulmonary edema (Option A) The surface tension generates a pressure that tends to collapse the sphere . In accordance with Law of Laplace - P=2T /r, where P - Collapsing pressure on alveolus (dynes /cm2) or Pressure required to keep alveolus open (dynes /cm2) T = Surface tension (dynes /cm) r = Radius of the alveolus (cm). Collapsing pressure is inversely related to radius i.e. large alveolus (one with a large radius) will have a low collapsing pressure and therefore will require only minimal pressure to keep it open . On the other hand, a small alveolus (one with a small radius) will have a high collapsing pressure and require more pressure to keep it open . By reducing surface tension, surfactant reduces the collapsing pressure for a given radius. Option B: Surfactant deficiency is an important cause of infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS ) also known as hyaline membrane disease , the serious pulmonary disease that develops in infants born before their surfactant system is functional. • In IRDS , there is high surface tension in the lungs resulting in atelectasis • Also, there is retention of fluid in the lungs . • During fetal life , Cl- is secreted with fluid by the pulmonary epithelial cells . At birth, there is a shift to Na+ reabsorption by these cells via ENaC and fluid is absorbed along with Na+. Prolonged immaturity of ENaC contributes to pulmonary edema in IRDS . Option D: Surfactant increases lung compliance , which reduces the work of expanding the lungs during inspiration. Increasing the compliance of the lungs reduces the collapsing force at any given volume so that it is easier for the lungs to expand.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A young lady at 35 weeks of gestation is at high risk of preterm delivery in the next 7 days. She is started on antenatal corticosteroid therapy to increase surfactant production in the fetus . What is the mechanism of action of this substance ?

options.a: Breaks the structure of water in alveoli
options.b: Lubricate the flow of CO2 diffusion

mcqs.explanation: The mechanism of action of surfactant is by breaking the structure of water in alveoli. When water forms a surface with air, the water molecules on the surface of the alveoli have a s trong attraction for one another. This pulls the molecules together , leading to high surface361 tension. The surfactant is amphipathic in nature (i.e., hydrophobic on one end and hydrophilic on the other). They align themselves on the alveolar surface , with their hydrophobic portions facing the alveolar lumen. The cohesive force between a water molecule and an adjacent pulmonary surfactant molecule is very low. So, they break up the attracting forces between water molecules lining the alveoli (which had been responsible for the high surface tension). Thus, they reduce surface tension.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Stability of alveoli is maintained by______.

options.c: Increased alveolar surface area by surfactant

mcqs.explanation: Stability of alveoli is maintained by increased alveolar surface area by surfactant. Surfactant reduces the lung's tendency to recoil so that they do not collapse easily and so the stability of the alveoli is maintained. Factors that maintain alveolar stability • Pulmonary surfactant: \023 surface tension within alveoli • Mechanical interdependence : prevents alveolar collapse Interdependence The tendency of one alveolus to collapse is opposed by the traction exerted by the surrounding alveoli. Thus, the collapse of a single alveolus stretches and distorts the surrounding alveoli, which in turn are connected to other alveoli. This support offered to lung units by those surrounding them is termed Interdependence .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A woman at risk for preterm delivery is planned for assessment of fetal lung maturity. At what gestational age will the surfactants be detectable in the amniotic fluid ?
mcqs.explanation: Surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation .362 By week 20 -24, primitive alveoli form and surfactant production begins but it does not reach the surface of the lungs until later. Mature levels of pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 wk of gestation . Clinical aspects : • Preterm infants develop respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease due to surfactant deficiency . • Antenatal corticosteroids are given to increase the production of surfactants. • Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio is a test for fetal lung maturity. L/S ratio > 2 is suggestive of a mature fetal lung.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A woman on multiple medications came for an antenatal check-up. Which among the following medications that she takes decreases surfactant production ?
mcqs.explanation: Inadequate Insulin intake in diabetic pregnant causes inadequate glucose control. This causes excess glucose in maternal plasma, crossing Placenta. Excess glucose in fetal plasma causes fetal pancreas to hypersecrete fetal Insulin. Excess insulin in fetal plasma decreases surfactant production . This is the reason for the increased incidence of hyaline membrane disease in infants of diabetic mothers. Factors increasing surfactant synthesis: • Glucocorticoids • Thyroxine • Stretching of lungs in infancy • Beta adrenergic agonist • Calcium • Regular exercise . Factors decreasing surfactant synthesis: • Smoking • Long term inhalation of 100 % oxygen • Occlusion of main bronchus/pulmonary artery.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which is the best metabolic function of the lung?

options.d: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II

mcqs.explanation: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II is the most significant metabolic function of the lungs. This is mediated by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), located on the surface of endothelial cells in the pulmonary capillaries . • Synthesized and used in the lungs363 • Surfactant • Synthesized or stored and released into the blood • Prostaglandins • Histamine • Kallikrein • Partially removed from the blood • Prostaglandins • Bradykinin • Adenine nucleotides • Serotonin • Norepinephrine • Acetylcholine • Activated in the lungs • Angiotensin I \032 Angiotensin II364

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A healthy 25-year-old software engineer participates in a 10 -km charity run. Which of the following muscle does this person use during expiration?
mcqs.explanation: In this scenario, the person has performed a strenuous exercise , so he will be using accessory muscles of respiration along with primary muscle of respiration. Internal intercostals and abdominal recti are the muscles involved.Muscles involved in Respirati on Primary inspiratory muscles DiaphragmExternal intercost al muscles Accessory inspiratory muscle s SternocleidomastoidScaleniA lae nasiSmall muscles of the head & neck Accessory expiratory muscles Internal intercostal musclesR ectus AbdominisInternal & e xternal obliquesTransversus abdominisClinical correlation: • The diaphragm is the chief muscle of inspiration. • It is supplied by the phrenic nerve ( C3-C5 ) • Hence transection of the spinal cord above the third cervical segment is fatal without artificial respiration, but transection below the fifth cervical segment is not fatal because , it leaves the phrenic nerves that innervate the diaphragm.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The intrapleural pressure is______

options.d: Negative at apex but positive at base

mcqs.explanation: Intrapleural pressure is usually negative . (normally -2.5 mmHg) During inspiration, it becomes more negative . (-6 mmHg). During forced expiration, contraction of the expiratory muscles raises intrapleural pressure to a positive value. Intrapleural pressure is the pressure of the fluid in the thin space between the visceral and parietal pleura.372

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The intrapleural pressure is negative both during inspiration and expiration because ______

options.b: Thoracic cage and lung recoil in opposite direction

mcqs.explanation: The intrapleural pressure is negative both during inspiration and expiration because the thoracic cage and lung recoil in opposite direction. The 2 factors that lead to a negative or subatmospheric intrapleural pressure are: • The lungs , with their elastic properties , tend to collapse , and the chest wall, with its elastic properties , tends to spring out. When these two opposing forces pull on the intrapleural space , a negative pressure , or vacuum, is created . • The continuous suction of excess fluid into the lymphatic channels.Applied aspect : In cases of pneumothorax, intrapleural pressure suddenly becomes equal to atmospheric pressure . Thus instead of its normal negative value, intrapleural pressure becomes zero. Hence lungs collapse and the chest wall spring out.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The intrapleural pressure (cm of H2O) at the beginning of inspiration is around
mcqs.explanation: The normal intrapleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration is about -3.4 cm H2O (-2.5 mmHg). Intrapleural pressure is the pressure of the fluid in the thin space between the lung pleura and the chest wall pleura . During normal inspiration, expansion of the chest cage pulls outward on the lungs with greater force and creates more negative pressure . At the peak of normal inspiration, it is about -8.15 cm H2O (-5.4 mm Hg). Note : 1mm Hg = 1.36 cm H2O373

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: With reference to atmospheric pressure , what is the alveolar pressure at the end of normal inspiration (in cms of H2O)?
mcqs.explanation: At the end of inspiration, the alveolar pressure is zero with reference to the atmospheric pressure . Whenever alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure , alveolar pressure is said to be zero. This happens when no air is moving in or out of the lungs . During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing the volume of the thorax to increase. As lung volume increases , the pressure in the lungs must decrease . (Boyle 's law states that P \327 V is constant at a given temperature .) Halfway through inspiration, the alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure (� 1 cm H2O). The pressure gradient between the atmosphere and the alveoli drives airflow into the lung. Air flows into the lungs until, at the end of inspiration, alveolar pressure is once again equal to the atmospheric pressure ; the pressure gradient between the atmosphere and the alveoli has dissipated, and airflow into the lungs ceases . During expiration, alveolar pressure rises to about +1 cm of H2O.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The transpulmonary pressure is the pressure difference between _______
mcqs.explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is intra-alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure . (Mnemonic TAP: Transpulmonary pressure = Alveolar pressure - Pleural pressure ) It is the pressure difference between that in the alveoli and that on the outer surfaces of the lungs , and it is a measure of the elastic forces in the lungs that tend to collapse the lungs at each instant of respiration, called the recoil pressure .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A man inspires 1000ml from a spirometer . The intrapleural pressure was -4cm H2O before inspiration and -12cm H20 at the end of inspiration. What is the compliance of lungs ?(ml/cm H20 )?
mcqs.explanation: 374 Compliance is change in volume per unit change in pressure . • C= \033V /\033P In this case, \033V = 1000 mL \033P= -12 -(-4) = -8 cm of H2O The minus sign indicates that the pressure has fallen by 8cms of H20 at the end of inspiration Therefore the compliance is, C= /8= 125 mL /cm of H2O

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old woman has pulmonary compliance of 0.2 L/cm H2O and an alveolar pressure of 4 cmH2O and an intrapleural pressure of -5 cmH2O at the beginning of inspiration. What is the transpulmonary pressure (in cmH2O) when this woman inhales 600mL of air ?
mcqs.explanation: The transpulmonary pressure would be 12 cmH2O when she inhales 600mL of air. Transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) is the difference between alveolar pressure (Palv ) and intrapleural pressure (Pip). It is given by the formula: Ptp = Palv-Pip. Inspiration causes a negative change in both the Palv and Pip. Lung compliance is the extent to which the lungs will expand for each unit increase in transpulmonary pressure . In a normal adult , the pulmonary compliance is 0.2 L/cmH2O or 200 mL /cmH2O of both lungs together . Hence , expanding the lungs by 200 mL of inspired air will require an increase in Ptp by 1 cm H2O. Given: Pulmonary compliance = 0.2 L/cm H2O = 200 ml/cm H20 Alveolar pressure at the beginning of inspiration = 4 cmH2O Intrapleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration = -5 cmH2O Volume of air inhaled = 600mL (0.6L ) Step 1: Calculate the initial transpulmonary pressure (Ptp). Transpulmonary pressure = Alveolar pressure - Intrapleural pressure ; Initial transpulmonary pressure = 4 cmH2O - (-5 cmH2O) = 9 cmH2O Step 2: Use the lung compliance formula to find the change in transpulmonary pressure . Lung compliance = Change in volume / Change in transpulmonary pressure . Pulmonary compliance is 0.2 L/cmH2O or 200 mL /cmH2O. Hence , to expand the lungs by 200 mL of inspired air, it will require an increase in Ptp by 1 cm H2O. So, for 600 ml inspired air, the compliance is = 600 mL / 200 mL /cm H2O = 3 cmH2O Step 3: Calculate the transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) after inhaling 600mL of air. During inspiration, the alveolar pressure ( Palv ) decreases , and the intrapleural pressure ( Pip ) becomes more negative . Final transpulmonary pressure = Initial transpulmonary pressure + change in transpulmonary pressure ; Final transpulmonary pressure = 9 cmH2O + 3 cmH2O = 12 cmH2O.375

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Compared to a gas-ventilated lung, a liquid-ventilated lung _____
mcqs.explanation: A liquid-ventilated lung is more compliant compared to a gas-ventilated lung. Compliance is a measure of distensibility. In a gas-filled lung, surface tension and elastic recoil forces act to collapse the lung and thus reduce compliance .• When the lungs are filled with air, there is an interface between the alveolar fluid and the air in the alveoli; so, there is surface tension. • But, in the case of the saline solution -filled lungs , there is no air–fluid interface and there is no surface tension, making it more compliant. • Hence , the pressure –volume curve obtained with saline measures only the tissue elasticity . • The difference in the curves generated during inflation and deflation , termed hysteresis , is not present in the saline-generated curves.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The factor responsible for hysteresis is _______
mcqs.explanation: Surfactant is the factor responsible for hysteresis . Difference between the curve of inflation (inspiration) and deflation (expiration) in a pressure –volume curve of the lung is termed as hysteresis . The alveolar environment and, specifically, the secreted factors that help reduce surface tension and keep alveoli from collapsing , contribute to hysteresis .376 Inspiration curve:Expiration curve:377

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The diagram below shows the pressure -volume curves for 3 different lungs . Which of the following is the best representation of compliance between the three lungs ?
mcqs.explanation: • The pressure -volume relationship is the fundamental relation between the work of breathing and lung mechanics. • The diagram depicts the change in volume with respect to the change in intrapleural pressure , which is compliance. Here, the change is more (steep curve) with B and least (flat curve) with C. • The "stiffer " lung displays a more horizontal curve (C), meaning that it takes a greater pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared with a normal lung (A). These lungs are called less compliant. • Curve (B) is more compliant as it takes lesser pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared to normal (A). Applied aspect : Compliance is increased in emphysema . The mechanism is shown in the flow chart below .378 Compliance is decreased in case of pulmonary edema or fibrosis.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In the pressure –volume graph shown below , compliance of lung is represented by _________.
mcqs.explanation: In the given pressure –volume graph: • A – Compliance of chest • B – Compliance of lung • C – Compliance of lung and chest wall The equilibrium position is at functional residual capacity (FRC), where the expanding force on the chest wall is exactly equal to the collapsing force on the lungs . FRC is also known as relaxation volume and represents the amount of air remaining in the lungs at the end of normal expiration.379 At the point where volume= FRC, • Intraalveolar pressure is equal to atmospheric pressure and considered as zero. • Intrapleural pressure is negative (-2.5 mmHg) • Transpulmonary pressure = Intraalveolar pressure – intrapleural pressure = 0 – (-2 .5 mmHg) = +2.5 mmHg. For compliance of lung – Pressure considered is Transpulmonary pressure . So at FRC, Transpulmonary pressure is positive (+2.5 mmHg). Hence , B indicates compliance of lung. For compliance of chest wall – Pressure considered is intrapleural – atmospheric pressure . At FRC, this value is -2.5 mmHg. Hence , A represents compliance of the chest wall. When the volume is FRC, the combined lung and chest -wall curve intersects the X-axis at an airway pressure of zero. Hence , C represents the combined chest wall and lung compliance .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is specific compliance of lung?
mcqs.explanation: Specific compliance is obtained by dividing compliance by functional residual capacity . Types of compliance : • Static compliance : It is measured at rest. • Dynamic compliance : It is measured during breathing. It considers airflow resistance or impedance into account. It is maximum in medium-sized bronchi. • Specific compliance : • Lung compliance is volume-dependent . • It is greater at low lung volumes than at high lung volumes. For this reason, the term specific compliance is often used to denote compliance with reference to the original lung volume. • The total compliance of a normal person near the normal end-expiratory lung volume (functional residual capacity [FRC]) is about 0.1 L/cm H2O. • The compliance of the lungs is about 0.2 L/cm H2O. Applied aspect : In case of emphysema , compliance is increased but specific compliance decreases (because FRC is severely elevated ).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Work done in quiet breathing is (kg-m/min)______
mcqs.explanation: Work done in quiet breathing is 0.5 kg-m/min. Estimates of the total work of quiet breathing range from 0.3 up to 0.8 kg-m/min. The work of breathing can be calculated from the pressure -volume curve.380 The value rises markedly during exercise , but the energy cost of breathing in normal individuals represents less than 3% of the total energy expenditure during exercise . Applied aspect : In the case of COPD, airway resistance increases (obstruction to outflow ). Hence , the patient should take slow , deep breathing. In the case of restrictive lung disease , viscous resistance increases. Hence , the patient is advised rapid, shallow breathing.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Work of breathing is mostly due to____
mcqs.explanation: Most of the work of breathing is due to surface tension elasticity . Work of Breathing: • Elastic /Compliance work (65%): Surface tension (2/3rd) + Tissue elasticity (1/3rd) • Non elastic work (35%): Tissue/Viscus resistance (7%) + Airway resistance (28%) Work of quiet breathing = 0.3 - 0.8 kg-m/min Maximum work of breathing = 10kg-m/min

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: If the lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume of the lung would be?
mcqs.explanation: If lung is allowed to undergo elastic recoil without the chest wall, the resultant volume of the lung would be minimum volume as the opposing force by the chest wall would be non existant.The yellow line in the above graph denotes the compliance of lungs alone. According to the graph, when the pressure (x axis) inside the lung is zero, there is some volume of air lesser than FRC still present (y axis) inside the lungs which is less than the functional residual capacity and residual381 volume which can be called as minimum volume.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Difference in trajectory between inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is due to:

options.a: Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration
options.b: Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration
options.c: Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration
options.d: Inspiration is active and expiration is passive

mcqs.explanation: The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis . It exists because a greater transpulmonary pressure is required to open a previously closed airway, due to a deficit of surfactant at the air-water interface , than to keep an open airway from closing, as then it has abundant surfactant.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following diagram shows the depth of respiration of a 45-year old man who suffered a head injury in an automobile accident . Identify the pattern of breathing.
mcqs.explanation: The pattern of breathing seen in the image is Cheyne –Stokes breathing. In this case, the person breathes deeply for a short interval and then breathes slightly or not for an additional interval. This pattern repeats itself about every minute. It is the most common type of periodic breathing seen most commonly in patients with heart failure and uremia, also seen in patients with brain disease and during sleep in normal individuals. This increased response occurs apparently due to the disruption of neural pathways that normally inhibit respiration. In such an individual, increased sensitivity to CO2 causes relative hyperventilation , lowering the arterial Pco2. During the resultant apnoea, the arterial Pco2 rises again to normal , but the respiratory mechanisms again over-responds to CO2. Breathing ceases , and the cycle repeats .382

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Oxygen comes from alveoli to blood by ______.
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli to blood along the concentration gradient i.e. passive process (ATP is not used ).387 It diffuses across respiratory membraneIt is governed by Fick's law of diffusion which is given in equation:Where • D is the diffusion rate • \033P is the partial pressure difference between the two ends of the diffusion pathway • A is the cross-sectional area of the pathway • S is the solubility of the gas • d is the distance of diffusion • MW is the molecular weight of the gas. (Diffusion coefficient of the gas, which is proportional to S/\016MW ).388

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the time taken (in seconds ) for blood to traverse the pulmonary capillaries at rest?
mcqs.explanation: Time taken by a red cell is about 0.75 seconds to traverse the pulmonary capillaries at rest and 0.3 seconds or less during exercise .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the percentage of systemic cardiac output which bypasses the pulmonary circulation (physiological shunt)?
mcqs.explanation: The percentage of cardiac output that bypasses the pulmonary circulation or physiological shunt is 2%. The fraction of mixed venous blood that does not become oxygenated as it moves from the right atrium to the left ventricle is called physiologic shunt. Causes of physiological shunt: • Extrapulmonary R->L Anatomic Shunt (normally ~ 1% of cardiac output ) • Intrapulmonary "True" Shunt • Flow past unventilated or collapsed alveoli (e.g., due to edema , pneumonia, atelectasis ) • Anatomic arterio-venous pathways - Mixing of unoxygenated blood in bronchial veins with oxygenated blood in pulmonary capillaries or vein reduces the final partial pressure of O2 in the arterial blood (PaO2). • Intrapulmonary regions with low ventilation/perfusion ratio: Alveolar ventilation is not zero, but blood is not completely oxygenated (A virtual shunt, not a "true" shunt).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man with shortness of breath is undergoing tests to assess lung function. Which of the following is used to measure lung diffusion capacity ?
mcqs.explanation: The diffusing capacity for CO (DLCO) is measured as an index of the diffusing capacity of the lung because its uptake is diffusion -limited . The diffusing capacity of the lung for a given gas is directly proportional to the surface area of the alveolo-capillary membrane and inversely proportional to its thickness.389 The normal value of DLCO at rest is about 25 mL /min/mm Hg. It increases up to threefold during exercise because of capillary dilation and an increase in the number of active capillaries .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The partial pressure of H2O at the body temperature (37\260 C) is (in mm Hg)_______
mcqs.explanation: The partial pressure of water vapor at a normal body temperature of 37\260C is 47 mm Hg. Humidification of air: • When dry air enters respiratory system it is humidified i.e. water molecules are continually escaping from the water surface (tissues) into the gas phase . • The partial pressure that the water molecules exert to escape through the surface is called the vapor pressure of the water. • The vapor pressure of water depends entirely on the temperature of the water. • The greater the temperature , the greater the kinetic activity of the molecules and, therefore, the greater the likelihood that the water molecules will escape from the surface of the water into the gas phase . • For instance, the water vapor pressure at 0\260C is 5 mm Hg, and at 100 \260C it is 760 mm Hg. • The most important value to remember is the vapor pressure at body temperature 47 mm Hg. (Once the equilibrium is attained after diffusion , vapour pressure is called partial pressure ).Gase s Inspired A ir Alveolar A ir Expired Air O2 158.0 100 .0 116 .0 CO2 0.3 40.0 32 .0 H2O 5.7 47.0 47.0390 Gase s Inspired A ir Alveolar A ir Expired Air N2 596.0 573.0 565 .0 Total 760.0 760.0 760.0

mcqs.question: What is the partial pressure of O2 in the alveolus?
mcqs.explanation: The partial pressure of O2 in the alveolus is 100 mmHg. The partial pressure of gases as they enter and leave the lungs is depicted below .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: If the tidal volume is 500 mL , PeCO2 is 30 mmHg and PaCO2 is 45 mmHg, calculate the dead space ?
mcqs.explanation: The Bohr-enghoff equation is used to calculate physiological dead space /total dead space . The original Bohr equation required measurement of the alveolar partial pressure of CO2 (PACO2).391 Later Enghoff modified the equation and replaced the PACO2 with PaCO2 (partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood). Enghoff 's modification of Bohr equation is:Where, • VD is the physiological dead space • VT is the tidal volume • PaCO2 is the partial pressure of CO2 in the arterial blood • PeCO2 is the average partial pressure of CO2 in the entire expired air. Substituting the values: Vd=(45-30/45) x 500=166 .66 ml392

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding dead space volume in a healthy individual?

options.a: Anatomical dead space > physiologic dead space
options.b: Anatomical dead space < physiological dead space
options.c: Anatomical dead space and physiologic dead space are almost equivalent
options.d: Anatomical dead space is not related to physiologic dead space

mcqs.explanation: In healthy individuals, anatomical dead space and physiologic dead space are almost equivalent, and can be estimated by body weight . Dead space is the volume of the airways and lungs that do not participate in gas exchange . Types • Anatomic dead space - Volume of the air-occupying conducting zone where no exchange of gases takes place . • Alveolar/functional dead space - the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood (wasted ventilation) • Total dead space /Physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar dead space . In healthy individuals: • Anatomical dead space = 150 mL . • Alveolar dead space is usually zero (increased in diseased conditions). Hence , • Physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar = 150 + 0 = 150 mL . • Physiological dead space = Anatomical dead space . • Radford's formula: Anatomical dead space in mL is approximately equal to the body weight in pounds. • Dead space can be measured by the following : • Single Breath N2 method (Fowler 's method ) • Bohr's equation

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: From base to the apex of the lung during standing, all the following decrease except ______

options.d: Intrapleural pressure (with respect to atmospheric pressure )

mcqs.explanation: V /Q ratio does not decrease from the base to apex of the lung while standing. • Normal differences in ventilation and perfusion of the lung in the upright position (refer figure ). Blood flow distribution in the lung PA: Alveolar pressure Pa: arterial pressure PV : venous pressureZones of lung Blood fl ow Pressure driving blood flow Zone 1 (near Ape x) Lowest PA> Pa> Pv Zone 2 Medium Pa> PA> Pv393 Zones of lung Blood fl ow Pressure driving blood flow Zone 3 Highest Pa> Pv > PAVentilation–perfusion ratio is not the same in all part of the lungs because of the effect of gravity. At the apex (Against gravity): Both ventilation and perfusion decrease since the flow is against gravity. But, a decrease in perfusion is higher than the decrease in ventilation. Hence , ratio increases (3.2). At the base of lung: Both ventilation and perfusion increase since the flow is towards gravity. Increase in perfusion is more than increase in ventilation, i.e., denominator increases. Hence , ratio decreases to 0.6. The average value of V /Q ratio throughout lungs is 0.8. Important points: • If the effect of gravity is eliminated , as in the supine position, the value is the same in all parts of the lung = 0.8. • V /Q ratio is infinity when perfusion is zero as in case of pulmonary embolism. • V /Q ratio is zero when ventilation is zero like in case of foreign body obstruction. • High V /Q ratio at apex leads to high pAO2 which favors the growth of microorganisms like tubercle bacilli. Intra -pleural pressure decreases as we move from the base to the apex of the lung i.e- becomes more negative as we move from the base to the apex of the lung.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Waterfall effect is seen in ____

options.a: Lower and middle portions of the lung

mcqs.explanation: Water fall effect has been used to describe the blood flow in the middle portion of lung.394 In this region blood flows in pulses . At first there is no flow because of obstruction at the collapsed venous end of the capillary bed . Pressure from the arterial side builds up until it exceeds alveolar pressure and flow resumes . This dissipates the capillary pressure and returns to the start of the cycle . The blood flow in this region is determined by the pulmonary artery–alveolar pressure difference . Blood "falls" into the pulmonary veins, which are compliant and take whatever amount of blood can flow into them. This has been called the waterfall effect . mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: V /Q = infinity holds true in which of the following conditions?

options.a: Foreign body obstruction in the bronchus
options.c: When O2 and CO2 ratio is equal
options.d: The PO2 of alveolar air is 159 mmHg and PCO2 is 40 mmHg

mcqs.explanation: VA /Q= infinity means that there is no exchange of O2 & CO2, which means the volume of the lung equals to dead space and the physiological effort of breathing is wasted . VA represents the ventilation in alveoli and Q represents the blood flow through the alveolus. The ratio of VA and Q explains the respiratory exchange when there is an imbalance between alveolar ventilation and alveolar blood flow . The ventilation-perfusion ratio is considered normal if there is an equal amount of blood flow & ventilation through the alveolus. VA /Q ratio is infinity when : • There is adequate ventilation but no perfusion . • No exchange of gases ( O2 and CO2 )through the respiratory membranes of corresponding alveoli. • The alveolar air equilibrates the humidified inspired air. • Partial pressures of the O2 and CO2 are 149 mmHg & 0 mm Hg respectively .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The O2-CO2 diagram shown below shows a ventilation-perfusion ratio curve for the normal lung. Which of the following options best describes the effect of decreasing the ventilation-perfusion ratio on the alveolar Po2 and Pco2?
mcqs.explanation: Decreased ventilation-perfusion ratio implies decreased oxygenation due to decreased ventilation with respect to perfusion . Hence , PAO2 decreases and Pco2 increases.395 A decrease in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (VA /Q) is depicted by moving to the left along the normal ventilation-perfusion line as shown in the figure (Zones here refer to the zones of variation in pulmonary blood flow and alveolar ventilation under influence of gravity) • Zone 1 - Zone 1 has the lowest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 3 but, in Zone 1 Ventilation (V)>>Perfusion (Q) hence V/Q is high • PAO2 is highest • PACO2 is lowest • Zone 2 - Ventilation (V) almost equal to Perfusion (Q) but slightly lower so V /Q is average (~0.8) • Zone 3 - Zone 3 has the highest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 1 but, in Zone 3 Perfusion (Q) >> Ventilation (V) hence V/Q is low • PAO2 is lowest • PACO2 is highest . *PAO2 - Alveolar partial pressure of oxygen *PACO2 - Alveolar partial pressure of CO2

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A person with normal lung at sea level (760 mm Hg) is breathing 50% oxygen . With a normal respiratory quotient of 0.8, what is the approximate alveolar Po2 (in mmHg)?
mcqs.explanation: Alveolar gas equation is used to calculate partial pressure of O2 in alveolar air. It is given by the formula:396 Where • PAO2 = Alveolar PO2 (mm Hg) • PIO2 = PO2 in inspired air (mm Hg) • PACO2 = Alveolar PCO2 (mm Hg), which is normally 40mmHg • R = Respiratory exchange ratio or respiratory quotient (CO2 production /O2 consumption) • Correction factor is usually negligible . Step 1: In the question PO2 in inspired air is not given directly . It has to be calculated using the formula: PIO2 = FIO2 (PB - PH20 ) Where • PIO2 = PO2 in inspired air (mm Hg) • FIO2 = Fraction of inspired O2 (50% or 0.5) • PB = Barometric pressure (760 mmHg) • PH2O = Water vapour pressure (47 mmHg) Substituting the values: PIO2 = 0.5 (760 - 47) = 0.5 \327 713 = 356.5 mmHg Step 2: PAO2 = PiO2 – (Pco2/R) = 356.5 – (40/0.8) = 356.5 – 50 = 306 .5 mmHg.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following decreases in a patient with emphysema ?
mcqs.explanation: In emphysema , the destruction of the alveolar walls brings down the diffusion area.397 Changes in Emphysema • Due to the destruction of the alveolar walls , there is a decrease in surface /diffusion area. • Cardiac output will be normal . • Pulmonary artery pressure may be elevated because the destruction of alveoli leads to loss of surrounding capillaries which forces blood into remaining capillaries , which tends to increase pulmonary artery pressure . • Alveolar Pco2 will tend to increase due to difficulty in expiration. Diffusion capacity of Lung for CO (DLCO): • In case of emphysema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of decreased surface area (trypsin destroys respiratory membrane) • In case of fibrosis or pulmonary edema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of increased thickness of membrane • In case of anemia – Decreased DLCO • Polycythemia , pulmonary hemorrhage – Increased DLCO.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes the mean arterial oxygen tension (pO2), carbon dioxide tension (pCO2) and pH in a healthy athlete during moderate exercise ?

options.a: \023 Arterial pO2, \023 Arterial pCO2, \023 Arterial pH
options.b: \023 Arterial pO2, \031 Arterial pCO2, \023 Arterial pH
options.d: No change in Arterial pO2, Arterial pCO2 or Arterial pH

mcqs.explanation: During moderate exercise , there is no change in arterial pO2, arterial pCO2 or arterial pH. Ventilation increases abruptly at the onset of exercise due to psychic stimuli and afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles , tendons , and joints. This is followed by a brief pause and then a gradual increase in ventilation. This gradual increase in ventilation is believed to be due to multiple factors such as an increase in body temperature , increase in plasma K+ level stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors , or the sensitivity of the neurons controlling the response to CO2. In strenuous exercise , at a certain point, the O2 uptake reaches its maximum levels , beyond which it cannot increase further. This leads to a rise in blood lactate levels . Buffering of lactic acid liberates CO2 which further increases ventilation. The increased production of lactic acid, increase in ventilation and CO2 production are proportional, and alveolar and arterial CO2 changes little to nil. This is called isocapnic buffering .398

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Transport of CO is diffusion limited because _____

options.a: Alveolar membrane is less permeable to CO
options.b: High affinity of CO to hemoglobin

mcqs.explanation: Transport of CO is diffusion limited because of the high affinity of CO to hemoglobin . Diffusion across the alveolocapillary membrane: • Blood takes 0.75s to traverse pulmonary capillaries . • CO diffuses into blood and combines with Hb with very high affinity. Thus the partial pressure of CO doesn 't rise (Only dissolved form of gas can increase the partial pressure , Gas which combines with Hb or plasma proteins cannot). Partial pressure gradient necessary for diffusion of CO is maintained for the whole 0.75s and hence it is Diffusion limited . • In the case of N2O it does not react and reaches equilibrium in about 0.1s. The amount of N2O taken up is not limited by diffusion but by the amount of blood flowing through the pulmonary capillaries ; that is, it is Flow -limited . • O2 is intermediate between N2O and CO; it is taken up by haemoglobin , but much less avidly than CO, and it reaches equilibrium with capillary blood in about 0.3 s. Thus, its uptake is Perfusion-limited . In the case of perfusion limited gases , an increase in pulmonary blood flow increases the amount of gas transferred. Hence O2 transport increases with an increase in pulmonary blood flow .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What is the percentage of O2 carried, chemically bound to Hb?
mcqs.explanation: 405 Percentage of O2 carried chemically (bound to Hb) is 97%. Oxygen is transported in the blood in two forms: • physically 3% - dissolved in plasma • chemically 97% - bound to hemoglobin. Remember: Gases are transported in 3 forms: • Dissolved gas - This is the form which contributes to partial pressure . Nitrogen is carried only in dissolved form in blood. • Bound gas - O2, CO are bound to Hb in RBC; CO2 is bound to Hb in RBC as well as plasma protein. • Chemically modified gas - CO2 in the form of HCO3-. Total gas concentration in solution is the sum of dissolved gas plus bound gas plus chemically modified gas.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The presence of hemoglobin in normal arterial blood increases its O2 concentration approximately by how many times ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of hemoglobin in normal arterial blood increases its O2 concentration approximately by 70 times • Normal arterial blood has Po2 of about 100 mm Hg. Amount of O2 transported in dissolved form (Calculated by using Henry's law): • Concentration of dissolved O2 = Partial pressure of O2 \327 solubility of O2 = 100 mmHg \327 0.003 mL O2/100 mL blood per mm Hg = 0.3 mL O2/100 mL • Hence 1L of plasma has 3mL of 02 in dissolved form. • 5L of plasma can carry maximum 15mL of 02 . • At rest, O2 demand is around 250mL/min. • Hence dissolved O2 alone is not sufficient to meet body demands . Amount of O2 transported bound to Hb: • Concentration of Hb is 15g/100 mL • Each gram of Hb binds to 1.34 mL of O2 • Hence , 15 g binds to 20 .1mL of O2/100 mL • On average, the 15 g of hemoglobin in 100 mL of blood can combine with a total of about 20 mL of O2. Thus, this value (20.1) in the presence of Hb is about 70 times the value (0.3) in the absence of Hb.406

mcqs.question: O2 delivery to tissues depends on all except _____
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen delivery is the volume of oxygen delivered to the systemic vascular bed per minute. It is the product of the cardiac output and the arterial oxygen concentration. Oxygen delivery to tissue depends on (refer flow chart)

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Each molecule of hemoglobin carries ______ molecules of O2.
mcqs.explanation: Hemoglobin has 4 subunits each of which has heme molecule and polypeptide chain. Ferrous in heme binds to a molecule of O2. Hence, hemoglobin binds to 4 molecules of O2. • Hemoglobin is a protein made up of four subunits . • Each subunit contains a heme moiety attached to a polypeptide chain. • Heme is a porphyrin ring complex that includes one atom of ferrous iron. • In normal adults , most of the hemoglobin molecules contain two �o and two \035 chains. • Each of the four iron atoms in hemoglobin can reversibly bind one O2. The iron stays in the ferrous state so that the reaction is oxygenation (not oxidation).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Most of the CO2 transported in the arterial blood is in the form of_____
mcqs.explanation: CO2 is carried in the blood in three forms: • Bicarbonate (HCO3� ) - Quantitatively the most important(70%) • Carbaminohemoglobin (23 %) • Dissolved CO2 (7%)407

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about hemoglobin is false ?

options.a: The T configuration of Hb does not favor O2 binding
options.b: The R configuration of Hb does not favor O2 binding
options.c: The R configuration of Hb favors O2 binding
options.d: Each Hb molecules carries 4 oxygen molecules

mcqs.explanation: A relaxed (R) configuration, exposes more O 2 binding sites . The quaternary structure of hemoglobin determines its affinity for O2. In deoxyhemoglobin , the globin units are tightly bound in a tense (T) configuration, which reduces the affinity of the molecule for O2. When O 2 is first bound, the bonds holding the globin units are released , producing a relaxed (R) configuration, which exposes more O2 binding sites . The net result is a 500-fold increase in O2 In tissues , these reactions are reversed, resulting in O2 dissociation .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The oxygen -haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid shape because _____

options.a: Binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules
options.b: Binding of one O2 molecule decreases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules

mcqs.explanation: The oxygen -haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid shape because binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules . The oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve relates percentage saturation of the O2 carrying power of hemoglobin (abbreviated as SaO2) to the Po2. It has a characteristic sigmoid shape due to the T–R interconversion. Combination of the first heme in the Hb molecule with O2 increases the affinity of the second heme for O2 and oxygenation of the second increases the affinity of the third, and so on, such that the affinity of Hb for the fourth O2 molecule is many times that for the first (Positive Co-operative Effect ). Option C: The effect of PCO2 and pH on the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is called the Bohr effect . Option D: O2 bound to hemoglobin changes its affinity for CO2, such that when less O2 is bound, the affinity of hemoglobin for CO2 increases . This is referred to as the Haldane effect .408

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Hb would be expected to become 100 % saturated with oxygen at Po2 of (in mmHg)_____
mcqs.explanation: When blood is equilibrated with 100 % O2, the normal hemoglobin becomes 100 % saturated . • In vivo , the hemoglobin in the blood at the end of the pulmonary capillaries is about 97.5% saturated with O2 (Po2 = 100 mm Hg). • Because of a slight admixture with venous blood that bypasses the pulmonary capillaries (i.e, physiologic shunt), the hemoglobin in systemic arterial blood is only 97% saturated . • Graph relates the percentage of saturated hemoglobin (SaO2) to PO2 and dissolved O2.Partial pressure of O2 Corresponding S pO2 99 - 100 % 89% 75 % 50%

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The normal value of P50 in an adult is(mm Hg)______
mcqs.explanation: Normal P50 is about 27 mm of Hg for adult Hb. P50 is the partial pressure of O2 at which Hb is 50 % saturated . P50 is an index of the affinity of Hb with O2. Higher the P50 value, lower is the affinity: Oxygen -Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve shifts to right. Lower the P50 value, the higher is the affinity: Oxygen -Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve shifts to left .409

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Decrease in pH shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to_____

options.d: On either side depending on other factors

mcqs.explanation: The pH decreasing from the normal value shifts the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, to the right. Oxygen -Hb dissociation curve (OHDC) • This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the % saturation of Hb with O2. • It is normally sigmoid-shape . • If OHDC is shifted to the right, it means that affinity of Hb for O2 has become less (which favors O2 delivery ) i.e. Higher the P50. (R - Right shift Releases oxygen ) Shift to the right is caused by: (Conditions with increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues ) • Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - Metabolically active tissues utilise O2 and tissues produce CO2 • \023 pH - Secondary to increased CO2 production • \031 in temperature , heat • \031 in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis • Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, androgen - by increasing 2,3 DPG • Sickle cell anaemia - reduced affinity for O2410

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Four molecules of myoglobin will bind how many molecules of oxygen ?
mcqs.explanation: 4 molecules of myoglobin will bind 4 molecules of oxygen . • Myoglobin : This is present in skeletal muscles . • 1 molecule of myoglobin binds 1 molecule of O2. Thus, 4 molecules of myoglobin will bind 4 molecules of oxygen • The shape of O2-myoglobin dissociation curve is the rectangular hyperbola . It lies to the left of Oxygen -Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC)(refer figure ).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Bohr effect
mcqs.explanation: 411 Facilitation of oxygen transport depends on the oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve, explained by the Bohr effect . When the metabolic activity of tissues increases, the production of CO2 increases. This CO2 diffuses into the blood and in turn, raises the blood H2CO3 and causes an increase in the H+ concentration and a decrease in pH. This decreases the affinity of Hb for O2, shifting the O2- hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. This facilitates the unloading of O2 in the tissues . The effect of Pco2 and pH on O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve is called the Bohr Effect . Conversely, in the lungs , CO2 diffuses from the blood to the alveoli and the H+ concentration decreases and theO2 hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the left increasing the affinity of Hb to O2. Note : Double Bohr effect occurring in the placenta : Oxygen –hemoglobin dissociation curve of fetal blood and maternal blood move in opposite directions . Mechanism: • The fetal blood entering the placenta carries large amounts of carbon dioxide , but most of it diffuse from the fetal blood into the maternal blood. • Fetal blood - loss of CO2 - reduced H+ - shift to left - loading of O2 i.e. oxygenation of fetal Hb. • Maternal blood - increase in CO2 - increase in H+ - shift to the right - Release of oxygen .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The level of 2,3 –DPG is decreased in______
mcqs.explanation: The level of 2,3–DPG is decreased in acidosis. 2,3-DPG is produced from 3-phosphoglycerate which is a product of glycolysis . Acidosis inhibits red cell glycolysis which decreases the levels of 2,3-DPG.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: High affinity of HbF to O2 is due to_____
mcqs.explanation: Increased affinity of HbF to O2 is due to decreased affinity of \025 chains of HbF to 2,3DPG. HbF is the fetal variant of hemoglobin . The \035 chains of adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) are replaced by \025 chains in HbF. This modification results in increased affinity of hemoglobin for O2, a left shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and decreased P50. The mechanism of the left shift is based on the binding of 2,3-DPG. 2,3-DPG does not bind as avidly to the \025 chains of HbF as it binds to the \035 chains of hemoglobin A. When less 2,3-DPG is bound, the affinity for O2 increases and facilitates the movement of O2 from the mother to the fetus . This increased affinity is beneficial to the fetus , whose PaO2 is low (approximately 40 mm Hg).412

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Haldane effect is _______

options.a: Binding of O2 to Hb favours release of CO
options.b: Binding of CO2 to Hb favours release of O
options.c: HCO3- leaving RBC in exchange for Cl-

mcqs.explanation: Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This effect is called the Haldane effect . (Remember - Haldane effect occurs in lungs and causes left shift of O2-Hb dissociation curve) Haldane Effect • Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This effect , called the Haldane effect , is important in promoting CO2 transport. • The Haldane effect results from the simple fact that the combination of O2 with hemoglobin in the lungs causes the hemoglobin to become a stronger acid. This displaces CO2 from the blood and into the alveoli.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: You are comparing the packed cell volume (PCV) obtained from an arterial and venous blood sample of the same patient . Why is PCV higher in venous blood?
mcqs.explanation: Hematocrit (PCV) of venous blood is normally 3% greater than that of the arterial blood because of 2 reasons: • Chloride shift • A small amount of fluid in the arterial blood returns via the lymphatics rather than the veins. Chloride shift:• Upon entering the red blood cell , CO2 is rapidly hydrated to H2CO3 by carbonic anhydrase. • H2CO3 is in equilibrium with H+ and its conjugate base, HCO3-. • H+ can interact with deoxyhemoglobin , whereas HCO3- can be transported outside of the cell via anion exchanger 1 (AE1 or Band 3). • In effect , for each CO2 molecule that enters the red cell , there is an additional HCO3- or Cl- in the cell .413 • Because of this chloride shift, the Cl – content of the red cells in venous blood is significantly greater than that in arterial blood. • Note that for each CO2 molecule added to a red cell , there is an increase of one osmotically active particles in the cell - either a HCO 3 – or a Cl – ion. Consequently , the red cells take up water and increase in size.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What makes CPDA superior than ACD for blood storage :

options.a: The fall in 2, 3 DPG is less

mcqs.explanation: The fall in 2, 3 DPG is less when the blood is stored in CPDA compared with ACD. 2, 3 DPG (2,3-diphosphoglycerate ) binds to deoxygenated haemoglobin . Therefore, an increase in 2,3 DPG causes increased release of O2 to the tissues . The equilibrium between Hb and O2 can be understood from the following equation: HbO2 + 2,3-DPG \037 Hb� 2,3-DPG + O2 In stored blood, the 2,3 DPG levels usually fall. As a result , stored blood releases less oxygen to the tissues than the normal circulating blood, thus limiting its use in hypoxic patients (Eg : anaemia). However, such a fall in 2,3 DPG is less when it is stored in a phosphate -containing solution like CPDA (Citrate, phosphate , dextrose , adenine ), rather than ACD (Acid citrate dextrose ). Therefore, the blood stored in CPDA, in comparison with blood stored in ACD has: • Higher 2,3 DPG concentration • More amount of deoxygenated blood bound to 2,3 DPG • Decreased affinity of Hb to the oxygen . • Increased release of oxygen to the tissues . • Raised P50 (PO2 at which Hb is half saturated ) • Shift in O2-Hb dissociation curve to the right

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The oxygen carrying capacity of a 18 year old boy with haemoglobin of 14g/dl is
mcqs.explanation: The oxygen carrying capacity of a boy with haemoglobin 14g/dl is 18. When blood is saturated with 100 % O2, the haemoglobin is also 100 % saturated and each gram of normal haemoglobin contains 1.39 mL of O2. However, blood normally contains some inactive haemoglobin derivatives, and the measured value in vivo is thus slightly lower hence, each gram of haemoglobin in vivo contains 1 . 31 mL of O2 (Hufner's constant). According to the above question, when Hb=14g/dl, O2= 1.31 *14= 18.34 The oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve • Demonstrates a progressive increase in the percentage of haemoglobin bound with oxygen as blood Po2 increases, which is called the percent saturation of haemoglobin .414 • Blood leaving the lungs and entering the systemic arteries usually has a Po2 of about 95 mm Hg, the usual oxygen saturation of systemic arterial blood averages 97 per cent. • Conversely, in normal venous blood returning from the peripheral tissues , the Po2 is about 40 mm Hg, and the saturation of haemoglobin averages 75 per cent.415

mcqs.explanation: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume. From the picture given below , (FRC = ERV + RV ).Lung Capacities : The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs . • The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level . • The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level . • The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath.

The functional residual capacity equals the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume. mcqs.question: A patient has a dead space of 150 mL , a functional residual capacity of 3L , tidal volume of 650 mL , expiratory reserve volume of 1.5 L, a total lung capacity of 8L, respiratory rate of 15 breaths/min. What is the rate of alveolar ventilation?

mcqs.question: Closing volume of the lung is_____

options.a: Above residual volume in upper portions of the lungs
options.b: Above the residual volume in dependent portions of the lungs

mcqs.explanation: The closing volume (CV) is the lung volume above the residual volume (RV ) at which the airways in the lower dependent parts of the lung begin to close off because of the lesser transmural pressure in these areas.427 In young adults , the closing volume is about 10 % of the vital capacity (VC). mcqs.question: Flow volume given below indicates _____
mcqs.explanation: The inspiratory flow -volume curve is truncated in patients with variable extrathoracic obstructions .428 • During a forced expiration, the cross-sectional area of a variable extrathoracic obstruction increases as the pressure inside the airway increases. • The expiratory flow -volume curve is therefore nearly normal or not affected . • However, during a forced inspiration, the pressure inside the upper airway decreases below atmospheric pressure , and unless the stability of the upper airway is maintained by reflex contraction of the pharyngeal muscles or by other structures , the cross-sectional area of the upper airway will decrease . mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Lung Volumes and Lung Function Tests
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes the changes in lung volume and thoracic volume in a case of pneumothorax, compared to normal ?
mcqs.explanation: In pneumothorax, lung volume is decreased and thoracic volume is increased . Both lungs and the chest wall (thoracic cage ) are elastic structures . Under normal conditions, the elastic tendency of the lungs to collapse is exactly balanced by the elastic tendency of the chest wall to expand. In pneumothorax, air is introduced into the pleural space , so the pleural pressure , which is normally subatmospheric , becomes equal to atmospheric pressure . The chest wall springs outward and the lungs collapse . This increases the thoracic volume and decreases the lung volume.

mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man inhaled as much air as possible and then expired with a maximum effort until no more air could be expired . This produced the maximum expiratory flow -volume curve shown in the following diagram. What is the forced vital capacity of this man (in liters)?
mcqs.explanation: The forced vital capacity of this man is 4.5 liters. The forced vital capacity (FVC), the largest amount of air that can be expired after a maximal inspiratory effort , is frequently measured clinically as an index of pulmonary function. Forced vital capacity (FVC) = Total lung capacity (TLC ) – Residual volume(RV ) • In the flow -volume curve, the point of intersection between abscissa and flow -volume curve gives the TLC and RV . • From the given flow -volume curve we can note that: • Total Lung Capacity (TLC ) = 5.5 L • Residual volume (RV )= 1.0 L • Thus,430 • FVC = TLC – RV = 4.5 L

These findings are consistent with which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: This is a case of asbestosis . Asbestosis is a restrictive lung disease characterized by diffuse interstitial fibrosis. In restrictive lung disease , the maximum expiratory flow volume (MEFV) curve begins and ends at abnormally low lung volumes. Note : In obstructive lung diseases , the airways are narrowed or radial traction of the airways is reduced , allowing them to close more easily . The lung volumes in these cases are higher than normal .
