mcqs.question: The maximum expiratory flow -volume (MEFV) curves shown in the figure below were obtained from a healthy man (purple curve) and a 57 -year-old man with shortness of breath (green curve). What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The green curve in the above image and the case scenario denotes that the diagnosis is likely to be emphysema . Maximum expiratory flow volume (MEFV): When a person expires with great force, the expiratory airflow reaches a maximum flow beyond which the flow cannot be increased anymore, even with greatly increased additional force. In obstructive airway disease like Emphysema , it is usually much more difficult to expire than to inspire because the closing tendency of the airways is greatly increased by the extra positive pressure during expiration. Due to the obstruction of the airways and because they collapse more easily than normal airways, the maximum expiratory flow rate is greatly reduced (But, total lung capacity and residual volume is increased ) which is shown in the green curve below . Other options given above will cause constricted lungs where the lungs cannot expand to a normal maximum volume. Hence , even with the greatest possible expiratory effort , the maximum431 expiratory flow rate will be reduced . (Note : here both the total lung capacity and the residual volume are reduced ), which is shown as the blue curve in the graph below . Following graph shows the MEFV of restrictive and obstructive lung diseases .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Lung Volumes and Lung Function Tests
mcqs.question: Which of the following increases in COPD?
mcqs.explanation: In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal. Hence, both 1 and 2 are correct. • In obstructive lung diseases , both FEV1 and FVC reduces , where the decrease in FEV1 is more than the reduction in FVC. As a result, the ratio of FEV1/FVC also decreases . • The total lung capacity is usually normal in chronic bronchitis, while increased in emphysema . • Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air present in the lungs at the end of passive expiration. In COPD, FRC is increased . Lung Capacities : The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs . • The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level . • The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level . • The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Lung Volumes and Lung Function Tests
mcqs.question: Which of the following factors is most likely to stimulate ventilation after strenuous exercise ?

options.a: Collateral impulses from higher than brain centres

mcqs.explanation: 432 The stimulus to ventilation after strenuous exercise is increased mean arterial H+. The respiratory rate after exercise does not reach a basal level until the O2 debt is repaid. The stimulus for ventilation is increased mean arterial H+ due to an increase in blood lactic acid levels . Most of the lactic acid is converted to glycogen and some amount is converted to CO2 and H2O.433

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which is the best parameter to analyze hypoxic hypoxia?

options.a: Partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (Paco2)
options.b: Partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (Pao2)

mcqs.explanation: Hypoxic hypoxia is characterized by low partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (Pao2), while other parameters like partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (Paco2) may remain normal . Ventilation–Perfusion Imbalance: • The patchy ventilation–perfusion imbalance is the most common cause of hypoxic hypoxia or hypoxemia . • If alveoli are not ventilated but perfusion is present - blood passing through that alveoli remains unoxygenated .439 • When this unoxygenated blood mixes with blood from normal or overventilated alveoli, there is a right to left shunt created . • This results in reduced partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2) i.e., hypoxemia and consequently hypoxia. Note : • Hypoxemia can be defined as a condition where arterial oxygen tension or partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2 ) is below normal . • Hypoxia is defined as the reduction of oxygen supply at the tissue level , which is not measured directly by a laboratory value. Scenario 1: • Generally , the presence of hypoxemia suggests hypoxia i.e. if there is less oxygen in blood, O2 supply to tissues will also be reduced . • But, in case of cyanide poisoning, there is hypoxia in the absence of hypoxemia , i.e., arterial O2 content is normal but tissues are not able to utilize it because cyanide interferes with aerobic metabolism in the tissues . Scenario 2: • Hypoxia may not be present in patients with hypoxemia if the patient compensates for a low PaO2 by increasing oxygen delivery . This is typically achieved by increasing cardiac output (by raising the heart rate) or decreasing tissue oxygen consumption. • Nevertheless , hypoxemia is definitely the most common cause of tissue hypoxia, and the correct diagnosis should be made because it is readily treatable .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which type of hypoxia does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors ?
mcqs.explanation: In the case of anemic hypoxia, O2 content is low but dissolved O2 is within normal limits, so it does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors . Peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid and aortic arteries sense changes in Po2(<60mm Hg), pH, and Pco2 and they respond to changes in dissolved O2(PaO2 ). Histotoxic hypoxia will lead to metabolic acidosis that will lead to an increase in H+ concentration, which in turn will stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors . Hemorrhage that produces hypotension leads to chemoreceptor stimulation due to decreased blood flow to the chemoreceptors and consequent stagnant anoxia of these organs. Note : In case of stagnant hypoxia, chemoreceptors can be stimulated if the resultant decreased oxygen delivery causes a significant drop in local tissue oxygen levels , which eventually can lower the PaO2 detectable by chemoreceptors . Therefore , they may not be significantly stimulated unless the reduction in oxygen levels is severe . Therefore, anaemic hypoxia is a better answer.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following is most likely in a patient with cyanosis?
mcqs.explanation: 440 In stagnant hypoxia, blood flow is very low; so, more oxygen is extracted causing an increase in reduced hemoglobin \032 cyanosis. Cyanosis - Cyanosis is the dusky bluish discoloration of the tissues occurring when the reduced hemoglobin concentration is more than 5g /dL. • Its occurrence depends upon • The total amount of hemoglobin in the blood • Degree of hemoglobin unsaturation • The state of capillary circulation Option a: In the case of anemia, the total hemoglobin content is low, so enough reduced hemoglobin cannot be formed. Option b: In histotoxic hypoxia, the amount of reduced hemoglobin formed is very less because the defect is in the tissue O2. Option c: In CO poisoning, there is the formation of carboxyhemoglobin, which is red in color obscure the color of reduced hemoglobin .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Administration of O2 has maximum benefit in:
mcqs.explanation: Administration of oxygen has maximum benefit in hypoxic hypoxia. Hypoxic hypoxia refers to a condition in which there is low atmospheric Po2, leading to low arterial Po2. Hence , supplemental O2 can be very beneficial when the cause of hypoxia is due to limited oxygen availability. Administration of oxygen -rich gas has limited value in anemic, histotoxic , and stagnant hypoxia because : Anemic hypoxia- Oxygen delivery is not beneficial because despite increasing the exogenous oxygen delivery , an anemic person will not have the capacity to carry more oxygen due to the hemoglobin / red blood cell deficit in anemia. Histotoxic hypoxia- The most common example is cyanide poisoning. Cyanide inhibits important enzymes in the oxidative phosphorylation process , which is essential to the survival of our cells . Additional oxygen supplementation will not be able to overcome this inhibition, and so it will have limited benefit . Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful to some extent . Stagnant hypoxia- Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient 's condition because it is the circulation that is affected . If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: In which of the following situations is oxygen therapy most beneficial provided the lung function is normal ?
mcqs.explanation: 441 With O2 therapy , increasing the inspired Po2 will result in an increased amount of dissolved O2. At high altitudes , there is low barometric pressure and so less Po2, hence , supplemental O2 will help . Option A: With anemia, the hemoglobin is fully saturated and O2 will have minimal effect . Treatment of anemia is more beneficial than providing oxygen to an anemic patient . Option B: With COPD there is CO2 retention due to difficulty in the expiration, and there will be a decreased Po2. So, there is a change in the regulation of respiration (drive for ventilation) from being under CO2 control to being driven by the decrease in O2. Giving supplemental O2 to such a person will increase arterial Po2, thus decrease the stimulus to breathe , resulting in patient stopping breathing. Option C: Cyanide poisoning results in decreased O2 utilization by the tissues and so additional O2 would be of no benefit .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is oxygen therapy not useful ?
mcqs.explanation: Oxygen therapy is not beneficial in central respiratory depression . High dose oxygen reduces the output of peripheral chemoreceptors . So, if given to patients who already have central respiratory depression, it will indirectly reduce the hypoxic drive to breathe even further, leading to a reduction in respiratory frequency and minute ventilation. Note : In acute severe asthma, a high concentration of oxygen should be given by face mask to achieve an oxygen saturation of >90%.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which of the points on the following figures represent arterial blood in a severely anemic person?
mcqs.explanation: When a person is anemic, there is decrease in O2 content of the blood (Fig 1-E) because of decreased number of RBCs and hence hemoglobin content in the blood. The oxygen saturation (Fig 2-D) of the available hemoglobin in the arterial blood is however normal and, the pO2 is also not affected by the hemoglobin concentration.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old woman is anemic with hemoglobin concentration of 6 g/dL. Which of the following set of changes have occurred in this case, compared to normal ?
mcqs.explanation: Normal Arterial Po2, \023Mixed venous Po2, \0312,3-DPG are the set of changes that will be seen in the above patient. The oxygen -carrying capacity of the blood is reduced in an anemic person, but the arterial Po2 and oxygen saturation are both normal . The decrease in arterial O2 content is compensated for by an increase in the extraction of oxygen f rom hemoglobin , which reduces the Po2 of the venous blood. The unloading of oxygen at tissue level is enhanced by an increased level of 2,3-DPG in an anemic patient because 2,3-DPG causes a right shift of the oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve.442

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curves corresponds to blood from an adult (dark blue line) and blood from a fetus (light blue line)?
mcqs.explanation: Curve C corresponds to blood from an adult (dark blue line) and blood from a fetus (light blue line). The fetal oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left relative to the adult curve. The fetal hemoglobin (Hb F) has a greater affinity for O2 than adult hemoglobin (Hb A). This facilitates the movement of O2 from the mother to fetus . The cause of this greater affinity is the poor binding of 2,3-DPG by \037 polypeptide chains that replace \035 chains in Hb F. The fetal oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curve is thus shifted to the left relative to the adult curve. Typically , fetal arterial Po2 is low, hence leftward shift enhances placental uptake of O2.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Which of the following oxygen -hemoglobin dissociation curves corresponds to blood during resting conditions (dark blue line) and blood during exercise ( light blue line)?
mcqs.explanation: The right shift of the oxygen -hemoglobin curve allows more oxygen to be released to the muscle at a given Po2 in the blood. The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right when factors like: • Increased temperature resulting from heat generated by the exercising muscle , • Higher carbon dioxide levels released from the muscle tissue , • Elevated 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), and • Increased hydrogen ions concentration in the muscle capillary blood Above factors decrease hemoglobin 's oxygen affinity. This shift promotes easier oxygen release to muscles and other tissues . Note : Despite the rightward shift, the maximum hemoglobin oxygen saturation at high oxygen levels remains unchanged . The plateau on the curve represents the maximal saturation achievable under optimal conditions, ensuring hemoglobin can still be fully saturated with oxygen .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Decompression sickness is seen in_____
mcqs.explanation: Decompression sickness is seen in pilots, mountaineers, and divers. Decompression sickness (DCS) or diver's disease , the bends , or Caisson disease is the name given to a variety of symptoms experienced by a person exposed to a reduction in the pressure surrounding their body. It can be seen in • Divers ascending rapidly from deep -sea (high pressure ) to the surface of the earth (low pressure ) • Pilots traveling in unpressurized aircraft or mountaineers, rapidly ascending from the surface of the earth (high-pressure zone) to a high altitude ( low -pressure zone). Under high-pressure , gases get compressed and their solubility increases. When a person is in a high-pressure zone like the deep sea for a long time, an increased amount of nitrogen gets443 dissolved in his or her body. If the person suddenly comes back to an area of atmospheric pressure or a low-pressure zone, the gases escape from a dissolved state and form bubbles . These bubbles are almost entirely made of nitrogen. The bubbles can plug many small blood vessels in different tissues .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: Nitrogen narcosis is due to_____

options.c: Increased solubility of nitrogen in nerve cell

mcqs.explanation: Nitrogen narcosis is due to increased solubility of nitrogen in the nerve cell . Concept : • Below the sea level , atmospheric pressure increases at the rate of 1 atm for every 33 feet depth . • According to Boyle 's law, as pressure increases, volume decreases . Hence , lungs tend to collapse . To prevent this and to keep lung expanded , gas is delivered at high pressure to the lungs . • According to Dalton's law, nitrogen contributes the maximum to barometric pressure and hence the amount of nitrogen entering alveoli increases. • Henry's law: As the partial pressure of nitrogen in alveoli increases, its concentration in blood also increases (dissolved form). Nitrogen is 5 times more soluble in fat compared to water. • As a result , nitrogen dissolves in the fatty substances in neuronal membranes, and because of its physical effect on altering ionic conductance through the membranes, it reduces neuronal excitability and produces the narcotic effect .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: During acclimatization at higher altitude , all of the following changes take place except ______.

options.d: Shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve to left

mcqs.explanation: A shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) to the right is seen in acclimatization. On ascension to higher altitudes over a period of days rather than a period of hours, the ability to breathe much more deeply and withstand lower atmospheric O2 concentrations is improved. This phenomenon is called acclimatization. Variation of pH in Acclimatization: Immediate exposure to low pO2 stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors . This increases alveolar ventilation. This immediate increase in pulmonary ventilation upon rising to a high altitude blows off large quantities of CO2, reducing the pCO2 and increases the pH of the body fluids . These changes inhibit the brain stem respiratory center and thereby oppose the effect of low PO2 to stimulate respiration through the peripheral arterial chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies . There is a reduction of bicarbonate ion concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid , as well as in the b rain tissues . This reduction , in turn, decreases the pH in the fluids surrounding the chemosensitive neurons of the respiratory center , thus increasing the respiratory stimulatory activity of the center . An important mechanism for the gradual decrease in bicarbonate concentration is compensation by the kidneys for the respiratory alkalosis. Gradually, the metabolic compensation of the kidney will shift the pH towards normal .444

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations in Hypoxia, Anemia and ...
mcqs.question: A person develops headache and breathlessness on a trekking expedition following rapid ascent to over 3000 metres above the sea level . Which of the following is not used in the treatment of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The symptoms of headache and breathlessness following rapid ascent indicate acute mountain/altitude sickness and IV digoxin is not used to treat this condition. On ascent to high altitudes , the low partial pressure of oxygen leads to hypoxia and systemic arteriolar dilatation. Consequently , the capillary pressure rises with increased transudation of fluid into the brain tissue and the following symptoms are seen : • Headache • Irritation • Insomnia • Breathlessness • Nausea and vomiting Treatment involves administration of oxygen , descent to a lower altitude and administration of acetazolamide . Acetazolamide counteracts hypoxia by stimulating respiration and also reduces the formation of cerebrospinal fluid , thereby reducing intracranial tension. Portable hyperbaric chambers are increasingly being used in the treatment of high-altitude illnesses when rapid descent is not possible . These chambers are available in armed forces hospitals in high altitude areas445

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Where is the pneumotaxic centre located ?
mcqs.explanation: Pneumotaxic center is located in upper pons. Neural regulation of respiration: It involves set of neurons located in pons and medulla : • Pons: • Pneumotaxic centre • Apneustic centre • Medulla : Pre-Botzinger complex • Dorsal respiratory group454 • Ventral respiratory group

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________

options.b: Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla

mcqs.explanation: Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing. • These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla . • These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration. • These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons. Breathing is under the control of both the following : • Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract) • Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex ). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle ). There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.Inspirati on Initiation Pre-Botzinger complex (Pace maker cells ) in Medulla Maintena nce Apneustic center in lower Po ns stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla455 Inspirati on Terminat ion Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic cent erRegulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process ; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise . Mnemonic DIVE : Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about the main respiratory control neurons?

options.a: Send out regular bursts of impulses to expiratory muscles during quiet respiration
options.c: Are unaffected by impulses from the cerebral cortex
options.d: Send out regular bursts of impulses to inspiratory muscles during quiet respiration

mcqs.explanation: The main respiratory control neurons called the pre- B\037tzinger complex (pre-BOTC), are located in the medulla. Pre-B\366tzinger complex (pre-B\326TC) is located on either side of the medulla , between the nucleus ambiguus and the lateral reticular nucleus They send out regular bursts of impulses to inspiratory muscles via phrenic nerve during quiet respiration. Option a: Expiration is passive during quiet breathing. There is no discharge of any neurons. Option b: Pain stimulates respiration. There are NK1 receptors and �M-opioid receptors in Pre-Botzinger complex , and, in vivo , substance P stimulates and opioids inhibit respiration. Option c: Impulses from cerebral cortex also influence the pre-Botzinger complex .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The rate of inspiration is controlled by _______

options.b: Ventral group of neurons in medulla

mcqs.explanation: The rate of inspiration is controlled by the pneumotaxic center . Pneumotaxic centre : Location: Upper pons (dorsally in nucleus parabrachialis) Function: • Transmits signals to the inspiratory area, i.e., it inhibits the apneustic center and thus the dorsal respiratory group of neurons, to stop inspiration. • It thus helps limit duration of inspiration and switching between inspiration and expiration. • This has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing because limiting the duration of inspiration also shortens the duration of expiration, and hence , the entire period of respiration.456

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Depth of inspiration is increased by_____

options.b: Ventral group of neurons in medulla

mcqs.explanation: Depth of inspiration is increased by the apneustic center . The apneustic centre sends signals to prevent switching off of inspiration maintained by the dorsal respiratory group of neurons, thereby increasing depth of inspiration. In contrast to this, the pneumotaxic center primarily limits inspiration by controlling the "switch off" point of the inspiratory ramp signal. A note on inspiratory ramp signal: The neural signals transmitted to the inspiratory muscle , mainly the diaphragm, is not the instantaneous burst of action potentials . Instead, it begins weakly and increases steadily in a ramped manner . The advantage of the ramp is that it causes a steady increase in the volume of the lungs during inspiration, rather than inspiratory gasps . Control of the limiting point at which the ramp suddenly ceases is the mechanism by which the respiratory centers control depth and rate of respiration. Option A: Pneumotaxic center of the pons regulates the rate and depth of breathing. Option B: Ventral group of neurons regulate expiration. Option C: Dorsal group of neurons regulate inspiration.457

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A young couple was spending their afternoon on a picnic. Suddenly , the woman got down on her knee, pulled out a ring, and proposed . The man was taken aback and began to hyperventilate . The overdrive mechanism observed is due to_____

options.b: Dorsal group of neurons (DRG) in the medulla
options.d: Ventral group of neurons (VRG ) in the medulla

mcqs.explanation: The ventral respiratory group contributes to the extra respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism) • During quiet breathing: Expiration is a passive process and the neurons from the ventral respiratory group remain almost totally inactive during quiet respiration. Unlike the dorsal respiratory group (DRG; dorsal group of neurons), VRG (the ventral group of neurons) does not appear to participate in the basic rhythmic oscillations that control respiration. • Extra-respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism): When the respiratory drive for increased pulmonary ventilation becomes greater than normal , for example , during exercise , respiratory signals spill over to VRG from DRG. So, VRG contributes to the extra respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism). • The neurons of VRG contribute to both inspiration and expiration; especially , they are important in providing powerful expiratory signals to the abdominal muscles during very heavy expiration. Dorsal and ventral respiratory group:Dorsal respiratory group Ventral respiratory group Locati on Nucleus Tractus Solitarius in medulla Nucleus Retro Ambigualis in medulla Funct ion Inspiratory ramp signals - Sti mulates inspiration Inactive during quiet breathi ng; Active during forced expi ration458

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Stimulation of the apneustic centre causes ______

options.a: Decrease in the inspiratory ramp signal

mcqs.explanation: The apneustic center is located in the lower pons and it stimulates the inspiratory center to increase inspiratory activity. The apneustic center of pons send signals to the DRG in medulla to delay the 'switch off' signal of the inspiratory ramp provided by pneumotaxic center of pons. It gets feedback from vagal afferents and also from other respiratory centers . The apneustic center is inhibited by vagal afferents from pulmonary stretch receptors aroused by inspiration so that stimulatory effect on the inspiratory neurons is switched off allowing expiration to supervene .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A few nights before the respiratory physiology exam, a student was suffering from a recurring nightmare. In this nightmare, a knife-wielding horse was chasing him through the streets and threatening to cut off his brainstem at the mid-pontine level . Assuming the horse was proficient in its threat, and performed a bilateral vagotomy as well , which of the following outcomes would occur?
mcqs.explanation: Transection of the brain stem at the mid-pontine level with bilateral vagotomy causes apneusis . At mid pontine level lesion, the apneustic centre is intact while the pneumotaxic centre is separated . Concurrent removal of vagus inputs causes this kind of abnormal pattern of breathing characterized by deep , gasping inspiration with a pause at full inspiration followed by a brief insufficient release .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors _____

options.a: Respond minimally to changes in PO2 under normoxic conditions
options.b: Respond to changes in arterial PO2 but not pH
options.c: Respond to changes on PCO2 slower than the central chemoreceptors
options.d: Are most important receptors causing an increased ventilation in response to a rise in PCO

mcqs.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond minimally to changes in PO2 under normoxic conditions. Because of the enormous blood flow per unit of tissue to the carotid bodies , the receptors are not stimulated in conditions such as anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, in which the amount of459 dissolved O2 in the blood reaching the receptors is generally normal , even though the combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased. Peripheral chemoreceptors are responsive to changes in arterial O2, CO2, and H+ ions. They are excited by a decrease in arterial O2. However, a graph plotted between the rate of firing of afferent neurons in the chemoreceptor vs. arterial pO2 shows they are most sensitive to changes in pO2 of less than 60mmHg. Thus, ventilation is driven by pCO2 and H+ under normoxic conditions. Other options : • Option B: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to changes in blood pH. They are excited by an increase in H+ ions (i.e decrease in pH) • Option C: The response of peripheral chemoreceptors to changes in Pco2 is faster than that of central chemoreceptors . Increase in arterial pCO2 stimulates respiration. However, the stimulation by way of peripheral chemoreceptors occurs 5 times as rapidly as that from central chemoreceptors . This helps increase the rapididty of response to CO2 at the onset of exercise . • Option D: Central chemoreceptors are more important than the peripheral chemoreceptors in the ventilatory response to increased CO2. Note : • Most potent stimulus for central chemoreceptor in blood: CO2 • Most potent stimulus for central chemoreceptor in CSF: H+ ions • Most potent stimulus for respiration: CO2

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors are primarily sensitive to_____
mcqs.explanation: The peripheral chemoreceptors , located in the carotid and aortic bodies , are primarily sensitive to decrease in arterial PO2, although high PaCO2 and low pH also stimulates them and enhance their sensitivity to hypoxia. Carotid body is more sensitive than aortic body.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated maximally by____
mcqs.explanation: Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia, and thus , by preventing the O2 utilization at the tissue level ; it acts as the powerful stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors . Even though Po2 level of blood is normal in case of cyanide poisoning the sensors in carotid and aortic bodies are not able to sense oxygen in blood because of blockade of cellular respiration and hence , they go in for hypoxic state and gets stimulated . • Option a: Acidosis (Increased H+ ions) stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors . • Option b : Increased pCO2 mainly stimulates central chemoreceptors . • Option c : The peripheral chemoreceptors have an enormous blood flow per unit tissue (2000mL /100g of tissue /min) because of which the O2 needs of the cells can be met by dissolved460 O2 Therefore, Carbon monoxide poisoning does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors because the amount of dissolved O2 is generally normal , even though the combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Carotid body chemoreceptors are stimulated by all of the following types of hypoxia except _____
mcqs.explanation: Anemic hypoxia does not stimulate carotid body chemoreceptors . In anemia, • Amount of dissolved O2 reaching the receptors is generally normal • Combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased . • The blood flow per unit tissue of carotid body chemoreceptors is enormous (2000mL /100g of tissue /min). Hence , O2 needs of the tissue can be met largely by dissolved O2 alone. Therefore, the receptors are not stimulated by conditions such as anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, in which the amount of dissolved O2 reaching the receptors is generally normal , even though combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased . These peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated when arterial pO2 is low.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Central chemoreceptors _____

options.a: Respond to both pCO2 and pO2 of blood
options.b: Are activated by changes in pH of the CSF
options.c: For a given rise in pCO2, the pH of the CSF falls less than that of blood
options.d: HCO3- concentration in CSF doesnt affect output of central chemoreceptors

mcqs.explanation: Central chemoreceptors are stimulated by changes in pH of the CSF. They are located on the ventral surface of medulla Option A: Central chemoreceptors do not respond to pO2 of the blood. Option C: For a given rise in pCO2, the CSF pH falls more than that of the blood because the CSF has less buffering. CO2 combines with H2O to form H2CO3 which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. H+ is buffered by combining with Hb. This buffering is less in CSF and hence pH falls. Option D: The HCO3- concentration of the CSF can affect the output of the central chemoreceptors by buffering the changes in pH. HCO3- can combine with H+ and thus neutralise it and alter pH and thus alter output of central chemoreceptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to the following change in the blood:
mcqs.explanation: Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased Pco2 in the blood. Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased Pco2 in the blood because CO2 moves into the CSF, where it is promptly hydrated to form H2CO3 that dissociates to increase the CSF H+ concentration. This stimulates the central chemoreceptors , which monitor CSF H+ concentration (not blood H+ concentration). Other options :461 • H+ in arterial blood penetrates the blood-brain barrier very slowly and hence has little effect on central chemoreceptors . • Arterial Po2 has no effect on central chemoreceptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The primary direct stimulus for excitation of central chemoreceptors which regulate ventilation is______
mcqs.explanation: The central chemoreceptors are primarily stimulated by an increase in the H+ in the CSF. CO2 readily penetrates the blood-brain barrier and is promptly hydrated in the CSF to form H2CO3 that dissociates so that local H+ concentration rises. The H+ concentration in the CSF parallels the arterial Pco2. So the effect of arterial Pco2 and CO2 in CSF is indirect or secondary. Arterial Po2 has no effect on central chemoreceptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Peripheral and central chemoreceptors may both contribute to increased ventilation that occurs as a result of decreased ______
mcqs.explanation: Both peripheral and central chemoreceptors contribute to increased ventilation that occurs as a result of decreased arterial blood pressure. • Decrease in arterial blood pressure \032 hypoperfusion \032 hypoxia \032 stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors . • Decrease in arterial blood pressure \032 CO2 retention \032 increased arterial PCO2 \032 \031 H+ concentration in the CSF \032 stimulation of central chemoreceptors Option a : Decreased arterial Pco2 doesnt stimulate chemoreceptors . It is increased Pco2 that stimulates central chemoreceptors . Option b : Decreased arterial Po2 stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors but has no influence on central chemoreceptors . Option d : Increased (not decreased ) H+ ions stimulate both peripheral and central chemoreceptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following do not stimulate either central or peripheral chemoreceptors ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypercapnia is a stimulus for central and peripheral chemoreceptors and not hypocapnia . Option b: The peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypoxia (hypoxic, stagnant and histotoxic but NOT anemic hypoxia)and exercise (increased K+ levels ). Option c: The central chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypercapnia and resultant acidosis. Option d: Low perfusion pressure produces hypoxia because the amount of O2 delivered to the receptors per unit time is decreased . This stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors .462

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The most important stimulus controlling the level of resting ventilation is_____

options.a: pH of CSF on central chemoreceptors

mcqs.explanation: The most important stimulus comes from the pH of the CSF on the central chemoreceptors . The CO2 that enters the brain and CSF is hydrated to H2CO3 and dissociates , leading to rising H+ levels . The CSF H+ concentration hence parallels the arterial CO2 levels . The effect of pO2 on peripheral chemoreceptors under normoxic conditions is very small. Changes in pCO2 do affect the peripheral chemoreceptors , but the magnitude is less than that for the central chemoreceptors . The effect of changes in the pH on peripheral chemoreceptors under normal conditions is small: and the changes in pO2 do not affect the central chemoreceptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following occurs after hyperventilation with 6% CO2 in inspired air?
mcqs.explanation: Hyperventilation with 6% CO2 is followed by continued hyperventilation till alveolar Pco2 drops towards normal . Ventilatory responses to CO2 There is a linear relationship between increase in % of CO2 in inspired air and respiratory minute volume . • The upper limit for this linearity is 6% of alveolar PCO2. • When the CO2 content of the inspired gas is >7%, the alveolar and the arterial PCO2 begin to rise abruptly in spite of hyperventilation leading to hypercapnia . • Hypercapnia depresses the central nervous system , including respiratory centers leading to CO2 narcosis (a headache , confusion and eventually coma). Mechanism: Increased CO2 in inspired air �� Increased Alveolar PCO2 �� Increased arterial PCO2 �� Stimulation of central chemoreceptors �� Stimulation of ventilation �� Alveolar PCO2 drops toward normal

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about the ventilatory response ?

options.a: CO2 major factor controlling the normal level of ventilation
options.b: Is not related to respiratory minute volume
options.d: Is increased if alveolar PO2 is raised

mcqs.explanation: The normal level of ventilation is controlled by the ventilatory response to CO2. Option b: There is linear relationship between respiratory minute volume and the alveolar Pco2, i.e. as alveolar Pco2 increases respiratory minute volume increases. Option c: The ventilatory response depends on peripheral chemoreceptors in addition to central chemoreceptors . Option d: The ventilatory response to CO2 is increased if the alveolar PO2 is reduced The ventilatory response is reduced also during sleep .463

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Hering-Breuer reflexes are mediated by ____________ .
mcqs.explanation: Hering-Breuer reflexes are mediated by slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers. Hering-Breuer inflation reflex : "Prolonged inspiration inhibits further inspiration" • Hyperinflation of lungs stimulates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers. • This signal inhibits the inspiratory ramp signals of the dorsal respiratory group of neurons (DRG), thus, inspiration is quickly inhibited and expiration follows . • Advantages of Hering-Breuer inflation reflex : It cuts down the inspiration time, and therefore , • It prevents overinflation of the lungs. • Lungs operate at lower lung volumes, thereby preventing wastage of energy . • The Hering-Breuer reflex is activated when the lung volume increases to more than three times the normal tidal volume (tidal volume = 0.5 liters/breath; So, lung volume > 1.5 liters per breath activates the reflex ). • It signifies that the reflex plays a protective role preventing the overinflation of the lung rather than regulating the normal ventilation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following statements about Hering-Breuer inflation reflex are true except _____

options.a: The impulses travel to the brain via vagus nerve
options.b: It results in further inspiratory efforts if the lung is maintained inflated
options.c: It is seen in adults at high tidal volumes
options.d: Abolishing the reflex in many animals causes slow deep breathing

mcqs.explanation: Hering-Breuer inflation reflex inhibits further inspiratory efforts if the lungs are maintained inflated . Mechanism- Stretch receptors �� Vagus �� Inhibit Dorsal Respiratory Group �� Phrenic & Intercostal Nerves �� Inspiration shortened , Expiration prolonged Option a: The impulses travel to the brain via the vagus nerve. Option c: HB Reflex activated when TV > 1.5L. The reflex is seen in adults at high tidal volumes . Option d: Abolishing the reflex by cutting the vagal nerves in experimental animals causes slow deep breathing.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about Head's paradoxical reflex ?

options.c: Plays an important role in normal respiration

mcqs.explanation: Head's paradoxical reflex is stimulated by hyperinflation of lungs . It refers to prolonged inspiration stimulating further inspiration. Hyperinflation of the lungs causes strong and long-lasting inspiratory effort (an effect opposite to the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex ). Physiological role: • Occasional deep breaths which are thought to counteract any tendency to atelectasis in quiet breathing and possibly in reinforcing the gasps or inspiratory efforts .464 • First cry after birth. • The possible explanation for this could be the inhibition of vagus nerve at cold temperatures (due to the presence of pulmonary fluid in the unaerated newborn lungs ). • Lack of inhibitory impulses from the pulmonary stretch receptors and vagus has an effect opposite to Hering-Breuer's inflation reflex .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The immediate response of J receptor stimulation is
mcqs.explanation: The immediate reflex response of J receptor stimulation is apnea. It is followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension (pulmonary chemoreflex ). Juxtacapillary receptors are the C fiber endings located close to the pulmonary vessels in the alveolar interstitium . They are not involved in quiet or normal respiration. They are stimulated by • Hyperinflation of the lung • Intravenous or intracardiac administration of chemicals like capsaicin P

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Moderate exercise being one of the most powerful stimulators of ventilation works by the way of_____

options.b: Low PO2 in mixed venous blood

mcqs.explanation: Moderate exercise does not reduce the arterial Po2, increase the arterial Pco2, or reduce the arterial pH. Option A: The brain , upon transmitting motor impulses to the exercising muscles , is believed to transmit collateral impulses into the brainstem at the same time to excite the respiratory center . This action is analogous to the stimulation of the vasomotor center of the brain stem during exercise that causes a simultaneous increase in arterial pressure . Option B: The Po2 of mixed venous blood does fall, but there are no known chemoreceptors that are stimulated as a result . Option C: Two points are important regarding pH during moderate exercise : • pH = pK + log ([HCO3-)/ [CO2]) • The pH of the blood is dependent only on the ratio of the amount of CO2 to the amount of HCO3-. The concentrations of both buffer components (HCO3- and CO2) are very large compared to the amount of H+ added to the blood during moderate exercise . Thus, any change in HCO3- due to the addition of H+ during moderate exercise is very tiny compared to the amount of HCO3- already present in the blood. Thus, the pH of blood during moderate exercise remains constant. • When sufficient oxygen is not available during exercise , there is increased accumulation of lactic acid, which initially leads to an increase in PaCO2. However , this is counteracted by the stimulation of ventilation and as a result , PaCO2 is decreased . This provides some respiratory compensation for further lactic acid production and prevents a decline in blood pH . Thus , blood pH remains constant in moderate exercise.465

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The exercise -induced hyperventilation during vigorous exercise is produced due to the receptors present in ______
mcqs.explanation: The exercise -induced hyperventilation during vigorous exercise is produced due to the receptors present in carotid bodies . When exercise becomes more vigorous, buffering of the increased amounts of lactic acid that are produced liberates more CO2, and this further increases ventilation. The additional increase in ventilation produced by the acidosis depends on the carotid bodies and does not occur if they are removed. Note : The abrupt increase at the start of exercise is presumably due to psychic stimuli and afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles , tendons , and joints.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In moderate exercise , the respiratory rate is increased at the beginning due to the response of______

options.b: Decrease in PO2 in arterial blood

mcqs.explanation: In moderate exercise , the respiratory rate is increased at the beginning due to the response of joint proprioceptor stimulation. Respiratory responses to exercise • During exercise , there is an increase in ventilatory rate that matches the increase in O2 consumption and CO2 production by the body. The stimulus for increased ventilation rate is the activation of joint proprioceptors at the beginning of the exercise . • The mean values for arterial Po2 and Pco2 do not change during exercise . Arterial pH does not change during moderate exercise , although it may decrease during strenuous exercise because of lactic acidosis. • On the other hand, venous Pco2 increases during exercise because the excess CO2 produced by exercising muscle is carried to the lungs in venous blood. • Pulmonary blood flow increases because cardiac output increases during exercise . As a result , more pulmonary capillaries are perfused, and more gas exchange occurs. The distribution of V /Q ratios throughout the lung is more even during exercise than when at rest, and there is a resulting decrease in the physiologic dead space. The abrupt increase at the start of exercise is presumably due to • Psychic stimuli • Afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles , tendons , and joints. The more gradual increase in ventilation is presumably due to • Increase in O2 consumption (Proportional increase) • Increase in body temperature • Increases in the plasma K+ level (Stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors ). • Sensitivity of the neurons controlling the response to CO2 is increased or that the respiratory fluctuations in arterial PCO2 increase so that, even though the mean arterial PCO2 does not rise , it is CO2 that is responsible for the increase in ventilation.466

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which among the following is not a function of pneumotaxic centre ?

options.b: Increase in the rate of breathing

mcqs.explanation: Respiratory rhythm generation is a function of dorsal respiratory group of neurons (and not pneumotaxic center ). Pneumotaxic center : • It is located dorsally in the nucleus parabrachialis of the upper pons and it transmits signals to the inspiratory area. • Primary effect of this center is to control the switchoff point of the inspiratory ramp, thus controlling the duration of the filing phase of the lung cycle . • Function of the pneumotaxic center is primarily to limit inspiration, which has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing, because limitation of inspiration also shortens expiration and the entire period of each respiration.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following ions is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors ?
mcqs.explanation: Potassium is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors . Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia. This reduces the K+ efflux , depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ in\037ux. The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following neurons predominantly fire during forceful expiration?
mcqs.explanation: Ventral groups of neurons fire, when forceful expiration is needed like during heavy exercise . Dorsal group of neurons control the normal inspiration and expiration. Pneumotaxic center limits the duration of inspiration.467

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: The windkessel effect is seen in___.
mcqs.explanation: The windkessel effect is seen in large elastic vessels . The aorta, the pulmonary artery, and their major branches have a large amount of elastin in their walls. Hence, they have a high elastic recoil effect . This property of elastic recoil is called windkessel effect (windkessel is a German word for the elastic reservoir). This recoil of the vessels that have been stretched during systole helps to propel the blood forward during diastole thus maintaining a continuous flow throughout the cardiac cycle .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: In the circulatory system , the highest velocity of blood flow is in the _____.
mcqs.explanation: In circulatory system , the highest velocity of blood flow is in the aorta. • The velocity of blood flow is inversely proportional to vascular cross-sectional area.474 v= velocity F= blood flow through the vessel A=vascular cross-sectional area • Aorta has the least cross sectional area (4.5 cm2) and capillaries have the maximum cross sectional area (4500 cm2). Thus, under resting conditions, the velocity is highest in aorta and least in capillaries .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: The largest compliance in the circulatory system is of ____.
mcqs.explanation: The largest compliance in the circulatory system is of veins. Vascular compliance /capacitance is the total quantity of blood that can be stored in a given portion of the circulation for each mmHg pressure rise. Vascular Compliance = distensibility X volume. The compliance of a systemic vein is about 24 times that of its corresponding artery because it is about 8 times as distensible and has a volume about 3 times as artery (8 \327 3 = 24).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: Bernoulli's principle states that___.

options.a: Sum of kinetic energy of flow and pressure energy is constant
options.b: Low tones produces maximum stimulation at the apex of cochlea
options.c: Magnitude of sensation felt is proportional to the intensity of stimulus
options.d: Force of contraction is proportional to stretch of the cardiac muscle

mcqs.explanation: The Bernoulli's theorem states that in a tube or blood vessel , the sum of the kinetic energy of flow and pressure energy is constant. Other options : • Option B: Travelling wave theory (Theories of hearing): Low tones produce maximum stimulation at the apex of the cochlea .475 • Option C: Weber—Fechner law: The magnitude of sensation felt is proportional to the log of the intensity of the stimulus . • Option D: Frank —Starling law of the heart: Force of contraction is proportional to stretch of the cardiac muscle .

mcqs.question: Which of the following increases turbulence in blood flow ?

options.a: Increase in diameter of blood vessel

mcqs.explanation: Turbulence in blood flow increases with increase in diameter of blood vessel . mcqs.explanation: The tendency for turbulent flow is greatest in the aorta. The turbulence of flow depends upon Reynold's number:477 v – velocity of flow – cm/sec \f – density of blood d – diameter of the vessel �M – viscosity of blood in poise In the proximal portions of the aorta and pulmonary artery, Reynold's number can rise to several thousand during the rapid phase of the ejection , which causes considerable turbulence due to the following : • High velocity of blood flow • Pulsatile nature of the flow • Sudden change in vessel diameter • Large vessel diameterReynold's num ber Type of blood flo w <2000 Laminar -3000 Transitional >3000 Turbulent

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: The main site of peripheral vascular resistance is ________
mcqs.explanation: The main site of peripheral vascular resistance is precapillary arterioles . Poiseuille —Hagen formula explains that small changes in the calibre of vessels cause large changes in total peripheral resistance .478 Where, R=resistance \020=viscosity L=length of the tube r=radius of the tube The resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: The factor favoring filtration at the arterial end of the capillary bed is ____.

options.b: Increase in hydrostatic pressure of the capillary
options.c: Increase in oncotic pressure of the capillary
options.d: Decrease in oncotic pressure of the interstitium

mcqs.explanation: The factor favoring filtration at the arterial end of the capillary bed is the increase in hydrostatic pressure of the capillary. The rate of filtration at any point along the capillary bed depends on the balance of the Starling forces, which are responsible for fluid movement. Net filtration pressure = (Pc-Pi)-(\021c- \021i) where , Pc=capillary hydrostatic pressure Pi=interstitial hydrostatic pressure \021c=capillary colloidal osmotic pressure \021i=interstitial colloidal osmotic pressure Glomerular filtration rate = k x NFP where , k= capillary filtration coefficient NFP= Net filtration pressure479

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: Which of the following factors tends to increase the lymph flow ?
mcqs.explanation: The factor tend to increase lymph flow is increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure . Since the lymph is derived from interstitial fluid , any factor that increases interstitial fluid pressure also increases lymph flow provided, the lymph vessels are functioning normally. The factors which increase interstitial fluid pressure include : • Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure • Increased interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure • Increased permeability of the capillaries • Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure All of the above factors increase the filtration at the capillary-interstitium interface and therefore increase the interstitial fluid volume and pressure .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: The coronary blood flow is regulated by ___.
mcqs.explanation: Coronary blood flow is regulated by adenosine . Blood flow through the coronary system is regulated mostly by local arteriolar vasodilation in response to the nutritional needs of cardiac muscle . \031local metabolism \032 \023in O2 \032 breakdown of ATP to form adenosine \032 vasodilation \032 \031local coronary blood flow .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: True about coronary flow during systole is:

options.a: No change in flow with systole .
options.c: Greater decrease in subendocardium than epicardium .
options.d: Greater decrease in epicardium than in subendocardium .

mcqs.explanation: The coronary blood flow in systole has a greater decrease in subendocardium than epicardium . The myocardial compression in systole compresses the subendocardial vessels to a greater extent , and the force is sufficiently dissipated in the epicardium to permit some flow in this region throughout the cardiac cycle .

mcqs.explanation: Based on the agglutination test shown in the image, the blood group is O positive . As agglutination is present only in 'Rh' and not with 'A' and 'B' hence the blood group is O Rh positive.480

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: Which of the following clotting factors would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy?
mcqs.explanation: Factor 2 would have decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in a patient on warfarin therapy . Activation of coagulation factors II , VII , IX, X is done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues . This is done by the enzyme \025-glutamyl carboxylase with the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor. This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue . This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase . This enzyme is inhibited by warfarin . Hence , warfarin indirectly inhibits the \025-carboxylation of vitamin K dependent clotting factors - Factors II , VII , IX, X by directly inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase . Thus leading to decreased gamma carboxyglutamate residue in these factors.481

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation I
mcqs.question: Which of the following has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation?
mcqs.explanation: Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation. The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava . From here, the blood enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium also receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava . This mixed blood is distributed to the body via aorta. Therefore, inferior vena cava has the highest concentration of oxygen in the fetal circulation.482

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: What is the most powerful activator of sympathetic vasomotor system ?

options.a: Posture of the body against gravity

mcqs.explanation: The most powerful activator of the sympathetic vasomotor system is CNS ischemic response . CNS ischemic response : When blood flow to the vasomotor center in lower brainstem (medulla ) is severely decreased , the local concentration of CO2 increases greatly and has a potent effect in stimulating the sympathetic vasomotor nervous control areas in the brain 's medulla . Blood pressure may increase till 250 mmHg. The strong activation may cause some peripheral vessels to occlude . It doesnt activate till arterial pressure drops to 60mmHg or less , hence it is principally a emergency mechanism. Note : Baroreceptors are the most common activators, but not the most powerful .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: During exercise , the organ experiencing the smallest decrease in blood flow is____.
mcqs.explanation: During exercise , the organ experiencing the smallest decrease in blood flow is brain .489 During exercise , the coronary and cerebral systems , are spared of vasoconstrictor effect because both these circulatory areas have poor vasoconstrictor innervation .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: An elderly man, with congestive cardiac failure, complains of shortness of breath when lying down. What is the mechanism behind this symptom ?

options.b: Reservoir function of veins in lower limbs.

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario describes orthopnea in congestive heart failure. It is due to reservoir function of pulmonary veins. Orthopnea is dyspnea occurring in the recumbent position. It results from redistribution of fluid from the splanchnic circulation and lower extremities (increased venous return) into the heart during recumbency . This increased venous return is not put out by the left ventricle and hence pools in the pulmonary veins that acts as capacitance vessels (reservoir function) adding to the already congested pulmonary vasculature resulting in breathing difficulty .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: The interstitial fluid pressure is negative in ______.
mcqs.explanation: The interstitial fluid pressure is negative in the lungs . The interstitial fluid pressure is slightly negative in the body except in the encapsulated organs. It is positive in • Rigid closed compartments- bone marrow, brain • Encapsulated organs - kidney, skeletal muscle This is due to the fact that in the kidneys, high-pressure vessels push the interstitial fluid against an unyielding fibrous capsule raising the pressure . The same principle applies to skeletal muscle surrounded by layers of fascia.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Blood flow per minute in pulmonary circulation is

options.a: Less than flow through systemic circulation
options.b: More than flow through systemic circulation
options.c: Equal to flow through systemic circulation

mcqs.explanation: Blood flow per minute in the pulmonary circulation is equal to flow through the systemic circulation so as to provide continuous blood supply to the body. If the flow rate is slower in the pulmonary circulation than systemic , then the left ventricle would soon empty completely . If the flow rate is faster in the pulmonary circulation then the left ventricle would be soon overloaded . Please note that because some blood flows into the bronchial arteries, the actual flow through the pulmonary circulation is slightly lesser than the flow through the systemic circulation. However, this question aims to state that the blood flow through both pulmonary and systemic circulation is largely equal.490

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: A patient was receiving a red cell transfusion following hip arthroplasty. Midway through the transfusion, she developed signs and symptoms of shock. What is the type of shock seen in her?
mcqs.explanation: The shock due to a transfusion reaction is distributive shock. During transfusion reaction, there is decreased systemic vascular resistance due to system -wide vasodilation mediated by release of histamine by mast cells in response to antigen bound IgE, leading to distributive shock. Types of circulatory shock: • Hypovolemic shock: due to decreased blood in vascular compartment. E.g., haemorrhage, dehydration. • Cardiogenic shock: due to decreased capacity of heart to pump . E.g., any pathology of heart decreasing its ability to maintain cardiac output . • Obstructive shock: due to conditions causing obstruction to blood flow in lungs and heart.E.g:pulmonary embolism. • Distributive/vasculogenic shock: excessive vasodilation leading to impaired organ perfusion . E.g: septic shock, SIRS , transfusion reaction, Addisonian crisis, neurogenic shock. Three stages of shock: • Non-progressive: also called compensated shock, where normal compensatory mechanism eventually causes full recovery without help from outside therapy . • Progressive: also called non-compensated , without therapy it gets steadily worse . • Irreversible: even therapy is inadequate to save life .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: During foetal life , blood vessel with maximum concentration of oxygen is ___.
mcqs.explanation: During fetal life , blood vessel with maximum concentration of oxygen is umblical vein.491

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Progressive hemorrhagic shock is characterized by ______.

options.a: Blood clots in the small blood vessels

mcqs.explanation: Progressive hemorrhagic shock is characterized by the presence of blood clots in the small blood vessels . The initiating cause of this blockage is sluggish blood flow in the microvessels . Tissue metabolites plus other deterioration products from the ischemic tissues causes minute clots in these vessels . Thus the microvasculature gets blocked by the sludged blood. In progressive hemorrhagic shock, there is increased lysosomal activity, decreased active transport of sodium and tissue acidosis.

mcqs.explanation: During rest, blood flow through skeletal muscle averages 3–4 mL /min/100 g of muscle . mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: The type of shock that has high cardiac output is _________.
mcqs.explanation: Septic shock is characterized by high cardiac output . High cardiac output in septic shock is caused by • arteriolar dilation in the infected tissues and • high metabolic rate and vasodilation (resulting from bacterial toxin stimulating cellular metabolism and from high body temperature).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Thin -walled and delicate vessels like capillaries are less prone to rupture . This can be explained by _______.
mcqs.explanation: Thin -walled and delicate vessels like capillaries are less prone to rupture and this can be explained by Laplace law.492 The principal reason for these vessels ' relative invulnerability is their small diameter . The protective effect of small size, in this case, is an example of the law of Laplace. Laplace law states that tension in the wall of a cylinder (T) is equal to the product of the transmural pressure (P) and the radius (r) divided by the wall thickness (w): T = Pr /w As the tissue pressure is low, P is equated to the pressure inside the blood vessel . W can be ignored as well as capillaries are thin walled . Hence : P = T/r In a thin-walled viscus, P = T divided by the two principal radii of curvature of the viscus: P = T (1/r1 +1/r2 ) In a cylinder such as a blood vessel , one radius is infinite, so P = T /r Hence , smaller the radius, lower is the tension necessary in the wall to balance the distending pressure .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about Cuthbertson 's metabolic ebb and flow responses to trauma?

options.a: The "ebb" phase is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption.
options.b: The "flow " phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock.
options.c: The "ebb" phase is aimed at reducing posttraumatic energy depletion .
options.d: The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute -phase response .

mcqs.explanation: The "flow " phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute -phase response . Cuthbertson 's ebb and flow response to trauma: The "ebb" phase lasts for a brief duration and is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption, aimed at reducing post traumatic energy depletion . The "flow " phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock, which leads to an increased metabolic turnover, activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute -phase response . This hypercatabolic condition leads to a significantly increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure .494

mcqs.question: Hering's nerve finally relays in ______.
mcqs.explanation: The Hering's nerve terminates in the medulla (Tractus solitarius). Baroreceptor reflexes • Carotid baroreceptors \032 Hering's nerve \032 the glossopharyngeal nerve \032 Tractus solitarius in medulla . • Aortic baroreceptors \032 Vagus nerve \032 tractus solitarius in medulla

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Microcirculation consists of__________.
mcqs.explanation: Microcirculation consists of capillaries, arterioles , venules and terminal lymphatics .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Mayer waves are due to ____.

options.a: Variation of arterial pressure during each systole .
options.b: Variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control of blood pressure
options.c: Variation of arterial pressure with changes in respiration.
options.d: Variation of arterial pressure with postural change.

mcqs.explanation: Mayer waves are due to the variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control of blood pressure . The most important mechanisms are as follows : I: Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflex : High pressure excites the baroreceptors -->inhibits sympathetic nervous system and lowers the pressure -->The decreased pressure, in turn, reduces the baroreceptor stimulation -->elevating the pressure to a high value (the response is not instantaneous , it is delayed until a few seconds later). This high pressure then initiates another cycle , and the oscillation continues . II : Oscillation of the CNS Ischemic Response :495 The cerebrospinal fluid pressure is raised to 160 mm Hg --> causes compression of cerebral blood vessels --> cerebral ischemia--> CNS ischemic pressure response raises the arterial pressure up to 200mm Hg -->the brain ischemia is relieved and the sympathetic nervous system becomes inactive -->the arterial pressure falls rapidly back to a much lower value, causing brain ischemia once again -->initiates another rise in pressure . This chain of events repeats itself cyclically as long as the cerebrospinal fluid pressure remains elevated .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Vasomotion refers to _____.

options.a: Venous drainage to RA by contraction of IVC .
options.b: Intermittent contraction of meta arterioles and precapillary sphincter .
options.c: Pulsatile action of arteries which help in lymphatic drainage.
options.d: Systolic pumping of blood by heart in to aorta.

mcqs.explanation: Vasomotion means intermittent contraction of meta arterioles and precapillary spinchter . Blood usually does not flow continuously through the capillaries . Instead, it flows intermittently , turning on and off every few seconds or minutes . This is vasomotion, which is responsible for flow of blood in capillaries . The main regulatory factor for vasomotion is tissue oxygen concentration.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: Ejection fraction in resting healthy man is approximately ___.
mcqs.explanation: Ejection fraction in resting healthy man is approximately 0.6. The fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected is called the ejection fraction, usually equal to about 60 %.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: The relation between ventricular stroke volume and end-diastolic volume is explained by ________
mcqs.explanation: 496 The relation between ventricular stroke volume and end-diastolic volume is explained by Frank Starling's law. Length–tension relationship in cardiac muscle is similar to that in skeletal muscle . when the muscle is stretched , the developed tension increases to a maximum and then declines as stretch becomes more extreme . Starling stated that "energy of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fibre". When cardiac output is regulated by changes in cardiac fibre length , this is referred to as heterometric regulation . Conversely, regulation due to changes in contractility independent of length is called homometric regulation .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.chapter: Vascular System and Regional Circulation II
mcqs.question: The best index of preload is _______.
mcqs.explanation: The best index of preload is left ventricular end diastolic volume. Preload - load that the left ventricle carries before the systole . Left ventricular end diastolic volume - blood remaining at the end of diastole , which determines stretch of the ventricle and thus force of contraction as explained by frank starlings law.497

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The basal cardiac output in adults is around ________
mcqs.explanation: The basal cardiac output in adults is around 5.5 litres. Cardiac output is given by, Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume. In a resting, supine man cardiac output averages about 5.0 L/min (70 mL \327 72 beats /min).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The cardiac output can be determined by all except :
mcqs.explanation: V /Q ratio not used to determine cardiac output . Measurement of cardiac output : • Fick principle • Dye dilution /thermodilution • Doppler plus echocardiograph • MRI

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Cardiac output in litre per minute divided by heart rate gives ______
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac output in litre per minute divided by heart rate gives stroke volume. Cardiac output is given by, Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume. The stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of each ventricle per beat , is about 70 mL from each ventricle in a resting man in the supine position.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Ejection fraction is
mcqs.explanation: Ejection fraction is SV/EDV. The amount of blood ejected by each ventricle per stroke at rest is 70–90 mL . The end-diastolic ventricular volume is about 130 mL . The ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic ventricular volume that is ejected with each stroke, is about 65%.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A patient with cardiac output 5L/min and body surface area 1.7m2. What will be the cardiac index (L/min/m2)?
mcqs.explanation: Cardiac index is the cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface . Cardiac Index = Cardiac output / body surface area.506 Therefore Cardiac index = 5L/min /1.7m2 = 2.94 L

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Volume determining preload is
mcqs.explanation: Volume determining preload is End diastolic volume. Preload is the initial stretch on muscle at the end of diastole . Preload is equal to End diastolic volume (EDV) and is determined by venous return to heart.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Starling's law implies :

options.a: Increased heart rate leads to increased cardiac output
options.b: Increased discharge leads to increased cardiac output
options.c: Increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output
options.d: Increased blood pressure leads to increased cardiac output

mcqs.explanation: Starling's law implies increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output . Frank -Starling law: The energy of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber. The length of the muscle fibers is proportional to the end-diastolic volume, which is determined by venous return.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is facilitated by all of the following factors except _____.

options.d: Increased arterial pressure due to gravitation.

mcqs.explanation: Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is not facilitated by increased arterial pressure . Factors that facilitate venous return to the heart: • Calf muscles contract and pump blood through veins. • Valves don't allow the retrograde flow of blood through veins. • Deep fascia by forming a supporting structure to veins.507 Note : The pulsations of artery helps in increasing lymph flow .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: When a person changes position from standing to supine , _______

options.b: Venous return to heart rises immediately
options.d: Decrease in blood flow to the lung apices

mcqs.explanation: When a person changes position from standing to supine , venous return to heart rises immediately. On standing, Gravitational pull causes venous pooling of blood in the legs . On supine position, this gravitational pull equalizes over body, causing the pooled blood to return back to heart. Other options : Option A: Heart rate decreases because of increased cardiac output and increased BP via baroreceptor reflex . Option C: Cerebral blood flow will remain constant due to autoregulation . Option D: Blood flow to the apex of lung will be high due to high cardiac output .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman has a resting heart rate of 70-beats /min. Her pressure -volume diagram of the left ventricle is given below . What is her cardiac output (in mL /min)? (Point 2 corresponds to 120 ml)
mcqs.explanation: In this case, the patient has a heart rate of 70-beats /min and the stroke volume can be determined from the given pressure -volume diagram. Point 2 corresponds to the EDV(End diastolic volume) = 120 mL Point 1 corresponds to the ESV(End systolic volume) = 50 mL Thus, stroke volume (SV) = EDV – ESV = 120 – 50 = 70 mL Therefore, Cardiac output = HR X SV = 70 X 70 = 4900 mL /min.508

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A sister donated one of her kidneys to her brother. What would be the effect on her cardiac output ?
mcqs.explanation: Surgical removal of kidney leads to decrease in cardiac output . Amputation of a limb or surgical removal of organs like kidney removes a parallel circuit thus increasing total peripheral vascular resistance . As the resistance increases, afterload increases hence decreasing stroke volume. CO= HR \327 SV , therefore decrease in stroke volume leads to decrease in cardiac output .
