In 1923 , the Nobel Committee decided to award Banting and Macleod the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine . The decision of the Nobel Committee made Banting furious. He felt that the prize should have been shared between him and Best .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: For cells of islets of Langerhans , which of the following is correctly matched ?
mcqs.explanation: The correctly matched pair is F-Pancreatic polypeptide . Cells of the endocrine pancreas are divided into: The close interrelations among these cells allow direct control of secretion of some of the hormones by the other hormones. For example : • Insulin inhibits glucagon secretion , • Amylin inhibits glucagon secretion , and • Somatostatin inhibits secretion of insulin and glucagon .Cell ty pe What they secrete A (alph a) Glucagon B (beta) Insulin and amylin718 Cell ty pe What they secrete D (delt a) Somatostatin F or P P Pancreatic polypeptid e

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 21 -year-old female is found in a semiconscious state . On initial evaluation, her CBG is 23mg/dL. Her parents tell that the patient is an athlete and was trying to gain weight recently . An evaluation of which of the following will help in establishing a diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette strongly suggests hypoglycemia due to surreptitious use of exogenous insulin, characterized by a low C-peptide level . Insulin abuse is a method for increasing muscle bulk and performance enhancement in athletes , although less common than anabolic steroid abuse . Exogenous insulin does not contain C-peptide . Therefore blood level of C-peptide will be low in such patients . On the other hand, endogenous production of insulin will be characterized by high C-peptide level in blood.Insulin is composed of two chains A and B, and a connecting peptide called C peptide . The insulin and C peptide are packaged in the secretory granules and secreted in equimolar amounts. Importance of C-peptide : • C peptide is measured by radioimmunoassay, and its level in the blood provides an index of beta-cell function in patients receiving exogenous insulin. If they are unable to produce insulin, they have greatly decreased levels of C peptide . • C peptide levels can be used to differentiate between an insulinoma (high C-peptide ) and exogenous insulin overdose (low C-peptide ) in a patient with hypoglycemia .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The half-life of insulin is ______ minutes ?
mcqs.explanation: 719 The half-life of insulin is 4-6 minutes . Insulin is degraded by the insulinase enzyme in the liver, and to a lesser extent , in the kidneys and muscles . Note : Half-life of C-peptide is 20 -30 minutes .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old diabetic man is initiated on a new hypoglycemic drug whose mechanism of action is extremely similar to the glucose -mediated insulin release mechanism. Which of the following best represents its mode of action?
mcqs.explanation: Glucose -mediated insulin release occurs through the closure of ATP sensitive K+ channels. Therefore the new drug being initiated is most probably a sulfonylurea which acts via a similar mechanism. Increased blood glucose concentration is the primary controller of insulin secretion . Inside the beta cells , glucose is converted to glucose -6-phosphate and later ATP is generated . This ATP closes ATP sensitive potassium channels, leading to a rise in K+ and depolarization. This in turn causes the opening of voltage -gated Ca 2+ channels and influx of Ca+. This ultimately leads to the secretion of insulin via exocytosis .Diazoxide keeps the ATP sensitive K+ channels open and prevents depolarization, resulting in a decreased insulin release . It is used in patients with insulinoma. Sulfonylureas cause closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channels, leading to increased insulin secretion . It is used in patients with diabetes mellitus .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Insulin mainly facilitates glucose uptake in which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin mainly stimulates glucose uptake by skeletal muscles . Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle , cardiac muscle and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent . In the presence of insulin, GLUT-4 receptors translocate to the cell membrane720 and hence , glucose uptake by the cell occurs. Most of the other GLUT transporters are not insulin sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. Ex: GLUT-1 in RBCs, brain and kidneys. (GLUT-3 is also present in the brain and kidneys) Note : Insulin promotes glucose uptake in the liver. However, this is done by increasing the activity of glucokinase and inactivating glycogen phosphorylase . The net effect is the synthesis of glycogen and decreased breakdown of glycogen .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Insulin acts on glucose metabolism by______

options.b: \023 permeability of glucose across cell membrane
options.c: \031 reabsorption of glucose from renal tubules

mcqs.explanation: Insulin stimulates the glucose entry into the cells via facilitated diffusion by increasing the number of glucose transporters (GLUTs) in the cell membrane. This type of insulin-dependent glucose transport via GLUT 4 is observed in skeletal muscle , cardiac muscle , and adipose tissues .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old diabetic man develops a gradually increasing demand for exogenous subcutaneous insulin therapy for glycemic control. His current insulin requirement is 130 IU/day. Downregulation of which of the following is associated with his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of insulin resistance , which is characterized by the downregulation of GLUT-4. GLUT-4 is an insulin-dependent GLUT. Other GLUTs are not insulin sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. An arbitrary but clinically useful benchmark considers patients insulin resistant if they require greater than 1 unit/kilogram/day of exogenous insulin to maintain glycemic control. Patients requiring greater than 200 units of exogenous insulin per day are considered severely insulin resistant.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presented with diabetic ketoacidosis . After the initial evaluation, he is started on intravenous insulin therapy via an infusion pump . He is at increased risk of developing which of the following electrolyte abnormalities?
mcqs.explanation: In patients who require intravenous insulin therapy , a rapid insulin infusion results in hypokalemia. Therefore such patients should undergo serum electrolyte level assessment at frequent intervals while on insulin infusion for prompt diagnosis and early correction of hypokalemia. Insulin increases the activity of Na-K ATPase in cell membranes so that more K+ is pumped into cells . Hence , serum K+ falls. Note : Since insulin decreases serum potassium level , insulin-glucose infusions are used to treat hyperkalemia.721

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following increases insulin secretion ?
mcqs.explanation: Arginine increases insulin secretion . Option B: \035-adrenergic blockers like propranolol inhibits insulin secretion . Option C: Epinephrine both stimulates (by beta -adrenergic agonistic action) and inhibits (by alpha-adrenergic agonistic action) the secretion of insulin. However, the inhibitory effect of epinephrine is more dominant than the stimulatory effect . Option D: Insulin promotes glucose uptake by cells , causing reduced serum K+. Low serum K+ does not cause an increase in insulin secretion .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Sympathetic stimulation has the following effect on insulin secretion ______
mcqs.explanation: Sympathetic stimulation inhibits insulin secretion . The regulation of insulin secretion can be controlled by alpha-adrenergic mediated response and beta -adrenergic mediated response . The stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptor (�o 2) plays an inhibitory role in insulin secretion . On the other hand, the stimulation of beta -adrenergic receptor (\0352) plays a stimulatory role in insulin secretion . Stimulation of the sympathetic nerves to the pancreas releases norepinephrine which predominantly acts on �o 2-adrenergic receptors , causing a decrease in insulin secretion . Note : If �o -adrenergic receptors are blocked , stimulation of the sympathetic nerves causes increased insulin secretion mediated by \0352-adrenergic receptors .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following decreases the secretion of both insulin and glucagon ?
mcqs.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits insulin and glucagon secretion . Note : Other actions of somatostatin: • Inhibits growth hormone secretion . Somatostatin is also known as growth hormone inhibitory hormone (GHIH ). • Decreases motility of the stomach, duodenum , and gallbladder . • Decreases both secretion and absorption in the gastrointestinal tract.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Insulin secretion is normally stimulated by_____
mcqs.explanation: Insulin secretion is normally stimulated by GLP -1. Glucagon -like peptide –1 (GLP -1) and glucose -dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) are called incretins and are potent stimulators of insulin secretion . They also inhibit glucagon secretion . They are released in the gastrointestinal tract after a person eats a meal. They then cause an "anticipatory" increase in blood insulin in preparation for the glucose and amino acids to be722 absorbed from the meal. Note : Drugs that mimic the action of incretins are used in the management of diabetes .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following compounds antagonizes the action of insulin?
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone is a hyperglycemic hormone and antagonizes the effect of insulin. Hyperglycemic Hormones • Glucagon • Epinephrine • Cortisol • Growth hormone • Thyroid Hormone

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In fetus , the insulin secretion begins by _____(months)
mcqs.explanation: In a fetus , the pancreatic islets are formed in the third month of the fetal life , while insulin secretion begins at about 5th month of fetal life . The exocrine pancreas starts functioning after birth.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: How many parts are there in insulin receptor ?
mcqs.explanation: An insulin receptor has 4 parts. It is a tetramer made up of two �o and two \035 subunits . The �o subunits are extracellular , whereas the \035 subunits penetrate through the cell membrane into the cytoplasm. The intracellular portions of the \035 subunits have tyrosine kinase activity. Once insulin binds to the alpha subunits, the portions of the beta subunits protruding into the cell become autophosphorylated . Autophosphorylation of the beta subunits , in turn, activates a local tyrosine kinase, which causes phosphorylation of multiple intracellular enzymes . The net effect is to activate some of these enzymes while inactivating others.723

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Regarding the action of insulin, which of the following is true?

options.a: Decreased K+ uptake in adipose tissue

mcqs.explanation: Insulin decreases ketogenesis in the liver. In the absence of insulin (Type -1 DM), diabetic ketosis may occur. Effects of insulin on various tissues :Tissue Increases Decreases Adipose tiss ue Increased glucose entryIncre ased fatty acid synthesisIncre ased glycerol phosphate synt hesisIncreased triglycerides d epositionActivation of lipopr otein lipaseIncreased K+ upt ake Inhibition of hormone-sensiti ve lipase Muscle Increased glucose entryIncre ased glycogen synthesisIncre ased amino acid uptakeIncre ased protein synthesis in ribo someIncrease ketone uptakeI ncrease K+ uptake Decrease protein catabolism Decrease release of glucogen ic amino acids Liver Increased protein synthesisIn creased lipid synthesisIncrea sed glycogen synthesis & glyc olysis Decrease ketogenesisDecreas ed glucose output due to decr eased gluconeogenesis General Increased cell growth

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: On giving a patient insulin, which of the following is expected to occur first?

options.a: Increased transport of K+ into adipocytes

mcqs.explanation: 724 Increased transport of K+ into adipocytes will occur first on giving an injection of insulin. Based on time on onset , actions of insulin are classified as: Rapid (seconds ): Increased permeability , leading to: • Increased transport of glucose , amino acids, and K+ into insulin sensitive cells Intermediate (minutes ): Changes in activity levels of intracellular enzymes , leading to: • Stimulation of protein synthesis • Inhibition of protein degradation • Activation of glycolytic enzymes and glycogen synthase • Inhibition of phosphorylase and gluconeogenic enzymes Delayed (hours to days): Changed rates of transcription of DNA, leading to: • Increase in mRNAs for lipogenic and other enzymes

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is incorrectly paired?
mcqs.explanation: The incorrect pair is thyroxine - decreased blood glucose . Thyroxine is a diabetogenic hormone leading to an increase in blood glucose levels . Effects Of Hormones On Carbohydrate Metabolism : • Catecholamines : Activation of glycogen phosphorylase and therefore glycogenolysis occurs. Hepatic glucose output is increased , producing hyperglycemia . • Glucocorticoids : Glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex elevate blood glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis and inhibiting glucose utilization by the cells . • Growth Hormone: The effects of growth hormone are partly direct and partly mediated via IGF-I (Insulin-like Growth Factor-I). The growth hormone mobilizes FFA from adipose tissue , thus favoring ketogenesis . It decreases glucose uptake into some tissues ("anti-insulin action"), increases hepatic glucose output , and may decrease tissue binding of insulin. Note : Infusing catecholamine (Epinephrine) mainly promotes glycogenolysis and it is also associated with enhanced rates of aerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscles during exercise (resulting in adenosine triphosphate production ).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A meal rich in insulin-stimulating amino acids but low in carbohydrates does not cause hypoglycemia because _____

options.a: Cortisol in the circulation prevents glucose from entering muscle .
options.b: Glucagon secretion is also stimulated by the meal.
options.c: The amino acids in the meal are promptly converted to glucose .
options.d: Insulin does not bind to insulin receptors if the plasma concentration of amino acids is elevated .

mcqs.explanation: A meal rich in arginine and alanine stimulates both insulin and glucagon secretion . Hence , hypoglycemia does not occur. Increased blood amino acids stimulate secretion of glucagon , which in turn causes the amino acids to get converted to glucose . So, the mechanism by which hypoglycemia is prevented after a protien rich meal is secretion of glucagon .725

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following would be least likely seen 14 days after a rat is injected with a drug that kills all of its pancreatic \035 cells ?

options.a: A rise in the plasma H+ concentration
options.b: A rise in the plasma amino acid concentration
options.c: A fall in the plasma amino acid concentration

mcqs.explanation: A fall is plasma amino acid concentration is least likely to be seen in this case. Injury to the beta cells of the pancreas impairs insulin production rendering the rat insulin deficient . Due to insulin deficiency , catabolism of proteins increases and amino acids in plasma increase. Insulin deficiency increases blood glucose levels , which lead to glycosuria and osmotic diuresis with extracellular dehydration . There is increase in the plasma osmolality . Insulin deficiency causes increased utilization of fats, excess production of ketoacids and metabolic acidosis. Metabolic acidosis - a rise in the plasma H+ develops .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an action of insulin?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin inhibits glucose -6-phosphatase . Insulin promotes liver uptake , storage, and the use of glucose . After a meal, insulin causes glucose to be rapidly stored in the liver in the form of glycogen . This occurs by: • Inactivation of liver phosphorylase , which is the principal enzyme that causes liver glycogen to split into glucose . • Enhanced uptake of glucose by the liver cells by increasing the activity of the enzyme glucokinase which causes phosphorylation of glucose after it enters the liver cells . Once phosphorylated , the glucose is temporarily trapped inside the liver cells because phosphorylated glucose cannot diffuse back through the cell membrane. • Increased activity of enzymes that promote glycogen synthesis , like glycogen synthase . When insulin levels drop (Ex: Fasting), glucose phosphatase gets activated. This causes phosphate to get detached from glucose phosphate , allowing free glucose from the liver cells to re-enter circulation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30 yr old male presents with recurrent attacks of sweating and dizziness. Further workup reveals hypoglycemia , elevated insulin and C-peptide levels . He is diagnosed with insulinoma and given diazoxide. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.a: Opening of the ATP Sensitive K+ channels
options.b: Closing of the ATP Sensitive K+ channels
options.c: Increase in number of GLUT-4 receptors
options.d: Opening of the voltage sensitive Ca2+ channels

mcqs.explanation: Diazoxide acts by opening ATP sensitive K+ channels and causing a decrease in insulin secretion . Glucose enters beta cells of the pancreas via GLUT-2 receptors . Once inside, it is phosphorylated by glucokinase (rate-limiting step ) to glucose -6-phosphate which is oxidized to form adenosine triphosphate (ATP ). This ATP causes closure of ATP -sensitive potassium channels and hence depolarization. This leads to opening voltage -gated calcium channels and Ca2+ influx. This stimulates fusion of the insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane and secretion of insulin into the extracellular fluid by exocytosis . Diazoxide keeps the ATP sensitive K+ channels open and prevents depolarization and subsequent insulin release. Sulfonylureas cause closure of the ATP sensitive K+ channels, leading to increased insulin secretion .726

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Coma occurs at a glucose level below _____.
mcqs.explanation: Coma occurs when glucose levels fall below 30 mg/dL.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones use receptor tyrosine kinase signalling?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin uses the receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to exert its functions. Other hormones acting in a similar fashion includes • Growth hormone • Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF727 • Prolactin • Leptin728

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones is secreted by the zona glomerulosa ?
mcqs.explanation: The zona glomerulosa secretes aldosterone . The adrenal cortex has three zones. From outer to inner, they are: • Zona glomerulosa : Secretes mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone ) • Zona fasiculata : Secretes glucocorticoids (Cortisol and corticosterone ) • Zona reticularis: Secretes sex steroids (dehydroepiandrosterone , androstenedione , estrogens, and glucocorticoids) The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not required for the formation of estradiol ?
mcqs.explanation: 11 \035 hydroxylase is not required for estradiol synthesis . \035 hydroxylase is required for the conversion of 11 -deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone , a compound formed in the mineralocorticoid synthesis pathway .735

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is statements is false ?

options.a: 90% of the cortisol is bound to plasma proteins
options.b: Cortisol has a half-life of 60-90 minutes .
options.c: Aldosterone has a half-life of about 20 minutes .
options.d: 80% of the aldosterone is bound to plasma proteins

mcqs.explanation: 60% of aldosterone is bound to plasma proteins , not 80%. 90% of cortisol is bound to plasma proteins . Most of it is bound to transcortin, a corticosteroid -specific �o 2 globulin , and the rest to albumin. This high degree of binding to plasma proteins slows the elimination of cortisol. Therefore, cortisol has a longer half-life of 60 to 90 minutes . Since only about 60% of aldosterone is in bound form, it has a relatively short half-life of about 20 minutes .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an action of cortisol?
mcqs.explanation: Cortisol suppresses the proliferation of T-lymphocytes and decreases the number of T-Lymphocytes . Actions of Cortisol: Metabolic effects : • Effect on carbohydrates : Exert an anti-insulin effect , leading to hyperglycemia • Increases gluconeogenesis • Increases glycogen synthesis • Decreases utilization of glucose in peripheral tissues • Effect on fat and appetite : promotes mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue in acute states . This mobilization increases the concentration of free fatty acids in the plasma, which also increases their utilization for energy , causing lipolysis . However, in chronic states cortisol increases appetite and food intake by inducing the synthesis of neuropeptide -Y which leads to an apparent lipogenic effect seen as buffalo humping and central obesity . • Effect on protein: Exerts a catabolic effect and causes proteolysis • Effect on water and electrolytes : Sodium water retention and diuresis Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects : • Induce the synthesis of lipocortin, an inhibitor of phospholipase A2 • Inhibit the release of histamine and serotonin • Inhibit the production of IL -2 and T lymphocytes , and depress cellular immunity Maintenance of vascular responsiveness to catecholamines : • Cortisol up-regulates �o 1 receptors on arterioles , increasing their sensitivity to the vasoconstrictor effect of norepinephrine

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following conditions increase cortisol except ______
mcqs.explanation: 736 Cortisol secretion is low during sleep . Any type of stress , physical or mental, can increase cortisol release .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man is being treated for severe COVID with dexamethasone . Which of the following mechanisms best explain the rationale for starting steroids in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Inhibition of phospholipase A2 is an anti-inflammatory effect of steroids , thus being the rationale for starting steroids in this patient . Patients with severe COVID are at high risk of developing a systemic inflammatory response . Steroids help in mitigating these deleterious effects . Phospholipase A2 is a precursor of arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is the precursor for prostaglandins and leukotrienes , which are involved in inflammation. Steroids induce the synthesis of lipocortin, which inhibits phospholipase A2 . Other anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of steroids are: • Inhibit the production of interleukin-2 (IL -2) and proliferation of T lymphocytes • Inhibit the release of histamine and serotonin from mast cells and platelets

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following effects is produced only at high levels of glucocorticoids ?

options.b: Increased excretion of a water load

mcqs.explanation: Inhibition of inflammatory response requires high levels of glucocorticoids . Anti-inflammatory and anti-allergic responses (inhibition of histamine from mast cells and basophils ) are produced only at high levels of glucocorticoids . These effects cannot be produced by normal circulating glucocorticoids in the body and thus require exogenous supplementation of steroids to produce them.737

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: ACTH level is higher during______
mcqs.explanation: ACTH level is higher during the early morning and low during late evening. % of the ACTH production occurs between 4:00 AM to 10 :00 AM. Note : Cortisol levels are also high in the early morning and low in the late evening.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: ACTH secretion is inhibited by______
mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoids inhibit ACTH secretion by a direct negative feedback mechanism. They also inhibit CRH secretion .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Aldosterone secretion is maximally stimulated by______
mcqs.explanation: Hyperkalemia and activation of renin-angiotensin system are the most potent stimulators of aldosterone secretion .738

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Mineralocorticoid receptors are present in all except ______
mcqs.explanation: Mineralocorticoid receptors are not present in the liver. They are present in kidneys, colon, hippocampus , salivary glands, and sweat glands. Mineralocorticoid activity increases the reabsorption of Na+ and potassium excretion from urine, sweat , saliva, and contents of the colon. Along with the Na+, there is water reabsorption and inturn ECF volume expansion.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In which of the following ways does aldosterone react with renal tubular cells ?

options.a: Increases transport of ENaCs from the cytoplasm to the cell membrane
options.b: Binds to steroid receptor inside the nucleus of renal tubular cells
options.c: Binds to ENaC's on the cell membrane and increase Na+ transport
options.d: Binds to G-protien coupled receptors on the cell surface

mcqs.explanation: Aldosterone increases transport of ENaCs (epithelial sodium channels) from the cytoplasm to the cell membrane. This is a rapid effect of aldosterone . Mechanism of action of aldosterone : • Aldosterone diffuses into the renal tubular epithelial cells and combines with a mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the cytoplasm . • The aldosterone -receptor complex diffuses into the nucleus and induces transcription. • The mRNA diffuses back into the cytoplasm and undergoes translation to form proteins . These have two effects - Rapid and Slow. • The slower effect is increase in synthesis of ENaCs. • The important products formed are: • Na+K+ATPase • membrane transport proteins like epithelial sodium channel739

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following has the greatest effect on plasma osmolality ?
mcqs.explanation: Vasopressin (also called ADH or anti-diuretic hormone) has the greatest effect on plasma osmolality . Two primary systems are especially involved in regulating the concentration of sodium and osmolarity of extracellular fluid : • The osmoreceptor -ADH system and • The thirst mechanism. Although aldosterone decreases the rate of sodium excretion by the kidneys, the concentration of sodium in the extracellular fluid rises only by a few mEqs. The reason for this is that when sodium is reabsorbed by the tubules , simultaneous absorption of equivalent amounts of water occurs. So, aldosterone does not cause a significant change in the plasma osmolality .740

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man is admitted with nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. On evaluation, he is hypotensive and has mucosal hyperpigmentation . Laboratory workup reveals the diagnosis of hypoaldosteronism . Which of the following is least likely to be found in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In a patient with hypoaldosteronism , alkalosis is least likely to be found. Hypoaldosteronism is rather responsible for causing metabolic acidosis. Patients with hypoaldosteronism have: • Hyponatremia- due to increased Na+ loss in urine • Hyperkalemia- due to K+ retention • Hypotension - due to reduced ECF volume • Mild metabolic acidosis because hydrogen ions are not secreted in the urine

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old female presents to the OPD with headaches and high blood pressure . On investigation, increased aldosterone levels with low renin levels are seen and a diagnosis of Conn's syndrome is made. Which of the following is least likely to be found in this patient ?

options.b: Rise of > 7meq/L in plasma Na+ level

mcqs.explanation: Rise in plasma Na+ level of > 7meq/L than the normal value is least likely to be found in this patient. Excess secretion of aldosterone causes only a modest increase in plasma sodium, usually a rise of less than 4-6 mEq/L . When sodium gets reabsorbed , water also accompanies it, resulting in plasma sodium remaining fairly normal . Conn's syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism is due to an aldosterone -producing tumour of the zona glomerulosa , causing: • Loss of potassium by the kidneys leads to hypokalemia. • Mild metabolic alkalosis. • A slight increase in extracellular fluid volume and blood volume. • A modest increase in plasma sodium concentration. • Hypertension .741

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following decreases aldosterone secretion ?
mcqs.explanation: Hypernatremia decreases aldosterone secretion .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Hormones that are increased in plasma during periods of stress include all of the following except _______
mcqs.explanation: Insulin does not increase during stress. In response to stress , the usual physiological functions like gluconeogenesis , lipolysis , and inhibition of insulin actions occurs, resulting in increased blood levels of fuel sources (glucose, fatty acids) needed to cope .742 Hormones that are increased in the blood by stress are CRH, ACTH, cortisol, \035-endorphin(to reduce pain), vasopressin, aldosterone, growth hormone, and glucagon .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the major adrenal androgen ?
mcqs.explanation: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is the major adrenal androgen. The androgens secreted from the adrenal gland are dehydroepiandrosterone and androstenedione.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 16-year-old female patient presents to the OPD with hirsutism and masculinization. Which of the following hormones of the adrenal cortex is the likely culprit ?
mcqs.explanation: Hirsutism and masculinization in a female suggest excessive androgens like dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). Adrenogenital syndrome is due to an adrenocortical tumor secreting excessive quantities of androgens that cause intense masculinizing effects . In boys, it presents as precocious puberty . In women, virile characteristics develop , including: • Growth of a beard • Deeper voice • Masculine distribution of hair on the body and the pubis and • Growth of the clitoris The excretion of 17-ketosteroids (which are derived from androgens) in the urine maybe 10 to 15 times elevated . This finding can be used in diagnosing the disease .743

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not directly controlled by ACTH?
mcqs.explanation: The secretion of the adrenal medullary hormones (epinephrine , norepinephrine , and dopamine) is not controlled directly by ACTH.Hormones secreted Regulated by Zona glomerul osa Mineralocorticoids (aldostero ne) Angiotensin II , K+, ACTH (m ild transient effect ) Zona fasiculata Glucocorticoids (cortisol, cort icosterone ) ACTH Zona reticulari s Sex steroids (DHEA, DHEA-S) ACTH Adrenal medul la Catecholamines (epinephrine , norepinephrine ) Diffuse sympathetic discharg e(stress )

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones is exclusively secreted by adrenal gland but not by the ovaries of females ?
mcqs.explanation: DHEAS is exclusively secreted from the adrenals but not by ovaries because ovaries lack the enzyme dehydroepiandrosterone -sulphotransferase needed to form DHEAS. 90% of DHEA is synthesised by the adrenals and 10 % comes from the ovaries.744

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following vitamins have a hormonal action?
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin D has hormonal action. In conjunction with parathyroid hormone, it is a major regulatory hormone for Ca2+ and phosphate metabolism .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The active form of vitamin D is______
mcqs.explanation: The active form of Vit D is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. Cholecalciferol is formed in the skin and converted to 25 hydroxycholecalciferol in the liver. This is hydroxylated in the kidney to form 1,25-dihyroxycholecalciferol .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding actions of vitamin D?

options.a: Vit D receptor -retinoid X receptor complex binds to DNA and activates transcription
options.b: Vit D increases absorption of calcium from the intestine by increasing calbindin
options.c: Phosphate flux through the gastrointestinal epithelium is enhanced by vitamin D
options.d: Vit D decreases phosphate reabsorption by the renal tubules

mcqs.explanation: Vit D does not decrease phosphate reabsorption by the renal tubules . It increases calcium and phosphate reabsorption by the renal tubules , leading to a decrease in excretion of these substances in the urine.752

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy was brought to the OPD with craniotabes, rachitic rosary and bowed legs . Diagnosis of rickets was made. To investigate the cause of rickets and to find the status of vitamin D in the body, which of the following should be measured ?
mcqs.explanation: Measurement of 25 hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol ) provides more accurate information about vitamin D levels . PTH is increased in vitamin D deficiency. PTH is a major stimulus for the 1�o -hydroxylase, so there is increased synthesis of the active hormone, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Paradoxically, levels of this hormone are often normal in severe vitamin D deficiency . Therefore, measurements of 1,25- dihydroxyvitamin D are not accurate reflections of vitamin D stores and should not be used to diagnose vitamin D deficiency in patients with normal renal function.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following decreases the conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol ?
mcqs.explanation: The conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol is done by enzyme 1�o -hydroxylase which is present in the kidney. In chronic renal failure (CRF), there is a deficiency of this enzyme and formation of the active form of vitamin D does not take place . Factors which increase activity of 1�o -hydroxylase are: • Ca2+ deficiency • Increased parathyroid hormone (PTH )

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which organ is not involved in calcium homeostasis ?
mcqs.explanation: The lung is not involved in calcium homeostasis . There are two sources of cholecalciferol in the body:753 • Diet • Synthesized in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol in the presence of ultraviolet light . Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated in the liver to form 25-hydroxycholecalciferol , which is further hydroxylated in the kidney to forn 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol . At higher calcium concentrations, when PTH is suppressed , the 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to a different compound —24,25dihydroxycholecalciferol— that has almost no vitamin D effect . Note : This is a controversial question because new evidence suggests an association between calcium homeostasis and pulmonary fibroblasts. Therefore: • If Lung is given in the options and spleen is provided as one of the choices instead of Kidneys , Skin , Liver or Intestine , then the best answer would be the spleen . • If other options are Kidneys , Skin , Liver, or Intestine , then the best answer would be Lung as the role of these organs in calcium metabolism is beyond doubt .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Increased calcium levels lead to______
mcqs.explanation: Increased calcium levels lead to an increase in 24,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol . The levels of calcium control formation of 1,25-dihydroxyxholecalciferol . When calcium is low, PTH (parathyroid hormone) promotes the conversion of 25hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25- dihydroxycholecalciferol? in the kidneys. At higher calcium concentrations, when PTH is sup - pressed , the 25hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to a different compound —24,25- dihydroxycholecalciferol — that has almost no vitamin D effect .754

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What would be seen in a patient whose diet is deficient in calcium?
mcqs.explanation: Low Ca2+ diet leads to hypocalcemia , which stimulates PTH release . Hence , this patient will have high PTH levels . Increased PTH causes • Hypophosphatemia due to increased excretion of phosphate via the kidneys. • PTH acts on the kidneys to increase the absorption of calcium. • PTH also increases the level of the enzyme 1-�o hydroxylase which leads to more production of the active form of Vitamin D- 1,25 dihydrocholecalciferol . In the presence of hypocalcemia , serum calcitonin levels decrease and active form of vitamin D increases .755

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In an experiment , a rat is infused with a small volume of a calcium chloride solution . Compared to the control condition, which of the following would result from the calcium load?
mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, increased formation of 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol will take place . Infusion of calcium chloride solution will lead to raised calcium concentration in blood. At higher calcium concentrations, PTH is also suppressed . So the 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to a different compound : 24,25dihydroxycholecalciferol — that has almost no vitamin D effect . When plasma calcium concentration is high, formation of 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol is also greatly depressed . Lack of 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol , in turn, decreases the absorption of calcium from the intestines , bones, and renal tubules , thus causing the calcium ion concentration to fall back toward its normal level . Option A: Since PTH levels are supressed bone demineralisation does not take place . Option B: Calcitonin is a calcium regulatory hormone whose level increases when the calcium concentration in plasma is high. Option C: Calcium ions are a part of the coagulation cascade and the blood coaguability either increases or remains the same with high plasma Ca+2 levels .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Calcium absorption takes place mainly from which of the following sites ?
mcqs.explanation: Calcium absorption is mainly from the proximal small intestine (duodenum ). Vit D and PTH are important factors that control calcium absorption.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an enhancer of calcium absorption from the intestine ?
mcqs.explanation: Ca 2+ absorption is enhanced by proteins. It is inhibited by phosphates , phytic acid, and oxalates because these anions form insoluble salts with Ca 2+ in the intestine .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the active form of calcium?
mcqs.explanation: Ionic calcium is the active form that is important for most functions of calcium in the body, including the effect of calcium on the heart, the nervous system , and bone formation. Most of the calcium (99%) is stored in the bones. Only about 0.1 percent of the total body calcium is in the extracellular fluid and 1 percent is in the cells and its organelles . From the 0.1% Ca+2 in the plasma, the distribution of calcium is as follows : • About 41 % is combined with the plasma proteins (non-diffusible through the capillary membrane)756 • About 9 % is combined with anionic substances of the plasma and interstitial fluids like citrate and phosphate in such a manner that it is not ionized (diffusible through the capillary membrane); and • The remaining 50 % of the calcium in the plasma is both diffusible through the capillary membrane and ionized.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells play a key role in bone resorption?
mcqs.explanation: Osteoclasts play a key role in bone resorption. The cells responsible for bone formation are osteoblasts and the cells responsible for bone resorption are osteoclasts . Osteoblasts are modified fibroblasts. Osteoclasts are the members of the monocyte family Osteoclasts erode and absorb the previously formed bone • They become attached to the bone via integrins forming a sealing zone where the bone resorption takes place • Proton pumps (H+ -ATPases) then move from the endosomes of the osteoclasts into the cell membrane as opposed to the sealing zone and acidify the area to pH 4.0. • The acidic pH dissolves hydroxyapatite , and the acid proteases secreted by the cell break down collagen .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: On infusing parathyroid hormone in experimental mice, there is increased resorption of bone due to stimulation of the osteoclastic activity. Which of the following is true regarding the cellular mechanism of osteoclastic activation?

options.a: The bone-resorbing osteoclast cells do not have PTH receptors
options.b: Osteoclasts produce osteoprotegerin (OPG) a cytokine that increases bone resorption
options.c: RANK ligand and M-CSF are necessary for formation of mature osteoblasts
options.d: Glucocorticoids promote osteoblast activity and inhibit bone resorption

mcqs.explanation: Osteoclast cells do not have PTH receptors . PTH stimulates osteoclast activity and bone resorption by an indirect mechanism.757 PTH has receptors on the osteoblasts in the bone. When PTH binds to these receptors , osteoblasts release cytokines like RANK-ligand and M-CSF. These cytokines allow the differentiation of macrophages to osteoclasts . Osteoclasts , in turn, cut the collagen in the bone, which is bound to calcium. This causes the release of calcium, phosphorus , and collagen breakdown products in the blood. Osteoblasts produce osteoprotegerin (OPG), or osteoclastogenesis inhibitory factor, a cytokine that inhibits bone resorption by preventing interaction of RANKL with its receptor . PTH decreases the production of osteoprotegerin (OPG). Glucocorticoids promote osteoclast activity and increase bone resorption by increasing RANKL production and decreasing the formation of OPG. On the other hand, the hormone estrogen stimulates OPG production .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A mouse is engineered to lack a transcription factor necessary for the normal development of osteoclasts . Compared to normal littermate mice, which of the following would be reduced in the knocked-out mouse ?
mcqs.explanation: Secretion of acid proteases would be decreased in the knocked-out mouse . Osteoclasts produce proteolytic enzymes and several acids necessary for bone resorption. The enzymes digest or dissolve the organic matrix of the bone, and the acids cause dissolution of the bone salts. A knocked-out mouse is a genetically modified mouse in which an existing gene is inactivated or 'knocked out' by replacing it with an artificial one. The control mice used in the above case are littermate mice i.e mice with genetically modified embryonic stem (ES) cell strains used to test whether specific genes control a disease or immunological phenomena (eg : normal osteoclastic development ) Option B: The acidic pH caused by the osteoclasts dissolves hydroxyapatite . In the knocked-out mouse , hydroxyapatite levels would therefore increase. Option A and C: Since the lineage of osteoclasts and osteoblasts is different , there is no decrease in the proliferation of osteoblasts . As the osteoblast levels are normal , phosphate deposition in bone also remains normal .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding calcium homeostasis ?

options.a: 90% of calcium is filtered from the glomerulus
options.b: Calcium is reabsorbed mainly from the late distal convoluted tubule (DCT)
options.c: Parathyroid hormone (PTH ) promotes calcium reabsorption from the renal tubules
options.d: Calcitonin promotes action of parathyroid hormone

mcqs.explanation: PTH promotes the reabsorption of calcium from the renal tubules . Option A: About 41 percent of the plasma calcium is bound to plasma proteins and is therefore not filtered by the glomerular capillaries . The rest of the calcium is filtered through the glomeruli into the renal tubules . Option B: Of the filtered calcium, approximately 90 percent is reabsorbed in the proximal tubules , l oops of Henle , and early distal tubules. However, when calcium levels are low and PTH levels rise, PTH promotes calcium reabsorption from the later DCT. Option D: Calcitonin tends to decrease plasma calcium concentration and, in general , has effects opposite to those of PTH .758

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an effect of parathormone?
mcqs.explanation: PTH does not increase phosphate reabsorption in kidney, rather it causes decreased phosphate reabsorption in the kidney.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following will be most likely seen in a patient with parathyroid deficiency after inadvertent damage to the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery?

options.a: High plasma phosphate , low Ca2+ levels and tetanus
options.b: Low plasma Ca2+ level , increased muscular excitability , and Trousseau sign
options.c: High plasma phosphate and Ca2+ levels and bone demineralization
options.d: Increased muscular excitability , a high plasma Ca2+ level , and bone demineralization

mcqs.explanation: In a patient with parathyroid deficiency due to inadvertent damage to the parathyroid glands, the clinical evaluation will show low Ca+2 level , tetany , trousseau sign, and high phosphate levels . PTH is released in response to low calcium levels . It increases the calcium levels by the following actions:Following signs can be elicited in hypoparathyroidism due to hypocalcemia (tetany ): • Chvostek sign: Contraction facial muscles on tapping over facial nerve in front of the tragus of the ear • Trousseau sign: accoucheur 's hand position and painful carpopedal spasm by applying a sphygmomanometer cuff to the arm and keeping the pressure above systolic blood pressure for 5 minutes Note - In option A, tetanus is different from tetany . Tetanus is caused by infection with the bacteria Clostridium tetani The image below is showing Trousseau sign.759

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of these cause hypocalcemia ?
mcqs.explanation: Calcitonin has calcium-lowering effects and may cause hypocalcemia . It does so by inhibiting bone resorption (direct effect ) Calcitonin is synthesized and secreted by parafollicular (clear) cells of the thyroid. Actions of calcitonin are as follows : • Inhibits osteoclasts , thereby decreasing bone resorption (direct effect ) • Increases renal calcium excretion • Decreases calcium absorption by the kidneys and intestines Under normal physiological conditions, calcitonin is more important in young individuals (compared to adults ), and it may play a role in skeletal development . In addition, it may protect the bones of the mother from excess calcium loss during pregnancy. Bone formation in the infant and lactation are major drains on Ca 2+ stores . They would cause bone loss in the mother if bone resorption were not simultaneously inhibited by an increase in the plasma calcitonin level.760

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old lady with metastatic breast cancer develops nausea, vomiting and confusion. Further evaluation reveals severe hypercalcemia. IV hydration is initiated and calcitonin is added to her treatment plan. Which of the following best represents the role of calcitonin in lowering serum calcium level ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of hypercalcemia of malignancy, most probably due to metastatic breast cancer. Calcitonin exerts its calcium-lowering effect mainly by inhibiting bone resorption and helps in the management of hypercalcemia . This calcium lowering action of calcitonin is direct , by inhibiting the activity of osteoclasts . However, calcitonin also increases renal calcium excretion and decreases calcium absorption by the kidneys and intestines .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old lady undergoes thyroidectomy due to suspected malignancy. A week after the surgery she develops a spasm of facial muscles on tapping over the facial nerve in front of the tragus. Which of the following is the reason behind her muscle hyperexcitability ?
mcqs.explanation: 761 The given clinical vignette is suggestive of chvostek sign, seen in hypocalcemia due to accidental parathyroid injury during thyroid surgery. The muscle hyperexcitability seen in hypocalcemia is due to increased permeability of cells to Na+. During thyroid surgery, parathyroid gland is prone to accidental injury due to proximity with the thyroid gland. Damage to the parathyroid gland will lead to a low PTH level and low Ca2+ level . When the ECF concentration of Ca2+ falls below normal , the nervous system becomes progressively more excitable . Because there is increased membrane permeability to Na+. This leads to easy initiation of the action potentials . The peripheral nerve fibres become so excitable that they begin to discharge spontaneously , initiating impulses that pass to the skeletal muscles to elicit tetanic muscle contraction. Tetany occurs usually when calcium concentration falls to 6 mg/dL.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding confounders affecting serum calcium level ?

options.a: Total calcium concentration is altered by variations in the serum albumin concentration.
options.b: Forearm exercise can lead to falsely elevated ionized calcium levels
options.c: Hemoconcentration due to tourniquet results in a rise of serum calcium
options.d: Acidosis causes a decrease in the ionized calcium levels

mcqs.explanation: Acidosis does not cause a decrease in the ionized calcium levels . Rather, alkalosis causes a decrease in the ionized calcium levels . Plasma proteins are more ionized when the pH is high (alkalosis), providing more protein anions to bind with and sequester free Ca2+. This causes a decrease in ionized calcium and may trigger symptoms of hypocalcemia . Option A: Total calcium concentration is altered by variations in the serum albumin concentration as 41% of calcium is bound to plasma proteins like albumin, hence changes in albumin concentration affects the serum calcium levels . The corrected calcium levels can be calculated as: Corrected calcium (mg/dL) = measured total Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 (4.0 - serum albumin [g/dL]), where 4.0 represents the average albumin level . Option B: Fist-clenching or forearm exercise can lead to falsely elevated ionized (free ) calcium levels . Option C: A tourniquet is usually avoided while drawing blood for calcium measurements since hemoconcentration also leads to an increase in serum calcium levels .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells is involved in the initiation and control of osteoclastic activity?
mcqs.explanation: Osteoblasts are involved in the initiation and control of osteoclastic activity. Osteoblasts produce receptor activator for nuclear factor \034B ligand (RANKL) and macrophage colony stimulating factor (M-CSF), which are necessary for formation of mature osteoclasts and hence osteoclastic activity . Specific receptors for parathormone are present only on the osteoblasts and not on osteoclasts .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of these is not a marker of bone resorption?
mcqs.explanation: 762 Serum bone specific alkaline phosphatase is a marker for bone formation. Other markers of bone formation are: • Serum osteocalcin • Serum type 1 procollagen (C-terminal/N-terminal) Markers for bone resorption are: • Urinary hydroxyproline • Urinary total pyridinoline (PYD) • Urinary free deoxypyridinoline (DPD) • Urinary collagen type 1 cross-linked N-Telopeptide (NTX) • Urinary or serum collagen type 1 cross-linked C-Telopeptide (CTX) • Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b International Osteoporosis Foundation has proposed serum CTX and serum PINP (Procollagen 1 N-terminal peptide ) to be used as reference markers of bone resorption and formation, respectively , for the assessment of fracture risk and monitoring therapy in clinical settings .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: Parathyroid adenoma is a benign tumor of the parathyroid gland, which causes primary hyperparathyroidism (not secondary). Secondary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by high levels of parathyroid hormone, to compensate for the low levels of serum calcium, due to some other underlying condition. Causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism, include : • Chronic kidney disease : The damaged kidneys are unable to produce sufficient amounts of the active form of vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol . This further causes hypocalcemia and triggers PTH secretion . • Vitamin D deficiency : Causes hypocalcemia, which triggers the increased secretion of PTH . • Lithium: May cause an increased set -point of calcium for parathyroid hormone suppression , which leads to parathyroid hyperplasia.763

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 32 year old lady is undergoing evaluation for polycystic ovary syndrome. Her sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is low. The decrease in sex hormone-binding globulin will have the maximum effect on which of the following hormones?
mcqs.explanation: The decrease in sex hormone-binding globulin will have the maximum effect on testosterone . Around 98% of the circulating testosterone is bound to plasma proteins such as sex hormone-binding globulin (65%) and albumin. So, the decrease in sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) or gonadal steroid -binding globulin (GBG) will have the maximum effect on testosterone levels by increasing the levels of its free form. Therefore patients with polycystic ovary syndrome will show features of hyperandrogenism (due to elevated free testosterone ).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Sertoli cells in testes have receptors for______
mcqs.explanation: Sertoli cells express FSH receptor , whereas Leydig cell express LH receptor Sertoli cells are the true epithelial cells of the seminiferous epithelium and extend from basal lamina to the lumen. Functions of Sertoli cells : • Express FSH receptor and androgen receptor . • Forms the blood-testis barrier . • Surround the sperm cells and provide structural support within the epithelium . • Guide sperm cells towards the lumen as they advance to later stages of spermatogenesis . • Produce inhibin and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS). • Produce androgen-binding proteins that maintain high androgen levels within the lumen of the seminiferous tubules and the proximal part of the male reproductive tract. • Perform phagocytic function by engulfing residual bodies (cytoplasm shed by spermatozoa during spermiogenesis ) and dead sperm cells . • Express aromatase, which converts testosterone to potent estrogen .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The negative feedback mechanism involving the Sertoli cells causes _____
mcqs.explanation: The negative feedback mechanism involving the Sertoli cells causes \023FSH. FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells . This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary . Thus, inhibin keeps FSH levels within a set point.772

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In men, LH controls secretion of______
mcqs.explanation: In men, LH controls the secretion of testosterone . LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone , which in turn inhibits LH by a negative feedback mechanism. FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to secrete inhibin, which in turn inhibits FSH by a negative feedback mechanism. Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus. Inhibin acts directly on the anterior pituitary to inhibit FSH secretion . FSH also stimulates the secretion of ABP (androgen-binding protein) and inhibin. FSH and androgens maintain the gametogenic function of the testes . Hypothalamic lesions in animals and hypothalamic disease in humans lead to atrophy of the testes and loss of their function.773

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Testosterone production is mainly contributed by ______
mcqs.explanation: Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells . Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol in the Leydig cells and also from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex. The diagnosis of testosterone deficiency should be made only on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms consistent with androgen deficiency , and consistently subnormal serum testosterone concentrations at 8 to 10 AM on three occasions. Testosterone has been used to treat primary or secondary hypogonadism in adult men.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: All of the following are androgens except ______
mcqs.explanation: 17�o hydroxy-progesterone is a progestin , not androgen. The term androgen means any steroid hormone that has masculinizing effects . Testosterone , Dihydrotestosterone , androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone are androgens. The sites of production : • Testes . • Adrenal gland. • Ovary (not significant). • Tumors of the adrenal androgen-producing cells etc . Both in the testes and in the adrenals, the androgens can be synthesized either from cholesterol or directly from acetyl coenzyme A.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following cells secrete anti mullerian hormone?
mcqs.explanation: (Anti Mullerian Hormone) is secreted by both sertoli cells and granulosa cells . Sertoli cells produce Anti Mullerian Hormone (Mullerian inhibitory substance ) during development. It induces the regression of the mullerian duct that is programmed to give rise to a female reproductive tract. Granulosa cells of the ovary produce AMH during the reproductive years. It limits the formation of primary follicles by inhibiting excessive follicular recruitment by FSH.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The blood-testis barrier is formed by______

options.a: Tight junctions between adjacent leydig cells
options.b: Tight junctions between adjacent sertoli cells

mcqs.explanation: 774 The blood-testis barrier is formed by the tight junctions between adjacent sertoli cells . This Sertoli-Sertoli cell tight junctions divide the seminiferous epithelium into 2 compartments: • Basal compartment - contains the spermatogonia and early-stage primary spermatocytes . • Adluminal compartment - contains later-stage primary spermatocytes and all subsequent stages of sperm cells . It imparts a selective permeability , allowing few substances such as testosterone to cross but preventing noxious substances that might damage the developing sperm. It also protects sperms from antibodies by creating a specialized, immunologically safe microenvironment for developing sperm. BELOW DIAGRAM - 1 basal lamina, 2 spermatogonia , 3 spermatocyte 1st order, 4 spermatocyte 2nd order, spermatid, 6 mature spermatid , 7 Sertoli cell , 8 tight junctions(Blood- Testis Barrier )

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Spermiogenesis refers to_______

options.d: Formation of secondary spermatocyte from primary spermatocyte

mcqs.explanation: Spermiogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids . Spermiogenesis is a process by which there is a formation of extremely specialized mobile spermatozoa from spermatids . This process requires extensive remodeling or packaging of cell elements . It occurs in the recesses formed by invaginations of the sertoli cell plasma membrane. Maturation from spermatids to spermatozoa depends on androgen acting on sertoli cells . When sperm maturation is complete , the cytoplasm of the sertoli cell around sperm retracts and sperms are released into the lumen to be bathed by the luminal fluid . The following changes occur during the formation ofspermatozoafrom spermatids : • The nucleus becomes eccentric and decreases in size, and the chromatin becomes condensed . • The cytoplasmic content is redistributed and discarded .775 • The acrosome buds from the golgi apparatus. • The centrioles migrate to the caudal pole and form a long axial filament made of microtubules . This becomes the axoneme or major portion of the tail. Spermiation is the release of the sperm from the sertoli cells . During spermiation, most of the remaining cytoplasm is shed in the form of residual bodies . Spermatogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatogonia .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Development of spermatozoa from spermatogonium takes how much time?
mcqs.explanation: The time required to produce mature spermatozoa from the earliest stage of spermatogonia is 65 to 70 days.776 Since several developmental stages of spermatogenic cells occur during this time frame, the stages are collectively known as the spermatogenic cycle .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Spermatogenesis is maintained by which hormone?
mcqs.explanation: All three of them (testosterone , FSH, LH ) are required for spermatogenesis . Pulses of hypothalamic GnRH stimulate the anterior pituitary to secrete FSH and LH , which then act on the testes FSH acts on the Sertoli cells to stimulate spermatogenesis and inhibin secretion . LH acts on the Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone secretion . Testosterone , acting locally on the Sertoli cells , is essential for maintaining spermatogenesis.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Role of growth hormone in spermatogenesis is _______
mcqs.explanation: The growth hormone specifically promotes the early division of spermatogonia . Hormonal factors that stimulate spermatogenesis : • Testosterone , secreted by the Leydig cells of the testis , is essential for growth and division of the testicular germinal cells , which is the first stage in forming sperm. • Luteinizing hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, stimulates the Leydig cells to secrete testosterone . • Follicle -stimulating hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, stimulates the Sertoli cells . Without this stimulation, the spermiogenesis will not occur. • Estrogens , formed from testosterone by the Sertoli cells when stimulated by FSH, are also essential for spermiogenesis . • Growth hormone is necessary for controlling the background metabolic functions of the testes . It specifically promotes early division of the spermatogonia themselves . In its absence , as in pituitary dwarfs, spermatogenesis is severely deficient or absent, thus causing infertility .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following provides a negative feedback in spermatogenesis ?
mcqs.explanation: Negative feedback in spermatogenesis is by inhibin. FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells . This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary . LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone , which in turn inhibits LH . Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH ) from the hypothalamus .777

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man is being evaluated for suspected infertility . His semen analysis shows a decrease in sperm count and motility . On physical examination, a 'bag of worms'-like structure is palpated in his scrotum, suggestive of varicocele. Which of the following is the most likely reason behind his decreased sperm count?

options.a: Lowered scrotal temperature , compared to core temperature
options.b: Rise in scrotal temperature , compared to core temperature

mcqs.explanation: The most likely reason behind decreased sperm count in this patient is rise in scrotal temperature, secondary to varicocoele. Normally, the testes occupy the scrotum, which lies outside the body cavity and is maintained at 35\260 to 36\260C, or 1\260 to 2\260C below body temperature . This lower temperature is essential for normal spermatogenesis . It is maintained by a countercurrent arrangement of testicular arteries and veins, which facilitates heat exchange . Enlarged veins around the testes , called varicoceles, cause infertility by raising the temperature in the scrotum and decreasing sperm production .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Sperm acquires motility in______
mcqs.explanation: Sperm is stored in the epididymis , where they undergo a process of maturation before they are capable of progressive motility and fertilization. Changes during the sperm maturation in the epididymis : • Progressive increase in forward motility • Increase ability to fertilize • Maturation of acrosome • Molecular reorganization of plasma membrane: Lipid (stabilization of plasma membrane) protein (shedding as well as the acquisition of new proteins ) • Ability to bind to zona pellucida • Acquisition of receptors for proteins of the zona pellucida778 • Increase disulfide bond between cysteine residues in sperm nucleoproteins • Topographic regionalization of glycosidic residues • Accumulation of mannosylated residues on periacrosomal plasma membrane • Decreased cytoplasm and cell volume

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: At which location does the capacitation of sperm take place ?
mcqs.explanation: Capacitation of sperm takes place in uterine tubes . Once ejaculated into the female genital tract, the spermatozoa move up the uterus to the isthmus of the uterine tubes , where they slow down and undergo final conditioning called capacitation. This process involves two components : • Increasing the motility of the spermatozoa • Facilitating their preparation for the acrosomal reaction.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following factors increases sperm motility ?
mcqs.explanation: Sperm motility is increased by vaginal secretions . On coming in contact with the fluids of the female genital tract, multiple changes occur that activate the sperm for the final processes of fertilization. These collective changes are called capacitation of the spermatozoa, which normally requires from 1 to 10 hours. The following changes are believed to occur: • The uterine and fallopian tube fluids wash away the various inhibitory factors that suppress sperm activity in the male genital ducts. • While the spermatozoa remain in the fluid of the male genital ducts , they are continually exposed to many floating vesicles from the seminiferous tubules containing large amounts of cholesterol . This cholesterol is continually added to the cellular membrane covering the sperm acrosome, toughening this membrane and preventing the release of its enzymes . • After ejaculation , the sperm deposited in the vagina swim away from the cholesterol vesicles upward into the uterine cavity, and they gradually lose much of their other excess cholesterol during the next few hours. In doing so, the membrane at the head of the sperm (the acrosome) becomes much weaker. • The membrane of the sperm also becomes much more permeable to calcium ions, so calcium now enters the sperm in abundance and changes the activity of the flagellum , giving it a powerful whiplash motion in contrast to its previously weak undulating motion. In addition, the calcium ions cause changes in the cellular membrane that cover the leading edge of the acrosome, making it possible for the acrosome to release its enzymes rapidly and easily as the sperm penetrates the granulosa cell mass surrounding the ovum, and even more so as it attempts to penetrate the zona pellucida of the ovum .779

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man suffering from prostate cancer is undergoing long-term androgen deprivation therapy . He is being treated with long acting GnRH agonist. After prolonged injection of GnRH, which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Prolonged injection of GnRH will lead to decreased LH levels . A constant administration of GnRH produces an initial agonistic action known as "flare", followed by a downregulation of GnRH receptors ( decrease in GnRH receptor concentration). This desensitizes pituitary to the action of GnRH and a hypogonadotropic -hypogonadal state is induced . This is characterized by low LH , low FSH levels and thereby reduced testosterone production (i.e., chemical castration).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The major contribution to semen is from which of the following organs?
mcqs.explanation: The major contribution to semen is from seminal vesicles . The seminal vesicles contribute ~60-70% of the volume of semen . Apart from sperm, the remaining 20 -40% represents epididymal fluids , as well as secretions of the prostate gland and bulbourethral glands. The seminal plasma originates primarily from the accessory glands (the seminal vesicles , the prostate gland, and the bulbourethral glands).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Normal pH of human semen is_____
mcqs.explanation: The normal pH of human semen is 7.4 (isotonic). The pH in the lumen of the epididymis is relatively acidic (6.5 to 6.8) as the result of H+ secretion by clear cells that are analogous to intercalated cells in the nephron. Addition of the relatively alkaline secretions of the seminal vesicles raises the final pH of seminal plasma to between 7.2 and 7.8. Spermatozoa generally tolerate alkalinity better than acidity . A pH near neutrality or slightly higher is optimal for the motility and survival of sperm cells in humans and in other species as well .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Prostaglandins in semen are secreted by which of the following organs?
mcqs.explanation: Prostaglandins in semen are secreted by seminal vesicle . The seminal vesicles secrete fluid that is rich in fructose , citrate, prostaglandins, and fibrinogen. The prostaglandins present in the seminal fluid may assist in fertilization in two ways: • Prostaglandins react with cervical mucus to make it more penetrable by sperm.780 • Prostaglandins induce peristaltic contractions in the female reproductive tract (i.e., the uterus and fallopian tubes ) to propel the sperm up the tract.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A couple is undergoing evaluation for their inability to conceive. In order to rule out male factor infertility, the consultant orders a semen analysis for the husband. Which of the following best estimates the normal sperm count in an adult ?
mcqs.explanation: Normal sperm count on an average is 100 million/ml (90-120 million/mL ). Note : The WHO 2010 minimal criteria for semen analysis requires a minimum sperm count >15 million/mL or >40 million/per ejaculate .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: In which part of the fallopian tube does fertilization take place ?
mcqs.explanation: In humans, fertilization of the ovum by the sperm usually occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: For how many hours does human sperm remain fertile in the female genital tract?
mcqs.explanation: After ejaculation , sperms have a maximal lifespan of 24-48 hours in the female genital tract. The activity and rate of metabolism of sperm increase markedly with increasing temperature causing its life to be considerably shortened . Sperm can be cryopreserved for years if agents such as glycerol are used to prevent ice crystal formation during freezing . Note : The ovum remains viable and capable of being fertilized , probably no longer than 24 hours after it is expelled from the ovary .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: For how long does the ovum remain viable following ovulation?
mcqs.explanation: The ovum remains viable up to 24hours following ovulation. If not fertilized , the ovum degenerates in the fallopian tube without leaving behind any trace after 24 hours.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones has no role for the attainment of puberty ?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin has no role in the attainment of puberty . GH, leptin and testosterone are all required for the onset of puberty . The onset of puberty is marked by enhanced androgenic activity. The growth spurt of adolescent males is influenced by a complex interplay between androgens, growth hormone (GH), nutrition, and genetic factors.781 Leptin, the satiety -producing hormone secreted by fat cells , may be the link between body weight and puberty.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones is responsible for pubarche ?
mcqs.explanation: Pubarche or the development of axillary and pubic hair is due to testosterone . The growth of pubic and axillary hair in both sexes is primarily due to androgens.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones play a permissive role in the attainment of puberty ?
mcqs.explanation: The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin . It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty . Leptin is a satiety -producing hormone secreted by adipocytes . High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure . Evidence for which is given by: • Obese ob/ob mice that cannot make leptin are infertile , and their fertility is restored by injections of leptin . • Leptin treatment also induces precocious puberty in immature female mice. • However, the way that leptin fits into the overall control of puberty remains to be determined . Leptin also accelerates GnRH pulsatility in neurons, fastening puberty .782

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones is not secreted by the ovary ?
mcqs.explanation: Gonadotropins (FSH, LH ) are not secreted by the ovary . They are secreted by the anterior pituitary. Ovaries secrete estrogen , progesterone , and inhibin B.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old lady has regular, infrequent menstrual cycles occurring at an interval of 35-36 days. What is the usual timing of ovulation in this lady?
mcqs.explanation: Ovulation occurs 14 days before menses , regardless of cycle length . If we calculate the day of menstruation from the beginning of the cycle , in a 28-day cycle , ovulation occurs on day 14 and in a 35-day cycle , ovulation will occur on day 22 .791 Option B: LH surge leads to ovulation. Ovulation does not occur before LH surge . Option C: The ruptured ovarian follicle (after ovulation) is converted into corpus luteum . Ovulation does not occur after corpus luteal maturation. Option D: Ovulation will occur 14 days before menstruation, i.e. on day 22 of a 35-day cycle . It does not occur 22 days before menstruation.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The corpus luteum starts regressing after how many days post ovulation?
mcqs.explanation: The human corpus luteum starts regressing ~10 days after ovulation. Ovulation occurs on day 14, and the day corpus luteum begins to regress on day 25 of the menstrual cycle . Therefore, Days after ovulation when corpus luteum starts regressing = 25-14 = 11 days The human corpus luteum is programmed to live for 14 days, plus or minus 2 days (corpus luteum of menstruation). Figure Events of the menstrual cycle :

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not seen in humans?
mcqs.explanation: Estrous cycle is not seen in humans. Mammals other than primates do not menstruate , and their sexual cycle is called an estrous cycle . It is named for the conspicuous period of "heat " (estrus ) at the time of ovulation, normally the only time during which the sexual interest of the female is aroused .792 In spontaneously ovulating species with estrous cycles , such as the rat, no episodic vaginal bleeding occurs, but the underlying endocrine events are essentially the same as those in the menstrual cycle . In other species , ovulation is induced by copulation (reflex ovulation).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the dominant hormone in the luteal phase ?
mcqs.explanation: • Progesterone is the dominant hormone during the luteal phase . • The corpus luteum in the non-pregnant woman secretes large quantities of progesterone and a small amount of estrogen , as well as inhibin. • In terms of ovarian function, the menstrual cycle may be divided into two phases approximately equal in length and separated by ovulation (Figure ): • The follicular phase , during which a mature follicle and secondary oocyte develop ; and • The luteal phase begins after ovulation and lasts until the death of the corpus luteum .Follicular phase (days 0–14) • A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage , with atresia of neighboring follicles . • LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells . • Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus . • FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary. • Progesterone levels are low. Ovulation (day 14) • Occurs 14 days before menses , regardless of cycle length . Thus, in a 28-day cycle , ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle , ovulation occurs on day 22 .793 • A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge ). • Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen -induced LH surge . • Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase ). • Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm. Luteal phase (days 14–28) • The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone . Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg . • Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center . • If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase . As a result , estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly . Menses (days 0–4) • The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone794

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones is responsible for the maintenance of endometrial thickness in the post -ovulatory phase ?
mcqs.explanation: Progesterone is mainly responsible for the maintenance of endometrial thickness in the post-ovulatory phase . The menstrual cycle consists of three phases : the menstrual phase , the proliferative phase , and the secretory , or progestational , phase Menstrual phase : This phase is characterized by the discharge of blood and endometrial debris from the vagina . • It coincides with the end of the ovarian luteal phase and onset of a new follicular phase . • Withdrawal of progesterone on the degeneration of the corpus luteum (CL) leads simultaneously to sloughing of the endometrium (menstruation) and development of new follicles in the ovary under the influence of rising gonadotropic hormone levels Proliferative Phase: Thus, menstrual flow ceases , and the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle begins concurrently with the last portion of the ovarian follicular phase . • When the menstrual flow ceases , a thin endometrial layer less than 1-mm thick remains. Estrogen stimulates proliferation of epithelial cells , glands, and blood vessels in the endometrium , increasing this lining to a thickness of 3 to 5 mm. • The estrogen -dominant proliferative phase lasts from the end of menstruation to ovulation.
