Tc-99m is a radioactive isotope that works by emitting gamma rays in the targeted tissue or organ. These gamma rays are then detected and recorded by specialized gamma camera for medical imaging purposes . The radioactive technetium can be chelated to several different compounds to create specific radiopharmaceuticals and optimize imaging of various structures . The half-life of Tc-99m is 6 hours. It produces gamma rays of 140 keV. It is a pure gamma emitter as it is in a metastable state . It decays to the stable isotope of ruthenium-99. Other options : Iodine-125, caesium -137, and iridium-192 are used in radiotherapy.406

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: An 84-year-old man has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease . Which of the following can be used to assess his cerebral perfusion ?
mcqs.explanation: Tc-HMPAO (technetium -99m hexamethyl propylenamine oxime) SPECT is used for the assessment of cerebral perfusion . In Alzheimer's disease , it shows reduced perfusion of the temporoparietal region. Other options : Option B: In -111 (Indium) DTPA is injected intrathecally to assess CSF flow . Option C: Tc-99m (Technetium) MIBI is used for parathyroid scintigraphy . Option D: Tl-201 (Thallium) is used in myocardial perfusion scanning.

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: An oncologist orders a bone scan to assess for bony metastases in a 49-year-old woman with breast cancer. The radioactive isotope of which of the following is used ?
mcqs.explanation: Technetium tagged to various substrates is used for bone scans. The patient is injected with a small amount of radioactive material such as 600 MBq of technetium -99m-MDP and scanned with a gamma camera, a device sensitive to the radiation emitted by the injected material. MDP (methyl diphosphonate ) adsorbs into the hydroxyapatite crystals and accumulates in the areas of active bone formation. Given below is a bone scan demonstrating bony metastasis in the pelvis.Other options : Phosphorous (P-32) and Iridium (Ir -192 ) are used in radiotherapy.

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old woman who underwent a renal transplant 4 months ago comes for follow -up. Which of the following would you perform to assess her renal function?
mcqs.explanation: 407 Tc-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine ) scan can be used in the evaluation of renal transplant function and may also be used in transplant obstruction. The imaging findings of acute rejection are characterised by diminished flow . Tc-99m MAG3 radioisotope is eliminated through the kidney through both glomeruli filtration and tubular excretion and is a measure of both. Indications for 99mTc -MAG3 dynamic renography are as follows : • To assess divided renal function and urinary drainage where the collecting system is significantly dilated . • To assess differential renal function following surgery or procedure , for example , post-pyeloplasty. • To assess for a urinary leak or possible obstruction following the renal transplant. Other options : Option A: Tc-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) is used to evaluate renal structure and morphology, particularly in pediatric imaging for detecting scarring and pyelonephritis . It is an ideal agent for the assessment of the renal cortex. Option B: Tc-99m DTPA (diethylene -triamine-pentaacetate ) is cleared only via glomeruli and has no tubular excretion. Hence , it is used for direct measurement of GFR. Option D: Captopril DTPA is used for screening in patients with renovascular hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: Technetium 99m labeled RBC scan is useful in which of the following patients ?
mcqs.explanation: Tc-99m labeled RBC scan would be useful in patients 1, 3, and 4. The uses of Tc-99m labeled RBC scan include assessment of the following : • Assessment of cardiac function in congestive cardiac failure and congenital heart disease • Occult gastrointestinal (GI) bleed • Vascular lesions like hepatic haemangioma • Ectopic splenic tissue (splenosis ) Other options : Tc-99m labeled leucocytes are used in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD ). 18-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan is used in tumors, including solitary pulmonary nodules .

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A DMSA scan can be performed in all of the following cases except :

options.a: To look for renal scarring in a child with vesicoureteric reflux
options.b: To evaluate a patient with a duplex renal collecting system
options.c: To assess renal perfusion in a man with renal artery stenosis
options.d: To confirm the presence of an ectopic kidney in a patient

mcqs.explanation: Tc-99m DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan cannot be used to measure renal plasma flow as it can be only seen on dynamic scans. The Tc-99m DMSA scan is used for the assessment of renal cortex as it binds to the sulfhydryl groups in proximal tubules with longer retention than other agents . It allows better assessment of differential renal function. It is a static scan as opposed to dynamic DTPA or MAG3 scans . It is408 used for the following : • Evaluation of renal structure and morphology • Detection of scarring and pyelonephritis • Evaluation of renal anatomical abnormalities Note : Captopril DTPA is used for screening in patients with renovascular hypertension .

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 61-year-old stroke patient is scheduled to undergo cerebral perfusion scanning. Which of the following would not be useful ?
mcqs.explanation: 18F-FDG is a metabolic tracer that is a glucose analog tagged with positron-emitting fluorine-18. It has no role in measuring cerebral perfusion . The following radiotracers are used for the measurement of cerebral perfusion : • 82RbCl (Rubidium chloride ) • 15O-H2O • 13N-NH3 (Ammonia )

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old child is brought with recurrent episodes of blood in his stool . Meckel 's diverticulum is suspected . Which of the following can be used to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Tc 99m pertechnetate scanning is used to confirm the diagnosis of Meckel 's diverticulum. Tc 99m pertechnetate scan, a radionuclide imaging more accurate in the pediatric age group than in adults for Meckel 's diverticulum. It has a very high sensitivity and specificity for bleeding Meckel diverticula but is of little value in children with no history of rectal bleeding . Other uses of Tc-99m pertechnetate include : • Thyroid imaging • Parathyroid imaging for distinguishing from the thyroid gland • Testicular imaging • Gastric emptying studies , intestinal and rectal functional studies .

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old woman is being evaluated for severe leg and back pain. CBC shows Hb of 7 g/dl and serum creatinine is 2.3 mg/dl. A plain X-ray of her femur reveals the following . A bone scan in this patient would likely show which of the following findings?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario and image showing multiple lytic lesions are suggestive of multiple myeloma . This condition presents with cold spots on bone scans as there is a lack of compensatory osteoblastic activity. Multiple myelomas are the most common primary malignant bone neoplasm in adults arising from red marrow due to the monoclonal proliferation of the plasma cells .409

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old man is rushed to the ED with severe chest pain and is diagnosed with acute myocardial infarction. Which of the following can be used to assess the area of infarction in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Technetium 99m pyrophosphate is used in hot spot imaging in acute myocardial infarction. It accumulates in the damaged myocardium and the area of infarct appears as a hot spot .

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman is referred from a PHC for the evaluation of nodular thyroid enlargement. As part of the evaluation, she is planned for a radio uptake scan. Which of the following isotopes is not used in this test ?
mcqs.explanation: Iodine-127 is the stable isotope and is not useful for thyroid imaging. The following isotopes are useful in thyroid imaging: • Iodine-123 : Functional scan of the thyroid • Iodine-124 : Produces positrons and is used in PET scans • Tc 99m pertechnetate

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: A 43-year-old woman presented with recurrent headaches , palpitations , and sweating . Her blood pressure was found to be 170/110 mm Hg. Further testing revealed elevated urinary metanephrines . An MRI was negative . What is the next best step in management?
mcqs.explanation: This clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma . The diagnosis can be confirmed by gallium-68 somatostatin receptor DOTATOC PET scan. Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy shows increased activity in paragangliomas and is a useful technique for identifying extra-adrenal phaeochromocytomas . The compounds often used in molecular imaging with PET include 68Ga-DOTATOC, 68Ga-DOTATATE , and 68Ga-DOTANOC. They bind to somatostatin receptors with varying affinity for different receptors . This investigation is useful in the diagnosis of new lesions in patients with or suspected neuroendocrine tumors. Other options : Option A: C11 methionine PET is a radiolabelled amino acid, and tumour uptake reflects cellular proliferation and microvessel density . It is used in the grading of brain tumors, differential diagnosis and identifying recurrence. Option B: 18F-NaF PET uptake reflects blood flow and bone remodelling . It is used for imaging bone pathology by detecting primary and secondary bone tumours. Option D: 99mTc pertechnetate is useful for thyroid nodules , and ectopic gastric mucosa. Note : The investigation of choice for adrenal phaeochromocytoma is contrast-enhanced MRI.

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: Technetium -99m labelled heat -denatured RBCs are used to diagnose pathology in which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Technetium -99m labelled heat -denatured RBCs are used for specific splenic assessment and is gold-standard in splenosis . The uses of Tc-99m labelled RBC scan include assessment of the following :410 • Assessment of cardiac function in congestive cardiac failure and congenital heart disease • Occult gastrointestinal (GI) bleed • Vascular lesions like hepatic haemangioma • Ectopic splenic tissue (splenosis )

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: What is PACS in medical imaging?
mcqs.explanation: Picture archiving and communication system (PACS) is a modality of imaging technology that helps in image transmission from the site of acquisition of images, to multiple different sites at different locations. This is not only economical (film-less department ), but is also convenient to access multiple modalities (radiographs, CT, MRI, ultrasound) simultaneously at multiple locations within the hospital or across the globe . Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) is a standard for handling, storing, printing, and transmitting information in medical imaging. DICOM is used worldwide to store, exchange , and transmit medical images.

mcqs.subject: Radiology
mcqs.question: Radioactive iodine uptake scan of a patient showed the following result . This is suggestive of which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows low radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) suggestive of subacute thyroiditis . High RAIU is caused due to Graves' disease , endemic iodine deficiency , and HCG-induced thyrotoxicosis. In non-pregnant, hyperthyroid patients with physical examination suggesting nodular thyroid disease , radioactive iodine should be the initial test to determine the etiology . Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications to radionuclide imaging.411

Surgery.desc: General surgery, GI, hepatobiliary, endocrine, vascular & trauma surgery

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the normal urine output in adults ?
mcqs.explanation: The average normal urine output is approximately 1500 mL /day. A minimum urine output of 400 mL/day is essential to excrete the end products of protein metabolism . Fluid loss occurs mainly by four routes : • Lungs: Approximately 400 mL of water is lost in expired air every 24 hours. • Skin : In a temperate climate the loss is between 600 and 1000 mL /day. • Urine: The normal urine output is approximately 1500 mL /day. • Faeces : About 60 and 150 mL of water are lost daily in patients with normal bowel function.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which parameter is the best guide to monitor the adequacy of fluid resuscitation in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 12 Urine output is the best measure of organ perfusion and the best monitor for adequacy of fluid resuscitation. Adequate end-organ perfusion is best indicated by urine output of >0.5 to 1 mL /kg/h. However, it does not give a minute-to-minute value. The level of consciousness is an important marker for cerebral perfusion . The only clinical indicators of perfusion of the gastrointestinal tract and muscular beds are measures of lactic acidosis (lactate and base deficit ) and mixed venous oxygen saturation. Other options : Option A: Central venous pressure (CVP ) is the mean pressure in the superior vena cava , used for estimation of preload and right atrial pressure . Normal CVP ranges from 2 to 7 mm Hg (3 to 9 cm H2O). A sick or injured patient with a CVP <3 mm Hg is presumed to be volume depleted and may be given fluids with relative safety . However, CVP is unreliable in assessing volume status or left ventricular function with respect to resusitation . Options C and D: Blood pressure and oxygen saturation do not reflect body fluid levels .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A surgery resident during the rounds advised the intern to monitor the burns patient for adequate fluid resuscitation and also instructed him to give a bolus of 10 mL /kg body weight if the patient showed signs of hypoperfusion . All of the following are indications to give bolus fluid , except :
mcqs.explanation: A low hematocrit does not indicate a need for fluid resuscitation . Instead, a high hematocrit is an indicator of hypoperfusion . Urine output is the best measure to monitor for the adequacy of fluid resuscitation . Urine output should be between 0.5 and 1.0 mL /kg body weight per hour. If the urine output is below this, the infusion rate should be increased by 50%. If the urine output is inadequate and the patient is showing signs of hypoperfusion , then a bolus of 10 mL /kg body weight should be given. Signs of hypoperfusion include : • Restlessness with tachycardia, • Cool peripheries • High hematocrit

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the source of endogenous fluids in the body?
mcqs.explanation: The source of endogenous fluids for the body is due to oxidation of solid foodstuff . Fluid is derived from both exogenous and endogenous fluids . • Exogenous fluids - Water from beverages , water from food, etc • Endogenous fluids - Water released during oxidation of solid foodstuff Eg : Glucose + O2 \037 CO2 + H2O + ATP The amount of endogenous fluids formed is normally less than 500 ml in 24 hours . Howe ver, during starvation, this amount is supplemented by water released from the breakdown of body13 tissues .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a stab wound to the abdomen underwent an emergency laparotomy. After the damaged intestine was resected , less than 100 cm of jejunum remained and a jejunostomy was made. Which of the following is not true?

options.a: The patient is a net secretor
options.b: Water intake should be less than a litre a day
options.c: Ensure adequate resuscitation with hypotonic fluids

mcqs.explanation: Net secretors are patients that have less than 100 cm of residual jejunum and a jejunostomy . They should not be given hypotonic fluids . The total amount of hypotonic fluids (water) is restricted to less than a liter a day. They are encouraged to take glucose and saline replacement solutions . Solutions that have a sodium concentration of at least 90 mmol/L (e.g.WHO cholera solution ) are given. Antisecretory drugs which include H2-receptor antagonists, proton pump inhibitors, and the somatostatin analog octreotide , are also used . The patients with short bowel syndrome who have had a jejunostomy and more than 200 cm of small bowel resected , are divided into two groups : • Net absorbers- These patients have more than 100 cm of residual jejunum. They absorb more water and sodium from the diet that passes through the stoma. These patients can be managed without supplementary parenteral fluids. • Net secretors - These patients have less than 100 cm of residual jejunum. As they lose water and sodium from their stoma, these patients require supplements .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with Crohn's disease has multiple skip lesions in the intestine . Surgical resection of damaged areas is being planned . Removal of which part will cause steatorrhoea ?
mcqs.explanation: Ileal resection may lead to steatorrhoea. The ileum is the only site of absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts. Following resection of the ileum , the loss of bile salts increases and is not met by an increase in synthesis . Depletion of the bile salt pool results in fat malabsorption that presents with steatorrhea . The efficiency of water absorption in the jejunum is 44% and in the is ileum 70%. Resection of ileum causes reduced conservation of fluid . Loss of bile salts into the colon affects colonic mucosa, causing a reduction in salt and water absorption, which increases stool losses . Small bowel motility is three times slower in the ileum than in the jejunum. In addition, the ileocaecal valve may slow the transit. Resection of the ileum results in a significant enhancement of gastric motility and acceleration of intestinal transit.14

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 66-year-old diabetic patient with a frail built comes to the OPD. His wife is concerned about his recent weight loss and lack of appetite . Which parameters will you consider while assessing his malnutrition using MUST?
mcqs.explanation: Age is not a criterion used in MUST. Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) is a five-step screening tool to identify malnourished adults or adults at risk of malnutrition.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of a Ryle's tube ?
mcqs.explanation: The best position for a conscious patient to be in during the insertion of Ryle's tube (RT ) is sitting with neck flexion. The described position helps in directing the RT towards the esophagus and also prevents it from coiling in the oropharynx or entering the trachea. RT , also known as nasogastric (NG) tube , measures 120 -125 cm. It has 4 markings at 40cm (cardia), 50cm (body), 60cm (pylorus), and 70 cm (duodenum ) to indicate the approximate position after the placement . Indications for NG tube : • Feeding in patients with dysphagia , decreased appetite , or those who are nil per os (NPO) for medical or surgical reasons. • Aspiration of gastric fluid • Gastric decompression in cases of intestinal obstruction and paralytic ileus . • Zollinger-Ellison syndrome • Bowel irrigation The absolute contraindications for an NG tube are severe midface trauma, recent nasal surgery, and basilar skull fractures15 Steps for the correct insertion of RT in an adult : • Examination of the patient 's nostril for any anatomical abnormalities and then instillation with 10 ml of 1% lignocaine • NEX method is used to measure the length of the RT : Place the exit port of the tube at the tip of the nose. Extend the tube to the earlobe, and then to the xiphisternum. • The patient is asked to sit upright with partial neck flexion. The tip of the Ryle's tube is lubricated and passed along the floor of the nasal passage until a resistance is felt (corresponds to nasopharynx) • The patient is subsequently asked to swallow water to guide the tube through the esophagus into the stomach until the marked length (based on the NEX method ). • NG tube is finally taped to secure it in place . Confirmation of the correct position is done by: • Auscultation in the epigastric area while injecting a bolus of air • X-ray chest to locate the lead markers • Aspiration of contents and subsequently confirming gastric origin (pH <6 indicates gastric placement )

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient in your ward is to be started on enteral nutrition. All of the following can be used as means of delivery, except :
mcqs.explanation: A peripherally inserted central venous catheter (PICC) line is used for providing parenteral nutrition. The term enteral feeding means the delivery of nutrients into the gastrointestinal tract. This can be achieved with oral supplements (sip feeding ) or with a variety of tube -feeding techniques such as nasogastric tubes (Ryle's), fine-bore feeding tubes , surgical or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG).16

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young female patient with dysphagia is started on enteral nutrition. Which of the following complications is least likely to occur in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The complication least likely to occur in a patient with enteral feeding is hypoglycemia . Metabolic complications related to decreased or increased feeding are commonly seen in total parenteral nutrition. Complications of enteral nutrition 1. Tube-related (most common): • Malposition • Displacement • Blockage • Breakage/leakage • Local complications (e.g. erosion of skin/mucosa) 2. Gastrointestinal : • Diarrhoea • Bloating, nausea, vomiting • Abdominal cramps • Aspiration • Constipation 3. Metabolic /biochemical : • Electrolyte disorders • Vitamin , mineral, trace element deficiencies • Drug interactions 4. Infective: • Exogenous (handling contamination) • Endogenous (patient )

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which dietary component is lacking in patients started on TPN?
mcqs.explanation: Fibers are not included in total parenteral nutrition. Total enteral or parenteral nutrition necessitates the provision of the macronutrients, carbohydrates, fat and protein, together with vitamins , trace elements , electrolytes , and water.17

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A peripherally inserted central catheter line(PICC) was placed in a patient to provide parenteral nutrition. Following the insertion, a chest X-ray was taken, which appeared as shown in the image below . Which of the following is the ideal position of the tip of this catheter ?
mcqs.explanation: The ideal position of the tip of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line, is superior vena cava . Peripherally inserted central catheters are commonly used for providing parenteral nutrition therapy. They are inserted through veins in the upper arm , and guided into the central venous system , such that the tip of the catheter enters the superior vena cava . A chest X-ray is taken to confirm the position of the tip. PICC lines have the advantage of minimizing inconvenience to the patients and clinicians. However, if the patient develops thrombophlebitis , the PICC line may be destroyed . The image below shows (A) a typical PICC line (B) an illustration showing insertion of PICC line (C) a patient with PICC line inserted through the upper arm .The image below shows the chest X-ray confirming the position of the tip of the PICC line (arrows), in the superior vena cava .18

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are asked to place a central line for providing parenteral nutrition to a critically ill patient . Which vein is the most suitable?
mcqs.explanation: The subclavian vein is considered the most suitable vein for parenteral nutrition, as the catheter lies flat on the chest wall, which optimizes nursing care. Moreover, the rate of infection with subclavian venous access is lowest when compared to jugular access and femoral access . Disadvantages of subclavian vein central venous access : • Subclavian vein stenosis • Pneumothorax

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient has been on total parenteral nutrition via a central venous catheter for 5 weeks . All of the following should be done, except:

options.a: Monitor for any signs of sudden glucose intolerance
options.b: Electrolytes must be checked every 2-3 days
options.c: LFT , BUN must be done once weekly
options.d: Change central venous catheter tube every two weeks

mcqs.explanation: A central venous catheter is changed only if the infection is suspected or the catheter is blocked . It need not be changed every 2 weeks . Total parenteral nutrition (TPN), also referred to as central parenteral nutrition, requires access to a large-diameter vein to deliver the entire nutritional requirements of the individual. The dextrose content of the solution given is high (15% to 25%). All macronutrients and micronutrients are deliverable by this route. To monitor or prevent complications , the following steps may be taken: • Infections • Use subclavian vein preferably • Monitor development of glucose intolerance as it is the earliest sign of systemic sepsis • Metabolic complications19 • BUN and LFTs weekly • Serum electrolytes every 2-3 days • Intestinal atrophy • Provide at least some nutrients enterally if feasible

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient on total parenteral nutrition may develop a deficiency of _______
mcqs.explanation: A patient on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) may develop a deficiency of zinc, among others. The commencement of TPN may precipitate or accentuate underlying nutrient deficiency by encouraging anabolism. Complications of TPN: • Infections • Highest risk - femoral vein • Lowest risk - subclavian vein • Metabolic complications • CO2 retention and respiratory insufficiency due to excess calorie infusion • Hepatic steatosis and marked glycogen deposition • Cholestasis and gallstones • Intestinal atrophy • Mucosal atrophy • Bacterial overgrowth • Impaired gut immunity

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following fluids contain lactate ?
mcqs.explanation: Ringer's lactate (sodium lactate solution ) or Hartmann 's solution is a mixture of sodium chloride , sodium lactate , potassium chloride , and calcium chloride in water. It is used for replacing fluids and electrolytes in those who have low blood volume or low blood pressure and to treat metabolic acidosis in cases other than those caused by lactic acidosis. It is also used to wash the eye following a chemical burn. The following table shows the composition of crystalloid and colloid solutions in (mmol/L ). *Composition of Gelofusine is incorrect in Bailey 27th edition .Solution Na K Ca Cl Lact ate Colloid Hartmann 's 131 5 2 111 2920 Solution Na K Ca Cl Lact ate Colloid Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) 154 Dextrose saline (4% dextrose in 0.18% saline) 30 Gelofusine * 120 Gelatin 4% Haemacel 145 5.1 <1 145 Polygelin 75 g/L Hetastarch Hydroxyethyl starch 6%

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the earliest sign of post -operative volume overload in a patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest sign of volume overload in a patient is weight gain. The administration of isotonic fluids in excess of actual needs commonly results in excess volume expansion. This may be due to the overestimation of third-space losses or due to ongoing GI losses that are difficult to measure accurately. The average postoperative patient who is not receiving nutritional support should lose approximately 0.11 to 0.23 kg/day from catabolism. Other signs of volume overload include : Cardiac: • Increased cardiac output • Increased central venous pressure • Distended neck veins • Murmur GI: Bowel edema Pulmonary: Pulmonary edema

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Ileus is common in patients that have conditions associated with __________
mcqs.explanation: Ileus may occur in conditions associated with volume deficit . Ileus is a disruption of the normal propulsive ability of the gastrointestinal tract. The term is usually restricted to those disruptions caused by the failure of peristalsis , rather than by mechanical obstruction. Hypoperfusion to the bowel in a volume deficit state may result in ileus . The following table shows various signs and symptoms , in general , in conditions associated with volume deficit or overload.21 System Volume deficit Volume overload Genera l Weight loss,Decreased skin t urgor Weight gain,Peripheral edem a Cardia c Tachycardia, orthostasis/hyp otension,Collapsed neck vein s Increased cardiac output and central venous pressure ,Dist ended neck veins,Murmurs Renal Oliguria, Azotemia Nothing specific GI Ileus Bowel edema Pulmo nary Nothing specific Pulmonary edema

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which electrolyte abnormality is expected in patients experiencing a post -operative rise in ADH?
mcqs.explanation: The post -operative rise in ADH (Antidiuretic hormone) may result in hyponatremia. Postoperative patients are usually prone to increased secretion of ADH, which causes an increase in reabsorption of free water from the kidneys resulting in volume expansion and hyponatremia. Dilutional hyponatremia occurs when there is an excess of extracellular water relative to sodium. However, it is self -limiting as both hyponatremia and volume expansion causes a decrease in ADH secretion .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an important cause of hypokalemia?
mcqs.explanation: Hypokalemia may occur as a result of metabolic alkalosis, not metabolic acidosis. The following are various causes of hypokalemia: • Inadequate intake • Diet , potassium -free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN • Excessive potassium excretion • Hyperaldosteronism • Medications • Potassium losses • Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea) • Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses ) • Metabolic • Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy Vomiting leads to hypokalemia via complex pathogenesis . The gastric fluid itself contains little potassium, approximately 10 mEq/L . However, vomiting produces volume depletion and metabolic alkalosis.22 Volume depletion leads to secondary hyperaldosteronism leads to enhanced cortical collecting tubule secretion of potassium in response to enhanced sodium reabsorption. Metabolic alkalosis further increases potassium secretion by the collecting tubule due to the decreased availability of hydrogen ions.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with pancreatitis is most likely to have which of the following electrolyte abnormalities ?
mcqs.explanation: Pancreatitis may lead to hypocalcemia . This is because inflammation of the pancreas, may lead to sequestration of the calcium via chelation with free fatty acids. Other causes of hypocalcemia : • Massive soft tissue infections such as necrotizing fasciitis • Renal failure • Pancreatic and small bowel fistulas • Hypoparathyroidism • Toxic shock syndrome • Abnormalities in magnesium levels • Tumor lysis syndrome

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A cachexic patient with a BMI of 14 was brought to a nursing care facility . Calorie-rich food through a nasogastric tube was started . On day 3 of therapy , the patient suddenly developed a seizure . An ECG showed dysrhythmia. Which of the following findings is most likely?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of refeeding syndrome which results in hypophosphatemia , hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia . Refeeding syndrome is a potentially fatal condition that may occur due to rapid and excessive feeding of patients with severe underlying malnutrition due to starvation , alcoholism, delayed nutritional support , anorexia nervosa, or massive weight loss in obese patients . With refeeding , a shift in metabolism from fat to carbohydrate substrate stimulates insulin release , which results in the cellular uptake of electrolytes , particularly phosphate , magnesium, potassium , and calcium. These electrolyte disorders can result in altered myocardial function, arrhythmias, deteriorating respiratory function, liver dysfunction , seizures , confusion, coma, tetany , and death . Severe hyperglycemia may result from blunted basal insulin secretion . It can occur with either enteral or parenteral nutrition but is more common with the latter.23

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true regarding the Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol?

options.b: It can be used after colorectal surgery
options.c: Waiting for one week to start oral feeding
options.d: Discharge planning is started before the patient is even admitted to hospital

mcqs.explanation: Waiting for one week to start oral feeding is not a part of the ERAS protocol . Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) is an approach designed to speed the clinical recovery of the patient and reduce the cost and length of stay in the patient . It is achieved by optimizing the patient's health before surgery and then delivering evidence-based best care in the perioperative period . It includes : • Early planned physiotherapy and mobilisation • Early oral hydration and nourishment • Adequate pain control using regular paracetamol, NSAIDs, epidural and nerve blocks • Discharge planning is started before the patient is admitted to hospital and involves support from stoma care nurses, physiotherapist . • Early removal of ryles tube and early feeding techniques24

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common type of shock:
mcqs.explanation: Hypovolemic shock is the most common type of shock and to some degree is a component of all other types of shock. Shock is defined as a systemic state of low tissue perfusion which is inadequate for normal cellular respiration. Shock can be classified as follows :Shock Inciting mechanism Hypovolemic sho ck Reduced circulating blood vo lume (eg ., hemorrhage, dehyd ration)31 Shock Inciting mechanism Cardiogenic shoc k Failure of the cardiac pump (e g., myocardial infarction, car diac dysrhythmias) Obstructive shoc k Mechanical obstruction of ca rdiac filling(eg ., cardiac tamp onade, tension pneumothora x) Distributive shoc k Systemic vasodilation leading to organ hypoperfusion (eg ., anaphylaxis due to histamine release , sepsis due to the rel ease of bacterial products , spi nal cord injury due to sympat hetic failure) Endocrine shock Combination of hypovolemic , cardiogenic or distributive s hock.(eg ., hypo and hyperthy roidism, adrenal insufficienc y)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is treated for hypovolemic shock following a motor vehicle collision. Which of the following is not a compensatory mechanism that is anticipated to occur in this patient ?

options.c: Reduced perfusion to the GI tract

mcqs.explanation: The compensatory mechanism in shock reduces the perfusion to the skin, muscle and gastrointestinal tract and not to the kidney. As shock progresses , the body's cardiovascular and endocrine compensatory responses reduce the blood flow to non-essential organs by vasoconstriction. This occurs in order to preserve preload and flow to the kidneys, lungs and brain .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old male patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident . On examination, he had multiple injuries over his body and was found to be in class II hemorrhagic shock. The percentage of blood loss would be between :
mcqs.explanation: The percentage of blood loss in class II hemorrhagic shock is 15–30%, which amounts to a loss of 750–1500 mL of blood. The class II hemorrhagic shock is considered as a mild shock with heart rate more than 100 . It is associated with orthostatic hypotension , and the patient is usually anxious at this stage .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Following a road traffic accident , a 23 -year-old man presents with breathlessness . On examination , he has hypotension and distended neck veins. On auscultation , muffled heart sounds are heard. What is this condition primarily associated with?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of Beck's triad (hypotension , distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds) is seen in cardiac tamponade . Shock due to cardiac tamponade is primarily an example of obstructive shock.32 Obstructive shock is characterized by a reduction in preload due to mechanical obstruction of the cardiac filling of the left and/or right sides of the heart, which in turn leads to fall in cardiac output . Common causes of obstructive shock include : • Cardiac tamponade • Tension pneumothorax • Massive pulmonary embolus or air embolus Cardiogenic shock is due to primary failure of the heart to pump blood. It may be due to myocardial depression as a result of infarction, cardiomyopathy , blunt myocardial injury. Patients with cardiac tamponade may eventually develop cardiogenic shock as the myocardium is stressed against the obstruction.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man sustained a spinal cord injury as a result of a road traffic accident . On examination , his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg. All of the following findings can be seen in the patient except ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock. It is associated with bradycardia and not tachycardia. Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds. Neurogenic shock is usually secondary to spinal cord injuries due to vertebral body fractures of the cervical or high thoracic region that disrupts the sympathetic regulation of peripheral vascular tone. Loss of vasoconstrictor impulses results in increased vascular capacitance , decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output .The classic description of neurogenic shock consists of: • Hypotension associated with bradycardia (absence of reflexive tachycardia due to disrupted sympathetic discharge ) • Warm extremities (due to loss of peripheral vasoconstriction)33 • Motor and sensory deficits indicative of a spinal cord injury • Radiographic evidence of a vertebral column fracture

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Modified shock index is calculated using?
mcqs.explanation: • Modified shock index = HR/MAP • Original shock index = HR/SBP The shock index is a hemodynamic stability indicator. In patients with shock, it is a better predictor of mortality than blood pressure or heart rate alone. A shock index >0.9 is indicative of higher mortality. The modified shock index is a more sensitive indicator of tissue perfusion than the original shock index. In critically ill patients , the DBP decreases earlier than SBP, hence , the modified shock index using MAP is better suited to assess the severity of shock.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The peripheral vascular resistance is decreased in ____________
mcqs.explanation: The peripheral vascular resistance is decreased in distributive shock. It is the condition of reduced oxygen delivery where the primary physiologic disturbance is a reduction in systemic vascular resistance. It is unique among the types of shock in that there is a compensatory increase in cardiac output . The most common cause of distributive shock is sepsis . The causes of vasodilatation in various types of distributive shock: The following Table shows cardiovascular and metabolic characteristics of different types of shock.Type of distributive shock Cause of vasodilatation Septic shock Release of bacterial products (endotoxin) and the activatio n of cellular and humoral co mponents of the immune sys tem. Anaphylactic shock Histamine release Neurogenic shock (spinal cor d injury) Failure of sympathetic outflo w and adequate vascular toneHypovole mia Cardioge nic Obstructi ve Distributive Cardiac output Low Low Low High (in septic and anaphyla ctic shock)Low (in neurogeni c shock) Vascular resistance High High High Low34 Hypovole mia Cardioge nic Obstructi ve Distributive Venous pressure Low High High Low Mixed venous saturati on Low Low Low High Base deficit High High High High

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who was admitted with third-degree burns presents with light -headedness and oliguria on the third day of admission. On examination, the peripheries are warm and capillary refill is brisk . His pulse rate is 138/min. In which of the following types of shock do you see this presentation ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical presentation is seen in septic shock. In distributive (septic ) shock, the peripheries are warm and capillary refill will be brisk , despite the profound shock. In early stages (compensated stage ) of septic shock, the patient has clammy, warm peripheries . The latter is a distinct feature from other types of shock where peripheral vasoconstriction leads to cold peripheries . The patient will have decreased vascular resistance , inadequate afterload , abnormally high cardiac output , and tachycardia. In the later stages (uncompensated phase ) of septic shock, there is reduced venous return, preload, and reduced cardiac output with low blood pressure .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An 82-year-old man with a history of recurrent urinary tract infection presents with fever, tachypnea , and tachycardia. On examination, he appears confused and has hypotension . Which of the following is used as the initial treatment for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of septic shock. Crystalloids are the initial fluid of choice in the resuscitation of severe sepsis and septic shock. Septic shock is also known as vasodilatory shock (But remember vasopressors are not the first line). Management protocol for septic shock: Step 1: Immediate evaluation - Securing the airway (if indicated ) and correcting hypoxemia and establishing venous access for the early administration of fluids and antibiotics are priorities in the management of patients with sepsis and septic shock. Step 2: Initial resuscitative therapy - aggressive administration of intravenous fluids (IVF ), usually crystalloids are given at 30 mL /kg (actual body weight ) within the first three hours following the presentation . Empirical antibiotic therapy started within first hour. Step 3: Intravenous vasopressors are useful in patients who remain hypotensive despite adequate fluid resuscitation or who develop cardiogenic pulmonary edema . Vasopressor agents such as phenylephrine , noradrenaline are indicated in distributive shock states which include septic shock, neurogenic shock, etc . where there is peripheral vasodilatation, and a low systemic vascular resistance, leading to hypotension . But they are not the first-line treatment .35

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are a medical officer at the blood bank and receive several units of packed RBCs, platelets , fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate following a blood donation camp. Which among the following components would you want to use at the earliest ?
mcqs.explanation: Platelets have a shelf life of only 5 days and hence they have to be used at the earliest . They are usually stored on a special agitator at 20 –24 \260C. They are given to the patients with thrombocytopenia or with platelet dysfunction who are bleeding or undergoing surgery. Packed cells (PRBCs) are stored in a SAG-M solution (saline–adenine –glucose –mannitol) and has a shelf life of 42 days at 2–6 \260C. (Older storage regimens included storage in CPD – citrate–phosphate –dextrose solutions which have a shelf life of 2–3 weeks .) Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is stored at � 40 to � 50\260C, while cryoprecipitate is stored at -30\260C, and both have a shelf life of one years.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of esophageal varices presents with hematemesis . What is the optimal level of hemoglobin to be maintained in this patient through blood transfusions?
mcqs.explanation: The optimal level of Hb to be maintained, in this case, is 8 gm/dL. The indications for blood transfusion are as follows : • Acute blood loss: To replace circulating volume and maintain oxygen delivery . • Perioperative anemia: To ensure adequate oxygen delivery during the perioperative phase . • Symptomatic chronic anemia: without hemorrhage or impending surgery.Haemoglobin level (g/d L) Indications <6 Probably will benefit from tra nsfusion 6–8 Transfusion unlikely to be of benefit in the absence ofblee dingor impending surgery >8 No indication for transfusion in the absence of other risk f actors

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old male patient was transfused with 2 units of fresh frozen plasma following a road traffic accident . Within 2 hours of the transfusion, he became breathless and his oxygen saturation dropped to 88%. Chest X-ray showed batwing appearance . This condition occurs due to which of the following ?

options.d: Preformed IgM Ab to ABO Ag

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI ). The presence of antibodies against the Human Leukocyte antigen (Anti-HLA Ab) in the donor blood is implicated in the development of TRALI . TRALI is defined as an acute lung injury that is temporally related to blood transfusion and causes non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. It occurs within the first six hours following a transfusion. Screening for HLA antibodies has been introduced to prevent TRALI . TRALI usually results from the transfusion of donor plasma that contains high-titer anti-HLA class II antibodies that bind to recipient leukocytes . The leukocytes aggregate in the pulmonary36 vasculature and release mediators that increase capillary permeability . Testing the donor's plasma for anti-HLA antibodies can support this diagnosis. The implicated donors are frequently multiparous women. The transfusion of plasma from male and nulliparous women donors reduces the risk of TRALI .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old male who is on warfarin prophylaxis for atrial fibrillation presents with massive uncontrolled haemorrhage following a fall from height . Which of the following blood components can be used for emergency reversal of warfarin therapy in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCCs) are indicated for the emergency reversal of anticoagulant (warfarin ) therapy in uncontrolled hemorrhage. PCCs are highly purified concentrates prepared from pooled plasma. They contain factors II , IX and X. Factor VII may be included or produced separately . Fresh frozen plasma and platelets are used in management of coagulopathy . Fresh frozen plasma is used if prothrombin time (PT) or partial thromboplastin time (PTT) >1.5 times normal . Platelets are transfused if platelet count <50 x103 /ul. However, in the presence of non-surgical haemorrhage these tests take time to arrange and may underestimate the degree of coagulopathy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Cryoprecipitate is stored at a temperature of ________
mcqs.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is a supernatant precipitate of FFP (fresh frozen plasma) and is rich in factor VIII and fibrinogen. It is stored at � 30 \260C and has a shelf life of two years. It is given in low fibrinogen states or factor VIII deficiency.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old male patient was brought to the emergency room following a road traffic accident . Upon arrival , the patient was unconscious with blood pressure of 90/64 mmHg and a pulse rate of 139 per minute. He was immediately transfused with 4 units of packed RBCs. All of the following complications can occur in this patient except :
mcqs.explanation: The complication of massive transfusion includes hypocalcemia , not hypercalcemia . The lethal triad of massive transfusion includes acidosis, hypothermia , and coagulopathy . Other complications which can be seen in massive transfusion are: • Hypocalcaemia • Hyperkalemia • Hypokalemia • Hypomagnesemia

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young patient is brought to the emergency room following a motorcycle collision. On examination , the patient is drowsy and has decreased blood pressure due to bleeding from multiple injuries. 1 unit of packed RBCs has been obtained from the blood bank . What is the correct procedure for blood transfusion?

options.a: The blood should be brought to room temperature before the transfusion
options.b: Transfusion should be started within one hour of removal from the refrigerator
options.c: Transfusion of PRBC should be completed within 4 hours
options.d: The rate of transfusion of PRBC is 50mL per hour

mcqs.explanation: 37 The transfusion of packed RBCs (PRBC ) should be completed within a maximum period of 4 hours after the removal from the blood fridge . There is an increased risk of bacterial proliferation and loss of the function of blood components after they are removed from the storage temperatures . Hence , the transfusion should be started within 30 minutes of receiving the components from the blood bank . The packed RBCs should be infused at a rate of 100 -150mL /hour. Warming of blood is not needed when the transfusion is at normal rates. The transfusion should be completed within a maximum period of 4 hours.Duration times for transfusio n Blood products Start transfusion Complete transfusion Whole blood / PRBC Within 30 minutes of removi ng from refrigerator \035 4 hoursDiscard unit if this period is exceeded Platelet concentrate Immediately Within 30 minutes Fresh frozen plasma As soon as possible Within 30 minutes Cryoprecipitate As soon as possible Within 30 minutes

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a road traffic accident presented to the emergency room and requires a large amount of fluids to be transfused . Which of the following IV cannula is preferred ?
mcqs.explanation: Grey coloured IV cannula is required for this patient in order to transfuse large amount of fluids . The ATLS 10th edition guidelines state that 2 cannulae of atleast 18G should be used to gain vascular access in trauma patients . In this scenario requiring large fluid transfusions, the grey (16G) cannula would be preferable to the green (18G) cannula due to the higher flow rate.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the size of the cannula shown in the below image?
mcqs.explanation: The given cannula is 20 gauge IV cannula as its color code is pink.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of qSOFA?
mcqs.explanation: Sepsis is defined as a "life -threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection ." It lies in the continuous spectrum between infection and septic shock. qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU). It uses three criteria, assigning one point each for • low blood pressure (SBP\035100 mmHg), • high respiratory rate (�o 22 breaths per min) • altered mentation (Glasgow coma scale, <15).38 The score ranges from 0 to 3 points. The presence of 2 or more qSOFA points is a simple prompt to identify infected patients outside the ICU who are likely to develop sepsis . The primary method to evaluate the risk of organ dysfunction (sepsis ) in patients with suspected infection is by determining the Sequential (sepsis -related ) organ failure assessment (SOFA) score; which includes assessment of: • Circulation - Systolic BP & need for vasopressors; platelet count • Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 & need for mechanical ventilation • Mentation - Glasgow Coma Score • Hepatic function - Bilirubin • Renal function - Creatinine Organ dysfunction is identified by a SOFA score of �o The SOFA score is limited by its requirement of multiple laboratory tests which makes it complex and time-consuming. In order to simplify the scoring process , the "Sepsis - 3" task force recommended the quick sepsis -related organ dysfunction assessment "qSOFA" score. SOFA Vs qSOFA : • SOFA is a more comprehensive and accurate scoring system which is particulary superior to qSOFA in the ICU setting . • qSOFA is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment of individuals at risk for sepsis particularly useful outside the ICU. setting (i.e. ward / emergency department ). However, note that it was originally designed as predictive tool that calculates the risk of death from sepsis rather than a diagnostic tool. Thereby, the best description of sepsis based on "Sepsis -3" task force recommendations would be : • Suspected or documented infection with SOFA score �o 2 Or • Suspected or documented infection with qSOFA score �o Another score that has been used is the NEWS(National Early Warning Score). It ranges from 0 to 20 and is based on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, use of supplemental O2, temperature, systolic blood pressure , pulse rate and level of consciousness . �o 5 out of 20 is considered a positive score. Other scoring systems for sepsis : The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) score is no longer recommended as is it not specific to infection . The Logistic Organ Dysfunction System ( LODS ) score is not recommended as it is complex and has too many variables.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: All of the following are features of SIRS except :
mcqs.explanation: Respiratory Rate > /minute or (Not and) PaCO2 < 32 mmHg (Not <35 mmHg) would be a feature of SIRS (Systemic inflammatory response syndrome).39 Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is an exaggerated defense response of the body to a noxious stressor (infection, trauma, surgery, acute inflammation, ischemia, or reperfusion ) to localize and then eliminate the endogenous or exogenous source of the insult. SIRS is diagnosed when any two of the following are present : • Hyperthermia (>38 Degree Celsius) or Hypothermia (<36 Degree Celsius ) • Tachypnoea (>20/min) or PaCO2 < 32 mmHg • Tachycardia (>90/min) • White cell count >12 x 109 /liter or <4 x 109 /liter or >10% Band forms Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection .40

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument:
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Babcock's forceps .63 In Babcock's forceps , the distal part of the distal blade is curved with a triangular fenestra which allows soft tissues to bulge out. The tip is non-traumatic with transverse serrations. It has a lock in the proximal part. It is used to hold tubular structures such as parts of the bowel , fallopian tube , appendix , ureter, etc.Option A: Allis tissue forceps have distal blades , not opposing each other. The tip has got teeth in each blade that are opposing . There is a lock in the proximal part. It is used to hold skin flaps , fascia, aponeurosis , and the bladder wall.Option C: Lane's tissue holding forceps have got stout and thick distal blades with oval fenestrae . It has an opposing tooth on the tip and a lock in the proximal part. It is used to hold bulky and tough structures and lymph nodes .64 Option D: Kocher 's hemostatic forceps - It is identified by the opposing tooth on the tip and serrations in the distal blades . It is used to hold pedicles , tough structures , and cut ends of muscles . It is also used to hold ribs during rib dissection , gauze for blunt dissection , and resected bowel .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: For which of the following would you use the instrument shown in the image?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a sponge holding forceps . It is used to: • Clean skin with a swab dipped in antiseptic solution during all operations • Remove laminated membrane and daughter cysts during operation of hydatid cyst . • Hold the fundus and Hartmann 's pouch of gall bladder during cholecystectomy65 • Swab an abscess cavity • Hold the cervix during cerclage .Ovum forceps is shown below . It is used to grasp products of conception and prevent the crushing of the conceptus . They have no catch and the blades are slightly bent and fenestrated . The absence of catch minimizes uterine injury if accidentally caught . It is introduced with the blades closed and opened up inside the uterine cavity to grasp the products . The instrument is taken out with a slight rotatory movement. The rotatory movement not only facilitates detachment of the products from the uterine wall, but also minimizes the injury of the uterine wall if accidentally grasped .Pile holding forceps are used to hold haemorrhoids.66 Cord holding forceps are typically used to hold spermatic cords.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You notice your surgery resident use the given instrument to remove gall stones . Identify the instrument.
mcqs.explanation: The above instrument is Desjardin's choledocholithotomy forceps and is used for bile duct stone removal. It may also be used during the removal of kidney, ureteric , or bladder stones . This is a long and slender instrument. There are finger bows but no catch. The shaft is curved. The blades are small, without serrations, and fenestrated centrally .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: For what purpose would you use the instrument shown in the image?

options.d: To hold tough tissue like skin and fascia

mcqs.explanation: 67 The above image is of Lister's sinus forceps which are used for blunt dissection . It is used during Hilton's method of abscess drainage to break the bacterial loculi . It is also used for inserting or removing packing in the sinus cavity.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument:
mcqs.explanation: Doyen's mouth gag is used to keep the mouth open for intraoral surgery when retraction of the tongue is not required or desirable . Mostly used for tongue surgery. It is applied on one side of the mouth on the molar teeth .Option A: Doyen's retractor is used to retract the abdominal wall in abdominal and pelvic surgeries to expose the field of operation.68 Option C: Doyen's intestinal occlusion clamp is used for resection and anastomosis of the intestine in cases of: • Strangulated hernia • Accidental injuries to the gut • Intestinal growths • Gastric/intestinal bypass surgeries .Option D: Joll's thyroid retractor is a self -retaining retractor used in thyroid surgeries to retract skin .69

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument given in the image below :
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a Morris retractor with a single , flat transversely curved blade and a blunt projecting ridge with backward projection. Morris retractor can be single or double -bladed . It is used to retract abdominal wall incisions, loin incisions, subcostal wounds or any wounds in depth . It can be used to improve visibility on one side of an incision. Thus, it is valuable during the initial phase of a laparotomy.Other options : Option A: Deaver's retractor is a question mark -shaped stout , atraumatic retractor with a broad, gently curved long blade . It is used to retract the abdominal wall and viscera. Moist mops should70 be kept underneath prior to placing this retractor. It is used for major abdominal surgeries , bladder surgeries and lumbar sympathectomy .Option C: Czerny's retractor is a superficial retractor with a thick and small blade on one side and a biflanged hook on the other side in opposite directions . It is used in hernia surgery and laparotomy, especially during closure .Option D: Double -hook retractor consists of two hooks with a handle. It is used in excision of swellings like lipoma, neurofibroma and cyst . It is also used to hold the skin flaps when raising them.71

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following instruments would be best suited to retract the liver out of the field of operation while performing an open cholecystectomy ?
mcqs.explanation: The Deaver's retractor would be most useful in cholecystectomy as it is specifically designed for holding the liver up and out of the way. Deaver's retractor is used carefully to avoid damaging the liver. Some surgeons protect the liver with an abdominal pack before placing the blade on top .Doyen's retractor - It is used to retract the abdominal wall as well as the bladder for proper exposure of the lower uterine segment during a cesarian section .72 Morris retractor is a large retractor useful for providing maximum exposure in large incisions e.g., abdominal incisions. It can be used to improve visibility on one side of an incision. Thus, it is valuable during the initial phase of a laparotomy.Czerny's retractor - This is a double -ended retractor used to retract wound edges for intermediate -type procedures . One end has a blade with a lip which helps to retract without the edge slipping . The other end has two prongs and helps to retract the ends of an incision.73

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: During thyroidectomy , the given instrument was used to retract the strap muscles . Identify the instrument:
mcqs.explanation: The above image is that of a Langenbeck retractor. It is used for holding open wounds , as in an open appendicectomy . Option B: Dyball retractor is used in major abdominal surgeries to retract deeper parts of the abdominal wall, bladder , or uterus while operating on the rectum and entering the rectovesical or rectouterine pouch . It has a lip at the bottom of the blade to prevent slippage . Care should be taken when it is used to retract the liver as it may damage the liver parenchyma.Option C: Goligher retractor is a self -retaining retractor used in operations on the sigmoid colon and rectum, such as anterior resection and the upper end of abdominoperineal resection . The retractor is inserted with the side blades to separate the edges of the abdominal wall. The central blade is then inserted to keep the small bowel away from the operation site .74 Option D: Travers retractor is a self -retaining retractor used for intermediate -type operations, such as: • Herniorrhaphy • Groin dissection for varicose veins • Femoral embolectomy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the given instrument.
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Kocher 's thyroid dissector which is used during a thyroidectomy to dissect the upper pole of the thyroid. The instrument is blunt and therefore damage to the superior thyroid artery or external laryngeal nerve is unlikely.75

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the size of the given blade used for incision and drainage of a superficial abscess ?
mcqs.explanation: The size of the surgical blade shown is the 11 -size blade (stab knife) that has a triangular shape with an oblique edge and a sharp-pointed tip. Uses : • Incision and drainage (I & D) of an abscess • Insertion of drains and arteriotomy. Other options : Option A: The 10 -size blade is used for skin incisions. It has a curved cutting edge that tapers to a pointed tip. Option C: The 22 -size blade is often used for abdominal incisions. It has a flat, unsharpened back edge and a curved front cutting edge . Option D: The 15-size blade is used for minor surgical procedures (lipoma excision) and precise skin incisions. It is a smaller blade with a small cutting edge .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The type of knot seen in the image is:
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the suture material exiting the knot is on the same side as the entry i.e no cross-over is seen . This is seen in a reef knot. A knot is a fastening made of threads intertwined together or on themselves . Each knot consists of- 2 half-hitches placed in sequential throws. Squaring refers to tightening the knot/half-hitch in a manner that the threads lay flat due to the alternating direction of half-hitches in adjacent layers. Types of knots:76 • Granny knot: half-hitch over a half-hitch in the same direction. It has better -holding power than half-hitch • Reef knot: half-hitch followed by a second half-hitch after squaring. • Triple throw knot: Reef knot with another half-hitch knot for added security . Knots made with prolene sutures require 6-8 throws to prevent slippage . • Surgeon's knot: Modification of the reef knot with two half-hitches in the first layer. • Slip knot: Modification of either granny/reef knot formed when one end of the thread is kept taut while tightening the knot.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man presents to the emergency with a clean lacerated wound on his forearm. You use the given suturing technique to close his wound . Which of the following statements is false?

options.a: This technique has the least cut through rate
options.b: The wound edges should be everted
options.c: Interrupted sutures are used to approximate the wound
options.d: After the first bite , the needle should emerge at the of center the wound

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows interrupted sutures . Horizontal mattress sutures , not interrupted sutures , have the least cut-through rate. In mattress suture , the initial suture is inserted as an interrupted suture , but then the needle either moves horizontally or vertically and traverses both edges of the wound once again as seen in the picture .77 Continuous suture : For a continuous suture , the first suture is inserted in an identical manner to an interrupted suture , but the rest of the sutures are inserted in a continuous manner until the far end of the wound is reached .Subcuticular sutures : Small bites of the subcuticular tissues are taken on alternate sites of the wound and then gently pulled together thus approximating the wound edges without the risk of the cross-hatched markings of interrupted sutures .78

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: During an intra-oral procedure , the resident uses the given suture material to place sutures on the soft palate . What is this suture material called ?
mcqs.explanation: The suture material shown in the image is plain catgut . It is a yellowish absorbable suture material. Chromic catgut is brownish in colour. Vicryl is a violet-coloured absorbable suture material.Silk is a black-coloured , multifilament , natural, braided, and non-absorbable suture material. It is derived from the cocoon of the silkworm larva .79 Prolene is a blue coloured , monofilament, non-absorbable suture .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about chromic catgut ?

options.a: It is made from cat gut
options.b: It is made from rabbit gut
options.c: It is absorbed by enzymatic degradation and macrophage phagocytosis
options.d: It is tanned with nickel salts to improve handling and to resist degradation in tissue

mcqs.explanation: Chromic catgut is absorbed through macrophage phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation within 90 days. It is made from collagen derived from healthy sheep or cattle . It is then tanned with chromium salts to improve handling and resist degradation in tissue . The tensile strength lasts for 21 -28 days. It has a moderate tissue reaction as compared to plain catgut , which has a high tissue reactivity. It is used to ligate superficial vessels , suture subcutaneous tissues , and is used for stomas and other tissues that heal rapidly. It is not used in tissues that heal slowly and require prolonged80 support .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young man presented to the ER with a facial injury following a fight with his brother. On examination , there is a 2 cm linear lacerated wound over his right cheek . The best method of management would be:
mcqs.explanation: The best method for the management of face laceration is a subcuticular suture with poliglecaprone (monocryl). Subcuticular sutures are used in the areas of the skin where the cosmetic appearance is important. The suture material is taken from the subcuticular layer and the edges are gently pulled together . The wound heals with minimal scarring.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old male patient presented to the emergency department with an injured femoral artery following a stab injury to the right thigh. Which of the following suture materials would be ideal for the repair of the artery?
mcqs.explanation: Polypropylene (prolene ), a non-absorbable monofilament, is the ideal suture material used for vascular anastomoses . Vascular anastomosis requires an accurate and watertight closure . A non-absorbable material that provides tensile strength for a longer period is best suited . The material should also be non-braided to avoid platelet adherence to the suture material.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The surgeon requests the given suture material while performing a bladder repair. Which of the following statements is true regarding it?

options.a: It is made of polyglycolic acid

mcqs.explanation: The image given is of polyglactin (vicryl). It is absorbed by hydrolysis . Complete absorption occurs by 60–90 days. It is a violet, braided multifilament absorbable suture . It is a copolymer of lactide and glycolide in a ratio of 90:10 , coated with polyglactin and calcium stearate . It is used mostly for gut anastomoses , vascular ligatures , subcuticular wound closures , and ophthalmic surgeries .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: After which procedure will you use the tube shown in the image?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Kehr's T tube used after choledochotomy . The horizontal limb is placed in the common bile duct while the vertical limb is brought out like a drain .81 It allows bile to drain while the sphincter of Oddi is in spasm postoperatively . Once the sphincter relaxes , bile drains normally down the bile duct and into the duodenum . Common bile duct T-tubes should remain in for 10 days. The 10 -day period is required to minimize the risk of biliary peritonitis . Once the T-tube cholangiogram has shown that there is a free flow of bile into the duodenum and that there are no retained stones , it is removed. Some surgeons like to clamp the T-tube prior to removal. Residual obstruction may be amenable to stone extraction via the T-tube .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following are used to stop esophageal variceal bleed ?
mcqs.explanation: All the given options can be used to stop esophageal variceal bleeding . Image A shows the Sengstaken -Blakemore tube . It has 3 lumens - one aspiration port and 2 inflation balloons. They are: • Gastric aspiration port • Gastric balloon port • Esophageal balloon port The gastric balloon is inflated and tension is applied to the gastroesophageal junction. If this does not control the haemorrhage, the esophageal balloon is inflated as well , compressing the venous plexus between them. Only gastric contents can be aspirated .82 Image B shows the Minnesota tube . It has 4 openings - 2 inflation tubes and 2 suction tubes i.e. both gastric and oesophageal aspiration ports are present , which allows the aspiration of both gastric and esophageal contents . Images C and D both show an upper GI endoscope . They are used to identify the source of bleeding and once identified , sclerotherapy and endoscopic variceal banding are performed , which have been shown to control hemorrhage effectively . Banding has a lower rate of complications . If bleeding does not stop by banding/sclerotherapy , balloon tamponade should be tried. The protocol for the management of esophageal varices is given below .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient has the catheter shown below inserted for draining a large liver abscess . All of the following statements are true except :

options.a: It is a self retaining catheter
options.b: It may be introduced into the urethra to relieve bladder retention
options.c: It can be placed percutaneously through an existing nephrostomy

mcqs.explanation: 83 A Malecot catheter is never introduced per-urethrally . It is a self -retaining catheter with an umbrella or flower tip. It contains sulfur, hence is radio-opaque . It can be sterilized by boiling. Uses : • Suprapubic cystostomy • Perinephric abscess • Pyonephrosis • Cabot's nephrostomy • Subphrenic abscess • Cholecystotomy • Infected pseudocyst of pancreas • Amoebic liver abscess • Gastrostomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are an intern asked to catheterize a patient using a 16F Foley 's catheter . You are unable to catheterize the patient and decide to use a slightly smaller catheter . The ward sister gives you the following four fresh catheters . Which one would you choose instead ?
mcqs.explanation: The Foley 's catheter having a green coloured ring in the ballon port is of size 14 F. If there is difficulty in catheterization , then a lower French number should be preferred . The French scale refers to the external diameter of the catheter , and 1Fr is 0.3 mm in diameter .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Foley catheter ?

options.a: French in foleys catheter refers to external diameter
options.b: Silicone foleys can be kept for maximum of 2 weeks
options.c: Three way foleys is used for instrumentation
options.d: If there is peri-urethral leakage of urine after inserting a foleys , first deflating the balloon is tried

mcqs.explanation: 84 French with respect to Foley catheter refers to the external diameter of the catheter , and 1Fr is 0.3 mm in diameter . Option B: Latex Foley catheter can be kept for one week whereas silicone Foley catheter can be kept for up to 6 weeks (some studies say 2-3 months). Option C: Three-way Foley catheter , shown below , is used for irrigation and helps in preventing clot retention following surgeries like TURP.Option D: If there is peri-urethral leakage of urine after inserting a Foley , inflating the balloon slightly more or using a larger-sized Foley are the corrective measures .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument:
mcqs.explanation: Veress needle is used to produce pneumoperitoneum in laparoscopic surgery.85 A blunt trocar is passed through the sharp needle . Insufflation of the abdomen is accomplished with a Veress needle held at its serrated collar with the thumb and forefinger . Since the linea alba is fused to the umbilicus , the abdominal wall is grasped with fingers or a penetrating towel clip to elevate it away from the underlying structures .Option A: An aneurysm needle (shown below ) is used to catch small vessels and nerves.86 Option C: Tracheal dilator is used to keep the tracheostomy open .Option D: Urethral dilator is used to dilate urethra.87

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding laparoscopic surgery?

options.a: Hasson approach preferred in patients with prior abdominal surgery
options.b: Monopolar diathermy is more effective in preventing electrosurgical injury
options.c: Heparin can be used routinely in irrigation fluid during laparoscopic surgery
options.d: Oral feeding can be initiated after 4-6 hours following an uneventful recovery period

mcqs.explanation: Bipolar diathermy is more effective than monopolar diathermy in preventing electrosurgical injury during laparoscopic surgery. Option A: During laparoscopic surgery, an artificial pneumoperitoneum is produced by insufflation of the abdominal cavity with CO2 through a temporary port created by carefully perforating the abdominal wall and peritoneum . As a common practice , blind insertion of a Veress needle is performed to enter the peritoneal cavity. However, in patients with prior abdominal surgeries , there is a higher chance of bowel adhesions and bowel wall injury during blind insertion of veress needle . Therefore the Hasson approach is used for direct visualization while establishing the intraperitoneal access . Option C: Clot formation may take place during laparoscopic surgery as a result of intraoperative bleeding . The routine use of 5000–7000 units of heparin per liter of irrigation fluid helps to avoid the formation of clots . Option D: If there is no contraindication for enteral feeding (e.g bowel resection ) and no sign of ileus postoperatively, oral feeding can be initiated 4-6 hours after surgery. Initially, a liquid diet is initiated , and if well -tolerated light meals can be initiated .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While assisting on laparoscopic cholecystectomy , you notice the given instruments are used to create a pneumoperitoneum . Select the true statement :

options.a: Proper placement of the needle can be seen by reaspirating injected saline
options.c: It is the most widely used open technique for creating pneumoperitoneum
options.d: It involves blind puncture of the peritoneum

mcqs.explanation: The image is that of a Veress needle and trocar which is involved in blind puncture of the peritoneum . There are two methods used for the creation of a pneumoperitoneum : • Closed method • Open method88 The closed method using the Veress needle has a small but significant potential for intestinal or vascular injury on the introduction of the needle or trocar. Proper placement of the needle can be determined by the inability to re-aspirate injected saline. The normal insufflation rate is 4-6 litres/min.The use of the open technique for creating a pneumoperitoneum avoids the morbidity related to a blind puncture . To achieve this, a 1 cm vertical or transverse incision is made at the level of the umbilicus , stay sutures are applied , and the fascia is dissected . Free penetration into the abdominal cavity is confirmed by the gentle introduction of a finger. A Hasson trocar, shown below , is inserted and anchored, and pneumoperitoneum is created . This is the Hasson or modified Hasson approach. This method is preferred for patients who have undergone previous abdominal surgeries as the small bowel may be adherent to the undersurface of the abdominal wound .89

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the following instrument.
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a rectal temperature probe. Option B: NAVA is Neurally Adjusted Ventilatory Assist is a mode of mechanical ventilation. The NAVA catheter detects electrical activity signalling on the diaphragm.Option C: Swan Ganz catheter / Pulmonary artery catheter is used for right heart catheterization .90 Option D: A CVP transducer is used in critical care settings to monitor the central venous pressure . It is connected to a central venous line and a monitor.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the instrument.
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a Humby's knife. This instrument is used to harvest a split skin graft. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humby's knife is 0.3 mm.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which mode does the following waveform of cautery represent ?
mcqs.explanation: 91 Cutting is a mode of diathermy/electrosurgery . The cut current is a low voltage , continuous waveform. Cutting occurs when sufficient heat is applied to the tissue to cause cell water to explode into steam. Coagulation is the sealing of blood vessels . In coagulation , a heating effect leads to cell death by dehydration and protein denaturation. Blend is the combination of cutting and coagulation . Fulguration refers to destructive coagulation of tissues with charring . The diathermy matching is set to coagulation and a higher effective voltage is used to make larger sparks jump an air gap thus fulgurating the tissues .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the following instrument?
mcqs.explanation: The given instrument is a unipolar cautery /monopolar cautery . Other options : Option B: The bipolar cautery contains two tips , unlike unipolar cautery which has only one tip.
