The current flows between these two tips and hence it does not need a return electrode , unlike the unipolar cautery .92 Option C: The harmonic scalpel (shown below ) is a surgical instrument used to simultaneously cut and cauterize tissue . Ultrasonic energy is used in Harmonic scalpel where ultrasonic energy is converted to mechanical energy at the active blade .Option D: LigaSure vessel sealing system (shown below ) is a bipolar apparatus for sealing vascular tissue . It applies a high coaptive pressure during the generation of tissue temperature under \260C, hydrogen cross-links are first ruptured and then renatured, resulting in a vascular seal that has high tensile strength .93

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the principle behind the wound -healing procedure shown in the image below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC ) device to promote healing in chronic wounds . Principle: An intermittent negative pressure of -125 mmHg hastens debridement and formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds . Indications: Chronic wounds (such as diabetic foot ulcers , stage III and IV pressure ulcers), traumatic wounds , flaps and grafts, and dehisced incisions. Contraindications: • Exposed vital structures (organs, blood vessels , or vascular grafts) • Preexisting infection • Inadequate debridement of devitalized soft tissue or bone increases the risk of infection . • The presence of malignancy (Marjolin's ulcer). • An allergic reaction towards the adhesive used to maintain the vacuum seal . Though not an absolute contraindication, there is no appreciable benefit for ischemic wounds .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The following drain is placed after mastectomy . Identify the type of drain.
mcqs.explanation: The Romo Vac drain, depicted in the image, is a closed type of drain commonly used after mastectomy. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely collect the air or fluids that may accumulate . This enhances wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains are prophylactic in elective surgeries and therapeutic in emergency surgeries . Drains can be -94 • Open - They are based on the principle of gravity • Semi-open - Their action is based on capillary effect • Closed - They carry out their actions through suction Suction drains are commonly used in chest , breast, abdominal, thyroid, and plastic surgeries . They remove intraperitoneal secretions , anastomotic leaks, and blood from hemorrhage at the surgical site . Romo Vac drain is a negative suction drain closed drain kept in the subcutaneous tissue . Romo Vac drain is indicated in modified radical mastectomy , subcutaneous swelling excision, and amputations . Special types of drains: • Chest drains are connected to an underwater seal to aid the exit of air from the pleural cavity. They are used in pneumothorax, pleural effusion , and hemothorax. • After surgical exploration of the bile duct , the sphincter of Oddi goes into spasm. To facilitate drainage of bile , a T tube may be used . Drain insertion site care: The site of insertion of the drain is kept clean by drying and patting the drain insertion site with a clean towel after bath. The dressing is changed daily with folded gauze pieces placed below and above the drain site . Removal of drains: The catheter at the site is milked for residual collections . It is then clamped and the suture holding the catheter is cut. The tube is then gently pulled out and any clots at the perforation end are removed. The time of removal of drains for various conditions is as given below . • Drains used in surgeries like thyroidectomy are usually removed within 24 hours. Their main purpose is to cover postoperative bleeding. • In a mastectomy , a drain is placed for 5 days to collect serous collections . • Drains used to cover the colorectal anastomoses are placed for 5-7 days. • Common bile duct T-tube drains are usually placed for 10 days. • Drains for infections are removed when the infection subsides or when the content of the drain is minimal. After the drain is removed, a folded gauze is placed over the drain insertion area. The dressing can be removed after 24 hours. The patie nt may be given an antibiotic ointment to apply over the area for a week .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The instrument given in the image is:
mcqs.explanation: The given image is of a Jackson -Pratt drain. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely drain the air or fluids that may accumulate . They promote wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains can be: • Open : They are based on the principle of gravity • Semi-open : Their action is based on capillary effect • Closed : They carry out their actions through suction95 Jackson -pratt drain is a closed , air-tight drainage system that operates by self -suction. The drain is sutured in place on the skin at the site of insertion to promote stability . There are two main parts to a JP drain: • Hollow tube • Collection bulb The drain should be emptied as often as possible to allow the bulb to be compressed fully in order to maintain suction. This is usually done every 4-6 hours the first few days.Other options : Option A: Hemovac is also a closed type of suction drain which can typically handle larger amounts of fluid than the JP drain. Option C: Minivac is a closed wound drainage system under negative pressure used in minor surgeries . Option D: Corrugated drain is an open drainage system to remove excess fluid from the operated site .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Match the following :
mcqs.explanation: 1-B, 2-C, 3-A, 4-D is the correct option. Urine bags are used for the collection of urine. They are usually attached to a Foley catheter placed to drain the bladder . An underwater seal bag is used for the collection of fluid from the thoracic cavity. It acts as a one-way valve. This system allows air to leave the pleural cavity, but it cannot be drawn back in by the negative pressure that is created in the intrathoracic cavity. Nasogastric tube /Ryle's tube is used for nasogastric feeding /stomach wash/aspiration.96 A metallic suction cannula is used to clear the operative field by suctioning secretions , blood, and fluid.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The instrument shown in the image is used for screening a 50-year-old patient with a family history of rectal cancer. Till which structure can this instrument visualize?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a flexible sigmoidoscope which allows visualization till the splenic flexure . It measures 60 cm. Factors like the mobility and redundancy of the sigmoid colon can limit the extent of the examination. Option A: An anoscope measures 8-10 cm in length and is used to visualize the anal canal.Option B: The rigid rectoscope is useful for examination of the rectum and distal sigmoid colon. It is occasionally used therapeutically . The standard rectoscope is 25 cm in length .97 Option D: Colonoscopes measure 100 to 160 cm in length and are capable of examining the entire colon and terminal ileum . Complete oral bowel preparation is necessary for colonoscopy . Sedation is required due to the duration and discomfort of the procedure .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The position of the patient in the image shown below is known as:
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows a reverse Trendelenburg position, where the patient 's head is elevated 15 - 30 degrees higher than the feet . It is named so, as the position is reverse of the Trendelenburg position, where the head end is lower and the feet are at a higher level . The Trendelenburg and reverse Trendelenburg positions are used in surgeries that are required to move the abdominal viscera, such as the small bowel , away from the operative field . Restraints and sideboards are placed to prevent the patient from sliding from the bed . In laparoscopic cholecystectomy , the patient is placed in a reverse Trendelenburg position slightly rotated to the left . This exposes the fundus of the gallbladder which is retracted towards the diaphragm. Other options : Option A: Lloyd Davies's position is a 30-degree Trendelenburg position with the hips flexed at 15 degrees . It is used for rectal and anal canal surgeries like low anterior resection and abdominoperineal resection . It can cause compartment syndrome of the calves.Option B: Jackknife position is a modified prone position where the patient 's hips are supported on a pillow and the table is flexed at a 90-degree angle with the head and feet at a lower level . It is not used anymore due to the chest compression causing impaired ventilation leading to positional asphyxia. It was used for hemorrhoids and fissure surgery.98 The image below shows commonly used patient positions in the operating room:

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding robotic surgery?

options.a: It is associated with less blood loss compared to laparoscopic surgery
options.b: Robotic surgery cuts down the operating time significantly
options.c: The learning curve is longer with robotic surgery
options.d: It is associated with a shorter length of hospital stay

mcqs.explanation: Even though robotic surgery has multiple advantages, the operating time is increased significantly compared to laparoscopic or open surgery. Advantages of robotic surgery include : • 3D vision • Tremor reduction • Scaling of movements • Finer dissection and suturing99 • Less intraoperative bleeding • Reduction in the length of hospital stay • Reduction of wound complications Disadvantages of robotic surgery include : • More expensive than other minimally invasive procedures • Longer operative time • Longer learning curve • Loss of tactile feedbackDa Vinci system for robotic surgery100

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An infant delivered at full -term by normal vaginal delivery , presented with respiratory distress immediately after birth. Chest X-ray showed the following picture . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 111 The above X-ray chest shows intra-thoracic bowel shadows along with mediastinal shift suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The common clinical presentation is as follows : • Respiratory distress • Dextrocardia • Scaphoid abdomen Prenatal diagnosis is done by ultrasonography . Lung-to-head ratio (LHR ) is used to assess severity in patients with left -sided CDH. An LHR value of <1 is associated with a very poor prognosis, whereas an LHR >1.4 predicts a more favourable outcome . Option A: Hyaline membrane disease is a syndrome in premature infants caused by developmental insufficiency of pulmonary surfactant production and structural immaturity in the lungs . Option B: Meconium aspiration syndrome is the aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid , which can occur before , during or immediately after birth. Meconium is the first intestinal discharge from newborns, a viscous, dark -green substance composed of intestinal epithelial cells , lanugo, mucus, and intestinal secretions . Option D: During normal delivery , the compression of the rib cage while passing through the mother's vaginal canal helps to remove fluid from the lungs . However, newborns who are delivered via cesarean birth may have excess fluid in the lungs and therefore be hypoxic and develop transient tachypnea .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding congenital diaphragmatic hernia?

options.a: Most CDH defects occur on the left side
options.b: Occurs due to failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal in the developing fetus
options.c: Pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension significantly affects the prognosis
options.d: The posterolateral variant of this hernia is known as Morgagni hernia

mcqs.explanation: The posterolateral variant of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is known as Bochdalek hernia while the anteromedian variant is called Morgagni hernia. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia results from the failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal in the developing fetus . Typically in CDH, there is a left -sided posterolateral diaphragmatic defect allowing herniation of abdominal viscera into the chest . 80% of CDH develops on the left side .112 The following sequence of events in CDH leads to the development of pulmonary hypoplasia .Pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary hypoplasia are the most important prognostic factors in congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Other poor prognostic indicators in CDH : • The presence of liver in the thoracic cavity • Early respiratory distress , within 24 h after birth • Need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation • Herniation to the contralateral lung (right-sided hernia) • Treatment of congenital diaphragmatic hernia:113 Variable period of time (24-72 hours) is to be allowed for stabilization before surgical repair. Immediate respiratory support should be provided, including rapid endotracheal intubation and sedation . Bag and mask ventilation is contraindicated in newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia because it causes distension of the stomach which in turn may limit the expansion of the already hypoplastic lung. During surgery, the viscera are reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is closed using interrupted , nonabsorbable sutures . In most cases (80%-90%), a hernia sac is not present . If identified , it is excised at the time of repair.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Most common organ that herniates in Morgagni's hernia is ______
mcqs.explanation: The transverse colon is the most common herniating structure in a Morgagni hernia. Morgagni Hernia: • A hernia in the anterior part of the diaphragm with a defect between the sternal and costal attachments • The most commonly involved viscus is the transverse colon. Morgagni hernia:114

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is not true regarding a Bochdalek hernia?

options.a: Early respiratory distress leading to early diagnosis and treatment is a good prognostic sign
options.b: The contents of hernial sac commonly includes retroperitoneal fat, left kidney or spleen
options.c: The condition is diagnosed prenatally by ultrasonography .
options.d: Pericardial cyst is a differential diagnosis.

mcqs.explanation: Early respiratory distress , within 6 hours of birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign. Features of a Bochdalek hernia: • Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). • Early respiratory distress , within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign. • Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter . • Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest , with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds . • The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred. • Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect . If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including stomach may herniate. Diagnosis: • Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis. • CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation ) • High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion. Ultrasonography findings: • Polyhydramnios • Chest mass • Mediastinal shift • Gastric bubble or a liver in the thoracic cavity • Fetal hydrops115 Differential diagnosis: • Eventration • Cystic lung lesion (pulmonary sequestration or cystic adenomatoid Malformation) • Group B streptococcal sepsis : associated with delayed onset of symptoms and a CDH often on the right side . • Pneumothorax: always occurs on contralateral to the side of CDH. Treatment: Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair The viscera are reduced into the abdominal cavity, and the posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is closed using interrupted , nonabsorbable sutures . In most cases (80%-90%), a hernia sac is not present . If identified , it is excised at the time of repair. Conventional mechanical ventilation, high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are the 3 main strategies to support respiratory failure in the newborn with CDH. Good relative indicators of stability are as follows : • Requirement for conventional ventilation only • Low peak inspiratory pressure • Fio2 <50 If the defect is too large, a porous polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) patch is used .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common Gastrointestinal atresia?
mcqs.explanation: The most common Gastrointestinal atresia is duodenal atresia (60%) followed by jejunal and ileal atresia (20%). Colonic atresia is the least common type (7-10%). Duodenal atresias are commonly associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome. It occurs approximately in 1/10 ,000 births.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 3-day-old neonate presented with recurrent bilious vomiting. An X-ray erect abdomen is given below . What is the next best step in managing this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Explanation: The given clinical history with an x-ray showing a triple bubble sign is suggestive of jejunal atresia. The next best step is to perform a contrast study to localize the site of obstruction. Small bowel atresias present with intestinal obstruction soon after birth. • Bilious vomiting is the dominant feature in jejunal atresia • Abdominal distension is more prominent in ileal atresia116 A small amount of pale meconium may be passed , despite the atresia. Plain abdomen radiographs in a jejunal/ileal atresia case will show multiple air-fluid levels and dilated loops. They don't reliably distinguish small and large bowels in neonates and hence contrast studies are often required to localize the obstruction. Water-soluble enemas (Gastrogaffin, Hypaque) are particularly useful in differentiating atresia from meconium ileus and Hirschsprung disease . Contrast studies also help to rule out distal intestinal obstruction and occasionally may act therapeutically to relieve obstructions . In most cases of jejunal/ileal atresia, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is done. If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated , it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis. Other options : Option A: CT is not recommended for neonates owing to the harmful effects of radiation. Option C: USG abdomen does not help to localize the site of obstruction and is more useful in the diagnosis of intussusception , where there is an abdominal mass. Option D: Explorative laparotomy is not done for diagnosing intestinal atresias.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Bishop-Koop anastomosis is done for which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Bishop-Koop Anastomosis and Mikulicz enterostomy are done for meconium ileus . Meconium ileus (also known as DIOS - Distal Intestinal Obstructive Syndrome) is defined as intestinal obstruction due to inspissated meconium within the terminal ileum . In the Bishop-Koop procedure , the proximal distended limb is joined to the side of the distal small bowel . This is vented by a 'chimney' to the abdominal wall. The Bishop–Koop operation with its irrigating stoma is now only rarely used .• Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is the standard operation for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis .117 • Kasai procedure is done for biliary atresia. • Duhamel , Soave, Swenson procedures are done in Hirschsprung's disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An infant presents with copious bilious vomiting and abdominal distension on the 5th day of life . He had not passed meconium for the first 3 days after birth. An abdominal radiograph shows the presence of dilated bowel loops . What is the gold standard investigation for the given condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of Hirschsprung's disease . A rectal biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of Hirschsprung's disease . A rectal biopsy 2 cm above the dentate line is the ideal area for a biopsy . Hirschsprung's disease is a developmental disorder characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus and submucosal (Meissner ) plexus . Most infants present with abdominal distention and bilious emesis with failure to pass meconium within the first 24 hours of life . The initial investigation is a contrast enema. The area between the dilated and contracted segments is referred to as the transition zone. The affected part shows the absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophy of nerve trunks in the rectal biopsy . Other investigations for Hirschsprung's disease include : • Water-soluble contrast enema - shows the presence of contracted aganglionic rectum, transition zone, and a dilated normally innervated colon. • Anorectal manometry - shows the failure of the relaxation of the internal anal sphincter . Definitive surgeries for Hirschsprung disease are as follows : • Swenson procedure , where aganglionic bowel is removed and a coloanal anastomosis is performed. • Duhamel procedure , where the aganglionic rectal stump is left in place and the ganglionated normal colon is pulled posterior. • Soave procedure , where endorectal mucosal dissection is done within the aganglionic distal rectum . The ganglionated normal colon is pulled through the remnant muscular cuff , and a coloanal anastomosis is performed .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old child is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain. On performing emergency exploratory laparotomy, the following finding is noted . Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.a: Can be a lead point for intussusception
options.b: The most common presenting symptom is bleeding in younger children
options.c: It is a false diverticulum which extends from the anti-mesenteric side
options.d: Most common heterotopic tissue is gastric mucosa

mcqs.explanation: Meckel 's diverticulum is a true diverticulum, which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel . The diverticula which contain all the layers of the intestine are called true diverticula. Meckel 's diverticulum is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5-7 of gestation. The rule of 2's (Mnemonic for Meckel 's diverticulum) : • 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic) • 2% incidence118 • located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve • approximately 2 inches in length • Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age The most common presentation is painless , massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years. Meckel 's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception . A bleeding Meckel 's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect ectopic gastric mucosa. Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel 's diverticulum. A simple V -shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach. The following diagram shows the various anomalies that arise as a result of the failure of normal regression of vitellointestinal duct :

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A surgery resident is examining a child born with the following defect . Which of the following statements regarding this defect is false ?

options.a: The central defect of the abdominal wall may be more than 4 cm
options.b: This defect is usually not associated with other congenital anomalies
options.c: The overlying sac is made of amnion and peritoneum
options.d: This defect is a component of the Cantrell's pentalogy

mcqs.explanation: Omphalocele is usually associated with other congenital anomalies whereas gastroschisis is rarely associated with other congenital anomalies. Omphalocele refers to a congenital defect of the abdominal wall in which the bowel and solid viscera are covered by the peritoneum and amniotic membrane. • During normal development of the human embryo, the midgut herniates outward through the umbilical ring and continues to grow. • Between 10th-12th week of gestation , the midgut returns to the coelomic cavity and undergoes proper rotation and fixation, along with the closure of the umbilical ring. • If the intestine fails to return, the infant is born with the abdominal contents protruding directly through the umbilical ring, with an intact sac covering the abdominal viscera, termed an omphalocele .119 The sac is composed of an outer layer of amnion and an inner layer of peritoneum . It is seen in omphalocele and not in gastroschisis . Omphalocele can vary from a small defect with intestinal contents to a giant omphalocele in which the abdominal wall defect measures 4 cm or more in diameter . It may even contain liver. Omphalocele occurs in association with special syndromes such as: • There is a 60% to 70% incidence of associated anomalies, especially cardiac anomalies (20–40% of cases ) and chromosomal abnormalities. • Exstrophy of the cloaca (vesicointestinal fissure ) • The Beckwith-Wiedemann constellation of anomalies (macroglossia, macrosomia, hypoglycemia, and visceromegaly and omphalocele ) • The Cantrell's pentalogy (lower thoracic wall malformations like cleft sternum, ectopia cordis, epigastric omphalocele , anterior midline diaphragmatic hernia, and cardiac anomalies).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old lady delivered a neonate with the following defect . Which of the following statements about the defect is false ?

options.a: The defect is generally located to the right of the umbilical cord
options.b: Herniation of liver is commonly associated with this condition
options.c: The incidence of this defect is more in preterm babies
options.d: Serial reduction of eviscerated intestines maybe done for management

mcqs.explanation: The above image shows gastroschisis . Herniation of the liver is more commonly seen with omphalocele than gastroschisis . Gastroschisis represents a congenital anomaly characterized by a defect in the anterior abdominal wall. The abdominal contents protrude through this defect . It is the most common anomaly seen in babies born to mothers under 20 years of age . Unlike omphalocele , there is no overlying sac and the size of the defect is usually <4 cm. An orogastric tube is placed to decompress the stomach. For primary closure , bowel loops are reduced , fascia and skin are approximated . If the viscera cannot be reduced into the abdomen, a silo is placed at the bedside as shown in the image. The eviscerated intestines are reduced serially during 5 to 7 days, followed by operative fascial closure .120

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common extracranial solid tumour in infants and children is _______.
mcqs.explanation: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumour of childhood . While brain tumours are the most common solid tumour of childhood . Neuroblastoma is a malignancy of neuroblast cells in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia and typically presents as an abdominal or paravertebral mass. Raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymoses ) are seen in neuroblastoma due to orbital metastasis . Shimada classification is used for classifying neuroblastoma. Blue subcutaneous nodules represent skin dissemination of tumour and are associated with the blueberry muffin syndrome.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common site of rhabdomyosarcoma in children is _______.
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of rhabdomyosarcoma in children is the head and neck. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common pediatric soft tissue sarcoma and accounts for approximately 3.5% of childhood cancers. These tumours may occur at virtually any anatomic site but are usually found in the head and neck (25%), genitourinary tract (24%), extremities (19%) and orbit (9%). Retroperitoneum and other sites account for the remainder of primary sites . Rhabdomyosarcomas are the most common soft tissue tumors among children younger than 15 years and can occur at any site comprised of striated muscle . Rhabdomyosarcoma is classified into three types - embryonal, alveolar, and pleomorphic. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common type .121

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common malignant brain tumor in children is ________.
mcqs.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in children. They are usually midline. Most of them occur in the cerebellum and present with symptoms of increased ICP. Most common tumours in children: • Brain tumours are the most common solid tumours. • Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common brain tumour (usually not malignant). • Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumour. • Rhabdomyosarcomas are the most common soft tissue tumours.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A female baby born at 30 weeks of gestation was admitted to NICU for prematurity and respiratory distress . She was placed on CPAP and enteric feeds were started . On day 5 of admission, she became lethargic and there was distension of the abdomen. A plain radiograph of the abdomen shows the following findings. Which statement about the condition is false ?

options.a: Antenatal steroids have shown to reduce the occurrence of this condition
options.c: Modified Bell's staging can be used for this condition
options.d: Surgery is the treatment of choice for all stages

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and radiological findings are indicative of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). The absolute indication for operative management of NEC is the presence of intestinal perforation. Milder cases can be treated with gut rest, antibiotics, and parenteral nutrition. The radiograph shows the presence of multiple air bubbles within the bowel wall. This is called pneumatosis intestinalis and is a pathognomonic sign suggestive of necrotizing enterocolitis . Necrotizing enterocolitis is the necrosis of a portion of the bowel and is the most common gastrointestinal surgical emergency in the neonatal period . The single most important risk factor is prematurity . Other contributing factors are enteral feeding , ischemia, and infection . Administration of antenatal steroids is known to reduce the occurrence of NEC. It usually occurs in the first few days of life after the initiation of the enteral feeds . Some clinical features include : • Lethargy • Feeding intolerance • Bloody stools • Abdominal distension • Abdominal tenderness . The radiograph may show pneumatosis intestinalis , portal venous gas, ascites , and the presence of free air. The modified Bell's criteria is used for staging the severity of NEC.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child presents with jaundice and abdominal pain. On examination, there is a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium. MRCP reveals multiple dilatations limited to the intrahepatic bile ducts . Which of the following statements about this condition is false ?

options.a: Todani classification is used for this condition
options.b: This condition is also known as Caroli's disease
options.c: Central dot sign is a characteristic CT finding associated with this condition
options.d: Endoscopic sphincterotomy followed by surveillance is the treatment of choice

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Caroli's disease (type V choledochal cyst ). Liver transplantation is the preferred treatment of choice here.122 Choledochal cysts are cystic dilations of the common bile duct (CBD). They present with a triad of jaundice , a palpable upper quadrant mass, and abdominal pain. There are mainly five types of choledochal cysts . The original classification for choledochal cysts by Alonso–Lej, has been modified by Todani. MRCP is the investigation of choice . The beaded appearance of intrahepatic bile ducts on HIDA scan and central dot sign on CT are characteristic findings associated with Caroli's disease . The arrows in the image given below are pointing to the central dot sign.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 10 -year-old child came with complaints of pain over the right lower quadrant and lower back pain. On examination, the patient had pain over the right side of the hip on passive extension with a mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical history of lower back pain, mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin and pain on passive extension of the ipsilateral hip is suggestive of a psoas abscess . Psoas abscess is a retroperitoneal abscess , caused due to various etiologies . Previously, tuberculosis of the spine was the most common cause secondary to spreading infection from the digestive or urinary tract, which can cause psoas abscess . Nowadays , Crohn's disease is the most common cause . Patients present with flank pain, fever and chills, malaise and weight loss. They can have referred pain to the hip, groin or knee. When the swelling extends across the groin and below the inguinal ligament along the course of the iliopsoas , it becomes cross fluctuant across the inguinal ligament . Imaging is done by a CT scan, which shows a low-density mass with surrounding inflammation and infiltration of surrounding fat and gas or air-fluid levels .123 Treatment is done by percutaneous CT-guided drainage and appropriate antibiotics. Other options : Option A: Pyelonephritis is usually associated with a history of urinary tract infection and sudden onset of pain in the flank and hypochondrium, not the lumbar region. Option C: Appendicitis (retrocaecal ) can present with pain on passive extension of the hip (psoas sign), but the presence of a mass in the right lumbar region pointing towards the groin makes it an unlikely diagnosis. Option D: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency condition presenting with sudden onset pain in the scrotum, groin and lower abdomen, tenderness , redness and edema of the scrotal skin.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 3-year child is brought to the pediatrician for the evaluation of the lateral neck mass. On examination , a painless , soft , fluctuating mass is found in the lateral side of the neck, as shown in the image. The slip sign is negative , and the swelling is brilliantly transilluminant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 124 A soft , painless , brilliantly transilluminant, fluctuating mass found in the posterior part of the neck in a child, is most likely to be a cystic hygroma. Cystic hygroma is a lymph-filled sac that results from the obstruction of the lymph vessels during their development . It is most commonly present in the posterior triangle of the neck. The mass may be apparent at birth or may appear in early childhood due to the increased accumulation of lymph. Since the sac is filled with lymph, it is soft , fluctuating , and brilliantly transilluminant. Treatment: • Aspiration of the contents , followed by excision once the sac or capsule gets thickened by fibrous tissue . • Single cysts can be treated with sclerosing therapy . Commonly used sclerosants include OK–432 or Picibanil, which is a mixture of group A Streptococcus pyogenes strain, pure ethanol , interferon alpha-2a, and doxycycline . • Complete excision is done in case of multiple cysts . Option B: A branchial cleft cyst also presents as soft fluctuant swelling . It is present in the anterior neck and at the junction of the upper third and middle third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle . Option C: Lipoma is less commonly seen in children. The swelling is non-fluctuant and when palpated , the edge slips under the finger. This is known as the slip sign. Option D: Cervical lymphadenopathy is seen in children with infections of the parotid and upper respiratory tract infections . On palpation, they are firm and non-fluctuant .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common location of cystic hygroma is ________.
mcqs.explanation: Cystic hygroma, also known as cystic lymphangioma and macrocystic lymphatic malformation, is a congenital multiloculated lymphatic lesion that can arise anywhere but is classically found in the left posterior triangle of the neck. The other common sites are the axillary, mediastinal, inguinal, and retroperitoneal regions. It occurs as a result of sequestration or obstruction of developing lymph vessels . The cysts are lined by endothelium and filled with lymph. The image below shows a newborn with cystic hygroma on the right side of the neck.125

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old girl presented with a slow -growing, rubbery, non-tender swelling on the side of the neck as shown in the image. Examination shows the presence of freckles and skin patches over the face and trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: A lateral neck mass in a pediatric patient, which is non-tender and present in association with freckles , and hyperpigmented skin patches (cafe -au-lait spots ) is suggestive of neural tumor i.e. neurofibroma. Neurofibroma is a benign tumor arising from the connective tissue of the nerve containing ectodermal , neural and mesodermal connective tissue components . It can be single or multiple . It is the most common intradural extramedullary spinal tumor. Neurofibromas can be local, generalized (von Recklinghausen's disease ) or plexiform types . Patients present with mild pain or a painless swelling usually in the subcutaneous or cutaneous plane with tingling, numbness and paraesthesia along the distribution of the nerve. Complications of neurofibroma include cystic degeneration , erosion into deeper planes, cord compression and paralysis (spinal neurofibroma) and sarcomatous changes . Treatment is excision under general or regional anesthesia . Indications for surgery in neurofibroma include symptomatic patients (pain and pressure symptoms ), cosmetic problems and malignant transformation (5%). Option A: Cystic hygroma is a type of congenital lymphangioma. This swelling is soft and partially compressible , which shows positive fluctuation and translucency test . Option B: Chemodectoma or carotid body tumor is a rare tumor, most commonly present in the fifth decade and there is an association with pheochromocytoma . These patients usually present with a slowly enlarging, painless lump at the carotid bifurcation. Option D: A lipoma is a soft painless swelling . It shows the characteristic slip sign and is freely mobile .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A first-born, 5-weeks -old male infant presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. The abdominal radiograph shows the following finding. Which of the following will be the preferred investigation in this case?
mcqs.explanation: 126 The given clinical vignette and the radiographic image showing the presence of an enlarged gastric gas bubble (single bubble ) are suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS). Ultrasound examination is the investigation of choice for this condition. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) is characterized by abnormal thickening of the pylorus muscles in the stomach leading to gastric outlet obstruction. First-born male infants are at the highest risk . Infants usually present with • Projectile , non-bilious vomiting due to gastric outlet obstruction, most commonly between 3 and 6 weeks of age . • Olive-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium . • Visible peristalsis after feeding , moving from left to right, followed by projectile vomiting. • Metabolic abnormalities include hypokalemic, hypochloremic , metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Ultrasound examination confirms the diagnosis of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) in the majority of cases . The diagnostic criteria for pyloric stenosis are a muscle thickness of �o 4 mm and a pyloric length of �o 16 mm. Ultrasound signs seen in Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric stenosis are: • Target sign (Hypoechoic thickened pyloric muscle with a hyperechoic central mucosa) • Cervix sign • Nipple sign. • Antral nipple sign The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected before proceeding to surgery. The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is the standard surgical procedure for its treatment .127 The ultrasound image given above shows hypertrophied pylorus resembling that of the uterine cervix (cervix sign) and double -layered hypertrophic mucosa protruding into the stomach, (Nipple sign).The ultrasound image given above shows redundant pyloric mucosa protruding into the antrum - Antral nipple sign.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 2-month-old baby is brought to the outpatient department for a facial defect . On examination , the following findings were noticed . The soft and the hard palate are intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate management in this child?

options.b: Cleft lip repair at 9 to 12 months
options.c: Cleft lip repair at 4 to 6 months

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical image is that of a child with a cleft lip on the left side . The most appropriate management for this patient would be a cleft lip repair at 4-6 months. Etiology of the cleft lip can include familial, protein and vitamin deficiency , rubella infection , radiation, chromosomal abnormalities, maternal epilepsy and drug intake during pregnancy (steroids /eptoin /diazepam) Majority of the cases are unilateral and cleft lip alone is uncommon. Millard Criteria (Rule of 10 ) is used to undertake surgery for cleft lip. • 10 pound in weight • 10 weeks old • 10g% Hemoglobin Millard cleft lip repair by rotating the local nasolabial flaps is done. The most appropriate management for this patient would be cleft lip repair at 4 to 6 months. According to Delaire timing of cleft surgery - unilateral cleft lip alone can be operated in one stage operation and is done at 4-6 months. The different types of facial clefts are shown below :128 • Unilateral cleft lip with alveolar involvement • Bilateral cleft lip with alveolar involvement • Unilateral cleft lip associated with cleft palate • Bilateral cleft lip and palate • Cleft palate only129

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not expected to increase as an immediate response to surgical stress or trauma?
mcqs.explanation: Insulin levels in plasma are decreased in the immediate ebb phase of surgical stress or trauma. There are three phases in the physiological response to injury: • Ebb phase • Flow phase • Recovery phase . The ebb phase begins at the time of injury and is characterized by hypovolemia and decreased basal metabolic rate. The predominant hormones regulating the ebb phase are catecholamines , cortisol, and aldosterone . The following mechanism leads to a reduction in insulin secretion during this phase :Pro-inflammatory cytokines like interleukin-1, tumour necrosis factor \033, IL -6 and IL -8 are produced within the first 24 hours of injury. In the later flow phase , insulin secretion begins to normalize i.e., relatively increases. However, insulin resistance by target cells occurs because of a defect in the insulin receptor /intracellular signalling pathway . Thus, the perioperative period is characterized by a state of functional insulin deficiency .136

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Following a mass casualty , how would you triage the following patients ?
mcqs.explanation: The patients should be triaged as follows : Triage means 'to sort'. It is done to categorize the need for priority of patients in cases of mass casualties . START triage scheme stands for Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment.Patient Triage color cod e A patient with tension pneu mothorax Red A patient with 95% third-deg ree burns Black A patient with a laceration on the forehead Green A patient with a degloving inj ury Yellow

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The components of the Revised Trauma Score (RTS) include which of the following :
mcqs.explanation: The Revised Trauma Score (RTS) is a physiologic scoring system based on the initial vital signs of a trauma patient. Revised Trauma Score (RTS) includes : • Glasgow coma scale • Respiratory rate • Systolic BP The score range is 0–12 . A lower score indicates a higher severity of injury.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Trauma and Injury Severity Score (TRISS ) includes which of the following components ?
mcqs.explanation: TRISS (Trauma and Injury Severity Score) includes : • Injury Severity Score (ISS) • Revised Trauma Score (RTS) • Age • Mechanism of injury (blunt/penetrating).137

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old man sustained a roller crush injury of his left arm up to mid-humerus and was brought to the casualty . The duty orthopedician uses the MESS score to decide about limb salvage. The score does not include which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Neurogenic injury is not included in the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS ). The Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS ) is useful in deciding about limb salvage. The components of the Mangled Extremity Severity score are: • The energy that caused the injury, skeletal and soft tissue injury • Limb ischemia • Shock • Age of the patient .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is being done in a patient with suspected hemoperitoneum . Which of the following statements is not true?

options.a: Presence of more than 100 ,000 RBCs/mm3 is a positive finding
options.b: Presence of more than 200 white cells /mm3 is a positive finding
options.c: Aspiration of at least 10 mL of gross blood is an indication for laparotomy
options.d: Amylase levels more than 175 units/dL is a positive finding

mcqs.explanation: The presence of more than 500 white cells /mm3 in blunt trauma indicates a positive finding of diagnostic peritoneal lavage. Diagnostic peritoneal lavage detects the presence of intraperitoneal blood. Its use has decreased to virtually nil at many centres with the advent of the FAST examination. Indications for diagnostic peritoneal lavage are: • Abdominal pain or tenderness • Low abdominal rib fractures • Unexplained hypotension • Spinal or pelvic fractures • Paraplegia or quadriplegia • Assessment hampered by altered mental status due to neurologic injury or intoxication. Procedure : It is performed through a small infraumbilical incision with the placement of the catheter under direct vision. The supraumbilical approach is indicated in pregnant patients and those with pelvic fractures. Aspiration of at least 10 mL of gross blood is an indication for laparotomy. If no blood is aspirated , a catheter is placed and 1 L of Ringer lactate solution is instilled into the peritoneal cavity and then allowed to drain by gravity. At least 200 mL of lavage fluid should be recovered to allow for accurate interpretation. Disadvantages: • Neither qualitative nor quantitative • Cannot identify the source of hemorrhage • Relatively small amounts of intraperitoneal bleeding may result in a positive study • May not detect small and large injuries to the diaphragm • Cannot rule out injury to the bowel or retroperitoneal organs.138

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old professional boxer was brought to the emergency department following a blow to the abdomen. On examination, his vitals were normal , and his abdomen was tender on palpation . Which among the following is the best modality to assess the injury to the abdominal organs for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: A contrast-enhanced CT scan is the best diagnostic modality (gold standard) for stable patients with blunt trauma to the abdomen. It is a non-invasive and sensitive investigation. It can identify haemorrhage, intraabdominal as well as retroperitoneal organ injury. However, performing CECT is time-consuming (when compared to FAST) and therefore it can be used only in stable patients . FAST ultrasound is a limited examination directed to look for intraperitoneal fluid or pericardial injury as a marker of the underlying injury. The best imaging modality for hemodynamically unstable patients with blunt trauma of the abdomen is FAST.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young man is brought to the trauma unit following a road traffic accident . He is hemodynamically unstable . As an adjunct to the primary survey, the managing surgeon decides to do a FAST. Which of the following areas would not be visualized in this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: The left lower quadrant is not assessed in FAST examination. FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma ) is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries. FAST also stands for Focussed abdominal sonography for trauma. However, since FAST is not only used to assess abdominal injuries but also to assess haemopericardium in cases of pericardial injuries, the expansion Focussed assessment with sonography for trauma is preferred . It can be performed within 2-4 minutes . Technique of FAST examination: With the patient in the supine position, a 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer is used . Four regions may be scanned: • Subxiphoid transverse view - To assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries • Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant - To assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morrison's pouch . • Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant - To assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury. • Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region - To assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas . In an extended FAST or eFAST scan, left and right thoracic views are used to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes the correct sequence of evaluation in the FAST technique ?

options.a: Pericardial sac \037 Perihepatic region \037 Perisplenic region \037 Pelvis
options.b: Perihepatic region \037 Perisplenic region \037 Pelvis \037 Pericardial sac
options.c: Pelvis \037 Pericardial sac \037 Perisplenic region \037 Perihepatic region
options.d: Perisplenic region \037 Perihepatic region \037 Pericardial sac \037 Pelvis

mcqs.explanation: The correct sequence of evaluation in the FAST technique is Pericardial sac \037 Perihepatic region \037 Perisplenic region \037 Pelvis.139

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a history of blunt trauma is brought to the casualty and an eFAST examination is performed . Which of the following statements about the investigation is false ?

options.a: B-lines indicate a normal ultrasonographic finding of the lung
options.b: Stratosphere sign seen in M-mode USG is indicative of pneumothorax
options.c: It can be reliably used to detect less than 100 mL of free blood
options.d: It is unreliable for the assessment of the retroperitoneum

mcqs.explanation: FAST is not reliable in detecting less than 100 mL of free blood. Disadvantages of FAST: • Does not directly identify injury to hollow viscus • Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma • Unreliable for the assessment of the retroperitoneum . B-lines or "comet trails" are echogenic bright linear reflections beneath the pleura that are usually lost with any air between the probe and the lung tissue . B-lines' are expected in normal aerated lung and are visualized moving along with the sliding pleura. Excessive 'B-lines', especially in the anterior lung, are abnormal and are usually indicative of interstitial edema . Therefore, the presence of B-lines along with seashore sign indicates the absence of pneumothorax . The image below shows the seashore sign.Barcode sign which is also known as the stratosphere sign and lack of sliding movement in the lungs diagnosed by an M-mode USG is suggestive of pneumothorax.140

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An intensivist is evaluating a patient for brain stem death in the ICU. Presence of which of the following features should not be misinterpreted as evidence for normal brainstem function in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Babinski reflex , tachycardia, and normal systolic blood pressure can be occasionally seen in patients with brain stem death . So, this should not be misinterpreted as evidence for normal brainstem function Brain death is not characterized by decerebrate or decorticate posturing , which is a brain -originating motor response . Brainstem death is defined as the irreversible loss of cerebral and brain -stem function. Ideal criteria for brain stem death contain three essential elements : • Widespread cortical destruction that is re\037ected by deep coma and unresponsiveness to all forms of stimulation • Global brainstem damage demonstrated by absent pupillary light reaction and by the loss of oculovestibular and corneal re\037exes • Destruction of the medulla manifested by complete and irreversible apnea. Brainstem death entails testing twice , by two clinicians, to demonstrate the absence of: • Response to pain • Respiratory drive (apnea despite arterial PCO2 �o 60 mm Hg ) • Pupillary light reflex • Corneal reflex • Vestibulo -ocular reflex • Oculo -cephalic reflex The following manifestations are occasionally seen in brain dead patients and should not be misinterpreted as evidence for brainstem function:141 • Normal systolic blood pressure >100 mmHg • Movements originating from the spinal cord or peripheral nerve may occur • Sweating , flushing , tachycardia • Deep tendon reflexes , superficial abdominal reflexes , triple flexion response • Babinski reflex • Spontaneous movements of limbs other than pathologic flexion or extension response • Respiratory-like movements (shoulder elevation and adduction , back-arching, intercostal expansion without significant tidal volumes).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false regarding imaging in the primary survey of a trauma patient ?

options.a: Hemodynamically unstable patient should not be sent for CT scan
options.b: All patients should have chest X-ray PA view only
options.c: X-ray of the pelvis is essential in primary survery
options.d: X-rays in primary survey must also be done in pregnant women

mcqs.explanation: Chest X-ray and X-ray pelvis are taken in AP view in the adjuncts to the primary survey of a trauma patient .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a part of the primary survey?

options.b: Removing clothes to inspect for wounds
options.c: Taking CT scan of the patient

mcqs.explanation: Taking a CT scan of the patient is a part of secondary survey. Primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life -threatening pathologies first. The secondary survey includes investigations that help identify all other injuries, excluding the apparent ones. This includes X-rays of the spine and extremities and a CT of the abdomen, head , chest , and spine .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who sustained an RTA was brought to the ER in a semiconscious state . He makes incoherent sounds, withdraws from painful stimuli, and opens his eyes to painful stimuli. Calculate his GCS score.
mcqs.explanation: The GCS score in this patient is 8. Withdraws from pain = 4 Incoherent sounds = 2 Opens eyes to painful stimuli = 2 Total GCS score = 4 + 2 + 2 = 8.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who was admitted after a road traffic accident is put on mechanical ventilation. He opens his eyes on verbal command and moves all four limbs spontaneously . Calculate his GCS.
mcqs.explanation: The patients GCS is Eyes -3, Verbal-NT, Motor-6. It is calculated as follows : • Eye opening : Opening to verbal command - 3142 • Verbal response : In the case of endotracheal intubation, the verbal response score is noted as NT (non-testable) • Motor respone : Movement of all 4 limbs spontaneously - 6 Total GCS score is not recorded since one of the components is non-testable .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is considered balanced resuscitation ?

options.c: Maintain ph by ensuring acid-base balance
options.d: Fluid resuscitation by giving colloids and crystalloids

mcqs.explanation: Permissive hypotension is a part of balanced resuscitation in trauma management to avoid bleeding . Damage control resuscitation (DCR) i.e. balanced resuscitation is used in the settings of major trauma. It aims to control hemorrhage and prevent coagulopathy prior to the development of the trauma triad of death (hypothermia , acidosis, and coagulopathy ). The components of DCR include : • Permissive hypotension until definitive surgical control • Minimize crystalloid based resuscitation • Early use of blood products (PRBCs, FFP, platelets , cryoprecipitate ) in the ratio of 1:1:1 • Use of hemostatic agents such as tranexamic acid, recombinant factor 7a, prothrombin complex concentrates DCR has the following advantages: • Minimizes the impact of trauma-induced coagulopathy • Limits blood product waste • Reduces the complications that occur with aggressive crystalloid resuscitation .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs have a significant role in the mortality reduction of trauma patients based on the CRASH-2 trial?
mcqs.explanation: The CRASH-2 trial has shown mortality reduction in bleeding trauma patients by early usage of tranexamic acid (preferably within the first 3 hours) with a loading dose of 1 g over 10 minutes and then infusion of 1 g over 8 hours.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In a patient with massive haemorrhage, damage control surgery is being performed . What does this consist of?
mcqs.explanation: Damage Control Surgery refers to performing limited surgical intervention in order to arrest hemorrhage, control sepsis , and protect from further injury. This concept of tailoring the operation to match the patient 's physiology and staged procedures to prevent physiological exhaustion is called Damage Control Surgery. Furthermore, definitive repairs are delayed and not until the patient is hemodynamically stable and physiologically capable of sustaining the procedure . Crystalloid and colloid infusions are143 limited in order to avoid dilutional coagulopathy . The term Damage Control Surgery is borrowed from the military, which ensures the continued functioning of a damaged ship above conducting complete repairs which would prevent a rapid return to battle .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young man sustained multiple injuries following a road traffic accident . On examination, his pulse rate is 100 /min and BP is 85/60 mmHg. He is diagnosed with pelvic fracture and is suspected to have retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Which of the following statements is true?

options.a: Coagulopathy is corrected in phase II of damage control surgery
options.b: Definitive repair of injuries is done 12 -24 hours after phase III
options.c: Internal iliac artery ligation is done in phase II
options.d: Hypothermia and acidosis are corrected in phase I

mcqs.explanation: Coagulopathy is corrected in phase II of Damage Control Surgery. Damage control surgery is minimal intervention done to stabilize the patient and do the definite surgery later. It centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries. It consists of three phases : • Phase I - Initial Exploration: This phase consists of an initial operative exploration to attain rapid control of active haemorrhage and contamination. • Phase II - Secondary Resuscitation : This phase focuses on secondary resuscitation to correct hypothermia, coagulopathy , and acidosis. • Phase III - Definitive Operation: It consists of planned re-exploration and definitive repair of injuries. This phase typically occurs 48 to 72 hours following initial and after successful secondary resuscitation .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of the trauma triad of death ?
mcqs.explanation: Shock is not considered to be a component of the trauma triad of death . The trauma triad of death is a combination of clinical features that are seen in exsanguinating trauma patients and contribute to the majority of trauma-related mortality and morbidities. The triad includes : • Hypothermia • Coagulopathy • Acidosis During the resuscitation phase of trauma, adequate precautions should be taken to prevent the development of these features . • Hypothermia is prevented by maintenance of ambient temperature within the patient 's room, usage of prewarmed iv fluids , blankets, etc . • Coagulopathy can be prevented by judicious use of i.v crystalloids (<1-1.5 Lit), early initiation of blood and blood products , usage of tranexamic acid, etc . • Acidosis can be prevented by correction of shock, ensuring adequate oxygenation , usage of sodium bicarbonate, etc .144

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: All of the following can be done to transport a polytrauma patient who is conscious except ?

options.a: Strap their thorax, abdomen and lower limbs on a stretcher
options.b: Place in prone position to prevent aspiration
options.c: Put patient on lateral position and shift him immediately
options.d: Roll the patient onto a hard board

mcqs.explanation: Patients with polytrauma are shifted into a supine or prone position (not in a lateral position) by laying them over a firm surface to restrict spinal movement. As per ATLS guidelines , in patients with trauma, airway management is first done along with cervical spine stabilization. All trauma patients until proven otherwise are considered to have an injured vertebral column. The patients are placed supine on a firm surface without rotating or bending the spinal column and a rigid cervical collar (philadelphia collar) is applied . Aspiration can be prevented by putting the patient in the prone position and strapping can be done to provide further stabilization.Long spine boards with straps are helpful in the rapid transport of the patient from one place to another. The patient can be put on the long spine board by log-rolling (a technique where four people hold the patient and roll the patient like a log without allowing rotation or bending of the spine ). Conscious and alert patient indirectly means that they don't need intubation and their airway is patent . If the patient is unconscious always check the airway and if needed , endotracheal intubation must be done immediately by various methods . Preferably by direct laryngoscopy and intubation.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A man met with a road traffic accident , which resulted in paralysis of both his upper and lower limbs. He has not passed urine and tenderness is elicited in the cervical region. What will you advise regarding radiography?

options.a: The patient should not be shifted and portable x-ray machine should be used after neck stabilization.
options.b: Instruct the radiographer to take cervical and chest x-ray.
options.c: Instruct the radiographer to take cervical x-ray AP and lateral view without any cervical support .
options.d: Order a cervical x-ray and shift the patient from the trolley by himself .

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical situation suggests a cervical spine injury due to trauma. The patient should not be shifted and a portable X-ray machine should be used for radiography after neck stabilization. Management in a trauma patient with a suspected cervical fracture involves the following steps :156 • Spinal immobilization with a rigid cervical collar and a long spine board is the immediate step in the management of blunt/penetrating cervical trauma cases . • It is followed by a gross assessment of spinal cord function by eliciting extremity movement. Tenderness over the injured vertebrae or the presence of a deformity is indicative of an associated fracture. • Imaging is done by X-ray or CT. Portable X-ray machines are preferred to avoid further injury while mobilizing the patient . They are useful in visualizing thoracic and lumbar vertebrae but not the cervicothoracic junction. Cervical CT has been made the modality of choice in most emergency departments owing to the high quality of images that can be obtained .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old construction worker sustained an injury to his neck after falling from the tenth floor of a construction site . The first aid team that rushed to his rescue log rolled him. According to ATLS , what is the minimum number of people required for log-rolling this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The 10th edition of ATLS recommends at least 4 people for the safe manoeuvre of log-roll in patients suffering from trauma. • The first person is assigned to restrict the motion of the head and neck. • The second person is positioned on the same side of the patient 's torso. He manually prevents segmental rotation, flexion, extension , lateral bending , or sagging of the chest or abdomen while transferring the patient . • The third person is responsible for moving the patient 's legs . • The fourth person removes the backboard and examines the back. Note : In a patient known to have a fracture of the extremities , a minimum of 5 people are required to safely perform the log-roll manoeuvre.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about acute spinal injury is false ?

options.a: Hypotension in acute spinal injury is due to the loss of parasympathetic tone
options.b: Immediate respiratory suppression can occur due to the involvement of the phrenic nerve
options.c: Canadian C-Spine rule and NEXUS help to determine the need for radiographic evaluation
options.d: Patients with neurological deficits should be removed from the backboard as soon as possible

mcqs.explanation: 157 Hypotension in acute spinal injury is due to loss of sympathetic tone. The classic presentation of neurogenic shock is hypotension in the setting of warm, well -perfused extremities in a paralyzed patient . This condition requires intravascular volume expansion and vasopressor support . Option B: High cervical spinal cord injury (SCIs) may have immediate respiratory suppression . This requires airway management and ventilatory support because of paresis of the phrenic nerves. Hypoventilation can occur from paralysis of the intercostal muscles (injury to the lower cervical or upper thoracic spinal cord) or the diaphragm (injury to C3 to C5). Option C: Canadian C-Spine rule and NEXUS are validated clinical decision tools to help determine the need for radiographic evaluation and to clinically clear the cervical spine . NEXUS criteria: There are five criteria included under NEXUS . If a trauma patient meets all five criteria, then no radiography is required and the cervical c-spine collar may be removed. However, if any one of the criteria is met then radiography is done to evaluate further. The NEXUS criteria include : • No posterior midline cervical spinal tenderness • No evidence of intoxication • A normal level of alertness • No focal neurologic deficit • No painful distracting injuries Option D: Patients with or without neurological deficits should be removed from the backboard as soon as possible . A patient who is allowed to lie on the hardboard for more than 2 hours is at high risk for pressure ulcers .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old college student sustained a superficial injury to his neck during a bar fight . What is the probable cause of sudden death in this patient ?

options.b: Air embolism through external jugular vein

mcqs.explanation: Air embolism through the external jugular vein is a cause of sudden death in patients with superficial neck injury. All other structures are deeper structures, hence are not involved much in superficial injuries of the neck.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man presented to the emergency department after suffering injuries in the neck during an armed robbery. On examination, several bleeding lacerated injuries are visible at the front and lateral aspects of the neck. Which of the following is not an indication for immediate surgical exploration?
mcqs.explanation: Fluid responsive hemorrhagic shock is not an indication for immediate surgical intervention. The following are the indications for immediate surgical exploration of neck trauma. They are also known as the hard signs of neck trauma: • Pulsatile bleeding • Expanding hematoma • Air bubbling from penetrating injury158 • Absent radial pulse • Respiratory distress • Presence of neurological deficit • Fluid resistant hemorrhagic shock • Audible bruit or palpable thrill • Signs of stroke/ cerebral ischemia The presence of any of these hard signs indicates major neurovascular/ airway injury and is an indication for surgical exploration of the trauma region as soon as possible . Neck trauma is classified based on the different regions of the neck. • Zone I: thoracic inlet to cricoid, associated with maximum mortality. It contains large vascular structures as well as the trachea and esophagus . • Zone II : cricoid cartilage to the angle of mandible, most commonly prone to injury and most easily accessible for surgery. It contains the carotid and vertebral arteries, jugular veins, and structures of the aerodigestive tract. • Zone III : angle of the mandible to the base of the skull. Structures within zone III include blood vessels that are difficult to expose surgically . Management : • If the patient is hemodynamically unstable : neck exploration • If the patient is stable : • Zone II injury: Conservative management • Zone I and Zone III : Angiography and angioembolisation are indicated . If it fails then neck exploration should be done.159

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after suffering a stab injury to the lower chest . On presentation , he had bradycardia and hypotension which did not improve despite IV fluid administration. Chest radiography showed clear lung fields . What is the next step in management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a patient with a stab injury and hypotension not responding to IV fluids indicates persistent hypotension due to ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST. Cardiogenic shock or hemorrhagic shock are the most likely causes of persistent hypotension in a trauma patient . Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed . In patients with persistent hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done. Evaluation of CVP or ultrasound of the IVC may further assist in distinguishing between cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock. It is mostly fatal if not controlled , and requires immediate management. Blood and plasma transfusions are provided in a ratio of 2:1. Patients with persistent hypotension requiring surgical intervention include : • Blunt trauma and massive hemothorax • Penetrating trauma • Hemoperitoneum • Gunshot injuries to the chest or abdomen • Penetrating weapon remaining in place . Other options : Options C and D: CECT can be done only when the patient is hemodynamically stable . Option B: Tube thoracostomy has no role in this patient 's management since the X-ray shows clear lung fields .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: eFAST is least helpful in diagnosing which of the following conditions?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , eFAST(extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma ) is least useful in diagnosing retroperitoneal hematoma as the sensitivity of ultrasound for detecting retroperitoneal hematomas is extremely poor. FAST is a rapid, noninvasive bedside test that uses sonography to detect free fluid in the abdomen and assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries. Technique: • The patient is placed in a supine position • With a 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer the following regions are scanned : • Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries • Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant : assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch160 • Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant : assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury • Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates Left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax. Computed Tomography (CT Scan) is the investigation of choice for retroperitoneal injury, but it can only be done in a hemodynamically stable patient .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department following a high-speed road traffic collision. His heart rate is 124 beats /min and BP is 78 /56 mmHg on the right arm , and 64/50 mmHg on the left arm . A portable chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum but normal lung and cardiac silhouette . Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of aortic injury. The investigation of choice in this hemodynamically unstable patient is transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). In hemodynamically stable patients , the investigation of choice is CECT or CT angiogram. Traumatic aortic injuries are commonly seen in deceleration injuries (e.g. road traffic accidents ). The most common site of aortic injury is the isthmus, near the attachment of ligamentum arteriosum. Clinical features of aortic injuries: • Hypotension • Difference in blood pressure in bilateral limbs • Absent pulse in the unilateral limb • Widened mediastinum on chest x-ray Management • Volume replacement : fluid therapy and blood transfusion • Permissive hypotension : Beta-blockers, such as esmolol • Immediate surgical repair: • Endovascular stenting , or • Open surgical repair with Dacron graft

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A young man was rushed to the casualty with multiple rib fractures. On examination, you notice a paradoxical movement of the chest , and the patient is diagnosed with respiratory failure. How would you manage him?

options.d: Internal operative fixation of the fractures segments

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of flail chest with respiratory failure. Management of this condition is IPPV (invasive positive pressure ventilation). A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage . This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures i.e., 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places . The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well .161 On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards, and therefore , less air moves into the lungs . On expiration, the segment moves outwards . This is known as paradoxical respiration. The diagnosis is made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm, the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment can be observed for several respiratory cycles and during coughing . Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure. The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax. Treatment: • Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided. • Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates ) or epidural analgesia, and physiotherapy. • IPPV (Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for patients developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen . Treatment algorithm of treatment of flail chest with respiratory failure:

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident says that his bike handle hit the right side of his chest. On palpation , he had tenderness in the right upper chest . Chest radiograph shows a fracture in the right third rib. Which of the following should you not do while managing him?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of a rib fracture. Strapping is not done for rib fractures because it prevents the patient from taking deep breaths. This can lead to lung collapse . The vital step in the management of rib fractures is to reduce pain and prevent the development of pneumonia. Rib fracture causes intense pain during breathing and increases the risk of pulmonary infections as the patient is not able to cough forcefully . In mild to moderate cases , pain can be managed by intravenous opioids . In severe cases , patients may require epidural analgesia.162 In addition to adequate analgesia, chest physiotherapy like deep breathing, frequent coughing , incentive spirometry should be encouraged in these patients . This prevents the development of pneumonia and lung collapse . When chest wall injuries result in respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation should be provided.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.chapter: Trauma - Spinal, Thoracic and Abdominal Injuries
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old female presents to the ER with a history of RTA . On examination, GCS is 15/15, heart rate = 110/min, BP = 90/60 mmHg, and there is elevated JVP . The right chest is hyperresonant on percussion with decreased breath sounds . The left chest appears normal . But the patient is dyspneic and ecchymosis is noted over the chest wall. The abdomen was soft . The probable diagnosis is:
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of trauma with decreased breath sounds and a hyper -resonant note on percussion indicates pneumothorax. The presence of tachycardia, hypotension and elevated JVP is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax develops when there is a parietal or visceral pleural tear. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e. air enters the pleural space from the lung or chest wall during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration, leading to the collapse of the affected lung. It is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea , acute dyspnea , sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness ), neck vein distention , tracheal deviation away from the side of injury, decreased chest movements on the affected side , hyper -resonance on percussion on the affected side and absent or decreased breath sounds on the affected side .
