mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presents with a painless swelling of the neck. The histology of the tissue is as given in the image below . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The slide shows the histopathology of Hashimoto thyroiditis , with: • Follicular destruction • Reduced colloid with increased interstitial connective tissue • Small lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration • A well -developed germinal centre may be seen • Hurthle (Askanazy ) cells that have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm lining the follicles291 Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is also known as struma lymphomatosa or lymphocytic thyroiditis . It is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure. Clinical features : • Most prevalent between 45-65 years of age • More common in females • Painless enlargement of the thyroid • Hashitoxicosis: When the auto-antibodies attack and damage the follicles , there is a sudden release of thyroid hormones from these follicles . This leads to a transient phase of thyrotoxicosis . • Hypothyroidism : Since the follicles are damaged and cannot form the hormones anymore, these patients tend to be in a state of hypothyroidism. Diagnosis: • T3 and T4 are low • TSH is raised • Autoantibodies against: • Thyroid receptors • Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) • Thyroglobulin These patients are managed with thyroid hormone replacement therapy . In patients with long-standing goiter , there is a risk of compressive features and the development of thyroid lymphoma. Such cases can be treated with total thyroidectomy . It may also predispose to papillary thyroid carcinoma . Other options : Option A: Histological features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include polygonal to spindle -shaped cells in the form of nests , trabeculae or follicles . Small, round anaplastic cells may be found in some cases and amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. The given slide below shows medullary carcinoma of thyroid:292 Option C: Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by hyperthyroidism due to circulating autoantibodies . The thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to the TSH receptors , causing overgrowth of the thyroid gland and increased thyroid hormone synthesis . Histologically , there is acinar cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia with the absence of normal colloid in the tall columnar epithelium (normally the epithelium is flat with colloid ). Lymphoid infiltrates , consisting predominantly of T cells , along with scattered B cells and mature plasma cells , are present throughout the interstitium . Germinal centers are common. The given slide below shows Grave's disease :

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A middle -aged female patient presented with malaise, fever, and painful neck swelling . She had recently recovered from an episode of upper respiratory tract infection . Lab reports show slightly elevated T4 and ESR was 100 mm/hr. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of De Quervain's thyroiditis for which NSAIDs is the treatment of choice . In this condition, T3 , T4 and thyroglobulin may be raised due to the release293 of preformed hormones from the destructed follicles . De Quervain's thyroiditis (subacute or viral thyroiditis ) is a granulomatous enlargement of the thyroid gland, usually following a viral infection . It is an inflammatory condition and not an infection as the thyroid gland is inherently resistant to infection due to its extensive blood and lymphatic supply , high iodide content, and fibrous capsule . It predominantly occurs in women between the ages of 30-40 years. The condition is self -limiting, and management is symptomatic i.e. aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are used for pain relief , but steroids may be indicated in more severe cases . Note : Acute suppurative thyroiditis mimics De Quervain's thyroiditis in that it is often preceded by a pyogenic upper respiratory tract infection or otitis media. However, acute suppurative thyroiditis is more common in children.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old lady, with a painless neck swelling , presented with palpitations and weight loss. Thyroid function tests revealed elevated T3 and T4, low TSH, and negative TSH-R Ab. Iodine scan showed multiple thyroid nodules with increased iodine uptake . Initial anti-thyroid treatment was given. What is the next step of management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of toxic multinodular goitre . The next step of management once a euthyroid state is achieved is a near-total thyroidectomy . Toxic nodular goiters are often large, uncomfortable , and are prone to recurrence. In a developing country like India, a near-total thyroidectomy eliminates the risk of recurrence and simplifies follow -up. However, it causes immediate thyroid failure and necessitates lifelong thyroxine replacement . Option A: Toxic multinodular goitres may show a decreased response to antithyroid drugs or may even enlarge further. Therefore, surgical management is recommended . Option B: Sub-total thyroidectomy has chances of recurrence and hence cannot be a definitive therapy. Option C: Large goiters show decreased response to radioactive iodine and the chances of recurrence are also high.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What will be the most likely associated condition with increased TSH and low T4 levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Increased TSH and low T4 levels are seen in primary hypothyroidism . Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the only cause of primary hypothyroidism in the given options . Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure. It is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. They also have autoantibodies against thyroid receptors , thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin . Other options : Option A: Hypoparathyroidism is generally not associated with hypothyroidism , except in certain congenital multisystem disorders such as DiGeorge 's syndrome. Option C: Grave's disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism . It is an autoimmune disorder caused due to autoantibodies against the TSH receptor . There will be elevated T3 and T4294 levels with low TSH levels . Option B: A TSH-producing pituitary adenoma can have increased TSH levels , but there will be elevated T3 , T4 levels as well .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old hypothyroid female patient presents with a painless , hard anterior neck mass, which progresses over weeks to years associated with dysphagia . Physical examination reveals a hard, "woody " thyroid gland with fixation to the surrounding tissues . Which of the following investigations will confirm the provisional diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Riedel 's thyroiditis , which is confirmed by an open thyroid biopsy . FNAC is inadequate due to the firm and fibrous nature of the gland. Riedel 's thyroiditis is invasive autoimmune fibrous thyroiditis where thyroid gland tissue is replaced by fibrous tissue . It is an IgG4-related systemic disease characterized by: • Elevated serum IgG4 levels • Lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate • Abundance of IgG4 bearing plasma cells It is associated with other focal sclerosing syndromes including mediastinal, retroperitoneal, periorbital, retro-orbital fibrosis, and sclerosing cholangitis . Clinical features : • Occurs predominantly in women between 30-60 years • Painless, hard anterior neck mass • Progresses over weeks to years to produce symptoms of compression: • Dysphagia • Dyspnea • Choking • Hoarseness • Symptoms of hypothyroidism and hypoparathyroidism as the gland is replaced by fibrous tissue • Physical examination reveals a hard, "woody " thyroid gland with fixation to surrounding tissues Treatment includes surgery, high-dose steroids , tamoxifen, and thyroxine replacement .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via :
mcqs.explanation: The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via the neck and the most common type of goitre approached is the secondary retrosternal goiter . A goiter is considered to be retrosternal if at least 50% of the thyroid tissue is located intrathoracically. They can be primary or secondary. Retrosternal goiter presents with dyspnoea , stridor, and dilated neck veins. Pemberton's sign (venous congestion of the neck on the raising of hands above the head ) is seen .295 Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the neck is performed to assess the location of the thyroid. The definitive treatment is surgical excision of the ectopic thyroid. Other options : Option B & C: Median sternotomy (via chest ) is indicated in: • Primary mediastinal goiter • Malignant retrosternal goiter • Very large retrosternal goiter • Recurrence in the mediastinumPrimary retrosternal goiter Secondaryretrosternal goiter Occurrenc e 1% Majorityof retrosternal goiter s Origin Arise fromectopic thyroid tiss uein the chestNo connection with the thyroid tissue in the neck Arise from thedownward exte nsion of cervical thyroid tissu ealong the fascial planes of th e neck Blood sup ply Intrathoracicblood vessels Superior and inferior thyroid arteries

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre ?

options.a: Operated in all patients regardless of symptoms
options.b: Sternal incision is always required to operate
options.c: It receives blood supply from the thoracodorsal artery
options.d: Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

mcqs.explanation: Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach). Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary. • Primary : rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels . It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck. • Secondary: they are the most common type ; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre . It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels . The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms . If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia , tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms . Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head ). CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice . Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck. Other options : Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia .296 Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in: • Primary mediastinal goiter • Malignant retrosternal goitre • Very large retrosternal goiter • Recurrence in the mediastinum For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest , resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated . Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided. Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter ).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following patients with thyroid swellings is least likely to require surgery?

options.a: A 22 year old woman with FNAC report of Bethesda category IV
options.b: A 66 year old man with a positive Pemberton's sign
options.c: A 58 year old man with an FNAC report of Thy
options.d: A 16 year old girl with recurrence of thyroid cyst

mcqs.explanation: FNAC report of Thy2 i.e. non-neoplastic is not an indication for surgery. Indications for surgical management of thyroid swellings include : • Neoplasia : FNAC positive Thy3–5 and clinical suspicion • Age • Male sex • Hard texture • Fixity • Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy • Lymphadenopathy • Recurrent cyst • Toxic adenoma • Pressure symptoms • Cosmesis • Patient's wishes

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Pick from the following the usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy :

options.a: Rough handling of thyroid during surgery

mcqs.explanation: The usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy is inadequate patient preparation before surgery. Patient preparation pre-operatively involves ensuring a euthyroid state . Rough handling of the thyroid in thyroidectomy does not cause a thyroid storm. Though a significant amount of thyroglobulin is stored in the acinar cells , they are inactive unless converted to thyroxine (T3 and T4).297

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with toxic adenoma is being prepared for surgery. Which of the following statements is wrong regarding this?

options.a: Iodine may be given pre-operatively with carbimazole
options.b: Beta blockers administered pre-operatively must be continued post operatively
options.c: Nadolol is given in a once daily regimen pre-operatively
options.d: The last dose of carbimazole must be given 24 hours before surgery

mcqs.explanation: The last dose of carbimazole may be given the evening before surgery. Toxic adenoma is a benign functioning thyroid tumour, which usually presents as a toxic solitary nodule . It is an autonomously functioning tumour that does not respond to TSH. Treatment involves antithyroid drugs or radioactive iodine. This is followed by hemithyroidectomy as the surrounding normal thyroid tissue regains normal function. Traditional preparation of a thyrotoxic patient aims to make the patient biochemically euthyroid . There are two methods of preparation that can be used : • Carbimazole 30-40 mg per day is the drug of choice . When euthyroid (after 8-12 weeks ), the dose may be reduced . Beta-blockers, if used preoperatively , must be given on the morning of surgery and continued for a week post -op. • Propranolol 40 mg TDS or a longer-acting nadolol 160 mg once daily may be given to achieve beta-blockade. It is important to continue treatment up to 7 days postoperatively . Iodine may be given with carbimazole or a beta -blocker 10 days before the operation. It produces transient remission and reduces thyroid vascularity.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man was posted for Hartley-Dunhill procedure . What is done in this procedure ?

options.a: Total resection of lobes on one side , with partial resection on the other side
options.b: Partial resection of each lobe removing the bulk of the gland
options.c: Total resection of one lobe with partial resection of three lobes
options.d: Resection of two lobes with the removal of the isthmus

mcqs.explanation: Hartley Dunhill procedure involves total lobectomy on the affected side with sub total resection on the less affected side . Indication: Asymmetrical multinodular goiters especially in older patients .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are performing thyroidectomy in a patient with thyroid neoplasia . Where will you make the Kocher 's incision?
mcqs.explanation: The structures marked as "A" and "B" in the above image are thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage respectively. A Kocher transverse collar incision is typically 3 to 5 cm in length and is placed parallel to a natural skin crease 1 cm below the cricoid cartilage , which is marked as "B". Rose position is preferred for thyroid surgery. The patient is supine with a towel roll below the shoulder to enable neck extension of 30 degrees . The advantage is a blood-less field as there is decreased venous congestion . However, there is an increased risk of air embolism.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: At which of the following points is the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the highest risk for injury during thyroid surgery?

options.a: At the level of Berry's ligament as it enters the larynx
options.b: In the tracheoesophageal groove as it forms one side of the Beahrs triangle
options.c: Under the tubercle of Zuckerkandl on the posterolateral portion of the gland
options.d: As the nerve loops around the aorta

mcqs.explanation: The point at which the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN ) is at the highest risk for injury during thyroid surgery is at its entry point into the larynx. This point is at the cricothyroid joint, at the level of Berry ' s ligament .298 The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve. On the left , it recurs over the arch of aorta, and on the right over the subclavian artery. Beahrs' triangle or recurrent laryngeal nerve triangle is formed by: • Common carotid artery • Inferior thyroid arteries • Recurrent laryngeal nerveNote : On the left side , the nerve has more distance in which to reach the transesophageal groove. Hence it runs in a medial plane . On the right, there is less distance and the nerve runs more obliquely to reach the groove.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In the post -op recovery room, a patient who had undergone a thyroidectomy suddenly experienced dyspnea with stridor. He was immediately sent back to the OT. What is the most likely cause for the patient 's condition?
mcqs.explanation: Development of a hematoma post -thyroidectomy may lead to venous edema of the larynx. This can cause airway obstruction and respiratory distress . It is evacuated promptly at bedside or through surgical re-exploration. Complications of thyroidectomy : • Haemorrhage - most common complication overall • Nerve injury • External laryngeal nerve - hoarseness (more common) • Recurrent laryngeal nerve - hoarseness if unilateral, life -threatening aspiration and aphonia if bilateral • Respiratory obstruction • Laryngeal edema - most common cause of respiratory obstruction • Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy299 • Laryngomalacia • Tension hematoma • Hypoparathyroidism - infarction of parathyroids • Thyroid storm - inadequately prepared for surgery • Hypothyroidism • Recurrent thyrotoxicosis • Wound infection , stitch granuloma, keloid Option C: Venous embolism typically occurs after a prolonged period of immobilization.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who had undergone a retro-oesophagal goitre resection was found to have partial ptosis and loss of hemifacial sweating . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Horner's syndrome. The cervical sympathetic trunk is at risk of injury in invasive thyroid cancers and retro-esophageal goitres and may result in Horner's syndrome.300

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the first investigation you would advise to a patient with a large thyroid swelling ?
mcqs.explanation: Assessing the biochemical function of the thyroid i.e. thyroid function test (TFT ) is the first investigation done in any thyroid condition. Assessment of TSH, T3 , and T4 is done. However, TSH is most helpful in determining the management plan, especially in patients with thyroid nodules who clinically appear to be310 euthyroid . Modalities for evaluation of thyroid swelling include : • Laboratory evaluation • TSH • T3 • T4 • Thyroid imaging • Ultrasound • Radioisotope scanning • CT/MRI • Biopsy techniques • Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) • Tru-cut/core-needle biopsy

mcqs.question: A patient presents with a 2.5 cm neck swelling which is firm, non-tender, and moves on swallowing . TSH, T3 , and T4 levels are normal . An ultrasound reports the swelling to be cystic and regular with low suspicion for malignancy. What is the next step in the management of this patient ?

options.a: Perform an fine needle aspiration biopsy
options.d: Reassure the patient and monitor periodically

mcqs.explanation: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy needs to be performed for further evaluation of the nodule . In cases where the FNAC is inconclusive, tru-cut or open biopsy can be done. However, this is rarely required. mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: FNAC is useful in all types of thyroid cancers except _____
mcqs.explanation: FNAC is not useful in the diagnosis of follicular carcinoma of thyroid as it cannot differentiate between benign and malignant follicular lesion. Trucut biopsy is used to differentiate between them as follicular thyroid malignancy is defined by capsular and vascular invasion . Limitations of FNAC in thyroid disorders: • Cannot distinguish between follicular carcinoma and adenoma • Cannot distinguish between Hurthle cell carcinoma and adenoma • Not useful in Reidel 's thyroiditis

mcqs.question: Which of the following carcinomas of the thyroid arise from the marked cells ?
mcqs.explanation: The cell marked in the image is a follicular cell of the thyroid gland. Papillary, follicular, and anaplastic thyroid carcinoma are all cancers of the follicular epithelium of the thyroid. Hurthle cell carcinoma is a variant of follicular thyroid carcinoma .312 Classification of thyroid neoplasms : • Benign - Follicular adenoma • MalignantOrigin Type Primary Follicular epitheliu m DifferentiatedPapillaryFollicu lar Poorly-differentiatedAnaplast ic Parafollicular cells Medullary Lymphoid cells Lymphoma Secondary Metastatic Local infiltration

mcqs.question: What is the most common thyroid malignancy in iodine-deficient regions?
mcqs.explanation: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy in iodine-deficient areas. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy in iodine-sufficient areas, children, and radiation-exposed areas.

mcqs.question: A 58-year-old man with a Thy3 lesion on FNAC was posted for hemithyroidectomy . Histopathology of the frozen section is given below . What is the next step of management?
mcqs.explanation: Capsular invasion as seen in the image confirms the presence of follicular carcinoma . Hence, total thyroidectomy is the recommended management.313 As FNAC shows Thy3 lesion which is a follicular neoplasm , the frozen section of the excised specimen has to be evaluated . The presence of capsular or vascular invasion confirms the presence of follicular carcinoma . options.a: Thyroglobulin levels can be used to monitor patients for recurrence
options.b: Hematogenous spread is more common than lymphatic spread
options.d: Mortality rate is twice that of papillary thyroid carcinoma

Thyroglobulin trends may be used to monitor patients with differentiated thyroid cancer for a recurrence . Following total thyroidectomy , thyroglobulin levels must be undetectable . options.d: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented with a thyroid nodule . The USG showed an irregular hypoechoic mass with microcalcifications. Lymph nodes were not involved. FNAC showed a follicular neoplasm with predominantly Hurthle cells . Intra -op frozen section confirms capsular invasion . What is the most appropriate management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hurthle cell follicular carcinoma . The most appropriate management is total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection . Hurthle cell carcinoma is a variant of follicular thyroid carcinoma .As compared to follicular thyroid cancer, it has a poorer prognosis as it is more likely to metastasize . It is often bilateral and multifocal . The histological picture consists of predominantly oxyphil (Hurthle , Askanazy ) cells containing abundant mitochondria. It cannot be diagnosed solely by FNAC as these cancers are characterized by vascular & capsular invasion . mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old woman came to the surgeon with a thyroid swelling that had developed a year ago. On examination, the swelling was 3 cm in size, firm and immobile. Further, lymphadenopathy was present . A biopsy of the swelling is given below . Which of the following is incorrect regarding management and post -op care in this condition?

options.c: Thyroxine is withheld after the surgery

mcqs.explanation: The given histological image depicts papillary formation with a fibrovascular stalk, characteristic orphan annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies , diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection would be the appropriate management in this condition, because there is lymphadenopathy , although the tumour size is less than 4 cm. Surgical management of differentiated thyroid cancers (DTCs) is as follows : The other options: Option 1: Post thyroidectomy , calcium supplementation is given to all patients to prevent hypocalcemia. mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following describes lateral aberrant thyroid?

options.a: Defective development of the fourth pharyngeal pouch
options.b: Metastatic thyroid cancer in lymph nodes
options.d: Cystic swelling of the thyroglossal duct

mcqs.explanation: Lateral aberrant thyroid almost always represents metastatic thyroid cancer in lymph nodes . Thyroid tissue situated lateral to the carotid sheath and jugular vein found along the course of the thyroglossal duct was previously termed lateral aberrant thyroid. It is associated with papillary thyroid cancer in the ipsilateral thyroid lobe . The image given below shows the lateral aberrant thyroid.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which type of thyroid cancer has the best prognosis?
mcqs.explanation: 318 Patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma have an excellent prognosis with a >95% -year survival rate.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man came to the surgery OPD with a midline neck swelling . He does not have any other complaints. The patient had received chemoradiation for Hodgkin's lymphoma nearly 20 years ago. On palpation , the mass is about 3 cm in size, non-tender, hard, fixed , and seems to arise from the right lobe of the thyroid. TSH levels were raised. A radioiodine uptake study showed cold nodule . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The history of radiation therapy to the head and neck for Hodkin's lymphoma and a cold nodule on radioiodine uptake scan are suggestive of papillary thyroid cancer. Radiation exposure is an identifiable aetiological factor in the development of differentiated thyroid cancer (follicular and papillary thyroid cancer). The most important factor, however, is irradiation of the thyroid before 5 years of age . Thyroid lymphomas are non-Hodgkin's B-cell lymphomas. They present with B-symptoms like fever, night sweats , and weight loss in addition to neck swelling . Thus, thyroid lymphoma is an unlikely diagnosis. Thyroid lymphomas often develop in the setting of lymphocytic infiltration.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland. Laboratory studies reveal low T3 , T4, high TSH and the presence of anti-TPO antibodies . FNAC from the gland shows enlarged cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm . Which of the following malignancies is commonly associated with this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical case scenario is suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis . Thyroid lymphoma or malignant lymphoma is associated with long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis . Thyroid lymphomas are usually non-Hodgkin's lymphomas, often associated with long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis ). The clinical features include : B - symptoms i.e. fever, night sweats , and weight loss As FNAC cannot characterize lymphoma, Tru-Cut biopsy is preferred . Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are often sufficient . Total thyroidectomy is indicated only in residual /recurrent disease . A chemotherapy regimen (RCHOP) is the first line of management. R - Rituximab C - Cyclophosphamide H - Hydroxydaunorubicin (Adriamycin) O - Oncovin (Vincristine) P - Prednisolone

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 72-year-old woman has a history of papillary thyroid carcinoma left untreated for 2 years. She complains that the rapid enlargement in her neck swelling over the last month has made it difficult for her to swallow and talk. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.a: Local invasion of the surrounding structures

mcqs.explanation: An elderly woman with rapidly enlarging neck mass and dysphagia in the setting of an untreated papillary carcinoma suggests a diagnosis of anaplastic thyroid cancer. Anaplastic thyroid cancer, a poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma , is the most aggressive cancer and has the worst prognosis of all thyroid malignancies.319 It usually occurs in elderly females . The typical manifestation is an with rapidly enlarging neck mass, dysphagia, and cervical tenderness . Patients usually have a history of untreated differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC). Local invasion to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) causes hoarseness . It may also cause tracheal obstruction. Distant metastasis is more common in the lungs via the hematogenous route. Diagnosis is made by FNAC. However, trucut /open biopsy is frequently used to confirm the diagnosis in cases of doubt . Management : • If metastasis is absent: Total thyroidectomy + LN dissection • If metastasis is present : Palliative care with chemotherapy and radiotherapy • If tracheal obstruction: Isthmectomy to relieve obstruction

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old woman was brought in a dehydrated state and complains of loose stools . On examination , a tender neck swelling was found which was found to be present for 1 year. Histopathology of the swelling shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Histopathology shows the presence of amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules . Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a tumor of parafollicular or C cells of the thyroid gland. They are derived from the neural crest cells of the ultimobranchial bodies . Most of the MTCs occur sporadically . However, around a quarter of the cancers are associated with familial MTC, MEN2A, and MEN2B. Patients with sporadic MTC present at an older age , whereas patients with familial MTC usually present at a younger age . Features of MTC include : • Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy • Dysphagia , dysphonia or dyspnea if locally invaded • Diarrhoea due to increased intestinal motility by serotonin • Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production • Metastasis is blood-borne • Microscopically , they consist of sheets of neoplastic cells separated by collagen and amyloid stroma It is diagnosed by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin, CEA levels , and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass. Total thyroidectomy with central neck node dissection is the treatment of choice in MTC patients . External beam radiotherapy can be used in patients with unresectable tumors. Targeted therapy can be considered using vandetanib, sorafenib, sunitinib, and cabozantinib. Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1year of age in MEN2B mutation.320

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Choose the substances secreted by medullary thyroid carcinoma :
mcqs.explanation: Medullary thyroid tumors secrete calcitonin, serotonin, histaminadases , and CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma is posted for surgery. He is nearly 6.5 ft tall, with a slender build and elongated digits . What is the screening test that should be done pre-operatively ?
mcqs.explanation: This patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma and features of marfanoid habitus (very tall patient with long, slender fingers and toes ) is suggestive of MEN 2B syndrome. Such patients are to be screened for pheochromocytoma by measuring urinary catecholamines . Pheochromocytoma, if present , should be treated first, and then MTC is to be treated next. A thyroid swelling with elevated calcitonin indicates a medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). MTC can either be sporadic (80%) or familial (RET gene mutation). In case of familial medullary thyroid carcinoma , stimulation with pentagastrin increases the release of calcitonin. This can be used for the screening of medullary thyroid carcinoma . MTC can be inherited as a part of autosomal dominant (AD) syndromes such as: • Familial MTC • MEN 2A • MEN 2B Prophylactic total thyroidectomy should be considered within 5years of age in MEN2A mutation and within 1year of age in MEN2B mutation. Note : Serum calcium is measured to screen for parathyroid adenoma in MEN 2A .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma . Which of the following could be used to screen the rest of her family?
mcqs.explanation: Screening of patients with familial MTC was historically done using pentagastrin stimulation test for calcitonin levels to make the diagnosis. Pentagastrin is a synthetic gastrin analogue . It acts on the CCK-B/gastrin receptor of the C cells and increases the basal rate of calcitonin secretion . Basal calcitonin level = total C cell mass x rate of secretion . Medullary thyroid tumors secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), but also other peptides such as calcitonin gene -related peptide , histaminadases , prostaglandins E2 and F2\033, and serotonin. Another test that can be used for screening is calcium-stimulated calcitonin levels .

mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old female was diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma . On USG paratracheal lymph node involvement was found. What is the best method of management of this patient ?

options.b: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection and RAI ablation
options.c: Total thyroidectomy with modified radical and central neck dissection
options.d: Total thyroidectomy with lateral and central neck dissection

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in patients with which of the following features :

options.b: Marfanoid habitus, multiple neuromas on the lip and familial pheochromocytoma ,
options.c: Dense lymphatic infiltration of the thyroid detected on FNAC

mcqs.explanation: Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated in MEN 2B syndrome as they can develop medullary thyroid carcinoma . This syndrome manifests as: • Pheochromocytoma • Marfanoid habitus • Mucosal neuromas • Medullary thyroid cancer. Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) can be inherited as familial MTC, MEN 2A or MEN 2B syndromes. These conditions are autosomal dominant and occur due to RET proto-oncogene mutation. As almost all cases of MEN 2B develop medullary thyroid cancer, a prophylactic thyroidectomy may be performed even during infancy. Option A: The most common malignancy in thyroglossal cysts is papillary thyroid carcinoma . In such a case, Sistrunk operation with total thyroidectomy is considered . Option C: Hashimoto's thyroiditis shows dense lymphatic infiltration of the thyroid detected on FNAC which is treated with thyroxine. However, total thyroidectomy is performed in malignant transformation to thyroid lymphoma. Option D: Upregulation of BRAF is associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma .

mcqs.question: What is the most common site of distant metastasis in patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: 322 Liver metastasis is more common in medullary thyroid carcinoma .Type of thyroid cance r Most common distant si te Papillary Lungs Follicular Bones Medullary Liver Anaplastic Lungs

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about the 8th edition AJCC staging of thyroid neoplasms?

options.a: In DTC, distant metastasis is IVB
options.b: In staging , age barrier is 55 years
options.d: N1a includes level VI and VII

mcqs.explanation: Minor extrathyroidal extension detected only on histological examination is removed from the definition of T3 disease and therefore has no impact on either T category or overall stage . Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: • The age cutoff used for staging is increased from 45 to 55 years of age at diagnosis. • N1 disease no longer upstages a patient to stage III . If < 55 years of age at diagnosis, N1 disease is stage I. If �o 55 years of age , N1 disease is stage II . • T3a is a new category for tumors > 4 cm confined to the thyroid gland • T3b is a new category for tumors of any size demonstrating gross extrathyroidal extension into strap muscles (sternohyoid , sternothyroid , thyrohyoid or omohyoid muscles ) • Level VII lymph nodes , previously classified as lateral neck lymph nodes (N1b) is re-classified as central neck lymph nodes (N1a) to be more anatomically consistent and because level VII presented significant coding difficulties for tumor registrars, clinicians and researchers. • In differentiated thyroid cancer, the presence of distant metastases (M1) in older patients is classified as IVB disease rather than IVC disease . Distant metastasis in anaplastic thyroid cancer continues to be classified as IVC disease . Minimal or occult /microcarcinoma are tumors 1 cm or less in size. They have no evidence of local invasiveness through the thyroid capsule or angioinvasion . Occult malignancies are usually not associated with lymph node metastases . However, about 25% of patients with these tumors have associated occult lymph node metastases . These are nonpalpable and are found incidentally at operative and histologic examinations or at autopsy . Anaplastic : • Unlike previous editions where all anaplastic thyroid cancers were classified as T4 disease , anaplastic cancers now use the same T definitions as differentiated thyroid cancer. • Intrathyroidal disease (T1 -3a) is stage IVA • Gross extrathyroidal extension (T3b ,T4) or cervical lymph node metastases (N1) is stage IVB • Distant metastases (M1) are stage IVC323 TNM staging 7th AJCC (2010 ) 8th AJCC (2018 ) Primary tumor(pT) TX Cannot be assessed -do- T0 No evidence of cancer -do- T1 Tumour \035 2 cm, intrathyroid alT1a : \0351 cm, intrathyroidalT 1b:1-2 cm, intrathyroidal -do- T2 2-4 cm, intrathyroidal -do- T3 >4 cm limited to the thyroid or any size with minimal extr athyroidal extension (muscle , soft tissue ) T3a :Tumor >4 cm limited to t he thyroidT3b: Gross extrath yroidal extensioninvading onl ystrap muscles (sternohyoid , s ternothyroid, thyrohyoid or o mohyoid muscles ) from a tu mour of any size T4 T4a Invades subcutaneous tis sue , larynx, trachea, esophag us, or RLNT4b Invades preve rtebral fascia or encases caro tid or mediastinal vessels -do- Regional lymph nodes (p N) NX Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed -do- N0 No lymph node metastasis -do- N1a Positive in level VI ; mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following will not be a treatment option for a pregnant patient with papillary thyroid carcinoma ?

options.b: Total Thyroidectomy plus Lymph node dissection

mcqs.explanation: Radioiodine ablation of thyroid is contraindicated in pregnant women due to risk of radiation exposure to the fetus . Therapeutic uses for radioactive iodine • In primary thyrotoxicosis after 45 years. • In autonomous toxic nodule after 45 years, it is useful as remaining gland still will function adequately after radiotherapy.325 • In follicular carcinoma of thyroid, after total thyroidectomy , if there are secondaries elsewhere in the body, as in bones or lungs , then I131 is given.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with papillary thyroid carcinoma underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection , a month ago. At present , a whole -body iodine scan is positive . What is the next step in management?
mcqs.explanation: Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole -body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma ). The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased , for example , by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks . A positive whole -body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation. A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue . They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin , TSH and USG-neck. If the tumour is resistant to radioiodine ablation, EBRT (external beam radiotherapy) is done.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A whole -body iodine scan is not useful in patients with which thyroid malignancy?
mcqs.explanation: After a total thyroidectomy , a whole -body iodine scan is not useful for detecting residual thyroid tissue or metastasis in medullary thyroid carcinoma . Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a tumour of parafollicular or C cells . These cells which are derived from neural crest cells , do not take up iodine. A whole -body iodine scan is useful in thyroid tumours derived from follicular cells that take up iodine.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following scales consider the completeness of surgical resection to determine the prognosis of a patient with thyroid cancer?
mcqs.explanation: MACIS scale includes completeness of the original surgical resection to determine the prognosis of the thyroid cancer. Prognostic indicators of well differentiated thyroid cancers: • AGES system - Age , histologic Grade, Extrathyroidal invasion , and metastases and tumor Size. • AMES system - Age (men <40 years old, women <50 years old), Metastases , Extrathyroidal spread, and Size of tumors (< or >5 cm). • DAMES - DNA aneuploidy + AMES • GAMES - Grade + AMES • TNM staging - Tumor , Nodal status , Metastases .326 • MACIS scale (postop modification) - distant Metastases , Age at presentation (<40 or >40 years old), Completeness of original surgical resection , extrathyroidal Invasion , and Size of original lesion (in centimeters ).327

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While performing a subtotal thyroidectomy , accidental ligation of which artery can potentially lead to hypoparathyroidism?
mcqs.explanation: Truncal ligation of the inferior thyroid artery can potentially result in hypoparathyroidism. Both superior and inferior parathyroid glands receive their blood from the335 inferior thyroid artery which arises from the subclavian arteries.Hence during thyroidectomy , only capsular branches closer to the thyroid gland should be ligated . The inferior parathyroid glands may have a variable blood supply , from either the ascending branch of the inferior thyroid arteries or the thyroid ima artery.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the correct pair based on their embryological development .

options.a: Thymus, Inferior parathyroid gland - Third pharyngeal pouch
options.b: Thymus, Superior parathyroid gland - Fourth pharyngeal pouch
options.c: Superior and Inferior parathyroid gland - Third pharyngeal arch
options.d: Thymus, Superior parathyroid gland - Fourth pharyngeal arch

mcqs.explanation: The thymus and inferior parathyroid glands originate from the third pharyngeal pouch . They migrate from the upper neck to the mediastinum during embryonic development . Inferior parathyroid glands have more variation in their anatomical position due to a long descent . The superior parathyroid glands originate from the fourth pharyngeal pouch . They are more constant in their position.336

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common site of ectopic parathyroid gland?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of the ectopic parathyroid gland is paraesophageal . The common sites of ectopic parathyroid glands are • Paraesophageal - most common • Mediastinal • Intrathymic • Intrathyroidal • Carotid sheath • High cervical or undescended Ectopic parathyroid is the most common cause of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism . In such cases , treatment involves surgical removal of the gland.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients ?
mcqs.explanation: Cancer is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients , whereas hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia detected incidentally in outpatients . The causes of hypercalcemia in cancer : • Cancers affecting bone like multiple myeloma, leukemia, bony metastasis - cause the bone to break down which releases excess calcium into the blood • Pseudohyperparathyroidism - tumours producing parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP ) cause the bone to release calcium into the blood. The most common carcinoma associated is squamous cell carcinoma of lung.337 • Cancers affecting kidneys - failure to remove excess calcium from the blood • Dehydration caused by nausea and vomiting - difficult for the kidneys to remove calcium from the blood properly • Lack of physical activity - causes bone breakdown, releasing calcium into the blood

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism ?
mcqs.explanation: A single adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism . They are most often located in the inferior parathyroid glands. Primary hyperparathyroidism is due to excess or non-suppressed PTH secretion from the following : • Single parathyroid adenoma • Multiple adenomas • Hyperplasia • Carcinoma Sporadic primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT ) is more common than familial (MEN syndrome/ familial HPT / Familial HPT with jaw tumor syndrome). Women are affected more commonly than men.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Lab investigations in a patient with fatigue and colicky abdominal pains show elevated PTH and calcium, and low serum phosphate . Which of the following ophthalmic findings is pathognomonic of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism . Band keratopathy is pathognomonic of this condition. It is due to the deposition of calcium phosphate crystals in the cornea. In patients with elevated PTH , calcium and phosphate levels are measured . Elevated calcium and decreased phosphate levels are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism . Normal calcium and elevated phosphate levels are suggestive of secondary hyperparathyroidism . The image given below shows band keratopathy.338 Option A: Kayser Fleischer rings are brownish-yellow rings in the corneoscleral junction due to the deposition of copper in the cornea. Option C: Ocular chrysiasis is the deposition of gold in the cornea, after repeated parenteral administration of gold salts. Option D: Hudson Stahli line is a superficial brown line at the junction of the upper 2/3 and lower 1/3 of the cornea in an otherwise normal cornea. It is attributed to the deposition of iron.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: During a clinical trial, it was found that some individuals who showed radioactive uptake on Sestamibi scan, showed no other evidence of hyperparathyroidism . They were instead found to be suffering from a Hurthle cell nodule of the thyroid gland. Which of the following radioactive tracer tests could be used to rule out the false positives ?
mcqs.explanation: A thyroid-specific tracer like 99Tc-Pertechnetate and subsequent subtraction images could be used to rule out the false positives caused by the solid thyroid nodules such as Hurthle cell nodule . The Sestamibi scanning is a nuclear-based imaging test used to localize the parathyroid glands. Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation that accumulates in mitochondria. Due to this, there is a difference in the rate at which it gets washed out depending upon the number of mitochondria in each tissue . Parathyroid adenomas often have a high concentration of oxyphilic cells with high mitochondrial content and they retain tracers and have a slower washout compared to the normal glands. In patients with nodular goiter or functional tumors of the thyroid gland, increased uptake of sestamibi by the thyroid gland makes parathyroid visualization difficult . There are two primary techniques to differentiate sestamibi uptake by abnormal parathyroid and thyroid tissue : • Dual-isotope subtraction imaging (with sestamibi and either iodine-123 or 99mTc pertechnetate ) - 99mTc pertechnetate is taken up only by the thyroid. The 99mTc pertechnetate scintigram is then digitally subtracted from the sestamibi scan to allow parathyroid localization. • Single -isotope dual-phase imaging (with sestamibi alone with early and delayed imaging) - since the rate of washout from the hyperfunctioning parathyroid gland is slower when compared to the thyroid gland. The image given below shows the dual-isotope subtraction imaging.339

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia , lethargy and abdominal pain. He had an X-ray taken a few days ago, which is given below . Which of the following investigations would not be useful in arriving at a diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with the X-ray showing nephrocalcinosis is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Angiography of renal arteries is not a useful investigation for hyperparathyroidism . Nephrocalcinosis occurs in this condition due to hypercalcemia . It decreases renal concentrating ability, which may cause polyuria and polydipsia . Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism: • Bones: • Pathological fractures • Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits , most common in radial aspect • Salt and pepper skull • Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen's disease of bone • Stones • Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common • Nephrocalcinosis • Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis • Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms • Band keratopathy • Features of hypercalcemia - • Vomiting • Confusion340 • ECG changes : increased PR interval, shortened QT interval The image given below shows salt and pepper skull seen in hyperparathyroidism .Investigations done in primary hyperparathyroidism : • Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands. • Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is also a widely used technique . Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue . • Dual-energy radiographic absorptiometry is a useful tool to demonstrate skeletal involvement in primary hyperparathyroidism. The image given below shows a radiolabeled Sestamibi scan.341

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In a patient with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism , when will you perform parathyroidectomy ?

options.a: If bone mineral density of > 2.5 SD above peak bone mass
options.c: In the presence of hypercalciuria but absence of nephrolithiasis
options.d: If creatinine clearance is reduced by 30%

mcqs.explanation: Reduction in creatinine clearance by 30% is an indication for parathyroidectomy in patients with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old lady with a history of multiple pathological fractures and renal stones was diagnosed with parathyroid hyperplasia involving all four glands. Which of the following treatment modalities will you use to treat her?

options.a: Complete removal of all four glands alone
options.b: Complete removal of three glands with a partial resection of the least affected gland
options.c: Partial resection of the affected glands with autotransplantation of the least affected gland

mcqs.explanation: Hyperplasia involving all four parathyroid glands is treated by complete removal of three glands with partial resection of the least affected gland (Subtotal parathyroidectomy ). Total cervical parathyroidectomy with heterotropic transplantation can also be done in this patient . Modes of treatment for parathyroid hyperplasia : • Subtotal parathyroidectomy - The affected glands are completely removed and the least affected gland is partially resected . The remnants left behind should ideally be 30 mg. A lower gland is preferred because its location reduces the risk of injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve. • Total parathyroidectomy with heterotopic transplantation - All 4 parathyroid glands are removed and parathyroid tissue is immediately transplanted to the non-dominant forearm. Pockets are made in the belly of the brachioradialis muscle , and one to two pieces of parathyroid tissue measuring 1 mm each are placed into each pocket . A total of 12 to 14 pieces are transplanted . Complications of parathyroidectomy include : • Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism • Hypoparathyroidism • Hungry bone syndrome • Injury to recurrent laryngeal nerve

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Autotransplantation was done after total parathyroidectomy in a patient with hyperplasia of all 4 parathyroid glands. Which of the following best describes this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: Parathyroid is transplanted heterotopically i.e. organ is implanted in another anatomic location. In total parathyroidectomy , all 4 parathyroid glands are removed and parathyroid tissue is immediately transplanted to the brachioradialis muscle in the non-dominant forearm.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Parathyroid gland post surgery is commonly transferred to:
mcqs.explanation: The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post -surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery. Parathyroidectomy is indicated in: • Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT ):342 • Asymptomatic primary HPT with: • raise in serum calcium >1mg/dl of the normal range • >400 mg urinary calcium in 24-hour urine test • < -2.5 Z-score of bone mineral density • Age <50yr and failed medical treatment • Severe cases of secondary HPT Parathyroidectomy is performed in neck hyperextension (semi-Fowler position). The thyroid gland is mobilized, and the parathyroid gland with adenoma is identified and resected . The parathyroid tissue is transplanted to the non-dominant forearm. Pockets are made in the belly of the brachioradialis muscle , and one to two pieces of parathyroid tissue measuring 1 mm each are placed into each pocket . A total of 12 to 14 pieces are transplanted . This is a type of heterotopic transplant. Miami criteria (confirm the absence of another hyperactive parathyroid): A drop of parathyroid hormone intraoperatively, to more than half the maximum value at 10 minutes postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma. However, if there is no drop in PTH level , then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration. Complications of parathyroidectomy include : • Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism • Hypoparathyroidism (presenting as hypocalcemia ) • Hungry bone syndrome • Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with complaints of numbness around the lips and a tingling sensation in her fingers. She underwent parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism one year ago. An ECG was done and is given below . What will be your immediate management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and ECG showing a prolonged QT interval (QT interval more than 0.43 seconds ) is suggestive of hungry bone syndrome i.e. hypocalcemia post parathyroidectomy . Acute symptomatic presentation of hypocalcemia is treated with IV calcium gluconate . Symptoms and signs of hypocalcemia : • Mild circumoral or digital numbness • Paresthesia • Laryngeal spasms • Cardiac arrhythmias • Chvostek sign: This is elicited by gently tapping over the facial nerve in front of the tragus of the ear. There is hyperexcitability of the facial muscles , manifesting as a contraction of the muscles . • Trousseau's sign: This is elicited by making the forearm ischemic by applying a sphygmomanometer cuff to the arm and keeping the pressure above systolic blood pressure (SBP) for 5 minutes . The hand goes into a painful carpopedal spasm and assumes the accoucheur ' s hand343 position. (shown in the image below )Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is an emergency and must be treated with: • 10 ml of 10 % calcium gluconate is given slowly through intravenous route • Calcium and vitamin D replacement is given orally • Magnesium supplementation may also be required due to the synergistic actions of calcium and magnesium The continuous need for calcium or vitamin D, 1-year postoperatively is called permanent hypoparathyroidism.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about secondary hyperparathyroidism ?

options.a: Lithium intake may cause secondary hyperparathyroidism
options.b: Calciphylaxis is seen in early stages

mcqs.explanation: Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy ) is a disseminated calcification seen late in the course of secondary hyperparathyroidism . In calciphylaxis , the underlying calcification in the vascular and arteriolar walls \037 ischemic necrosis \037 ulceration and gangrene \037 sepsis \037 death . It presents as an expanding cutaneous lesion which is predominantly seen in the extremities and lower abdomen. Prognosis is poor and an urgent parathyroidectomy is shown to increase median survival . Causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism: • Chronic renal failure (most common) • Vitamin D3 deficiency • GI malabsorption • Lithium intake344 To minimize the risk of missing parathyroid glands, transcervical thymectomy should be considered as a routine part of total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation and subtotal parathyroidectomy . In addition, careful cervical exploration for secondary hyperparathyroidism should be carried out. The image below shows calciphylaxis .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old patient with chronic renal failure presents to the OPD with complaints of recent onset pain in her feet . Blood investigation showed elevated PTH levels and normal serum calcium values. All of the following mechanisms contribute to elevated PTH in this patient except _____

options.a: Stimulation of parathyroid cells by hyperphosphatemia
options.b: Increased secretion of FGF-23 by osteocytes
options.c: Reduced expression of Vitamin D receptors and CaSR (calcium-sensing receptor ) in bones
options.d: Interference with parathyroid kinase C signal transduction pathway and Wnt pathway

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario described here showing elevated PTH and normal calcium levels is that of secondary hyperparathyroidism due to renal failure. Interference with parathyroid kinase C signal transduction pathway and Wnt pathway is the proposed mechanism of secondary hyperparathyroidism in the setting of lithium consumption and not renal hyperparathyroidism . Causes for increased PTH in secondary hyperparathyroidism due to renal failure: • Abnormal renal tubular reabsorption \037 hyperphosphatemia \037 stimulation of parathyroid cells \037 elevated PTH • Increased FGF-23 secretion from osteocytes \037 decreased 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D \037 decreased intestinal absorption of calcium \037 elevated PTH • Normally, ECF calcium controls PTH secretion by interacting with CaSR. Stimulation of CaSR by high calcium suppresses PTH secretion. In chronic renal disease , there is reduced expression of Vitamin D and CaSR by bones \037 increased skeletal resistance to PTH \037 elevated PTH .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old female patient is undergoing focussed parathyroidectomy for parathyroid adenoma. According to the Miami criteria, for the resection to be considered adequate , the intraoperative drop in parathyroid hormone should be ______.

options.a: More than one third the maximum preoperative value in 10min
options.b: More than one third the maximum preoperative value in half an 30 min
options.c: More than half the maximum preoperative value in 10min
options.d: More than half the maximum preoperative value in 30 min

mcqs.explanation: Drop of parathyroid hormone to more than half the maximum value at 10 min postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma by the Miami criteria.345 Most of the patients with primary hyperparathyroidism have single adenoma, and therefore undergo a focused or minimally invasive parathyroidectomy , where the localized abnormal parathyroid gland is removed. Once the gland is removed, the surgeon can ensure that there is no other hyperactive gland remaining by performing an intraoperative PTH assay for Miami criteria. It is based on the principle that the half-life of the PTH is 3-5 minutes . In a single -gland disease , once the gland is removed the PTH levels should drop to >50% of the preoperative PTH level within 10 minutes . However, if there is no drop in PTH level , then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with complaints of fatigue , vomiting, abdominal cramps and bone pain. She had undergone total parathyroidectomy and heterotopic autotransplantation for the same complaints 8 months ago. Sestamibi scan was done and found to be normal . What is the next step in management?

options.b: Post her for bilateral neck exploration
options.d: Label her as persistent hyperparathyroidism and start her on medical management

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of recurrent hyperparathyroidism which could be due to recurrence in the neck or graft (graft hyperplasia ). The next step would be to perform Casnova test to differentiate between them, as Sestamibi scan has ruled out ectopic parathyroid. Casanova test involves selective venous sampling for PTH levels from neck veins and brachial veins. If PTH from the brachial venous sample is >20 times that of neck vein sample , graft hyperplasia is confirmed. Persistent parathyroidism is defined as hypercalcemia that fails to resolve after parathyroidectomy i.e. within 6 weeks of surgery. Recurrent parathyroidism is hyperparathyroidism that occurs after an intervening period of at least 6 months of biochemically documented normocalcemia. Causes of persistent /recurrent hyperparathyroidism include : • Ectopic parathyroid • Unrecognized hyperplasia - graft site hyperplasia • Missed adenoma in normal position • Incomplete resection • Familial hyperparathyroidism • MEN -1 syndrome The image below summarises the management protocol for a case of persistent /recurrent hyperparathyroidism. *FHH stands for Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia346

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: All of the following are indications for surgical intervention of tertiary hyperparathyroidism except ____

options.c: Nodular hyperplasia of the parathyroid gland

mcqs.explanation: Reduced serum phosphate is not an indication for surgical intervention in tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Renal transplantation in patients with chronic kidney diseases may be associated with autonomous functioning of the parathyroid gland. This is called tertiary hyperparathyroidism where there is hypercalcemic hyperparathyroidism . The indications for surgical intervention in tertiary hyperparathyroidism are as follows : • Subacute severe hypercalcaemia (>3 mmol/L ) • Impaired graft function • Nodular hyperplasia of the parathyroid gland(s) • Progressive symptoms for >2 years following transplantation • Worsening bone disease - pain, fractures, bone loss • Renal stones /nephrocalcinosis • Soft tissue or vascular calcifications

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 75 -year-old lady with type 2 diabetes mellitus , hypertension , and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presents with hypercalcemia , hyperphosphatemia , and elevated PTH . What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The patient 's long-standing renal failure and elevated calcium, phosphate , and PTH are suggestive of tertiary hyperparathyroidism . This form of hyperparathyroidism can be life -threatening , and all patients with it should be referred for surgical intervention. The surgical procedure of choice for tertiary hyperparathyroidism is subtotal parathyroidectomy . In subtotal parathyroidectomy , the affected glands are completely removed and the least affected347 gland is partially resected . Option A: Total parathyroidectomy without an autograft is not a treatment option due to the postoperative and persistent difficulties in managing the associated hypocalcemia . Option C: Minimally invasive approaches commonly refer to the removal of a localized abnormal parathyroid gland through an incision less than 3cm in length . It is based on the principle that over 80% of individuals with primary hyperparathyroidism have a single adenoma. It is contraindicated in multi-glandular disease , lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism , and hyperparathyroidism associated with familial syndromes. Option D: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic used in the treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism . The use of calcimimetics in tertiary hyperparathyroidism remains controversial and has not been approved for this indication.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 41-year-old man with a history of treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma in childhood presents with severe abdominal cramps and right flank pain. He has a firm 2x2cm mass in the front of his neck. He has a Calcium of 15.2 mg/dl, normal TSH, markedly elevated PTH , and PGP9.5+ on immunohistochemistry . What is the leading cause of mortality in his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism . With early-onset , neck mass, and positive IHC for PGP9.5+, it is concerning for parathyroid cancer. Hypercalcemia is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with parathyroid cancer. Parathyroid cancer is a rare malignancy and makes up 1% of cases of primary hyperparathyroidism. History of prior neck radiation is considered to be a risk factor. Patients usually present a decade earlier than primary hyperparathyroidism (5th - 6th decade ), with an equal preponderance in males and females. Patients may present with a neck mass and severely elevated calcium and PTH levels . Treatment is focused on controlling hypercalcemia and surgery is the mainstay. Option B: Cardiovascular disease is a major contributing cause of mortality in patients with hyperthyroidism and chronic kidney disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In patients with parathyroid carcinoma , which of the following treatment modalities would you not consider?

options.c: En-bloc excision of the tumor and ipsilateral thyroid lobe with MRND

mcqs.explanation: Etelcalcetide has no role in the treatment of parathyroid carcinoma . It is ineffective . Etelcalcetide is a calcium-sensing receptor agonist used to treat secondary hyperparathyroidism in adult patients with chronic kidney disease undergoing dialysis . Treatment modalities for parathyroid carcinoma : • Surgical - Bilateral neck exploration + En-bloc excision of the tumor and ipsilateral thyroid lobe with/without MRND (Modified radical neck dissection ) in presence of lymph node metastasis . • Pharmacological: • Cinacalcet hydrochloride , a calcimimetic , can reduce PTH levels by directly binding to the CaSR (calcium-sensing receptor ) cells on the parathyroid gland ; used to control hypercalcemia in refractory parathyroid carcinoma .348 • Azidothymidine (telomerase inhibitor) • Octreotide • Anti-parathyroid hormone immunotherapy • Radiation therapy - for unresectable disease or for palliation of bone metastases Risk factors for parathyroid carcinoma incude : • Radiation exposure • Hyperparathyroidism jaw bone syndrome • HPRT gene or parafibromin inactivation

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man presents with severe hypercalcemia . His father had similar complaints and was found to have hyperparathyroid -jaw tumour syndrome. Which of the following is pathognomonic of his condition?
mcqs.explanation: Ossifying jaw fibromas are a pathognomonic feature of hyperparathyroid -jaw tumour syndrome. It arises due to inactivating mutations in the HRPT2 gene on chromosome 1 q21 -32 , encoding parafibromin . It is a rare cause of primary hyperparathyroidism with an early onset (32 years) which presents with severe hypercalcemia . It is associated with an increased risk of parathyroid carcinoma and other conditions like polycystic kidney disease . Surgical intervention may be considered to remove all enlarged glands. Osteitis fibrosa cystica is a feature of hyperparathyroidism but is not considered pathognomonic of any condition.349

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following conditions is correctly matched with its layer of origin?
mcqs.explanation: The area marked '2' depicts the zona fasciculata , which secretes glucocorticoids . In ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome, excess cortisol is produced from this layer. Parts of the adrenal glands: • The adrenal cortex is arranged in a zonal configuration in three zones - • Outer zona glomerulosa - secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone ) • Middle zona fasciculata - secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone ) • Inner zona reticularis- secretes androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone ) • The adrenal medulla - stores and secretes catecholamines (epinephrine , norepinephrine )355 On histological examination, the different layers are identified as: • Outer zona glomerulosa - small, compact cells • Central zona fasciculata - larger lipid -rich cells arranged in radial columns • Inner zona reticularis - pigmented , compact cells • Adrenal medulla - thin layer of large chromaffin cellsOption A: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine producing tumour derived from chromaffin cells and arises from the adrenal medulla . Option C: In Conn's syndrome, excess aldosterone is secreted from zona glomerulosa . Option D: Neuroblastoma arises from the adrenal medulla .356

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An adrenal incidentaloma was detected in a patient who underwent evaluation for renal calculi. Which of the following statements are true regarding this condition?

options.a: The majority of these adrenal masses are functional tumours
options.b: The likelihood of the adrenal mass being an adrenocortical carcinoma is independent of the size of the mass
options.d: The only indication for biopsy of this adrenal mass is to confirm adrenal gland metastasis

mcqs.explanation: The only indication for an adrenal gland biopsy is to confirm adrenal gland metastasis . An adrenal incidentaloma is defined as a clinically unapparent adrenal lesion that is incidentally detected on imaging performed for indications other than evaluation for adrenal disease . The majority of these lesions are non-functional tumours i.e. benign. The likelihood of an adrenal mass being an adrenocortical carcinoma increases with the size of the mass (25% chance if size >4 cm). Incidentalomas are evaluated to classify them as functional and non-functional. Non-functional incidentalomas <4cm are managed conservatively with MRI surveillance every 3-6 months. If >4cm, laparoscopic adrenalectomy is done. Note : An adrenal mass should never be biopsied until a pheochromocytoma has been biochemically excluded .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient being evaluated for primary aldosteronism underwent selective adrenal venous sampling. A comparison of the samples obtained from both the adrenal veins showed a significant difference in the aldosterone -cortisol ratio. What is the preferred line of treatment for this patient ?

options.c: Medical treatment with spironolactone and supplemental antihypertensives

mcqs.explanation: During selective adrenal vein sampling, a significant difference in the aldosterone -cortisol ratio on one side indicates unilateral hyperaldosteronism. In this case, unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice. Primary hyperaldosteronism (PHA) is characterized by hypersecretion of aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin levels (due to the negative feedback ). The most frequent cause of PHA is unilateral adenoma. CT or MRI is used to detect the tumour. In a patient with bilateral micronodular hyperplasia , there could be a unilateral non-functioning tumour. Selective adrenal vein sampling can be done to differentiate between unilateral and bilateral disease . Conservative management with 3-6 months of MRI surveillance is done in non-functional adrenal tumours of < 4cm. Medical management is done in patients with bilateral disease , the commonly implemented therapeutic approach is treatment with spironolactone and antihypertensive medication. Surgical management is done in unilateral and asymmetrical bilateral disease by unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy . A subtotal resection can be considered in the case of a typical single Conn's adenoma. However, it is not superior to unilateral adrenalectomy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are asked to perform sequential adrenal vein sampling in a patient with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia . Which of the following is the correct sequence of veins that you will go through to test the left adrenal gland?

options.a: Femoral vein\037IVC \037right renal vein\037right adrenal vein
options.b: Femoral vein\037IVC \037left renal vein\037left adrenal vein
options.d: Femoral vein\037IVC \037left gonadal vein\037left adrenal vein

mcqs.explanation: The correct sequence encountered during sequential venous sampling is femoral vein\037IVC \037left renal vein\037left adrenal vein. On the right side , the order is femoral vein\037IVC \037right adrenal vein.357

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient was found to have an elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol level and elevated ACTH. On administration of high-dose dexamethasone , ACTH levels were suppressed . MRI of the pituitary gland shows no enlargement . What is the next best step ?

options.a: CT scan of the chest and abdomen
options.b: CT scan/ MRI to assess the adrenals
options.c: Venous sampling from the inferior petrosal sinus

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario of elevated ACTH levels that respond to high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is indicative of a pituitary source of hypercortisolism . Since the MRI pituitary is inconclusive, the next best step is to perform a venous sampling from the inferior petrosal sinus. The stepwise approach to hypercortisolism is as follows : • Confirmation: This includes 2 steps : • Tests to detect hypercortisolism (�o 2 abnormal test results ): • Midnight salivary or serum cortisol • 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion • Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) • Low dose DST • Test to rule out pseudo Cushing's syndrome: • Low-dose DST + CRH stimulation test • Identifying the source • Localizing the lesion358

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with Cushing's syndrome presents with deep vein thrombosis. Which of the following mechanisms do not contribute to this?
mcqs.explanation: Increased factor V does not contribute to the risk of thromboembolic complications like DVT in a patient with Cushing's Syndrome. There is increased factor VIII , vWF , and decreased fibrinolysis in Cushing's syndrome patients which causes an increased risk of developing thromboembolic complications . Patients with Cushing's Syndrome are at a greater risk of acquiring hospital -acquired infection , thromboembolic and myocardial complications . Therefore, prophylactic anticoagulants and antibiotics constitute an essential component of pre-operative management.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Bilateral adrenalectomy is advised in all of the following conditions except

options.c: Unlocalised primary tumour of the adrenals

mcqs.explanation: Unilateral adrenalectomy is done in adrenal incidentaloma with a size >4cm. Bilateral adrenalectomy is advised in: • Bilateral ACTH-independent disease • Ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing's Syndrome • Irresectable or unlocalized primary tumor Adrenalectomy is done as a surgical measure in severe hypercortisolism or Cushing's disease . The adrenalectomy can be unilateral or bilateral depending on whether the tumor autonomously secrete hormones that could have a detrimental effect on health or If the adrenal mass benign or malignant.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old male patient has undergone unilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's syndrome and you have been asked to start him on cortisol supplementation , post -surgery. What is the rationale behind it?

options.a: Remaining adrenal gland has insufficient reserve
options.b: Contralateral adrenal gland is suppressed by prolonged cortisol over-secretion

mcqs.explanation: 359 The rationale behind cortisol supplementation after the surgical removal of the adenoma is that there is suppression of the contralateral adrenal gland by the pre-operative elevated cortisol levels . This causes primary adrenal insufficiency . Patients undergoing unilateral adrenalectomy typically require exogenous steroids for up to a year, which is usually the duration the remaining adrenal gland takes to recover adequate function. In bilateral adrenalectomy , steroids are required indefinitely , and patients may also require mineralocorticoid replacement therapy . Option A: The remaining adrenal gland usually has sufficient reserve to maintain homeostasis . Option C: A deficiency of ACTH causes secondary adrenal insufficiency . However, the adrenal insufficiency post adrenalectomy is primary i.e due to the hyposecretion of cortisol from the gland itself . Option D: Waterhouse –Friderichsen syndrome is a bilateral adrenal infarction associated with meningococcal sepsis and is rapidly fatal unless immediately treated .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the OPD with complaints of new-onset hyperpigmentation of the skin. He had undergone bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease 2 years ago. Which of the following statements is not true regarding his current condition?

options.a: It is characterized by elevated ACTH
options.b: Glucocorticoid replacement has to be continued
options.d: Screening is done using brain MRI

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of new-onset hyperpigmentation post -adrenalectomy is suggestive of Nelson 's syndrome. The first-line and definitive management is surgical resection of the pituitary adenoma. Nelson 's syndrome is a rare complication of total bilateral adrenalectomy (TBA ). TBA is a procedure used to control hypercortisolism in Cushing's disease (due to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) when resection of the primary tumor is not possible . The loss of feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic -pituitary -adrenal axis following TBA increases CRH.
