This leads to stimulation of ACTH-secreting corticotroph cells , causing enlargement of the original pituitary tumor or formation of a new one. Nelson 's syndrome is associated with a clinical triad of: • Hyperpigmentation • Excessive ACTH secretion • Corticotroph adenoma Screening is done with fasting plasma ACTH levels and MRI brain performed at regular intervals. Prophylactic pituitary irradiation may be recommended to prevent its incidence . The primary treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Patients will also require life -long glucocorticoid replacement , as they do not produce cortisol. The use of steroidogenic inhibitors in the treatment of Cushing's disease has decreased the need for bilateral adrenalectomy these days.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Pheochromocytoma is a ten percent tumor. Which of the following statements is false about pheochromocytoma ?

options.d: 10 % of pheochromocytomas are seen in children

mcqs.explanation: 10 % of pheochromocytomas are bilateral.360

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male patient admitted for evaluation of treatment -resistant hypertension and paroxysmal palpitations was found to have elevated metanephrines on urine screen. What is the next best step in the clinical management of this patient ?

options.a: Imaging study with an MRI scan
options.b: Medical pre-treatment with phenoxybenzamine followed by laparoscopic resection
options.c: Imaging study with a contrast CT scan

mcqs.explanation: In this scenario, the elevated urinary metanephrines point towards the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. Hence , the next best step is an MRI to localise the site of the tumour. MRI is preferred for the localization of pathologies because contrast media used for CT scans can provoke paroxysms. Classically , pheochromocytomas show a 'Swiss cheese ' configuration. 123 Iodine-MIBG (metaiodobenzylguanidine ) single -photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is essential for the detection of multiple extra-adrenal tumours and metastases , but PET scan using FDG or DOPA is more sensitive in detecting metastatic foci. The image given below shows MRI (marked B and C) and high uptake on 123I -mIBG scintigraphy (marked D and E)Laparoscopic resection is now a routine in the treatment of pheochromocytoma . An \033-adrenoreceptor blocker, phenoxybenzamine , is used pre-operatively to block excess catecholamine and its consequences during surgery. \031-blocker is added if there is tachycardia or arrythmia .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Germline mutations of which of the following genes is not associated with hereditary pheochromocytoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Germline mutation in NF2 gene is associated with neurofibromatosis type 2, and not hereditary pheochromocytoma. Hereditary pheochromocytomas are associated with NF1 germline mutations. Pheochromocytomas can occur in isolation or can be associated with hereditary tumor syndromes with the specific germline mutations such as: • Neurofibromatosis type 1 - mutation in NF1 gene361 • Familial paraganglioma syndrome - mutations within succinate dehydrogenase complex subunit B (SDHB), SDHD, SDHC genes • Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) - activating germline mutations of RET proto-oncogene • Von Hippel -Lindau syndrome - mutations in VHL gene

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 15-year-old boy undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma . On the third postoperative day, the boy feels lethargic and tired. Blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, there is no sign of bleed . What could be the cause of this?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life -threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones. Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal or addisonian's crisis) is a medical emergency caused due to a precipitating illness unmasking insufficiency or trauma or severe sepsis causing adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse -Friderichsen syndrome) or surgical removal of the glands. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as shock with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypocalcemia and electrolyte imbalances. It may be often misdiagnosed as an acute abdominal emergency . Adrenal insufficiency can be primary (due to adrenal pathology ), secondary (due to pituitary pathology - lack of ACTH) or tertiary (due to hypothalamus pathology - lack of CRH). Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide . Tuberculosis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in India. Adrenal crisis requires immediate intervention owing to its high mortality rate. Immediate rehydration is initiated with a saline infusion at 1 litre/hr with continuous cardiac monitoring. Glucocorticoid replacement is initiated with an initial bolus injection of hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, preferably by continuous infusion or alternatively by IV or IM injections. Mineralocorticoid replacement is initiated once the daily dose of hydrocortisone has been reduced to <50 mg, since hydrocortisone at higher doses provides sufficient stimulation of mineralocorticoids.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Neuroblastoma can originate in all of the following except
mcqs.explanation: Neuroblastoma does not originate in the adrenal cortex. Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumour of the sympathetic nervous system . These tumours arise during fetal or early postnatal life from sympathetic cells derived from the neural crest. Therefore, tumours can originate anywhere along the path which neural crest cells migrate, including: • Adrenal medulla - most common site • Paraspinal sympathetic ganglia • Sympathetic para ganglia such as the organ of Zuckerkandl362 Note : Neuroblastoma is the most common abdominal (extradural) tumour in children and the most common overall tumour in infants.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 2-year-old girl child with failure to thrive was found to have a palpable , firm, irregular abdominal mass that crossed the midline. CT revealed a calcified mass near the left kidney which on biopsy showed Homer-Wright pseudorosettes . Which of the following is not true regarding this condition?

options.a: 70% patients present with metastasis at diagnosis
options.b: Urine homovanillic acid is used for screening
options.c: Amplification of N-myc gene is a good prognostic factor
options.d: Abdominal mass is a common presentation of the condition

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of neuroblastoma and amplification of N-myc gene is an indicator of poor prognosis. Neuroblastoma arises from the adrenal medulla . Homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid(VMA) are elevated in the urine of approximately 95% of patients and are used to diagnose and monitor this tumor. Clinical features : • Abdominal mass (retroperitoneal or hepatic ) • Periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes," from periorbital ecchymosis caused by orbital metastases ) • Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome • Hypertension - due to secretion of catecholamines Metastatic disease is present in more than 70% of patients at presentation .Histopathology is the gold standard for diagnosis. Histologically , classic neuroblastomas are composed of small, immature ganglion cells with dark nuclei . Typically , Homer-Wright pseudorosettes can be found which are tumour cells concentrically arranged about a central space filled with neuropil. The mainstay of treatment is resection of the tumour and chemotherapy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common presentation of adrenal carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: 363 The most common presentation in patients with adrenal carcinoma is Cushing's syndrome due to excess cortisol. Patients with non-functioning tumours frequently complain of abdominal discomfort or back pain (large tumours). Mc Farlane classification is used for staging adrenal carcinoma . Treatment involves complete resection of tumour and chemotherapy.364

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A full -term infant with a history of polyhydramnios in utero presents with respiratory distress soon after birth. On examination, the child has frothing of saliva and the resident suspects tracheoesophageal fistula . What is the most common type of fistula likely to be present in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Type C is the commonest variety of tracheo-esophageal fistula (TEF). A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal communication between the esophagus and trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF. The proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF. Tracheoesophageal fistula is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal , renal, and limb) anomalies. Drooling of saliva, inability to pass a nasogastric tube and history of polyhydramnios suggest a diagnosis of oesophagal atresia with or without TEF. This can be confirmed with a chest X-ray image showing a coiled nasogastric tube in the oesophagal pouch as shown in the image below .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A neonate was brought by his mother with complaints of regurgitation of the feeds given to him. The nasogastric tube could not be passed to the stomach. Radiograph is shown below . The birth weight of the neonate was 2.7kg. There is no current evidence of pneumonia. What is the most suitable management in this case?
mcqs.explanation: 377 The above scenario along with the radiograph is suggestive of a type -E or H-type tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The management for this case would be Cameron Haight's surgery. Management of TEF is based on Waterson's criteria: Diagnosis of TEF: Confirmatory - Contrast study (Iohexol) Investigation of choice for H-type - Combined tracheo-esophagoscopy Definitive surgery for: • Types B, C, D, and E - Cameron Haight surgery • Type A - Anastomosis with/without gastrostomyCateg ory Weight/Comorbidities Management A Birth weight > 2.5kg Definitive surgery B Birth weight 1.8-2.5kg or pne umonia or congenital anomal y Needs stabilization before su rgeryAntibiotics + Build up n utrition C Birth weight < 1.8kg or sever e pneumonia or congenital a nomaly Staged repairAntibiotics + ga strostomy

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the following image of a barium swallow suggestive of?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a markedly dilated esophagus and characteristic bird's beak appearance (distal narrowing), which is suggestive of achalasia cardia. Achalasia cardia is caused due to the degeneration of the neurons in the myenteric plexus of the esophagus . This degeneration results in the failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) on swallowing . The patients present with a classic triad of dysphagia , regurgitation , and weight loss. The dysphagia initially begins with liquid foods and then progresses to solid foods . As the food gets accumulated in the esophagus , patients may complain of halitosis. With further progression of the disease , the patients may develop pneumonia, lung abscess , etc . The initial diagnosis is made by barium swallow or endoscopy , which shows the presence of dilated esophagus due to the constriction of the lower esophageal sphincter (bird-beak appearance ). The gold standard test to confirm achalasia cardia is esophageal manometry.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is normal peristalsis not seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Achalasia cardia does not show normal peristalsis .378 Manometric features of achalasia cardia are as follows : • Incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation • Aperistalsis of the esophageal body • Elevated LES pressure Diffuse esophageal spasm is characterized by simultaneous multi-peaked contractions of the esophagus . The contractions are spontaneous and may be of abnormally high amplitude (>120 mmHg) or long duration. Intermittent normal peristalsis is seen . Nutcracker esophagus is characterized by high amplitude (�o 180 mmHg) contractions with an increased mean duration. The peristaltic sequence is normal . Hypertensive lower esophageal sphincter is characterized by elevated LES pressure (�o 26 mmHg). Normal peristalsis is seen in the body of the esophagus .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young woman was admitted with chief complaints of dysphagia since adulthood which worsened in the last three months followed by odynophagia , nausea, and vomiting of undigested food. Her barium swallow shows features suspicious of achalasia and she is advised to undergo esophageal manometry. Which of the following will not be seen ?

options.d: Absent peristalsis of the esophageal body

mcqs.explanation: There is increased esophageal baseline pressure in achalasia cardia. Manometric features of achalasia cardia are as follows : • Incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation • Absent peristalsis of the esophageal body • Elevated LES pressure • Increased intraesophageal baseline pressures relative to the gastric baseline pressure High-resolution manometry (HRM) is a gastrointestinal motility diagnostic system that measures intraluminal pressure activity in the gastrointestinal tract using a series of closely spaced pressure sensors. For a manometry system to be classified as high-resolution instead of classic, the pressure sensors must be spaced at most 1 cm apart.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about Chicago classification ?

options.a: The classification is based on readings obtained by classic manometry
options.c: Type l achalasia exhibits panoesophageal pressurization pattern
options.d: Per oral endoscopic myotomy is the definitive treatment for type I achalasia

mcqs.explanation: Type III achalasia in Chicago classification is also known as spastic achalasia. Achalasia cardia is a motility disorder of the esophagus in which the LES (lower esophageal sphincter ) fails to relax due to loss of ganglion in the myenteric plexus . Chicago classification of esophageal motility divides achalasia cardia into 3 types . This classification is based on the readings obtained by high-resolution manometry (HRM). Type I achalasia cardia does not show pressurization pattern. Treatment options : • Pneumatic dilatation • Laparoscopic myotomy • POEM (per-oral endoscopic myotomy)379 The definitive treatment for Achalasia is surgical myotomy (Hellers myotomy) + fundoplication.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old male was diagnosed with achalasia cardia. High-resolution manometry revealed massive, simultaneous , high-pressure contractions of the distal oesophagus . According to the \037Chicago classification , the patient has which type of achalasia?
mcqs.explanation: The given features are suggestive of type III achalasia cardia. Type III achalasia cardia is characterised by massive, simultaneous , high-pressure contractions of the distal esophagus . Achalasia cardia occurs due to the loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of GIT . During swallowing , the food bolus normally triggers a primary peristaltic wave, which is responsible for carrying the bolus to the stomach, accompanied by the relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to allow esophageal emptying into the stomach. Achalasia is characterized by a disruption of this normal process . Failure of relaxation of the LES causes an elevated median integrated relaxation pressure and a complete failure of peristalsis . The esophagus becomes progressively more tortuous , leading to a megaesophagus .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old woman presented with long-standing complaints of dysphagia which was getting worse for the past 4 months. A barium swallow was performed and it showed the following finding. Which of the following is the definitive treatment of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The patient likely has achalasia cardia and the definitive treatment is Heller 's myotomy. Surgical management is the first-line treatment modality . Achalasia or 'failure to relax' in Greek occurs due to the lack of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus (Auerbach's). The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax leading to dysphagia , regurgitation of food, and progressive dilation of the esophagus proximal to the constriction. Barium radiology shows hold-up in the distal esophagus , abnormal contractions in the oesophageal body, and a tapering stricture in the distal esophagus often described as a 'bird's beak'. Laparoscopic Heller 's myotomy is the procedure of choice . Here, the muscles of the lower esophagus and cardia are cut. However, this can cause iatrogenic gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) due to damage to the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). Thus, newer techniques involve a partial fundoplication like Dor's procedure to reinforce the sphincter and reduce GERD symptoms . Endoscopic myotomy is a newer , alternate procedure . Here, a submucosal tunnel is formed in the mid esophagus region that allows a long myotomy.380 Option A: Calcium channel blockers can be given in the initial stages of the disease . They relieve the chest pressure that occurs around mealtimes . However, they are not permanent treatments and can be used while waiting for surgery. Option B: Botulinum toxin injection can be used as a treatment in patients who may not be candidates for surgery or dilatation. Limitations to botulinum toxin injections are that the effect is short-lived (6-12 months) and patients often require multiple treatments . Option C: Pneumatic dilatation of the LES has is successful in 75 % of patients . It involves using a balloon to stretch the LES and improve competence . It requires multiple sessions and has a low risk of esophageal perforation.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following esophageal carcinomas is most likely to develop in patients with long-standing achalasia cardia?
mcqs.explanation: The most common type of carcinoma associated with this condition is squamous cell carcinoma . Achalasia is a premalignant condition. It becomes malignant due to long-standing, retained, undigested fermenting food in the body of the esophagus , causing mucosal irritation . Adenocarcinoma may also arise in the setting of achalasia but is less common as compared to SCC. Small cell carcinoma is a rare type of neuroendocrine esophageal carcinoma more common in the lower esophagus . It is very aggressive and the 5-year survival rate is 8%. Carcinoid tumors are slow -growing tumors of neuroendocrine cells that form in the GI tract, mainly in the rectum, small intestine , or appendix .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In which of the following conditions is peroral endoscopic myotomy done?
mcqs.explanation: Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM ) is used in achalasia cardia.381 Treatment options : • Pneumatic dilatation • Laparoscopic myotomy • POEM (per-oral endoscopic myotomy) With the use of an operating endoscope , the mucosa of the esophagus is divided around the mid to the distal third, and a submucosal tunnel is created . Through this tunnel , the muscular layer of the distal esophagus , lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and cardia are visualized and divided , effectively performing an endoscopic myotomy. The major downside of POEM is that an effective anti-reflux valve cannot be created , exposing the patient to a 40%–50% risk of post -procedural gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented with complaints of crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and dysphagia . It starts whenever he has ice cream and he takes sublingual nitroglycerin which provides him relief . He underwent manometry which showed simultaneous multi-peaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mm Hg). What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario with episodes triggered by cold foods and manometric findings are suggestive of a diffuse esophageal spasm (DES). Diffuse esophageal spasm is a hypermotility disorder of the esophagus . It is caused by spontaneous , abnormal contractions seen more in the distal two -thirds of the esophageal body. It is more common in women. Patients usually present with dysphagia and chest pain. Pathologically , there is marked hypertrophy of the circular muscles . It is often triggered by cold foods . It mimics symptoms of myocardial infarction and also shows improvement when sublingual nitroglycerin is administered . It causes smooth muscle relaxation of the esophagus . A barium swallow shows a corkscrew esophagus . However, manometry (high-resolution manometry is preferred ) is the gold standard test for diagnosis. In classic manometry, if there are simultaneous , multi-peaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mmHg) or long duration (>2.5 seconds ) it is suggestive of diffuse esophageal spasm.382 On high-resolution manometry, a DCI (distal contractile integral) >450 mmHg is suggestive of DES. The distal contractile integral (DCI) is an index of contractile vigor in high-resolution manometry, calculated as the product of amplitude , duration, and span of the distal esophageal contraction. Hypertensive lower esophageal sphincter - It is achalasia in evolution. Shows increased LES pressure but normal peristalsis . Nutcracker's esophagus - It is the most common motility disorder of the esophagus . In conventional manometry, it shows a high-amplitude peristaltic contraction ( >180mmHg) and a longer duration of contraction (>7sec ). In high-resolution manometry, a DCI > 8000mmHg is suggestive of nutcracker's esophagus .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with dysphagia was evaluated with a barium swallow as given in the image. Which of the following is false regarding the management of this condition?

options.a: Calcium channel blockers and nitrates are first line therapy
options.b: Pneumatic dilatation only provides short term relief
options.c: Myotomy of only the affected segment is done
options.d: Endoscopic botulinum injection is given when medical therapy is contraindicated

mcqs.explanation: The given image is suggestive of diffuse esophageal spasm (DES). Myotomy involves the entire length of the affected segment along with a margin of several centimeters to the spastic region to prevent remnants of spasticity . First-line therapy is with calcium channel blockers and nitrates. Endoscopic botulinum toxin injection and pneumatic dilation are second -line therapies . Calcium-channel antagonists, vasodilators, and endoscopic dilatation have only transient effects . Botulinum toxin injection is also considered an effective and low-risk procedure but for short-term symptom relief . Pneumatic dilation is targeted at the exact anatomic site of narrowing . Surgical treatment includes extended myotomy of the esophageal body or peroral endoscopic myotomy . Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM ) is a safe and effective treatment for patients , especially those who are refractory to medical therapy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 72-year-old female patient presented to the hospital with complaints of difficulty swallowing and generalised weakness for 4 months. Peripheral smear revealed the following and an esophagography was done as given below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario with microcytic hypochromic anemia and characteristic esophagogram is suggestive of Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Plummer-Vinson syndrome/Paterson–Kelly syndrome has a triad of: • Post-cricoid webs • Dysphagia • Iron -deficiency anemia The webs are made up of fibrovascular stroma and esophageal epithelium . Glossitis , angular stomatitis, koilonychia are also associated with this condition. Laboratory investigations reveal microcytic-hypochromic blood picture and barium esophagography or esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) will help detect post -cricoid webs . Treatment includes correcting the iron- deficiency anemia which may improve dysphagia and pain. Esophageal bougies can be used during upper endoscopy to dilate the post -cricoid webs and allow383 normal swallowing and passage of food. Complications include the risk of perforation during dilatation and also malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma . The image below shows endoscopic appearance of post -cricoid web .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old male presented with intermittent dysphagia for the past 3 months. Barium swallow showed the following characteristic appearance . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Schatzki's ring. The barium swallow shows a thin circumferential ring in the distal esophagus , which is suggestive of Schatzki's ring.Schatzki's ring is a benign condition wherein there is a concentric, fibrous thickening and narrowing of the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ), with squamous epithelium above and384 columnar cells below . Schatzki's ring is made up of mucosal and submucosal layers. It causes dysphagia and is associated with gastroesophageal reflux disorder (GERD). It is most commonly seen in the lower third of the esophagus . Treatment is endoscopic dilation with antireflux therapy and repeated dilation is often necessary . Persistent strictures should always raise suspicion for malignant disease . The image below shows endoscopic appearance of the Schatzki's ring.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of nonprogressive dysphagia for solids with no previous similar episodes . Barium swallow revealed fixed narrowing of the esophagus at the level of the aortic arch. CT angiography revealed the following . Which anomaly is most commonly seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The above image shows the origin of the aberrant right subclavian artery (red arrow) causing extrinsic compression of the esophagus that is suggestive of dysphagia lusoria. In dysphagia lusoria, the right subclavian artery arises as the fourth branch of the aortic arch instead of branching from the brachiocephalic artery. It then courses behind the esophagus to supply blood to the right arm . This causes pressure on the esophagus and results in dysphagia . It is diagnosed by CT angiography. A barium swallow shows fixed narrowing of the esophagus at the level of the aortic arch without mucosal abnormality. Treatment is surgical repair either by reconstruction or ligation of the aberrant right subclavian artery.385

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old man presents with halitosis and swelling in the lateral aspect of the neck. He also complained of persistent cough and regurgitation of food remnants shortly after consumption. He underwent a barium swallow which is given below . Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.b: Occurs in the midline posteriorly and as sac enlarges lies on the left side
options.c: Dohlman's procedure is indicated when size > 2-5 cm
options.d: Herniates through the thyropharyngeus and cricothyroid muscle

mcqs.explanation: The above scenario is suggestive of a Zenker 's diverticulum or pharyngeal pouch . It is caused due to herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the space between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus . This space is known as Killian's triangle, which is a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor in the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is a pulsion diverticulum, formed due to increased intraluminal pressure forcing mucosa and submucosa to herniate. A small Zenker 's diverticulum < 2cm is managed by diverticulectomy and cricopharyngeal myotomy . Large diverticulum > 2-5cm is treated by endoscopic diverticulopexy (Dohlman's procedure ) or by a diverticulectomy with cricopharyngeal myotomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which among the following is a true esophageal diverticulum?
mcqs.explanation: Mid esophageal diverticula is a true diverticula. It involves all three layers of the esophageal wall such as mucosa, submucosa , and muscularis. Esophageal diverticula are herniations of the esophagus that extend into neighbouring structures . They occur as a result of primary motor disturbance or abnormality of the esophageal sphincters . They are classified based on their location into: • Zenker 's diverticulum (hypopharyngeal) • Mid esophageal (parabronchial) • Epiphrenic (supradiaphragmatic)386 Epiphrenic and Zenker 's diverticula are false diverticula involving herniation of only the mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer of the esophagus . Midesophageal diverticula may be caused by traction on the esophagus from adjacent inflammation and fibrosis (classically tuberculosis ). They are most common on the right side due to an overabundance of structures in the left mid-thoracic region. Zenker 's diverticulum:Epiphrenic diverticula as 1 and 2:

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man presented with complaints of chest pain and a feeling of food getting stuck in the esophagus , after a meal. He has asthma and is under treatment . PPIs were prescribed but it did not resolve the problem so a barium swallow was done and showed the following . What is the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario and imaging findings are suggestive of eosinophilic esophagitis .387 Eosinophilic esophagitis is an idiopathic condition commonly affecting the proximal one-third of the esophagus . There is migration of eosinophils to the esophagus and they contribute to extensive tissue damage and inflammation. Clinical features include swallowing difficulty , food impaction, vomiting, and heartburn. Barium swallow shows the presence of a series of rings in the esophagus which is suggestive of eosinophilic esophagitis . These rings appear as stripes on the cat and is also known as the feline esophagus . Feline esophagus :The definitive diagnosis requires biopsy with a histologic finding of >15–20 eosinophils per high-power field . Treatment includes oral corticosteroids and immunotherapy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department after the ingestion of a large amount of household cleaning liquid. She complained of a burning sensation in the throat and severe abdominal pain. She has a history of depression for the past 1 year. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.a: It is a risk factor for esophageal carcinoma
options.b: Early endoscopic evaluation is recommended to assess the grade of mucosal injury
options.c: Prophylactic antibiotics improve the clinical outcome
options.d: Acids only cause superficial damage to the esophagus

mcqs.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics have not been shown to improve the clinical outcome of acute corrosive esophagitis and are not recommended. Corrosive esophagitis is caused due to the ingestion of alkali or acid and can be accidental or from attempted suicide . The injury caused by alkali ingestion is deeper due to the process of saponification of fats and dehydration. The injury caused by acids is more superficial because they cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation, which prevents the deeper penetration of the acid. The acids also cause severe pylorospasm and therefore more gastric damage compared to alkali due to the accumulation of the contents in the antrum. Severe corrosive injury may lead to esophageal perforation, bleeding , stricture , and death . It is a risk factor for esophageal carcinoma . Therefore, early endoscopic evaluation is recommended to assess mucosal injuries even if there is no signs of oral injury.388 Management of corrosive esophagitis : • Hemodynamic stabilization and management of patient 's airway • Endoscopic evaluation of injuries • Surgical management includes laparotomy and • Esophageal stenting and jejunostomy for limited hemorrhage and superficial ulceration • Esophagogastric resection and jejunostomy for extensive necrosis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common site for pill-induced esophagitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site for pill-induced esophagitis is in the mid esophagus near the crossing of aorta or carina . These structures externally compress the esophagus and prevent the movement of the pills . Pill-induced esophagitis is caused when the pill lodges within the lumen of the esophagus . This pill causes direct damage to the mucosa. The risk factors for pill-induced esophagitis include poor pill-taking habits, consuming inadequate liquids, and lying down immediately after consuming the pill. Drugs causing esophagitis are: • Doxycycline • Quinidine • Phenytoin • NSAIDs • Bisphosphonates

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Esophageal endoscopy of a patient reveals the presence of serpiginous ulcers . This finding indicates :
mcqs.explanation: The image showing serpiginous ulcers in the otherwise normal mucosa of the distal esophagus is suggestive of cytomegaloviral esophagitis .389

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A middle -aged man presented to the emergency department with upper abdominal pain after having a heavy meal. On clinical examination, upper abdominal tenderness was noted . On chest radiography widening of the mediastinum with pneumomediastinum was seen . What is the probable diagnosis?

options.d: Rupture of emphysematous bulla of lung

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of spontaneous perforation of the esophagus . In a perforated peptic ulcer, patients develop sudden onset severe generalized abdominal pain, tenderness , and board-like rigidity and an erect plain chest X-ray shows gas under the diaphragm (Option B). The foreign body in the esophagus can be asymptomatic or may present with perforation after ingestion . The radiopaque foreign body can be seen with a chest X-ray (Option C). Rupture of emphysematous bullae of the lung will lead to secondary pneumothorax, which manifests as chest pain and dyspnoea . A plain chest X-ray shows air in the thorax, and the mediastinum is pushed to the opposite side (Option D). Spontaneous perforation of the esophagus needs immediate diagnosis and intervention due to the higher mortality associated with it. The most common site of perforation is the lower esophagus towards the left esophageal cavity. Causes : • Iatrogenic perforation (most common) • Boerhaave's syndrome (spontaneous emetogenic perforation) • Sharp foreign body • Corrosive ingestion • Esophageal carcinoma It usually manifests as severe pain in the chest or abdomen after a meal or after a bout of drinking , commonly associated with dyspnoea . On clinical examination, there is rigidity and tenderness in the upper abdomen. The diagnosis is usually confirmed by a chest radiograph which shows pneumomediastinum , pneumoperitoneum , and pneumothorax. Subcutaneous emphysema can be seen in Boerhaave's syndrome. Patients with sepsis will have a fever, tachycardia and tachypnea .390 Treatment includes adequate drainage, antibiotics, closure of the perforation site if possible and supportive measures .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man was brought to the casualty with a history of severe chest pain radiating to the back and difficulty in breathing following several episodes of vomiting. PR- 110bpm and BP- 80/50 mm of Hg. On examination, there is palpable crepitus over the chest wall. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.a: Most common in lower third of esophagus
options.b: Iohexol is used as contrast agent
options.c: Cervical esophagostomy and gastrostomy is done in early presentation
options.d: Most common cause of mortality is mediastinitis

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario points to Boerhaave's syndrome. Primary closure is done in stable patients presenting within 24 hrs and not cervical esophagostomy with gastrostomy . Boerhaave syndrome is the spontaneous perforation of the esophagus caused due to episodes of vomiting. During vomiting, the pressure in the esophagus rises rapidly and the esophagus ruptures at the weakest point. They usually have a history of heavy meal intake and alcohol abuse . Clinical features include Mackler's triad: • Retching • Chest pain • Subcutaneous emphysema The diagnosis is made by contrast esophagogram (iohexol) in unstable patients or contrast-enhanced CT scan, in stable patients . Treatment includes primary closure within 12 hours of the injury for a better prognosis. If the patient is unstable or presents late , the perforated part is resected and cervical esophagostomy is performed . A T-tube is placed into the esophagus along with appropriately located drains and a feeding jejunostomy or gastrostomy is performed for nutrition. Most common cause of mortality in Boerhaave syndrome is mediastinitis (40% to 50%).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 47-year-old woman underwent endoscopy for the evaluation of dysphagia . After the procedure , she developed severe chest pain radiating to the back and respiratory distress . What is the initial investigation you will perform on this patient to identify the cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of esophageal perforation following endoscopy . The initial investigation that is performed in this condition is a contrast esophagogram which will show the extravasation of the contrast. Water-soluble contrast (iohexol) should be used instead of barium contrast to prevent barium-related inflammation of the mediastinum if there is perforation. If the esophagogram is normal , contrast-enhanced CT is useful in identifying the injury. If the radiological investigations are normal and suspicion of esophageal perforation is high, then endoscopy can be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following cases of esophageal perforation will you not manage surgically ?

options.a: Crepitus in the neck and difficulty breathing after nasogastric tube insertion
options.b: Severe chest pain and breathing difficulty following several episodes of vomiting
options.c: Septic shock due to pyothorax and mediastinitis on left side of lower esophagus
options.d: Epigastric pain radiating to the shoulder with air under the diaphragm

mcqs.explanation: The patient with crepitus in the neck and difficulty breathing after nasogastric tube insertion most likely has perforation of the cervical esophagus . Instrumental perforations in the cervical esophagus are usually small and can nearly always be managed conservatively.391 Esophageal perforation is mostly due to spontaneous or iatrogenic causes . Iatrogenic instrument-induced perforation is the most common cause of esophageal perforation and is most common in the cervical esophagus in the cricopharyngeal area. Clinical features include pain as the most common presentation . Crepitus may be present . Hamman sign is heard during auscultation which is a crunching, rasping sound, synchronous with the heartbeat . Investigations include : • X-ray chest • CT scan • Esophagogram • Thoracentesis • Serum amylase level may be raised. Treatment is primary closure within 24 hours of injury and conservative treatment in selected cases . Complications of esophageal perforation are pneumothorax and empyema (most common in the left side of the chest and bilateral in 10 % of cases ). Option B: The patient with severe chest pain and breathing difficulty following several episodes of vomiting most likely has Boerhaave syndrome which affects the lower third of the esophagus and requires primary closure within 24 hours of the injury for a better prognosis. Option C: Patients presenting with septic shock due to an infection in the chest (pyothorax or mediastinitis) following an esophageal perforation require emergency surgical stenting , debridement , or drainage. Option D: The presence of epigastric pain radiating to the shoulders with air under the diaphragm point to a diagnosis of abdominal esophagus perforation. It requires immediate surgical intervention to restore the integrity of the esophagus .Consideration for interventio n in esophageal perforation Indications for non-operative management Indications for operative ma nagement Small septic load Large septic load Minimal cardiovascular upset Septic shock Confinedtomediastinum Pleura breached Perforation ofcervical esopha gus Perforation of the abdominal esophagus Perforation by flexible endos cope Boerhaave's syndrome

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old woman presented with dysphagia and postprandial chest pain that is relieved on loud belching . On examination, the patient had pallor. Chest radiography showed an intrathoracic gas bubble . Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 392 The above clinical scenario is suggestive of a hiatus hernia. Hiatus hernia is the protrusion of any abdominal structure other than the esophagus into the thoracic cavity through a widening of the hiatus of the diaphragm. Type 1 - sliding hernia: Gastroesophageal junction or cardia migrates into the thoracic cavity. The length of intra abdominal esophagus is reduced leading to GERD. Most of the patients are asymptomatic . The treatment of choice in symptomatic patients is fundoplication . Type 2 - rolling hiatus hernia: Gastroesophageal junction or cardia is normal but a portion of the stomach migrates into the thoracic cavity. The length of intra abdominal esophagus remains the same in a true rolling hiatus hernia. Clinical features : • Chest pain or fullness relieved on belching . • Dysphagia . • Longitudinal ulcers (Cameron's ulcer) that bleeds , leading to anemia. Surgical reduction of hernia and tightening of diaphragmatic crura is the best treatment modality even in asymptomatic patients to avoid life -threatening complications like volvulus. Type 3 - mixed hiatus hernia: A combination of sliding and rolling hiatus hernia. Treatment is the same as rolling hiatus hernia. Type 4 hiatus hernia: Other contents of GIT herniates into the thoracic cavity. Eg : Colon. CT with oral contrast is the best method of diagnosis of hiatus hernia. It highlights gastric anatomy and also helps to identify other structures involved. Chest X-ray shows an intrathoracic gas bubble .393

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most important pathophysiological factor implicated in GERD?
mcqs.explanation: Frequent transient lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation accounts for more than 90% of the cases of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a condition that develops when there is a retrograde flow of stomach contents back into the esophagus . It can present as non-erosive reflux disease or erosive esophagitis . A hiatal hernia is the next common cause of GERD. Factors contributing to the high pressure in the LES zone: Factors contributing to the high pressure in the LES zone: • Intrinsic musculature of the distal esophagus and sling fibers of the cardia of stomach which are in tonic contraction • During inspiration, the anterposterior diameter of the crural opening of diaphragm is decreased (increases LES pressure )400 • Transmitted pressure of the abdominal cavity on the LES zone

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following foods will you recommend to a patient to reduce symptoms of GERD?
mcqs.explanation: Protein increases the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure , thereby allowing the closure of the sphincter and reducing reflux. Other options : Option A: Chocolate and coffee both contain methylxanthine , which causes muscles to relax and lowers the LES pressure . In addition, coffee can stimulate gastric secretions , which can promote reflux. Option C: Fatty foods have been found to delay gastric emptying and decrease the LES pressure , thereby prolonging the esophageal exposure time to the stomach acid and the volume available for reflux. Option D: Alcohol, mint, citrus, tomatoes , and/or carbonated beverages may cause further irritation to the damaged esophageal mucosa but have not been found to cause reflux themselves .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old male patient presented with a feeling of fullness and sensation of a lump in the throat for the past 3 weeks . He has no other complaints like weight loss or dysphagia . Rigid endoscopy showed no growth or foreign body in the throat. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.a: Lump in the throat only felt during swallowing
options.c: Does not interfere with eating or drinking

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of globus hystericus . It is a feeling of fullness or lump in the throat that is felt always and not only when swallowing . Globus hystericus or globus pharyngeus is a persistent abnormal sensation in the throat in the absence of any observable pathology . The exact cause of globus sensation is uncertain. The sensation is often relieved by the act of swallowing and it does not interfere with eating and drinking . Examination and investigations may be carried out to exclude any other underlying problem. It is often attributable to GERD. Reassurance that there is no serious underlying problem may be all that is needed in terms of treatment .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 67-year-old man presented to the physician with complaints of heartburn and a sour taste in the mouth for the past 1 year. He was prescribed proton pump inhibitors, but the symptoms did not improve. What is the immediate next step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: This is a case of dyspepsia not responding to PPIs. So the best management for this patient is endoscopy . In case of an unexplained dyspepsia • If the patient is >60 years - Endoscopy is the investigation of choice • If the patient is <60 years - A test for H.pylori infection is done (stool antigen and urease breath test ) and eradication treatment is given. Endoscopy is done only if any one of the alarming signs are present . Alarming signs401 • Odynophagia or dysphagia • Unexplained weight loss • Massive GI bleeding • Recurrent vomiting • Jaundice • Palpable mass or adenopathy • Family history of GI malignancy

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 48-year-old woman presented with dysphagia and postprandial chest pain that is relieved by loud belching . On examination, the patient had pallor. Chest radiography showed an intrathoracic gas bubble . What is the investigation of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with X-ray findings showing a retrocardiac gas bubble are consistent with the diagnosis of a hiatus hernia. A CT scan with oral contrast is the best method of diagnosis. It highlights the gastric anatomy but also helps to identify other structures involved in the hiatal hernia. Hiatus hernia is the protrusion of any abdominal structure other than the esophagus into the thoracic cavity through a widening of the hiatus of the diaphragm. Types of hiatus hernia: Type 1- sliding hernia Gastroesophageal junction or cardia migrates into the thoracic cavity. The length of intra abdominal esophagus is reduced leading to GERD. Most of the patients are asymptomatic . The treatment of choice in symptomatic patients is fundoplication . Type 2- rolling hiatus hernia: Gastroesophageal junction or cardia is normal but a portion of the stomach migrates into the thoracic cavity. The length of the intraabdominal esophagus remains the same in a true rolling hiatus hernia. Clinical features : • Chest pain or fullness relieved on belching . • Dysphagia . • Longitudinal ulcers (Cameron's ulcer) that bleed lead to anemia. Surgical reduction of hernia and tightening of diaphragmatic crura is the best treatment modality even in asymptomatic patients to avoid life -threatening complications like volvulus. Type 3- mixed hiatus hernia: A combination of sliding and rolling hiatus hernia. Treatment is the same as rolling hiatus hernia. Type 4 hiatus hernia: Other contents of GIT herniates into the thoracic cavity. Eg : Colon.402 Note : This is a controversial question as some books give barium swallow as the investigation of choice for hiatal hernia. But Bailey's 28th edition clearly mentions that a CT scan with oral contrast is the answer. The image below shows a retrocardiac gas bubble on an X-ray that is consistent with hiatus hernia.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common complication of Nissen's fundoplication ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common complication of Nissen's fundoplication is gas-bloat syndrome. Fundoplication is the procedure in which the fundus of the stomach is wrapped around the lower end of the esophagus .403 After this procedure , most patients are unable to belch gas from the stomach into the esophagus . This causes increased gas in the stomach resulting in bloating sensation, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence . This is known as gas bloat syndrome and occurs more commonly with Nissen total fundoplication . Pneumothorax is the most common complication that occurs intraoperatively.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The fundus is wrapped (270 degrees ) around the posterior aspect of the esophagus in which of the following corrective procedures for GERD?
mcqs.explanation: Partial posterior fundoplication between 180 to 270 degrees is called Toupet fundoplication . It is used in the surgical management of GERD. Partial anterior fundoplication is Dor's fundoplication and total fundoplication is Nissen's fundoplication .404

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common benign tumor of the esophagus ?
mcqs.explanation: Leiomyomas are the most common benign tumors of the esophagus . Leiomyomas are benign tumors that arise from the muscularis propria. They are found in the mid to distal esophagus . They are more common in males and small, asymptomatic lesions are observed, while symptomatic lesions are enucleated .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for developing squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus ?
mcqs.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is a risk factor for adenocarcinoma of the lower end of the esophagus , not for squamous cell carcinoma . Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of esophageal carcinoma . Risk factors for SCC: • Tobacco • Alcohol • HPV • Plummer–Vinson syndrome • Achalasia • Tylosis • Caustic ingestion Risk factors for adenocarcinoma: • Barrett's esophagus • GERD405 • Smoking • Obesity

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true about Barrett's esophagus ?

options.a: It is the intestinal metaplasia of esophagus
options.b: Mucus secreting foveolar cells are characteristic
options.c: Alician blue is used in the staining of biopsy specimen
options.d: It is a reversible cell adaptation

mcqs.explanation: Mucus -secreting goblet cells (not foveolar cells ) are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus , as there is intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus . Foveolar cells are the mucus-secreting cells in the stomach. Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it is estimated to occur in about 10 % of individuals with symptomatic GERD. Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation and sometimes dysphagia . Obese white men over the age of 60 years represent the highest -risk group. Intestinal metaplasia in the esophagus occurs due to chronic irritation of the esophagus in GERD (option A) since intestinal epithelium is better suited to handling gastric acid exposure . Hence , mucus-secreting goblet cells are characteristic of Barrett's esophagus . Since all metaplasia are reversible, Barrett's esophagus is also reversible (option D). Only 0.2 to 1% of Barrett's esophagus leads to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.Alician blue is used in the staining of the biopsy specimen , as it stains the goblet cells (option C). Mucicarmine is the specific stain. Seattle protocol is used for the management of Barrett's esophagus .406

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Investigation of choice for cardia metaplasia in Barrett's esophagus is
mcqs.explanation: The investigation of choice for Barrett's esophagus showing cardia metaplasia is endoscopy with methylene blue . Barrett's esophagus is a metaplastic change (squamous to columnar change) in the lower end of the esophagus as a result of long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease . Barrett's esophagus can be- • Classical Barrett's esophagus - > 3cm of columnar epithelium in the distal esophagus . • Short segment Barrett's esophagus - < 3cm of columnar epithelium in the distal esophagus . • Cardia metaplasia - microscopic Barrett's in the GE junction. In cardia metaplasia due to lack of macroscopic changes , an endoscopic biopsy is difficult . So chromoendoscopy is the ideal investigation. Here mucosa is first stained by methylene blue to highlight abnormal mucosa. Investigation of choice : endoscopic biopsy Management : Seattle protocol is ideally followed to detect early dysplastic changes in Barrett's esophagus . Here a 4 quadrant biopsy specimen is taken 1- 2 cm apart throughout the area of intestinal metaplasia . • No signs of dysplasia - continue 2 yearly surveillance. • Low-grade dysplasia - APC or RFA or EMR followed by 6 monthly surveillance. • High-grade dysplasia - APC or RFA or EMR followed by 3 monthly surveillance. APC - Argon photo coagulation RFA - Radiofrequency ablation EMR - Endoscopic mucosal resection Lugol's iodine is used for squamous cell carcinoma .407

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Endoscopic biopsy of a patient with GERD revealed high-grade dysplasia of esophageal mucosa proximal to the GE junction. What is the appropriate management for this patient ?

options.a: Radiofrequency ablation and 6 monthly follow up
options.b: No intervention now and follow up every 2 years
options.c: Argon photocoagulation and 3 monthly follow up

mcqs.explanation: Ablation of abnormal mucosa and 3 monthly endoscopic protocol is the appropriate management in cases of high-grade dysplasia of esophageal mucosa due to GERD.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An 80-year-old male patient was recently diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the esophagus . The tumor is present in the distal esophagus , within 1 to 5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. According to the Siewert classification , which type does this tumor belong to?
mcqs.explanation: Siewert type I lesions include tumors of the distal esophagus with the center located within 1 - 5 cm above the anatomic esophagogastric junction.408

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly male presented with significant weight loss and an inability to swallow food. A barium swallow was done and showed the following . Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.a: Dysphagia is the most common symptom
options.b: T1a tumor is restricted to sub mucosa
options.c: Barium swallow shows rat tail appearance
options.d: Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is used to confirm diagnosis

mcqs.explanation: The above clinical scenario with rat-tail appearance on barium swallow is suggestive of esophageal carcinoma . T1a tumor is restricted to the muscularis mucosa. Esophageal carcinoma is more commonly seen in men. Tobacco use and alcohol are strong risk factors. Adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus are the two most common types . Clinical features include : • Dysphagia (most common) • Regurgitation • Vomiting • Odynophagia • Weight loss In the advanced stage , there can be hoarseness of voice due to recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy , horner's syndrome, chronic spinal pain, and diaphragmatic paralysis. Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Other Investigations include barium swallow which shows a rat-tail appearance due to irregular narrowing or ulceration. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis . Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS ) is the investigation of choice to assess tumor invasion and lymph node metastasis . TNM staging :Primary Tumor (T) TX Tumor cannot be assessed409 Primary Tumor (T) T0 No evidence of tumor Tis High-grade dysplasia T1 Tumor invades the musculari s mucosa (T1a )or submucosa (T1b ) T2 Tumor invades into but not b eyond the muscularis propria T3 Tumor invades the adventitia T4a Tumor invades adjacent struc tures that are usually resecta ble (diaphragm and pericardi um) T4b Tumor invades unresectable structures Regional Lymph Nodes (N) NX Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed N0 No regional lymph node met astasis N1 Metastasis in 1-2 regional ly mph nodes N2 Metastasis in 3-6 regional ly mph nodes N3 Metastasis in �o 7 regional lym ph nodes Distant Metastasis (M) M0 No distant metastasis M1 Distant metastasis

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the blood supply of the conduit in gastric pull up done during esophagectomy ?

options.a: Right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries
options.b: Right gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries
options.c: Left gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries
options.d: Left gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries

mcqs.explanation: The blood supply to the gastric conduit is based on the right gastric and right gastroepiploic arteries. A gastric pull -up is done during esophagectomy for esophageal carcinoma . It is a surgical procedure where the stomach is pulled up into the thoracic cavity that now acts as a new passage (conduit ) instead of the esophagus . During the esophagectomy , the proximal stomach and lymph nodes are typically resected along with the segment of the esophagus . The gastric conduit is then fashioned by tubularization of the stomach. The right gastroepiploic artery is preserved and the other arteries are ligated to make ample length and mobility for the conduit .410 It is of utmost importance the right gastroepiploic artery is preserved as ischemia to the stomach will result in anastomotic leakage , stricture , and even dehiscence . The rich supply of submucosal vascular networks can preserve the stomach on this single vessel .Approaches of esophagectomy : 1. Mckeown approach • Done for upper 1/3rd and mid 1/3rd tumors (above aortic arch) • Anastomosis site is in the neck • Three incisions made (abdominal, thoracic, and left neck) 2. Transhiatal approach (Orringer) • Done for tumor of lower 1/3rd and mid 1/3rd of the esophagus • Anastomosis site is in the neck • The most common complication is atelectasis and mortality is due to an anastomotic leak 3. Ivor lewis approach • Done for mid 1/3rd(below aortic arch) and lower 1/3rd esophagus tumors • Anastomosis site is in the thorax

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with esophageal carcinoma . Radiological investigations show a 2 cm tumor in the middle part of the esophagus . The tumor extends up to the submucosa with the involvement of mediastinal lymph nodes , there is no distant metastasis . What is the best treatment modality in his case?
mcqs.explanation: Chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy is the best treatment modality for tumors extending to the submucosa (T1b ) with regional lymph node involvement (N1). EMR (endoscopic mucosal resection ) is done for small tumors confined to the mucosa, with no lymph node involvement. (T1aN0 ) Esophagectomy \261 chemoradiation is done when the tumor extends into the submucosa , with no lymph node involvement.411 Chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy is done for tumors extending into the submucosa or beyond with lymph node enlargement Chemoradiation therapy alone is done as a palliative measure in case of advanced esophageal carcinoma or in those patients unfit for surgery. Esophageal stent placement is done in patients with advanced cancer and severe dysphagia that is not resolved by chemoradiation therapy. SEMS (self -expanding metallic stent ) is the treatment of choice in malignant tracheoesophageal fistula .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old woman presented with a history of dysphagia and weight loss for the past 1 year. Endoscopic ultrasonography done showed a tumor of size 4 cm in the mid esophagus above the aortic arch. Which of the following is the best approach?
mcqs.explanation: The best surgical approach for a mid-esophageal carcinoma above the aortic arch is Mckeown's esophagectomy . Approaches of esophagectomy : 1. Mckeown 's approach • Done for upper 1/3rd and mid 1/3rd tumors (above aortic arch) • Anastomosis site is in the neck • Three incisions were made (abdominal, thoracic, and left neck) 2. Transhiatal approach (Orringer's approach) • Done for tumor of lower 1/3rd and mid 1/3rd of the esophagus • Anastomosis site is in the neck 3. Ivor Lewis approach • Done for mid 1/3rd(below aortic arch) and lower 1/3rd esophagus tumors • Anastomosis site is in the thorax • The most common complication is atelectasis • The most common cause of mortality is due to an anastomotic leak leading to mediastinitis . In esophagectomy , a proximal margin of 10cm and a distal margin of 5cm is taken.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An male patient with stage IV esophageal carcinoma is taken up for esophageal stent insertion as a palliative measure . Which of the following is the most common complication of this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common complication of placing a stent in the esophagus is the migration of the stent . Palliative treatment in advanced stages of esophageal carcinoma includes esophageal stent placement , enteral nutrition support , or the use of chemotherapy and radiation. Complications of esophageal stent placement : • Migration of stent (most common) • Odynophagia • Tumour ingrowth and overgrowth412 • Chest pain • Severe reflux
