mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A neonate presented with features of intestinal obstruction. The X-ray showed the following image. What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The above plain abdominal radiograph shows a typical double -bubble sign suggestive of duodenal atresia. The double -bubble represents dilatation of the stomach and the proximal duodenum . Duodenal atresia is often associated with trisomy 21 /Down syndrome, prematurity , maternal polyhydramnios, cardiac malformations, and malformations of the hepatobiliary system . It is caused due to failure of recanalization or partial recanalization of the duodenum or failure of vacuolization of the duodenum from its solid cord stage . The anatomic variants are as follows : • Type I: • most common • mucosal web with intact muscle wall (so-called windsock deformity ) • Type II : • two ends separated by a fibrous cord, but muscle continuity present • Type III : • complete separation of two ends with a gap within the duodenum Clinical features : • Obstructive features such as • bilious emesis (due to duodenal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater)425 • postprandial emesis • upper abdominal distension with a scaphoid lower abdomen • Delayed passage of meconium Abdominal radiographs show the double -bubble sign. If distal air is present , an upper GI contrast study should be considered to exclude midgut volvulus. Treatment: • The initial treatment of infants with duodenal atresia includes nasogastric or orogastric decompression. • IV fluids and parenteral nutrition are started to prevent acid-base imbalance. • Echocardiography , renal ultrasound, and radiology of the chest and spine should be performed to evaluate for associated anomalies. • Definitive correction of the atresia is done by duodenoduodenostomy . This procedure is also preferred in cases of the concomitant or isolated annular pancreas.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An infant with Edward 's syndrome presents with the following radiological finding. Which of the following is false about this condition?

options.b: Mostly presents as vomiting within 1 week
options.c: Erythromycin exposure in the first 2 weeks of life can lead to this condition
options.d: Palpation of the pyloric olive is pathognomonic for this condition

mcqs.explanation: The radiographic image showing the presence of an enlarged gastric gas bubble (single bubble ) is suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS). It most commonly presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting between 2-8 weeks of age and is only rarely seen after 13 weeks . Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet . First-born male infants are at the highest risk . Risk factors for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis : • Turner syndrome • Edwards syndrome426 • Erythromycin or azithromycin exposure in the first 2 weeks of life either orally or via mother's milk. Palpation of the olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium is considered pathognomonic. USG criteria for diagnosing hypertrophic pyloric stenosis - pyloric muscle thickness of >3-4 mm or a pyloric length >15-18 mm in the presence of functional gastric outlet obstruction is diagnostic .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An abdominal mass in a patient with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is best seen _________.

options.c: During palpation over the left hypochondrium

mcqs.explanation: In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant . Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age . Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet . Male infants are at a higher risk . Clinically, when the infant is given a test feed , an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen. Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). All infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are evaluated with an ultrasound (investigation of choice ). It confirms the diagnosis in the majority of cases . Management : Rehydration and metabolic correction prior to definitive surgery - Ramstedt 's pyloromyotomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child is diagnosed with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis . Which among the following statements is true regarding her condition?
mcqs.explanation: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) most commonly presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2-8 weeks of age . When the infant is given a test feed , visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right, followed by projectile vomiting. Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-). The kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreti ng Na+ and HCO3-. However, the loss of sodium stimulates the secretion of aldosterone via the RAAS pathway . The aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions. Loss of potassium ions leads to the development of hypokalemia. Loss of H+ ions in urine lowers the urinary pH resulting in aciduria. It is called paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially lost H+ ions due to loss of HCl, and instead of427 compensating that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine. The cervix sign and nipple sign are signs of CHPS seen on ultrasonography : • Double -layered hypertrophic mucosa protrudes into the stomach, creating the so-called nipple sign. • The sonographic appearance of the hypertrophied pylorus resembles that of the uterine cervix and is sometimes referred to as the cervix sign. The given ultrasound image shows thickened pylorus , with cervix sign and nipple sign.Treatment: • The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality has to be corrected preoperatively . • The Ramstedt pyloromyotomy is the standard surgical procedure for its treatment .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which part of the GIT is most sensitive to ischemia following a hypovolemic insult?
mcqs.explanation: Tonometry studies have shown that of all the parts of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT ), the stomach is most sensitive to ischemia following a hypovolemic insult and is also the slowest to recover. This may explain the high incidence of stress ulceration in the stomach. The Griffiths point (or Griffiths critical point) refers to the site of watershed anastomosis between the ascending left colic artery and the marginal artery of Drummond occurring in the region of the splenic flexure . Most anatomy texts describe its location as two -thirds along the transverse colon. The Sudeck point (or Sudeck critical point) refers to a specific location in the arterial supply of the rectosigmoid junction, namely the origin of the last sigmoid arterial branch from the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).428

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of upper GI bleeding is peptic ulcer. The causes of upper GI bleed in decreasing order of frequency: • Ulcers • Esophageal (6%) • Gastric (21 %) • Duodenal (33%) • Erosions • Mallory–Weiss tear • Esophageal varices • Tumour • Vascular lesions

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man came with complaints of dark -colored stools to the OPD. After undergoing endoscopy , the patient was diagnosed with an upper GI bleed . Which of the following structures is used as a demarcation point to differentiate it from a lower GI bleed ?
mcqs.explanation: The ligament of Treitz is used as the demarcation point to differentiate between upper gastrointestinal bleeding and lower gastrointestinal bleeding . It is a part of the duodenojejunal junction. Upper GI bleeding refers to bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, and lower GI bleeding refers to bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz.429

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic, with a history of binge drinking and multiple episodes of vomiting, presents with hematemesis . On endoscopy , a longitudinal mucosal tear is found in the gastroesophageal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Mallory Weiss tear. It is due to a longitudinal tear in mucosa or submucosa of the gastroesophageal junction. It is most commonly seen in alcoholics , following forceful vomiting, retching, coughing , or straining. The left gastric artery is the most common vessel to bleed . The investigation of choice is endoscopy . Management of Mallory Weiss tear • Conservative, as it is usually is self -limiting. • Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy . • Angiographic embolization - if endoscopy fails. • High gastrotomy - if all these maneuvers fail. Boerhaave syndrome is characterized by spontaneous perforation of the esophagus . Here all layers are involved. Clinical features include Mackler's triad • Retching • Chest pain • Subcutaneous emphysema Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE) is characterized by dilated venules in the submucosa of the antrum. On endoscopy : Watermelon stomach.430 Management of GAVE • Endoscopic argon photocoagulation (APC) • If persistent - antrectomy. Dieulafoy lesion is a vascular malformation (dilated submucosal arterioles ) that is seen along the lesser curvature of the stomach. The investigation of choice is endoscopy .Management of Dieulafoy lesion: • Endoscopic electrocoagulation or sclerosant therapy • Angiographic embolization.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old male patient presented to the OPD with complaints of increasing heartburn and dyspepsia for the past several months. He was prescribed PPIs for one month but he has no relief . You perform a urea breath test which is found to be positive . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 431 The given clinical scenario and the positive urea breath test are suggestive of a Helicobacter pylori infection which is most commonly associated with Type B gastritis. Type B gastritis usually affects the antrum. Intestinal metaplasia associated with chronic pan-gastritis and atrophy is seen . It has greater potential for malignancy as compared to Type A gastritis. Type A gastritis affects the fundus with antral sparing. Its features can be easily remembered by 4 'A's: • Autoimmune condition - has circulating antibodies to parietal cells • Atrophy of parietal cell mass • Achlorhydria - causes chronic hypergastrinemia and microadenomas of enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells • Anemia - leads to pernicious anemia, due to malabsorption of Vit B12 (as the intrinsic factor is also produced by parietal cells )

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following causes gastritis in patients with AIDS?
mcqs.explanation: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) gastritis is secondary to infection with cryptosporidiosis . Other specific types of gastritis: • Eosinophilic gastritis appears to have an allergic basis and is treated with steroids and cromoglycate . • Granulomatous gastritis is seen rarely in Crohn's disease and also may be associated with tuberculosis . • Phlegmonous gastritis is a rare bacterial infection of the stomach, found in patients with severe intercurrent illnesses .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of gastric ulcer?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of gastric ulcer is the lesser curvature near incisura. Approximately 60% of ulcers are in this location and are classified as type I gastric ulcers . These ulcers are generally not associated with excessive acid secretion and may occur with low to normal acid output .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which type of gastric ulcer has increased gastric acid levels ?
mcqs.explanation: Gastric ulcers of Types II (gastric body with duodenal ulcer) and III (prepyloric ) are associated with increased gastric acid levels .432

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A biopsy was obtained from a patient with chronic peptic ulcer disease . The pathological slide is given below . Identify the false statement regarding the causative agent of this condition.

options.b: Causes the most common type of gastritis
options.c: Associated with causation of gastric MALToma
options.d: Considered by WHO as class I carcinogen

mcqs.explanation: The given slide shows the GI mucosa, stained with Warthin -Starry silver stain, infected with Helicobacter pylori. H. pylori cause hypergastrinemia . The ammonia released by H. pylori acts on the antral G-cells and releases gastrin. This is responsible for hypergastrinemia in these patients resulting in type B gastritis (the most common type of gastritis). Urea breath test and antibodies to H. pylori help us with diagnosis. The gold standard investigation for H. pylori is a tissue biopsy . H. pylori is classified by the WHO as a class I carcinogen because of the production of certain cytotoxins, notably the Cag A and Vac A, which are implicated in gastritis, peptic ulceration, and cancer.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common complication that you expect in patients suffering from peptic ulcer disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common complication of peptic ulcer disease is bleeding , followed by perforation and obstruction. The most common site for perforation of peptic ulcers is the first part of the duodenum . Complications of peptic ulcers are • Bleeding - It is the most common complication of posterior duodenal ulcer. • Perforation - It is the most common complication of anterior duodenal ulcer and gastric ulcer. • Obstruction • Hour-glass deformity of the stomach - Large long-standing gastric ulcers can lead to fibrosis. fibrosis if present can cause hourglass constriction of the stomach. Barium meal shows double pouched stomach. • Tea-pot deformity (handbag stomach) - It is caused by cicatrization and shortening of the lesser curvature. • An ulcer can erode posteriorly into the pancreas and anteriorly into the liver. • Malignancy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used for the classification of the endoscopic appearance of bleeding peptic ulcers in a patient with peptic ulcer disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Forrest classification is used for classifying the endoscopic appearance of bleeding peptic ulcers . It stratifies the risk of rebleeding based on observed stigmata of recent hemorrhage. Forrest classification is clinically very significant as it provides prognostic information to the surgeon about the need for endoscopic therapeutic intervention and the risk of rebleeding .433 Option B: The Glasgow –Blatchford bleeding score (GBS) is a screening tool to assess the likelihood that a patient with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) will need medical intervention such as a blood transfusion or endoscopic intervention. It incorporates the patient 's blood urea level , hemoglobin level , blood pressure , and other clinical parameters. Option C: Rockall score assesses the risk of rebleeding and in-hospital mortality in patients with an upper GI bleed . Option D: The Bismuth–Corlette classification system provides an anatomic description of the tumor location and longitudinal extension in the biliary tree .Stigmata of Recent Hemorrh age Forrest Classification Active Spurting I A Active Oozing I B Non-bleeding vessel II A Adherent Clot II B Flat Pigmented Spot II C Clean Based Ulcer III

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most commonly involved vessel in patients with bleeding peptic ulcers on the posterior wall?
mcqs.explanation: The most common vessel responsible for bleeding in peptic ulcer disease is the gastroduodenal artery. Ulcers located in the posterior wall can erode the mucosa and the gastroduodenal artery, leading to hematemesis and melena.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old woman was admitted to the burns ward with an involvement of 45% of the body surface area. She is at an increased risk of developing ulcers in which of the following parts of the stomach?
mcqs.explanation: 434 A patient with burn is at risk of developing Curling's ulcers (stress ulcers ). Stress ulcers in the stomach are located most commonly in the fundus . Stress gastritis occurs after a physical trauma, shock, sepsis , hemorrhage, or respiratory failure. It is characterized by multiple superficial (non-ulcerating) erosions that begin in the proximal or acid-secreting portion of the stomach and progress distally . They are almost always seen in the fundus of the stomach and usually develop within 1 to 2 days after a traumatic event. The stress -induced splanchnic vasoconstriction causes systemic hypotension and reduced blood flow leading to mucosal injury. On microscopic examination, they appear as wedge -shaped mucosal hemorrhages, with coagulation necrosis of the superficial mucosal cells . Stress ulcers present as painless upper GI bleeds . Note : Cushing ulcers arise in individuals with intracranial disease . They occur in the stomach, duodenum , and esophagus and carry a high incidence of perforation. They occur due to gastric acid hypersecretion from direct vagal nerve stimulation.

mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency room with complaints of severe abdominal pain. On examination, his vitals are stable and there is abdominal rigidity and tenderness . The erect X-ray of the abdomen is suggestive of pneumoperitoneum and the patient is posted for emergency laparotomy. It reveals the presence of a perforated type I gastric ulcer. How will you manage this patient ?

options.a: Perform distal gastrectomy with Billroth I anastomosis
options.b: Closure of the perforation with Graham's patch repair

mcqs.explanation: In stable patients without operative risks, Perforated type I gastric ulcers are best managed by distal gastrectomy with Billroth I anastomosis (with or without vagotomy). If the patient is hemodynamically unstable or unfit for surgery, simple patch repair with biopsy preferred .Type of Gastric Ulce r Management Type I Distal gastrectomy Type II and III Distal gastrectomy + Vagoto my Type IV Csendes procedureorPauchet procedureorKelling - Madlen er procedure

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Kelling -Madlener procedure is done for _____
mcqs.explanation: The Kelling -Madlener procedure is done for type lV Gastric ulcers . Surgical management of type lV gastric ulcer • Kelling -Madlener procedure - involves antrectomy and excision of gastric ulcer. • Pauchet 's procedure - involves distal gastrectomy with a selective sleeve -like extension to the lesser curvature to remove the ulcer. • Csendes Procedure - subtotal gastrectomy with sleeve -like extension to the lesser curvature.435 Management of gastric ulcerTypes of gastric ulcer Management Type l Distal gastrectomy Type ll & lll Distal gastrectomy + Vagoto my Type lV Pauchet 's procedureOrKellin g-Madlener 's procedureOrCs endes procedure

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man on SSRI presented with hematemesis and abdominal pain. An endoscopy was performed immediately which showed an actively bleeding ulcer of size 2cm in the posterior wall of the duodenum . What is the next best step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The next best step to manage the above scenario is endoscopic electrocoagulation . Management of bleeding peptic ulcer For actively bleeding ulcers or non-bleeding visible vessels , • Endoscopic therapy with a combination of epinephrine injection and electrocoagulation is done. Surgery is done only when 2 attempts of endoscopic therapy fail. • Surgical management includes duodenostomy and under-running of the vessel . Duodenal ulcers also show a good response to acid-reducing surgery or vagotomy. Medical management includes PPIs and H.pylori eradication therapy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the preferred approach for treating a patient who has a duodenal ulcer with a perforation of 2.5cm?

options.a: Primary closure and buttress with well -vascularised omentum

mcqs.explanation: The preferred treatment of perforations between 1–3 cm in size is a Graham patch repair.436 Treatment of perforated duodenal ulcer: • <1 cm: Primary closure + buttress with well -vascularised omentum • 1–3 cm: Graham patch repair • >3 cm: Closure of defect using omentum or jejunal serosa + pyloric exclusion + gastrojejunostomy

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about the type of vagotomy shown in the image below ?
mcqs.explanation: The picture depicts Highly Selective Vagotomy (HSV ). Post-procedure acid reduction is minimum in HSV . It involves resection of crowfoot branches , 6cm from the gastroesophageal junction but stopped 7cm from the pylorus . The nerve of Latarjet from the anterior and posterior vagal trunk supplies the acid pepsin areas of the stomach. It is spared in HSV . Usually , the motor branch to the pylorus is also preserved . There are 3 types of vagotomy • Highly selective vagotomy • Truncal vagotomy + gastrojejunostomy • Truncal vagotomy + antrectomy. Highly selective vagotomy • Acid reduction is minimum. • Highest ulcer recurrence rate. • Minimum postoperative complications . Truncal vagotomy + antrectomy • Acid reduction is maximum. • Least ulcer recurrence rate. • Maximum postoperative complications . Note : Vagal nerves are motor to the stomach and denervation of the antro-pyloro-duodenal segment results in gastric stasis after truncal vagotomy. Hence , a drainage procedure , most commonly Heineke –Mikulicz pyloroplasty or gastrojejunostomy is done along with vagotomy. The criminal nerve of Grassi is a branch of the posterior vagal trunk that arises at the gastroesophageal junction and supplies the fundus of the stomach. It is called a criminal nerve because it is often missed during vagotomy procedures and can result in recurrent peptic ulcer disease .437

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the surgical procedure shown below .
mcqs.explanation: The procedure illustrated in the image is Billroth II gastrectomy . Following resection , the distal end of the stomach is narrowed by the closure of the lesser curve aspect of the remnant. The greater curve aspect is then anastomosed , usually in a retro-colic fashion, to the jejunum. Option A: In Billroth I gastrectomy , the lower half of the stomach is removed, and the cut end of the stomach is anastomosed to the first part of the duodenum . Option C: Braun modification of classical Billroth II gastrectomy is Billroth II reconstruction with jejunojejunostomy. Option D: Roux-en Y gastrojejunostomy is a gastric bypass surgery where a loop of jejunum is anastomosed to a proximal gastric pouch.438

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain. Guarding is present on per abdomen examination. HR is 110bpm and BP is 88/60mmHg. Erect abdominal X-ray is shown below . Which of the following would you proceed with, for managing this case?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) is suggestive of gastrointestinal perforation. It is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy. It is a surgical emergency . Management includes : • Adequate preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids followed by correction of electrolyte imbalance, instituting broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and • Early surgical intervention/laparotomy to address the cause for pneumoperitoneum and stop further contamination of the peritoneal cavity.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 54-year-old man presented with acute onset of abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting. Examination revealed tenderness over the right iliac fossa. USG showed gas around the right kidney. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pneumoretroperitoneum caused by a perforated duodenal ulcer. Posterior duodenal ulcer perforates into the retroperitoneum , and the contents leak through the right paracolic gutter into the right iliac fossa, mimicking appendicitis . This is called Valentino syndrome. On USG, gas can be seen around the right kidney known as the renal veil sign.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 30-year-old actress who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity , presents with complaints of sweating , palpitations , epigastric fullness , and loose stools which start immediately after meals. Which of the following would you not associate with her condition?

options.a: It is precipitated by carbohydrate rich food.
options.b: It is more common after partial gastrectomy with the Billroth II reconstruction.
options.d: It is relieved by lying down.

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of early dumping syndrome. Hypoglycemia \037 does not occur in early dumping syndrome. Hypoglycemia is seen in late dumping syndrome secondary to raised insulin levels . Dumping syndrome is a complication occurring post gastrectomy . It can be early or late . Early dumping syndrome is due to the high osmotic load that reaches the small bowel , leading to sequestration of fluid from the circulation into the gastrointestinal tract (GIT ). This fluid shift induces autonomic responses . It is characterized by more GI and fewer cardiovascular effects such as: • Epigastric fullness • Sweating • Lightheadedness • Tachycardia • Diarrhea Symptoms are aggravated by having more food and relieved by lying down.439 Late dumping syndrome is due to an increase in insulin levels and secondary hypoglycemia . This hypoglycemia causes a catecholamine surge , which results in predominantly cardiovascular effects such as: • Diaphoresis • Tremulousness • Light-headedness • Tachycardia • Confusion The symptoms are aggravated by exercise and relieved by having food. The principal treatment for both types of dumping syndrome is dietary manipulation. Meals based on fat and protein are known to work the best . Octreotide before meals is useful .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the casualty with severe upper abdominal pain and recurrent retching with minimal vomiting. A nasogastric tube insertion was tried but it was unsuccessful . A chest X-ray showed diffuse distension of bowel loops and a left -sided diaphragmatic defect . Which of the following statements regarding this condition is false ?

options.b: Organoaxial type is associated with a diaphragmatic defect
options.c: Surgery is performed through a transabdominal approach

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of gastric volvulus. Organoaxial gastric volvulus is more common (66%) than mesenteroaxial volvulus (33%). Organoaxial gastric volvulus: Torsion occurs along the longitudinal axis of the stomach and often occurs acutely . It is associated with a diaphragmatic defect . Mesenteroaxial gastric volvulus: Torsion occurs along the vertical axis. It is partial (<180 degrees ) and recurrent. It is not associated with a diaphragmatic defect .The Borchardt triad is seen in gastric volvulus: • Sudden -onset severe upper abdominal pain • Recurrent retching with production of little vomitus • Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube440 Management involves reduction and uncoiling of the stomach through a transabdominal approach.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male presented to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain, diarrhea, loss of appetite , and loss of weight . On examination, the patient had peripheral edema and ascites . Laboratory studies showed decreased serum albumin but normal serum levels of transaminases and gastrin. Upper GI endoscopy showed the following appearance of the stomach. Which of the following is true about the condition?

options.b: Gastrectomy is the treatment of choice in severe cases
options.c: Caused by overexpression of TNF alpha

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the image showing the presence of hypertrophied gastric mucosal folds are characteristic of Menetrier 's disease . Gastrectomy is the treatment of choice in severe cases of Menetrier 's disease . Menetrier 's disease is a premalignant condition. The disease seems to be caused by overexpression of transforming growth factor-alpha i.e., TGF-alpha (not TNF-alpha), which stimulates the EGFR pathway , resulting in increased proliferation of mucus cells /foveolar hyperplasia . This results in gross hypertrophy of the gastric mucosal folds , mucus production, and hypochlorhydria . The antrum is usually spared . There is a loss of albumin (up to 10 g/day), across the gastric mucosa leading to hypoproteinemia . Secondary symptoms include weight loss, diarrhea, and peripheral edema . Histologically , it is characterized by hyperplasia of foveolar mucous cells . The glands are cystically dilated and elongated with a corkscrew-like appearance as shown in the image below .Cetuximab , an EGFR inhibitory antibody, is now considered the first-line treatment for Menetrier's disease , leaving total gastrectomy for severe disease with persistent and substantial protein loss refractory to cetuximab .441

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following factors will increase the risk of a patient developing gastric carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma . Aspirin, which is a COX inhibitor, is protective against gastric cancer. Eating refrigerated food has reduced the need for salting of food for preservation, and thus reduced the incidence of gastric cancer. Males are more commonly affected as compared to females .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of gastric adenocarcinoma in the Asian population ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of gastric adenocarcinoma in the Asian population is the antrum. This is because H. pylori infections are relatively more prevalent in Asian countries and are associated with carcinoma of the body and distal stomach than the proximal stomach. However, in western countries , the proximal stomach is the most common site . This is attributed to a lesser prevalence of untreated H.pylori infections and a greater burden of chronic GERD and obesity in western countries .448

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man presents to the hospital with a 3-day history of haematemesis . Upper GI endoscopy reveals multiple gastric polyps and a positive urease breath test . Which type of polyp is he most likely to have?
mcqs.explanation: The given history and investigations are suggestive of Helicobacter pylori infection . The polyps most commonly associated with H. pylori infection are hyperplastic polyps . Hyperplastic polyps usually regress following H. pylori eradication therapy . Benign gastric polyps are classified into two groups : • Neoplastic : • Adenoma • Fundic gastric polyp • Non- neoplastic : • Hyperplastic polyp (most common) • Inflammatory polyp • Hamartomatous polyp Note : The terms hyperplastic polyp and metaplastic polyp refer to the same lesion, however, 'hyperplastic polyp ' is a preferred term.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly patient who presented with abdominal discomfort and weight loss was diagnosed with type I gastric cancer according to Lauren's classification . Which of the following is not true regarding this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Type I gastric cancer is associated with hematogenous spread . Lauren's system classifies gastric cancer pathology as either type I (intestinal) or type II (diffuse ), based on differences in etiology , epidemiology , and pathology . Intestinal type of gastric cancer shows hematogenous spread , whereas diffuse -type shows transmural and lymphatic spread .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following genetic mutations is least likely to be seen in a patient with an intestinal type of gastric cancer?

options.b: Loss of heterozygosity in the APC gene
options.c: Under expression of transforming growth factor \
options.d: Loss of heterozygosity at the bcl-2 gene

mcqs.explanation: In the intestinal type of gastric cancer, several growth factors may be overexpressed , including transforming growth factor \033, the epidermal growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). Molecular pathologies seen in Intestinal type : • Mutation or loss of heterozygosity in the APC gene or in \031-catenin • Inactivation of p53 • Loss of heterozygosity at the BCL -2 gene • Microsatellite instability Molecular pathologies seen in diffuse -type :449 • Mutation of E- cadherin • Inactivation of p53

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man, presented with multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting containing undigested food particles within one-hour post meals. On physical examination, he was found to be anemic and cachexic. CECT abdomen revealed diffuse infiltration of a neoplastic growth into the stomach wall. What Bormann 's classification does this tumor belong to?
mcqs.explanation: The history and investigation findings are suggestive of gastric outlet obstruction caused by a diffusely infiltrating type of gastric carcinoma . This is commonly known as linitis plastica and it is classified as type IV in Bormann 's classification system .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient was found to have a tumor extending up to 1cm below the gastroesophageal junction on EUS . According to the Siewert classification , which stage of carcinoma does she have?
mcqs.explanation: The patient is likely to have a Siewert type II lesion. This include tumors with the center located 1 cm above and 2 cm below the GE junction. • Type I: Adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus - the epicenter of the lesion is 1-5 cm above GEJ • Type II : Adenocarcinoma of the cardia - the epicenter of the lesion is up to 1 cm above and 2 cm below GEJ • Type III : Subcardial type adenocarcinoma - the epicenter of the lesion is 2-5 cm below GEJ

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A woman presented to the gastroenterology OPD with significant weight loss, fatigue , and a bloating sensation for the past 8 months. A detailed workup was done, and she was diagnosed with early gastric carcinoma . All of the following structures can be involved in this stage except :
mcqs.explanation: In early gastric cancer, there is no involvement of muscularis propria. Gastric cancer can be classified as early and advanced gastric cancer, based on the extent of involvement. Early gastric cancer involves: • Mucosa (including muscularis mucosa) • Submucosa • +/- lymph nodes Advanced gastric cancer involves: • Muscularis layer • +/- adjacent structures450

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An Asian man who is a known smoker presented to the OPD with dysphagia , nausea, and loss of appetite . Endoscopy revealed a tumor arising from the stomach. Which of the following statements is false regarding TNM staging for this condition?

options.a: In T4 lesions , tumor perforates the serosa.
options.b: Metastasis in 1-5 lymph nodes is N1 disease .
options.c: Tumor invades adjacent organs in T4 lesions .
options.d: Metastasis in > 15 lymph nodes is N3b.

mcqs.explanation: The clinical features and endoscopy findings point to a diagnosis of gastric carcinoma . According to TNM staging of gastric carcinoma , N1 disease refers to metastasis to 1-2 regional lymph nodes .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A positive Troisier's sign refers to the involvement of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Troisier's sign refers to the enlargement of left supraclavicular lymph nodes , which is also known as Virchow nodes . It is seen in patients with gastric cancer metastasis , caused by the spread of the tumor via the thoracic duct into the left supraclavicular lymph nodes . It is a sign of advanced cancer. It is one of the atypical presentations of gastric carcinoma . Other atypical presentations of gastric carcinoma include • Sister Mary Joseph nodule • Due to periumbilical metastasis . • See in both gastric cancer (most common) and ovarian cancer. • Krukenberg's tumor • Bilateral ovarian metastasis • Due to retrograde lymphatic spread • Irish nodule • Left axillary lymphadenopathy . • Blumer shelf nodules • Pelvic metastasis into the pouch of Douglas / retrovesical pouch451 • Sign of advanced gastric carcinoma • Felt on digital palpation • Trosseau syndrome • Migratory thrombophlebitis • Leser Trelet sign • Multiple seborrheic keratoses • Resolves after gastrectomy • Tripe palms • Hyperkeratosis palm. The image below shows an elderly man with left supraclavicular lymph nodes enlarged .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A male patient who was diagnosed with early gastric cancer is planned for endoscopic mucosal resection. Which of the following features would make him a poor candidate for this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: Endoscopic mucosal resection for gastric cancer should not be performed in case of ulcerated gastric cancer. Indications for endoscopic resection of early gastric cancer: • Tumor smaller than 2cm • Tumor limited to the mucosa • No lymphovascular invasion • No ulceration • Well or moderately well -differentiated histopathology . If any of these are not fulfilled , then gastrectomy with lymph node dissection is indicated .452 For a proximal gastric carcinoma a total gastrectomy is done and for distal gastric carcinoma , subtotal gastrectomy is ideal . For advanced carcinoma gastrectomy can be done as a palliative treatment .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: According to the Japanese classification for gastric carcinoma , which of the following is the level 5 lymph node?
mcqs.explanation: Suprapyloric nodes are the level 5 gastric lymph nodes . The japanese classification for gastric carcinoma (JCGC) staging system divided lymph nodes into 16 groups based on the likelihood of metastasis from the primary tumor and removal of lymph nodes during gastrectomy . The surgery for gastric cancer involves the removal of the primary tumor and lymph nodes . Depending on the extent of lymph node stations removed, the surgery may be either D1 or D2 gastrectomy . D1 gastrectomy involves the removal of lymph node stations 1-6. D2 gastrectomy involves the removal of lymph node stations 1-11 .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with gastric adenocarcinoma is posted for surgery. What is the extent of negative margin you should remove around the tumor for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In surgical resection of gastric cancer, at least 5cm of negative margin should be removed around the tumor.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented with vague abdominal pain and feeling of a lump in the abdomen for the past 1 year. He was found to have a tumor arising from the stomach on CT scan. Biopsy of the lesion showed tumor cells positive for CD117 and CD34. What is the most likely origin of the tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical and histopathological features are suggestive of gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST ). They arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.453

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a component of Carney's triad?
mcqs.explanation: Carney's triad does not include pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Carney's triad consists of: • Extra-adrenal paraganglioma • Gastrointestinal stromal tumor • Pulmonary chondroma

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents with epigastric pain and intermittent vomiting for 2 months. He was inadequately treated for H. pylori infection 3 months back. The patient is HIV positive and is on ART for the same. Endoscopy reveals a fungating mass arising from the stomach. Biopsy of the lesion shows tumor cells positive for CD20 . Which of the following is false regarding this tumor?

options.a: Stomach is the most common organ involved.
options.c: Fundus is the most common site involved
options.d: It is associated with H. pylori infections

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of gastric lymphoma. The most common type of gastric lymphoma is non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL). Among NHL, the most common type is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL ) (55 %), followed by gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT ) lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, mantle cell and follicular lymphoma. Immunodeficiencies and H. pylori infections are risk factors for the development of primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The antrum is the most common site for gastric lymphoma. The stomach is the most common organ to develop lymphoma in the GI system . Treatment: • Combined modality - chemotherapy , surgery, and/or radiotherapy • The most common chemotherapeutic combination for DLBCL is R-CHOP [Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide , Hydroxydaunomycin (doxorubicin), Oncovin (vincristine), prednisone ].

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not an indication for surgery in a patient with gastric lymphoma?
mcqs.explanation: Intractable pain is not an indication for surgery in the case of gastric lymphoma. Indications for surgery in gastric lymphoma: • Patients with symptomatic recurrence or treatment failure • Patients who develop complications , such as bleeding , gastric outlet obstruction, and perforation

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A woman underwent a total gastrectomy 5 months ago for gastric carcinoma . Which of the following is the most common metabolic complication expected in her?
mcqs.explanation: The most common metabolic complication seen after gastrectomy is iron deficiency anemia.454 Although absorption of iron occurs primarily in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, it needs an optimum acidic environment for absorption. Hence , due to a combination of decreased iron intake, impaired iron absorption, and chronic blood loss, there is iron deficiency anemia. The addition of iron supplements to the patient 's diet corrects iron deficiency anemia. Complications of gastrectomy : • Dumping syndrome: early and late • Nutritional deficiencies - Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vit B12 deficiency , and osteoporosis • Diarrhea • Duodenal stump leak/blow out • Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis • Gall stones • Roux syndrome

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old male presented with upper GI bleeding , abdominal pain, and a palpable abdominal mass. An endoscopic biopsy revealed a 5 cm tumor, with a high mitotic rate and c-KIT positivity in the body of the stomach. Which of the following is the best treatment of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of GIST with a high risk of malignancy (high mitotic rate). The best treatment modality in the given scenario is surgical resection (with negative margin) followed by imatinib. Imatinib is a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor. Option A: Surgical resection + surveillance is done for GIST with a low risk of malignancy. The risk of malignancy is determined by 2 factors - the size of the tumor and mitotic index. Option C: Lymphadenectomy (D2 gastrectomy ) is not done in GIST as it does not show lymph node metastasis. Option D: GIST is radioresistant and does not respond to conventional chemotherapy . It only responds to imatinib. If imatinib resistant, sunitinib or sorafenib is given.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The gastrectomy specimen of a 56-year-old woman who underwent total gastrectomy showed HER2/neu positivity . Which among the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Trastuzumab is the drug of choice in carcinoma stomach with HER2/neu mutation. Trastuzumab is a HER2 receptor antagonist. Chemotherapy options in carcinoma stomach: • With HER2/neu mutation - Trastuzumab/Herceptin • With PD-L1 gene mutation - Pembrolizumab • Oral chemotherapy drugs: • Tegafur • Oteracil • Gimeracil455 • Conventional chemotherapy drugs used are 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin. Chemotherapy is offered for patients with lymph node-positive disease and advanced gastric carcinoma (T3 and beyond ) as part of palliative treatment .456

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old female patient of asian ethnicity with a BMI of 34 kg/m\262 has decided to seek surgical options to reduce her weight . She has multiple comorbidities . Which of the following would make her unsuitable for bariatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Severe depression would make her unsuitable for bariatric surgery. The patient should be psychologically stable before undergoing bariatric surgery. Psychological instability makes the patient incapable of understanding the implications of the procedure . It becomes difficult for the patient to understand the lifestyle changes necessary for optimal outcomes .461 The indications for bariatric surgery as per international standards as well as the modifications specific for Asian and Indian populations are as follows : The criteria for Asian and Indian patients has been modified by reducing the BMI by 2.5 points. This modification takes into account the geographical differences in food, lifestyle , and genetic make-up of patients .International criteria Asian-specific modification i n BMI 1.BMI �o 40 kg/m2regardless of obesity -related comorbiditi es BMI �o 37.5kg/m2 2. BMI �o 35 kg/m2with obesit y-related comorbidities, such asHypertensionType 2 DMCo ronary artery disease (CAD)D yslipidemiaObstructive sleep apnea (OSA): Pickwickian sy ndromeArthritis and function al impairment BMI �o .5kg/m2 3. Has failed to lose weight d espite :Lifestyle modifications PharmacotherapyPsychother apy 4. Is psychologically stable 5. Motivated and capable of u nderstanding lifestyle change s

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a contraindication for bariatric surgery?

options.a: Failure to lose weight despite psychotherapy

mcqs.explanation: Failure to lose weight by an obese patient despite psychotherapy , pharmacotherapy, and lifestyle modifications is an indication for metabolic surgery. Potential contraindications to metabolic and bariatric surgery include : • Severe medical disease making anesthesia or surgery prohibitively risky (American Society of Anesthesiologists class IV ) • Mentally incompetent to understand the procedure • Inability or unwillingness to change lifestyle postoperatively • Drug, alcohol, or other addiction (including smoking) • Active problem of bulimia or other eating disorder • Psychological instability (schizophrenia, severe depression ) • Unsupportive home environment462

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: For a patient being considered for bariatric surgery, which of the following will you not include when calculating the Obesity Surgery-Mortality risk score (OS-MRS score)?
mcqs.explanation: Type-2 Diabetes mellitus (DM) is not a component of the Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score (OS-MRS). Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS) and Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score (OS-MRS) are used to discuss with patients the likely prognosis without surgery, and the risk of complications . Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score (OS-MRS): Note : Uncontrolled diabetes is considered a risk factor, as in any other surgery. However, it is not considered under the OS-MRS scoring system .Risk factor Scor e Age �o 45 yr BMI �o 1 Male gender Hypertension DVT (Deep Vein Thrombosis) / PE(Pulmonary Embolism) 1Risk Catego ry Scor e Post-op mortalit y A (Low) 0-1 0.3 B (Moderat e) 2-3 1.7 C (High) 4-5 3.2

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old male patient with a BMI of 42 kg/m\262 with central obesity is scheduled to undergo bariatric surgery. As preparation for surgery, he is advised to follow a low-carbohydrate, low-fat, and moderate -protein meal, for two weeks . On follow -up, he is found to be non-compliant with the diet . What is the next best step ?
mcqs.explanation: Psychological re-evaluation is necessary to address the underlying psychological blocks in a patient who is unable to comply with the diet . Morbidly obese individuals, especially those with central obesity , have large livers that make surgery impossible . Liver shrinkage diet helps reduce the size of the liver. This allows mobility for the surgeon and increases the chances of a safer procedure . Liver shrinkage diet : • Low-carbohydrate, low-fat and moderate protein diet • Started at least 2 weeks prior to the surgery463 The ability to comply with the diet and lose weight suggests that the patient is willing to make an effort to adopt lifestyle modifications. Failure to do so must arouse suspicion of important underlying psychological blocks, which need addressing .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a bariatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Pyloric exclusion with gastrojejunostomy is not a bariatric surgery. It is a technique used in the repair of duodenal and pancreatic injuries. Based on their mechanism of action, bariatric surgeries are categorized as follows :Mechanism of action Common procedures Purely Restrictive Laparoscopic adjustable gastr ic bandingSleeve gastrectomy Intragastric balloon placeme nt Predominantly Malabsorpti ve Biliopancreatic diversion (BP D)Duodenal switch (DS) Restrictive + Malabsorptive Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy (gastric bypass )

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a reversible bariatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Laparoscopic gastric banding and intra-gastric balloon placement surgeries are considered to be reversible bariatric surgeries . It is because the gastric band or the intragastric balloon can be removed once the desired weight loss or metabolic benefit is achieved .464 An inflatable band is placed just below the GE junction \030 A small virtual stomach pouch is created \030 Reduces hunger (probably vagally mediated ) \030 Reduced consumption of food \030 Weight loss Complications of LAGB include : • Prolapse / Slippage (most common) • Band erosion of the stomach wall and rupture • Increased risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism (highest risk within 1 month of surgery), managed with early ambulation, pressure stockings and LMWH .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In recent years, what is the most commonly performed bariatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Sleeve gastrectomy is the most commonly performed bariatric surgery, in recent years.A vertical sleeve is created , resecting most of the greater curvature \030 Restriction of stomach capacity \030465 Early satiety \030 Reduced consumption of food \030 Weight loss Advantages of sleeve gastrectomy : • Less challenging procedure • Preservation of pylorus (avoids gastric dumping ) • No need for serial adjustments (as seen with gastric banding) • Reduction in internal hernias (as seen with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass ) Complications of sleeve gastrectomy : • Bleed from the staple line • Leakage from staple line (close to the angle of His)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old woman with diabetes and a BMI of 46 kg/m\262 underwent laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). On the second postoperative day, she developed fever, tachycardia, and blood reports show leucocytosis . What is the next best step in her management?

options.a: Send blood for culture and sensitivity
options.b: USG abdomen to locate the septic focus

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of fever, tachycardia, and leucocytosis in a postoperative patient of LSG should raise suspicion for leak along the gastric staple line. The next best step in the management of this patient is to perform a contrast-enhanced CT. Leaks following LSG most commonly occur in the proximal third of the stomach, close to the angle of His. Early leaks are due to tissue trauma and staple misfire, and late leaks are usually due to ischemia and high intragastric pressure. Management of the leak involves providing nutritional support to the patient and adequate drainage. Once the leak is diagnosed , the patient should be kept nil per oral. Total parenteral nutrition and antibiotic therapy should be started in the patient . Drainage can be done either by CT-guided percutaneous catheter placement , endoscopic stenting , or operative procedures . Note : Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a risk factor for an anastomotic leak. Treatment with continuous positive airway pressure might reduce this risk .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in bariatric surgery?

options.a: Gastric pouch is created at the lesser curvature.
options.b: Biliary limb is 100 -150 cm in length
options.c: It is a purely restrictive type of procedure .

mcqs.explanation: Gastric pouch is created at the lesser curvature in Roux-en-Y gastric bypass .466 A small proximal gastric pouch is created at the lesser curvature \030 Create a shorter biliary limb of 30 - 50 cm (duodenum ); Create a longer Roux limb of 75 - 150 cm (jejunum) \030 Bowel continuity is restored by a Y - jejunojejunostomy \030 Restrictive + Malabsorptive mechanism \030 Weight loss Note : Biliary limb is usually kept short (30-50 cm) in order to reduce vitamin and mineral deficiencies .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old woman presented to the casualty with vomiting and severe colicky pain in the abdomen for the past 48 hours. She had undergone a weight reduction surgery six months ago and had achieved around 30% weight loss. Her plain X-ray abdomen is given below . Which of the following bariatric procedures was most likely done in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and radiograph (dilated bowel segments with valvulae conniventes in the left upper quadrant ) are suggestive of small bowel obstruction. Bariatric surgery, specifically , Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery is associated with the creation of mesenteric defects . The small bowel can herniate through these defects (internal hernia) and get strangulated , resulting in bowel obstruction. In addition, as the person loses weight (due to the bariatric procedure ), the protective , space -occupying effect of the mesenteric fat is lost and hernia spaces open up, further increasing the risk of internal hernia. The laparoscopic procedure has a higher risk compared to open surgery since fewer adhesions form to tether small-bowel loops and prevent them from467 herniating. Adequate closure of the mesenteric defects by the surgeon at the time of operation significantly reduces the risk of internal hernia. Other complications specific to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass : • Nutritional deficiencies : iron (most common), folate , Vitamin A, D, K and B12 • Anastomosis site leak • Bleeding from the site of gastrojejunostomy • Dumping syndrome • Marginal ulcers • Increased risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism Option A: Sleeve gastrectomy is often complicated by staple line leak. Option B: Laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding is associated with band slippage and erosion. Option D: Endoluminal stapling is also used to create a gastric sleeve . It is associated with postoperative nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and transient dysphagia .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who previously underwent biliopancreatic diversion surgery has been having excessive malabsorption and is now being planned for a revisional procedure to increase the length of the common channel. What is the usual length of the common channel?
mcqs.explanation: The usual length of the common channel in biliopancreatic diversion (BPD) is 50 cm (0.5 m). Revisions increase common channel by up to 150 cm. The length of the common channel plays a significant role in the amount of weight loss achieved with BPD procedure . A shorter common channel implies a greater length of the bypassed small bowel . This induces more malabsorption and thereby greater weight loss.Distal hemigastrectomy is performed to create a residual gastric pouch \030468 Terminal ileum is divided 250 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve \030 Gastroileostomy : Proximal anastomosis between the distal end of divided ileum and residual gastric pouch \030 Ileoileostomy : Distal anastomosis between the proximal end of divided ileum and terminal ileum \030 A common channel of 50 cm is established \030 Malabsorption \030 Weight loss Prophylactic cholecystectomy is usually performed since there is an increased incidence of gallstones due to malabsorption of bile salts. Complications of biliopancreatic diversion surgery: • Anastomosis site leak • Nutritional deficiencies : Iron ; folate ; vitamins A, D, K, and B12 • Marginal ulcers • Bleeding • Increased risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism (maximum risk within 1 month of surgery), managed with early ambulation, pressure stocking, and LMWH

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a surgical step that will be done during a duodenal switch procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: In duodenal switch (DS) surgery, gastroduodenostomy is not performed .469 Sleeve gastrectomy is performed \030 Duodenum is divided 2 cm beyond the pylorus ; Terminal ileum is divided 250 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve \030 Duodenoileostomy : Proximal anastomosis between the distal end of divided ileum and duodenum \030 Ileoileostomy : Distal anastomosis between the proximal end of divided ileum and terminal ileum \030 A common channel of 100 cm is established \030 Malabsorption \030 Weight loss Prophylactic cholecystectomy is usually performed since there is an increased incidence of gallstones due to malabsorption of bile salts. Complications of duodenal switch surgery: • Anastomosis site leak and bleeding • Nutritional deficiencies - Iron , folate , Vitamin A, D, K and B12 • Increased risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism (maximum risk within 1 month of surgery) - managed with early ambulation, pressure stocking, and LMWH In comparison to BPD, the incidence of marginal ulcers is negligible470

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of death in patients who undergo bariatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: Pulmonary embolism is the most common cause of death in patients of bariatric surgery. Pathogenesis : Obesity \030 Increased levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 \030 Blocks conversion of plasminogen to plasmin \030 Decreased fibrinolytic activity \030 Hypercoagulable state \030 Increased risk for VTE Morbidly obese patients are physically inactive. Restricted mobility post -surgery potentiates this risk of developing deep vein thrombosis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In patients who undergo gastric bypass surgery (bariatric surgery), what is the 3-year percentage of diabetes remission?
mcqs.explanation: The 3-year percentage of diabetes remission for gastric bypass surgery is 50%. Different Bariatric surgeries and their Outcomes :Protein/Calorie Malabsorp tion 3 year % Excess Weight L oss (EWL ) 3 yr % Diabetes remis sion Gastric band No 40 -50 % % Gastric bypass No 50 - 60 % 50 % Sleeve gastrectomy No 50 - 60 % 50 % Biliopancreatic diversion / Duodenal switch Yes 70 -80 % 80 %471

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the surgical anatomy of the small intestine ?

options.a: The duodenum is demarcated from the jejunum by the ligament of Treitz.
options.b: The ileum makes up three -fifths of the small intestine .
options.c: The blood supply to the jejunum may have four or five separate arcades with shorter vasa recta
options.d: The jejunum has a larger circumference, is thicker than the ileum

mcqs.explanation: The jejunum receives its blood supply from long, straight vasa recta arising from only one or two arcades. The blood supply to the ileum may have 4-5 separate arcades with shorter vasa recta.The ligament of Treitz or the suspensory muscle of the duodenum is found at the junction of the duodenum and jejunum. It also forms the line of demarcation for gastrointestinal bleeding : • Upper GI bleeding - refers to bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz • Lower GI bleeding - refers to bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz.484

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In a plain X-ray of the abdomen, the small bowel is said to be dilated if the diameter is more than ______.
mcqs.explanation: The small bowel is said to be dilated if the diameter is more than 3 cm in a plain X-ray. The following triad of findings is specific for small bowel obstruction on plain X-ray imaging of the abdomen: • Dilated small bowel loops (>3 cm in diameter ) • Air-fluid levels seen on upright films • A paucity of air in the colon.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In a suspected case of bowel obstruction, the presence of which of the following helps you to distinguish the small intestine from the large intestine ?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of valvule conniventes (plicae circulares) helps to distinguish the small intestine from the large intestine . They are prominent mucosal folds seen in the gross examination of the small intestine and are also visible radiographically. They are more prominent in the jejunum. Radiological differences between small bowel and large bowel obstruction are: Investigation of choice : CECT abdomen (adults ); USG abdomen (children)Radiological feature s Small bowel Large bo wel Valvulae connivente s Present in jejunu m Absent No of Loops Many Few Distribution of loops Central Peripher al Haustra Absent Present Diameter 3-5 cm >5 cm485 Radiological feature s Small bowel Large bo wel Solid faeces Absent Present

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 42-year-old man with past history of inguinal hernia presented with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain that started 4 hours ago. His abdomen was tender and rigid along with a lump in the inguinal region with purplish skin changes . Which of the following is the ideal management for this patient ?

options.a: Resuscitative measures and arrange for immediate laparotomy
options.b: Conservative management with a nasogastric tube and IV fluid , assessment every 24 hrs
options.c: Perform an oral contrast study , followed by pneumatic decompression

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of intestinal obstruction, due to a strangulated inguinal hernia. The ideal management is exploratory laparotomy as soon as possible with ongoing resuscitative measures until surgery. Bowel strangulation is a type of mechanical bowel obstruction, associated with complete cessation of blood supply leading to irreversible loss of viability of the affected bowel segment . Inguinal hernias, most commonly of non-reducible type , are associated with a high chance of strangulation and need urgent medical intervention. Bowel strangulation can be suspected in the presence of • constant severe abdominal pain, • abdominal tenderness with rigidity and peritonism, • signs of shock, and lack of response to conservative management. • Reduced bowel wall enhancement on CT When strangulation occurs in an external hernia, the lump is tense , tender , and irreducible with overlying skin changes (erythema or purplish discoloration). Supportive management: • IV fluids • Nasogastric tube to decompress the bowel and reduce abdominal distention • IV antibiotics (adequate coverage required for gram -ve and anaerobes)486 • Analgesia Definitive management: • Continue supportive management up to 72 hrs if suspicious of adhesions . Surgical exploration and adhesiolysis should be done if there is no improvement. • Immediate surgical exploration and resection of non-viable gut segments if suspicious of any of the following : • Obstructed external hernia • Clinical features suspicious of intestinal strangulation • Obstruction in a 'virgin ' abdomen (i.e no prior history of intraabdominal surgery)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A surgeon sees a necrotic bowel when operating on a child for an inguinal hernia. What is true about the resection and anastomosis of the bowel ?

options.a: The surgeon must use chromic catgut
options.b: The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures
options.c: The surgeon must use the single -layer, extramucosal suture technique
options.d: The surgeon must use the single -layer seromuscular suture technique

mcqs.explanation: The standard technique used currently for resection anastomosis of the bowel is a one-layer extra mucosal suture technique since it causes the least tissue necrosis and luminal narrowing . Interrupted and continuous single -layer suture techniques are adequate and safe . The extra mucosal suture must also include the submucosa because this layer has a high collagen content and it is the most stable suture layer in all sections of the gastrointestinal tract. Catgut has now been replaced with absorbable synthetic polymers . Stapling devices can be used when speed is required.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 5-year-old child who underwent an appendicectomy is brought to the emergency with abdominal distension and vomiting. The mother tells that the child passed stools that looked like currant jelly . The ultrasound finding is shown below . What is the most likely location of this pathology in this child?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette and the USG showing the doughnut sign (target sign) are suggestive of postoperative intussusception and the most likely location is ileoileal in postoperative cases . Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment . The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic . However, ileoileal is the most common location of intussusception postoperatively and in Henoch–Sch\366nlein Purpura. Causes of intussusception are: • Idiopathic (most common cause in children) • Pathological lead points such as enlarged submucosal Peyer's patch, lymphoma, intestinal polyp , leiomyomas, etc . • Meckel 's diverticulum • A recent upper GI or respiratory infection , rotavirus vaccination has also shown some association with intussusception in children. The characteristic clinical triad includes : • Pain • Palpable sausage -shaped mass487 • Red currant jelly stools USG findings in intussusception include : • Target sign (also known as the doughnut sign)- The appearance is generated by concentric alternating echogenic (submucosa and serosa) with hypoechogenic bands (muscularis propria). • Pseudokidney sign: this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel : • the edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and • the mesentery which is dragged into the intussusception resembles the renal hilum. • Crescent in a doughnut sign. Barium enema shows the characteristic coiled spring appearance . Treatment: • Reduction of intussusception should be done immediately after the diagnosis. • Radiologic hydrostatic reduction has a success rate of 80-95% in cases of ileocolic intussusception • Surgical reduction is only done in the presence of refractory shock, suspected bowel necrosis or perforation, peritonitis , and multiple recurrences .The above image shows the coiled spring appearance

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 3-day-old neonate presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. An erect X-ray of the abdomen is done and shown below. The neonate is taken up for surgery and an apple -peel bowel with loss of dorsal mesentery is seen . Which type of ileal atresia has this feature ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image showing a triple bubble appearance and associated finding of apple -peel bowel with loss of dorsal mesentery is a feature of type 3 ileal atresia. Small bowel atresias present with intestinal obstruction soon after birth. Bilious vomiting is the dominant feature in jejunal atresia whereas abdominal distension is more with ileal atresia.488 Plain abdominal radiographs show a variable number of dilated loops of bowel and fluid levels according to the level of obstruction. • Jejunal/ileal atresia - Triple bubble appearance • Duodenal atresia - Double bubble appearance A contrast study is the next best investigation to exclude other bowel anomalies. In jejunal/ileal atresia, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is possible . If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated , it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis. Classification of Jejunoileal atresia:Type Feature Type Mucosal web or diaphragm Type With an atretic cord between two blind ends of bowel with intact mesentery Type 3 a Complete separation of the bl ind ends of the bowel by a V - shaped mesenteric gap Type 3 b Anapple peelorChristmas tre e deformitywith a large mese nteric gap Type Multiple atresias, with a strin g of sausage appearance489

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child with complaints of abdominal pain and vomiting for the past 24 hours associated with tenderness over McBurney's point undergoes open appendicectomy . However, during surgery, the appendix was found to be normal . On exploration of the ileum , the following finding is seen . Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?

options.a: It is a lead point for intussusception
options.b: Gastric mucosa is the most common heterotropic tissue
options.d: Located 60 cm proximal to ileocecal valve

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of Meckel 's diverticulitis . It arises from the antimesenteric border of the small intestine . Meckel 's diverticulum is the most commonly encountered congenital anomaly of the small intestine . Meckel 's diverticulum is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct or omphalomesenteric duct that develops during weeks 5 to 7 of gestation . It contains all 3 layers of the intestine and hence it is a true diverticulum. It is located 45 to 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve. The most common heterotopic tissue within the Meckel 's diverticulum is gastric mucosa (50%) followed by pancreatic mucosa(5%) and colonic mucosa. Most Meckel 's diverticula are benign and are incidentally discovered . Its clinical features include : • Gastrointestinal bleeding (most common) • Intestinal obstruction, which may occur as: • Volvulus • Intussusception (ileo-ileal or ileo -colic) • Incarcerated Littre's hernia. Complications of Meckel 's diverticulum are: • Diverticulitis - presents like appendicitis • Perforation - resembles a perforated duodenal ulcer • Peritonitis • Neoplasms - neuroendocrine tumour (most common) > adenocarcinoma > GIST > lymphoma.490

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common presentation of Meckel 's diverticulum?
mcqs.explanation: The most common presentation of Meckel 's diverticulum is lower gastrointestinal bleeding . Clinical features of Meckel 's diverticulum include : • Lower GI bleeding (most common in children and overall) • Abdominal pain • Vomiting Another common presentation is an intestinal obstruction (most common in adults ), which may occur due to: • Volvulus • Intussusception (ileo-ileal or ileo -colic) • Incarcerated Littre's hernia.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following cannot be used to increase the sensitivity of the Tc-pertechnate scan in Meckel 's diverticulum?
mcqs.explanation: Metoclopramide is not used to increase the sensitivity of the Tc-pertechnate scan in Meckel 's diverticulum. Metoclopramide stimulates gastric motility and decreases the time available for the uptake of Tc-pertechnate . Hence it reduces sensitivity . 99mTc -pertechnetate is preferentially taken up by the mucus-secreting cells of the gastric mucosa and ectopic gastric tissue . The sensitivity of the Tc-pertechnate scan is increased by:491 • Glucagon : Relaxes the smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract. This decreases peristalsis , causing enhanced detection of the ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel 's diverticulum • Pentagastrin: Potent stimulator of gastric secretions . Increases uptake and secretion of pertechnetate by the gastric mucosa • Cimetidine : Increases radionuclide uptake , and decreases peptic secretion and the release of pertechnetate from the diverticular lumen. This results in higher radionuclide concentrations in the wall of the diverticulum.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What will be the investigation of choice in a child suspected to have Meckel 's diverticula?
mcqs.explanation: The investigation of choice in a child suspected to have Meckel 's diverticulum is a 99mTc -pertechnetate radionuclide scan. The radionucleotide is preferentially taken up by the mucus-secreting cells of the gastric mucosa and ectopic gastric tissue in the diverticulum. In adults , there is a reduced prevalence of ectopic gastric mucosa. Hence it is less accurate and barium studies are preferred . The image below depicts a 99mTc radionuclide scan showing Meckel 's diverticulum.Most of the Meckel 's diverticula are discovered incidentally . In the absence of bleeding , Meckel 's diverticula are rarely diagnosed prior to the time of surgical intervention. Other investigations for Meckel 's diverticulum: • Angiography is used to locate the site of bleeding in an acute hemorrhage. • CT scan has a very low sensitivity . • Enteroclysis has an accuracy of 75 % but is usually not applicable during acute presentations .492

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While performing an inguinal hernia repair in a 3-year-old boy, you notice Meckel 's diverticulum as the content of the hernial sac. What is this hernia called ?
mcqs.explanation: Meckel 's diverticulum found in inguinal or femoral hernial sacs is known as Littre's hernia. It can cause intestinal obstruction.Option A: Amyand's hernia is an inguinal hernia in which the hernia sac contains a normal or acutely inflamed appendix . Option B: Narath's hernia is seen in patients with congenital dislocation of the hip. It is a femoral hernia seen behind the femoral vessels . Option C: Cloquet 's hernia is a type of femoral hernia where the sac lies under the pectineus fascia.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While performing a laparotomy, the surgeon incidentally notices a narrow -mouthed , thickened Meckel 's diverticulum. What is the treatment of choice ?
mcqs.explanation: In a narrow -mouthed , thickened Meckel 's diverticulum, resection of the diverticulum is the treatment of choice . When Meckel 's diverticulum is found in the course of abdominal surgery: • In cases of narrow -mouthed , thickened Meckel 's diverticulum, resection of the diverticulum is the treatment of choice • If it has a wide mouth and is not thickened , it can safely be left alone. Rarely, Meckel 's diverticulum is complicated by a meso-diverticular band, which is believed to be a remnant of a vitelline artery. In such symptomatic cases , the treatment is diverticulectomy with the removal of associated bands connecting the diverticulum to the abdominal wall or intestinal mesentery . Segmental resection of the ileum that includes both the diverticulum and the adjacent ileal peptic ulcer should be performed if: • There is bleeding from the diverticulum493 • The base is inflamed or perforated • The diverticulum contains a tumour.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common site for acquired diverticula in the small intestine ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site for acquired diverticula in the small intestine is the second part of the duodenum (Windsock's diverticulum). The colon is the most common site for acquired/false diverticula overall, followed by the duodenum . Meckel 's diverticulum is the most common true congenital diverticulum of the small bowel . A barium swallow showing a well -defined diverticulum in the second part of the duodenum (Windsock's diverticulum) is shown below .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man presents with dull aching abdominal pain for the past few weeks accompanied by loss of weight and appetite . A barium meal follow -through image is shown below . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the barium study showing a shrunken caecum pulled -up away from the right iliac fossa is most likely suggestive of intestinal tuberculosis . The most common site of intestinal tuberculosis is the distal ileum and cecum .494 The yellow color arrow marks indicate the shrunken caecum , stricturous narrowing of the terminal ileum and ileocaecal junction, and proximal ileal dilatation.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A respiratory therapist presents to the OPD with abdominal pain. He also complains of low-grade fever, night sweats , and loss of weight . You investigate him for intestinal tuberculosis . Which of the following radiological signs are expected to be seen in him?
mcqs.explanation: Creeping fat sign and apple core sign are not the radiological findings seen in intestinal tuberculosis . The creeping fat sign refers to the widely separated bowel loops due to fibrofatty proliferation seen in Crohn's disease . The apple core sign describes a short segment irregular circumferential stricture of the large bowel that has abrupt shouldered margins resembling an apple core. This appearance is classically seen in a stenosing annular colon carcinoma .495

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Match the following radiological signs in intestinal tuberculosis with their respective appearance:
mcqs.explanation: The correctly matched option is 1 - C, 2 - B, 3 - D, 4 - A.Sign Appearance Sterlein sign Narrowing of the terminal ile um with a shortened cecum Gooseneck deform ity Loss of ileocecal angle with d ilated terminal ileum String sign A persistent narrow stream o f barium Fleischner sign Thickening of the valve lips, with narrowing of the termin al ileum

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young man presented with pain abdomen, diarrhoea, and fever gradually increasing in a step ladder pattern over the past 2 weeks . A Widal test confirmed the diagnosis and he was admitted . A few days later, he developed intestinal perforation and was taken up for exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following findings would you see in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Typhoid causes longitudinal ulcers . Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi . It presents with step -ladder fever and abdominal pain after an incubation period of 10 –20 days. Over the next week , the patient can develop : • Distension • Diarrhoea • Splenomegaly • Characteristic rose spots on the abdomen caused by a vasculitis Surgical complications of typhoid are: • Paralytic ileus • Intestinal haemorrhage • Free ileal perforation (characteristically occurs during the third week of the illness ) • Cholecystitis • Longitudinal ulcers (usually situated in the distal ileum ) Diagnosis of typhoid is confirmed by culture of blood or stool . Treatment is by antibiotics, usually chloramphenicol . Perforation requires surgery to wash out and close the ulcer. Intestinal resection is usually avoided. In unstable patients , with evidence of septic shock, the bowel should be exteriorized and the perforation closed after recovery.
