Paratyphoid infection also resembles typhoid fever and is treated in a similar manner .496 Note : Transverse ulcers with stricture formation are seen in tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A lady underwent a left hemicolectomy for colon cancer 5 days back. She now complains of abdominal discomfort and bloating. She is still unable to pass gas. On examination, the abdomen is distended and no bowel sounds are heard. X-ray shows gas-filled loops of the intestine with multiple air fluid levels . Which of the following will be part of the management plan of the patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given post -op scenario after 72 hours of laparotomy with no passage of flatus , absent bowel sounds, and X-ray findings are suggestive of paralytic ileus . Initiation of oral intake and emergency laparotomy is not done in paralytic ileus . The return of normal motility post -surgery occurs in the following sequence : Small intestine (within the first 24 hours) \037 Stomach (within 48 hours) \037 Colon (3 to 5 days). Paralytic ileus is an adynamic/functional obstruction in which there is a failure of transmission of peristaltic waves. This is secondary to neuromuscular failure in the myenteric (Auerbach's) and submucous (Meissner 's) plexuses . Since there are no rigorous contractions, there is no colicky pain. The resultant stasis leads to the following clinical features : • Abdominal distension - marked and tympanitic • Effortless vomiting • Absence of bowel sounds • Absolute constipation Paralytic ileus takes on clinical significance if any of the following are observed at 72 hours after laparotomy after handling of the bowel : • No return of bowel sounds on auscultation • No passage of flatus Radiologically , the abdomen shows gas-filled loops of the intestine with multiple air fluid levels in an erect X-ray. A CT scan is more accurate for differentiating functional from mechanical obstruction Paralytic ileus is managed by nasogastric tube decompression and restriction of oral intake until bowel sounds and the passage of flatus return. Electrolyte balance must be maintained.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 22 -year-old male presents with purulent discharge from the umbilicus . He underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy 6 months back. X-ray sinogram of the patient reveals an enterocutaneous fistula tract as shown below . Which of the following aids in the spontaneous closure of the fistula ?

options.b: Foreign body in the fistula tract

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the X-ray sinogram showing a fistula tract connecting the skin opening and the small intestine are suggestive of an enterocutaneous fistula . In this case, it is most likely due to the umbilical port used during appendicectomy . Fistula track length >2.5 cms is likely to heal. Enterocutaneous fistulas of length <2.5 cm are unlikely to heal and close . Enterocutaneous fistulas are classified according to their location and volume of daily output . These factors determine the treatment and mortality rates. Proximal fistulas are associated with higher output , greater fluid and electrolyte loss. Distal fistulas tend to have lower output , making497 them easier to manage and more likely to close spontaneously .Type of fistula Output /da y High-output fistula >500 mL Intermediate fistul a - 500 mL Low-output fistula <200 mL

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old man, who underwent exploratory laparotomy for acute abdomen develops a fever on the 5th postoperative day. The sutured site is erythematous and on the removal of two skin sutures , there is a leakage of gastrointestinal contents through the wound . An electrolyte panel done shows hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic acidosis. What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of an enterocutaneous fistula . From the electrolyte panel showing hyponatremia, hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis, a diagnosis of duodenal fistula can be made. The electrolyte abnormalities with gastric fistula are hypochloremia , hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Enterocutaneous fistulas are classified according to their location and volume of daily output . • Proximal fistulas are associated with higher output , greater fluid , and electrolyte loss, and greater loss of digestive capacity . • Distal fistulas tend to have lower output , making them easier to manage and more likely to close spontaneously . Although both gastric and duodenal fistulas are proximal fistulas , duodenal fistulas receive an additional 1 to 2 litres of enzymes , electrolytes , and water from the pancreatic and bile ducts . Hence duodenal fistulas are at greater risk for more electrolyte imbalance than gastric fistulas . The management of enterocutaneous fistula is based on well -established principles known as SNAP which includes : • S - Sepsis elimination and skin protection • N - A period of parenteral nutrition may well be required • A - Anatomical assessment • P - Definitive planned surgery

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old bride-to-be presented with nausea, vomiting, and recurrent episodes of postprandial epigastric pain. She has lost nearly 25 kgs in the last 6 months to look good in her wedding dress . Proton pump inhibitors were tried but were unsuccessful . A barium meal follow -through of the patient is given below . Which of the following is false about her condition?

options.a: Weight gain is part of the management
options.b: Lying in prone position postprandially improves symptoms
options.d: The second part of duodenum is commonly involved

mcqs.explanation: The false statement about her condition is that the second part of the duodenum is commonly involved. The given clinical scenario with rapid weight loss and the barium follow -through demonstrating dilation of the duodenum with an abrupt cut-off at its third part, coinciding with the line of the superior mesenteric artery is suggestive of superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome. The third498 part of the duodenum is involved in SMA syndrome. SMA syndrome (also known as Wilkie's syndrome) is usually seen in young asthenic women. It is a rare condition characterized by compression of the third portion of the duodenum by the SMA against fixed retroperitoneal structures. SMA syndrome is associated with: • Rapid childhood growth • Profound weight loss • Abdominal surgery • Inflammatory diseases of the abdomen • Short ligament of Treitz • Immobilization in a cast that increases lordosis (cast syndrome) Its clinical features include : • Episodic vomiting • Profound nausea • Abdominal distention • Postprandial epigastric pain Upper gastrointestinal barium swallow or hypotonic duodenography demonstrates abrupt or near-total cut-off of the flow of barium from the duodenum to the jejunum. CT and magnetic resonance (MR) arteriography can also be used for additional anatomical detail . The normal aortomesenteric angle is between 28-65 degrees . This is reduced to less than 25 degrees in SMA syndrome. A CT scan showing the reduced aortomesenteric angle is given below :In SMA syndrome, initial conservative management includes : • Frequent small feedings • Lying in a prone position or on the left side postprandially499 • Weight gain (to increase mesenteric fat pad and thereby increase the aorto-mesenteric angle) • Removal of a body cast in cast syndrome Laparoscopic lysis of the ligament of Treitz is beneficial in few cases . If all the above treatments fail, duodenojejunostomy is done.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young male, who wishes to pursue his higher studies abroad gets a chest X-ray done as a part of the immigration clearance. X-ray shows air under bilateral domes of the diaphragm. He is currently asymptomatic with normal vital signs. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with an asymptomatic patient having air under the diaphragm without evidence of peritonitis (sterile pneumoperitoneum ) is suggestive of pneumatosis intestinalis . Pneumatosis intestinalis presents as multiple gas-filled cysts of the gastrointestinal tract. It is usually located in the subserosa , submucosa, and rarely the muscularis layer. The common sites are jejunum > ileocecal region > colon. It represents one of the few cases of sterile pneumoperitoneum . Pneumatosis in neonates is usually associated with necrotizing enterocolitis . Predisposing factors include : • Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease • Immunocompromised state • Inflammatory , obstructive , or infectious conditions of the intestine • Endoscopy and jejunostomy • Ischemia • Diabetes Patients can be asymptomatic . Symptoms if present , is usually nonspecific like: • Diarrhoea • Abdominal pain500 • Abdominal distention • Nausea , vomiting • Weight loss • Mucus in stool Diagnosis can be made on the basis of: • Plain X-ray showing radiolucent areas within the bowel wall (appear as grape-like clusters or tiny bubbles ) • Barium contrast • CT studiesTreatment involves: • Management of the uncomplicated primary disease . • When symptoms demand treatment , the first line is intermittent high flow oxygen therapy , providing a concentration of 70% continuously for 5 days by nasal specula . • The cysts may also resolve with antibiotics, particularly metronidazole . • In resistant cases , maintenance treatment with sulfasalazine may be helpful . The prognosis in most patients is that of the underlying disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man with IHD presents with sudden , severe , generalized abdominal pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, the pulse rate is 118bpm, rhythm is irregularly irregular, BP is 90/60 mmHg. The abdomen appears soft , non-distended , and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following could be a likely diagnosis in this case?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia. Mesenteric ischemia may be acute or chronic. The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is most likely affected . An embolus is the most common cause of SMA occlusion . Possible sources for SMA501 emboisation include : • Left atrium in atrial fibrillation • Previous history of ischemic heart disease /myocardial infarction • Vegetations on mitral and aortic valves associated with endocarditis • An atheromatous plaque from an aortic aneurysm. Other causes of mesenteric ischemia include : • Atherosclerosis of mesenteric vessels • Vasculitides • Venous thrombosis in factor V Leiden mutation • Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia due to alterations in splanchnic blood flow . The most important clue to an early diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain in a patient with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis . The pain is typically in the central abdomen and out of proportion to the physical findings. Associated clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distension , peritonitis, and the passage of bloody stools . The gold standard for the diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is angiography, and management is laparotomy. The goal of operative exploration is to resect the compromised bowel and restore blood supply via embolectomy . Other options : Option B: A pulsatile abdominal mass is seen in the case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation. Options A and D: Acute severe pancreatitis and peptic ulcer perforation have no association with atrial fibrillation. They usually present with pain over the upper abdomen associated with guarding and rigidity on examination.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the minimum dose of radiation that can cause radiation enteritis of the small intestine ?
mcqs.explanation: The minimum radiation dose in the small intestine that can cause radiation enteritis is 4500cGy. Radiation enteritis is a common complication of radiation treatment aimed at the abdomen and pelvis. It causes diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramps. The amount of radiation appears to correlate with the probability of the development of radiation enteritis. In general , serious late complications are unusual if the total radiation dosage is less than 4000 cGy. Morbidity risk increases with dosages exceeding 5000 cGy. The table below shows various parts of GIT and the radiation doses that can cause enteritis .Part of GIT Radiation dose (in cGy) Esophagus 6000 to 7500502 Part of GIT Radiation dose (in cGy) Stomach 4500 to 5000 Small intestine & colon 4500 to 6500 Rectum 5500 to 8000

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient who is a known case of Crohn's disease underwent ileal resection for a stricture . Which of the following is not a part of the management of postoperative complications in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Administration of folic acid is done in jejunal resection . Ileal resection causes vitamin B12 deficiency which requires administration of parenteral vitamin B12 . Extensive resection of the small intestine (<150 cm of remaining small intestine ) can result in metabolic and nutritional consequences . This is known as short bowel syndrome. The presentation of the patient is dependent upon the site and extent of intestinal resection . The ileum is the only site of absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts. Following resection of the ileum , the loss of bile salts increases resulting in fat malabsorption and diarrhea. Other complications of resection include : • Peptic ulcers - Due to gastric hypersecretion • Cholelithiasis - Due to interruption of the enterohepatic cycle of bile salts Initial treatment priorities include repletion of fluid and electrolytes lost in severe diarrhoea by initiating TPN. Long-term management involves: • Administration of oral cholestyramine to bind with bile salts • Dietary fat restriction • Parenteral vitamin B12 • Proton pump inhibitors to lower gastric pH • Octreotide to reduce the volume of GI secretions • Antimotility agents such as loperamide hydrochloride to delay small-intestinal transit Small intestine lengthening procedures done to increase absorption and transit time are: • Longitudinal intestinal lengthening and tailoring procedure (LILT ) • Serial transverse enteroplasty procedure (STEP) Intestinal transplantation is indicated only in complicated cases .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about the Tillaux sign?

options.a: Mass is felt in the periumbilical region
options.c: Mass is mobile perpendicular to mesentery attachment line

mcqs.explanation: Tillaux's sign is said to be positive if the mass/swelling is mobile perpendicular to the mesentery attachment line. Tillaux's sign is seen in a mesenteric cyst . Mesenteric cysts occur either in the small intestine (60%) or the colon (40%) and can be classified as the following:503 • Chylolymphatic (most common type ) • Enterogenous • Urogenital remnant • Dermoid • Other causes : traumatic hematoma and cyst formation, tuberculous cold abscess of mesentery and hydatid cyst of the mesentery They most commonly occur in adults with a mean age of 45 years. It is more common in females than males (2:1). The most common presentation is a painless abdominal swelling near the umbilicus , which is smooth and not moving with respiration with Tillaux's triad: • Soft, smooth swelling in the umbilical region • Freely mobile in a direction perpendicular to the mesentery (Tillaux's sign) • Zone of resonance around the cyst Other presentations include recurrent attacks of abdominal pain due to temporary impaction of a food bolus in a segment of the bowel narrowed by the cyst and vomiting. Complications of mesenteric cyst include torsion, rupture , infection and hemorrhage into the cyst. Ultrasonography and CT are used to demonstrate mesenteric cysts . Treatment: • Chlyolymphatic cyst is managed by enucleation . • Enterogenous cyst is managed by removal of the cyst with resection of the adjacent bowel as it arises as a diverticulum or duplication from the adjacent bowel . In cases where complete excision is not possible due to the close proximity to vital structures , partial excision or marsupialization should be performed .504

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the investigation of choice in a patient suspected to have a small bowel tumor?
mcqs.explanation: Enteroclysis is the investigation of choice in patients with small bowel tumours. Enteroclysis is a barium study in which the contrast agent is put directly into the duodenum through a nasogastric tube . Continued infusion of 500 to 1000 mL of thin barium sulfate and methylcellulose suspension is done and then viewed continuously with the use of either fluoroscopy or radiographs taken at frequent intervals. This technique is a double -contrast procedure that allows detailed imaging of the entire small intestine . Enteroclysis has a sensitivity of over 90% in the detection of small bowel tumours and is the investigation of choice , particularly for tumours located in the distal small bowel . Advantages of enteroclysis : • The contrast is administered at a controlled rate directly in the small bowel , bypassing the regulatory action of the pylorus . • The entire small bowel is demonstrated in a distended state , allowing better diagnosis. As a result of the dilatation, the following can be visualised : • Mild strictures • Small sinus tracts and fistulas • Minimal extrinsic compressions • Skip lesions • Proximal and distal extent of diffuse diseases . • The examination can be completed in 15–30 minutes , thus reducing patient waiting time.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of breathlessness , dull aching abdominal pain, and diarrhea. On examination, his face and chest appear flushed . CT scan of the abdomen shows a tumor in the terminal ileum with liver metastasis . An increased levels of 5-HIAA is seen in a 24-hour urinary sample . Which of the following is false regarding the management of this patient ?

options.a: Surgery should be done as soon as the diagnosis is made.
options.b: MRI is the best method for staging of the disease .

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome caused by a carcinoid tumour. The best method for the staging of a carcinoid tumour is the octreotide scan. They are neuroendocrine tumours of the gastrointestinal tract. They arise from the enterochromaffin cells . They metastasize early to the regional lymph nodes and the liver. Abdominal symptoms include : • Pain • Abdominal distension • Lower GI bleeding Metastasis in these patients can cause increased production of serotonin leading to carcinoid syndrome with features like: • Flushing • Diarrhoea505 • Bronchospasm • Cardiac symptoms because of stenosis and insufficiency of the cardiac valves The diagnosis is made by an assessment of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) in a 24-hour urine sample . It is positive in larger tumours only if metastases are present . Ultrasonography , CT scan, and MRI may show the primary tumour and metastases . The best method for staging carcinoid tumours is by octreotide scan or somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS). Treatment: • Somatostatin and its analogues are used in the symptomatic treatment of carcinoid syndrome. • Surgery should be undertaken as soon as the diagnosis is made, even in the presence of liver metastases . • Resection of the primary tumour and mesenteric lymph node metastases is done. • In the presence of liver metastasis - liver resection , transarterial embolization (TAE), chemoembolization (TACE), chemotherapy , and liver transplantation can be done.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a false statement about abdominal lymphoma?

options.a: MALT lymphoma is associated with H.pylori infection .
options.b: Primary small-intestinal lymphomas are most commonly located in the jejunum.
options.c: Lymphoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of spleen .
options.d: Stomach is the most common site for extranodal lymphoma.

mcqs.explanation: Primary small-intestinal lymphomas are most commonly located in the ileum . Option A: Primary gastric lymphomas are derived from B-cells and classified as diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (DLBCL ) and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT ). Both DLBCL and MALT are thought to be associated with chronic Helicobacter pylori infection . This linkage is better established for MALT , whereas the association between H. pylori infection and DLBCL is more controversial. Option C: Lymphoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of the spleen . Option D: Gastric lymphoma accounts for the majority of extranodal lymphomas, representing approximately 50–75 % of primary gastrointestinal lymphomas.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding lymphoma of the small intestine ?

options.b: It is the most common tumour of the small intestine in children
options.c: Resection is indicated in all symptomatic patients
options.d: Burkitt's lymphoma affects the ileocaecal junction

mcqs.explanation: B-cell lymphomas are chemo-sensitive. T-cell lymphomas are chemo-resistant. Approximately one-third of GI lymphomas occur in the small bowel . In the small intestine , most commonly they are found in the ileum . In children <10 years, lymphomas are the most common intestinal neoplasm . In adults , they constitute up to 25% of small bowel malignant tumours. Patients with celiac disease and immunodeficiency are at increased risk for the development of primary small intestine lymphomas.506 Clinical features include : • Pain • Weight loss • Nausea • Vomiting • Bleeding • Change in bowel habits • Intestinal obstruction Small intestine lymphomas are usually larger than 5 cm. They may extend into the mucosa. Microscopic examination shows diffuse infiltration of the intestinal wall. In the absence of symptoms , they are often chemo-responsive and do not require surgery. In symptomatic patients , resection is indicated . • B-cell lymphomas are more chemosensitive and have high remission rates, with or without surgery. • T-cell lymphomas are more resistant to therapy and will progress to symptoms of obstruction or perforation if not resected . Small intestine lymphomas cause complications like haemorrhage and perforation. The best prognostic indicator is a response to systemic therapy . The five-year survival rate is 50% to 60% Note : • The stomach (50–75 %) is the most common site of lymphomas in the gastrointestinal system . • Burkitt's lymphoma can aggressively affect the ileocaecal region. • Lymphoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of the spleen .507

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the earliest sign in Crohn's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Aphthous ulcers , surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa, are the earliest lesions seen in a patient with Crohn's disease during endoscopy . Crohn's colitis usually spares the rectum and is most severe in the ileocaecal region. • In early Crohn's disease , small, punched -out aphthous ulcers are often seen (the result of submucosal lymphoid follicle expansion). • In moderate disease , the aphthous ulcers coalesce into larger ulcers , which may take on the appearance of a star (stellate ulcers ). • As disease severity increases, submucosal edema and injury can result in cobblestoning of the mucosa (option A) and eventually the formation of serpiginous ulcers , which are typical findings in Crohn's disease . Thorn -like extraluminal projections in barium studies are known as rose-thorn appearance , and are a typical sign of Crohn's disease . They represent deep penetrating linear ulcers or fissurings typically seen within stenosed terminal ileum with a thickened wall. (Options C and D)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about Crohn's disease ?

options.a: For effective treatment of a Crohn's mass, only antibiotics are prescribed .
options.b: Symptomatic relapse after surgery is not related to the presence of disease during resection .
options.c: The proximal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease .
options.d: On endoscopic examination, continuous lesions are visualised , which are diagnostic of Crohn's disease .

mcqs.explanation: Symptomatic relapse of Crohn's disease after surgery is not related to the presence of the disease during resection. The course of the disease after surgery is unpredictable since surgery does not cure Crohn's disease . Instead, the probability of relapse increases with the time since resection . Other options : Option A: Antibiotics alone cannot treat a Crohn's mass effectively . Abscesses can be treated with metronidazole and ciprofloxacin and should also undergo drainage (and resection if needed ). Option C: The terminal ileum is most commonly involved in Crohn's disease . Option D: On endoscopic examination, discontinuous "skip" lesions are visualized. These are irregular areas of inflamed mucosa that are ulcerated with mucopurulent exudate separated by intervening, normal -appearing intestinal mucosa.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old female patient presents with a 9-month history of weight loss, abdominal cramps, and intermittent diarrhea. On examination, a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen is found. Stool cultures are normal . Colonoscopy shows the presence of skip lesions . Biopsy showed the presence of non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: 520 The clinical scenario and the biopsy showing the presence of non-caseating granulomas are diagnostic of Crohn's disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old patient was brought to the casualty ward with high fever and pain abdomen. He had a history of bloody diarrhea for several months. His past history was negative for long-term medications and previous surgeries . The abdominal X-ray image obtained is shown below . What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and the radiograph are suggestive of toxic megacolon . Toxic megacolon may present with fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension . Abdominal radiography shows transverse or right colonic dilation of >6 cm and loss of haustrations. It is usually associated with ulcerative colitis as indicated by history of chronic bloody diarrhoea. It can be triggered by electrolyte imbalance and narcotics which interfere with gut motility . Features of secondary bacterial infecton and sepsis may be present . It can be complicated by intestinal perforation. It usually resolves with supportive treatment (correcting electrolyte imbalance, fluids , and bowel rest ) and medical therapy which includes glucocorticoids , anti-inflammatory drugs, and antibiotics. However, an urgent colectomy is indicated in patients who do not show signs of improvement. Indications for urgent surgery include : • Frank intraperitoneal peritonitis , secondary to perforation • Life-threatening hemorrhage or increasing transfusion requirements • Worsening systemic toxicity • Worsening colonic dilatation Other options : Option B: Volvulus occurs when the air-filled segment of the colon twists around the mesentery . The sigmoid colon is the most commonly involved part of the large intestine (90%). The patient can present with abdominal distension , nausea and vomiting. X-ray abdomen shows a bent inner tube or coffee bean appearance .521 Option C: Ogilvie syndrome, also known as colonic pseudo -obstruction is a functional disorder with colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction. It occurs commonly in hospitalized patients and is associated with narcotics, bed rest and comorbid disease . X-ray shows dilatation of the colon (predominantly transverse colon) with absent mechanical obstruction.Option D: Pneumatosis intestinalis is the presence of gas within the bowel wall seen in any part of the GI tract but most commonly in the jejunum. It is a pathognomic feature of necrotizing enterocolitis . X-ray of the abdomen will show intramural gas in the bowel .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are doing an emergency laparotomy for a case of intestinal obstruction. Which organ will you first visualize to know if this is a case of small bowel or large bowel obstruction?
mcqs.explanation: The cecum is the first organ to be visualized to differentiate between the small and large bowel in cases of intestinal obstruction.522 Distension of the cecum will confirm large bowel involvement. The identification of a collapsed distal segment of the large bowel and its sequential proximal assessment will lead to the identification of the cause .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man presented to the OPD with complaints of intermittent constipation and a sense of heaviness in his lower abdomen. His barium enema film is given below . Which of the following statements is false about the pathology responsible for his condition?

options.a: Commonly occurs along the mesenteric side of the colon
options.b: Sigmoid colon is the most common site
options.c: It is characterized by true diverticula

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and X-ray film showing saw-toothed appearance of the colon are suggestive of colonic diverticulosis . They are false diverticula. Diverticulosis refers to the herniation of the mucosa and muscularis mucosa through the colonic wall, usually at the point where the nutrient artery enters the colon (mesenteric side ). The condition is usually asymptomatic until complications arise. They may be detected incidentally . On a barium X-ray, the colon with diverticular disease will have a saw-toothed appearance . Colonic diverticula are more often acquired than congenital . They are common in developed countries that have a low fiber diet . A low fiber diet results in low stool volume. As the colon generates higher intraluminal pressure to propel smaller volumes of stools , low stool volumes cause an increase in colonic wall tension and segmentation of the colon. Prolonged colonic contractions and high pressures (directed radially along the colonic wall) results in the formation of pulsion diverticula. The sigmoid colon is the most common site . Note : True diverticulum involves the herniation of all the layers of the intestine whereas false diverticulum involves the herniation of only the mucosa and submucosa .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding left -sided diverticulitis ?

options.a: It is often an incidental finding during surgery
options.b: Appendicitis is an important differential diagnosis
options.c: Left sided diverticulitis is more common than right
options.d: The anatomical location is given by the Hinchey classification

mcqs.explanation: In the general population , left -sided diverticulitis is more common. The sigmoid colon (left colon) involvement is more common than the right colon involvement.523 Diverticulitis is the inflammation and infection of the diverticulum. It most commonly presents with • left lower abdominal pain (often termed as left -sided appendicitis ) • fever • a change in bowel habits • anorexia, nausea • urinary urgency if there is an associated inflammation of the bladder etc . Right-sided diverticulitis occurs more often in younger patients of Asian descent than in other populations and presents with pain in the right lower quadrant . Patients presenting with these symptoms are often thought to have acute appendicitis , and often the diagnosis of right-sided diverticulitis is subsequently made in the operating room. The Hinchey classification is used to describe the severity of the diverticular disease , complicated by perforation.Hinchey classification : Stage 1 Mesenteric or pericolic absce ss Stage 2 Pelvic abscess Stage 3 Purulent peritonitis Stage 4 Fecal peritonitis

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 38-year-old man is brought to the casualty with severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain for the last two days. You suspect right-sided diverticulitis due to the relatively long history and lack of migration of pain. However, your co-resident is convinced it is appendicitis . Which is the best investigation to rule in your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis is now considered by most to be the standard modality for the evaluation of acute diverticulitis . Contrast enema studies are the most accurate way to find out the colonic diverticula. However, because of the risks of extravasation of barium from the perforation and aggravation of inflammation, it is avoided. In contrast to barium enema, a CT scan demonstrates both the intraluminal and extracolonic manifestations of acute right-sided diverticulitis. CT findings include pericolic soft tissue stranding, colonic wall thickening and pericolic fat infiltration (streaky fat).524 Barium enema in diverticulosis shows a saw-tooth appearance .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While performing surgery on a patient who presented with clinical features suggestive of peritonitis, a diverticular perforation is seen along with fecal peritonitis . What is the Hinchey's stage ?
mcqs.explanation: Fecal peritonitis belongs to grade 4 in the Hinchey classification . Diverticulitis refers to the inflammation and infection associated with the diverticula. Hinchey classification is the most commonly used classification for the severity and complication of acute diverticulitis . It is used additionally to guide the overall management of acute diverticulitis .Hinchey classification : Stage 1 Mesenteric or pericolic absce ss525 Hinchey classification : Stage 2 Pelvic abscess Stage 3 Purulent peritonitis Stage 4 Fecal peritonitis

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man with past history of diabetes mellitus , hypertension , and chronic constipation presented with right lower abdominal pain associated with fever. CT abdomen findings are suggestive of acute diverticulitis with 6 cm fluid accumulation in the paracolic region. What is the most appropriate management for this patient ?

options.a: Oral antibiotics, bowel rest and continued monitoring
options.b: iv antibiotics, bowel rest, and continued monitoring
options.c: Laparotomy for abscess drainage and surgical resection
options.d: CT guided percutaneous drainage with iv antibiotics

mcqs.explanation: The elderly patient with multiple comorbidities and complicated acute diverticulitis (fluid collection >5 cm) should ideally be managed with CT-guided percutaneous drainage with iv antibiotics. Acute diverticulitis management: Outpatient care • Initiated for young patients with no comorbidities • It includes : • Liquid diet • Analgesia • Regular follow -up Inpatient care • Should be initiated if CT shows complicated diverticulitis characterized by: • Perforation • Abscess formation • Obstruction or • Fistulization . • Can also be initiated if CT shows uncomplicated diverticulitis but the patient is of high risk such as • Sepsis at presentation • Elderly patient • Immunosuppression • Presence of comorbidities • Failure of outpatient care • Inpatient care includes the following : • Bowel rest • IV fluids • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics526 • Antibiotic therapy can be continued with careful monitoring if fluid collection is <5 cm • CT guided percutaneous drainage if antibiotic therapy fails or fluid collection is > 5 cm • Surgical exploration and resection if there is perforation, obstruction, or fistulization • Regular follow -up with imaging Note : Oral antibiotics have no proven benefit in the outpatient management of acute uncomplicated diverticulitis .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 55 -year-old man is brought to the casualty with a history of fever and abdominal pain. The pain was initially in the left lower quadrant for 2 days but is diffuse and severe for the past 4 hours. The erect X-ray of the chest showed the presence of pneumoperitoneum . Emergency laparotomy was performed . It showed the presence of perforated left -sided diverticulitis with fecal peritonitis . How will you manage the patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of fecal peritonitis due to perforation of left -sided diverticulitis . This is managed by Hartmann 's procedure . It involves segmental resection , a proximal-end colostomy , and closure of the rectal stump . If the perforation of the diverticulitis leads to a localized pericolic abscess formation, then it is treated with antibiotics alone or along with percutaneous drainage.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly male patient presents to the hospital with complaints of abdominal pain, increased frequency of micturition, and passing of air bubbles in urine. He was diagnosed with diverticulitis 2 years before and was treated with antibiotics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The history of diverticulitis and pneumaturia point towards a diagnosis of colovesical fistula . The patients present with the symptoms of urinary tract infection caused by colonic flora, pneumaturia (air bubbles in urine), and fecaluria (foul -smelling and brownish material in the urine). Complications of diverticular disease : • Bleeding • Perforation leading to a pericolic abscess or generalized peritonitis527 • Intestinal obstruction due to fibrosis • Fistula formation (colovesical, coloenteric, colovaginal) Emphysematous cystitis can also present with pneumaturia. It is caused by urinary tract infection (UTI) with a gas-forming organism, especially in people with diabetes or patients with urinary tract outflow obstruction.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A CECT confirmed severe acute diverticulitis in a 34-year-old brought to the emergency with lower abdominal pain. A Foley 's catheter was promptly placed to prevent a certain complication. Which of the following statements is false regarding the complication?

options.b: Contrast enema is used to identify the course the pathology
options.c: Previous hysterectomy may increase the risk
options.d: It more commonly occurs in females

mcqs.explanation: The colovesical fistula is more common in men than in women because the uterus prevents the sigmoid from adhering to the bladder . Hence , females who have undergone hysterectomy are at increased risk . Clinical features of a colovesical fistula are: • Pneumaturia (flatus in urine) • Fecaluria (feces in urine) • Suprapubic pain • Dysuria • Urgency • Frequency • Gross hematuria (rare) Pneumaturia is usually appreciated toward the end of urination because the collection of gas usually sits at the top of the bladder . The finding pneumaturia or fecaluria is virtually pathognomonic for urinary tract fistulas , and patients presenting with this condition should be presumed to have a colovesical fistula and investigated accordingly. Over time, cystitis associated with a colovesical fistula may evolve to pyelonephritis . An abdominopelvic CT with oral or rectal contrast is the investigation of choice . A contrast enema may be used to identify the course of the fistula .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presented with fever, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. She has a history of recent intensive care unit admission for sepsis which required prolonged antibiotic therapy . Sigmoidoscopy findings are given below . Choose the false statement regarding the given condition.

options.a: Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is done in fulminant disease
options.b: IV vancomycin is used for treatment of recurrent disease
options.c: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an emerging treatment option
options.d: Stool sample is used for PCR detection of toxins

mcqs.explanation: A history of diarrhea associated with prolonged antibiotic treatment and characteristic adherent pseudomembranes in the colon is highly suggestive of pseudomembranous colitis . Oral Fidaxomicin is commonly used in recurrent pseudomembranous colitis . The causative antibiotic agent must be discontinued and infection control measures must be taken for all patients . • Initial episode - non severe : WBC \03515,000 /mm3 , Creatinine < 1.5 mg/dL • Oral Fidaxomicin(drug of choice ) or Vancomycin • Oral Metronidazole can be given if Vancomycin /Fidaxomycin is not available528 • Initial episode - severe : >15,000/mm3 , Creatinine >1.5 mg/dL • Oral Fidaxomicin or Vancomycin • Consider fecal microbiota transplantation • Initial episode - fulminant • Hypotension , ileus or megacolon • Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole • Rectal Vancomycin can be used if ileus present • Overwhelming sepsis , colonic perforation, or peritonitis • Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy • First recurrence • Repeat course of antibiotics for another 10 -20 days • Oral Fidaxomicin(drug of choice ) or Vancomycin can be used . • Repeated recurrence • Consider fecal microbiota transplantation Option A: Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is the procedure of choice for patients requiring surgery for severe colitis or toxic megacolon. It allows for disease control, stabilization, and preservation of reconstruction options for the future . Segmental colectomy , ileostomy , or colostomy alone does not address the pancolonic nature of the disease . Option C: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is emerging as a promising treatment option for recurrent and recalcitrant C. difficile infection . Using FMT, donor stool is administered to the patient through one of a variety of described routes (nasogastric tube , colonoscopic lavage, or upper endoscopy ) to restore colonic flora. Option D: Pseudomembranous colitis is caused by Clostridium difficile which is a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic microorganism . The pathogenesis is mediated by the enterotoxins - toxin A and toxin B. They can be detected in the stool using PCR

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly male patient is brought to the casualty with complaints of vomiting and severe abdominal pain. The abdomen appears grossly distended , is tender to touch , and percussion reveals hyper -resonance. His X-ray abdomen is shown in the image below . What is the next best step in the management of this patient ?

options.b: Laparotomy followed by sigmoid resection alone
options.d: Insertion of a rectal tube through a flexible sigmoidoscope

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the X-ray radiograph showing characteristic coffee bean appearance are highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus. Non-operative decompression followed by insertion of a rectal tube through a rigid proctoscope or a flexible sigmoidoscope is the next best step in the management of this patient . Sigmoid volvulus is a cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon . Symptoms include constipation , abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. Onset may be acute or chronic. It occurs more commonly in patients with a history of mental illness and chronic constipation . X-ray abdomen shows a large , dilated loop of the colon , often with a few air-fluid levels . Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. CT may reveal large gas-filled loop without haustral markings , forming a closed -loop obstruction.529 Non-operative decompression is successful in treating 90% of the patients . The rectal tube should be left in place for 1-2 days to allow complete decompression and to prevent immediate recurrence of the volvulus. This should be followed by bowel cleansing with cathartics and a complete colonoscopic examination. In patients with signs of colonic necrosis or in whom endoscopic detorsion has failed , sigmoid colectomy with the closure of the rectum and end colostomy (Hartmann procedure ) maybe required. Even if detorsion of the sigmoid is successful , elective sigmoid resection is indicated to prevent recurrence.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A lady is brought to the casualty department with a 2-day history of diffuse abdominal pain. She has had several episodes of bloody diarrhea for the past 8 hours and appears dehydrated . On examination, her pulse is feeble and BP is 80/55 mmHg. An abdominal x-ray shows the "thumbprinting sign." What could be the likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The thumbprinting sign is seen in both ischemic colitis and pseudomembranous colitis . Bowel wall "thumbprinting" (the appearance of thumbprint-shaped projections ) is a radiological sign of submucosal thickening of the colonic wall. It can result from any process that leads to edema of the bowel wall, including pseudomembranous colitis , ischemic colitis , non-infective inflammatory bowel disease , other infective bowel diseases , as well as submucosal /intramural hemorrhage. The plain abdomen x-ray given below shows submucosal thickening with crescentic margins of the colon described as "thumbprinting" sign.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 44-year-old female patient presents to the casualty with complaints of sudden onset of pain in the abdomen. On examination, there is a palpable tympanic swelling in the left side of the abdomen. X-ray abdomen of the patient is given below . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette and the X-ray findings are suggestive of caecal volvulus. It is differentiated from sigmoid volvulus as there is only a single air-fluid level and the apex of the volvulus pointing towards the left upper quadrant . It is commonly seen in females in the 4th and 5th decade who can present with partial or complete intestinal obstruction. The clinical features include : • Marked abdominal distention530 • Abdominal pain • Obstipation • Nausea and vomiting etc . On examination, a palpable tympanic swelling in the midline or the left side may be seen . If there is strangulation or perforation of the obstructed bowel segment , peritoneal signs (rigidity, rebound tenderness etc .) can be present. Radiological findings include caecal dilatation, single air-fluid level , and absence of gas in the distal colon. On X-ray abdomen, the apex of the cecal volvulus points towards the left upper quadrant ( vs apex pointing towards the right upper quadrant in sigmoid volvulus) CECT abdomen is the investigation of choice that shows a whirl sign (also seen in the midgut volvulus). Management of cecal volvulus includes supportive therapy with nasogastric tube , iv fluids , antibiotics etc . and early surgical intervention. • Perforated or strangulated cecal volvulus should be treated with right hemicolectomy • If there is no sign of perforation or strangulation, either cecopexy or right hemicolectomy can be performed. Option B: Sigmoid volvulus (image shown below ) is a cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon . X-ray abdomen shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels . Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. On X-ray abdomen, the apex of the sigmoid volvulus points towards the right upper quadrant .Option C: Toxic megacolon (image shown below ) is defined as the dilatation of the transverse colon to a diameter of more than 6 cm. It is usually associated with severe ulcerative colitis . It can be triggered by electrolyte imbalance and narcotics as they interfere with gut motility .531 Option D: Fecal retention is an accumulation of a large amount of stool within any bowel segment , most commonly within the colon usually due to chronic constipation . A colonic distention with fecal material is often called fecal loading on the radiograph. It can be complicated by fecal impaction and subsequent bowel obstruction.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A middle -aged woman underwent an open repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The procedure was uneventful . However, on the 2nd postoperative day, the patient developed symptoms of acute abdomen and bloody diarrhea with significant guarding. The patient was taken up for an exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following areas is most likely to be involved?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of ischemic colitis and it occurs most commonly at the splenic flexure . Ischemic colitis occurs due to interruption or decrease in colonic blood flow . It may occur with many different conditions, including embolism from cardiac disease , low-flow states such as congestive heart failure, sepsis , and vasopressor use . Major vascular surgery (both open and endovascular repair), especially involving the abdominal aorta, is a well -known risk factor for developing ischemic colitis . Although any area of the colon may be affected , the watershed areas of the splenic flexure (Griffith's point) and the rectosigmoid (Sudeck 's point) are the most prone to ischemia because of the often incomplete anastomoses of the marginal artery in these locations. The next most common area afflicted is the cecum , secondary to low blood flow in the terminal branches of the ileocolic artery. Splenic flexure (also known as Griffith's point) is a watershed area between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. Sudeck point is a watershed area between the sigmoid arterial branch from the inferior mesenteric artery and the superior rectal artery (branch of Inferior mesentric artery).532 The marginal artery of Drummond runs parallel to the colon, connecting the SMA and IMA circulation - the majority of blood flow to the left and sigmoid colon in case of occlusion of the IMA. Arc of Riolan is a variable collateral vessel that connects the SMA (middle colic vessel ) to the IMA (left colic).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient had a painless episode of profuse per rectal bleeding . After initial stabilization, a colonoscopy was performed . The findings are given below . What is the most common site of this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario and colonoscopy findings are suggestive of angiodysplasia . The cecum is the most common site of angiodysplasia followed by the colon. In the colon the angiodysplasia can occur anywhere , however it is commonly found in the right colon than the transverse and the left colon.533

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient being evaluated for recurrent lower GI bleeding secondary to colonic angiodysplasia is suspected to have Heyde syndrome. What are the other common features associated with the condition?

options.c: Aortic stenosis and von Willebrand disease

mcqs.explanation: Heyde 's syndrome is a multisystem disorder characterized by the clinical triad of: • Aortic stenosis • Gastrointestinal bleeding from angiodysplasia • Acquired type 2 vWD (secondary to valvular stenosis , returns to normal once the valve is replaced ) Dilated mucosal and submucosal veins are usually seen on colonoscopy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old infant presented with constipation since birth. On a per rectal exam, a sudden release of feces was seen . A contrast enema showed a dilated descending colon leading to a constricted segment . Which of the following is involved in the pathogenesis of the disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario, with a positive blast sign (sudden release of feces on PR examination) and characteristic barium enema findings, are suggestive of Hirschsprung disease . Patients with Hirschsprung's disease have an increased frequency of mutations in certain genes such as glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GCDNF). GDNF promotes the survival , proliferation, and migration of neural crest cells in culture . GDNF is expressed in the gut in advance of migrating neural crest cells and is chemoattractive for neural crest cells in culture . Mutations are also seen its receptor Rearranged during Transfection (RET), or its coreceptor Gfra-1 (GDNF family receptor alpha-1). Gene mutations in chromosomes 10 and 13 , family history, and Down's syndrome are also factors associated with Hirschsprung's disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A neonate was brought to the pediatrician on day 5 of life with bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium. On examination, the abdomen was distended . and X-Ray showed distended bowel loops . Due to suggestive family history, the resident suspected Hirschsprung's disease . What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: A rectal biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease . It shows the following : • Absent ganglia • Hypertrophied nerve trunks • Positive immunostaining for acetylcholinesterase • Calretinin immunostaining (superior to acetylcholinesterase staining) Anorectal manometry is an important screening tool. It shows the absence of rectoanal inhibitory reflex .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: From which of the following sites should a rectal biopsy be taken in order to confirm the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease ?
mcqs.explanation: 534 The ideal site to obtain a rectal biopsy in a patient with Hirschsprung's disease is from a point that is at least 2 cm above the dentate line. The internal sphincter extends up to 2 cm above the dentate line. This region is normally devoid of ganglionic cells . Hence , biopsy in this region may lead to errors in the results . Rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation in patients with Hirschsprung's disease . It shows the presence of hypertrophied nerve trunks and the absence of ganglion cells .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: All of the following are surgeries you may plan in a child with aganglionic megacolon , except ?
mcqs.explanation: Heineke -Mikulicz's operation is a type of pyloroplasty and is not done for aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung disease ). Surgery is the treatment of choice for Hirschsprung disease . A multi-stage approach may be adopted . A colostomy is done in the newborn period , followed by a definitive pull -through operation after the child is over 10 kgs. Definitive surgeries for Hirschsprung disease are as follows : • Swenson • Duhamel • Soave

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common problem that arises postoperatively following surgery for Hirschsprung's disease ?
mcqs.explanation: Constipation is the most common postoperative problem after surgery for Hirschsprung disease . Other problems are soiling, incontinence, and postoperative enterocolitis .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Up to what length from the anal verge will you be able to visualize through a flexible sigmoidoscope?
mcqs.explanation: Flexible sigmoidoscope is 60 cm in length and can be used to visualize the rectum and sigmoid colon. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is a procedure involving the following steps : A sigmoidoscope is inserted through the anus and the distal colonic mucosa (up to 60 cm from the anal verge) is visualized. Diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers are performed , as needed .535 Scope Length Anoscope 8 cm Proctoscope 15 cm Rectoscope 25 cm Flexible sigmoidosco pe 60 cm Colonoscope –16 0 cm

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which structure would you trace to identify enlarged paracolic lymph nodes ?

options.c: Main branches of the superior mesenteric artery
options.d: Named branches of inferior mesenteric artery

mcqs.explanation: Paracolic lymph nodes are located along the marginal artery.536

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presents with 2 episodes of bleeding per rectum over the past 2 hours. His vitals are stable . Per rectal examination was normal except for trace evidence of fresh blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: In case of suspected lower GI bleeding or hematochezia , if the hemodynamic status of the patient is stable , colonoscopy with appropriate bowel preparation should be done at the earliest . A patient with hematochezia or fresh blood per rectum should be managed in the following way: Hemodynamically unstable on initial assessment (or suspected massive UGI bleed ): • At first, resuscitation with iv fluids , blood transfusion, and volume replacement • Perform EGD (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy ) • Consider getting gastro surgery/interventional radiology consult • If a source is not found on EGD, • Perform angiography \261 embolization if still hemodynamically unstable • Perform colonoscopy if the patient is hemodynamically stable or, if a source was not identified on initial angiography • If colonoscopy did not identify a bleeding source , consider further evaluation with • Capsule endoscopy • Tagged red blood cell scan • Repeat EGD, etc . Hemodynamically stable on initial assessment : • Bowel preparation and perform colonoscopy • If a source was not found on colonoscopy , EGD should be performed • If a source was not found even on EGD, consider further evaluation with • Capsule endoscopy537 • Tagged red blood cell scan • Repeat colonoscopy , etc .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old man with weight loss and pallor comes to the physician. A CBC and Fe studies indicate iron deficiency anemia. The patient denies any history of bleeding disorders or changes in diet . A guaiac test is advised. What parameter does it test ?
mcqs.explanation: Guaiac test is used for testing occult blood in the stool . New -onset iron deficiency anemia in middle -aged men should be thoroughly evaluated for colorectal carcinoma , even in the absence of other symptoms . Principle: Guaiac is a colorless organic compound that turns blue upon oxidation by oxidants, peroxidases, or pseudoperoxidase of hemoglobin . The test is more sensitive for lower GI bleed . Fecal hemoglobin must exceed 10 mg/g of stool (blood loss of 10 ml daily), for the test to be positive in 50% of the cases , although the test can be positive in some cases even if hemoglobin is <1mg/g of stool .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: 99mTc -labeled red blood cell scan can be used to detect gastrointestinal bleeding as low as __________.
mcqs.explanation: 99mTc -labeled red blood cell scan can detect gastrointestinal bleeding as low as 0.1 mL /min. Selective angiography, using the superior or inferior mesenteric artery, can detect hemorrhage in the range of 0.5 to 1.0 mL /min.538

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common anatomical position of the appendix ?
mcqs.explanation: Retrocaecal is the most common position of the appendix . Positions of appendix : • Retrocaecal : 74% • Pelvic: % • Sub-cecal : 1.5% • Pre-ileal: 1% • Post-ileal: 0.5%548

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not true regarding the various anatomical positions of the appendix ?

options.a: Tenderness may be elicited on the immediate right of the umbilicus in post -ileal appendicitis
options.b: The most common location of the base of the appendix is retro-caecal
options.c: An inflamed pelvic appendix may cause an increase in frequency of micturition
options.d: Post-ileal appendicitis may have diarrhoea as a presenting complaint

mcqs.explanation: The base of the appendix is found at the confluence of the three taeniae coli of the caecum . Its position is constant. Conversely, the tip of the appendix can be found in many positions ( retrocaecal being the most common) The taeniae coli fuse to form the longitudinal muscle coat of the appendix . During surgery, gentle traction at the taenia coli, leads the surgeon to the base of the appendix .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: During an appendectomy , the mesoappendix is divided and ligated . Which of the following is false about the major vessel ligated in this step ?

options.b: It is a branch of upper division of the ileocolic artery
options.d: Thrombosis is most common at the tip

mcqs.explanation: 549 During appendectomy , the appendicular artery is the major vessel that is ligated when the mesoappendix is divided . It is a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery.The appendicular artery transverses behind the terminal ileum and enters the mesoappendix away from the base of the appendix . It lies along the free border of the mesoappendix . The terminal part or the tip of the artery lies on the wall of the appendix and may become thrombosed in appendicitis , resulting in distal gangrene or necrosis. It supplies only the appendix and is an end-artery. An accessory appendicular artery called the artery of Seshachalam may be present . It anastomoses at the base of the appendix with a branch of the posterior cecal artery.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While assisting a laparoscopic appendectomy , you observe the resident use the Fold of Treves as a guide while coagulating vessels in the mesoappendix . Which of the following best describes the anatomical landmark ?

options.a: Mucous membrane projecting into the ileal lumen
options.b: The ilio-cecal fold of the peritoneum
options.c: The fold of the mucous membrane around appendiceal orifice
options.d: The fold of the peritoneum over ascending colon

mcqs.explanation: 550 Fold of Treves is an antimesenteric ileocecal fold of peritoneum . A clinical aid useful for detecting the location of the appendix through small abdominal incisions is the identification of the fold of Treves. It marks the junction of the ileum and cecum . As it does not contain any vessel , it is referred to as the bloodless fold of Treves. It is also used as a guide to determine the extent of coagulation during an appendectomy . This prevents thermal injury to adjacent structures .Jackson Membrane: Adhesion from the right abdominal wall to the anterior tenia of the ascending colon. Gerlach valves: A mucosal fold covering the appendiceal orifice.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The CECT findings of a patient who presented with a positive McBurney's sign show a dilated appendix , appendicular wall thickening, and fat stranding. What is the initiating event that leads to his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of appendicitis . The initiating event in the development of appendicitis is luminal obstruction. Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, known as McBurney's sign, is a sign of acute appendicitis. McBurney's point is a point at one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine and umbilicus . It is where the appendix is commonly located . Due to the relatively small diameter of the appendicular lumen, it is easily obstructed . Usually, due to fecoliths. This leads to the buildup of mucus secretions and air due to bacteria. With progressive dilation, venous drainage may get hampered , leading to full -thickness ischemia and perforation. Obstructed lumen of appendix \037 Retained secretions with distension of lumen \037 Secretions get infected \037 Venous occlussion due to increased pressure \037 Bacterial translocation \037 Gangrene & perforation \037 Appendicular abscess551

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the earliest symptom in a patient with acute appendicitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Symptoms of acute appendicitis begin as periumbilical pain followed by anorexia and nausea. Acute appendicitis begins with poorly localized colicky abdominal pain, first noticed in the periumbilical region. This is due to midgut visceral discomfort (T8 to T10 dermatomes ) in response to appendiceal inflammation and obstruction. Over the next 12 -24 hours, it localises to the right lower quadrant due to local peritoneal inflammation.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the casualty with right lower abdominal pain, nausea, and fever. On examination , there is increased pain in the right lower quadrant when palpating the left lower quadrant . What is this sign is called ?
mcqs.explanation: The given triad of clinical features , namely fever, nausea and right lower abdominal pain is Murphy's triad. It is suggestive of acute appendicitis . Deep palpation of the left iliac fossa can cause pain in the right iliac fossa. This sign is called Rovsing's sign. This pain is due to the backflow of gases from the colon into the inflamed right intestine when the left lower abdomen is palpated .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are examining a patient suspected to have appendicitis . During the given manoeuvre, you notice that the patient has sharp right-sided abdominal pain. Which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: This sign elicited is known as Psoas Sign
options.b: It is commonly associated with pelvic appendicitis
options.c: Flexion of the hip against resistance may be done instead
options.d: Pain is due to contact of inflamed appendix with the psoas muscle

mcqs.explanation: The manoeuvre in the given image shows hyperextension of the hip joint. It can induce abdominal pain when there is irritation of the psoas muscle by the inflamed appendix . This is known as the psoas sign and is commonly seen in retrocecal appendicitis . Flexion of the hip against resistance also elicits the psoas sign.Pain elicited on hip flexion and internal rotation is called the obturator sign. It is commonly seen in pelvic appendicitis .552

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young boy was brought to the casualty with a history of fever and abdominal pain. On examination , he was febrile and his pulse rate was 104 beats /min. The CT scan image is shown below . Which of the following signs is not seen in this disease ?
mcqs.explanation: The patient 's history and radiological findings are indicative of acute appendicitis . Ballance sign is not seen in acute appendicitis . Findings on CT that are suggestive of acute appendicitis include : • Appendiceal dilatation (>6 mm in diameter ) • Appendiceal wall thickening (>3 mm) and enhancement Ballance sign is seen due to a ruptured spleen . The ballance sign is positive if there is a fixed dullness to percussion in the left flank and shifting dullness to percussion in the right flank. The fixed dullness is due to the presence of coagulated blood near the lacerated spleen while the shifting dullness is due to the presence of blood in the peritoneal cavity. Option A: Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, known as McBurney's sign, is a sign of acute appendicitis. McBurney's point is a point at one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine and umbilicus . Option B: Rovsing sign is seen in appendicitis . Deep palpation of the left iliac fossa may cause pain in the right iliac fossa. Option C: Psoas sign is seen in appendicitis . Occasionally , an in\037amed appendix lies on the psoas muscle , and the patient will lie with the right hip \037exed , for pain relief .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the casualty with a history of abdominal pain and vomiting for the past 4 hours. On examination, the patient is febrile . Rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa is seen . Which among the following is the preferred imaging modality in this patient ?

options.d: Erect X Ray of the abdomen

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute appendicitis . In the pediatric population , ultrasound of the abdomen is the preferred imaging modality to identify the presence of an inflamed appendix . It avoids the risk of radiation exposure .553 In adults , the best imaging modality is a CT scan.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: For which of the following criteria on the Alvarado system , will you assign 2 points to a patient with features of appendicitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The Alvarado score is a clinical scoring system used in the diagnosis of appendicitis . In the Alvorado scoring system , leukocytosis �o \327 109 cells /L and tenderness right iliac fossa have two points.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following organisms is most commonly isolated in patients presenting with perforated appendicitis ?
mcqs.explanation: Bacteroides fragilis is the most common anaerobe and Escherichia coli is the most common aerobe isolated from perforated appendicitis.Type of bacteria Patients (%) Anaerobic Bacteria Bacteroides fragilis Bacteroides thetaiotaomicro n Bilophila wadsworthia 55 Peptostreptococcusspp . Aerobic Bacteria E. coli Streptococcus viridians 43 Group D streptococci 27 Pseudomonas aeruginosa 18

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presents with fever and right lower quadrant pain for the past week . On examination , tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa are present . An ill-defined abdominal mass is also palpated . CBC reveals leucocytosis . What is the next step in management?
mcqs.explanation: In appendicular mass, the inflammatory process is already localized and any surgical intervention may be difficult and dangerous . Hence , if the general condition is satisfactory , the conservative Ochsner–Sherren regimen is used .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the incision made on a patient while performing an appendicectomy .
mcqs.explanation: Lanz incision is a transverse skin crease incision for appendicitis 2 cm below the umbilicus, centered on the midclavicular–mid inguinal line554 Option A: Gridiron incision is an oblique muscle -splitting incision in the right lower quadrant . It is also called McBurney incision. Option C: Rutherford–Morrison incision is an oblique muscle -cutting incision with its lower end over McBurney's point and extending obliquely upwards and laterally as necessary (Shown on the left side in the image for the sake of clarity) Option D: Rockey–Davis incision is a transverse right lower quadrant incision.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A surgeon performs an appendicectomy with a grid iron incision. He later converts the incision to Rutherford Morrison incision. Which of the following are cut?
mcqs.explanation: The structures cut when the initial incision gridiron incision (McBurney's incision) is converted to the Rutherford Morrison incision are the external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis muscles . When the preoperative diagnosis is reasonably certain, the widely used incision for appendectomy is known as the gridiron incision. It is made perpendicular to a line connecting the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus , with its center at McBurney's point. When better access is needed , the gridiron incision can be converted to a Rutherford Morison incision by extending the incision obliquely upwards and laterally . Rutherford Morison's incision is suitable for a para- or retrocecal appendix that is fixed . It is an oblique muscle -cutting incision starting from McBurney's point and extending upward and laterally as needed . All layers (skin, subcutaneous tissues , external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, and the peritoneum ) are divided along the incision line. In recent years, the transverse skin crease (Lanz ) incision has gained popularity due to improved exposure and ease of extension when necessary . This incision is placed approximately 2 cm below the umbilicus along the midclavicular-midinguinal line, with its length adjusted according to the patient 's size and obesity . If required, the incision can be extended medially by retracting or dividing the rectus abdominis muscle (statement 4).555 When there is uncertainty in the diagnosis, especially in the presence of intestinal obstruction, a lower midline abdominal incision is preferred over a right lower paramedian incision.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: As a surgical resident performing an appendectomy , what is the maximum stump size that you can leave behind in order to prevent stump appendicitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The residual appendiceal stump should be no longer than 5 mm, so as to minimize the possibility of stump appendicitis in the future . Stump appendicitis is a complication that occurs after an appendectomy . It is caused by the inflammation of the residual appendiceal tissue after the appendix is removed. The clinical presentation of stump appendicitis is similar to acute appendicitis . Factors predisposing for stump appendicitis : • Inadequate identification of the appendicular base due to severe local inflammation • Leaving a long stump due to fear of cecal injury or difficult dissection • Local ulcerations due to fecoliths .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 19-year-old boy is taken up for open appendicectomy . Which of the combinations of the following instruments is best suited for his procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: Babcock's forceps , 22 size blade , and Langenbeck retractor are used in open appendicectomy . The image below shows Babcock's forceps , where : • Distal part of distal blade is curved with a triangular fenestra which allows soft tissues to bulge out. • Tip is non traumatic with transverse serrations on it. • It has got a lock in proximal part. Uses :556 • Hold any part of Bowel , Fallopian tube, Appendix , Ureter , Cord, etc .The below image is that of a Langenbeck Retractor: • Useful for holding open wounds , as in an open appendicectomy . • Often used in pairs (one in each of the assistant's hands). • The width of the lip of the retractors varies.557 The 11 -blade is used for skin incisions (eg . incision and drainage) and arteriotomy The 22 -blade is often used for abdominal incisions 15-blade for minor surgical procedures. Deaver's Retractor is specifically designed for holding the liver up out of the way during a cholecystectomy . It needs to be used carefully to avoid damaging the liver.558 Lane's tissue holding forceps • It has got stout and thick distal blades with oval fenestra in each blade • Apposing tooth in the tip • Lock in proximal part Uses : • Hold bulky and tough structures , hold lymph nodes . Tracheal dilator is used to keep tracheostomy open .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common post -operative complication that may arise in patients who undergo an appendectomy ?
mcqs.explanation: Wound infection is the most common postoperative complication of appendectomy .559

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common neoplasm of the appendix ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common neoplasm primarily identified in the appendix are carcinoid tumors. They account for approximately 66% of all tumors of the appendix . They are detected in 0.3 to 0.9% of appendectomy specimens . Adenocarcinoma of the appendix is very rare, accounting for 0.5% of all gastrointestinal cancers. The adenocarcinoma malignancies are three subtypes : • Mucinous • Colonic type • Adenocarcinoid Mucinous is the most common subtype whereas Adenocarcinoid is the rarest.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false about carcinoid tumours of appendix ?

options.a: Size appears to be the best predictor of malignant behavior and metastatic potential
options.b: Arise from Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberk\374hn
options.c: Most common location is the base of the appendix

mcqs.explanation: The most common location of the carcinoid tumour of the appendix is the tip of the appendix i.e., the distal third of the appendix . A carcinoid tumour, also known as argentaffinoma, arises in argentaffin tissue (Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberk\374hn). It often presents with symptoms of subacute or recurrent appendicitis . On gross examination, it is a moderately hard, yellow tumour between the intact mucosa and the peritoneum . Microscopically , tumour cells are small, arranged in small nests within the muscle , and have a characteristic pattern using immunohistochemical stain for chromogranin B. Carcinoid tumours are the most common appendiceal tumours but they rarely metastasize . Treatment includes appendicectomy . Indications for right hemicolectomy along with appendectomy are : • Involvement of the cecal wall • Tumour is 2 cm or more in size • Lymph nodes are involved.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old female patient is admitted to the hospital for complaints of pain and tenderness in the right iliac fossa. She underwent an appendicectomy . A 2.5 cm tumor was encountered at the base of the appendix which was found to be carcinoid on histopathological examination. What is the next step in management?

options.b: Send the urine for 5- hydroxy indole acetic acid levels

mcqs.explanation: The carcinoid tumors of the appendix which are more than 2 cm in size are treated with right hemicolectomy. Management of carcinoid tumors: • <1 cm – Appendicectomy560 • 1-2 cms - Appendicectomy or right hemicolectomy depending on the individual tumor characteristics. • >2 cm – Right hemicolectomy Irrespective of size, it is recommended to perform a right hemicolectomy in: • Carcinoids at the appendiceal base (<2 cm from the base) • Lymphatic invasion or lymph node involvement • Spread to the mesoappendix • Tumor -positive resection margins • Cellular pleomorphism with a high mitotic index.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Following an appendectomy , the specimen was sent for HPE. A well -circumscribed, yellowish tumor measuring 0.5 cm in diameter at the tip of the appendix was seen . The stained sections revealed a typical carcinoid tumor of the appendix . The specimen had a tumor-free margin on all sides . The base of the appendix , the mesoappendix , and nodes were not involved. What is the next step of management?
mcqs.explanation: The size of the carcinoid tumour is 0.5 cm (<1 cm), the margins of the resected specimen are tumour free , and there is no involvement of appendix base, mesoappendix , or lymph nodes . The best management approach here is observation. Carcinoid tumour may be detected in ~0.5% of appendectomy specimens . Appendectomy is adequate in the treatment of cases with a diameter of <1 cm and in those with a diameter of 1-2 cm without lymphovascular invasion . If a tumour is found after appendicectomy : • If it is an adenocarcinoma, perform right hemicolectomy . • If it is a carcinoid tumour, treatment differs according to the tumour size: • <1 cm – Observation • 1–2 cm – Right hemicolectomy if a lymphovascular invasion is seen • >2 cm – Right hemicolectomy Right hemicolectomy treatment is indicated even in tumours < 2 cm in case of: • Tumours localized at the base of the appendix • Invasion of lymphatic ducts , serosa and mesoappendix • Presence of regional lymph node metastasis • Positive surgical margins • Mucin production (mucinous carcinoid tumours) • High mitotic fast cellular pleomorphism

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old presented with right lower quadrant pain and fever for 1 day. An appendicitis was suspected and the patient was prepared for surgery. During the surgery, a normal appendix was found but mesenteric lymph nodes were enlarged . What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Yersinia enterocolitica causes inflammation of the terminal ileum , appendix , and cecum , alongwith mesenteric lymphadenopathy. It is the most common differential diagnosis of acute561 appendicitis . Acute mesenteric lymphadenitis manifests as acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain associated with mesenteric lymph node enlargement and a normal appendix . Diagnosis is made after exploration of the abdomen of a patient suspected of having acute appendicitis , which reveals a normal appendix and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes . It usually occurs in children and young adults .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A postmenopausal lady diagnosed with mucinous cystadenoma appendix is unwilling for surgery.
