mcqs.question: During a cricket match, a batsman controls his urge to urinate as he is unable to take a break in-between . While batting, he suffers a sudden blow as the ball hits him in the suprapubic region. He presents to the emergency department with severe hypogastric pain and the inability to pass urine. He collapses suddenly during the examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.d: Pubic diastasis with bulbar urethra rupture

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a history of injury to a full bladder , inability to pass urine, and syncope are suggestive of intraperitoneal rupture of the bladder . Bladder rupture can be of two types : Pubic diastasis refers to the separation of the pubic symphysis without concomitant fracture. Pubic diastasis with bulbar urethra rupture usually occurs due to straddle injury and presents with blood at the tip of the meatus .Extraperitoneal rupture Intraperitoneal rupture More common(80%) Less common (20 %) Cause Penetrating traumaPelvic fra ctureSurgical damageAssocia ted withproximal urethral inj ury Direct blow or fall on adisten ded bladder926 Extraperitoneal rupture Intraperitoneal rupture Clinical features Pelvic urinoma (encapsulated collection of extravasated uri ne) is seenBlood at the tip of the meatus Sudden severe pain in the hy pogastriumSyncopePeritoniti s Treatment Catheter drainage for 7–10 d ays LaparotomyRepair of bladder Bladder drainage

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient was rushed to the casualty after sustaining a suprapubic injury. On examination, no blood is seen at the meatus . On inserting Foley 's catheter , gross hematuria is noted . His vitals are stable and his pelvic X-ray is given below . What will be the next step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a bladder injury. Open book fracture is most likely suggestive of an intraperitoneal bladder injury. CT cystogram will be the next step in the management to confirm the type of bladder injury. In unstable patients , a cystogram will be the investigation of choice . If an associated urethral injury is suspected , retrograde urethrogram (RGU) is done.Note : Closed book pelvic fractures are more commonly associated with urethral injuries than bladder injuries.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly man was rushed to the casualty at midnight with complaints of severe suprapubic pain and inability to pass urine for the past 24 hours. The abdominal examination finding of the patient is given below . A smooth and enlarged prostate was felt in the per-rectal examination. While attempting to insert a 16-F Foley catheter in this patient , you feel resistance and fail to catheterize . What will be the next step in the management?

options.b: Insert a smaller sized Foley catheter

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute retention of urine, possibly because of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The next step would be to insert an 18-Fr Coud \351 catheter . In men, the BPH especially the middle lobe enlargement obstructs the insertion of Foley 's catherter. Hence , a Coude catheter is advised over suprapubic catetherization as the immediate next step as larger Fr Coude catheter is helpful in negotiating past the angulation in the prostatic urethra.927 (Note : In acute urine retention , urethral strictures should be suspected when there is resistance at the urethral meatus as the strictures are more common in distal urethra than proximal urethra) Bladder outlet obstruction is usually the most common cause of acute retention of urine. Its clinical features include : • Inability to pass urine • Severe suprapubic pain • A distended , palpable , and tender bladder Acute urinary retention is managed by placing a urethral catheter as early as possible . Usually in BPH, smaller catheters will not pass through the angulation of the prostatic urethra as they are flexible and kink . Hence in BPH, the Coud \351-tip catheter , which has a rigid and angulated tip, can be used to overcome the urethral obstruction. If urethral catheter placement is not successful , suprapubic catheterization should be done. If there is a urethral stricture , a council tip catheter is used to dilate it using a cystoscope , guide wires, and urethral dilators.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You are asked to remove a Foley 's catheter after a procedure but you are unable to deflate the balloon. The surgeon himself tries to remove it after cutting the sidearm but is unsuccessful as well . What should be the next step of management?

options.a: CT-guided rupture of bulb of Foley 's
options.b: Inject ether to dissolve the balloon and pull it out
options.c: Inject water to over distend the balloon until it bursts and remove the catheter
options.d: Inflate with 20ml of water and under USG guidance , locate and prick the balloon

mcqs.explanation: USG-guided rupture of the balloon percutaneously after inflating it with 20ml water should be the next step of management. The failure of the balloon to deflate may be caused by: • Faulty valve mechanism • Blockage of the inflation channel by debris • Crystallization of the fluid within the balloon (when saline is used ) The next best step in the management of a retained Foley 's catheter is to further inflate the balloon with 20mL of water, following which the inflated balloon is ruptured percutaneously with928 a needle under USG guidance . A suprapubic approach is used in males, while in females , either a transurethral or transvaginal route can be used . A cystoscopy should be done to ensure that all fragments are removed. Other methods of approach include cutting the sidearm of the catheter , thereby disabling the valve mechanism, or advancing a ureteric stylet or fine-gauge wire through the inflation port to dislodge debris or puncture the balloon. But these are often unsuccessful . Option A: CT is not routinely used in most settings with retained Foley 's. Option B: Injection of ether through the balloon port causes the rupture of the balloon within seconds . But this technique causes significant bladder irritation . Option C: Balloons should not be overinflated until they rupture . This may cause severe pain and could cause bladder rupture .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In the given picture of a Foley 's catheter , what is the function of the tube marked 'A'?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a three -way Foley 's catheter . The tube marked 'A' is used for continuous irrigation of the bladder to remove debris & blood clots . This is most commonly used after any prostate surgery or conditions with bleeding in the bladder . The central tube is used for the drainage of urine and the tube on the right is used for inflating the balloon.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the earliest sign seen on cystoscopy in a patient suspected to have bladder tuberculosis ?
mcqs.explanation: The earliest sign of tuberculosis of the bladder observed by cystoscopy is the pallor of the mucosa around the ureteric orifice due to submucous edema . Subsequently , tubercles may be seen . In long-standing cases , there is marked fibrosis and the capacity of the bladder is greatly reduced (thimble bladder). This is managed by augmentation cystoplasty . The following X-ray KUB shows a thimble bladder :929 Ureteric lesions can also be seen in genitourinary tuberculosis . They include : • Kerr's kink - kinking of the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) • Ureteral stricture • Beaded ureter • Shortening of the ureter • Golf hole ureter - Longitudinal fibrosis leading to shortening of the ureter and pulling up the orifice as a gaping hole . Reimplantation of ureter is done.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man comes with complaints of hematuria and difficulty in urination for the past few weeks . Microscopic examination of urine samples shows parasitic eggs as shown in the image. Which type of bladder carcinoma is the patient most likely to develop ?
mcqs.explanation: 930 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of schistosomiasis . The patient is most likely to develop squamous cell carcinoma as it is associated with schistosomiasis . The image shows oval-shaped eggs with the terminal spine which is characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium. Schistosomal bladder cancers can also be adenocarcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma (less frequently ). Primary bladder tumors usually originate from the transitional epithelium of the bladder (90%). Sometimes , they arise from connective tissue . Secondary tumors of the bladder arise from the sigmoid and rectum, the prostate , the uterus , or the ovaries. Carcinoma of the bladder & associated risk factors:Histological subtype Risk factors Transitional cell carcinoma ( urothelial ) SmokingExposure to anilined yesCyclophosphamidePelvic i rradiation Squamous cell carcinoma SchistosomiasisChronic irrita tion caused by stone disease Bladder diverticulaChronic U TISmoking Adenocarcinoma Persistent urachus or trigone of the bladder

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs causes carcinoma bladder ?
mcqs.explanation: Cyclophosphamide (an alkylating agent ) causes bladder cancer The risk of bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of cyclophosphamide treatment . Phosphoramide mustard is the primary mutagenic metabolite that causes bladder cancer in patients exposed to cyclophosphamide . Painless, gross hematuria is the most common symptom that is indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise . Depending upon the depth of invasion, bladder carcinoma can be divided into • Flat, non-invasive carcinoma in situ (CIS) • Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (70% of cases ) - does not invade detrusor muscle but can invade lamina propria. • Muscle -invasive bladder cancer - invades the detrusor muscle . Diagnosis is by cystourethroscopy (directly visualizing the growth ) and biopsy . Management is as follows : • Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer: • Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT ) followed by intravesical chemotherapy with mitomycin C or epirubicin931 • Immunotherapy with regular intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) in high-risk tumors. • Muscle invasive bladder cancer: Radical cystectomy along with urinary diversion procedure and lymph node dissection +/- neoadjuvant chemotherapy Other options : Option B: Cisplatin is an anticancer drug used to treat testicular cancer. It is associated with an increased risk for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Option C: Taxane is an anticancer drug and is the main component in the treatment regimens of metastatic cancers. Taxane's adverse effects are neutropenia and fluid retention (pulmonary edema ). Option D: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and is used in the treatment of estrogen -dependent breast cancer. Due to its partial agonistic activity, it is known to increase endometrial cancer in post -menopausal women.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the incorrect statement regarding bladder carcinoma .

options.a: Painless hematuria is the most common symptom
options.b: Inactivation of the Rb gene is implicated in the cancer formation
options.d: The most important prognostic factor is the size of the tumor

mcqs.explanation: The most important prognostic factor in bladder carcinoma is the depth of invasion . Activation of oncogenes such as ras, c-erbB, E2F3, and inactivation of tumor-suppressor genes such as p53, p21, p16, and Rb gene is implicated in the cancer formation of the bladder . Clinical features of bladder carcinoma include : • Painless gross haematuria - Most common symptom and is indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise • Urinary retention • Constant pelvic pain • Increased urinary frequency • Discomfort while urinating • If there is nerve involvement, pain is referred to the suprapubic region, groins, perineum , and thighs. Investigations done for bladder cancer are: • Urine cytology - Low sensitivity • Intravenous urography - Not frequently used nowadays. Replaced by non-contrast CT and MRI • Cystourethroscopy and biopsy - The best investigation

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the treatment of choice for a patient with non-invasive bladder carcinoma of stage pT1?

options.c: Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor

mcqs.explanation: Since the pathological staging of the tumor is given (pT1), it implies that transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT ) has already been done. Therefore, this patient should be managed932 by instillation of intravesical BCG. TURBT is done for the pathologic staging of the tumor. This staging helps us to decide the further plan of treatment. Intravesical therapy (using chemotherapy or immunotherapy) is done within 24hrs of TURBT in order to kill any residual cancer cells . It only affects the lining of the bladder and is not useful for cancers that have spread into the deeper layers. pT stage : Pathological stage Treatment of carcinoma bladder : M-VAC chemotherapy regime consists of: • Methotrexate • Vinblastine • Adriamycin • CisplatinpT sta ge Extent of the tumor Tx Primary tumor cannot be ass essed T0 No evidence of primary tumo r Ta Noninvasive papillary carcin oma Tis Carcinoma in situ T1 Tumor invades subepithelial connective tissue (lamina pro pria) T2 Tumor invades muscularis pr opria bladder wall T3 Tumor invades perivesical tis sue T4 Tumor invades any of the foll owing: Prostate, uterus , vagi na, pelvic wall and abdomina l wallpT stage Treatment Low-grade pTa Intravesical chemotherapywit h mitomycin, thiotepa , and a driamycin may be started aft er TURBT High-grade pTapTis pT1 Intravesical BCGis started aft er TURBT933 pT stage Treatment pT2 Radical cystectomyfollowed b yradiotherapy pT3pT4 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy ( M-VAC ), radical cystectomy , and radiotherapy

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with carcinoma in situ of the urinary bladder is posted for intravesical therapy . What is the strain of mycobacteria that will be used in this therapy ?
mcqs.explanation: An attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis is used in intravesical BCG therapy . Intravesical BCG is used for the treatment of non-invasive (no invasion into the muscle layer) urinary bladder tumors. It induces a strong local inflammatory response against the attenuated bacteria, which helps in the destruction of the tumor cells . Option d: Mw vaccine for multibacillary leprosy patients and their contacts is extracted from Mycobacterium indicus pranii. It is also used as an adjunct to chemotherapy for category II tuberculosis .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which laser is preferred for performing transurethral resection of the bladder tumor?
mcqs.explanation: The Nd: YAG laser is preferred for the resection of minimally invasive bladder tumors.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly man on follow -up for treatment of bladder cancer presents with painless hematuria. Which of the following assays should be done on this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: An NMP 22 assay should be done in this patient to detect the recurrence of bladder carcinoma . NMP 22 is a nuclear matrix protein that is used to form cell nuclei . It is shed into the urine and has a higher concentration in the urine of bladder cancer patients . NMP-22 cutoff levels for bladder cancer detection is > 10 units/mL.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Urinary diversion is indicated in all the following clinical conditions, except :
mcqs.explanation: Urinary diversion is not done in cases of bladder hematoma. Urinary diversion procedures are performed to divert urine from the bladder to a new exit site . It is of two types : • Cutaneous urinary diversion (External diversion): Urine drains through an opening created in the abdominal wall and skin • Ileal conduit - urine is diverted by implanting ureters into a loop of ileum that is led out through the abdominal wall.934 • Cutaneous ureterostomy - ureters are directed through the abdominal wall and attached to an opening in the skin. • Continent urinary diversion (Internal urinary diversion): A portion of the intestine is used to create a new reservoir for urine. The internal pouch is placed inside the abdomen. The ureters are attached to the internal pouch , and the internal pouch is attached to the urethra or to a stoma in the abdomen with a valve. Indications of urinary diversion: • Post cystectomy • Carcinoma of the urinary bladder • Distal obstruction • Neurogenic bladder • Ectopia vesicae, Incurable fistula • Irremovable obstruction • Trauma to the ureters and urethra

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient presents to the emergency department with confusion and drowsiness . He underwent cystectomy with urinary diversion for bladder carcinoma 8 weeks back. ABG analysis and electrolyte values are given below . Which of the following urinary diversion conduits was most likely done in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: A uretero -sigmoid diversion was most likely done in this patient as it frequently results in hyperchloremic hypokalemic acidosis. Hypokalemia is less common with ileal diversions because the ileum reabsorbs some of the potassium from the urine while the colon does not. The order in which the hyperchloraemic hypokalemic acidosis occurs is sigmoid colon > colon/ileum. Electrolyte abnormalities based on the part of intestine involved:935 Stomach Jejunum Ileum/colon Hypokalemia Hyperkalemia Hypokalemia Hypochloremia Hypochloremia Hyperchloremia Metabolic alkalosi s Metabolic acidosi s Metabolic acidosi s

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old lady experiences increased frequency of urination and lower abdominal pain which is relieved by micturition. Urinalysis is normal . Cystoscopy reveals fissures and punctate hemorrhages in the bladder mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with normal urinalysis and cystoscopy findings are suggestive of interstitial cystitis . Interstitial cystitis is a persistent , painful form of chronic cystitis , occurring most frequently in women. It is also known as chronic pelvic pain syndrome or bladder pain syndrome. Its clinical features include : • Severe suprapubic pain • Urinary frequency • Urgency • Hematuria • Dysuria without evidence of bacterial infection Cystoscopic findings seen in bladder mucosa are: • Fissures • Punctate hemorrhages (glomerulations) • Ulcerations in the fundus of the bladder (Hunner's ulcer) The image shows Hunner's ulcer seen in interstitial cystitis :936 Treatment options include : • Conservative - Patient education about the chronicity of the condition, behavioral modification (timed voiding, bladder training), stress reduction , dietary alteration (avoidance of caffeine and spicy and acidic foods ) and physical therapy should be the initial management for all patients . • Pharmacological - Neuropathic analgesics (e.g. amitriptyline , pregabalin) are used for those with a significant pain component , whereas antimuscarinics and \0313-agonists are used for frequency, nocturia and urgency symptoms . • Surgical - For those with Hunner lesions, fulguration or laser to these lesions can be beneficial . Cystodistension as a treatment has variable evidence for success . If these options fail to improve symptoms major surgical reconstruction can be considered in selected cases . Option b: Malakoplakia is a distinct form of inflammatory reaction seen in chronic cystitis . It appears as soft , yellow , slightly raised mucosal plaques . Option d: Cystitis cystica occurs due to chronic irritation of the bladder mucosa. Cystoscopy reveals cystic lesions in the bladder .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child with recurrent urinary tract infection undergoes voiding cystourethrogram . It shows reflux of urine into the pelvis and calyces , without dilation of the ureter. What is the grade of vesicoureteric reflux?
mcqs.explanation: Reflux of urine into pelvis and calyces without dilatation is Grade II vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). VUR is the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the upper urinary tract. VUR is a common clinical entity . The investigation of choice for VUR is micturating cystourethrogram (MCU ). VUR is graded as follows :GRA DE DESCRIPTION I Reflux into a non-dilated uret er937 GRA DE DESCRIPTION II Reflux into the pelvis and cal yces without dilatation of the ureter III Reflux is associated with mil d to moderate dilatation of th e ureter, renal pelvis, and cal yces , with minimal blunting of the fornices IV Moderate ureteral tortuosity and dilatation of the pelvis a nd calyces V Gross dilatation of the ureter, pelvis, and calyses ; loss of pa pillary impressions; ureteral tortuosity

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following will be seen in a patient with Marion's disease ?

options.a: Hypertrophy of the internal sphincter of the bladder
options.b: Hypertrophy of the external sphincter of the bladder
options.c: Congenital obstruction of the prostatic urethra

mcqs.explanation: Hypertrophy of the internal sphincter of the bladder is seen in Marion's disease . This leads to bladder outlet obstruction. Its clinical features include voiding and storage symptoms (usually associated with BPH). Therefore it is also called prostatism sans prostate : • Increased urinary frequency • Urgency • Dribbling of urine • Hesitancy • Intermittent stream938 • Nocturia It is commonly seen in young patients . Bladder outlet obstruction can occur due to 2 causes : • Muscular causes • Congenital hypertrophy of internal sphincter , i.e., Marion's disease • Dyssynergic contraction of the smooth muscle of the bladder neck (bladder neck dyssynergia ) • Fibrosis of bladder neck following transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding the condition shown below ?

options.a: Bilateral in more than 50% of the cases
options.d: Affects males more often than females

mcqs.explanation: The given intravenous urography (IVU) image depicts cobra head /adder head deformity which is a classic sign of ureterocele . It is associated with dysplastic renal tissue . Ureterocele : A ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is thought to be caused due to ureteric orifice atresia. It is observed more in females than males in a 4:1 preponderance and is bilateral in about 10 % of the cases . They are similar to ectopic ureters wherein the upper pole of the kidney is drained. This condition is typically associated with dysplastic and non-functional renal tissue . Clinical presentation : • Children with ureterocele usually present with infection . • Adults present with renal stones . Diagnosis: • IVU shows a classical cobra head sign but is relatively infrequently performed these days. • Cystoscopy shows a bulging , translucent swelling involving the ureteric orifice where there is urinary stasis. It is emptied by ureteric peristalsis . Treatment: • Surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter is the treatment of choice for simple ureterocele . • Renal stones associated with ureterocele are removed using an endoscopic incision • An advanced disease that causes hydronephrosis or pyonephrosis is an indication for nephrectomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements regarding bladder stone is false ?

options.a: Primary bladder stone develops in sterile urine
options.c: Uric acid stones occur in patients with ileostomies
options.d: Triple phosphate calculus occurs in urine infected with urea-splitting organisms

mcqs.explanation: A cystine calculus occurs only in the presence of cystinuria and is radioopaque because of its high sulfur content .939 Primary bladder stone : • Develops in sterile urine in the absence of any known functional, anatomic, or infectious factors and does not necessarily imply that stones have formed de novo in the bladder . • Most common in children younger than 10 years of age • Most vesical calculi are mixed • Ammonium acid urate, calcium oxalate , uric acid, and calcium phosphate are the most common components of primary bladder calculi Secondary bladder stone : Forms during infection , due to bladder outflow obstruction, impaired bladder emptying , or the presence of a foreign body. Types : • Calcium oxalate stones • Uric acid stones - occur in patients with gout but are also observed in patients with ileostomies or with bladder outlet obstruction • Cystine stones - in cystinuria • Triple phosphate stones - occur in urine infected with urea-splitting organisms940

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following are storage symptoms of BPH?
mcqs.explanation: Urgency , enuresis and frequency are storage symptoms . Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) can be classified as:Storage Voiding Frequency(earliest symptom in BPH)NocturiaUrgencyUrg e incontinenceNocturnal inco ntinence (enuresis ) HesitancyPoor flowIntermitt ent streamDribblingSensatio n of poor bladder emptyingE pisodes of near retention948 Storage symptoms are seen in conditions where the bladder is irritated. Voiding symptoms are common in conditions causing bladder outlet obstruction. In benign prostatic hyperplasia , both storage and voiding symptoms are present .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 60-year-old man presented with fever, chills, and dysuria. On per-rectal examination, his prostate was tender and boggy . His PSA level was 7.4 ng/dl. What is the next best step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute bacterial prostatitis and should be managed by antibiotics. A rigorous and prolonged treatment for 2-6 weeks with an antibiotic that penetrates the prostate wall is indicated (trimethoprim, ciprofloxacin or aminoglycoside ). Incomplete infection eradication lead to recurrent attacks and chronic prostatitis . Acute bacterial prostatitis is usually caused by an ascending urinary tract infection (UTI) or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts . The most common organism is Escherichia coli. An associated increase in levels of PSA(>4ng/ml) may be present due to prostate inflammation. Catheterization and prostatic massage are contraindicated in patients with suspected acute prostatitis, as they increase the chance for bacteremia and sepsis . Instead, suprapubic tap should be performed to alleviate retention . Chronic bacterial prostatitis is the sequela of inadequately treated acute prostatitis . Diagnosis includes : • Three-glass urine test - If the first glass with the initial urine sample is clear, but the second and third samples contain prostatic threads and leukocytes , it indicates the presence of prostatitis . • Digital rectal examination - Prostate may be normal , boggy , or tender . • Prostatic fluid examination - post -prostatic massage fluid shows pus cells and bacteria.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which is the most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is Escherichia coli. It is commonly caused by an ascending urethral infection or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts . Sexually transmissible infections and other urinary pathogens , such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus faecalis may also be responsible . The patient presents with fever, perineal pain, chills and rigor, and dysuria. Per rectal examination will reveal a tender , boggy prostate . Care should be taken to avoid aggressive palpation or prostatic massage as it can lead to bacterial dissemination and sepsis . Urine examination and culture should be done. Urine examination reveals threads in urine. Management : Patients with systemic signs of infection should be admitted for IV antibiotics , hydration , and monitoring of laboratory parameters. Patients who have no signs of systemic infection , who can tolerate oral intake, and who have no urinary retention can be treated with oral antibiotics. Antibiotics are given for 2-6 weeks to ensure949 the eradication of the infection as antibiotics don't penetrate the prostate capsule easily . For outpatient therapy : Ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral every 12 hours or levofloxacin 500 mg OD or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double -strength tablet oral every 12 hours can be used . For hospitalized patients : Intravenous ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin with or without an aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin) or intravenous beta -lactam with or without an aminoglycoside . Gram-positive infections are treated with cephalosporins (cephalexin , cefazolin) or dicloxacillin and vancomycin .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of following compounds form endogenous prostatic calculi?
mcqs.explanation: Endogenous calculi are most commonly composed of calcium phosphate . Exogenous calculi are urinary calculi that are arrested in the prostatic urethra. They are relatively rare.Corpora amylacea are benign histological findings in prostate glands. Prostatic calculi are thought to develop from the calcification of corpora amylacea.

options.d: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors act best when the gland is small.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings is not an indication to perform prostatectomy in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia ?
mcqs.explanation: Increased frequency alone is not an indication for prostatectomy . Increasing difficulty in micturition, with considerable frequency during both day and night, delay in starting, and a poor stream are the usual symptoms for which surgery is advised. Other indications include the following : • Acute retention • Chronic retention and renal impairment • Residual urine of �o 200 mL • Raised blood urea • Hydroureter or hydronephrosis • Complications of bladder outflow obstruction • Stone • Infection • Diverticuli • Hemorrhage - Venous bleeding from a ruptured vein overlying the prostate

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the approach for surgery of the prostate as shown in the image:
mcqs.explanation: The image shows the transvesical approach, also known as Freyer approach. In this approach, the bladder is opened and the prostate is enucleated by putting a finger into the urethra, pushing forward towards the pubes to separate the lateral lobes , and then working the finger between the adenoma and the false capsule . Among the other approaches , TURP is most commonly performed .951

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: As a first-year surgery resident , you have scrubbed in to assist a urologist on a TURP procedure . Up to what distal anatomical landmark do you expect him to resect ?
mcqs.explanation: Verumontanum is used as the distal -most border of the resection in transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). This prevents damage to the external urethral sphincter which is located just distal to the verumontanum. Damage to the external urethral sphincter leads to urinary incontinence. The bladder neck is the proximal limit of resection .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient in your ward is scheduled for monopolar-TURP . Which of the given fluids should be used for irrigation during the procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: The best irrigating fluid for M-TURP is 1.5% isotonic glycine .952 M-TURP removes tissue with a wire loop that has an electrical current flowing in one direction (monopolar). The surgical site is irrigated with a non-conducting non-ionic fluid as the use of an ionic solution leads to dissipation of the cutting current and poor cutting efficacy . Thus, normal saline and N/5 saline cannot be used . The use of distilled water in TURP leads to the water-intoxication syndrome. Bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate (B-TURP ) uses a specialized resecting loop that incorporates both the active and the return portions of the circuit on the same electrode and an ionic irrigating solution such as normal saline can be used safely .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 70-year-old patient with benign prostatic hypertrophy underwent TURP. An hour later, he was found to have an altered sensorium and had several bouts of vomiting. What is the most probable cause ?
mcqs.explanation: The most probable cause for the above-mentioned symptoms is water intoxication also known as transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) syndrome. Absorption of water into the circulation at the time of transurethral urethral resection can lead to : • Hyponatremia, which may manifest as confusion, nausea, and vomiting • Congestive cardiac failure • Hemolysis It is managed by fluid restriction. The use of isotonic glycine for irrigation during resection reduces the incidence of water intoxication.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man presents with a history of minimal ejaculation at sexual climax and passing cloudy urine after. He is a known diabetic and underwent TURP 6 months ago. What is the mechanism leading to this complication?

options.a: Injury to the external urethral sphincter
options.b: Disruption of the autonomic nerve supply to the corpora of the penis
options.c: Over use of coagulating diathermy during the procedure

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario above suggests the patient has retrograde ejaculation . The most likely mechanism of its development is disruption of the bladder neck. Retrograde ejaculation is the most common complication of transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Option A: Injury to the external urethral sphincter causes incontinence following TURP. Option B: Disruption of the autonomic nerve supply to the corpora of the penis causes impotence . Option C: Overuse of coagulating diathermy following TURP causes bladder neck contracture. Other complications of TURP include : • Transurethral resection of prostate (TUR) syndrome • Primary and secondary hemorrhage • Perforation of the bladder or the prostatic capsule • Sepsis • Urethral stricture953 Note :Transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), Transurethral needle ablation (TUNA), and laser vaporization are less invasive methods used for the treatment of BPH. They have a decreased incidence of ejaculatory dysfunction and hemorrhage.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 68- year-old patient presents with difficulty in initiating micturition. A DRE reveals an enlarged nodular prostate with adherent rectal mucosa. PSA was found to be 25 ng/ml and a biopsy result was suggestive of adenocarcinoma. Which of the following statements is false regarding his condition ?

options.a: PSA is a not specific marker for the condition.
options.b: Gleason score correlates with the pathological stage
options.c: It is associated with decreased % free PSA
options.d: It arises from the transitional zone of the gland.

mcqs.explanation: Prostatic carcinoma , as indicated in the clinical scenario, arises from the peripheral zone of the gland. Anatomically, the prostate is divided into three zones. • The peripheral zone lies posteriorly and has an abundance of prostatic glands. • The central zone lies posterior to the urethral lumen and above the seminal vesicles as they course through the prostate . • The transitional zone is periurethral. Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises from the transitional zone.954 Gleason grading may be used after biopsy to evaluate the stage of histopathological specimen . Gleason scores range from 6 to 10 where 6 is low risk for prostate cancer while 10 is high risk . PSA (prostatic specific antigen) is a glycoprotein peptidase that facilitates the liquefaction of semen. It is useful for screening and for monitoring response to therapy but is neither specific nor sensitive to the condition as it can be elevated due to old age and benign conditions such as prostatitis and BPH. Slightly elevated total PSA (between 4.0 and 10 .0 ng/mL ) and low free PSA (<25%) is suspicious for prostate cancer.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 63-year-old patient comes to the urology OPD with hesitancy , incomplete voiding, and pelvic pain. On a digital rectal examination, an irregularly enlarged prostate with a nodular surface is felt . The rectal mucosa does not move freely over it. A biopsy using an automated gun is planned . How many biopsy cores should be obtained ?
mcqs.explanation: Ideally , 12 systematic biopsy cores are obtained in patients with suspected prostatic cancer. A 12 -core systematic biopsy that incorporates apical and far-lateral cores in template distribution allows maximum cancer detection . It also avoids detection of insignificant prostate cancers and the need of a repeat biopsy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 77 -year-old man was evaluated for a nodule found on his prostate . His PSA levels were 15 ng/dl and a transrectal biopsy indicated a malignancy. Which of the following statements is false regarding its spread ?

options.a: Local spread can occur to the seminal vesicles .
options.b: Direct involvement of rectum is common.
options.c: Obturator nodes are most commonly involved.
options.d: Spread by bloodstream usually occurs to the bones.

mcqs.explanation: Palpable nodules over the prostate with raised PSA are highly suggestive of carcinoma . direct involvement of the rectum is rare but it may become stenosed by the tumor infiltrating around it. Option A: Local invasion occurs upwards , first involving seminal vesicles , bladder neck, and trigone; this is followed by distal invasion to the external sphincter . Obstruction of one or both ureters can occur resulting in anuria . Option C: Lymph nodes involved are obturator lymph nodes , external iliac nodes , and occasionally retroperitoneal , mediastinal, and supraclavicular lymph nodes . Option D: Spread by the bloodstream occurs mostly to the bones; the bones involved most frequently in carcinoma of the prostate are the pelvic bones and the lower lumbar vertebrae.

mcqs.question: Orchidectomy is used as treatment for which of the following stages of prostate cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Orchidectomy is performed to carry out androgen ablation in the treatment of locally advanced disease in the elderly . It is also done to manage metastatic disease . mcqs.question: A 77 -year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. The X-ray revealed the given lesions The patient had undergone an orchidectomy three years ago to manage his prostatic carcinoma . However, recent serial estimations of PSA have shown an increasing trend. What is the treatment of choice for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: Blastic lesions on X-Ray after surgical castration (therapeutic orchidectomy ) in patients with prostatic carcinoma is suggestive of hormone-resistant bone metastasis . The treatment of choice for hormone-resistant bone metastasis is radiopharmaceutical therapy with radium-223 . Radium-223 is a radioactive isotope that emits low levels of alpha-particle radiation. mcqs.question: Which of the following vaccines is used in the treatment of prostate cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Sipuleucel -T (Provenge) is an autologous prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP)-loaded dendritic cell vaccine. It is approved for patients with hormone-resistant, metastatic prostate cancer with minimal or no cancer-related symptoms . Other immunotherapies in prostate cancer include : • GVAX allogeneic recombinant whole-cell vaccine • Immune checkpoint inhibitors such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor • CTLA -4 inhibitor Option A: Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) has demonstrated therapeutic activity in melanoma. Option B: Bacillus Calmette –Gu\351rin is used for bladder carcinoma . Option D: Algenpantucel -L is used as immunotherapy in pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used in laser enucleation of the prostate ?
mcqs.explanation: Ho-YAG laser is the most common laser used in enucleation of the prostate . The procedure is known as Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP). Laser reduce the duration of the procedure and the risk of harmorrhage . KTPA green light laser is the best laser that can be used . It causes vaporisation of prostatic tissue . As it is hemostatic in nature, it can be safely used in patients on anticoagulants .959

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Where does urethral stricture most commonly occur?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of urethral stricture is the bulbar urethra. A urethral stricture is a narrowing of the urethra caused by scarring, which functionally causes obstructive voiding dysfunction of the lower urinary tract. The most common cause of urethral stricture is trauma. It can also be iatrogenic due urethral catheterization and infections . These patients present with features of the hesitancy of micturition, straining to void, and poor urinary stream. The most common complication of urethral stricture is urinary tract infection .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the investigation and the lesion depicted in the image given below .

options.a: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
options.b: Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
options.d: Micturating cystourethrography with prostratic urethra stricture

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture. The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU ).967 In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities. The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture :In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter , the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the OPD with complaints of difficulty to start urination and that he has to strain to maintain a proper flow . He gives a history of pelvic injury one year back. Investigations reveal a stricture of length 1.5 cm at the bulbar urethra. What will be the best management for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a short bulbar urethral stricture (<2cm) due to trauma, will be best managed by excision with end-to-end urethroplasty . It is the gold standard for the repair of968 anterior urethral stricture . The management of a urethral stricture depends on the site , the length , and the cause of the stricture. They include : • Endoscopic urethrotomy - The stricture is released using a knife passed through a rigid urethroscope . • Urethroplasty - Excision of the stenosed length of the urethra and re-anastomosis is done. A buccal mucosa graft can be used to bridge the gap. It is considered when a stricture is due to trauma or recurred following endoscopic treatment . • Urethral dilation - The urethra is stretched using urethral dilators. This is a blind procedure and it can cause injury. Hence , it is not done frequently . • Intermittent self -dilatation - In patients with recurrent strictures who are unable to undergo urethroplasty , then intermittent self -dilatation with soft hydrophilic catheters is done on a daily basis.

On examination, blood was seen at the tip of the urethra, and swelling of the penis and scrotum was seen . What is the site of injury?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a history of a blow to the perineum , blood at the tip of the meatus , swelling of the penis and scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra. Urethral injuries can be classified into: Note : Urinary bladder rupture occurs due to an injury to the suprapubic region. mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old was brought to the ER after falling off his bicycle . His vitals were stable , but he had a bruise over the perineum and he has not passed urine yet . Blood was seen at the meatus and the bladder was not palpable . What will be the next step in the management of this patient ?

options.d: Wait for bladder to fill and urge to urinate

mcqs.explanation: The clinical features such as perineal bruise and blood at the urethral meatus following a fall from the bicycle are suggestive of a bulbar urethral injury. In this case, as the bladder is not palpable969 the best option would be to wait for the bladder to fill and urge to urinate. Once the bladder is full the urine should be drained by a suprapubic catheter . Foleys catheter insertion should not be done in cases of suspected urethral injury, as it can convert a partial tear into a complete tear.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A worried mother brings her 18-month-old son to OPD with complaints of repeated urinary tract infections . During diagnostic work-up, pelvic USG shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with the USG showing the key-hole sign is suggestive of the posterior urethral valve (PUV). It is seen due to dilatation of the bladder and the proximal urethra. The posterior urethral valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit, which lies just distal to the verumontanum. They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow . The posterior urethral valve is the most common congenital cause of bladder outlet obstruction in males . PUV is classified into three types based on Young 's classification . Diagnosis is made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder . If the diagnosis is not made antenatally , then neonates typically present with urinary infection or uremia and renal failure. The investigation of choice for a posterior urethral valve is micturating cystourethrography (MCUG ). Initially, the obstruction is relieved by catheterization to preserve renal function. Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with lifelong supportive treatment . The following VCUG shows vesicoureteric reflux due to posterior urethral valves:970

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A newborn was found to have a following anomaly of the penile urethra while being examined by a pediatrician. Identify the incorrect statement regarding the condition.

options.a: It is the most common congenital abnormality of the urethra
options.b: Circumcision should be done to remove the excess skin
options.c: It does not cause urinary obstruction
options.d: Ventral chordee is a common association

mcqs.explanation: The image showing a newborn having a urethral meatus that opens on the underside of the penis is indicative of hypospadias . Circumcision should not be done in hypospadias as the foreskin will be used for surgical reconstruction. Hypospadias is the most common congenital abnormality of the urethra. It is characterized by the combination of: • A ventrally placed urethral meatus (underside of penis or perineum ) • Poor development of the ventral aspect of the prepuce (resulting in hooded foreskin) • Ventral chordee (bending of the penis )971 Hypospadias does not cause either obstruction or urinary tract infection and surgery is recommended for sexual , urinary stream, or cosmetic reasons. Note : In hypospadias , ventral chordee is seen , whereas , in epispadias , dorsal chordee is seen . The image below shows a hooded prepuce :The image below shows epispadias with bladder exstrophy :

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the appropriate age at which corrective surgery should be done for the defect shown in the image?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows penoscrotal hypospadias . Operations for hypospadias are routinely performed when the patient is between 6 and 18 months of age . The infant has good tolerance to surgery by the age of 6 months. The child is well aware of his genitalia and will be toilet trained by the age of 18 months.972 Surgery in hypospadias is done to correct problems with the urinary stream and for cosmetic reasons. The main principles of surgery in hypospadias include : • Orthoplasty - Chordee correction • Urethroplasty - To reposition the urethral opening • Glanuloplasty - Reconstruction of glans • Skin cover and scrotoplasty Surgery depends on the site of the hypospadias . Tubularized incised plate (TIP ) urethroplasty is the most commonly done procedure . It is done for distal hypospadias . Complications of hypospadias surgery include : • Urethrocutaneous fistula (most common) • Recurrence of chordee • Urethral stricture • Meatal stenosis • Infection
