mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of erectile dysfunction ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of erectile dysfunction (ED) is stress . It can also be associated with diabetes , hypertension , dyslipidemia , and smoking. The most common pathological cause of ED is vascular disease affecting the penile arterial blood flow. Evaluation of ED involves confirmation of the diagnosis by history taking, assessing the patient for underlying risk factors, and physical examination of the genitalia . Measurement of the blood pressure and assessment of the secondary sexual characteristics is also done. Biochemical assessment of the blood sugar, the serum lipid profile , and the serum testosterone is done in all cases . Treatment involves the use of phosphodiesterase -V inhibitors (sildenafil ) with an intra-cavernosal injection of alprostadil . Vacuum erection devices and penile implants are reserved for resistant cases . The most common cause of erectile dysfunction in: • Middle -aged men: Psychological974 • Older men: Organic (atherosclerosis ) • Overall: Psychological

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: All of the following are indications to perform circumcision in children, except :
mcqs.explanation: A tight frenulum and physiological phimosis are not indications of circumcision in children. Physiological phimosis is seen in children that are less than 6 years of age (2-6 years) due to natural adhesions between the glans and inner preputial skin. It rectifies on its own. Circumcision is the surgical removal of the foreskin that covers the glans penis . Indications of circumcision in children: • True phimosis (associated with a white , scarred preputial orifice, most common just before puberty ) • Paraphimosis • On request (most common) • Balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO) • Recurrent UTI with abnormal upper urinary tract • Recurrent balanoposthitis Indications of circumcision in adults : • Recurrent balanitis • Tight frenulum (Splitting of frenulum can occur during sexual activity) • Inability to retract the foreskin for intercourse975

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old boy was catheterized for a surgical procedure , and an intern noticed the following finding when he removed the catheter . A manual reduction was attempted and was not successful . What will be the next step in the management of this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical history and the image showing swollen glans are suggestive of paraphimosis. If manual reduction of the skin is unsuccessful , a dorsal slit procedure should be performed . Paraphimosis is the inability to place back the retracted preputial skin. This creates a ring-like constriction, and the glans tend to be swollen , and edematous , with severe pain and tenderness . Paraphimosis is precipitated after sexual intercourse or iatrogenically after urethral catheterization . The first line of treatment includes manual reduction of the skin by applying lignocaine jelly . Ice bags and injection of a solution of hyaluronidase in normal saline may help to reduce the swelling . If this fails, an initial dorsal slit is made to relieve the edema and compression. Antibiotics and analgesics are also given. Circumcision is performed after 3 weeks .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In patients with which of the following symptoms is Nesbitt 's procedure done?

options.a: Penile deformity , painful erection and palpable penile plaques
options.b: Downward directed stream of urine with bending of penis
options.d: Popping sound during sexual intercourse , painful and flaccid penis

mcqs.explanation: Penile deformity , painful erection , and palpable penile plaques are features associated with Peyronie's disease . Nesbitt 's procedure is the most common procedure done for this condition. Peyronie's disease is caused due to injury to tunica albuginea resulting in microhemorrhages. This leads to excess collagen deposition , calcification, and penile plaques . Hence , the penis bends towards the side of the plaque. This causes difficulty during sexual intercourse . It is also associated with Dupuytren 's contracture.976 Nesbitt 's procedure corrects the deformity by plicating the opposite side of the deformity , thereby straightening the penis . This procedure is done once the active phase subsides as the bend increases during the active phase (18-24 months). Option B: Downward directed stream of urine with bending of the penis are symptoms of hypospadias. Option C: Persistent erection lasting longer than 4 hours is called priapism. Option D: Popping sound during sexual intercourse , painful and flaccid penis is suggestive of fracture of the penis . There will be bluish discoloration of the penis and scrotum due to extensive bruising (eggplant deformity ). Management is mainly surgery for evacuation of hematoma and repair of corpora. The image below shows eggplant deformity in fracture of the penis :977

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Heineke -Mikulicz principle is used in which of the following procedures ?
mcqs.explanation: The Heineke -Mikulicz principle is used in both preputioplasty and frenuloplasty . The Heineke -Mikulicz principle involves the use of a longitudinal incision followed by a transverse closure , or vice-versa. In preputioplasty , it allows for the retraction of the foreskin, and in frenuloplasty , it allows the lengthening of the frenulum. Heineke -Mikulicz's pyloroplasty also uses the same principle . Here, a longitudinal incision is done through the pylorus , with extension to the duodenum and gastric antrum. This incision is then closed transversely. It is done for gastric outlet obstruction and along with highly selective vagotomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding carcinoma of the penis ?

options.a: Balanitis xerotica obliterans is a pre-malignant condition
options.c: Jackson staging is used to stage the disease

mcqs.explanation: Superficial inguinal lymphadenopathy in the context of carcinoma of the penis more often reflects infection rather than metastatic disease. It is usually a painless condition and the patient presents late because of embarrassment or misdiagnosis. They may present with: • Large fungating lesion • Foul, bloody discharge (secondary to infection ) • Non-retractile prepuce • Enlarged inguinal lymph nodes (often due to infection ) • Erosion of inguinal lymph nodes Jackson staging is used for the staging of penile carcinoma : • Stage I - Only glans / prepuce involved • Stage II - Tumour extending into the body of penis • Stage III - Tumour having mobile inguinal nodes • Stage IV - Tumour spreading to adjacent structures / fixed nodes Premalignant lesions of penile squamous cell carcinoma include • Bowen disease - Reddish papules in the shaft of the penis • Erythroplasia of Queyrat - Reddish papules involving glans and prepuce • Condyloma acuminatum - Usually benign, but can undergo a malignant transformation (Buschke–L\366wenstein tumor) when associated with HPV 16, 18, , 33, 35, and 39 • Balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO) - White, thickened foreskin which forms a constricting band. This prevents retraction and later develops into carcinoma • Leukoplakia The following image shows erythroplasia of Queyrat :978

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 52-year-old man came to the urology OPD with complaints of a slow -growing ulcerative lesion in the penis for the past few months. On examination, a fungating mass in his glans penis was seen and lymph nodes were not palpable . He was suspected to have penile carcinoma . Which of the following statements is false regarding the management of the patient ?

options.a: MRI is the investigation of choice for staging
options.b: 1cm margin of normal tissue must be removed
options.c: Sentinel lymph node biopsy should be done
options.d: If stump is < 3cm, total amputation of the penis is done

mcqs.explanation: In penile carcinoma , total amputation of the penis is done if the stump is < 2cm. The investigation of choice for penile carcinoma is a biopsy from the primary tumor. For staging , MRI is the investigation of choice . The first lymph node to be involved is the superficial inguinal lymph node and thus , the sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB ) is helpful for evaluating the spread of penile cancer. The management is divided into treatment of the primary tumour and the treatment of the lymph nodes . The main principles of penile cancer surgery are to remove a 1cm margin of normal tissue and have at least a 2cm stump after surgery. Surgery is the mainstay treatment of penile cancer. Chemotherapy regime includes 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin. Radiotherapy can be done for inguinal lymph nodes if lymph node dissection is not done.979

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most important prognostic factor in patients with penile cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Inguinal lymph node status is the most important prognostic indicator in penile carcinoma . The prognosis for tumors confined to the penis is good with 5-year survival rates in excess of 80%. With nodal involvement, the 5-year survival rate falls to around 40%.980

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common site of ectopic testis ?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site of ectopic testes is the superficial inguinal pouch . Testes develop from the genital ridge in the retroperitoneum at 3 months of intrauterine life . They descend into the scrotum by 9 months of age due to differential abdominal growth , pull of the gubernaculum , and the effect of testosterone . Cryptorchidism refers to the absence of one or both testes in the scrotal sac. The descent of the testis can be arrested in its usual path of descent (true undescended testis ) or can migrate from the usual path of descent (ectopic testis). The image below shows the possible sites of the testes in cryptorchidism:A retractile testis can also lie in the inguinal canal and needs to be differentiated between an ectopic testes . It is present in the scrotum and occasionally moves into the inguinal canal.990 An ectopic testis is treated with orchidopexy , while a retractile testis requires no intervention as it resolves spontaneously .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the OPD for consultation regarding an empty scrotal sac. On examination B/L inguinal masses are palpable . What is the ideal age for orchidopexy in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Orchidopexy is ideally performed before the boy reaches 12 months of age . Orchidopexy is done before 12 months of age to avoid the following complications : • Infertility • Malignancy (Risk may still exist post surgery) • Hernia • Testicular torsion • Infection The management for undescended testes that are not palpable is:

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 1-year-old child was brought to the OPD as the mother noticed that the scrotum contained only one testicle . On examination, the testis is not palpable in the inguinal region or abdomen. A diagnostic laparoscopy reveals abdominal testes and orchiopexy is done. Which of the following tumors is most likely to develop in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The tumor most likely to develop in this patient is seminoma. The tumor that develops most commonly in undesceded testes is germ cell tumor in situ or intratubular germ cell tumor. It commonly progresses into seminomas. In patients with a nonpalpable testicle, diagnostic laparoscopy is performed . If testis is still not visualised , the spermatic cord or testicular artery is traced at the deep inguinal ring to locate it. If a blind ending spermatic cord is found instead , vanishing testis syndrome (or testicular regression syndrome) is suspected . It is the partial or total absence of testicular tissue often due to an ischemic event in foetal life .991 The testis once found can be delivered into the scrotum, and an orchidopexy is performed .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A newborn was diagnosed with undescended testes . Due to the intra-abdominal location of the testes , a two -stage Stephen -Fowler 's orchiopexy was planned . Which of the following is performed during the first stage of this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: In the first stage of a two -stage Stephens -Fowler approach, the testicular vessels are clipped . Clipping of the testicular artery promotes neo vasculogenesis along the vas deferens . It does not result in ischemia of the testis due to the presence of collaterals from the cremasteric artery and the artery to the ductus deferens (deferential artery). Several months later, after collaterals are established , the second stage is performed during which the testis and its new blood supply is mobilized into the scrotum. Stephen -Fowler 's approach is done when an intra abdominal testes is located too far to reach the scrotum. Alternatively, Silbar's orchiopexy may be done. In this procedure , microvascular anastomosis of the testicular vessels with internal illiac vessels is done after the testis is mobilised to the scrotum.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of testicular torsion?

options.b: Presence of remnant of mullerian duct
options.d: Pedicle between epididymis and body of testis

mcqs.explanation: High investment of the tunica vaginalis is the most common cause of torsion of testis . It causes the testes to hang within the tunica like a clapper in a bell . This is the most common cause of testicular torsion in adolescents . Bell clapper testes are typically bilateral. The image below shows the bell -clapper deformity of the testes :992 Other abnormalities that cause torsion of the testes : • Inversion of the testis : The testis is rotated so that it lies transversely or upside down. • Pedicle between epididymis and body of testis : Separation of the epididymis from the body of the testis by a pedicle allows torsion of the testis on the pedicle that connects the testis with the epididymis . An appendix testis is a small vestigial appendage located on the upper pole of the testis . Twisting of the appendage causes testicular appendix torsion. In it, a classic blue dot sign is seen on the upper pole of the testis . It is seen as a hard tender nodule with a blue discoloration on the superior aspect of the testis . This is a remnant of the Mullerian duct , that regresses on development . The image below shows the blue dot sign on the testis :993

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with acute onset of pain in his scrotum. He previously had similar pain that would subside spontaneously but the pain this time is unbearable. Physical examination shows a swollen erythematous scrotum. Cremasteric reflex is absent. What is the next best step in management?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of testicular torsion. In cases of high clinical suspicion, the next best step is to explore surgically . Clinical features of testicular torsion are painful scrotal swelling , erythema , nausea, and vomiting, testis seems high in the scrotum and the twisted cord can sometimes be palpated . Signs seen on torsion of the testis are: • Deming's sign: Spasm of the cremaster muscle due to twisting of the spermatic cord causes the affected testis to be positioned higher than the normal testis . • Angell 's sign: The testis on the normal side lies horizontally because of the mesorchium between the testis and epididymis . • Cremastic reflex : Absent on the side of the affected testis Doppler ultrasound scanning can confirm the absence of the blood supply to the affected testis , but the false positives are high and hence it is not routinely recommended . Manual detorsion of the testes is usually difficult because of acute pain during manipulation. Nonoperative manual detorsion is not a substitute for surgical exploration.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child presents with pain and swelling in the right side of his scrotum and testicular torsion is suspected . Which is the most appropriate management?

options.a: Immediate exploration on both symptomatic and asymptomatic side
options.b: Immediate exploration on symptomatic side only
options.c: Delayed exploration on both symptomatic and asymptomatic side
options.d: Delayed exploration on symptomatic side only

mcqs.explanation: In a case of suspected testicular torsion, immediate exploration needs to be done on both the symptomatic as well as the asymptomatic side . After the de -torsion, the adequacy of the blood flow has to be assessed by Doppler . In testicular torsion, the blood supply to the testicle is compromised due to the twisting of the spermatic cord within the tunica vaginalis, resulting in ischemia of the epididymis and the testis . The patient usually presents with acute onset pain and swelling of the scrotum. On examination, the cremasteric reflex is lost, and the scrotum looks asymmetrical. Prehn's sign is used to differentiate epididymitis from testicular torsion. Prehn's sign is said to be positive when the pain gets relieved on lifting the testis , and it is seen in epididymo -orchitis. At the time of surgical exploration, contralateral testes also must be explored and fixed to the dartos fascia in order to prevent possible torsion occurring in this testes . More than 80% of the testis can be salvaged if surgery is performed within 6 hours. If the testis is f ound to be necrosed on scrotal exploration, orchidectomy of the necrosed testis and orchidopexy of the contralateral testis is done.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young man presents to the emergency with a painful scrotum. On examination, the patient is febrile and a Prehn's sign is positive . What is the most likely cause of the patient 's condition?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute epididymitis .994 A positive Prehn's sign is used to differentiate epididymis from testicular torsion. A Prehn's sign is said to be positive when the pain gets relieved on lifting the testis . If it persists , it is likely to be testicular torsion. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of acute epididymitis in young, sexually active males . In older men(>40yrs) with bladder outflow obstruction, epididymitis results from urinary infection , most commonly due to Escherichia coli. Acute epididymitis is managed by antibiotics and scrotal support .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A young male patient presented with painless swelling of the scrotum. Examination revealed a firm, enlarged epididymis along with beading of the vas deferens . Testes were normal . What is the next best step in management?

options.b: Send urine or semen for PCR

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, a firm enlarged epididymis , beading of the vas deferens , and a normal testis on palpation indicate secondary tubercular epididymo -orchitis. The next best step is confirmation with polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Beading of the vas deferens is due to subepithelial tubercle formation and is specific to genital tuberculosis . A scrotal USG will reveal an enlarged epididymis but does not have diagnostic value. Chest, kidney , and upper urinary tract imaging may reveal a primary focus . Tuberculous epididymo -orchitis is usually secondary and resolves once the primary focus is treated . Hence , a course of anti-tubercular therapy must be completed even if there is no evidence of disease elsewhere . If resolution does not occur within two months, epididymectomy or orchidectomy is advisable.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old diabetic patient presented with a painful, malodorous, discolored scrotum as shown in the image. The patient was febrile and in extreme pain. Which of the following statements is true about his condition?

options.b: Managed by antibiotics and scrotal support
options.c: Staphylococcus is the most common causative organism
options.d: The condition is usually self limiting

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of Fournier's gangrene in which the testis is classically spared . It lies naked following debridement of the gangrenous skin and is tucked subcutaneously into the thigh. It is also called "shameful exposure of the testis ." Fournier's gangrene is a surgical emergency. It is a life -threatening disease , with a mortality of over 40% even with treatment . It is due to a mixed infection of both aerobic and anaerobic bacterial flora. Concurrent illnesses that diminish the host defense , especially diabetes mellitus and alcoholism, predispose patients to the development of Fournier's gangrene . It is managed by debridement , wide surgical excision, IV fluids , and antibiotics.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 24-year-old presents with a scrotal swelling as shown in the image. The swelling is brilliantly transilluminant and the testes cannot be palpated separately . Which additional clinical finding is most likely to be present ?
mcqs.explanation: The scrotal swelling is most likely a hydrocele . Due to the movement of fluid , a fluctuation test is positive .995 Hydrocoele is an accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. It is brilliantly transilluminating and testes will not be separately palpable . As it arises in the scrotum, it is possible to get above the swelling . It is irreducible and cough impulse is absent. A USG will show anechoic reflection due to fluid collection .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of a secondary hydrocele ?
mcqs.explanation: A secondary hydrocele is most commonly caused by an acute or chronic epididymo -orchitis. Other causes of secondary hydrocele include torsion of the testis and testicular tumors.Primary vaginal hydrocele Secondary vaginal hydrocele Due to defective absorption o f fluid Due to increased secretion of fluid Tense swelling Lax swelling Testis not palpable separately Testis palpable separately Transillumination positive (cl ear fluid present ) Transillumination negative (t urbid fluid present )

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with hydrocele is scheduled for Lord 's plication. Which of the following is false regarding the procedure ?

options.a: The procedure can be performed under local anesthesia
options.b: Increased risk of hematoma formation as compared to Jaboulay's
options.c: Preferred for small to medium sized swellings
options.d: Tunica vaginalis is bunched to obliterate the hydrocoele sac

mcqs.explanation: Lord 's plication has a lower risk of hematoma formation as compared to Jaboulay's procedure . Hydrocele may be managed surgically by various techniques . Lord 's plication and Jaboulay's eversion of the sac are most commonly performed . Jaboulay's eversion of the sac is preferred for large hydroceles . In this method , the tunica vaginalis sac is everted around the testis. Although it has a shorter operative time, the risk of hematoma formation is more. Congenital hydroceles are managed by a herniotomy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 32 -year-old male patient presented with a scrotal swelling . On examination, the testis is felt separate from the scrotal swelling and the swelling is brilliantly transilluminant, as shown in the image below . What is the probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario of a transilluminant scrotal swelling palpated apart from normal testes is suggestive of an epididymal cyst . An epididymal cyst is a multilocular cyst formed due to is the cystic degeneration of the epididymis . Multiple cysts formed posterior to the epididymis can feel like a bunch of grapes on palpation . Due to the presence of crystal clear fluid , an epididymal cyst brilliantly transilluminates and has a Chinese lantern appearance. The image shows the Chinese lantern appearance on transillumination:996 It can be differentiated from a hydrocele , where the testis is not separately palpable . Option A: Varicoceles present with dragging discomfort in the scrotum on standing and characteristic 'bag of worms' feel on palpation. Option C: Spermatocele is a unilocular transluminant retention cyst formed at the epididymal head. Due to the presence of spermatozoa, barley-water fluid is seen . Although transilluminant, the cyst does not have a Chinese lantern appearance . Option D: Chyloceles are formed due to the rupture of lymphatic varix and the discharge of chyle into the hydrocele . Fluid rich in cholesterol is seen and the swelling is not transilluminant.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 33-year-old man was referred to the surgery OPD from the infertility clinic. On inspection , the scrotum appeared as in the image. On palpation , a bag of worms sensation was felt . What is the appropriate management?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of a varicocele. As this patient is young and infertile , varicocelectomy is indicated and a Palomo procedure may be performed . Varicocele may present with a dull aching scrotal pain and enlargement . Additionally , patients may have infertility . A bag of worms, which gets prominent on Valsalva 's maneuver is palpated due to the engorged pampiniform plexus. Often , patients may be asymptomatic and do not require treatment . Left-sided varicocele is more common. Isolated right-sided varicocele should always raise suspicion of renal cell carcinoma . (Note : Varicoceles occurs on left side more commonly as the left spermatic vein opens at sharp angle to the left renal vein, whereas , on the right side , the right spermatic vein opens into a larger Inferior vena cava and an isolated Right-sided varicocele may indicate a tumour that compresses the venous return in the inferior vena cava ) Treatment of young patients includes surgical ligation of the gonadal vein. It may be achieved through embolectomy or varicocelectomy . Approaches to varicocelectomy are: • Inguinal ( Ivanisevic method )997 • Retroperitoneal (Palomo procedure ) • Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery through the transvesical route In older patients , NSAIDs and scrotal support are adequate .Grades of varicocel e Grade 1 Varicocele only palpable on V alsalva's maneuver Grade 2 Varicocele palpable without Valsalva 's maneuver Grade 3 Varicocele is seen on inspecti on of the testis

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for developing testicular carcinoma ?
mcqs.explanation: Benzopyrene exposure is not associated with an increased risk of developing testicular cancer but with an increased risk of developing scrotal carcinoma . Shale oil exposure (a petroleum byproduct ) is also associated with an increased incidence of scrotal carcinoma . Undescended testes , history of contralateral testicular tumor, and Klinefelter 's syndrome are known to increase one's risk to develop testicular cancer. Note : Patients with Klinefelter 's syndrome also have an increased risk of developing extragonadal germ cell tumors.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which among the following are germ-cell tumors?
mcqs.explanation: Germ-cell tumors (90–95%) include seminoma, embryonal cell carcinoma , yolk-sac tumor, teratoma, and choriocarcinoma . Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors are non-germ-cell tumors.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 45-year-old male patient who presented with a scrotal swelling underwent an orchidectomy . The image below shows the histopathology findings. What is your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Based on the gross and microscopic appearance of the specimen , the diagnosis is seminoma. The gross specimen shows a well -circumscribed, pale , gray-white , fleshy , homogenous mass, with a lobulated cut surface , usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology shows uniform tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and large central nuclei . There is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. Classically, they have a fried egg appearance . Other options :998 Option B: Yolk-sac tumor has a yellowish -white , mucinous appearance . Histologically , they are typically composed of a lace-like (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal , flattened , or spindled cells , which generally show less cytologic atypia than embryonal carcinoma . In approximately 50% of tumors, structures resembling endodermal sinuses (Schiller-Duval bodies ) may be seen ; these consist of a mesodermal core with a central capillary and a visceral and parietal layer of cells resembling primitive glomeruli .Option C: Embryonal cell carcinoma appears variegated with foci of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histologically , the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns , sometimes with papillary folds . More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells with cleft -like spaces . The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance , are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli . The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable variation in cell and nuclear size and shape (pleomorphism). Mitotic figures and tumor giant cells are frequently seen .999 Option D: Teratomas also have a variegated appearance but have cysts reflecting the multiplicity of tissue types . Histologically , collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures originating in all 3 germ layers can be seen . Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues ) or immature (sharing histologic features with fetal or embryonic tissue ).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding testicular tumors?

options.a: They may present as an abdominal lump.
options.b: Testicular biopsy is done to diagnose testicular carcinoma .
options.c: Seminomas metastasize predominantly via the lymphatic system .
options.d: Elevated tumor markers are found almost exclusively in non-seminomatous germ-cell tumors.

mcqs.explanation: There is no role of testicular biopsy in the diagnosis of testicular tumors. This is due to the risk of seeding tumor cells onto the scrotal wall. In testicular tumors, the most common site of lymphatic spread is retroperitoneal lymph nodes which may present as an abdominal lump. Elevated tumor markers are found almost exclusively in non-seminomatous germ-cell tumors. Few seminomas may have elevated placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP ) or beta -human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG). Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH ) can be used as a marker of tumor bulk. Seminomas are radiosensitive tumors that metastasize via lymphatics . Non-germ-cell tumors arise from Sertoli or Leydig cells and follow a more benign course . Approximately only 10 % are malignant.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a left -sided testicular tumor is being evaluated for metastasis . Which group of lymph nodes is most likely to get involved first?
mcqs.explanation: The first sites of metastasis in left -sided testicular tumors are the para-aortic lymph nodes . Testicular tumors metastasize first to the retroperitoneal nodes . Right-sided tumors metastasize primarily to the interaortocaval nodes. Left-sided tumors metastasize primarily to the left para-aortic nodes .1000 Deep inguinal lymph nodes receive drainage from the perineum and lower extremity . Inguinal lymph nodes may be involved if the testicular tumor spreads to the skin of the scrotum.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 25-year-old male patient presented with a hard painless testicular lump with a dragging sensation. The blood investigations showed raised AFP levels . Which of the following is least likely to be included , in further management of this case?

options.c: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) of the testis . Orchidectomy via a scrotal approach is not done due to fear of seeding the tumor in the scrotal skin. Instead, an inguinal approach is used . Raised AFP levels point towards the diagnosis of non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) of the testis . Ultrasound of the testis should be done in all suspected cases of testicular tumor. Tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH ) are measured for the staging of cancer. CT of the chest , abdomen, and pelvis is done to detect metastasis .Management of testicular tu mors Stage Non-seminomatous Seminomatous Stage ITumor confined to tes tis Orchidectomy and chemothe rapy Orchidectomy and Active Sur veillanceIf poor prognostic fe atures* are seen , chemothera py with a single agent , cisplat in for 1-2 cycles Stage IINodal disease confine d to nodes below the diaphra gm Orchidectomy and chemothe rapyRetroperitoneal lymph n ode dissection for residual di sease Orchidectomy andradiothera pyIf residual lymph node dis ease is present , chemotherap y Stage IIINodal disease prese nt above the diaphragm Orchidectomy ,radiotherapy, and chemotherapyIf residual lymph node disease is presen t, retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is done Stage IVMetastasis Orchidectomy and chemothe rapy In testicular tumors, the BEP regimen is followed withbleo mycin, etoposide , cisplatin.*P oor prognostic factors followi ng orchidectomy are:No decr ease or change in tumor mar ker values or tumor sizePoor follow up

mcqs.question: A patient with Stage I seminoma underwent an orchidectomy 3 months ago. On a follow -up visit, elevated LDH levels were seen . What is the most appropriate line of management?

options.d: Regular scanning using CT and tumor marker measurement

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is brought to the casualty following a head injury. He is unconscious and is not able to open his eyes . He also has no verbal or motor responses . What will be his GCS score?
mcqs.explanation: The GCS score in this patient will be 3. The lowest possible Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 3 and never zero.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is confused , opens his eyes on painful stimuli, flexes one limb on painful stimuli, and can localize the stimulus with the other limb. His Glasgow Coma Score is ________
mcqs.explanation: The GCS in this patient is 11 . • The score for verbal response : 4, because he is confused . • The score for eye -opening : 2, because his eyes are opening to only painful stimuli. • The score for best motor response : 5, because he can localize pain. Therefore, the GCS score is (4+2+5) = 11 .1011

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An 18-month-old child is brought to the ER after sustaining a head injury from a fall. On examination , she moans to pain. What is her verbal response score on the GCS scale ?
mcqs.explanation: The verbal response of "moans to pain" in a child <2 years of age is 2. mcqs.explanation: Motor response of 3 indicates decorticate posture or abnormal flexion to pain stimulus .

mcqs.question: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the casualty ward with a history of road traffic accident and head trauma. She opens her eyes to pain, moans, can localize her limb towards the pain stimulus on the left hand and away from the pain stimulus on the right hand and both the legs are in extended posture . Calculate her GCS.
mcqs.explanation: The GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale ) of this patient is E2V2M5, which comes to a total score of 9. • E2 - Eye opens to pain • V2 - Moans • M5 - Localizes to pain on the left hand (the score represents the best performance elicited , which would be localized towards the pain stimulus )

mcqs.question: Which of the following head injury patients need not undergo head CT at this point in time?

options.a: An RTA victim with GCS score of
options.b: A patient with an episode of vomiting
options.c: A child with an episode of seizure post -trauma
options.d: A biker with suspected skull fracture

mcqs.explanation: A single episode of vomiting after a head injury is not an indication for immediate CT brain . However, more than one episode mandates a scan.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old batsman was rushed to the ER when he fell unconscious after a cricket ball hit his head . He regained consciousness later but started to deteriorate rapidly. A plain CT of the patient is shown below . What is the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of lucid interval in this patient and the CT image are suggestive of extradural hematoma. The above CT scan shows a large extradural hematoma (hyperdense biconvex/lentiform shape ) with a mass effect . Extradural hemorrhage (EDH) is the accumulation of blood between the skull and the dura. It usually results from arterial disruption, especially of the middle meningeal artery. It lies behind the pterion, which is the thinnest part of the skull. In EDH, the patient is initially unconscious from the concussive aspect of the head trauma. The patient then awakens and has a "lucid interval," while the hematoma sub-clinically expands . As the volume of the hematoma grows, intracranial pressure (ICP) increases, and the patient rapidly becomes lethargic and herniates. Uncal herniation from an EDH classically causes ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiparesis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An alcoholic patient was brought to the casualty after he was found lying near a ditch. He had a laceration over his scalp . His GCS on arrival was 13 and after a few minutes , it dropped to 10 . A plain CT scan was done and given below . What will be your diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and the plain CT scan showing a concavo-convex shaped hematoma on the left side with a midline shift to the right is suggestive of subdural hematoma (SDH).1013 An acute SDH is the result of the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. It is usually due to the rupture of bridging veins running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses . The level of consciousness is usually impaired at presentation and may deteriorate further as the hematoma expands . Elderly and alcoholic patients are at a higher risk of acute SDH formation after head trauma due to brain atrophy. Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following : • Thickness >1 cm • Midline shift >5 mm • Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) drops by two or more points from the time of injury to hospitalization.

mcqs.question: A 70-year-old man presents with headache , vomiting, and altered sensorium for the past 6 hours. His wife reports him having a fall in the bathroom 4 weeks ago. On evaluation, the following funduscopic findings are noted . What will be your provisional diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and fundus examination are most probably suggestive of chronic subdural hematoma. The fundoscopic image shows dilated veins with a blurred disc margin which is suggestive of papilledema . Chronic SDH is a collection of blood breakdown products that are at least 2 to 3 weeks old. It occurs in patients without a clear history of head trauma, as they may arise from a minor head injury. Alcoholics , the elderly , and patients on anticoagulation are at higher risk for developing chronic SDH than others. Patients may present with headaches , seizures , confusion, contralateral hemiparesis , or coma. A chronic SDH >1 cm or any symptomatic SDH should be surgically drained.Nomencla ture Time Acute SD H <3 day s Subacute SDH 4–21 d ays Chronic S DH > 21 da ys

mcqs.question: A 50-year-old man presented with a sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. His medical record revealed he has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease . On examination, pulse - 100 bpm, BP - 190 /110 mm Hg, marked neck rigidity was present and no neurological deficits were noted . What could be the most likely cause of the symptoms ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) due to the rupture of a berry aneurysm. It is an extrarenal manifestation of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease .1014 Clinical features of SAH: • Sudden -onset severe headache (thunderclap headache ) • Rapid onset vomiting • Confusion or a lowered level of consciousness • Seizures • Meningitic features of neck stiffness and photophobia often develop over hours. The most common cause is trauma and is managed conservatively. The second most common cause is a rupture of a berry aneurysm. CT scan is the investigation of choice . A hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space . Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region.A lumbar puncture should be performed if the CT scan fails to establish the diagnosis of SAH. It will show xanthochromic CSF. Delayed ischemic neurological deficit (DIND) is attributed to vasospasm of the cerebral vasculature typically developing 3–10 days following ictus . It is the main cause of a poor outcome . Management : • Endovascular treatment ("coiling") is generally preferred over craniotomy and clipping for aneurysms amenable to this approach. • The combination of induced hypertension , hypervolemia, and hemodilution (Triple-H therapy ) is often utilized to prevent and treat cerebral vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Note : The combination of subarachnoid hemorrhage and vitreous hemorrhage (subhyaloid) is known as Terson syndrome.1015

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding delayed ischemic neurological deficit ?

options.a: It is seen in subarachnoid haemorrhage
options.c: It is attributed to cerebral vasospasm

mcqs.explanation: Delayed ischemic neurological deficit (DIND) usually occurs between 3 and 10 days after the SAH. It is a delayed complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage characterized by the fluctuating decline in consciousness and appearance of neurological deficits . It is attributed to ischemia resulting from reactive cerebral vasospasm. Patients with a larger blood load (in the subarachnoid space ) are at higher risk of vasospasm. Medical management strategies aim to minimize secondary brain injury, through avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension and control of ICP. The incidence of DIND can be lowered by prophylaxis with nimodipine (60 mg, 4 hourly) and hypervolemia (8 hourly normal saline).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 26-year-old formula one driver was rushed to the casualty , unconscious , following a heavy crash from a side -impact collision during a racing event. The CT scan was normal . However, MRI showed multiple small hemorrhages, especially in the corpus callosum and the dorsolateral midbrain , with no midline shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario with a normal CT and MRI showing evidence of hemorrhages in the corpus callosum and midbrain is probably due to a diffuse axonal injury. A diffuse axonal injury is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents . It is caused by damage to axons throughout the brain due to rotational acceleration and then deceleration . Axons may be completely disrupted and then retract, forming axon balls. Small hemorrhages can be seen in more severe cases , especially on MRI (investigation of choice ). Hemorrhage is classically seen in the corpus callosum and the dorsolateral midbrain . The prognosis is very poor. MRI showing multiple hypointense punctate foci within the subcortical and deep white matter within the corpus callosum is characteristic of diffuse axonal injury.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: According to the Glasgow Outcome Score, what score will you give to a patient who is in a persistent vegetative state following a head injury?
mcqs.explanation: 1016 A persistent vegetative state is given a score of 2, according to the Glasgow Outcome Score. The Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) is different from the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), and it is used to quantify the degree of recovery achieved after a head injury, especially for research purposes . The scoring system is as follows :Patient condition Scor e Good recovery Moderate disability 4 Severe disability Persistent vegetative state 2 Dead 1

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is recovering from a spinal shock after a fall from height . Which of the following is the first reflex that you will expect to reappear in him?
mcqs.explanation: Bulbocavernosus reflex is the first reflex to return after the spinal shock has resolved . It is elicited by squeezing the glans penis in males and applying pressure to the clitoris or pulling the Foleys catheter in females . Any of these will lead to anal sphincter contraction. Spinal shock is a condition of transient physiologic reflex depression of spinal cord function (motor, sensory, tone, reflexes ) below the level of injury. It usually results from a high-impact, direct trauma to the spinal cord. When the level of injury is above T6, it can result in hemodynamic changes such as hypotension and bradycardia (due to loss of sympathetic tone and unopposed parasympathetic function). The resolution of spinal shock occurs over a period of days to months, when the areflexia slowly transitions to hyperreflexia and spasticity. Reflexes return sequentially rather than simultaneously . The resolution of the somatic component of spinal shock is classically signaled by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex, a polysynaptic cutaneous spinal reflex (mediated by the conus medullaris ) which is then followed by monosynaptic deep tendon reflexes (e.g. ankle jerk).1017

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not used for managing a patient with raised intracranial pressure following a head injury?
mcqs.explanation: Steroids are not used in severe head injury, since they are associated with increased mortality. Initial management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP): • Airway protection • Positioning the head up 20 –30\260 (reverse Trendelenburg positioning ) • A bolus of mannitol up to 1 g/kg for free water diuresis (the effect is delayed by 20 min) • Hypertonic saline (3% or 5%) • Maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance • Seizure control • Sedation using a combination of opiates and barbiturates • Ventriculostomy and/or craniectomy may be needed for definitive decompression . ICP normally varies between 4 and 14 mmHg. Sustained ICP levels above 25 mmHg can injure the brain . The goal of therapy in raised ICP is to maintain the ICP 20 - 25 mmHg. Note : Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centers , classically producing Cushing's triad. It is comprised of: • Bradycardia • Raised blood pressure • Irregular respirations.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In patients with head trauma, which of the following is least likely to cause secondary brain injuries?
mcqs.explanation: 1018 Hypercapnea (and not hypocapnea ) is a cause of secondary brain injury. It is essential to avoid hypercapnia in patients with head injury since it will raise intracranial pressure (ICP). While hyperventilation is an effective way of managing acute intracranial hypertension , it should be remembered that it can produce a dangerous decrease in cerebral blood flow , especially if cerebral perfusion pressure is low. Primary brain injury (focal and diffuse ) results from mechanical injury at the time of the trauma. Secondary brain injury is caused by the physiologic responses to the initial injury. This is thought to involve a cascade of events, with edema and hematomas leading to increased intracranial pressure , which leads to compression and deformation of surrounding brain tissue and further damage . Causes of secondary brain injury: • Hypoxia • Hypotension • Raised ICP >20 mmHg • Low cerebral perfusion pressure • Hypercapnea • Hyperthermia • Seizures • Metabolic disturbance (hyperglycemia)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a head injury presents to the casualty with rapidly deteriorating sensorium and progressive dilatation and fixation of the pupil . Neurosurgeon and CT scan are not available. The duty surgeon decides to make a burr hole . What will be the management plan?

options.a: Make a hole in the temporal region, contralateral to the side of pupillary dilatation.
options.b: Make a hole in the midline, if both pupils are equal or it is not known which side dilated first.
options.c: If no localizing sign is found, make a hole in the left temporal region.
options.d: Refer to higher center if both pupils are equal or it is not known which side dilated first

mcqs.explanation: In the given situation, no localizing sign is found and it is not known which side dilated first. So, the best choice would be to do a burr hole in the dominant hemisphere (most commonly, the left temporal region).1019

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding post -traumatic seizures in patients with head injury?

options.a: Use of antiepileptics in late post -traumatic seizure patients is recommended
options.b: Prolonged seizures cause primary brain injury post head trauma
options.c: Occurrence of seizures after 2 weeks of head injury is called late post -traumatic seizures
options.d: Initiation of antiepileptics in early post traumatic seizure patients reduces the likelihood of developing post -traumatic epilepsy

mcqs.explanation: The use of antiepileptics in late post -traumatic seizure (PTS) patients is recommended . Post-traumatic seizures (PTS) are seizures that result from traumatic brain injury (TBI ). They are classified into early and late . Early PTS occurs within 1 week and late PTS occurs after 1 week of trauma (Option C). Early PTS are acute symptomatic events, attributed to a direct reaction to injury and hemorrhage. Risk factors for early PTS are: • Younger age (especially <5 years) • Moderate to severe head injury (measured by GCS) • Acute intracerebral hematoma • Subdural / Subarachnoid hemorrhage • Depressed skull fractures • Diffuse cerebral edema • History of alcohol abuse • Penetrating head injury Late PTS usually occurs due to underlying permanent structural and physiologic changes within the brain . Patients with late PTS may develop post -traumatic epilepsy (PTE). It refers to recurrent and unprovoked PTS that occur at least 1 week after TBI . Risk factors for PTE are: • Early PTS • Severe head injury • Older age (especially >65 years) • Focal neurological deficit • Intracranial hemorrhage • Intracranial infection • Abnormalities on EEG • Alcohol-related head injury Prolonged seizures (30 to 60 minutes ) can cause secondary brain injury, not primary (Option B). Hence , it is imperative to control acute seizures as soon as possible . The initiation of antiepileptics in early PTS patients is to prevent damage due to seizures themselves . It does not reduce the likelihood of developing PTE (Option D). For patients who develop late PTS, because of the high risk of seizure recurrence after the first episode of late PTS, the use of antiepileptic medication is recommended even after a single late seizure episode . The long-term sequelae of head injury are headache , raised ICP, impaired short-term memory, lack of concentration, emotional disinhibition, and depression .1020 Prophylaxis for PTS is indicated in patients at risk of early PTS, for 7 days and is stopped without tapering the dose if no seizures have occurred during this duration. Prophylaxis is not recommended for late PTS.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding basilar skull fractures?

options.a: Racoon eyes is one of the earliest signs to develop
options.b: Battle sign is associated with posterior cranial fossa fractures
options.c: CSF leaks should be promptly managed by surgical intervention
options.d: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation should be avoided

mcqs.explanation: Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation should be avoided in patients with basilar skull fractures due to the risk of pneumocephalus . Signs in basilar skull fractures: • Hemotympanum : Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of basilar fracture. • Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes ): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes , associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. • Retroauricular or mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign): Pooled blood behind the ears in the mastoid region is associated with fractures to the middle cranial fossa. • CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: "Halo" sign, a double -ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen. Battle sign and raccoon eyes are both typically not present during the initial evaluation and are delayed by 6 hrs up to 3 days after head injury. CSF leaks may be delayed hours to days after the initial trauma. Fluid suspicious for CSF is confirmed by testing for \0312 transferrin. Most CSF leaks are conservatively managed. Persistent leaks >7 days have a heightened risk of meningitis and are often surgically repaired. Nasopharyngeal airways and nasogastric tube insertion are relatively contraindicated in basilar skull fractures due to the risk for intracranial placement . NIPPV is avoided due to the risk for pneumocephalus . The image below shows the 'battle ' sign.1021 The image below shows 'racoon' eyes .The image below shows pneumocephalus .

mcqs.question: A man is brought to the ER with a depressed skull fracture and a clean overlying scalp laceration. There are no focal neurological deficits . CT scan revealed that the degree of depression was less than the thickness of the adjacent skull bone. What is the next step in the management of the patient ?

options.a: Surgically elevate the depressed segment and close the laceration with sutures
options.b: Provide prophylactic antibiotics and discharge the patient
options.d: Apply dressing and discharge the patient

mcqs.explanation: In the given scenario, the next step is to close the laceration with suture . The management of the depressed skull fractures: • The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion. • The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery ) if: • The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull1022 • The wound is are open and grossly contaminated • There are focal neurological deficits • Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present .

mcqs.question: Identify the type of herniation labelled as '1' in the given image.
mcqs.explanation: The type herniation labelled as '1' in the given image shows herniation of the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri, which is known as subfalcine herniation. mcqs.question: A 25-year-old football player had a fall followed by one episode of vomiting, a day before his final match. When brought to the casualty , he was awake and conscious but could not recall events after the fall. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient ?

options.b: Discharge home and advice adequate rest before playing the final match
options.c: Observe for 6 hours in the ED and refrain from playing for one week
options.d: Admit to intensive care for intracranial pressure monitoring

mcqs.explanation: The given history of fall and anterograde amnesia with no focal neurologic deficits points towards the diagnosis of concussion. Observation followed by a gradual return to play is the current recommendation for a concussion. It is defined as an alteration of consciousness as a result of closed head injury. It is the most common type of traumatic brain injury, which can result from vehicle accidents , falls, sports injuries, etc . Clinical features of concussion include : • Anterograde amnesia/post -traumatic amnesia - a hallmark of a concussion. In this type of amnesia, the events following the injury cannot be recalled . • Confusion • Headache • Dizziness • Nausea • Vomiting Observation in the emergency department is essential following the clinical exam to look for alterations in mental status or focal neurological signs. The presence of either of which may signal more serious underlying pathology (e.g., intracranial bleeding ). Following discharge , the patients are advised to not return to contact sports e.g., football , boxing, etc. which carries the risk of further injury, for at least a week . Then, there should be a gradual, stepwise increase in physical activity. Option A: There are no focal neurological deficits to warrant an NCCT of the brain . Option B: Immediate discharge and return to intense physical activity following mild TBI are inappropriate. Because those who are symptomatic after a head injury, are vulnerable to a repeat impact. Due to disturbed cerebral autoregulation , even a minor second injury may trigger a form of malignant cerebral edema refractory to treatment . Option D: Admission to the intensive care unit for intracranial pressure monitoring would be appropriate in patients with severe TBI , for which elevated intracranial pressure is a serious concern due to brain edema and/or bleeding . Severe TBI is characterized by a GCS \035 8. Here the patient has a GCS of >14.1024

mcqs.question: In patients with confirmed sialolithiasis , what is the most common location of stone formation?
mcqs.explanation: The most common site for salivary gland stone formation is the submandibular gland due to highly viscous secretions . 80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque, while parotid duct stones are usually radiolucent and rarely visible on plain radiography. Parotid gland sialography is usually required to identify the stone . A stone located in the collecting duct or within the gland may be managed by either endoscopic retrieval or lithotripsy ; in rare cases , surgical removal via a parotidectomy approach may be required. The below USG image shows a stone in the Wharton duct of the submandibular gland.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding management considerations in a patient with submandibular gland stones ?

options.a: Surgical gland excision is the treatment of choice if patient is unresponsive to conservative management
options.b: Associated chronic sialadenitis is a contraindication for sialendoscopy
options.c: Conventional radiography is mostly useless as more than 80% of submandibular stones are radiolucent
options.d: Stones proximal to the lingual nerve can be removed via an intra-oral approach

mcqs.explanation: If the stone is proximal to the lingual nerve, stone retrieval can be done via an intraoral surgical approach under general anesthesia . 80% of submandibular stones are radio-opaque. Conventional radiography is useful in the initial workup of salivary stones , but ultrasound, CT, MRI, and sialendoscopy are required for accurate diagnosis and localization (especially for smaller and parenchymal stones ). The only contraindication for sialendoscopy is acute sialadenitis . This is because sialendoscopy and ductal dilation is more difficult in the setting of inflammation and there will be a greater likelihood of ductal trauma and potential spread of infection . Management of sialolithiasis should begin with conservative measures , oral hydration, analgesia, massaging of gland, sialogogues , and antibiotics (if there are signs of infection ). If unsuccessful , the next step is based on the sialolith 's size, number, and location: • Small stones (<4mm) - endoscopic removal using Dormia basket.1039 • larger stones - external shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL ) + fragment removal or Open surgery and stone removal • Surgical excision of the gland should always be a last resort If distal to lingual nerve: Make a longitudinal incision over the duct . Remove the stone . Suture the duct using absorbable suture . If proximal to lingual nerve: intraoral approach The image below shows a stone in the submandibular salivary duct .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 56-year-old man presented with complaints of recurrent bilateral painless swelling over the parotid glands. FNAC done showed acinar cell hypertrophy without any inflammatory signs. All of the following are associated with this condition except ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and FNAC report of acinar hypertrophy are suggestive of sialadenosis . Hyperthyroidism is not associated with sialadenosis . Sialosis (sialadenosis ) is defined as an asymptomatic , non-inflammatory, non-neoplastic parenchymal salivary gland disease . It is accompanied by a persistent painless bilateral swelling of the salivary glands, most commonly involving the parotid glands. Most cases of sialadenosis are observed in patients between 40 to 70 years of age , and the salivary gland swellings are often soft and symmetrical. On FNAC, acinar cell hypertrophy is seen without any inflammatory signs. Sialadenosis is associated with the following conditions: • Nutritional disorders • Bulimia nervosa • Vitamin deficiency • Endocrine disorders • Diabetes mellitus • Hypothyroidism1040 • Metabolic disorders • Obesity • Cirrhosis • Malabsorption • Autoimmune disorders • Sj\366gren disease • Drug-induced • Valproic acid • Thiourea • Pregnancy • Alcoholism

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man on routine dental checkup was found to have the following finding on orthopantomogram. What is the reason for the finding marked with the arrow?
mcqs.explanation: The given orthopantomogram shows a right-sided clearly demarcated radiolucent lesion suggestive of a stafne bone cyst . It is the most common type of ectopic salivary tissue . It presents as an asymptomatic , clearly demarcated radiolucent lesion at the angle of the mandible, characteristically below the inferior dental neurovascular bundle . It is more common in males. Usually , no treatment is required. A dentigerous cyst is a cyst in relation to an unerupted tooth . Most commonly involves the 3rd molar. It is managed by enucleation and removal of the tooth .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 5 year-old-boy was brought to the OPD by his parents with a painless , soft , translucent swelling under the tongue . On examination, the swelling is as seen below . Which of the following statements best describe his condition?

options.a: Mucous retention cyst from a minor salivary gland
options.b: Mucous extravasation cyst from sublingual gland
options.c: Mucous extravasation cyst from a minor salivary gland
options.d: Mucous retention cyst from sublingual gland

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and image points to a diagnosis of an oral ranula. It is a mucous extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland. Ranula is a transilluminant mucocele . It is also known as "frog's belly ", as it resembles the vocal sacs of a frog. It is of two types : • Oral ranula - It is a benign cystic lesion formed by extravasation of mucus, involving the sublingual gland. Clinically present as cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth. On examination fluctuation test and transillumination test is positive . It is conservatively managed by marsupialisation. Definitive management is excision of the cyst . Some may resolve spontaneously . • Cervical or plunging ranula- is a rare type of retention cyst arising from the sublingual gland. The mucous passes through the mylohyoid muscle diaphragm to enter the neck. Clinically present as intraoral and cervical swelling . Diagnosis is made by USG or MRI. Management includes excision of sublingual gland + aspiration of saliva out of the sac.1041 Note : Oral ranulas located in the floor of the mouth can often be confused with an epidermoid cyst.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true regarding salivary gland tumors?

options.a: 90% of the minor salivary gland tumors are malignant
options.b: The submandibular gland is the most common site for salivary tumors
options.c: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the salivary gland
options.d: A salivary gland tumor with perineural invasion is mucoepidermoid carcinoma

mcqs.explanation: 90% of the minor salivary gland tumors are malignant, and the common sites are the upper lip, palate , and retromolar regions. Option B: The most common site for salivary tumors is the parotid gland, mostly involving the superficial lobe . Option C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the salivary gland. Option D: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is known to be associated with perineural invasion .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man presents with a slowly progressive swelling over the past 1 and 1/2 years. On examination , it has a variable consistency and appears as shown in the image. What is the probable cause ?
mcqs.explanation: A slowly progressive swelling , with a variable consistency , lifting the ear lobe , is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland. Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, primarily affects the parotid gland, particularly its superficial lobe . It is also referred to as a mixed tumor due to its combination of epithelial and mesenchymal components . This tumor most commonly occurs in females around the age of 40. Clinical features : • Painless, slow -growing swelling • Lobulated , firm, variable in consistency • Lifts the earlobe • No facial nerve involvement • Curtain sign positive - cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone. • In case of deep lobe involvement, tonsils, and faucial pillars will be pushed medially . • Features of malignancy - a sudden increase in size, ulceration of the overlying skin, facial nerve palsy (involvement of facial nerve), painful swelling , and restriction of jaw movements. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the investigation of choice in diagnosing pleomorphic adenoma. Open biopsy is contraindicated due to the chances of injury to the facial nerve. All tumors of the superficial lobe of the parotid gland should be managed by superficial parotidectomy. Radical parotidectomy is performed for malignant pleomorphic adenoma. Other options : Option A: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumor that usually presents with pre-tibial pain and swelling since it most commonly affects the tibial diaphysis . Option B: Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types :1042 • Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development . • Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube /duct • Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma • Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto , meso, and endoderm ) Option D: Sebaceous cysts are retention cysts of the sebaceous glands that present as smooth, non-tender , non-transillumination swelling with a punctum (in 70% of the patients ).
