mcqs.question: A 45-year-old woman presented with painless swelling in front of the left ear for the past 2 years. On examination, her left earlobe was lifted and the curtain sign was positive . Which of the following is false about the condition?

options.a: Treatment of choice is total radical parotidectomy
options.d: Malignant form shows LMN facial palsy

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma. The treatment of choice is superficial parotidectomy . Clinical features : • Painless, slow -growing swelling • Lobulated , firm, elastic -to-hard in consistency • Lift the ear lobe • Free from deeper structures • With no facial nerve involvement • Curtain sign positive - cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone Pleomorphic adenoma involves the superficial lobe of parotid gland and should be managed by superficial parotidectomy . Types of Parotidectomy • If only the superficial lobe is involved: • Superficial parotidectomy - only superficial lobe removed. Usually done in benign conditions. • If both lobes are involved: • Total conservative parotidectomy - both lobes are removed but the facial nerve is preserved . • Total radical parotidectomy - both lobes and facial nerve removed. Sometimes it may undergo malignant transformation . The malignant form is mixed malignant tumor or carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma (most aggressive salivary malignancy). Signs of malignant transformation • A rapid increase in size • Pain and ulceration • Facial nerve involvement (LMN) • Lymph node involvement • Restricted jaw movements1043

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Technetium -99m pertechnetate scintigraphy done for a patient with a chronic painless facial swelling is shown below . Which of the following statements is false regarding this tumor?

options.a: This tumor has no malignant potential
options.b: Superficial parotidectomy is the treatment of choice
options.c: Histology shows a double layer of epithelial cells with dense lymphoid stroma
options.d: It is the most common unilateral benign tumor of the parotid gland

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and image are suggestive of Warthin 's tumor. These tumors appear as hot spots on radionuclide scans because of the high mitochondrial content in oncocytes that incorporate technetium -99m. The most common benign tumor of the parotid gland is pleomorphic adenoma. Warthin 's tumor or papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum usually presents as a unilateral tumor. It is usually seen in the lower poles of the parotid and is commonly associated with smoking. It occurs most often in elderly males. It has no malignant potential . Histology shows tumor cells lined by a double layer of neoplastic epithelial cells resting on the dense lymphoid stroma. FNAC is the preferred investigation. Superficial parotidectomy is the treatment of choice .Note : Both pleomorphic adenoma and Warthin 's tumors commonly present as unilateral tumors. A bilateral presentation is usually rare. However in rare cases , if there is a bilateral benign salivary tumor, the tumor is most likely to be a Warthin 's tumor.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Match the following
mcqs.explanation: Godwin's tumor • Benign lymphoepithelial tumor of the salivary gland. • It is associated with CMV. • < 5% shows malignancy - known as Eskimoma. Kuttner 's tumor is chronic sclerosing sialadenitis of the submandibular gland. Oncocytoma (oxyphil adenoma) - • Usually benign, originating from oncocytes .1044 • Grossly - tan-colored small, well -circumscribed, and encapsulated . • Microscopically - large oncocytes with swollen granular cytoplasm . • Appear as a hotspot on Technetium -99m pertechnetate scintigraphy due to an abundance of mitochondria.Tumor Description Godwin's tum or Benign lymphoepithelial tum or Eskimoma Malignant salivary gland tum or Kuttner 's tum or Chronic sclerosing sialadeniti s oncocytoma Hotspot on 99Tc scintigraph y

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly woman presents with recent onset facial asymmetry and a lump over the roof of the mouth for the past 1 year. On examination, a solitary erythematous swelling with diffuse borders is seen over the left hard palate . Biopsy of the lesion reveals a swiss cheese pattern. Which of the following conditions is she likely to have?
mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and biopsy finding is suggestive of adenoid cystic carcinoma . Facial asymmetry points to the perineural invasion of the tumor into the facial nerve, which is characteristic of adenoid cystic carcinoma . It is the second most common malignant tumor of the parotid gland. It is a slow -growing tumor most commonly involving the parotid and submandibular glands. Histology shows a swiss cheese pattern. The tubular type has the best prognosis, while the solid type has the worst. It has a deceptively benign histologic appearance characterized by indolent , locally invasive growth with a high propensity for local recurrence and distant metastasis . The most common site of distant metastasis is the lung. Treatment involves removal of the gross tumor, with radiation therapy for the microscopic disease .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common malignant tumor involving the parotid gland?
mcqs.explanation: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor, while pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumor of the parotid gland. Histological classification and incidence of tumors of salivary glands: NOS: Not otherwise specified .Benign Tumors Incide nce Malignant tumors Incide nce Pleomorphic aden oma 50% Mucoepidermoid carcin oma 15% Warthin 's tumor 5–10% Adenocarcinoma (NOS) %1045 Benign Tumors Incide nce Malignant tumors Incide nce Oncocytoma 1% Acinic cell carcinoma 5% Other adenomas 5–10% Adenoid cystic carcino ma 5% Basal cell adenom a 1-2% Malignant mixed tumor 3–5% Canalicular adeno ma 1% Squamous cell carcino ma 1% Ductal papillomas - Other carcinomas 2%

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: As a 1st year resident assisting in a superficial parotidectomy , you have been asked to identify the facial nerve trunk. All of the following structures can be used for its localization except :
mcqs.explanation: The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle is not used as an anatomical landmark for the identification of the facial nerve trunk. There are two methods for localization of the facial nerve trunk: 1. Anterograde method : In this method, the facial nerve trunk is identified based on the anatomical landmarks after it exits from the stylomastoid foramen. The anatomical landmarks include : • Conley 's pointer is the inferior portion of the cartilaginous canal. The facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and inferior to its tip. • Posterior belly of digastric- The facial nerve lies superior to the upper border of the muscle . • Mastoid process - Upon drilling it, the nerve is identified proximally. • Squamotympanic fissure is a fissure in the temporal bone, which runs from TMJ to the tympanic cavity. The facial nerve runs through this fissure . • Styloid process - The facial nerve lies superficial to it. 2. Retrograde method : In this method , the main branches of the facial nerve trunk are identified and are then traced proximally until the main tunk is identified . Some of the main branches that are commonly used for tracing the facial nerve trunk include : • Buccal branch lies in relation to the parotid gland • Marginal mandibular branch lies in relation to the facial vessels • Temporal branch The given image points to the facial nerve (marked by arrow).1046

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is scheduled to undergo a total parotidectomy with selective node dissection of levels Ib, IIa , IIb , and III . Which of the following groups of lymph nodes will be removed during the procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , only submandibular (Level Ib) and middle jugular nodes (Level III ) nodes will be removed. The other nodes that will be removed in the procedure will be upper jugular nodes (Level IIa and IIb ). Selective neck dissection has been used in the treatment of patients with cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract (oral cavity, pharynx, larynx), cancer of the thyroid gland, cutaneous malignancies, and cancer of the salivary gland. The type of selective neck dissection used varies depending on the lymphatic drainage and metastatic pattern associated with the primary cancer site .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with pleomorphic adenoma is posted for submandibular gland excision. Which of the following nerves is least likely to be injured during this procedure ?

options.a: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve

mcqs.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve is the nerve least likely to be affected by submandibular surgery. Nerves at risk for injury during removal of the submandibular gland include : • Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve • Lingual nerve • Hypoglossal nerve An important landmark in submandibular gland dissection is the posterior border of the mylohyoid muscle . Once identified , it can be retracted to reveal the deep lobe of the gland. The hypoglossal nerves lie deep to the submandibular capsule and should not be damaged during intracapsular dissection . The facial artery is ligated twice during the surgery.1047

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which nerve is involved in Frey's syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating ). Frey's syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery. It is caused by an aberrant regeneration of post -ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers crossed along the sympathetic pathways to the sweat glands near the parotid region. Clinical features are due to the result of salivary stimulation (by the smell or taste of food) leading to the sweating and flushing of the periauricular region on the involved side of the face . A starch iodine test is used for diagnosis. Treatment ranges from antiperspirants (in mild cases ) to tympanic neurectomy or botulinum toxin injection (in severe cases ). It can be prevented by incorporating careful extracapsular dissection and closure of the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer during parotidectomy .1048 Other options : Option A: Facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve that supplies the muscles of the face , and results in facial paralysis if injured during parotidectomy Option B: Oculomotor is the 3rd cranial nerve which supplies the extraocular muscles . If injured during ophthalmic surgeries , it results in ocular paralysis and the eye pointing down and out. Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: After parotidectomy patients complains of loss of sensation while shaving. Which nerve is most likely affected ?
mcqs.explanation: After parotid surgery, the nerve involved in the loss of sensation while shaving is the great auricular nerve. The great auricular nerve (GAN) originates from the second and third nerve roots of the cervical plexus (C2-C3). It supplies the skin over the lower pinna, pre-auricular region, and angle of the mandible (image below ). The main trunk passes over the sternocleidomastoid and into the anterosuperior portion of the parotid glands and branches into the anterior and posterior GAN. The anterior branch of GAN is often injured during parotid surgery during the initial elevation of the skin flap. When GAN is injured, it can cause reduced sensations in the earlobe , pre-auricular skin, and the angle of the mandible that can interfere with habits such as shaving, wearing earrings, etc .1049 Other options : Option A: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3 of trigeminal) supplies the posterior part of the temple , tragus, and adjoining auricle. It does not supply the area where a person is likely to shave. However, the injury to the auriculotemporal nerve resulting in aberrant regeneration would result in Frey's Syndrome (gustatory sweating ). Option C: Though the facial nerve is the most common nerve affected during parotidectomy , any damage would result in facial paralysis and not loss of sensation of the face . Option D: The mandibular nerve is a branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V ) that supplies the skin over the mandible, lower lip, and cheek . However, they are not injured during parotidectomy .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: At what age should the congenital defect (shown in the image below ) be ideally repaired?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a unilateral cleft lip. Repair of cleft lip (primary palate ) along with associated nasal deformities is done at 3–6 months of age .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child with a cleft lip is posted for surgery. Which of the following methods is not used to repair this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Wardill's method is not a method of cleft lip repair. It is a technique for hard palate closure . Cleft -lip repair techniques : • Millard's rotation advancement technique (most common) • Thompson • Le Mesurier • Tennison–Randall1050 Techniques of hard palate closure include the use of the following : • Unipedicled hard palate mucoperiosteal flaps as in the Wardill-Veau-Kilner repair • Bipedicled hard palate mucoperiosteal flaps as in the von Langenbeck repair

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which among the following is an oral cavity lesion with a high-risk of malignant transformation ?
mcqs.explanation: Speckled erythroplakia has a high risk of malignant transformation . Malignancy risk : High-risk lesions Erythroplakia (homogenous /speckled ) • Seen as red velvety lesions • Speckled type is the most aggressive • The treatment of choice is surgical ablation Proliferative verrucous leucoplakia • A white patchy lesion that cannot be rubbed off. • Speckled leucoplakia has an erythematous base • The treatment of choice is excision Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis • White patches that can be rubbed off with a hyperaemic border. • Management includes prolonged treatment with topical antifungals or systemic antifungal therapy. If no improvement or if there are any signs of dysplasia , surgical excision is done. Medium risk lesions Oral submucous fibrosis • Hypersensitive reaction to betel nut product . • Other risk factors are - tobacco, chili, vitamin deficiency • Clinical features - trismus, ankyloglossia, soreness , and burning sensation in the mouth. • Management includes antioxidants, intralesional triamcinolone, and surgical excision. Syphilitic glossitis • Associated with tertiary syphilis Low-risk lesions Oral lichen planus • Reticulate fine lace-like pattern. • Management is topical corticosteroids. Discoid lupus erythematosus1051 Discoid keratosis congenita Speckled erythroplakia:

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man presented with complaints of difficulty in opening his mouth, restricted tongue movements, and a burning sensation in the mouth while eating food. He is a smoker and chews pan masala. On examination, scarring is present in the oral cavity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is oral submucous fibrosis. It is a premalignant lesion of the oral cavity, in which fibrous bands are formed beneath the oral mucosa. Risk factors are • Betel nut • Chilli • Tobacco • Vitamin deficiency Clinical features include ankyloglossia, trismus, soreness , and a burning sensation in the mouth while eating. Management includes intralesional steroids, vitamin supplements , and surgical excision. Option A: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by post cricoid web that is associated with iron deficiency anemia, glossitis , and koilonychia. It usually presents as dysphagia . Option B: Proliferative verrucous leucoplakia appears as a white patchy lesion, that cannot be rubbed off. Option D: Erythroplakia is seen as bright red velvety plaque in the oral cavity.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 57 -year-old male patient presents to the surgery OPD, with a 7cm lesion over the left buccal mucosa and difficulty opening the mouth. On examination, the right cervical lymph node is 4cm in size with overlying skin involvement. What is the TNM staging of this lesion?
mcqs.explanation: 1052 The TNM staging in this patient is T4bN3bMX. A 7-cm primary tumor in the oral cavity with difficulty in opening mouth denotes a locally advanced tumor: T4b. Contralateral cervical lymph node involvement with skin involvement (extranodal extension -positive ): N3b Note : Here the skin invasion corresponds to ENE positive , and hence , the N staging is N3b instead of N2c (contralateral lymph nodes , <6 cm and ENE \037negative ).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the given incision used for maxillectomy .
mcqs.explanation: The image shows Weber–Ferguson incision which is used to access the floor of the maxillary sinus in the case of maxillary carcinoma . The rest of the options are incisions used for modified radical neck dissection (MRND).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is this approach used in the treatment of oral cancer?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows the visor approach. In the visor approach, an incision is made extending from one end of the mandible to the opposite side and subplatysmal flaps are elevated superiorly over the mandible (like a visor of a helmet ). This approach provides a wide exposure to remove larger lesions involving the anterior oral cavity that is not amenable to a peroral approach. This avoids a lip-splitting incision but has the disadvantage of anesthesia of chin/lower lip (due to the sacrifice of submental nerves). The surgical approach selected for excision of oral cavity tumors depends on the size of the tumor, location (anterior vs posterior), proximity to bone (mandible or maxilla), and the need to perform neck dissection . The most commonly employed approaches are as follows : • Peroral - accessible early-stage tumors • Lower cheek flap - tumors requiring partial mandibulectomy or large posterolateral tumors that cannot be accessed via a peroral approach1053 • Upper cheek flap - tumors requiring partial maxillectomy or those involving the hard palate , upper gum, upper gingivobuccal sulcus and anterior soft palate • Mandibulotomy - larger tumors of the posterior oral cavity, tumors that involve the base of the tongue or pharyngeal wall. • Visor flap - larger lesions of the anterior oral cavity involving the anterior floor of the mouth and lower gum that are not amenable to a peroral approach Commando operation is the combined mandibular resection and neck node dissection . It is used mainly for carcinoma of the tongue .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: You will use an Abbe-Estlander flap for the reconstruction of which of the following structures ?
mcqs.explanation: Abb\351- Estlander flaps are used for the reconstruction of the lip. They are lip switch flaps based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves the commissure, the Estlander flap is used , and the Abb\351 flap is used for more midline defects .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A woman from Himachal Pradesh, presented with complaints of neck swelling for the past 1 year. On examination, a firm, non-tender, pulsatile mass was palpated on the left side of the neck. The mass is mobile from side to side , but not up and down. A carotid angiogram of the patient is shown below . Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.b: Shamblin classification is used for staging
options.d: FNAC is the initial investigation of choice

mcqs.explanation: The given scenario and carotid angiogram showing splaying of the bifurcation of the carotids, also known as lyre sign points to a diagnosis of chemodectoma . Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is contraindicated when a chemodectoma is suspected . Chemodectoma is also known as carotid body tumor (aka potato tumor). It is a benign tumor of the neuroendocrine tissue of the carotid body. It has a higher incidence at high altitudes because of chronic hypoxia, which leads to carotid body hyperplasia . The tumor presents as a slowly enlarging mass that is firm, rubbery, pulsatile , mobile from side to side but not up and down. A bruit may be heard. Family history can be present in 10 % of the1054 cases . Shamblin classification is used for staging carotid body tumors.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common site of branchial cyst is ______.

options.a: Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle
options.b: Junction of middle and lower third of the sternomastoid muscle
options.d: Between the two heads of the sternomastoid muscle

mcqs.explanation: The most common site of a branchial cyst is at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border. The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst .Branchial cyst develops due to the persistence of the cervical sinus. The cervical sinus is formed when the 2nd arch mesoderm overgrows the succeeding arches and overhangs them as shown in the image. The space between the overhanging 2nd pharyngeal arch and the 3rd, 4th, and 6th arches is called the cervical sinus. The cavity of the cervical sinus is lined by ectoderm and1055 normally gets obliterated . Branchial cysts are usually lined by squamous epithelium and contain thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate when it contains clear fluid . A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital . The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid (option B). An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture , and it is seen at the same site as the cyst .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: To which group of lymph nodes does a tumor limited to the glottis of the larynx spread commonly?
mcqs.explanation: Tumors limited to the glottis usually do not spread to any lymph nodes , as there are no lymphatics in the vocal cords. However, if the tumor invades the supra- or the infra-glottic spaces , lymph node spread can occur. The most common malignant tumor of the larynx is squamous cell carcinoma . Glottis is the most common site of laryngeal cancer.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Radical neck dissection spares which of the following structures ?
mcqs.explanation: Digastric muscle is spared in radical neck dissection (RND). RND is used in the treatment of malignant lesions of the neck with local spread or metastasis . In 1905, Crile described RND where Level I-V LN, sternocleidomastoid (SCM), internal jugular vein (IJV ), and XI cranial nerve (spinal accessory nerve) are removed. In 1962 , Suarez described modified RND (MRND) where Level I-V LNs are removed and the following are preserved : • MRND I - XI cranial nerve1056 • MRND II - XI cranial nerve and IJV • MRND III - XI cranial nerve, IJV , and SCM Note : RND with an additional LN/muscle/nerve is called extended RND.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient is posted under your unit for type 2 modified radical neck dissection . Which of the following structures will you preserve during this procedure ?
mcqs.explanation: In type 2 modified radical neck dissection (MRND), internal jugular vein and spinal accessory nerve will be preserved .1057

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which among the following are indications to shift a patient to the burn center ?
mcqs.explanation: > 5% BSA burnt is not an indication to send a patient to the burns center . Guidelines for referral to a burn center : • Partial-thickness burns greater than 10 % body surface area (BSA). • Burns involving the face , hands, feet, genitalia , perineum , or major joints. • Third-degree burns in any age group. • Electrical burns, including lightning injury. • Chemical burns. • Inhalation injury. • Burn injury in patients with complicated pre-existing medical disorders. • Patients with burns and concomitant trauma in which the burn is the greatest risk . If the trauma is the greater immediate risk , the patient may be stabilized in a trauma center before transfer to a burn center . • Burned children in hospitals without qualified personnel for the care of children. • Burn injury in patients who will require special social, emotional, or rehabilitative intervention.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following are false regarding first-degree burns?

options.c: Protective functions of the skin are intact
options.d: No residual scar after injury heals

mcqs.explanation: First-degree burns involve only the epidermis , are painful, but do not blister , protective functions of the skin are intact and heals without a scar. Second -degree burns have dermal involvement and are extremely painful and blister . Third-degree burns are leathery , painless , and non-blanching.1070

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man accidentally took a bath with overheated water. A few hours later, he developed the given lesion on his shoulders and chest . Following spontaneous rupture 3 days later, the base of the lesion was erythematous and blanches on touch . What is the time taken by these wounds to heal?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of second -degree superficial burns. They usually heal with minimal scarring in 10 –14 days unless they become infected . Second -degree burns are divided into two types : • Superficial Dermal burns are erythematous and painful, blanch to touch , and often blister . They heal in 10 –14 days. • Deep dermal burns involve the reticular dermis, appear more pale with erythmatous regions, do not blanch to touch , but remain painful to pinprick. They heal in 4–8 weeks .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which layer is involved in blister formation in a superficial partial thickness burn?
mcqs.explanation: The papillary dermis is involved in blister formation in a superficial partial-thickness burn. First-degree burns involve only the epidermis , with pain, redness , and mild swelling . Second -degree (partial thickness) burns involve the epidermis and some parts of the dermis (also known as partial-thickness burns). Further divided into: • Superficial second -degree burns - involves the upper part of the dermis (papillary) and shows pain, blisters, and severe swelling . • Deep second -degree burns - extends up to the reticular layer of the dermis and appears more pale and mottled , does not blanch to touch , but remains painful to pinprick. Third-degree or full -thickness burns involve the full thickness of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue . Fourth-degree burns involve deep structures such as muscle and bone.1071

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient has presented to you with a burn wound as seen in the image below . With regards to Jackson 's zones of tissue injury, which of the following statements is false ?

options.a: Area 2 is the most severely burned portion
options.b: The outer area of a burn is called the zone of hyperemia
options.c: Vasodilation is seen in the area
options.d: Area 1 heals with minimal or no scarring

mcqs.explanation: Vasoconstriction (not vasodilation) is seen in red region or zone of stasis (marked zone 3). Jackson zones of tissue injury following burns has three zones: • The zone of coagulation is the most severely burned portion and is typically in the center of the wound. • Peripheral to that is a zone of stasis, with variable degrees of vasoconstriction and resultant ischemia. • The last, outermost area of a burn is called the zone of hyperemia , which will heal with minimal or no scarring and is most like a superficial or first-degree burn. It is characterized by vasodilation from inflammation surrounding the burn wound .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While examining the burns on this patient , you find a lack of sensation and capillary refill at the burnt site . What is the degree of burn?
mcqs.explanation: The characteristic features of full -thickness burns (third-degree burns) are lack of sensation in the burned skin, lack of capillary refill, and a leathery texture that is unlike normal skin. Deep dermal and full -thickness burns require excision with skin grafting for the patient to heal the wounds properly .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A chemical engineer burnt his fingers as shown in the image while working with hydrofluoric acid. What is the most appropriate way to manage this patient ?

options.a: Topical application of calcium gluconate gel along with ECG monitoring
options.b: Irrigation with Dakin 's solution followed by surgical excision of the burn site
options.c: Immediate intrarterial injection of calcium gluconate
options.d: Copious irrigation with normal saline and application of mafenide acetate

mcqs.explanation: Following irrigation of the burn site , topical application of calcium gluconate gel along with ECG monitoring is the most appropriate management.1072 Hydrofluoric acid is the strongest inorganic acid and it can cause liquefaction necrosis of deeper tissues (since the acid is highly lipophilic ). Pain out of proportion to physical examination is a hallmark finding in HF burns. Systemic absorption of fluoride ions can result in intravascular chelation of calcium causing hypocalcemia . Depletion of calcium causes inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump , leading to hyperkalemia and subsequent life -threatening arrhythmias. Therefore ECG monitoring is imperative. ECG abnormalities that can occur include prolonged QTc (from hypocalcemia ) and QRS widening (from hyperkalemia). Following copious irrigation of the burn site with water, the mainstay of treatment is with topical application of calcium gluconate gel . If the pain does not subside , or if systemic signs ensue , an intraarterial injection of calcium gluconate can be given in the affected extremity .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: 20 % of a patient 's total body surface area was burnt from an overhead electric supply line. What is leading cause of death in such burns?
mcqs.explanation: The leading cause of death in electrical injuries is cardiac arrest. This is because alternating current injuries interfere with normal cardiac pacing. The electricity itself does not usually cause significant underlying myocardial damage . So resuscitation, if successful , should be lasting. The domestic electricity supply comprises a low voltage alternating current.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: ABG of a patient with extensive burns shows pH: 7.29, pCO2: 38mmHg, HCO3: 16.5, and elevated lactate of 5mmol/L. As part of initial fluid resuscitation , which fluid would be the best to initiate in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The best fluid used for burns is Ringer's lactate or Hartmann 's solution . Ringer lactate (crystalloid ) is a mixture of sodium chloride , sodium lactate , potassium chloride , and calcium chloride in water. It prevents metabolic acidosis that may occur in burns. Crystalloids are said to be as effective as colloids for maintaining intravascular volume and are given during the initial 24 hours. Option A: Normal saline may be used , but large quantities of saline can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, worsening this patient 's existing acidosis. Option D: Human albumin solution is a colloid . Colloids should be ideally be given after the first 12 hours of burn because before this period , the massive fluid shifts cause proteins to leak out of the cells .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An adult whose both lower limbs are charred along with genitalia has ____ burns.
mcqs.explanation: Using Wallace's Rule of 9, the % total burn surface area: • One lower limb = Thigh (9%) + leg (9%) = 18% • Genitals = 1%1073 Hence , in this patient , one lower limb+ other lower limb + genital = 18% + 18% + 1% = 37%.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 3-year-old is brought with superficial and deep second degree burns on his chest . What is the most accurate method to assess the total body surface area involved ?

options.c: Using the child's palm as reference

mcqs.explanation: Lund and Browder chart gives a more accurate accounting of the true burn size in children. Unlike the Wallace rule of nines, the Lund and Browder chart takes into consideration the age of the person, by decreasing percentage BSA (Body Surface Area) for the head and increasing percentage BSA for the legs as the child ages , making it more useful in pediatric burns.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient comes to your clinic with a superficial partial-thickness burn. Which of the following statements regarding the management is false ?

options.a: Superficial burns generally do not require the use of topical antibiotics
options.b: Blisters on second degree burns should not be burst
options.c: All topical antibiotics retard wound healing
options.d: Facial burns of the same degree will require a hydrocolloid dressing

mcqs.explanation: Facial burns do not require a hydrocolloid dressing . Exposure therapy (no dressings are applied over the wound ) is typically used on the face and head . All topical antibiotics retard wound healing to some extent so they are used only in second or third-degree burns or wounds , which have a high risk of infection . Blisters on second -degree burns should not be burst as they may cause an infection . Topical treatment of deep burns: • 1% silver sulphadiazine cream • 0.5% silver nitrate solution • Mafenide acetate cream • Silver nitrate, silver sulphadiazine and cerium nitrate

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While starting fluid resuscitation on a patient with burns, it is important to keep in mind that all of the following parameters will be decreased , except :
mcqs.explanation: 1074 Capillary permeability and afterload is increased after severe burns. Significant burns is associated with massive release of inflammatory mediators, both in the wound and in other tissues . These mediators produce vasoconstriction and vasodilation, increased capillary permeability , and edema locally and in distant organs. Cellular and humoral immunity are decreased in burns (increased risk of infection ). Changes in various systems in burns: CVS • Massive edema • Increased afterload • Decreased venous return • Decreased cardiac output Renal • Low volume concentrated urine • Decreased urinary sodium • Myoglobinuria • Renal ischemia • Acute tubular necrosis • Acute renal failure GI • Reflex Ileus • GI Ulcers (Curling's Ulcer ) Endocrine and Metabolism • Increased glucagon , cortisol • Protein catabolism • Ureagenesis • Lipolysis • Increased gluconeogenesis • Lactic acidosis Hematological • Anaemia • Initial thrombocytopenia then thrombocytosis • Decreased capacity of neutrophil phagocytosis • Overall lymphopenia • Relative increase in T-Suppressor Cells1075

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient has rushed to your clinic after she spilled hot tea on her hand. What should be the ideal temperature of the water used to cool her injuries?
mcqs.explanation: In temperate climates , cooling should be at about 15 \260C, and hypothermia must be avoided. Moreover, studies show that ice cold water increases tissue damage . Water at 15 \260C provides analgesia and delays the microvascular damage in burns. It should occur for a minimum of 20 minutes and is effective up to 1 hour after the burn injury. Particularly important in scalds .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While fixing faulty wiring, an electrician sustains the given burn. Which of the following is false ?

options.a: Electric burns are usually third degree burns
options.b: Urine output should be monitored for volume and deposits
options.c: ECG should be monitored even in low voltage burns
options.d: Fluid requirement is less as compared to other burns

mcqs.explanation: Fluid requirement is more as compared to other burns. All electric burns are managed by resuscitation at 4mL /Kg /%TBSA (which means 4mL for every Kg for every %TBSA). This is double what the ATLS guidelines advise for other burns as electrical burns may cause myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury. Most of the electrical burns are of severe degree and cause third-degree burns. The fluid resuscitation is done to ensure urine output of 100 mL /hr in adults and 1–1.5 mL /kg/hr in children < 30 kg, until the urine clears from pigmentation . The IV fluid is then titrated down to ensure the urine output of 0.5 mL /Kg /hr. Electrical injuries are usually divided into low and high-voltage injuries. • Low voltage injuries cause small, localized , deep burns. • High voltage injuries damage by flash (External burn) and conduction (Internal burn) The myocardium may be directly damaged without pacing interruption. Thus, ECG must be monitored for arrhythmias.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man with severe burn injuries is admitted to the ward. Proton-pump inhibitors are started . Which ulcer is being prevented ?
mcqs.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors are used in burns patients to prevent Curling's ulcer. It is an acute gastric erosion that is a complication from severe burns when reduced plasma volume leads to ischemia and cell necrosis of the gastric mucosa. Marjolin's Ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma occurring in a long-standing burn scar or any chronic ulcer. Cushing's ulcer is a gastric ulcer occurring in elevated intracranial pressure . Buruli's Ulcer is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 34-year-old electrician sustains electrical burns while at work. On arrival he is hemodynamically stable , and he is placed on ECG monitoring and initial fluid resuscitation is initiated . His urine is collected for routine labs and appears as below . Which of the following lab abnormalities may be seen in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: 1076 The tea-colored urine in the clinical vignette in the setting of an electrical injury is suggestive of rhabdomyolysis following electrical burns. Elevated creatine kinase is seen in rhabdomyolysis . AC injuries are more commonly seen and this current creates tetany within the muscles . This sustained contraction can lead to muscle injury and resulting in rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria, presenting as tea-colored urine. Damage to the underlying muscles in the affected limb can also cause the rapid onset of compartment syndrome. The release of the myoglobins will cause myoglobinuria and subsequent renal dysfunction . Therefore, during the resuscitation of these patients , efforts must be made to maintain a high urine output of up to 2 mL /kg body weight per hour. Biochemical features of rhabdomyolysis are: • Elevated CPK, BUN, Cr • Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia , hypocalcemia .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A woman, weighing 58 kg, has second -degree burns covering 20 % of the total body surface area. Which of the following formulae would you use to calculate the amount of fluid to be given?

options.a: Percentage of burns \327 weight (kg) \327 2 = volume in mL
options.b: Percentage of burns \327 weight (kg)/2 = volume in mL
options.c: Percentage of burns \327 weight (kg) \327 4 = volume in mL
options.d: Weight + 1500 ml/m2 \327BSA burnt = volume in mL

mcqs.explanation: According to the latest ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support ) 10th edition 2018 , resuscitation formula for second and third-degree thermal burns in the first 24 hours is given by the following equation: Total percentage body surface area burned \327 weight (kg) \327 2 = volume (mL ). Half this volume is given in the first 8 hours and the second half is given in the subsequent 16 hours. This has been recommended to reflect concerns about over-resuscitation when using the traditional Parkland formula. Adequacy of fluid resuscitation is assessed by monitoring for a urine output of 0.5-1.0 mL /kg/hr. However, in cases of electrical burns, the formula is: Total percentage body surface area burned\327 weight (kg) \327 4 = volume (mL ). Parkland and Modified Parkland formula: • Parkland 's formula for resuscitation in the initial 24 hours is given by = Total percentage body surface area \327 weight (kg) \327 4 = volume (mL ). • Modified Parkland 's formula provides more specific recommendations for the second 24 hours, advising colloid infusion of 5% albumin at the amount of 0.3-1.0/mL /kg/%BSA/hr. The management of the first 24 hours remains the same.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following formulas will you use to calculate the amount of albumin to be administered to a patient with burns?
mcqs.explanation: The most commonly used colloid -based formula is the Muir and Barclay formula: • 0.5 \327 percentage body surface area burnt \327 weight = one portion • A total of six portions are given in 36 hours • Three portions: One portion for every 4 hours in 12 hours.1077 • Two portions: One portion for every 6 hours in the next 12 hours. • One portion: Remaining one portion in the last 12 hours. Colloid -based resuscitation using the Muir-Barclay formula results in the administration of lower volumes of fluid than Parklands formula and carries a lower risk of complications from over-resuscitation. However, colloids (4.5% Albumin) are deferred for the first 8 hours when capillary permeability is highest and the benefit is questionable . So, the 36-hours schedule of the Muir and Barclay formula would begin after the first 8 hours of burn. Options A and C: Parkland formula and Evan's formula are used to calculate the crystalloid volume to be given in the first 24 hours. Option D: Wallace's rule of nine is used to calculate the percentage of the burnt body surface area (%TBSA ).

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient was brought to the hospital after being rescued from a burning house where he was trapped for 4 hours. The patient has a few minor burns but is coughing extensively . His voice is hoarse and he is able to drink water with some difficulty . What is the safest strategy of management?

options.b: O2 therapy with well -fitting face mask

mcqs.explanation: For a patient who presents with a history or suspicion of inhalational burn injury, elective endotracheal intubation is the safest strategy . Delay can make intubation very difficult because of airway edema and can lead to airway obstruction. One should be ready to perform an emergency cricothyroidotomy if intubation is delayed . Recognition of the potentially burned airway: • A history of being trapped in the presence of smoke or hot gases • Burns on the palate or nasal mucosa, or loss of all the hairs in the nose • Deep burns around the mouth and neck American Burn Life Support (ABLS ) indications for early intubation include : • Signs of airway obstruction (hoarseness , stridor, accessory respiratory muscle use , sternal retraction) • The extent of the burn (TBSA > 40%–50%) • Extensive and deep facial burns • Burns inside the mouth or difficulty swallowing • Significant edema or risk for edema • Signs of respiratory compromise: Inability to clear secretions , respiratory fatigue , poor oxygenation or ventilation • Decreased level of consciousness where airway protective reflexes are impaired • Anticipated patient transfer of large burn with airway issue without qualified personnel to intubate en route

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 12 -year-old boy presented to the OPD with a scald injury of his arm . The lesion was pink, oozing, and painful to moving air and touch . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
mcqs.explanation: 1078 Scald injury (damage from contact with hot liquids) that appears pink in colour, has oozing, and pain is suggestive of a 2nd-degree burn (i.e. partial-thickness burn). Collagen dressing is the most appropriate management for this injury. The best dressing for burn wounds is skin; collagen is a good substitute for skin, especially in partial-thickness burns. For full -thickness burns, sequential excision and grafting should be considered . Initial treatment for burns includes cleaning burnt areas and removing loose dead skin. Blisters are de -roofed and an appropriate dressing is applied . Biological dressing (collagen dressings , amniotic membrane, etc .) is the preferred dressing material, especially in partial thickness burns. If this is not available then a non-adhesive dressing like paraffin gauze impregnated with silver sulfadiazine (SSD) cream, colloidal silver, ionic silver cream, or silver nitrate cream can be applied . Since increased resistance to SSD has recently emerged , it should be judiciously used and reserved for deep dermal, full thickness, infected , and old neglected burns.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following antibiotics will be most appropriate for managing the burn wound in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The image shows a burn eschar. Among the given topical antibiotics, only mafenide acetate penetrates burn eschar to reach the interface with the patient 's viable tissue . This agent has the disadvantage that it is quite painful on any partial thickness areas, and it is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and can potentially cause metabolic acidosis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 58-year-old homeless man was brought to a PHC in Himachal Pradesh during late winter. He was found unresponsive. His rectal temperature was 23 degrees C, pulse was not measurable , heart rate was 30 per minute and respiratory rate was 6. Rewarming with an electric blanket was started . Which organ is most susceptible to dysfunction in this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hypothermia . The heart is the organ most sensitive to cold and is subject to ventricular fibrillation or asystole when the temperature drops to 21 –24 \260C.1079 Hypothermia affects the dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin , so less oxygen is released to the tissues . Other complications are coagulopathies and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), pancreatitis , and acute renal failure. Classification of hypothermia :Trau ma Acciden tal Mild 36-3 4oC 35-32oC Mode rate 34-3 2oC -28oC Sever e <32o C <28oC

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Sweating is usually absent in _____
mcqs.explanation: Sweating is usually absent in classic (epidemic ) heatstroke (CHS). Heatstroke occurs as a result of an imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation (sweating ). The skin is pink or ashen and sometimes , paradoxically, dry and hot. Dry skin in the presence of hyperpyrexia is virtually pathognomonic. It is of 2 types : • Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures , usually without adequate training. • Sedentary heatstroke (CHS) is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises. Heat Cramps: • These are painful spasms of voluntary muscles which follow strenuous work in a hot atmosphere. • Caused by loss of water and salt in profuse sweating . Heat exhaustion /heat prostration: • Collapse without any elevation of body temperature • Occurs due to exposure to high temperature in closed environment • Precipitated by muscular exercise and unsuitable clothing • Extreme exhaustion with peripheral vascular collapse with scanty sweating .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A marathon runner was training on a hot afternoon when he experienced leg cramps and dizziness. He fainted and was taken indoors by his coach. His temperature was 104 .8 F, pulse 126 per minute and BP 90/60 mm of Hg. Despite an hour of rest and cold sponging , he did not improve. Which of the following is false regarding his condition?

options.a: Is a result of imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation
options.b: The patient should be cooled rapidly

mcqs.explanation: The heat stroke may be either exertion induced or sedentary heatstroke .1080 Heat stroke occurs as a result of an imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation . • Exertion-induced heat stroke is seen in people with prolonged exposure to or physical exertion in high temperatures , usually without adequate training. • Sedentary heat stroke is a disease of elderly or infirm people whose cardiovascular systems are unable to adapt to the stress of a hot environment and release sufficient heat such that body temperature rises. The body temperature must be measured rectally . Treatment is rapid cooling by spraying the patient with water at 15 \260C.1081

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: If histopathological examination of a 2-day-old forearm laceration is done, which of the following would be seen ?
mcqs.explanation: Neutrophil peak is seen on day 2 of the inflammatory phase of wound healing. Wound healing has three phases : The inflammatory phase , proliferative phase , and maturation phase. The inflammatory phase lasts 2-3 days.1094

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient 's wound has the given appearance 1 week after the injury. Which cells are predominantly found in this stage of wound healing?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows granulation tissue formed during the proliferative stage of wound healing. Fibroblasts are the predominant cell during the proliferative stage . Fibroblasts are specialized cells that differentiate from resting mesenchymal cells into connective tissue . The primary function of fibroblasts is to synthesize collagen . The proliferative stage of wound healing is characterized by the formation of granulation tissue , which consists of a capillary bed , fibroblasts, macrophages , and a loose arrangement of collagen , fibronectin, and hyaluronic acid.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an anti-inflammatory cytokine involved in wound healing?
mcqs.explanation: Interleukins 1, 6 and 8 are pro-inflammatory cytokines, whereas IL -10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following events of wound healing will be altered in a patient with scurvy?
mcqs.explanation: Dietary deficiency of vitamin C (scurvy) results in poorly formed collagen and affects the early matrix scaffolding . Type I and Type III collagens are both present in the extracellular matrix of normal skin (in an 8:1 ratio). However, during the proliferative phase of wound healing, the dominant collagen that is laid is Type III . This stage is also known as early matrix scaffolding . Type III collagen is gradually replaced by type I collagen (during the final remodeling phase ) until a ratio (type I: type III ) of 4:1 is achieved .1095

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: In patients presenting with non-healing surgical incisions, what is the most common underlying cause ?
mcqs.explanation: All the factors listed impair wound healing, but local infection is the most common underlying cause of non-healing surgical incisions. To reduce the chances of infection ,the surgeon should make every effort to remove all devitalized tissue and leave a clean wound for closure . Factors affecting wound healing: • Site of the wound • Structures involved • Mechanism of wounding (crushing, incision, avulsion) • Contamination • Loss of tissue • Local factors (vascularity, previous irradiation , pressure ) • Systemic factors (malnutrition, anemia, steroids , AIDS, smoking)

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child with a grazed knee comes to your clinic for first aid. He has a history of nephrotic syndrome and is on oral prednisolone therapy . Which stage of wound healing would be most affected by his medication?
mcqs.explanation: While all of the given options are inhibited by steroids , the major effect of steroids is to inhibit the initial inflammatory phase of wound healing (angiogenesis , neutrophil and macrophage migration, and fibroblast proliferation) and the release of lysosomal enzymes . The stronger the anti-inflammatory effect of the steroid compound used , the greater the inhibitory effect on wound healing. Steroids used after the first 3 to 4 days post -injury do not affect wound healing as severely as when they are used in the immediate postoperative period . In addition to inhibiting collagen synthesis , steroids also inhibit epithelialization and contraction and contribute to increased rates of wound infection , regardless of the time of administration. Steroid delayed healing of cutaneous wounds can be stimulated to epithelialize by topical application of vitamin A.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following findings in a long-standing ulcer would indicate malignant transformation ?
mcqs.explanation: Everted edge around a chronic wound is a sign of malignant transformation . The majority of wounds that have not healed in 3 months are considered chronic and are prone to malignant changes . Malignant wounds are differentiated clinically from non-malignant wounds by the presence of overturned edges . Biopsy of the wound edges should be performed to rule out malignancy. Malignant transformation can occur in any long-standing wound . The image shows a Marjolin's ulcer with everted edges . It is squamous cell carcinoma that develops on a long-standing burn.1096

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 21 -year-old man came to the casualty 12 hours after sustaining a laceration on his leg from a trekking accident . On closer examination, other than dirt, you do not notice any pus or signs of infection . What is the most appropriate management?

options.a: Closure after granulation tissue has formed
options.b: Delayed closure 2 days after removal of devitalised tissue
options.c: Primary closure after adequate wound toileting and debridement
options.d: Wound debridement , topical antibiotics and dressing

mcqs.explanation: Contaminated wounds older than 6 hours should be managed with delayed primary closure . The wound is cleaned , debrided , and left open for a few days. This allows soft tissues to drain and also ensures no infection is present before surgical closure can be done. Wound closure is categorized into primary, secondary, or tertiary: Primary closure is done for clean wounds with minimal tissue loss that are amenable to approximation of wound edges . Healing occurs by primary intention. Primary closure is ideally performed within 6 to 8 hrs of trauma, but wounds in vascular areas (e.g. face ) may be delayed to up to 24 hours after trauma. Secondary closure allows healing by secondary intention. The wound is left open to heal largely by the formation of granulation tissue and contraction. These wounds often have significant tissue loss precluding tension-free approximation of edges , with devitalized edges . Wound dressings are changed daily to aid in the formation of granulation tissue and subsequent contraction. Tertiary closure , also known as delayed primary closure , results in a combination of healing by primary and secondary intention. The wound is thoroughly irrigated, debrided , and left open for 2 to 5 days before surgical closure . It is used for wounds that are grossly contaminated without significant tissue loss.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Stage the bedsore in the following image:
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows complete skin loss that involves muscles and shows exposed bone indicating a stage 4 pressure sore. Pressure sores are skin or soft tissue injuries that occur due to prolonged pressure over specific areas of the body. An external pressure of >30 mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores.1097 The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are the ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel , malleolus (lateral followed by medial), and occiput . Pressure sores can be prevented with good skincare, the use of air-fluidized beds , special pressure -dispersion cushions, or foams. Repositioning the patient every two hours can lessen the pressure on the area. Ulcers of stages 1 and 2 often do not require operative measures . They are managed with regular wound cleaning and dressing with a good antibiotic cover. Stage 3 and 4 ulcers are adequately debrided , and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC ) is used to promote the growth of granulation tissue required for surgical closure . Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the most common site of pressure sores ?
mcqs.explanation: Pressure sore frequency in descending order: • Ischium • Greater Trochanter • Sacrum • Heel • Malleolus • Occiput

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: An elderly paraplegic patient admitted to a nursing home, developed an ulcer on her gluteal region. All of the following are true regarding the management of this patient except :

options.a: Diet and nutritional support should aim to establish a positive nitrogen balance
options.b: Following debridement , exposure of the wound is recommended
options.c: Tensor fascia lata flap with an intact nerve supply may be used for covering the defect
options.d: Frequent change in position and air mattresses can help in preventing further sores

mcqs.explanation: The given image is that of a grade 3 bedsore . A grade 3 pressure sore requires dressing following debridement. Preoperative management involves adequate debridement , and the use of vacuum-assisted closure (VAC ) to provide a suitable wound for surgical closure . Alginates , foams, hydrocolloids , hydrogels are other options that are available. The aim of surgery is to fill the dead space and to provide durable sensate skin. Large skin flaps that include muscle are best and, occasionally, an intact sensory innervated area can be included (e.g. extensor fascia lata flap with the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh). Nutritional optimization with high caloric and protein diet should be done to establish a positive nitrogen balance. Frequent changes in position and air mattresses can also help in preventing further sores.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A meshed skin graft was used to cover a defect and vacuum-assisted closure of the transplant was done. What is the pressure generated within the dressing ?
mcqs.explanation: The pressure used in vacuum-assisted closure for wound healing is –125 mmHg.1098 Applying negative pressure appears to hasten debridement and the formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds and ulcers . It acts by decreasing edema , by removing interstitial fluid , and as a result , helps in decreasing bacterial counts and cell proliferation increases.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A man who had undergone an exploratory laparotomy 6 months ago came for a follow -up visit. Which of the following statements about healed incision is false ?

options.a: Disorganized collagen fibers become aligned along stress lines
options.b: Strength of the scar is in their weave rather than in their amount
options.c: By the first week it is held by sutures and a weak type 3 collagen matrix
options.d: Tensile strength is about 60-80% of normal skin by 3 months

mcqs.explanation: During the first week , a surgical wound has minimal inherent strength because the dermal edges are held together solely by a hemostatic plug and sutures . During the second postoperative week , fibroblasts proliferate rapidly and begin to produce type I collagen in addition to type III . The strength of the wound is still limited to less than 10 % of its final strength . By week 6, the concentration of strong collagen fibers begins to resemble that of intact skin. As the collagen matures and becomes denser , the scar becomes almost acellular as the fibroblasts and blood vessels reduce .The disorganized collagen fibers become aligned along stress lines with their strength being in their weave rather than in their amount. Most of these changes occur over the first three months but a scar will continue to mature for 1 to 2 years. Tensile strength will continue to increase but would not be expected to exceed 60–80% of that of normal skin.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The forearm of a patient admitted to the psychiatric ward is shown in the image. Which of the following is true about the healed injury?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows hypertrophic scars which have developed on possible sites of self -inflicted cuts. Type 3 collagen fibers are arranged parallelly in hypertrophic scars. This is in contrast to a keloid where the collagen fibers are more and randomly arranged. Hypertrophic scars rise above the skin level but stay within the confines of the original wound and often regress over time. They have no racial or genetic predilection . Difference between keloid and hypertrophic scar:Features Hypertrophic scar Keloid Genetic predispositio n Not familial Maybe familial - Autosomal d ominant with incomplete pen etration Age Children Adolescents . Middle age Race No predilection African American, Asian, His panic Site Anywhere (more common on extensor surface ) Neck, chest , ear lobes , should ers, upper back Timings 4–6 weeks postinjury Symptom-free interval; may appear years after injury1099 Features Hypertrophic scar Keloid Symptoms Raised, some pruritus, respec ts wound confines Pain, pruritus, hyperesthesia , growth beyond wound margi ns Regression Frequent spontaneous No Contracture Frequent Rare Histology Parallel orientation of collage n fibers Hypocellular , thick, wavy coll agen fibers in random orient ation

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements are true with regards to a keloid scar?

options.a: The extent does not cross the wound margins
options.b: Wide excision of the keloid scar prevents recurrence
options.c: Histopathology of a keloid scar shows reduced collagen and increased vascularity
options.d: A keloid scar forms due to increase in the level of growth factors

mcqs.explanation: Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factor leading to increased proliferation of fibrous tissue . A keloid scar is defined as excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound (option A) and rarely regresses on its own. It is more common in darker-pigmented ethnicities . It can arise from surgery, burns, skin inflammation, infections , ear piercing, and even spontaneously . It occurs 3 months to years after the initial insult with even minor injuries causing keloid formation. It most commonly occurs on the skin of the earlobe , deltoid , presternal , upper back, and rarely extends into the subcutaneous tissue .The histology of keloid scars shows excess collagen and hypervascularity with collagen fibres arranged haphazardly in loose sheets (option C). Treatment: Keloid scars do not improve spontaneously with time and excision alone has a high rate of recurrence (option B). The following can be done:1100 • Pressure - local moulds or elastic garments. • Silicone gel sheeting . • Intralesional triamcinolone injection. • Excision and steroid injections. • Excision and postoperative radiation (external beam or brachytherapy ). • Intralesional excision. • Laser to reduce redness . • Vitamin E and palm oil massage . Differences between Keloids and Hypertrophic scars:Keloid Hypertrophic scar Incidence Rare Frequent Ethnic groups African, American, Asian, Hi spanic No predilection Prior injury Yes Yes Site predilection Neck, chest , earlobes , should ers, upper back Anywhere Genetics Autosomal dominantwith inc omplete penetration No Timing Symptom-free interval; may appear years after injury 4-6 weeks post -injury Symptoms Pain, pruritus, hyperesthesia , growth beyond wound margi ns Raised, some pruritus, respec ts wound confines Regression and contractur e No, and rare Frequent Histology Hypocellular , thick, wavy coll agen fibres inrandom orienta tion Parallel orientationof collage n fibres

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient has been treated for the lesion shown in the picture below for the past 12 months but there has been no response to treatment . What is the next line of treatment for this patient ?
mcqs.explanation: Surgical excision in combination with adjuvant therapy is advised to patients with refractory keloids . The adjuvant therapy usually includes radiation.The risk of malignancy attributable to keloid radiation therapy is minimal Treatment of keloids : • First-line treatments include silicones in combination with pressure therapy and intralesional corticosteroid injections.1101 • Intralesional 5-fluorouracil, bleomycin , and verapamil should be used in accordance with established treatment protocols . • Refractory cases after 12 months of therapy should be considered for surgical excision in combination with adjuvant therapy . • Excision alone results in a high recurrence rate of 50% to 100 % and enlargement of the keloid. • Immediate postoperative electron beam irradiation or brachytherapy with iridium-192 reduces recurrence rates. The risk of malignancy attributable to keloid radiation therapy is minimal. • An additional new invasive treatment modality is internal cryotherapy , in which a metal rod is introduced into the keloid and the subsequent extreme cooling leads to tissue necrosis.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following techniques will you use to reduce suture marks and scars?
mcqs.explanation: Fine sutures (6/0 or smaller) placed close to the wound margins tend to cause less scarring . Subcuticular suturing avoids suture marks on either side of the wound or incision. Suture marks can be minimized using monofilament sutures that are removed early (3–5 days). Wounds can be strengthened post -suture removal by the use of sticky strips.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is not a skin substitute ?
mcqs.explanation: Duoderm is a hydrocolloid and not a skin substitute . Skin substitutes are skin products made of cells , extracellular matrix components , or a combination of the two . Integra is a bilayered membrane skin substitute . Alloderm is a acellular cadaveric dermis. Apligraf is a living bilayered biologic dressing composed of neonatal dermal fibroblasts on a collagen matrix. Trancyte is a tissue -engineered skin substitute is made from a nylon mesh and a silastic semi-permissible and biocompatible layer.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Identify the procedure shown in the image.
mcqs.explanation: The image depicts a fasciotomy of the lower limb. Fasciotomy involves incising the deep muscle fascia and is best carried out via longitudinal incisions of skin, fat, and fascia. The muscle is seen bulging out through the fasciotomy opening . The lower limb can be decompressed via two incisions, each being lateral to the subcutaneous border of the tibia. This gives access to the two posterior compartments and to the peroneal and anterior compartments of the leg .1102

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A catheter is inserted into the limb of a patient suspected to have compartment syndrome. What minimum reading on the pressure monitor will prompt an immediate fasciotomy?
mcqs.explanation: The pressure threshold for doing a fasciotomy in a case of suspected compartment syndrome is 30 mmHg Fasciotomy involves incising the deep muscle fascia and is best carried out via longitudinal incisions of skin, fat, and fascia.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: While performing a fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, the following layers are incised :

options.c: Skin , Subcutaneous tissue , Superficial fascia and Deep fascia
options.d: Skin , Subcutaneous tissue , Superficial fascia, Deep fascia and a few muscular fibres

mcqs.explanation: The incision for a fasciotomy involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue , superficial fascia, and deep fascia. Fasciotomy involves incising the deep muscle fascia and is best carried out via longitudinal incisions of skin, subcutaneous fat, and superficial and deep fascia. The muscle will be seen bulging out through the fasciotomy opening. The lower limb can be decompressed via two incisions, each being lateral to the subcutaneous border of the tibia. This gives access to the two posterior compartments and the leg 's peroneal and anterior compartments.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The lower limb of this patient was run over by a car. Identify the type of injury.
mcqs.explanation: Degloving injury occurs when the skin and subcutaneous fat are stripped by avulsion from its underlying fascia, leaving neurovascular structures , tendons , or bones exposed . It may be open or closed .1103 A tidy wound is a clean incised wound with seldom tissue loss whereas an untidy wound is one that is crushed , avulsed , contaminated often with tissue loss.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: What is the most likely diagnosis of the lesion shown in the image below ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image which shows a punched -out ulcer with regular margins on the plantar surface of the dry, crackled foot is suggestive of a neuropathic ulcer. Neuropathic ulcers occur as a result of repeated trauma to the insensitive part due to peripheral neuropathy . There is a lack of sensation over the pressure points, leading to unnoticed microtrauma , wounds or cuts which develop into an ulcer. Causes of neuropathic ulcers include diabetic neuropathy , B12 deficiency , alcoholism, hypothyroidism , leprosy , peripheral nerve injury, transverse myelitis and myelomeningocele . Other options : Option D: Tuberculous ulcers occur when a cold abscess from bone and joint tuberculosis breaks out on the surface . The most characteristic feature of this ulcer is its edge which is thin and undermined . mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 68-year-old diabetic presented with a foot ulcer that he first noticed 1 month ago. The edges are irregular with sloped margins. The ulcer does not bleed to touch . Peripheral pulses are felt and an arterial doppler does not indicate a compromised blood flow . Which growth factor has been formulated and approved for treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of a diabetic foot ulcer. At present , PDGF (platelet -derived growth factor)-BB is currently approved by the FDA for the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers . Application of recombinant human PDGF-BB in a gel suspension to these wounds increases the incidence of total healing and decreases healing time.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following procedures leaves a clean-contaminated wound ?

options.b: Repair of an old duodenal perforation

mcqs.explanation: 1106 Elective procedures in uninfected respiratory, genital , urinary , and gastrointestinal tracts such as elective cholecystectomy produce clean-contaminated wounds . Option A: Thyroidectomy leaves a clean wound . Option B: Repair of an old duodenal perforation is a contaminated wound . Option D: Emergency appendectomy is usually performed in the setting of an inflamed appendix and results in a dirty surgical wound .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: ASEPSIS wound scoring takes all of the following into consideration except :
mcqs.explanation: ASEPSIS wound score does not take induration into consideration. Instead, the I in ASEPSIS stands for the isolation of bacteria from the wound . ASEPSIS wound score and Southampton wound score are used to determine the severity of the surgical site wound infection (SSI). ASEPSIS score includes : • Additional treatment • Antibiotics for wound infection • Drainage of pus under local anesthesia • Debridement of the wound under general anesthesia • Serous discharge • Erythema • Purulent exudate • Separation of deep tissue • Isolation of bacteria from the wound • Stay as inpatient prolonged over 14 days as a result of wound infection

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: Which of the following is used for wound infection grading?
mcqs.explanation: Southampton wound grading system is used to score the severity of wound site infection . Southampton wound grading system : • Grade 0 - Normal healing • Grade I - Normal healing with different grades of erythema • Grade II - Erythema with other signs of inflammation at different parts of the wound . • Grade III - Clear or serosanguinous discharge at different sites • Grade IV - Pus discharge Other options :1107 Option A: American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grading is used in pre-anesthetic checkups to assess a patient 's physical health and fitness for anesthesia and surgery. Option B: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a set of clinical criteria used to identify and monitor critically ill patients with high-grade burns, severe trauma, and other major surgeries . Option D: Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II ) is a scoring system used to assess the severity and predict the outcome of pancreatitis .1108

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A scar excision followed by reconstruction with a split skin graft was performed on the forearm of a 28-year-old man. The survival of the graft during the first 48 hours will be mainly dependent on ________.
mcqs.explanation: Skin grafts survive by imbibition during the first 48 hours. The stage of imbibition is the first stage of graft uptake during which the graft draws nourishment from the plasma exudate at the host site (by simple diffusion ). After this inosculation and revascularization take over.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A patient with a leg injury was treated with a skin graft as shown below . Which of the following statements is false regarding this type of skin graft?

options.a: Degree of contraction is dependant on amount of dermis in graft
options.b: Healing with abnormal pigmentation are more common.
options.d: Meshing grafts improve their ultimate cosmetic appearance

mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a meshed , split-thickness skin graft. Split grafts are meshed to expand the surface area that can be covered but it does not improve the cosmetic appearance . Less dermis in the split -thickness skin graft translates into less primary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks in surface area after harvesting and before grafting) and more secondary contraction (the degree to which a graft shrinks during healing).1117 Less dermis also translates into a better chance of graft survival . Thin split grafts have a low primary contraction, high secondary contraction, and high reliability of graft take. However, they tend to heal with abnormal pigmentation and poor durability. mcqs.question: A 34-year-old man sustains facial burns and is being planned for reconstruction with a skin graft. Which type of graft should he receive to achieve a better cosmetic appearance and minimal contraction?
mcqs.explanation: The patient should receive a Wolfe graft to achieve a better cosmetic appearance and minimal contraction. Wolfe grafts are full -thickness skin grafts that are used for small areas of skin replacement where good elastic skin that will not contract is required (such as fingers, eyelids , and facial parts). Option B: Partial-thickness skin grafts or split -thickness grafts are called Thiersch grafts. They consist of the epidermis and a portion of the dermis. They tend to heal with abnormal1118 pigmentation and result in suboptimal cosmetic appearance . Option C: Composite grafts are grafts that contain skin and fat or skin and cartilage . They are often taken from the ear margin and useful for rebuilding missing elements of the nose, eyelids , and fingertips . mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The most common cause of skin graft failure is ____

options.d: Poor quality of the recipient bed

mcqs.explanation: The most common cause of skin graft failure is hematoma under the graft, where the blood clot is a barrier to contact of the graft and bed for revascularization . Other causes are shearing or movement of the graft on the bed , infection , poor quality of the recipient bed , and characteristics of the graft itself , such as thickness or vascularity of the donor site .

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A 20 -year-old lady sustained extensive burns over her left forearm for which a split -thickness skin graft was planned . During surgery, after obtaining a skin graft from the anterior thigh, the patient became hemodynamically unstable and a transplant to the forearm could not be completed . What would you do with the harvested graft?

options.a: It must be discarded and fresh graft harvested before repeat surgery
options.b: It can be stored for up to 2-3 days at +4\260C in saline
options.c: It can be stored for up to 2-3 weeks at +4\260C in saline
options.d: It can be stored for 2-3 months at +4\260C in saline

mcqs.explanation: The harvested graft can be stored at +4\260C in refrigeration after wrapping it in a sterile gauze pad moistened with saline. The process of harvesting and storing skin grafts is called skin banking . Skin banks store grafts using various methods . Most commonly preferred is to store the graft for up to 2-3 weeks at +4\260C.1119

mcqs.question: Which of the following is true with respect to a skin graft harvested from the post -auricular area?
mcqs.explanation: Graft harvested from the postauricular area is a full -thickness skin graft. As it involves harvesting the complete dermis donor site needs to be sutured following harvest. mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: A child is being prepared for a Millard's repair as seen in the image. The factors influencing the development of his condition are all except __________________.
mcqs.explanation: 1120 Vitamin A deficiency during pregnancy is not a factor influencing the development of cleft lip/palate . Millard's repair is the most common surgical repair of cleft lip and is usually performed between 3 to 6 months of age . The cause of orofacial clefting is felt to be multifactorial. Factors that likely increase the incidence of clefting include increased parental age , drug use and infections during pregnancy, and smoking during pregnancy.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The given image shows a forearm flap harvested for the reconstruction of the oral cavity of a 45-year-old patient with squamous cell carcinoma . Identify the type of flap.
mcqs.explanation: The picture shows a radial forearm free flap. Fasciocutaneous radial forearm free flap is the most common free flap used in head and neck reconstruction. A flap defines the tongue of tissue whereas a pedicle is used to describe the base or stem with the vascular supply . In a free flap, the blood supply is isolated , disconnected , and then reconnected using microsurgery at the new site . Other Eg for free flaps : free fibular flap, DIEP flap (Deep inferior epigastric perforators) Option A: Axial flaps are much longer and are based on known blood vessels . Eg : Latissmus Dorsi flap, TRAM (Transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous ) flap. Option B: An islanded flap is that in which the axial blood supply is swung round on a stalk. Option D: A random flap includes three sides of a rectangle , bearing no specific relationship to where the blood supply enters . Eg : V-Y plasty , Z plasty , Limberg, or rhomboid flap.

mcqs.subject: Surgery
mcqs.question: The flap shown in the picture is which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: The given image shows a serratus anterior flap. The serratus anterior flap is a highly reliable flap with a consistently long pedicle . Its anatomy permits coverage of complex wounds .
